visits.text: Explore Colmar, renowned for its beautifully preserved Old Town featuring half-timbered houses and idyllic canals in the Alsace region of France. The colorful facades and flower-bedecked bridges create a fairy-tale atmosphere that has made this one of France's most photogenic towns. The medieval and Renaissance architecture has survived remarkably intact.

Visit the Unterlinden Museum, housed in a 13th-century Dominican convent, to see the famous Isenheim Altarpiece. This masterpiece of German Renaissance art by Matthias Grünewald is considered one of the most important works of Western painting, its vivid colors and emotional intensity still captivating visitors five centuries later.

Wander through La Petite Venise (Little Venice), where traditional half-timbered houses line the canals of the Lauch River. This picturesque district, best explored by boat or on foot, captures the essence of Alsatian charm with its pastel-colored buildings reflected in the still waters.

Little Venice follows the Lauch for a few hundred meters—half-timbered houses with ochre, pink, and blue façades are reflected in the canal, geraniums spill from every balcony, flat-bottomed boats glide beneath the bridges. It's the most photographed site in Alsace, and the crowds know it. Arrive early in the morning if you want the reflections to yourself.

The Unterlinden Museum occupies a former 13th-century convent of Dominican nuns. Its centerpiece is the Isenheim Altarpiece, painted by Matthias Grünewald between 1512 and 1516 for the Antonine commandery at Isenheim—a hospital for patients suffering from Saint Anthony's fire. This seven-panel polyptych is one of the most expressive works in Western painting: the Crucifixion depicts Christ's body with wounds meant to comfort the sick by making them feel understood in their suffering. It survived two world wars hidden alternately in banks and Périgord châteaux. Book your ticket in advance—the line can be long during the tourist season.

The Collegiate Church of Saint-Martin's two unequal spires have risen above the old town since the 13th century—its construction lasted from 1235 to 1365. Look up at the carved west portal and its gargoyles before entering to see the stained glass and the Alsatian Gothic nave.

The Pfister House, built in 1537 for a draper named Ludwig Scherer, is one of the finest Renaissance residences in Alsace. Its corner oriel, wall frescoes, and long carved wooden gallery give it the air of stone lacework. Note that it now houses a wine cellar — you can go inside for a tasting.

Make a detour through the Quartier des Tanneurs, on rue de la Poissonerie. These narrow half-timbered houses, built in the 16th and 17th centuries, had upper floors open to the air to dry hides. Also look at the Maison des Têtes: its façade, dating from 1609, is decorated with more than a hundred grotesque faces.

activities.text: Sample the rich culinary tradition of Alsace, exploring local specialties and wines that reflect the region's unique Franco-German heritage. The town's gastronomic scene celebrates centuries of culinary tradition.

Board a flat-bottomed boat for a trip along the Lauch from Little Venice. Operators offer these outings during the tourist season—allow around twenty minutes to glide past the colorful façades and see them from the water.

Wander the lanes of old Colmar looking for details that go unnoticed: the carved figure of a cloth merchant on a façade along rue des Marchands, the wrought-iron shop signs, the medieval inner courtyards. The tourist office offers themed routes that help you miss nothing.

Late in the day, step into a winstub—a traditional Alsatian wine tavern—to try a flammenkueche (tarte flambée) or baeckeoffe with a glass of Riesling or Pinot Gris. It's the best time to soak up the local atmosphere away from the peak tourist hours.

visits.text: Discover Dijon, the historic capital of Burgundy, set in the heart of the Burgundy vineyards. The city boasts a rich heritage as the seat of the powerful Dukes of Burgundy, with the Palace of the Dukes now housing the outstanding Musée des Beaux-Arts. Medieval and Renaissance buildings line the pedestrian streets of the remarkably well-preserved centre.

Follow the Owl Trail (Parcours de la Chouette), a walking route marked by bronze owl plaques embedded in the pavement that leads past 22 historic landmarks. This self-guided tour reveals the city's architectural treasures, from Gothic churches to elegant hôtels particuliers.

Explore the gastronomic heritage for which Dijon is famous worldwide, including its renowned mustard and exceptional Burgundy wines. The city is the birthplace of fine Burgundy cuisine, where traditional recipes have been perfected over centuries.

Take the Route des Grands Crus (D122) between Beaune and Dijon - 60 km of UNESCO-listed vineyards (the “Climats de Bourgogne”, listed in 2015). You will pass through Pommard, Volnay, Meursault, Nuits-Saint-Georges, Vosne-Romanée and Gevrey-Chambertin. Stop at the Clos de Vougeot: this 50-hectare walled estate was established by the monks of Cîteaux in the 12th century. The road is narrow and winding - take your time. Plan a round trip during the day from Dijon to explore the vineyards around Beaune.

In Dijon, head for the Palace of the Dukes and Estates of Burgundy, which dominates the Place de la Libération (designed by Hardouin-Mansart between 1681 and 1686). The Musée des Beaux-Arts, housed in the palace, is one of France's oldest museums—and it's free. If you have the stamina, climb the 316 steps of the Tour Philippe le Bon (15th century, 46 m high) for panoramic views over the entire city.

Don't miss the Church of Notre-Dame in Dijon—you'll see the Jacquemart, an automaton stolen from Courtrai in 1382 by Philip the Bold. In 1651, the people of Dijon added a wife (Jacqueline), then a son in 1714 (Jacquelinet) and a daughter in 1884 (Jacquelinette). On a buttress of the church, stroke the little carved owl with your left hand while making a wish—it's been a tradition since the 15th century.

Second day in Dijon—start with Saint-Bénigne Cathedral. You'll descend into the 11th-century Romanesque crypt, one of the few of its type still standing in France. Three levels descend into the ground around a columned rotunda. It's austere and powerful.

Head to the Halles de Dijon, built in a metal architectural style attributed to Gustave Eiffel (opinions differ, but the structure is characteristic). The market on Tuesday, Friday and Saturday mornings is spectacular: Époisses cheeses, mustard, gingerbread, snails and blackcurrants.

Visit the Cité Internationale de la Gastronomie et du Vin—you'll discover the Gastronomic Meal of the French (inscribed on UNESCO's intangible heritage list in 2010) through interactive exhibitions, cooking workshops, and a tasting cellar. Opened in 2022 in the former General Hospital. Allow at least 1 hour 30 minutes.

If you love sculpture, continue to the Chartreuse de Champmol, a former monastery founded by Philip the Bold in 1383. Only the church portal (with statues by Claus Sluter) and the Well of Moses remain—six life-size prophets carved in stone, with astonishing realism for the 14th century.

activities.text: Sample the celebrated wines of Burgundy, from the grand crus of the Côte de Nuits to the village appellations that surround the city. The vineyards of this region produce some of the world's most sought-after Pinot Noir and Chardonnay wines.

Follow the Owl Trail—22 stops marked on the ground by bronze plaques that guide you through Dijon's protected heritage district (97 hectares, UNESCO-listed). You'll pass the private mansions of Rue des Forges, the 15th-century Maison Millière, the Law Courts, and Saint-Bénigne Cathedral. Pick up the guidebook at the Tourist Office. Allow an hour of walking.

End the day with a tasting of crème de cassis—you'll learn that it originated in Dijon in the 19th century. Try a kir (Aligoté white wine + crème de cassis): it was Canon Kir, former mayor of Dijon, who popularized this cocktail in the mid-20th century.

visits.text: Begin the Alsace Wine Route at Marlenheim, the northern gateway to 170 kilometers of winding roads through charming villages and picturesque vineyards. This celebrated route leads through the foothills of the Vosges Mountains, where the unique microclimate produces some of France's finest white wines.

Sample local wines including Riesling, Gewürztraminer, Pinot Gris, and Muscat - the noble grape varieties that have made Alsace famous worldwide. The roadside cellars and tasting rooms offer opportunities to discover these exceptional wines directly from the producers.

activities.text: Enjoy the idyllic landscape of vine-covered hillsides, medieval villages, and distant mountain views. The warm hospitality of the winemaking families adds a personal dimension to discovering this renowned wine region.

visits.text: Discover Ribeauvillé, a quintessential Alsatian village crowned by three castle ruins towering over the medieval town. These fortress remnants - Saint-Ulrich, Girsberg, and Haut-Ribeaupierre - date from the 11th to 14th centuries and offer panoramic views of the vine-covered slopes and Rhine plain beyond.

Stroll through the historic Old Town along the Grand'Rue, lined with Renaissance and Gothic buildings housing artisan shops and traditional restaurants. The town's medieval heritage is visible in its fortified gates, fountain squares, and half-timbered houses decorated with wrought-iron signs.

Twelve metres of Romanesque portal, fantastic animals, human figures and interlacing - the portal of Andlau Abbey Church has a density of sculpture rarely seen in Alsace. The church dates back to the 9th century, and the crypt houses the tomb of Saint Richardis, wife of Charles the Fat. Andlau is also one of the few villages to have three grands crus within its boundaries: Kastelberg, Moenchberg and Wiebelsberg. Allow for a drive from Ribeauvillé to reach Andlau.

Three medieval gates still standing, ramparts nearly complete—Dambach-la-Ville is one of Alsace's best-preserved fortified towns. Its grand cru Frankstein grows on pink and beige granite that geologists come to study as much as sommeliers. Less frequented village than its neighbors: take advantage.

600,000 visitors a year—which gives you an idea of the July line. Perched at 755 meters since the 12th century, Haut-Koenigsbourg burned in 1633 during the Thirty Years' War, remained in ruins for two and a half centuries, then Wilhelm II had it restored from 1900 to 1908. Result: not entirely medieval, but striking. The view over the Alsatian plain—and on clear days to the Alps—is worth admission. Arrive at opening (9 a.m.) or after 4 p.m.

It's here, in this library, that the American continent received its name for the first time. Waldseemüller's Cosmographiae Introductio, published in Saint-Dié in 1507, is preserved here—with the first printed mention of the word 'America.' Beatus Rhenanus's personal library, intact since 1547, was UNESCO-listed in 2011. Paid admission, closed Mondays.

activities.text: Explore the surrounding vineyards that have produced wines here since Roman times. The Alsace Wine Route passes directly through Ribeauvillé, offering opportunities to sample exceptional Rieslings, Gewürztraminers, and Pinot Gris at local cellars.

Marc Kreydenweiss has practised biodynamics since 1989 - one of the first in Alsace. His Rieslings and Pinot Gris grown on Andlau granite are among the region's most talked-about wines. Ask for the Wiebelsberg cuvée, a grand cru on pink Vosges sandstone. Cellar visits are by appointment only. Allow for a drive from Ribeauvillé to reach Andlau.

Sélestat market on Tuesday morning, in the town center on the Neja Waj: local producers, cheeses, cured meats and prepared dishes. Less touristy than Colmar and more local. A good opportunity to fill the trunk before Ribeauvillé. Arrive before 10 a.m.

visits.text: Visit the Notre-Dame du Haut chapel in Ronchamp, designed by legendary architect Le Corbusier and declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site. This revolutionary masterpiece of modern architecture, completed in 1955, breaks all conventions with its sculptural white walls, mushroom-shaped roof, and seemingly random window openings that create dramatic interior lighting.

Experience the spiritual atmosphere created by Le Corbusier's masterful manipulation of light and space. The chapel's organic forms and pilgrimage setting combine modernist architecture with ancient religious traditions, creating a contemplative environment that continues to inspire architects and visitors alike.

Le Corbusier's Notre-Dame-du-Haut Chapel, a masterpiece of modern architecture and Haute-Saône's only UNESCO site, revolutionized 20th-century religious architecture. Built between 1953 and 1955 on Bourlémont hill, it replaces a sanctuary destroyed by 1944 bombings. The architect drew inspiration from a crab shell for the reinforced concrete roof's shape.

Cross the chapel's threshold to discover an intimate space where light sculpts forms. The 27 windows piercing the 2.72-meter-thick south wall create shafts of colored light. The 18th-century statue of the Virgin and Child, spared by the war, is backlit in the east wall.
Admire the steel campanile created in 1975 by Jean Prouvé, bearing three bells. This elegant structure harmoniously completes the architectural ensemble.

Renzo Piano's contemporary buildings have complemented the site since 2011: the Sainte-Claire monastery partially buried in the hill and the reception gatehouse. The landscaping designed by Michel Corajoud brings the spaces into harmony with green roofs.

activities.text: Explore the surrounding grounds designed by Renzo Piano, including the Monastery of Saint Clare and the gatehouse. The peaceful hilltop setting offers views of the Vosges Mountains and the charming landscapes of the Bourgogne-Franche-Comté region.

From Bourlémont hill, admire the panorama that captivated Le Corbusier during his first visit. Views open onto the first Jura mountains to the south and the Vosges to the north, creating what the architect called 'the four horizons.'

Throughout the year, the hill hosts concerts, exhibitions, conferences, and theatrical performances that make this pilgrimage site an essential cultural venue, visited by 65,000 people from 60 countries annually.

places.name: Strasbourg

visits.text: Explore Strasbourg, the capital of Alsace and seat of the European Parliament, featuring a stunning Gothic cathedral and well-preserved Old Town designated as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The cathedral's 142-meter spire was the world's tallest building for over two centuries, while its intricate facade and astronomical clock continue to amaze visitors.

Wander through La Petite France, the most picturesque quarter of Strasbourg, where half-timbered houses from the 16th and 17th centuries line the canals of the Ill River. Former tanners' and fishermen's homes now house restaurants and shops, their flower-bedecked balconies reflected in the still waters below.

Visit the European Parliament building, where the European Union's directly elected assembly meets. Guided tours reveal the workings of this important democratic institution and the stunning hemicycle chamber where 705 members from 27 nations deliberate.

You've saved the best for the penultimate day. Strasbourg, self-proclaimed 'Christmas Capital' since 1992, hosts France's oldest Christmas market — the Christkindelsmärik (in Alsatian: 'Christ Child's Market'), existing since 1570. Its history begins with the Protestant Reformation: in December 1570, Pastor Johannes Flinner preached against the Saint Nicholas tradition deemed 'papist,' and the Town Council decided to transfer gifts to the Christ Child and move the market to just before Christmas. The Christkindelsmärik was born. Today it's held at Place Broglie — where it's been anchored since 1871 — with hundreds of wooden chalets in a model imposed by the municipality to guarantee visual harmony.

Don't miss the Cathédrale Notre-Dame — one of the Gothic world's tallest, with its 142-meter pink sandstone spire, and whose sculpted façade is a picture book carved in stone. In December, its tapestries commissioned by Richelieu for Louis XIII (14 pieces on the Virgin's life) are exhibited in the choir — they're only visible between Advent and Epiphany. The Petite France quarter, with its 16th and 17th-century tanners' half-timbered houses reflected in the Ill river, is even more beautiful beneath December garlands.

Climb Place Kléber's grand Christmas tree — no, you can't literally, but stay to contemplate it from a winstub (traditional Alsatian bistro) terrace overlooking the square. This monumental tree, different each year, has been Strasbourg's Christmas symbol for decades. In the evening, when it lights up simultaneously with the Aubette façade, it's the iconic image of Christmas in Alsace.

This final day in Strasbourg deserves exploring the city from a different angle — fewer markets, more heritage, with the serenity of a winter Sunday. The Musée de l'Œuvre Notre-Dame, installed in medieval buildings behind the cathedral, houses original sculptures from the portals (copies are outside to protect them), 12th-century stained glass, and an extraordinary collection of Rhenish art. It's one of Strasbourg's most overlooked and most beautiful museums.

The Musée Alsacien, installed in an ensemble of 17th-century patrician houses in the Grande-Île, recreates authentic Alsatian interiors from the 18th to 20th centuries — kitchens, bedrooms, artisan workshops — with a unique collection of everyday objects. In December, the museum offers Christmas storytelling sessions in Alsatian for children (ages 3-7). The Palais Rohan, an 18th-century former episcopal palace that welcomed Napoleon and Marie-Antoinette, houses three museums including the Musée des Arts Décoratifs — its 'Cardinal's Apartment' is one of France's most refined rococo interiors.

activities.text: Discover Strasbourg's rich culinary heritage, from traditional winstubs to Michelin-starred restaurants. The city's cuisine reflects its unique position at the crossroads of French and German culture, producing distinctive dishes found nowhere else.

Strasbourg deploys over 300 chalets across a dozen UNESCO-listed Grande-Île squares and streets. Each has its theme: local crafts at Place des Meuniers, Alsatian gastronomy at Place du Marché aux Cochons de Lait, decorations at Place de la Cathédrale. Allow at least half a day for the complete circuit — and stay until nightfall for illuminations that transform medieval façades into fairy tale settings.

In the evening, enjoy free concerts resounding in all Strasbourg churches during Advent — Catholic, Protestant, Orthodox. The cathedral, the Église Saint-Thomas (which houses Marshal de Saxe's Mausoleum by Pigalle), the Église Saint-Pierre-le-Jeune: each December evening, a church lights up and fills with voices. It's the spiritual dimension of this Alsatian Christmas sometimes forgotten behind the chalets.

For a final view of illuminated Strasbourg, climb to the Barrage Vauban terrace — this 17th-century dam spans the Ill at the entrance to Petite France and offers a 360° panorama over the old town's rooftops, the cathedral, and the Vosges. Access is free. In December, with low afternoon light, it's the most beautiful postcard.

Finish this final afternoon strolling one last time through the Village de l'Avent at Place Broglie, and treat yourself to a final mulled wine in a Petite France winstub before heading to the TGV station or airport. Strasbourg is served by direct TGV from Paris (1 hour 50 minutes) and by Strasbourg-Entzheim international airport. It's one of Europe's best rail hubs for departing to any destination.

visits.text: If you finish in Wissembourg, the Saints-Pierre-et-Paul abbey church offers one last pause amid stone architecture before departure. Its stained-glass windows and cloister continue the thread of religious visits begun in Worms, with a different Gothic vocabulary. Stop by after you arrive if the church is open; otherwise, view the exterior, then enjoy the town center before nightfall.

Start with the Abbey Church of Saints Peter and Paul, founded around 660 by Austrasian nobles on an island in the Lauter River—an island because the monastery was wedged between two branches of the river linked by a canal whose location corresponds to today's Rue Stanislas. Rebuilt in Gothic style between 1262 and 1293 under Abbot Édelin, it's the second-largest Gothic church in Alsace after Strasbourg Cathedral. Don't miss the Saint Christopher fresco covering an entire nave wall: 11 meters tall, it's the largest medieval full-length figure in France and Germany. The Christ of Wissembourg stained-glass window has been moved to the Strasbourg museum—but the 12th-century Romanesque rose window depicting the Virgin and Child remains in place.

Wander through the historic center crossed by the Lauter and its canals. The 15th- and 16th-century half-timbered houses line narrow streets that quickly give the impression of straddling the Franco-German border—which isn't far from the truth, since Germany is two kilometers away. Spot the statue of King Dagobert along your way, legendary founder of the abbey according to an apocryphal 12th-century charter. Wissembourg is also the home of Hans Trapp, the Alsatian Christmas figure who punishes naughty children, whose legend originates with a odious local lord who dammed the Lauter to deprive the town of water.

Walk the circuit of medieval ramparts — they date from the 13th to 18th centuries and encircle the old town for several hundred meters. The tower known as Schartenturm (15th century) to the southwest and the Powder Tower (13th century) are the best preserved. From the walkway, the view over Alsatian rooftops and the Lauter winding below is worth the detour.

activities.text: Follow the pedestrian loop along the ramparts and canals—about 3 to 4 kilometers of easy walking that covers the essentials of the old town. If you're there in the morning, local bakers offer pretzels and rye bread before 8 a.m. Plan an hour for a leisurely stroll.

Climb the wooded heights northwest of town for panoramic views of the Palatinate Forest on the German side and Alsatian vineyards on the French side. Marked trails from the Club Vosgien depart directly from the town center and lead to several viewpoints in under an hour.

visits.text: Fontenay Abbey draws all its power from its austerity. Founded in 1118 by Saint Bernard, this Cistercian abbey in Marmagne is the oldest surviving example, with its Romanesque church with bare walls, cloister, dormitory and forge. UNESCO-listed in 1981. No superfluous decoration: here, only light dresses the stone.

The gardens of Fontenay Abbey, awarded the “Jardin remarquable” label in 2004, surround the buildings in a green setting. Two hectares of lawns, paths and rose bushes spread across the hollow of the valley. The walk is included in the ticket. In autumn, the century-old trees turn bright yellow.

activities.text: If you visit in summer, look out for candlelit evening openings at the abbey. You can discover the great forge, a rare remnant of medieval industry, along the route. Regular guided tours run without booking during the season. Bring good shoes; the valley is damp.

visits.text: Valloires Abbey, founded in the 12th century by monks from Cîteaux, is the only fully preserved 18th-century Cistercian abbey in France. Its baroque church surprises with choir screens, suspended papier-mâché angels, and Louis XV rocaille woodwork. Visits are guided only, as the abbey still accommodates children in social care facilities. Allow an hour for the complete circuit, cloister included.

In spring, the avenue of Japanese cherry trees at the Jardins de Valloires forms a white, airy canopy that alone justifies the detour. Designed by landscape architect Gilles Clément across 8 hectares, these gardens hold the Jardin Remarquable designation and bring together over 5,000 species in five distinct settings, including the Jardin des Cinq Sens, designed for children. There is an elevation difference of more than 25 meters between the site's upper and lower sections. Check opening hours by email before traveling.

visits.text: "In the age of raw concrete, blessed be such an encounter": this is how Le Corbusier hailed the Abbey of Thoronet in 1953. Built between 1160 and 1230, this Cistercian abbey is considered the "marvel" of the three Provençal sisters, alongside Sénanque and Silvacane. Its remarkable acoustics—over ten seconds of reverberation—have inspired generations of architects, from Fernand Pouillon to John Pawson. Entry runs around €9, free for those under 26.

The trapezoidal cloister of Thoronet Abbey unfolds four asymmetrical round-arched galleries, adapted to the slope of the terrain. The neighboring chapter house, with six rib vaults on two central columns, is among the earliest in the south of France. The acoustics of the abbey church, with a reverberation time of about twelve seconds, are best experienced during a visit with a small group, outside peak hours.

visits.text: The people of Bergues still call the neighboring hill “la butte,” where the ruins of the Benedictine abbey of Saint-Winoc stand. Its square tower and pointed tower have dominated the town for centuries, proudly standing in ruins. Below, the Musée du Mont-de-Piété, housed in a 17th-century building, displays Flemish, French, and Italian paintings. The two sites combine well into a single afternoon outing.

visits.text: The Saint-Vulfran collegiate church's Flamboyant Gothic facade has stood since 1488. Its towers received their bells in 1524, and construction spanned two centuries.

From the street, view the belfry dating from 1209, one of the oldest in France. The Musée Boucher-de-Perthes is closed for renovation; its archaeological and fine arts collections, spanning the Middle Ages to the 20th century, are not accessible.
Jacques Boucher de Perthes, the father of prehistory, left the town his collections of stone tools and Gallo-Roman objects.

activities.text: Abbeville's parks and gardens offer green spaces in the heart of the town rebuilt after 1940.

visits.text: Agay means favorable in Greek, and sailors have never disputed that: the bay, tucked between Cap Dramont and Pointe de la Baumette, is one of the best sheltered on the coast. Three sandy beaches, the Rastel d'Agay and its red rocks in the background, and a small marina. In season, parking spaces fill up before 10am.

The arrival of the railway in 1860 made Agay a stopover for artists: Maupassant, Louis Valtat, Vincent d'Indy, Saint-Exupéry. A fountain dedicated to the Little Prince pays tribute to him in the hamlet. At the foot of the Baumette lighthouse, a stele marks the spot where his plane was last spotted, on July 31, 1944.

activities.text: Paddle from Agay beach toward the Estérel coves: kayaks and paddleboards are available to rent on site, the water is clear and the red rock drops straight into the sea. The beach slopes gently and has Handiplage and AudioPlage certification, with a lifting hoist and wheelchairs for entering the water. Dogs are prohibited from June 15 to September 15.

days_plan.itin_title: Roquebrune-sur-Argens: sea, villages and the Var in 10 days

visits.text: Start with Saint-Caprais Cathedral, built in the 12th century on the foundations of a 6th-century basilica sacked by the Normans in 853. Its history is eventful: converted into a hay store for the horses of the revolutionary army in 1791, it did not officially become a cathedral until 1802, after the destruction of the former Saint-Etienne Cathedral. Listed as a historic monument in 1862 and inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List as part of the Routes of Santiago de Compostela since 1998, it is worth visiting for its interior, painted from floor to ceiling. The decoration was created between 1845 and 1869 by Jean-Louis Bezard, a pupil of Ingres, who depicted the martyrs of Agen, including Saint Caprais himself. Do not miss the grand Stoltz organ with its 45 stops, said to have been donated by Empress Eugenie in 1858.

The Pont-Canal is Agen’s other source of pride and one of the most spectacular structures in south-western France. Built between 1839 and 1847 from dressed Quercy stone, it measures 539 metres, has 23 arches and carries the Canal latéral à la Garonne across the river. Its foundation stone was laid with great ceremony by the Duke of Orléans, son of Louis-Philippe, on 25 August 1839. It remained France’s longest canal bridge until the Briare Canal Bridge opened in 1896. Walk across it or follow it from the riverbanks: the view along its arches is well worth seeing, especially in the late morning.

The 13th-century Jacobins Church has housed part of the Fine Arts Museum’s collections since 2025 while the museum is closed for renovation. Housed in four 16th- and 17th-century townhouses, the museum is one of the most important in south-western France. Its collections notably include five paintings by Goya, bequeathed in 1899 by the Count of Chaudordy, French ambassador to Spain. Goya’s self-portrait, dating from around 1783, is its centrepiece, alongside the Venus of Mas-d’Agenais, a Gallo-Roman sculpture from the 1st or 2nd century discovered in 1876. Check the progress of the collections’ relocation to the Jacobins Church before your visit.

Wander along Rue des Cornieres with its medieval arcades and half-timbered houses. It is Agen's historic shopping street, where shops and cafes follow one another beneath covered galleries typical of the bastides of south-western France. A cafe terrace under the arcades is the obvious place to watch local life go by.
Head to the place des Laitiers, which marks the site of the former Saint-Étienne cathedral, destroyed during the French Revolution. Today it is a lively square where a market is held.

activities.text: Visit the Halle du Pin market or Place Durand to taste Agen prunes, a speciality linked to the introduction of the Ente plum by the monks of Clairac in the 14th century. You will also find hazelnuts, foie gras, Buzet wines and farmhouse cheeses. The covered and open-air markets operate from Tuesday to Sunday morning.

Follow the Canal de Garonne by bicycle or on foot along the towpath from the canal bridge. The greenway runs beside the water for several kilometres in a setting lined with plane trees. If you have time, continue to the village of Le Passage-d’Agen: the finest view of the canal bridge is from the opposite bank.

days_plan.itin_title: Lot-et-Garonne Road Trip: Bastides and Villages

visits.text: Ramparts of Aigues-Mortes, perfectly preserved 13th-century medieval fortified walls. The mile-long crenellated walls punctuated by 20 towers completely encircle the town. The walkway accessible along the entire perimeter offers panoramas over Camargue, pink salt marshes, and Mediterranean Sea. Military architecture designed under Louis IX (Saint Louis) illustrates medieval defensive art with loopholes, hoardings, and machicolations. Fortified gates—Porte de la Gardette, Porte de l'Organeau—controlled access to the port town. Sunset sets ablaze ochre stones of ramparts creating magical atmosphere.

Tour de Constance, 131-foot cylindrical keep dominating Aigues-Mortes since 1248. The massive tower served as state prison from the 17th century, imprisoning Protestants after Revocation of the Edict of Nantes. The upper room with impressive vaults imprisoned Marie Durand for 38 years, who carved "resist" on the well rim. The 196-step spiral staircase leads to circular panoramic terrace. The visit evokes the prison-tower's history and moving testimonies of female captives. The monument symbolizes Huguenot resistance and religious intolerance.

Salins d'Aigues-Mortes, 26,700-acre salt exploitation producing Camargue salt. Salt pans in pink hues due to halophilic microalgae create spectacular colorful landscapes. Camelles, white salt mountains rising 65 feet, sparkle in sunlight. Thousands of pink flamingos frequent evaporation basins feeding on brine shrimp and algae. Discovery circuit by small train tours industrial and natural site explaining ancestral harvest. Boutiques sell artisanal salt—fleur de sel, grey salt, flavored—and derivative products.

Historic center of Aigues-Mortes, medieval bastide with preserved grid plan. Straight streets intersect at right angles following regular 13th-century urbanism. Place Saint-Louis bordered by café terraces honors the king-builder who departed on crusade from the port. Notre-Dame-des-Sablons church in southern Gothic style shelters relics and marine ex-votos. Limestone houses with colorful shutters align facades along paved streets. Artisan shops offer Camargue specialties: fougasse, gardiane, rice, salt.

Plage de l'Espiguette at Le Grau-du-Roi, sand desert with wild dunes classified as Grand Site de France. The 3,700 acres of mobile dunes reach 40 feet high shaped by winds and tides. The six-mile nearly deserted beach offers Mediterranean swimming far from urbanization. Marram grass, glasswort, and immortelles anchor sand in fragile dune ecosystem. The Espiguette lighthouse, 89-foot white tower, marks channel entrance. The wild, preserved atmosphere contrasts with neighboring seaside resorts.

activities.text: Excursion in Gard Camargue discovering fauna and landscapes. Roads traverse expanses of reeds, rice paddies, marshes, and lagoons populated with birds. Pink flamingos, grey herons, egrets, ibis, and avocets allow observation from ornithological observatories. Herds of Camargue bulls and white horses graze in wet meadows. Traditional Camargue farmhouses dot preserved territory. Camargue Regional Natural Park protects 212,000 acres of internationally important wetlands. The changing light transfigures aquatic landscapes stretching to infinity.

Visit salt marshes by tourist train touring salt pans and evaporation basins. The 45-minute narrated circuit reveals seawater crystallization process from seawater pumping. Small wagons wind between salt mountains, pink and green basins according to saline concentration. Explanations detail mechanized harvesting, storage, and salt packaging. Stops allow photographing flamingos in surreal colored décor. Boutique offers tastings and purchases of locally produced flavored salts.

Taste gardiane de taureau at a typical Camargue restaurant. Traditional stew simmers Camargue bull meat AOC with red wine, black olives, garlic, and aromatic herbs. The rustic dish accompanied by Camargue rice IGP illustrates authentic regional gastronomy. Restaurants near ramparts also serve tellines, local shellfish, brandade, grilled fish. Vins des sables IGP produced on Camargue terroir pair with specialties. Fougasse d'Aigues-Mortes, brioche with orange blossom seeds, concludes traditional meal.

Bike ride on cycle paths between Aigues-Mortes and Le Grau-du-Roi. Developed paths traverse salt marshes, canals, reedbeds, and beaches in horizontal Camargue landscape. The flat six-mile route accessible to all follows lagoons reflecting the sky. Stops allow observing flamingos, photographing pink salt pans, and enjoying marine panoramas. Bike rental in Aigues-Mortes facilitates day family excursion. Wind can blow hard requiring extra effort but guaranteeing invigorating fresh air.

days_plan.itin_title: Gard Circuit: Roman Nîmes, Pont du Gard and Camargue
Côte Bleue and Camargue: the lower coastal route in 7 days

visits.text: Aiguèze awaits you just beyond the gorges, on the Gard side—its name comes from the Occitan “aigo,” water in the rock, referring to the numerous wells in the limestone cliff. The first village in Gard to join Les Plus Beaux Villages de France in 2005, it was founded as a fortress by Charles Martel after the Battle of Poitiers in 732 to control the ford across the Ardèche. The 11th-century Saracen tower is one of the village's oldest structures—it was intended to defend against attacks by the Arab-Berber tribes whose name it bears. It is connected to the 13th-century round tower and the 12th-century rectangular keep: together, these three towers perched on a blade of Urgonian limestone form one of the most characteristic silhouettes of the Lower Ardèche.

The rampart walk is Aiguèze's unmissable experience: it follows the old fortification along the cliff and passes the castle (private), the Saracen tower and the keep. The view from this path over the Ardèche gorges below and, on clear days, toward the distant silhouette of Mont Ventoux is one of the finest on this circuit. Note a characteristic architectural detail: the ground floors of the houses are medieval, while the second floors are Renaissance—the Hundred Years' War had left the village with only nine surviving inhabitants around 1382, and reconstruction proceeded gradually on the ruins.

Saint-Roch church, with its Renaissance portal and bell tower restored in Gothic style, deserves a stop for its neo-Gothic interior frescoes. The main street paved with Ardèche pebbles is the village's backbone—its golden stone houses with Romanesque vaults and mullioned windows invite you to slow down and observe the carved details.

activities.text: From Aiguèze, a hike toward the rock of Castelviel leads to a remarkable view over the gorges from above: allow 2 hours round trip on a marked garrigue trail of moderate difficulty. The view of the bend in the Ardèche beneath your feet is well worth the effort. Closed-toe shoes are essential.

Aiguèze is at the heart of the Côtes du Rhône vineyards. Operators offer tastings in village cellars or excursions to neighboring estates. In the evening, Place du Jeu de Paume beneath the century-old plane trees, with its pétanque games and stone terraces, is the ideal spot to unwind.

days_plan.itin_title: Cèze Valley and Ardèche Gorges Circuit

places.name: Aiguines

visits.text: Your first glimpse of Aiguines is from the lake: its turrets with conical roofs covered in multicolored glazed tiles from Moustiers-Sainte-Marie mark out the village from afar on its rocky spur. Perched at an altitude of 800 meters, it overlooks the turquoise waters of the lake with the Valensole plateau as a backdrop—on clear days, you can even make out Mont Ventoux on the horizon. The château, built in the early 17th century by Balthazar de Gauthier during Henry IV's reign, covers 3,300 m² on a twenty-hectare estate. It remains private, but its surroundings and the view are freely accessible. Don't try to enter—enjoy it from the small square facing the towers.

Climb up to the Saint-Pierre chapel overlooking the village from its promontory. The panoramic orientation panel on its esplanade lets you identify Lake Sainte-Croix, the Valensole plateau, the Prealps, and the Luberon range. This is one of the widest panoramas in the entire Verdon region—plan to be there in late afternoon for the low-angle light on the water.

The Musée des Tourneurs sur Bois, designated a “Musée de France”, tells an unusual story: in the 16th century, Aiguines was the largest woodturning center in southeastern France, using timber from the cliffs of the Verdon. Its most surprising specialty? Studded balls — turned boxwood spheres covered with hundreds of small nails, the forerunners of pétanque balls. The museum is open from May to September; from October to April, check its opening days before your visit. If you are here outside the main season, artisan shops keep the tradition alive in the narrow streets.

Stroll around the Place de la Fontaine, Aiguines' heart with its wrought-iron bell cage and pastel-hued façades, its sundial and historic fountain. The parish church of Saint-Jean preserves a crucifix classified as a Historic Monument. The village has around 300 winter residents — a number that explodes in summer, but the square retains its authentic Provençal village character.

activities.text: The D71 road, known as the “Balcons du Verdon”, winds along the corniche from Aiguines, with viewpoints offering breathtaking views of the canyon. The limestone cliffs plunge 300 meters down to the river. Stop at the viewpoints — particularly at the Col d'Illoire. Allow at least 2 hours for this drive with stops.

Aiguines is the rock climbing capital of the Verdon, with routes for all levels on the limestone walls. The cliffs are oriented east–west, allowing climbing year-round. Local providers offer supervised introductory sessions for beginners and guided outings for experienced climbers.

days_plan.itin_title: Lake Sainte-Croix and Verdon Circuit
Alpine Hinterland and Verdon Gorges: From Thorenc to Riez
Southeast France Road Trip: Perched Villages and Gorges
Var in 4 Days: From Bormes to the Most Beautiful Villages of the Verdon

visits.text: Ailhon is a forest village in green Ardèche, more secret than its gorge neighbors but precious for its authenticity. The Romanesque church at the village's mineral core is discreet but refined—look for the sundials painted on some village house facades, including a notable one marked in the center. The network of lanes and shaded squares invites unhurried wandering, far from the summer bustle of the south.

Ailhon's scattered hamlets deserve the detour. Between maritime pine undergrowth and clearings, dry-stone walls still border old paths. This type of bocage landscape, typical of Ardèche's chestnut groves, was gradually abandoned during 20th-century rural exodus—many hamlet houses have since been restored as second homes or gîtes.

The forest edges around the village shelter remarkable Mediterranean flora in all seasons. From high points in the territory, on clear days, views carry to the first Cévennes foothills westward and the Coiron basalt plateaus northward.

activities.text: The Ailhon hamlets loop (4 to 6 km) starts from the village and links several hamlets scattered in the forest. The path crosses chestnut groves and clearings, with sections on old mule tracks bordered by walls. Prefer this walk in the morning when light filters through the undergrowth.

The heritage circuit around the church and Ailhon sundials is signposted and short (about 1h30). It reveals the village's architectural details—dated lintels, armorial doors, fountains—while gathering information on village history through explanatory panels.

days_plan.itin_title: The 18 Most Beautiful Villages of Ardèche

visits.text: Ainhoa is a bastide town founded in the 13th century—its single street lined with red-and-white half-timbered houses ranks among the most photogenic in the Basque Country. Classified as one of France's Most Beautiful Villages, the town preserves its church with typical wooden galleries and its pelota court. Walk to the far end of the street where the facades close in—that's where Ainhoa is at its most beautiful.

A 10-minute drive brings you to Espelette, where facades are draped with garlands of red peppers drying (late August through November). Espelette pepper earned AOC status in 2000—you'll taste it in every form at the village producers.

activities.text: From Ainhoa, hike up to the Chapelle de l'Aubépine via the marked trail—allow an hour round trip. The view across the valley and frontier ridges is magnificent, and you'll likely have it to yourself.

days_plan.itin_title: Nouvelle-Aquitaine Loop: Villages, Vineyards & Dordogne

visits.text: The Saint-Pierre Abbey Church in Airvault is a monument often underestimated by passersby. Built in the 11th, 12th, and 13th centuries, it features 180 historiated capitals depicting scenes of everyday life, biblical stories, and geometric motifs—a rare wealth of sculpture. The Romanesque nave is covered by Plantagenet Gothic vaults added in the 13th century: the combination is surprisingly harmonious. Look for the Elders of the Apocalypse on the tympanum of the screen facade. Inside, be sure to see the early 12th-century Romanesque altarpiece and the mechanical barrel organ built in Mirecourt around 1830, listed as a historic monument—it still plays during visits. Ask the reception staff to set it in motion.

The cenotaph of Pierre de Saine Fontaine, the abbey’s founder, who died in 1110, depicts nine people beneath arches—faceless figures, stone silhouettes of pilgrims. It is one of the region’s most moving examples of Romanesque church furnishings.

Continue to the underground fountain, accessible with a key borrowed from the town hall’s heritage department. Its blue-green waters have inspired many local legends. This is one of those tucked-away places that hurried visitors miss—and locals cherish.

The 19th-century market hall and the 15th- and 16th-century half-timbered houses around Place Saint-Pierre form a cohesive group of historic secular buildings. Also climb up to the old castle for a panoramic view of the town and the Thouet Valley.

activities.text: Follow the Chemins d’Aldéarde, routes marked by medallions set into the pavement that guide you through Airvault’s urban heritage. Allow 1 hour 15 minutes for the full circuit.

As you leave Airvault heading south, stop at the Romanesque Vernay Bridge over the Thouet. Legend has it that the fairy Mélusine flipped it over with a kick—a short detour worth making for the river view.

days_plan.itin_title: Deux-Sèvres Tour: Marais Poitevin and Romanesque Heritage

places.name: Aix En Provence

visits.text: The Château de Tarascon is one of the most complete fortified castles in France—precisely because it served as a prison from 1481 to 1926, 445 years of continuous use as a prison, which discouraged demolitions and remodeling. Built in the 14th and 15th centuries, completed under King René of Anjou. In the cells: thousands of prisoners' graffiti carved in stone from the 16th to 19th centuries—ships, coats of arms, portraits, names and dates. One of the most important collections of prison graffiti in France, preserved intact. And during the Revolution, local sans-culottes threw between 18 and 23 counter-revolutionary prisoners from the ramparts into the Rhône below (30-meter drop, June 25, 1794). Documented in the archives of the Revolutionary Tribunal of Marseille. No commemorative plaque. Ticket €7.50, allow 2 hours.

The Collégiale Sainte-Marthe, a 14th-century Gothic collegiate church 30 meters east of the castle, houses in its crypt the 3rd-century early Christian sarcophagus presented as the tomb of Saint Martha. The legend: arriving from Palestine with her sister Mary Magdalene around AD 48, she supposedly tamed the Tarasque—an amphibious monster that devoured passersby along the Rhône—with a simple sprinkling of holy water and a rosary, before the villagers stoned the monster. Saint Martha's historical presence in Provence is largely legendary, but the Tarasque festival (last weekend of June) has been inscribed on UNESCO's intangible heritage list since 2005 and has continued since the 15th century. Access to the crypt is free.

The Abbaye Saint-Michel-de-Frigolet, 20 minutes northeast of Tarascon in the Montagnette, sits isolated among the rocks as if the world had stopped at the edge of the forest. It is still home to a Premonstratensian community of around twenty monks. In 1880, the decrees against religious congregations sent the army to its gates: the monks barricaded themselves in and held out for several days before surrendering. They returned in 1923. If you arrive at a time of prayer, the silence of the forest and the Gregorian chant create an effect that is hard to reproduce any other way. Guided tour €5, allow 1 hour.

Cézanne's Studio (9 avenue Paul Cézanne) has been preserved as it was at his death in 1906—the easel, the smocks, the wax apples, the skulls that appear in several still lifes. Cézanne had been painting Mont Sainte-Victoire from this city for 40 years when he collapsed outdoors in an October 1906 thunderstorm and was brought home in a laundryman's cart. He died of pneumonia a week later, on October 22, at 67. The Large Bathers, painted here between 1902 and 1906, is at the National Gallery in London. Ticket €7, allow 45 minutes.

Saint-Sauveur Cathedral (center) is an architectural layer cake: founded in the 5th century, it bears Romanesque, Gothic and Baroque elements side by side, sometimes in the same wall. Its 5th-century early Christian baptistery is one of the oldest in France—an octagonal baptismal pool surrounded by eight marble columns of Roman origin. This unintended blend of everything Provence has lived through over fifteen centuries is worth the stop. Free admission.

The Château de Lourmarin (about 39 km north of Aix-en-Provence, 40 minutes by road, in the Luberon) is the first Renaissance château built in Provence, dating from the 15th–16th centuries, now home to the Fondation Laurent-Vibert—an artists' residence active since 1925. Writers, painters and musicians have stayed there for a century. And several of them, notably the Provençal writer Henri Bosco (a regular resident in the 1940s–1950s), recorded in their journals footsteps in the south wing and a figure at the north window, identified by village tradition as a 15th-century woman who died in childbirth. Bosco was not a man easily impressed. These journals are kept on site. Ticket €8, allow 1.5 hours.

Lourmarin cemetery: Albert Camus is buried here, under a simple white slab—first name, years, nothing else. He had bought a house in the village in 1958 with the money from his 1957 Nobel Prize in Literature because he passionately loved the Luberon. He died on January 4, 1960, in his publisher Michel Gallimard's Facel-Vega on the N5 near Sens—he had an unused train ticket in his pocket. The manuscript of The First Man was in the car (published posthumously in 1994). His wife Francine rests beside him. The grave is freely accessible.

activities.text: Lunch in Tarascon: Le Bistrot des Anges on the main square, unpretentious Provençal cooking, €25–40. The atmosphere of the square—facing the castle, a stone's throw from the Rhône—is better than at any fine-dining restaurant on that day's itinerary.

Arrival in Aix-en-Provence at the end of the day, 1 hour's drive southeast via the A7–A8. Accommodation: Hôtel Le Pigonnet (€200–400), or Hôtel des Augustins—a converted 12th-century former convent, €130–220, the most fitting choice for this trip. Dinner at your leisure: Le Petit Verdot or L'Épicurien, €40–60.

The Château de Lacoste, 30 minutes north of Lourmarin: the former estate of the Marquis de Sade, where he stayed between 1771 and 1778 between two spells in prison, and where the orgies that led to his convictions are documented in court records. Ransacked and burned in 1792 during the Revolution. Bought in 2001 by Pierre Cardin, who restored it and holds a summer opera festival there. He also bought 5 other houses in the village to lodge the festival's artists, which turned Lacoste into a village largely inhabited by a single owner. Open on certain days, ticket €10, allow 1 hour.

Return to Aix-en-Provence for a farewell dinner. Restaurant Mickaël Féval for fine dining (€90–150), or Le Petit Verdot for something hearty and unpretentious (€40–60). Aix TGV station is 15 minutes south of the center: TGV Aix–Paris in 3 hours 20 minutes.

visits.text: Annecy, about 35 km and a 35-minute drive from Aix-les-Bains, deserves some time in the morning. The old town, with its canals lined with colorful houses, is often compared to Venice - that is an exaggeration, but the charm is real. Start with the Palais de l'Isle, the unusual galley-shaped building on a rocky island in the middle of the Thiou. Built in the 12th century, it served as a prison, courthouse, mint, barracks and even a home for older people before being saved from demolition in 1900. The cells are at water level - imagine the prisoners' conditions.

In Annecy (about 35 km from Aix-les-Bains, a 35-minute drive), continue to the Pont des Amours, at the entrance to the Pâquier. From there, the view of the lake framed by mountains is Annecy's classic postcard scene. Early in the morning, when the water is as smooth as a mirror, it is even better.

In Aix-les-Bains, the Musée Faure, housed in the Villa des Chimères, is closed to the public for renovation. Its collection includes sculptures by Rodin and paintings by Degas, Cézanne, Pissarro, Sisley and Renoir, but it cannot be visited during the work. Continue on foot through the town center around the Casino Grand Cercle. Look at the Belle Époque facades and the Arc de Campanus, visible from outside, then head to the esplanade beside the lac du Bourget for a lakeside walk. This lets you discover the center of Aix-les-Bains and its lakeside setting without planning a museum visit.

Finish with a stroll along the Lake Bourget esplanade. It's France's largest natural lake—18 km long—and the late afternoon light there is superb. As you pass through the town center, take a look at the Arc de Campanus (1st century), the Casino Grand Cercle inaugurated in 1850, and the Belle Époque facades on Rue de Genève. Queen Victoria came here for spa treatments three times—the English left their mark.

activities.text: In Annecy (about 35 km from Aix-les-Bains, a 35-minute drive), walk or cycle part of the way around the lake from the Pâquier. The cycle path follows the western shore for several kilometers. The water of the lac d'Annecy is among the purest in Europe - if it is summer, a swim is a must.

If time allows, board a short cruise in Annecy (about 35 km from Aix-les-Bains, a 35-minute drive) on the lac d'Annecy. Boats depart from quai Napoléon III and make the circuit in about 1 hour. The view of the mountains from the lake completely changes your perspective.
