Savoie from Lakes to Glaciers: Yenne to Haute-Maurienne
Grand Tour Ain & Savoie Mont-Blanc: Lakes, Mountains and Heritage
Lyon to Annecy Road Trip: Heritage and Alpine Lakes
From the Alps to the Ardèche Gorges: Lakes, Peaks and Garrigue

visits.text: The Église Sainte-Croix, built in the 13th century, owes its name to a legend: a pilgrim returning from Jerusalem reportedly rested here with a fragment of the True Cross. Its Limousin portal and three naves shelter a remarkable treasure of 21 reliquaries, including two champlevé enamel shrines from the 13th century.
The Tour Jeanne d'Albret, listed as a historic monument, is the last surviving remnant of the fortified castle built on the rocky spur overlooking the confluence of the Aixette and the Vienne.

The Pont de Malassert, called the 'Roman bridge,' spans the Aixette with a single stone arch dating from the 14th century. The sole remnant of a former wooden plank bridge, it reveals itself along a shaded path.

Head to the Sanctuaire d'Arliquet, a neo-Gothic brick chapel unique in Limousin, built between 1865 and 1868. Its contemporary stained glass by Francis Chigot replaces the 19th-century windows. Four large reliquary shrines hold martyrs' relics brought from Rome in 1870.
The sanctuary park invites you to enjoy a quiet moment. A Way of the Cross with 14 stations winds among the trees, through a landscape of woodland and rocks.

activities.text: Aixe sits at the crossroads of GR 4 (Royan-Grasse) and GR 654 (Vézelay-Compostela). Follow a section of the trail along the Vienne for a 5 km hike between riverbanks and meadows.

Stroll through the old town's lanes, among the remnants of the three medieval gates—Lavaud, Auroux, and Guingand—which had protected the town since the Middle Ages. Aixe was a strategic point on the via Lemovicensis to Compostela.
Settle in the medieval garden laid out along the Vienne for a break. The riverbanks offer a peaceful setting for a picnic facing the river.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Vienne Tour: Limoges, Porcelain and Villages

visits.text: Start at the Maison Bonaparte on rue Saint-Charles—this is where Napoleon was born on August 15, 1769, in a family home that came into Bonaparte ownership in 1743. The tour begins on the second floor with Corsica's history and portraits of Charles and Letizia, then descends to the birth chamber on the first floor. The Directoire furniture purchased by Letizia Bonaparte in Marseille in 1798 is still there, including Milanese commodes gifted by Joseph. Listed as a historic monument in 1923 and opened as a national museum in 1967, the house is open daily except Mondays. Arrive in the morning to beat the cruise ship crowds.

The Cathedral of Our Lady of the Assumption, steps away from the Maison Bonaparte, is where Napoleon was baptized on July 21, 1771—nearly two years after his birth, which was common practice at the time. The 16th-century building houses a Virgin of the Sacred Heart said to have belonged to Letizia Bonaparte. The polished marble floors and light filtering through the stained glass make for a calm interlude between visits.

Climb up to the Place d'Austerlitz at the top of town to see the artificial grotto built under Napoleon III on the spot where young Bonaparte used to retreat as a child. A statue of the Emperor crowns a monumental staircase. The view from the esplanade over the Gulf of Ajaccio and the Sanguinaires Islands is one of the finest in the city.

Make the detour to Pointe de la Parata, 12 km west of Ajaccio—from the parking area, a 10-minute trail leads to a 16th-century Genoese tower overlooking the Sanguinaires archipelago. In late afternoon, the setting sun ignites the pink granite rocks and the water turns orange—this is one of Corsica's most photographed sunsets.

This last day in Ajaccio before heading to the airport is a chance to stroll through neighborhoods you did not see on arrival. The quartier des Cannes, above the cours Napoléon, is the Ajaccio of the locals - away from the Napoleonic circuit, with its Corsican grocery stores, bakeries and neighborhood cafés.

If time allows before heading to the airport, return to the Pointe de la Parata for a last view of the îles Sanguinaires - the morning light is different from sunset and the site is almost deserted before 9 a.m. Allow for a round trip by road from Ajaccio before continuing to the airport. It is a simple way to complete your tour of the island at the same starting point, but from a different perspective.

activities.text: The Ajaccio market takes place on Place Foch and along the quays every morning (until 1 PM). Corsican cheese shops, charcuterie, smoked figatellu, maquis honey—take your time; the producers love to chat. It's the best place to assemble a picnic or bring home island specialties.

The Musée Fesch, housed in the palace of Cardinal Joseph Fesch—Napoleon's uncle—holds France's second-largest collection of Italian paintings after the Louvre: Botticelli, Titian, Bellini, Veronese. Allow at least 1.5 hours. Open Tuesday through Sunday; closed Mondays.

Tour operators offer boat excursions from Ajaccio harbor to the Sanguinaires Islands. The trip lasts about two hours and follows the coast out to the archipelago. Book the day before in summer—boats depart in the morning between 9 and 10 AM.

Final tasting at Ajaccio market, Place Foch and Quai Napoléon: figatellu, lonzu, coppa, brocciu, strawberry tree honey, citron jam, white wine canistrelli. If you haven't yet tasted Corsican charcuterie, this is your last chance. The producers selling directly in the morning aren't the same as the evening tourist shops.

Corsican wine tour from Ajaccio: the Ajaccio region wine route follows the hillsides north of the city for 30 km. Corsica has 9 AOCs—Ajaccio, Patrimonio, Muscat du Cap Corse, Porto-Vecchio, Sartène, Figari, Corse, Calvi, Corse-Coteaux-du-Cap-Corse. Estates offer tastings; favor those producing white vermentino, which is very floral and typical of the island.

days_plan.itin_title: Complete Tour of Corsica
Complete Tour of Corsica
Southern Corsica Tour: Bonifacio, Porto-Vecchio and Mountains

visits.text: Alba-la-Romaine is a doubly remarkable village. Its medieval architecture first: all facades are built in a checkerboard of black stone (volcanic basalt) and white stone (limestone), giving the village a unique atmosphere among Ardèche villages. In 1948, painter André Lhote published an enthusiastic article about "these checkerboard walls, where black and white stones alternate randomly," launching an artistic resurrection movement for the village. Its ancient history second: Alba was the capital of the Helvii, a Gallic people, and became an episcopal seat at the end of the 4th century AD.

Make the detour to the archaeological site of Alba Helviorum, the former Gallo-Roman capital that extended over 30 hectares. The ancient theater, dated to the 2nd century and able to accommodate up to 3,000 spectators, is one of the best-preserved in the region. It's still used each summer for Festival d'Alba, a contemporary circus festival organized by La Cascade, the national circus center. MuséAl, an archaeological museum opened in October 2013, presents objects from excavations—mosaics, sculptures, everyday items—with 3D video reconstructions.

The Château d'Alba-la-Romaine crowns a volcanic dyke at the village entrance—that is, a former solidified lava conduit that surrounding soft rocks eroded around, leaving the basalt in relief. This type of geological formation is characteristic of Ardèche and visible at several locations in the department. The castle itself hosts contemporary art exhibitions in season.

activities.text: The village loop between ramparts and lower quarters (2 to 3 km) is signposted with interpretive panels. Look for the basalt clock tower, the Trappe gateway (last remnant of the four medieval enclosure gates), and the lintels with sculptures classified as Monuments Historiques. The free circuit is available at the tourist office.

In July-August, themed guided tours "Sous les vignes, une ville antique" (Beneath the vines, an ancient city) blend modern and ancient viticulture, starting from the archaeological site through the surrounding vineyard. An original way to understand that Pliny the Elder himself already mentioned Alba's vines in 65 AD. Check times at the tourist office.

days_plan.itin_title: The 18 Most Beautiful Villages of Ardèche

visits.text: The basilica of Notre-Dame de Brebières was rebuilt after 1918 with its gilded statue at the top. More than 2,000 shells hit it during the Battle of Albert.
Descend 10 meters underground into the Somme 1916 Museum, set within 250 meters of tunnels. Realistic scenes recreate life in the trenches during the 1916 offensive.

activities.text: Albert marks the starting point of the Circuit of Remembrance toward Thiepval, Beaumont-Hamel, and the Newfoundland and Australian memorials.
The town rebuilt in the 1920s showcases Art Deco architecture bearing witness to resilience.

days_plan.itin_title: Somme Road Trip: Bay of Somme and War Remembrance

visits.text: Pass through the Porte de Savoie, a remnant of the 14th-century ramparts, to enter the medieval citadel of Conflans. Built on a rocky spur at the confluence of the Arly and Isère rivers, this upper town guarded the entrance to Tarentaise. Cobbled lanes, artisan workshops, and colorful facades have kept their charm intact.

The Maison Rouge, a listed 14th-century building, houses the Musée d'Art et d'Histoire d'Albertville (labeled Musée de France). Gallo-Roman archaeology, baroque sacred art, rural Savoyard objects, and early skiing equipment form a diverse collection.

The église Saint-Grat de Conflans, recognizable by its onion-dome bell tower, was rebuilt in the early 18th century. Its baroque interior—gilded altarpiece, carved woodwork—illustrates the importance of this art in the Savoyard valleys.

The Tour Sarrasine, built between the 11th and 12th centuries, is the sole vestige of the Château de la Cour. From the garden surrounding it, the panorama embraces Albertville, the Isère valley, and alpine summits.

Descend to the lower town to discover the "Tremplin 92, Mountain and Olympism" visitor center. The space recounts the 1992 Winter Olympics through documents, artifacts, and testimonies. The Halle Olympique, renovated in 2015, remains a venue for cultural and sporting events.

activities.text: Guided tour of Conflans with a guide from the Pays d'Art et d'Histoire. The route details the fortified gates, Château Manuel de Locatel (16th century, built by a noble merchant from Bergamo), and the 1390 Château Rouge.
Want to gain altitude? A paragliding flight above the valley lets you soar over the confluence of the Arly and Isère, with the Tarentaise peaks as backdrop.
Taste Savoyard specialties in Conflans inns: crozets gratinéed with Beaufort, diots in white wine, and polenta. Terraces offer plunging views over the valley.

days_plan.itin_title: Savoie from Lakes to Glaciers: Yenne to Haute-Maurienne

places.name: Albi

visits.text: Sainte-Cécile Cathedral commands attention as a single imposing mass: the world's largest brick cathedral, its single nave rises 30 meters high. The Italian paintings on the vault cover more than two hectares, and the 15th-century Last Judgment occupies the entire western wall.

Step into the Palais de la Berbie, a 13th-century episcopal fortress built of brick. It houses the museum dedicated to the painter born in Albi in 1864: posters, lithographs, early canvases, and scenes of Parisian cabarets form the world's largest collection devoted to this artist.

Descend into the palace gardens, awarded the Jardin Remarquable label. The terraces overlook the Tarn and offer panoramic views of the Pont-Vieux, one of France's oldest bridges, and the wild riverbanks below.

The Saint-Salvi collegiate church blends stone and brick, Romanesque and Gothic styles. Its cloister, hidden in the heart of the city, reveals Romanesque arcades and an enclosed garden where tranquility contrasts with the bustling streets nearby.

Cross the Pont-Vieux, built in the 11th century, then take up a spot on the right bank at square Botany Bay: the view of the episcopal city, with the cathedral and palace reflected in the Tarn, is Albi's most iconic.

Lose yourself in the narrow streets of the UNESCO-listed historic center. Half-timbered houses stand alongside Renaissance mansions, testaments to the wealth generated by the trade in woad, a plant used to produce a blue pigment.

activities.text: Board a gabarre, a flat-bottomed boat that once transported goods along the Tarn. From the river, the episcopal city reveals another side: mills, quays, and a lockkeeper's house.
Follow the Échappée Verte, a 4 km urban hiking trail along the Tarn riverbanks. The route connects downtown to green spaces along the GR 36.
Head to the covered market hall to taste local products: Lacaune cured meats, sheep's milk cheeses, and pink garlic from Lautrec. The market is liveliest on Saturday mornings.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Garonne Road Trip: From Toulouse to the Pyrenees
Tarn Road Trip: Albi & Hilltop Villages
Southeast France Road Trip: Perched Villages and Gorges

map_keywords: Jardins du Palais de la Berbie Albi

places.name: Alencon

visits.text: The Museum of Fine Arts and Lace occupies the former Jesuit college. Its flagship section displays the Point d'Alençon, a needle lace inscribed by UNESCO in 2010. A 19th-century bridal veil, 3.50 m long, required up to 500,000 hours of work.

Step through the doors of Notre-Dame Basilica. Its three-bay Flamboyant Gothic porch, built in the early 16th century, is one of the finest in Normandy. Inside, the 15th-century nave houses stained glass dating from 1530.
The Halle au Blé, a circular building erected between 1811 and 1819, surprises visitors with its impressive glass dome. Today it hosts cultural events.
Head to the Maison d'Ozé, a medieval mansion from 1450 and former residence of the Duke of Alençon. It now houses the tourist office and a heritage orchard.
The Château des Ducs d'Alençon preserves its machicolated towers, remnants of the medieval fortress. Its entrance pavilion sets the tone for this ducal town.

Wander the lanes of the Saint-Léonard quarter, Alençon's oldest neighborhood. Half-timbered houses, spiral staircases, and wrought-iron balconies line the Grande Rue. Don't miss the Maison des 7 Colonnes with its vividly painted timbers.

activities.text: Browse the town-center market on Thursdays or the Place Courteille market on Sunday mornings. Norman cheeses, cider, and regional produce fill the stalls.
Alençon is crossed by the Véloscénie, a cycle route linking Paris to Mont-Saint-Michel. Ride a section of it along the Orne and its landscaped banks.
The Écouves massif, approximately 15 km from Alençon, a 15-minute drive away, reaches 413 m at the Signal d'Écouves. Its stands of oak and beech are home to deer and roe deer.

days_plan.itin_title: Orne Road Trip: Norman Bocage and Stud Farms

map_keywords: Musée des Beaux-Arts et de la Dentelle Alençon

visits.text: Mine-témoin d'Alès, preserved historic mining site testifying to the Cévennes coal epic. Underground gallery descent recreates 19th-20th century miners' working conditions. Underground workings reveal extraction techniques, tools, wagons, and timbering. Museography traces industrial history of the Alès coal basin that employed up to 15,000 people. Collections display mine lamps, measuring instruments, installation models. The metal headframe dominates the site classified as Historic Monument. One-hour guided tours recount the dangerous daily life of the coal miners.

Saint-Jean-Baptiste Cathedral of Alès, 19th-century neoclassical building in the rebuilt city center. The monumental facade with Corinthian columns draws inspiration from Rome's Pantheon. The sober interior lit by a dome shelters a majestic organ and religious paintings. The cathedral quarter preserves Haussmannian buildings testifying to industrial urbanism. Place Gabriel-Péri bordered by cafés animates downtown. The neighboring Protestant temple recalls Protestantism's importance in Cévennes territory.

Musée-bibliothèque Pierre-André Benoît, modern and contemporary art collection installed in the former bishop's palace. The collection gathers 5,000 works by 20th-century creators: Picasso, Miró, Braque, Giacometti, Dubuffet. Artists' books, prints, drawings illustrate dialogue between poets and painters. Temporary exhibitions explore avant-garde artistic movements. The sculpted Mediterranean garden offers a plant setting for works. Free admission democratizes access to art.

Fort Vauban of Alès, 17th-century citadel dominating the city from Saint-Julien hill. The bastioned fortification designed by Vauban surveilled the Protestant region after Revocation of the Edict of Nantes. Pentagonal ramparts and casemates testify to classical military architecture. The panoramic site embraces the Alès agglomeration, Cévennes plain, and first mountain foothills. Ramparts now host walks and cultural events. Free access allows discovering fortifications and belvedere.

activities.text: Alès market at Place de la Mairie, daily gathering under Belle Époque metal halls. Cévennes producers offer organic vegetables, goat cheeses, charcuterie, honey, seasonal fruits. Colorful stalls overflow with olives, tapenades, flavored oils, Cévennes wines. The southern atmosphere resonates with singing accents and animated conversations. Rotisseries emit appetizing aromas of roasted chickens and paella. The particularly abundant Saturday morning market attracts residents throughout the agglomeration.

Evening at Le Cratère, Alès national performing arts center programming quality shows. The cultural center offers contemporary theater, dance, concerts, comedy, circus in a 500-seat modular hall. Eclectic programming mixes nationally significant productions and emerging artists. Artist meetings, workshops, and residencies enrich cultural offerings. The café-restaurant welcomes audiences before and after performances. Box office allows reserving seats for varied artistic evenings.

Walk towpaths along the Gardon d'Alès. Developed banks invite walks on foot or by bike in preserved natural setting. Century-old plane trees shade paths following the clear river. Equipped picnic areas allow bucolic breaks. Anglers practice their passion in calm banks. The route discovers Mediterranean fauna and flora: herons, kingfishers, tamarisk, poplars. The flat route accessible to all offers green escape near downtown.

days_plan.itin_title: Cèze Valley and Ardèche Gorges Circuit
Gard Circuit: Roman Nîmes, Pont du Gard and Camargue

visits.text: In 52 BC, this is where Vercingetorix surrendered to Caesar: the MuséoParc Alésia recounts the siege on the very site of the battle, in Alise-Sainte-Reine. The interpretation centre, a circular building by Bernard Tschumi, presents more than 600 objects and immersive displays. Ticket valid two days. Closed part of winter: check the calendar.

The Gallo-Roman vestiges of Alesia spread across the Mont-Auxois plateau, above the museum. After the Gallic defeat, a prosperous Roman town developed here in the 1st century. Theatre, forum, and houses can be made out on the ground; a free 3D tablet helps reconstruct them. Open April to November only.

activities.text: Climb to the monumental statue of Vercingetorix, a few minutes' walk away. Over six metres tall, it was erected under Napoleon III in the 1860s, during the construction of the Gallic myth. Access is free. The panorama over the plain explains at a glance why Caesar was able to encircle the stronghold.

days_plan.itin_title: Eastern France by Train from Paris

visits.text: The "Potence" of Allègre: this name designates the spectacular ruins of the 14th-century feudal castle, built atop the Baury volcano. Two towers linked by a cornice of trefoil machicolations remain balanced above the void. Classified as a Historic Monument in 1935.
The original castle counted 23 towers across 3 enceintes. Built by Morinot de Tourzel starting in 1385, it was one of Auvergne's most imposing. A chimney fire ravaged it on November 15, 1698.
Pass through the Porte de Monsieur, the south entrance to the fortified town. It has retained its two towers, the portcullis housing, and the hinges of the original gate.
On the Place du Marchédial, surrounded by fortified houses, the Chapelle Notre-Dame-de-l'Oratoire shelters a 16th-century Pietà.
Allègre, labeled a "Petite Cité de Caractère," reveals itself through its charreyrons: narrow lanes once used by water carriers between houses staggered on the slopes of Mont Baury.

activities.text: Climb to the summit of Mont Bar (1,175 m / 3,855 ft), unique in Europe: it's the only strombolian volcano sheltering a peat bog in its crater. An interpretive trail circles this Natura 2000 classified zone.
From the orientation table at the foot of the Potence, take in the Devès volcanoes, Mont Bar facing you, and the Velay mountains in the distance.
Allègre is the gateway to the Livradois-Forez Regional Natural Park. Several marked trails radiate from the village to explore the surrounding countryside.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Loire Road Trip: Le Puy-en-Velay and Volcanoes

visits.text: Ambérieu-en-Bugey marks the gateway to mountainous Bugey. This transit town and important railway junction has preserved a few old houses in its historic centre. The Neo-Gothic church and covered market bear witness to the 19th-century architecture of the period when the town developed following the arrival of the railway.

The Musée du Cheminot explores the railway history that shaped Ambérieu-en-Bugey. Its collections of objects, documents, equipment and reconstructions recount the work of railway employees and the development of the railways. The museum preserves the memory of the major railway junction around which the modern town developed.

Discover the railway heritage that shaped Ambérieu's identity. The old facilities, red-brick buildings and metal bridge spanning the Albarine tell the story of the railway adventure. The station, still in operation, sees freight trains and TGV services connecting Lyon to Geneva.

The immediate surroundings reveal the first foothills of Bugey. Limestone hills, deeply incised valleys and the first plateaux signal the region's mountainous character. Winding roads climb towards hilltop villages where a preserved rural atmosphere still prevails.

activities.text: Explore the nearby Dombes ponds. These artificial bodies of water, created in the Middle Ages for fish farming, are home to exceptional birdlife. Herons, egrets, ducks and migratory birds populate the reed beds and banks. Hiking trails allow you to observe this aquatic environment without disturbing protected species.

Fish in the Albarine or the nearby ponds. The fish-rich waters teem with trout, pike and carp. Local anglers share their secret spots and fishing techniques suited to Bugey's waterways. Angling associations organise competitions and events throughout the year.

Taste pike quenelles, an essential Bugey speciality. These light preparations made with fish flesh, flour and eggs are generally served coated in Nantua sauce made with crayfish butter. Local restaurants preserve the tradition of this emblematic recipe, which requires skill and expertise.

Travel along country roads towards the first villages of Bugey. Each hamlet has its own church, washhouse and stone farmhouses. Scattered settlements, hedgerows and grazed meadows form an authentic rural landscape where extensive farming maintains biodiversity.

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip from Bresse to Bugey via Beaujolais and Lyon

visits.text: The Moulin Richard de Bas, nestled in the Laga valley at the heart of Parc Livradois-Forez, is Auvergne's last paper mill. Since the 15th century, it has continued making rag paper by hand using ancestral methods dating back to 1326. Two hundred sheets a day still emerge from its vats, paper of such quality that it was used to print Diderot and d'Alembert's encyclopedia and is still used to restore works of art. Awarded the Entreprise du Patrimoine Vivant label, the mill can be visited in an hour with a guide who reveals the secrets of making paper pulp.

Ambert's round town hall is unique in Europe. This 19th-century circular building, whose shape recalls a wheel of Fourme d'Ambert cheese, houses administrative services, the municipal council chamber, and a wedding hall at the building's center. The ground floor's circular exhibition traces the town's history. Classified as a Historic Monument in 1975, the town hall was immortalized in Jules Romains' 1913 novel Les Copains.

The Maison de la Fourme d'Ambert presents the production, history, and tasting of this PDO blue cheese, one of France's oldest. Ambert is so closely tied to fourme that the town is twinned with Gorgonzola in Italy, another blue cheese town. The Plus Beaux Détours de France label distinguishes this medieval town with its narrow lanes, half-timbered houses, and Art Nouveau architecture.

The Gothic Saint-Jean church dominates Ambert's historic center, rising above its medieval lanes. The old quarter reveals varied built heritage, where half-timbered houses, Renaissance facades, and Art Nouveau features stand side by side, testifying to the past prosperity of this papermaking and cheesemaking town.

activities.text: Workshop to make a sheet of handmade paper at the Moulin Richard de Bas. Each participant dips the mold into the pulp vat and creates their own sheet using the centuries-old techniques of master papermakers. The mill shop offers notebooks, cards, printed texts, and paper with pressed flowers.

Journey on the AGRIVAP tourist train between Ambert and La Chaise-Dieu. This historic line crosses the rolling landscapes of Livradois-Forez, passing high-altitude meadows, fir woods, and small granite villages, offering an unusual view of the regional nature park from the railway.

Explore the Parc naturel régional Livradois-Forez around Ambert. Marked hiking trails, forest roads, and backroads lead through moderately elevated mountain terrain where granite plateaus, deep valleys, and conifer forests alternate.

days_plan.itin_title: Volcanoes and Auvergne traditions

visits.text: Fort Ambleteuse, built by Vauban between 1683 and 1690 at the mouth of the Slack, is the only sea fort still standing from Cherbourg to the Belgian border. An artillery tower protected by a horseshoe-shaped rampart, it was meant to defend a military harbour planned by Louis XIV—a project abandoned due to silting.

At high tide, the fort is surrounded by the sea—a striking spectacle. At the top of the tower, a viewpoint map helps you identify the English coast in clear weather. Six relief models recount Ambleteuse's history, from Henry VIII's citadel to the seaside resort.

Napoleon restored the fort in 1803 to prepare for the invasion of England, developing the Slack estuary with jetties and quays. The Germans installed artillery casemates there during the Second World War. Listed as a Historic Monument in 1965, it was bought for a token franc by an association of volunteers who have been restoring it ever since.

The Slack estuary is a remarkable habitat where fresh and salt water mingle. A breeding ground for marine wildlife and a stopover for migratory birds, it can be explored along unobtrusive paths among reeds and salt marshes.

Villa Robinson (also called villa Flé), listed as a Historic Monument, is the work of architect Louis Bonnier. It is part of the modest seaside architectural heritage that survived the destruction of the Second World War—many villas were destroyed during military exercises.

activities.text: The Slack dune system extends over more than 200 ha—an ecological complex with no equivalent on the European coast. The area close to the sea is accessible; the inland dune, fragile and sensitive to trampling, is protected.
Ambleteuse's communal meadow, a 60 ha regional nature reserve, offers common grazing inherited from a 1209 charter. Meadows, ponds, nesting birds: a bucolic walk away from the beach.
Ambleteuse's Second World War museum displays uniforms, documents and everyday objects. A direct complement to a visit to the fort and the coastal bunkers.

days_plan.itin_title: Opal Coast Villages and Flemish Heartlands
The Most Beautiful Villages from Flanders to the Bay of Somme

places.name: Amboise

visits.text: Stop in Vouvray, six miles east of Tours en route to Amboise. The AOC Vouvray vineyard, nearly 5,000 acres on the right bank slopes of the Loire, produces chenin blanc wines—dry, semi-dry, sweet or sparkling—aged in troglodyte caves carved from tufa. These underground galleries, stretching for miles, maintain a constant temperature of 54°F.

The royal Château d'Amboise, perched on its promontory above the Loire. Favorite residence of Charles VIII, who died here in 1498 after striking a door lintel, then of François I who invited Leonardo da Vinci. The Saint-Hubert Chapel, a jewel of Flamboyant Gothic, houses Leonardo's presumed tomb. From the rampart balcony, sweeping views over the river and town.

The Clos Luce, Leonardo da Vinci's final home, a third of a mile from the chateau. The Tuscan genius lived here from 1516 until his death in 1519, invited by Francois I who gave him this pink-brick manor. The workshops recreate his study. In the seventeen-acre park, forty giant models of his inventions, swing bridge, armored vehicle and aerial screw, line the path.

The old town of Amboise stretches at the château's foot between Loire and hillside. Medieval lanes, Renaissance mansions and a covered market compose an authentic setting. The Clock Tower, former city gate, dates from the 15th century.

Amboise conceals remarkable troglodyte heritage. The granaries of Caesar, carved into the limestone hillside, served as grain silos since antiquity. Further on, troglodyte dwellings inhabited until the 20th century show the ingenuity of these houses—cool in summer, warm in winter—carved from soft tufa rock.

activities.text: Tasting in the troglodyte cellars of Vouvray, about 16 km from the stopover town, 15 minutes by road. The winegrowers welcome visitors into their underground galleries to reveal the range of chenin blanc: mineral dry, fruity off-dry, golden sweet or lively sparkling. Traditional-method sparkling Vouvray is the local pride.

Leonardo's inventions trail at the Clos Lucé. The Leonardo da Vinci park displays full-scale models in a verdant setting. Children operate drawbridges, gears and propellers. Underground, digital painting galleries immerse you in Leonardo's work.

A stroll on the Île d'Or, between the two arms of the Loire facing the castle. This shaded park offers the finest view of the castle's north front and its gardens. Picnicking by the river is possible.

Excursion to the Pagoda of Chanteloup, two miles from Amboise. This 144-foot folly, inspired by 18th-century chinoiserie taste, is the sole vestige of the Duke of Choiseul's château. The climb to its summit offers panoramas over forest and valley.

days_plan.itin_title: Indre-et-Loire Road Trip: Loire Valley Châteaux, Secret Valleys & Touraine Vineyards

map_keywords: Clos Lucé Léonard de Vinci Amboise

visits.text: Notre-Dame Cathedral rises 145 meters and has the largest interior volume of any cathedral in France. Built in the 13th century, it houses medieval sculptures and a labyrinth set into the floor.
Small colorful houses line the canals of the Somme in the Saint-Leu quarter. Once home to medieval craftsmen, the lanes now house art galleries and antique shops.
Glide in a barque à cornet along the 65 kilometers of canals in the Hortillonnages. These floating gardens cover 300 hectares farmed for 800 years and are home to market gardeners' huts and herons.
Jules Verne lived for 18 years in this house with a tower, where he wrote more than 30 novels. His study on the second floor still has its original furniture.
The Picardy Museum displays collections spanning from Prehistory to the 21st century in a palace built between 1855 and 1867, modeled after Napoleon III's Louvre.

activities.text: Visit the marché sur l'eau on Saturday morning to buy fruit and vegetables from the market gardeners.
The Jules Verne circus, built in 1889, hosts shows and concerts in its round building, listed as a historic monument.
The Perret Tower rises 104 meters opposite the train station, Europe's first reinforced concrete skyscraper erected in 1952.
Ten kilometers away, Samara park recreates dwellings from Prehistory to the Middle Ages across 30 hectares with demonstrations of ancient crafts.

days_plan.itin_title: Somme Road Trip: Bay of Somme and War Remembrance

visits.text: The Jardin des Faïenciers in Sarreguemines extends the museum visit outdoors across 8,000 m². Created in 2009 by landscape architect Philippe Niez, it combines industrial heritage with contemporary planting. Dye plants used to produce glazes, including madder and woad, aquatic species along the Blies stream and katsura trees (Cercidiphyllum) with their gingerbread scent create a sensory journey through the seasons. Glass cubes house changing plant arrangements.

Walygator Grand-Est amusement park offers its thrills with 40 attractions across 45 hectares of forest. Three roller coasters, including the Anaconda with its 36-metre loop, thrill rides and family attractions are laid out on different levels in a preserved woodland setting. Thrill seekers will enjoy the Monster (35 m of free fall) and the vertiginous drops at 90 km/h. A water zone, shows and entertainment complete the offering.

activities.text: Amnéville Thermal Baths offer a relaxing break in 2,500 m² of thermal-water pools heated to 34°C. A hammam, Finnish sauna, Roman caldarium and eight outdoor hot tubs provide relaxation after sightseeing. The thermal centre also offers 60 treatments and massages by reservation, as well as approved spa programmes for rheumatic and respiratory conditions. The Vitalis relaxation area has a water slide and a counter-current river.

Walk along the Orne Valley, a former iron-and-steel industrial area converted into a 15 km green corridor. Hayange’s vegetation-covered slag heaps and the former wastelands around the blast furnaces bear witness to the region’s metallurgical past. Nature is reclaiming the area, with wild orchids and rare butterflies, while peaceful trails lead walkers through a landscape combining heritage and biodiversity.

days_plan.itin_title: 4-Day Moselle Tour: Metz, Bitche Citadel and Chagall’s Stained Glass

places.name: Ampuis

visits.text: Better preserved than Rome's Pantheon - yes, really. The Temple of Augustus and Livia in Vienne has survived intact since the 1st century BC, partly because it served as a courthouse, then a church, then a grain depot depending on the era. The Corinthian facade and its fluted columns dominate Place du Palais, right in the city center. Free entry, explanatory panel in front - allow 20 minutes, longer if you're curious.

Vienne's ancient theater, carved into Pipet hill following its slope, could seat 11,000 spectators in the 1st century. It's still in use—the Jazz à Vienne festival has been held here every July since 1981 and attracts world-class headliners. Outside festival season, climbing to the upper tiers offers a panorama of the Rhône that few tourists see: they all stay down below.

On the right bank of the Rhône facing Vienne, the museum of Saint-Romain-en-Gal presents one of France's richest Gallo-Roman collections—mosaics measuring 200 m², frescoes, tools, workshop reconstructions. The site is the former commercial port of Roman Vienne, excavated since the 1960s over 7 hectares. Under your feet, intact archaeological layers still remain. Closed Mondays.

Côte Brune and Côte Blonde, just above Ampuis—one on brown soils of mica and amphibole, the other on decomposed pale granite—produce two different styles of Syrah 500 meters apart. This is where it gets serious. The terraces with slopes steeper than 40°, some so narrow only a single hiker can pass at a time, explain why certain plots are still worked with winches. Pull over by the roadside to look: the vines literally cling to the cliff face.

activities.text: Maison Guigal is the ultimate benchmark for Côte-Rôtie. In 1978, Marcel Guigal released his first 'La Mouline', 'La Landonne', and 'La Turque' cuvées - three wines that put the northern Rhône on the world map. The cellar tour is carefully planned, educational, and truly impressive. Book on the website; places are limited.

Dinner in Ampuis or Condrieu on the Rhône riverbank. The river is calm at this point, and lights from villages on the opposite bank reflect in the water. If you want a simple local restaurant, the riverside inn in Condrieu will do—save your culinary ammunition for Le Beau Rivage tomorrow.

days_plan.itin_title: Rhône Valley: From Northern Syrahs to Southern Grenaches

map_keywords: Temple of Augustus and Livia Vienne

visits.text: The Château d'Ancy-le-Franc is a masterpiece of Italian Renaissance architecture in Burgundy. Designed around 1542 by architect Sebastiano Serlio for Antoine III de Clermont, brother-in-law of Diane de Poitiers, it's the only French château to adopt a perfectly square plan with four identical wings. The interior frescoes, created by artists from the Fontainebleau school (including Primaticcio and Nicolò dell'Abate), cover more than 4,000 square meters—a unique ensemble in France. Allow 1.5 hours for the guided tour.

Take time to stroll through the château's park: French-style parterres, a canal, and classical vistas. The estate has recently been restored and the gardens replanted in the Renaissance spirit. From the terraces, the view over the village rooftops and the Auxois countryside is restful.

Head down to the Canal de Bourgogne, which runs through the village. The lock and the plane-tree-lined canal reaches create a landscape typical of Burgundy's waterways. If you see a barge maneuvering through the lock, stop and watch—it's always a little spectacle.

activities.text: Hop on a bike along the Canal de Bourgogne cycle route—the section between Ancy-le-Franc and Tonnerre is flat, shaded, and virtually car-free. Rental shops offer bikes near the lock. Allow 1.5 hours for the round trip.

If you have time, continue to the château de Tanlay, about 17 km by road northwest of Ancy-le-Franc. Another Renaissance gem, it preserves a trompe-l'oeil gallery in the Tour de la Ligue, where Admiral de Coligny gathered Protestant leaders during the French Wars of Religion.

days_plan.itin_title: Burgundy's 15 Most Beautiful Villages

visits.text: Andlau's abbey church was founded around 880 by Richardis, wife of Emperor Charles the Fat, before becoming a powerful chapter of canonesses. Its carved Romanesque frieze, one of the richest in Alsace, blends biblical scenes and animal figures along the porch. Above the village, the ruins of the Château du Haut-Andlau and its two round towers provide an opportunity for a walk through the surrounding vineyards.

activities.text: The Musée de la Folie Marco, housed in an 18th-century townhouse, displays furniture and regional objects typical of Andlau. A peaceful alternative to the castle walk on rainy days.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Villages of Alsace in 4 Days

visits.text: Bambouseraie en Cévennes in Générargues, a unique botanical garden in Europe created in 1856. The giant bamboo forest covers 84 acres sheltering over 1,000 bamboo varieties reaching 82 feet high. The Zen Japanese garden with red bridge, stone lanterns, and koi carp offers a meditative interlude. The reconstructed Laotian village presents traditional stilt houses surrounded by banana trees and lotus flowers. Tropical greenhouses gather tree ferns, orchids, and exotic plants. The maze-like park invites shaded strolling, refreshing in summer.

Village of Anduze, traditional Cévennes town and gateway to the Cévennes at the Gardon confluence. Tortuous medieval alleyways climb from quays bordering the river. The Protestant temple clock tower overlooks a covered square hosting weekly markets. Corbelled houses with colorful facades testify to traditional Cévennes architecture. Workshops perpetuate manufacture of famous Anduze vases, monumental glazed pottery adorning gardens since the 17th century. Shops offer chestnuts, Pélardon, chestnut honey, and local products.

Steam Train of the Cévennes, historic tourist line connecting Anduze to Saint-Jean-du-Gard. Century-old locomotives pull Belle Époque carriages for eight miles along the Gardon de Mialet. The winding route crosses tunnels, viaducts, and spectacular Cévennes landscapes. Commentary relates the railway's history, created in 1880 to transport silk, wood, and chestnuts. Restored stations preserve period railway architecture. The one-hour round trip plunges into retro railway atmosphere.

activities.text: Canoe-kayak descent of the Gardon River from Anduze. The clear river winds between limestone cliffs and pebble beaches under forest cover. Moderate rapids alternate with calm sections suitable for swimming. Rental companies offer routes from 4 to 15 miles depending on level and available time. The Gardon canyon reveals caves, emerald pools, and preserved wild landscapes. Cliffs shelter reintroduced griffon vultures soaring over gorges. The family activity allows discovering the Cévennes from the river.

Exploration of the Trabuc cave, an underground network of 8 kilometres of which 1.2 km are laid out for visits. The galleries reveal thousand-year-old formations: stalactites, stalagmites, limestone draperies in ochre tones. The lake of the Hundred Thousand Soldiers astonishes with its 100,000 thread-like stalagmites, unique in the world. The cathedral chambers impress by their size and exceptional geological formations. The constant temperature of 14°C offers welcome coolness in summer. The 45-minute guided tours recount the use of the cave as a refuge for the Camisards. The cave is about 11 km from the stopover town, 17 minutes by road.

Taste Cévennes products at local farms and producers. Pélardon AOC, small aged goat cheese, comes plain, ash-covered, or with aromatic herbs. Dried, creamed, or candied chestnuts illustrate the historic importance of the chestnut tree, the Cévennes "bread tree." Full-bodied chestnut honey, heather, or wildflower comes from transhumant apiaries. Sweet onions of the Cévennes AOC cook as confit or raw in salads. Artisan canneries offer terrines, confits, and traditional Cévennes dishes.

days_plan.itin_title: Gard Circuit: Roman Nîmes, Pont du Gard and Camargue

visits.text: Château d'Anet, jewel of the French Renaissance built in 1548 for Diane de Poitiers, mistress of King Henry II. Philibert Delorme, Benvenuto Cellini, and Jean Goujon created a masterpiece that led Joachim Du Bellay to call it the “paradise of Anet”. The surviving wing houses period furniture and sumptuous tapestries.

Diane de Poitiers' funerary chapel, built by her daughter to house her magnificent tomb, the work of Pierre Bontemps. After centuries of upheaval, her remains were identified and returned here in 2010. The trompe-l'œil dome and checkerboard floor create a striking illusion.

Château entrance gatehouse, a veritable triumphal arch in the classical style with its four Doric columns. The monumental clock shows the phases of the moon, a symbol of Diana the huntress. The sculpted group depicting Diana embracing a stag is a copy of the original in the Louvre.

Royal chapel of the château, a masterpiece with a Greek cross plan featuring a coffered dome and checkerboard floor creating a mirror effect. A unique example of Renaissance architecture where geometric decoration draws the eye toward the celestial heights.

activities.text: Walk through the royal Eure valley around Anet, where the river winds between meadows and groves. This bucolic landscape inspired Renaissance poets who praised the 'garden carpeted with eternal greenery' of Diane's estate.

Discover the village of Anet and the Church of Saint-Cyr-Sainte-Julitte, whose construction was financed by Diane de Poitiers. The stained glass windows and furnishings testify to the royal favorite's generosity toward her parish.

days_plan.itin_title: Eure-et-Loir Tour: Chartres, Châteaux and Proust

visits.text: The château commands the Maine from its promontory. Its 17 towers of black schist and sandstone enclose the Apocalypse Tapestry, 103 metres of medieval tapestry listed by UNESCO.
The château gardens combine a Renaissance kitchen garden and vines, with panoramic views over the city and the Maine valley.
Saint-Maurice Cathedral shows the domed vaults typical of Angevin Gothic. Its stained-glass windows date from the 12th century.

The 13th-century Toussaint abbey church houses the David d'Angers Gallery. A contemporary glass roof floods the local sculptor's monumental works with light. His original plaster casts served as models for the works displayed in the Panthéon and Père-Lachaise.
Step through the door of the Maison d'Adam, a 15th-century half-timbered house decorated with carved woodwork.
The Museum of Fine Arts occupies the 15th-century Logis Barrault, presenting collections spanning from the Middle Ages to contemporary art.

activities.text: Terra Botanica is the first European park devoted to plants. Its 5,000 species from five continents are spread over 22 hectares. The tethered balloon lifts you 150 metres up to take in the whole park.
Stroll along the banks of the Maine and reach the Doutre quarter by the bridges. The quays offer a unique perspective on the château.
The Saumur wine cellars, about 44 km from the stopover town, 45 minutes by road, produce crémants and white wines. Several estates offer tastings in their troglodyte cellars.

days_plan.itin_title: Maine-et-Loire Road Trip: Anjou and Loire Valley Châteaux

visits.text: Angles-sur-l'Anglin has been listed among the Plus Beaux Villages de France since 1982—the only one in the Vienne department. Medieval houses cluster together on a rocky spur between the river and the plateau.
The 11th-century fortress dominates the village from 40 meters above the Anglin. Its majestic ruins—towers, walls, chapel—offer panoramic views over the valley and the village rooftops below.

The Roc-aux-Sorciers Interpretation Center presents a reconstruction of a 20-meter sculpted frieze, 15,000 years old. Considered the "Lascaux of sculpture," the original site is closed to the public for conservation reasons.

Step into the village's artisan workshops. The Jours d'Angles embroidery technique, invented here, provided a livelihood for over 300 female workers in the 1950s. Demonstrations are offered in season.

activities.text: Canoe or kayak down the Anglin. The rental center offers equipment on-site, a few kilometers from the village.
Hike along the cliffs of the Anglin and then the Gartempe. The trail passes by troglodyte dwellings near Saint-Pierre-de-Maillé.
Want a fun outing? The Tèrra Aventura app offers "Les Jours d'Angles sont contés," a geolocated treasure hunt through the village.

days_plan.itin_title: Vienne Road Trip: Futuroscope and Romanesque Heritage

visits.text: The Cité internationale de la BD occupies a former wine cellar on the banks of the Charente. Over 20,000 original comic pages, cutting-edge temporary exhibitions, and Europe's largest comic book library. Allow 2 hours to make the most of it.

The Cathédrale Saint-Pierre is Romanesque, not Gothic — and that changes everything. The sculpted 12th-century façade tells the story of the Ascension and the Last Judgement across 70 stone figures. The contemporary Treasury by Jean-Michel Othoniel is worth a detour.

The ramparts walk offers a full panorama over the Charente below. Angoulême sits on a rocky spur — you can see why it served as a stronghold. It's also the best vantage point for spotting the comic book murals.

Over 30 monumental murals in the streets: Titeuf on a gable end, Lucky Luke at a crossroads, Blake and Mortimer around the corner of a narrow lane. Free map at the tourist office. Kids love them, and so do adults.

Under the Halles centrales, producers sell pineau, rillettes and cagouilles (local snails). Around them, cobbled lanes climb towards the town hall housed in the former counts' castle. Good bistros in the area.

activities.text: Guided tour “Comics in the City”. The qualified tour guides know the stories behind every mural: who painted what, why there, the hidden details. Duration: 1 hour 30 minutes, departure from the tourist office.

Walk along the Charente riverbanks. The towpath runs from the Cité BD along the river. Canoe hire available at the watersports centre in season. Quieter option: traditional gabare boat with commentary.
Musée d'Angoulême in the former bishop's palace, behind the cathedral. Varied collections: Charente archaeology (the famous gold Agris helmet), African arts, regional paintings. Small but well done.

days_plan.itin_title: Charente Tour: Cognac and Romanesque Heritage in 4 Days

places.name: Annecy

visits.text: Annecy deserves its reputation as the “Venice of the Alps”—and the nickname isn't just a tourist pitch. The Thiou river, which flows from the lake, crosses the old town feeding canals that were already running in the Middle Ages to power mills and trip hammers. The Palais de l'Isle, perched on a triangular islet in the middle of the canal since the 12th century, has successively been the seat of the lords of the Isle, a mint (the County of Geneva minted coins here from 1356 to 1392), a courthouse and a prison—it was still used as a prison during World War II. Listed as a historic monument in 1900, it now houses the Centre d'Interprétation de l'Architecture et du Patrimoine. It's the city's most photographed building—and with good reason.

The Château d'Annecy overlooks the old town from a hill: built between the 12th and 16th centuries, it was the residence of the counts of Geneva, then the dukes of Genevois-Nemours when Savoy bought it in 1401. The Tour de la Reine, the oldest part (13th century), sets the tone for its long history. Now a museum, it presents collections on Alpine archaeology and regional heritage—but it's especially from its esplanades that you'll understand why Annecy looks the way it does: a turquoise lake framed by peaks, the ocher-roofed old town below, the Pre-Alps in the background. Head up toward the end of the day for the light.

The Albigny–Sévrier area offers direct views of the lake with the mountains in the background. The Pont des Amours, a footbridge spanning the canal du Vassé between the Jardins de l'Europe and the Pâquier, is a classic viewpoint overlooking the canal and the île aux Cygnes—according to legend, a kiss exchanged here guarantees eternal love. You decide.

Head up to the Col de la Forclaz—at an altitude of 1,147 meters, around twenty kilometers south of central Annecy, about a 30-minute drive from Annecy. The road is spectacular, and the final hairpin bends even more so. Once at the top, the entire lake spreads out before you: turquoise waters framed by peaks, the village of Talloires below, and dozens of paragliding wings silently soaring overhead. This is one of the world's most renowned free-flight sites—on some fine days, more than a thousand takeoffs are recorded. The view is absolutely breathtaking, whether you take to the air or not. Restaurants at the pass serve the customary fondues and tartiflettes.

As you descend back toward Annecy, detour to the Château de Menthon-Saint-Bernard, perched on its promontory above the lake like something from a fairy tale. Built between the 10th and 18th centuries, it's been the residence of the same family for nine hundred years—and it's said that Bernard of Menthon, born here in 923, became the patron saint of mountaineers and founded the Great St. Bernard Hospice. The visit, enlivened by actors in period costume, is particularly suited to families. Reserve ahead in summer—slots fill quickly.

activities.text: Rental operators offer electric boats, pedal boats and paddleboards right by the lake, at the Pâquier and at several water sports centers around the lake. Booking is recommended in July and August, when demand is very high.

An introductory tandem paragliding flight at the Col de la Forclaz is Annecy's most memorable activity—flying above an alpine lake at an altitude of 1,100 meters while watching the mountains pass beneath your feet is hard to forget. Providers approved by the Fédération Française de Vol Libre operate from the pass and from the Planfait site, with landings on the lakeshore. Allow about an hour for preparations, travel and the flight itself. Reserve ahead, spots go quickly from spring onward.

The cycling greenway around the lake between Annecy and Saint-Jorioz (a round trip of about 20 km) is the ideal alternative for those who prefer to keep their feet on the ground: a path entirely separated from traffic, constant lake views, and direct access to several free beaches where you can take a dip along the way. Bike rentals are available in central Annecy, at the station and in several lakeside towns. In summer, leave early in the morning before the crowds.

visits.text: Annot sits at an altitude of 700 metres at the foot of a jumble of rocks designated an Espace Naturel Sensible since 1921 — sandstone blocks formed 35 to 40 million years ago by underwater avalanches, then fractured during the formation of the Alps. The village itself is medieval: its 11th-century ramparts are still clearly visible, and the houses in local sandstone give the lanes a very distinctive warm hue. Look for carved lintels, corbelled houses and vaulted passages — every façade detail tells of a trade or a date.

The Grès Trail (starting at the station, 6 km loop, 350 m elevation gain, about 3 hours) is the highlight of the stop. It first crosses the Jardins du Roi — cantilevered rock formations — then reaches the Chambre du Roi, a cave in the cliffs where, according to legend, a lord and his princess hid until a traitor gave them away. The natural arch of Les Portettes marks the descent; the Espaluns viewpoint offers the best view down over the village. Hiking boots are essential — the trail can be slippery.

activities.text: The Grès d'Annot cliffs are considered the benchmark for traditional climbing in France: no artificial holds, and climbers place their own protection in the bare rock. Local operators offer introductory sessions for beginners or guided outings on equipped routes. Even if you don't climb, watching the climbers from below in this forest of century-old chestnut trees is worth the detour.

If you're passing through between May and October, check the timetable for the Train à Vapeur des Pignes: volunteers from GECP (Groupe d'Étude pour les Chemins de fer de Provence) run a steam locomotive on selected weekends. Annot is the terminus for these heritage trains — boarding or simply watching the engine manoeuvre at the station is a special experience.

places.name: Ansouis

visits.text: Ansouis has been officially labeled one of France's Most Beautiful Villages since 1982—and the distinction is richly deserved. Its houses cling in a semicircle to the southern flank of a rocky spur facing the Mourre Nègre, the highest point of the Luberon. As you wander through its stone lanes (calades), be sure to visit the Balcon du Barri, the commanding panoramic viewpoint from the medieval ramparts overlooking the Lourmarin valley and the Luberon foothills. Claude Berri filmed several scenes from Jean de Florette and Manon des Sources here in 1986—and gazing at this landscape, you'll immediately understand why.

The Chateau d'Ansouis has dominated the village since the 10th century. Originally a military fortress, with its square keep and four towers, it passed to the powerful Sabran family in 1178. The 17th century transformed it into a pleasure residence with some of the finest plasterwork decoration in Provence. It has been classified as a Historic Monument since 1948 and is still inhabited by its passionate owners, who personally conduct the guided tour. Book ahead: it is open from April through All Saints' Day, with weekend time slots. Allow at least 1.5 hours to appreciate the armoury hall, the terraced gardens, and the small 18th-century house known as the Hermitage, tucked away at the heart of the chateau.

At Château Turcan, the Museum of Wine Arts and Trades displays over 3,000 tools related to viticulture, including one of Provence's oldest wine presses (18th century) and an oenology laboratory dating from 1900. A genuine curiosity, especially if you're interested in traditional winemaking techniques.

activities.text: Walking loop through vineyards, olive groves and cherry orchards at the foot of the village (approximately 1h15). The trails along the stone lanes lead toward the Aigues valley, with open views across the southern Luberon foothills.

Late in the day, climb up to the Barri viewpoint for the end-of-afternoon light over the valley. It's one of the finest panoramas in the southern Luberon—locals call it their terrace overlooking Provence.

map_keywords: Musée des Arts et Métiers du Vin Château Turcan Ansouis

visits.text: In 1946, Picasso accepted curator Dor de la Souchère's invitation and set up his studio on the 2nd floor of Grimaldi Castle—the former acropolis of the Greek city of Antipolis, founded in the 4th century BC. He worked there from mid-September to mid-November 1946, with Françoise Gilot at his side. In two months of intense work, he created dozens of works including “La Joie de Vivre,” a major painting from this period. When he left for Paris, he placed 23 paintings and 44 drawings in the city's care. The castle officially became the “Picasso Museum” on December 27, 1966—the world's first dedicated to the artist. Allow 90 minutes. Closed Mondays.

The Vieil Antibes stretches around its ancient ramparts reinforced by Vauban: Provençal lanes, pastel façades, the cathedral of the Immaculate Conception combining Romanesque and Baroque styles (a 1515 altarpiece by Louis Bréa in the side chapel). The Provençal market on cours Masséna is held every morning, except Mondays from September to May - one of the most beautiful on the Côte d'Azur, with a flower market and a craft market alternating.

Fort Carré, built in the 16th century on a rocky peninsula, raises its four bastions 26 meters above the sea. Napoleon Bonaparte was briefly imprisoned here in 1794, during the Revolution. Panoramic view from the ramparts over the Baie des Anges, Nice and the Pre-Alps—even more spectacular from the northern bastions. Access on foot from the port, 15 minutes.

Port Vauban, one of the largest marinas in the Mediterranean with 1,650 berths. Yachts over 50 meters are moored at the “billionaires' quay” on the northwest side. The Belle Époque architecture facing the basin contrasts with the ultramodern lines of the boats—a spectacle in itself, especially in early evening.

The Safranier quarter, wedged between the ramparts and the cathedral, has proclaimed itself a “free commune” since 1966—humorous signs, flower-decked facades, a bohemian atmosphere. A few dozen houses, quiet streets a short walk from luxury shops. Inhabited year-round, lively and authentic.

activities.text: The Tire-Poil path runs along Cap d'Antibes for about 5 km between cliffs and turquoise sea. Coves accessible by climbing over rocks, sumptuous villas hidden in vegetation on the landward side. One of the Côte d'Azur's most beautiful coastal walks. Arrive early in summer—the parking lot at Plage de la Garoupe fills up quickly. Closed-toe shoes.

Swimming at Plage de la Gravette, Old Antibes' only free sand beach: directly at the ramparts' foot, protected by the port. Generally calm water. A rarity on this stretch of coast where private beaches dominate.

Garoupe Lighthouse at the summit of Cap d'Antibes: 73 km range, one of the Mediterranean's most powerful. One hundred steps, then 180° view over the sea, Mercantour and Estérel. The neighboring Notre-Dame de Bon Port chapel houses a touching collection of fishermen's ex-votos from the 16th to 20th centuries.

Discover Villa Eilenroc on Cap d’Antibes, a neoclassical residence designed by Charles Garnier in 1867 and surrounded by an 11-hectare park featuring an olive grove and a rose garden. The villa is currently open to the public on Saturdays from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., with last admission at 4:30 p.m. Admission costs €2 for adults and is free for children under 12. Check the opening hours before your visit.

visits.text: Parc de Sceaux extends south to Antony. The Grenouillère pavilion offers dining by the Grand Canal.
The Saint-Saturnin church dates back to the 12th century. The Romanesque bell tower testifies to Antony's ancient history.

activities.text: The Vallée aux Loups shelters Chateaubriand's House. The writer lived here from 1807 to 1818 and penned his Memoirs from Beyond the Grave. The landscape park preserves centuries-old trees.
The Bièvre river flows through the wooded valley. Once polluted, the stream is gradually recovering its purity in preserved natural areas.

days_plan.itin_title: Hauts-de-Seine Road Trip: Royal Heritage & Gardens

visits.text: Antraigues-sur-Volane perches at 470 meters on a basalt outcrop between three rivers. This designated village full of character offers a striking panorama over the Cévennes valleys and volcanic massifs.

activities.text: The Festival Ferrat celebrates lyric-focused French chanson every summer in July. Free and ticketed concerts bring the village to life for three days.

days_plan.itin_title: Ardèche Road Trip: Wild Gorges and Villages with Character

visits.text: Saint-Just Church, visible from afar thanks to its ocher-yellow stone bell tower reaching 60 meters. The Romanesque building consists of three naves with galleries and numerous side chapels. The architecture testifies to Arbois's rich wine-growing past. The warm stone color gives this monument dominating the wine town its distinctive character.

Louis Pasteur's House, preserved in the state the scientist knew it. Pasteur returned here regularly throughout his life and set up a private laboratory where he developed the famous pasteurization process. The museum presents his research work and his connection to the region. Fun science workshops for families are organized during school holidays, making science accessible to the youngest visitors.

Wine and Vine Museum at Château Pécauld, a medieval building that was part of the old fortifications. The visit begins in the vineyards planted around the château. The rooms trace the work of the vine, the social history of winemakers, and the vinification of Jura grape varieties: Poulsard, Trousseau, Chardonnay, Vin de Paille, Macvin, and Vin Jaune. The collections explain why Arbois became France's first AOC in 1936.

Fruitière Vinicole d'Arbois at Château Béthanie. This cooperative founded in 1906 during the wine crisis testifies to the collaborative work of winemakers. It contributed to improving Jura wine quality and obtaining the AOC designation. The 14th-century cellars host tastings of Arbois and Côtes du Jura wines. The venue also organizes vineyard walks with audio guides via QR codes.

Cascade des Tufs at Planches-pres-Arbois, at the foot of a vast reculee. A family-friendly walk leads to this marvel gushing in an invigorating environment. Water cascades over tufa limestone formations covered with mosses and lush vegetation. The forest trail offers immersion in Jura nature just moments from the village.

Pont des Capucins, an 18th-century pedestrian bridge under which flows the Cuisance. Locals also call it the lovers' bridge. The view of the town from this tranquil spot reveals the Gloriette Tower, a square fortification from the 13th to 17th centuries standing 17 meters high. The bucolic setting invites contemplation away from the bustle of the center.

activities.text: Cellar visits and Jura wine tasting. Winemakers open their doors to introduce Savagnin, Chardonnay, Poulsard, Trousseau, and local specialties like Vin Jaune aged six years and three months under veil, Vin de Paille with its candied fruit aromas, and Macvin, a typical aperitif. The centuries-old vaulted cellars create the ideal atmosphere for understanding these exceptional wines.

Walk through the vineyards to Pupillin, 3 kilometers away. This village boasts an impressive concentration of winemakers per square kilometer and is considered the world capital of Poulsard. The south-west-facing slopes offer magnificent panoramas over plots that turn green, yellow, and russet with the seasons. The belvedere above the village opens a striking view over the vineyard and Bresse Comtoise.

Exploring Arbois's alleyways on foot. The yellow-ocher stone of the old town gives it a distinctive character perfect for wandering. Welcoming squares, beautiful winegrowers' houses, private mansions, romantic gardens, and arcades compose the scenery. The Cuisance bubbles and winds through the alleyways, adding a refreshing touch to the stroll.

days_plan.itin_title: Jura Road Trip: Lakes, Waterfalls & Mountains
Burgundy-Franche-Comté: The Most Beautiful Villages in 7 days

visits.text: Royal Saltworks of Arc-et-Senans, masterpiece by Claude-Nicolas Ledoux inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list since 1982. This unique monument built between 1775 and 1779 commissioned by Louis XV was Europe's first monumental factory. The 11 buildings arranged in a semicircle within a 13-hectare park housed places of production and habitation according to a rational and hierarchical organization. The neoclassical architecture reflects the Enlightenment ideal of progress with its columns, pediments, and harmonious proportions.

The Ledoux Museum presents 60 models of projects built or dreamed up by this visionary architect. Theatres, mansions, toll houses, the ideal city of Chaux with its cemetery, house of pleasure, schools, prisons and industrial buildings reveal the scale of his utopian vision. The works, with their futuristic roundness, show a mind ahead of its time.

Lumières Center in the Berne Est, a 1,500-square-meter hall where the extraction boilers were located. Eight 3D films projected continuously transport visitors to UNESCO sites around the world through digital modeling. Palmyra, Leptis Magna, and other threatened or inaccessible treasures come to life in this immersive experience inaugurated in 2023. The impressive framework evokes that of an overturned ship.

Salt Stories exhibition tracing salt's origins, production, trade, and uses. The extremely rich and well-designed permanent exhibition explains how brine was extracted at Salins-les-Bains then transported 21 kilometers by wooden salt pipeline to Arc-et-Senans between 1780 and 1895. The Chaux forest provided fuel to evaporate the saltwater in the pans. Salt, the white gold of the 18th century, generated considerable revenues via the salt tax.

Un Cercle immense, a 13-hectare landscape development completing Ledoux's project. No fewer than 400 trees planted, 10 educational gardens on themes of seeds, soil, climate, recycling, vegetable garden, and biodiversity, plus 10 permanent gardens compose this second plant-filled semicircle. The harmonious dialogue between stone and vegetation restores to the monument the spirit of its creator. The garden festival transforms the site each summer with ephemeral creations.

activities.text: Stroll through the landscape and vegetable gardens bordering the buildings. The shaded paths invite contemplation of the architecture in its plant setting. Themed gardens illustrate different approaches to cultivation and biodiversity. Strategically placed benches allow admiration of the perfect arc of buildings from different angles. The harmony between nature and construction illustrates Ledoux's global vision.

Break at the café with a view of the hemicycle. The terrace offers an unbeatable perspective on the architectural ensemble. The exceptional setting transforms a simple coffee into a privileged moment. The local products served recall the territorial anchoring of this classified monument. The peaceful atmosphere of the park invites you to extend your stop.

days_plan.itin_title: Doubs Road Trip: Nature and Heritage of Franche-Comté
Jura Road Trip: Lakes, Waterfalls & Mountains

visits.text: Arcachon's Ville d'Hiver is a unique district created in the 19th century to welcome visitors seeking health treatments. Over 300 Belle Époque villas with eclectic architecture are tucked away in a wooded park on higher ground. Styles vary: colonial, Moorish, neo-Gothic, Swiss chalet. A stroll through the lanes reveals these architectural gems. Costumed guided tours are regularly organized by the tourist office.

The Dune du Pilat is Europe's highest dune at 104 meters tall and 3 km long. A member of the Grands Sites de France network, it's in perpetual motion, advancing 1 to 5 meters per year toward the forest. A 160-step staircase facilitates the climb from April to November. The panorama from the summit is spectacular: on one side the Atlantic Ocean and Banc d'Arguin, on the other the Landes forest stretching endlessly. Allow 30-45 minutes to climb and descend.

Arcachon Bay is a 155 km² lagoon connected to the ocean by channels. At its center, Île aux Oiseaux and its two stilt huts are the symbol of the bay. The large tidal range (up to 4 meters) transforms the landscape: at low tide, the oyster beds are accessible on foot. The circuit around the bay by road is about 80 km and lets you discover the different oyster-farming villages.

Jetée Thiers extends 250 meters into the bay from Arcachon's central beach. It's the embarkation point for boat excursions to Île aux Oiseaux, Banc d'Arguin, and Cap Ferret. Built in 1865, it has been rebuilt several times after storms. The pier's end offers beautiful views of the Ville d'Hiver and villas. A pleasant stroll at any hour, particularly at sunset.

From Arcachon, allow for a boat crossing to Cap Ferret, followed by travel to the villages. The oyster-farming villages of Cap Ferret (L'Herbe, Le Canon, La Vigne) have retained their authenticity. The oyster farmers' colorful huts line the pontoons. You can taste fresh oysters directly from the producers, with your feet in the water facing the bay. The atmosphere is peaceful, away from the tourist bustle. The village of L'Herbe, with its little Algerian chapel, is particularly photogenic.

Pereire Beach is one of Arcachon's four beaches, on the bay side. Quieter than the central beach, it's appreciated by families for its shallow waters and absence of waves. Colorful huts line the seafront. The beachfront promenade offers beautiful views of the bay and boats. Several restaurants and ice cream shops are located along the waterfront.

activities.text: Oyster tasting in an oyster farmer's hut. Arcachon Bay produces over 8,000 tonnes of oysters annually. Oyster farmers welcome visitors directly to their huts for tastings. You'll taste oysters facing the bay, accompanied by bread, butter, and lemon, with a glass of white wine. Some huts also offer seafood platters. Authentic atmosphere and affordable prices.

Boat excursion on Arcachon Bay. Several companies offer trips with commentary to Île aux Oiseaux and its stilt huts, Banc d'Arguin, or Cap Ferret. Some cruises include onboard oyster tasting. Duration varies from 1 to 3 hours depending on the route. Boats generally depart from Jetée Thiers in Arcachon. Remember to check tide times, which influence departures.

Cycling around Arcachon Bay. The bike path network totals over 220 km around the bay. The complete circuit measures 80 km but you can choose shorter sections. The route is mostly flat and crosses the pine forest. You'll pass the oyster-farming villages, beaches, and the Dune du Pilat. Bike rentals available in all municipalities around the bay.

Excursion to Banc d'Arguin, a nature reserve at the foot of Dune du Pilat. This 4 km long sandbank emerges at low tide and hosts numerous migratory bird species. Access is by boat only (departures from Arcachon or Cap Ferret). On site, you can swim in shallow waters, picnic, and birdwatch. Pay attention to tide times for the return trip.

Climb to the top of the Cap Ferret lighthouse. From Arcachon, allow for a boat crossing to Cap Ferret, followed by travel to the lighthouse. This red-and-white-striped lighthouse is 53 meters tall. You must climb 258 steps to reach the top, but the 360° panorama is worth the effort. You can see Arcachon Bay, the Conche du Mimbeau, the Dune du Pilat, the oyster beds and the ocean. On clear days, visibility extends up to 40 km. Souvenir shop at the foot of the lighthouse.

A tidal outing with an oyster farmer. This unique experience gives you an inside look at oyster farming. You'll board the boat to go and work on the oyster beds at low tide. The oyster farmer explains the stages of farming, the daily work, and the challenges of the trade. The outing typically ends with a tasting. Duration 3 to 5 hours depending on tides. Reservations required several days in advance.

Swimming on the beaches of Arcachon. The town has four beaches on the bay side (Eyrac, Thiers, Pereire, Abatilles). The bay's beaches are ideal for children, with calm, shallow water. Sun loungers and parasols are available to rent on the main beaches.

days_plan.itin_title: Gironde Circuit: Bordeaux, Vineyards & Arcachon Bay
Bordeaux to Toulouse Road Trip: Ocean, Pyrenees and Heritage

places.name: Argentan

visits.text: The Church of Saint-Germain, a listed historic monument since 1862, blends Gothic, Renaissance, and Classical styles. Its facade, richly adorned with expressive gargoyles, dominates the town centre. The Gothic nave contrasts with the Renaissance chancel.

The Château des Ducs, rebuilt in the 14th century after the Hundred Years' War, was a royal residence of François I. Catherine de Medici and Henri IV stayed here. Nighttime lighting highlights its architecture.

Climb to the top of the Tour Marguerite, a 12th-century vestige of fortifications erected under Henry I Beauclerc, son of William the Conqueror. Its rampart walk offers a 360° panorama over the town and the Argentan plain.

The Maison des Dentelles, housed in a 19th-century bourgeois residence beside the Parc de la Noé, traces the history of Argentan needlepoint. From 17th-century pieces to contemporary creations, the collection spans four centuries of needlepoint lace.
The Church of Saint-Martin, dating from the 15th to 17th centuries, preserves beautiful old stained glass. Its Flamboyant Gothic style completes the town's religious heritage.

The Fernand Léger–André Mare Museum, in the childhood home of the Cubist painter, honors these two 20th-century artists from Argentan. Interactive exhibits and digital tools make modern art accessible to all.

activities.text: At the Abbey of the Benedictines, the nuns perpetuate the art of Argentan needlepoint. This lacemaking technique, distinct from Alençon needlepoint, was prized by the courts of France and Spain in the 17th and 18th centuries.
Along the Orne, a landscaped promenade passes Fernand Léger's birthplace. Verdant banks and a pond compose a peaceful waterside route.
Argentan lies at the heart of horse country. The surrounding stud farms and the racecourse set the rhythm of local equestrian life. The Haras du Pin is only 15 km away.

days_plan.itin_title: Orne Road Trip: Norman Bocage and Stud Farms

map_keywords: Musée Fernand Léger André Mare Argentan

visits.text: Quai Lestourgie. A row of houses with wooden balconies and stone-slab roofs testifies to Argentat's past as a center of riverboat transport. It was the main loading port and departure point for Aquitaine—gabares were also called “argentats” because many were built here. Three historic ports line the Dordogne.
Maison du Patrimoine. Exhibition on the history of the riverboatmen and life in the Dordogne valley in the past, before the construction of the dams.

activities.text: Gabare cruise through the Dordogne gorges. Theatrical cruises with an actor departing from Grafeuille (a 10-minute drive from Argentat). Duration: 1 hour 15 minutes, minimum 8 people per departure. A storyteller brings the epic tale of the riverboatmen to life in the wild gorges upstream of the town.

Canoe trip down the Dordogne. Several routes are possible from Argentat: a challenging 8 km route (1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours) with class 2 rapids to Monceaux, or an adventure route of 22–25 km (full day) to Beaulieu. Wild landscapes, Corrèze forests, and the option of a picnic break on pebble beaches.

“Tous sur le pont” Festival. On the first weekend of July, Argentat celebrates its riverboat heritage with entertainment, reenactments and the legend of the Coulobre, a monstrous serpent that terrorized boatmen.

days_plan.itin_title: Corrèze Road Trip: Villages and Dordogne Valley

visits.text: Old bridges and Creuse riverbanks. Nicknamed the Venice of Berry, Argenton features houses with galleries suspended above the Creuse River. The old bridges offer the finest views of this architectural ensemble. A promenade along the right bank allows you to walk past picturesque mills and discover old alleyways.

Bonne-Dame Chapel. Perched on high ground, this chapel crowned with a gilded statue of the Virgin Mary offers a remarkable panorama over the town's rooftops and the Creuse valley. The site provides the best vantage point for appreciating Argenton's townscape.

Saint-Sauveur Church. This 19th-century neo-Gothic church dominates the town center. Its bell tower above the entrance porch is visible from afar, and the interior houses a remarkable organ. The building testifies to the town's development during the industrial era.

Musée de la Chemiserie et de l'Élégance masculine. From 1860 onwards, Argenton became a major center for textile manufacturing. The museum traces this story through modern displays presenting the expertise of female shirtmakers, leading fashion houses, and local working-class history. Collections of catalogs, fashion designers' engravings, and old machines illustrate this industry that formed the economic heartbeat of the town.

activities.text: Argentomagus archaeological site in Saint-Marcel. A neighboring Gallo-Roman city, Argentomagus testifies to the ancient town's major role on Gaul's commercial routes. The museum built over monumental remains presents a domestic altar unique in Gaul and immersive reconstructions. Outside, you can wander among the ruins: temples, houses, theaters, and ancient roads.
Greenway. This former railway line turned cycle path runs through Argenton and lets you reach Le Blanc. The route crosses the Creuse valley through green countryside, perfect for walking or cycling.

Traditional market. On Saturday mornings, the market brings the town center to life with local produce from Berry. Goat cheeses, local wines, seasonal vegetables and artisan specialties come together in a friendly atmosphere.

days_plan.itin_title: Indre Road Trip: Secret Berry and the Vallée Noire

visits.text: As the road winds down into the valley, Arlempdes appears without warning: an 80-meter basalt dyke crowned by a medieval castle, encircled by the young Loire in a dramatic meander. The sight is breathtaking. This village, ranked among France's Most Beautiful Villages, sits barely thirty kilometers from the river's source — earning it the nickname 'first castle on the Loire,' built here from the 13th century onward by the Lords of Montlaur.
