The fortress has witnessed its share of drama: in 1429, Anna de Montlaur made it part of her dowry when she married Charles III de Poitiers, whose granddaughter Diane de Poitiers — King Henri II's mistress — served as Lady of Arlempdes from 1550 to 1566. In 1585, the Huguenots took the castle by surprise after bribing a guard to open a secret door on the riverside.

Push open the door of Saint-Jacques chapel (12th century) at the heart of the castle ruins, then walk down to the village's Saint-Pierre church — a 12th-century Romanesque building with a single nave and a bell-gable with four arches, elegant and unadorned like all Auvergnat Romanesque architecture. Inside, look for a 16th-century Pietà. Don't miss the 11th-century postern gate at the village entrance, with its soaring broken-barrel vault — it's been listed as a Historic Monument since 1971.

Walk the loop along the castle walls that follow the basalt columns — remarkably regular prisms that look almost machine-cut, though they're entirely natural volcanic formations. Descend to the banks of the Loire: from the pebble beach, the view of the castle clinging to its sheer rock face is dizzying. Bring good shoes for the climb back up.

activities.text: The Arlempdes gorge loop (3–4 km, with sections along balcony paths above the Loire) starts right from the village. It follows basalt flows that sometimes form volcanic organ pipes and offers perspectives on the meander the river has carved through the rock. Allow 1h30 at a gentle pace — the trail is waymarked and not technical.

Every July, the Théâtrales du Velay festival takes over the castle ruins for several weeks of performances. If you're visiting during this period, check the programme: watching a play inside a medieval fortress once owned by Diane de Poitiers beats any indoor theatre in the world.

days_plan.itin_title: Auvergne Circuit: Perched Villages and Volcanoes
Haute-Loire Road Trip: Le Puy-en-Velay and Volcanoes

visits.text: The Arles arena, a Roman amphitheatre from the 1st century AD, has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1981. Measuring 136 metres long and 107 metres wide, it could hold 21,000 spectators. In the Middle Ages it was turned into a residential quarter with more than 200 houses and two chapels inside, visible on old engravings. Today it hosts the Easter and Whitsun ferias.

The Saint-Trophime cloister, built from 1150, is a masterpiece of Provençal Romanesque art: twin columns, sculpted capitals illustrating the Old and New Testaments, galleries whose first two date to the mid-12th century. UNESCO-listed since 1981, it's remarkable for the perfect balance of its volumes and the fineness of its statuary. Climb to the roof terrace for a view of the church bell tower and Arles rooftops.

The Alyscamps is a UNESCO-listed paleo-Christian and medieval necropolis. For several centuries, the Alyscamps was the largest Christian cemetery in the West: sarcophagi from the 4th to 11th centuries were transported here from throughout the region. The main alley bordered by cypresses, sarcophagi, and the Saint-Honorat church (12th century) possesses a unique melancholy beauty. Van Gogh and Gauguin painted here side by side in 1888.

The Museon Arlaten was created in 1896 by Frédéric Mistral with proceeds from his Nobel Prize (1904) to preserve Provençal traditions and ethnography. Relocated to the Laval-Castellane palace, it assembles costumes, furniture, work tools, and religious objects that reconstruct 19th-century Provençal life. Contemporary museography is currently renovating certain sections — check which sections are open during your visit.

activities.text: Walk along the Rhône quays at sunset: from Trinquetaille Bridge to the Jardin d'Été, the quays offer direct views of the Grand Rhône with late-day raking light. Here Van Gogh came to paint the river, notably Starry Night over the Rhône (1888). Restaurant terraces on Quai Marx Dormoy come alive from 7 PM.

Visit to Arles' ancient theater (1st century BC): a few meters from the arena, this open-air theater yielded the famous Venus of Arles in 1651 (now at the Louvre). Only a few tiers and two columns called "the Two Widows" remain, but the space is used for summer shows — notably the Rencontres d'Arles (photography) and Suds à Arles (world music).

days_plan.itin_title: Alpilles, Aix-en-Provence & Arles Circuit
Roman Provence Road Trip: Ancient Remains and Villages
Southeast France Road Trip: Perched Villages and Gorges
Côte Bleue and Camargue: the lower coastal route in 7 days

visits.text: Pompadour Castle. Fortress rebuilt in the 15th century by the Hélie family. In 1745, Louis XV bought the estate and gave it with the title of Marquise to his favorite Jeanne-Antoinette Poisson—who never visited it, deeming the property too far from the court! She resold it in 1761. The following year, Louis XV regained it and transformed it into a royal stud farm. Tour of 11 rooms including the library, with furniture, Aubusson tapestries and Limoges porcelain.
Marquise's Stables and Orangery. They house the National Stud's horses. The Orangery hosts equestrian shows in summer.

Chignac Estate Broodmare Stud. France's only national broodmare stud, birthplace of the Anglo-Arab breed created in Pompadour in the 19th century. You can see foals being born and growing (present from March to October). Visit to discover breeding and selection methods.

activities.text: Horse racing at the racecourse. Classified as category 1 for jump racing and category 2A for flat racing, it's one of the most beautiful racecourses in France with its 2,000-meter natural sand track facing the castle. 11 race days per year in summer.

Equestrian shows at the castle. In July–August, equestrian cabaret shows are organized in the evening on the castle terraces or in the Orangery riding hall. The company “Christophe et Max Hasta Luego,” in particular, offers internationally renowned shows.
Horse Festival - August 15. Major annual day of events: Saint Hubert Mass at the racecourse, show jumping competition, horse races, demonstrations and equestrian shows.
Route de la Pomme du Limousin. Pompadour is also the starting point of this route through the orchards producing apples under the Pomme du Limousin PDO. Farm visits are possible in summer.

days_plan.itin_title: Corrèze Road Trip: Villages and Dordogne Valley

visits.text: Built in 1470 by Louis Malet de Graville, the Arpajon market hall stretches 35 meters. Its oak and chestnut framework rests on sandstone bases.
Classified as a historic monument in 1921, the hall hosts a traditional market every Friday and Sunday. The Sunday market features about twenty stalls selling fresh produce.
Since 1922, the Foire aux Haricots has been held in mid-September beneath the market halls. This regional event celebrates the Chevrier bean, a local flageolet variety discovered in 1872.
The old town preserves historic houses around the place du Marché.

activities.text: Follow the banks of the Orge River downstream from Arpajon. The river flows through the valley between meadows and groves, creating a peaceful setting for hiking.
The area's market gardening heritage can be discovered nearby. The Arpajonnais was long known for growing vegetables destined for Les Halles in Paris.

days_plan.itin_title: Essonne Tour: Castles and Valleys

visits.text: The Grand'Place and the Place des Héros in Arras form the best-preserved Flemish baroque ensemble in northern France — 155 baroque gabled façades rebuilt exactly as they were after the total destruction of 1914-1918. The oldest house on the Grand'Place, at number 49, dates from the 15th century. Wander beneath the arcades: each façade is slightly different, yet they all come together in a harmony of brick and white stone that is best seen at night, when the lighting turns them into a theatre set.

The 75-metre belfry is the French people's favourite monument — it won that title in 2015, and it deserves it. Built from 1463 under Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, and completed in 1554, it has been listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2005 (along with 55 other belfries in France and Belgium). Destroyed by German bombardment in 1914, it was rebuilt exactly as before between 1927 and 1931 — with reinforced concrete hidden beneath the dressed stone. Take the lift up to 55 metres, then climb the remaining steps: the view over the two squares and their tiled rooftops is breathtaking.

Descend 12 metres underground into the Boves, chalk quarries dug from the 10th century onwards beneath the whole town. The underground network stretches for 24 km, but only part of it can be visited, on a 40-minute guided tour departing from the tourist office. In 1917, these galleries were used to shelter thousands of Allied soldiers before the offensive. Each gallery holds its own graffiti and inscriptions left by soldiers — some of them are poignant.

The town hall, rebuilt after 1914 in 15th-century Gothic style for the façade facing the Place des Héros (and in classical style on the Place de la Vacquerie side), houses on its ground floor the giants Colas, Jacqueline and Dédé — the town's guardian figures. Its 2-metre-high gilded lion, installed under Louis XIV as a symbol of communal power, is a replica of the original kept in the Musée des Beaux-Arts.

Take a look from the outside at the 18th-century Abbaye Saint-Vaast, home to the Musée des Beaux-Arts. The museum and its collections are currently closed for the abbey's renovation works, so the belfry's original lion is not accessible to the public.

activities.text: The Wellington Quarry plunges you 20 metres underground into tunnels dug by New Zealand sappers ahead of the Battle of Arras in April 1917. In secret, they fitted out these galleries so that 24,000 soldiers could emerge straight into enemy lines on the day of the attack. It is one of the most moving memorial museums in northern France — booking ahead is advisable.

Wander beneath the arcades of the Grand'Place to sample local specialities: the coeur d'Arras (a heart-shaped creamy cheese), chocolate rats, or waffles from the Wednesday and Saturday market. The chocolate rat speciality recalls the town's capture by the French from the Spanish occupiers in 1640 — the townspeople had taken refuge underground and held out thanks to the rats living in the Boves.

Visit the Vauban Citadel, built on the orders of Louis XIV between 1668 and 1672. Nicknamed “la Belle Inutile” (the beautiful useless one) by the military of the time because of its poor strategic position, it is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site (since 2008) and hosts the Main Square festival in summer. You may spot deer in the moat.

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip Pas-De-Calais: The Opal Coast and Belfries

visits.text: Arreau, at an altitude of 700 meters, occupies an exceptional position at the confluence of the Aure and Louron valleys, where the Neste d'Aure meets the Neste du Louron. Former capital of the Quatre Vallées and seat of the judiciary until the 16th century, then of the lieutenancy until 1789, the town was an important economic center thanks to its fairs, markets, and cloth-making industry. Designated a Grand Site Occitanie and Pays d'Art et d'Histoire, it is protected by a heritage protection zone created in 1995 covering the entire municipal territory.

The Maison des Lys, classified as a Historic Monument, is a 16th-century Gothic building whose half-timbered facade is adorned with fleurs-de-lis in homage to Louis XI. Its base is made of gray Pyrenean marble, and its two jettied stories give it a slender silhouette characteristic of the valley's medieval secular architecture.

The Chapel of Saint-Exupère, classified as a Historic Monument, is distinguished by its 16th-century Gothic bell tower that dominates the village. Its Romanesque entrance consists of six columns topped by a tympanum adorned with a Chi-Rho monogram. Inside, the stained glass, colored ceiling, and statues reflect devotion to Saint Exuperius, 5th-century Bishop of Toulouse and supposed native of Arreau—the 16th-century school adjoining the chapel is said to be his birthplace.

The Church of Notre-Dame, listed as a Historic Monument since 1989, features a square bell tower and houses a remarkable 16th-century Pietà. Nearby, the chapels of Saint-Michel de Garian (12th century) and Notre-Dame-du-Bon-Rencontre, the latter called the “pilgrims' chapel,” complete the town's religious heritage.

The Château des Nestes, on the banks of the Neste du Louron, is a former 17th-century sawmill symbolizing the union of the two rivers. It now houses the Pyrénées2vallées Tourist Office and the Musée des Cagots, dedicated to this community, which was marginalized from the Middle Ages to the Ancien Régime. The museum is open daily. Two hundred meters away via rue Saint-Exupère, the Château de Ségure retains a 16th-century square tower built directly on rock, replacing a keep four hundred years older. It is now the headquarters of the Communauté de Communes Aure Louron.

Arreau's remarkable houses line the narrow streets: the Maison Foche (or Maison Pic-Molié), Maison Feraud, Maison Laguens, Maison Ducuing-Forgue, and others testify to rich secular architecture from the Middle Ages to the 19th century. The Halle-Mairie, built in 1932 to replace a 16th-century wooden market hall, hosts a traditional market every Thursday beneath its remarkable roof structure.

activities.text: Tour the town on foot following the heritage trail: from the Maison des Lys to the Chapel of Saint-Exupère, then along the Neste du Louron to the Château des Nestes, each facade tells a chapter in the history of the Quatre Vallées.
Visit the Musée des Cagots in the Château des Nestes to discover the little-known history of this excluded community that lived in the Pyrenean valleys for centuries.
On Thursday mornings, shop at the market under the Halle-Mairie to taste valley products: mountain cheeses, charcuterie, gâteau à la broche, and Pyrenean honey.

Climb the Col d'Aspin (1,489 m) via the D918, legendary stage of the Tour de France cycling race, for a panorama over peaks and valleys - cyclists can attempt the ascent from Arreau, about 12 km of climbing.
Families will enjoy the Aigles d'Aure, a Pyrenean bird of prey center in Arreau, where free-flight demonstrations are presented in a mountain setting.

days_plan.itin_title: Hautes-Pyrénées Circuit: From Tarbes to Cirques and Valleys

visits.text: The remains of the Mulberry B artificial harbour emerge from the sea like sleeping giants. At low tide, the concrete Phoenix caissons reveal the scale of this technical feat that enabled the landing of 2.5 million men and 4 million tonnes of equipment. The floating pontoons and breakwaters bear witness to Allied daring.

Explore the fully renovated D-Day Museum, facing the remains it documents. The large 28 m² animated model and projection mapping precisely illustrate the construction and operation of the Mulberry harbour. Archive films and period artefacts complete this immersive experience lasting 1 hour 30 minutes.

At the Arromanches 360° circular cinema, immerse yourself in the history of the Battle of Normandy. Images projected across nine screens envelop you in the story of the 100 days following the landings through to the liberation of Paris.

activities.text: Climb to the museum's panoramic terrace. The viewpoint takes in the entire Bay of Arromanches and conveys the sheer scale of Operation Overlord.
Discover Norman gastronomy in the seafront restaurants. Moules-frites, sole meunière and farmhouse cider are enjoyed against the backdrop of the artificial harbour remains.
Visit the Battle of Normandy Museum in nearby Bayeux. This museum deepens your understanding of the Normandy campaign with its collections of vehicles and uniforms.

days_plan.itin_title: Calvados Tour: D-Day Beaches and Normandy
Cotentin, Pays d'Auge: 5 days exploring the most beautiful villages

visits.text: The Château des Allymes raises its medieval silhouette above the plain. This 13th-century fortress commands the passages between Bugey and Dauphiné. Allow for a round trip during the day from Artemare.
The Cerveyrieu Waterfall tumbles through the Thurignin Gorges with a thunderous roar. A viewing platform allows admiration of this spectacular cascade.
Set off to discover the Clairefontaine Waterfall nestled in a green setting. The forest path leads to this curtain of water that cools the summer air.
The Niaz Waterfall surges from a rocky crack in a wild setting. Hikers appreciate this preserved site far from the beaten path.
Thirty-five minutes by road, the Glandieu Waterfall is undoubtedly the most beautiful in the Ain. Its 60-meter drop impresses visitors.
The Grand Colombier peaks at 1,534 meters offering a 360-degree panorama of the Alps, Jura, and Ain plain. On clear days, Mont Blanc stands out on the horizon.

activities.text: The Groin Gorges attract canyoning enthusiasts. Roped and helmeted, they navigate pools and natural slides.
The Lèbe Observatory offers fun astronomy activities for stargazing far from urban light pollution.
Experienced cyclists challenge the Grand Colombier slopes, a legendary pass used by the Tour de France.
Rent bikes and ride the Lock circuit winding to Belley, capital of Bugey.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour Ain & Savoie Mont-Blanc: Lakes, Mountains and Heritage

visits.text: Royaumont Abbey is the largest Cistercian abbey in Île-de-France. Founded in 1228 by Louis IX (later Saint Louis) and his mother Blanche of Castile, it housed up to 114 monks at its height. After the French Revolution, it was converted into a cotton mill, then a novitiate, before being purchased by the Goüin family in 1905. In 1964, the family established the Fondation Royaumont, which still owns it. The purity of the Cistercian spaces strikes you immediately: the Gothic cloister, the monks' refectory with two aisles and six rib-vaulted bays - the abbey's best-preserved room - and the romantic ruins of the abbey church, destroyed during the Revolution. Augmented reality glasses reconstruct the lost church. Open daily, 10 am-6 pm (April-October), 10 am-5:30 pm (November-March).

The Royaumont park extends over 6.5 hectares irrigated by a canal network dug by the monks themselves. Three distinct gardens: the cloister garden, the garden of 9 squares (medieval-inspired, featuring plants from Hildegard of Bingen's pharmacopoeia), and the Potager-Jardin. Don't miss the music library, accessible by guided tour, which houses 1,300 manuscripts and scores by Debussy, Fauré, Schubert, and Bach collected by pianist François Lang.

activities.text: The Saison Royaumont offers concerts and performances every Sunday afternoon at 2 PM in the abbey's spaces—classical and contemporary music, and dance. Check the program at royaumont.com and book ahead; performances fill up quickly on weekends.

Sunday brunch in the former lay brothers' refectory (last Sunday of the month): an all-you-can-eat meal with monument access and a guided tour included. An unusual way to have lunch beneath 13th-century Gothic vaults.

days_plan.itin_title: Val-d'Oise Tour: Impressionist Villages and Heritage

visits.text: The Château d'Aubenas dominates the town from its strategic rocky outcrop. Listed as a Monument Historique, this much-transformed building bears the mark of six seigneurial families from the 12th century to the Revolution.

activities.text: The weekly market brings Aubenas to life every Saturday morning in the town center. Stalls overflow with Ardèche specialties: Sabaton and Imbert chestnut cream, goat cheeses, chestnuts, and regional products.

days_plan.itin_title: Ardèche Road Trip: Wild Gorges and Villages with Character

visits.text: The Church of Notre-Dame-des-Vertus, listed as a historic monument since 1908, retains a 17th-century organ still in use. In 1336, a young girl prayed for rain here and saw the eyes of the statue of the Virgin begin to stream: this miracle made Aubervilliers a major pilgrimage site until the 18th century.
The church's stained-glass windows, remade after the destruction of World War I, illustrate the various miracles that occurred here. The baroque facade was built by Louis XIII in 1628.

Les Laboratoires d'Aubervilliers occupy 900 m² of a former precision metalwork factory in the Quatre Chemins neighborhood. This transdisciplinary artistic creation venue features a garden designed by landscape architects, with a terrace, greenhouse, and pergola.
Aubervilliers town hall, housed in a former 19th-century farm, contains a ceremonial reception room adorned with neoclassical frescoes depicting allegories of work and abundance.
The Théâtre de la Commune, a national performing arts venue, has presented contemporary productions since the 1960s. Its understated building blends into the downtown urban fabric.

activities.text: Walk along the banks of the Saint-Denis canal on the Aubervilliers side to admire the footbridges left by the Paris Games: the Pierre-Larousse footbridge made of recycled steel and the Lucie Bréard footbridge, 13 meters wide, dedicated to nonmotorized travel.
Square Stalingrad, in the heart of downtown, offers a green retreat with a fountain. Settle on a bench before setting off to explore the shopping streets.
Want to discover an unexpected world? Aubervilliers's Chinese wholesale district is one of Europe's largest wholesale trading centers.

days_plan.itin_title: Seine-Saint-Denis Tour: Basilica and Urban Culture

visits.text: The underground church of Saint-Jean: 27 m long, 16 m wide and almost 20 m high, carved into the cliff in the 12th century. A monumental nave, a reliquary carved into the rock and some 170 tombs in the floor. Striking.

The church of Saint-Jacques at the top of the village: Romanesque façade with Hispano-Moorish carvings, a reminder of pilgrims passing through on their way to Compostela. Portal with finely carved archivolts.

The village rises in tiers like an amphitheatre above the Dronne. Pebble-paved lanes, white houses with tiled roofs, Spanish-style flower-decked balconies. Listed among the Plus Beaux Villages de France since 1993.
The Place Ludovic Trarieux, heart of the village, honours the founder of the League of Human Rights, born here. Lime-tree-shaded terraces, shops, artisans. The spot for a coffee.

activities.text: Visit to the monolithic church. Open year-round except 25 December and 1 January. Bring a cardigan — it's cool inside. The exceptional acoustics occasionally attract concerts.
Swimming in the Dronne. The managed beach below the village has sand, a shaded lawn, slides. Lifeguards in summer. Canoe hire on site.
Canoeing and kayaking on the Dronne. Gentle routes from the village watersports base. Clear water, wooded banks. Return by shuttle.
Artisan workshops. The village is home to potters, painters, sculptors. Shops with workshops open in summer. One-off pieces, opportunities to meet the makers.

days_plan.itin_title: Charente Tour: Cognac and Romanesque Heritage in 4 Days
Nouvelle-Aquitaine Loop: Villages, Vineyards & Dordogne

visits.text: Aubigny-sur-Nère was Scottish for 250 years. In 1423, Charles VII granted the lordship to John Stuart of Darnley, commander of the Scottish army who had come to fight the English. The Stuart castle, built in the 16th century, now houses the town hall and the Auld Alliance Interpretation Centre. There you discover this military alliance signed in 1295 between France and Scotland — and why there is a red telephone box in the town centre.

Aubigny's town center burned down in 1512. Robert Stuart allowed the inhabitants to rebuild using timber from his forests. This explains the 16th-century half-timbered houses: Maison François Ier (1519), Maison du Bailli and Maison de la rue des Foulons. The diamond-patterned façades combine late Gothic and early Renaissance styles.

The Grands Jardins d'Aubigny were designed by a pupil of Le Nôtre at the request of Louise de Kéroualle, the castle's last owner in the 17th century. French-style parterres, lime-tree avenues, ponds — a verdant setting for the Fêtes Franco-Écossaises in July.

activities.text: The Fêtes Franco-Écossaises (mid-July) transform Aubigny for three days. Parades of kilted pipe bands, Highland Games, Celtic rock concerts, Scottish market, medieval encampments. You taste haggis (stuffed sheep's stomach) and the local whisky “The Aubigny Auld Alliance”. 10,000 visitors each year — book accommodation well in advance.

The Aubigny Pipe Band, founded in 1993, is the only bagpipe ensemble in Berry. Some twenty musicians practise year-round and take part in the Festival Interceltique de Lorient. Outside the July festivities, you can sometimes hear them rehearsing at the castle.

The Auld Alliance Monument, opposite the castle, honours Scots who died for France. A plaque recalls the bonds between Aubigny and Scotland — bonds that endure: the town has been twinned with East Kilbride since 1990.

days_plan.itin_title: Cher Loop: Romanesque Berry and the Route Jacques-Cœur

visits.text: The Cité internationale de la tapisserie, opened in 2016, celebrates six centuries of expertise inscribed on UNESCO's intangible heritage list since 2009. In the converted former École Nationale d'Art Décoratif, the Nef des tentures, covering 600 m² and standing 7 meters high, displays masterpieces in a theatrical setting. From medieval tapestries to contemporary creations inspired by Tolkien or Miyazaki, the immersive tour fascinates.

The “Mains d'Aubusson” section within the Cité reveals what the UNESCO inscription covers: interpretive tapestry, the result of an artistic project meeting a craftsperson's expertise. Visitors discover the daily lives of tapestry weavers, dyers, tapestry cartoon designers, and restorers. A workshop lets visitors observe the dexterity essential to tapestry weaving on a low-warp loom.

The Cité's resource center, which inherited the former ENAD library, holds Europe's foremost documentary collection on tapestry: 16,500 publications, artist files, and visual archives. Researchers and enthusiasts can consult unique documentation on this textile art.

The old town of Aubusson nestles in a bend of the Creuse. Weavers' houses with steeply pitched roofs line the quays. The Clock Tower, a remnant of the fortifications, overlooks the historic center. On Place d'Espagne, outdoor seating invites a break. The peaceful atmosphere of this country town charms visitors with its enduring authenticity.

activities.text: Aubusson's tapestry workshops, around twenty of which are still operating, sustain an industry providing 180 local jobs: spinning mills, dye works, tapestry cartoon designers, weavers, and restorers. Some open their doors by appointment. The Cité offers immersive 24-hour “textile tours” to explore Aubusson's textile ecosystem.

The banks of the Creuse in Aubusson offer a pleasant walk. A trail follows the river from the town center, passing under old bridges. The reflections of houses in the water create a peaceful scene that the Impressionist painters of the neighboring valley would have appreciated.

days_plan.itin_title: Creuse Tour: Valley of the Painters and Aubusson Tapestries

visits.text: Sainte-Marie Cathedral in Auch, an imposing monument stretching 345 feet, was built starting in 1489 on a plan inspired by Notre-Dame de Paris. Its 18 stained-glass windows by Arnaud de Moles rank among the finest Renaissance stained glass in France. The oak choir features 113 carved stalls where more than 1,500 figures narrate the Old and New Testaments. Listed as UNESCO heritage as part of the Ways of Saint James.

Auch's monumental staircase plunges 115 feet between the upper and lower town. Built starting in 1863 on the model of Italian staircases, it counts 374 steps in total—though 233 suffice for the direct ascent. On one landing, Jaume Plensa's sculpture "l'Observatoire du temps" recounts the flood story in Latin.

Halfway up the staircase, d'Artagnan's statue faces the Gers valley. This bronze by Firmin Michelet (1931) represents the most famous Gascon, born Charles de Batz de Castelmore around 1613 in Lupiac, 35 miles away. Auch, historic capital of Gascony, proudly claims the musketeer.

The Tower of Armagnac, 130 feet tall, rises southeast of the cathedral on Place Salinis. Built in the 14th century as the archbishop's prison, it counts seven floors each containing a cell of 40-50 square feet. Today it houses the cathedral treasury museum.

The Jacobins Museum, housed in a former convent, contains France's second-largest collection of pre-Columbian and Latin American art, bequeathed by patron conservator Guillaume Pujos. Ceramics, textiles and metalwork from Latin American civilizations sit alongside collections of sacred art and Egyptian antiquities.

Get lost in the pousterles, those narrow, steep medieval lanes that tumble down the hillside between upper and lower town. Medieval houses, stone stairways, vaulted passages—a picturesque labyrinth that Auscitains have navigated for centuries.

activities.text: Guided tour "Auch, capital of Gascony." The Pays d'art et d'histoire du Grand Auch offers commentary-led circuits: cathedral, cloister, Tower of Armagnac, pousterles and townhouses. Auch was the seat of an archbishopric whose authority stretched from the Pyrenees to the Atlantic.

Auch market on Saturday mornings. On Place de la Libération and adjacent streets, producers spread out foie gras, duck breast, confits, Gascon pastis and armagnac. The department's largest market, lively and delicious.

Stroll along the Gers River in the lower town. From the foot of the monumental staircase, follow the shaded riverbanks. Turn around to admire the silhouette of the cathedral and Tower of Armagnac perched on the hillside—the finest view of the town.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Garonne Road Trip: From Toulouse to the Pyrenees
Gers Road Trip: Gascon Bastides, Armagnac & Musketeers

visits.text: Audresselles has that rare charm of villages that never tried to please. This fishing port of roughly 650 residents has kept its flobarts beached on the entry roundabout, reminders of a lobster and crab fishing tradition practiced since the late 19th century. Whitewashed lanes wind down to the beach, split in two by the Noirda rock. The best moment remains sunset, far from the crowds of the Deux Caps.

activities.text: Put on your boots and head to Audresselles' rocky intertidal shore, known for its mussels, brown shrimp and velvet swimming crabs at low tide. The sentier du pêcheur follows the main street and tells the village's maritime history, one information panel after another. Check the tide times before venturing onto the rocks.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Villages from Flanders to the Bay of Somme

visits.text: The Church of Saint-Sulpice, built in the 12th century by stonemasons in service to the Abbey of Cluny, is Aulnay-sous-Bois's oldest structure. Its Romanesque transept and choir are listed as historic monuments.
The Vieux Pays neighborhood preserves the atmosphere of a village within the city. Around the church, the Ferme du Vieux-Pays and a few old houses bear witness to Aulnay's rural past.
The Demeure Gainville, likely the town's oldest house, was inhabited by the chemist who contributed to the discovery of bleach. It now hosts a space dedicated to art exhibitions.
Aulnay features lovely early-20th-century buhrstone villas inspired by Art Nouveau. Exposed brick, ceramics above windows, wrought-iron railings: set out to discover them along the streets.
Parc Dumont, laid out around the former villa of the priest who founded the housing development, offers a verdant setting with an adjoining municipal library.

activities.text: The departmental Parc du Sausset covers 200 hectares north of the town. Its varied landscapes—meadows, woods, bodies of water—make it an ideal playground for walking, cycling, and birdwatching.
Reach Aulnay from Paris via the Ourcq canal bike path. Around ten pleasant kilometers through the landscapes of northeast Paris.

days_plan.itin_title: Seine-Saint-Denis Tour: Basilica and Urban Culture

visits.text: Follow the scenic roads winding towards the Étang de Lers, in the heart of the Ariège Pyrenees Regional Nature Park. The landscape shifts gradually into high mountain terrain, beech forests giving way to upland meadows. The Col d'Agnès, at 1,570 metres, offers a sweeping vantage point over the Couserans valleys and the Pyrenean ridges.

Étang de Lers at 1,274 meters elevation spreads its natural lake beneath Mont Béas, Mont Ceint, and the majestic Pic des Trois Seigneurs rising to 2,199 meters. Vast gently sloping meadows reveal lherzolite, a rare magmatic rock giving the landscape a lunar appearance. A protected Natura 2000 site, the lake is bordered by summer pastures where cows, sheep, and Mérens horses graze. A site renowned for fishing, paragliding, and cross-country skiing in winter.

Aulus-les-Bains, a charming thermal village nestled at 750 meters in the Garbet valley, displays stone houses beneath slate roofs. A spa town renowned since the 19th century for its sulfated waters treating cholesterol and metabolic conditions, the village has 200 permanent residents, creating a friendly atmosphere. The exceptional mountain setting blends forests, streams, and lush green meadows.

The hike to the Cascade d'Ars begins on the edge of Aulus along the D8, at the first hairpin above the spa. The forest trail climbs at a steady grade along the Garbet, then the Ars, before joining the GR10 long-distance path. Past the Artigous bridge, the ascent steepens into switchbacks through beech and fir woods. This natural wonder drops 246 metres in three successive tiers and ranks among the finest waterfalls in the Pyrenees. At snowmelt in May and June it reaches its peak, a swollen torrent thundering down the rock faces. Allow 3.5 to 4 hours there and back, with roughly 600 metres of ascent; proper hiking boots are essential.

activities.text: Around the Col d'Agnès and the Lers plateau, settle into observation points to watch Pyrenean wildlife. Raptors soaring on updrafts, chamois bounding across rocky crests, Mérens horses galloping through summer pastures, marmots whistling at approaching hikers. Dawn and dusk offer the best conditions for observing this preserved wildlife.

At the foot of the Cascade d'Ars, the refreshing spray creates an ideal microclimate for a restorative picnic. Settle on the flat boulders or on the shaded grassy patches facing the waterfall's three tiers. The return follows the same trail, or the GR10 for a longer loop through fir woods with wide views over the valley.

days_plan.itin_title: Ariège Circuit: Cathar Castles, Prehistoric Caves & Mountain Lakes

visits.text: Aumont-Aubrac is a major stop on the GR65, the Via Podiensis pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostela, inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List. The village sits at the crossroads of the ancient Roman Via Agrippa (Lyon-Toulouse) and the Santiago trail.

Saint-Étienne Church blends Romanesque and Baroque. Its 11th-century semi-circular apse is the oldest part, with a half-dome vault on pointed-arch ribs. The 14th-century nave has ribbed vaults resting on corbels carved with human and grotesque figures.
The Maison du Prieuré, a 1684 building with a pointed-arch portal and mullioned windows, houses the Tourist Office. Its vaulted cellar hosts exhibitions and regional product sales.

Javols-Anderitum, 6 km away, was the Gallo-Roman capital of the Gabali, a Gaulish people whose territory corresponds to present-day Lozère. The archaeological site covered 40 hectares in the 2nd century. A trail of 19 panels and a virtual reality app, 'Javols 3D', reconstruct the forum, the baths and the theatre-amphitheatre.

The archaeological museum at Javols presents two major pieces: a limestone milestone and a life-size statue of Silvanus-Sucellus, a Gallo-Roman forest god, carved from local red sandstone—a unique artifact.

The statue of Christ the King, erected in 1946 on the Truc del Fabre hilltop, commemorates the absence of civilian casualties in the village during World War II. The promontory offers sweeping views across the Aubrac and Margeride ranges.

activities.text: Reach the Aubrac plateau via the route des Lacs from Nasbinals, about 20 km from the stopover town, 30 minutes by road. Vast pastures, stone burons (old shepherds' huts), Aubrac cows with their made-up eyes. The Déroc waterfall drops 33 m into a basalt chaos.

Taste aligot, the Aubrac's emblematic dish: mashed potatoes worked at length with fresh Laguiole AOP tome cheese and garlic. Village restaurants prepare it by hand, in the dining room, in front of guests.

Hike the GR65 between Aumont-Aubrac and Nasbinals (27 km). The path crosses vast high pastures and passes the Domerie d'Aubrac, a hospice founded in 1120 for pilgrims, and its bell of the lost, which guided travellers who had strayed in the mist.

days_plan.itin_title: Lozère Circuit: Tarn Gorges and Cévennes

visits.text: In the former Ursuline chapel, the Simon Segal Museum displays over 280 canvases donated by Bruno Bassano, an Italian patron exiled in France under the Mussolini regime. Three schools of painting coexist here: Toulon, Paris, and Bourges. A small Resistance museum occupies the rear of the building, dedicated to the local history of the 5th Company of Provence. Plan for 45 minutes.

activities.text: At the Maison de la Truffe, housed in the 17th-century former Hospice Saint-Jacques, you'll discover the secrets of the black truffle, a specialty of Aups, nicknamed “the truffle capital of Haut-Var.” The Provençal market on Wednesdays and Saturdays offers truffles in season, from November to March. Out of season, the Maison de la Truffe remains the best way to understand this product.

days_plan.itin_title: Var in 4 Days: From Bormes to the Most Beautiful Villages of the Verdon

visits.text: Descend the Loch ramps toward Saint-Goustan harbour—the view of tightly packed rooftops and the Auray river is superb. The harbour has existed since the 12th century; in the Middle Ages it was one of Morbihan's busiest for the salt, wine and grain trade. Today pleasure yachts have replaced the coastal traders, but the cobbled quays and granite houses remain unchanged.

Linger on the old stone bridge crossing the Loc'h, which links upper town to harbour. Its current form dates to 1752, though a crossing has existed here since medieval times. This bridge witnessed the clash between royalists and Bonapartists in June 1815, during the Chouan uprising of the Hundred Days.

On Place Saint-Sauveur, colourful half-timbered and corbelled houses date from the 15th century. Look for the commemorative plaque: Benjamin Franklin landed here on 4 December 1776, forced ashore by headwinds that prevented him sailing up the Loire to Nantes. He spent the night at number 8 on the quay—which now bears his name—before heading to Versailles to seek Louis XVI's support for American independence.

Climb the Saint-Sauveur and Saint-René alleys—narrow cobbled passages home to artist galleries and craft studios. Push open the doors of those inviting you in: potters, weavers and wood sculptors keep centuries-old techniques alive in this quarter. It's the sort of place where an hour vanishes without notice.
Saint-Gildas Church, listed as a Historic Monument in its entirety, preserves traces of medieval fortification in its structure. Take a moment to admire the altarpiece and stained glass inside.

Six kilometres north, Sainte-Anne-d'Auray basilica is Brittany's premier pilgrimage site. The current neo-Gothic basilica dates to the 19th century, but the story began in 1624 when a peasant claimed to find a statue of Saint Anne in a field. The cloister, miraculous fountain and World War I memorial to Breton dead complete the complex. Detour even if you're not religious—the architecture and setting reward the effort.

activities.text: The big Monday-morning market fills Auray's centre. In summer, hundreds of stallholders gather here. Seafood, farmhouse cheeses, crepes and the scent of kouign-amann butter drift through the air. Arrive around 8am to enjoy the quiet and the best stalls.
Follow the Loch river north from Franklin Quay. The wooded areas flanking the ria harbour shelducks and grey herons. The path is flat and shaded—perfect for walking off the market.

From Port-Blanc in Baden, about 12 km from the stage town, 12 minutes by road, board the ferry to the Île aux Moines for a 5-minute crossing. Nicknamed the pearl of the Gulf, it offers 17 km of coastal paths to explore on foot or by bike. Don't miss the Kergonan cromlech, a semicircle of standing stones out in the open countryside. Allow at least half a day.

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip Morbihan: Gulf, Carnac and Breton Coast

visits.text: The listed keep of the Château Saint-Étienne has stood in the heart of the town since medieval times. Within its volcanic stone walls, the Muséum des Volcans offers 600 m² of permanent exhibitions on the geology of Europe's largest stratovolcano: interactive models, rocks, minerals and collections of 30,000 pieces tell the story of Earth's upheavals. The garden terraces offer a panoramic view over the town.

The Abbatiale Saint-Géraud bears witness to Aurillac's religious prestige dating back to the 9th century. Founded by Count Saint Géraud, it marked a major stop on the Way of Saint James. Admire the majestic nave, the Romanesque remains and the 18th-century organ that still resounds during concerts.

The historic centre reveals its Renaissance townhouses, witnesses to the past prosperity of the Cantal capital. Stroll through lanes where lava stone lends the façades an austere elegance. The Place du Square is home to the statue of Pope Gerbert, an illustrious local son who became Sylvester II.

activities.text: The covered market reveals Cantal's gastronomic treasures inside its hall built in 1890. Local producers offer PDO cheeses, artisanal cured meats and regional products. On Saturday mornings, the outdoor market spills across the town centre squares in a warm and authentic atmosphere.

The International Street Theatre Festival transforms Aurillac into a giant stage every August. Companies from around the world take over streets and squares for free shows blending circus, dance and theatre in a festive atmosphere with broad public appeal.

days_plan.itin_title: Cantal Road Trip: Auvergne Volcanoes and Mountain Traditions

visits.text: Autoire - It's called “the Little Versailles of the Lot” because notables from Saint-Céré had second homes built here as early as the Renaissance. The village, listed among the Plus Beaux Villages de France, is nestled at the bottom of a cirque enclosed by limestone cliffs 150 to 200 meters high. Start at the dolphin fountain in the center, then go up the narrow streets to admire the turreted manor houses: the Château de Limargue (15th century, built for a companion-in-arms of Charles VIII), the Château de Busqueilles, the Laroque-Delprat manor. The Church of Saint-Pierre, originally Romanesque (11th century), was remodeled in the 16th century.

Loubressac - If you have time, make a detour to this hilltop village 5 km from Autoire, also listed among the Plus Beaux Villages de France. From its ramparts, the view extends over the valleys of the Dordogne, the Bave and the Cère, with the towers of Castelnau-Bretenoux castle in the background.

activities.text: Hike to the Autoire waterfall - From the parking lot at the edge of the village, a shaded 1.2 km trail leads to the waterfall: a 30-meter drop, the highest in the Lot department. The site is designated an Espace Naturel Sensible. Warning: the waterfall is spectacular after rain (fall/winter), but can dwindle to a trickle during a dry summer. Wear proper shoes; the ground is slippery. Swimming is prohibited.

Tour of the Autoire cirque and Château des Anglais - For hikers, a 6 km loop circles the cirque along the ridges, with dizzying views over the village and valley. Along the way, you'll pass the ruins of the Château des Anglais (or Roque d'Autoire), a fortress built partly into the rock against the cliff, used as a hideout by mercenary companies during the Hundred Years' War. The viewpoint above the waterfall is the highlight of the route.

days_plan.itin_title: Midi-Pyrénées Circuit: Bastides, Cliffs and Abbeys
The Most Beautiful Villages of Lot and Périgord in 6 Days

visits.text: Autrans is set in the northern part of the plateau, around its church and large Dauphiné farms with crenellated roofs. Since the early 20th century, Autrans has hosted international cross-country skiing competitions: the Nordic events of the 1968 Grenoble Olympics took place here—50 km cross-country and other Nordic events on the panoramic trail. Today the Nordic domain totals 180 km of trails and is ranked France's 3rd Nordic domain for the 2024-2025 season.

The meadows and plateau forests around the village are the natural habitat of the Nordic Vercors: firs, beeches, snow-covered combes in winter, and alpine grasslands in summer. The "Gève plateau," nicknamed "little Scandinavia," can be discovered on foot or skis depending on season. A perfect stopover village to admire traditional farm architecture before resuming the route.

activities.text: The easy forest loop to plateau clearings (4-6 km) follows marked paths that serve as Nordic trails in winter. In summer, they're shaded paths between beech groves and meadows. The viewpoint on La Molière, accessible by chairlift (operating outside winter by reservation), offers one of the Vercors' broadest panoramas.

The heritage circuit of the center and old Autrans farms (2 km loop) shows different generations of plateau construction: large 19th-century farms with crenellated roofs, early 20th-century vacation homes, and contemporary resort buildings. Map available at the tourist office.

days_plan.itin_title: Royans-Vercors Road Trip: Hilltop Villages and Gorges

visits.text: Autrey Abbey is the only listed historic abbey in the Vosges still inhabited by a religious community—and you can feel it. Founded in 1149 by Cardinal Étienne de Bar, bishop of Metz, upon his return from the Second Crusade, it has weathered the centuries with a turbulent history: a wire-drawing factory during the Revolution, a home for the elderly, a war hospital in 1914, then complete abandonment until 1982. Since then, the Community of the Beatitudes has undertaken spectacular restoration work. If you only see one thing, it should be the Saint-Hubert chapel to the northeast of the transept: its carved coffered ceiling in 16th-century Renaissance style is described as unique in the Vosges. Plan to arrive before 5 pm for the visit.

The abbey gardens are labeled Jardin Remarquable and extend over 4 hectares with 3,500 varieties of trees, shrubs, old roses, perennials and medicinal plants. Don't just skim through them — allow at least an hour. Open from April to November, generally from 2 pm to 5 pm except Mondays.

activities.text: Take the hiking trail that follows the Mortagne from Autrey toward Rambervillers (8 km north). Walk there and return by road if you don't want to cover the trail twice. The alluvial vegetation along the river and the calm of this little-visited valley contrast pleasantly with the solemnity of the abbey. Choose the second half of the day—the filtered light under the trees is more beautiful.

days_plan.itin_title: Vosges Abbey Trail: Monastic Heritage

visits.text: The so-called Temple of Janus still has two walls of its square cella standing more than 20 meters high, beyond the ancient city walls. The deity actually worshipped here remains unknown—the name “Janus” stems from a mistaken interpretation of the place-name La Genetoye. Listed on France's very first register of historic monuments in 1840.

The Cathedral of Saint-Lazare, consecrated in 1130, is a masterpiece of Cluniac Romanesque art. Its Last Judgment tympanum, signed by the sculptor Gislebertus—an exceptional occurrence in the Middle Ages—is considered one of the pinnacles of Romanesque sculpture. The Reclining Eve, the Flight into Egypt, and the Sleep of the Magi are among the most celebrated capitals.

The ancient theater of Augustodunum could accommodate 20,000 spectators. Built against the hillside, it overlooks the Vallon lake. In summer, the sound and light show “Augustodunum - Cité des Gaules” brings 2,000 years of history to life.

The Porte d'Arroux, one of two Roman gates still standing from the original four, opens onto the river of the same name. Two passages for vehicles, two for pedestrians, and an upper arcaded gallery that inspired Cluniac builders twelve centuries later. The 4.5 km of surviving Gallo-Roman ramparts make Autun the foremost ancient site north of the Loire.

The Musée Rolin, housed in the 15th-century mansion of the Chancellor to the Duke of Burgundy, is closed for renovation. During the works, a selection from its collections is displayed at the Muséum d'Autun, on impasse Rollet, in the exhibition “Merveilles choisies : du musée Rolin au Panoptique”. Highlights include Ève and some of the museum's best-known paintings.

activities.text: Guided tour of Gallo-Roman and medieval Autun. The circuit links the Temple of Janus, the Porte d'Arroux, the Roman theater, and the cathedral in a loop lasting about 3 hours. The Espace Gislebertus, near the cathedral, offers a remarkable immersive 3D experience of Romanesque sculpture.
Walk along Autun's ramparts. The wall walk offers panoramas of the cathedral, the Arroux valley, and the Morvan hills. The Tour des Ursulines and Tour Marchaux punctuate the route.
Autun market, Friday mornings on Place du Champ de Mars. Charolais beef, Burgundy snails, Morvan cheeses, and Côte Chalonnaise wines fill the stalls. A lively Burgundian atmosphere.

days_plan.itin_title: Saône-et-Loire Road Trip: Bibracte, Cluny, Solutré & the Mâconnais Vineyards

places.name: Auvers Sur Oise

visits.text: Start with the Château d'Auvers, built in 1635 for Zanobi Lioni, an Italian banker at the court of Marie de' Medici, and purchased by the Val-d'Oise Department in 1987. Inside, the immersive exhibition “Vision Impressionniste, Naissance et Descendance” features 600 m² of digital projections on Monet, Pissarro, Cézanne, Van Gogh, Seurat, and their artistic heirs. The 9-hectare park, with its Italian-, French-, and English-style gardens, is accessible for free. Open Tuesday–Sunday, 10 AM–5 PM, closed Mondays.

The Auberge Ravoux - known as Van Gogh's House - is the only house where the painter lived that has been preserved in its original state. Van Gogh arrived on May 20, 1890, rented a 7 m² attic room for 3.50 francs per day, and painted more than 74 paintings in 70 days before dying on July 29, 1890. Room No. 5 has never been rented out since. The visit lasts about 30 minutes and includes an audiovisual presentation about the painter's stay. Open Wednesday-Sunday from March to November, 9:30 AM-6 PM. Book ahead in high season.

The Church of Notre-Dame d'Auvers-sur-Oise is a Romanesque and Gothic building from the 12th–13th centuries, made famous in 1890 by Van Gogh, who painted its chevet in one of his best-known paintings—the original is in the Musée d'Orsay. The monument is listed. Go inside to see the chancel and bell tower; Van Gogh's viewing angle is easily found by walking around the chevet.

The Auvers cemetery, at the top of the village, holds the graves of Vincent and Theo van Gogh side by side beneath ivy, amid the wheat fields Van Gogh painted just before his death. It's an austere place, without embellishment—exactly what the place should be. Visit in late afternoon for quiet and low-angled light.

activities.text: Follow the marked painters' trail that connects locations immortalized by Van Gogh, Daubigny, Cézanne, and Pissarro in the village and surrounding areas. Reproductions of the paintings are installed at the exact spots where the painters worked. Allow 2 hours for the complete circuit. Leave in mid-afternoon for the light.
Dinner on the village square, around the Town Hall. The terraces buzz with activity on weekends in season - reserve if you're there on a Saturday evening in July or August.

days_plan.itin_title: Val-d'Oise Tour: Impressionist Villages and Heritage

map_keywords: Auberge Ravoux Maison de Van Gogh Auvers-sur-Oise

visits.text: Pass through the 17th-century clock tower to enter Auvillar, listed as one of Les Plus Beaux Villages de France since 1994. You emerge onto a triangular square with a circular grain market on Tuscan columns at its centre, built in 1824 and listed as a historic monument. It is the only round market hall in southwestern France - look for the wooden inscriptions naming the grains (maize, wheat, rye and buckwheat), still legible beneath the roof.

Push open the door of Saint-Pierre church, a former Benedictine priory from the 12th-14th centuries attached to Moissac Abbey. Inside, don't miss the baroque altarpiece with twisted columns and the colorful rose window. Auvillar is a major stop on the Way of St. James (GR 65)—you'll likely cross paths with pilgrims in the narrow streets.

The Museum of Old Auvillar, housed in the Clock Tower, displays nearly 500 pieces of local faience manufactured between 1739 and 1909. Auvillar was one of the largest faience production centers in the southwest during the 18th century—a craft that has vanished but is magnificently preserved here. If you're there on a Sunday morning, the farmers' market beneath the hall is worth catching.

activities.text: Walk down to Auvillar's port on the Garonne riverbank. You'll see the Sainte-Catherine chapel, patron saint of boatmen, a remnant of the village's river navigation past. From the Place du Château at the top of the village, the panorama sweeps across miles of the Garonne valley—the Quercy hillsides on one side, the gateway to Aquitaine on the other.

days_plan.itin_title: Tarn-et-Garonne Road Trip: Bastides and Orchards
Southeast France Road Trip: Perched Villages and Gorges

visits.text: Saint-Etienne Cathedral has towered over Auxerre since the 13th century. Its unique 68-meter tower can be seen from afar. Inside the Romanesque crypt lies the only known depiction of Christ on horseback.

Descend into the Carolingian crypt of Saint-Germain Abbey, built between 841 and 859. Its 9th-century frescoes—including the stoning of Saint Stephen—rank among France's oldest surviving wall paintings.
The Clock Tower, erected in the 15th century, marks the heart of the old town. Its two Gothic dials display both the hours and lunar phases—a symbol of Auxerre's communal independence.
Saint-Eusèbe Church, built in the 12th century, preserves a Romanesque bell tower and remarkable stained glass. It once housed Saint Germain's relics before their transfer to the abbey.

Head to Place Charles Surugue, the former pillory square. A fountain crowned by a statue of Cadet Roussel—a local bailiff turned folk-song hero—stands at its center, surrounded by colorful half-timbered houses.
Step into the Museum of Art and History, housed in the former monks' dormitories of Saint-Germain Abbey. The collections span from prehistory through contemporary times.

activities.text: Stroll along the Yonne riverbanks in the Marina quarter. Moored barges and evening views of the illuminated cathedral and abbey create Auxerre's iconic panorama.
Follow the 'In the Footsteps of Cadet Roussel' trail: 67 curiosities dot the old town, winding through cobbled lanes, half-timbered houses, and Renaissance façades.
Cycle to the Caves de Bailly-Lapierre, birthplace of Crémant de Bourgogne, set in a former underground quarry spanning 4 hectares, 60 meters beneath the earth.

days_plan.itin_title: Yonne Circuit: Northern Burgundy & Chablis
Burgundy Road Trip: Cathedrals, Vineyards and Villages

visits.text: The Collegiate Church of Saint-Lazare, founded in the 12th century, preserves a Romanesque portal of exceptional richness. Spiral columns, archivolts carved with a zodiac and labors of the months, scrollwork and Greek key patterns rival Vézelay and Autun.
The Clock Tower, erected in 1456, rises 49 meters high. A former municipal belfry, it marks the entrance to the old town. Its clock mechanism still functions.
The medieval ramparts, flanked by six circular towers, bastions, and sentry boxes, encircle the rocky promontory. The Gaujard Tower (1438) and Escharguet Tower (1522) are among the best preserved.
The Jean Després Museum of Avallonnais presents archaeological collections from Arcy-sur-Cure caves, Art Deco goldsmith works, and an ensemble of Yao people costumes.

The House of the Lords of Domecy, on the collegiate square, dates from the 15th century. Its corbelled turret houses a spiral staircase. The neighboring 1490 salt granary now hosts temporary exhibitions.
Avallon's terraced gardens, cultivated since the 10th century, descend in tiers beneath the ramparts. These green spaces offer multiple viewpoints over the Cousin valley below.

activities.text: Descend into the Cousin valley via the Petite Porte promenade. The 70-meter elevation drop under linden trees opens a panorama over the first Morvan hills and converted old mills.
Follow the 'Frog Circuit,' a 3-km urban route marked by bronze studs in the ground. It passes all of Avallon's major monuments: Clock Tower, ramparts, collegiate church, and historic squares.
On Saturday morning, market day, the upper town comes alive. Morvan producers offer cheeses, charcuterie, and local specialties under the covered market and on the square.

days_plan.itin_title: Yonne Circuit: Northern Burgundy & Chablis
Burgundy Road Trip: Cathedrals, Vineyards and Villages

visits.text: TGV Lyon Part-Dieu to Avignon TGV: 1h10 direct, €40–75. The TER shuttle (la Virgule) connects Avignon TGV to Avignon Centre in 5 minutes for €1.60 (or included if your TGV ticket arrives at Avignon Centre). The walled old town is barely 1 km across. Staying intra-muros is worth it for the atmosphere at night.

The Palais des Papes, the world's largest Gothic palace at 15,000 m². Between 1309 and 1377, seven successive popes ruled from Avignon after Clement V relocated the papacy from Rome — the Hundred Years' War and the insecurity of Rome explain the move. Twenty-five rooms to visit: chapels with frescoes by Matteo Giovannetti (1343–1348), private apartments, the Great Audience Hall. €12, combined ticket with the Bridge €14.50.

Pont Saint-Bénézet — the Pont d'Avignon of the famous song. Originally 920 metres long with 22 arches, built 1177–1185 by the Frères Pontifes. According to legend, the shepherd Bénézet built it on divine orders. Repeated flooding of the Rhône (notably in 1668) swept away most of the arches. Only four remain today, along with the two-storey Chapel of Saint Nicholas. €5.

Rocher des Doms, a three-hectare garden on the limestone spur overlooking the Rhône. Neolithic traces were found here. A formal French garden with a pond, ducks and peacocks. The panorama: Pont Saint-Bénézet below, Villeneuve-lès-Avignon across the river (where the cardinals had their residences), Mont Ventoux in the distance, the Alpilles on clear days. Free access, magical at sunset.

Musée du Petit Palais, former 14th-century archbishops' palace. Three hundred medieval Italian and Provençal paintings and sculptures — one of the finest collections of early Italian masters outside Italy. Botticelli, Sienese and Florentine altarpieces, the Avignon School (Enguerrand Quarton). €6, free on the first Sunday of the month. Closed Tuesdays.

Rue des Teinturiers — well off the tourist trail. It follows a canalized stretch of the Sorgue and retains four old waterwheels, remnants of the 14th-to-19th-century dye mills. Centuries-old plane trees, penitents' chapels, weathered façades, bohemian cafés. Pierre Boulle — author of Bridge over the River Kwai and Planet of the Apes — lived here.

Morning at the Pont du Gard. Bus liO line 115 from the PEM interchange next to Avignon Centre station: 40 minutes to 1 hour depending on stops, €2 payable on board. Timetables vary by season (school term, holidays, summer) — check lio.laregion.fr before setting out, as services are limited (a handful of buses per day). The aqueduct is one of the most impressive monuments of ancient Gaul — built in the 1st century AD (40–60 AD) to supply Nîmes with water from Uzès, 50 km away, with an average gradient of just 24 cm per kilometre.

The Pont du Gard: 275 metres long, 48 metres tall (the highest Roman aqueduct bridge ever built), three tiers of arches in local limestone, some blocks weighing 6 tonnes, all assembled without mortar. The masons' technical marks are still visible (FR for Frons Dextra). UNESCO since 1985. Five kilometres of footpaths, an archaeological museum, swimming in the Gardon in summer. €11.50 site + museum.

Back to Avignon by around 1pm, quick lunch, then TER from Avignon Centre to Arles: 20 minutes, €8. Arles is 40 km south. Founded in 46 BC by Julius Caesar as a Roman colony, it became one of the largest cities in the Empire in Gaul. Eight UNESCO-listed monuments in the Arles Roman and Romanesque Monuments ensemble, listed since 1981.

The Arles Amphitheatre, built around 90 AD under Domitian — 25,000 spectators, one of the largest in Gaul (136 × 107 m). Converted into a fortress in the Middle Ages, with 200 houses built inside and four towers added. Cleared from 1825 onwards. Bullfights during the Easter Feria and the Rice Feria (September). €9.

The Ancient Theatre of Arles, built around 25 BC under Augustus, with 10,000 seats. Used as a quarry for stone over the centuries, leaving only a partial façade with two Corinthian columns known as the Two Widows. The Venus of Arles (1st century, discovered in 1651) is now in the Louvre. Combined ticket with the amphitheatre: €12.

Arles town centre: Place du Forum with its statue of Frédéric Mistral (Nobel Prize for Literature 1904, champion of the Provençal language), and the vividly yellow Café Van Gogh (the subject of Terrasse du café le soir, painted in 1888 — Van Gogh lived here for 15 months and produced 300 works). Place de la République: the Saint-Trophime Cathedral (12th-century Romanesque, UNESCO) with its spectacular sculpted portal and cloister. The underground cryptoporticos beneath the town hall.

activities.text: Dinner: avoid Place de l'Horloge (too touristy). Head instead to Rue de la Bonneterie, Rue des Teinturiers or Place des Corps-Saints. La Fourchette (Rue Racine), €35–50. L'Épicerie (10 Place Saint-Pierre), Provençal cuisine. Specialities: Avignon-style daube, soupe au pistou, aïoli. Wines: Côtes du Rhône, Châteauneuf-du-Pape (15 km away), Tavel rosé. €35–55.

Walk the 14th-century ramparts — 4.3 km with towers and gates, a rare survival in France (most towns demolished their walls in the 19th century). In July, the Festival d'Avignon takes over courtyards, cloisters and squares. Book well ahead if you plan to visit then.

For photography enthusiasts: the Fondation Vincent Van Gogh (35 Rue du Docteur Fanton) in a 15th-century mansion. No permanent collection but excellent temporary exhibitions. €10. Or LUMA Arles — the Maja Hoffmann foundation in a former railway yard, anchored by Frank Gehry's spectacular tower (2021, 56 m, 11,000 steel panels). Park free, exhibitions €18.

Return to Avignon by TER in the early evening. Provençal dinner intra-muros — tapenade, brandade de morue (from Nîmes), courgette-flower fritters in season, a goat's cheese board with a Gigondas or Vacqueyras.
