visits.text: The Scriptorial is the only museum in Europe devoted to the manuscripts of Mont-Saint-Michel. Its collections include 200 volumes from the 8th to the 15th century, 70 of them produced directly by the abbey's scriptorium. The Treasure Room displays the most precious pieces, changed every three months to protect the parchment.

Climb up to the Jardin des Plantes, suspended above the Norman bocage. Created in 1796 for botanical experimentation and opened to the public in 1802, it is made up of twelve themed spaces: camellia garden, hydrangea collection, meadow of flowering cherry trees. From the belvedere, the panorama takes in the whole bay of Mont-Saint-Michel.

Saint-Gervais Basilica holds the relic of the skull of Saint Aubert, founder of Mont-Saint-Michel in 708. According to tradition, the hole visible in the frontal bone was left by the finger of the Archangel Michael, who came three times to order the bishop to build a sanctuary on the rock.

Climb the keep and walk the ramparts of Avranches castle. From the wall walk, the view reaches over the town's slate roofs and, on a clear day, as far as the silhouette of Mont-Saint-Michel on the horizon.

The Hortus medieval garden, at the foot of the ramparts, recreates an orchard and a kitchen garden of the Middle Ages. Aromatic, medicinal and dye plants sit alongside an orchard of old varieties, including the Louise Bonne d'Avranches, a pear born in the region.

The Patton Memorial, on the square of the same name, commemorates the breakthrough of 31 July 1944 that allowed Allied forces to break the German front during Operation Cobra. A Sherman tank stands in the middle of the square.

activities.text: At the Scriptorial, take part in a calligraphy or medieval illumination workshop. The techniques for making parchment and vellum are explained following the methods of the copyist monks.
Avranches market is held on Saturday mornings, on place Littré and in the adjacent streets. Produce from the bay, salt-marsh lamb, cider and perry from the bocage.
Head to the viewpoint of the Avranches platform at sunset. During the great tides, the sight of the sea encircling Mont-Saint-Michel is striking: the water comes in at the speed of a galloping horse.

Set off on a guided crossing of the bay of Mont-Saint-Michel from the shores near Avranches. Barefoot in the quicksand, naturalist guides explain the tidal phenomena and the wildlife of the foreshore.

days_plan.itin_title: Manche Road Trip: Cotentin Peninsula & Mont-Saint-Michel
Normandy's Bay of Mont-Saint-Michel: Coastal Drives & the Sacred Abbey

visits.text: In the heart of Ax-les-Thermes, the Bassin des Ladres steams in the open air: a stone basin from the 13th century fed by springs at 77 degrees. Its name comes from the ladres, the lepers: the adjoining hospital, founded in 1260 by Count Roger IV of Foix at the request of Saint Louis, treated soldiers who returned sick from the Crusades. Listed as a historic monument in 1979, it now serves as a free public footbath. Soak your feet like the locals do, it's tradition.

With nearly 70 hot springs, Ax is one of France's oldest spa towns. To move from footbath to full immersion, the Bains du Couloubret offer indoor and outdoor pools, jets, and hammams facing the mountains. Perfect at the end of the day after yesterday's hike. Booking recommended on weekends and school holidays.

activities.text: Ax is also at the foot of a ski resort: Ax 3 Domaines, accessible directly by cable car from town, becomes a hiking and mountain-biking terrain in summer, a family-friendly ski area in winter. The rest of the year, stroll along the Ariège River on shaded banks where the glacial waters tumble through rapids and gorges. Enough to fill half a day depending on weather and season.

days_plan.itin_title: Ariège Road Trip: Cathars and Prehistoric Caves

visits.text: Aÿ is a grand cru village, and Bollinger is its most illustrious resident. The house was founded on 6 February 1829 and has remained family-owned and independent ever since. Its hallmark: vinification in oak barrels and its own cooperage with 4,000 casks — the last one still operating in Champagne. The cellar tour gives access to Clos Saint-Jacques, one of two plots never affected by phylloxera, from which the extremely rare “Vieilles Vignes Françaises” champagnes are made. Bollinger is also James Bond's champagne — but the house prefers people to talk about that as little as possible. Booking well in advance is essential.

The Deutz cellars run more than 20 metres beneath the hill of Aÿ, across 3 kilometres of galleries. Founded in 1838 by two Germans from Aachen, Wilhelm Deutz and Pierre-Hubert Geldermann, the house now belongs to the Rouzaud family (Louis Roederer). The champagnes are made with 80% grand cru grapes, which gives a very precise, mineral style.

The Henry IV wine press is a listed monument from the 16th century. Henry IV was a great admirer of Aÿ's wines — the village was his personal property and he owned this press there. A rare testament to Champagne viticulture before the invention of champagne as we know it today.

activities.text: Visit Pressoria, housed in Pommery's former press rooms at Aÿ. This isn't a traditional cellar tour — it's an immersive journey engaging all the senses to tell the story of the vine, the soils, the seasons and champagne production. You can even blend your own cuvée. The final tasting room overlooks UNESCO-listed hillsides — a very beautiful setting.

Walk through the grand cru plots surrounding the village. Aÿ produces pinot noirs recognised as among the most powerful and structured in the Marne valley. Vineyard paths allow you to walk freely between the plots — stroll around, observing the different grape varieties and aspects.

days_plan.itin_title: Marne Road Trip: Reims, Épernay and Champagne

visits.text: The Château de Villandry, last of the great Renaissance châteaux built in the Loire Valley (1532). Inside, beautiful 18th-century decor and a collection of Spanish paintings await. But Villandry's true glory lies in its gardens: seven spaces arranged on terraces, redesigned in the early 20th century by Joachim Carvallo in the Renaissance spirit.

Villandry's ornamental kitchen garden is the masterpiece: nine geometric squares where cabbages, chard, eggplants and celery create a polychrome tapestry. Two plantings per year refresh the colors. From the terrace of the medieval keep, the patterns reveal themselves as if seen from above. Love gardens, water garden, labyrinth and sun garden complete the ensemble.

The Château d'Azay-le-Rideau, "a faceted diamond set in the Indre," as Balzac called it. Built from 1518 to 1524 on a river island for Gilles Berthelot, treasurer to François I, it blends French Gothic tradition with Italian influences. Its straight-flight staircase was one of the first in France. The white tufa façades reflect in two ornamental pools created in the 19th century.

The Azay-le-Rideau landscape park, twenty acres of English-style garden shaped by the Marquis de Biencourt in the 19th century. Giant sequoias, Lebanese cedars, and Virginia tulip trees line winding paths. The trails lead to ornamental pools where the château appears to float—the finest view is from the south bank.

activities.text: Guided tour of Villandry's gardens with a gardener. Discover the organic techniques used since 2009, crop rotations, and the secrets behind the colorful compositions. The vegetable garden peaks in September.

Walk along the Indre from Azay-le-Rideau. The river winds between willows and poplars through the valley beloved by Balzac. Two miles away, Chateau de l'Islette, Azay's "little brother," sheltered the romance between Rodin and Camille Claudel.

Wine tasting of AOC Azay-le-Rideau. This small vineyard produces elegant dry whites and rosés from chenin blanc and grolleau grapes. The troglodyte caves carved into the hillside offer an authentic setting.

days_plan.itin_title: Indre-et-Loire Road Trip: Loire Valley Châteaux, Secret Valleys & Touraine Vineyards
The Essential Châteaux of the Loire Valley

visits.text: The Baccarat Collection displays nearly 700 pieces along the Meurthe river. Chandeliers, tableware, and perfume bottles trace 260 years of craftsmanship since 1764.
The Harcourt glass commissioned by Louis-Philippe in 1841 ranks among the iconic pieces. Charles X's ewer and the Tsarina's candelabra testify to royal commissions.
The crystal armchair purchased by a Maharaja illustrates the relationship with India. The crystal works opened an office in Bombay in the 1880s.
Église Saint-Rémy forms a triangle symbolizing the Holy Trinity. Nicolas Kazis rebuilt it between 1953 and 1957 on the ruins of the old church.
Approximately 20,000 crystal plates compose Saint-Rémy's windows. The 150 different hues required 18 months of work by the Baccarat crystal works.

activities.text: Rue des Cristalleries features boutiques showcasing Baccarat crystal and Lorraine artisan creations.
Café Collection Baccarat overlooks the Meurthe river and Église Saint-Rémy. The terrace offers valley views.

days_plan.itin_title: Meurthe-et-Moselle Road Trip: Art Nouveau Nancy & Fortified Cities

visits.text: Bagnères-de-Bigorre, a spa town nestled at the entrance to the upper Adour valley and overlooked by Pic du Midi, was known as early as Roman times as “Vicus Aquensis.” The town retains forty recorded springs. A terrible earthquake in 1660 destroyed all the homes, which were rebuilt in the same style. Construction of the Grands Thermes began in 1823, and they were inaugurated in 1828; the arrival of the railway in 1862 accelerated the development of resort tourism. In 1993, a “facade” restoration campaign restored the town's colors.

The Tour des Jacobins, classified as a Historic Monument in 1932, is all that remains of the former church and Dominican convent built around 1373. This thirty-five-meter-high Flamboyant Gothic belfry has a square base extending over two stories, followed by an octagonal section. Its first-story openings feature 15th-century moldings with round arches topped by ogee arches and finials. Partially destroyed by lightning, it was rebuilt in the 16th century.

The Church of Saint-Vincent, classified as a Historic Monument in 1990, is a building of primary importance for architecture in the Hautes-Pyrénées after the 14th century. Built outside the walls in the 13th century on the site of older buildings, it was extensively altered between the late 14th and early 16th centuries. Its bell gable, portal, vaults combining stone and wood, and timber roof structures are remarkable.

The Musée Salies, listed as a Historic Monument in 2014, occupies an Art Deco building designed by architect Léon Jaussely and completed in 1931, on place des Thermes. Its facade is inspired by the 1925 Paris International Exhibition of Decorative Arts, with allegorical figures and bas-reliefs of female nudes. Collections include paintings from major 19th-century Paris salons, obtained thanks to member of parliament Achille Jubinal and his friendship with Princess Mathilde, as well as the collection of Blanche Odin (1865–1957), a watercolorist nicknamed “the Fairy of Roses and Flowers,” and Pyrenean folk art objects bequeathed by Jeanne Sayous.

The Musée du Marbre, housed in the former Thermes du Salut whose main building dates from 1781, presents the Jacques Dubarry de Lassale collection: marbles from 320 European sources, including about a hundred Pyrenean quarries ranging from the Spanish Basque Country to Languedoc. The historical gallery preserves original marble bathing cubicles and bathtubs, paving, and entrance steps testifying to Pyrenean marble-working expertise. It is the only collection of this type displayed in France. The museum also houses an area dedicated to bats, with an infrared camera allowing observation of colonies roosting in the attics in summer.

The Médous Caves, located between Bagnères and Campan in the municipality of Asté, were discovered by speleologist Norbert Casteret. The visit lasts approximately forty-five minutes to an hour, takes place at 13 °C, and passes through the Galerie des Merveilles, with a succession of mineral formations, helictites, petrified waterfalls, rimstone pools, and cave draperies, including a column twenty meters in circumference. The visit ends with a boat ride on the underground river in the cave's largest chamber.

activities.text: Walk through Bagnères city center starting from the Tour des Jacobins toward the Baltard-style covered market (1896) with its metal framework and glass roof, then along the Grands Thermes in classical style to the Musée Salies.

Visit the Musée du Marbre in the Vallon de Salut, then continue the walk along the 4.5 km walking route linking the Vallon to the Allées Maintenon, a protected natural site lined with beautiful trees and named in honor of Louis XIV's second wife.
Descend into the Médous Caves for the underground boat crossing - a magical moment that delights children and adults alike, to combine with a stop at the Allées Maintenon leading to the site.
For an exceptional panorama, reach the Pic du Midi de Bigorre by cable car from La Mongie, or simply climb up to the Parc Bédat for a transition from the town to wild nature.

For additional visits, the surrounding area offers the Grottes de Gargas in Aventignan, a prehistoric sanctuary with hand stencils dating back 27,000 years, the Grottes d'Esparros with their aragonite formations and the Château de Mauvezin, a medieval fortress. For each of these sites, allow for a day excursion there and back from Bagnères-de-Bigorre.

days_plan.itin_title: Hautes-Pyrénées Circuit: From Tarbes to Cirques and Valleys
Pyrenean Thermal Route: Spa Towns

visits.text: The thermal baths of Luchon rank among France's most renowned. Renovated in 2023, they treat rheumatological and respiratory conditions using the hottest sulfurous waters in the Pyrenees. Cures last 18 days but 5-day mini-cures are available. The Ressources & Vous spa, with its thermal water pools and its vaporarium unique in Europe, is open to all.

The lime-tree-lined Allées d'Étigny link the baths to the town center. Created in the 18th century by the intendant of Auch, they give Luchon its spa town character. The Belle Époque façades of hotels and the casino testify to the golden age of thermal tourism.
The old town preserves 17th and 18th-century houses. The church of Notre-Dame-de-l'Assomption has a 12th-century Romanesque portal. The 19th-century covered market is still active.

activities.text: The Superbagnères ski resort is accessible by gondola from Luchon's center. In winter, 32 runs spread between 1,440 and 2,260 meters. In summer, the gondola operates for access to high-altitude hikes. The view from the summit embraces the entire Pyrenean chain.

The Lys valley is one of the most beautiful Pyrenean valleys. The road leads to the Hospice de France at 1,385 meters. From there, hikes depart toward high-altitude lakes and peaks over 3,000 meters. The Lys cirque with its waterfalls is spectacular.

Hikes around Luchon are countless. From Col de Peyresourde to Port de Venasque, passing by Lacs d'Oô or the Quayrats, there's something for every level. Trails are well marked and mountain refuges enable multi-day traverses.
The Luchon market operates daily in summer and three times weekly the rest of the year. You'll find mountain cheeses, artisan charcuterie, and local products.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Garonne Road Trip: From Toulouse to the Pyrenees

visits.text: The Belle Époque Quarter, designed by Albert Christophle in 1886, unfolds its boulevards lined with sumptuous villas. Slate roofs, Armorican sandstone, sculpted balconies, and bay windows: a true open-air museum of the early 20th century.
Lake Bagnoles, shaped by human hands in the 17th century, is the heart of the resort. The casino from 1927, built on its shores, reflects Art Deco elegance in the calm waters.

The thermal establishment draws on a spring of aquamarine water, rich in trace elements, that has flowed for centuries. The first spa buildings date to the 17th century; the resort reached its peak in the years 1920-1935 with the arrival of the European aristocracy.

The Château de la Roche-Bagnoles, built in 1855 in neo-Renaissance style, is today the town hall. Its 6-hectare arboretum shelters more than 150 tree species, including a giant sequoia among the tallest in France.

Climb to the Roc au Chien, a natural lookout on a rocky outcrop of the Armorican Massif. The view sweeps over the lake, the thermal baths, and the forest. Two local legends surround the site—one involves a lord and his steed revived by the spring.

activities.text: The thermal spa treatments use natural mineral water with recognized benefits for phlebology and rheumatology. Half-day spa packages, hammam, or massage: the only thermal resort in northwest France.

The Andaines State Forest covers 5,400 hectares around Bagnoles. Its trails cross oak and beech groves; the Hippolyte oak is said to be over 300 years old. Arthurian legends are attached to the gorges of Villiers.
The 26 km cycling route starting from Bagnoles runs through the Andaines forest and suits the whole family. The Vélo Bocage, a 20 km greenway, links the resort to Briouze station.

days_plan.itin_title: Orne Road Trip: Norman Bocage and Stud Farms

visits.text: Built between 1704 and 1707 at the top of the village, Bagnols-en-Forêt's Saint-Antonin church is surprisingly bright: 30 meters long, 10 wide, tall, broad windows and two Louis XIII-style altarpieces. Its style combines Romanesque and Renaissance elements. The church square, shaded by horse chestnut trees, is the best place in the village to catch your breath.

The former millstone quarries of Bagnols-en-Forêt are reached along the ridges amid red rocks. Stone was cut there from prehistory until the 18th century. In clear weather, the view stretches to the sea. Start from the village, but access to the hills is restricted in summer: check the day's decree before setting out.

activities.text: Follow the Chemin de notre mémoire through the lanes of Bagnols-en-Forêt: old photos displayed on façades compare the village then and now. The route passes along rue en Calade, the main medieval approach from Fréjus, and past the Siagnole fountain. Free, one hour, best done first thing in the morning before the heat.

days_plan.itin_title: Roquebrune-sur-Argens: sea, villages and the Var in 10 days

visits.text: Bagnols-sur-Cèze holds a surprise few people expect: a museum of Post-Impressionist art, housed on the third floor of the town hall, on Place Mallet. The Albert-André Museum has a story worthy of a novel. Founded in 1859 by Léon Alègre as France's first cantonal museum, it changed completely when the painter Albert André became curator in 1917. A friend of Renoir, Monet and Matisse, he “hit up his friends”—as he put it himself—to rebuild the collection destroyed in a fire accidentally caused by the town's firefighters in 1924. The result: an outstanding group of works by Renoir, Matisse, Bonnard, Signac, Marquet, Valadon, Van Dongen, Picasso, Camille Claudel and Rodin. Free, open almost all year round.

Place Mallet is the medieval heart of Bagnols—its arcades, old facades and private mansions tell a tale of past prosperity. Founded in 1223, the town has preserved some narrow streets and alleys from its old center. The Wednesday morning market is one of the area's largest.

activities.text: The banks of the Cèze downstream from Bagnols offer swimming areas in limestone pools accessible on foot from town (20 minutes). Kayaking spots on the Cèze can be reached from Bagnols—operators offer equipment rental and return shuttles.

Bagnols-sur-Cèze's Wednesday market is one of the valley's culinary gatherings. Wine producers from the Gard part of the Côtes du Rhône, market gardeners and cheesemakers from the region have permanent stalls there.

days_plan.itin_title: Cèze Valley and Ardèche Gorges Circuit

visits.text: You'll follow the shore of Écalgrain Bay along the customs officers' path, between heather moorland and gorse that earn this part of La Hague the nickname little Norman Ireland. The pebble beach, wild and largely undeveloped, is best appreciated at low tide. Bring good shoes, as the path can be slippery.

days_plan.itin_title: Cotentin, Pays d'Auge: 5 days exploring the most beautiful villages

visits.text: You couldn't make up a name like that: legend links the name Baie des Trépassés, wedged between Pointe du Raz and Pointe du Van, to the bodies of shipwreck victims deposited there by currents. Today it's mainly a consistent surf spot: the westerly swell rolls in unobstructed, even in moderate wind. Lifeguarded swimming in summer only, and strong rip currents near the rocks.

days_plan.itin_title: Brittany 7 days: Pink Granite, Lighthouses & Peninsulas

visits.text: Balazuc ranks among the Most Beautiful Villages of France and richly deserves the title. Clinging to a limestone cliff that drops vertically into the Ardèche, the village was already inhabited in Neanderthal times. Its name comes from the Gaulish Baladunum—"the high fortified rock." The medieval lordship of Balazuc extended over much of lower Vivarais, as far as Vogüé, Largentière and Saint-Montan. Enter the village through the medieval gate and let the cobbled lanes guide you—some passages are carved directly into rock. The village is entirely pedestrian. In 1890, an exceptional flood reached 15 meters above the bridge's normal level—a plaque still attests to this today.

The church of Sainte-Madeleine, built in the 11th and 12th centuries, is listed as a Monument Historique. Climb its bell-arcade tower for a circular panorama over the village, castle and cliffs: this is where you best appreciate the site's verticality. The church also houses an early Christian sarcophagus. Next door, the Château de Balazuc, whose rectangular keep dates to the 11th century with 13th-century additions, is listed as a Monument Historique—it sometimes hosts temporary exhibitions.

The Muséum de l'Ardèche, housed in Balazuc, presents over 600 original fossils tracing the region's geological history from 300 million years ago, with a gallery dedicated to dinosaurs. It's a short but surprising visit, ideal for understanding why these limestone cliffs are so rich in fossils. Workshops are offered for children.

activities.text: Walk down from the village to the hamlet of Viel Audon via the shaded trail along the river—15 minutes' walk. This cooperative hamlet restored by a community of volunteers since the 1970s offers educational activities around sustainable development, a teaching garden and light organic refreshments. Access is on foot or by boat only.

From Balazuc beach, local operators offer canoe descents toward Pradons or Ruoms. Passing beneath the village cliffs from the river is a different experience: from water level, the site's verticality is even more impressive than from the lanes. Supervised swimming areas July-August are set up below the bridge.

days_plan.itin_title: Ardèche Road Trip: Wild Gorges and Villages with Character
The 18 Most Beautiful Villages of Ardèche

visits.text: Banne is a Cévennes village set on a hillside terrace, its castle ruins and parish church overlooking the surrounding countryside. The castle hill carrying those ruins offers a wide panorama over the hills and garrigue of the Cévennes rim. The village has a more austere feel than the gorge villages: grey stone, straight streets, no mass tourism.

The circuit between the two villages (upper and lower) and cultivated terraces reveals a territory deeply shaped by traditional agriculture: dry-stone terraces in restanques, vine and chestnut cultivation on slopes. The neighboring plateau shelters dolmens testifying to dense prehistoric occupation.

Dolmens and megaliths on the plateau around Banne are numerous—Ardèche is France's second department for dolmen density, with over 700 recorded. The nearest monuments are accessible on foot in under an hour from the village. Ask for the megalith map at the tourist office.

activities.text: The panoramic loop around the castle hill (3 to 4 km) circles the ruins with viewpoints over the village, plateau and surrounding hills. The climb toward the hill summit is fairly steep for the last 200 meters but the view from the ruins is worth the effort. Allow 1h30.

The terraces and clapas route on the garrigue edge (2 to 3 km, 1h) follows old cultivated fields on the village's western slopes. A discovery circuit of Ardèche rural heritage that helps understand how generations of peasants developed these harsh slopes.

days_plan.itin_title: The 18 Most Beautiful Villages of Ardèche

places.name: Bar Le Duc

visits.text: Bar-le-Duc's Upper Town district constitutes one of France's most remarkable Renaissance urban ensembles. Clinging to a rocky promontory, it unfolds mansions with sculpted pediments, fluted pilasters, and 16th-century gargoyles along Place Saint-Pierre and rue des Ducs de Bar.

Step through the doors of Saint-Étienne church in Flamboyant Gothic style. It houses Ligier Richier's Transi, a macabre sculpture depicting a flayed skeleton holding its heart toward heaven - one of the most striking works of the Lorraine Renaissance, commissioned for René de Chalon's funerary monument.

The Barrois Museum occupies remnants of the former castle of the Dukes of Bar and Lorraine. Nicknamed the "little Louvre," it presents archaeological objects from ancient Nasium, paintings from the Middle Ages to the 20th century, weapons and armor, and works by Ligier Richier and Ipoustéguy.

The Clock Tower, one of the rare remnants of 10th-century medieval fortifications, dominates the upper district. Circular at its construction, it received a clock oriented toward castle inhabitants in 1381. Its arrow slits and embrasures recall its defensive purpose.

The Gilles de Trèves college, built from 1573 to educate the duchy of Bar's youth, is a remarkable example of Renaissance school architecture. Its ornate roofs are discovered during a walk around the ramparts, between Upper and Lower Town.
Head to Lower Town and rue du Bourg, the city's Gallo-Roman cradle. Saint-Antoine and Notre-Dame churches preserve stained glass that, in the evening, shine with vivid colors.

activities.text: Discover the centuries-old know-how of seeding currants with a goose quill, an artisanal tradition attested since 1344. Local jam makers perpetuate this technique that gives "Bar caviar" its incomparable texture.
Stroll along the Ornain, the river crossing Bar-le-Duc. The bridges, squares laid out in the 18th century, and boulevard de la Rochelle reveal another facet of the town, more intimate and bucolic.
Visit the Sacred Way's zero milestone, the historic starting point of the supply route to Verdun during the 1916 battle. The monument recalls Bar-le-Duc's strategic role as a rear-front zone.

days_plan.itin_title: Meuse Circuit: Verdun and the Citadels
Grand Est Road Trip: Vineyards, Ramparts and Forests

map_keywords: Église Saint-Étienne Transi Ligier Richier Bar-le-Duc

visits.text: A Small Town of Character nestled at the Champagne-Burgundy border, Bar-sur-Seine stretches its half-timbered facades along the still-modest Seine. At 118 Rue de la Résistance, the 1580 Renaissance House displays a statue of Saint Roch and his faithful dog, its gable carved with the town's motto: Better a little with justice than great wealth without equity. Medieval remnants (17th-century Châtillon Gate, Clock Tower commanding the rooftops) and flower-lined walks compose the urban décor.

A jewel of Bar-sur-Seine, Saint-Étienne Church is remarkably bold: built between 1505 and 1616, it combines Flamboyant Gothic architecture with Renaissance touches over a length of 56 meters. Listed as a Historic Monument in 1907, this true glass lantern displays 16th-century stained glass from the Troyes School depicting the life of Christ, allegories of the Church and legends of the saints. The exceptional statuary—attributed to the workshops of Primaticcio and Dominique le Florentin—makes the building a sacred museum combining glass and sculpted stone.

The Croc Ferrand promenade follows the banks of the Seine, lined with cadoles—charming holiday pavilions surrounded by flower gardens where 19th-century notables entertained guests; the Goncourt brothers stayed there. The grounds of the Château du Val de Seine provide free access to gardens, playgrounds and picnic areas. On the heights, the Neo-Gothic Notre-Dame du Chêne chapel, built in 1867, marks the place where Saint Bernard is said to have meditated in 1153—a pilgrimage site that is peaceful today.

activities.text: The Côte des Bar Tourist Office organizes 1½-hour themed guided tours covering the development of timber-framed architecture from the Middle Ages to the Renaissance, the romantic Seine riverbanks and Belle Époque cadoles, or the artistic treasures of Saint-Étienne. In July and August: Thursdays at 2:30 p.m. Price: €6. Reservations on 03 25 29 94 43.

Bar-sur-Seine marks the entrance to the Côte des Bar, Champagne's southern wine-growing area, which forms an arc southeast of Troyes. Family-run cellars and estates open their doors to showcase Pinot Noir-dominant champagnes produced on steep slopes with Kimmeridgian soils—the same terroir as Chablis. The Union Auboise and its Devaux brand offer a complete wine-tourism experience in an 18th-century manor on the banks of the Seine: cellar tour, tasting and shop.

days_plan.itin_title: Aube Tour: Champagne, Medieval Heritage and the Lakes of the Forêt d'Orient

places.name: Barbentane

visits.text: The Tour Anglica dominates Barbentane at 28 meters — built in 1365 by Archbishop Grimoard (brother of Pope Urban V), it was the episcopal castle's keep. Classified as a historic monument, it was celebrated by Frédéric Mistral in the Iscles d'Or. Just beside it, the Maison des Chevaliers dates from the 12th century with 15th-century modifications — it's classified as a historic monument and constitutes one of the oldest seigneurial residences in the region. The 12th-century Romanesque church, with its beautiful classified bell tower, completes the medieval ensemble at the village heart.

The Château de Barbentane is nicknamed the "Little Trianon of the Sun" or "the most Italian of Provençal châteaux." Built from 1674, it was decorated in the 18th century by Joseph-Pierre Balthazar de Puget, Louis XV's ambassador to Florence, who brought back stucco work, Carrara marble, and Louis XV and XVI period furniture. Miracle: it suffered no damage during the Revolution because its owner agreed to become a Republican general. It's still inhabited by the marquis's descendants. Regular visits have not been offered since 2014, but the château opens exceptionally during Heritage Days in September.

3 km into the Montagnette, the Abbey of Saint-Michel de Frigolet is a monastery still inhabited by Premonstratensian monks. Its name comes from thyme (ferigoule in Provençal) that grows wild in the wooded hills surrounding the edifice. Frédéric Mistral studied here. The 12th-century Romanesque chapel is visible within the enclosure. The Montagnette forest surrounding it is closed from July to mid-September (fire risk).

activities.text: Walk at the edge of the Montagnette from Barbentane: marked trails starting from the village (or Frigolet abbey) follow pine forests and holm oaks of this 4,000-hectare state forest. Access regulated in summer — inquire at town hall. Outside the risk period, a 2-hour loop offers openings onto the Rhône plain and Alpilles.

Tour of townhouses and sculpted doorways in Barbentane center: several 17th-18th century residences line the main streets, some with door frames sculpted with plant motifs or coats of arms. The Bretoule Mill (1774), perched on the hill, owes its name to the fact that its founder, a stuttering miller (bret in Provençal), gave it his nickname. Its sails stopped in 1845, defeated by the steam engine.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpilles, Aix-en-Provence & Arles Circuit

map_keywords: Château de Barbentane Petit Trianon Provence

visits.text: The Auberge Ganne, heart of the Barbizon Painters Museum, welcomed generations of artists between the 1820s and 1860s. On the ground floor, the dining rooms and grocery store recreate the atmosphere with period furniture and panels decorated by the artists themselves.
Climb to the inn's first floor: bedroom walls preserve drawings, paintings, and humorous graffiti applied directly by visiting artists. The permanent collection brings together a hundred works.
Théodore Rousseau's house-studio, where the landscape painter lived his last twenty years until his death in 1867, hosts temporary exhibitions alternating with displays related to the painter's work.
Wander down Barbizon's Grande Rue, a former woodcutters' hamlet that became an artists' colony from 1830. Art galleries and shops occupy the old stone houses.
At the forest edge, painters found their subjects among centuries-old oaks and sandstone chaos. The same intact landscape still inspires artists who come to set up their easels today.

activities.text: Join an open-air sketching workshop, regularly organized by the museum. Charcoal or watercolor in hand, set up facing the same landscapes that inspired the Barbizon School.
Take forest trails from Barbizon to reach the Apremont boulders, one of the most accessible climbing sites in the massif. Color-coded circuits indicate difficulty levels.
Explore Barbizon's contemporary art galleries. The village maintains an active artistic life, with open studios and outdoor exhibitions.

days_plan.itin_title: Seine-et-Marne Circuit: Fontainebleau and Châteaux

places.name: Bareges

visits.text: The Col du Tourmalet is a cycling legend: since its first appearance in the Tour de France in 1910, it has been crossed over 80 times by the Grande Boucle. At 2,115 meters elevation, it's the highest road pass in the French Pyrenees. From Bagnères, the climb via La Mongie is a steady high-mountain ascent — allow about 45 minutes driving from the base. At the summit in summer, a statue of the Giant of the Tour welcomes cyclists and hikers. The view opens onto Pic du Midi, Barèges, and the surrounding massifs.

From La Mongie, a cable car climbs to Pic du Midi de Bigorre at 2,877 meters elevation. The astronomical observatory at the summit houses one of the world's largest solar telescopes, and the panoramic terrace offers views reaching the Bay of Biscay on clear days. In winter, the site is also accessible, with the stars of the Pic visible during organized astronomy nights. Bring warm clothing even in summer — temperatures drop significantly at altitude. Book the cable car in advance during peak season.

activities.text: Barèges is home to the highest continuously working spa town in France: 1,250 meters elevation, with a therapeutic tradition going back to the Roman legions and carried on under Madame de Maintenon, who during her stay in 1675 gave the village its present name by dating her letters from "Barèges." In this remarkable setting the Ciéléo spa offers a thermal water pool under a glass dome, a hammam, a sauna and a panoramic jacuzzi facing the Col du Tourmalet. The thermal water is polymetallic and sulfated, valued for its anti-inflammatory and healing properties. After a day in the mountains, it is hard to do better.

days_plan.itin_title: Pyrenean Thermal Route: Spa Towns

map_keywords: Pic du Midi de Bigorre La Mongie

visits.text: First stop at Omaha Beach in Saint-Laurent-sur-Mer. On June 6, 1944, 34,000 American soldiers landed here. Losses were so heavy that the sector was nicknamed 'Bloody Omaha.' On the beach, Anilore Banon's sculpture 'Les Braves,' installed in 2004 for the 60th anniversary, emerges from the sand facing the sea. Arrive early in the morning - the place is particularly poignant in silence.

Just above on the cliff, the American cemetery at Colleville-sur-Mer aligns 9,389 white crosses over 70 hectares facing the sea. It's the first American cemetery established in France during World War II, inaugurated as early as June 8, 1944. Don't miss the Wall of the Missing where 1,557 names of soldiers whose bodies were never recovered are engraved. Entry and parking are free. Allow at least 1.5 hours.

Head next to Pointe du Hoc in Cricqueville-en-Bessin. On June 6, 1944, 225 American Rangers scaled these 30-meter cliffs under enemy fire to neutralize a German battery of 155mm guns. By day's end, only 90 were still combat-effective. You'll literally walk on a frozen battlefield: bombing craters, shattered bunkers, trenches. A granite monument stands atop the command bunker. Plan for an hour on site - and good shoes.

Continue to Utah Beach, where the D-Day Museum in Sainte-Marie-du-Mont is located. This is where the US 4th Infantry Division set foot on June 6. The museum traces the operation with period equipment, including an authentic B-26 bomber. The beach itself, long and flat, contrasts with Omaha's cliffs - you understand why losses were lower here.

Late in the day, head to Barfleur, classified as one of France's 'Most Beautiful Villages.' This small port built of gray granite was the most important port in Normandy during the Middle Ages - from here the dukes crossed the Channel. Edward III destroyed it in the 14th century and it never regained its splendor. Walk around the harbor, peek into Saint-Nicolas church, and get lost in the 'Coche des amoureux,' a tiny alley beside the church.

If time allows, head to the Gatteville lighthouse 5 minutes away by car. It's the second tallest lighthouse in France and Europe - 75 meters tall, built between 1829 and 1835 with 11,000 blocks of pink granite from Fermanville. The anecdote: it supposedly has as many steps as days in the year (365), as many windows as weeks (52), and as many levels as months (12). In reality, it has only 349 steps - but the view from the top over the Barfleur Race is worth every step.

activities.text: In the evening, stroll along Barfleur's dike and pier. If you're there between June and October, look for the 'Blonde de Barfleur' in the harbor restaurants - a renowned local wild mussel, served with cider or Norman cream. No guarantee of finding it (it's a wild species), but Norman mussels are always available.

Complete Normandy Road Trip: Cliffs, D-Day Beaches and Mont-Saint-Michel
The 20 Most Beautiful Villages in Normandy
Cotentin, Pays d'Auge: 5 days exploring the most beautiful villages

places.name: Barjac

visits.text: Barjac is a Renaissance town designated a “Village de Caractère,” perched on a rocky spur between the Cèze and Ardèche gorges. Its history is marked by the Wars of Religion—the town switched several times between Protestantism and Catholicism, and Louis XIII stopped here on his way to the Peace of Alès in 1629. The Château des Comtes du Roure is the central monument: it actually consists of three buildings from different eras, the oldest being a lord's tower dating to the second half of the 10th century. The new residential building, built between 1634 and 1639, is where Richelieu stayed. Owned by the municipality since 1982, it now houses the town hall, the multimedia library and rooms for cultural activities. Go up to the terrace—the view over the Cévennes is unobstructed.

On the old main square, the Renaissance Tower is one of the village's architectural jewels: slender and narrow, it was most likely built in the 16th century, and its singular form makes it instantly recognizable. Seven other towers punctuate the tour of the old center, including that of the Bellet mansion (1580) with its spiral staircase. The ramparts from 1379 left some vestiges, and in the walls of houses, you can spot Roman sculptures salvaged from the Gallo-Roman estate of Malhac, rediscovered in the 1860s.

The Capuchin chapel, established in 1633 to bring the town back to Catholicism, and Saint-Laurent church complete the heritage tour. Don't miss the market hall and the market square with its century-old plane trees—every Friday morning, Barjac's Provençal market extends over almost the entire village and ranks among the most renowned in northern Gard.

activities.text: About ten kilometers from Barjac, the Aven d'Orgnac is one of the Grands Sites de France: gigantic mineral formations rise several dozen meters high in chambers reaching 250 meters long. The adjoining Cité de la Préhistoire traces 350,000 years of human occupation in the valley. Allow half a day to combine both visits. Book online in high season.

Every year in late July, the courtyard of Barjac castle becomes a stage for 'Barjac m'en chante', a festival of French songs with a focus on lyrics, in an intimate atmosphere. The antiques fairs (Easter and August) and the Friday organic market are essential fixtures of local life.

days_plan.itin_title: Ardèche Road Trip: Wild Gorges and Villages with Character
Cèze Valley and Ardèche Gorges Circuit

map_keywords: Château des Comtes du Roure Barjac

visits.text: Barneville-Carteret unites two towns: Barneville inland and Carteret facing the sea. Cap de Carteret offers a panorama of Cotentin's west coast and the Channel Islands.
Carteret's harbor, protected by a granite jetty, welcomes fishing boats and the maritime link to Jersey. The atmosphere remains that of an authentic fishing village.
Barneville's Saint-Germain Church, from the 11th century, presents a beautiful Romanesque portal and a seaside cemetery facing the coast.
The Hatainville dunes, classified as a nature reserve, stretch 6 km south of Barneville. A rare dune ecosystem shelters wild orchids and green lizards.
Climb to the summit of Cap de Carteret via the customs officers' path. The orientation table identifies Jersey, Sark, and the Écréhous on the horizon.

activities.text: Coastal walk on the Cap de Carteret path. The trail passes between moorlands, sandstone cliffs, and fine sand beaches, with views of Jersey.
Seafood tasting at Carteret's harbor. Lobsters, spider crabs, and clams are caught locally.
Swimming or stroll on Barneville's long sandy beach. At low tide, the foreshore extends hundreds of meters.

days_plan.itin_title: The 20 Most Beautiful Villages in Normandy

visits.text: The Old Harbor unfolds its ochre and salmon facades around quays where fishing boats bob gently. Dominated by the Church of Saint-Jean-Baptiste with its twin bell towers soaring 70 meters high, it invites leisurely strolls along the Quai des Martyrs de la Libération. Bar and restaurant terraces come alive from early morning when the boats return.

The Terra Nova Citadel towers over the sea from its rocky promontory. Founded in 1380 by Genoese governor Leonello Lomellini, it houses the Palais des Gouverneurs with its ochre facade now home to the Bastia Museum. Through the cobbled lanes, the baroque Sainte-Marie Cathedral (17th-18th centuries) reveals its marble and stucco work, including the monumental statue of the Assumption cast in solid silver weighing nearly half a ton.

The Oratory of Sainte-Croix preserves its venerated Black Christ. Built in 1542, this baroque edifice contrasts with the austerity of the ramparts. The Romieu Garden connects the Citadel to the Old Port via a monumental staircase planted with Judas trees, bella sombra trees, and spindle trees offering shaded respite.

Place Saint-Nicolas stretches 300 meters long and 90 meters wide. Lined with plane trees and palms, it holds the war memorial, the statue of Napoleon as a Roman emperor and a bandstand built at the end of the 19th century.

activities.text: The Aldilonda, a suspended walkway above the sea, hugs the citadel's rocky base for 200 meters. Inaugurated in 2020, it offers spectacular views of the ramparts and continues as the Spassimare promenade all the way to Arinella beach. Best experienced at sunrise over the Tyrrhenian Sea.

The market at Place du Marché buzzes to life on Saturday and Sunday mornings. Corsican producers offer charcuterie, sheep's cheese, maquis honey, and fresh vegetables. The authentic local atmosphere reveals Bastia far from the tourist circuits.

Arinella beach spreads its fine sand along Bastia's southern edge. The only true urban beach in the city, it's easily reached on foot or by bike via the Spassimare promenade. Clear waters and nearby amenities make it a popular spot for a swim break.

days_plan.itin_title: Upper Corsica Road Trip: Cap Corse and Balagne
Complete Tour of Corsica

visits.text: Saint-Guénolé Church in Batz-sur-Mer can be spotted from far off thanks to its 60-meter tower, built between 1660 and 1677 to replace a wooden bell tower struck twice by lightning. Climb the 184 steps of the spiral staircase: on clear days, the panorama sweeps from the island of Noirmoutier to Belle-Île. The Breton Gothic interior is also worth the detour—the organ, whose case dates from the 17th century, is among the oldest in the Pays de la Loire region. The tower is open from April to September. Access is managed by a local association.

The Musée des Marais Salants, founded in 1887 by Adèle Pichon, a nun and daughter of a salt worker, ranks among Brittany's oldest museums of folk traditions. Closed in 1970, it reopened in 1984 and now has 800 m² of exhibition space in former salt storehouses. You'll find scale models of salt marshes, salt workers' tools made entirely of wood, and a recreation of a 19th-century Batz-sur-Mer interior. A good introduction before heading out for a walk in the marshes.

The Notre-Dame-du-Mûrier Chapel, steps from the church, deserves a stop. Its name comes from the Breton word murié, meaning brine—not from the mulberry tree, contrary to a local legend about a castaway guided to shore by a statue in a mulberry. Built in the 15th century, it features a beautifully sculpted porch. Then head to La Govelle Beach for a break facing the Atlantic.

activities.text: Walk the salt marshes between Batz and Guérande. The tourist office offers several marked trails, including a 4.3-kilometer salt worker village circuit crossing Kervalet, a hamlet of tall terraced houses in white stone that seems frozen in the 19th century, complete with its own Saint-Marc chapel where mass was held in high summer to spare salt workers the trek to town. Informational signs along the trails explain the ecosystem and harvesting techniques.

days_plan.itin_title: Loire-Atlantique Road Trip: Nantes and the Côte de Jade

visits.text: Bauduen rises in tiers in an arc on the Défens hillside, giving every house a direct view of the lake. It would almost look like a Mediterranean port if the cliffs of Haute-Provence did not surround the landscape. Wander the narrow, shaded lanes—you'll find well-preserved Renaissance-style doorways, mullioned windows, and fragments of medieval ramparts. The village as a whole is remarkably authentic for a place that has lived primarily from tourism since the dam deprived it of its agricultural land in 1973.

The 16th-century Romanesque church of Saint-Pierre is open to visitors. Alongside it, the 15th-century Saracen tower is one of the few remnants of the village's defenses still standing. Don't miss the 19th-century sundial—it bears Louis XIV's motto: “Nec pluribus impar” (“Above all others”). A small irony in this peaceful village, far from any royal court.

The ruins of the medieval château overlooking the bay are worth the climb — from up there, the 180° view across the lake is spectacular. The dam's original plans called for flooding Bauduen like Les Salles, but the presence of the Fontaine-l'Évêque vauclusian spring (which still flows at the bottom of the lake) raised fears of a siphon effect and saved the village. This spring is now invisible beneath the waters, but its story is known to all the residents.

activities.text: Bauduen's large pebble beach and its jetty — which resembles a Mediterranean harbor quay — are the best spots for enjoying the lake. Swimming, sailing, canoeing, kayaking, paddleboarding, and electric boats are all available from the village's water sports center. Providers offer half-day or full-day rentals. Sunday mornings, the market sets up on the lakefront esplanade from 8 AM to 1 PM.

The Circuit du Défens, a marked hiking trail starting from Bauduen, offers a panoramic 20 km loop around the hill and lake. A shorter version of about 8 km is accessible to hikers of all levels. Ask for a map at the local tourist office.

days_plan.itin_title: Lake Sainte-Croix and Verdon Circuit

visits.text: The Abbey of Baume-les-Dames was founded around the 5th century by Saint Germain, Bishop of Besançon. It was around it that the city developed. In the 7th century, Saint Odile, blind daughter of the Duke of Alsace fleeing death, was baptized there and regained her sight. The current abbey church, rebuilt in the 18th century by architect Nicolas Nicole, features a profusion of pink and white marble, black Arguel stone, and gilding. To enter this monastery, one had to prove 16 quarters of nobility.

Baume-les-Dames, a character town labeled Station Verte, owes its name to the caves ('baume' in Celtic) and the canoness ladies of the abbey. The historic center preserves the 17th-century Saint-Martin church, the Hôtel des Sires de Neufchâtel (Renaissance) with its reconstructions of medieval life, and mullioned houses. The Affiche Moilkan typography workshop perpetuates the art of traditional printing.

The Cusancin valley and the château of Belvoir are worth a detour from Baume-les-Dames. The castle, guardian of the Sancey valley with its perched medieval outline, offers a tour of its rooms and a remarkable viewpoint. The 14th-century covered market hosts evening markets in summer. About 20 km from the base town, a 30-minute drive.

activities.text: The EuroVelo 6, the famous river cycle route connecting the Atlantic to the Black Sea, runs along the Doubs at Baume-les-Dames. The flat route on the old towpaths allows you to discover the valley in complete tranquility. The town is also a river stopover for boaters.

The Baume cliffs offer 460 climbing routes from levels 4 to 9, a renowned climbing ground in the region. For hikers, the viewpoint of the Virgin of Cholera offers the prettiest view of the historic heart of Baume-les-Dames. The Sous-Buen caves, accessible on foot or by bike, invite exploration.

days_plan.itin_title: Doubs Circuit: Watchmaking and Swiss Border

visits.text: Imperial Abbey of Baume-les-Messieurs, a Cluniac site founded in the 9th century by Abbot Bernon before the creation of Cluny Abbey. The abbey church of Saint-Pierre preserves an exceptional 16th-century Flemish altarpiece made of carved oak wood decorated with gold leaf. This masterpiece ranks among the most remarkable in Europe with its profuse details. The three courtyards, tomb chapel, and abbot's lodging can be visited to understand monastic life.

Caves of Baume-les-Messieurs winding 120 meters underground with a 70-meter entrance worthy of a church nave. The hour-long guided tour crosses a succession of chambers with ceilings 20 to 80 meters high shaped by the Dard, an underground river. Stalactites and stalagmites adorn the galleries developed over 600 meters. The constant temperature of 11 degrees requires warm clothing even in summer. Some chambers serve for exceptional acoustic concerts.

Tufa Waterfall of Baume-les-Messieurs at the back of the cirque. The Dard emerges after its underground journey creating a magical spectacle in the midst of verdant landscape. Crystal-clear water cascades over mosses and limestone rocks in a luminous environment with sumptuous colors. A small trail allows you to pass above the waterfall to witness the crystalline purity of the water. The lush vegetation adds to the enchanting character of the place.

Reculée of Baume-les-Messieurs, a geological cirque over 200 meters high typical of limestone rock collapse. The vertical cliffs dominate the village nestled at the confluence of three valleys. This particularity offers a natural setting enhancing the abbey and houses with flagstone roofs. The belvederes of Granges-sur-Baume and Crançot overlook this grandiose landscape inscribed in the network of remarkable sites of Bourgogne-Franche-Comté.

Village of Baume-les-Messieurs, one of France's Most Beautiful Villages and doubly labeled as a Cité de Caractère. Picturesque lanes wind between blonde stone houses vying in charm. The village of 200 inhabitants has preserved its authenticity far from modern bustle. The soothing atmosphere protected by the rock invites wandering between gardens, fountains, and covered passages.

activities.text: Hike to the belvederes overlooking the cirque. The trail climbs via the Échelles de Sermu, steep but secured stairways, to spectacular viewpoints. From atop the cliffs, the plunging view reveals the village, abbey, and three cirques converging on this unique site. The route crosses deciduous forests and undergrowth before descending toward the caves. Count on a half-day for the complete loop.

Échappée Jurassienne trail crossing the site. This emblematic 300-kilometer itinerary links Dole to Les Rousses station passing through the major sites of the Jura. The portion near Baume allows hikes suited to walkers of all levels through landscapes of cirques, forests, and high-altitude meadows. The marked trails regularly offer panoramas over the surroundings.

days_plan.itin_title: Loop Around Lyon: Villages and Pierres Dorées
Jura Road Trip: Lakes, Waterfalls & Mountains
Burgundy-Franche-Comté: The Most Beautiful Villages in 7 days

visits.text: Bavay's Ancient Forum is the largest Roman forum discovered in France. This 2.5-hectare archaeological site, classified as a Historic Monument and Site of National Interest, reveals the complete plan of a Gallo-Roman city: a judicial basilica nearly 100 metres long, a temple on a terrace, shops and civic buildings.

The cryptoporticus is the site's most imposing element. These semi-underground vaulted galleries, preserved to a height of over 10 metres, are protected by a monumental 6,400 m² roof – a contemporary architectural feat that enhances the ancient remains.

The archaeological museum presents 800 objects from the excavations: the bronze Jupiter statuette, Corinthian capitals in local limestone, marble tessera mosaics, tableware, jewellery and coins that recount the daily life of the inhabitants of Bagacum.

What did Bagacum look like two thousand years ago? The 3D projection “Retour à Bagacum” reconstructs the ancient city in computer-generated images – from the seven Roman roads converging on the city to details of daily life on the forum's streets.

Seven Roman roads converged on Bavay, a strategic crossroads founded between 19 and 15 BC as capital of the Nervii. Milestone markers still line certain routes visible in the surrounding landscape, witnesses to this road network that connected Bavay to Cologne, Reims and Boulogne-sur-Mer.

activities.text: Wander the archaeological site beneath the great protective cover. The outdoor route lets you walk between the judicial basilica's foundations and shop remains, following the exact layout of ancient streets.
The Roman garden, laid out near the museum, recreates plant species grown in Gallo-Roman gardens: aromatic herbs, medicinal plants and ornamental species. An adjacent picnic area extends the visit.
Bavay regularly hosts workshops introducing archaeology and ancient mosaic work. Visitors reproduce Roman geometric patterns with tesserae, following techniques documented by site excavations.

days_plan.itin_title: Nord Tour: Lille, Belfries and Flemish Culture

visits.text: Start with Arromanches-les-Bains. From the beach, you'll see the caissons of the Mulberry artificial harbor still lying in the sea—80 years after D-Day. This harbor, prefabricated in England, enabled 2.5 million men to land in 100 days. The museum (renovated in 2023, 1,200 m²) traces the operation in 7 sections. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes.

Continue to Pointe du Hoc, approximately 29 km from Bayeux, a 25-minute drive. On June 6, 1944, 225 American Rangers climbed this 30-meter cliff under enemy fire. The site has remained as it was: bomb craters, shattered bunkers and uneven ground. Wear sturdy shoes.

You'll then reach the American Cemetery at Colleville-sur-Mer, overlooking Omaha Beach. 9,387 white crosses and Stars of David perfectly aligned facing the sea. The visitor center traces the events of June 6. Explore independently, with free admission. Then walk down to Omaha Beach—the sculpture “Les Braves,” consisting of three steel blades planted in the sand, has become the symbol of the site.

Morning in Bayeux. Bad news: the Tapestry Museum is closed until October 2027. But don't pass it by—Notre-Dame Cathedral is worth the detour. Begun in the 11th century in Romanesque style and enlarged in the 13th in Gothic style, the cathedral housed the 70-meter embroidery for centuries. The Romanesque crypt beneath the choir is remarkable.

Bayeux was miraculously spared the bombings of 1944—it's one of the few Norman towns to have kept its medieval fabric intact. Stroll along rue Saint-Martin and rue Saint-Malo: half-timbered houses, 15th–16th-century mansions, a watermill on the Aure River.

If you want to understand what happened after D-Day, step into the Battle of Normandy Memorial Museum. It covers operations from June 7 to August 29, 1944, with period vehicles, uniforms, and animated maps. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes. Right next door, the British Military Cemetery has 4,648 graves laid out in rows in an immaculate garden.

Mont-Saint-Michel is 1 hour 40 minutes from Bayeux. Arrive before 9 a.m. Park at the main lot and take the free shuttle or walk 2.5 km along the footbridge. A UNESCO site since 1979, the Mont welcomes 3 million visitors a year. The silhouette reveals itself gradually—first the ramparts, then the village, then the abbey at the summit.

Climb via the Grand-Rue through the medieval village, then up to the abbey. The story begins in 708 when the Archangel Michael is said to have appeared in a dream to Bishop Aubert. Benedictine monks settled in 966. The “Merveille”—the 13th-century Gothic building clinging to the north face—has three levels of rooms stacked atop one another and is an architectural marvel. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes with the audio guide.

Walk around the ramparts. Built from the 12th to 14th centuries, they enabled the Mont to withstand the English siege from 1423 to 1434—one of the few Norman sites never to be taken. The West Terrace offers the most unobstructed view of the bay, which experiences continental Europe's greatest tides (a tidal range of up to 15 meters).

activities.text: On the way back to Bayeux, stop at the Longues-sur-Mer battery—the only Atlantic Wall battery whose 150 mm guns are still in place in their casemates. The fire control post, perched on the cliff facing the sea, offers an unobstructed panorama.
Visit the Battle of Normandy Memorial Museum. Military vehicles, uniforms, and dioramas trace the 77 days of combat that liberated Normandy.
Stroll along the Aure River as it winds through the town. Watermills and old washhouses line this bucolic walk.
Explore the Saint-Loup quarter and its local craft shops. Norman cheeses, farm ciders, and Bayeux lace perpetuate regional traditions.

If tide times permit, stay to watch the incoming waters from the causeway bridge—you won't regret it. Legend says the sea rushes in "at the speed of a galloping horse"—in reality it's about 6 km/h, but it's still striking when the water encircles the rock.

places.name: Bayonne

visits.text: Construction of the Cathedral of Saint Mary in Bayonne began in the 1240s under Champenois influence — the architect drew on the plans of Reims for the choir and of Soissons for the chapels. It was only more or less completed in 1451, when the French took Bayonne back from the English. Its two 85-metre spires were finished in the 19th century. Inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1998 as part of the Roads to Santiago, it deserves at least an hour — look at the coloured keystones representing the different quarters of Bayonne.

The Rayonnant Gothic cloister adjoining the cathedral is one of the largest in France. Built between the 14th and 16th centuries, in the Middle Ages it was a meeting place for the guilds and the quarter assemblies. Its galleries preserve enfeus (tombs set into the walls) and funerary slabs from the 14th to the 18th century. Freely accessible, it offers a rare space of calm in the heart of the busy town.

The Basque Museum and Museum of the History of Bayonne occupies a 16th-century house on the banks of the Nive. Its collections trace Basque culture from the Neolithic to the 20th century: costume, pelota, architecture, maritime traditions. Allow an hour and a half to go round it all.

Walk the Vauban ramparts that have encircled Grand Bayonne since the late 17th century. From the Mousserolles bastion, the view takes in the confluence of the Nive and the Adour. Bayonne was long the main stronghold of the Southwest, and its fortifications are part of the network of Vauban sites.

activities.text: Petit Bayonne is packed with pintxo bars and restaurants along the Nive. Pintxos — Basque tapas on toasted bread — are ordered standing at the counter, as tradition has it. The quarter is liveliest in the evening, especially on Thursdays and Fridays. Take the chance to try veal axoa, piperade and local anchovies.

Bayonne chocolate dates back to the 17th century — in 1609, Jewish craftsmen driven out of Portugal by the Inquisition brought the secrets of cocoa making to Bayonne. The town has been known as France's chocolate capital ever since. Several artisan chocolate makers carry on a four-century-old tradition under the arcades of the rue Port-Neuf. Look for a dark chocolate with a high cocoa content, sometimes flavoured with Espelette pepper.

Visit the Halles de Bayonne to find Bayonne ham IGP — salted with salt from Salies-de-Béarn and air-dried in the Pyrenees for at least 7 months. The tradition goes back to the Middle Ages; the Bayonne ham fair has been held since 1462. Every year at Easter, the Ham Festival draws thousands of visitors to the quays of the Adour.

Road Trip Pyrenees-Atlantiques: Basque Country and Bearn

map_keywords: Cathedral of Saint Mary Bayonne UNESCO

visits.text: Beauchastel closes the circuit beautifully: this medieval village sits at the exact confluence of the Rhône and Eyrieux, perched on a hillside in an exceptional Mediterranean microclimate. Its name comes from Latin Bel Castrum—"beautiful castle"—erected in the 12th century by lords Retourtour and Briand. By order of Louis XIII in 1622, the keep and ramparts were demolished; only the Maison des Seigneurs remains, a fine 16th-century dwelling with mullioned windows built by the powerful Tournon family. The old village, restored since the 1970s by the association Enfants et Amis de Beauchastel, lines up houses in schist and Eyrieux pebbles in paved lanes and vaulted passages facing south. It was elected "Mon beau village d'Ardèche" in 2023.

Follow the signposted heritage circuit (map available at the information point on the town hall square) so you miss nothing: the Fontaine du Chat (legend says a healer lived beside it), the impasse du bac that once led to the Eyrieux ferry crossing, the La Succulente space (the former girls' school of 1842, now an exhibition venue), and the 18th-century church of Saint-Jean-l'Évangéliste, wedged among the houses on the square. From the heights of the old village, the panorama over the confluence of the Rhône and the Eyrieux is striking.

The Chemin de Gurlhie, in the square beside the town hall, gathers sculptures and totems created by Alphonse Gurlhie (1862–1944), a local artist. Other creations have been installed in the old village in his honor. It's a fine example of artistic heritage integrated into Ardèche public space.

activities.text: The ViaRhôna—cycle route linking Lake Geneva to the Mediterranean over 815 km—crosses Beauchastel. The section climbing the Rhône northward, between Beauchastel and La Voulte-sur-Rhône (10 km), is particularly pleasant with views over both river banks. Bike rental can be found in neighboring communes. Even a 5 km round trip on the Ardèche bank is worth the ride.

La Dolce Via, a 35 km greenway laid out on the old Eyrieux railway line, is 15 minutes from Beauchastel by bike. Local operators offer bike rentals and shuttles. The section between Beauchastel and Le Cheylard is the wildest, crossing wooded gorges. It makes an excellent conclusion to this itinerary, between old Ardèche stone and unspoilt nature.

days_plan.itin_title: The 18 Most Beautiful Villages of Ardèche

visits.text: The Musée Japy chronicles the dynasty's industrial story. Housed in the former Pendulerie clock factory dating from 1892, it displays clocks, typewriters, pumps, and a diverse range of products. From a simple factory in 1777, the company grew to become France's second-largest industrial concentration under the Second Empire, employing 5,000 workers.
Seven Japy châteaux survive in Beaucourt out of the thirteen the family had built. These opulent industrialists' residences were erected during the company's golden age in the 1880s.

The Japy workers' housing estates exemplify 19th-century industrial paternalism. Six complexes have been studied as part of the heritage inventory: workers' housing, communal kitchens, and private schools.
The Protestant church built by the Japy family recalls founder Frédéric Japy's Anabaptist origins. The Protestant community shaped Beaucourt's social life.

activities.text: Japy heritage walking circuit (5 km): Pendulerie clock factory, industrialists' châteaux, workers' housing estates, church. A brochure is available at the museum to explore Japy's influence on the town's layout.
Cycle the FrancoVéloSuisse route toward Delle and Porrentruy. This 37-km cross-border itinerary follows the Allaine valley into the Swiss canton of Jura.

days_plan.itin_title: Territoire de Belfort Road Trip: The Citadel and the Lion

visits.text: Beaufort-sur-Doron stretches along its river, between footbridges and mountain-architecture houses. The "Beaufort Through Time" trail, marked by 18 panels, guides your walk: Château de Randens (15th century, now town hall), Pont Morens repeatedly swept away by floods and rebuilt, the former imperial gendarmerie of Napoleon III.

The baroque église Saint-Maxime, built on the rock since 1171 and remodeled in the 18th century, strikes with its carved wooden doors and gilded altarpiece. The interior testifies to the baroque exuberance of the Savoyard valleys.

The Beaufortain dairy cooperative reveals the secrets of Beaufort AOP, a pressed cooked cheese made from raw milk of Tarine and Abondance cows. Tour of the aging cellars followed by a tasting of summer and winter Beaufort, paired with a Savoie wine.

Take the road to Lac de Roselend (1,557 m altitude). The dam, built between 1955 and 1962, measures 804 meters long and 150 meters high. Its turquoise waters mirror the peaks of Beaufortain, including Pierra Menta.

The Romanesque Chapelle Sainte-Marie-Madeleine de Roselend, sole vestige of the old hamlet submerged when the dam was filled, was dismantled stone by stone and rebuilt on the lake's shores. A place of contemplation facing the mountains.

activities.text: Hike around Lac de Roselend. The trail follows turquoise shores through alpine pastures where herds of Tarine cattle graze. From Plan de la Laie, a 15-minute detour leads to an unusual curiosity: a red telephone booth perched in the middle of the mountains.

Panoramic road over the Cormet de Roselend (1,968 m), about 15 km from the stopover town, 25 minutes by car. This pass links the Beaufortain to the Mont-Blanc massif and is famous for its Tour de France crossings. The hairpin bends offer spectacular views over the lake and the snow-capped peaks.

Discover the Beaufortain alpine pastures. In summer, Tarine cows—brown coats and gentle eyes—climb to altitude to produce milk for Beaufort d'alpage. Trails cross flower-filled meadows with Mont Blanc in the background.

days_plan.itin_title: Savoie from Lakes to Glaciers: Yenne to Haute-Maurienne

visits.text: Caesar's Tower is Beaugency's oldest monument: this square Romanesque keep was built by Lancelin I, lord of Beaugency, between 1015 and 1030. It stands 36 metres high and commanded both the citadel's defences and control of the bridge over the Loire. In 1567, a fire during the Wars of Religion gutted the interior — only the shell of the four walls remains. The Tower is only accessible during Heritage Days, but its silhouette dominates the town from any street. Historians compare it to the keep of Loches, from the same period.

Beaugency Château has housed a digital art centre since 2021. Originally built in the 15th century by Jean de Dunois — the Bastard of Orléans, Joan of Arc's companion-in-arms — it later belonged to the Dukes of Orléans until the Revolution. In the 19th century it served as a poorhouse, then for decades as the Orléanais Museum. Today, its medieval and Renaissance halls host immersive light and digital installations. An unexpected experience within 15th-century architecture. Buy tickets in advance during peak season.

The Notre-Dame abbey church dates from the 12th century — it's where two councils were held that changed the history of France: in 1104, Philip I was ordered to separate from Bertrade of Montfort; in 1152, Louis VII the Young had his marriage to Eleanor of Aquitaine annulled, and she wed Henry II of England a few weeks later, indirectly triggering the Hundred Years' War. Push open the door to see the 12th-century carved capitals and the still-intact Romanesque choir.

Beaugency's old bridge spans the Loire on some twenty stone arches. The first mention of a bridge at this spot dates to 1145. It's one of the rare old bridges still standing on the Loire. From the bridge, the view of the medieval town's towers — Caesar's Tower, the abbey church belfry — is the classic photo of Beaugency. Go at the end of the day for the light.

activities.text: Walk along rue du Pont and its half-timbered houses from the 15th and 16th centuries. The Renaissance town hall — listed as a Historic Monument as early as 1840 — is worth a stop: upstairs, the ceremonial hall holds eight 17th-century embroidered hangings. The climb toward the château offers open views over the Loire and the slate roofs.

Rent a bicycle and follow the Loire à Vélo path on the levees between Beaugency and Meung-sur-Loire. The track is flat, waymarked and hugs the river between vineyards and wooded islands. Plan 15 to 20 km depending on your halfway point. Bike rental is available in town.

days_plan.itin_title: Loiret Road Trip: Orléans and the Châteaux of the Loire

places.name: Beaujeu

visits.text: Beaujeu, the historic capital of Beaujolais, gave its name to the entire wine region. The lords of Beaujeu ruled these lands from the 11th to the 15th century, developing the vineyards and laying the foundations of local viticulture. The town retains a remarkable architectural heritage from this glorious period, with medieval lanes and Renaissance residences.

The Hospices de Beaujeu, an 18th-century building, bear witness to the organisation of charitable care in the past. Their classical architecture contrasts with the surrounding medieval houses. Inside, the preserved apothecary's shop and period furnishings recreate the atmosphere of an old hospital where nuns and doctors cared for the destitute.

Saint-Nicolas Church, a Romanesque building of Cluniac inspiration constructed in the 12th century, stands in the heart of Beaujeu. Its restrained architecture and solid proportions reflect the Romanesque art of the period. Its façade and square bell tower rise above the rooftops of the former capital of Beaujolais.

The Musée des Arts et Traditions populaires Marius Audin is closed to the public for renovation. Part of its collections can be seen at the Maison du Terroir Beaujolais through its off-site exhibitions. The objects on display explore the history of Beaujeu, local trades and everyday life in the Beaujolais. This visit offers an introduction to the region's rural and wine-growing heritage without going to the museum's closed galleries.

activities.text: Wander through the old town's lanes, where timber-framed houses stand alongside private mansions. Each façade tells a story: that of a merchant enriched by the wine trade, a local notable or an ordinary winegrower. Projecting upper storeys, carved lintels and inner courtyards create a preserved medieval setting.

Visit the Sources du Beaujolais, a modern wine centre in a historic setting. Interactive museum displays present the history of the vineyards, winemaking techniques and the different terroirs. Tasting workshops help you understand the diversity of Beaujolais wines, from Beaujolais nouveau to crus suitable for ageing.

Explore the vineyard-covered hillsides surrounding the town. Marked trails wind between the plots of vines, offering views over the valley and the Beaujolais mountains. In autumn, the landscape becomes a palette of colours, with the yellow, orange and red vine leaves contrasting with the green of the surrounding forests.

Enjoy the weekly market, where local producers offer their specialities. Alpine cheeses, artisan charcuterie, seasonal fruit and, of course, Beaujolais wines create a symphony of flavours. The friendly atmosphere and conversations with producers embody the Beaujolais way of life.
