visits.text: Beaulieu is a peaceful village in southern Ardèche, surrounded by vines, garrigue and light woods. Its heritage is modest but sincere: the chapel and traces of the old priory constitute the village's micro-religious heritage, complemented by stone houses and paths bordered by walls. This is a village to visit without a tight schedule, taking time to notice architectural details.

The network of old paths bordered by walls and clapas (stone piles from field clearing) around Beaulieu is characteristic of traditional Ardèche agriculture. Some walls date to the 19th century, when peasants transformed cumbersome stones into parcel boundaries. These structures run alongside vines and oak groves, making magnificent hiking trails.

From heights around the village, views carry over a typically southern Ardèche landscape: garrigue-covered hills, rows of vines on south-facing slopes, silhouettes of first Cévennes reliefs on the horizon. Beaulieu is a good starting point for exploring the surrounding countryside on foot or by bike.

activities.text: The rural loop of 5 to 7 km around Beaulieu crosses vines and light oak woods, with sections on old mule tracks bordered by walls. Ideal in spring (garrigue flowers) or autumn (harvest, colors). Map available at the town hall or tourist office.

The hamlet circuit around Beaulieu reveals traditional Ardèche buildings: houses with aître (exterior covered gallery), dovecotes, communal bread ovens. A rural heritage reading circuit is signposted from the village—allow 1h30.

days_plan.itin_title: The 18 Most Beautiful Villages of Ardèche

visits.text: The 13th-century press, a listed Historic Monument, is one of the oldest in Europe. Made of solid oak without metal parts, it weighs 30 metric tons and could crush 3,000 kg of grapes. It remained in operation until the late 19th century.
Saint-Rouin church, rebuilt in 1880 in neo-Gothic style, houses the relics of Saint-Rouin and Saint-Maurice in two reliquaries on either side of the transept.
Reach the orientation table at the summit of the promontory. The view embraces the Meuse valley, the Argonne forests and the wind turbines that dot the horizon.
The half-timbered houses of this street-village testify to Argonne's architectural identity. Some are built with cut stone recovered during the demolition of the abbey in 1790.

In the forest, the Saint-Rouin chapel (1954) surprises: cubic concrete blocks on stilts, inspired by Le Corbusier. Colored stained glass by a Japanese artist softens the geometric rigor. An 18th-century Assumption altarpiece, the only vestige of the abbey church, stands in the open air nearby.

activities.text: Take the Abbey loop starting from the village. The marked trail crosses the state forest to the Saint-Rouin hermitage and its miraculous fountain.
For walkers, the Saint-Rouin loop (15 km, GR14) crosses ponds, valleys and deciduous woods—territory of the red kite and osprey.
The village, awarded 4 flowers, lends itself to wandering: an English garden along the street-village, a row of linden trees including three planted for the bicentennial of the Revolution.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Est Road Trip: Vineyards, Ramparts and Forests

visits.text: Saint-Pierre Abbey Church and its Romanesque tympanum. Founded in the 9th century, the Benedictine abbey features a tympanum sculpted around 1125 representing the Parousia (Christ's return at the end of time). It's one of the masterpieces of Limousin Romanesque sculpture, comparable to Moissac or Conques. Christ in Majesty is surrounded by apostles, angels and monsters symbolizing evil.
Penitents' Chapel. On the banks of the Dordogne, this 12th-century chapel with its bell gable is reflected in the water. Iconic view of Beaulieu from the river.
Renaissance House. 16th-century turreted residence in the village center, witness to the prosperity of the era.

activities.text: Gabare boat ride on the Dordogne. The gabare “Adèle et Clarisse,” built in 2002 using traditional methods, offers 45-minute guided boat trips about the history of the boatmen. These boatmen once transported wood, Auvergne cheeses and coal to Bordeaux.
Tasting of Beaulieu strawberries. The mild climate of the “Limousin Riviera” allows strawberry cultivation. Local producers at the Wednesday market.

days_plan.itin_title: Corrèze Road Trip: Villages and Dordogne Valley

visits.text: Villa Kérylos is one of the French Riviera's most bewildering curiosities. Built between 1902 and 1908 by archaeologist Théodore Reinach and architect Emmanuel Pontremoli, it's a complete reconstruction of a Greek dwelling from the island of Delos from the 2nd century BC—but with Belle Époque running water and central heating. The library bears a Greek inscription: "Here I create for myself a peaceful retreat in immortal beauty." Reinach bequeathed the villa to the Institut de France at his death in 1928. During World War II, the Gestapo searched the villa and sent family members to Auschwitz. Classified as a Historic Monument, open year-round except May 1st and December 25th.

Beaulieu's seafront merits a stroll: its Belle Époque palaces, promenade with direct views of Saint-Jean-Cap-Ferrat, and Fourmis Bay make this resort one of France's most sheltered—the microclimate is so mild it rivals Menton as the country's warmest town.

activities.text: Promenade Maurice Rouvier: seaside path linking Beaulieu to Saint-Jean-Cap-Ferrat (about 2 km, flat, easy). Constant views over the roadstead and rocks. Ideal in late afternoon for the light.
Petite Afrique Beach: a small, well-sheltered beach that is rarely crowded outside the high season. The calm, shallow waters are ideal for family swimming.

days_plan.itin_title: The 15 Gems of the French Riviera and Backcountry

visits.text: If you're looking for a quiet stop between Beuvron and Honfleur, Beaumont-en-Auge, a small hilltop town in the Pays d'Auge, fits the bill. Place de Verdun, lined with half-timbered houses, retains an unspoilt rural character, far from the bustle of the major D-Day sites. The village is also known as the birthplace of astronomer Pierre-Simon de Laplace.

days_plan.itin_title: Cotentin, Pays d'Auge: 5 days exploring the most beautiful villages

places.name: Beaune

visits.text: Gevrey-Chambertin is about 30 km from Beaune, a 30-minute drive. Gevrey-Chambertin is the first village in the Côte de Nuits worth a stop. Napoléon demanded that his chambertin be served at every meal; he even took it on campaign, diluted with water. The village has 9 grand cru appellations covering 87 hectares, more than any other in Burgundy. Walk up rue du Chambertin to the vineyards: in 10 minutes on foot, you will be facing the plots that created the legend.

The Château du Clos de Vougeot is about 20 km from Beaune, a 20-minute drive. Its 50.6 hectares have been enclosed by the same wall since 1336; Cistercian monks built this clos in the 12th century and enlarged it over 400 years. The result is Burgundy's largest enclosed grand cru, with four wine presses dating from the 13th to the 16th centuries still in working order inside the buildings. Since 1934, the Confrérie des Chevaliers du Tastevin has held its costumed chapters here, with 600 guests, a Burgundian menu and mock-Latin speeches. The 1-hour guided tour is available without a reservation outside chapter periods.

Romanée-Conti is about 20 km from Beaune, a 20-minute drive. A wire fence. A stone cross. 1.8 hectares of vines a few metres from the road. That is all you will see of Romanée-Conti; no visit is possible without a professional introduction, and even then. The estate produces between 6,000 and 8,000 bottles a year depending on the vintage, at more than €20,000 each and €100,000 for older vintages. The plot has belonged to the same estate since 1869. The photo stop lasts 5 minutes; the memory of being there will remain.

Nicolas Rolin, chancellor to the Duke of Burgundy, founded the Hospices in 1443 - some historians say he wanted to atone for a lifetime of political compromises, others that he was simply wealthy and devout. Either way: the building treated patients until 1971, 528 years of continuous operation. The glazed tile roof (gold, ochre, black, red lozenges) ends up on every postcard, but it's the Grande Salle des Pôvres that takes your breath away - 72 meters long, oak four-poster beds recreated identically, and at the back Van der Weyden's Last Judgment polyptych, commissioned by Rolin himself. Every November, the Hospices wine auction sets the global barometer for Burgundy prices.

Kengo Kuma designed the building in 2021, right across from the ramparts - wood, stone, diagonal lines evoking the slopes of the hillsides. Inside, two hours of serious content: Kimmeridgian geology explained with samples, the 1,247 distinct UNESCO-listed parcels visualized on an interactive table, the history of négociants, an introduction to tasting with eight glasses. It's more rigorous than Dijon's Cité de la Gastronomie, less touristy than expected. Book tickets online, full on weekends in season.

Dijon mustard has no geographical requirement - any factory in China can legally make it. Fallot, however, has been grinding in Beaune since 1840 with stone millstones, the last artisanal mustard mill in Burgundy to maintain this technique. The 45-minute tour ends with a tasting of 8 varieties: classic, tarragon, lemon, Burgundy blackcurrant. That last one divides people radically - you're either for it or against it, no middle ground possible.

activities.text: Nuits-Saint-Georges is about 15 km from Beaune, a 15-minute drive. Taste wines at Domaine Faiveley in Nuits-Saint-Georges, a house founded in 1825 with 120 hectares of its own vineyards, from Gevrey to Mercurey. The guided tasting, by reservation, compares appellations from the same vintage, a highly instructive exercise for understanding why 200 metres between two plots can justify a tenfold price difference.

Grand Crus Route at slow speed: from Marsannay-la-Côte to Nuits-Saint-Georges, the D122 runs alongside the vineyards at the foot of the slope for 25 km. Free stops in front of appellation signs - each parcel is identified by its name and classification. Villages follow one another (Fixin, Brochon, Morey-Saint-Denis, Chambolle-Musigny) each with their own cellar open to the public.

1720: Champy is the oldest négociant house still active in Burgundy - it survived the Revolution, two wars, a dozen owners. The guided tasting does what few cellars honestly do: explain prices. Why a Pommard village at €25 and a Pommard premier cru at €65? The difference shows in the glass, the guide puts words to it. Allow 1h30, reservation recommended. Ask to see the 18th-century vaulted cellars - they're not always offered automatically.

Walk around Beaune's ramparts: the medieval fortifications are virtually intact over 2 km - bastions, round towers, moats. The path winds between gardens and négociant cellars whose chimneys barely rise above ground level. Perfect in late afternoon when golden light hits the stone. Free, always open.

visits.text: Saint-Pierre Cathedral has the highest Gothic vault ever built, with a height of 48.50 metres beneath the keystone. Begun in 1225 and never completed, it surpasses Amiens by four metres but has only one nave bay.
The choir collapsed in 1284, twelve years after its completion. Vibrations caused by resonance in the upper structures during violent winds brought down the vaults.
The Flamboyant Gothic transept was built between 1500 and 1548 by Martin Chambiges. Sixty metres long, it displays the achievements of late Gothic art before the style was abandoned.
The 153-metre lantern tower, built between 1569 and 1573, made Beauvais the world's tallest human-built structure. It collapsed four years later in 1573, destroying two 13th-century pillars.
Auguste Lucien Vérité's astronomical clock stands 12 metres high and 6 metres wide. Ninety thousand synchronised components bring this 19th-century mechanical masterpiece to life.
The Basse-Œuvre survives as witness to the former Notre-Dame cathedral from the year 1000. This Carolingian nave stands beside the unfinished Gothic edifice in a coexistence unique in France.

activities.text: Admire the 13th-century stained glass in the radiating chapels and clerestory windows of the chevet. Enguerand Leprince's 16th-century work illuminates the south transept.

days_plan.itin_title: Oise Circuit: châteaux, forests and history

visits.text: The island of Béhuard emerges from the Loire, entirely liable to flooding except for the church that sits on its rock. Classed a Petite Cité de Caractère, it welcomes 150,000 visitors a year.

Notre-Dame Church has stood on a rock since the 5th century, when Saint Maurille placed a statue of the Virgin here. Louis XI had the present building rebuilt in 1469 after being saved from drowning in the Charente.
The sanctuary has two naves set at right angles. The rock breaks through inside the church itself, beneath the statue of the Virgin and Child.
The 15th-century stalls and the stained-glass windows from the 15th to the 19th centuries decorate the building. Louis XI made fifteen pilgrimages here between 1470 and 1479.
The picturesque village is discovered on foot. Cobbled lanes and old houses line the island, where a bucolic atmosphere reigns.

activities.text: The Loire à Vélo route crosses Béhuard. The cycling itinerary links the island to the châteaux of Anjou along landscaped paths.
The banks of the Loire invite a stroll. Guinguettes and terraces open up in fine weather.
The interpretation trail starts on the church square. It reveals the island's treasures and its thousand-year history.

days_plan.itin_title: Maine-et-Loire Road Trip: Anjou and Loire Valley Châteaux

visits.text: Belcastel Castle dates from the 11th century with its square keep and corner towers. Fernand Pouillon restored it from 1975 to 1982, involving numerous local craftsmen. Visit the water-filled moat, medieval chapels, and art galleries exhibiting contemporary works.

Alzias de Saunhac had the bridge built in the 15th century. It connects the Sainte-Madeleine Church to the village on the other bank of the Aveyron river. Passers-by once paid for their crossing with prayers and offerings at the altar stone.

The 15th-century Sainte-Madeleine Church houses the tomb of Alzias de Saunhac with its recumbent effigy. You will also see the Saunhac family coat of arms and four statues listed as historic monuments. Casimir Ferrer created an extraordinary Stations of the Cross for the church.

activities.text: The Maison de la Forge is over 200 years old and displays the tools of the blacksmith, farrier, clog-maker, and fisherman. Guides explain the use of the twitch to restrain horses and the tail docker.
Climb to the Roc d'Anglars located 500 m upstream from the village. This 5th-century fort occupies the heights above the Lourdou cave. The 3 km hike offers views of the village and the Aveyron river.

days_plan.itin_title: Aveyron Road Trip: Causses, Tarn Gorges and Villages
The Most Beautiful Villages of Lot and Périgord in 6 Days

places.name: Belfort

visits.text: Bartholdi's Lion measures 22 meters long and 11 meters high. Carved from pink Vosges sandstone between 1875 and 1880, it commemorates Belfort's resistance during 103 days of siege in 1870–1871.
Pass through the Porte de Brisach, the only remaining gate from Vauban's fortifications. Carved fleurs-de-lis and the Sun King's motto adorn its facade.
The Citadel has dominated the town since the 17th century. Vauban designed this fortress to control the Belfort Gap between the Vosges and Jura mountains.
The Grand Souterrain offers an audiovisual tour beneath the ramparts. Projections and exhibition staging trace the military history of the stronghold.
The Citadel's keep houses the History Museum. Collections on the 1870 siege, scale models of fortifications, and military memorabilia testify to Belfort's strategic past.
The Cathédrale Saint-Christophe dates from the 18th century. A listed historic organ and restrained neoclassical architecture.
Wander around the Place de la Grande Fontaine and through the lanes of the old town. Colorful Vosges sandstone facades and squares laid out according to Vauban's plan.

activities.text: Climb to the Tour de la Miotte, a medieval remnant perched on high ground. The panorama takes in Belfort, the Savoureuse valley, and the southern Vosges.
Follow the banks of the Savoureuse on foot or by bike. The cycling path winds through residential neighborhoods and green spaces.
The Étang des Forges lies to the east of town. Walking paths, a playground, and birdwatching in this 7-hectare urban park.
Follow the Hauts de Belfort circuit (7 km) downhill from the Miotte towards the Fort de la Justice. Views over the city and the southern Vosges.

days_plan.itin_title: Territoire de Belfort Road Trip: The Citadel and the Lion
Territoire de Belfort Road Trip: The Citadel and the Lion

map_keywords: Place de la Grande Fontaine Belfort

visits.text: The Église Notre-Dame de l'Assomption de Bellac, formerly the chapel of the counts of La Marche, has two parallel naves: the 12th-century Romanesque nave once opened onto the keep of the now-vanished castle, while the 14th-century Gothic nave bears a 25-meter granite spire. The whole is listed as a historic monument.

Inside the church, the enameled shrine dating from around 1130 is Limousin's oldest. This sarcophagus-shaped reliquary in gilt copper bears 14 medallions in domed champlevé enamel: Christ, the evangelists, the Virgin, and the Lamb. Its colors—dark blue, green, turquoise, whitish pink—and cabochon semiprecious stones testify to Limoges' first enamel workshops.
The Chapelle du Cardinal, adjoining the church, opens through a 15th-century Flamboyant Gothic window. Its limestone carving is remarkably delicate for the region.

Walk down to the Pont de la Pierre, a 13th-century medieval granite bridge over the Vincou. It's one of France's oldest preserved bridges. Below, the former 15th-century hide-drying shed evokes the tannery tradition that sustained the town for centuries.

Writer Jean Giraudoux's birthplace, at 4 Rue Jean-Jaurès, has been transformed into a museum with interactive and immersive installations. An escape game called 'Secrets d'État(s)' invites you to investigate the circumstances of his mysterious death.

activities.text: Explore old Bellac on foot around the church: half-timbered houses, Renaissance windows, winding lanes, and former merchants' shops. The town, a commercial crossroads between Limousin, Marche, Berry, and Poitou, preserves traces of its medieval prosperity.
The Festival national de Bellac, founded in 1953, programs theater, dance, and music annually in late June through early July. Performances take over the old town's squares and courtyards.

Interested in megaliths? The Monts de Blond, a granite massif rising to 514 meters, lie 15 minutes away. The megalith circuit from Ceinturat (11 km) leads to the Pierre Branlante de Boscartus—a boulder weighing 120 tonnes used in the Middle Ages as an ordeal stone—then to the Roche aux Fées, a Neolithic shelter and necropolis.

The village of Mortemart, 11 km from Bellac, is among the “Plus Beaux Villages de France”. Its Augustinian convent, wooden market halls, and Carmelite convent transformed into artists' workshops are worth a detour.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Vienne Tour: Limoges, Porcelain and Villages

visits.text: The Pertes de la Valserine offer a fascinating geological spectacle. The river enters a maze of narrow limestone canyons before reappearing farther downstream. The turbulent water rushes through the rock with a deep rumble. This karst phenomenon, typical of the Jura, captivates geologists and visitors who come to admire the power of natural forces.

Fort l'Écluse, a strategic military stronghold, has guarded the Rhône gorge between the Jura and the Vuache since the 13th century. This multi-level fortress, altered and enlarged over the centuries, controlled the route between France and Savoy. Its ramparts, casemates and underground passages can be visited, recounting centuries of military history. The terraces offer views over the Rhône valley and the Jura Mountains.

The Valserine gorges reveal their vertiginous limestone walls. The road through them, cut into the cliff, overlooks the river by several dozen metres. The visible geological strata tell the story of how these mountains were formed. Waterfalls and rapids punctuate the turbulent course of the Valserine, which carved these gorges over thousands of years.

Bellegarde-sur-Valserine, now part of the municipality of Valserhône, preserves an industrial heritage linked to hydropower. Former factories, the power station and dams reflect the use of water to generate energy and economic activity. Local heritage tours recount the industrial development that transformed the town into a prosperous working-class centre.

activities.text: Hike through the gorges along the trails laid out beside the Valserine. Metal footbridges cross the river, while the paths cling to the steep slopes. The route passes through beech and fir forests, rocky scree and high-altitude meadows. The plunging views over the gorges provide a dizzying thrill for experienced hikers.

Go rock climbing on the limestone cliffs lining the valley. The equipped rock faces offer routes for every level, from beginner climbs to demanding multi-pitch routes. The compact, grippy limestone of the Jura provides an ideal surface for climbers. Local climbing schools offer courses and guided outings to introduce you to this vertical sport.

Explore the exceptional geological heritage of this contact zone between mountain ranges. Folded, faulted and eroded rocks tell the story of Alpine tectonics. Exposed fossils bear witness to the ancient seas that once covered the region. Amateur geologists will find a fascinating field of study here for understanding the formation of the Jura Mountains.

Visit Fort l'Écluse at night during the summer events. The illuminated ramparts, sound-and-light shows and historical reenactments bring the site's military epic back to life. The special atmosphere of these evenings, blending history and enchantment, delights young and old alike in the majestic setting of this hilltop fortress.

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip from Bresse to Bugey via Beaujolais and Lyon

visits.text: The Church of Saint-Sauveur, a listed historic monument, dominates Bellême's main square. Classical in style, it holds refined liturgical furnishings and has watched over the town since the 17th century.
Pass through the Porte Saint-Sauveur, a remnant of the medieval fortifications. This vaulted gateway recalls the era when Bellême was a stronghold of the Counts of Perche.
The moats and Clock Tower complete the town's defensive architecture. From the heights, panoramic views sweep across the Perche hills and the state forest.
Stroll down the Rue Ville Close, a picturesque street lined with 17th- and 18th-century townhouses. The ochre and rose facades typical of Perche architecture now house antique dealers and brocantes.
The Chapel of Notre-Dame, also called Saint-Santin, is the oldest religious building in the Perche. A quiet detour off the beaten path.

activities.text: The Bellême State Forest covers 2,400 hectares of centuries-old oak and beech groves. The Pierre des Druides trail offers an easy 2 km family walk through the woods.

Head to the Étang de la Herse, deep in the forest. This classified natural site features a fountain with Latin inscriptions dedicated to Venus, Mars, and Mercury—the Gauls believed it had healing powers.
In autumn, the Bellême forest hosts the International Mycology Festival: guided mushroom forays, lectures, and exhibitions celebrating the 1,100 fungal species recorded here.
Visit the nearby village of La Perrière, designated a Petite Cité de Caractère. Its cut-stone houses and bocage views are well worth the detour.

days_plan.itin_title: Orne Road Trip: Norman Bocage and Stud Farms

places.name: Belley

visits.text: Belley was the historic capital of Bugey before giving birth to Brillat-Savarin, father of French gastronomy. Ancient alleyways preserve the charm of an episcopal city.
Saint-Jean-Baptiste Cathedral displays its 19th-century neo-Gothic style. The richly frescoed interior houses an 18th-century Virgin statue miraculously spared by the Revolution.
The 18th-century Episcopal Palace lines up its imposing classical facade on Rue des Cordeliers. French-style gardens extend this architecture of power.
The 16th-century Bailliage Hotel now houses the Tourist Office. Push the door to admire its stone staircases and coffered ceilings.
The Hotel of the Dukes of Savoy displays its octagonal stone tower, witness to Bugey's belonging to the duchy before joining France in 1601.
The Old Gate on Rue Sainte-Marie is not a former town entrance but an elevated passage built to allow monks to reach their garden without crossing the public road.
The Lavours Marsh House Museum presents the flora and fauna of this nature reserve where reconstituted aurochs graze.

activities.text: Follow the heritage circuit from the tourist office to discover mansions with arcades and exterior staircases characteristic of the area.
Taste Tome de Belley, a local raw-milk cheese that pairs wonderfully with Bugey wines.
The Lavours Marsh nature reserve can be explored on foot along boardwalk trails. Reconstituted aurochs graze in the wetland meadows.
Continue to the Glandieu waterfall to admire this cascade. Allow for a round trip during the day from Belley.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour Ain & Savoie Mont-Blanc: Lakes, Mountains and Heritage

map_keywords: Hotel of Dukes of Savoy Belley

visits.text: Belvédère, perched at 838 m, guards the entrance to the Gordolasque valley, a wild tributary of the Vésubie. The tall Piedmontese Alpine-style houses, with covered passages and old porches, give the village a true mountain identity.

The 17th-century Saint-Pierre-et-Saint-Paul church is flanked by a square tuff stone bell tower. Inside, the 17th-century gilded wood high altar, listed in 1925, and a painted wood pulpit are worth the stop. Visits by request at the tourist office.
The Milk Museum occupies the former dairy cooperative from 1911, itself installed in an old grain mill. You can see old-time utensils and understand why transhumance shaped the village economy.
Four rural chapels survive around the village—Saint-Antoine, Saint-Blaise, Le Planet, and Saint-Grat higher up in the Gordolasque. Saint-Roch only opens on Wednesday afternoons.

activities.text: From Belvédère, the road climbs past the Countet bridge, the classic starting point for the Nice refuge. The full climb to the refuge takes 4h one way, so 8h round trip, and 900 m elevation gain.
The Gordolasque waterfalls trail, more accessible, follows the river past several cascades. Budget 1h30—flat to moderate.
Ibex spotting, reintroduced to the Mercantour, works well early morning or late afternoon toward the Countet bridge and the slopes above. Binoculars useful.
For food, local mountain tomme and potato fritters can be found at village producers. Don't confuse this with the Madone de Fenestre, which is in Saint-Martin-Vésubie, not here.

days_plan.itin_title: Secret valleys of the Nice hinterland in 6 days

activities.text: Climb to the Belvédère des Roches in Crançot to take in the entire blind valley of Baume-les-Messieurs and its tufa waterfall at a glance. Morning is best: the waterfall has a greater flow and the site is less crowded.

days_plan.itin_title: Burgundy-Franche-Comté: The Most Beautiful Villages in 7 days

visits.text: Saint-Cado island, a tiny jewel set on the Étel ria, is reached by a nine-arch stone bridge. According to legend, the Welsh monk Cado had this bridge built by the devil in one night - then tricked him by giving a cat instead of the promised soul.
Saint-Cado's Romanesque chapel, from the 11th century, is one of the oldest in Brittany. Its rough granite walls, calvary, and small seaside cemetery create a scene of deeply moving simplicity.
Behind the chapel, a stone bed placed on the foreshore is said to be 'saint Cado's bed.' Tradition holds that the deaf come to place their ear there to regain hearing.
The Étel ria forms a 9 km inlet, with alternating mudflats, islets, and oyster beds. The Étel bar at the mouth is one of Brittany's most dangerous maritime passages—currents reach 8 knots.
Small fishermen's houses with blue or green shutters line the island's quay. At low tide, boat hulls and flat-bottomed boats rest on the mud, creating a timeless landscape.

activities.text: Walk around Saint-Cado island - it takes less than 30 minutes. The path passes the blue-hulled house, one of Brittany's most photographed, sitting alone on its rock facing the ria.
Follow the Étel ria on the coastal path southward. The trail crosses old salt marshes and oyster beds before reaching the Nestadio peninsula dunes.
Embark on a boat tour of the Étel ria. Narrow channels between islets, gray herons, and little egrets create a Breton mangrove landscape.

days_plan.itin_title: Brittany Road Trip: Villages with Character, Sea and History

visits.text: Bergerac's old town has been a protected historic sector since the 1970s. Cobbled streets wind past half-timbered houses from the 15th through 17th centuries and elegant stone townhouses built by prosperous wine merchants. Two statues of Cyrano—the fictional poet-swordsman—grace Place Pélissière and Place de la Myrpe, though the real Cyrano de Bergerac never set foot here.

The Tobacco Museum, housed in the 17th-century Maison Peyrarède, traces 3,000 years of tobacco's global journey. The collection—unique in Europe—includes Native American artifacts, pipes from every era, and the history of tobacco cultivation in Périgord. To be clear: the museum documents tobacco's cultural history; it doesn't promote smoking.

The Récollets Cloister, a 17th-century architectural gem built by Franciscan monks, now houses the Bergerac Wine House. The tasting room offers 140 wines from the region's 13 appellations: Bergerac, Monbazillac, Pécharmant, Montravel, and more. Tastings are available on-site—an excellent introduction to these underappreciated wines.

activities.text: Quai Cyrano gathers the tourist office, the Wine House, and a museum space dedicated to the character of Cyrano de Bergerac. Historical footnote: the real Savinien de Cyrano never visited Bergerac. His ancestors owned a small estate called 'Bergerac' in the Yvelines, near Paris. The town adopted the fictional hero anyway—and who can blame them?

The Bergerac wine route winds through the surrounding countryside to Monbazillac Castle, a 16th-century fortress encircled by vineyards. Monbazillac sweet wine, made from grapes affected by noble rot, is a luscious golden nectar traditionally paired with foie gras. Cellar visits and tastings reveal why these wines deserve wider recognition.

days_plan.itin_title: Dordogne: Prehistoric Caves, Medieval Fortresses & Périgord Delights

places.name: Bergheim

visits.text: Bergheim is protected by a double circuit of medieval defensive walls erected from 1311, among the best preserved in Alsace. Its walls extend over more than 2 kilometers and include nine towers still visible today. The Porte Haute or Obertor, erected in the 14th century and remodeled in the 16th, is the only one of the three old gates to survive. From the walkway on the north side—the most spectacular flank, with its five flanking towers and outer moat—the view looks down over Gewurztraminer vineyards and toward the Vosges peaks. Bergheim was voted Village Préféré des Français in 2022, after Eguisheim (2013) and Kaysersberg (2017)—a longstanding Alsatian presence in these awards.

The House of Witches, housed in a building from 1550, traces with historical rigor the 40 witchcraft trials that took place in Bergheim between 1582 and 1683. Forty women were condemned to the stake, including 22 in the space of five months for the year 1630 alone. The last trial occurred in 1683, one year after Louis XIV issued an ordinance decriminalizing witchcraft. The museum relies exclusively on preserved historical archives and raises the question of intolerance without any folklore. Open late June to October.

Don't leave Bergheim without finding the Tanzlinde—a linden tree planted in 1313, designated an Arbre Remarquable since 2017, whose trunk exceeds 1.80 meters in diameter. Popular festivals took place beneath its branches as early as the 14th century. The neo-Romanesque synagogue from 1863, rebuilt at the exact location of a 14th-century medieval synagogue, can also be visited: it's the only synagogue in Alsace never to have left its original site.

activities.text: Walk the complete circuit of the ramparts along the walkway—about 2 to 3 km of pleasant walking offering panoramas over the vineyards and the Vosges. The 4 km hike along the Altenberg and Kanzlerberg Grands Crus trail, just outside the town, features information panels about the terroir. A tasting at a local winemaker's is a must—Bergheim's Gewurztraminer is among the finest on the Wine Route.

days_plan.itin_title: The 15 Most Beautiful Villages of Alsace
Grand Est Road Trip: Vineyards, Ramparts and Forests
The Most Beautiful Villages of Alsace in 4 Days

map_keywords: Remparts Bergheim XIVe siècle Porte Haute

visits.text: Bergues' belfry, a UNESCO World Heritage site, has stood at the heart of this Flemish town since the 13th century. Rebuilt after its 1944 destruction, it houses a 50-bell carillon whose melodies punctuate residents' lives. From the top, after 206 steps, the panorama sweeps across the entire Flemish plain.

The Mont-de-Piété Museum occupies a jewel of Flemish baroque art, built between 1629 and 1633 by Wenceslas Cobergher. Its two richly decorated gables house a collection of 16th- to 18th-century Flemish paintings, including the masterly Hurdy-Gurdy Player with a Dog by Georges de La Tour – the largest surviving painting by this artist.

Over 2,000 sheets make up the museum's collection of drawings, the region's second collection after Lille. Works by Van Dyck, Poussin and Le Brun come largely from the 1877 donation of Verlinde, a painter and restorer born in Bergues.

The remains of Saint-Winoc Abbey, founded in 1022 by the counts of Flanders, dominate the town from their hill. Only the square tower and pointed tower survive, but these two silhouettes, spared as navigation landmarks, remain the city's guardians.

Bergues preserves nearly all its ramparts – over five kilometres of walls blending medieval fortifications and Vauban bastions. The gates, towers – including the Couleuvrinier tower – and canal-bordered moats trace a remarkably well-preserved defensive perimeter.

Bergues' yellow brick houses line rue Faidherbe and rue Carnot. These façades characteristic of maritime Flanders, with stepped gables and mullioned windows, give the town its "little Bruges of the North" appearance.

activities.text: Follow the ramparts circuit on foot from wooded bastions to moats where grey herons and little egrets nest. Casemates and underground passages shelter hibernating bats – Bergues is home to half of the Nord's amphibian species.
Stroll along the canal de Bergues. It links the town to Veurne and once made it possible to flood the marshy plain through a system of locks in the event of a siege.

Bergues sausage and cheese are the town's two emblematic specialities. The sausage, made of pure pork and Spanish spices, dates from the 16th century, when the town was under the rule of the Spanish Netherlands. Sample both in an estaminet on the market square.

Every mid-Lent Sunday, Bergues carnival sees thousands of revellers parade through the streets to the sound of the “marching band”. The Drum Major sets the procession in motion, cheese is thrown from the town hall balcony – a lively and joyfully unbridled Flemish tradition.

days_plan.itin_title: Nord Tour: Lille, Belfries and Flemish Culture
Opal Coast Villages and Flemish Heartlands
The Most Beautiful Villages from Flanders to the Bay of Somme

places.name: Bernay

visits.text: Notre-Dame Abbey Church of Bernay. Normandy's oldest Romanesque church still standing, it was built between 1013 and 1050 at the initiative of Judith of Brittany, William the Conqueror's grandmother, under the direction of builder monk Guillaume de Volpiano. Its three levels, exceptional for the era, and sculpted capitals (human masks, leafy heads, monsters) bear witness to the blossoming of Norman Romanesque art.

Bernay, City of Art and History. Eure's only town bearing this label, Bernay has preserved its historic center with 15th and 16th-century half-timbered houses. The 'Water, Stone, and Wood' trail guides visitors through winding alleys, old doorways, and manor houses via 62 pictograms scattered throughout the town.

Notre-Dame de la Couture Basilica. Becoming a pilgrimage site after the miraculous discovery of a Virgin statue, this Gothic church begun in 1340 houses funeral slabs and apostle statues from Le Bec-Hellouin Abbey, including a remarkable 15th-century Entombment.

Bernay Museum of Fine Arts. Housed in the former abbatial lodging, this museum presents collections ranging from archaeology to decorative arts. Contemporary art temporary exhibitions in the abbey's exceptional setting.
Cordeliers Convent. Two hundred meters from the abbey church, this 13th-century Franciscan convent preserves some cloister remnants in a private courtyard accessible from Rue de la Comédie.

activities.text: Walk along the Charentonne. This river flows through Bernay and gives the town its particular charm. Developed riverbanks invite strolling between stone bridges and old mills.

Bernay Market. Every Saturday from 8am to 1pm, the market animates Rue Thiers and Place Sainte-Croix. Norman regional products, cider, Camembert, and teurgoule (oven-baked rice dessert) delight food lovers.

days_plan.itin_title: Eure Road Trip: From Giverny to Normandy's Most Beautiful Villages

map_keywords: Basilica of Notre-Dame de la Couture Bernay

places.name: Besancon

visits.text: Start with the Doubs riverbanks and the loop around the historic center. Besançon nestles within a meander of the Doubs so perfectly circular that Julius Caesar himself described it in The Gallic War: “the Doubs almost entirely surrounds the town in a circle that looks as though drawn with a compass.” The Grande-Rue, the Roman Porte Noire gate, and the drapers' mansions trace several centuries of history. Allow 1.5 hours to stroll to the Battant bridge and return along the quays.

The Museum of Fine Arts and Archaeology, 1 place de la Révolution, is the oldest public museum in France—its collection was established in 1694, nearly a century before the Louvre. Its 5,500 drawings (Dürer, Rembrandt, Rubens, Courbet) make it one of the country's finest print rooms. Don't miss the paintings by Courbet, a native of the region, including the imposing The Stag at Bay. The museum is closed Mondays.

Just steps away, the Museum of Time occupies the Granvelle Palace, a jewel of the French Renaissance built in the 16th century by Nicolas Perrenot de Granvelle, Charles V's chief adviser. Since 2002, it has housed Besançon's watchmaking collections, including the celebrated Leroy 01 watch, long considered the most complicated in the world. Don't miss the Foucault pendulum over 13 meters long that swings in the palace tower.

Step through the door at 140 Grande-Rue: this is where Victor Hugo was born on February 26, 1802. The Victor Hugo House, opened in 2013, doesn't resemble an ordinary museum—it's a multimedia exhibition centered on the socially committed writer's campaigns against the death penalty and for the rights of peoples and freedom of expression. A short visit (45 min), but packed with content.

The Citadel of Besançon is the most visited monument in Franche-Comté, with 250,000 to 300,000 visitors per year. Completed in 1684, Vauban's masterwork for Louis XIV, it extends over 11 hectares on Mount Saint-Étienne more than 100 meters above the Doubs. The first stone was laid on September 29, 1668, when Besançon still belonged to the Spanish crown—Vauban transformed it into a royal fortress after the Treaty of Nijmegen in 1678. UNESCO-listed since 2008 along with eleven other Vauban sites, it houses three museums with the Musées de France label. Allow at least half a day.

Don't miss the Museum of the Resistance and Deportation within the Citadel, completely redesigned in 2023. The Citadel served as an execution site for Resistance fighters during the German Occupation between 1941 and 1944. The museum pays tribute to their memory with primary-source archival materials and objects.

activities.text: Operators offer boat trips on the Doubs from the river port. It's the best way to grasp the city's unique geography, enclosed within its river loop with the citadel dominating everything. Allow 1 hour on average.

From the Citadel's rampart walks, the 360° panoramas over the six wooded hills around Besançon are spectacular. To extend the experience, the Chaudanne and Brégille forts, accessible on foot or by car from the city, offer viewpoints over the Doubs loop and the old town rooftops.

Doubs Road Trip: Nature and Heritage of Franche-Comté
Doubs Road Trip: Nature and Heritage of Franche-Comté

Musée du Temps palais Granvelle Besançon

Musée de la Résistance et de la Déportation Besançon

visits.text: The medieval town of Besse-et-Saint-Anastaise stands at an altitude of 1,000 meters on an ancient lava flow and holds the Petite Cité de Caractère label. Its cobbled lanes wind among volcanic stone houses dating from the 12th–16th centuries, the belfry, remnants of ramparts, and the Château du Bailli. Saint-André church, half Romanesque and half Gothic, contains historiated capitals and a remarkable dome. The town was a Medici fief, and the Maison de la Reine Margot now houses a ski museum.

Lac Pavin, metropolitan France's youngest crater lake, occupies a 6,900-year-old maar created by an explosion when molten lava met groundwater. Its nearly perfect circular shape, 800-meter diameter, and 92-meter depth make it a major geological site. The dark waters turn turquoise blue in summer, and local legend tells of a submerged city said to lie in its depths. A 2.7 km trail circles the lake through a centuries-old beech forest.

Super-Besse, seven kilometers from the village, is the municipality's sports and leisure resort. In summer, the water sports center, swimming pool, summer luge, and downhill mountain biking bring the resort to life. The Besse-Pertuyzat Nordic area has a total of 75 km of cross-country ski trails and four snowshoeing routes in winter.

activities.text: Circle Lac Pavin on the 2.7 km marked trail that threads beneath century-old beeches. The walk, accessible to all, offers changing perspectives on the crater's dark waters and the basalt columns that ring it. Swimming is forbidden, but boat fishing is permitted under conditions: trout, perch, and Arctic char populate the lake.

Climb the basalt columns at Lac Pavin. Twenty-four equipped climbing routes traverse a 25-meter cliff made of basalt columns. The site attracts beginner and experienced climbers in an exceptional natural setting.

Taste farmhouse Saint-Nectaire at farms around Besse. The municipality holds the Site remarquable du goût label for this PDO cheese, whose production from raw cow's milk continues on farms in the Sancy summer pastures. The Monday market offers an opportunity to meet local producers.

Visit the summer exhibition at Lac Pavin on fish, microorganisms, and scientific advances. Research conducted on this meromictic lake—whose deep waters never mix with surface waters—makes it a natural laboratory for scientists worldwide.

days_plan.itin_title: Volcanoes and Auvergne traditions

visits.text: Lake Bethmale, at 1,074 metres, reveals crystalline emerald waters cradled in dense greenery. This small lake, tucked into the Ariège Pyrenees Regional Nature Park, is ringed by deciduous woodland that turns the landscape copper in autumn. A shaded footpath loops right around it in 45 minutes. Wooden walkways and viewpoints punctuate the route, opening onto the finest angles over those emerald reflections. Legend tells of a witch hunted down by the villagers who threw herself into the lake: her emerald-green dress, left on the bottom, is said to have given the water its colour ever since.

Saint-Girons, capital of the Couserans at the meeting of the Lez and the Salat, stretches along landscaped riverbanks. The 16th-century Pont Vieux, with pavements of local marble, spans the river and offers a picturesque view of the traditional houses. The Champ de Mars, lined with 72 century-old plane trees, hosts every Saturday morning one of the largest markets in the region. Wander the lanes of the historic centre, where the Saint-Girons, Villefranche and Lédar districts meet, witnesses to a rich papermaking industrial past. Allow about 25 km from the overnight town, roughly 35 minutes by road.

activities.text: The forest walk around Lake Bethmale meanders through centuries-old beeches and firs in peaceful tranquility. The trail accessible to all, even stroller-friendly thanks to wooden boardwalks, follows the lake's three basins clockwise. Spread your picnic facing the emerald waters, pause on panoramic benches to contemplate reflections changing throughout the day. Swimming and water sports are prohibited to protect the fragile ecosystem, but the setting invites contemplative relaxation and observation of rainbow trout, brown trout, and brook char.

days_plan.itin_title: Ariège Circuit: Cathar Castles, Prehistoric Caves & Mountain Lakes

visits.text: The belfry of Béthune is one of the oldest stone sentinels in the region. A first wooden belfry was built in 1346 — it was during the Hundred Years' War, and the burghers had just gained the right to build a gaol for thieves. Destroyed by fire, it was rebuilt in sandstone in 1388 under the authority of Marquis William I of Namur. Raised higher in 1437 (133 steps for a 33-metre tower, plus a 17-metre bell turret), enriched with a carillon by the aldermen in 1546, then again by Charles V with bells from Thérouanne in 1553 — its history reads layer upon layer. Listed by UNESCO in 2005, it now stands alone at the centre of the Grand-Place since the Cloth Hall burned down in 1664.

Béthune's Grand-Place lines up its Flemish façades, rebuilt after 1918, all listed as historic monuments. Its atmosphere is more intimate than in Arras — it's a living market square, not a museum. Note the golden dragon crowning the belfry's bell turret since 1503: a weathervane converted in the 17th century that still indicates the wind direction.

Saint-Vaast church, rebuilt from 1924 to 1927 to plans by architect Louis-Marie Cordonnier, blends neo-Gothic and Art Deco. Its 68-metre tower dominates the town. Inside, the stained-glass windows illustrate the story of Saint Vaast, apostle of Artois in the 6th century. Some stones from its former façade, destroyed in 1918, were reused to rebuild the belfry — so the two monuments share the same stones.

Wander through the lanes of the historic centre and spot the remains of the medieval ramparts that once encircled the town. Béthune controlled one of the strategic routes between Flanders and Artois, and its fortifications were fought over for centuries. Philosopher Jean Buridan, born here in 1292, is said to have got the idea for his famous indecisive donkey while watching horses pass beneath the belfry.

activities.text: Stroll through the 5-hectare public garden at the heart of the town. It's the most pleasant green space in Béthune for a break between visits — sports grounds, children's play areas and benches beneath the trees.

Explore the lanes of the historic centre, rebuilt in the regionalist and Art Deco styles after the First World War. Brick façades, local shops and estaminets — this is authentic Béthune, the one passing tourists never see.
End the day in a local estaminet to sample the region's craft beers — the brewing tradition is as strong in the Béthune area as elsewhere in Flanders.

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip Pas-De-Calais: The Opal Coast and Belfries

visits.text: Beuvron-en-Auge is tiny. Its central square, bordered by 17th- and 18th-century half-timbered houses with polychrome facades, is one of the most photographed in Normandy.
The old manor, at the back of the square, raises its richly carved half-timbered facade. Local produce shops and artisans occupy the former outbuildings.
The village is a stop on the Pays d'Auge Cider Route. High-stem apple orchards surround the town, providing the raw material for cider, calvados, and pommeau.

In Saint-Pierre-sur-Dives, the medieval timber-framed market hall, rebuilt identically after the fire of 1944, covers 1,500 sq m. The weekly Monday market has been held there since the Middle Ages. About 17 km from the stage town, 17 minutes by road.

The abbey church of Saint-Pierre-sur-Dives, founded in the 11th century, blends Romanesque and Gothic. Its medieval floor of polychrome terracotta tiles is unique in Normandy. About 17 km from the stage town, 17 minutes by road.

The corbelled houses of the town of Saint-Pierre have kept facades from the 15th and 16th centuries. The capitals of the abbey church deserve a close look. About 22 km from the stage town, 25 minutes by road.

activities.text: Tasting at cider and calvados producers in the Pays d'Auge. The Cider Route links about twenty farms between orchards and manor houses.
Walk or cycle between apple orchards and bocage hedgerows of the Pays d'Auge. In April-May, apple blossoms offer a white and pink spectacle.
Saint-Pierre-sur-Dives market on Monday morning under the hall: cheeses (livarot, pont-l'évêque, camembert), farm poultry and bottled cider. About 17 km from the stage town, 17 minutes by road.

days_plan.itin_title: The 20 Most Beautiful Villages in Normandy
Cotentin, Pays d'Auge: 5 days exploring the most beautiful villages

visits.text: Beynac Castle crowns a 150-meter cliff in one of the most commanding positions in medieval France. Built in the 12th century, it served as a French stronghold during the Hundred Years' War, facing off against the English-held fortress of Castelnaud across the Dordogne River. The river itself marked the border between rival kingdoms—an uneasy frontier for generations.

The States Hall of Périgord, where the nobility of the four great baronies (Beynac, Biron, Bourdeilles, Mareuil) once gathered, preserves a Renaissance fireplace and 15th-century frescoes. Walk the castle's wall walk for sweeping views across the 'valley of five castles'—a landscape defined by medieval power struggles.

The village of Beynac-et-Cazenac, classified among France's Most Beautiful Villages, cascades down the cliff in steep, narrow alleys called 'barry.' The ochre stone houses with slate roofs epitomize Périgord Noir architecture. Filmmakers love Beynac—it's appeared in Les Visiteurs, Jeanne d'Arc, and Ridley Scott's The Last Duel (2021).

activities.text: Castelnaud Castle, Beynac's historic rival, now houses the Museum of Medieval Warfare. The collections include weapons, armor, and full-scale reconstructions of siege engines: trebuchets, mangonels, and battering rams. In summer, costumed demonstrators fire the weapons and explain medieval siege tactics.

Hot air balloon flights at sunrise or sunset drift silently over the valley of five castles. Departures launch from Beynac, weather permitting. The aerial perspective reveals the strategic logic of these cliff-top fortresses. Booking several days in advance is essential.

days_plan.itin_title: Dordogne: Prehistoric Caves, Medieval Fortresses & Périgord Delights
Nouvelle-Aquitaine Loop: Villages, Vineyards & Dordogne
The Most Beautiful Villages of Lot and Périgord in 6 Days

visits.text: The Bèze rises right in the village center at a spectacular resurgent spring—water emerges from an underground network stretching several kilometers. It's one of the most beautiful springs in Burgundy. Stop by the pool: the water is a translucent blue-green, surrounded by lush vegetation.

Descend into the Grottes de Bèze, accessible by boat on an underground river. The navigable passage extends beneath the village—the experience is unique in Burgundy. Check opening hours; the caves are only accessible in season (April to October).

Stroll through the village: vestiges of the Abbey of Saint-Pierre founded in the 7th century (one of the oldest in Burgundy), washhouses, alleyways lined with gardens, and limestone houses. Bèze has an understated charm—it's the quietest stop along the route.

activities.text: Follow the Bèze river on foot downstream from the village, between wet meadows and pastures. The path runs alongside the water for 3 km—a bucolic atmosphere is guaranteed, with occasional gray herons fishing in the shallows.

If you're traveling by car, make a detour through the vineyards of Marsannay or Fixin, at the gateway to the Côte de Nuits, 30 minutes south. A tasting at a winemaker's is a good way to prepare for the next part of the journey toward the Route des Grands Crus.

days_plan.itin_title: Burgundy's 15 Most Beautiful Villages

visits.text: The Allées Paul Riquet form the grand plane-tree-shaded promenade at Béziers's heart. They bear the name of Pierre-Paul Riquet, designer of the Canal du Midi and Béziers native. The central median is bordered by cafés and restaurants with lively terraces. It's locals' favorite promenade and the city's meeting point. Markets regularly set up here. The southern atmosphere and 19th-century architecture bordering the avenue are pleasant.

The Fonséranes Locks are a 17th-century engineering masterpiece on the UNESCO-listed Canal du Midi. This water staircase of 8 oval locks overcomes a 21-meter elevation change. Built between 1676 and 1680, it still functions today. You can walk along the canal, watch barges pass through, and understand the ingenious system imagined by Riquet. A museum and educational trail explain the canal's history. It's a remarkable, highly photogenic site. Sunset here is magnificent.

Saint-Nazaire Cathedral dominates Béziers from its promontory. This 13th-century Gothic fortress replaced the old church destroyed during the 1209 sack of Béziers. The architecture is austere with massive towers and crenellations. The southern Gothic interior is sober yet luminous. The adjoining cloister offers a haven of peace. From the esplanade, you enjoy exceptional panoramas over the wine plain, the Orb River, and the Pyrenees on clear days. It's Béziers's finest viewpoint.

The Pont-Vieux has spanned the Orb since the 12th century. With its 12 arches, it linked the medieval town to the suburb and was fortified. Now pedestrian, it offers fine views of the Orb, the cathedral on its rock and the historic district. It is a pleasant place for a stroll, especially at the end of the day. The banks of the Orb below have been laid out for walking. The bridge is a listed Historic Monument and bears witness to the medieval past of Béziers.

activities.text: Boat cruise on the Canal du Midi. Several companies offer cruises departing from Béziers to discover the canal and its environment. You navigate at a slow pace, passing through locks and engineering works. Passage through the Fonséranes Locks from the boat is impressive. Commentary recounts the canal's history and construction. The plane-tree-shaded banks and wine landscape glide peacefully by. Duration varies from 1 hour to half a day.

Wine tasting in Béziers cellars and surroundings. The Béziers region is at the heart of Languedoc vineyards with several appellations: Languedoc, Faugères, Saint-Chinian. Cooperative cellars and wine estates offer tastings and direct sales. You'll discover Mediterranean grape varieties: Syrah, Grenache, Carignan for reds, Viognier and Roussanne for whites. Prices are affordable. Some estates organize guided tours of vineyards and cellars.

Cycle along the Canal du Midi. The landscaped cycle route follows the canal for hundreds of kilometers. From Béziers, you can pedal west toward Carcassonne or east toward Agde and the Mediterranean. The plane-tree-shaded route is flat and easy. You'll pass locks, canal bridges, and barges. Bike rentals available in Béziers. Allow 2-3 hours for a leisurely ride to the locks or toward Villeneuve-lès-Béziers.

days_plan.itin_title: Hérault Road Trip: Montpellier, Beaches and the Hinterland

visits.text: Start at Virgin's Rock, the iconic symbol of Biarritz. This rock, tunneled through by Napoleon III in 1864, is connected to the shore by a 76-meter metal footbridge built in 1887 by the Schryver workshops of Haumont — not by Eiffel, contrary to local legend. The statue of the Virgin Mary, installed in 1865, commemorates according to tradition the miraculous return of Biarritz whalers guided by a light during a storm. Go in late afternoon: the light on the ocean from the rock is spectacular, and in rough seas waves crash just meters below your feet.

The Biarritz Aquarium has occupied an Art Deco building facing Virgin's Rock since 1933. Its aquariums recreate the depths of the Bay of Biscay — sharks, rays, octopuses — with a dedicated seal zone that appeals to children. Plan about 1.5 hours for a complete visit.

Climb the Biarritz Lighthouse for the most complete view of the city. Built from 1830 and in service since 1 February 1834, this cylindrical tower, 47 metres tall, stands 75 metres above sea level on the Pointe Saint-Martin. Its 248 steps lead to a 360° panorama: to the north the Landes beaches, to the south the rocky Basque coast, and on clear days the Pyrenees on the horizon. Its copper dome is adorned with twelve bronze lion heads, each one different.

Stroll along the Grande Plage, set between the Casino Municipal and the Hôtel du Palais — the former imperial residence of Napoleon III and Eugénie, who made Biarritz the fashionable European resort of the Second Empire. The promenade offers a sweeping view over the bay, the lighthouse and the Belle Époque villas stepping down the cliff.

activities.text: The Côte des Basques is the birthplace of surfing in Europe: it was here, in 1957, that Peter Viertel rode the first French wave. The beach is still one of the busiest spots on the continent today. Operators offer beginner lessons for all levels, summer and winter alike. Arrive early in the morning in July and August — the beach fills up fast.

The Cité de l'Océan offers an interactive immersion in the marine world: a surf simulator, 3D animations and the Seaborg, a recent immersive installation. Ideal for families or on rainy days — Biarritz gets a few even in season.

Cross the Port-Vieux at low tide. This small sheltered cove between the cliffs is Biarritz's first harbour, used for centuries. In calm weather it is the town's most protected swimming spot — far quieter than the Grande Plage.

Road Trip Pyrenees-Atlantiques: Basque Country and Bearn

visits.text: The oppidum of Bibracte, capital of the Celtic Aedui tribe, crowns Mont Beuvray at an altitude of 821 meters. Founded around 100 BC, this fortified city covered 135 hectares—a 5.2 km rampart encircled streets, artisan quarters, and aristocratic residences. Here Vercingetorix was proclaimed leader of the Gallic coalition, and Caesar wrote part of The Gallic War.

The Bibracte Museum, designed by architect Pierre-Louis Faloci and opened in 1995, nestles into the beech forest at the site's foot. Animated models, digital reconstructions, and thousands of excavated artifacts bring to life the daily routines of the city's 10,000 inhabitants: blacksmiths, bronze-workers, enamelers, and coin-strikers.

The Porte du Rebout, the oppidum's main gateway, preserves a reconstructed section of the murus gallicus—that nearly indestructible rampart of earth, stone, and interlocking timbers that so fascinated the Romans. Beyond, the remains of the Pâture du Couvent and the Rebout Quarter reveal themselves beneath the forest canopy.

The summit of Mont Beuvray offers a 360-degree panorama over the Morvan, the Pilat massif, and, on clear days, Mont Blanc. The Celtic sacred precinct (nemeton) was discovered beneath the current 19th-century chapel. Century-old beech trees with twisted shapes—the “queules”—have dotted the forest for centuries.

activities.text: Guided tour of the Bibracte archaeological site. Your guide leads you through the forest to active excavation sites, the foundations of Gallic houses, and the reconstructed rampart. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes to 2 hours for the complete circuit.

Hike the GR 13 trail around Mont Beuvray. The footpath follows the first line of fortifications through the beech forest. The atmosphere is entrancing—forest floors carpeted with dead leaves, absolute silence—the exact opposite of the bustle that reigned here 2,000 years ago.

“Gallic” lunch at the Chaudron de Bibracte. Dishes are inspired by recipes reconstructed by archaeologists: bostia, mocco, and beer brewed exclusively for the site. You eat without forks—kids love it.

days_plan.itin_title: Saône-et-Loire Road Trip: Bibracte, Cluny, Solutré & the Mâconnais Vineyards

places.name: Biot

visits.text: The Fernand Léger National Museum is as much an architectural curiosity as an artistic one. Inaugurated in 1960 under the patronage of Picasso, Braque, and Chagall, it was designed around a 400 m² mosaic originally intended for the Hanover stadium (never built). The colored glass tesserae shimmer according to sunlight—the edifice itself is a work of art. The interior traces Léger's entire career, from cubist research to the large colored compositions of the 1950s. Léger had purchased the neighboring land a few months before his death in 1955 to install ceramic sculptures there. Free the first Sunday of the month.

Biot has held the "Villes et Métiers d'Art" label for its glassmaking tradition since 1997. In 1956, Eloi Monod founded the Verrerie de Biot and invented bubble glass, now the village's signature. The Glass Ecomuseum offers glassblowing demonstrations and workshops. The medieval village, with its Place des Arcades and Sainte-Marie-Madeleine Church (15th century, with a remarkable altarpiece of the Virgin of the Rosary), is worth an hour's stroll.

activities.text: Trail along the Brague in the departmental park: 9 km of easy, shaded walking among alders, ash trees, and scrubland, at the bottom of a valley a few kilometers from the sea. One of the few genuinely cool and wild places near the French Riviera coast.

Heritage circuit in the village: medieval gates, shaded squares, jewelers' and ceramicists' galleries create a lively route. Biot has kept a more authentic atmosphere than Saint-Paul-de-Vence because it remains inhabited year-round.

French Riviera Art Museums and Galleries: An 8-Day Journey

visits.text: Seaplane Museum: 1,250m² tracing the saga of transatlantic seaplanes at the former Latécoère base. From 1930 onward, engineer Pierre-Georges Latécoère chose the lake for his routes to America and the West Indies. Mermoz, Saint-Exupéry and Guillaumet took off from these waters. Collection of restored seaplanes, period uniforms, models, engines and giant propellers. Interactive experiences and documentary films.

Lac de Cazaux-Sanguinet: 5,600 hectares. Clear waters with turquoise reflections nicknamed Biscaraïbes. Fine sandy beaches (Maguide, Navarrosse, Caton) lined with pine trees. A gently sloping sandy bottom ideal for families. Unobstructed views of the Dune du Pilat to the north in clear weather.

Petit étang de Biscarrosse: Unspoiled fishing reserve in the forest's heart. Wild banks and absolute calm. Hiking trails allowing a complete loop. Wildlife observation: ducks, moorhens, herons. Access from the D652, designated parking area.

activities.text: Seaplane discovery flight: Takeoff and water landing on the lake from the Latécoère seaplane base. A 20-minute flight over lakes, forest and ocean. Unique sensation of flying just above the water. Experienced pilots and maintained aircraft. Booking required, weather permitting.

Water activities on the lakes: Sailing, windsurfing, paddleboarding, water skiing. Several water sports centers around Lake Cazaux. Hourly or half-day rentals. Sailing lessons for children and adults in July-August. Designated zones for each activity. Mandatory life jackets provided.

Aquapark on the lake: Giant floating inflatable structures (slides, trampolines, obstacle courses). Suitable for swimmers aged 6 and up. One-hour sessions that can be extended. Life jackets provided and mandatory. Supervisors on site. Open June to September depending on the weather.

Bike paths: 145km of greenways connecting Biscarrosse to neighboring towns and the Vélodyssée. Flat and shaded routes through the forest. Lake-beach-town loops. Standard and electric bike rental downtown and near beaches. Picnic areas along the routes.

days_plan.itin_title: Landes Road Trip: Ocean, Pine Forest and Landes Traditions

visits.text: Bitche Citadel crowns a pink sandstone spur at an altitude of 300 m. This military masterpiece was built to plans by Vauban between 1679 and 1697, then rebuilt by Cormontaigne between 1741 and 1754. Its 500 m of underground galleries carved into the rock contain an immersive 50-minute audiovisual tour recounting the heroic siege of 1870-1871, when 2,400 French soldiers under Commander Teyssier resisted 20,000 Prussians for 230 days, a French record ahead of Belfort’s 104 days. The 1794 relief model, listed as a historic monument, reproduces the fortress in minute detail at a scale of 1:600 across 42 m².

The rampart walk runs for 980 m around the pink sandstone fortifications, offering unrivalled views over the town of Bitche, 300 m below, and the forests of the Vosges Regional Nature Park stretching up to 15 km into the distance. Twelve information panels describe the evolution of military architecture from Vauban to the Maginot Line. Viewing points on the Saint-Sébastien, Bourbon and Sainte-Catherine bastions punctuate this free route, which is accessible to everyone.

activities.text: The Altschlossfelsen raises its 30-metre red sandstone cliffs on the Franco-German border, about 14 km from the stage town, 20 minutes by road, a popular climbing site with 80 routes and a natural viewpoint over the forests of the Palatinate. The waymarked paths of the Vosges club wind between erratic blocks with fantastic shapes carved by wind erosion over 250 million years. Ruins of the thirteenth-century medieval castle perch at the summit at 389 m.

The Pays de Bitche invites visitors to hike through the forests of the Northern Vosges Regional Nature Park, a UNESCO biosphere reserve since 1988 covering 130,000 hectares. Ponds created by Cistercian monks in the 12th century, ancient peat bogs harbouring carnivorous sundews and stands of century-old beech trees reaching 40 m form unspoilt landscapes where roe deer, wild boar and lynx roam freely. The area has 1,500 km of marked trails, including the GR53.

days_plan.itin_title: 4-Day Moselle Tour: Metz, Bitche Citadel and Chagall’s Stained Glass

visits.text: Blaye Citadel is a military fortress designed by Vauban between 1685 and 1689. With 38 hectares of fortifications, 1.5 km of ramparts, and four bastions, it's an impressive defensive complex. UNESCO-listed along with Fort Pâté and Fort Médoc, it forms the Verrou de l'estuaire, which was intended to protect Bordeaux from maritime invasions. The citadel now houses shops, restaurants, and accommodations. Free entry; guided tours of the underground passages carry a fee.

The citadel ramparts offer spectacular panoramas over the Gironde estuary, Europe's largest. On clear days, you can see Fort Pâté on its islet and Fort Médoc on the opposite bank. The rampart walk circles the entire citadel. Several viewpoints and panoramic information boards help you get your bearings. Sunset from the ramparts is particularly beautiful with reflections on the estuary.

The Château des Rudel, inside the citadel, is a medieval remnant dating from the 12th century. It was the fortified castle overlooking Blaye before Vauban incorporated its ruins into the new fortifications. The famous troubadour Jaufré Rudel is said to have been born here. Some of the towers and curtain walls survive. Panoramic views from the remains of the towers.

The Couvent des Minimes, built under Henry IV in the early 17th century, served as a place of worship for the garrisons. Integrated into the citadel by Vauban, it retains its original architecture, including the cloister and monastic buildings. It is now a vacation center and event venue. The chapel can be visited and hosts temporary exhibitions. The cloister is a peaceful haven with its central garden.

Blaye Citadel's underground passages form a network of defensive galleries carved into limestone rock. The guided tour (about 45 minutes) reveals this ingenious system designed by Vauban. You'll explore the galleries and vaulted rooms and learn about the defense strategy. The temperature stays at 14°C year-round; bring warm clothing. Reservations recommended through the tourist office.

activities.text: The Route de la Corniche fleurie connects Blaye to Bourg-sur-Gironde over 10 kilometers. This small road winds between limestone cliffs, dry-stone walls and the estuary. The scenery is magnificent, with views of the carrelets (fishing huts on stilts), the silvery waters of the Gironde and the vineyards. There are numerous places to stop and take photographs. The road is narrow; drive slowly.

Wine tasting in Blaye. The Blaye Côtes de Bordeaux appellation mainly produces powerful red wines and dry whites. Several wine cellars and châteaux in the region offer tastings. The Maison du Vin de Blaye presents a selection from the appellation and organizes guided tastings. The Printemps des Vins de Blaye in April brings together more than 300 winegrowers in the citadel.

Cruise on the Gironde estuary. Boat excursions depart from Blaye to discover the Verrou Vauban: you'll pass Fort Pâté on its islet and Fort Médoc on the Médoc bank. Cruises with commentary explain the history of the defensive system and navigation on the estuary. Some outings include a stop at Fort Médoc. Duration 2 to 3 hours. Departures vary by season and tides.

Blaye market. The market takes place on Wednesday and Saturday mornings in the lower town, at the foot of the citadel. You will find local products: fruit and vegetables, cheeses, honey, wines, oysters from the estuary and fish. The atmosphere is friendly and authentic. It is a good opportunity to talk with producers and discover the region's specialties. The Saturday market is the largest.

Horse-drawn carriage or small train ride through the citadel. These guided tours reveal the citadel's history and monuments in a fun way. The small tourist train circles the ramparts with audio commentary. Carriages offer rides in and around the citadel. It's a pleasant option for families with children or people with walking difficulties. Regular departures in season.

days_plan.itin_title: Gironde Circuit: Bordeaux, Vineyards & Arcachon Bay

visits.text: Direct TER from Paris Austerlitz to Blois-Chambord, 1h25 to 1h40, €16–35 depending on how far ahead you book (OUIGO Train Classique from €16, full-fare TER/Intercités around €34). Trains every 1–2 hours. Blois town centre is a 10-minute walk from the station. Drop your bags near the Place Louis XII — you'll be right in the thick of things. Head straight for the royal château that towers over the town.

The Royal Château of Blois is a rare thing: four châteaux in one, built around a single courtyard across different eras. Start with the Louis XII wing (1498–1501) in red brick and stone, flamboyant Gothic with Italian touches. Inside, the Fine Arts Museum displays works by Rubens, Ingres, and Boucher. €15, allow 2 hours.

The François I wing (1515–1524) is the showpiece. Its monumental open spiral staircase, placed on the façade like a stage set, is a pure Renaissance invention. Look for crowned salamanders everywhere — the emblem of François I. It was at Blois that he launched his great architectural ambitions before Chambord.

The Salle des États Généraux — the oldest part of the château, 13th century. A vast Gothic civic hall measuring 30 × 18 metres, one of the largest surviving in France. The Estates General met here in 1576 and 1588. On 23 December 1588, Henri III had the Duke of Guise assassinated in this very room for threatening his throne.

Across the square, the Maison de la Magie Robert-Houdin. Every half hour, six giant mechanical dragons emerge from the windows and breathe steam. Jean-Eugène Robert-Houdin (1805–1871), a native of Blois, is considered the father of modern magic — Houdini took his stage name as a tribute. €12.

Walk down towards the Loire. The Saint-Louis Cathedral, rebuilt after a hurricane in 1678, preserves a 10th-century Carolingian crypt. Behind it, the Jardins de l'Évêché — a formal terraced garden with a sweeping view over the town and the river. The Denis-Papin staircase, 120 steps, leads down to the square and its statue.

Rémi bus (line 2) from Blois-Chambord station to Chambord in about 35 minutes, €2 per journey (Rémi fare). Arrive at opening time, 9am. Chambord reveals itself along a 4.5 km approach: a cascade of turrets, chimneys, and pinnacles. 426 rooms, 77 staircases, 282 fireplaces. UNESCO World Heritage Site. €16.

François I began Chambord in 1519. The largest Loire château was originally a hunting lodge — he spent only 72 nights here in his entire life. The central double-helix staircase is attributed to Leonardo da Vinci, who died just a few months before construction began. Two interlocking spirals: two people can go up and down simultaneously without ever crossing paths.

Climb to the rooftop terraces. The forest of 800 sculpted pinnacles evokes the skyline of an oriental city — historians have identified Leonardo's Italian influence throughout. The Greek cross floorplan was inspired by St Peter's Basilica in Rome. Views over the 5,440-hectare enclosed estate.

Back to Blois around midday. Quick lunch, then TER to Chenonceaux — about 1h20 total with a change at St-Pierre-des-Corps (the TGV hub for the Tours area), €14–29. Chenonceaux station is 400m from the château, five minutes on foot.

Chenonceau, the Ladies' Château. Built between 1513 and 1517 by Katherine Briçonnet on a fortified mill. Given by Henri II to Diane de Poitiers in 1547, reclaimed by Catherine de' Medici in 1559. The gallery spanning the River Cher — 60 metres long, 18 windows, built 1570–1576 — makes it the world's only château-bridge. €17.

Inside: the Chamber of the Five Queens, the Guard Room, the Chapel, and the Green Study from which Catherine de' Medici governed France as regent. Flemish tapestries, paintings by Rubens, Primaticcio, Correggio, and Van Dyck. In 1914–1918, Gaston Menier (of the chocolate fortune) converted the gallery into a military hospital, treating 2,254 wounded soldiers. In 1939–1945, it was the only crossing point between the Occupied Zone and the Free Zone.

The gardens are equally remarkable. Diane de Poitiers' garden (12,000 m²) was laid out in 1559. Catherine de' Medici's garden is more intimate. A 1,500 m² maze of 2,000 yew trees. The flower garden supplies 70 bouquets a day to the rooms inside. In November, pumpkins take over for Halloween.

activities.text: Dinner in the old town. L'Orangerie du Château, next to the monument, serves gastro cuisine at €45–70 in an 18th-century setting. More affordable: Le Castelet (Rue des Trois Marchands, €18–25). Try rillettes de Tours, Selles-sur-Cher AOP goat's cheese, and tarte Tatin — invented at Lamotte-Beuvron, 45 km away, in 1889.

April to September: son et lumière show at the Royal Château after dark. 45 minutes of projections across the four façades of the inner courtyard — 1,500 projectors, original score. Off-season: an evening stroll along the illuminated Loire embankment and over the Pont Jacques-Gabriel (1724, listed).
Return to Blois by TER in the late afternoon, about 1 hour via St-Pierre-des-Corps. Last connections around 7–8pm — check on SNCF Connect. In winter, Chenonceau closes at 4:30pm, so plan accordingly.

Last dinner in Blois. Cheverny or Touraine wine on a terrace. To extend your Loire stay by a day: Cheverny (10 km, the château that inspired Tintin's Moulinsart), Amboise (Clos Lucé, where Leonardo da Vinci died in 1519), and Chaumont-sur-Loire (garden festival) are all reachable by TER or shuttle.
