visits.text: The MC93, Bobigny's national performing arts venue, occupies a building designed by architects Fabre and Perrotet in exposed concrete, steel, and sandstone. The main Oleg Efremov auditorium seats 800. Since the 1970s, this theater has hosted productions by international directors.

The Seine-Saint-Denis prefecture, built between 1968 and 1971, marks the emergence of modern administrative architecture. Its buildings are organized around a square dominated by the triangular 1974 town hall, resembling a beehive.

The Memorial to the former Bobigny deportation station, inaugurated in 2023, occupies the site from which 21 convoys of Jewish deportees departed between July 1943 and August 1944. An educational trail traces this dark chapter of history.
The Bourse du Travail de Bobigny, designed by the Brazilian architect, displays characteristic curves in white concrete. Its auditorium regularly hosts cultural events.

Cross the town's wooded park to reach the Church of Saint-André. The route runs alongside boules courts and opens onto Place de la Libération, bordered by the former town hall converted into a music conservatory.

activities.text: The Cité de l'Abreuvoir, designed in the 1950s by architect Émile Aillaud as a garden city of 1,500 housing units, has been awarded the “Architecture contemporaine remarquable” label. Walk its paths to understand the post-war social housing utopia.
Head to the banks of the Ourcq canal on the Bobigny side. The towpath links Pantin to Bondy through a changing landscape punctuated by murals and new developments.

days_plan.itin_title: Seine-Saint-Denis Tour: Basilica and Urban Culture

visits.text: The Rouquan woods, near Vidauban, contain a restored pitch kiln. Until the mid-19th century, pitch was produced here to seal the hulls and ropes of ships from Toulon and Saint-Tropez. The loop is an easy 4.1 km. It starts 8 km from the village, on the D48 toward La Garde-Freinet.

activities.text: Walk the Rouquan woods loop, staying on the tracks throughout: the area is part of the Plaine des Maures Nature Reserve, a refuge for Hermann's tortoise. Start at the rest area, near the second water tank on the right. Let's be frank: you come for the kiln, not the panorama.

days_plan.itin_title: Roquebrune-sur-Argens: sea, villages and the Var in 10 days

visits.text: Bonifacio's Upper Town stands on 70-meter limestone cliffs dominating the sea. Medieval ramparts protect cobbled lanes, a 12th-century citadel, and centuries-old churches. The Bastion de l'Étendard houses a museum tracing the town's history. The walk along the fortifications offers vertiginous views over the Strait of Bonifacio and Sardinia.

The King of Aragon Staircase has 187 steps cut into the limestone cliff, according to legend in a single night during the 1420 siege. The steps plunge toward the sea down a spectacular sheer cliff. The climb reveals sea caves and geological formations sculpted by erosion. The panorama from the top takes in the strait and white cliffs.

The 12th-century Sainte-Marie-Majeure church dominates the historic center with its bell tower. The interior blends Romanesque and Gothic styles; the underground cistern testifies to medieval ingenuity. The Gothic Saint-Dominique church preserves relics and 13th-century architecture. The seaside cemetery offers a unique perspective on the cliffs and the Mediterranean.

Le Gouvernail de Corse can be visited near Bonifacio's marine cemetery. A tunnel with 168 steps cut into the cliff descends to a former military observation post. The underground room offers a view of the Bouches de Bonifacio, the limestone cliffs and Sardinia.

activities.text: Boat excursions reveal Bonifacio's sea caves inaccessible by land. Sdragonato cave has an opening in its ceiling shaped like Corsica. Tours include the Lavezzi Islands in their protected nature reserve. Crystalline turquoise waters invite swimming in wild coves.

Beaches around Bonifacio offer alternating stretches of white sand and rocky coves. Piantarella's shallow turquoise waters are ideal for families. Petit Sperone and Rondinara Beach form perfect arcs of fine sand. All offer panoramas over the Lavezzi Islands and Cavallo.

Bonifacio's waterfront district comes alive around its natural harbor sheltered in a deep calanque. Seafood restaurants line the quays where sailboats and yachts moor. Artisan shops offer Corsican products and souvenirs. The Mediterranean atmosphere flourishes in the evening along the waterfront.

days_plan.itin_title: Complete Tour of Corsica
Southern Corsica Tour: Bonifacio, Porto-Vecchio and Mountains

visits.text: The kitchen garden of Bonnétable is one of Sarthe's most pleasant surprises. Laid out in 1885 over 13,000 m² by brothers Denis and Eugène Bühler—the landscape architects who also designed Thabor Park in Rennes—it was commissioned by the Duke of La Rochefoucauld-Doudeauville for his Château de Bonnétable. Surrounded by walls covered with old roses and clematis, it houses a heritage orchard, heirloom vegetables, a Mediterranean garden, a medicinal herb garden, and magnificent greenhouses. At the back of the park, a Bollée windmill from the late 19th century—a wind turbine invented in 1868 by Ernest Sylvain Bollée to pump water—is one of the finest examples still standing in France. Free access during tourist office hours.

The Château de Bonnétable, built in the 15th century then remodeled in the 19th for the Dukes of Doudeauville, dominates the village with its re-dug moats and park. The old stables, with their preserved stalls and saddlery, now house the tourist office and a temporary exhibition hall.

The Church of Saint-Sulpice, whose origins date back to the 11th century, preserves a wooden organ from 1850 and beautiful 19th-century stained glass windows illustrating the life of Saint Sulpice. The 1856 covered market, on Place du Vieux Château, deserves a look for its campanile with two clocks.

activities.text: The Transvap is a tourist railway operated by passionate volunteers who run steam locomotives and vintage railcars on the 17 km of the former Mamers-Saint-Calais line—nicknamed the Dukes' line because it was originally financed by the region's château owners. The journey between Bonnétable and Beillé crosses the Jousse valley through the Sarthe bocage. Trains run in summer on Sundays and holidays. Check the calendar before coming—the Transvap sometimes has technical closures.

The Forest of Bonnétable extends over several hundred hectares north of the village. Marked walking and cycling circuits allow you to stroll beneath centuries-old oaks and beeches. It's an ideal outing to finish this circuit gently, away from the bustle, before rejoining Le Mans 30 km away.

days_plan.itin_title: Sarthe Road Trip: Le Mans and the Loir Valley

visits.text: Bonneval, nicknamed the Little Venice of Beauce for its canals fed by the Loir. This medieval town founded in 857 around Saint-Florentin Abbey has preserved its water-filled moats, ramparts, and picturesque streets. An oasis of greenery in the heart of the Beauce plain.

Former Benedictine Abbey of Saint-Florentin-et-Saint-Hilaire, classified as a historic monument since 1883. The pointed-arch entrance gate from the 13th century remains, topped by the 15th-century abbot's lodging, with its checkerboard wall of white stones, bricks, and flint flanked by three towers.

Church of Notre-Dame de Bonneval, a jewel of early Gothic architecture built between the 12th and 13th centuries. It houses two paintings from the abbey's former refectory, including a copy of a canvas by Nicolas Poussin. Its bell tower dominates the medieval town's rooftops.

Medieval fortifications of Bonneval with the 15th-century Porte Saint-Roch and the 13th-century Tour du Roi, a former 22-meter-high keep. The ramparts still encircle the old town, offering a walk along the flower-lined moats.

activities.text: Electric boat ride on Bonneval's canals, a unique experience to discover the town from the water. These small boats require no license and allow you to pass under medieval bridges and admire age-old washhouses. In the evening, the illuminations of “Bonneval, lumières au fil de l'eau” enhance the journey.
Walk along Bonneval's medieval moats, where ducks and moorhens come to greet strollers. The 19th-century washhouses punctuate the route while old houses are reflected in the calm waters of the Loir.
Tasting of local Beauce products at Vergers de Beauce, a shop offering exclusively local products through short supply chains. A gourmet stop to discover the authentic flavors of Eure-et-Loir.

days_plan.itin_title: Eure-et-Loir Tour: Chartres, Châteaux and Proust

visits.text: Bonneval-sur-Arc is the only Savoyard village classified among France's Most Beautiful Villages. Perched at 1,800 m altitude at the far end of Haute-Maurienne, it lines up stone houses with 80-cm-thick walls, roofed with lauze slabs on larch timbers. No antenna or satellite dish disturbs the village silhouette.

The parish church raises its tower bell-spire of stone above the rooftops. Originally a simple chapel, it was enlarged in the 16th century to accommodate the parish newly established by the Bishop of Maurienne.

Push on to the hamlet of l'Écot, 4 km from the village (2,000 m). Classified as a historic site in 1971, this cluster of abandoned chalets and its Chapelle Sainte-Marguerite (Romanesque, adorned with medieval frescoes) served as a film set for Belle et Sébastien adaptations.

The Espace Neige et Montagne recounts daily life in the high mountains of yesteryear: wood crafts, pottery, weaving, and the beginnings of mountaineering at Bonneval. The old-timers heated themselves with "grébons," molded briquettes made from sheep dung.

Stop at the cooperative fromagerie to taste Bleu de Bonneval, a local blue-veined cheese, and Beaufort AOP d'alpage. Cows graze here between 1,800 and 2,500 m altitude, in the pastures of Vanoise National Park.

activities.text: Hike to the Cirque des Évettes. From l'Écot, the trail climbs alongside the Arc torrent to a glacial amphitheater dominated by the Albaron (3,637 m). Facing the Évettes glacier, silence and immensity reward every step.
Family walk on the Sentier des Agneaux, between the village and the hamlet of l'Écot. The path follows pastures where flocks spend the summer, with views of the border peaks of Italy.
Canyoning in the gorges of l'Écot. One of the Alps' finest spots: descent in the Arc's waters with natural slides, jumps, and rappels supervised by instructors.

days_plan.itin_title: Savoie from Lakes to Glaciers: Yenne to Haute-Maurienne

visits.text: Drive to Bordeaux (3 hours 15 minutes via the A10). Get settled and set out to explore the historic center, a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2007. Start with the Place de la Bourse, designed by architect Jacques Gabriel between 1730 and 1755—it's the first open square in the history of French urban planning. Opposite, the Miroir d'eau (3,450 m², the world's largest) reflects the 18th-century façades. Every 15 minutes, 900 misters create a fog effect—magical late in the day.

Walk up to the Saint-André Cathedral, begun in the 11th century and expanded through the 15th. This is where Eleanor of Aquitaine married the future Louis VII in 1137. Climb to the top of the Pey-Berland tower (66 meters, 231 steps) for the panorama over Bordeaux's rooftops.

Continue to the Grand Théâtre (1780), one of Europe's finest. Its 12 Corinthian columns and monumental staircase inspired Charles Garnier for the Paris Opera. Guided tours are rare—check availability.

Morning at the Marché des Capucins, the "belly of Bordeaux." This covered market operates daily except Monday. You'll taste Arcachon oysters, entrecôte bordelaise, canelés, and cheeses. The atmosphere is lively and working-class—Bordelais do their shopping here.

Head to La Cité du Vin, opened in 2016 on the banks of the Garonne. It's not a conventional museum but an immersive experience in the world of wine. The glass-and-aluminum building designed by XTU Architects evokes a twisted vine trunk. The interactive journey lasts 2 hours. The belvedere on the 8th floor offers a panoramic view and includes a tasting with your ticket.

Late afternoon, wander down rue Sainte-Catherine, Europe's longest pedestrian street (1.2 km). Pass beneath the Grosse Cloche, a medieval belfry from the 15th century with its two 40-meter towers—the 7,800 kg bell rings only for special occasions. The Saint-Pierre quarter behind it is the most charming in old Bordeaux.

Head to Saint-Émilion this morning, 45 minutes from Bordeaux. This medieval village perched amid the vines has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1999—the world's first "viticultural jurisdiction" to receive this distinction. Start with the Monolithic Church, entirely carved out of limestone rock between the 8th and 12th centuries. It's Europe's largest underground church—38 meters long, 20 wide. Accessible only by guided tour (departure from the tourist office).

Stroll the village's cobbled lanes—the view from the King's Tower (13th-century keep) sweeps across vineyards to the horizon. The ramparts, cloisters, and golden stone houses create an atmosphere that the tourist crowds can't quite spoil.

Day at the Arcachon Basin, 1 hour from Bordeaux. Start with the Dune of Pilat—Europe's highest sand dune: 100 to 110 meters high depending on the year (it moves!), 2.9 km long, 616 meters wide. Climb via the wooden staircase (installed March to November) or on foot through the sand. The panorama from the summit sweeps across the ocean, pine forest, and Banc d'Arguin. Arrive early—the parking lot fills quickly in summer.

Head down to the oyster-farming village of Gujan-Mestras or Le Canon, on the Cap-Ferret peninsula. The colorful huts of the oyster farmers serve oysters straight from the basin, with a glass of white wine and rye bread. It's simple, fresh, and the best value of your trip.

Your last morning in Bordeaux. If you have not already done so, visit the Bassins des Lumières, housed in the former German submarine base from World War II. The immersive exhibitions change regularly. The pools reflect the projections and create a dizzying effect.

Cross the Pont de Pierre to the right bank and the Darwin quarter, a former military barracks converted into an alternative eco-space—skatepark, urban farm, craft brewery, organic restaurants. This is dynamic Bordeaux, far from the classicism of the left bank.

activities.text: Treat yourself to a stroll along the Garonne quays late in the day. The 4.5 km of quays redeveloped since 2009 have become the Bordelais' favorite gathering place—joggers, cyclists, families. The Pont de Pierre (1822), with its 17 brick-and-stone arches, is at its most photogenic when viewed from the quays. Legend has it that the number of arches corresponds to the letters in “Napoléon Bonaparte”—an appealing story, but historians have debunked it.
In the evening, try a wine bar downtown—Bordeaux has dozens, from the most traditional to the most trendy. Ask for a glass of Saint-Émilion or Pessac-Léognan to stay local.

Book a tasting at one of the wine châteaux around Saint-Émilion. Most estates welcome visitors by appointment—allow 1 hour to 1 hour 30 minutes for a tour of the cellars and a tasting of 3–4 wines. Saint-Émilion Grand Cru appellations are among the world's most prestigious.

On the way back, if you enjoy vineyard landscapes, make a detour via Pomerol—Bordeaux's least-known appellation. No village, no monumental château, just vines and understated estates producing some of the world's most expensive wines.

If weather permits, take a tour by pinasse (traditional flat-bottomed boat) around the Île aux Oiseaux and its cabins on stilts—two cabins that have become the symbol of the Basin. Operators offer 2-hour outings from the port of Arcachon or Cap-Ferret.

Treat yourself to a final coffee on an outdoor terrace along the quays before departure. Bordeaux-Mérignac airport is 20 minutes from downtown, and Saint-Jean station offers TGV trains to Paris in 2 hours 4 minutes.

visits.text: A 12th-century medieval village listed among the Plus Beaux Villages de France, Bormes unfolds its flower-lined alleys, its “cuberts” (vaulted passages), and its ochre-tinted facades. Over 700 plant species color the village, from bougainvillea in summer to mimosa in winter.

Climb up to the 13th–14th-century castle, a listed historic monument since 1931. From the village's highest point, the panorama takes in Lavandou Bay, the islands of Levant and Port-Cros, La Favière harbor, and Cap Bénat.

Saint-Trophyme Church, built in the 18th century in a Provençal Romanesque style, replaced the old church near the castle, which had become too small. In the heart of the village, it stands out for its sober stone façade and typically Provençal atmosphere.

Parc Gonzalez, awarded the Jardin Remarquable label, brings together plants from Australia and around the world across 3,000 m², including 250 species arranged by landscape designer Gilles Augias. The terraces offer views over the Mediterranean.
The Museum of History and Art of Bormes, housed in the former town hall, offers an augmented reality tour via the HistoPad. The rooms reveal the village's secrets through the centuries.

activities.text: Fort de Brégançon, a state residence overlooking the sea, can be glimpsed from the coast. Head to Cabasson beach below: white sand, crystal-clear water, and a direct view of the fort.
Nine wine estates and one cooperative cellar offer tastings of AOC Côtes de Provence wines. The Vignobles & Découvertes label guarantees a quality welcome in the cellars.
From La Favière harbor, boat excursions head to Port-Cros, Porquerolles, or offshore to watch dolphins. Departures run from April to October.

days_plan.itin_title: Var Road Trip: French Riviera & Provence Verte
Var in 4 Days: From Bormes to the Most Beautiful Villages of the Verdon

visits.text: Boucieu-le-Roi is the "village of a thousand secrets," as its inhabitants call it. The name comes from its history: in 1291, Philip IV the Fair created a royal court of justice here whose jurisdiction covered all of Haut-Vivarais, from the Eyrieux to the north of the department. The village was thus a small judicial and commercial capital. The Maison du Bailli, listed as a Monument Historique, is the emblematic building of that period, its projecting watchtower recognizable at a glance. It housed the high court of justice. The 16th-century Wars of Religion put an end to this prosperity.

Go down to the Pont du Roi, listed as a Monument Historique, probably built in the 15th century to ensure the link with northern Vivarais. It spans the Doux in a wild setting below the village—allow 15 min on foot. Below flows the Doux, a river classified as Espace Naturel Sensible since 2015, renowned for its water quality and protected species (Grand Murin bats, orchids). Climbing to the convent on the heights, you visit the Musée Pierre Vigne, devoted to the Ardèche missionary priest (1670-1740) beatified by John Paul II in 2004, who found in Boucieu a resemblance to Jerusalem and in 1714 built a Stations of the Cross with 39 station-chapels.

The small exhibition room at the village entrance traces the history of Boucieu and Vivarais through photos and old documents—useful context before wandering the lanes. The craft art exhibition "Les Arts à la Cure" in July-August opens the doors of one of the village's oldest houses.

activities.text: The Vélorail des Gorges du Doux offers panoramic descents of 8, 12 or 20 km on the historic Train de l'Ardèche line (built 1891), above the gorges. You pedal on 2- or 4-person rail bikes, the climb by train. The route is accessible to all and landscapes are cut off from the road—the only places where you'll see the Doux gorges from the bank. Absolutely book ahead in July-August.

The Train de l'Ardèche—nicknamed the Mastrou—is a historic steam train linking Tournon-sur-Rhône to Lamastre over 28 km climbing the wild Doux gorges. Boucieu-le-Roi is one of the intermediate stations. Half a day suffices for the Étroits or Viaduct descent from Boucieu. An original experience to discover otherwise inaccessible landscapes.

days_plan.itin_title: The 18 Most Beautiful Villages of Ardèche

visits.text: Bouges Castle. This 18th-century château, nicknamed the Petit Trianon of Berry, appears at the end of a 2 km bridle avenue lined with two-hundred-year-old plane and horse chestnut trees. The elegant residence has remained furnished and decorated with refinement, giving the impression that the owners have just stepped out. The salons, dining room, and bedrooms illustrate the French art of living during the Age of Enlightenment.

French formal gardens. Designed by the celebrated landscape architects Duchêne, these formal gardens feature borders of boxwood and cone-shaped yews, surrounded by a double row of linden trees. The view along the pool leads to the nymphaeum's cascading fountain, while at the center of the lawn stands a white marble sculptural group depicting Hercules.

Cutting garden. This flower garden created by Renée Viguier in the early 20th century draws inspiration from the Belle Époque spirit. Organized along two main axes around a circular pool, it offers a variety of annual flowers for the bouquets that adorn the château's rooms. The propagation greenhouses grow plants for the floral displays. Visit from June to October, with full bloom in July–August.

English landscape park and stables. The 80-hectare park features an open woodland landscape with plantings whose colors change: sweetgums, tulip trees, purple beeches, American red oaks, and sumacs set the pond ablaze with golden reflections in autumn. The stables house a museum of horse-drawn carriages and testify to the importance given to horses in the 19th century.

activities.text: Family activity booklet. A free, fun trail allows children to discover the gardens while enjoying themselves. Puzzles and treasure hunts designed for ages 6–12 punctuate the walk through the park and gardens.

Park stroll. The 80 hectares of greenery offer many opportunities for walks. The Ensemble Arboré Remarquable label recognizes the exceptional quality of the century-old trees. The pond provides a soothing focal point for a contemplative pause.

days_plan.itin_title: Indre Road Trip: Secret Berry and the Vallée Noire

visits.text: Boulbon is a village with tight-knit streets clinging to its limestone promontory. Its vaulted passages at the hill's foot — typical of medieval Rhône-side architecture — create an atmosphere from another time. Climb to the château ruins (11th-12th centuries) for a view simultaneously embracing the Rhône to the west, the Montagnette to the north, and the Alpilles ridges to the southeast. Few villages of this size offer such amplitude of landscape.

The Saint-Marcellin chapel, at the village's base, is an 11th-century Romanesque structure of remarkable sobriety. It's known for the "procession of bottles" held here every June 1st for centuries: the village men carry wine bottles and have them blessed to protect the vines from diseases and storms. This archaic ritual linked to the cult of Saint Marcellin is one of the last of its type in Provence.

activities.text: Climb to Boulbon's castle promontory: a steep 20-minute path from village center leads to the château ruins. The panorama over the Rhône, Tarascon, and Alpilles is exceptional. Bring good shoes and arrive late afternoon for golden light on the Alpilles.

Chapel loop around Boulbon: several 16th-17th century rural oratories and chapels dot the paths between Boulbon and Barbentane. A marked heritage route of 7 km explores these discreet structures against a backdrop of garrigue and pine forests.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpilles, Aix-en-Provence & Arles Circuit

visits.text: The Musée des Années 30 displays 3,000 m² of Art Deco and modern art. Paintings, sculptures, and furniture by Ruhlmann and Leleu testify to Boulogne's artistic ferment in the interwar years.
Île Seguin housed the Renault factory from 1929 to 1992, employing 30,000 workers. La Seine Musicale, inaugurated in 2017, now occupies the downstream tip, a work by Japanese architect Shigeru Ban.
Stroll along the Seine embankments between Boulogne and Sèvres. The redesigned quays offer views of Île Seguin and former industrial sites.

activities.text: The 4-hectare Albert Kahn gardens compose landscape scenes: a Japanese garden with tea pavilion brought over in 1909, Vosges forest, English garden, and French formal garden. The museum preserves 72,000 autochrome photographs from the Archives of the Planet.
Parc de Boulogne stretches across the southern commune. Perfect for a nature break.

days_plan.itin_title: Hauts-de-Seine Road Trip: Royal Heritage & Gardens

visits.text: Nausicaá opened its extension in May 2018, after 70 million euros of work. Its main tank of 10,000 m³ — the equivalent of four Olympic swimming pools — recreates Malpelo Island off the coast of Colombia. You can watch sharks, manta rays and shoals of glittering fish through a glass wall 20 metres long and 5 metres high. Allow a full day: the complete tour of the three areas (Journey on the High Seas, Shores and Mankind, In the Eye of the Climate) takes 4 hours 30 minutes. In 2024, the aquarium welcomed 916,000 visitors — arrive at opening time in summer.

The nineteenth-century Notre-Dame basilica dominates the upper town with its dome visible from the sea. Its crypt of 1,400 m² is the largest in France — a maze of 20 underground rooms spanning two levels, including a fourteenth-century Romanesque crypt adorned with thirteenth-century frescoes. Pick up the audio-guided tablet offered at the entrance, essential for finding your way around.

Walk along the thirteenth-century ramparts — the only intact medieval town wall in the north of France. The wall-walk circles the old town completely in 30 minutes and offers 360-degree views over the Boulonnais and the sea. Within these walls, the upper town has kept its cobbled streets and eighteenth-century houses.

The thirteenth-century comital castle, built on the foundations of a Roman camp, houses the Boulogne museum. Its collections are eclectic — from ancient Egypt to Pacific tribal art — with some remarkable Gallo-Roman pieces from local excavations.

The belfry, a former twelfth-century keep standing 37 metres tall, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1926. It is the oldest of the six listed belfries of Pas-de-Calais — and the only one to have kept its function as a medieval keep until the nineteenth century. It symbolises Boulogne's communal independence.

activities.text: Wander along the harbour promenade and visit Boulogne's fish auction market, France's leading small-scale fishing port. The smell of the tide, the boats at the quayside and the crates of fresh mackerel, herring and scallops give a foretaste of what you will find in the evening's restaurants.

Climb the Grande Armée column, erected 3 km north of Boulogne in honour of Napoleon, who camped here with 150,000 men in 1804 while preparing the invasion of England. The 53-metre bronze column (263 steps) rises on a knoll overlooking the Channel. The view over the Boulonnais, the sea and the cliff is outstanding.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Villages from Flanders to the Bay of Somme
Road Trip Pas-De-Calais: The Opal Coast and Belfries

visits.text: The Château de Bourbon (13th–14th centuries), cradle of the Capetian house of Bourbon which reigned from 1589 to 1848, rises atop a rocky spur with its three northern towers and the “Qui Qu'en Grogne” tower. Nine rooms with surprising décor evoke medieval life and the arts of the period. From the top of the battlements (24 metres), the panorama takes in the Bourbonnais bocage. A listed historic monument since 1862.

The Thermes de Bourbon-l'Archambault, listed as a historic monument, reveal their intact Belle Époque décor: an ornate coffered wooden ceiling and ceramic panels in shimmering colours with exotic influences. Built on the site of ancient baths, these 19th-century baths have welcomed spa guests since antiquity. Muscle-relaxing and sedative waters treat rheumatic and gynaecological conditions.

The 12th-century Church of Saint-Georges, in Burgundian Romanesque style, displays its rounded portal and fifty historiated capitals. Until the Revolution, the Holy Cross chapel housed precious relics (a fragment of the True Cross and a thorn from Christ's crown). A Romantic organ with 16 stops (1892) adorns the nave.

The Musée Augustin Bernard occupies the former neoclassical casino, which housed a gaming room, theatre and ballroom. The Sainte Chapelle district, within the medieval enclosure, is lined with picturesque houses built against the ramparts. The Allées Montespan, planted by Marshal de la Meilleraye, and the spa park offer unique views of the town and castle.

activities.text: Courses of thermal treatment or spa packages (fitness, wellbeing) offer the chance to enjoy the beneficial waters known since antiquity. Short treatment courses of 5 to 12 days, health stays or treatments for a single day: there is an option for everyone. The Belle Époque setting of the baths adds to the charm of a moment of relaxation.

The Casino de Bourbon-l'Archambault, in its Belle Époque setting, offers 77 slot machines, a table games area (blackjack, English roulette) and electronic roulette. Located in the heart of a tree-filled park in the spa town, it invites visitors to enjoy a festive and friendly atmosphere after a day of sightseeing.

The guided town tour reveals its heritage along a route with eleven heritage markers. On foot or by horse-drawn carriage, discover spa villas, canons' houses, castle officers' residences and traces left by famous spa guests such as Madame de Sévigné or Talleyrand. This Petite Cité de Caractère® reveals its rich spa history.

days_plan.itin_title: Allier Road Trip: Vichy, Thermal Baths and Bourbonnais Bocage

visits.text: The thermal water of Bourbonne-les-Bains surfaces at 66°C: it descends more than 2,000 metres underground before rising again, loaded with sodium chloride, calcium and magnesium. The Romans were already here: Julius Caesar, so the story goes, sent his wounded centurions to be treated. In 1735, Louis XV set up a military thermal hospital there, which later treated the wounded of the Napoleonic and colonial wars. Today the spa, approved for rheumatology and respiratory conditions, welcomes between 5,000 and 7,000 spa patients a year, from March to November.

The municipal museum, accredited under the Musée de France label, has occupied the park of the former medieval castle since 2003. Don't miss the archaeology gallery, which houses Gallo-Roman remains unearthed from Bourbonne's own soil: two sculpted Gallic heads in wood, votive stelae, and ritual objects discovered during excavations at the military hospital. These finds rank among the region's finest.

The castle park overlooks the town from the heights. A 16th-century porch opens onto avenues lined with century-old trees. This is also where the Montmorency Arboretum stands, with 250 different species, a perfect place for a stroll between two treatments.

activities.text: Book a wellness package at the thermal springs. Short stays without medical prescription are available for non-patients: invigorating baths, stimulating showers, massages, and hammam. If you're coming for a rejuvenating weekend, contact the spa directly in advance, as capacity is limited.

A few kilometers from town, the 150-hectare Bannie animal park lets visitors roam semi-freely among red deer, does, fallow deer, wild boar, and peacocks set within a forest you can explore in part. An excellent way to stretch your legs before or after spa treatments.

Hike the marked trails winding through the Champagne bocage. Circuits starting from the city snake between forests and meadows. The tourist office provides maps and suggestions tailored to your preferred distance.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Marne Circuit: Langres and Heritage

visits.text: The Royal Monastery of Brou stands like the Taj Mahal of Bresse, built as a monument to love between 1506 and 1532. A masterpiece of Flamboyant Gothic architecture, it captivates visitors with its lace-like stonework, three princely tombs and poignant history: Margaret of Austria commissioned this mausoleum for her husband, Philibert the Fair, who died too soon. Three cloisters and a Fine Arts Museum complete the visit to this listed monument.

Notre-Dame Church displays the Flamboyant Gothic architecture typical of Savoyard Bresse. Built of carrons, the region's characteristic Savoyard bricks, it bears witness to the town's medieval past. Its bell tower has watched over the town centre for centuries, providing a landmark visible from the surrounding cobbled streets.

Stroll through the streets of the historic centre, where timber-framed houses tell the story of this former capital of Bresse. Place Carriat and its terraces invite you to watch the daily bustle of Bourg-en-Bresse's residents. Colourful façades and arcades house craft shops that preserve local expertise.

The Ferme du Sougey, a listed historic monument, is one of the oldest timber-framed farms in Bresse, dating from the 15th century. Plan a round trip from Bourg-en-Bresse for this visit. Converted into a museum of local rural heritage, it presents traditional Bressan housing and houses a farm raising AOC Bresse poultry. The surrounding 35 hectares of hedgerow countryside bear witness to the area's longstanding agricultural traditions.

activities.text: Discover AOC Bresse poultry, the only poultry in the world to have held an appellation d'origine contrôlée since 1957. At local farms and restaurants, taste its delicate, marbled meat, from birds raised outdoors in Bresse's hedgerow countryside. Local gastronomy celebrates this blue-legged chicken, the pride of the region.

Lose yourself in the cobbled streets of the Brou district. The old houses, secret passages and small inner courtyards preserve a medieval atmosphere. Every façade tells a story, and every stone bears witness to the passing centuries in this town of weavers and merchants.

Every Saturday morning, the market halls bustle with activity as local producers gather. Bresse poultry, alpine cheeses, cured sausages and thick crème fraîche: the stalls overflow with local produce. The friendly atmosphere and conversations with producers keep Bresse's agricultural tradition alive.

Visit the apothecary's shop at the Hôtel-Dieu in Bourg-en-Bresse, established in these buildings in the late 18th century. This former pharmacy houses an exceptional collection of earthenware jars, including pieces from Meillonnas, and period medical instruments. Its intact laboratory and the dispensary's oak panelling bear witness to the medicine of the past.

days_plan.itin_title: Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes Road Trip: Monasteries, Mountains & Lakes
Grand Tour Ain & Savoie Mont-Blanc: Lakes, Mountains and Heritage
Road Trip from Bresse to Bugey via Beaujolais and Lyon

visits.text: Bourges Cathedral startles you from the moment you enter: no transept, five naves that sweep unbroken for 120 metres. This feature, extremely rare in a Gothic cathedral, creates a vertiginous perspective found nowhere else in France. Built between 1195 and 1230, it rivals Notre-Dame de Paris. The central portal of the Last Judgement repays close attention: smiling resurrected souls, grimacing damned, sculpted with striking realism.

The 13th-century stained glass ranks among the finest surviving medieval ensembles. In the ambulatory, the Last Supper and the Vision of Saint John have not moved in 800 years. The crypt holds the marble recumbent figure of Duke John of Berry (1422) and the remains of the rood screen destroyed in the Revolution. Guided tour mandatory, departures every hour.

396 spiral steps lead up the Tour de Beurre to a panoramic terrace. The ascent is steep, but the 360° view over Bourges, medieval roofs and the Berry countryside rewards the effort. You can make out marshes to the north and the first slopes of the Sancerrois to the east. Access limited to July–August, set hours, limited places.

The Jacques-Cœur Palace is one of the finest secular Gothic buildings in France. Built between 1443 and 1451 by Charles VII's treasurer, it comprises 43 rooms across 4,000 m². Jacques Cœur slept there only 8 nights before his disgrace. The street façade shows two sculpted figures leaning on the sills of false windows — they seem to have been watching passers-by for 600 years. Inside, the upturned ship's-hull roof frame and monumental fireplaces speak to the opulence of the age.

Jacques Cœur's motto — “To a stout heart, nothing is impossible” — is carved throughout the palace, accompanied by sculpted shells and hearts. The chapel preserves a stained-glass window depicting one of his merchant ships. The feasting hall, with its gallery for musicians and a fireplace bearing the royal arms, gives a sense of the lavish receptions he was never able to hold here.

activities.text: The Jardin de l'Archevêché, attributed to Le Nôtre, offers a clear view of the cathedral's east end. French-style lawns, geometric parterres and shaded benches: the perfect spot for a rest after sightseeing. Free access year-round.

Bourges's old town is easily explored on foot. Half-timbered houses on Rue Bourbonnoux, the Hôtel Lallemant (Renaissance), Notre-Dame church with its contemporary stained glass. The cobbled streets around the cathedral retain their medieval layout.

The Nuits Lumière de Bourges (May 7 to September 19, 2026): a free nighttime route with projections on historic façades. The cathedral, the Palais Jacques-Cœur and several historic mansions light up at nightfall. Allow 2 hours for the full route.

days_plan.itin_title: Cher Loop: Romanesque Berry and the Route Jacques-Cœur

places.name: Boussac

visits.text: Boussac Castle stands atop a cliff overlooking the Petite Creuse. Built in the 15th century by Jean de Brosse, Joan of Arc's comrade-in-arms, it was the site of a major discovery: here, George Sand identified the Lady and the Unicorn tapestries during her stays between 1840 and 1870. The writer convinced her friend Prosper Mérimée, inspector of historic monuments, to have them listed as historic monuments. The six panels entered the Cluny Museum's collection in 1882.

George Sand's bedroom in the castle has been reconstructed with touching attention to detail: a half-open book on the table, slippers at the foot of the bed, a hair clip on the nightstand. The writer wrote her pastoral novel Jeanne here. A reproduction of the “À mon seul désir” tapestry recalls the medieval masterpiece discovered within these walls.

The castle now houses a remarkable collection of more than 40 tapestries, from the 15th century to the present day. An entire room is devoted to Dom Robert, a Benedictine monk whose colorful cartoons depict cheerful wildlife. The works of Jean Lurçat, including the “Liberté” tapestry inspired by Paul Éluard's poem, testify to the revival of textile art in the 20th century.

activities.text: The Pierres Jaumâtres, a natural jumble of granite boulders on Mont Barlot, offer a fantastical landscape of strangely shaped rocks. George Sand set a scene from her novel Jeanne here. The blocks stacked by erosion evoke petrified creatures. A maintained trail winds between the rock formations, offering a panoramic view of the Marche hills.

The town of Boussac retains some old houses and a 12th-century church. A stroll through the narrow streets lets visitors appreciate the atmosphere of this small Creuse town. The weekly market brings the central square to life.

days_plan.itin_title: Creuse Tour: Valley of the Painters and Aubusson Tapestries

map_keywords: Château de Boussac Lady and the Unicorn

places.name: Bouxwiller

visits.text: Bouxwiller is the secret market Alsatians jealously guard for themselves. Former capital of the County of Hanau-Lichtenberg, this small Bas-Rhin town preserves exceptional architectural heritage — half-timbered houses, colorful façades, cobbled streets — and its Christkindelsmärik was voted 'most authentic Christmas market in Alsace' by France Bleu Alsace listeners. The reason? Here, the 200 exhibitors are exclusively Alsatian, no imported products appear on stalls, and selection is absolutely rigorous. Just three days in December (Friday-Saturday-Sunday), 50,000 visitors, and a soul that big markets have sometimes lost.

The Musée du Pays de Hanau presents a 'Christmas Window' each year: figures and decorations fashioned by the territory's glass artisans, with Christmas tree ornaments dating from the 19th and 20th centuries. The 'Christmas Treasure Hunt' exhibition in the old town streets allows discovering heritage while having fun — booklet available at the tourist office. Bouxwiller also organizes the Grand Est's only labeled truffle market, coinciding with the Christkindelsmärik — a gastronomic curiosity not to be missed.

activities.text: The wanderings of the Hàns Tràpp and the Christkindel are Bouxwiller market's signature entertainments. The Christkindel, this young girl dressed in white wearing a fir crown on her head, distributes sweets to good children at day's end. The Hàns Tràpp — a dark and frightening character, the Alsatian counterpart of Père Fouettard — is meant to scare naughty children. The small steam train that traverses Place du Château carrying the winemaker from the Domaine des Trois Sorciers completes the festive tableau.

The fire show 'The Dragon's Legend' on Place du Château at day's end is one of the route's most spectacular moments — flames, music, and narration in the Alsatian night. Pastry workshops (bredele making) and floral workshops are offered throughout the weekend, perfect for families with children.

days_plan.itin_title: Alsace's Most Beautiful Christmas Markets

map_keywords: Musée du Pays de Hanau Bouxwiller

visits.text: The village of Bouzigues stretches along the Thau lagoon with its colorful oyster shacks. Oyster farming has been practiced here since antiquity, as evidenced by archaeological excavations at the nearby Roman villa of Loupian. The port shelters oyster farmers' boats working on the oyster beds visible offshore. The village has retained its authenticity despite tourist influx. A walk along the quays lets you observe producers at work. The atmosphere is peaceful, far from the bustle of seaside resorts.

The Musée de l'Étang de Thau in Bouzigues traces the history of the lagoon and shellfish farming activities. The collections present oyster and mussel farming techniques, the evolution of tools and trades, and the daily life of fishermen and oyster farmers. Models illustrate the organization of water-based farms. The museum also raises awareness about protecting Thau's unique ecosystem. The visit complements a tasting at producers' farms nicely. Modest admission fee.

activities.text: Paddleboard or kayak outing on the Thau lagoon. Several rental companies offer craft to paddle among the oyster beds. The lagoon's calm water is ideal for this activity accessible to all. You glide between shellfish tables while observing water birds. The view from the water offers a different perspective with Mont Saint-Clair in the background. Bring a hat and sunscreen as there's no shade. Allow 2-3 hours for a leisurely outing.

Discover artisan workshops around the Thau lagoon. The villages of Bouzigues, Mèze, and Marseillan are home to potters, painters, and sculptors inspired by the Mediterranean environment. Some open their workshops to visitors. You can observe creative work and purchase unique pieces. It's a wonderful way to discover local creativity and bring home an authentic souvenir. Galleries and shops are often concentrated in village centers.

days_plan.itin_title: Hérault Road Trip: Montpellier, Beaches and the Hinterland

places.name: Bouzonville

visits.text: Start the route in Schwerdorff, right on the German border—the nearest German villages are less than two kilometers away. Notre-Dame-de-l’Assomption Church, built in 1886 in the Romanesque Revival style, holds a surprise: its carved oak paneling bears the epitaphs of the lords of Haen and the de Villers family, allowing you to trace the entire history of the village’s castle owners. During the Christmas season, it hosts an exhibition of miniature nativity scenes from around the world, accompanied by pieces played on the restored Dalstein-Haerpfer organ. While you are there, take a look at the Gallo-Roman remains visible within the municipal boundaries.

Sainte-Croix Abbey Church in Bouzonville is the landmark of this first day. It was founded in 1033 by Count Adalbert of Alsace—a little-known fact: his direct descendants founded the Ducal House of Lorraine and the city of Nancy. The current building was completely rebuilt in the Gothic style between 1342 and 1375 after a fire. Listed as a Historic Monument since September 8, 1999, the abbey church surprises visitors with its restrained sandstone facade, which contrasts with the splendor of its interior. Its Christmas nativity scene is one of the route’s most remarkable: the figures come from Oberammergau in Bavaria, a village world-famous for its Passion Play. Do not miss the Last Supper, created in 1925 by a local artisan and restored in 2020, or the Garnier organ, an instrument unique in the region.

Take a detour to the Maison Lorraine d’Oberdorff in Oberdorff. In this house with a 15th-century vaulted room, you will find an old 18th-century nativity scene from Saint-Martin Church in Odenhoven, several nativity scenes from the Pays de Nied—in wax, terra-cotta, wood, and paper—and a collection of angels and shepherds on the mantelpiece. A showcase of Lorraine’s Christmas craftsmanship in an authentic setting.

activities.text: From the abbey church, follow the Stations of the Cross uphill toward Belle Croix, the town’s highest point. This walk takes you through the historic center and past the Town Hall, built in 1719 and topped with a bell tower with an onion dome typical of Lorraine. It is a lovely way to see the 18th-century houses of the “Pearl of the Nied” illuminated by Christmas decorations.

In December, Bouzonville holds its Christmas market and welcomes Saint Nicholas, who arrives by horse-drawn carriage in the square in front of the Town Hall. Concerts at the abbey church—particularly December’s Christmas concert featuring organ and soprano—are free and worth the trip. Check the town’s event program before your stay.

days_plan.itin_title: Christmas Nativity Scene Route in Moselle

map_keywords: Stations of the Cross Belle Croix Bouzonville

visits.text: Brancion is perched on a fortified spur overlooking the pass linking Cluny to the Saône—a strategic position that explains everything. The castle alone brings together a thousand years of Burgundian military architecture: the residence from around the year 1000 (early 11th century, one of the rare examples of a large Carolingian lord's hall in France), the 12th–13th-century lord's castle with its 23-meter keep, and the 14th-century ducal residence with its trefoil openings. In 1259, the Brancion family—ruined by the Crusades—sold their castle to Hugh IV, Duke of Burgundy, who made it a ducal castellany for two centuries. The castle has been listed as a historic monument since 1977. From the top of the keep, the view over the Saône-et-Loire plain is exceptional.

The Saint-Pierre church, at the end of the spur, is a Romanesque masterpiece from the second half of the 12th century. It houses late-13th-century wall paintings and the recumbent effigy of Josserand de Brancion, who died at the Battle of Mansurah in 1250 during the 7th Crusade alongside Saint Louis—before selling the castle, the family had already spent everything on the Crusades. Next door, the medicinal herb garden recreated by a local association features 80 medieval plants.

activities.text: Loop through viewpoints and woodland edges above the village (2–3 km, ~1 hour). The trail runs alongside the Mâconnais vineyards and offers alternating views over the Grosne valley and the hills of southern Burgundy.
Interpretive tour of the castle site and church with an audio guide available in 4 languages (included in the castle admission ticket). In July, medieval festivals bring the site to life.

days_plan.itin_title: Loop Around Lyon: Villages and Pierres Dorées
Burgundy's 15 Most Beautiful Villages
Burgundy-Franche-Comté: The Most Beautiful Villages in 7 days

visits.text: Erbalunga spreads its fishermen's houses tightly across a rocky peninsula. The ruined 16th-century Genoese tower dominates the small harbor while salt-weathered facades reveal authentic charm. The baroque-fronted Church of Saint-Érasme protects the processional crosses used during Holy Week.

The hamlets of Brando climb in tiers through the valley: Castello with its feudal castle ruins, Pozzo and its flagstone quarries, Mausoleu and its cipolin marble quarries. The Chapel of Notre-Dame-des-Neiges preserves 14th-century frescoes. A journey back in time among fountains and dry-stone washhouses.

The Lavasina sanctuary has drawn pilgrims for centuries. The ex-voto museum can be visited by reservation and tells the story of the miracle. The former Franciscan convent overlooks a small pebble beach facing the sea.

activities.text: The coastal path from Erbalunga winds along coves between maquis and black rocks. Kayak rentals available at the harbor for exploring caves and wild inlets. Diving clubs offer trips to the protected waters of the Cap Corse Marine Natural Park.
Erbalunga beach and Campinca cove offer swimming in a pristine setting. Fine sand and transparent waters bordered by rocks. Family-friendly atmosphere far from the crowds of beach resorts.

days_plan.itin_title: Upper Corsica Road Trip: Cap Corse and Balagne

visits.text: Legend credits Charlemagne with founding Brantôme's Benedictine abbey in 769 AD. Whether or not the emperor passed through, the 11th-century Romanesque bell tower—among France's oldest—still stands on the rock outcrop above the abbey church. Monks carved living spaces directly into the limestone cliff: a dovecote, Saint Sicaire's miraculous fountain, and austere monastic cells that speak to centuries of devotion.

The Cave of the Last Judgment, hewn into the cliff face during the 15th century, harbors two monumental bas-reliefs: Christ in glory surrounded by apocalyptic scenes. The atmosphere inside is haunting and profound. Nearby, the remnants of troglodyte dwellings reveal where monks lived as early as the 9th century—before the abbey was even built.

Brantôme earned the nickname 'the Venice of Périgord' for good reason: the Dronne River winds through the town, crossed by arched bridges and lined with riverside terraces. The angled medieval bridge, the Renaissance pavilion, and the abbey mill create postcard-perfect reflections in the water. It's a place made for strolling and lingering.

activities.text: The Dronne River offers gentle canoeing and kayaking—Class I water suitable for beginners and families. Routes range from one to five hours, paddling beneath Brantôme's bridges and alongside limestone cliffs. Local outfitters provide gear and shuttle service back to town.

days_plan.itin_title: Dordogne: Prehistoric Caves, Medieval Fortresses & Périgord Delights
Nouvelle-Aquitaine Loop: Villages, Vineyards & Dordogne

visits.text: Bressuire Castle has one of the largest medieval defensive enclosures in western France. First mentioned in written records around 1030—when Thibaud de Beaumont, its first known lord, had a church built there—it was gradually fortified until a 700-meter circuit of walls punctuated by 38 towers was established in the 13th century. These walls, much of which still survive, withstood du Guesclin in 1370, the Hundred Years’ War, and the Wars of the Vendée. Now owned by the town, the grounds are accessible year-round. Walk along the walls to appreciate the scale of the site.

The romantic ruins of the 15th-century residence, with its fine mullioned windows and granite fireplaces, bear witness to the splendor of the era of Jacques de Beaumont, chamberlain and adviser to Louis XI. The 19th-century Neo-Gothic residence hosts temporary exhibitions.

Notre-Dame Church was founded in the late 11th century by Thibaud de Beaumont. It was remodeled in the 12th century with domed Angevin-style vaults in the nave, then again in the 16th century with the construction of the choir and the 56-meter Renaissance bell tower—dated 1538 and inspired by the bell tower of Saint-Gatien in Tours—which dominates the town like a stone beacon.

activities.text: From the castle esplanade, enjoy the view of Saint-Cyprien Chapel and the former 19th-century slaughterhouses, reminders of the town’s economic history.
Local providers offer tours of the town and castle, particularly during Heritage Days in September. Outside these events, a self-guided tour route is marked from the tourist office.

days_plan.itin_title: Deux-Sèvres Tour: Marais Poitevin and Romanesque Heritage

visits.text: Océanopolis, a national center for ocean science and culture, unique in Europe. The Brittany pavilion unveils the ecosystem of Armorican coasts with its otter trail and recreated aquariums. The new Oceanauts City offers an interactive, sensory experience to understand marine biodiversity. Themed gardens add a botanical dimension to this oceanographic immersion.

Recouvrance Bridge, iconic lifting bridge spanning the Penfeld with its twin 70-meter-tall pylons. Inaugurated in 1954, it connects the contrasting Siam and Recouvrance districts. The crossing provides a plunging view over the military Arsenal and the river that once sheltered France's greatest fleets. The urban cable car, installed in 2016, crosses the Penfeld in 3 minutes with spectacular panoramas over the roadstead.

Recouvrance Quarter, Brest's historic soul on the Penfeld's right bank. Cobbled lanes climb the heights while Breton houses testify to the district's working-class maritime past. The Tour Tanguy, a 14th-century medieval keep, houses a museum retracing Brest's history before its 1944 destruction. The Breton-speaking quarter contrasts with the rebuilt city center, offering an authentic village atmosphere.

Brest Castle and the National Maritime Museum, a Vauban fortress overlooking the entrance to the Penfeld for more than 1,700 years. The castle houses a collection of maritime objects with ship models, navigation instruments and mementoes of the great age of the royal navy. The ramparts offer a stunning view over the roadstead, one of the most beautiful and largest bays in the world.

activities.text: Sailing trip on Brest roadstead aboard a traditional tall ship like La Recouvrance, a replica of a 19th-century dispatch vessel. The schooner, crewed by five professional sailors, navigates this immense 180 km² bay surrounded by rugged coastlines. Excursions reveal islets, military forts, and changing perspectives on surrounding peninsulas. Wind fills the sails as the crew shares maritime anecdotes and old-fashioned maneuvers.

Stroll along Cours Dajot, a panoramic terrace overlooking Brest roadstead since the 18th century. This esplanade, developed by convict labor, offers unobstructed 180° views embracing the narrows, fortifications, and the comings and goings of military and commercial vessels. Benches invite contemplation of sunsets while palm trees testify to the oceanic climate's mildness. Cafés below animate the atmosphere in the evening.

Discovery of Les Ateliers des Capucins, 18th-century arsenals transformed into a cultural and leisure venue. The monumental 70-meter-high hall houses shops, restaurants, a media library, and exhibition space across 17,000 m². The preserved industrial architecture creates a unique atmosphere between heritage and modernity. The cable car directly connects this district to downtown, soaring over the Penfeld.

days_plan.itin_title: Finistère Circuit: Breton Headlands, Islands & Artists' Villages
Brittany 7 days: Pink Granite, Lighthouses & Peninsulas

visits.text: Briançon's Cité Vauban coils within its ramparts at 1,326 meters: it's France's highest city, perched at the convergence of five valleys. Its fortifications, inscribed on UNESCO's list since 2008 among Vauban's twelve major sites, were built from 1713 to 1734 according to plans left by the engineer. Steeply sloped cobbled streets, vaulted passages, fountains, and the famous Grande Gargouille that rushes down through the center. Allow plenty of time—the upper town is best savored slowly.

The defensive system extends beyond the walls: four high-altitude forts (Salettes, Trois-Têtes, Dauphin and Randouillet) crown the heights around the town. Linking them all is the Pont d'Asfeld, an engineering feat with a single arch spanning the Durance gorges. The view from the bridge alone is worth the climb.

The Notre-Dame-et-Saint-Nicolas collegiate church has a clever story behind it: Vauban placed it on the most exposed bastion, betting that a Christian enemy would not dare bombard a church. Consecrated in 1726, its two bell towers rise above the upper town, and it houses gilded altarpieces and listed historic organs. Also look out for the 80 sundials painted on Briançon's facades, created by Italian and French artists since the seventeenth century.

activities.text: Hike up to Fort des Salettes along the historic military path: an hour's climb rewarded with a view down over Briançon and its converging valleys. The fortification, envisioned by Vauban as early as 1692 and built from 1709, guards the flat area that stood dangerously above the city. Good shoes, water, and a windbreaker: it's often windy up there.

To understand the town, nothing beats a guided tour of the Cité Vauban with a certified Ville d'Art et d'Histoire guide: ramparts, fortified gates, powder magazines and secret passages. Allow 1.5 to 2 hours; tickets are available at the tourist office. It is also an opportunity to enter fortifications that are sometimes closed to unguided visitors.

The Maison du Parc national des Écrins, in the upper town, presents the massif's fauna, flora, and alpine environments through interactive exhibits, screenings, and activities. A good introduction before the hikes of the following days, especially with kids. Generally free admission, hours vary by season.

days_plan.itin_title: Hautes-Alpes Road Trip: High Mountains and Alpine Valleys

places.name: Briare

visits.text: The Briare canal bridge is the must-see monument of eastern Loiret. Built between 1890 and 1894 by the Gustave Eiffel company for the masonry and Daydé & Pillé for the metal trough, it was inaugurated on 16 September 1896. Its 662 metres in length, its 14 piers in the Loire and its 72 lamp posts make it the largest metal canal bridge in France — for a century it was the longest in the world, overtaken only in 2003 by the Magdeburg canal bridge. Crossing it on foot, you have the canal water at your feet and the Loire 11 metres below. The effect is striking. Listed as a Historic Monument in 1976, it draws 300,000 visitors each year.

The Musée des Deux Marines retraces the history of river navigation on the Loire and the canals. Models of flat-bottomed boats, photographs of the boatmen and onboard objects reconstruct life on the water in the 19th century, when the Briare Canal — one of France's oldest canals, opened in 1642 — linked the Loire to the Seine across 54 kilometres and 38 locks.

activities.text: Operators offer electric boats for hire without a licence to navigate the canal running alongside the Loire and pass beneath the canal bridge from the water. It's the best way to understand the structure from the inside. Allow around 2 hours for a comfortable round trip.

Settle on a terrace by the marina to watch the pleasure barges pass through the locks. Briare has 7 locks and 14 bridges — its boatmen called it the town of 14 bridges. The Briare Canal still links the Loire to the Loing Canal and the Seine basin today.

days_plan.itin_title: Loiret Road Trip: Orléans and the Châteaux of the Loire

map_keywords: Museum of Two Maritime Traditions Briare

visits.text: An imperial town in Champagne, Brienne-le-Château intertwines its destiny with the Napoleonic legend. Three key moments stand out: from 1779 to 1784, the young Napoleon Bonaparte, aged 10 to 15, studied at the Royal Military School, far from his native Corsica; in 1805, he made a triumphant return before his coronation as King of Italy; and in January 1814, the Battle of Brienne opened the tragic Campaign of France. The hilltop château, cobbled streets and half-timbered houses preserve this history. Rochet's statue of the young Bonaparte stands opposite the town hall, funded by a bequest of one million gold francs sent from Saint Helena.

Housed in the former Royal Military School, the Napoleon Museum explores the imperial epic through four themes: military triumphs—Austerlitz, Marengo and Wagram—image and propaganda, Napoleon's vast reform program—the Civil Code, still in force, the Bank of France, land registry, baccalauréat and Legion of Honor—and the private life of Bonaparte. Bearing the Musée de France label, it displays 350 objects across 250 m² of renovated space: the legendary bicorne, the young student's prize books, sculptures, paintings and touching personal belongings.

activities.text: Brienne-le-Château belongs to the Imperial Towns network, and the 1814 Campaign of France can be read here on the ground. On 29 January 1814, the Battle of Brienne pitted Napoleon's troops against the Prussian army: explanatory panels now line the battlefield. On its hill, the neoclassical château de Brienne served as the Emperor's headquarters during the fighting. Today it houses a mental health facility and opens only for occasional guided tours in summer and autumn, on reservation. Maps and information at the Tourist Office.

Brienne-le-Château lies beside the Aube, with landscaped riverbanks ideal for peaceful country walks. The trails cross wet meadows, willow groves and quiet river meanders. At the gateway to the Forêt d'Orient Regional Natural Park, these flat paths are suitable for families. Views over the Champagne countryside, riverside wildlife and pastoral serenity are guaranteed.

days_plan.itin_title: Aube Tour: Champagne, Medieval Heritage and the Lakes of the Forêt d'Orient

visits.text: The Cité Radieuse conceived by Le Corbusier has stood in the forest since 1961. This vertical village, 110 meters long and 56 high, holds 339 duplex apartments across 17 floors.
Rough concrete frames the colorful loggias. André Wogenscky led the construction following Le Corbusier's Modulor principles.
Six interior streets traverse the building constructed on stilts. The association La Première Rue opens model apartments furnished in 1960s style.
The 13th-century Église Saint-Gengoult testifies to Briey's medieval past. This Gothic gem, a listed monument, dominates the old town.
Briey-Haut's historic center preserves ramparts and remains of the county castle. Cobbled lanes wind between old houses.

activities.text: The Sangsue lake offers swimming and water sports. A 2.6-kilometer trail circles the lake.
The forest trails of Mance and Mancieulles offer loops from 5 to 15 kilometers. The forest surrounds the Cité Radieuse.

days_plan.itin_title: Meurthe-et-Moselle Road Trip: Art Nouveau Nancy & Fortified Cities

visits.text: Pontusval Lighthouse in Brignogan-Plages doesn't stand on a jetty but directly on a granite block at the edge of the beach, amid a jumble of rocks emerging from the water. It's automated and closed to visitors, but the approach along the shore is worth the detour. At the village entrance, the Men Marz menhir, nearly three meters tall, was Christianized by a cross planted at its summit. Easy parking outside July–August.

activities.text: The GR34 between Meneham and Pontusval Lighthouse in Brignogan-Plages follows a jumble of rocks set in water that is strikingly turquoise in fine weather. Allow an hour one way, with no difficulty, on sand and flat rock. The automated lighthouse stands on a rock at the edge of the beach. Best done at low tide for access to the small coves.

days_plan.itin_title: Brittany 7 days: Pink Granite, Lighthouses & Peninsulas

visits.text: The Basilica of Saint-Julien is the largest Romanesque church in Auvergne, built between the 11th and 12th centuries over a 4th-century martyr's tomb. Its polychromy of red sandstone, basalt, granulite, and gray marbles is utterly unique.
Look up: roughly 300 Romanesque capitals populated with foliage, symbolic animals, and knights follow one another down the nave. The sculpted cycle in the choir evokes the Passion and Resurrection.
Look down at the pavement of basalt and quartz pebbles, rediscovered in 1963. Arranged in flowers, rosettes, and waves, these river stones form a two-tone mineral carpet.

The 37 contemporary stained-glass windows by Father Kim En Joong, created by the Loire Workshops of Chartres in 2008, flood the nave with colored light. The dialogue between Romanesque and contemporary art is striking.
Take rue du 4-Septembre to admire the Maison de Mandrin (12th-20th c.), its corbelled façade of brick and half-timbering, and its rib-vaulted room bearing coats of arms.
The Saint-Julien Fountain, on Avenue d'Auvergne, marks according to legend the site of the saint's beheading. Its capitals reportedly date back to the 10th century.

activities.text: Brioude sits on the Via Arverna linking Clermont-Ferrand to Santiago de Compostela. Walk a stretch of this thousand-year-old pilgrimage route in the surrounding area.
Wander the lanes of this "Petite Cité de Caractère" (Small Heritage Town): mansions, turrets, half-timbered houses, and shaded squares punctuate your stroll.
Looking to cool off? Head down to the banks of the Allier. The river, one of the last wild rivers in Europe, flows at the town's doorstep at the entrance to its gorges.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Loire Road Trip: Le Puy-en-Velay and Volcanoes

visits.text: The Château de Brissac is the tallest in France with its 7 floors and 204 rooms, which have earned it the nickname Giant of the Loire Valley. Its 50 metres of height dominate the Aubance valley.

The two medieval towers stand alongside the Renaissance façade, evidence of building work that was never finished. Charles II de Cossé commissioned a new palace in 1606, but his death in 1621 halted the works for good.
The Belle Époque theatre was built in 1890 by Jeanne Say, Marquise de Brissac and a renowned singer. This opera hall welcomed the artistic elite of Paris.

Gold-leaf ceilings, precious tapestries and period furniture make up a sumptuous setting. The Louis XIII chamber preserves the memory of the reconciliation between the king and Marie de Médicis in 1620.
The 16th-century chapel has frescoes painted by Coppin Delf. Sixteen musical angels glorify the Virgin Mary and Christ.
The 250-metre water tunnel diverts the Aubance beneath the park. Its schist vault is reflected in the water, creating an illuminated underground spectacle.

activities.text: The 70-hectare romantic park invites a stroll. Century-old cedars, the mausoleum avenue, the Jeanne Say waterfall and vines make up a bucolic landscape.
The village of Brissac-Quincé nestles in a vineyard bordered by the Aubance. The 16th-century church and the winegrowers' houses testify to the local wine tradition.
Every year in late August the Montgolfiade draws thousands of visitors to the château park to watch the hot-air balloons rise at sunset.

days_plan.itin_title: Maine-et-Loire Road Trip: Anjou and Loire Valley Châteaux

visits.text: Labenche Museum. Located in a 16th-century Renaissance mansion listed as a Historic Monument, this art and history museum has 17 rooms. A collection unique in France of 10 tapestries from the English royal Mortlake tapestry works (17th century). Also features the piano that belonged to Claude Debussy, prehistoric and Gallo-Roman archaeological collections, and sections on local traditions.
Saint-Martin Collegiate Church. 12th-century Romanesque church in the heart of the old town. The 6th-century baptistery, discovered during excavations, testifies to the site's antiquity.
Saint-Libéral Chapel. 15th-century Gothic building converted into a contemporary art space, with programming managed by the Labenche Museum.

activities.text: Brive Market. On Saturday mornings, it's one of the most renowned in the region. In the Georges Brassens market hall and on the surrounding squares, local producers and market gardeners offer regional specialties. Don't miss Brive's purple mustard, a specialty made with grape must.

Tasting of Corrèze specialties. The region offers hearty cuisine: farcidures (grated potato dumplings with bacon), mique (a poached dough ball served with salted pork), millassou (potato pancake), tourtous (buckwheat crepes), potato pie, flognarde (apple flan).

days_plan.itin_title: Corrèze Road Trip: Villages and Dordogne Valley

visits.text: Place des Halles in Brou, the beating heart of this town between Beauce and Perche. The current market hall from 1846 replaces the former 16th-century wooden structure that housed one of the region's most important calf markets. 15th-century half-timbered houses frame this lively square.

Church of Saint-Lubin in Brou, built in the 12th century and expanded in the 15th and 16th centuries. Its 18th-century furnishings and religious statues testify to this trading town's past prosperity. The bell tower dominates the historic center's rooftops.

Listed half-timbered houses in Brou, notably the 15th-century one on Place des Halles and the houses on rue des Changes with their beams carved with figures. These last vestiges of the medieval town have miraculously survived through the centuries.

activities.text: Weekly market in Brou on Wednesday mornings, one of the region's most important. Place des Halles, rue des Changes, and rue de la Chevalerie come alive with local producers offering cheeses, charcuterie, and vegetables from Beauce and Perche.

Walk along the millrace on the banks of the Ozanne, where late-19th-century washhouses follow one another in a bucolic setting. This river crosses Brou from west to east and joins the nearby Loir, offering peaceful rural views.

Explore the rural character of Perche-Gouët around Brou, a transitional region between the grain-growing plain of Beauce and the hedgerow-lined hills of Perche. Traditional farms and Percheron horse breeding farms dot this authentic landscape.

days_plan.itin_title: Eure-et-Loir Tour: Chartres, Châteaux and Proust

visits.text: The Château Vieux, built in the 13th century on the site of a Roman castrum, overlooks the 90-meter cliff.
The Château Jeune was built between 1485 and 1510 by Maffre de Comminges. Its restored rooms house an exhibition on prehistory and the filming of The Old Gun with Romy Schneider.
The tower of Queen Brunehaut dates from the 12th century. Legend attributes the founding of the village to this Merovingian queen.
Walk the pebble-paved lanes lined with limestone residences from the 15th, 16th, and 17th centuries. Climbing roses and lilacs adorn the facades.
Discover the exhibition dedicated to Bruniquel Cave. Structures built 176,500 years ago make this site the oldest human construction in an underground setting.

activities.text: Explore the terraced gardens spreading across 6 hectares around the castles. The view takes in the Aveyron and Vère valleys.
Head to the panoramic viewpoint. The cirque de Bône reveals the Aveyron's meanders nestled among the limestone cliffs. Plan a round trip during the day from Bruniquel.
Visit the arts and crafts workshops housed in the village. Painters, sculptors, and ceramicists bring life to the bastide, listed among the Plus Beaux Villages de France since 1994.

days_plan.itin_title: Tarn-et-Garonne Road Trip: Bastides and Orchards

visits.text: Walk along the Planches de Cabourg, the iconic 4 km promenade stretching along the fine sandy beach. The Belle Époque atmosphere permeates this seaside resort with its unique fan-shaped layout. The villas with their bow windows, loggias and colourful ceramics showcase the architectural refinement of the 1900s.

The Grand Hôtel de Cabourg stretches its 300-metre façade facing the sea. Opened in 1907, this Belle Époque luxury hotel welcomed Marcel Proust, who stayed each summer in room 414 from 1907 to 1914. The writer composed passages of In Search of Lost Time here, renaming Cabourg “Balbec”.

activities.text: Explore the Villa du Temps retrouvé, a museum evoking the Belle Époque, housed in the former Villa Bon-Abri. Exhibitions, collections and recreations immerse you in the way of life in 1900.
Follow the promenade Marcel Proust, named after the writer. The Méridien de l'Amour marks this romantic spot popular with couples.
Try your luck at the Cabourg casino, next to the Grand Hôtel. Rebuilt in 1911 in a neoclassical style, it carries on the tradition of elegant entertainment at the resort.

days_plan.itin_title: Calvados Tour: D-Day Beaches and Normandy

visits.text: The Abbaye aux Dames, founded around 1060 by Matilda of Flanders, houses the queen's tomb beneath a black marble slab in the Trinity Abbey Church. A masterpiece of Norman Romanesque art, the abbey transports you to the Middle Ages with its capitals carved with fantastical animals and its crypt with its forest of columns. The 18th-century conventual buildings, the seat of the Normandy Region, can be visited with enthusiastic guides.

The Caen Memorial, a leading museum on the Second World War, presents a gripping journey from the D-Day landings to the Cold War. Period films, reconstructions and testimonies plunge you into 20th-century history through immersive exhibition design. Temporary exhibitions enrich this essential place of remembrance.

William the Conqueror's Castle, one of the largest medieval fortified enclosures in Europe, commands the city centre from its thousand-year-old ramparts. Inside, the Normandy Museum and the Museum of Fine Arts house remarkable collections. The ruins of the ducal palace evoke the power of the conqueror of England.

Explore the Abbaye aux Hommes, where William the Conqueror has rested since 1087. The Saint-Étienne abbey church masterfully combines Romanesque and Gothic architecture. The 18th-century cloister, now the town hall, can be discovered during daily guided tours.

activities.text: Wander through the Vaugueux quarter, the medieval heart of Caen. Its narrow lanes lined with half-timbered houses are home to traditional restaurants and lively terraces.
Visit the marina right in the city centre. Accessible from Ouistreham via the Orne Canal, it offers an unexpected maritime atmosphere just steps from the castle.
Savour Caen's specialities in a traditional cider house. Tripes à la mode de Caen, andouille de Vire and teurgoule are enjoyed with a farmhouse cider from the Pays d'Auge.

days_plan.itin_title: Calvados Tour: D-Day Beaches and Normandy
Complete Normandy Road Trip: Cliffs, D-Day Beaches and Mont-Saint-Michel

places.name: Cagnes Sur Mer

visits.text: Climb to Haut-de-Cagnes, the medieval quarter perched on its rocky spur. Renoir, Soutine, Modigliani, and Klein fell in love with it. The Grimaldi castle-museum, erected in 1309 by Rainier Grimaldi (Admiral of France appointed by Philip the Fair) then transformed into a baroque palace around 1620, now houses the Olive Museum, a donation of 40 portraits of cabaret singer Suzy Solidor painted by Foujita, Van Dongen, Lempicka, and Cocteau, and ceilings painted in trompe-l'œil on the theme of Phaethon struck down by Zeus. Take free shuttle #44 from the bus station to avoid the walk uphill.

Renoir Museum at Domaine des Collettes: in 1907, Pierre-Auguste Renoir purchased this land of century-old olive trees in Cagnes, seduced by the light. He lived there until his death in 1919, painting despite severe rheumatism that had fused his fingers—some witnesses report he had brushes tied to his hands. The house-studio remains in its original state: studio, kitchen, olive grove—everything breathes the end of a life devoted to painting. Open daily except Tuesdays.

activities.text: Promenade de la Plage along the seafront: Cagnes has 3.5 km of promenade along the Baie des Anges between Cagnes-sur-Mer and Saint-Laurent-du-Var. Panoramic view of the snow-capped Mercantour in winter. Accessible by bike (rental on site).

If the calendar allows, the Hippodrome de la Côte d'Azur (one of France's rare seaside racetracks) hosts trotting and galloping races in winter. The esplanade offers an interesting view of the bay year-round.

days_plan.itin_title: The 15 Gems of the French Riviera and Backcountry
7-Day French Riviera Circuit: Villefranche to Antibes
French Riviera Art Museums and Galleries: An 8-Day Journey

map_keywords: Renoir Museum Domaine des Collettes Cagnes-sur-Mer

visits.text: The Pont Valentré has spanned the Lot River since 1308. Three defensive towers rise 40 meters above the water, linked by eight stone arches stretching 172 meters. Look for the carved devil perched atop the central tower—a reminder of the legend about the architect's pact with Satan. The bridge is UNESCO-listed as part of the Way of Saint James pilgrimage routes.

Step inside the Cathedral of Saint-Étienne, consecrated in 1119. Two massive domes on pendentives cover the nave—the largest in the medieval southwest, soaring over 30 meters high. The western dome preserves 14th-century murals depicting the stoning of Saint Stephen and eight prophets. The northern portal, carved between 1140 and 1160, illustrates Christ's Ascension.

Behind the cathedral, the Flamboyant Gothic cloister was built between 1493 and 1553. Its galleries feature delicately carved arches sheltering sculptures and coats of arms of successive bishops. The Chapel of Saint-Gausbert, in the former chapter house, contains the Holy Coif—a relic believed to have wrapped Christ's head.

Wander the narrow streets of old Cahors: half-timbered medieval houses, Renaissance twin windows, and soleilhos—those distinctive open-air attics typical of Quercy. Rue Nationale, Place Saint-Urcisse, and the Badernes quarter showcase the finest facades. Beneath the underground parking, you can glimpse the remains of a 1st-century Gallo-Roman amphitheater.

Climb Mont Saint-Cyr for the most breathtaking panorama of Cahors. From 260 meters elevation, your gaze sweeps across the entire meander of the Lot, the cathedral domes, and the Pont Valentré far below. The walk takes 45 minutes with 120 meters of elevation gain.

activities.text: Follow the towpath along the Lot at the foot of Pont Valentré. The trail passes the Chartreux Fountain, a former resurgent spring, and the Maison de l'Eau, a converted 19th-century pumping station. Unobstructed views of the bridge's arches from the riverbank.

Visit Cahors market on Wednesday and Saturday mornings. Stalls fill the area around the cathedral and the market hall, ranked among France's exceptional markets. Rocamadour cheese, Périgord walnuts, Quercy lamb, melons, saffron, pastis quercynois, and Cahors wines.

The Cahors AOC vineyards spread across the hillsides surrounding the town. Malbec, the region's signature grape, produces deep, full-bodied wines nicknamed "black wine." Several estates offer tastings by appointment.

days_plan.itin_title: Lot Itinerary: Cahors, Rocamadour & the Lot Valley
