visits.text: Calais belfry, listed by UNESCO in 2005, rises to 75 metres beside the town hall. Outside the town hall stand Les Bourgeois de Calais — Rodin's sculpted group, unveiled in 1895, commemorates the sacrifice of six notables who offered themselves as ransom to the English in 1347, ropes round their necks, to end Edward III's siege. The sculpture refused to immortalise these men as triumphant heroes: Rodin showed them hesitant, stooped, exhausted — and that is why it still moves people today.

Calais town hall, built between 1911 and 1925, blends Flemish style with Art Nouveau. Its 75-metre belfry is UNESCO-listed. Climb it for a 360° panorama over Calais, the strait and, on a clear day, the English coast. The clock's four faces and the carillon still mark the rhythm of the town's life.

The Cité internationale de la dentelle et de la mode occupies a former lace factory built in 1870. Calais has been producing lace since 1816, when English workers secretly brought in Leavers looms to get round the British law banning their export. Even today, 70% of the world's lace is made in Calais. The original 19th-century machines are still in working order.

The Mémoire 39-45 museum, housed in the former German command bunker, traces the Occupation in Calais through 21 rooms and authentic artefacts: uniforms, photographs, equipment. Operation Dynamo and the evacuation of Dunkirk in May 1940 are recounted in exhaustive detail.

Head down to Calais's long sandy beach to watch the constant coming and going of ferries bound for Dover. On a clear day, the English cliffs are plainly visible. This is where Louis Blériot took off on 25 July 1909 for the first cross-Channel flight — a memorial marks the departure site at Sangatte, a few km to the west.

activities.text: Visit Calais lighthouse: 53 metres high and 271 steps for a breathtaking view over the busiest strait in the world. Built in 1848, it survived the Second World War and remains fully operational. Check opening times, which depend on weather conditions.

Explore the Saint-Pierre-lès-Calais district and its former lace factories. This working-class quarter grew up around the industry that has made Calais world-famous since the 19th century. A few factories are still in operation — some offer tours.

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip Pas-De-Calais: The Opal Coast and Belfries

visits.text: Calvi's citadel dominates the bay from its granite spur—a 15th-century Genoese fortress whose motto inscribed on the ramparts, “Semper Fidelis,” says everything about the city's attachment to Genoa. In the paved lanes of the upper town, a plaque on some ruins claims “Christopher Columbus was born here in 1441.” Historians agree the explorer was probably Genoese, but the people of Calvi won't hear anything else—the legend is far more entertaining. Also visit the Saint-Jean-Baptiste cathedral in the citadel's center, which houses an organ and artworks from the Genoese period.

Notre-Dame de la Serra, 5 km from Calvi along a road climbing through the maquis, is a chapel perched on a rocky outcrop 200 meters above sea level. The view from its forecourt takes in the whole bay of Calvi, the citadel below and, in clear weather, the coast of Liguria on the horizon. Access on foot from the road takes 20 minutes.

The Revellata peninsula, beyond the beach, contains a lighthouse and several wild coves accessible on foot or by kayak. It's also one of Balagne's best diving spots, with posidonia meadows and rocky bottoms down to 30 meters. Tour operators offer diving outings from Calvi harbor.

activities.text: Calvi beach stretches for 4 km of white sand. It is well equipped with lifeguard stations, water sports equipment rental operators and beach bars. Arrive before 9:30 a.m. to find a spot; in July and August, the parking lot fills up within an hour.

The Bonifatu forest is about 20 km from Calvi, a 30-minute drive. It is the starting point for hikes to the high peaks of Balagne. An easy 2-hour trail follows the Figarella river to natural pools where you can swim. The pine and oak forest offers welcome coolness after the beaches.

days_plan.itin_title: Upper Corsica Road Trip: Cap Corse and Balagne
Complete Tour of Corsica

visits.text: Vauban Tower of Camaret, inscribed on UNESCO World Heritage since 2008. Built in 1689 to defend the Brest narrows, this red sandstone fortification has watched over Camaret cove for over 300 years. The 17th-century military architecture testifies to Vauban's genius adapted to maritime constraints. Interior exhibitions trace the history of coastal defense and naval battles. Views from the ramparts embrace the harbor, trawler wrecks, and ocean.

Notre-Dame-de-Rocamadour Chapel, a 16th-century edifice poised facing the ocean. Orange granite walls blaze under the setting sun creating a mystical atmosphere. The interior honors sailors with ex-votos and model boats suspended from the vault. The chapel marks the beginning of the Breton Way of Saint James. The forecourt offers privileged views over the harbor and colorful boats.

Camaret boat cemetery, melancholic alignment of old trawlers beached on the sand bar. Hulls rusted by time and sea spray testify to the glory days of lobster fishing. These metallic carcasses create a photographic post-industrial setting facing the waves. The site illustrates the difficult reconversion of old Breton fishing ports. Low tide reveals submerged structures adding to the location's poetic dimension.

Pointe du Toulinguet and its marine caves accessible at low tide. Carved cliffs shelter deep cavities where the sea rushes in with a roar. The coastal path winds to the semaphore offering panoramas over Pen-Hir and the Molène archipelago. Vegetation typical of Breton headlands colors the rocks yellow and purple according to seasons. Crested cormorants nest on vertical walls.

activities.text: Stroll through Camaret's Artists' Quarter where painters and sculptors have installed studios and galleries. Lanes bordered by colorful houses reveal murals and artistic installations. The bohemian atmosphere contrasts with the port's industrial past as a lobster fishing center. Cafés and restaurants offer terraces facing the sea in a relaxed atmosphere. The weekly market animates the town with stalls of local products.

Watching the sunset from Camaret pier, a long jetty extending into the sheltered cove. Final rays set the Vauban Tower and chapel ablaze in spectacular golden light. Pleasure boats rock gently while gulls wheel in the reddening sky. Anglers take advantage of the rising tide to catch bass and pollock. The peaceful atmosphere invites contemplation.

Boat excursion to marine caves and the Crozon Peninsula nature reserve. Boats departing from the harbor reveal the coast from the ocean with vertiginous cliffs and inaccessible coves. Commentary enlightens about geology, marine fauna, and local legends. Dolphins and seals can sometimes be spotted offshore. The maritime perspective reveals the full grandeur of the peninsula's landscapes.

days_plan.itin_title: Finistère Circuit: Breton Headlands, Islands & Artists' Villages
Brittany 7 days: Pink Granite, Lighthouses & Peninsulas

visits.text: Cambrai's belfry, a UNESCO World Heritage site, towers 62 metres above the city. The former bell tower of Saint-Martin Church dates from 1447–1474 and served as a watchtower until 1934 – lookouts were still posted there to signal fires.

Step inside Notre-Dame-de-Grâce Cathedral, a vast 18th-century edifice housing Fénelon's tomb. This funerary monument, sculpted by David d'Angers, depicts the archbishop kneeling, draped in his chasuble.

Saint-Géry Church preserves a Rubens Entombment in a sumptuous baroque altarpiece. Built between 1698 and 1745, it features richly ornamented interiors with a monumental rood screen and 18th-century carved woodwork.

The Porte de Paris, built between 1685 and 1692, was the fortified city's main entrance. A remnant of Spanish fortifications, this imposing stone and brick arch attests to the defensive role of Cambrai, an episcopal seat since the 6th century.

What remains of old Cambrai? The Maison Espagnole, dating from 1595, is a timber-framed house. Its exposed timber framing and projecting upper floors contrast with the surrounding brick façades. Today it houses the tourist office.

CambraiScope, an interpretation centre in the former Jesuit college, unveils the city's history through a relief model and immersive displays. The models show how the city appeared within its ramparts.

The Museum of Fine Arts occupies a 1720 private mansion. Its rooms present a collection of 17th-century Dutch and Flemish paintings, sculptures and archaeological objects found in the Cambrésis region.

activities.text: Descend into the catiches, underground passages carved in white chalk beneath the city centre. Quarried since the Middle Ages then used as civilian shelters until 1944, these cool galleries maintain a constant temperature year-round.

The Bêtise de Cambrai, born around 1830 from a manufacturing error, is a caramelised sugar sweet striped with mint. Watch confectioners work the mixture into long ribbons – a craft passed down for nearly two centuries in the city.

Circle the ramparts along the tree-lined boulevards encircling the historic centre. The route follows the former moats, passes the Porte de Paris and offers clear views of the city's bell towers, with Cambrai holding the Ville d'Art et d'Histoire designation.

Taste Cambrésien specialities in a city-centre estaminet. Local cuisine blends Flemish and Picard influences: maroilles flamiche, potjevleesch, carbonnade – generous dishes suited to the climate of the Nord.

days_plan.itin_title: Nord Tour: Lille, Belfries and Flemish Culture

visits.text: Port de la Houle and Oyster Market. Cancale's oyster-farming port comes alive year-round with around ten producers offering their cupped and flat oysters directly at market stalls. Designated a Site Remarquable du Goût, this is the place to taste the Cancale flat oyster, a rare pearl with an incomparable briny flavor, accompanied by a glass of Muscadet overlooking Mont-Saint-Michel Bay. The oyster beds visible at low tide stretch for kilometers along the jetty, testifying to seven centuries of oyster-farming tradition. The authentic port atmosphere, seagull cries, and ballet of boats create a living tableau of maritime Brittany.

Pointe du Grouin. This granite spur juts out into the sea at a height of 40 meters, offering one of Brittany's finest panoramas. To the east, the view takes in the entire Mont-Saint-Michel Bay as far as the Normandy coast, while to the west, headlands and beaches line the Emerald Coast as far as Cap Fréhel. Île des Landes opposite, a designated bird sanctuary, shelters colonies of cormorants and gulls. The coastal lookout station still watches over these waters, among Europe's most dangerous, where the continent's greatest tides clash. Legends tell that Saint Michael and the devil are said to have fought here, leaving their footprints on the rocks.

Village and Saint-Méen Church. Cancale's upper town has gray stone houses and picturesque alleys around Place de la République. The fontaine des Laveuses d'Huîtres pays homage to the hard labor of women who cleaned shellfish and crustaceans by hand. The church overlooks the port from above, offering a view down over the bay. The Musée des Arts et Traditions Populaires, housed in the former 18th-century church, recounts the epic story of the Newfoundland fishermen and the history of fishing off Newfoundland that made Cancale wealthy.

activities.text: Customs Officers' Path (GR34), Cancale - Pointe du Grouin. This spectacular 11-kilometer section winds along the coast from Port de la Houle to Pointe du Grouin, crossing wild coves and picturesque small ports: Port Briac, Port Mer, Port Pican. The trail alternates between fine sand beaches, jumbles of granite boulders, and cliffs covered with coastal heath, offering changing panoramas of Mont-Saint-Michel Bay and the archipelago of islands off Cancale. The diversity of coastal flora, seabirds, and the preserved authenticity of fishing hamlets make it one of the Emerald Coast's most beautiful hikes. The cumulative elevation gain of 468 meters is spread across successive climbs and descents along the undulating route.

Ferme Marine and Oyster Bed Tours. Founded in 1989, the Ferme Marine offers an introduction to the secrets of oyster farming through guided walking tours of the beds at low tide. The oyster-farmer guide explains the oyster's entire life cycle, from reproduction to packing in baskets, discusses the history of flat oysters, and reveals modern farming techniques. The view of Mont-Saint-Michel Bay from the exposed beds adds to the magic of this authentic experience. Reservations are essential; boots or old shoes are needed.

Dolphin-Watching Boat Excursion. Boat trips depart from the port to observe dolphins that regularly frequent the bay, notably bottlenose dolphins and common dolphins. The 2–3-hour outings also follow the coast to Pointe du Grouin and Île des Landes, revealing unique perspectives on the shoreline. Sightings are never guaranteed, but encounters remain frequent, particularly in spring and autumn.

days_plan.itin_title: Brittany Road Trip: Villages with Character, Sea and History
Normandy's Bay of Mont-Saint-Michel: Coastal Drives & the Sacred Abbey
Ille-et-Vilaine Tour: Saint-Malo, Dinard and the Emerald Coast

visits.text: The Oniria Aquarium spans 3,500 m² with 83 tanks. Inaugurated in 2021, this immersive journey follows the water cycle from Canigou's summit to the ocean abyss. Over 3,500 animals from 660 species populate ten worlds.
The marina has 2,200 berths. Sheltered by two jetties, it offers three basins, a modern harbor office and facilities for sailing and powerboating.
The fine sandy beach stretches for six kilometers. Blue Flag certified for over 25 years, it guarantees the quality of the bathing water and the environment.
The étang de Canet is a protected wetland. It is home to remarkable Mediterranean flora and fauna.

activities.text: Enjoy water sports at the marina. Diving and sailing schools, a jet-ski center, and sailboat and catamaran rentals for exploring the coast.
Watch the fish auction at the fishing port. The comings and goings of boats returning from sea offer a traditional spectacle from dawn.
Enjoy the beach clubs along the shoreline. Beach volleyball, lounging, and entertainment enliven the six kilometers of sand.
Walk the seafront promenade. Restaurants, bars, and terraces bring the boulevard facing the Mediterranean to life.

days_plan.itin_title: Pyrénées-Orientales Road Trip: French Catalonia and the Côte Vermeille

visits.text: La Croisette stretches for two legendary kilometers between sandy beaches and Belle Époque luxury hotels. The boulevard was laid out in the 19th century on the site of a wayside cross (“croisette” means little cross). Walk on the sea side to avoid crowded sidewalks and watch giant yachts offshore. The three luxury hotels—Carlton (1913), Majestic (1926), Martinez (1929)—line up their white facades facing the bay. Spectacular, especially in the evening when the facades light up.

Cobbled streets climbing toward the 12th-century Tour du Mont Chevalier, authentic views over the bay: Le Suquet is the original Cannes, perched on its hill. The Musée de la Castre, in the former castle, presents archaeological and ethnographic collections from around the world (Africa, Oceania, Americas). The ascent is as worthwhile for the view as for escape from Croisette crowds.

The modernist Palais des Festivals has stood facing the sea since 1982 (the previous building, the “Palais Croisette,” was farther along the Croisette). Climb the famous red steps where stars parade each May during the Cannes Film Festival, created in 1946. On the Allée des Étoiles, look for celebrity handprints set in concrete (like the Hollywood Walk of Fame, but more modest).

The Old Port and Quai Saint-Pierre offer Cannes' other face, that of colorful fishing boats alongside the piers for the Lérins islands. This is residents' Cannes, far from the Croisette's luster. Restaurant terraces serve the best fish of the day.

activities.text: Head for the Lérins islands, 15 minutes by boat from the Old Port. Île Sainte-Marguerite houses the Fort Royal, where the mysterious Man in the Iron Mask was imprisoned between 1687 and 1698—his identity remains unknown. Île Saint-Honorat has been home to a community of Cistercian monks since the 5th century; they produce wine and liqueur (Lerina). Regular boats all day. Plan your visit to Saint-Honorat for Wednesday morning for sung Lauds.

Swimming on Croisette beaches or in the wild coves of the Lérins islands: translucent water, seabed often visible down to 5 meters. The public beaches at Pointe Croisette are less mobbed than central ones.

Forville market is the real belly of Cannes: flowers, regional fruits and vegetables, alpine cheeses, fish from the local auction, marinated olives. This is where grand hotel chefs stock up at dawn. Every morning except Monday (antiques market).

Cannes' painted walls pay tribute to cinema throughout the city: giant murals celebrating great film posters in different neighborhoods. A walking route lets you discover them, with a map available at the tourist office. A nice way to combine a stroll with film culture.

Spend the evening on the Croisette to round off the road trip: illuminated grand hotels, the window displays of major fashion houses, the subdued atmosphere of the terraces. Even without spending anything, it is a spectacle.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpes-Maritimes Road Trip: Riviera and Mercantour, 13 days

visits.text: The wind blows here almost constantly, and that is precisely what makes Cap Blanc-Nez so vibrant. Its chalk cliffs rise to 134 meters, facing the English coast, which is visible in clear weather, in the heart of the Grand Site de France des Deux-Caps. Old bunkers from World War II still line the trails. Wear sturdy shoes: the paths can be slippery after rain.

activities.text: If weather permits, take the GR120, nicknamed the customs officers' path, linking Cap Blanc-Nez to Cap Gris-Nez along the coast. The family-friendly 4.5-kilometer loop around the cape explores the site's geology without serious difficulty. The Grand Site des Deux-Caps encompasses eight coastal villages across 7,500 protected hectares. Set out in the morning to avoid the crowds on fine summer weekends.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Villages from Flanders to the Bay of Somme

visits.text: Built in 1959, the Cap Couronne lighthouse is the only one on the Côte Bleue: a white tower with a red top, 33 metres above the sea, with a range of 26 nautical miles. It's not open to visitors, but from its base you look out over a coastline indented with small coves. Automated, its keeper long gone.

Plage du Verdon, below the Cap Couronne lighthouse, is the largest beach on the Côte Bleue, a wide ribbon of sand at the back of the cove. Pay car park, summer lifeguards, access for people with reduced mobility. It's the family beach of the area: don't expect solitude in August.

activities.text: Put on beach sandals before entering the water at the foot of the Cap Couronne lighthouse: the rocks are slippery and covered with sea urchins. The Cap Couronne marine reserve, the largest in the park at 210 hectares, begins just offshore, marked by yellow buoys.

days_plan.itin_title: Côte Bleue and Camargue: the lower coastal route in 7 days

visits.text: Low-growing heath scorched by wind, unlike anything else in Brittany: Cap de la Chèvre closes off the Crozon peninsula to the south, facing the bay of Douarnenez. At the top, a wing-shaped memorial honors naval aviation crews. In clear weather, your eye can follow the coast as far as Cap Sizun. Free parking, five minutes' walk to the viewpoint.

At Saint-Hernot, on the road to Cap de la Chèvre, the Maison des Minéraux explains why the Crozon peninsula is an open-air geology textbook: hundreds of millions of years of folding readable directly in the cliffs. The fluorescence room, with minerals under ultraviolet light, leaves a lasting impression on children. Allow an hour. Limited opening outside the season: check which days it's open before heading up.

activities.text: The round trip on the GR34 from Saint-Hernot to the tip of Cap de la Chèvre covers about 6 km, with no real difficulty but often waterlogged ground. Views over the bay of Douarnenez come one after another, and the heath turns violet in late summer when the heather blooms. Closed-toe shoes, two hours.

days_plan.itin_title: Brittany 7 days: Pink Granite, Lighthouses & Peninsulas

visits.text: The only blue pebble beach around: Débarquement beach, at the foot of Cap Dramont, owes its stones to esterellite, while all the surrounding landscape is red. On August 15, 1944, more than 20,000 GIs from the Texas 36th Division landed there. A commemorative stele marks the place. Supervised swimming in season, and good waves for surfing.

Built in 1860 on the ruins of a 1562 watchtower, the coastal lookout station at Cap Dramont still monitors the sea, including for pollution control. The building itself is closed to the public. The viewpoint just behind it, however, overlooks the bay of Saint-Raphaël, the Île d'Or and the Estérel massif. That's why you make the climb.

activities.text: Walk around Cap Dramont along the coastal path, from Camp Long to the Poussaï fishing port: about 3.5 km from Débarquement beach, with QR codes on the rocks explaining the wildlife, plants and geology. The beach parking lot is undergoing work and may start charging: bring change.

days_plan.itin_title: Roquebrune-sur-Argens: sea, villages and the Var in 10 days

visits.text: Cap Fréhel's cliffs plunge 70 meters into emerald seas. Pink sandstone and schist form natural ramparts among the most spectacular in Brittany. On clear days, views extend to the coasts of Jersey and Bréhat Island. The site has been classified since 1967 and holds the Grand Site de France label.

Cap Fréhel lighthouse, rebuilt in 1950 after being dynamited in 1944, rises 103 meters above the sea. Its beam reaches 50 km, sweeping the night with two flashes every ten seconds. Beside it, the old lighthouse built under Louis XIV in 1687 testifies to how far back maritime signaling goes here.

Fort La Latte, also known as the Château de la Roche Goyon, has stood on a rocky headland since the 14th century. Two drawbridges, a barbican, a keep and a cannonball furnace tell the story of seven centuries of coastal defense. Remodeled by Vauban in the 17th century, it offers a 360° view of the Côte d'Émeraude from the keep.

La Fauconnière bird reserve occupies Cap Fréhel's cliffs. Common guillemots, razorbills, herring gulls, and northern fulmars nest in sandstone crevices. In spring and summer, the colonies reach their peak—bring binoculars.

activities.text: Hike the coastal path from Cap Fréhel to Fort La Latte. The GR34 follows the cliffs between gorse and heather moorlands, each bend revealing a new sea panorama. Allow 1 hour 15 minutes one way, 2 hours 30 minutes round trip with photo stops.

Visit Fort La Latte. The route passes through the stables, guardroom, chapel, 20,000-liter cistern, and keep. The shot furnace heated projectiles red-hot before firing. Also discover the menhir called “Gargantua's finger” on the access path.
Sunset at Cap Fréhel. The site takes on copper tones as the sun descends to the horizon. The pink sandstone cliffs become incandescent. One of Brittany's finest spots for golden hour.

days_plan.itin_title: Côtes-d'Armor Road Trip: Dinan, Pink Granite Coast, Bréhat Island & Lake Guerlédan

visits.text: Commissioned in 1957, the lighthouse of Cap Gris-Nez marks the closest French point to England, just over thirty kilometers away. At its base, CROSS Gris-Nez keeps watch, a monitoring center that tracks one of the world's busiest straits day and night. Unlike Blanc-Nez, this cape doesn't feature dramatic chalk cliffs but offers a rawer experience, right at water level. The path from Audinghen is accessible to all.

activities.text: From the viewpoints at Cap Gris-Nez, a furtive movement on the rocks below often betrays the presence of seals. The site, redesigned in 2008, remains a prime spot for observing migratory birds in spring and fall. The headland is now accessible to people with reduced mobility. Bring binoculars; the animals are hard to spot and don't show up at every tide.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Villages from Flanders to the Bay of Somme

visits.text: If the weather permits, extend your walk along the customs officers' path to Cap Lévi lighthouse, a 28-metre square tower in pink granite rebuilt in 1948 after the first structure was destroyed in 1944. The grounds of the neighbouring Napoleonic fort, built between 1801 and 1806, are open to visitors.

days_plan.itin_title: Cotentin, Pays d'Auge: 5 days exploring the most beautiful villages

places.name: Capbreton

visits.text: Estacade: a 189m wooden pier built under Napoleon III and completed in 1860, rebuilt and altered several times throughout its history. Built using 600 pine trees, it marks the harbor entrance and faces the Gouf de Capbreton. The lighthouse added in 1950 has a range of 14 miles. Walking along the wooden decking offers a striking view of the ocean.

Port of Capbreton: The Landes department's only fishing harbor and marina, with 1,000 moorings. Successor to the former Port d'Albret, which prospered until the Adour was diverted toward Bayonne in 1578. The port's 19 boats sell their catch directly at the fish market without an auction. Sea bass, sole, sea bream and small squid, depending on the season.

Gouf de Capbreton: Underwater canyon opening right in front of the pier, comparable to the Grand Canyon and carved by tectonic activity over 270km. It gradually reaches a depth of nearly 4,000m offshore. This unique geological phenomenon shapes the waves and local marine life. The Journée du Gouf during the Journées du Patrimoine features talks and activities.

Historic center: Pedestrian street lined with medieval half-timbered houses testifying to Capbreton's maritime past. The Maison de l'Oralité et du Patrimoine tells the story of the port and local traditions. The Boudigau, which follows the former bed of the Adour, now winds through the town as a developed canal.

activities.text: Fish market: Daily direct sales by fishermen, depending on the catch landed, from 9am to noon and 3pm to 7pm. Ultra-fresh line-caught fish, langoustines, sole. Authentic atmosphere on the docks. Fishermen advise on preparation. Prices vary by season and weather.
Dune trail: discover the dune and its distinctive flora along an educational path. Information panels explain the Landes dune ecosystem. Panoramic view from the top over ocean and forest.

Fish restaurants at the port: Lunch facing the boats with freshly caught specialties. Ttoro (Basque fish soup), griddle-cooked small squid, grilled sea bream. Lively terraces in season. Reservations recommended on weekends and in July–August.

Bike paths to Hossegor and Labenne: A flat, connected network for exploring the coast. Routes through the forest and along the beaches. Loops possible by combining several routes. Bike rental downtown.

days_plan.itin_title: Landes Road Trip: Ocean, Pine Forest and Landes Traditions

map_keywords: Maison de l'Oralité et du Patrimoine Capbreton

visits.text: There are places where the numbers alone tell the story. Eleven months under siege. Two hundred Cathars who refuse to renounce their faith. A pyre at the foot of the pog on March 16, 1244. No trace of bodies - the fire was so intense that it left only ashes. The castle visible today is not the Cathar castrum of 1244, demolished after the capture and rebuilt by Guy II de Lévis, the French lord installed by the king. But the pog, the elevation change, the Pyrenees in the background - all that remains intact since the 13th century. From Carcassonne, plan a round trip by car to the parking area, followed by a climb on foot to the castle. The climb from the parking area takes about 30 minutes on an uneven limestone path: walking shoes are essential. In October, with the Ariège mist at the bottom of the valley and the wind on the plateau, the place needs nothing added. Admission €7.

Plan a round trip by car from Carcassonne for this visit to Montségur. The Prat dels Cremats - Occitan for Field of the Burned - is 200 meters below the parking area, with free access. A 1960 memorial stone bears the inscription: 'Als catars, als martirs del pur amor crestian. 16 de març 1244.' No monument, no museum, just a field and a stone. Among the names known from Bernard de Caux's records: the Cathar bishop Bertrand Marty, the deacon Raymond Aiguilher, and Esclarmonde de Péreille - the castle lord's daughter, born after 1224, so under 20 when she was burned. Of the 200 people who died that day, historians have identified 64 names. The other 136 are anonymous. This is where the journey takes on its full meaning.

Plan a round trip by car from Carcassonne to visit the village of Montségur. The archaeological museum of Montségur, in the village below, is small and unpretentious - ceramics, coins, arrowheads from the siege of 1243-1244. The arrowheads in particular leave the strongest impression: found in the precise archaeological layer of the siege, where they fell. However much you already know, holding a catalog and seeing a photograph of a 13th-century arrowhead still embedded in the earth of the pog changes your perspective. Allow 30 minutes.

Touristy, but sincere - and far more impressive at night. The medieval city of Carcassonne (UNESCO 1997): 3 km of ramparts, a double ring of walls, 52 towers, 2,500 years of continuous occupation since the Gallic oppidum. A detail few guides mention: the pointed slate roofs of the towers are an invention of Viollet-le-Duc (restoration 1853-1879), not a medieval feature. The Visigothic towers of the 5th century had flat roofs. Viollet-le-Duc restored them 'in the style of the period', which gave him a certain freedom. During the day, 3 million visitors a year. After 7 p.m., once the coach groups have left: the lanes to yourself, the ramparts in silence, the sound of swifts. If you stay inside the fortified city, it is the defining experience of the journey.

The Château Comtal is the former residence of the Trencavel viscounts. Between 1234 and 1330, the Inquisition of Carcassonne tried more than 5,000 people according to the records in the Archives de l'Aude - 900 death sentences and 2,000 sentences of life imprisonment. Raymond-Roger Trencavel, the viscount who surrendered his city in August 1209 after 15 days of siege, died in captivity in his own castle. Probably poisoned. Castle + ramparts admission €11.50, allow 2 hours.

The Inquisition Museum (7 rue Saint-Jean, 12th-century building in the citadel) presents the complete procedure - anonymous denunciation, arrest, interrogation, torture, sentence - and the instruments that went with it. The most striking case exhibited here: Bernard Délicieux, Franciscan (circa 1260-1320), who publicly contested the Carcassonne Inquisition's methods for twenty years. He was tried, sentenced to life imprisonment in the Inquisition Tower, and died there. A monk who opposes the Inquisition ends up exactly where the Inquisition puts its suspects. Ticket €9, 45 minutes.

activities.text: Plan a round trip by car from Carcassonne to reach the village of Montségur. Lunch in Montségur village: Auberge du Lys or Le Costumé, straightforward Ariège cuisine, €25-40. The aligot and local dried sausage are worth the detour.

Optional stop at the château de Puivert (plan a round trip by car from Carcassonne) - another less-visited Cathar fortress, allow 2 hours for the visit. Overnight in Carcassonne. For the fullest atmosphere: Hôtel de la Cité inside the medieval city, €280-500; you have the ramparts to yourself from 7 p.m., once the coach groups have left. Alternatively, Le Donjon (€130-220) or Hôtel Le Trois Couronnes in the lower town (€90-150). Dinner inside the fortified city: Comte Roger or Auberge des Lices, €35-55.

Lunch in the medieval citadel: Comte Roger or L'Adresse, regional Aude cuisine, €35–50. Corbières lamb in season, cassoulet from Castelnaudary (40 km away) served throughout the region—this is the real version, rather than an imitation.

Before the TGV: two options depending on the time available. The Châteaux de Lastours (30 minutes to the north) - four Cathar fortresses lined up on a ridge, all captured during the Crusade, views over the Montagne Noire, admission €7. Or the Abbaye de Saint-Hilaire (20 minutes to the south) - founded in the 8th century, where the monks are said to have invented blanquette de Limoux in 1531, a century before champagne, a €5 visit with a tasting in neighboring wine cellars. Carcassonne TGV station - TGV to Paris in 5 hours 30 minutes, or to Toulouse in 1 hour for the return flight.

days_plan.itin_title: Aude Road Trip: Carcassonne, Cathar Country & the Mediterranean
Aude Road Trip: Carcassonne, Cathar Country & the Mediterranean
Haunted Southwest - 5 Days from Périgord Noir to the Cathar Castles
Haunted Southwest - 5 Days from Périgord Noir to the Cathar Castles

visits.text: Saint-Spyridon Greek Church, built between 1868 and 1874, dominates the waterfront with its neo-Gothic façade. The neoclassical interior displays a finely decorated wooden iconostasis donated in 1886. The east-facing Eastern sanctuary faces the Latin church in a unique architectural dialogue. Services continue the Greek Byzantine rite observed since Greek colonists settled in 1676.

The Church of the Assumption, known as the Latin church, was built between 1822 and 1828 and stands opposite the Greek church. The neoclassical building has a nave flanked by side chapels and a bell tower topped by an octagonal lantern. The interior preserves 19th-century liturgical furnishings and paintings. The two churches symbolize the peaceful coexistence of Latin and Greek rites in Cargèse.

The harbor of Cargèse comes alive around its marina basin and colorful boats. The houses of the village, founded in 1773, descend toward the sea in an amphitheater. Descendants of Greek colonists from Vitylo perpetuate traditions and surnames like Stephanopoli or Frimigacci. The unique Mediterranean atmosphere blends Greek and Corsican heritage.

activities.text: Beaches around Cargèse offer alternating stretches of fine sand and rocky coves. Peru Beach near the center extends its golden sand for several hundred meters. Chiuni Beach to the north offers crystalline waters in a wild setting. Menasina and Stagnoli beaches to the south nestle in sheltered inlets. All benefit from transparent turquoise waters.

The hike to Omigna tower follows the coastal trail from Peru Beach. The 16th-century Genoese tower, listed as a historic monument, dominates the peninsula of the same name. The 1-hour route offers panoramic views over the Gulf of Sagone, Capo Rosso, and the Îles Sanguinaires. The restored tower provides access to its terrace for a 360° panorama.

Maritime excursions from Cargèse harbor explore the Gulf of Porto and Gulf of Sagone. Circuits toward the Calanques de Piana and Capo Rosso reveal red cliffs and sea caves. Trips toward the Scandola reserve cross protected waters rich in marine life. Scuba diving reveals remarkable seabeds with groupers and coral.

days_plan.itin_title: Complete Tour of Corsica
Southern Corsica Tour: Bonifacio, Porto-Vecchio and Mountains

visits.text: Start with the Ménec alignments: 1,099 standing stones arranged in 11 nearly parallel rows, stretching over a kilometre. The stones are ranked by descending height—those at the west end reach 4 metres. The site opens with a partially preserved megalithic hemicycle. Erected around 4500 BCE, these are France's most celebrated alignments. Arrive early to beat the crowds.

At Kermario, over 1,000 standing stones align across 10 rows spanning 1,200 metres. Here stand the site's most imposing stones. Climb to the old Kermaux mill nearby—the panoramic view over the entire alignment is unbeatable. In season, favour morning or late afternoon visits.

The Manio Giant rises 6.5 metres in a wood between Kermario and Kerlescan—Carnac's tallest menhir. Early 20th-century archaeologist Zacharie Le Rouzic re-erected it. Beside it, the Manio quadrilateral, a rectangle of metre-high granite blocks, once enclosed an ancient burial mound. The spot is quiet and somewhat hidden; follow signs from Kermario.

The Saint-Michel tumulus is colossal: 125 metres long, 60 metres wide and 10 metres high. Built in the 5th millennium BCE, it held burial chambers where archaeologists discovered polished jade axes and variscite beads—exceptionally precious objects for the era. The interior is no longer accessible, but climb to the top.

Climb to the top of the tumulus: the Saint-Michel chapel (rebuilt in 1925) offers a 360° panorama over Quiberon Bay, Belle-Île-en-Mer, the alignments and the hinterland. Local tradition says sailors' wives once swept the chapel in the direction they wanted the wind to blow.

Don't overlook the Kerlescan alignments: 555 standing stones in 13 rows, the smallest site but best preserved. They're preceded by a still-visible semicircular cromlech. Push on to the Petit Ménec on neighbouring La Trinité-sur-Mer, which extends this ensemble into wilder country.

Carnac's Prehistory Museum holds one of Europe's richest prehistoric collections. From the Palaeolithic period to Gallo-Roman times, displays present tools, ornaments and reconstructions that bring sense to what you've seen outdoors. Budget at least 1.5 hours if the subject captivates you.

activities.text: Begin at the Maison des Mégalithes, facing the Ménec site. Free entry, video presentation and scale models orient you before walking the alignments. It's also the departure point for guided tours allowing entry into the enclosures—otherwise off-limits in season. Book ahead between April and September.

Explore the alignment circuit by bike: roughly 15 kilometres of cycle paths link the three main sites through heathland and pine forest. Rental shops near the alignments offer bikes and mountain bikes. The route is flat and enjoyable, even with children.

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip Morbihan: Gulf, Carnac and Breton Coast

visits.text: The Synagogue of Carpentras, founded in 1367, is the oldest in France still in use. Remodeled in the 18th century with luminous rococo decor, it preserves in its basement a medieval 14th-century mikveh, a ritual bath carved into the rock.

The 15th-century southern Gothic Cathédrale Saint-Siffrein contains twelve side chapels with baroque decoration. The flamboyant Gothic Porte Juive recalls forced conversions. Inside, the treasury holds the Saint Mors, a relic attributed to Emperor Constantine.
The 1st-century Roman arch, embedded in the cathedral walls, bears bas-reliefs of chained captives. It's the only monumental vestige of ancient Carpentorate.

The 18th-century Hôtel-Dieu houses the Bibliothèque-Musée Inguimbertine. Its pharmacy preserves Moustiers faience jars aligned in period woodwork, and the museum displays paintings, manuscripts, and natural history collections.

The Passage Boyer, a 19th-century covered arcade, cuts through a block of buildings beneath an elegant glass roof. A few shops and cafés bring life to this Haussmann-style passage in the heart of Provence.

activities.text: Friday morning's market spreads across several squares with over 350 vendors. Candied fruits from Apt, Carpentras berlingots, goat cheeses, and vegetables from the Comtat Venaissin.
From mid-November to March, the truffle market convenes every Friday morning. Brokers negotiate Ventoux black truffles in hushed voices, following an unchanging ritual.
Sample Carpentras berlingots, artisanal candies in mint, anise, or violet flavors. Confectioners continue a craft documented since the 14th century.
Cycle along the Via Venaissia, the greenway that crosses Carpentras towards Pernes-les-Fontaines and Velleron. The path follows the old railway line through vineyards and orchards.

Take the scenic road through the Gorges de la Nesque between Villes-sur-Auzon and Monieux, about 20 km from the town for this stage, a 20-minute drive. Over twenty-two kilometers, tunnels cut into the rock and viewpoints follow one another above the canyon. Stop at the Castellaras viewpoint facing the Rocher du Cire, a dizzying 300-meter cliff listed as a Biosphere Reserve.

days_plan.itin_title: Vaucluse: Avignon, Luberon Villages & Ventoux Routes

visits.text: The smell of iodine and crushed ice from 8:30am: the Carro harbour fish market sets up on the stones of the quay, run by fishermen's wives while the boats come in. Ten to fifteen stalls depending on season and weather. No boats out, no market: don't plan your morning around it.

A spot for waves a stone's throw from a power station: Plage de Carro embraces the contrast. Narrow, a mix of sand and pebbles, it's renowned among Côte Bleue surfers and windsurfers. Free parking nearby via Rue des Ragues.

activities.text: Walk the Carro botanical loop, 800 metres through the heart of the village, with information panels on garrigue and pine forest. Short, flat, perfect with children before lunch. Little shade at midday.

If the wind picks up, the Arnettes spot at Carro becomes a gathering place for windsurfers: the shoal produces serious waves in south-west and east winds. A free spectacle from the shore. Swimming not recommended on those days.

days_plan.itin_title: Côte Bleue and Camargue: the lower coastal route in 7 days

places.name: Carros

visits.text: Carros village is perched on a rocky peak overlooking the lower Var valley, with 360° views over sea and Mercantour. It's a good pivot point between the mountains and the coastal plain.

The castle of Carros, medieval (12th century) then remodelled, has housed the CIAC, International Centre for Contemporary Art, since 1998. Free entry, 12 exhibition rooms, a rich collection of several hundred works representing Côte d'Azur creativity.
The Notre-Dame des Selves chapel, set away from the village, features a bell tower and an ancient core. It's one of the oldest religious buildings in the area, worth seeing in passing.
The old village lanes climb in stairways and vaulted passages up to the castle square. Parking is at the bottom—plan for the 200 m climb on foot.

activities.text: The CIAC in the castle is the main stop of the day. Two temporary exhibitions per year, a permanent collection, and the castle itself which can be visited in parallel. Budget 1h.
The Balcons de Carros circuit is a family-friendly hiking loop around the village with views over the Var valley. Best done late afternoon for the light.
The summer night market, Friday evenings, brings the lanes alive with producers and artisans. Good option if you're passing through July-August.

days_plan.itin_title: Secret valleys of the Nice hinterland in 6 days

map_keywords: International Centre for Contemporary Art Carros

visits.text: The Château de Carrouges, a listed historic monument, unfolds seven centuries of architecture—from the 14th-century keep to the Renaissance entrance pavilion, Normandy's first. Encircled by water-filled moats, it houses a state bedroom, a unique hunting collection in Europe, and the chamber where Louis XI stayed in 1473.

The château park covers 10 hectares. Wrought-iron gates from the 17th century, groves, an orchard, and medieval-inspired gardens invite you to wander. The ground-floor hunting rooms and the keep are freely accessible.

The Collégiale du Chapitre, founded around 1480 by Jean Blosset, Seneschal of Normandy, served as the burial place of the lords of Carrouges for three centuries before becoming the seat of the Regional Natural Park.

activities.text: The Maison du Parc et du Géoparc Normandie-Maine offers an interactive museum space on the geology and landscapes of the area. A local products shop, cultural programming, and a starting point for walks.

From Carrouges, marked trails lead into the Écouves forest. The Andaines forest lies approximately 20 km from Carrouges, a 20-minute drive away. The Regional Natural Park covers 257,000 hectares of hedgerows, forests and ridges in the Armorican Massif.

days_plan.itin_title: Orne Road Trip: Norman Bocage and Stud Farms

visits.text: Welcome to Carry-le-Rouet, nicknamed the "Pearl of the Blue Coast." Its marina nestles at the back of a calanque inlet and forms the town's lively heart — restaurant terraces, a cinema (the only casino on the Blue Coast), and the scent of sea spray. This is where actor Fernandel spent his summer holidays with his family and moored his wooden boat, the "Camera," which you can still see at the quayside since its return in 2024. Inhabited since the Paleolithic era (a coastal settlement discovered during excavations in 1991), the town flourished in 1915 with the arrival of the Miramas-Marseille railway that ended its isolation.

The Carry-le-Rouet Marine Reserve has protected 85 hectares of coastline since 1983, as part of the Côte Bleue Marine Park. Cap Rousset beach, at the heart of the reserve, has a marked underwater trail: if you have a mask and fins, don't miss exploring the shallows. The Marine Park runs free guided snorkelling outings in July and August, ask at the tourist office.

The Calanque des Eaux Salées awaits after a 20-minute walk from downtown (Lizard Trail, Quai Maleville). Framed by limestone cliffs sculpted by sea spray, this wild creek set in an Aleppo pine forest owes its name to a brackish spring on the site. A century-old listed railway viaduct spans the site — a photographic composition that painters particularly favor. Bring good shoes: the polished pebbles can be slippery.

activities.text: Walk along the coastal path between the port and the Calanque de la Tuilière (about 3 km one way). The trail follows limestone cliffs, passes the Pain de Sucre lighthouse, and offers views of the Sausset-les-Pins calanques. Allow 1h30 round trip.

Sea Urchin Festival (if your visit falls on the first Sunday of February): since 1960, Carry-le-Rouet fishermen have organized a sea urchin tasting at the Cap Rousset calanque. Expect around 5,000 visitors during this event that has made the town famous. Outside this date, the port fish market allows you to buy the morning's catch directly from fishermen.

Snorkeling or swimming in the marine reserve (Cap Rousset beach): translucent waters, sea urchins, rock fish, and posidonia meadows. Beach access goes through the private Barqueroute housing development (signposted path from Rouet beach). Uncrowded, it's one of the best spots in the Mediterranean for independent exploration of the seabed.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpilles, Aix-en-Provence & Arles Circuit
Côte Bleue and Camargue: the lower coastal route in 7 days

visits.text: The Autoire waterfall plunges from the rock wall that closes off the amphitheater, about twenty minutes on foot from the village along a marked trail. The flow varies greatly with the season: the display is more abundant in spring than in midsummer.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Villages of Lot and Périgord in 6 Days

visits.text: Caseneuve is one of the most discreet villages in the eastern Luberon—and that's precisely what makes it precious. Perched at 555 meters altitude, it overlooks the Apt valley with an unbeatable view of the Luberon massif. The site has been inhabited since Roman colonization. The present château, a towering 32-meter fortress with ramparts, great towers and high weathered stone walls, took its place between the 10th and 12th centuries under the lords of Agoult-Simiane, who held it for centuries. First mentioned in 978, Caseneuve was never attacked—only the Plague of 1720-21 claimed eighteen victims among its inhabitants. The château is private and not open to visitors, but its silhouette is impressive.

At the village entrance, the Saint-Jean oratory is a curiosity not to be missed: built in 1830 after a Franciscan mission, it's the largest oratory in Provence. Its pointed-arch facade with columns and pilasters gives it a deceptive Romanesque appearance. From the forecourt, there's an open view over the Luberon countryside. In the village, the 17th-century Maison Commune (former seat of the Town Council) and the Church of Saint-Étienne complete the heritage picture.

activities.text: Loop on the plateau edge (approximately 1h). Moors and lavandin fields depending on the season, with open views over the Luberon range. The Colorado Provençal de Rustrel, just 4 km away, makes an ideal afternoon excursion from Caseneuve.

Spotting the old drailles (drove roads) and clapas (stone piles used to mark parcels or shelter shepherds) in the landscape around the village. Caseneuve is part of the Luberon Geological Nature Reserve—the subsoil regularly reveals vestiges of intense Gallo-Roman colonization.

days_plan.itin_title: The 15 Most Beautiful Villages of the Luberon

visits.text: Cassel, voted France's Favourite Village in 2018, is perched at 176 m on the highest hill in Flanders. Napoleon reportedly declared that the hill offered “the most magnificent picture that nature has drawn in a land of plains”. In clear weather, the view extends up to 80 km—from the mining basin's slag heaps to the Artois hills.

The departmental Museum of Flanders, unique in Europe, occupies the Hôtel de la Noble Cour, a 16th-century Renaissance building listed as a Historic Monument. A façade carved with grimacing masks, lions' heads and fantastical animals. Inside, the collections cover Flemish art from the 15th century to the present—Joos de Momper, Jan Gossaert, Pieter Coeke van Aelst—with displays arranged in thematic pairs.

The Kasteel Meulen (“castle mill”), a landmark windmill, stands at the top of the hill. Until the early 20th century, some twenty wooden mills dotted the slopes. This rebuilt mill recalls Flanders' agricultural role—cereals, flax and rapeseed.

Notre-Dame de la Crypte collegiate church, at one end of Grand-Place, preserves a 16th-century statue before which Marshal Foch prayed daily when he installed his headquarters in Cassel in 1914. His kepi, gifted after the war, is exhibited in the museum.

The public garden, at the top of the hill, is a maze of small spaces: a vegetable garden, a formal French garden, a contemporary garden and viewpoint maps. The UNESCO-listed giants Reuze Papa (6.25 m) and Reuze Maman (5.85 m) parade at the winter carnival and at Easter.

activities.text: The “Cassel par rues et ruelles” route winds through cobbled streets, past Flemish houses, the 19th-century rampe alpine and Marshal Foch's statue. Yellow-brick architecture, crow-stepped gables and estaminet signs create an intact setting.

Flemish estaminets—le Breughel, le T'Kasteelhof—serve carbonnade flamande, potjevleesch, Welsh rarebit, and homemade chips in an atmosphere of wood panelling and beer. A gastronomic experience inseparable from the visit.
The Mont des Récollets garden, 5 minutes away by car, is a lush private garden open to visitors. Flower-filled terraces, botanical collections and a panoramic view over the Flemish plain.

days_plan.itin_title: Opal Coast Villages and Flemish Heartlands
The Most Beautiful Villages from Flanders to the Bay of Somme

visits.text: Arrive early in Cassis - the parking lots fill up fast in high season. The port is delightful, with its pastel façades, its terraces and its rows of pointus. From there, look up at Cap Canaille to the east: at 394 meters, it is the highest sea cliff in France. The ochre-red color of the rock at sunset is a show in itself.

Head on foot toward Port-Miou calanque, 20 minutes from the center. This long 1,400-meter fjord, bordered by remains of an old limestone quarry operated from the 18th century until 1981, now serves as a natural harbor for hundreds of sailboats. In Provençal, “Port-Miou” means “good harbor”—it's the perfect shelter on windy days.

Continue on the GR98 trail to Port-Pin—allow 40 minutes from Port-Miou. You'll recognize it by its small sand and pebble beach framed by Aleppo pines (hence its name). The water is translucent, turquoise—you'd think you were in the Caribbean. If you're there early morning, you'll have the beach almost to yourself.

For motivated hikers, push on to the En-Vau belvedere—170 meters above the sea, aligned with the canyon. En-Vau is considered the massif's most beautiful calanque: vertical white cliffs 100 meters high plunge into impossibly blue water. Warning: the descent to the beach is steep and technical (Portalet passage, fixed rope), bring good shoes. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes to 2 hours from central Cassis.

activities.text: If hiking doesn't appeal, board a cruise from Cassis harbor. Boats depart every 30 minutes in season for a calanques tour—3, 5, or 8 calanques depending on the formula. You'll see Port-Miou, Port-Pin, and En-Vau from the sea, which lets you appreciate the cliff heights. Allow 45 minutes to 2 hours depending on the route.

Late afternoon, take the Route des Crêtes between Cassis and La Ciotat (D141). Over 15 km, this cliff road winds along the top of the Soubeyranes cliffs with viewpoints offering plunging views over Cassis on one side and La Ciotat bay on the other. Warning: the road closes in strong wind (mistral over 60 km/h). Best time is late afternoon for the light.

days_plan.itin_title: From Marseille to Aix-en-Provence: Calanques, Hilltop Villages and Provençal Light

visits.text: Casteljaloux is the only spa town in Lot-et-Garonne, nestled among the Landes pines on the edge of the Landes de Gascogne. The Bains de Casteljaloux are the focal point of a stay here: the thermal water is drawn from a depth of more than 1,200 metres and emerges naturally at 42°C, rich in chloride and sulphate minerals. It is recognised for its effects on joint pain, lower-back pain and neuralgia. The modern thermal centre opened in 1995, but the reputation of its waters dates back to the 19th century, when the town was known as ‘Casteljaloux-les-Bains’. Two pools, one indoor and one outdoor, along with hot tubs, a sauna and a hammam make up the thermal leisure area, ideal for a restorative stop at the end of the road trip.

The Church of Notre-Dame-de-l'Assomption is listed as a historic monument. Built in the 15th century and altered in the 17th, it contains fine stained-glass windows and overlooks the old centre of the town. Casteljaloux was a Protestant stronghold under the Albret family: Jeanne d'Albret and her son Henri of Navarre stayed here regularly, making the town a bastion of Protestantism until the revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685.

The 16th-century Maison du Roy now houses the tourist office. Its name comes not from Henri IV but from Louis XIII and Louis XIV, who stayed here when passing through the region. The building has kept its handsome half-timbered facade.

Walk through the lanes of old Casteljaloux to find the 15th- and 16th-century half-timbered houses with overhanging upper floors. Around ten survive, one of which is listed as a historic monument. Remnants of the 14th-century ramparts still partially surround the historic centre.

activities.text: Lake Clarens, 2 km south-west of the town, is Casteljaloux’s recreational lake. It was created between 1974 and 1976 and opened in 1977. Its 15 hectares are bordered by fine sandy beaches and pine-covered shores, with supervised swimming in summer, fishing, pedal boats and canoeing. A walking trail circles the lake; allow 45 minutes for a leisurely circuit.

In season, the Lake Clarens leisure centre offers giant inflatable structures on the water, treetop adventure courses, zip lines and an orienteering trail through the pines. Operators also offer flyboarding and paddleboarding. It is ideal for a final active day before continuing your journey.

Treat yourself to half a day at the thermal baths or book an individual session in the thermal leisure area. You do not need to be undergoing medical treatment to enjoy it. The outdoor thermal-water pool at 34°C is particularly pleasant at the end of the day. Book online or directly at reception.

Waymarked trails through the Landes de Gascogne forest start in Casteljaloux. The maritime pine forest stretches endlessly to the south. Walking or cycling for a few kilometres beneath the pines, amid the quiet scents of resin and moss, provides a striking contrast with the medieval bastides visited since the beginning of the trip.

days_plan.itin_title: Lot-et-Garonne Road Trip: Bastides and Villages

visits.text: Follow the winding path leading to Notre-Dame-du-Roc chapel, lined with wayside shrines marking the Stations of the Cross. The sanctuary stands atop a limestone rock roughly 184 meters high overlooking Castellane. The panorama takes in the village rooftops, the Verdon and the first foothills around the gorges.

The Verdon gorges display their vertiginous canyon with emerald waters. Cliffs 700 meters high frame Europe's largest canyon. The river has sculpted this geological masterpiece in white Jurassic limestone over millennia.

The Route des Crêtes winds along the edge of sheer drops; allow for a round trip from Castellane within the day. Viewpoints follow one another, offering dizzying views down into the canyon. Each bend reveals a new perspective on the turquoise meanders of the Verdon and the steep rock faces.

The old village of Castellane preserves its medieval gates and 14th-century ramparts. Walk through cobbled streets where Provençal houses line up. Place Marcel-Sauvaire brings the town center to life with its market and shaded terraces.
Saint-Victor Church combines Romanesque and Baroque architecture. The restored frescoes illuminate the nave with their vivid colors.

activities.text: Canyoning plunges you into the heart of the Verdon's secondary gorges. Natural slides, jumps into pools and rappels punctuate the descent. Rocky walls enclose crystal-clear streams, creating the atmosphere of a cathedral of stone.

The Martel trail crosses the canyon floor for 16 kilometers; allow for a round trip from Castellane within the day to reach this hike. The legendary route follows in the footsteps of the explorers of 1905 between Chalet de la Maline and Point Sublime. Tunnels carved into the rock, metal ladders and exposed sections mark this exceptional hike.
Rafting on the Verdon offers thrills in the rapids. Boats glide between canyon walls in a magnificent setting. Calm stretches let you admire cliff-dwelling wildlife and the vertiginous cliffs.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpes-de-Haute-Provence Tour: Lavender and Hilltop Villages
Forcalquier & Verdon Gorges Road Trip
Alpine Hinterland and Verdon Gorges: From Thorenc to Riez

places.name: Castelnou

visits.text: Castelnou crowns an Aspres hill, dominated by its 10th-century viscounty castle whose plan forms an irregular pentagon adapted to the rock. The village hasn't changed silhouette since the Middle Ages: schist houses with canal-tiled roofs, steep lanes, ramparts three meters thick.

The viscounty castle served as residence to the Vallespir viscounts from the 10th to 14th centuries. Classified as a Historic Monument, it's open to visitors: discover a collection of medieval weapons, recreated furniture, and a plunging view over the Roussillon plain to the Mediterranean.

From the battlements, the view reaches Mount Canigou (2,784 m), the Catalans' sacred mountain. In clear weather, snowy foothills stand out to the southwest. To the northeast, the plain of Thuir and Aspres vineyards stretch to Perpignan.
The church of Santa Maria del Mercadal, 12th-century Romanesque, stands outside the ramparts. Its name recalls the market (mercadal in Catalan) once held at the village foot.

Two main lanes structure the village: the carrer d'avall (lower street) and carrer del mig (middle street). Brown schist façades, sometimes enhanced with pink marble lintels, testify to Catalan builders' expertise.
Artist galleries and potter workshops occupy old shops. The village counts a dozen permanent creators whose productions draw inspiration from local materials: terracotta, schist, olive wood.

activities.text: Marked trails around Castelnou cross the Aspres maquis, covered with holm oaks, rockroses, and strawberry trees. The castle loop offers an aerial view of the fortified village.
The Aspres terroir produces AOC Côtes du Roussillon wines. Several estates around Castelnou and Thuir offer tastings of grenache, syrah, and mourvèdre grown at Canigou's foot.
The priory of Serrabona, about thirty kilometers into the Aspres, preserves a carved pink marble tribune from the 12th century, considered a masterpiece of Catalan Romanesque art.

days_plan.itin_title: Occitanie's 13 Most Beautiful Villages

map_keywords: Église Santa Maria del Mercadal Castelnou

visits.text: Saint-Sauveur Church has stood on Place de la Raison since 961. Rebuilt in 1254, it served as a priory of Moissac Abbey until 1626. Its hexagonal bell tower and 19th-century stained glass illustrate southern Gothic architecture.
Cross the Eiffel Footbridge spanning the Canal de Garonne. This metal structure built by the Eiffel company connects the train station to the marina.
Port Jacques-Yves Cousteau has welcomed barges since 1998. A Corten steel sculpture pays tribute to the commander, and the flower-lined banks invite a stroll.
The Town Hall has occupied the former Carmelite convent since 1791. Rebuilt between 1824 and 1827 after a fire, it was completed in the 19th century with a clock and two statues.
The grain market hall retains its traditional architecture. Markets were held here from the time the town was founded in the Middle Ages.

activities.text: Head up to the belvedere overlooking the Garonne. The view stretches across the valley and the surrounding hillsides.
Walk along the Canal des Deux Mers. Plane trees line the banks, where cyclists and walkers come and go.
From November to April, visit the market for fattened poultry and foie gras held every Thursday morning. Foie gras, confits and specialties from southwestern France are displayed in the market hall.

days_plan.itin_title: Tarn-et-Garonne Road Trip: Bastides and Orchards

visits.text: The Goya Museum occupies the former episcopal palace, built in 1675 to designs by Versailles' architect. It's France's only museum entirely devoted to Hispanic art: Goya, Velázquez, Murillo, Picasso, Dalí, and Miró share 23 rooms.

The houses on the Agout River are Castres' emblem. From Quai des Jacobins, admire their pastel façades—white, green, blue, orange—plunging directly into the water. Former homes of tanners, dyers, and weavers, they evoke a little Venice of Languedoc.

At the foot of the Goya Museum, the jardins de l'Évêché were designed by Le Nôtre, Louis XIV's gardener. This listed French formal garden offers a carefully arranged geometric perspective, visible from the palace's second floor.

Place Jean Jaurès, bordered by handsome granite façades and arcades, is the city's beating heart. The market sets up here four days a week with local products, amid the lilting accents of southwestern France.

The national center and museum dedicated to the public orator born in Castres in 1859 traces his political career and pacifist struggle. Documents, photographs, and personal objects shed light on this major figure in French history.

Explore the old town's narrow streets: mullioned windows, corner turrets, and Renaissance mansions like Hôtel de Viviès or Hôtel Nayrac reveal the past wealth of this town with the Ville d'Art et d'Histoire designation.

activities.text: Board a river passenger boat, a faithful reproduction of 17th-century river stagecoaches. The wooden boat takes you upstream along the Agout to parc de Gourjade, the city's green lung.
Taste nougatine castraise, the city's emblematic crunchy confection, in one of the downtown pastry shops. It's a classic local specialty.

Drive to the Sidobre, a granite plateau east of Castres, about 30 minutes by car from the town. Rocks with extraordinary shapes - the Peyro Clabado (780 tonnes balanced in place), the Rocher Tremblant des Sept Faux - dot the forests and rivers.

days_plan.itin_title: Tarn Road Trip: Albi & Hilltop Villages

visits.text: Notre-Dame Church in Caudebec — Called "the finest chapel in the kingdom" by Henry IV, this flamboyant Gothic church from the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries displays a lace-like stone façade with 333 statues. Its Renaissance organ and stained glass rank among Normandy's artistic treasures.

Templars House — This thirteenth-century half-timbered medieval house, among Normandy's oldest, houses a local history museum. Its carved beams and low rooms testify to the civil architecture of the Middle Ages.

activities.text: MuséoSeine — This modern museum opened in 2015 traces the history of the river, of navigation, and of the tidal bore that surged over Caudebec until 1963. Scale models of Viking ships, gabare sailing barges, and river barges evoke 2,000 years of river history.

Seine quayside at Caudebec-en-Caux — Along the river, the walkway follows the quays and opens onto a clear view of the meanders and of the cargo ships heading up toward Rouen. A simple moment to grasp the bond between the town and the Seine.

Boucles de la Seine Normande Regional Nature Park — This 89,000-hectare park protects the Seine's meanders, the Brotonne and Roumare forests, the marshes, and the orchards. Hiking, bird-watching, and discovery of Normandy's rural heritage.

days_plan.itin_title: Seine-Maritime Road Trip: The Cliffs of Étretat, Rouen & Jumièges Abbey

visits.text: Notre-Dame Church from the 13th century displays southern Gothic architecture. Its brick bell tower dominates the bastide.
Place de la Mairie preserves the arcades where merchants once traded. The town hall occupies an 18th-century bourgeois mansion.
The grain market hall hosts the traditional market. Caussade was the hat-making capital in the 19th century, producing straw hats exported worldwide.

activities.text: Explore the morning market that brings the bastide to life. Producers and artisans display specialties from Quercy.
Learn the history of Caussade hat-making. Workshops produced up to 3 million hats annually in the early 20th century.

days_plan.itin_title: Tarn-et-Garonne Road Trip: Bastides and Orchards

visits.text: The Pont d'Espagne, at 1,500 meters altitude and seven kilometers south of Cauterets, is a stone bridge from 1886 spanning the confluence of the Gave de Gaube and the Gave du Marcadau. A former pastoral route linking France to Spain via mountain passes, it marks the entrance to the heart of the Pyrenees National Park. The waterfall beside it is accessible in a few minutes' walk from the parking lot.

Lac de Gaube, nestled at an altitude of 1,725 meters, has turquoise waters facing the north face of Vignemale, the highest peak of the French Pyrenees at 3,298 meters. Accessible on foot in one hour and fifteen minutes from Pont d'Espagne via the GR10, or by chairlift followed by a twenty-minute walk, it is one of the most photographed sites in the Hautes-Pyrénées.

The Chemin des Cascades connects La Raillère to Pont d'Espagne over approximately four kilometers through the forest. Six waterfalls lie one after another along the Gave de Jéret: the Lutour waterfall, the Mauhourat waterfall above the old sulfur baths, the Escane-Gat waterfall (literally “cat strangler” in Gascon), the Ceriset waterfall with its enormous balancing rock, the Pouey Bacou waterfall, which you can get right up close to, and the Boussès waterfall.

The spa village of Cauterets retains its 19th-century resort architecture, from the era when the aristocracy came to take the waters. Victor Hugo, George Sand, and Chateaubriand stayed here. The spa center offers treatments and a balneotherapy area.

The Marcadau Valley opens out beyond Pont d'Espagne toward the Clot plateau and the Wallon mountain hut. This sector of the National Park is home to numerous high-altitude lakes—Aratille, Nère, Pourtet, Cambalès—in an unspoiled high-mountain setting where Pyrenean chamois and marmots are regularly encountered.

The Lutour valley, south of Cauterets, leads toward La Fruitière and Lac d'Estom in a wild setting of waterfalls, forests, and high-altitude meadows. The shaded route from Cauterets takes about four hours round trip.

activities.text: Hike the Chemin des Cascades from La Raillère: allow an hour and a half for the shaded climb through the forest, with 550 meters of elevation gain, to reach Pont d'Espagne, discovering each waterfall along the trail.
From Pont d'Espagne, climb to Lac de Gaube on foot (one hour and fifteen minutes via the GR10) or by chairlift, then picnic by the lake facing Vignemale.
For a longer day, continue beyond Lac de Gaube toward the Oulettes mountain hut via the trail that follows the mountain stream—Vignemale draws closer with each step.
End the day by relaxing at the Cauterets baths, in a renovated spa setting that combines indoor and outdoor hot pools facing the mountain.

days_plan.itin_title: Hautes-Pyrénées Circuit: From Tarbes to Cirques and Valleys
Pyrenean Thermal Route: Spa Towns

visits.text: The royal abbey of Celles-sur-Belle is one of Aquitaine’s most surprising: an Augustinian priory elevated to an abbey in 1137, rebuilt on the orders of Louis XI after the Hundred Years’ War, almost entirely destroyed by the Huguenots in 1568, then rebuilt in the 17th century by architect François Le Duc, known as Toscane. The facade’s arrangement is immediately clear: above, the Louis XIV-style bell tower over the porch; below, wedged between the rebuilt sections, a 12th-century Romanesque portal with six multifoil archivolts—the only remnant of the original abbey. These lobes, showing Eastern influence and ending in a trefoil and a human or animal head, are a rare curiosity in Poitou. Step inside the church: the height of the pillars and the light-filled nave contrast with the austere portal.

The monastic building, an imposing structure nearly 83 meters long built of rusticated stone with recessed joints, bears the inscription “Me fecit Anno 1682 par François le Duc”. Inside, the refectory with ribbed vaults spanning six bays, the ambulatory, and the crypt of the former Saint-Hilaire church—the only Romanesque section still visible—tell the story of successive building campaigns. One floor up, the museum recreates the abbot’s room and a monastic cell.

activities.text: Stroll through the abbey’s three gardens: the formal French garden created from François Le Duc’s plans, the herb garden with its medicinal plants, and the insect garden with its vegetable patch. A pleasant break between visits.

In an annex of the abbey, the vintage motorcycle museum displays a collection of nearly 200 vehicles dating from the 1900s to the 1960s, bequeathed to the town by a collector from Niort. A museum as unexpected as it is bewildering in this abbey setting.

days_plan.itin_title: Deux-Sèvres Tour: Marais Poitevin and Romanesque Heritage

places.name: Centre Pompidou

visits.text: The historic Centre Pompidou building is closed to the public for renovation until 2030. You can still view its architecture from the piazza, with its blue, green, yellow and red exterior pipes, designed by Renzo Piano and Richard Rogers. Collections and activities continue at various off-site venues, so check the current program before your visit. The interior spaces and the sixth-floor panorama are inaccessible during the works.

activities.text: The Piazza Beaubourg in front of Centre Pompidou is one of Paris's liveliest squares year-round: acrobats, street musicians, sketch artists. Head down Rue Rambuteau toward the Marais to reach Rue des Francs-Bourgeois and the neighborhood galleries.

days_plan.itin_title: The Great Museums of Paris

map_keywords: Musée national d'Art moderne Pompidou Paris

visits.text: The harbor of Centuri nestles in a cove lined with colorful houses. France's premier lobster fishing port, multicolored nets dry on the quays. Slate roofs and ochre facades compose a picturesque tableau. The round Genoese tower has stood watch since the 16th century near the Chapel of Saint-Antoine.

The seven hamlets of Centuri stretch in an arc between 110 and 130 meters elevation. Camera reveals the Church of Saint-Sylvestre from the 6th century with its separate square bell tower and the Chapel of Sainte-Croix. Ortinola houses the blue Mattei house, an "American's home" built by Corsicans who returned from Puerto Rico.

The Mattei Mill dominates the western point of the Cape from the D80. Restored in the early 20th century, it symbolizes the Cap Corse aperitif created by Louis-Napoléon Mattei in 1872. Exceptional panorama over the sea on both sides of the Cape and the village of Centuri below.

activities.text: The harbor restaurants serve freshly caught lobster, simply grilled or tossed with pasta. A culinary tradition perpetuated for centuries by fishing families. Reservations recommended in high season.

The Roman road connects Centuri to Macinaggio via the Col de Cataro at 192 meters. An old mule track crossing abandoned sheepfolds and fragrant maquis. A 12-kilometer section lined with dry-stone walls bearing witness to past agricultural activity.

days_plan.itin_title: Upper Corsica Road Trip: Cap Corse and Balagne

places.name: Cerdon

visits.text: Cerdon's cellars hold the secret of sparkling rosé wine made using the ancestral method. In the cool galleries, winegrowers explain this unique process with no added sugar or yeast: natural fermentation, slowed by the cold and then resumed in the bottle, creates this delicate effervescence. A blend of Gamay and Poulsard, local grape varieties, produces this aromatic, fruity nectar with an alcohol content of 8%. Tastings reveal a light wine with notes of raspberry and blackcurrant.

The Grottes du Cerdon prehistoric park leads visitors through an underground landscape shaped during the great ice ages. The route crosses galleries, cathedral-like chambers and narrow passages carved by water. Outside, workshops recreate life in the Magdalenian period through flint knapping, fire lighting and the use of spear-throwers. Excavations have revealed a major archaeological site containing tools and bones that attest to human occupation 15,000 years ago.

The village of Cerdon spreads its stone houses along the Veyron valley. Its lanes climb towards the church and offer views over the steep terraced vineyards. The twenty fountains dotted through the streets reflect the abundance of springs in this karst region. The Maison at the place known as La Suisse, Château d'Epierre and flour mill form a remarkable architectural heritage.

The Mémorial du Val d'Enfer pays tribute to resistance fighters killed in the fighting of 1944. The 4-kilometre historical trail crosses forests and clearings to reach this emotionally charged site. Memorial stones and commemorative plaques recall the sacrifice of these resistance fighters who fought for freedom. The peaceful natural surroundings contrast with the violence of the events commemorated.

activities.text: Taste ancestral-method Cerdon at independent winegrowers' estates on the steep hillsides. Each producer offers a distinctive version of this sparkling rosé, shaped by a unique clay-limestone terroir. Small family-run holdings, often covering 3 to 5 hectares, preserve expertise handed down from generation to generation. The legendary hospitality of Bugey winegrowers makes every visit an authentic moment of sharing.

Go caving in the numerous cavities that pierce the limestone massif. Vertical shafts, chasms and underground networks offer every level of difficulty for enthusiasts of underground exploration. Local clubs organise introductory outings and expeditions to discover formations, underground rivers and majestic galleries. The equipment provided and supervision by qualified guides ensure safety and enjoyment.

Walk along the vineyard slopes around Cerdon, between vine plots and woodland edges. The steep slopes reveal the vineyard landscape and its terraces. Head to Notre-Dame de Carmier, the protective Virgin perched on the heights, to look out over the village and surrounding hillsides. This walk offers a chance to explore the terrain and wine-growing landscapes without taking the prohibited access routes to the cascades de la Fouge.

Discover the industrial history of the copperworks, which gained worldwide renown in the 19th century. Cerdon exported silverware for hotels, stills and trays around the world. A few workshops still preserve this ancestral expertise in working hammered copper. Demonstrations of metal spinning and chasing fascinate with the precision of the movements and the beauty of the objects produced.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour Ain & Savoie Mont-Blanc: Lakes, Mountains and Heritage
Road Trip from Bresse to Bugey via Beaujolais and Lyon

map_keywords: Memorial of the Valley of Hell

visits.text: Expanded in 2022, the Museum of Modern Art houses 53 works by Picasso, 14 drawings by Matisse, and canvases by Chagall, Miró, and Soutine. Nicknamed the Mecca of Cubism, Céret drew all the great names of the 20th century.
The Devil's Bridge has spanned the Tech River since the 14th century. Legend has it that a cat was sacrificed to the Devil for its construction.
The Nine Jets Fountain dates from 1313. Its nine spouts supplied water to the different quarters of the medieval town.
Pass through the Porte d'Espagne, remnant of the medieval fortifications. Its arch marks the southern entrance to the old town.
The church of Saint-Pierre houses a baroque altarpiece and works by the Catalan sculptor.

activities.text: Experience the Saturday morning market. Local produce, crafts, and Catalan atmosphere fill the main square.
In May and June, taste Céret's cherries. The first fruits are traditionally sent to the French President during the cherry festival.
Follow the Chemins Sublimés route. Reproductions of paintings are placed in situ where the artists worked.
Explore the art galleries in the town center. Céret perpetuates its artistic tradition with a vibrant contemporary scene.

days_plan.itin_title: Pyrénées-Orientales Road Trip: French Catalonia and the Côte Vermeille

visits.text: Start with Dani Karavan's Axe Majeur - a 3.2 km urban sculpture designed from 1980 and completed in 2009, after almost thirty years of construction. The work has 12 stations (12 like the months and the hours) that descend gradually from the plateau to the Oise: the 36-meter Tour Belvédère leaning at 1.5°, the twelve columns of the Esplanade de Paris, the amphitheater, the red footbridge, the astronomical island and the pyramid. At night, a green laser beam leaves the top of the tower and runs along the 3.2 km axis. Awarded the Patrimoine d'intérêt régional designation in 2020, it is entirely free to access. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes to walk along the section accessible on foot.

Next, head down to Port Cergy on the Oise. This revitalized marina on the river bend is the starting point for walks along the towpath—a walk or bike ride of about ten kilometers follows the Oise toward Pontoise. The area is lively during the day, with café terraces along the quays.
