In the evening, head back up to the Axe Majeur-Horloge district to watch the Tour Belvédère switch on its laser beam. The laser projects from the tower's roof at nightfall and traces the entire axis—a free, often understated spectacle that few visitors wait to witness.

For this final day, take a detour through Wy-dit-Joli-Village—one of the best-preserved villages in the French Vexin, whose name is said to come from Henry IV who, lost during a hunt around 1590, reportedly exclaimed “Ah, what a pretty village!” upon discovering the place. Its stone houses hidden behind high walls, the Church of Saint-Romain (12th century, listed), the Saint-Romain fountain, and the Musée de l'Outil—housed in a farm where 1976 excavations uncovered a Gallo-Roman bathhouse—make it an authentic stop far from tourist circuits.

From Cergy, take a trip to Vétheuil (about 36 km, 35 minutes by car) - a wine-growing village on a bend in the Seine where Claude Monet lived from 1878 to 1881 and painted a famous series of views of the village in icy conditions during the winter of 1879-1880. The church of Notre-Dame de Vétheuil, whose facade he painted many times, overlooks the river from its promontory. Park at the bottom of the village and walk up - the view of the bend in the Seine from the church forecourt is worth the few minutes' walk.

End at Port Cergy on the Oise—the itinerary's starting point—for a final stroll along the quays or dinner by the water. The port is livelier in the evening during the season; reserve a table with a view of the Oise for weekend evenings.

activities.text: From Cergy-Saint-Christophe station, walk along the Oise promenade to the Cergy-Neuville lakes - bodies of water created during the new town's development that now form a water sports center. Operators offer kayaking and stand-up paddleboarding in season (spring through autumn). Allow about 2 hours for the round trip from the Tour Belvédère.

Sunset walk along the Oise towpath from Port Cergy. Leave around 6 PM in summer to catch the golden light on the river. Reflections and herons await; the view toward Pontoise opens up as you move away from the port.

Cycling in the Vexin: rental shops offer bikes in Cergy-Pontoise, and a cycle path connects the urban area to the Vexin Regional Natural Park via the Oise banks. The Cergy-La Roche-Guyon route through the Seine Valley is about 40 km, doable in a day.
Farewell dinner on the Oise at Port Cergy: riverside quay restaurants are most pleasant in the evening. Reserve for weekend evenings in season (May-September), waterside terraces fill quickly.

days_plan.itin_title: Val-d'Oise Tour: Impressionist Villages and Heritage
Val-d'Oise Tour: Impressionist Villages and Heritage

visits.text: Quick stop in Auxerre to walk along the Yonne riverbanks - the Saint-Etienne Cathedral reflects in the water, its Carolingian crypt dates from the 9th century, but we're not lingering. Head southeast to Chablis, 20 km away: 2,500 inhabitants, no chateau, no Michelin-starred restaurant, and yet the world's most imitated dry white wine. The secret lies in the soil - Kimmeridgian limestone, a 150-million-year-old marine rock that gives this Chardonnay a razor-sharp acidity and an almost briny minerality impossible to replicate elsewhere. Taste a glass, then compare it with a Macon from the same vintage: you'll instantly understand why terroir isn't just marketing speak.

If you only visit one estate in Chablis, make it Fèvre. 15 hectares spread across all 7 grands crus, vinification in stainless steel tanks to preserve the fruit without interfering oak, and a guided tasting that does what no book really does: lets you feel the difference between a Valmur and a Blanchot side by side. Founded in 1959, acquired by Groupe Henriot in 1998 - corporate takeovers often kill the soul, but not this one. Book online, morning slots fill up first.

A 15-minute walk from the center brings you face to face with the 7 grands crus lined up on the right bank of the Serein - Blanchot, Bougros, Les Clos, Grenouilles, Preuses, Valmur, Vaudésir - 100 hectares total, sitting here since the 12th century when Cistercian monks understood what this slope was worth. The interpretive panel on site is well done: read it before tasting, not after. Morning or evening light reveals the slope of the parcels better than any map.

Nobody comes to Chablis to see a church - which is exactly why Saint-Martin is worth the detour. In the portal, horseshoes are nailed into the stone: ex-votos left by merchants who shipped their wine to Paris by river and thanked the draft horses for making the journey. The nave dates from the 12th century, the silence is total on weekdays. Twenty minutes, free entry, and you leave with an image of medieval wine trade that no cellar will give you.

activities.text: Lunch at Bistrot des Grands Crus, Place du Général de Gaulle: no-fuss Burgundian cooking - house terrine, grilled andouillette, chocolate fondant. Honest value for the region. Arrive before 12:30, the dining room is small.

Walking through the vineyards: from the center of Chablis, a marked trail (about 6 km round trip) runs along Petit Chablis and Premier Cru parcels up to the viewpoint. In May, the still-bare rows expose the Kimmeridgian soil - white pebbles that crunch underfoot. In September, the grapes are there and so are the harvesters.

days_plan.itin_title: Yonne Circuit: Northern Burgundy & Chablis
Burgundy's 15 Most Beautiful Villages
Burgundy Road Trip: Cathedrals, Vineyards and Villages
Burgundy Grand Crus Route - 7 Days from Chablis to the Mâconnais

visits.text: Pommard and Volnay are about 20 km from Chagny, a 20-minute drive. Pommard followed by Volnay: two consecutive villages, two radically different styles. Pommard is full-bodied, tannic and long on the palate, a favourite among lovers of lively pinot. Volnay is silky, with violet aromas and an almost ethereal finish. Five minutes by car separate the two villages; a decade separates them in the glass.

The Château de Meursault is about 15 km from Chagny, a 15-minute drive. The cellars of the Château de Meursault date from the 14th century and extend over two underground levels, with hundreds of thousands of bottles lined up in vaulted galleries kept at a constant 12°C. It is one of the most spectacular visits on the Côte, not because of the château itself, an unsurprising 19th-century building, but because of what lies beneath it.

Alexandre Dumas said Montrachet should be drunk on one's knees with head uncovered. 8 hectares shared between Puligny and Chassagne, bottles at €500 minimum, a waiting list at producers measured in years. The villages themselves are tiny and silent - before 11am, you see more tractors than tourists. That's exactly why you should stop: see what a grand cru blanc looks like in its actual context, not in a tasting room.

Santenay closes the Côte de Beaune to the south. Less famous than its neighbors, the village produces reds at still-reasonable prices and houses a thermal spa active since Roman times - the lithium and sodium-rich waters were already being exploited in the 1st century. The casino gaming room, installed in a Belle Époque spa hotel, is one of the region's most endearing incongruities.

activities.text: The Voie des Vignes, a 13 km bike path between Beaune and Santenay, is one of the rare routes where you pedal between rows of vines without sharing the road with cars. Minimal elevation, asphalt or packed gravel depending on sections. Bike rental in Beaune (several providers in the city center). One way takes about 1h30 at a leisurely pace.

Meursault is about 15 km from Chagny, a 15-minute drive. Have lunch in Meursault, where the village has several good restaurants. Le Soufflot serves carefully prepared bistro cuisine with a list of local wines at producer prices. Booking is strongly recommended; the village is small, and so are its restaurants.

days_plan.itin_title: Burgundy Grand Crus Route - 7 Days from Chablis to the Mâconnais

visits.text: Chalencon is perched at 700 meters altitude on the heights of the Boutières massif, in the heart of Parc Naturel Régional des Monts d'Ardèche. A former Gallic oppidum, Roman garrison, then one of Vivarais's oldest baronies, the village was battered by Wars of Religion between the 16th and 17th centuries. Wander paved lanes to observe granite houses with mullioned windows, armorial doors and grain measures on the temple square—these measurement standards testify to the village's important commercial role in the Middle Ages.

From the Place du Valla viewpoint, the panorama is one of Ardèche's broadest: on clear days, you see the Alps and Vercors eastward, Cévennes and Gerbier-de-Jonc westward, Mont Mézenc southwest. Rampart remnants include the Tour de la Potence (19th century) and especially the Porte des Autrichiens, classified Monument Historique—one of the 12th-century village entry gates. The mysterious square tower called Tour de Diane is associated with Diane de Poitiers, who owned a castle at Chalencon and established in 1551 four annual fairs and a weekly market.

The church of Saint-Pierre, of Romanesque layout, and the 19th-century Protestant temple (which houses a dismountable Chaire du Désert, used during clandestine Protestant meetings when the religion was outlawed) illustrate Ardèche's complex religious history, divided between Catholicism and Protestantism. The Châteauvieux geosite at the village entrance, classified by PNR and UNESCO, tells the territory's geological formation in ten thematic panels.

activities.text: The Chemin des Crêtes et des Châteaux (12.8 km, 3h45) winds around the village and opens up wide views over the Eyrieux valley and the surrounding hills. Along the way you pass the old village gates and the Tour des Pendus. For a shorter option, the Oppidum loop (40 minutes there and back from the tourist office) reaches the remains of the Gallo-Roman rampart on the granite dome above the village.

La Dolce Via—a 35 km greenway developed on the old Eyrieux railway—is accessible 15 minutes from Chalencon by bike. Bike rental is available in neighboring communes. The section following the Eyrieux valley toward La Voulte-sur-Rhône offers a pleasant descent with panoramas over the river.

days_plan.itin_title: The 18 Most Beautiful Villages of Ardèche

visits.text: Head to the market in Challans on Tuesday morning—one of the region's largest markets. Stalls overflow with live poultry (Challans duck is renowned), local products from the Marais Breton area, mogettes and brioche vendéenne. If you are not there on a Tuesday, the Saturday market is also very lively.

Stop in Sallertaine, a village of craftspeople on the Île aux Artisans. At Moulin de Rairé, you will discover the only windmill in France that has never stopped operating since it was built in 1555. It was constructed for the lord of La Garnache, Jacques de La Touche, and the Burgaud-Billet family, descendants of a long line of millers, continue to grind wheat using wind power. The mill stands 12 meters high and produces organic flour. The guided tour lasts around 45 minutes—try the crêpes made with the mill's flour before leaving.

activities.text: Explore the Marais Breton by canoe from Sallertaine. The channels snake through 45,000 hectares of wet grassland where storks, herons and egrets nest. It's calm and flat, and you stand a good chance of spotting nutrias and migratory birds. Allow 2 hours for a leisurely paddle.

If you prefer to stay on land, pull on your boots to gather shellfish at low tide during spring tides. Periwinkles, cockles and clams can be gathered on local beaches—check the tide times and comply with the statutory minimum sizes.

days_plan.itin_title: Vendée Itinerary: Noirmoutier Island, Puy du Fou and the Coastline

visits.text: The Nicéphore Niépce museum, on the banks of the Saône, honors the inventor of photography, born in Chalon in 1765. The collection covers the entire history of the medium, from its origins to digital techniques. One of the most important photography museums in the world.

The Cathedral of Saint-Vincent, built from the 11th to the 15th century, blends Romanesque and Gothic with a neoclassical façade added in the 19th century. The Romanesque capitals of the narthex and the 15th-century stained glass are worth a visit. The partially preserved cloister offers a moment of calm.

Île Saint-Laurent, in the middle of the Saône, is home to a concentration of the city's oldest half-timbered houses. The polychrome 15th- and 16th-century façades are reflected in the river. Cross the bridge to reach the left bank and its quays lined with terraces.

Place Saint-Vincent, the heart of the old town, is framed by half-timbered houses and the cathedral's façade. Bars, restaurants, and the market enliven daily life in Chalon. In summer, the Saône quays host riverside bistros and open-air concerts.

activities.text: Visit to the Musée Nicéphore Niépce. From the earliest daguerreotypes to digital cameras, the tour traces 200 years of the history of images. Temporary exhibitions are world-class. Free admission.

Stroll through the old town and Île Saint-Laurent. Medieval lanes, interior courtyards, and covered passages give Chalon a discreet charm. The island's half-timbered houses photograph best from the quays on the right bank.

Côte Chalonnaise wine tasting. The appellations Mercurey, Givry, Rully, and Montagny produce distinctive wines at more accessible prices than the neighboring Côte de Beaune. Wine cellars are a short drive into the surrounding countryside.

days_plan.itin_title: Saône-et-Loire Road Trip: Bibracte, Cluny, Solutré & the Mâconnais Vineyards

places.name: Chalons En Champagne

visits.text: The Collegiate Church of Notre-Dame-en-Vaux is the symbol of the city — its two spires are reflected in the Mau and are visible from afar. Built between the 12th and 15th centuries, it blends Romanesque and Gothic art in rare harmony. Its four-level nave lets in exceptional light. Listed as a historic monument since 1840 and inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage list as part of the Routes to Santiago de Compostela, it was a stopping point for pilgrims. Entry is free.

The collegiate church's carillon has 56 bells, one of the largest in Europe. Cast in 1858 by the Bollée foundry in Le Mans, it has sounded automatically every quarter of an hour since it was installed. Concerts are held in summer and guided tours allow visitors to get close to the original mechanism, still in working order.

The Cloister Museum, on the north side of the collegiate church, displays the statue-columns from the 12th-century cloister destroyed by the canons themselves in the 18th century. Rediscovered during excavations in 1973, these high-quality Romanesque sculptures are now shown in a dedicated museum. Do not miss it.

The Cathedral of Saint-Étienne, a short walk away, is renowned for its stained glass from the 12th to 19th centuries, including some medieval windows among the region's finest. The nave is simpler than the collegiate church, but the glass is worth the visit.

activities.text: Take a boat trip on the Mau canal. The reflections of the collegiate church's spires dance on the water — the best angle for photographing the building. This harmony between water and monuments earned Châlons-en-Champagne the nickname “little Venice of Champagne”.
At the end of the day, walk along the gardens bordering the Marne. Châlons has numerous green spaces along the water — a pleasant stroll to finish the day before dinner.

places.name: Chambery

visits.text: On the route between Lyon and Chambéry, stop at Lake Aiguebelette—one of France's most pristine lakes. Here, boats with internal combustion engines have been banned since 1967: the silence on the water is a rare experience. Covering 545 hectares, it owes its emerald-green color to its shallow depth and clear waters. The Épine mountain protects it from wind year-round, giving it the reputation of being one of France's warmest natural lakes (up to 28°C in July). The Maison du Lac in Nances offers an immersive exhibition on the site's history and ecology. Take the opportunity to snap some photos from the shore viewpoints: the view of the two small islands and reflections of the Chartreuse mountains is worth the stop.

In Chambéry, start with the Château des Ducs de Savoie—residence of the counts and then dukes of Savoy since Chambéry became capital of the States of Savoy in 1295. It has housed the Savoie prefecture since 1860, giving it a somewhat unusual status: a functioning administrative building and a historic monument at once. The Sainte-Chapelle, built in the 15th century to replace a chapel that was too small, housed the Holy Shroud from 1502 to 1578—the relic whose presence attracted pilgrims and sovereigns from across Europe. The carillon of the Tour Yolande, composed of 70 bells (41 tonnes), is one of Europe's most important—a concert takes place on the first and third Saturdays of each month at 11am. The cour d'honneur and Sainte-Chapelle can only be visited on guided tours.

Stop at place des Éléphants to see the most unusual fountain in Chambéry—and perhaps in France (it was voted France's most beautiful fountain in 2023). Erected in 1838 by Grenoble sculptor Pierre-Victor Sappey in tribute to General Count de Boigne, a benefactor of the town, it stands 17.65 meters tall. Four cast-iron elephants joined at their hindquarters pour water from their trunks into an octagonal basin—the animals recall the count's Indian campaigns. The Chambériens nicknamed it “The Four without Backsides”, with a sense of humor that even the Henoo guide had to acknowledge. The rue de Boigne, which leads straight from here to the château beneath its Turin-style arcades, is also worth a stroll.

Saint-François-de-Sales Cathedral dates from 1779 and holds a surprise: it's unusually small for a cathedral, due to marshy soil that forced builders to drive more than 30,000 larch piles into the ground to secure the foundations—and reduce the dimensions accordingly. Inside, trompe-l'œil paintings that bring the walls to life give the impression of a space much larger than it is. The square in front of the cathedral is one of the liveliest in Chambéry's historic center.

activities.text: At Lake Aiguebelette, rental companies offer canoes, paddleboards, pedal boats and sailboats from the various developed beaches. The total absence of internal combustion engines makes boating silent and relaxing—you can approach the two small islands with a few paddle strokes. Outside summer, cycling around the lake on the northern bike path (a leisurely half-day) is a fine alternative. Worth knowing: beaches charge admission in high season and shore access is regulated—the lake is privately owned by EDF and a family.

Savoie from Lakes to Glaciers: Yenne to Haute-Maurienne
Lyon to Annecy Road Trip: Heritage and Alpine Lakes

Château des Ducs de Savoie Chambéry

visits.text: Lake Chambon is one of Auvergne's great volcanic lakes—its formation is recent on the geological scale. Some 5,000 to 8,000 years ago, Tartaret volcano erupted and its lava flow dammed the bed of the Couze river, creating this 60-hectare lake. Today its beaches, awarded Blue Flag status since 2016, surrounded by forests with Murol castle as backdrop, make it one of Auvergne's most photogenic lakes.

A few kilometers to the south, the Chaudefour valley is a national nature reserve of striking beauty. Carved into the Sancy massif by Quaternary glaciers, this U-shaped valley features sheer basalt cliffs with evocative names: the Dent de la Rancune, the Puy de Cacadogne. It is one of the most spectacular geological sites in the Massif Central. A waymarked path along the valley floor (accessible without difficulty) lets you observe the solidified lava flows.

activities.text: The day at Lake Chambon naturally lends itself to swimming and water activities. Outfitters offer canoe, pedal boat, and stand-up paddleboard rentals. The main beach is supervised July-August. At low water, pebble zones allow you to walk along the lake.

For hikers, the loop around Lake Chambon in roughly 2h30 (8 km, easy) lets you see the lake from every perspective—beach side, forest side, Tartaret lava flow side—all with Murol castle on its pinnacle in sight.

days_plan.itin_title: Auvergne Volcanoes Road Trip: Puy de Dôme and Lakes

visits.text: The Abbey Church of Sainte-Valérie in Chambon-sur-Voueize is surprisingly imposing for this small village. This 11th-century Romanesque church, one of the largest in Limousin, houses the reliquary bust of Saint Valerie, a young Christian who, according to legend, was beheaded for refusing a marriage. Tradition has it that she carried her head to Saint Martial, who placed it back on her shoulders.

The village of Chambon-sur-Voueize is worth a stroll through its old narrow streets. Old shops, the Romanesque bridge spanning the Voueize, and houses full of character create a picturesque scene. Walk up the Grande Rue du Puy for an overview of the village and its majestic abbey church.

activities.text: The Voueize gorges offer an unspoiled natural setting for hiking. Marked trails follow the river through dense vegetation. The cool woodland shade and the murmur of the water create a soothing atmosphere, ideal for observing local wildlife.

days_plan.itin_title: Creuse Tour: Valley of the Painters and Aubusson Tapestries

visits.text: Château de Chambord rises at the heart of Europe's largest walled park. This architectural masterpiece commissioned by Francis I after his victory at Marignano impresses with its colossal dimensions: 440 rooms, 282 chimneys, and 77 staircases. The double-helix staircase attributed to Leonardo da Vinci forms the centerpiece of the keep, allowing two people to ascend and descend without ever meeting. The terraces offer 360-degree views over the 5,440-hectare park encircled by 32 kilometers of walls. The restored French formal gardens feature 600 trees, 800 shrubs, and 15,000 plants in front of the north façade.

Chambord Forest Park extends across 5,440 hectares entirely enclosed by a 32-kilometer wall. The 800 hectares open to the public offer hiking trails and cycling paths through century-old oak woods and wild meadows. Abundant wildlife includes red deer, wild boar, roe deer, and numerous forest birds. Purpose-built observation points let you admire animals without disturbing them, creating special moments amid unspoiled nature. The estate is a national hunting and wildlife reserve.

Chambord's French formal gardens have been recreated from historical plans from the reign of Louis XIV. The 6.5 hectares of geometric parterres feature intricate boxwood patterns, topiary, and immaculate lawns in front of the château's north façade. The main axis, 4.5 kilometers long, extends the vista from the double-helix staircase to the canal. Trees planted in quincunx patterns and bridle paths give the grounds a harmonious structure. Flowerbeds and clipped shrubs change with the seasons, creating fresh scenes of greenery.

activities.text: Bicycle rental to explore the Chambord estate and surrounding forests. Rental shops offer conventional and electric bikes for riding the forest trails and the route around the canal. Dedicated cycling paths allow visitors to observe wildlife and enjoy views of the château from different angles. The 4-kilometer circuit around the château offers changing perspectives on its Renaissance architecture. Surrounding villages like Maslives can be explored by bike in an unspoiled rural setting.

Deer watching during rutting season in Chambord forest from mid-September to mid-October. The estate shelters approximately 700 deer whose powerful bellowing echoes at dawn and dusk throughout the forest. Purpose-built observation points let you witness this impressive natural spectacle while respecting wildlife. Males clash in spectacular combat to win the hinds. Booking is highly recommended for guided outings organized by the estate with specialized guides.

Electric boat ride on the Chambord canal running alongside the château. This peaceful activity allows visitors to admire the north façade from the water, from a unique viewpoint that is rarely accessible. The 1.8-kilometer canal dug in the 18th century reflects the monumental architecture and French formal gardens. The silent boats make it easier to observe waterbirds nesting in the reeds. Boats are rented by the hour for a contemplative family ride in an exceptional setting.

days_plan.itin_title: Loir-et-Cher Itinerary: Royal Châteaux and the Loir Valley

visits.text: Chamonix-Mont-Blanc nestles at the foot of Western Europe's roof. This world capital of mountaineering has attracted travelers fascinated by glaciers and granite needles since 1741.
The Aiguille du Midi peaks at 3,842 meters, accessible by the Alps' most vertiginous cable car. The panoramic terrace offers a breathtaking view of Mont Blanc and surrounding peaks.
Step into the Void suspends visitors above 1,000 meters of emptiness in a glass cage. The experience guarantees thrills.
The Panoramic Mont-Blanc gondola links the Aiguille du Midi to Pointe Helbronner in Italy. This aerial journey flies over the Vallée Blanche and its seracs.
Chamonix town center blends traditional chalets with mountaineering shops. The statue of Jacques Balmat points to the summit he first conquered in 1786.
Saint-Michel Church raises its steeple facing the peaks. The neighboring cemetery holds the graves of mountaineers who died in the mountains.
The Montenvers Train has climbed the mountainside since 1908 to the Mer de Glace. This rack railway offers spectacular views of Chamonix's needles.
The Mer de Glace spreads its 7-kilometer glacier, France's longest. The Drus, Grandes Jorasses, and Grépon dominate this river of ice with their vertiginous walls.
The Ice Grotto is visited inside the glacier itself. Carved each summer as the glacier advances 70 meters per year, it reveals ephemeral ice sculptures.
The Glaciorium explains glacier formation and retreat due to climate change. This interpretation center raises awareness about environmental issues.
From the Montenvers station, admire Les Drus, the Grandes Jorasses and the Chamonix aiguilles rising above the Mer de Glace. The viewing terraces open up broad vistas over this glacial landscape.
The Mer de Glace gondola now links the Montenvers site to the edge of the glacier. It provides access to the Ice Cave without using the former long staircase from the station.

activities.text: Treat yourself to the Aiguille du Midi ascent at day's end to watch the sunset over the Mont Blanc range.
Glaciers can also be discovered on guided hikes with mountain guides who share their passion for the massif.
The QC Terme spa offers hot baths facing the Alpine panorama. Steam from outdoor pools creates a magical atmosphere in winter.
The pedestrian street abounds with mountaineering gear shops and souvenirs. Café terraces offer constant spectacle of the peaks.
The Montenvers station panoramic restaurant offers unbeatable views of the Drus and Grandes Jorasses during lunch.
Experienced hikers can descend on foot to Chamonix via the Montenvers trail through the forest.
In winter, the 20-kilometer Vallée Blanche ski descent is a legendary adventure on the glacier.
The Mont-Blanc Tramway from Saint-Gervais climbs to Nid d'Aigle at 2,372 meters, starting point for climbers.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Savoie Road Trip: Alpine Lakes & Mont Blanc
Grand Tour Ain & Savoie Mont-Blanc: Lakes, Mountains and Heritage
Grand Tour Ain & Savoie Mont-Blanc: Lakes, Mountains and Heritage

visits.text: Lake Chalain, about 13 km from the stopover town, 20 minutes by road, the largest natural lake in the Jura with its 232 hectares of turquoise, lagoon-like water. This glacial lake at the foot of the first Jura plateau spreads its green reflections between Fontenu, Marigny and Doucier, lined with limestone cliffs and conifer forests. The fine sandy beaches offer a change of scene worthy of an exotic destination. The Neolithic site has revealed remains of lake dwellings 5000 years old. Waymarked footpaths go all the way round the lake.

The Hérisson waterfalls, about 16 km from the stopover town, 24 minutes by road, a listed natural site in the Grands Sites de France network, in the Hérisson valley and the Plateau of the 7 lakes. The lively torrent fed by the lakes of Bonlieu and Ilay creates 31 successive drops over 3.7 kilometres, including 7 main waterfalls. The Éventail waterfall takes its name from its very distinctive shape, 60 metres high. The Grand Saut majestically dominates the route. Pure water gushes out in a magical green setting.

The Maison des Cascades, about 16 km from the stopover town, 24 minutes by road, an audiovisual and museum space plunging into the heart of the valley's heritage. The geological origins of the site, its history and its legends are presented in a playful way. Entry is free with the car park ticket. The explanations help to understand how these spectacular falls were formed and the fragile ecosystem around them.

Joux Forest, one of Europe's most beautiful fir forests extending over several thousand hectares. The president firs, remarkable trees over 45 meters high and 4 meters in circumference, impress with their majesty. Forest trails wind beneath the dense canopy creating a plant cathedral atmosphere. The filtered light and silence conducive to wildlife observation invite contemplation.

activities.text: Full walk of the Hérisson waterfalls from the Maison des Cascades, about 16 km from the stopover town, 24 minutes by road. The 7-kilometre round trip takes about 3 hours and remains accessible all year. The well-laid-out path climbs alongside the torrent with steps and footbridges to admire the falls from different angles. The less sporty can opt for the easy 1.6-kilometre stroll from the Ilay car park. Bring good shoes, as it is slippery in winter.

Swimming at Lake Chalain on the laid-out beaches, about 13 km from the stopover town, 20 minutes by road. The clear water is inviting on hot summer days. The gentle terrain around the lake and the chance to combine walking and swimming make it a perfect family destination. Pedalos, kayaks and windsurf boards can be hired for water sports fans. Supervised swimming areas ensure safety.

Tour of Lake Chalain on foot or by bike on the waymarked paths, about 13 km from the stopover town, 20 minutes by road. The full route of about 10 kilometres follows the shore through forests and meadows. The viewpoints offer varied perspectives over the turquoise water and the cliffs. The relatively flat path suits families with children. Picnic stops at the laid-out areas make the most of the natural setting.

days_plan.itin_title: Jura Road Trip: Lakes, Waterfalls & Mountains

places.name: Champlitte

visits.text: Château de Champlitte, listed as a Historic Monument since 1909, displays its elegant Renaissance façade flanked by two 18th-century neoclassical wings. French formal gardens laid out in 2008 enhance the main courtyard.

The Musée départemental des Arts et Traditions Populaires transports you into Haute-Saône's rural society at the end of the 19th century. Explore 40 rooms featuring immersive recreations of peasant interiors, artisan workshops (leather, hemp, iron, lace), and shops (grocery store, café, pharmacy). The collection founded by Albert and Félicie Demard preserves objects and furniture threatened by the rural exodus.
The château's salon evokes the wealth of the Toulongeon family, owners until 1825. Panoramic wallpaper from 1804 titled “Les Sauvages de la Mer Pacifique” still adorns the walls of the oval salon.

activities.text: Enjoy an immersive experience with the escape game “Les bijoux de la comtesse”, which transports you to 1751 in a château room furnished in period style. Solve puzzles to recover the precious jewels of Countess Anne-Prospère Cordier de Launay.

Explore the vineyards still cultivated in Champlitte. Follow the Sentier des Pierres Sèches aux Cabordes to discover how humans have shaped these limestone wine-growing landscapes while enjoying magnificent panoramas.

Walk in pilgrims' footsteps along the Via Francigena, a Cultural Route of the Council of Europe linking Canterbury to Rome. Champlitte houses the European Association's office and is a major stop on this pilgrimage route.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Saône Tour: Comtois Plateaus and Heritage

map_keywords: Museum of Arts and Popular Traditions Champlitte

visits.text: The Château de Champs-sur-Marne, an 18th-century gem, illustrates aristocratic living under Louis XV. Its furnished and decorated interiors—painted paneling, chinoiserie, and refined furniture—are among the best preserved in Île-de-France.
The formal garden, attributed to Claude Desgots, nephew of Le Nôtre, unfolds its embroidered parterres facing the château. Geometric perspectives frame pools and sculpted topiaries.
The English-style landscape park, laid out in the 19th century, contrasts with the formal garden's rigor. Large centuries-old trees border rolling lawns and winding paths.
The château has served as a backdrop for numerous historical films and series. Its salons, staircases, and gardens recreate the Enlightenment atmosphere.

activities.text: Picnic in the château park, beside the Marne. The shaded lawns offer a peaceful setting to conclude your Seine-et-Marne circuit.
Walk to the Marne riverbanks from the château. The towpath follows the river, offering a bucolic stroll at the gates of Paris.

days_plan.itin_title: Seine-et-Marne Circuit: Fontainebleau and Châteaux

visits.text: Chanaz nestles along the Savières Canal linking Lake Bourget to the Rhône. This picturesque village is nicknamed the little Venice of Savoy for its quays lined with flower-bedecked houses.
The navigable canal invites waterside wandering. Pleasure boats pass former salt storehouses converted into artisan workshops.
Steep lanes climb between stone houses with colorful shutters. The village antique shop overflows with treasures collected over decades.
The walnut oil mill still operates the old way. Stone millstones crush the kernels to produce oil with an incomparable taste.
The Romanesque church raises its bell tower above the slate roofs. Interior frescoes date from the 12th century.

activities.text: Rent a canoe-kayak to glide along the Savières Canal to nearby Lake Bourget.
Guided cruises reveal the canal and its wild banks where herons and kingfishers nest.
Push open the doors of artisan workshops housed in former shops: potters, weavers, and wood carvers.
The canalside restaurant serves Savoyard specialties facing the water reflections and colorful facades.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour Ain & Savoie Mont-Blanc: Lakes, Mountains and Heritage

visits.text: The Château de Chantilly comprises the 16th-century Renaissance Petit Château and the Grand Château, rebuilt between 1875 and 1880. It passed from Louis d'Orléans to the princes of Condé and then to the Duke of Aumale, and was bequeathed to the Institut de France in 1886.

The Musée Condé holds the second-largest collection of Old Master paintings after the Louvre. Eight hundred works by Raphael, Fra Angelico, Poussin, Watteau and Ingres are displayed in a 19th-century arrangement that respects the Duke of Aumale's testamentary wishes.

The Cabinet des Livres brings together 19,000 volumes and 1,500 illuminated manuscripts. The Très Riches Heures du duc de Berry shines among the bibliophilic treasures bequeathed by the Duke of Aumale.
The Grandes Écuries were raised to the plans of Jean Aubert between 1719 and 1735. Two hundred and forty horses and five hundred dogs were housed in two 70-metre naves crowned by a 28-metre dome.

The Musée du Cheval displays two hundred objects across fifteen rooms in the Grandes Écuries. The harnesses from the coronation of Charles X in 1825 and the equestrian collections tell the story of equestrian history.
The Park spreads across 115 hectares designed by Le Nôtre. The 2.5-kilometre Grand Canal runs through formal French gardens, an Anglo-Chinese garden and an English garden.

activities.text: Wander through the Hameau among five rustic thatched cottages built in 1773. These Norman-style cottages inspired Marie-Antoinette's hamlet at the Petit Trianon.

days_plan.itin_title: Oise Circuit: châteaux, forests and history

visits.text: Thirty kilometers south of Troyes, Chaource spreads its limestone houses across a setting of wet meadows typical of the hedged landscapes of Champagne. The town gave its name to the famous soft, bloomy-rind cheese created in the Middle Ages under the influence of the Cistercian monks of Pontigny. The Cheese Museum recounts this dairy story through period objects, a documentary film and a final tasting, introducing visitors to this gastronomic heritage awarded AOC status in 1970.

Saint-Jean-Baptiste Church is worth the detour in its own right. Built in stages between the 12th and 17th centuries, this Gothic building houses a dazzling collection of Renaissance sculptures. In the crypt lies the 1515 Entombment by the mysterious Master of Chaource—a polychrome sculpted group that attracts art lovers from around the world. A 16th-century gilded wooden Nativity scene, a majestic organ and sculptures combining Champagne art with Italian influences form an exceptional museum collection within the walls of a parish church.

activities.text: Artisan cheesemakers preserve ancestral techniques: 2 to 4 liters of whole milk from local cows are needed to make a single Chaource. Slow coagulation lasting at least 12 hours, delicate hand-ladling—never mechanized—dry salting and at least 14 days of aging in a cool, damp cellar create this creamy cylinder with a runny center. On the palate: notes of fresh hazelnut and double cream. Chaource was already delighting the royal court at the table of Francis I. Visits are available by reservation.

Around Chaource stretches a network of waymarked trails crossing state forest, preserved bocage and hidden valleys. Family loops and routes for experienced hikers criss-cross this area where broadleaf woods, grazed meadows and viewpoints over the Champagne countryside alternate. GPS tracks and paper maps are available at the Othe Armance Tourist Office to explore these rolling landscapes between Champagne and Burgundy on your own.

days_plan.itin_title: Aube Tour: Champagne, Medieval Heritage and the Lakes of the Forêt d'Orient

visits.text: Clermont chapel can be reached from Beuvron-en-Auge along a footpath lined with beech trees several centuries old. Built from the 12th century onward, it houses an 11th-century stone altar and offers a panorama over the Dives valley as far as the hills of Mont Pinçon.

days_plan.itin_title: Cotentin, Pays d'Auge: 5 days exploring the most beautiful villages

visits.text: The oldest church in Bagnols-en-Forêt is not in the village: the 11th-century Romanesque Saint-Denis chapel stands apart, at the end of a one-kilometer trail through vineyards. It has been listed as a historic monument since 1974, and its chancel retains frescoes. It was built on the remains of a Gallo-Roman villa.

activities.text: Walk the kilometer separating Bagnols-en-Forêt from the Saint-Denis chapel: the trail crosses vineyards, with views of the countryside and the Estérel hills. Allow just under an hour for the round trip. The interior isn't always open: ask at the tourist information office on boulevard du Rayol.

days_plan.itin_title: Roquebrune-sur-Argens: sea, villages and the Var in 10 days

visits.text: The former church of the vanished village of Oberkirch, the Saint-Sébastien chapel overlooks Dambach-la-Ville from the Frankstein vineyard, with a 12th-century ossuary attached to its Romanesque tower. The first document mentioning it dates from 1285. From the forecourt, the view extends south to Sélestat and, on clear days, all the way to Strasbourg Cathedral's spire. Access is unrestricted and free of charge; the walk from the village takes about fifteen minutes.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Villages of Alsace in 4 Days

visits.text: A mummy and a Chagall in the same room: the Sainte-Roseline chapel, built in the 11th century and listed in 1980, displays the remains of Roseline de Villeneuve in a crystal reliquary, opposite the mosaic Le Repas des Anges, donated by Marc Chagall and unveiled in 1975. Stained glass by Bazaine and Ubac, bronzes by Diego Giacometti. Open only in the afternoon, closed Mondays.

Restored in 1969 thanks to Marguerite Maeght's patronage, the Sainte-Roseline chapel adjoins the cloister of the former monastery of La Celle-Roubaud. Marguerite Maeght had to go to court to have the site opened to the public. You can visit the cloister when access is available: ask on site, as it isn't always open.

activities.text: Walk down the avenue of plane trees to Château Sainte-Roseline, a Côtes de Provence cru classé right next to the chapel. Tastings and sales amid the vineyards surrounding the site. There's a large parking lot almost opposite: it's the simplest way to visit both without getting back on the road.

days_plan.itin_title: Roquebrune-sur-Argens: sea, villages and the Var in 10 days

visits.text: Charenton-le-Pont occupies 1.85 km² — one of Val-de-Marne's smallest and densest communes. It sits exactly at the confluence of the Seine and Marne. Julius Caesar mentions it in The Gallic Wars. The bridge has been rebuilt 18 times since the 7th century — Wars of Religion, 1870 war, World War II. Go down to the quays to see the confluence with your own eyes: this is where the Marne disappears into the Seine, 200 meters from the Bois de Vincennes.

The Charenton asylum—now replaced by the Esquirol hospital in Saint-Maurice—housed the Marquis de Sade from 1803 until his death on December 2, 1814. Transferred as “insane” to avoid Bicêtre, which his family considered too disgraceful, he lived there with his companion and organized theater performances for the insane and Parisian high society, with the director's authorization. Peter Weiss immortalized this period in his play Marat/Sade. The site of the old buildings is visible on the Saint-Maurice side.

Charenton's church played a role in the Wars of Religion: the town had been designated by the Edict of Nantes to house Paris's Protestant church. In 1621, during the Protestant uprising, worshippers were massacred there after the failed siege of Montauban. A violent and little-known episode in French religious history.

activities.text: Walk or bike around the quays between the Seine and Marne—the Carrières neighborhood along the banks and the village of Conflans as you head north. In 1990, excavations uncovered dugout canoes in the Seine dating from 4500 BC. The objects are at the Musée Carnavalet in Paris, but the walk along the quays reminds you that this confluence has been inhabited since the Neolithic.

Charenton is 10 minutes from central Paris by metro line 8—convenient for ending the circuit. If you have time, Gare de Lyon is less than 20 minutes away: the Neolithic dugouts passed through there on their way to the Musée Carnavalet.

days_plan.itin_title: Val-de-Marne Road Trip: Castles and the Banks of the Marne

visits.text: Place Ducale. This 17th-century royal square unfolds its pink brick and white stone arcades across 126 meters on each side, designed by the Clément Métezeau brothers and inspired by the Place des Vosges. The galleries shelter cafés and boutiques beneath centuries-old vaults. At the center, the equestrian statue of Duke Charles of Gonzaga recalls the princely foundation of 1606.

Rimbaud Museum. In the Old Mill overlooking the Meuse, discover the universe of the rebellious poet born in Charleville in 1854. Original manuscripts, rare editions, and biographical exhibits trace the dazzling creative journey of this precocious genius. The room dedicated to A Season in Hell evokes the intensity of his visionary writing.

Basilica of Notre-Dame d'Espérance. The neo-Gothic edifice dominates the city with its twin 72-meter spires. The interior bathed in colored light reveals magnificent 20th-century stained glass windows illustrating the life of the Virgin. The grand organ resonates during regular concerts.

Ardennes Museum. In the former ducal palace, immerse yourself in local history from prehistoric times to the World Wars. Collections of ancient weapons, ceramics, and artisan tools testify to Ardennes craftsmanship. The section devoted to metalworkers traces the industrial importance of the département.

activities.text: World Festival of Puppet Theatres. Every two years in September, the city comes alive with this unique event where puppeteers from around the world take over squares and theaters. Street performances, contemporary shows, and children's workshops celebrate this ancient art. The International Puppetry Institute perpetuates this living tradition.

Stroll along the Meuse quays. The river winds peacefully between landscaped banks where poplars and weeping willows offer shade. Follow the towpath to the Mont Olympe district to admire reflections of facades in the calm water. Moored barges and fishermen compose a bucolic scene.

Visit the ramparts and fortifications. Remnants of the old ramparts tell the defensive history of this frontier city. Walk the paths along the ancient walls to discover fortified gates and preserved bastions. Explanatory panels detail the evolution of defensive systems from the Middle Ages to Vauban.

days_plan.itin_title: Ardennes Road Trip: Forests & Fortresses (3 Days)

visits.text: Benedictine Abbey. Founded around 875 and affiliated with Cluny Abbey in 932, this listed monastic complex stands out for its exceptional architectural qualities. The great 12th-century portal, whose decoration is inspired by the Book of Revelation, is a masterpiece of Romanesque art. The late 15th-century cloister opens onto the chapter house through a Romanesque colonnade. The prior's chapel and the courtyard of the Hôtel du prieur date from the early 16th century. The Tour Philippe Auguste, a defensive keep more than 21 meters high and 11 meters in diameter, dominates the complex. Excavations have revealed the foundations of three successive churches built in the 9th, 10th and 11th centuries. The abbey celebrates the 1,150th anniversary of its foundation in 2025.

Silk Museum. Housed in a former weaving workshop, the museum traces the textile history of Charlieu, once a major center of silk production. The silk-weaving industry became established in the town in 1827. Working looms, sumptuous fabrics and demonstrations help visitors understand the artisans' expertise. Temporary exhibitions complement the permanent displays. This living museum highlights the international reputation Charlieu gained through its textile creations.

Medieval Old Town. Awarded the Village de Caractère and Plus Beaux Détours de France labels, Charlieu has retained its 13th-century stone houses and picturesque 14th- and 15th-century timber-framed houses with overhanging upper stories. Renaissance and classical residences line the medieval streets. The first mention of the town dates to 994. Established under the abbey's protection on the edge of the Duchy of Burgundy, the town's strategic position led French kings to fortify it, as Philip Augustus did in 1180. A prosperous town populated by merchants and artisans, particularly weavers.

activities.text: Charlieu Andouille Tasting. A source of local gastronomic pride, andouille is made using traditional expertise passed down from generation to generation. Smoked over beechwood and lightly spiced, it is enjoyed hot or cold. Restaurants in the town center serve it as a specialty. Local charcutiers carry on the tradition.

Walk or Ride along the Véloire. The greenway connects Roanne to Paray-le-Monial in Saône-et-Loire. From Briennon, a short 1.2 km stretch of shared roadway allows you to cross the Loire to reach Pouilly-sous-Charlieu, then 4.9 km of greenway leads to Charlieu. A family route for cycling or walking along the canal and through the countryside.

days_plan.itin_title: Loire Circuit: Wild Gorges and Industrial Heritage

places.name: Charroux

visits.text: Charroux, Allier's only village with the Plus Beaux Villages de France designation, crowns a hill at an altitude of 413 m. Its cobbled lanes wind between carved stone façades (15th–18th centuries) and timber-framed houses from the 14th century. The Porte d'Orient and Porte d'Occident mark the location of the former fortifications of this medieval town, once a stronghold and commercial hub of the Bourbonnais.

The 12th-century Saint-Jean-Baptiste church intrigues visitors with its truncated bell tower, a mystery finally solved: lightning struck off its top over the centuries. In the heart of the village, the Cour des Dames reveals its unique circular architecture, a grassy inner courtyard where façades seem to curve to create a mysterious space. An astonishing place accessible through narrow passages.

The Musée de Charroux et de son Canton occupies 14 rooms spread across two buildings of the former fortifications. Collections of objects, documents, sculptures and furniture trace the history of Charroux from the Gallo-Roman period to the 20th century.

Since 1990, the Moutarderie de Charroux has kept alive a craft that disappeared in the mid-20th century. Seeds crushed on a stone mill are blended with white wine from Saint-Pourçain (Tressallier grape variety), giving this wholegrain mustard its unique character. Awarded a Coq d'Or, it appeals to leading chefs and is exported as far as Japan.

activities.text: Artists' and craftspeople's studios enliven the village: RAL-certified candles (the only ones in France), an organic jam maker with 180 recipes, wire creations and local pottery. Each shop reveals authentic craftsmanship, turning a stroll into a discovery of local crafts. Local products make a better alternative to standardised souvenirs.

The panorama from the village heights takes in the Limagne plain to the north and Auvergne's mountains to the south. This strategic position explains why Charroux became a medieval stronghold. Terraced gardens offer excellent views over the surrounding Bourbonnais bocage.

The weekly market and events punctuate the year: a giant flea market in late April (400 exhibitors, 30,000 visitors), the Fête de la Soupe in November, when 50 homemade soups can be sampled in the streets, and the Journée des artistes in early August. Charroux pulses to the rhythm of its convivial traditions.

days_plan.itin_title: Allier Road Trip: Vichy, Thermal Baths and Bourbonnais Bocage

map_keywords: Museum of Charroux and Its Canton

visits.text: Notre-Dame de Chartres Cathedral, a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1979 and an absolute masterpiece of French Gothic art. Its 176 stained glass windows from the 12th and 13th centuries cover 2,600 m² of exceptionally well-preserved glazing, including the famous Chartres blue. The two asymmetrical spires dominate the Beauce plain and can be seen from nearly thirty kilometers away.

Cathedral labyrinth, a geometric pattern inlaid in the nave's paving stones since the 13th century. This symbol of the tortuous path to salvation is one of Europe's largest, with a 261-meter route. Pilgrims still follow it on their knees on certain occasions.

Cathedral crypt, the world's third-largest crypt. It forms the lower cathedral and houses the puits des Saints-Forts along with the Veil of the Virgin, a relic given by Charles the Bald in 876. One of the most popular Marian pilgrimage sites of the medieval West.

Royal Portal of the cathedral, a marvel of 12th-century Romanesque sculpture. The jamb statues frozen in eternity embody a transition between Romanesque and Gothic art that is unique in the world. The 13th-century north and south portals bear witness to the elegance of the era.

Ascent of the cathedral's north tower to access the immense metal framework and discover a view looking down over the city and the Beauce plain. A dizzying experience revealing the construction secrets of medieval builders.

Saint-Piat Chapel, reopened in 2024 after 24 years of restoration. It now houses the cathedral treasury with nearly 150 precious liturgical objects and contemporary stained glass by Korean artist Bang Hai Ja. An architectural jewel bridging medieval heritage and contemporary creation.

activities.text: Chartres en lumières, the world's largest event showcasing heritage through light. From April to January, 21 heritage sites light up every evening from dusk until 1 AM. A magical free route through the historic heart of the city with projection mapping on the cathedral.

A stroll through the old town of Chartres, between the upper town around the cathedral and the lower town along the Eure. Discover the half-timbered houses such as the Maison du Saumon, a witness to the medieval merchant tradition. The cobbled lanes reveal a well-preserved heritage.

Walk along the banks of the Eure in the lower town, where stone bridges, medieval washhouses, and timber-framed houses follow one another in a bucolic setting. The cathedral's silhouette in the background offers romantic views at every turn.

Visit the Bishop's gardens behind the cathedral, laid out in the former episcopal palace. The beautifully maintained French-style garden offers panoramic views over the old town, the Eure riverbanks, and Chartres' outskirts. An ideal relaxation spot after visiting the cathedral.

days_plan.itin_title: Eure-et-Loir Tour: Chartres, Châteaux and Proust

visits.text: Remote, austere, nearly forgotten: the Chartreuse de la Verne nevertheless stands as one of the most striking sites in the Massif des Maures. Founded in 1170 by the bishops of Toulon and Fréjus, it burned three times before the association “Les Amis de la Verne” began restoring it in 1968. The volcanic marble entrance door sets the tone: this monastery is visited in silence, out of respect for the monastic community still living there. The access road, narrow and winding, closes on high fire-risk days in summer.

activities.text: You'll continue your visit through the great cloister, a 90-meter gallery leading to the nuns' cells, then to the monastic crafts shop housed in the old cellar. Entry is free for children under 12. Observe the silence requested throughout the route.

days_plan.itin_title: Var in 4 Days: From Bormes to the Most Beautiful Villages of the Verdon

visits.text: Village of Château-Chalon, one of France's Most Beautiful Villages, perched on a rocky spur at 400 meters altitude overlooking the Seille valley. Cobbled lanes wind between blonde stone winegrowers' houses and tiled roofs. Vestiges of the old Benedictine abbey and medieval keep recall that in the 7th century, the nuns planted the first Savagnin vines that gave birth to Vin Jaune. The vaulted cellars tell the wine-growing story through the centuries.

Saint-Pierre Church, an 11th-century Romanesque edifice located in the village heart. The simple yet elegant architecture testifies to the influence of the abbey that dominated the site. The stones weathered by time and austere vaults create an atmosphere conducive to contemplation. The church houses several sacred artworks and offers a viewpoint from its parvis.

Maison de la Haute-Seille in a historic village mansion. This fun and interactive discovery of the Jura vineyard presents through video projections, audio testimonies, and touch screens the Château-Chalon AOC reserved exclusively for Vin Jaune. The 60 hectares of steep vineyards spread across four communes produce approximately 35 hectoliters per hectare of this rare wine aged a minimum of six years and three months.

Four belvederes offering different perspectives on the vineyard and valley. From these strategic viewpoints, the gaze embraces the steep slopes planted with Savagnin protected by limestone cliffs from northern and eastern winds. The south-southwest orientation provides maximum sunshine. The wine-growing villages of Domblans, Ménétru-le-Vignoble, and Nevy-sur-Seille compose the appellation with their abrupt slopes.

activities.text: Hike through the Sous-Roche and Puits-Saint-Pierre vineyards at the mouth of the Baume-les-Messieurs cirque. The trail meanders through these two emblematic terroirs where everything is difficult for the vines and winemakers. These constraints and an exceptional environment create the outstanding wine that is Château-Chalon. The route passes beneath the famous yellow rock and offers plunging views over the Seille valley.

Vin Jaune tasting at winemakers' estates. The 62-centiliter clavelin contains this wine ranked among the world's five best whites. After a minimum of six years and three months in oak barrels without racking or topping up, the yeast veil protects the wine and gives it its characteristic aromas of walnuts, spices, curry, and dried apples. Passionate winemakers explain this unique and ancestral process.

Lunch at a village restaurant with views over the vines. Terraces come alive on sunny days for savoring regional specialties like chicken with Vin Jaune and morels, or morel croûte. The pairing of Vin Jaune with an aged slice of Comté creates a perfect marriage. The peaceful atmosphere of this belvedere village invites you to linger over your meal.

days_plan.itin_title: Jura Road Trip: Lakes, Waterfalls & Mountains
