places.name: Chateau Chinon

visits.text: Le Calvaire rises to 609 meters on the site of the former castle destroyed during battles between Charles the Bold and Louis XI in 1475. Three mission crosses dominate the site.
The panorama offers 360° views of the Morvan mountains, the Bazois plain, and the Yonne valley. The orientation tables were inaugurated in 2014.
The François Mitterrand Memorial, set in an oak forest facing the Bazois plain, is a place of remembrance dedicated to the former president. He loved to contemplate the horizon opening westward.
The Septennat Museum, housed in the former 18th-century Sainte-Claire convent, displays official and personal gifts received by François Mitterrand during his two presidential terms (1981-1995).
The Porte Notre-Dame, built in the 16th century with stones from the destroyed castle, remains the sole witness to the era when the castle overlooked the town.
The Château-Chinon Fountain, a monumental work by Niki de Saint Phalle and Jean Tinguely inaugurated in 1988, numbers among the five examples worldwide.

activities.text: Walk the 4.4-kilometer François Mitterrand trail, the former president and mayor of Château-Chinon's (1959-1981) regular route. Fifteen points of interest mark the itinerary.
Hike in the Morvan from Château-Chinon, the massif's capital. Marked trails wind through oak and beech forests, valleys crossed by rushing streams.
Discover the "From Earth to Sky" project at Le Calvaire: exhibition on meteorites and Morvan minerals, weather station history since 1934, climate evolution.

days_plan.itin_title: Nièvre Road Trip: Morvan and Ducal Heritage

map_keywords: Niki de Saint Phalle fountain Château-Chinon

visits.text: Bought in 1893 by merchant Louis Prat-Noilly, the Château d'Avignon was transformed into a hunting lodge crammed with technology: electricity, central heating, hot running water. The original bastide dates back to the 18th century and the d'Avignon family. Listed as a Historic Monument in 2003. The château only opens on the 1st Sunday of the month, by reservation.

The real highlight of the Château d'Avignon isn't the drawing room, it's the pumping station: the late-19th-century pump still irrigates the estate's former lands. A water tower, wash-houses and settling tanks complete the complex, in the middle of a landscaped park of more than 20 hectares. Free access to the park.

activities.text: If the mistral exceeds 70 km/h, the Château d'Avignon estate closes to the public because of the park's branches and trees. Call before travelling the 24 km from Arles. The estate opens Wednesday to Sunday in season, with free entry and audio guides available.

days_plan.itin_title: Côte Bleue and Camargue: the lower coastal route in 7 days

visits.text: Chambord emerges from the marshy Sologne lands. 128 meters of façade, 282 chimneys, 440 rooms, and 83 staircases. Francis I ordered its construction in 1519 to engrave his power into white tuffeau limestone.

At the center of the keep, the double-helix staircase remains the marvel of the place. Two helical ramps coil around an open core: two people climb simultaneously without ever meeting. The design is attributed to Leonardo da Vinci's inspiration.

On the second floor, the coffered vaults bear the emblems of Francis I: the salamander and the letter F are repeated several hundred times on walls and ceilings. Some monograms are drawn in reverse so that God can read them from heaven.

Climb to the terraces for a 360-degree view. This “celestial village” bristling with turrets, sculpted dormers, and monumental chimneys forms a striking contrast with the restrained façades. The lantern tower rises to 56 meters.
The royal residence houses a collection of 4,500 art objects in refurnished apartments. The 18th-century kitchens and the state apartments round out the more than 70 rooms open to visitors.

activities.text: The formal French gardens, recreated in 2017 across 6.5 hectares at the foot of the château, have regained their Louis XIV-era layout. The 19th-century English garden unfolds along curved paths among cedars and sequoias.
The 5,500-hectare estate is Europe's largest enclosed forest park, surrounded by a 32-kilometer wall. Nature outings in all-terrain vehicles allow observation of deer, wild boar, and raptors.

days_plan.itin_title: The Essential Châteaux of the Loire Valley

visits.text: The château de Champchevrier, surrounded by moats and woods, is one of the few estates in Touraine where hunting with hounds is still practiced. Its long 17th-century classical façade overlooks a preserved forest park.
The reception salons preserve 17th and 18th-century furniture: Flemish tapestries, Louis XV commodes, family portraits, and hunting trophies compose an authentic aristocratic décor.

The hunting room traces several centuries of hunting with hounds. Antler tines, hunting horns, whips, and period attire testify to a tradition passed down from generation to generation by the family that owns the estate.
The château's old kitchens and outbuildings open their doors. Copper cookware, serving utensils, and larders recreate the domestic organization of an aristocratic estate.

activities.text: The pack of hunting hounds, fed daily in the château's kennel, can be observed during the visit. Ask at reception for the feeding schedule to witness this centuries-old tradition.

days_plan.itin_title: The Essential Châteaux of the Loire Valley

visits.text: Chenonceau spans the Cher on five arches. Nicknamed the "Ladies' Château," it was shaped by Katherine Briçonnet, Diane de Poitiers, Catherine de Medici, and Louise of Lorraine, each leaving her architectural mark.
The two-story gallery built by Catherine de Medici over the Cher extends 60 meters. During World War I, it served as a military hospital. During World War II, the south bank led into the Free Zone.

Pass through the richly decorated rooms: Catherine de Medici's green study, Diane de Poitiers' chamber with its monumental fireplace by Jean Goujon, and Francis I's chamber with its Renaissance furniture.

The Louis XIV salon preserves a portrait of the king painted by Rigaud, offered during his visit in 1650. The neighboring chapel holds stained glass windows by Max Ingrand installed after World War II.
The painting collection assembles works by Primaticcio, Rubens, Tintoretto, and Murillo. The Gallery of Domes exhibits paintings by European old masters.
The kitchens occupy the château's lower levels, at water level. A pantry, staff dining room, larder, and butcher's room illustrate the domestic organization of a grand Renaissance residence.

activities.text: Diane de Poitiers' gardens spread out in geometric beds bordered with lavender along the Cher. Facing them, Catherine de Medici's more intimate gardens are arranged around a central pool.
Get lost in the 1-hectare hedge maze, planted with 2,000 yews. At the center, a raised gazebo offers a view down over the winding paths.

days_plan.itin_title: The Essential Châteaux of the Loire Valley

visits.text: Cheverny dazzles with the perfect symmetry of its façades made of Bourré stone, a tuffeau limestone that whitens with time. Built in a single campaign between 1620 and 1640, it pioneered the French classical style that would dominate under Louis XIV.

Seventeen richly furnished rooms are open. 17th-century Gobelins tapestries, Louis XIV and Louis XV furniture, old master paintings, and gilding create an interior so well preserved it seems still inhabited. The Hurault de Vibraye family has resided here for six centuries.
The arms room houses a collection of armor, crossbows, and arquebuses. Heavy swords and shields recall the era of medieval tournaments.

Hergé drew inspiration from Cheverny's façade to draw Marlinspike Hall. He simply removed the two side pavilions. The permanent exhibition “The Secrets of Marlinspike Hall” occupies 700 m² in the outbuildings.

Crypt, Marlinspike drawing room, Tintin's bedroom, Professor Calculus's laboratory: the life-size recreations from the exhibition plunge young and old into the comic book universe with sound and light.

activities.text: Board an electric boat to glide along the park's canal. The avenue of 157 Atlas cedars and the Louisiana bald cypresses are reflected in the calm water.
Six themed gardens can be discovered through the seasons: a vegetable and cutting garden, a tulip garden in spring, and a laurel maze. Electric carts tour the 100-hectare estate.
Fancy a gourmet break? L'Orangerie behind the château offers artisanal ice creams and cold drinks beneath the park's canopy.

days_plan.itin_title: The Essential Châteaux of the Loire Valley

visits.text: It's impossible to be unmoved by the Château de Fleckenstein, which literally clings to a 30-meter-high red sandstone spur and is partly carved into the rock itself. The second most visited castle in Alsace after Haut-Koenigsbourg, this 12th-century fortress built partly into the rock overlooks the forest of the Parc naturel régional des Vosges du Nord. Allow around two hours for the round trip from the castle parking lot, and wear good shoes for the stairs cut into the stone.

activities.text: The marked trail leading to the castle parking lot continues toward other ruins in the Northern Vosges, such as Lutzelhardt, for walkers who want a longer outing. Bring water—there is little shade on the rocky ridge in summer.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Villages of Alsace in 4 Days

visits.text: The château de Gizeux stretches along 250 meters of façades, making it the longest residence in Angevin Touraine. Owned by the du Bellay family for 350 years (including the poet Joachim du Bellay), it's now inhabited by the de Laffon family.

The Francis I Gallery, on the first floor, was entirely painted by Italian artists around 1585. One can distinguish Marie d'Yvetot's monogram, mythological scenes inspired by Ovid's Metamorphoses, and flower bouquets.

During the Revolution, the villagers helped cover the paintings with a daub wall to hide royal symbols from vandals. The covering, intended to be temporary, was only rediscovered in the 20th century by a child playing in the château.
The Galerie des Châteaux du Roy, restored between 2013 and 2019, displays 400 m² of 17th-century murals depicting the great royal châteaux: Chambord, Versailles, Fontainebleau, and Gizeux itself.

On the ground floor, the small salons with 18th-century woodwork illustrate the comfort of Renaissance life. The dining room, kitchen, and vaulted cellars complete the circuit through this still-inhabited residence.

activities.text: In summer, the owners dress in costume on Tuesdays at 9 PM for a candlelit tour. By flickering light, the painted galleries, Cordovan leathers, and gilding take on a theatrical dimension.
The château's vaulted cellars host tastings of Bourgueil wines, an appellation produced on neighboring hillsides. The estate once owned its own vines, lost to phylloxera in the early 20th century.

days_plan.itin_title: The Essential Châteaux of the Loire Valley

places.name: Chateau De La Ferte Saint Aubin

visits.text: At the edge of Sologne, the château de La Ferté-Saint-Aubin presents its 17th-century brick-and-stone façades above moats that once regulated the Cosson River upstream of Chambord. A gateway flanked by two pavilions opens onto the main courtyard.

A private residence inhabited for over 350 years, the château opens more than 15 furnished rooms to visitors. From vaulted cellars to the roof space, the route takes in the guards' hall, the dining room, the drawing rooms, and the attics.

The grand kitchens in the basement are the star attraction. The 19th-century stove still works: a cook in period costume prepares madeleines with Sologne honey, baked over a wood fire, and offers them for tasting.
On either side of the courtyard, the Grandes Écuries (riding horses) and the Petites Écuries (working horses), built by Henri II de la Ferté Sennectère, are open to visitors.
Behind the château, on a small island in the moats, stands a 19th-century chapel. Its reflection in the still water creates one of the estate's most photogenic views.

activities.text: Explore the 40-hectare park in Sologne. Mini-golf, life-size wooden games, and a puzzle trail through the vegetation fill half a day with the family.

days_plan.itin_title: The Essential Châteaux of the Loire Valley

places.name: Chateau De Langeais

visits.text: The château de Langeais stands two buildings side by side: the ruins of Fulk Nerra's keep (994), one of France's oldest stone keeps, and Louis XI's residence, built from 1465, a stern fortress on the town side and an elegant residence on the garden side.
The Langeais drawbridge is one of the few still in working condition in France. Its mechanism of chains and counterweights operates just as it did in the 15th century.

Fifteen richly furnished rooms recreate late-15th-century seigneurial life. Millefleurs tapestries, carved chests, canopy beds, and monumental fireplaces furnish the rooms from ground floor to upper story.

The scene of the marriage of Charles VIII and Anne of Brittany, celebrated here on December 6, 1491, is recreated with life-size wax figures in period costumes. This event sealed Brittany's incorporation into the kingdom of France.
The covered rampart walks offer an elevated walk with views of the Loire and the town rooftops. The machicolations and crenellations recall the building's defensive purpose.

activities.text: The medieval-inspired gardens occupy the terrace between the château and the keep ruins. Dye plants, herbs, and medicinal plants are cultivated in boxwood-bordered squares according to medieval horticultural treatises.
Walk through the ruins of Fulk Nerra's keep. This 10th-century remnant, set against the main tower, commands a panoramic view of the Loire.

days_plan.itin_title: The Essential Châteaux of the Loire Valley

map_keywords: Mariage Charles VIII Anne de Bretagne Langeais

visits.text: Perched at 528 meters above Ribeauvillé, the Château de Saint-Ulrich, also called Grand-Ribeaupierre, is the largest of the three fortresses overlooking the town. A chapel dedicated to Saint Ulrich, Bishop of Augsburg, has given the site its name since the 11th century. You can explore freely, but at your own risk, as the ground among the ruins is sometimes unstable. Allow roughly two and a half hours for the Three Castles circuit from the parking lot, via the GR5.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Villages of Alsace in 4 Days

visits.text: The château de Talcy appears as a “country house” in the heart of Beauce. Behind the square gate tower with its turrets and crenellations, the cobbled courtyard reveals a Renaissance gallery with four basket-handle arches inspired by the one at Château de Blois.

Here the poet Ronsard met Cassandre Salviati, daughter of the Florentine banker who owned the estate, at a ball in Blois. He dedicated his famous verses to her: “Darling, let us go see if the rose...” Her niece later inspired the poet Agrippa d'Aubigné.

About fifteen rooms are open to visitors. The 18th-century furniture remains in place: the room known as Charles IX's chamber preserves its Hungarian-stitch tapestries, while painted decorations imitating printed cotton fabrics adorn the drawing rooms' paneling.
The late-15th-century circular dovecote holds 1,400 nesting holes. Its original rotating ladder still provides access to the nests. It's one of the largest in the region.
In the 17th-century barn, an impressive 6.7-meter-high wine press testifies to the estate's viticultural past, when it produced up to 25,000 liters of wine annually.

activities.text: Visit the conservation orchard designated Jardin Remarquable. Across 6 hectares, hundreds of heritage apple and pear varieties are trained into artistic forms: palmettes, tridents, lattices, and cordons.

days_plan.itin_title: The Essential Châteaux of the Loire Valley

visits.text: The château de Valençay blends Renaissance architecture and classicism in an imposing façade dominated by a round keep crowned with an Italian-style dome. It's the former residence of Charles-Maurice de Talleyrand-Périgord, Napoleon's diplomat.

The state drawing rooms preserve the Empire-style furniture commissioned by Talleyrand. The Grand Salon, the bedroom of King Ferdinand VII of Spain (detained here from 1808 to 1814), and the gallery testify to diplomatic splendor.
The small theater with First Empire décor could accommodate 150 spectators. Talleyrand had plays performed there to entertain his illustrious guests and the captive Spanish princes.
The château kitchens display the copper cookware and utensils needed for lavish receptions. Talleyrand, a renowned gastronome, employed the celebrated chef Carême.
The museum presents Talleyrand memorabilia: diplomatic documents, personal objects, and portraits trace the career of the man who served every regime from Louis XVI to Louis-Philippe.

activities.text: The terraced formal French gardens descend toward a vast 53-hectare park populated with fallow deer, peacocks, and black swans. The Duchess's garden and the Spanish garden offer contrasting atmospheres.
The Napoleon maze, planted in the park, invites children to find their way through trimmed hedges, with historical references and navigation games along the way.

days_plan.itin_title: The Essential Châteaux of the Loire Valley

visits.text: Villandry is the last of the great châteaux built on the Loire's banks in the Renaissance. But its fame rests above all on its gardens, recreated in the early 20th century across six levels of terraces descending toward the Cher.

The ornamental vegetable garden comprises nine geometric squares planted with vegetables, flowers, and aromatic plants. The colors change twice yearly: spring and then summer plantings completely transform the scene.
The ornamental gardens feature four squares symbolizing forms of love: tender love, passionate love, fickle love, and tragic love. Patterns in clipped boxwood illustrate each theme.
Inside, the furnished rooms include an oriental drawing room adorned with a 13th-century Mudéjar ceiling from Toledo, collections of Spanish paintings, and furniture from the 17th and 18th centuries.
The water garden, at the top of the terraces, surrounds a large pool shaped like a Louis XV mirror. Linden trees and clipped hornbeam hedges create a cool, serene space above the rest of the gardens.

activities.text: Head to the belvedere at the top of the terraces for an overall view of the gardens, the château, and the confluence of the Cher and Loire. The viewpoint is the best spot to photograph the entire site.
The hornbeam maze, at the heart of the gardens, invites you to test your navigation skills among the hedges. The shaded paths lead to a raised central platform.
Guided garden tours by the estate's gardeners explain the techniques of pruning, planting, and maintaining this horticultural masterpiece labeled Jardin Remarquable.

days_plan.itin_title: The Essential Châteaux of the Loire Valley

visits.text: The château de Villesavin was Chambord's “site hut.” Jean Le Breton, secretary of finance to Francis I, had it built between 1527 and 1537 to oversee work at the royal construction site a few kilometers away.
Modeled on an Italian villa with a U-shaped plan and square pavilions, the château preserves in its main courtyard a Florentine Carrara marble basin, a gift from Italian craftsmen to Jean Le Breton.

The chapel holds murals from the second half of the 16th century depicting the Passion cycle. Chubby infants bearing the instruments of the Passion form an iconographic detail as surprising as it is fascinating.

The 16th-century white stone dovecote holds 1,500 nesting holes and preserves its original rotating ladder and chestnut timber framework. A symbol of judicial power, it's one of the best preserved in the Loire Valley.

The marriage museum recreates the stages of a wedding day between 1840 and 1950. More than 1,500 original objects: costumes, trousseau, bridal chamber. This collection is considered the world's largest on this theme.
The collection of horse-drawn carriages and 19th-century baby carriages completes the visit in the château's outbuildings.

activities.text: Wander through the 27-hectare English-style park. A nectar-rich garden houses beehives, while a mini-farm has donkeys and draft horses from Easter to All Saints' Day.

days_plan.itin_title: The Essential Châteaux of the Loire Valley

places.name: Chateau Du Clos Luce

visits.text: The Clos Lucé was Leonardo da Vinci's final home. Invited by Francis I in 1516, the Florentine master lived here for his last three years. His reconstructed bedroom overlooks the garden he walked through daily.
Leonardo da Vinci's workshop has been recreated with his easels, brushes, and sketches. He is believed to have completed some of his last paintings and continued his scientific research in this room.
The chapel adorned with frescoes attributed to Leonardo's disciples preserves a contemplative atmosphere. Pictorial details recall the master's style, particularly in the treatment of light.
Forty scale models of machines built from Leonardo da Vinci's drawings punctuate the route: a swing bridge, a tank, a flying machine, and an aerial screw. Visitors can operate some of the mechanisms.
The Renaissance kitchen, with its period dishes and monumental fireplace, evokes the meals prepared for the master and his guests. Italian recipes mingled with Touraine fare of the era.

activities.text: Descend into the 7-hectare Parc Leonardo da Vinci. Full-scale machines are installed outdoors: the swing bridge, the paddle boat, and Archimedes' screw. Sound and visual effects bring the route to life.
A tunnel connected the Clos Lucé to the royal château of Amboise, allowing Francis I to visit his friend Leonardo. The passage is visible from the estate's gardens.

days_plan.itin_title: The Essential Châteaux of the Loire Valley

map_keywords: Parc Leonardo da Vinci Clos Lucé
Machines Léonard de Vinci Clos Lucé
Atelier Léonard de Vinci Clos Lucé

visits.text: Built around 1246 by Eberhard d'Andlau to watch over the valley, the Château du Haut-Andlau's two granite towers still stand on a narrow rocky spur at an altitude of 451 meters. Inhabited by the Andlau family until the early 19th century, it was partially dismantled after 1806 before becoming family property again in 1822. Allow about fifteen minutes for the walk through the forest from the parking lot at the Maison forestière du Hungerplatz.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Villages of Alsace in 4 Days

visits.text: Haut-Koenigsbourg castle is history within history. First mentioned in 1147, razed by Swedish troops after a 52-day siege in 1633, it lay in ruins for two and a half centuries before the city of Sélestat offered it in 1899 to Emperor Wilhelm II of Hohenzollern. He saw in it a symbol of Alsace's Germanic identity and entrusted the restoration to architect Bodo Ebhardt—a project from 1900 to 1908 that resurrected the castle as it was around 1500, in the Thierstein era. Pass through the high gate: two-thirds of the walls are medieval, the rest reconstructed using documented methods. Nearly 550,000 visitors per year.

The castle's lower court houses a forge, water mill, and reconstructed inn—a village within the village, which functioned self-sufficiently during sieges. The ramparts extend 270 meters. Two artillery towers flank the great bastion. Climb to the bastion terrace for the panorama: the Alsace plain, the Black Forest to the east, the Vosges to the west, and on exceptional days the Swiss Alps. Bring warm clothing—even in summer, it's often 5°C cooler than in the plain.

The banquet hall—called the 'Kaiser's Hall'—is the castle's most overtly political room. Wilhelm II had it enlarged beyond its original dimensions (a gallery indicates the initial height) and covered with heraldic frescoes by Léo Schnug illustrating Alsace's Germanic character. The imperial eagle dominates the coats of arms of Alsatian cities. Propaganda in stone worth seeing for what it reveals about the restoration's political ambition.

The medieval garden arranged in the lower enceinte cultivates aromatic and medicinal plants according to medieval methods—squares bordered by woven branches called 'plessis,' which protected against wild animals. Jean Renoir filmed a scene from 'La Grande Illusion' (1937) here, and illustrator John Howe, who worked on 'The Lord of the Rings,' says he was inspired by the castle.

activities.text: Theatrical tours animate the castle in season, with costumed actors reenacting scenes from medieval life. Check the castle's website program before your visit—time slots are often limited and animations vary by day and season.

days_plan.itin_title: Alsace and the Wine Route: Strasbourg to the Vosges

visits.text: The château du Rivau rises in the Touraine countryside, combining a medieval fortress and a Renaissance residence. Its fairytale silhouette, with crenellated keep and drawbridge, was mentioned by Rabelais in Gargantua.

The 15th-century royal stables are listed as a historic monument. Joan of Arc came here to collect horses before the Battle of Chinon. Their impressive dimensions testify to the site's military prestige.
The interior mixes classical décor and contemporary art. Artists' installations engage with tapestries and antique furniture in the vaulted halls and towers. The contrast is striking and intentional.
The Potager de Gargantua takes up the château's Rabelaisian theme. Giant vegetables and heritage varieties compose a kitchen garden of Pantagruelian proportions.

The château rose garden brings together more than 450 varieties of roses. Designated a “Collection nationale” by the Conservatoire des Collections Végétales Spécialisées, it perfumes the air from May to October.

activities.text: Explore the 14 fairytale gardens labeled Jardin Remarquable. Each tells a tale: the enchanted forest, Melusine's garden, Sleeping Beauty's path. Artistic installations blend into the vegetation.

days_plan.itin_title: The Essential Châteaux of the Loire Valley

places.name: Chateau Gontier

visits.text: Château-Gontier-sur-Mayenne, classified among France's Most Beautiful Detours, was born around the year 1000 from Count of Anjou Foulque Nerra's strategic decision to establish a fortress facing the Bretons. The castle, entrusted to officer Gontier, has disappeared, but the town has preserved abundant heritage on both sides of the river, with 18 protected historic monuments and a 58-hectare Remarkable Heritage Site.

Saint-Jean-Baptiste church, built in the 11th century in flint and roussard stone by Benedictines from Saint-Aubin Abbey in Angers, is the town's oldest church. Its Romanesque interior strikes with its purity: wooden-vaulted nave, rare dome on pendentives above the choir, ten-column crypt and fine ensemble of 12th-13th century mural paintings.

Hôtel Fouquet, an elegant 17th-century townhouse at the intersection of Grande Rue and Rue Jean Bourré, houses the Museum of Art and Archaeology. Nearby, spot the Hôtel de Lantivy (17th c., classified MH), Hôtel du Tertre de Sancé (15th c., listed MH) and half-timbered houses in medieval lanes.

Cross the Mayenne to discover the Ursuline convent in the Azé suburb. Founded in 1634 in a 15th-century manor house, expanded by Laval architects Pierre and Gilles Corbineau from 1642, it boasts a majestic cloister, a Jesuit-style church and convent cells. Since 1999, it has housed the National Stage Le Carré in a 530-seat theater integrated into the cloister.

Push open the gate to the Garden of the End of the World, perched on a rocky spur above the Mayenne. This flower-filled park with century-old trees shelters a 17th-century ice house and mischievous goats. The view over the river and town rooftops is worth the visit.

The Garden of Scents, on the Mayenne's banks, displays 80 varieties of fragrant and medicinal plants: lavender, mint, oregano, thyme. The Medieval Garden of the Spring, at the foot of old ramparts, completes this plant journey. Château-Gontier has earned four flowers in the Flowered Towns and Villages competition.

activities.text: Walk down the Mayenne quays along the river from the river stop. In summer, ephemeral riverside cafés set up on the banks with concerts and dining.
The Perrettes circuit (marked) winds between the Mayenne quays, the Ursuline convent, old quarters and the Garden of the End of the World—an ideal loop to embrace all the town's faces.
Thursday mornings, Château-Gontier's traditional market invades the town center squares. It's also the continent's largest calf fair—a vibrant tradition of this livestock-raising land.

days_plan.itin_title: Mayenne Circuit: Hedgerows and Medieval Towns

map_keywords: Jardin du Bout du Monde Château-Gontier

visits.text: Baroque trompe-l'oeil painted ceilings, cool 14th-century stone, and in the midst of it all: Suzy Solidor in forty portraits. The Grimaldi Castle Museum in Haut-de-Cagnes was built around 1300 by Admiral Rainier Grimaldi, transformed into a noble residence in the 17th century. The singer donated about forty of her portraits in 1973, signed by Cocteau, Dufy, Foujita, Lempicka, Picabia, Van Dongen. Also worth seeing: the ethnographic museum of the olive tree on the ground floor.

activities.text: Climb on foot through the lanes of Haut-de-Cagnes—the castle is worth the effort. The medieval village spirals around the keep, cobblestone alleys, vaulted passages, shaded squares. Twenty minutes is enough to tour it before or after your visit. Parking is difficult at the top; park in the lot below and climb up.

days_plan.itin_title: French Riviera Art Museums and Galleries: An 8-Day Journey

visits.text: The royal château of Amboise overlooks the Loire from atop its promontory. The favorite residence of Charles VIII and then Francis I, it was the cradle of the French Renaissance. The terrace offers a 360-degree view of the river and town.

The Chapel of Saint-Hubert, a flamboyant Gothic masterpiece, houses Leonardo da Vinci's presumed tomb. Its sculpted lintel depicts the legend of Saint Hubert facing the stag bearing a cross between its antlers.

The Tour des Minimes, with its five-meter-wide helical ramp, allowed riders and carriages to climb directly from the Loire's edge to the château terrace. Its counterpart, the Tour Hurtault, offers the same ascent on the opposite side.

The royal residences feature rooms furnished with period pieces: the Council Hall adorned with Gothic pillars, Henry II's chamber with its Renaissance furniture, and the Estates Hall where royal audiences were held.
From the ramparts, spot the traces of the immense medieval palace that once occupied the entire promontory. Only one-tenth of the original edifice remains, the rest demolished under Napoleon.

activities.text: The château's panoramic gardens, redesigned in the 19th century, blend flowerbeds, cedars of Lebanon, and trimmed boxwoods. The linden avenue drops steeply toward the Loire below.
In summer, the château offers themed guided tours, children's workshops, and illuminated evening visits that highlight the Gothic and Renaissance architecture under enchanting lighting.

days_plan.itin_title: The Essential Châteaux of the Loire Valley

visits.text: The royal château of Blois unites four wings from four eras in one monument: the 13th-century Gothic of the Estates Hall, the Flamboyant Gothic of Louis XII, the Renaissance of Francis I, and the 17th-century classicism of Gaston d'Orléans.

The monumental staircase of the Francis I wing is a feat: an octagonal spiral staircase housed in a tower with three sides open to the courtyard. Sculptures of salamanders, pilasters, and medallions ornament each floor.

The royal apartments recreate daily court life in the 16th century. The chamber of King Henry III is marked by the assassination of the Duke of Guise on December 23, 1588, an event recounted in the displays.
Catherine de Medici's study preserves its 237 carved wood panels. Four panels conceal secret compartments, long presented as her "poison cabinets."
The Museum of Fine Arts, housed in the Louis XII wing, exhibits paintings, sculptures, and tapestries from the 16th to 19th centuries. The queen's gallery offers views of the Façade des Loges.
The Façade des Loges, facing the Loire, displays its Italian-style stacked galleries. From the garden below, the view takes in the full height of this Renaissance façade.

activities.text: The château de Blois sound and light show projects major episodes from the site's history onto the façades of the inner courtyard. The walls come alive with colors and stories for 45 minutes.

days_plan.itin_title: The Essential Châteaux of the Loire Valley

visits.text: Jean de La Fontaine's birthplace, listed as a Historic Monument and awarded the Maison des Illustres label, reopened in January 2026 after three years of renovation. The 16th-century mansion retains its intertwined crescents of Diane de Poitiers, decorated pilasters, and sculpted band. The famous fabulist was born here on 8 July 1621 and spent his childhood here.

The renovated museum offers an immersive tour featuring interactive displays, restored works, audio narratives and visual projections. Collections spanning the 17th to the 20th century illustrate the poet's work: engravings by Marc Chagall, a painting by Léon Lhermitte and a bronze clock depicting The Milkmaid and the Milk Pot. The reconstructed study evokes his role as Master of Waters and Forests.

The medieval castle dominates the Marne from a hilltop. Remnants include the imposing Saint-Jean Gate, ramparts punctuated with towers, and the former keep. The route along the walls offers superb views of Château-Thierry's rooftops and the valley. Information panels line the walk through the 2.5-hectare grounds.
The American Monument on Hill 204 commemorates World War I battles. American soldiers fought in this sector in 1918. The memorial site overlooks the region.

activities.text: The slopes of Château-Thierry produce Champagne under the appellation. Several Champagne houses offer cellar tours and tastings. The Champagne Route winds through the vineyards and wine-producing villages of the Marne valley.
Wander through the town centre's streets, dotted with 17th- and 18th-century mansions. La Fontaine's statue stands proudly in the renovated square. The façades tell the story of this literary town.
The Jean de La Fontaine Festival brings the city to life every May. Music, theatre, and dance celebrate Château-Thierry's cultural heritage during this artistic event.

days_plan.itin_title: Aisne Itinerary: Gothic Cathedrals and the Picardy Countryside
Marne Road Trip: Reims, Épernay and Champagne

visits.text: The way into Chateaudouble is a spectacle in itself: the road runs 40 meters through a tunnel cut into the rock before coming out at the perched village. Mentioned as early as 1021 under the name "Castellum Diaboli" — the devil's castle, because of a site the Romans judged impregnable — the village owes its present name to the two castles it had in the Middle Ages, one on each side of the Nartuby. It stands 130 meters above the gorges, and from Place Beausoleil at the top of the village the view over the limestone cliffs and the gorges cut by the river is dizzying. Climb the cobbled lanes to the remains of the 12th-century square keep on the Sainte-Anne plateau — you can also see the ruins of a second castle on the far side of the gorges.

Nostradamus himself mentioned Chateaudouble in one of his prophecies: "Chateaudouble, double castle, the river shall be your tomb", seeing in the Nartuby the natural force able to wear away the cliffs that protect the village. The floods of 2010 did indeed carry off the gorge road. Wander the narrow cobbled lanes between the medieval houses and look at the carved pediments — Templar crosses are still visible on some facades, a reminder of their presence in the 13th century. The church of Notre-Dame de l'Annonciation, built in 1550 and enlarged in 1678, holds three listed altarpieces and 16th-century baptismal fonts.

activities.text: The Nartuby gorges are a classified site and playground for climbing enthusiasts — 5 sites with 350 routes from grade 4 to 8b+. For non-climbers, hiking trails follow the gorge edges from the hamlet of Rebouillon at Châteaudouble's base. Golden eagles and other raptors nesting in the cliffs are regularly spotted.

days_plan.itin_title: The 10 Most Beautiful Villages of the Haut-Var

visits.text: Château de Châteaudun, first of the Loire châteaux for those arriving from Paris. Standing more than 60 meters above the Loir, this fortress was the home of Jean de Dunois, companion-in-arms of Joan of Arc. The building spans eight centuries of architecture, from the medieval keep to Renaissance staircases.

Circular keep from the 12th century, one of the best preserved in the world at 31 meters high with walls 4 meters thick. The magnificent 15th-century roof structure with its radial timber framing crowns this defensive tower where the Counts of Blois resisted Norman assaults.

Gothic Sainte-Chapelle of the château, founded by Jean de Dunois in the 15th century. It preserves fifteen polychrome statues of saints and a mural painting of the Last Judgment. This private sanctuary testifies to the piety of Joan of Arc's companion.

Longueville wing from the 16th century, where the first signs of the Renaissance emerge. The grand state rooms house an exceptional collection of 17th-century tapestries. The monumental staircase already heralds the wonders of the Loire châteaux.

activities.text: Medieval-inspired garden at the foot of the keep, laid out in the former moats. Fourteen themed beds present 150 varieties of medieval plants: aromatic, medicinal, edible, and dye plants. An immersion into the art of medieval gardens.

Promenade du Mail offering an exceptional panorama over the Loir valley and the château perched on its rocky spur. The hanging gardens, the first of their kind in France and inspired by the Italian model, complete this exploration of the grounds.

Wander through Châteaudun's old town with its houses from the 15th and 16th centuries that survived the fire of 1723. Rue Saint-Lubin and its half-timbered facades lead to the Foulon caves, a fascinating geological site with concretions and marine fossils.

days_plan.itin_title: Eure-et-Loir Tour: Chartres, Châteaux and Proust

visits.text: You'll spot Châteauneuf from afar—the village and its fortress perch on a rocky spur visible from the A6 highway. Listed among the Plus Beaux Villages de France, the town has preserved its 14th-century medieval castle, one of the last remnants of Burgundian military architecture in its original state. Climb the keep for views over the Auxois valley and the Canal de Bourgogne, 200 meters below.

Explore the cobbled streets lined with merchants' houses from the 15th–16th centuries. The Maison Bichot, Maison du Mouton, and their sculpted facades testify to the prosperity of Burgundian merchants at the end of the Middle Ages. In summer, the village hosts contemporary artists in the old residences—don't be surprised to stumble upon an art installation in a 15th-century courtyard.

activities.text: Walk down to the Canal de Bourgogne via the trail that leaves from the village. The towpath follows the reaches and locks—a flat, soothing walk after climbing to the château. Pleasure barges pass regularly, especially in summer.

If you've rented bikes, the Canal de Bourgogne makes for beautiful rides. The stretch between Châteauneuf and Vandenesse-en-Auxois is particularly pretty, passing flower-decked locks and rolling countryside.

days_plan.itin_title: Burgundy's 15 Most Beautiful Villages

visits.text: Only two wall sections remain of the Avignon popes' castle—the rest was dynamited in 1944 by retreating Germans. But from these ruins on the hill above the village, the view over the vineyard and the Rhône below is beautiful enough to justify the climb. The famous “rounded pebbles of Crau”—those large white pebbles carried by the glacial Rhône—are visible from here, white and round in the plots below. They store the sun's heat and release it to the vines at night. That's Châteauneuf.

13 permitted grape varieties - grenache, syrah, mourvèdre, but also cinsault, counoise, vaccarèse, terret noir, and six others. The Musée Brotte in the heart of the village explains the history of the appellation, a pioneer in France: in 1923, rules defining the geographical boundaries for wine production were drawn up here, a forerunner of the AOC system. A small museum, free admission, informative in 45 minutes.

Tavel, on the right bank of the Rhône, is France's oldest rosé appellation. This is no fashionable pale rosé: it is a powerful grenache rosé, with 13.5 to 15% alcohol, that ages well for two to three years and confidently accompanies a slow-cooked beef stew or lamb. In neighboring Lirac, the reds often offer better value for money than Châteauneuf wines. Allow for a round trip from Châteauneuf-du-Pape to Tavel and Lirac.

activities.text: Château de Beaucastel is the biodynamic benchmark for Châteauneuf—and one of the rare estates to truly use all 13 authorized grape varieties in its blends, not just the three main ones. The Perrin family has run the estate since 1909. The tour is serious, the tasting rigorous. Expect wines that demand patience: standard Beaucastel red needs 8 to 12 years to be at its best. Booking required.

Lunch on the terrace at Le Verger des Papes, beneath the walls of the destroyed castle, with views over the vineyard. Straightforward Provençal cuisine—tapenade, lamb, local cheeses—and a wine list centered on village producers. Not the most ambitious restaurant on the route, but the location more than makes up for it. Book a table on the terrace.

days_plan.itin_title: Rhône Valley: From Northern Syrahs to Southern Grenaches

visits.text: Less spectacular than a reconstruction, the Château de Châteauneuf is all the more authentic for it: the 12th-century keep, Philippe Pot's lodgings, and the chapel with its wall paintings can be visited almost unchanged. The viewpoint on the rocky spur offers the best view of the Burgundy Canal.

activities.text: Wander through the village lanes before heading down to the canal for a waterside stroll. The medieval garden at the postern gate, free to visit, complements the château tour.

days_plan.itin_title: Burgundy-Franche-Comté: The Most Beautiful Villages in 7 days

visits.text: The medieval castle of Châteauneuf has vanished. Only the name and presumed site near the current fairground remain. However, the Logis de Barqueville (15th century) facing the church forms a handsome ensemble with the square. Pleasant walk along the shaded riverbanks.

The church of Saint-Pierre (12th century) boasts one of the finest façades in the Charente: three sculpted tiers, a horseman representing Constantine crushing paganism. Inside, carved Romanesque capitals and a little snail hidden in high relief.
The river port brings the town to life. A stop on the Charente for pleasure boaters and canoeists. Café terraces, shaded picnic area. Watersports centre in summer.

activities.text: Canoeing on the Charente. The watersports centre hires out kayaks and canoes with a return shuttle. Routes from 2 hours to a full day. Calm water, swimming possible at designated stops.

Swimming at the Bain des Dames. The leisure area, with its Station Sport Nature designation, offers the only beach with facilities on the River Charente within the Cognac destination area. Lawn, toilets, snack bar. Free.
Fishing on the Charente. Quiet spots upstream and downstream of town. Zander, pike, carp. Daily fishing licence available at the tobacconist and newsagent.

days_plan.itin_title: Charente Tour: Cognac and Romanesque Heritage in 4 Days

visits.text: At the summit of Griffon Hill stands the feudal fortress of the Counts of Provence — two medieval towers from the 12th and 15th centuries classified as historic monuments. It's one of the rare medieval fortresses in the Arles region still standing to a significant height. The guided tour of the furnished rooms reveals the life of Benedict XIII, the controversial Avignon pope who stayed here, and the defensive architecture of this strategic site. From the terraces, the view over Mont Ventoux, the Alpilles, and the Durance plains is striking. Count 263 steps from the church.

Châteaurenard's town center developed at the foot of the château over the centuries. A quiet public garden surrounds the base of Griffon Hill, with permanent views of the two medieval towers. The town is also known for its major produce market — one of the largest in the region — supplying restaurants in Avignon and the Alpilles.

activities.text: Châteaurenard weekly market: the lively town center market (check days at town hall) is where market garden producers from the plain gather. Châteaurenard lies at the heart of one of France's densest horticultural zones — tomatoes, melons, cherries, zucchini. A morning market tour provides insight into the agricultural economy structuring the entire Rhône corridor.

Walk along the Durance dikes: from the area around Griffon Hill, an eastward promenade reaches the banks of the Durance and its riparian forests of poplars and alders. In autumn, thousands of ducks and wading birds frequent these wetlands. The Durance is the Rhône's most important left-bank tributary, with flow varying between 30 and 3,000 m³/s.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpilles, Aix-en-Provence & Arles Circuit

visits.text: Château Raoul. Founded in the 10th century by Raoul le Large, who gave the town its name, this castle rises above the ramparts and the Indre valley. Rebuilt in stone in the 12th century after two fires, it was the seat of power in Lower Berry. Seven lords bearing the name Raoul succeeded one another here. Owned by the Indre department, the castle can be visited on guided tours in summer and during Heritage Days.

Bertrand Museum. Housed in the mansion of General Henri-Gatien Bertrand, Napoleon's faithful companion, this museum presents highly diverse collections across 26 rooms. The aviary brought back from Saint Helena, the Aboukir saber carried by Bonaparte, the original plaster version of Sakuntala by Camille Claudel, a cabinet of curiosities and Egyptology, Flemish and Dutch paintings, and Gallo-Roman and medieval works form an exceptional collection. The Empire collections bear witness to the Napoleonic epic.

Couvent des Cordeliers. This former medieval friary now houses cultural spaces and testifies to the town's religious past. The building's Gothic architecture contrasts with the contemporary fittings within.

Historic center. From Château Raoul to rue des Pavillons, from place Monestier to place de la République, Châteauroux reveals a thousand years of history. The medieval quarter preserves numerous ancient half-timbered dwellings. Place Sainte-Hélène and place Napoléon evoke the town's connection with the Imperial epic.

activities.text: Indre riverbanks and Saint-Gildas meadow. Below Château Raoul, this 17-hectare natural area harbors remarkably rich fauna and flora. A marked discovery trail allows you to observe European pond turtles, kingfishers, beavers, large copper butterflies, and numerous other species. The garden city with its four-flower rating well deserves its title.

Saturday market. The weekly market brings the town center to life with products from Berry. Goat cheeses, local wines, seasonal vegetables, and artisanal specialties create a friendly atmosphere typical of this prefectural town in Berry.

Art Deco and Belle Époque facilities. Châteauroux has preserved several buildings testifying to its development during the Belle Époque. The Art Deco architecture of certain public facilities illustrates the urban modernization of the early 20th century and contrasts with the medieval heritage.

days_plan.itin_title: Indre Road Trip: Secret Berry and the Vallée Noire

visits.text: The Pont Henri IV, in Renaissance style, has spanned the Vienne since 1611. An emblem of Châtellerault, it offers picturesque views of the river and quays. It's one of the city's two bridges listed as historic monuments.

The Auto Moto Vélo Museum occupies La Manu, a former arms factory that employed up to 8,000 workers in the early 20th century. Across 4,000 square meters, over 200 vehicles are on display: Bugatti, Delage, Ferrari, Terrot, and rare prototypes like the 1953 Longchamps-Decouçy.
The Théâtre Blossac, a 19th-century Italian-style theater, was fully restored to its original state in 2013. Its intimate auditorium with gilded balconies hosts a regular program of performances.
Saint-Jacques Church, a stop on the route to Compostela, houses a listed carillon of 52 bells. Its neo-Romanesque façade dominates the town.
The Maison Descartes, 16th-century residence of René Descartes' grandparents, speaks to the city's intellectual past. The visit sheds light on the philosopher's life and his connection to Poitou.

activities.text: Board the riverboat for a narrated cruise on the Vienne, from Châtellerault toward the Chitré mill. Offered in summer only.
Cycle along the Ligne Verte, a 40 km cycle path laid out on a former railway line. Information panels about the region's history line the route.
Stroll along Châtellerault's quays at twilight. The reflection of the Pont Henri IV in the Vienne is a classic photographic subject in the city.

days_plan.itin_title: Vienne Road Trip: Futuroscope and Romanesque Heritage

visits.text: Châtenois's fortified cemetery, rare in Alsace, preserves its medieval enclosure pierced with loopholes. At the center, the 12th-century Saint-Georges church presents a squat Romanesque bell tower and a porch with sculpted décor.
The Tour des Sorcières (13th century), former rampart keep, owes its name to the witchcraft trials held in the region. Its massive silhouette dominates the old town.
The partially preserved ramparts and medieval gates frame an ancient core of half-timbered houses. The village is a southern gateway to the Alsace Wine Route.
A few kilometers away, Sélestat houses the Humanist Library, registered in UNESCO's Memory of the World registry, and the Romanesque Sainte-Foy church (12th century).

activities.text: Châtenois's wine trail winds between plots of Riesling and Pinot Noir. Educational panels and viewpoints over the plain line the route.

Head up to Haut-Koenigsbourg Castle, around a twenty-minute drive from Châtenois, a medieval fortress restored in the early 20th century, perched at 757 m with views over the Alsace plain, the Black Forest and the Vosges.
Châtenois cellars produce excellent Rieslings. The clay-limestone terroir yields mineral and chiseled wines.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Est Road Trip: Vineyards, Ramparts and Forests

visits.text: Stroll through cobbled lanes lined with elegant timber-framed houses featuring red brick and projecting upper storeys. This medieval town, awarded the Plus Beaux Détours de France and Ville Fleurie Quatre Fleurs designations, has preserved its exceptional architectural heritage. The colourful façades are reflected in the peaceful waters of the Chalaronne, which flows through the historic centre.

The 15th-century market halls, an 80-metre-long wooden cathedral, host one of France's most beautiful markets every Saturday morning. Enormous oak pillars support the massive timber framework, rebuilt to the original design after the fire of 1670. Beneath these centuries-old vaults, poultry, cheeses and produce from the Dombes create a ballet of flavours and colours.

Saint-André Church displays its Flamboyant Gothic architecture in the heart of the town. Built of Savoyard bricks, it bears witness to Châtillon's former association with Savoy. Its colourful stained-glass windows illuminate the nave, while the pointed vaults create an airy, bright space conducive to contemplation.

The former hospital, whose present buildings were constructed in 1732, houses a remarkable apothecary's shop with a unique collection of 120 Meillonnas earthenware jars. The carved woodwork, period containers and historic medical instruments recreate the atmosphere of an old pharmacy. Do not miss the Lamentation Triptych of 1527, an exceptional work preserved within these history-filled walls.

activities.text: Follow the flower-decked bridges spanning the Chalaronne. Each footbridge overflows with geraniums, petunias and floral arrangements that earned the town the Grand Prix National du Fleurissement. Shaded riverbanks invite leisurely strolls, offering photographic views of old houses reflected in the calm water.

Explore the Porte de Villars, an imposing remnant of the medieval ramparts that once encircled the fortified town. This historic monument now houses a guest house where remarkable old wallpapers are preserved. From the top of the old castle ramparts, the view takes in the town's rooftops and the surrounding Dombes landscape.

Visit the Arboretum, which brings together 342 exceptional tree varieties across several hectares. The educational apiary explains the importance of bees for biodiversity, with Châtillon being France's first bee-friendly town, with around sixty hives. Botanical trails cross this plant conservatory, where every tree species is identified and documented.

Taste Dombes specialities in the restaurants of the town centre. Farm-raised poultry, pond fish and local cheeses form a generous cuisine rooted in the terroir. Dombes-Bresse cuisine blends Savoyard and Lyonnais influences in recipes handed down from generation to generation.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour Ain & Savoie Mont-Blanc: Lakes, Mountains and Heritage
Road Trip from Bresse to Bugey via Beaujolais and Lyon

visits.text: The Source du Par emerges at 82°C. This exceptional geothermal feature, used since Roman antiquity, still supplies the spa town's district heating today. The bubbling water steams in the purpose-built basin, where visitors try the traditional experiment: cooking an egg in 15 minutes in this naturally scalding water.

The Caleden thermal centre makes the most of Chaudes-Aigues' 32 hot springs in a modern complex combining spa therapy and wellness. The mineral waters with pain-relieving and relaxing properties treat rheumatic conditions. The thermal leisure area, open to children from 9 months of age, offers pools at 32–37°C, a jacuzzi, waterfalls and massage jets in a setting for family relaxation.

The Musée Géothermia tells the exceptional story of this spa town, the first city in Europe to use a geothermal district heating network as early as the Middle Ages. Models, historical documents and interactive displays explain how residents have used these springs for heating, healthcare and daily life since antiquity.

activities.text: The spa walk through the town reveals Auvergne's stone architecture and stone-slab roofs. Touch the warm water in the fountains brought back into use, discover the hot-water wash house fed by the Lestande spring (62°C), and warm up in winter in the Saint-Martin-Saint-Blaise church, whose underfloor heating is supplied by geothermal springs. The “De Par en Par” trail guides you through this unique thermal heritage.

Hiking on the Aubrac plateau is a must on the doorstep of Chaudes-Aigues. These vast wild highland spaces reveal lush pastures, traditional burons and herds of Aubrac cattle in an unspoilt landscape of mid-altitude mountains. Waymarked trails offer panoramas stretching to the Truyère gorges and the Cantal mountains.

days_plan.itin_title: Cantal Road Trip: Auvergne Volcanoes and Mountain Traditions

visits.text: The Chaumont Viaduct ranks among Europe's most impressive 19th-century engineering feats: 600 meters long, 52 meters high, 50 arches, 60,000 cubic meters of masonry. Built in just fifteen months between August 1855 and November 1856, it was France's first construction site lit by electricity, enabling night work for 2,500 laborers and 300 horses. On August 31, 1944, German forces dynamited two arches to sever the rail line; service resumed by December 1944. Since 2012, 430 LED projectors illuminate the structure nightly with an ever-shifting color ballet.

Saint-Jean-Baptiste Basilica deserves a long stop. The nave and the facade date from the 13th century. The transept and the choir, rebuilt between 1517 and 1543, boldly mix Flamboyant Gothic vocabulary with the first Renaissance grammar. Look for the Entombment from the late 15th century: this sculpted group is one of the most moving works in Haute-Marne. The Tree of Jesse, carved around 1530, is 4.5 metres tall. The Cavaille-Coll organ of 1872 is one of the best known in the region.

The medieval keep crowns the rocky promontory that gave the city its name—the "bald hill" that became Chaumont. It marks the former seat of the Counts of Champagne. Descending toward the basilica, detour through the old town's winding lanes: manor houses testify to Chaumont's past as a glove-making capital, a craft that sustained the city until the 20th century.

activities.text: Walk to the viaduct from the town centre in about twenty minutes. If you are lucky enough to be there at sunrise or sunset, the limestone masonry takes on exceptional golden tones. A pedestrian walkway on the first level lets you cross the viaduct and appreciate its height from the inside. Freely accessible and free of charge.
Permanent and temporary exhibitions at the Chaumont Museum of Art and History round out the cultural offering.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Marne Circuit: Langres and Heritage

visits.text: The International Garden Festival of Chaumont-sur-Loire has run from April to November since 1992. A globally recognized laboratory for contemporary landscape design, it presents around thirty ephemeral gardens each year, created around a theme by landscape designers, designers and architects from all over the world. Bold planting designs combine rare plants, unusual flowers and distinctive pairings in a leafy setting covering several hectares. Six permanent gardens complete the experience: the English-inspired woodland garden, the extraordinary greenhouse and playful children's gardens. The immersive sensory journey evolves through the seasons.

Château de Chaumont-sur-Loire overlooks the Loire from its promontory at a height of 40 meters. Built between the 15th and 16th centuries, it combines Gothic defensive features with Renaissance comfort. Catherine de' Medici acquired it in 1550 before exchanging it with Diane de Poitiers for Chenonceau. Richly furnished interiors testify to the splendor restored in the 19th century by the Prince de Broglie. The apartments reveal tapestries, period furniture, and refined art objects. Temporary exhibitions in the historic rooms present internationally renowned contemporary artists.

Chaumont's stables and historic park, the latter created by landscape architect Henri Duchêne between 1884 and 1888. The stables, among the most remarkable of their era, now house contemporary art exhibitions in their vast vaulted halls. The 32-hectare park has shaded paths dotted with sculptures and artistic installations. Century-old cedars, giant sequoias, and carefully planned vistas create a remarkable green setting. Views of the Loire and château offer exceptional opportunities to pause and contemplate.

activities.text: A stroll through the Festival's creative gardens explores current trends in international landscape design. Each ephemeral creation offers an original vision combining plants, stone, and artworks in bold compositions. The installations invite reflection on our relationship with nature and the contemporary environment. Light effects, vistas, and planting arrangements reveal the designers' talent. A children's activity booklet transforms the visit into a fun botanical adventure with riddles to solve in each garden.

Viewpoints offering stunning views of the Loire. The château's terraces reveal 180-degree panoramas of the valley, dotted with wooded islands and shifting sandbanks. The silvery meanders wind between meadows and forests towards the distant horizon. The historic park features carefully planned openings that frame the landscape like living paintings. Sunsets setting the river ablaze create unforgettable scenes from the heights of the estate overlooking the valley.

Discovering contemporary art exhibitions in the stables, outbuildings, and estate park. The Saison d'Art presents monumental sculptures, photographs, and artistic installations by leading international artists. Works scattered throughout the park create an open-air museum where nature and artistic creation engage in continuous dialogue. Temporary exhibition rooms in historic buildings showcase paintings, videos, and digital creations. The estate brings architectural heritage and contemporary creation together in a novel and stimulating dialogue.

days_plan.itin_title: Loir-et-Cher Itinerary: Royal Châteaux and the Loir Valley
The Essential Châteaux of the Loire Valley

visits.text: The abbey of Saint-Jean-des-Vignes raises its two slender spires to over 75 metres. Founded in 1076 and rebuilt in the 13th century, it rivals the nearby cathedral in size. The twin-towered façade with its three portals, the large rose window and the rich sculptural decoration testify to the ambitions of the abbots who built it. Viollet-le-Duc compared it to a cathedral, so impressive is its scale. Allow for a return trip to Soissons from Chauny, the town for this stage.

The large Gothic cloister of the abbey of Saint-Jean-des-Vignes offers refined sculptural decoration, with plants and animals bringing its galleries and capitals to life. The monks' spacious, elegant refectory now hosts exhibitions. Allow for a return trip to Soissons from Chauny, the town for this stage.

Construction of the cathedral of Saint-Gervais Saint-Protais began in 1176 and ended in 1479. Its 300 years of building span two periods of Gothic architecture. The south tower alone rises above the asymmetrical façade. Rubens' Adoration of the Shepherds and the stained-glass windows restored in 2021 enrich its exceptional collection of furnishings and artworks. Allow for a return trip to Soissons from Chauny, the town for this stage.

The crypt of Saint-Médard houses the tombs of Clovis' descendants in the abbey founded in the 6th century by Chlothar. Only this crypt remains of the Merovingian monastic complex. The guided tour takes you back to the roots of French history. Allow for a return trip to Soissons from Chauny, the town for this stage.

activities.text: Explore the 25 stencils by C215 scattered around the town. Street artist Christian Guémy created these portraits of major historical figures during an artist residency: Louise Michel, Chlothar I, Joan of Arc and Rubens enliven the walls of Soissons. Allow for a return trip to Soissons from Chauny, the town for this stage.

The banks of the Aisne invite you to stroll from the town centre to the lock. The path follows the river through greenery, offering opportunities to watch waterbirds. The Cuffies bridge provides a view of the lock, whose mechanism fascinates curious visitors. Allow for a return trip to Soissons from Chauny, the town for this stage.

The Saint-Léger museum occupies the former abbey founded in 1139. The refurbished displays present medieval sculptures from the Soissonnais and works from the 19th and 20th centuries, including superb busts by local artists. The archaeological collections testify to the rich history of the Aisne valley. Allow for a return trip to Soissons from Chauny, the town for this stage.

The fort of Condé is a fine example of late 19th-century military architecture. Allow for a return trip from Chauny, the town for this stage. The landscaped grounds offer opportunities to discover nature and an arboretum. Historical escape games immerse you in the world of 1944.

days_plan.itin_title: Aisne Itinerary: Gothic Cathedrals and the Picardy Countryside

visits.text: Five fortified castles stand on the same rocky spur in Chauvigny—a rare concentration in Europe. The Bishops' baronial castle, built in the 11th century, dominates the Vienne Valley from the promontory's edge.

The Saint-Pierre Collegiate Church, a 12th-century jewel of Romanesque art, is world-renowned for its polychrome capitals. Signed by master sculptor Gofridus, they depict scenes from Christ's life, monsters, and fantastical beasts.
The Château d'Harcourt, best preserved of the five fortresses, dates from the 13th century. Its curtain walls and towers provide a clear glimpse into medieval military architecture.
Enter the Gouzon keep, topped by a small modern glass lookout. It houses the Espace d'Archéologie Industrielle.

Hidden in a cemetery of Merovingian origin, Saint-Pierre-les-Églises Church contains some of Western Europe's oldest frescoes, dating from between 780 and 980. The Nativity is depicted in an original way.

activities.text: Watch the Géants du Ciel show in the setting of the Bishops' Castle. Eagles, vultures, and falcons fly free above the medieval ruins.
Hop on a VéloRail along the old railway line for 17 km of scenic riding through woods, over viaducts, and along the river—with breathtaking views of the medieval city.
Head down to the lower town to walk along the Vienne riverbanks. The trail offers a striking perspective on the fortress-crowned rocky spur.

days_plan.itin_title: Vienne Road Trip: Futuroscope and Romanesque Heritage

visits.text: The Chateau de Chenonceau, nicknamed the "Ladies' Chateau," spans the Cher on its elegant arches. Diane de Poitiers had the bridge built over the river, and Catherine de' Medici added the two-story gallery, 200 feet long above the water. It is the most visited privately owned chateau in France.

Chenonceau's interiors unfold like a museum: Diane de Poitiers' bedroom with its fireplace by Jean Goujon, Catherine de Medici's bedroom with coffered ceiling, vaulted kitchen in the bridge piers, gallery transformed into a military hospital during World War I. The collection includes works by Rubens, Primaticcio and Correggio.

The gardens compete in symmetry. Diane de Poitiers' garden, terraced by the Cher, aligns its flower beds protected by moats. Catherine de Medici's garden, more intimate, surrounds a round pool. The flower vegetable garden, labyrinth and caryatid statues complete the 170-acre estate.

The Gallery of the Domes, former orangery, houses a collection of wax figures and historical souvenirs. Don't miss the 16th-century wine cellar or the floral workshop where the château's vase arrangements are created each morning with flowers from the estate.

activities.text: Visit to Chenonceau's château and gardens. Allow 2 hours minimum for the complete experience. In summer, the "Nocturnal Promenades" illuminate the château and gardens with a thousand lights set to music—a magical spectacle.
Walk along the Cher at Chenonceau. The banks offer unique perspectives on the château's arches reflecting in the river. In summer, boats are available to approach the monument from the water.
Taste Touraine wines in the cellars of the Chenonceau estate.

days_plan.itin_title: Indre-et-Loire Road Trip: Loire Valley Châteaux, Secret Valleys & Touraine Vineyards

visits.text: Head to Cherbourg this morning. Settle in and make your way to the Cité de la Mer, housed in the former Art Deco transatlantic ocean-liner terminal. The highlight of the visit is the nuclear submarine Le Redoutable, France's first SSBN, launched in 1967 - you explore its interior from the conning tower to the torpedoes. The abyssal aquarium (the deepest in Europe) and the Titanic exhibition complete an attraction that easily warrants 3 hours.

After the Cité de la Mer, stroll along the marina to Place Napoléon. The roadstead of Cherbourg, the world's second-largest artificial harbor (1,500 hectares), was commissioned by Louis XVI and completed under Napoleon III. The central breakwater measures 3.7 km long. From the quay you'll spot the forts guarding the entrance.

Take a stroll through the town center: the Basilique Sainte-Trinité, founded in the 11th century and remodeled in the 15th–16th centuries, is often overlooked by tourists—unjustly. The neighborhood around Rue du Commerce and Place de Gaulle is where you'll find the best places to visit. Cherbourg was liberated on June 26, 1944, three weeks after D-Day, and its port was vital for supplying the Allies.

Head toward eastern Cotentin this morning. Barfleur is 30 minutes from Cherbourg. This little gray granite harbor is listed among the Plus Beaux Villages de France. Low houses with slate roofs frame a harbor where boats settle on the bottom at low tide. The Église Saint-Nicolas at the end of the quay has watched over the port since the 17th century. It was from Barfleur that William the Conqueror supposedly embarked in 1066 to conquer England.

Continue to the Gatteville lighthouse (about 29 km from Cherbourg, a 30-minute drive). The lighthouse is 75 meters tall and has 365 steps. If you have the stamina, climb it: the view of the pointe de Barfleur and the tidal-race currents is spectacular. Beside it, the small original lighthouse (1774) serves as a landmark.

Head to Saint-Vaast-la-Hougue (about 31 km from Cherbourg, a 30-minute drive). This oyster-farming port is dominated by the Vauban tower, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2008. Saint-Vaast's port is renowned for its oysters: you will find them to taste on the quay.

If the amphibious shuttle schedule permits, embark for Île Tatihou (10 min crossing). The island holds a second Vauban tower, a maritime botanical garden and a natural history museum. The ticket includes the crossing. Check times in advance—the shuttle depends on the tide.

A day in the wild landscapes of La Hague, the northwestern tip of the Cotentin Peninsula. Start with the Nez de Jobourg: plan a day trip from Cherbourg, parking your car before continuing on foot along the coastal path. The cliffs plunge 128 meters into the sea - among the highest in continental Europe. The coastal path follows the edge for about 2 km. In clear weather, you can see the Channel Islands. Beware of the wind: it blows hard here even in summer.

Continue north to Goury. The little sheltered harbor is dominated by the Phare de la Hague—an automated lighthouse you'll see from the coast, perched on a rock in open water. The SNSM lifeboat station building at the end of the jetty is a reminder that this sea passage (the Raz Blanchard) is one of the Channel's most dangerous, with currents reaching 12 knots.

Detour to Port Racine, 5 minutes from Goury. It's said to be France's smallest harbor—room for no more than about ten boats in a granite cove. The place is tiny and charming. Walk down the steps to the water.

Finish with the dunes of Biville on the west coast, planning a day trip from Cherbourg. This wild dune belt stretches for several kilometers beside a vast beach where you will probably be alone. The sand is fine and the sea powerful - swimming is not recommended (currents), but the walk is magnificent. If you enjoy windsurfing or kitesurfing, this is a well-known spot.

Head down the west coast of Cotentin to Barneville-Carteret (1 hour from Cherbourg). The Cap de Carteret is a windswept rocky promontory where an old signal station keeps watch over the sea. The customs officers' path circles the cape in 45 minutes—the view of Jersey in clear weather is the reward. The lighthouse at the summit offers a viewing point over the dunes and the Havre de Carteret.

Go back down to Barneville-Carteret beach. It's a large beach of fine sand stretching for kilometers to the south. At low tide the tidal inlet (estuary) empties and the channels in the sand form changing patterns. Much less crowded than the Calvados beaches.

activities.text: In the evening, if weather permits, head up to Fort du Roule on the hill overlooking Cherbourg. The view down over the roadstead, port and city is the finest on the peninsula. The fort houses a Liberation museum with free admission.

At low tide in Saint-Vaast, head down onto the seawall and observe the oyster beds as they are exposed. The oyster farmers tend their oyster bags directly in the water—it's a rare sight most visitors don't take time to see.

The road between La Hague's sites crosses landscapes of heathland and stone walls that recall Ireland. Stop frequently—sea views appear at every turn. Don't miss Baie d'Écalgrain, a wild cove accessible by a short path.

Walk north to the dunes of Hattainville, north of Carteret. It's one of Normandy's finest dune systems—marram grass (dune grass) stabilizes the sand across hundreds of hectares. A 5 km loop between dunes and beach gives you the feeling of being at the world's edge. No buildings on the horizon.
