visits.text: The Château de Cheverny has stayed in the same family for more than six centuries: the Hurault de Vibraye, who still live there. Built between 1624 and 1630 in a uniform classical style in Bourré stone, it is considered the most magnificently furnished château of the Loire, with its Gobelins and Flemish tapestries, its Louis XIV and Louis XV commodes and its period furniture still intact. The tour reveals sumptuous rooms such as the arms room with its carved paneling, the king's bedchamber and the grand salon with portraits by master painters. The château inspired Hergé's design for Marlinspike Hall in Tintin.

Cheverny's kennels house a pack of approximately 120 tricolor Anglo-French hunting hounds, descended from the English Foxhound and the French Poitevin. These magnificent dogs take part in hunts with hounds during the season. The dogs' feeding in the late afternoon is a fascinating spectacle: the animals are fed in the converted former stables according to a tradition kept up for generations. Visitors discover aristocratic hunting traditions. In spring, the puppy naming festival invites the public to propose names for the new arrivals, depending on the annual program.

Cheverny's gardens comprise six themed areas across nearly 100 hectares. The English-style garden has winding paths lined with majestic century-old linden trees. The botanical garden presents a rich collection of varied, labeled species. The vegetable and cutting garden designed by the marquise combines vegetables and flowers in a harmony of colors and innovative materials. The hedge maze challenges visitors to reach its heart. In spring, 120,000 multicolored tulips form a spectacular floral ribbon. Contemporary artworks punctuate the landscaped walks.

activities.text: The permanent exhibition Les Secrets de Moulinsart spans 700 square meters and recreates Tintin's world at full scale. The crypt, underground passage, drawing room, Tintin's bedroom, and Professor Calculus's laboratory immerse young and old in the famous reporter's adventures. Interactive sets with sound effects and models allow visitors to step literally into the comic panels. The dedicated 100-square-meter shop delights collectors with figurines, plush toys, and exclusive collectibles. This fun visit enchants families and rekindles adults' nostalgia.

Electric boat and cart rides on the canal and through Cheverny's park. The 115-meter canal dug in the 18th century allows a peaceful ride between shaded banks. Electric carts travel along the estate's paths, offering a comfortable tour of the 100-hectare park without fatigue. Changing views of the château reveal the harmony of its classical architecture. The 2-hectare vineyard producing white wine can be discovered during the ride through the estate's ancillary grounds.

Discovering the surrounding Sologne with its characteristic landscapes of heaths, ponds, and pine forests. Winding roads pass through villages with typical red-brick houses and past châteaux hidden behind foliage. Shimmering ponds attract varied birdlife, including herons, egrets, and wild ducks. This region rich in game has always been a favored hunting ground of kings and nobles. Sologne's farmhouses bear witness to preserved vernacular architecture. These landscapes inspired writer Maurice Genevoix.

days_plan.itin_title: Loir-et-Cher Itinerary: Royal Châteaux and the Loir Valley

visits.text: The royal fortress of Chinon, perched on its rocky spur, unfurls its ramparts for nearly a third of a mile. Three enclosures, Fort Saint-Georges, Chateau du Milieu and Fort du Coudray, chronicle ten centuries of history. Henry II Plantagenet stored his treasury here in the 12th century. It was here, on February 25, 1429, that Joan of Arc recognized Charles VII among his courtiers and convinced him to march to Reims.

The royal lodgings, restored after 200 years as ruins, recreate the apartments of Charles VII and Marie d'Anjou. The Histopad tablet offers 360° augmented reality reconstructions: Henry II Plantagenet's Christmas court, the Recognition scene with Joan of Arc, medieval war machines.

The old town of Chinon, at the fortress's foot, lines up half-timbered houses and tufa mansions in a maze of cobbled lanes. Rue Voltaire, the main artery, leads to Place Jeanne-d'Arc. François Rabelais, native son, set several episodes of Gargantua here. The collegiate church of Saint-Mexme preserves a 10th-century nave.

Stroll the quays of the Vienne for panoramic views of the fortress crowning the town. The river winds between vineyards—Chinon's 5,700-acre vineyard, on both banks, produces some of the Loire's most renowned cabernet franc reds.

activities.text: Visit to troglodyte wine caves and AOC Chinon tasting. Ancient tufa quarries, carved into the hillside, house naturally cool cellars. Chinon's cabernet franc reds are the perfect match for Tours rillettes and fouées.
Chinon market on Thursday morning, Place Jeanne-d'Arc. Goat cheeses, rillettes, fouées, garden vegetables and Chinon wines. Authentic Touraine market atmosphere.
Cruise or canoe on the Vienne. The calm river invites lazy paddles with views of the fortress and vineyard slopes. Several outfitters offer routes from one hour to half a day.

days_plan.itin_title: Indre-et-Loire Road Trip: Loire Valley Châteaux, Secret Valleys & Touraine Vineyards
Loire Valley Wine Route in 8 days

visits.text: Chiroubles nestles at the highest point of the Beaujolais vineyards, at an altitude of 400 metres. The winegrowing village spreads its terraced vineyards across steep slopes that catch every ray of sunshine. This high-altitude setting gives the wines a unique aromatic freshness, with a floral bouquet of violet and peony that makes the most delicate Beaujolais cru renowned.

The village's panoramic terrace offers views down over the tiered vineyards and, in the distance, the majestic outline of the Alps. On clear days, Mont Blanc appears on the horizon, creating a striking contrast between the green vines and snow-covered peaks. This natural viewpoint takes in the entire Chiroubles terroir at a glance.

The village church watches over the stone houses clinging to the slope. Narrow lanes wind between winegrowers' homes, whose cellars carved into the rock hold barrels. Each façade bears witness to a family history linked to the vines, handed down from father to son for generations.

The communal wine cellar and private estates offer tastings of this light, fragrant Chiroubles. The winegrowers explain the characteristics of the high-altitude granite terroir that produces these light, floral wines with a pale ruby colour. Elegance and finesse characterise this cru, often described as feminine by connoisseurs.

activities.text: Walk the vineyard trails that criss-cross the steep hillsides. Vines cultivated on the mountain slopes create a mosaic landscape where each plot has its own exposure and microclimate. The byways reveal the different named vineyard sites that make up the appellation, each contributing its nuances to the finished wine.

Enjoy Alpine panoramas from the heights of the vineyards. Benches at strategic viewpoints invite you to contemplate the mountain range silhouetted against the horizon. The scene changes with the seasons: green vines in spring, golden in autumn and bare in winter, revealing the hillside's terraced structure.

Taste Chiroubles wines from independent producers. This cru is characterised by its lightness for a Beaujolais, its intense floral aromas and its ability to be enjoyed young while also keeping for a few years. Passionate winegrowers describe the difficulty of working these steep slopes, where harvesting by hand remains the norm.

Visit the neighbouring villages of Fleurie and Morgon, reached by small roads winding through the vines. The Beaujolais crus circuit lets you compare styles and terroirs within a radius of a few kilometres. Each village has its own character, architecture and, of course, winegrowing personality.

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip from Bresse to Bugey via Beaujolais and Lyon

visits.text: The Museum of Art and History devotes its history gallery to the great moments of the Choletais region since Gallo-Roman times. A major focus is on the Vendée Wars, which deeply marked the town.
The Textile and Fashion Museum occupies the former cloth-bleaching factory built in 1881. Demonstrations on century-old looms and a look at the stages of fabric manufacture.
The museum workshop still weaves Cholet's famous red handkerchief. Red for the blood shed during the Vendée Wars, white for the monarchy, this local symbol has been sung about since 1900.
Notre-Dame Church stands in the town centre. Its architecture testifies to the rebuilding of Cholet after the destruction.
The Parc Oriental de Maulévrier, a few kilometres from Cholet, is the largest Japanese garden in Europe at 29 hectares.

activities.text: Puy du Fou is 25 km from Cholet. Voted Best Theme Park in the World, it offers grand historical shows and enchanting settings. The night-time Cinéscénie brings together 2,400 volunteer actors.
Cholet's market, held on Saturdays, is one of the most important in Anjou. Local produce and regional specialities are on offer.
Parc de Moine and Lac de Ribou offer natural spaces to recharge. Hiking and water activities are available.

days_plan.itin_title: Maine-et-Loire Road Trip: Anjou and Loire Valley Châteaux

visits.text: The Choranche cave is the most spectacular natural site in the northern Vercors. In 1871, drought drove villagers to follow a dry streambed; at the foot of the Presles cliffs (300 meters high), they entered a cavity from which water flowed. It wasn't until 1897 that Oscar Descombaz, speleology pioneer, conducted the first explorations. Open to the public since 1967. Choranche's distinctive feature: thousands of tubular stalactites—"calcite straws" exceeding 3 meters—cover the vaults. They've grown only 5 cm in 100 years. No site in Europe concentrates so many. Bring a sweater: it's permanently 10°C.

Along two underground rivers, you'll encounter olms in their aquariums: blind, depigmented cave amphibians from Slovenia, capable of fasting for months and living up to 80 years. The visit concludes in the Cathedral Room—40 meters in diameter, 25 meters high—with a sound and light show projected onto millennia-old walls. Book ahead in high season.

The cave's outdoor site offers exceptional views of the Presles cliffs and limestone cirque. Before or after the visit, walk the developed path at the foot of the walls: karst geology is visible to the naked eye, with Jurassic limestone strata exposed for hundreds of meters.

activities.text: The balcony trail overlooking the Bourne valley starts from Choranche village and climbs 3-5 km in marked aerial passages along the cliffs. Across the way, the Presles walls with their climbing routes, and below, the river emerging from rock. One of the Vercors' most striking routes—bring hiking shoes.

days_plan.itin_title: Royans-Vercors Road Trip: Hilltop Villages and Gorges

places.name: Cite De L Architecture Et Du Patrimoine

visits.text: The Cité de l'Architecture et du Patrimoine, in the east wing of Palais de Chaillot, is a surprising museum: its gallery of plaster casts presents life-size reproductions of cathedral portals, sculptures, and frescoes from great French monuments—from Chartres to Vézelay, from Conques to Notre-Dame de Paris. You literally walk through the façade of Chartres at 1:1 scale. The gallery of murals and stained glass, contemporary architecture collections, and a direct view of the Eiffel Tower from the windows complete the ensemble. Allow at least 2 hours.

activities.text: Palais de Chaillot, built for the 1937 Universal Exposition on the site of the former Trocadéro, also houses the Maritime Museum and the Museum of Mankind—plan a second visit if these themes interest you. The central terrace between the two wings offers the most perfect view of the Eiffel Tower and the Champ-de-Mars.

places.name: Cite Des Sciences Et De L Industrie

visits.text: The Cité des Sciences et de l'Industrie, inaugurated in 1986 in the former La Villette slaughterhouses transformed by Adrien Fainsilber, is Europe's largest science museum: 30,000 m² of permanent and temporary exhibitions, a planetarium, a real submarine to visit, and the Géode—a steel sphere 36 meters in diameter with a 1,000 m² hemispherical screen. The interactive exhibitions are calibrated for all age groups. If you're coming with children, block out the entire day. Without children, 2 hours allows you to see the essentials.

activities.text: Parc de la Villette (55 hectares), Paris's largest urban park, surrounds the Cité des Sciences. It houses the Philharmonie de Paris, the Grande Halle, red follies designed by Bernard Tschumi, and themed gardens. In summer, the outdoor cinema is free. A walk from the Cité to the Canal de l'Ourcq takes 30 minutes.

visits.text: Saint-Nicolas Church in Civray has one of the most ornate Romanesque façades in Poitou, alongside Notre-Dame-la-Grande. Built in the 12th century, it displays the Wise and Foolish Virgins, the Assumption of the Virgin, the Labors of the Months, and the signs of the Zodiac across two tiers.

Step inside to see the 13th-century fresco recounting the legend of Saint Giles in the south transept. The rest of the interior was painted in the 19th century by Amédée Brouillet, creating a highly colorful atmosphere beneath the octagonal lantern tower.
The Hôtel de la Prévôté, built in the late 15th century, hosted King Louis XIII and his young wife in 1616. Several private mansions line the town's streets.

Fifteen minutes from Civray, the village of Charroux preserves a tall octagonal tower—a remnant of the 11th-century Saint-Sauveur Abbey—plus a cloister and chapter house. The village holds the Petite Cité de Caractère designation.

activities.text: Walk along the Charente River in Civray. A path leads to the leisure area and Île Foin, a 10-minute walk from the center. The town holds the Station Verte designation.
Visit local producers in the Civray region: farmhouse cheeses, artisanal apple juice, and Poitevin charcuterie can be found within a few kilometers.

days_plan.itin_title: Vienne Road Trip: Futuroscope and Romanesque Heritage

visits.text: In a clear valley that gave the site its name, Clairvaux Abbey-Prison unfolds 900 years of confinement across 30 hectares. On June 25, 1115, Bernard of Fontaine—the future Saint Bernard—founded the third daughter house of Cîteaux there with twelve companions. The abbey flourished, housing as many as 900 monks at its peak and founding 80 daughter abbeys across Europe. Rebuilt in the 18th century in a classical style by prosperous monks, it changed purpose during the French Revolution. In 1808, Napoleon I purchased the site to turn it into France's largest prison, holding 3,500 inmates during the 19th century. Closed in 2023, it is finally revealing its secrets to visitors.

A masterpiece of Cistercian architecture, the 12th-century Lay Brothers' Building, 74 meters long, embodies Saint Bernard's ideal: restraint, light and purity of line. A rib-vaulted cellar with semicircular arches occupies the ground floor, while the upper floor contains a dormitory with groin vaults. Begun before the founder's death, it bears witness to the first medieval Clairvaux. It contrasts completely with the 18th-century Refectory-Chapel, with its stucco ceilings decorated with trophies, painted paneling and black-and-white checkerboard floors. Converted into a chapel for prisoners in the 19th century, it combines classical splendor with its later prison use.

The most striking building is the Disciplinary Wing, dating from the second half of the 19th century and used until December 2017. Cramped isolation cells measuring 1.5 m by 2 m, metal walkways and windowless punishment cells recount the detention conditions endured by the thousands of men who lived here. This moving visit delves into the history of the French prison system: revolts, escapes and daily prison life. A powerful experience. Restricted to visitors over 11 and limited to 18 people.

activities.text: Extended 2.5-hour tours combining the historic abbey and the disciplinary wing give a complete picture of monastic and then penal confinement. Tours of the restoration site, with access to the scaffolding on the south front of the Great Cloister, reveal the colossal challenges of preservation. Passionate guides recount Victor Hugo denouncing the death penalty here (Claude Gueux), mutinies and famous inmates. Closed flat shoes are compulsory on the worksite. Booking strongly advised.

Clairvaux comes alive with a bold cultural program: classical and contemporary music concerts benefiting from the exceptional acoustics of the lay brothers' dormitory, art exhibitions, a giant live-action Cluedo game and treasure hunts for families. The Renaissance de l'Abbaye de Clairvaux association organizes these events throughout the year, creating a dialogue between centuries-old heritage and contemporary works. Program available at abbayedeclairvaux.com.

days_plan.itin_title: Aube Tour: Champagne, Medieval Heritage and the Lakes of the Forêt d'Orient

visits.text: Clairvaux-les-Lacs consists of two lakes with very different destinies: the Grand Lac (64 hectares, maximum depth 28 meters) is open to the public with its fine sand beach labeled Blue Flag for over ten years, its diving boards at 3, 5 and 7.50 meters and its water activities (pedal boat, canoe, windsurfing). The Petit Lac (21 hectares) is private — swimming and fishing are prohibited there. In summer, the water of the Grand Lac reaches 25°C: a warmth that few Jura bodies of water can claim to reach. Arrive when the parking opens to get a spot — the site is very busy in July-August.

The shores of the Clairvaux lakes have been inhabited since prehistory — underwater excavations have revealed stilt dwellings between 5000 and 500 BC. These sites have been inscribed as UNESCO World Heritage Sites since 2011, just like the Chalain site. An archaeological exhibition space on lake cities is open in July-August. Don't miss either the tower of the former 12th-century castle that dominates the village, and the entire street dedicated to wood artisans (wooden toys, cutlery, regional products) — this is the "Village du Bois" (Wood Village).

activities.text: Bike ride around the lakes on marked cycling routes: the gentle topography around the Clairvaux lakes is ideal for a family bike outing. The Langard circuit (10 km around the Petit Lac) passes through wooded areas and panoramas over the recesses. Local providers offer bike and mountain bike rentals in the village.

Relaxing time kayaking or stand-up paddling on the Grand Lac: local providers set up on the shores of the Grand Lac offer rentals of non-motorized craft. Motorized navigation is prohibited (except electric engines), which guarantees calm water and visibility to the bottom. Water quality is regularly monitored — the Blue Flag label attests to this.

days_plan.itin_title: Jura Lakes Route: Emerald and Turquoise Waters

visits.text: The Museum of Art and History occupies the birthplace of Romain Rolland, winner of the 1915 Nobel Prize for Literature, and the 17th-century Hôtel du Duc de Bellegarde. It holds the "Maisons des Illustres" label.
The log-floating room evokes the activity that supplied Paris with wood from the Morvan for 400 years. In 1804, over 3,500 timber rafts arrived in Paris from Clamecy.
The museum preserves 6,000 posters by Charles Loupot, a 20th-century advertising giant—the world's most complete collection. Clamecy earthenware and Gallo-Roman archaeology round out the collections.

The Collegiate Church of Saint-Martin, built between the 13th and 16th centuries, dominates the town with its two towers. Its Flamboyant Gothic portal and ancient stained glass windows are worth the detour.
Bethlehem Church, a fortified Romanesque building, once served as the parish church for log floaters. Its square bell tower and thick walls recall its defensive role.

activities.text: Walk along the Nivernais Canal, opened in 1841 after three tunnels were cut. The towpath offers a shady stroll between locks and unspoiled landscapes.
Visit the Log Floating Ecomuseum where enthusiasts teach you how to build a timber raft. Discover the epic of the floaters who descended the Yonne to Paris.
Relax in Parc Vauvert, a green haven in the heart of Clamecy. Its century-old trees and paths invite relaxation after the museum visit.

days_plan.itin_title: Nièvre Road Trip: Morvan and Ducal Heritage

visits.text: Droiteval Abbey has more to it than meets the eye, deep in the Darney forest. Founded in 1130 by Lord Aubert de Darney—who wanted, according to the texts, to atone for his sins—it is a Cistercian abbey that became a priory in the 15th century, then national property during the Revolution. A royal forge was established there, followed by a scythe factory. Restored in the 19th century, it became private property again in 1987 and has housed an art and culture center since the 2000s. Check opening hours before coming—they vary according to the season and current exhibitions.

activities.text: The Darney forest surrounds the abbey site and offers forest paths that are easy to explore on foot. If you have energy, continue to Châtillon-sur-Saône, about twenty kilometers south: it's an exceptionally well-preserved Renaissance village, with 16th- and 17th-century mansions that have hardly changed since. Little known, rarely crowded—go in the afternoon.

days_plan.itin_title: Vosges Abbey Trail: Monastic Heritage

visits.text: Leaving the Mont-Saint-Michel area, stop in Mortain for the Grandes Cascades - the highest in western France, with a 25-meter drop in a green setting. The access path descends through a beech forest. Right next door, the Abbaye Blanche (12th century), a former Cistercian abbey, can be visited from outside - the terraced gardens offer a view of the Cance valley.

Welcome to Suisse Normande - don't expect the Alps, but the steep Orne valleys have surprises in store. The Rocher de la Houle, above Clécy, offers a viewpoint over the Orne's meanders and wooded hills. It's the sector's most photographed vantage point.

Continue to Rocher des Parcs, another viewpoint accessible by a short ridge trail. The view plunges to the river below and the schist cliffs bordering the valley. In autumn, the colors are spectacular.

The Roches d'Oëtre are Suisse Normande's most impressive natural site. From the viewpoint, you overlook the Rouvre gorges from 118 meters. The rock profile, seen from the right angle, draws a human face - look for it. A marked trail circuits the site in 45 minutes.

activities.text: Hike the Orne ridges on a marked route starting from Clécy. You'll follow the high points with views over the valley, river and bocage meadows. This is Normandy's green heart, far from beaches and tourists.

days_plan.itin_title: Complete Normandy Road Trip: Cliffs, D-Day Beaches and Mont-Saint-Michel
Cotentin, Pays d'Auge: 5 days exploring the most beautiful villages

visits.text: Saint-Samson Church has a Rayonnant Gothic façade dating from the 13th and 14th centuries. Its sculpted portal and rose window dominate the Place d'Armes from the hill overlooking the Brèche valley.
The municipal belfry has stood since the 12th century as a symbol of civic freedoms. Rebuilt in the 16th century, it marks the town's independence from the Counts of Clermont.
The Town Hall occupies a 16th-century Renaissance building. Its stone and brick façades testify to the town's prosperity during the Wars of Religion.

activities.text: Follow the remains of medieval ramparts around the historic centre. The 12th-century fortifications protected the town perched on its limestone spur.

days_plan.itin_title: Oise Circuit: châteaux, forests and history

visits.text: Notre-Dame-de-l'Assomption Cathedral crowns the historic center's hilltop with its black lava silhouette. Construction began in 1248 under Jean Deschamps, making it the first major edifice built entirely from Volvic stone, whose exceptional strength allowed remarkably slender pillars. Inside, a unique collection of stained glass from the 12th to 19th centuries floods the nave with colored light. The twin 96-meter spires, added by Viollet-le-Duc in the 19th century, signal the monument from every quarter of the city.

In the old merchant quarter of Portus, Notre-Dame-du-Port Basilica radiates the warm glow of golden arkose stone—a striking contrast to the dark tones of the ubiquitous lava. Built in the first third of the 12th century and inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site as part of the Santiago de Compostela pilgrimage routes, it ranks among the five great Romanesque churches of Auvergne. Its pyramidal east end adorned with lava stone mosaics, its 250 capitals with narrative carvings, and its sculpted portal stand as some of the finest examples of Romanesque art in France. In the crypt, pilgrimage to the Black Madonna has been documented since 1614.

The musée Bargoin is closed to the public for renovation work. Its archaeological collections trace the Auvergne region from prehistory to the Gallo-Roman period: the Bronze Age Trésor de Manson, a monumental bronze foot and the Gallic votive offerings from the source des Roches in Chamalières illustrate their richness. To discover this heritage during the closure, museum workshops and activities are offered in the former bibliothèque Lafayette premises on boulevard Lafayette in Clermont-Ferrand, according to the program.

Across 2,000 square meters of exhibition space, L'Aventure Michelin traces more than a century of industrial history that began in Clermont-Ferrand. From the Michelin brothers' first pneumatic tires to contemporary innovations, the visitor route combines spectacular vehicles, interactive screens, cinemas, and exploration notebooks. The story of Bibendum, the worldwide mascot, unfolds through archival documents and unusual objects. The museum is bilingual in French and English, with audio guides in several languages.

Place de Jaude, Clermont-Ferrand's largest esplanade, brings the city's bustle together around its fountains and magnolia trees. The equestrian statue of Vercingetorix by Bartholdi—the sculptor of the Statue of Liberty—dominates the square with its triumphant posture. The 19th-century theater, Saint-Pierre-des-Minimes church, and Galeries de Jaude line this square, where strolling visitors mingle among café terraces and seasonal markets.

Vulcania immerses visitors in the telluric forces that shaped Auvergne. This European volcano park, set in the Chaîne des Puys, combines immersive experiences, shows and educational workshops on volcanoes, geology and natural phenomena. Among the flagship attractions: La Chaîne des Puys racontée, le Réveil des géants and Premier envol, a spectacular flight over the volcanoes. The park can be reached by shuttle from the Clermont-Ferrand railway station, about 15 km from the stopover town, a 20-minute drive.

Puy de Dôme rises to 1,465 meters, the highest point in the Chaîne des Puys, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Panoramique des Dômes electric rack railway makes the 500-meter ascent in fifteen minutes, with departures every 20 to 40 minutes depending on the season. At the summit, the 360-degree panorama takes in 80 dormant volcanoes, the Limagne plain, and, on clear days, the Massif du Sancy. Three themed trails traverse the site: the Chemin des pèlerins, the Chemin des conquérants, and the Chemin des curieux.

The ruins of the Temple of Mercury atop Puy de Dôme constitute the largest mountain sanctuary in Roman Gaul. Built in the 2nd century, this monumental temple testifies to the site's religious importance since antiquity. An interactive museum space presents the sanctuary's history and the results of archaeological excavations. A treasure hunt with three difficulty levels, Les Reliques du Temple, offers a fun way to discover the site.

activities.text: Wander through the two historic centers of Clermont and Montferrand, brought together by the union of two rival cities in 1630. In Clermont, medieval lanes wind around the cathedral among Renaissance mansions, sculpted fountains, and volcanic stone facades. Montferrand's protected quarter preserves its bastide grid plan and exceptional private mansions, including the celebrated Maison de l'Apothicaire.

Discover Clermont's street art on an urban trail that leads from mural to mural through downtown streets. Five major works created in the city coexist with more discreet pieces scattered along the lanes, like the one on rue des Bohêmes evoking Lascaux's cave paintings. The Such'Art route, designed by the Sommet Urbain Clermontois association, guides curious visitors among art galleries, antique dealers, and murals.

Taste Auvergne's culinary specialties in the historic center's restaurants. Truffade, potée auvergnate, stuffed cabbage, tripoux, and potato pie are part of the local culinary repertoire. The PDO cheeses—Saint-Nectaire, Bleu d'Auvergne, Cantal, Fourme d'Ambert—accompany meals or can be enjoyed on their own.

Hike the sentier des Muletiers to reach Puy de Dôme's summit on foot. This historic 5 km path offers a strenuous but accessible climb with 420 meters of elevation gain. The route crosses moorland and high-altitude meadows before opening onto the summit panorama.

Witness the Brocken specter phenomenon from Puy de Dôme's summit when conditions are right. This optical illusion projects the observer's shadow onto the sea of clouds, surrounded by a circular rainbow. Free seasonal activities include guided walks with interpreters, summit concerts, and yoga sessions with volcano views.

Paragliding from Puy de Dôme's summit for thrill-seekers. The site ranks among France's most renowned for free flight thanks to regular updrafts and an exceptional panorama over the volcanic chain. Introductory flights supervised by certified instructors.

days_plan.itin_title: Auvergne Circuit: Perched Villages and Volcanoes
Auvergne Volcanoes Road Trip: Puy de Dôme and Lakes
Volcanoes and Auvergne traditions
Volcanoes and Auvergne traditions

visits.text: Clisson Castle has watched over the Sèvre Nantaise from an elevated position since a wooden castle stood here in the 9th century—the stone fortress you see today was built over five centuries, from the 12th to the 17th. This is where two great figures of Breton history were born: Olivier V de Clisson, Constable of France, and Francis II, the last Duke of Brittany and father of Anne of Brittany. Burned during the Vendée Wars, the castle was bought in 1807 by the sculptor Lemot, who turned it into a romantic setting for his artist friends. Its ruins, today preserved across four hectares, offer a remarkable panorama over the town below.

Then cross the old stone bridge over the Sèvre and wander the cobbled streets: ochre houses, Roman-style barrel tiles, umbrella pines, and round arches make you forget you're in Loire-Atlantique. After the destruction of the Vendée Wars, Clisson was rebuilt in the 19th century in a neoclassical style of Italian inspiration, driven by the Cacault brothers and the sculptor Lemot—one of a kind in France. Notre-Dame Church, rebuilt in the 19th century on the model of an Italian Romanesque church, is the most striking example, with its Tuscan campanile.

The wooden medieval market halls, built in the 14th century, rank among France's largest and oldest. They still host a market on Tuesday and Friday mornings—if you're there, it's the best place to buy local produce. Then venture into the Domaine de la Garenne Lemot on the opposite bank: an English-style landscape park, a temple, follies, and views of Clisson create a beautifully romantic scene.

activities.text: The Clisson vineyards produce one of the most renowned Muscadets of the Nantes region. The Clisson communal cru, recognized in 2011, comes from old vines on granite—the Armorican bedrock, weathered into granite sand, gives the wines their notes of smoke, candied citrus, and sweet spices. Head to the cellars of the wine estates to taste this Muscadet suitable for aging, aged on its lees for at least two years. Plan to book your tasting in advance.

Follow the river on foot or by canoe from the Pont Caffino site. The river winds between granite cliffs, watermills and vineyards: the scenery changes around every bend. If you are here in June, check the dates of Hellfest, the metal festival that turns Clisson into the world capital of the genre for several days and has attracted hundreds of thousands of festivalgoers since 2006.

days_plan.itin_title: Loire-Atlantique Road Trip: Nantes and the Côte de Jade

visits.text: Cluny Abbey, founded in 910 by William the Pious, was the center of the largest monastic order in the West. At its peak around 1100, the Cluniac order ruled over 10,000 monks and 1,500 monasteries across Europe. The Cluny III abbey church, the largest church in Christendom before St. Peter's in Rome, measured 187 meters long.

Only 8% of the immense abbey church remains after its destruction during the Revolution—it was sold as a stone quarry in 1798 and dynamited by an unscrupulous contractor. The great transept, the Eau-Bénite bell tower, and the world's tallest Romanesque vaults still testify to its enormous scale.

The Farinier, a 13th-century monastic building, houses the capitals from the curved end of Cluny III's choir—carved around 1095, they represent the eight modes of Gregorian chant and the seasons. The 3D digital reconstruction lets you visualize the abbey church in its original dimensions.

The Palais Jean de Bourbon, Museum of Art and Archaeology, is a rare example of a lord's residence in the Flamboyant Gothic style. Monumental fireplaces, state rooms, and medieval sculptures from the town and abbey. Don't miss the full-scale reconstruction of the Great Portal of Cluny III.

Climb the 120 steps of the Tour des Fromages, a former tower in the abbey's perimeter walls, for an exceptional panorama over the abbey town, Cluny's rooftops, and the Burgundian countryside. The monastic town below has rows of Romanesque and Gothic houses—a rare urban ensemble.

activities.text: Guided tour of the abbey. Your guide recreates the scale of the vanished building through the remains, augmented reality terminals, and an immersive 3D film. The screens act as windows revealing the past in the present.
Grands Crus de Bourgogne music festival. Every summer, concerts in the monks' Farinier and the abbey cloister. Classical and early music in an exceptional medieval setting.

Stroll through the town of Cluny. Romanesque and Gothic houses, two parish churches, the Hôtel-Dieu, and the national stud farm make up a rich urban heritage. The École nationale supérieure d'arts et métiers occupies the 18th-century monastic buildings.

days_plan.itin_title: Saône-et-Loire Road Trip: Bibracte, Cluny, Solutré & the Mâconnais Vineyards
Burgundy's 15 Most Beautiful Villages
Burgundy-Franche-Comté: The Most Beautiful Villages in 7 days

visits.text: The Hennessy house offers the most spectacular tour: solar-powered boat crossing of the Charente, ageing cellars where the “angel's share” floats in the air, guided tasting. Booking essential.

Martell, the oldest of the great houses (1715), has renovated its historic site with its Art Deco tower. Tour of the century-old cellars and the founder's house. A more intimate atmosphere than at Hennessy.
The Château de Cognac, birthplace of Francis I, houses Baron Otard cognacs. Renaissance vaulted cellars, rooftop view over the Charente. French history entwined with the story of cognac.
Old Cognac can be explored on foot: medieval houses with walls blackened by the cognac fungus (the famous Torula), merchants' townhouses, quays where gabares loaded barrels.
The Musée des Arts du Cognac traces the history of this spirit: stills, cooperage, vintage labels, retro advertisements. A good complement to cellar tours. Housed in two townhouses.

activities.text: Tour of a major cognac house. Hennessy for the immersive experience, Martell for intimacy, Rémy Martin for connoisseurs (expert tours available). Allow 1 hour 30 minutes to 2 hours including tasting.
Cruise on the Charente. Traditional gabares with commentary (1 hour 30 minutes) or electric boat hire with no licence required. The river at the pace of the barrels of old.
Cycling along the Charente. The Flow Vélo (national route) passes through Cognac. Bike hire available in town. Flat route to Jarnac (15 km) or Saint-Brice (8 km).

days_plan.itin_title: Charente Tour: Cognac and Romanesque Heritage in 4 Days

places.name: Colleville Sur Mer

visits.text: Perched on the cliff overlooking Omaha Beach, the American Cemetery at Colleville-sur-Mer spreads its 9,387 white crosses in perfect rows across an emerald lawn. The headstones face westward towards the homeland, while at the centre, the bronze statue “The Spirit of American Youth Rising from the Waves” watches over this haven of peace. The chapel, the Garden of the Missing and the Visitor Centre movingly recount Operation Overlord and the sacrifice of an entire generation.

Walk down to Omaha Beach, the scene of “Bloody Omaha” on 6 June 1944. The fine sand stretches peacefully today, but the remains of blockhouses and memorials recall the 2,500 American soldiers who fell in a single day. The calm sea contrasts with the memory of waves laden with men and equipment, creating a uniquely contemplative atmosphere.

At Pointe du Hoc, the 30-metre cliffs bear the indelible marks of bombardment. Moon-like craters, shattered bunkers and gaping casemates bear witness to the heroic assault by Colonel Rudder's 225 Rangers, who scaled these walls at dawn on D-Day. The site, managed by the American administration, offers a striking panorama over the English Channel and illustrates the ferocity of the fighting.

activities.text: Walk the coastal path between Omaha Beach and Pointe du Hoc. Toposcopes line this historic route offering spectacular views of the cliffs and the sea.
Attend the flag-lowering ceremony at the American Cemetery. Every day at 4 pm, the American flag is retired to the sound of Taps in reverent silence.

days_plan.itin_title: Calvados Tour: D-Day Beaches and Normandy

map_keywords: Coastal Trail Omaha Pointe du Hoc

visits.text: The Royal Castle has plunged its stone walls into the Mediterranean since the 13th century. Built by the Kings of Majorca then remodeled by Vauban, it offers a panoramic view in all directions over the bay and the Albères.

The Church of Our Lady of the Angels rises from the waves with its 17th-century lighthouse-bell tower. Its baroque altarpiece by Joseph Sunyer, covered in gold leaf, features 97 figurines and statues.

Fort Saint-Elme overlooks the bay with a 360° panorama. This fortress dating from 1538 controlled the passage between Collioure and Port-Vendres. Closed to visitors since 2023, it can only be viewed from outside.
La Vitrine sur le Fauvisme displays reproductions and documents about Matisse and Derain. It's the starting point for the Chemin du Fauvisme.
Step inside the Chapel of Saint Vincent, perched on its rocky outcrop. It houses the patron saint's relics brought back from Rome in 1700.

activities.text: Follow the Chemin du Fauvisme. Reproductions mark the exact spots where Matisse and Derain set up their easels in 1905.
Get lost in the narrow streets of Mouré and Port d'Avall. The ochre-pink facades capture the light that seduced the painters.
Admire the colorful Catalan boats on the pebble beach. Fishermen still haul in their nets from 5 a.m. onward.
Taste Collioure's AOC anchovies. The 16th-century cellars preserve Banyuls and Collioure wines, fortified on site.

days_plan.itin_title: Pyrénées-Orientales Road Trip: French Catalonia and the Côte Vermeille

visits.text: Built in the 12th century, the humpbacked Pont-Vieux straddles the Réal Collobrier at the heart of Collobrières, the chestnut capital of the Massif des Maures. Ducks paddle against the gentle current beneath the gaze of old houses with colored shutters. It's the village's must-have postcard shot. A bench nearby lets you linger without blocking pedestrians where the passage is narrow.

If you climb above the village, the ruins of Saint-Pons church, medieval in origin, still overlook the rooftops of Collobrières. The 19th-century Gothic building that replaced it now houses the original bell from the Chartreuse de la Verne, moved here in the 1800s. The climb is short but steep—good shoes recommended.

activities.text: Locals will tell you: don't leave the village without stopping at the Confiserie Azuréenne, which has been making candied chestnuts and chestnut cream since 1945. Collobrières is known as the chestnut capital of the Massif des Maures. The Chestnut Festival is held on the last three Sundays of October—the liveliest time but also the most crowded.

days_plan.itin_title: Var in 4 Days: From Bormes to the Most Beautiful Villages of the Verdon

visits.text: Saint-Pierre Church and its sculpted tympanum. Romanesque building from the 11th century with a rare detail: the tympanum representing Christ's Ascension is made of white Turenne limestone, which contrasts with the surrounding red sandstone. The octagonal gabled bell tower exceeds 20 meters. The church was divided in two during the Wars of Religion to accommodate both religious services simultaneously.

Penitents' Chapel (Saint-Maximin). This 14th-century Gothic chapel served as a burial place for noble families including the Maussacs (coat of arms visible on a vault keystone). From the mid-17th to the late 19th century, the Black Penitents brotherhood met here. Saved from ruin in 1927 by the Amis de Collonges, it houses a stained glass window by Francis Chigot (1937) depicting the Resurrection, and two contemporary stained glass windows by Didier Mencoboni and Olivier Juteau (2016).

Castel de Vassinhac. Built in 1583, this manor house belonged to the lords of Collonges, who were also governors of the Viscounty of Turenne. The façade features mullioned windows typical of the Renaissance, and two round towers flank the building.

Maison de la Sirène. 16th-century residence that owes its name to the mermaid sculpted to the right of the entrance door. It houses a small museum of folk arts and traditions with a reconstruction of a Corrèze interior from days gone by.

16th-century grain hall. The wine and walnut oil market was held under this covered hall. The floor is paved with red sandstone. It was here that Charles Ceyrac, former mayor, launched the Plus Beaux Villages de France association in 1982. Collonges was the first village to receive the label.

activities.text: Walk through the narrow streets with 25 towers. Allow 2 hours for the complete tour. The noble houses with blue stone-slab or slate roofs were built by officers of the Viscounty of Turenne between the 15th and 16th centuries. Vines climb the red facades—the green/red contrast is striking. The red sandstone comes from a geological fault between Brive and Meyssac, rich in iron oxide.
Tasting of Corrèze straw wine. This sweet wine is produced from grapes dried on straw racks. A few local producers offer tastings in the village or around Meyssac.
Meyssac Market. 1.5 km from Collonges, the neighboring village holds a market on Tuesdays and Fridays year-round, and on Sundays in July-August.

days_plan.itin_title: Corrèze Road Trip: Villages and Dordogne Valley
Nouvelle-Aquitaine Loop: Villages, Vineyards & Dordogne
The Most Beautiful Villages of Lot and Périgord in 6 Days

visits.text: Colmars-les-Alpes sits at an altitude of 1,250 metres in the Haut-Verdon valley, where Alpine and Provençal influences meet: medieval ramparts, fountains adorned with flowers, sundials on the façades and tall houses with colourful shutters. Founded by the Romans under the name Collis Martis, the town received its first fortifications in 1382, when the neighbouring village of Allos passed to the Duchy of Savoy. It was awarded the Plus Beaux Villages de France designation in September 2025; start by wandering through its lanes and along the 500-metre rampart walk encircling the town.

Fort de Savoie is the landmark monument: built between 1693 and 1696 by the engineer Creuzet de Richerand (following plans by Vauban, who never came to the site), it guarded the border with Savoy. Listed as a Historic Monument since 1923, it houses an immersive exhibition with projections and reconstructed scenes about the history of Colmars. The guided tour lasts about 1 hour 30 minutes and is offered in July and August. Fort de France, on the downstream side, can be seen clearly from the ramparts.

In the house museum beside the rampart walk, a recreated 19th-century middle-class apartment immerses you in the daily life of the fortified town. And if you have 20 minutes, head to the Jardin de l'Apothicaire: dedicated to the village's 17th-century apothecary, it brings together aromatic and medicinal plants from the Haut-Verdon — a peaceful and fragrant garden just steps from the ramparts.

activities.text: The Cascade de la Lance can be reached on foot from the village in 20 minutes (an easy, waymarked trail suitable for families). On the way back, take the Canal de l'Adroit trail (4 km loop, 2 hours, information panels on the fortified heritage) for an elevated view of the ramparts and the Mercantour peaks.

Colmars stands at the gates of Mercantour National Park: in summer, half-day hikes lead to alpine pastures and high-altitude lakes. Operators also offer canyoning outings in the nearby gorges — a fine option if the weather is warm.

days_plan.itin_title: Forcalquier & Verdon Gorges Road Trip

visits.text: The Charles de Gaulle Memorial, inaugurated in October 2008 by Nicolas Sarkozy and Angela Merkel for the 50th anniversary of the Fifth Republic, is designed as the base of the Lorraine Cross. Over 1,600 square metres, the display retraces the history of the 20th century through the General's life: immersive sets, films on giant screens, multimedia terminals. This is not a traditional museum, there is no object that belonged to the General, but a living interpretation centre. Allow two hours.

The Lorraine Cross rises 44.3 meters in reinforced concrete sheathed in pink granite, visible from 15 kilometers away. In 1954, speaking to André Malraux while viewing the hill, de Gaulle said: "Look at that hill. It's the highest. When I am gone, they will erect a Lorraine Cross there." He added with characteristic wit: "No one will visit… save rabbits to mount a resistance." Inaugurated on June 18, 1972, two years after his death.

La Boisserie can be visited on a combined ticket with the Memorial. De Gaulle bought this former brewery turned family home in 1934, halfway between Paris and his eastern garrisons. It was here that he received Konrad Adenauer in September 1958, the first historic Franco-German meeting of the Fifth Republic. It was also here that he died on 9 November 1970, in his study in the hexagonal tower. The General's grave, in the village cemetery, respects the wish for simplicity he had expressed: a plain white slab, far from official honours.

activities.text: Follow the interpretive trails that start from the Cross of Lorraine: three waymarked routes lead through the Dhuits forest and the Champagne landscapes de Gaulle described in his Memoirs. In autumn, you may well hear the stags belling.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Marne Circuit: Langres and Heritage

visits.text: Combourg Castle. A granite fortress built in the 11th century on a hillock overlooking Lac Tranquille, this medieval castle with its four pepper-pot towers is the birthplace of French Romanticism. François-René de Chateaubriand spent his childhood and adolescence here, sleeping in the tour du Chat, which he said was haunted by the ghost of a peg-legged count and a black cat. The guided tour passes through rooms with period furnishings, reveals the writer's bedroom, then climbs to the crenellated rampart walk, offering magnificent views over the 25-hectare park and surrounding countryside. The mysterious atmosphere that deeply affected young François-René still permeates the dark corridors and turret staircases, creating total immersion in the Romantic world of Memoirs from Beyond the Grave.

Lac Tranquille and Romantic Park. This vast pond, fed by a natural spring, lies at the foot of the castle, creating enchanting reflections of the fortress in its calm waters. Chateaubriand named it Lac Tranquille in reference to the tranquility that came over him during boat rides at twilight. The English landscape park designed in the 19th century by the Bühler brothers draws inspiration from Memoirs from Beyond the Grave: Cour Verte, Grand Mail and Petit Mail, and avenues of oaks, lindens, and horse chestnuts recreate the atmosphere described by the writer. The 250-year-old false cypress designated an Arbre Remarquable, the Rose Chateaubriand, and the cross of Lucile (his sister) mark the literary walk. The gazebo on the lake's north shore completes this perfect Romantic tableau.

Combourg, a Petite Cité de Caractère. The town developed between the castle and Notre-Dame Church around three medieval centers: the settlement belonging to the lord, the parish settlement, and the Trinité priory founded by Benedictine monks. The Maison de la Lanterne, illuminated by torches during the Angevine fair until the Revolution, the Cour des Templiers, and the Relais des Princes testify to a prosperous past linked to the cloth trade and tanning. Cobbled streets, half-timbered houses, and a tranquil atmosphere invite a timeless stroll.

Literary Trails and Chateaubriand. Three walking routes follow in the writer's footsteps: the Patrimoine route reveals architectural treasures, the Chateaubriand route follows the places where he lived and meditated, and the Littéraire route makes a complete circuit of Lac Tranquille. Interpretive panels along the routes quote Memoirs from Beyond the Grave and explain how this setting forged the Romantic sensibility of this literary movement's founding father. The statue of Chateaubriand by Alphonse Terroir has stood in Place du Lac since 1930.

activities.text: Ille-et-Rance Canal and Water Sports. A few kilometers away, this 85-kilometer canal links Rennes to Saint-Malo via Dinan, offering an ideal setting for kayaking, canoeing, paddleboarding, or cycling on the towpath. Rental operators offer self-guided or guided trips downstream lasting several hours, allowing visitors to discover the Breton countryside from the water in a bucolic atmosphere. Old locks, stone bridges, and the villages along the route create an enchanting setting.

Dinard-Dinan Greenway. This former railway line, converted into a safe bike path, crosses the Breton countryside for 17 kilometers between Dinard and Dinan, passing through the village of Tréméreuc and running along the Rance. Perfectly flat and shaded, it suits families with children and allows cyclists to reach Dinan from the coast without using roads. Hedgerow landscapes, converted old stations, and views of the estuary make the ride particularly pleasant.

days_plan.itin_title: Brittany Road Trip: Villages with Character, Sea and History
Ille-et-Vilaine Tour: Saint-Malo, Dinard and the Emerald Coast

places.name: Commercy

visits.text: Château Stanislas de Commercy, classified as a Historic Monument, was embellished by the Prince of Vaudémont then by Stanislas Leszczynski, former King of Poland and Louis XV's father-in-law. Architects Boffrand and Dorbay gave it its current appearance. Partly destroyed in 1944, it was identically rebuilt from 1957 to 1977.

Cross the semicircular Place du Fer à Cheval, bordered by two symmetrical buildings extending the castle. The stables redesigned by architect Héré recall the pavilions of Place Stanislas in Nancy: continuous rustication, semicircular bays, and balustrades adorned with trophies.
Saint-Pantaléon church blends a 17th-century nave with a 19th-century choir in Champagne Gothic style. Its sober interior contrasts with the richness of liturgical furnishings.

The Museum of Ceramics and Ivory is housed in the former municipal bathhouses in Art Deco style (1930), inspired by Stanislas's royal pavilion. It holds one of France's most important ivory collections, from the 17th to 19th centuries, complemented by porcelains and earthenware.
Place Charles de Gaulle houses the former Town Hall built under Stanislas. Nearby, a 1903 pharmacy with Art Nouveau decor testifies to the town's elegance at the turn of the century.

activities.text: Step into an artisanal madeleine factory to watch the making of these small shell-shaped cakes, born in the kitchens of Stanislas's castle in the 18th century. Tasting on site.

Walk along the Meuse following the Promenade Stanislas, which crosses the town's different districts within 18th-century boundaries. The river draws meanders bordered by willows and classical architecture.
Visit the Priory of Breuil, founded in the 11th century, which occupies an important place in Commercy's religious history. Guided tours trace its successive transformations.

days_plan.itin_title: Meuse Circuit: Verdun and the Citadels

map_keywords: Place du Fer à Cheval Commercy

visits.text: The Château de Compiègne has neoclassical façades built between 1751 and 1788 by Ange-Jacques Gabriel. Louis XV, Louis XVI, then Napoleon I and Napoleon III made it a major residence alongside Versailles and Fontainebleau.

The Imperial Apartments showcase the unified First Empire décor of 1808–1810. Architect Louis-Martin Berthault completely remodelled the interior, with Jacob-Desmalter responsible for the furniture and Girodet for the painted decorations.

The Ballroom Gallery was built in 1810 for the arrival of Marie-Louise of Austria. Napoleon welcomed his future wife there on 27 March 1810, exactly as Marie-Antoinette had been received forty years earlier.

The Second Empire Museum evokes Napoleon III's famous series of gatherings. Each autumn, one hundred guests came in succession over four to six weeks for hunts, concerts and plays in an almost private imperial setting.

The Clairière de l'Armistice is the site where the armistices of 1918 and 1940 were signed. Its memorial displays a carriage from the same series, fitted out identically; the original carriage was destroyed in 1945. On 11 November 1918 at 5:15 a.m., Marshal Foch received the German surrender here in dining carriage 2419D of the Compagnie des wagons-lits.

The Armistice Memorial displays carriage 2439D, fitted out identically after the original carriage was destroyed in 1945. Hitler had demanded that the June 1940 armistice be signed in the same place to avenge the 1918 humiliation.

activities.text: Wander through the Forest of Compiègne among stands of mature beeches and century-old oaks. Fourteen thousand hectares of forest stretch just a short walk from the château.

days_plan.itin_title: Oise Circuit: châteaux, forests and history

visits.text: The Ville Close of Concarneau, a 15th-century walled town still fully inhabited. The granite ramparts enclose 350 meters of cobbled lanes reached through two fortified gates. The remarkably preserved medieval architecture lines up fishermen's houses, craft shops and restaurants in a maze of alleys. The wall walk offers panoramas over the fishing port, the bay and the surrounding beaches. The Vauban fortifications testify to the strategic importance of this stronghold.

The Fishing Museum, housed in a former trawler listed as a historic monument. The visit on board reveals the living and working conditions of fishermen in the 20th century: holds, cabins, engine room, wheelhouse. Thematic displays trace the evolution of fishing techniques, fish processing and the history of the port of Concarneau, the third in France. The aquariums present local species and Breton marine ecosystems.

Concarneau fishing harbor, France's third landing port with 30,000 tons annually. Quays bustle with returning trawlers unloading tuna, monkfish, sole, and langoustines. The computerized fish auction can be visited early morning revealing sale mechanisms and fish traceability. Artisan canneries perpetuate canning know-how. The fishermen's quarter retains typical architecture of fishermen's houses with colorful façades.

Fine sand beaches around Concarneau, seaside resorts prized since the Belle Époque. Sables Blancs unfolds 200 meters of golden sand facing the Glénan Islands. Cabellou beach nestled in a rocky cove offers calm, transparent waters. The GR34 coastal path connects various beaches through pine forests and flowering moorlands. Nautical clubs offer sailing, kayaking, and windsurfing in ideal conditions.

activities.text: Participating in the Blue Nets Festival in late August, a historic festival created in 1905 to support fishermen in distress. For four days, Breton costume parades, fest-noz, concerts, and entertainment invade the Ville Close and quays. The Grand Parade gathers thousands of participants in traditional dress with banners and bagadoù. Stalls offer gastronomic specialties and local crafts. Harbor fireworks close the event in a festive, popular atmosphere.

Visiting Concarneau fish auction at dawn, a fascinating spectacle of fish arrivals. From 6:30 AM, professional buyers evaluate crates of fresh fish landed during the night. The computerized descending auction system accelerates transactions. Guides explain species, fishing techniques, and the fishing industry chain. The bustling quay atmosphere contrasts with early morning calm. Harbor restaurants then offer fishermen's breakfasts.

Boat excursion to the Glénan archipelago, a string of paradise islands 10 miles offshore. Turquoise waters rivaling the tropics surround immaculate white sand beaches. Saint-Nicolas island, the only inhabited one, houses an international sailing school. Crystalline depths attract divers and snorkelers discovering seagrass beds, multicolored fish, and lobsters. The Glénan narcissus, an extremely rare endemic flower, blooms April-May. Boats offer round trips or full days with multiple stops.

days_plan.itin_title: Brittany Road Trip: Villages with Character, Sea and History
Finistère Circuit: Breton Headlands, Islands & Artists' Villages
Brittany 7 days: Pink Granite, Lighthouses & Peninsulas

visits.text: Condom's Saint-Pierre Cathedral has watched over the Baïse River since the 16th century. Built on the site of an 11th-century abbey church, it follows the classic plan of southern Gothic churches: a single wide nave flanked by lateral chapels squeezed between buttresses. Its 19th-century choir draws inspiration from Albi's Sainte-Cécile Cathedral. Bossuet briefly served as bishop here in 1669-1670.

The 16th-century cloister adjoining the cathedral unfolds vast galleries with elegant flamboyant Gothic arcades. It once led bishops to their private chapel. The eastern gallery houses three pointed arches adorned with nine painted keystones bearing the coats of arms of the lord bishops. On the square outside, the Musketeers statue crosses swords: Athos, Porthos, Aramis and d'Artagnan together.

The Armagnac Museum occupies the outbuildings of the former bishop's palace. Built around a monumental 19th-century beam press, the rooms trace the complete production cycle of Gascony's signature brandy: viticultural techniques, alembic distillation and barrel-making. France's oldest eau-de-vie certainly deserves its own museum.

Wander through the lanes of the old episcopal city. The 17th and 18th-century townhouses—Polignac, Cugnac—display their stone façades and wrought iron flourishes, witnesses to the wealth of armagnac merchants. The Baïse, once nicknamed the "silver river," carried barrels downstream to Bordeaux.

Head to the marina quays along the Baïse. Developed in the 18th century for river trade, the waterway remains navigable and offers a peaceful setting bordered by plane trees. Condom is listed among Occitanie's Grand Sites under the title "Armagnac, Abbey and Cities."

Larressingle, nicknamed the "little Carcassonne of Gers," is France's smallest fortified city. Its 13th-century ramparts stretch 900 feet and rise 20 to 26 feet high, enclosing a castle-keep, a Romanesque church dedicated to Saint Sigismond and a handful of golden stone houses. Cross the restored drawbridge and step back seven centuries.

Larressingle's Saint-Sigismond Church displays sober Romanesque architecture with a typically Gascon bell-wall. Curious detail: the saint's statue, commissioned from a Toulouse workshop, is actually a scaled-down version of Aimé Millet's Vercingétorix. A rather odd mustachioed Gaul watches over this medieval village.

Flaran Abbey, a Cistercian monastery founded in 1151 in the Baïse valley, ranks among the best-preserved in southwestern France. Romanesque church, cloister, chapter house, refectory and gardens compose a monastic ensemble of remarkable legibility. In 1913, the Gers archaeological society prevented its cloister from being dismantled and shipped to New York's Cloisters museum.

In the former monks' dormitory at Flaran, the Simonow Collection displays over 300 works of European art from the 16th to 20th centuries. Cézanne, Renoir, Picasso, Monet, Braque, Rodin—a small Gascon Louvre assembled by an Anglo-Saxon philanthropist who fell in love with the Gers. The department's most visited site.

Montréal-du-Gers, the first bastide of Gascony, founded in 1255 by Alphonse de Poitiers, brother of Saint Louis. Perched on a rocky promontory, it has kept its grid layout, its stone arcades, its pointed fortified gateway and its half-timbered houses. Listed among the Most Beautiful Villages of France. About 14 km from the base town, 15 minutes by road.

A few kilometres from Montréal, the Gallo-Roman villa of Séviac reveals a vast fourth-century palace. Rooms opening one into the next, marble colonnades, lavish baths and floors paved with polychrome mosaics. Motifs of flowers, vine shoots and birds unfurl like sumptuous carpets.

activities.text: Guided tour of the episcopal city. The tourist office offers commentary-led circuits unveiling the secrets of the cathedral, cloister, townhouses and the Way of Saint James that passes through town.

Armagnac tasting in the town's cellars. Producers open their doors to explain the distillation process and offer guided tastings. Floc de Gascogne—a blend of grape must and armagnac—is served chilled as an aperitif.

Stroll along the Armagnac greenway, built on a former railway line. This flat, shaded path is perfect for cycling or walking, connecting Condom to neighboring villages through vineyards and hillsides.

Medieval siege camp at the gates of Larressingle. Life-size catapults, trebuchets, stone-throwers and crossbows: operate medieval war machines. Firing demonstrations and activities for the whole family.
Hike from Larressingle to Condom on the GR 65, the Way of Saint James. Three miles through vineyards and hillsides, passing the UNESCO-listed Artigues bridge. A pilgrim's path accessible to everyone.

Montréal-du-Gers market on Friday morning. Under the arcades of the bastide, producers offer foie gras, shepherds' cheeses, seasonal vegetables and Côtes de Gascogne wines. Gascon atmosphere guaranteed. About 14 km from the base town, 15 minutes by road.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Garonne Road Trip: From Toulouse to the Pyrenees
Gers Road Trip: Gascon Bastides, Armagnac & Musketeers
Gers Road Trip: Gascon Bastides, Armagnac & Musketeers

visits.text: Condrieu, ancient city of river merchants on the Rhône's right bank, had connections with the Phocaeans of Massalia. Its steep hillsides carry one of the Rhône Valley's most prestigious appellations: 540 acres of Viognier clinging to granite rock on narrow terraces supported by dry-stone walls—the 'chaillées.'

Condrieu's vineyard, an AOC since 1940, nearly vanished in the 20th century: after phylloxera, wars, and industrialization, only about 25 acres remained in the 1950s. Passionate winegrowers saved it by replanting abandoned hillsides in the 1980s. Viognier expresses itself here like nowhere else.

The Rhône riverbanks at Condrieu offer a peaceful walk between river and vineyards. The landscape of terraced hillsides, supported by centuries-old walls, ranks among the most spectacular in French wine country. Across the river on the left bank, the village of Les Roches-de-Condrieu reflects in calm waters.

Three miles north, Ampuis is the birthplace of Côte-Rôtie appellation, one of the world's greatest Syrah crus. Slopes steepen to 60%! The 'cheys,' stone walls supporting the vines, sometimes date to Roman times. The landscape bears the Vignobles & Découvertes label.

activities.text: Tasting of Condrieu and Côte-Rôtie in winegrowers' cellars. Condrieu, 100% Viognier, unfolds aromas of peach, apricot, and honeysuckle. Côte-Rôtie, Syrah on vertiginous slopes, is an age-worthy red of remarkable depth.

Walk through Condrieu's terraced vineyards. Trails between dry-stone chaillées lead to natural viewpoints over the Rhône valley. Work is almost entirely manual—mechanization is impossible on these slopes.

Water sports on the Rhône and Condrieu lake. Paddleboarding, kayaking, wakeboarding, and inflatable obstacle courses at the leisure base. The water ski cable system lets you learn water skiing without a boat.

days_plan.itin_title: Rhône Road Trip: Lyon, Golden Stone Villages of Beaujolais & Condrieu Vineyards

visits.text: The Pont-Vieux in Confolens has spanned the Vienne since the 11th century (on ancient foundations). Postcard view of half-timbered houses reflected in the water. This is where the Goire meets the Vienne — hence the name 'confluent'.
The old town climbs the hill in winding lanes. Medieval half-timbered houses, craft shops, small shaded squares. The Saint-Barthélemy quarter keeps its old-world atmosphere.
The church of Saint-Maxime overlooks the upper town. Sculpted Romanesque doorway, square bell tower typical of Poitou. Inside, historiated capitals and contemporary stained glass. Free entry.

activities.text: Walk along the Vienne. The towpath leads from the Pont-Vieux towards the countryside. Anglers, grey herons, abandoned locks. Peaceful atmosphere guaranteed.
Canoeing on the Vienne. The watersports centre offers routes from 2 hours to a full day. Calm water, no technical difficulty. Hire includes life jackets and watertight containers.

Confolens Festival (mid-August). Since 1958, France's biggest folklore festival. Troupes from around the world, costumed parades, free concerts. If you're passing through at this time, it's unmissable.

days_plan.itin_title: Charente Tour: Cognac and Romanesque Heritage in 4 Days

visits.text: The Sainte-Foy Abbey Church was built from 1041 by Abbot Odolric. The Last Judgement tympanum features 124 sculpted figures on 24 blocks of yellow limestone. The interior contains 250 Romanesque capitals spread over two levels.

The Treasury houses the reliquary statue of Saint Foy, a unique piece of Carolingian goldsmith work set with gold and precious stones. This collection bears witness to nine centuries of pilgrimage on the Way of Saint James.

Pierre Soulages worked from 1987 to 1994 to create 104 stained glass windows for the abbey church. He carried out nearly 700 trials with master glassmaker Jean-Dominique Fleury to achieve a unique translucent glass. The light changes throughout the day thanks to variations in grain size.

activities.text: The Conques Nocturnes take place from May to October to illuminate the polychrome tympanum. The reimagined polychromy reveals the restored medieval colours.

Visit the abbey church galleries to get up close to the Soulages stained glass windows. The guided tour lasts 45 minutes and explores the painter's creative approach. Booking recommended, open to visitors aged 12 and above.

days_plan.itin_title: Aveyron Road Trip: Causses, Tarn Gorges and Villages
The Most Beautiful Villages of Lot and Périgord in 6 Days

visits.text: Conques-en-Rouergue - The village appears around a bend, nestled in a shell-shaped valley (“conca” in Occitan) above the Dourdou. Listed among the Plus Beaux Villages de France since 1982, it's a major stop on the Way of St. James (Le Puy route). Wander the sloping streets among the half-timbered houses and stone-slab roofs. The place was “discovered” in 1837 by Prosper Mérimée, who launched the restoration of the abbey church.

Abbey Church of Sainte-Foy - Take your time here: this is one of the masterpieces of French Romanesque art. Built from 1041 onwards by Abbot Odolric, it served as a prototype for the great pilgrimage churches (such as Saint-Sernin in Toulouse or the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela). The Last Judgment tympanum, carved in the 12th century on 24 limestone blocks, shows 124 figures arranged in three registers - the saved on the left, the damned on the right and Christ in the center. Look for traces of the original polychromy. Inside, there are 250 sculpted Romanesque capitals on two levels. Since 1994, the 104 stained glass windows by Pierre Soulages - born in Rodez in 1919, 40 km away - have bathed the nave in a unique translucent light. Soulages spent eight years (1986-1994) and carried out hundreds of trials to create this special glass with varying grain sizes. If you are here between April and mid-October, return for the Nocturnes: the tympanum is illuminated at 22:15, and the upper galleries can be visited with music at 21:30.

Treasury of Conques - Don't leave Conques without visiting the south wing of the cloister. This collection of medieval goldsmiths' work is the richest in France. The centerpiece: the Majesty of Sainte Foy, a Carolingian-era reliquary statue covered in gold, silver and precious stones. The relics of the young martyr from Agen (beheaded in 303) were “borrowed” by a Conques monk in the 9th century—a pious theft that brought prosperity to the place. Allow 30 to 45 minutes to tour it.

activities.text: Bancarel viewpoint - For the best overall view of Conques, head down from the abbey along the GR 62, cross the footbridge and climb about a hundred meters. From this promontory opposite the village, you can take in the entire medieval settlement, its stone slab roofs, the abbey church and the valley. It is also the classic postcard viewpoint.

Pont des Pèlerins over the Dourdou - Descend to this medieval bridge (called “Roman”) below the village. The walk along the Dourdou is peaceful and gives you a different perspective on the abbey church that dominates the valley. This is where pilgrims arrived—and still arrive—on the Compostela route.

days_plan.itin_title: Midi-Pyrénées Circuit: Bastides, Cliffs and Abbeys

visits.text: The Thermes de Contrexéville occupy a remarkable neo-Byzantine building, with its columns in shades of blue and its domes. Contrexéville water has been recognized by the Académie de Médecine since 1903.

The Galerie thermale, designed by Charles Mewes (architect of the Guerlain building in Paris), has a row of neo-Byzantine columns facing the park. At its center, the Rotonde houses the statue des Verseuses beneath a copper dome.
The Pavillon des Sources lets you taste the mineral water at the source. The kiosk and its fountains stand in the 4-hectare thermal park, a promenade for spa-goers for over two centuries.
The Russian Orthodox chapel (1909) and the Protestant church (1893), built for foreign spa guests, recall the international clientele the resort attracted during the Belle Époque.
The Art Déco Casino of Contrexéville stands in the heart of the spa town. Its architecture makes it a focal point for evening entertainment.

activities.text: Cycle to the Lacs de la Folie via the bike path from the center. Free supervised swimming in summer, pedal boats, treetop adventure courses, and picnic areas in a wooded setting.
Treat yourself to a half-day at the Spa des Thermes: a thermal leisure pool at 32 °C, a salt-brick sauna, a mosaic hammam with fiber optics imitating a starry sky, and outdoor jacuzzis.

Contrexéville is the “capital of slimming,” the first resort to receive Gastronomie Saveur-Minceur certification. Restaurants offer balanced menus created by chefs, proof that you can eat light and well.

days_plan.itin_title: Vosges Road Trip: Lakes, Mountains & Thermal Spas

visits.text: The 19th-century Grands Moulins dominate the Essonne River with their industrial metal architecture. Saint Louis had his castle built here before leaving on crusade.
Founded in 957 to house the relics of Saint Exuperius, the Cathedral of Saint-Spire blends Romanesque and Gothic styles. Its bell tower dominates the river.
The marble recumbent effigy of Count Haymon rests in the choir. This 14th-century sculpture rivals those at Saint-Denis in its delicacy.
The 17th-century organ was restored after its destruction by the Prussians. The stained glass windows trace the history of the relics preserved in the original church.
The former Church of Saint-Jean-en-L'Isle housed a commandery of the Knights of the Order of Malta. No longer used for worship, it has been listed as a historic monument since the 12th century.

activities.text: Take a walk along the Essonne in Corbeil-Essonnes. The river flows through the town center before joining the Seine; its banks offer a way to discover the urban landscape.
Corbeil-Essonnes Jazz Festival takes place between June and July with several days of open-air concerts.
La Nacelle Park and Chantemerle Park offer over 200 hectares of green spaces. The town has earned three flowers in the Flowered Towns competition.

days_plan.itin_title: Essonne Tour: Castles and Valleys

visits.text: The two 55-meter towers of the Saint-Pierre abbey church stand over the valley. Founded in the 7th century by Queen Bathild, it holds early Christian relics from the 3rd century.
The 18th-century high altar and choir stalls show the power of the Benedictine abbey, whose influence spread across Europe through its scriptorium.

activities.text: Follow the Circuit du Souvenir between Albert and Péronne, marked by the British poppy, past memorials and cemeteries from the First World War. Plan a round-trip drive from Corbie during the day.
The Somme valley offers towpaths and ponds ideal for bike rides.

days_plan.itin_title: Somme Road Trip: Bay of Somme and War Remembrance

visits.text: Built from 1754, Saint-Léonard Abbey towers over Corbigny in all its height. A listed historic monument, it opens broadly to the sky, with light flooding its galleries.

The abbey hosts contemporary art and artist companies in residence. Krijn de Koning's blue room, Lawrence Weiner's works, and Vincent Mauger's wooden sphere dialogue with the centuries-old architecture.
The relics of Saint Leonard, a monk who died in 570, were transported to Corbigny in 882. The abbey took his name, as did the town that grew around it.

Saint-Seine Church, in Flamboyant Gothic style with three naves, was built in the early 16th century and consecrated in 1537. The high altar in pink and white marble comes from the former abbey church.
Ancient choir stalls line the choir, while cast iron holy water fonts and 18th-century baptismal fonts marry pink marble and copper.
The remains of the abbey's former fortified entrance on Rue de l'Abbaye protected the dependencies in the Middle Ages. The site served as a military hospital during World War I.

activities.text: Attend performances and artistic residencies by the La Transverse Association. The "Scène Ouverte aux Arts Publics" project transforms the entire town into a living stage.
Stroll along the Anguison, a tributary of the Yonne that flows through Corbigny. The peaceful banks invite relaxation at the gates of the Morvan Regional Natural Park.
Follow the Route Buissonnière, the Way of St. James. Corbigny was one of the first stops for pilgrims departing from the Basilica of Vézelay.

days_plan.itin_title: Nièvre Road Trip: Morvan and Ducal Heritage

visits.text: Cordes-sur-Ciel reveals itself on foot as you climb its cobbled lanes through five fortified walls. A bastide founded in 1222 by Count Raymond VII of Toulouse, it is one of the oldest in Occitanie.

Stop before the Maison du Grand Fauconnier: its 13th-century Gothic façade is carved with fantastical creatures and mythological scenes. Next door, the Maison du Grand Veneur displays hunting bas-reliefs of remarkable precision.
The church of Saint-Michel dates from 1269. Its southern Gothic architecture with a single nave was expanded twice in the 14th and 15th centuries. The side chapels deserve careful attention.

Step inside the Charles-Portal Museum, housed in the Porte des Ormeaux, a classified medieval military structure. Here you'll find carved falcons, an old 16th-century town hall door, and films about the market hall's well, which plunges more than 100 meters deep.

Under the 14th-century market hall—Cordes' commercial heart for seven hundred years—locate the vertiginous well that drops more than 100 meters beneath your feet. The surrounding terraces remain the townspeople's gathering place.
The Jardin des Paradis, classified as a Remarkable Garden, occupies the top of the town behind a white stone wall. Botanical squares, forgotten species, and cooling pools compose a timeless retreat.

Forty minutes by road, Bruniquel perches atop a cliff overlooking the Aveyron gorges. Two castles face each other: the Old (13th century) and the Young (15th century), separated by a wall born of family feuds lasting three centuries.

In the Old Castle, the Renaissance gallery overlooks the Aveyron 90 meters below. The knights' hall preserves 13th-century paired windows and sculpted capitals. One room recounts the discovery of Bruniquel Cave, whose structures date back 176,500 years.

activities.text: Follow Cordes' heritage trail (roughly 2-hour loop). The route offers views of the town from the surrounding hills and passes through the five remaining fortified gates out of the original fifteen.

Rise early to admire Cordes from the Cerou valley: on certain mornings, mist envelops the hill and only the town emerges from the clouds. This spectacle inspired its name 'sur-Ciel' (in the sky) in 1993.
Artisan workshops—ceramicists, jewelers, wood sculptors, leather craftspeople—line the upper town's lanes. Push open their doors and discuss their craftsmanship.
The AOC Gaillac vineyard spreads at Cordes' foot, with over 2,000 years of winemaking history. Nearby estates offer tastings of reds, dry whites, sparkling wines, and rosés.

days_plan.itin_title: Tarn Road Trip: Albi & Hilltop Villages
Occitanie's 13 Most Beautiful Villages
Midi-Pyrénées Circuit: Bastides, Cliffs and Abbeys
The Most Beautiful Villages of Lot and Périgord in 6 Days

visits.text: Château de Cormatin, built between 1605 and 1616, preserves the most sumptuous Louis XIII painted apartments in France. The marquise's cabinet of curiosities, with blue-and-gold ceilings covered in allegorical scenes, is a jewel of Mannerism. The French and English gardens, boxwood mazes, and intricately patterned parterres complete the picture.

The gardens of Château de Cormatin, which have won several awards, extend across 12 hectares of greenery. The flowering kitchen garden, labyrinth, and medicinal herb garden are arranged around water features and classical vistas. An ideal setting for a stroll after touring the interiors.
