Brancion, a fortified village perched on a rocky spur, dominates the Grosne valley. Its castle (10th–14th century), medieval lanes, and Romanesque church of Saint-Pierre (12th century) with interior frescoes form a remarkably preserved ensemble. No cars in the village—you climb on foot.

Brancion's Romanesque church, simple and luminous, preserves 12th-century frescoes depicting Christ in Majesty and the apostles. The recumbent effigy of a lord of Brancion, in armor, lies in the nave. From atop the castle keep, views extend to the Bresse, the Jura, and sometimes the Alps.

activities.text: Guided tour of Château de Cormatin. Guides reveal the details of the painted ceilings, the symbols hidden in the allegories, and the turbulent history of this residence that passed through multiple owners' hands.

Exploration of Brancion. The village is explored on foot, from the parking area below up to the keep. The path passes through the ruins of the covered market and the fortified gates, among medieval houses. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes for the castle, church, and panorama.
Côte Chalonnaise wine tasting. The appellations Mercurey, Givry, and Rully produce distinctive Pinot Noirs and Chardonnays. Wine cellars abound in the surrounding villages.

days_plan.itin_title: Saône-et-Loire Road Trip: Bibracte, Cluny, Solutré & the Mâconnais Vineyards

visits.text: Perched on its rocky peak above the Cèze, Cornillon is a medieval village listed in the inventory of protected sites, still little known. Its history is directly linked to the turbulence of the Avignon papacy: in the 14th century, Guillaume II Roger de Beaufort, brother of Pope Clement VI, purchased the lordship. At his death in 1380, the castle inventory revealed 40 rooms, two chapels and a 6-level keep tower. But in 1632, the Duke Henri II de Montmorency, owner of the castle, was beheaded in Toulouse for conspiring with Gaston d'Orléans against Richelieu. His property was destroyed: Cornillon castle was dismantled. The remaining walls, pierced with large windows, still dominate the valley from the village heights.

Walk along the ramparts to Place du Barry: a viewpoint guide helps you identify the hamlets and landforms in the verdant Cèze plain. The current church occupies one of the castle chapels, whose outer wall is formed by the old ramparts. Below the village, near the washhouse, you can see medieval sarcophagi found near the old church—destroyed by Protestant troops in the 16th century.

Since 2013, the festival “Cornillon se la joue au château” has taken over the courtyard during the first week of August each year for open-air theater performances in a unique setting. Outside the season, the ruins can be accessed freely from outside—the view from the courtyard over the valley alone justifies the detour.

activities.text: The trail that descends from the village toward the Cèze gorges (4 km loop, about 1 hour 30 minutes, easy difficulty) runs alongside abandoned agricultural terraces, dry stone walls and olive trees. The river below offers swimming spots in limestone pools—much less crowded than those at Aiguèze or La Roque-sur-Cèze.

A few kilometers from Cornillon, the Saint-Sauveur chapel in the hamlet of Saint-Gély (12th century) is accessible on foot via marked trails. It's characteristic of rural Romanesque art in Gard, simply built in light limestone.

days_plan.itin_title: Cèze Valley and Ardèche Gorges Circuit

places.name: Correncon En Vercors

visits.text: Corrençon-en-Vercors separated from Villard-de-Lans in 1857 to form its own commune. It's the southernmost village of the Villard-Corrençon ski domain—the Vercors' largest alpine ski domain, linked since 1984, with 125 km of trails from 1,143 to 2,050 meters altitude. The alpine village is smaller and quieter than Villard, with its chalets, flagstone walls, and small squares. It's a good starting point for the High Plateaus, a Nature Reserve since 1985.

Clearings and trail heads to high combes open just outside the village. The view of the Grande Moucherolle and Roc Cornafion (2,049 m) from the pastures above Corrençon is one of the most beautiful in the Isère Vercors. From these heights you understand this massif's uniqueness: a plateau closed on all sides by cliffs, a natural fortress that explains the 1944 maquis.

activities.text: The panoramic loop at the High Plateaus edge (6-8 km) starts from Clos de la Balme, Corrençon's ski base, and climbs to the first ridges of the Nature Reserve. The path to Grand Veymont (Vercors' highest point at 2,341 m) is glimpsed in the distance. This walk is the perfect conclusion to a Royans-Vercors circuit: you look back toward the Isère plain you left 14 days earlier.

The heritage walk through the village—flagstone and wood-shingle roofs, dry-stone walls, fountains, and squares—takes 30-45 minutes and reveals the vernacular architecture of the Isère Vercors before leaving the massif. A map is available at the Villard-de-Lans tourist office, 10 km away.

days_plan.itin_title: Royans-Vercors Road Trip: Hilltop Villages and Gorges

map_keywords: Réserve naturelle des Hauts Plateaux Vercors

visits.text: Correns is France's first entirely organic-certified village — a revolution launched in 1997 when its mayor, a winemaker and agronomist, proposed that all farmers convert together to organic agriculture during the height of the wine crisis. Since then, the local economy has thrived on organic Côtes-de-Provence vineyards, chicken and goat farming, honey and olive oil. Wander the cobbled lanes that spiral upward around Fort Gibron, a 12th-century priory of the Abbey of Montmajour in Arles — its 2-meter-thick walls of Correns stone are a fine example of Provençal Romanesque art. The Fort now houses a cultural center with concerts and exhibitions. At the village's base, the 14th-century Porte Saint-Germain with its portcullis gives access to the old quarter — legend has it that Saint Germain stopped here on his return from Rome.

The single-arch stone bridge spanning the Argens connects the old village on the right bank with the suburb on the left. From the bridge, several houses in the center look directly onto the river — the typical image of Correns in summer, with gardens reaching down to the water. The 18th-century baroque church conceals in its choir a gilded wooden high altar topped with a glory, an altarpiece of rare quality for the region.

activities.text: The Vallon Sourn, between Correns and Châteauvert, is one of the Var's most beautiful natural sites. The Argens winds for 4 km at the foot of limestone cliffs renowned for their climbing routes, through protected riparian woodland. Shaded pebble beaches line the river — ideal for family swimming away from crowds. Local outfitters offer canoe trips on the Argens from Correns, descending the valley and passing the Benedictine lock. Check ahead on access conditions during fire-risk periods.

Several organic wine estates in Correns open their cellars for tastings and visits. The white wines of the Côtes-de-Provence appellation are the local specialty. Check with the tourist office for estates that welcome visitors without reservation.

days_plan.itin_title: The 10 Most Beautiful Villages of the Haut-Var

places.name: Corte

visits.text: Corte is the only inland city—and the former capital of independent Corsica between 1755 and 1769, when Pascal Paoli made it the seat of his government and founded a university there. The citadel, perched on a rocky spur 100 meters above the confluence of the Restonica and Tavignano, is the only one of Corsica's seven citadels built inland. Climb to the belvedere for the 360° view over both valleys and the triangular bell tower of the Annunciation church. The Museum of Corsica, in the Serrurier barracks at the citadel's heart, houses 3,000 objects of traditional Corsican ethnography collected by Father Doazan—open since 1997, it's the island's best museum for understanding the island's culture. Your Corte train ticket entitles you to a discount.

Place Gaffory, in the old town, contains the house of General Jean-Pierre Gaffory—the man who liberated Corte from the Genoese before being assassinated in 1753. The bullet impacts visible on his house's façade aren't decoration: they date from the 1750 Genoese siege, when Gaffory was defending his own home with his wife while the Genoese held his son hostage.

The Restonica gorges begin 2 km from the center of Corte, reached by a narrow mountain road. The road no longer allows you to drive to the Grotelle sheepfold. In season, a shuttle runs from Corte to La Frasseta; the upper section is reached on foot. The pools and natural swimming holes between the gorges and the Grotelle sheepfold are among Corsica's most beautiful - the water is icy even during a heat wave.

activities.text: Hike to lac de Melo: in season, take the shuttle from Corte to the La Frasseta bridge, then continue on foot via the Grotelle sheepfold (1,375 m). The former parking area at the end of the Restonica valley is inaccessible by car. Allow six to seven hours of walking round trip from La Frasseta to reach lac de Melo at 1,711 m, along a marked rocky trail. Cliffs surround the lake and its water is an intense, cold blue. In summer, local shepherds sell their tomme cheese directly at the sheepfold - do not miss this stop.

Swim in the Restonica pools on the way back from Grotelle. The best pools are halfway along the valley; reach them on foot from the shuttle stops in season, as the road is cut off toward Grotelle. The water flows directly down from lac de Melo - expect 10°C in midsummer.

days_plan.itin_title: Upper Corsica Road Trip: Cap Corse and Balagne
Complete Tour of Corsica

map_keywords: Citadelle Corte musée de la Corse

visits.text: The Loire Museum occupies the former Augustinian convent, a historic monument listed in 1977. Its collections trace the history of traditional river trades: boatmen, fishermen, washerwomen, sand dredgers.
The museum's fine arts collection brings together works by renowned artists. The museum holds the "Musée de France" designation.
Founded in 1735 by Pierre Babaud de La Chaussade, the royal forges produced anchors and cannons for the Royal Navy. They employed 3,500 workers in the 18th century before closing in 1871.

The "Sévigné" portal, the entrance gate to the former forges dating from the late 17th century, bears a plaque citing Madame de Sévigné's visit in 1677. The riverside site has retained its historic façades.
Saint-Agnan Church dominates the town. Built in the 12th century, it preserves Romanesque and Gothic elements. Its bell tower serves as a visible landmark from the quays.

activities.text: Stroll along the Quai du Maréchal Joffre by the Loire. The river once facilitated transport of goods produced at the forges.
Discover the Eden Cinema, listed as a historic monument. Its Art Deco façade and Briare enamel sign make it an unmissable photo stop on the old N7 road.
Walking tour through town: former medieval castle with its keep (Rue Duguet), remnant rampart tower (Rue Chollet), boatmen's quarter.

days_plan.itin_title: Nièvre Road Trip: Morvan and Ducal Heritage

visits.text: Cotignac has been listed among France's Most Beautiful Villages since 2022 — and the moment you first catch sight of the tufa cliff, 80 meters high and 400 meters wide, standing over the village rooftops, you understand why. This ochre wall, shaped by the Cassole river in the Quaternary era, is pierced with dwellings hollowed straight out of the rock. A secured path lets you explore these cavities from the foot of the cliff — allow an hour for the full visit. You will find old stables, oil mills and even grain silos, all cut into the tufa by the villagers of the Middle Ages. If you can, take the guided tour offered in summer: the stories about daily life in these caves are worth it.

At the cliff's summit stand the two so-called Saracen towers, built in the 12th century — they're actually the remnants of the feudal castle constructed from 1033 onwards by Boniface de Castellane. Climb up to them via the cobbled paths for a 360° panorama sweeping across the entire plain stretching to Carcès and Entrecasteaux. The medieval village below is equally worth exploring on foot: its 16th and 17th-century stone lanes open onto flower-decked squares, and its 17 fountains — including the famous Cascade fountain — bear witness to the water abundance that built Cotignac's prosperity.

About 1.5 km from the center, the Notre-Dame de Graces sanctuary is worth the detour. In 1519 the Virgin is said to have appeared here to a woodcutter on Mont Verdaille. Louis XIV himself came on pilgrimage on February 21, 1660, with his mother Anne of Austria, to give thanks to Mary for the birth of the Dauphin. The site is quiet, shaded and offers a fine view over the hills.

activities.text: Rise early on Tuesday morning for the Cotignac market, held on Cours Gambetta beneath the centuries-old plane trees. This is one of the most flavorful markets in the Haut-Var: bottarga, lavender honey, hillside olive oil, goat cheese and all-natural soaps. Arrive before 9:30 AM to have your pick and chat with the producers without the crowds.

Head out for an hour's walk in the hills around Cotignac to see the vineyards (Coteaux Varois en Provence appellation) and olive groves encircling the village. Local estates offer tastings — check with the tourist office for opening hours.

days_plan.itin_title: The 10 Most Beautiful Villages of the Haut-Var
Var Road Trip: French Riviera & Provence Verte
Var in 4 Days: From Bormes to the Most Beautiful Villages of the Verdon

visits.text: The ruins of Coucy Castle have dominated the rocky outcrop since the 13th century. Enguerrand III sought to rival the kings of France by building this colossal fortress. The keep, destroyed in 1917, was the largest tower in the Christian West, standing 54 metres high and measuring 31 metres in diameter. The four corner towers, 2,000 metres of ramparts, and remains of the Gothic palace still testify to the power of the lords of Coucy.

The small museum at the castle entrance traces the site's history from its foundation through its successive destructions. Illustrated panels and reconstructions help visitors imagine its vanished splendour. The lords' motto still echoes: “I am neither lord, nor king, nor duke, nor count. I am the Lord of Coucy.”

The Soissons Gate opens onto the medieval town. Cobbled streets wind between old houses to the Church of Saint-Sauveur. The medieval garden at the foot of the ramparts includes a vegetable garden, an orchard and a medicinal herb garden cultivated according to ancestral traditions.
Walk along the outer ramparts to appreciate the scale of the fortifications. A herd of goats uses the ruins as a playground. The path offers stunning views of the Ailette valley below.

activities.text: The nighttime show Coucy la Merveille brings the castle's glorious past back to life every summer. More than 300 volunteers stage medieval dances, knights' battles, equestrian jousts, and fire performances. The history of the lords of Coucy resounds beneath the stars in a grand historical spectacle.

A short family walk circles the ramparts. The accessible path starts at the Soissons Gate and follows the walls, offering panoramic views of the surrounding countryside. Allow 1.5 hours for an easy stroll.

days_plan.itin_title: Aisne Itinerary: Gothic Cathedrals and the Picardy Countryside

visits.text: The Commanderie des Templiers de Coulommiers, built between the 12th and 15th centuries, is the best preserved north of the Loire. The rectangular courtyard serves the Tithe Barn, dovecote, commander's lodging, and Sainte-Anne Chapel.
Enter the Sainte-Anne Chapel: its 13th-century wall paintings are among the rare preserved medieval decorations in the region. A permanent exhibition traces the history of the Knights Templar.

The Parc des Capucins, considered one of the most beautiful parks in Île-de-France, occupies the site of the former château of the Duchess of Longueville, who inspired "La Princesse de Clèves". The château remnants and Notre-Dame-des-Anges Church are classified Historic Monuments.
The Capucins Municipal Museum, housed in the former convent chapel, preserves the last vestiges of the tannery industry that made Coulommiers prosper for 800 years.

The Halle aux Fromages (Cheese Market Hall), labeled Heritage of Regional Interest, was built in 1887 in cast iron modeled after Paris's Les Halles. It was the trading and sales place for Brie cheeses.

activities.text: Walk along the Grand Morin's brassets, small canals created in the Middle Ages by Champagne tanners. Thirty-six bridges and footbridges span these waterways that earn Coulommiers the nickname "Little Venice".
The Commanderie's medieval garden recreates a vegetable patch, medicinal plants, and cut flowers cultivated in the Middle Ages. A 4,000-square-meter space to explore at your own pace.
Taste Coulommiers cheese at one of the local fromageries. Smaller and creamier than Brie de Meaux, this soft cheese is best enjoyed when aged on-site.

days_plan.itin_title: Seine-et-Marne Circuit: Fontainebleau and Châteaux

visits.text: The Maison du Marais Poitevin occupies the former Maison de la Coutume, a building once used to collect tolls for passage along the Sèvre. A one-hour visit traces ten centuries of marsh history: how the abbeys dug the first canals in the 11th century, and how the bataillards transformed this sea inlet into a network of narrow waterways. You will understand why Coulon is called the “capital of Green Venice”—this Grand Site de France spans 100,000 hectares across Vendée, Deux-Sèvres, and Charente-Maritime.

Step inside Sainte-Trinité Church, founded in 830 by monks from Charroux Abbey, pillaged by the Normans, rebuilt in the 11th century, remodeled in the 15th, and restored in the 19th. Do not miss the tower with a canopy on the south side: despite the story often told, it is not an outdoor preaching pulpit, but simply a stair tower that replaced a ladder used to ring the alarm bell. The black funerary band painted around the nave dates from the 18th century and recalls the right of lords with high judicial authority to be buried in churches.

Coulon’s narrow lanes deserve a leisurely stroll. Low houses with whitewashed walls and blue or green shutters create a distinctive atmosphere—at once rooted in the land and shaped by the water. Head to Quai Louis Tardy in the late afternoon: the light on the moored boats and their reflections in the Sèvre creates one of Poitou’s most photographed scenes.

activities.text: Board a traditional boat at Quai Louis Tardy. Local boatmen tell you about the marsh’s wildlife—otters, purple herons, and kingfishers—the canals dug in the Middle Ages, and the vegetation of century-old pollarded ash trees. Morning or late afternoon is the best time to watch birds. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes for a guided outing.

Rent a flat-bottomed boat (a “batais”) or a canoe to explore the maze of narrow waterways on your own. Maps are provided at every boat landing. The narrowest canals are accessible only to lightweight boats: this is where the marsh reveals its most beautiful colors. Allow at least 2 hours.

days_plan.itin_title: Deux-Sèvres Tour: Marais Poitevin and Romanesque Heritage

visits.text: Acquired in 1552 by Cosme Clausse, the Château de Courances was rebuilt between 1622 and 1630. Baron de Haber restored it in the 19th century, adding the horseshoe staircase inspired by Fontainebleau.
Go upstairs to the Galerie des singes, adorned with tapestries depicting little monkeys clowning around. The guided tour reveals six rooms used by the de Ganay family.
Fourteen springs feed the park. The 600-meter Grand Canal predates Fontainebleau's by a century. Louis XIII came here to go boating.
The stepped pools, the Miroir reflecting the château, the decagonal Gerbe, and the sculpted water spouts give the Renaissance water system a theatrical quality.
The Japanese garden created in 1930 by the Marquise de Ganay sits beside the 3-hectare vegetable garden. Organic fruits and vegetables are grown for sale throughout Île-de-France.

activities.text: Explore the 75-hectare park along its grassy paths. The great gardener de Noailles described it as the only park in France that is both classical and romantic.
Visit the Foulerie tea room, housed in the former hemp mill. The building is reflected in the canal of the same name.
The landscape architects Achille Duchêne redesigned the park in the early 20th century to restore its classical layout. Each generation of owners has left its mark.

days_plan.itin_title: Essonne Tour: Castles and Valleys

visits.text: Notre-Dame Cathedral in Coutances is a masterpiece of 13th-century Norman Gothic, built over an 11th-century Romanesque structure still visible beneath the facing. Its dizzying lantern tower floods the transept crossing with light. The two spires on the façade reach 75 and 77 metres.

Take the guided tour of the cathedral's upper parts. The route passes through the inside of the Romanesque towers, the galleries, the medieval timber frames and the walkways of the nave. From up there, the 13th-century stained glass appears at eye level.

The Jardin des Plantes in Coutances, listed as a Historic Monument since 1992, combines French, English and Italian styles on a single site. Italian-style terraces, English-style groves and a plant labyrinth follow one another. The purple beech, 4.90 m in girth, and the tulip tree are among its notable trees.

The Quesnel-Morinière Museum occupies a 17th-century mansion bequeathed to the town in 1850. Its seven permanent rooms present paintings from the 17th to the 20th century, a collection of Norman ceramics and works of 'Le Pou qui grimpe', a local art movement of the early 20th century. Admission is free.

Saint-Pierre Church, rebuilt after the Hundred Years' War in the 15th century, shows the transition from Flamboyant Gothic to the Renaissance. Its tracery windows and sculpted portal are worth a stop.
Founded before 1238 by Hugues de Morville, Saint-Nicolas Church stands outside the old town walls. The 13th-century chapel was enlarged in the 14th to become the parish church of the suburb.

activities.text: The Jazz sous les Pommiers festival has taken over Coutances every Ascension week since 1982. More than 50 concerts unfold in the cathedral, the theatre, the halls and the schoolyards. Jazz, soul, world music and street performances set the rhythm of the week.
Wander the medieval lanes of Coutances around the cathedral. Inner courtyards, vaulted passages and half-timbered houses make up an old centre spared by the bombing of 1944.
Coutances market is held every Thursday morning, on place Saint-Nicolas and around the cathedral. Cotentin cheeses, teurgoule, Isigny butter and fish from the coast.
The Jardin des Plantes' tradition of mosaiculture, practised since the late 19th century, is discovered along the flower beds. The geometric designs change every season.

days_plan.itin_title: Manche Road Trip: Cotentin Peninsula & Mont-Saint-Michel

visits.text: Craon Castle, nicknamed 'little Versailles of Mayenne,' stands on Guinefol hill overlooking the town. This elegant late 18th-century tuffeau edifice, built by the Marquis d'Armaillé on the ruins of a feudal lodge destroyed by the Wars of Religion then by Henri IV, is still inhabited by the same family.

The guided tour opens salons with finely carved woodwork and furnishings that belonged to Marie-Antoinette. The architecture, inspired by Versailles' Petit Trianon, illustrates the art of living in the Age of Enlightenment.

The French formal garden surrounds the castle with perfect symmetry. Water mirrors reflect the façade and light. The English-style park, planted in 1830, unfolds 47 hectares of greenery and over 150 plant species along 6 km of tree-lined alleys with century-old specimens.
Don't miss the large walled kitchen garden (over a hectare), the 19th-century greenhouses, the ice house, the wash-laundry and the dovecote—all preserved in their original state.

In town, Saint-Nicolas church and the market halls merit a detour. Craon was also a major center for Mayenne horse racing, a tradition rooted in this horse-breeding land symbolized by Pegasus, the red winged horse, emblem of the department.

activities.text: Walk the castle park following the 6 km of alleys. A treasure hunt is offered to children. Along the paths, encounter horses, goats, swans, geese and perhaps deer or squirrels that populate the estate.
Follow the Oudon river that borders the park. Its two bridges offer romantic viewpoints of the castle through the grove.

days_plan.itin_title: Mayenne Circuit: Hedgerows and Medieval Towns

visits.text: The Gallé-Juillet Museum showcases fine earthenware from Creil and Montereau produced between 1797 and 1895. Black stencil-printed and polychrome tableware sets illustrate the golden age of the Creil pottery factory.
The former earthenware factories lined the banks of the Oise from the late 18th century. The ceramic industry made Creil's reputation with patterns inspired by Antiquity and the Orient.
Saint-Médard Church has a 16th-century Flamboyant Gothic bell tower. Rebuilt after the Hundred Years' War, it preserves Renaissance stained glass and furnishings.

activities.text: Banks of the Oise.
Industrial heritage.

days_plan.itin_title: Oise Circuit: châteaux, forests and history

visits.text: Don't miss Crémieu's market hall—it's the centerpiece of the visit. Dated to 1434 through dendrochronological analysis of its structural timbers, it's unique in Isère and hasn't changed in appearance in six centuries. At the back, you'll notice four carved stone troughs: these are the grain measures from medieval fairs (the “bichet” equaled 19.5 liters). A stone's throw away, the Augustinian convent, founded in the 14th century by Dauphin John II, houses the current town hall. But step inside the church: it preserves a set of Augustinian paintings uncovered since the 2000s, unique in France, notably depicting a double Apostolic and Prophetic Creed. The organ mentioned in the archives in 1785 is the oldest in Isère. On July 20, 1315, Dauphin John II granted Crémieu a charter of privileges—one of the most comprehensive in the Dauphiné—marking the beginning of two centuries of prosperity.

Climb to the 12th-century castle of the Dauphins, perched on the Saint-Laurent hill overlooking the town. While the castle interior isn't open to visitors, the climb through the medieval lanes offers a beautiful panorama over the Dauphiné plain. Along the way, observe the roofs of flat limestone slabs—a distinctive local architectural feature that's gradually disappearing.

activities.text: Circuit of gates and ramparts within the walls (3 km, ~1 hour 30 minutes): the Porte de la Loi, restored in 2023, marks the main entrance to the town. A free numbered map, available at the tourist office, helps you avoid missing anything. In September, the “Médiévales” take the town back to its past in the Dauphiné with a market, fights, and entertainment.

Walk in the Isle Crémieu beyond the walls: this “triangle” between the Rhône, ponds, and limestone cliffs is home to more than 1,300 plant species and 187 bird species. Marked trails lead from the town toward the surrounding gorges and limestone caves.

days_plan.itin_title: Loop Around Lyon: Villages and Pierres Dorées

visits.text: Climb the 257 steps leading to the summit of France's tallest keep. Standing 52 meters high, the Tower of Crest is an architectural masterpiece comprising three nested towers. Transformed into a state prison from the 17th to 19th centuries, it held Protestants, libertines, and insurgents. From the top, enjoy exceptional 360° panoramas over the Drôme valley, Saou forest, and Vercors mountains.

Wander the narrow, winding alleys of the medieval old town that snake beneath the tower. Discover calades paved with river stones, covered passages, and remnants of ancient ramparts. The Saint-Sauveur church with its Romanesque bell tower stands as a remarkable edifice.

activities.text: Experience something unique with the immersive audio system. A 19th-century guard guides you through nine centuries of history. Discover prisoners' living conditions, escape attempts, and hundreds of poignant graffiti covering the walls.
For the truly daring, attempt the 44-meter rappel down the east wall, reliving Philippe Rivoire's 1789 escape attempt. Supervised by certified instructors, you'll enjoy an incredible view over Crest.
Take the Ramparts Path that climbs from downtown to the Tower. This steep ascent offers beautiful valley views. Below, stroll along the emerald-watered Drôme riverbanks.

days_plan.itin_title: Drome Provencale Road Trip: Villages and Terroirs

visits.text: Créteil Lake spans 42 hectares, born from a gypsum quarry that operated from 1940 to 1976—when excavators hit the Champigny aquifer, pools formed naturally and urban planners had the good idea of turning them into a lake. The result: 1,500 meters long, 6 meters deep, with a continuous 4 km walking route around the shore since 2019. Be warned in summer: cyanobacteria regularly invade the surface, the water turns greenish, and some activities get suspended. Check the lake's status before visiting.

MAC VAL in Vitry-sur-Seine is France's only museum entirely devoted to the French art scene from the 1950s to today—not a single Spanish Picasso or American Warhol. 2,500 works including pieces by Kader Attia, Christian Boltanski, Niki de Saint Phalle, and Agnès Varda. Jacques Ripault's white building (2005) opens onto a 10,000 m² garden where sculptures from the collection are placed as though it were perfectly ordinary. No barriers between you and the artworks—museum policy. Allow at least 2 hours; the display changes every 18 months. Take tram T9 to the Musée MAC VAL stop.

activities.text: The Île de loisirs de Créteil has surrounded the lake since 1980: kayaking, windsurfing, catamaran sailing, dinghy sailing—all are available on the lake between June and August with certified instructors. Swimming in the lake has been banned since 1982 (prefectural decree), but the 1,300 m² wave pool makes up for it. Check seasonal hours before heading out.

In the late afternoon, walk around the lake's east side and look up: Créteil's residential towers nicknamed “the cabbages”—for their flower-shaped balconies—date from the 1970s and have become an inadvertent symbol of the new town. The lake is reflected between the facades. A strange view, somewhat sci-fi, totally Créteil.

days_plan.itin_title: Val-de-Marne Road Trip: Castles and the Banks of the Marne

places.name: Crozant

visits.text: The fortress of Crozant rises on a rocky spur at the confluence of the Creuse and Sédelle, a strategic site that fascinated George Sand as early as 1827. The romantic ruins of the Lusignan castle, built in the 12th–13th centuries, stretch along a kilometer of ramparts punctuated by ten towers. The Colin Tower, a figurehead above the precipice, has a striking silhouette. Listed as a historic monument and a stop on the Way of St. James.

The Hôtel Lépinat, a meeting place for Impressionist painters from 1880 onward, has become the museum of the Valley of the Painters. In this legendary inn where Guillaumin, Picabia, and so many others stayed, an immersive 1.5-hour tour plunges visitors into the world of the Crozant School through new technologies, atmospheric sets, and more than 100 original works. Visitors discover how 500 painters came here in succession from 1850 to 1950.

The Moulin de la Folie, on the banks of the Sédelle, was one of the most frequently painted subjects in the valley. Paul Madeline depicted it realistically, while Francis Picabia used it as inspiration for works with abstract outlines. The mill and its stone bridge remain, although vegetation has replaced the rocky scree that fascinated the artists. A trail follows the stream to the mill.

activities.text: The Sentier des Peintres de Crozant offers a circuit dotted with interpretive markers displaying the paintings created at each viewpoint. Enameled stoneware medallions reproduce details of artworks, engraved plaques tell the valley's history, and glass windows invite playful visual interaction with the landscape. A discovery booklet extends the experience with practical exercises.

A boat tour with commentary lets visitors discover the Creuse gorges from the water. From Crozant to the Éguzon dam, the 1.5-hour trip offers a unique perspective on the cliffs and lush vegetation that has replaced the rocky landscapes painted by the Impressionists before the waters rose in 1926.

days_plan.itin_title: Creuse Tour: Valley of the Painters and Aubusson Tapestries

map_keywords: Museum of the Valley of the Painters Crozant

visits.text: Pointe de Pen-Hir, spectacular natural site culminating 63 meters above the Iroise Sea. Armorican sandstone cliffs plunge vertiginously into the ocean while the Tas de Pois, enormous aligned rocks offshore, shelter seabird colonies and seals. The monumental Cross of Lorraine pays homage to Free French Bretons. On clear days, the panorama extends from Pointe Saint-Mathieu to Pointe du Raz over 50 kilometers.

Lagatjar megalithic alignments in Camaret, 87 menhirs erected facing the sea for 5,000 years. These Neolithic standing stones evoke Carnac alignments in a more intimate atmosphere. The site overlooks Camaret Bay offering views of the Vauban Tower and trawler wrecks. Bare moorland accentuates the mystical dimension of these prehistoric monuments witnessing vanished civilizations.

Île Vierge Beach, a white pebble cove considered one of Europe's most beautiful beaches. Nestled in a rocky cliff amphitheater at Pointe de Saint-Hernot, it reveals translucent emerald waters. Access requires 20 minutes walking through blazing yellow broom. The preserved site prohibits swimming but offers a striking natural tableau where ochre rock contrasts with turquoise sea.

Cap de la Chèvre, the peninsula's southern extremity closing Douarnenez Bay. Pine forests clinging to cliffs create a unique landscape where Mediterranean vegetation meets Breton moorland. The semaphore watches over maritime traffic while GR34 trails wind along 20 kilometers of wild coastline. Panoramas embrace oceanic immensity and Breton mountain foothills in the background.

activities.text: Hiking the GR34 along sandstone cliffs between Pointe de Pen-Hir and Pen-Hat beach. The customs officers' path winds along heights offering plunging views over deserted coves and rock formations sculpted by 60 million years of erosion. Pen-Hat's immense beach unfolds its fine sand facing a turquoise Iroise Sea where swimming is forbidden due to dangerous currents. Caves along cliff faces reveal themselves at low tide, creating translucent pools colonized by mussels.

Sea kayaking to discover Morgat's marine caves. Cap de la Chèvre harbors a dozen cavities carved by sandstone erosion, including the Altar Cave extending 80 meters deep. Sunlight illuminates quartz walls creating magical multicolored reflections. Boats departing from Morgat also offer guided circuits revealing legends associated with each cave. The Île Vierge cove completes this maritime discovery of natural heritage.

Visit to the Ménez-Hom, a sacred mountain rising to 330 meters, about 20 km from Crozon, 20 minutes by road. From its summit, the 360° panorama takes in the Crozon peninsula, the Brest roadstead, the bay of Douarnenez and the Montagnes Noires. Popular with paragliders, it offers exceptional flying conditions facing the ocean. Hikers follow the marked paths crossing moorland and granite chaos. The site has had a spiritual dimension since Celtic times.

days_plan.itin_title: Finistère Circuit: Breton Headlands, Islands & Artists' Villages

visits.text: Cruis is an understated village set on the southern slope of Montagne de Lure — the “little sister of Ventoux” dear to Jean Giono. Its large Church of Notre-Dame-et-Saint-Martin is actually the former church of an abbey founded around the year 1000 by Augustinian canons. Around it, remnants of the cloister and traces of the abbey recall that the village owes its development to this institution, which was very wealthy until the Hundred Years' War and the Great Plague ruined it in the 15th century. Wander the quiet stone lanes, cool in summer — the tall houses with carefully crafted lintels reveal the past prosperity of families of travelling druggists.

A few kilometres north of Cruis, the Abbey of Notre-Dame de Lure (12th century) nestles at the bottom of the Morteiron valley, beneath century-old walnut and lime trees. It was one of the essential stops for travelling medicinal-plant sellers who roamed the mountain gathering medicinal plants — lavender, wormwood, thyme — and reselling them as far away as the Beaucaire fair. This trade was so well established here that the Pays de Forcalquier had 45 travelling medicinal-plant sellers in 1779 (compared with 3 in 1707) — their descendants became pharmacists in the 19th century.

activities.text: Three waymarked routes called “Sur le chemin des plantes de la montagne de Lure” allow you to discover aromatic and medicinal plants in their natural environment (the Graves site, the Lure ridges). A discovery guide is available from the Forcalquier tourist office. If you are there between June and August, the Ronde des Jas (10 km, 4 hours 30 minutes, starting in Cruis) leads to the mountain pastures and high-altitude sheepfolds, with exceptional views of the Alps.

A tasting of essential oils and Provençal herbs at local producers in the Pays de Forcalquier is a good introduction to the region's flavours — some estates near Cruis offer visits to lavender distilleries in season.

days_plan.itin_title: Forcalquier & Verdon Gorges Road Trip

visits.text: Dambach-la-Ville has one of the largest areas under vine of any municipality in Alsace, with the celebrated Frankstein grand cru on its granite slopes. The surviving medieval ramparts encircle 16th-century half-timbered houses. Above the village, the Romanesque Saint-Sébastien chapel houses a baroque altarpiece and serves as the starting point for several vineyard trails.

activities.text: The Sentier des Grands Crus crosses the Frankstein vineyard between Dambach and the Saint-Sébastien chapel, with explanatory panels about the local Riesling. Count on around 40 minutes of easy walking among the vine rows.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Villages of Alsace in 4 Days

visits.text: The Château de Darney (18th century, on 10th-century foundations) houses the Franco-Czechoslovak Museum. It was here that President Poincaré recognized Czechoslovak independence on June 30, 1918, before 6,000 legionnaires from Camp Kléber.

The Franco-Czechoslovak monument stands at the town entrance. The museum preserves Poincaré's original speech, a painting gifted by the National Museum of Prague, and a replica of the first Czechoslovak flag.
On the château's ground floor, the Musée Damia is dedicated to this 1930s singer nicknamed "the tragedienne of song," whose grandparents lived in Darney. Period posters, costumes, and records.

The Musée du verre d'Hennezel-Clairey (10 km), in the heart of Darney Forest, traces the history of the gentleman glassmakers. The 1448 Glassmakers' Charter ennobled glass artisans. There were as many as 30 glassworks in the forest.

activities.text: Explore Darney Forest, a major natural site in the Vôge, a region of wooded plateaus. A marked circuit with 8 stops links the Hennezel museum to the remains of glassworks, Droiteval Abbey, and the arboretum.

The glassworks in Passavant-la-Rochère, south of Darney in Haute-Saône, is the oldest glassworks in France still in operation. Allow for a return trip from Darney for the visit. The glassblowers work in full view of the public.
The Saône flows peacefully through the Vosges a few kilometers away. Its banks lend themselves to trout fishing and bucolic strolls in a landscape of rolling meadows.

days_plan.itin_title: Vosges Road Trip: Lakes, Mountains & Thermal Spas

visits.text: Dauphin sits on its hilltop between the Luberon and the Valensole plateau, 9 km from Forcalquier. The village was established there in the Middle Ages for protection from marauders, leaving below the remains of Gallo-Roman villas and mosaics along the Via Domitia, which crossed the municipality. Pass under the Pourcheirieu gate — the sole remnant of the fortified walls — and climb to the old castle viewpoint: to the north, the domes of the Saint-Michel Observatory, the village of Mane and the Forcalquier citadel; to the south, the wooded Luberon. The view is one of the most comprehensive over the Pays de Forcalquier.

The Church of Saint-Martin, a former castle chapel that became the parish church in 1524, houses an exceptional Baroque organ: restored and enhanced with numerous stops by organ builder Michel Deluz, it's renowned for its acoustics and attracts organists each summer for concerts (Bach, Buxtehude, Handel, Frescobaldi). Concerts take place from July to September. If you're not there for a concert, the nave is worth visiting for its 19th-century paintings on canvas by Esprit Michel Gibelin and its mullioned windows.
In December, the church displays one of the oldest nativity scenes in the Pays de Forcalquier: 11 dressed figurines from the 18th century in their original condition.

activities.text: The village is home to working craftspeople — potters, ceramicists, ornamental ironworkers and woodturners. A late-morning stroll through the cobbled lanes often gives you the chance to enter their workshops. The Fête du Fer et du Feu, held on the last weekend of March, is the main event celebrating these crafts.

The Via Domitia runs along the municipality: from the village, it's easy to join the GR 653 (Way of St James), which follows the old Roman route. A 2-hour walk through olive groves and oak forests, heading north towards the Forcalquier plateaus, offers beautiful panoramas.

days_plan.itin_title: Forcalquier & Verdon Gorges Road Trip

visits.text: Fontaine Chaude: Gushing at 64°C since Roman times, this spring supplies the spas of Dax, France's leading spa town and one of Europe's most important. The neoclassical building erected between 1814 and 1818 houses the Nèhe spring. Peloid, mud derived from Adour River silt, has been used for rheumatological treatments for 2,000 years.

Archaeological crypt: Remains of a 1st-century civic basilica bearing witness to ancient Aquae Tarbellicae (the waters of the Tarbelli). The mosaics and Roman foundations reveal the importance of this ancient spa town. Guided tours organized by the Borda Museum on Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday at 3pm from February to December.

Notre-Dame Cathedral: Built between 1662 and 1894 in an imposing Greek Revival classical style. The Apostles' Portal, a 13th-century Gothic remnant, contrasts with the overall architecture. The Gallo-Roman ramparts are still visible nearby, recalling the ancient city's fortifications.

Art Deco heritage: The Atrium and Hotel Le Splendid testify to the golden age of the 1930s. These buildings designed by Parisian architects Granet and Expert illustrate the splendor of grand spa resorts. The Parc du Sarrat, a remarkable 3.5-hectare garden, shelters over 1,000 trees and 130 species.

activities.text: Heritage circuit: A 2-hour urban route taking in the Fontaine Chaude, Gallo-Roman ramparts and cathedral. The tourist office offers themed guided tours (Art Deco, spa heritage, bullrings). Dax has held the Ville d'Art et d'Histoire designation since 2019.

Dax markets: The market halls, renovated in 2021, offer local products on Saturday and Sunday mornings. Fattened ducks, Landes asparagus, Tursan wines and Bayonne ham. The friendly atmosphere and local producers make these markets essential stops.

Banks of the Adour: Walk along the river at Parc Théodore-Denis. The landscaped banks offer a peaceful setting for walking or running. Fishing possible with permit. Sunsets over the water create a special atmosphere.

Feria de Dax in August: 5 days of entertainment with courses landaises, street bands, concerts and parades. The city transforms completely during this festive period. Accommodation booking essential several months beforehand. The bullring hosts bullfights and other bull-related shows.

days_plan.itin_title: Landes Road Trip: Ocean, Pine Forest and Landes Traditions
Bordeaux to Toulouse Road Trip: Ocean, Pyrenees and Heritage

visits.text: The Planches de Deauville, a legendary 643-metre boardwalk made of azobé wood, runs alongside the beach dotted with multicoloured parasols. The 450 bathing cabins bear the names of stars who attended the American Film Festival. The Art Deco Bains Pompéiens complex completes this postcard setting immortalised by Claude Lelouch.

Admire the Hôtel Normandy Barrière and its green half-timbering in the Anglo-Norman style. This five-star luxury hotel built in 1912 embodies the elegance of the Côte Fleurie. Just steps away, the Casino Barrière has been glowing with golden lights for over a century.

Visit Les Franciscaines, an innovative cultural hub set in a former convent. Museum, temporary exhibitions, media library and documentation spaces explore horses, cinema, photography and the Norman art of living.

activities.text: Attend horse racing at the Deauville-La Touques racecourse. Inaugurated in 1864 by the Duke of Morny, this temple of racing hosts the most prestigious Group 1 events during the August meeting.
Enjoy the beach and its water sports. Land sailing, swimming and sunbathing set the rhythm of summer days on Deauville's fine sand.
Browse the luxury boutiques in the town centre. Deauville cultivates the art of elegant shopping, with fashion houses and designers side by side.
Unwind at the spa or thalassotherapy centre. Deauville's wellness establishments offer marine treatments and massages overlooking the sea.

days_plan.itin_title: Calvados Tour: D-Day Beaches and Normandy

visits.text: Built on a rocky island, Decize is nicknamed "little Venice." You must cross five bridges to go from one end to the other: Nivernais Canal, Aron, Vieille Loire, Loire, and lateral canal.

The confluence brings together the Nivernais Canal, Aron, Vieille Loire, and Loire at the end of the Promenade des Halles. This waterway crossroads offers magnificent views of the Saint-Léger-des-Vignes dam.
Saint-Aré Church honors the former Bishop of Nevers who wished to be placed in a boat at his death. It miraculously sailed up the Loire to Decize where he was buried.
The ramparts (12th century) preserve a watchtower, two towers, and a former drawbridge gate. The ruins of the former château of the Counts of Nevers are topped by a statue of the Virgin.
The Vieille Loire bridge (1777) allows the D981 to cross the waterways. One arch was demolished by the retreating French army on June 18, 1940, then repaired.

The Promenade des Halles, created in the late 18th century and extended in 1810, stretches nearly a kilometer. Three rows of century-old plane trees and lindens run along the confluence between town and waterways.

activities.text: The Port de la Jonction, awarded the Blue Flag label, accommodates 80 boats. This crossroads connects all French navigable waterways: Nivernais Canal, Loire, and lateral canal.
Walk the Vieille Loire interpretive trail with its twenty educational panels. Quizzes and mini-games explore the Loire ecosystem and South Nivernais natural heritage.
Follow the EuroVelo 6 along the Loire or the Nivernais Canal bike route. Decize is a hub for river and cycling tourism.
Fish in the waterways that earned Decize the nickname "Fisherman's Paradise." Pike-perch, chub, perch, pike, and catfish frequent these fish-rich waters.

days_plan.itin_title: Nièvre Road Trip: Morvan and Ducal Heritage

visits.text: The international station at Delle, reopened in 2018, serves the Belfort–Bienne line via Delémont. Located 1,600 meters from Boncourt in Switzerland, it is the terminus for CFF trains and provides connections to TGV services from Belfort-Montbéliard.

The railway heritage testifies to Delle's strategic role since 1868. After the annexation of Alsace in 1870, the line bypassed German territories to maintain the Franco-Swiss connection without passing through Mulhouse.

activities.text: Cross the border on foot or by bike to Boncourt. Explore the Swiss canton of Jura: Porrentruy lies 15 km away with its medieval old town and castle.

The Malsaucy leisure centre (about 35 km from Delle, a 40-minute drive) offers sailing, kayaking and stand-up paddleboarding from April to October. A 6000 m² beach with lifeguards and free access from June to August. The Eurockéennes festival takes place in early July (100 000 spectators).

days_plan.itin_title: Territoire de Belfort Road Trip: The Citadel and the Lion

visits.text: Admire these exceptional 3rd-century ramparts, witnesses to the grandeur of Dea Augusta Vocontiorum. These fortifications extend nearly 2 kilometers with a thickness of 3.6 meters and rise up to 14 meters high. The Saint-Marcel Gate, the only Roman monument still standing in the department, ranks among France's best-preserved.

Visit this listed cathedral built between the 12th and 13th centuries atop the vestiges of an ancient Roman temple. The building blends Romanesque and Gothic architecture. The remarkable 12th-century Romanesque portal ranks among the finest in the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes region.

Discover an exceptional treasure in this chapel of the former episcopal palace: the 12th-century Romanesque mosaic of the Four Rivers. This unique altar carpet in France offers a symbolic representation of the universe according to medieval cosmogony.

Housed in an 18th-century mansion, the municipal museum designated a Museum of France holds archaeological collections dating back to the Neolithic. The Gallo-Roman period shines through taurobolic altars listed as Historical Monuments.

activities.text: Head to the cellars to taste the famous Clairette de Die, granted AOP status in 1942. This naturally sparkling wine is made using the ancestral Die method dating back to Gallo-Roman times. The Jaillance cooperative cellar, founded in 1950, brings together more than 240 winegrowers.

Wander through the medieval cobbled streets of the historic center with its colorful old houses. Admire the Protestant temple housed in a former 18th-century Jesuit chapel. Enjoy the Wednesday and Saturday morning markets to discover Clairette, Picodon PDO, and local products.

A few kilometers from Die, visit the Notre-Dame de Valcroissant Abbey, a listed monument founded in the late 12th century. Though partially ruined, it still presents a cloister surrounded by an abbey church in a preserved natural setting testifying to over 800 years of history.

days_plan.itin_title: Drome Provencale Road Trip: Villages and Terroirs

visits.text: Dieppe Castle-Museum — This fortress of sandstone and flint, built in the fifteenth century on the cliffs, overlooks the port and the beach. Its collections of carved ivories, a Dieppe tradition since the sixteenth century, rank among France's richest with over 2,000 pieces.

Saint-Jacques Church in Dieppe — A flamboyant Gothic masterpiece from the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, this maritime church features carved friezes depicting distant peoples, testifying to the voyages of Dieppe's navigators to Africa and Brazil.

Dieppe Waterfront and Beach — France's oldest seaside resort, visited by the Duchess of Berry as early as 1824, Dieppe stretches 1.8 km of pebbles before a lawn where the international kite festival takes place every two years.

activities.text: Varengeville-sur-Mer — This artists' village overlooking the sea is home to the seaside cemetery where Georges Braque rests, the Church of Saint-Valéry with stained glass by this same Cubist painter, and Shamrock Garden with 2,000 varieties of hydrangeas.

Saturday Market in Dieppe — One of Normandy's largest markets takes place every Saturday on the Grande Rue and the town center squares. Fresh fish from the port, local Pays de Caux produce, and antique dealers have enlivened the town since the Middle Ages.

Le Pollet District — This fishermen's quarter on the port's east bank preserves its colorful houses and working-class atmosphere. The Church of Notre-Dame-de-Bon-Secours has watched over sailors since the seventeenth century.

days_plan.itin_title: Seine-Maritime Road Trip: The Cliffs of Étretat, Rouen & Jumièges Abbey

visits.text: Stroll down the pedestrian shopping street running from the Protestant temple to the clock tower. Designated a City of Art and Crafts, Dieulefit concentrates workshops, boutiques, museums, and galleries. The village sits beside the Jabron River. The riverside house façades have been repainted in pastel tones creating a colorful, joyful atmosphere.

Discover the 40 pottery and ceramics workshops, heirs to a 2,000-year tradition. Dieulefit's pottery history begins in Gallo-Roman times thanks to clay renowned for its qualities. Today, the Dieulefit region perpetuates this tradition with a revival of contemporary production. Enter galleries to admire original creations bearing the Dieulefit Original label.

Visit this cultural center created in 1995 in Baume Park that presents the region's pottery history. The museum space displays over 200 pieces illustrating local production evolution, particularly the great 19th-century era. Discover pottery's various uses through the ages and manufacturing techniques employed.

Spend the morning completing your artisan souvenir shopping in village boutiques. Utilitarian or decorative pottery, unique pieces created by local ceramists stamped with the Dieulefit Original label, local products like Picodon PDO, lavender honey, and essential oils.

activities.text: Get hands-on during a pottery initiation workshop offered by the House of Ceramics or a local potter. Discover coiling, slab building, modeling, and throwing. You can create your own unique piece guided by passionate artisans.

Tour the workshop circuit open to the public in downtown and surroundings. Engage with artisans in their workspaces, observe shaping techniques, discover kilns and various firing methods. Each artisan has developed their own style and specialty.

Enjoy the orienteering sport space set up by the department to discover the old village in a fun family way. The goal is to find wooden markers shown on the map. Three routes of varying difficulty exist. Cool off along the Jabron's banks, whose source lies in neighboring Comps.

Savor one last stroll through Dieulefit's colorful alleys, enjoy a café terrace along the Jabron's banks, soak in the peaceful atmosphere of this artists' village nestled in Drôme Provençale. If departing on Sunday, enjoy the small local market.

Hit the road home carrying memories of this magnificent journey through Drôme Provençale. From Roman ramparts to lavender fields, from medieval villages to sun-drenched olive groves, you've discovered this region's exceptional terroir and heritage.

days_plan.itin_title: Drome Provencale Road Trip: Villages and Terroirs
Drome Provencale Road Trip: Villages and Terroirs

visits.text: The Haute-Provence Geological Reserve reveals its fossil treasures. Marine impressions emerge from the limestone, bearing witness to a vanished ocean. The geological trail takes you past ammonite slabs and fossilized ichthyosaurs.

The Gassendi Museum combines contemporary art and natural sciences in an unexpected dialogue. Natural history collections sit alongside installations by resident artists. Light from above floods the main gallery, where Andy Goldsworthy's works and geological specimens interact.

Discover the limestone rock that rises above Digne-les-Bains like a stone ship. Steep trails lead to the summit, where the view takes in the spa town and surrounding valleys. The hilltop chapel has watched over the town since the Middle Ages.
The Digne thermal baths use sulfurous waters that emerge at 42°C. The spa offers treatments and balneotherapy.

The old town unfolds its ochre facades and shaded little squares in tiers. Stroll through the medieval lanes where fountains murmur, bringing a sense of coolness. Boulevard Gassendi brings the town center to life with its Provençal craft shops and welcoming terraces.

activities.text: The Train des Pignes winds from Digne to Nice through the Pre-Alps. The historic route passes through tunnels and across vertiginous viaducts. Landscapes shift from olive trees to fir trees, offering a unique railway spectacle in Provence.
Digne-les-Bains is the ideal starting point to explore the Verdon gorges. Scenic roads lead toward Castellane and the canyon entrances. Plan a full day for this memorable excursion.
Hiking trails crisscross the surrounding hills. Mont Saint-Pancrace offers a moderate ascent rewarded by a 360-degree panorama. Oaks and Aleppo pines punctuate the routes with their welcome shade.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpes-de-Haute-Provence Tour: Lavender and Hilltop Villages
Forcalquier & Verdon Gorges Road Trip

visits.text: Dinan's ramparts stretch 2.7 km around the town—the largest surviving medieval walled enclosure in Brittany. Built between the 13th and 15th centuries, they still feature 10 towers and 4 monumental gates. A walk along the wall walk offers views down into the Rance valley.
Dinan Castle, built between 1380 and 1384 by Duke Jean IV of Brittany, served as a residential tower and fortress. From the top, a sweeping panorama takes in the town's rooftops and the Rance.

Follow rue du Jerzual, the steep street that has connected the upper town to the port for ten centuries. Its half-timbered houses contain artists' studios, galleries, and craft shops. Weavers and tanners once worked here—the bustle still revolves around crafts.

The Saint-Sauveur Basilica, constructed in the second half of the 12th century, blends Romanesque and Gothic influences across its western facade. It preserves the heart of Bertrand Du Guesclin, Constable of France, in a reliquary in the north chapel. The Romanesque portal displays Oriental-Byzantine motifs rarely seen in Brittany.

Dinan's port, at the foot of the ramparts, was a trading crossroads as early as the 11th century. Commerce with England, Flanders, and later Spain built the town's prosperity. Now a marina, its quays lined with outdoor seating have a quiet atmosphere in the morning and come alive in the evening.

The Clock Tower, a 15th-century belfry, dominates the town from its 46-meter height. Duchess Anne's bell still rings today. Climb the stairs for a 360° panorama over the slate rooftops and surrounding countryside.

activities.text: Guided tour of the medieval city. Expert guides reveal stories behind the 130 half-timbered houses, the murder holes, gun ports, and counterscarps of the ramparts. A journey from daily medieval life to the present day.

Cruise on the Rance from Dinan port. The boat sails up the estuary toward Léhon or down toward Saint-Malo, between wooded banks and granite manor houses. The ramparts viewed from the river offer a spectacular perspective.

Dinan's weekly market, Thursday mornings. Stalls fill Place du Guesclin and adjacent streets. Local Breton products: galettes-saucisses, farmhouse cider, salted butter, buckwheat crêpes. A lively and colorful atmosphere.

days_plan.itin_title: Côtes-d'Armor Road Trip: Dinan, Pink Granite Coast, Bréhat Island & Lake Guerlédan
Brittany Road Trip: Villages with Character, Sea and History

visits.text: Belle Époque Villas and Promenade du Clair de Lune. Dinard has 407 listed villas testifying to the seaside splendor of the Belle Époque, when British and American aristocrats made it Europe's most elegant resort. The Promenade du Clair de Lune winds along the coast between palm trees and exotic gardens, offering sublime views of the sea and Saint-Malo across the water. The extravagant architecture blends Anglo-Norman, neo-medieval, and Art Nouveau styles: bow windows, verandas, turrets, and ornate facades vie for originality. The villa Les Roches Brunes, a historic monument built in 1893 in neo-Louis XIII style, is regularly open for visits, and its terrace suspended above the waves offers a dizzying panorama.

The Beaches of Dinard. Écluse Beach, the resort's main beach, has fine sand between the blue-and-white striped tents and retro beach huts that give Dinard its charm. Its pontoon allows visitors to dive at high tide, while the heated Olympic-size seawater pool draws swimmers all year round. Farther west, Saint-Énogat Beach offers a family-friendly setting with its water sports club and miniature golf course, while Prieuré Beach appeals for its tranquility. Spring tides reveal an impressive foreshore scattered with rocks.

Pointe du Décollé and Coastal Path. This rocky point marks the western tip of Dinard, offering a grand panorama of Saint-Malo Bay, Dinard, Saint-Lunaire, and on clear days to Cap Fréhel. The GR34 coastal trail runs along the cliffs between wild coves and perched villas, revealing new Emerald Coast landscapes at every turn. The surprising Mediterranean vegetation (palms, agaves, mimosas) testifies to Dinard's exceptionally mild climate.

Town Center and Covered Market. The market hall's glass enclosure comes alive three times a week with up to 300 vendors offering seafood, Breton cheeses, and local specialties. The Belle Époque architecture of the Barrière Casino, Palais des Arts, and shopping streets preserves the elegance of yesteryear. Seaside café and restaurant terraces invite visitors to savor seafood and oysters in a refined setting that still evokes aristocratic seaside vacations.

activities.text: British Film Festival. Each autumn in October, Dinard celebrates British cinema for a week with a competition, premieres, and meetings with directors and actors. A jury of prominent figures awards the Hitchcock d'Or to the best film. Even outside the festival, British influence permeates the town through its gardens, architecture, and afternoon tea traditions in the lounges of grand hotels.

Rance Dam and Tidal Power Station. Between Dinard and Saint-Malo, this 750-meter dam, inaugurated in 1966, was the world's first tidal power station to harness tidal energy. Site visits (with registration at the tourist office from June to September) explain this unique system, which produces electricity for 225,000 inhabitants. The panorama from the dam takes in the Rance estuary with its islets and wooded shores, particularly photogenic at sunset.

days_plan.itin_title: Ille-et-Vilaine Tour: Saint-Malo, Dinard and the Emerald Coast

visits.text: Disneyland Park, opened in 1992, centers around Sleeping Beauty Castle. Five themed lands recreate worlds ranging from the Victorian Wild West to science fiction, with attractions for all ages.
Walt Disney Studios Park plunges into the backstage of cinema and animation. Immersive attractions recreate large-scale movie sets.

activities.text: Disney Village, a free-access zone between the two parks, offers restaurants, shops, and evening shows. The atmosphere comes alive especially after the parks close.
The nighttime spectaculars project onto Sleeping Beauty Castle a show blending fireworks, fountains, lasers, and video projections.

days_plan.itin_title: Seine-et-Marne Circuit: Fontainebleau and Châteaux

visits.text: Saint-Samson Cathedral. This jewel of Breton Gothic architecture has dominated the Dol marshes since the 13th century, blending an elegant interior with a fortress-like exterior. The great eastern window, the oldest in Brittany, illuminates the 39-meter nave with its medieval stained glass depicting the Last Judgment. The Renaissance tomb of Thomas James, a 15th-century bishop, comes alive with a strange phenomenon at the summer solstice: at noon, a sunbeam strikes the carved vial of immortality precisely. The cathedral also possesses the only curiosity of its kind in Europe: a double well dating first from Roman and then medieval times, forming an underground passage that testifies to the builders' ingenuity. The unfinished north tower feeds legends about Saint Michael's battle with the Devil.

Cathédraloscope. Opposite the cathedral, this unique interpretation center explores the world of Gothic cathedral construction through 12 rooms and 800 m² of interactive exhibitions. Videos, animated models, and reconstructions of building sites reveal the builders' techniques, the trades of architects and stonemasons, and the symbolism of stained glass and sculptures. The Pillars of the Earth room brings together 20 models of France's greatest cathedrals in a spectacular presentation. A fun trail with puzzles captivates children, while stone-cutting demonstrations by a genuine journeyman complete the experience.

Grande Rue des Stuarts and the Medieval Town. Designated a Petite Cité de Caractère, Dol reveals a remarkable heritage in its narrow lanes. Grande Rue des Stuarts, a reminder that Dol was the cradle of that dynasty, is lined with 15th–17th-century half-timbered houses and private mansions. The Maison des Petits Palets, dating from the 12th century, is one of the oldest houses still standing in Brittany. The Hôtel de Quengo, which served as a revolutionary prison and later as a town hall and post office, hides its Renaissance facade in the ruelle du Robinet. Colorful facades and lively shops give this beautifully preserved medieval town a warm atmosphere.

Champ-Dolent Menhir. Two kilometers south of Dol, this 9.3-meter granite giant has stood enigmatically in the middle of a field since the Neolithic period. Listed as a historic monument since 1889, it's one of Brittany's largest standing menhirs. Legends variously associate it with Saint Michael's battle against the Devil or with a funerary or commemorative monument. According to local tradition, it is said to sink one inch into the ground each century, and the day it disappears completely would mark the end of the world.

activities.text: Mont-Dol. This 65-meter granite islet rises from the Dol marsh, offering an exceptional 360° panorama of Mont-Saint-Michel Bay, from Cancale to Granville, with Mont-Saint-Michel as a backdrop. The site, inhabited for 700,000 years, yielded mammoth, rhinoceros, and cave bear bones during 19th-century excavations. Breton legends recount that Saint Michael confronted the Devil here: their footprints, along with the demon's seat and claw marks, are said to remain visible on the rocks. The 12th-century Saint-Pierre Church, with its restrained Romanesque style, houses 15th-century frescoes depicting medieval Hell. The mill and Saint-Michel chapel crown the summit, creating a characteristic silhouette.

Promenade des Douves and Ramparts. The garden laid out along the former line of the medieval ramparts offers a peaceful walk with views of the Dol marsh and Mont-Dol. The three garden levels create varied perspectives, combining a shaded walkway with planted spaces. It's also the starting point for several hiking routes in the white marsh, a birdwatching paradise where herons, egrets, and wild ducks cross paths.

days_plan.itin_title: Ille-et-Vilaine Tour: Saint-Malo, Dinard and the Emerald Coast

visits.text: Chat Perché Circuit: a 4-kilometer trail through 35 waypoints spanning eight centuries of Dole's history. Brass plaques depicting a cat guide your steps through cobbled lanes. You'll discover the Collégiale Notre-Dame dominating the skyline, Renaissance townhouses, the tranquil Tanners' Canal with its still reflections, and Rue du Collège de l'Arc. The circuit offers a free map at the Tourist Office, also available as an audio guide.

Louis Pasteur's birthplace, located at 43 rue Pasteur on the banks of the canal des Tanneurs. Louis Pasteur was born there on 27 December 1822 in the family home of his father, a tanner. The visit reveals the life of this scientist who revolutionized microbiology and hygiene. One room displays the pastel portraits he made as a teenager, evidence of his little-known artistic talents.

Collégiale Notre-Dame, the religious edifice dominating the town, built between the 13th and 18th centuries. Its imposing yellow stone bell tower can be seen from several kilometers away. The interior houses three naves with galleries and richly decorated side chapels. The church testifies to Dole's prosperity when it served as capital of Franche-Comté until 1678. The stained glass windows and liturgical furnishings tell the story of the city's religious history.

Tanners' Canal and river port. This historic quarter has kept the three-storey houses of the tanners, with cellars opening onto the pavement through a trapdoor. The passage Raynaud conceals an architectural surprise. Renaissance façades are reflected in the still water of the canal, where dozens of pleasure boats are moored.

Fine Arts Museum with a non-conformist approach to art history. Collections from the 16th to 19th centuries sit alongside contemporary artworks that break chronology. The Barbizon school and Comtois masters like Courbet, Pointelin, Brun, and Adler occupy pride of place. Dole's prosperity as capital of Franche-Comté shines through in the richness of Burgundian and Comtois art collections from the Renaissance to the 18th century.

activities.text: Walk at the confluence of the Doubs and the Loue, approximately 10 km from the stopover town, a 10-minute drive. The landscaped riverbanks offer an idyllic setting for walking or cycling. The confluence of the two rivers creates a rich ecosystem observed by anglers and naturalists. The towpaths lead away from the town center toward unspoiled countryside.

Covered market halls on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays. The unique atmosphere of this market offering a wide choice of food stalls attracts both locals and visitors. Local producers sell Comté cheese, Morteau sausages, Jura wines, and fresh farm products. Conversations between vendors and customers create a warm atmosphere conducive to gastronomic discoveries.

days_plan.itin_title: Jura Road Trip: Lakes, Waterfalls & Mountains

visits.text: Listed as early as 1910, the Agriotier dolmens stand at an altitude of 198 meters in the hills above Les Issambres. They remind us that the valley was inhabited well before the Romans and their fish ponds. You reach them along trails climbing from the coast. Bring water: shade is scarce and access to the hills is restricted from June 21 to September 20.

activities.text: Climb to the Agriotier dolmens from the coast at Les Issambres: the slope is steep and the trail passes through cork oaks and mimosas. The view looks down over Saint-Aygulf and the Estérel. Bring water: there's nowhere to get supplies along the way, and the sun beats down hard in summer.

days_plan.itin_title: Roquebrune-sur-Argens: sea, villages and the Var in 10 days

visits.text: Acquired by the Conservatoire du littoral in the 1970s, the Domaine de la Palissade extends over 702 hectares at the mouth of the Grand Rhône. It lies entirely outside the dikes. Salt flats, reed beds, lagoons and riverside woodland.

activities.text: Climb the viewing tower on the Clos d'Argent trail at the Domaine de la Palissade: the mosaic of habitats becomes clear at a glance. Short circuit, interpretive panels, observatory. Pets forbidden on the trails.

If you have half a day, the Sableuse-Grande Palun trail leads to a lagoon: about 8 km, flat, with a hide at the end. Kayaking on the Rhône and horse rides are offered from April to November, with advance booking.

days_plan.itin_title: Côte Bleue and Camargue: the lower coastal route in 7 days

visits.text: The ruins of Domfront castle stand on a sandstone spur reaching 211 m. The 12th-century keep, 25 m high, the shell curtain wall, and the ramparts testify to a stronghold that controlled the routes to Mont-Saint-Michel, Maine, and Brittany. Dismantled in 1610 by order of Sully.

At the fortress's foot, the Church of Notre-Dame-sur-l'Eau is a jewel of Norman Romanesque art, dating to the late 11th century. Its choir welcomed illustrious guests: Louis IX and Louis XI on pilgrimage, Thomas Becket, and Henri II Plantagenet, who baptized his daughter here in 1162.

The Church of Saint-Julien, built in 1924–1926, is a unique structure: reinforced concrete, square plan, and neo-Byzantine decoration. Its mosaics in geometric gold-and-blue forms, by Gaudin, create a striking atmosphere. Listed as a historic monument in 1993.

Roam the cobbled lanes of the medieval town, one of the few in Orne to preserve its medieval urban plan. Covered passageways, interior courtyards, half-timbered houses, and townhouses follow one after another.
The 11 towers and gates of the old town punctuate the Rue des Fossés Pusson. These remnants of the ramparts frame a preserved medieval urban fabric.

activities.text: From the Place du Panorama and the castle's orientation table, views extend from the Maine landscapes to the borders of Brittany. The Domfront bocage spreads below, dotted with centuries-old pear trees.
Domfront is the capital of poiré, a fermented pear drink with AOP status. Visit a producer to discover Domfront calvados as well, which blends pears and apples—a unique particularity.
Domfront sits at the crossroads of the Vélo Francette (Ouistreham–La Rochelle) and the Véloscénie (Paris–Mont-Saint-Michel). Ride a section through Norman bocage.
The Medieval Festival of Domfront, held every two years, plunges the town into the fervor of the 12th century: shows, activities, and historical reenactments.

days_plan.itin_title: Orne Road Trip: Norman Bocage and Stud Farms

visits.text: Domme is a royal bastide founded in 1281 by Philip III the Bold, perched 150 meters above the Dordogne on a rocky promontory. Unlike the checkerboard layout typical of bastides, Domme's trapezoidal plan adapts ingeniously to the clifftop terrain. The Porte des Tours—a gateway flanked by two massive towers—preserves enigmatic graffiti carved between 1307 and 1318.

The graffiti inside the Porte des Tours have long been attributed to Knights Templar imprisoned here after Philip the Fair dissolved the order in 1307. Crosses, human figures, and mysterious symbols cover the stone walls. Historians continue to debate whether these carvings are truly Templar—or the work of other prisoners—but the mystery endures.

Domme Cave, accessible directly from the central market square, is the largest developed cave in Périgord Noir. Its 450 meters of galleries are adorned with stalactites, stalagmites, and flowing draperies. The exit is through a panoramic elevator carved into the cliff, emerging at the belvedere with stunning views across the valley.

activities.text: The Belvedere de la Barre offers one of the finest panoramas in all of Périgord: a sweeping 180-degree view over the Dordogne Valley, the villages of La Roque-Gageac and Beynac, and the castles of Castelnaud and Marqueyssac. The esplanade sits right at the cliff edge—bring your camera.

Domme's market convenes Thursday morning at Place de la Halle, where local producers sell foie gras, walnuts, seasonal truffles, and Domme wine. The vineyard, replanted in 1990 after phylloxera devastated it a century earlier, now produces wine again—a small triumph of agricultural revival.

days_plan.itin_title: Dordogne: Prehistoric Caves, Medieval Fortresses & Périgord Delights
The Most Beautiful Villages of Lot and Périgord in 6 Days

visits.text: The Basilica of Bois-Chenu is not medieval—people often forget that. The foundation stone was laid on November 3, 1881, on the hillside where Joan, then a shepherdess, is said to have heard her voices. She was not yet canonized at the time, and the building was initially dedicated to Saint Michael. Designed by architect Paul Sédille and subsequently completed by the Demay family, with work continuing until 1926, it blends pink Vosges granite and white Euville stone in a striking combination of colors. Inside, mosaics cover everything from floor to vault—a decorative program carried out from 1891 to 1934. In the crypt, look for the statue of Notre-Dame de Bermont, the Virgin whom Joan came to pray to every week 3 km from here. The building is illuminated every evening—if you pass by at nightfall, the view from the valley is striking.

500 meters from the basilica, the birthplace of Joan of Arc (born around 1412) is one of the most visited monuments in the Vosges. What's remarkable: it survived thanks to a tax exemption granted by the Duchy of Lorraine as early as the 15th century to preserve the dwelling. Joan spent her entire childhood here before leaving in 1429 to liberate Orléans. An adjoining museum traces the Maid's history with original documents and objects.

activities.text: Climb to the Bois-Chenu hillside after visiting the basilica and walk on the heights overlooking the Meuse valley. If you have time, continue to the chapel of Notre-Dame de Bermont in Greux, 3 km north: this is the pilgrimage site that Joan visited every Saturday from Domrémy, in all weather. A quiet, almost forgotten place that makes a change from the village's tourist sites.

days_plan.itin_title: Vosges Abbey Trail: Monastic Heritage
Grand Est Road Trip: Vineyards, Ramparts and Forests

visits.text: Port-Museum of Douarnenez, a unique maritime site in Europe with its fleet of afloat historic vessels. Traditional ships moored in Port Rhu harbor testify to the diversity of European navigation: Breton lobster boat, Norwegian dundee, Loire river barge, British tugboat. Pontoons allow boarding to explore holds, cabins, and decks. Land-based exhibitions trace navigation history and fishing techniques through the centuries.

Tristan Island, a private islet facing the harbor accessible only during spring tides or summer guided visits. The former Richelieu family estate harbors archaeological remains, 16th-century fortifications, and a preserved cannery. Botanical gardens group Mediterranean and tropical species benefiting from the island's microclimate. The walk across the exposed foreshore reveals mudflats, seagrass beds, and marine fauna. Views from the island embrace Douarnenez Bay and the Plomarc'h headlands.

Sables Blancs Beach, a large urban beach of fine sand framed by Belle Époque villas. Turquoise waters sheltered in the bay allow safe swimming. The coastal promenade connects various beaches and coves to Tréboul. Nautical clubs offer sailing, kayaking, and paddleboarding in ideal conditions. The seaside district retains its retro charm with colorful beach cabins.

Plomarc'h and the customs officers' path to Pointe du Millier. The GR34 trail winds along cliffs offering panoramas over Douarnenez Bay and Cap Sizun. Rocky coves alternate with short grasslands where gorse and heather bloom. The preserved site shelters seabirds and rare plants. Remains of the old semaphore testify to the location's strategic importance.

activities.text: Discovering Douarnenez's sardine heritage, formerly France's leading sardine port. Converted canneries line the harbor testifying to the fishing industry's golden age in the early 20th century. The Tréboul district reveals typical fishermen's house architecture with nets drying at windows. Industrial wastelands now house artists' studios and cultural spaces. Social history marked by the great 1924 strikes is reflected in the urban fabric.

Attending the fish auction return and fresh fish tasting at the harbor. Douarnenez remains an active fishing port with trawlers landing bass, pollock, hake, and crustaceans. Quayside restaurants offer the day's catch simply prepared: grilled fish, Breton cotriade stew, seafood platters.
