The authentic atmosphere of port bistros contrasts with downtown gastronomic addresses. Artisan canneries perpetuate the canning know-how.

End of the day at the Sables Blancs beach in Douarnenez, facing the bay. The coastal promenade links the coves and beaches of the seaside district. The sailing clubs offer outings under sail and by kayak depending on the season. The seafront terraces make it easy to linger into the evening facing the sunset.

days_plan.itin_title: Haunted Brittany in 6 days: From Brocéliande to the Lands of the Ankou
Finistère Circuit: Breton Headlands, Islands & Artists' Villages
Brittany 7 days: Pink Granite, Lighthouses & Peninsulas

visits.text: Completed in 1222 by Philip Augustus, Dourdan Castle is one of the few 13th-century fortresses in Île-de-France that retain their structures: keep, towers, and dry moats.
Climb the 36-meter circular keep for a 360° view of the town and forest. The ramparts offer a unique perspective on this defensive system in the style of Philip Augustus.
The municipal museum occupies the former salt storehouse. Tactile models, digital tablets, and a film trace the castle's evolution from royal residence to prison.
The Church of Saint-Germain l'Auxerrois dates from the 12th and 13th centuries. Its Gothic architecture reflects Dourdan's importance as a royal residence.
Houses built from sandstone cobbles and decorative rockwork surround the castle. The historic center has preserved its medieval character.

activities.text: The Dourdan State Forest stretches across thousands of hectares. Once a royal forest prized for hunting, it offers numerous hiking trails.
Follow the Fontaines Bouillantes circuit along the Orge River. These three ponds, created in the 1950s, form a bucolic landscape between town and forest.
The Haute Vallée de Chevreuse Regional Nature Park begins at Dourdan's doorstep. Perfect for cycling and nature walks.

days_plan.itin_title: Essonne Tour: Castles and Valleys

visits.text: Saint-Benoît d'En Calcat Abbey, founded in 1890, is home to some forty Benedictine monks. The abbey church, open to all, is bathed in light filtered through colored stained-glass windows whose colors are reflected on the stone columns.

1,200 meters away, Sainte-Scholastique Abbey has been home to a community of Benedictine nuns since 1890. Community life, prayer, and work form the pillars of their daily routine, shared with passing visitors.

Head to Sorèze, a few kilometers away. The Abbaye-école, a former royal college founded in the 8th century, now houses the museum devoted to contemporary tapestries by the monk-artist, a major figure in 20th-century textile art.

From Dourgne, head to the small church in the village of Massaguel. It houses the only mural painted by Dom Robert, along with seven stained-glass windows dating from 1957. An unassuming but moving detour.
Explore downtown Dourgne, a small town close to nature at the foot of the Montagne Noire. Its stone and brick houses, fountains, and unspoiled atmosphere make it a peaceful stop between two abbeys.

activities.text: Attend a sung service at En Calcat Abbey. The liturgy, celebrated in French with passages of Gregorian chant, is open to the public. The chants resonate beneath the abbey church's vaults.
Browse the Siloë-Saint Benoît bookstore at the abbey. You'll find religious works, tapestry reproductions, art cards, balms, and craft products made by the monks.
Hike the Montagne Noire trails starting from Dourgne. Paths cross beech and oak forests, with open views over the Lauragais hills and Toulouse plain.

days_plan.itin_title: Tarn Road Trip: Albi & Hilltop Villages

places.name: Draguignan

visits.text: The Clock Tower, rebuilt in 1662 and listed as a historic monument, rises on the town's central rock. Its 79 steps lead to a campanile offering a panoramic view over the landscape around Draguignan. The monument stands 24 meters tall.

The Dolmen de la Pierre de la Fée, dated to 2,500 BCE, is one of the most imposing in Provence: 60 tonnes, three slabs over 2 meters supporting a 6-meter-long capstone. Listed as a historic monument since 1889, it backs onto a centuries-old oak.

The Musée des Arts et Traditions Populaires de Moyenne Provence, awarded the Musée de France label, holds one of the country's finest collections of ethnographic objects. Its exhibitions are developed in partnership with the greatest museums in the world.

The Museum of Fine Arts, located in the heart of the historic center, displays a collection of artworks and historical artifacts, including the ceremonial armor of François de Montmorency, restored by the Research Center of the Museums of France.
The Rhône American Cemetery and Memorial, established in August 1944, gathers the graves of 861 soldiers who died during the reconquest of southern France. A sober and moving place of remembrance.

activities.text: In Trans-en-Provence, cross the 70-meter footbridge overlooking the Nartuby gorges. The route offers lovely views of the river, waterfalls, and gorges.
Climb up to the Malmont viewpoint map for a 360-degree panorama over the region. The trail starts from the town center and winds between garrigue and pine forest.
Wander the medieval lanes of the old town, between the old houses of the Maison de la Reine Jeanne and the Saint-Hermentaire chapel. Parc Chabran, with its century-old trees, invites you to relax.

days_plan.itin_title: Var Road Trip: French Riviera & Provence Verte

map_keywords: Dolmen Pierre de la Fée Draguignan
Musée des Arts et Traditions Populaires Draguignan

visits.text: The Drancy Shoah Memorial, opened in 2012, faces the Cité de la Muette. Video testimonies, archival documents, and period photographs trace the history of France's main internment and transit camp for Jews between 1941 and 1944.

The Cité de la Muette, built in the 1930s by Beaudoin, Lods, and Bodianski, was at the forefront of collective housing with its fourteen-story towers, France's tallest at the time. Requisitioned by the Nazis, it became an assembly camp from which 63,000 people departed for the extermination camps. It has been designated a protected site since 2001.

In front of the housing project, Shelomo Selinger's deportees' monument consists of three 3-meter blocks of pink granite forming the Hebrew letter Shin. The central block depicts ten figures gripped by flames.

The memorial railcar, inaugurated in 1988 and protected as a historic monument, is connected to the monument by rails. It is identical to those that transported thousands of deportees to the camps in Poland.

activities.text: Every Sunday at 3 PM, a free guided tour of the Memorial is offered. It includes the permanent exhibition and an outdoor route facing the Cité de la Muette.
Take a break in Ladoucette Park in Drancy. Walk around the Château de Ladoucette, among the park's lawns and trees.

days_plan.itin_title: Seine-Saint-Denis Tour: Basilica and Urban Culture

visits.text: Royal Chapel of Saint-Louis in Dreux, necropolis of the Orléans family since the 19th century. This masterpiece of neo-Gothic architecture houses about fifty burials including that of Louis-Philippe, the last King of the French. The stained glass windows from the Sèvres Manufactory, signed by Ingres and Delacroix, are exceptionally beautiful.

Sculpted tomb effigies of the royal chapel, a veritable museum of 19th-century sculpture. Admire particularly the tomb of Sophie-Charlotte of Bavaria, sister of Empress Sissi, who died tragically in the Bazar de la Charité fire in 1897. Her effigy by Walhain depicts burning pieces of wood.

Remains of Dreux's medieval castle on the counts' former estate. The ramparts flanked by defensive towers and the 13th-century Tour Grise bear witness to over a thousand years of history at the borders of Normandy and the Loire Valley.

Dreux belfry, a symbol of medieval municipal power. This 15th-century square tower, topped with a Renaissance campanile, offers a panorama over the city and the royal estate's parks. A testament to the city's commercial importance in the Middle Ages.

activities.text: Stroll through the parks of Dreux's royal estate, laid out in the 19th century in the English landscape garden style. These 6-hectare spaces feature remarkable tree species and offer panoramic views over the city from the heights of the former fortress.

Tour of Dreux's historic center with its half-timbered houses and the 16th-century Saint-Pierre church. The Art and History Museum presents archaeological and artistic collections tracing the history of this royal city.

days_plan.itin_title: Eure-et-Loir Tour: Chartres, Châteaux and Proust

visits.text: Dun-sur-Auron's belfry impresses: six storeys of 13th-century stone, a remnant of the second fortified wall. Also called the Porte de l'Horloge, it guarded the entrance to this former royal stronghold. Sections of ramparts are still visible along the Auron.

The Saint-Étienne Collegiate Church, founded in the 11th century, is recognisable by its reddish façade — local limestone is rich in iron oxide. The bell tower above the entrance porch dates to the 14th century. Inside, sculpted columns illustrate the Old and New Testaments with touching naïveté.

The Berry Canal Museum occupies the former gatekeeper's lodge of the Châtelet. Models, towing tools and period photographs tell the story of this canal linking the Loire to the Allier. Decommissioned in 1955, it now serves as a greenway.

activities.text: The Contres Marsh, the largest in the Centre-Val de Loire region, stretches south of Dun. A preserved wetland, renowned fishing spot, observation trails. Herons, ducks, dragonflies — the marsh teems with life in spring.

Dun-sur-Auron is the walnut capital of Berry. Local mills produce an artisanal walnut oil with a pronounced flavour. You'll find it in the grocers in the town centre, perfect for dressing Berry lentils.
The “Dun-sur-Auron, la tradition du Calon” loop covers 16 km through bocage landscapes and sleepy hamlets. Starts from the town centre, yellow waymarks. Allow 4 hours of easy walking.

days_plan.itin_title: Cher Loop: Romanesque Berry and the Route Jacques-Cœur

visits.text: Climb Dun-Haut hill (81 m above the town), an ancient Gallic oppidum then Roman castrum. Notre-Dame de Bonne Garde church, built in 1346 by the lords of Apremont, is the only surviving monument from the old fortress. This Gothic jewel possesses a sumptuous 18th-century organ case and furnishings.

Inside the church, two monumental sculptures by contemporary artist Ipoustéguy, native of Dun-sur-Meuse, surprise with their expressionism: Death of Bishop Neumann (1976) and a tormented Christ. The church is part of the European "Open Churches" network.

Walk through remnants of ramparts built from the 10th century. A round tower and a square tower survive, along with the 1402 Porte des Chevaux. From the church square, the view plunges over the Meuse valley, the river's meanders, and surrounding fields.

In the lower town at Doulcon, the Ipoustéguy cultural center exhibits marbles and bronzes by this sculptor who won the Bright Award at the Venice Biennale in 1964 and installed a monumental bronze on the Berlin Congress Palace forecourt in 1978.
Five kilometers away, Mont-devant-Sassey's 12th-century Romanesque church stands beside the Meuse in a majestic setting. Its young heritage ambassadors offer passionate summer tours.

activities.text: Follow the Dun-le-Chastel ramparts circuit, a one-hour pedestrian walk punctuated with explanatory panels between archaeology, heritage, and gardens. Medieval remains blend with valley panoramas.
The "Old Meuse and Green Lake" green circuit winds along ponds and the old Meuse. The Natura 2000 classified zone shelters remarkable fauna and flora, between gray herons and water lilies.
Lake Dun offers supervised summer swimming and daily boat rentals. The marina allows peaceful navigation on the water body.

days_plan.itin_title: Meuse Circuit: Verdun and the Citadels

visits.text: Duras Castle overlooks the Dropt Valley from a rocky spur. Its origins date back to the 12th century, when a viscount of Bézaume built a fortress on this outcrop. The building belonged to Pope Clement V through his brother Gaillard de Got before passing to the Durfort family, dukes of Duras, who transformed it into a country residence in the 17th century. The first duke, Jacques Henri de Durfort, began rebuilding the main residential wings in the late 17th century according to the architectural conventions of the period. Listed as a historic monument in 1970, it now contains 35 rooms refurnished in medieval and Grand Siècle styles through a partnership with the Mobilier national launched in 2016. The view from the terraces over the Dropt vineyards is one of the finest in the region.

Inside, do not miss the recently refurnished Great Hall of the Marshals and the Kitchen of the Hundred Bundles. Two figures dominate the visit: the first Marshal of Duras and Claire de Kersaint, Duchess of Duras and friend of Chateaubriand, whose correspondence is presented in the apartments.

The Maison des Vins de Duras, in the town itself, offers an introduction to the Cotes de Duras vineyard. The appellation, granted in 1937 among the first in France, covers around 1,230 hectares across 15 communes. Francois I himself described this wine as a 'nectar'. Dry whites, sweet whites, roses and reds: the range is complete.

Look for the Clock Tower, the only listed remnant of the former fortifications of the Duras bastide. It once guarded access to the plateau from the lower town. A walking route then follows the cobbled streets of the town, where white-stone houses and winegrowing façades bear witness to 800 years of vine cultivation.

activities.text: Taste the Cotes de Duras at the Maison des Vins. Reds with aromas of blackcurrant and pepper, crisp dry whites or golden sweet wines: the winegrowers on hand introduce a terroir that is often overlooked and well worth the detour. Exports to the Netherlands took off from the revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685, carried by the Protestants driven out of the region.

Local operators offer visits to nearby wine cellars, with guided tastings and tours of the wineries. This is where the appellation reveals its different terroirs: Agenais molasse for the white wines and limestone-clay soils for the reds. Book ahead if you are visiting as a group or outside the high season.
The Monday morning market in the town of Duras is modest but authentic. Local producers, regional wines and a few craftspeople bring the aisles to life in a typically French village atmosphere.

days_plan.itin_title: Lot-et-Garonne Road Trip: Bastides and Villages

places.name: Ecouen

visits.text: The Château d'Écouen is one of the little-known jewels of the French Renaissance. Built starting in the 16th century for Anne de Montmorency, Constable of France and a close associate of Francis I, it has housed France's only museum entirely dedicated to the Renaissance since 1977. The collections come largely from the Musée de Cluny: gold and silver objects, Limoges painted enamels, Italian majolica (over 500 pieces), furniture and paintings from the 15th to 17th centuries. The centerpiece is the David and Bathsheba tapestry series—ten tapestries woven in Brussels around 1515–1520, believed to have belonged to Henry VIII of England, displayed across 75 meters in the Galerie de Psyché. The château is open Mon, Wed, Thu, Fri and weekends from 9:30 AM to 5:45 PM; closed Tuesdays, January 1 and December 25. Free for under-26s, and on the first Sunday of the month.

Don't leave without touring the château's park, 19 hectares with free access. From the southern terraces, the view over the Plaine de France is remarkable - on clear days, you can spot the Basilica of Saint-Denis. The French-style avenues and hunting vistas recall the atmosphere of great 16th-century seigneurial estates. The park opens at 8 AM, before the museum itself.

activities.text: Guided lecture tours of the château take place Saturdays and Sundays at 11 AM and 3:30 PM (duration 1 hour 30 minutes, surcharge on admission price). They provide access to rooms normally closed and tell the story of Anne de Montmorency—a figure who owned 130 châteaux at his death in 1567.

In late afternoon, climb to the viewpoint from the château steps on the southern side: the Plaine de France stretches endlessly toward Paris. The low-angle light in late afternoon is particularly beautiful in autumn.

days_plan.itin_title: Val-d'Oise Tour: Impressionist Villages and Heritage

map_keywords: Musée national de la Renaissance Château d'Écouen

places.name: Eguilles

visits.text: From the esplanade of Château d'Éguilles (17th century, now the town hall), the panorama is one of the most expansive in the Aix region: to the west the Étang de Berre — France's largest lagoon at 155 km² — and to the east Sainte-Victoire. The château, built by the last lord of Éguilles, Vincent de Boyer, after the Wars of Religion ruined the medieval fortress, is flanked by a clock by Paul Odobez that has been running for over 131 years.

Descend into the narrow streets to find the Jardin d'Éguilles, 950 m² of sculptures by designer Max Sauze — books, paper, metal, snails, and pebbles mingle with Mediterranean vegetation. This garden, labeled "Remarkable" since 2005, is freely accessible. Walking up Rue des Jasses, you'll find a former 17th-century vaulted oil mill converted into a Provençal café-bookshop — ideal for a break.

500 meters south of the village, on the Pierredon hillock, stands the Celto-Ligurian oppidum of Pierredon, classified as a historic monument. Occupied from the 6th century BC, this strategic site at the edge of the limestone plateau is one of the best-preserved in the region. Walk around the promontory's perimeter for unobstructed views over the Éguilles countryside.

activities.text: Heritage walk through the old center (cobblestone streets, passageways, fountains). Follow the former moat protecting the fortified château, now Rue Saint-Antoine, then climb the Four stairs to the château esplanade. The old wash house, oratories, and blonde stone facades from the 17th-18th centuries line the route. Allow 1 hour for a complete tour.

Garrigue paths toward the olive groves: agricultural tracks start from the lower village between cypress hedges and olive groves of the Coteaux d'Aix-en-Provence PDO. A tasting at the Éguilles cooperative cellar or at the Cellier d'Éguilles (PDO and Coteaux d'Aix certified) can pleasantly complete the walk.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpilles, Aix-en-Provence & Arles Circuit

map_keywords: Esplanade Éguilles vue étang de Berre

visits.text: Eguisheim is laid out in concentric circles around its central castle—a unique configuration in Alsace that makes it a truly enchanting maze. The octagonal castle at the center of place Saint-Léon dates to 720, when Count Eberhard of Alsace, nephew of Saint Odile, had his residence built here. Bruno of Eguisheim was born within these walls in 1002 and would become Pope Leo IX in 1049—one of the few French popes in history. The Saint-Léon fountain in the square honors him. In 2013, Eguisheim was voted France's Favorite Village—the village had already held the Plus Beaux Villages de France designation since 2003.

The Church of Saint Peter and Saint Paul combines a Romanesque transept and a Gothic nave on a 12th-century base built up over the centuries. Its square yellow sandstone tower is the village's most visible landmark from the vineyards. Inside, look for the 13th-century shrine Madonna—a statue of the Virgin whose belly opens to reveal a carved Trinity.

Follow rue du Rempart Sud, which traces the old medieval moat. The village's oldest house—dated 1479—stands on this street. Look at the carved lintels and inscriptions in old Alsatian dialect on the façade beams that record the names of winegrowing families.

At the edge of the village, the Parc des Cigognes has several active nests. The white stork, emblem of Alsace, had nearly disappeared from the region in the 1980s—a reintroduction program brought about its recovery. Here you can observe the storks up close on their nests perched above the enclosures.

activities.text: The Eichberg Grand Cru vineyard trail winds across south-facing limestone slopes. This grand cru has been renowned since Roman times for its Rieslings and Gewurztraminers. Explanatory panels in French and English mark the 3-kilometer circuit and present the seven Alsatian grape varieties as well as the winegrowers' work through the seasons. The panoramic view of Eguisheim and its ramparts from the top of the slope is worth the detour alone.

Step into a winegrower's cellar to taste the local grands crus. Eguisheim has about thirty independent winegrowers—cellars are generally open without an appointment during the week. The Grands Crus Eichberg and Pfersigberg are the village's jewels: guided tastings offer an opportunity to understand why this particular terroir produces age-worthy wines.

days_plan.itin_title: The 15 Most Beautiful Villages of Alsace
Haut-Rhin Road Trip: Colmar and the Southern Wine Route
Alsace's Most Beautiful Christmas Markets
Grand Est Road Trip: Vineyards, Ramparts and Forests
The Most Beautiful Villages of Alsace in 4 Days

visits.text: The Cathedral of Saint Eulalia and Saint Julia has dominated the town since the 11th century. A major monument of Catalan Romanesque art, it served as the bishopric seat from the 6th to 17th century. Blue marble portal and barrel-vaulted nave.

The white marble cloister veined with blue was built from the 12th to 14th century. Listed as a historical monument in 1840, it displays the evolution of medieval Roussillon sculpture between Romanesque and Gothic.
The Terrus Museum celebrates Étienne Terrus, a painter born in Elne in 1857. Friend of Matisse, Maillol, and Derain, he captured Roussillon landscapes in watercolor. Over 100 works on display.
The archaeology museum in the Saint-Laurent chapel presents artifacts from the Neolithic to the Middle Ages. Three 6th-century Visigothic marble sarcophagi adorn the east gallery.
The Swiss Maternity Hospital, built in 1901, sheltered children of all nationalities between 1939 and 1944. A historical monument bearing witness to solidarity and hope.

activities.text: Stroll from the Porte Balaguer. Panoramic views take in the surrounding mountains and Canigou, the Catalans' sacred peak.
Wander through the old town's maze. Glassblowers, art restorers, and galleries perpetuate the artistic tradition.
Visit the Jardin des Métiers d'Art. Catalan artists and local artisans open their workshops: ceramics, chocolate making, rousquilles.
Enjoy the market three times a week. Produce from vineyards and orchards recalls Elne's agricultural role.

days_plan.itin_title: Pyrénées-Orientales Road Trip: French Catalonia and the Côte Vermeille

visits.text: Notre-Dame-du-Réal Cathedral is the largest religious edifice in the French Alps, built between 1170 and 1225—a contemporary of Notre-Dame de Paris. Its Lombard porch, the Réal, rests on two stone lions and once sheltered a fresco said to be miraculous, a pilgrimage site where more than 200 miracles were recorded. Inside, a play of black schist and white limestone, a fifteenth-century rose window, and the grand organ gifted by Louis XI in 1464, among the oldest in France. Free access year-round.

The cathedral treasury, kept in the Sainte-Anne chapel, is one of France's richest: nearly 500 objects, liturgical vestments embroidered with gold and silver, reliquaries, ornaments from the fifteenth to nineteenth centuries. A remnant of an archiepiscopal city whose influence once reached from the Alps to the Mediterranean. Access is mainly through guided tours run by the heritage service, which opens the chapel for them. Allow an hour.

Wander Embrun's medieval core: cobbled lanes, colorful facades, and the Tour Brune, the former archiepiscopal keep that dominates the old town (check its opening status—it's had closures). Across from the cathedral, the Maison des Chanonges, one of the city's oldest buildings (thirteenth century), hosts exhibitions. Pause in the Jardin de l'Archevêché for the view over the Durance. Embrun enjoys a microclimate, nearly 300 days of sun a year.

activities.text: Embrun's lake, 27 hectares of water separated from Lake Serre-Ponçon by a dike with a promenade, is the town's number-one summer spot. Grassy Blue Flag beaches, supervised swimming in July and August, and three water-sports centers offering kayaking, rowing, sailing and windsurfing. It is also the swimming course for the famous EmbrunMan triathlon. A lit 2.6 km trail circles the lake, perfect at sunset. Two kilometers from the center, with a free shuttle in summer.

Embrun is an outdoor base camp: cycling and mountain-bike routes, easy walks around the Roc and the lake, tougher hikes on the heights at the gates of Écrins National Park. The shores of Serre-Ponçon, coves and beaches, are a few minutes' drive. Enough to fill half a day of activity depending on your fitness and the weather.

days_plan.itin_title: Hautes-Alpes Road Trip: High Mountains and Alpine Valleys

visits.text: Enghien-les-Bains is Île-de-France's only spa town—a town created from scratch in 1850, its entire existence revolving around its lake and sulfurous waters discovered in 1766 by Abbé Cotte. Stroll along the 350-meter wrought-iron promenade built in 1911, cantilevered over the lake with its century-old plane trees. From there, the view of the casino and Belle Époque hotels is the town's most spectacular. Louis XVIII had an ulcer on his leg treated here—the spring was renamed “Source du Roi” and the resort's reputation was made.

The Casino Barrière, France's top-grossing casino, occupies a building constructed in 1909 after its 1901 predecessor—shaped like a white sailboat launching onto the lake—literally took on water. The current façade, renovated in 2005 by architect Louis Soors with its immense glass atrium, faces directly onto the lake. Mistinguett, Coco Chanel, and Baron de Rothschild made appearances here during the Belle Époque. Admission is charged.

Then spend an hour exploring the Belle Époque villas scattered along the avenues around the lake. In 150 years, Enghien has accumulated every architectural style since the Restoration: neo-Gothic cottages, Art Nouveau villas with ceramic façades, neo-Renaissance manors with towers and gables. The tourist office offers a walking circuit from the station or lakeside—the best way to catch the finest examples tucked into side streets.

activities.text: Rent pedal boats or small boats on the lake in Enghien from spring through fall (available from the quays, from April to early November). In the morning, the lake is calm and the reflections are perfect. Allow about 45 minutes to go around it by pedal boat.
Show or evening at the Casino d'Enghien: theater, concerts, or simply the atmosphere of the grand hall. Check the program in advance and book - weekend evenings often sell out.

days_plan.itin_title: Val-d'Oise Tour: Impressionist Villages and Heritage

visits.text: Entraygues comes from the Occitan entraigas meaning between the waters. The Lot and the Truyère rivers meet here at an altitude of 219 metres. Two 13th-century Gothic bridges link the banks from the medieval castle.

The historic centre retains half-timbered houses from the 15th and 16th centuries. The cantous are small covered passageways running beneath the houses. Some façades still shelter craftsmen's workshops.

The Entraygues-Le Fel vineyard covers 20 hectares of terraces between schist and granite. Five winemakers carry on a winemaking tradition dating back to the Roman occupation. The AOC was granted in 2011, following the VDQS classification of 1965.

activities.text: The Espace EDF Truyère occupies the former control room of the Couesques dam power station. This 600 m² educational trail explains how hydroelectricity works and the industrial adventure built around water.

The Calvaire viewpoint offers a panorama of the confluence of the Lot and the Truyère. Head towards Aurillac, cross the Cambeyrac dam and stop after a hairpin bend. A 5-minute path leads to the viewpoint marked by a large cross.

days_plan.itin_title: Aveyron Road Trip: Causses, Tarn Gorges and Villages

visits.text: The Chateau d'Entrecasteaux is one of the fine surprises of the Var hinterland. Built on a rocky spur, it has stood 20 meters above the village since the 11th century, but it is above all its 16th- and 17th-century facade that strikes you, with its balanced proportions and its wrought-iron balustrades. Its history is full of scandal and adventure: in 1669 it passed to Francois Adhemar de Castellane, son-in-law of Madame de Sevigne. Le Notre himself is said to have given the marquise the plans of the Orangery garden at Versailles so that her son-in-law could reproduce them here. In 1784 the Marquis Jean-Baptiste de Bruny murdered his wife and fled abroad, ending his life in Portuguese jails. His brother, Admiral Bruny d'Entrecasteaux, born in the castle in 1737 and sent by Louis XVI in search of La Perouse, died of scurvy in 1793 during his expedition in the South Pacific.

The French formal garden, freely accessible year-round, is a gem often overlooked by guidebooks. Designed according to plans inspired by Versailles, it extends below the château's south façade in geometric terraces. Take time to sit and admire the perspective — it's particularly beautiful in late afternoon when golden light strikes the stone façades. Following the village lanes afterwards, you'll discover handsome medieval houses with tall, narrow façades, vaulted passages and Provençal fountains. The fortified church of Saint-Sauveur and the 18th-century Pont Saint-Pierre over the Bresque complete the visit.

activities.text: The Bresque flows through Entrecasteaux for several kilometers before joining Sillans — upstream and downstream from the village, paths following the river offer cool, shaded walks, ideal in summer. Natural swimming spots exist along the river depending on water levels.

days_plan.itin_title: The 10 Most Beautiful Villages of the Haut-Var
Var in 4 Days: From Bormes to the Most Beautiful Villages of the Verdon

visits.text: Cross the drawbridge over the Var — two towers flank the Porte Royale built in 1658 — and you'll enter one of the few medieval towns in Provence to have remained intact. Entrevaux has been a royal town since 1541 (Francis I granted it total tax exemption that year) and has held the Plus Beaux Villages de France designation since 2023. Wander the narrow lanes between tall houses, fountains and medieval shops: every stone tells the story of three centuries of life within the fortifications.

The Cathedral of Notre-Dame de l'Assomption is worth stepping inside: built between 1604 and 1667, it forms part of Vauban's fortifications via the Porte d'Italie. The exterior is austere, but the Provençal Baroque interior surprises — carved decoration, gilded altarpieces and a contemplative atmosphere. Don't leave without seeing the old dungeons right at the town's entrance.

Climb to the citadel — allow 30 minutes for the walk up the paved zigzag path that Vauban had built starting in 1693 (before him, soldiers climbed up a ladder!). The fortress itself dates from the 11th century and was reinforced between 1683 and 1702 on Louis XIV's orders: 150 metres above the village, the 360° panorama over the Var valley and surrounding ridges makes the effort worthwhile. During the First World War, the citadel served as a prison for German officers — graffiti from that period remain visible on the walls.

activities.text: The ideal way to arrive is aboard the Train des Pignes from Nice: the Chemins de Fer de Provence line (151 km, metre gauge) is a spectacle in itself, with its viaducts and tunnels. Entrevaux station, on the right bank of the Var opposite the ramparts, offers a striking first view of the town. Take time to pause on the platforms and photograph the fortifications from below.

From the opposite bank of the Var, a marked trail leads to the two old 18th-century mills (flour and oil) — one is still operating, which is rare in Provence, and both are open to the public. The path offers the best views of the fortified town from outside: allow 45 minutes for the round trip.

days_plan.itin_title: Forcalquier & Verdon Gorges Road Trip
Alpine Hinterland and Verdon Gorges: From Thorenc to Riez

visits.text: The Avenue de Champagne is a kilometre and a half of neoclassical, neo-Gothic and Art Deco façades belonging to the world's greatest champagne houses. Beneath your feet, 110 kilometres of galleries and 200 million bottles. UNESCO-listed in 2015 as part of the 'Champagne Hillsides, Houses and Cellars', it deserves a slow walk to take in the architectural details of each mansion. Start at the top of the avenue: the view over the Marne from the end of the park is magnificent.

The Moët & Chandon cellars are the largest in the whole of Champagne: 28 kilometres of galleries, dug between 10 and 30 metres below the limestone ground beneath the avenue. The house was founded in 1743 by Claude Moët, and it is in the main courtyard that the statue of Dom Pérignon greets visitors. Worth seeing in particular: the Réserve des Grands Millésimes, to which only the cellar master holds the key. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes with the tasting. Book well ahead in high season.

The Mercier cellars offer a different experience: you visit the 18 kilometres of underground galleries aboard a small electric train, 30 metres below ground. The house was founded in 1858 by Eugène Mercier, a marketing figure ahead of his time. Do not miss the giant cask he had built for the Paris World's Fair of 1889, a 200,000-litre barrel so large that it took 24 oxen and 18 days to haul it to Paris.

The 60-metre De Castellane tower has stood at the end of the avenue since 1905. Climb its 237 steps to take in at a single glance the Avenue de Champagne, the rooftops of Épernay and, on a clear day, the hillsides silhouetted on the horizon. The effort is rewarded.

activities.text: At Aÿ-Champagne, a few minutes from Épernay, don't miss Pressoria — an immersive exhibition space housed in Pommery's former press rooms. The tour engages all your senses to tell the story of champagne production, from soils to cellars, from the grape harvest to the final tasting. A very different format from traditional cellar visits, accessible and fun.

In late afternoon, head for the hillsides overlooking the Marne valley. Vines rise in tiers on the UNESCO-listed chalk slopes — here, between Épernay and Hautvillers, the Champagne landscape is at its most spectacular. Stop at the Champillon viewpoints for the view.

days_plan.itin_title: Marne Road Trip: Reims, Épernay and Champagne

visits.text: You'll find the Basilica of Saint Maurice right in the heart of the old town, and it's going to surprise you. Built between the 11th and 13th centuries, it blends Rhenish Romanesque, Champagne Gothic and Burgundian Gothic within a single structure—a rare combination in Lorraine. Look for the Portail des Bourgeois on the north side: its apses are offset at 45° from the church's main axis, a layout so unusual in Romanesque art that only a handful of equivalents exist in France. Inside, the nave rises to 14 meters and the Virgin and Child on the trumeau dates from the 13th century. The church only received its title of basilica in 1933—a thousand years of history for one ceremony.

If you think Épinal prints are old-fashioned, the Musée de l'Image will change your mind. Over 110,000 printed pieces from the 17th century to today—the largest collection of its kind in Europe—are preserved in this glass building facing the old Pellerin workshops. A tablet is provided at the entrance to help you find your way through the rooms. In summer, don't miss the Chemin des Images: an urban art trail through the streets of Épinal that connects the museum to the rest of the city's heritage—a good way to end the day on foot.

Prepare yourself for a rather unusual visit: at Chaumousey, 10 km southwest of Épinal, almost nothing remains of the abbey. Founded in 1090 by a priest named Séhère with the support of Lord Thierry and his wife Hadevide, it was sold as national property in 1796 and dismantled stone by stone to serve as a quarry. What remains—a section of wall, two statues embedded in house facades, an open burial vault—is still enough to gauge what was once one of the most powerful Augustinian abbeys in Lorraine. What makes the place endearing: this is where Saint Peter Fourier celebrated his first Mass on June 24, 1589, before becoming the great reformer of the canons regular of Lorraine. And the Baroque high altar from the abbey church, saved by parishioners during the Revolution, still stands in the church of Girancourt 5 km away—if you want to see it, make the detour.

activities.text: Head up to Parc du Château in late afternoon — the former medieval fortress of the bishops of Metz towers over the rooftops of Épinal and offers a direct view of the Basilica of Saint Maurice and the Moselle below. Then walk back down into the historic quarter and spot the few remaining sections of 13th-century ramparts still standing near the Tour du Chapitre. The raking evening light on the pink sandstone is particularly beautiful.

Head to Lake Bouzey at Sanchey, a few minutes from Chaumousey. This artificial body of water created to supply the Canal de l'Est has a dark history: on April 27, 1895, its dam suddenly gave way and the resulting flood killed about a hundred people in the valley. Panels along the banks tell the story of the disaster. The loop around the lake is about 5 km and can be walked without effort—ideal in late afternoon before returning to Épinal.

days_plan.itin_title: Vosges Abbey Trail: Monastic Heritage
Vosges Abbey Trail: Monastic Heritage
Vosges Road Trip: Lakes, Mountains & Thermal Spas

visits.text: The Jean-Jacques Rousseau Park extends over 62 hectares created between 1763 and 1775 by the Marquis de Girardin. It was inspired by Rousseau's Julie, or the New Heloise.

The Île des Peupliers holds the cenotaph of Jean-Jacques Rousseau, who died in 1778. Before his remains were transferred to the Panthéon in 1794, this tomb became a destination for Romantic pilgrimage from across Europe.
The Temple of Philosophy has unfinished columns dedicated to Newton, Descartes, Voltaire, Rousseau, Montesquieu and Penn. This rotunda symbolises the perpetual progress of thought.
The Royal Abbey of Chaalis preserves its 13th-century Cistercian ruins and 16th-century frescoes. The Jacquemart-André collections and Rousseau's autograph manuscripts enrich the visit.
The Forest of Ermenonville spreads across 3,300 hectares of Scots pines and jumbled sandstone boulders. The Pierre de la Sorcière and the Bruyères du Frais Vent emerge among the trees.

activities.text: Follow the Sentier des Écrivains for three kilometres between Rousseau Park and Chaalis Abbey. This trail crosses the Launette valley in the footsteps of Rousseau, Senancour and Nerval.

days_plan.itin_title: Oise Circuit: châteaux, forests and history

places.name: Espelette

visits.text: The Castle of the Barons d'Ezpeleta has dominated the village since the year 1000 — the Barons d'Ezpeleta came from a noble family of Navarre. In 1694, their last descendant, Baroness Juliana Henriquez, gave the castle to the villagers. Now the town hall, it also houses a permanent exhibition on Espelette pepper. Listed as a Historic Monument since 1993, it was renovated in 1998. The adjoining cemetery contains the Art Deco tomb of Agnès Souret, the first Miss France, elected in 1920.

Construction of the Church of Saint Stephen began in 1593. Its fortified keep-like bell tower and its interior galleries on three levels are typical of Labourdin churches. The Baroque gilded wood retable, the entirely painted 17th-century ceilings and a painting attributed to José de Ribera deserve a careful stop. It has been listed as a Historic Monument since 1925.

Wander through the lanes of Espelette to see the white facades with red shutters of the Basque Country — a colour known as euskal gorria. From late August to November, strings of scarlet peppers hang on the facades, drying in the sun before being ground into powder. Espelette pepper obtained AOC status in 2000 — it covers ten municipalities of the Labourd and rates 4 on the Scoville scale, less hot than cayenne pepper but far more aromatic.

activities.text: The village market sets up in the morning. Ossau-Iraty sheep's cheese, veal axoa, gâteau basque and pepper in every form — powdered, on strings, as jam, in chocolate — fill the stalls. On the last Sunday in October, the Pepper Festival turns the whole village into a giant market with concerts and cooking contests.

Hike the Mondarrain, which peaks at 749 metres. Part of the Natura 2000 network, this massif is home to semi-free-roaming pottoks, griffon vultures and protohistoric remains (a cromlech) visible on the summit rocks. From the top, the view takes in the Atlantic coast, the Pyrenees and the Basque villages stretching towards Spain. Allow about 3 hours for the loop.

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip Pyrenees-Atlantiques: Basque Country and Bearn

map_keywords: Castle of the Barons d'Ezpeleta Espelette town hall

visits.text: Built in the 13th century and then rebuilt in 1606, the château d'Esquelbecq stands at the corner of the Grand'Place with its eight round towers and broad moat. This village was voted the French people's favorite village in 2023, a distinction it fully deserves.

Modest from the outside, the Église Saint-Folquin hides origins dating back to the 10th century, rare for a Flemish hallekerke. Restored to its original state after the 1976 fire, it preserves an 18th-century meantone organ and 19th-century stained glass. It faces the château from the other side of the Grand'Place Alphonse Bergerot. Entry is free, though it's best to visit on a weekday for peace and quiet.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Villages from Flanders to the Bay of Somme

visits.text: Nestled among the vineyards of the Côte des Bar, Essoyes lives in remembrance of Pierre-Auguste Renoir. The Du Côté des Renoir Cultural Center—housed in the former stables of the château overlooking the Ource—begins the visit with a 20-minute film, a permanent exhibition on the family saga—Pierre the actor, Jean the filmmaker and Claude the ceramicist—and a temporary exhibition room. For thirty summers, from 1888 to 1919, the Impressionist master found incomparable light, willing models and a peaceful life here, far from the turmoil of Paris.

The family house acquired in 1896 reveals the private world of the Renoirs: period furniture, wallpapers recovered identical to the originals, everyday objects frozen as if the family had just stepped out. The garden walk leads to the 1906 studio, built at the far end of the property so as not to disturb the children at play. Beneath the exposed beams bathed in overhead light: easel, brushes, wheelchair (Renoir went on painting despite his deformed hands), traveling trunk for Paris. Listed as a Maison des Illustres, the house still breathes the painter's soul.

Throughout the village, large-format reproductions mark the places where Renoir set up his easel: the silver reflections of the Ource, the washhouse where the washerwomen posed, the church and the market square. This self-guided route allows visitors to see Essoyes through the master's eyes. Pierre-Auguste, Aline and the entire family are buried in the village cemetery, a simple and moving final testimony to this family of artists' deep attachment to this corner of Champagne.

activities.text: The two-hour guided tours organized by the Du Côté des Renoir association weave together the complete story: the Cultural Center, house, garden and studio. Passionate guides explain how Renoir discovered Essoyes through Aline Charigot, a native of the village, why he returned every summer and how the villagers became affordable models. Anecdotes, technical details and family secrets turn the visit into an immersive experience. Departures at 10:30 a.m. and 2:30 p.m. Reservation required.

The Accord Parfait initiative brings art and champagne together: nine Côte des Bar houses have paired nine cuvées with nine reproductions of works by Renoir. In the partner cellars, guided tastings explore blends of Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Pinot Meunier from the Champagne hillsides while visitors contemplate the master's paintings. A subtle marriage of bubbles, aromas and Impressionist art—an original sensory experience in the heart of the vineyards.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Est Road Trip: Vineyards, Ramparts and Forests
Aube Tour: Champagne, Medieval Heritage and the Lakes of the Forêt d'Orient

visits.text: Estaing Castle dates back to the 13th century with its octagonal keep surrounded by turrets. The d'Estaing family owned it for eight centuries before it was acquired by Valéry Giscard d'Estaing in 2005. The exhibition retraces the presidential term and the advances of his mandate.

François d'Estaing had the Gothic bridge built in the early 16th century. This UNESCO-listed structure is crossed each year by pilgrims heading to Santiago de Compostela. The wrought-iron cross in the middle is a symbol of Aveyron craftsmanship.

The 15th-century Church of Saint-Fleuret holds the relics of the Bishop of Clermont who died here in the 5th century. The saint is known for his miraculous healings. Grey-blue schist houses with lauze stone roofs line the narrow streets.

activities.text: The Maison de la Vigne, du Vin et des Paysages tells the story of the vineyard. The Vignerons d'Olt cultivate 20 hectares that earned the AOC Estaing designation in 2011. The wine was once shipped throughout Europe via the Lot river.

The Saint-Fleuret procession takes place on the first Sunday of July. Locals wear costumes representing saints, angels, and members of the d'Estaing family. This historical and religious re-enactment brings the whole village to life.

days_plan.itin_title: Aveyron Road Trip: Causses, Tarn Gorges and Villages

visits.text: The Church of Saint-Basile dates from the 12th century. Its imposing bell tower and stained glass windows make it a jewel of Gothic architecture in Étampes.
The Tour Guinette rises 27 meters above its plateau. This four-lobed 12th-century keep, built by Louis VII, served as Queen Ingeborg's prison from 1201 to 1213.
From the plateau of the Tour Guinette, enjoy the view of Étampes and its four Gothic churches. The valleys of the Juine, Louette and Chalouette stretch out below.
Discover the church of Notre-Dame du Fort in Étampes and take a look at its bell tower and façades. The visit offers an opportunity to explore the town's religious heritage.

The Saint-Blaise chapel decorated by Cocteau in Milly-la-Forêt can be visited on an excursion from Étampes; allow for a return trip during the day. Its frescoes of medicinal plants adorn the walls of this former leper hospital.

activities.text: The Dourdan Forest extends to the west. Formerly a royal forest, it served as a hunting ground for the kings of France. Marked hiking trails.
Follow the Orge Valley on the GR11 trail. Old washhouses and mills dot this pastoral route through meadows and woods.
The forest of Fontainebleau can be explored on an excursion from Étampes; allow for a return trip during the day. Its climbing rocks and hiking trails attract outdoor enthusiasts.

days_plan.itin_title: Essonne Tour: Castles and Valleys

visits.text: Locals call it little Camargue: the Villepey ponds, in the Argens delta, form one of the few coastal wetlands between the Camargue and the Italian border. About 260 hectares, owned by the Conservatoire du littoral following acquisitions in 1982 and 1997, and designated under the Ramsar Convention in 2008. Flamingos, herons and egrets depending on the season.

More than 220 bird species have been recorded at the Villepey ponds, including notable breeding species such as the little bittern. The European pond turtle also hides here, keeping a lower profile. The Vasière bird hide lets you watch without disturbing the wildlife. March and early September, during migration: that's when it's worth the trip.

activities.text: Park at the Esclamandes beach parking lot and follow the Villepey ponds trail: 7.8 km, 14 meters of elevation gain, two hours and fifteen minutes. Wooden walkways, reed beds and a dune belt. Some bridges remain inaccessible after flooding, and one section closes from June 15 to September 15: plan an out-and-back walk rather than a loop.

Sea daffodils grow in the sand of the dune belt at the Villepey ponds, alongside sea holly and prickly parsnip. A one-kilometer loop on the Esclamandes side is enough to see them. These plants are protected: look, don't pick them, and stay on the marked trail.

days_plan.itin_title: Roquebrune-sur-Argens: sea, villages and the Var in 10 days

visits.text: Saint-Pierre Abbey at Étival is the oldest in the Pays des Abbayes—its first monastery dates back to the 7th century. Pass through the 18th-century classical facade (built in 1726 by architect Nicolas Pierson) and prepare for a surprise: behind it lies a Romanesque abbey church from around 1200, with its Romanesque capitals, its Gothic choir remodeled between 1510 and 1516, and its 18th-century choir stalls. It was the Premonstratensian monks who settled here in 1147 who founded the first Vosges paper mill in 1512—the direct ancestor of the Clairefontaine paper mills whose notebooks you used in school. The abbey is fortified and you can still see it in its thick walls. Free self-guided visits every day from 9 am to 6 pm; guided tours on Wednesdays in July–August at 10:30 am and on the first Saturday of each month, with advance registration at the Tourist Office.

activities.text: Climb to the Pierre d'Appel, a rock at 492 meters that overlooks the valleys of the Meurthe, Rabodeau, Hure and Valdange. Excavations have revealed a Celtic presence in prehistoric times—the Gauls already used it as a lookout and warning post. On clear days, you'll see the rounded Vosges summits on the horizon. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes round trip from the village, on a marked trail.

days_plan.itin_title: Vosges Abbey Trail: Monastic Heritage

places.name: Etretat

visits.text: Yport nestles in the hollow of a valleuse. A few capstans and brightly colored boats recall its past as a fishing port, when sailors set out for the Grand Banks of Newfoundland.
Saint-Martin Church in Yport was built by the villagers themselves in brick and flint. Its inverted ship's hull ceiling and maritime ex-votos are worth the detour.

The Porte d'Aval at Étretat forms an immense arch carved by waves into white chalk. At its feet, the Needle rises 55 meters above the sea—Maurice Leblanc imagined it hollow in the adventures of Arsène Lupin.
Climb the Amont cliff by the 263-step staircase. The Notre-Dame-de-la-Garde chapel, rebuilt after World War II, offers a complete panorama of the Needle, Porte d'Aval, and Manneporte.
The Gardens of Étretat, perched on the Amont cliff, blend topiary and contemporary art. Each themed garden frames a different view of the cliffs.
The Clos Arsène Lupin, Maurice Leblanc's former villa, offers an immersive visit into the gentleman burglar's universe. Puzzles and secret passages punctuate the tour.
The Halles d'Étretat, rebuilt in 1926 with old timbers, host Thursday morning's market. Seafood, farmhouse cider, and Norman terrines.

activities.text: Hike the cliff path between the Porte d'Aval and Manneporte. The GR21 follows the summit of chalk cliffs with plunging views over the sea.
Sea kayaking or paddleboarding along the cliffs. Unique view of the arches from water level, with access to beaches unreachable on foot at high tide.
Sunset from the Amont cliff: the low-angle light sets the white chalk and Needle ablaze. Monet painted about 90 canvases of the cliffs under different lights.

days_plan.itin_title: Complete Normandy Road Trip: Cliffs, D-Day Beaches and Mont-Saint-Michel
The 20 Most Beautiful Villages in Normandy
Seine-Maritime Road Trip: The Cliffs of Étretat, Rouen & Jumièges Abbey

map_keywords: Notre-Dame de la Garde Chapel Étretat

visits.text: Château d'Eu — King Louis-Philippe's favorite residence, where he received Queen Victoria in 1843 and 1845, this sixteenth-century castle transformed into a Romantic palace houses the Louis-Philippe museum. Its collections trace the history of the July Monarchy and royal visits.

Notre-Dame-et-Saint-Laurent Collegiate Church in Eu — Founded in 1186 by Henry II Plantagenet to atone for the murder of Thomas Becket, this Gothic collegiate church houses the effigies of the Counts of Eu and an eleventh-century Romanesque crypt. The Duke of Guise married Catherine of Clèves here in 1570.

activities.text: Eu Forest — This state-owned forest of 9,300 hectares, one of Normandy's largest, offers hiking trails through a centuries-old beech and oak woodland. The rides laid out for royal hunts converge at star-shaped junctions.

Jesuit College Chapel — Built in the seventeenth century for Jesuits settled by Catherine of Clèves, this Baroque chapel houses the tombs of the Dukes of Guise and a remarkable timber roof shaped like a ship's keel.

days_plan.itin_title: Seine-Maritime Road Trip: The Cliffs of Étretat, Rouen & Jumièges Abbey

visits.text: Évaux-les-Bains, Limousin's only thermal spa town, traces its history back to antiquity. Around 50 BC, Caesar's legions were already using the hot springs of Ivaonum, a name derived from Ivaos, the Gallic deity of water. The remains of the Gallo-Roman baths, listed as historic monuments as early as 1840, testify to this ancient occupation. The ancient spring collection system is still in use.

The Abbey Church of Saint-Pierre-et-Saint-Paul, a masterpiece of Romanesque art, was built in the 11th century over the relics of Saint Marien, the hermit who protected the town. Its five-story entrance bell tower, clad in chestnut shingles, dominates the town. The interior is surprising in its grandeur and simplicity. Partially destroyed by a fire in 1942, it remains the pride of the people of Évaux-les-Bains.

The modern thermal spa, completely renovated in 2001, occupies an Art Deco building with red and white bricks arranged in geometric patterns. The waters emerge at 60°C and are used to treat rheumatism and venous conditions. The recently opened “Les Bains d'Evahona” spa offers a hammam, sauna, Jacuzzi, and outdoor thermal pool, the gentlest in France.

activities.text: The 6-kilometer Rochers de Bord circuit starts at the tourist office and passes through a remarkable natural site. Allow two hours to discover the rock formations and enjoy an unobstructed view of the Tardes Viaduct, a metal structure built between 1882 and 1885 under the direction of Gustave Eiffel.

The spa park, a green haven in the heart of town, invites a stroll. The century-old trees of the former convent and shaded paths offer a restful setting between treatments or after a visit. The Grand Hôtel, a building typical of spa towns, overlooks the park.

days_plan.itin_title: Creuse Tour: Valley of the Painters and Aubusson Tapestries

visits.text: Explore this spectacular natural cirque in the Sixt-Fer-à-Cheval nature reserve, about 43 km from the stopover town, 1 hour by car. The cirque forms an amphitheatre 4 to 5 kilometres across with walls 500 to 700 metres high. More than thirty waterfalls pour from its cliffs, at their most impressive in spring when the snow melts.

Visit the legendary spring discovered in 1789 that made Évian famous worldwide. The magnificent Buvette Cachat, an Art Nouveau masterpiece built in 1905, is covered by a dome of glazed tiles. The water flows continuously at a constant temperature of 11.6°C.

Admire this sumptuous building constructed in 1902 to serve as a thermal establishment. A former spa turned cultural center since 2007, it impresses with its Belle Époque architecture and its immense glass dome more than 30 meters high.

Discover the former summer residence of the Lumière family, inventors of cinema, which became Évian's Town Hall in 1927. Rich in woodwork, bronzes, and marquetry, the building can be visited freely during office opening hours.

activities.text: Follow the family trail that runs up the valley floor from the car park to the Bout du Monde, about 43 km from the stopover town, 1 hour by car. This almost entirely flat walk crosses a magnificent landscape with views of the sheer walls and the many waterfalls.
Stroll along Évian's flower-lined quays, which follow Lake Geneva for nearly 3 kilometers. Flowering gardens, fountains, and a bandstand punctuate the route. The sunsets are particularly magical.

Ride the historic funicular free of charge, in service since 1907. This gem of railway heritage links the town center to the heights over 750 meters. At the upper station, you can visit the historic engine room.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Savoie Road Trip: Alpine Lakes & Mont Blanc
Grand Tour Ain & Savoie Mont-Blanc: Lakes, Mountains and Heritage

visits.text: The Gorges de Spelunca connect Évisa to the village of Ota via a 5 km mule track carved into the gorges of the Porto and Tavulella rivers. The descent winds between orange granite walls and crystal-clear pools. Along the way you'll pass the Zaglia bridge—a 15th-century Genoese arch listed as a historic monument, built of pink granite over the river. It's one of Corsica's most beautiful low-mountain trails; count on 2.5 hours for the descent. Bring water and a swimsuit.

If you still have energy after the gorges, climb up into the Aïtone forest above Évisa: century-old laricio pines 40 to 50 meters tall, filtering the light into a green and gold checkerboard. A marked trail follows the waterfalls and natural pools of the torrent—the water is icy even in mid-August. It's the most popular swimming spot in the region, so avoid Sunday morning.

activities.text: Swimming in the natural pools of the Gorges de Spelunca: midway along the trail between Ota and Évisa, several basins carved in granite allow you to plunge into transparent water. It's a popular family picnic spot on weekends—come during the week or arrive early in the morning for peace and quiet.

Hike in the Aïtone forest from the village of Évisa: the trail gradually climbs under the pines to viewpoints over the Gulf of Porto. The forest is cool even in midsummer—ideal if you're looking for an alternative to the coastal heat. Count on 2.5 hours for a complete loop.

days_plan.itin_title: Complete Tour of Corsica

places.name: Evreux

visits.text: Notre-Dame Cathedral of Évreux. A jewel of Gothic art, this vast sanctuary brings together every style from the 11th to the 16th century. Its 70 stained glass windows constitute a masterpiece of the art of glass, including the famous 'Évreux Yellow', a silver-salt color invented in the 14th century whose golden brilliance has never been equaled. The flamboyant north portal by Jehan Cossart and the lantern tower with its 'silver steeple' complete this treasure. The contemporary organ by Pascal Quoirin sports a futuristic case designed by Bruno Decaris.

Évreux Belfry (Clock Tower). The sole vestige of medieval fortifications, this 44-meter flamboyant Gothic belfry built between 1490 and 1497 houses the 'Louyse' bell cast in 1406. Unique in Normandy, it symbolizes the communal freedoms of the Middle Ages and offers a panorama over the city.

Saint-Taurin Abbey Church. Founded in the 10th century by Richard the Fearless, this former Benedictine abbey preserves a priceless treasure: the shrine of Saint Taurin, a masterpiece of 13th-century medieval goldsmithing, considered one of France's most precious.

Museum of Art, History, and Archaeology. Housed in the former 15th-century episcopal palace flanking the cathedral, this museum traces Évreux's history from Gallo-Roman times (when it was called Mediolanum Aulercorum) to modern Reconstruction.

Iton riverbank promenade. This developed path along the river crosses Évreux's historic heart. Old washhouses, rampart remains, stone bridges, and a reflecting pool offer a romantic perspective on the cathedral and episcopal palace.

activities.text: Gisacum Archaeological Site. A few kilometers from Évreux, this Gallo-Roman site reveals the vestiges of an exceptional 2,000-year-old city. The interpretation center offers guided tours, children's workshops, and themed events.

Évreux–Le Bec-Hellouin Greenway. This 42 km pastoral route follows an old railway line through woods, bocage, and villages. Accessible on foot, by bike, or on rollerblades, it passes near Château du Champ de Bataille.

days_plan.itin_title: Eure Road Trip: From Giverny to Normandy's Most Beautiful Villages

map_keywords: Museum of Art History and Archaeology Évreux

visits.text: The Basilica of Notre-Dame de l'Épine in Évron is Mayenne's most significant medieval religious building. According to legend, a 7th-century pilgrim returning from Jerusalem deposited a relic of the Virgin's milk in a hawthorn bush; its miraculous overnight flowering led Saint Hadouin to found a monastery here in 642.

The architecture offers a complete panorama of medieval religious art: a 10th-century crypt, an 11th-century Romanesque nave, a 12th-century fortified tower-porch, and a 13th-century Gothic choir with soaring proportions. Listed as a Historic Monument since 1840.

Don't miss the 12th-century Saint-Crepin chapel, an Arabo-Byzantine jewel inspired by Spanish Moorish architecture, decor found nowhere else in western France. Also admire the mural paintings, stained glass and ornate reliquary containing the Virgin's milk.

The basilica's history is turbulent: destroyed by Bretons and Vikings in the 9th century, rebuilt in the 10th, pillaged during the Wars of Religion in 1562. A Festival of Sacred Arts brings the naves to life each summer in July.

activities.text: Go hiking in the Charnie forest, south-east of Évron, about 15 km from the overnight town, 15 minutes by road. This woodland is one of the largest in the Mayenne and offers many waymarked paths through oak and beech groves.
The Coëvrons territory around Évron offers over 500 km of marked trails for hiking, mountain biking or horseback riding through hedgerow countryside and green hills.

days_plan.itin_title: Mayenne Circuit: Hedgerows and Medieval Towns

places.name: Evry Courcouronnes

visits.text: The only cathedral built in France during the 20th century. Its 38-meter brick cylinder crowns 24 silver lime trees symbolizing the hours of the day and resurrection.
Discover the 12 stained-glass windows in different colors, the work of the priest Kim en Joong. Each evokes one of the twelve apostles.
The white Carrara marble altar stands at the center of the choir beneath a modern stained glass window depicting a tree. The cylindrical baptistery allows for baptism by immersion.
Place des Droits de l'Homme brings together three modern brick buildings: cathedral, town hall, and chamber of commerce. Pools and water jets enliven the esplanade.

activities.text: Explore the parc des Coquibus on foot in Évry-Courcouronnes. Its paths run through a wooded area near the town center, and the playgrounds give children somewhere to stop during the walk.
The Évry 2 shopping center and the Agora border the cathedral district. Perfect for a shopping break in this new town.

days_plan.itin_title: Essonne Tour: Castles and Valleys

map_keywords: Place des Droits de l'Homme Évry

visits.text: Climb to the summit of old Eygalières village through cobbled streets lined with limestone houses — no pastel tones here, only the raw rock of the Alpilles. At the top, the Clock Tower built in 1672 with stones from the château symbolizes the village's independence. Its story: in 1660, the villagers paid the ransom of their lord, the Duke of Guise, taken hostage by the Spanish. In exchange, the duke ceded them the seigneurial rights. The tower, erected 12 years later, celebrates this emancipation.

Of the medieval keep (13th century), only the vaulted ground floor and the base of a tower remain, topped with a statue of the Virgin placed in 1893 to commemorate an apparition reported by a young village girl. Beside it, the Pénitents Chapel from 1581 served as a charnel house during the great plague of 1720. It now houses the Maurice Pezet Local History Museum.

1.4 km east of the village, the Saint-Sixte chapel, perched on a knoll and framed by cypresses, is one of the most photographed images of Provence. Its sober Romanesque style, built in 1581, contrasts with the surrounding olive fields. The climb is easy and the view from its forecourt over the Alpilles ridges is splendid. A pilgrimage is still held here on Easter Tuesday, a centuries-old tradition.

activities.text: Provençal market on Friday morning: one of the best markets in the Alpilles, heavily frequented by residents of surrounding farmhouses. PDO Vallée des Baux olive oils, IGP Alpilles wines, goat cheeses, and broken olives flavored with wild fennel. Arrive before 9 AM to enjoy the local atmosphere before passing visitors.

Loop around the Calanquet from Eygalières: marked route of about 10 km that descends into the olive plain along the ridges. The trail captures the geological structure of the Alpilles — a compressed limestone massif whose arid crests emerge abruptly from fertile plains. Allow 3 to 3h30.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpilles, Aix-en-Provence & Arles Circuit

visits.text: Eyguières takes its name from the abundance of its springs — "aiguières" in Provençal — and several fountains punctuate its streets and squares as testimony. The village sits at the foot of the Alpilles massif, within which its entire territory lies in the Regional Natural Park. Its medieval feudal gate, its cobblestone Rue Calade with ancient paving, and the remains of the château of the de Sade family (11th century) deserve a leisurely hour-long stroll.

2 km north of the village, the Castellas de Roquemartine is a medieval fortress from the 12th-13th centuries that belonged to the d'Albe family of Tarascon — the same who controlled the strategic passage between the Durance and the south of the Alpilles massif. The architectural ensemble includes a double curtain of ramparts and a church dedicated to Saint-Sauveur. The ruins are accessible on foot and offer a commanding view over the plain.

For geology enthusiasts, don't miss the Tour des Opies, the Alpilles' highest point at 498 meters, visible from the village. It was a medieval watchtower that allowed surveillance of movements across the entire plain. From this summit, the panorama covers the Maures, Sainte-Victoire, Mont Ventoux, and, on clear days, the Mediterranean.

activities.text: Hike to Tour des Opies (498 m): from the village, a marked trail climbs to the Alpilles' highest point in about 2h30 round trip. The panorama over the entire limestone massif, the Crau plains, and distant Camargue is well worth the effort. Hiking shoes and water essential.

Eyguières market on Tuesday morning, Place Monier. Small village market very pleasant for stocking up on Provençal products — PDO Alpilles olive oil, seasonal fruits, local crafts. The atmosphere is more local than touristy, which is rare in the region.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpilles, Aix-en-Provence & Arles Circuit

visits.text: Eyragues is a village of traditional Provence with quiet charm — its ochre-rendered houses and plane-tree-shaded squares welcome you to an atmosphere of deep Provence, far from tourist flows in the neighboring Alpilles. Wander the center's streets, spot the sculpted doorways of bourgeois houses and stone fountains. This is where Frédéric Mistral situated certain characters from his Provençal works.

A few minutes from the center, a 4.5-hectare bamboo forest opens its doors: a signposted path through a collection of varied bamboos forms a surprising plant tunnel, complemented by a wide diversity of trees and flowering shrubs blooming year-round. An unusual detour in this agricultural plain landscape.

activities.text: Cycling loop toward Maillane (quiet roads, flat terrain): the D5 and secondary roads linking Eyragues to Maillane cross a peaceful agricultural plain — orchards, wheat and corn fields, cypress hedges. Allow 30 minutes by bike one way to reach Mistral's native village.

Photo tour of Eyragues doorways and small squares: the old center's houses often have carved door frames and dated lintels from the 17th-18th centuries. A walking tour will reveal architectural details that few visitors notice — sculpted heads, acroteria, worn coats of arms.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpilles, Aix-en-Provence & Arles Circuit

visits.text: Èze clings to a rocky peak at an altitude of 429 meters, on the Moyenne Corniche between Nice and Monaco. The village is 100% pedestrian and 100% vertiginous—medieval cobbled streets, artisan shops, views that suddenly open onto a 400-meter drop toward the sea. Visit before 10 AM or late in the day to avoid buses carrying cruise passengers. Park at the Moyenne Corniche parking lot; access to the village is a steep climb.

The Jardin Exotique d'Èze crowns the ruins of the medieval castle razed by Louis XIV in 1706. Created in 1949 by mayor André Gianton, it gathers cacti, agaves, aloes and euphorbias clinging to the rocks, punctuated since the 2000s by Jean-Philippe Richard's terracotta female sculptures. The summit belvedere overlooks the Mediterranean at 429 m—on clear days, Corsica is visible at 170 km. Best in the morning.

Notre-Dame de l'Assomption Church, rebuilt in the 18th century in restrained Baroque style, marks the village center. An unpretentious ochre facade, a cool interior that contrasts with the heat of the streets. A quick 10-minute stop, but welcome in high summer. A short walk away, the 14th-century Chapelle des Pénitents Blancs houses painted panels from the Nice school.

The Fragonard and Galimard perfumeries, located at the village entrance, offer free guided tours of their laboratories: copper stills, a maceration demonstration, bottling. The tours are short, pleasant and informative—Galimard began operating in 1747, making it the oldest perfume house in Grasse still in business. The shop is of course part of the tour, but there is no obligation to buy.

activities.text: The Friedrich Nietzsche path connects Èze-Village to Èze-sur-Mer via the southern slope of the peak, with 400 meters of elevation change over 2.4 km. The philosopher took it during his stays in the region in 1883—it is said that he conceived part of “Thus Spoke Zarathustra” on these slopes, beneath the olive trees and pines. Descent: 1 hour. Ascent: 75 minutes minimum, strenuous. Closed-toe shoes are essential; the terrain is rocky and slippery. Return train from Èze-sur-Mer to Nice.

Perfume creation workshop at Fragonard or Galimard in Èze: guided by a “nose,” you learn about fragrance families and blend your own bottle of perfume from 127 essences. 1 to 1.5 hours, around €60. Booking essential in high season.

Summit belvedere of the exotic garden: the 360° view covers the sea, the Alpes-Maritimes and the coastal arc from Nice to Bordighera (Italy). Photographers: the light is better in late afternoon when the sun grazes the facades from the west.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpes-Maritimes Road Trip: Riviera and Mercantour, 13 days
The 15 Gems of the French Riviera and Backcountry
7-Day French Riviera Circuit: Villefranche to Antibes

places.name: Falaise

visits.text: Falaise Castle, birthplace of William the Conqueror, who was born in 1027, towers above the town with its three imposing keeps. The medieval fortress majestically combines Caen stone and Norman architecture. The virtual tour recreating the castle in the time of the dukes offers spectacular immersion in the 11th century.
Explore the historic centre of Falaise and its medieval remains. The ramparts, Saint-Gervais Church and half-timbered houses recount the history of this strategic ducal city.

activities.text: Visit the Mémorial des civils dans la guerre, unique in France. It tells the story of civilians' daily lives during the Occupation and the Liberation.
Discover the Automates Avenue museum, home to an astonishing collection of Belle Époque automata and antique toys. The magic of these mechanisms delights visitors of all ages.

days_plan.itin_title: Calvados Tour: D-Day Beaches and Normandy

map_keywords: Memorial of Civilians in War Falaise

visits.text: Abbey Church of the Holy Trinity — 127 meters long, this Benedictine abbey founded in 658 houses the Precious Blood, a relic brought back from the Holy Land. Its Gothic lantern tower has overlooked the town since the thirteenth century.

Bénédictine Palace — A neo-Gothic and neo-Renaissance masterpiece built between 1882 and 1900 by architect Camille Albert, this "Versailles of industry" houses the Bénédictine liqueur distillery. The 27 plants in the secret recipe created in 1510 by monk Dom Bernardo Vincelli are revealed in the spice room.

Cap Fagnet — The highest point of the Alabaster Coast at 110 meters, this promontory offers a panorama over Fécamp, the cliffs, and the Channel. Remains of the Atlantic Wall and a sailors' chapel recall the site's turbulent history.

activities.text: Fisheries Museum — Housed in a former cod-drying warehouse, this museum traces the epic of Fécamp's Newfoundland fishermen who sailed to the Grand Banks from the sixteenth to twentieth centuries. Collections of scale models, tools, and testimonies of this maritime adventure.

Fécamp Port — This natural harbor wedged between two cliffs was France's leading cod-fishing port until the 1970s. Today, trawlers and pleasure boats share the quays with construction sites for the offshore wind farm visible on the horizon.

Fécamp Cliffs — The coastal trail allows you to walk along the chalk cliffs framing the town. Head north toward Senneville or south toward Yport: spectacular hikes on the GR21 with views over the Channel and layers of flint.

days_plan.itin_title: Seine-Maritime Road Trip: The Cliffs of Étretat, Rouen & Jumièges Abbey

visits.text: Felletin has shared Aubusson's tapestry tradition since the 15th century. This small working-class town has retained a few workshops where tapestry weavers carry on age-old techniques. The Moutier Church, in the Romanesque style, is worth a visit for its carved capitals. The Creuse River runs through the town, offering charming views of the old weavers' houses.

On the banks of the Creuse, Felletin's former diamond-cutting cooperative bears witness to a little-known industrial past: for nearly a century, diamonds were cut here, a few steps from the tapestry workshops. The restored building is open to visitors and tells the story of the craft practiced by Felletin's diamond cutters.

activities.text: The tapestry workshops of Felletin sometimes open their doors to visitors. Watching a tapestry weaver work at a low-warp loom, choose threads from thousands of shades, and interpret an artist's cartoon reveals why this expertise is inscribed on UNESCO's intangible heritage list. Information about available visits can be obtained at the tourist office.

The Millevaches plateau, with Felletin as one of its gateways, offers landscapes of moorland, peat bogs, and forests. Hiking trails let visitors explore this “water tower” of France, where several rivers have their source. The altitude (up to 1000 meters) guarantees cool temperatures and clean air.

days_plan.itin_title: Creuse Tour: Valley of the Painters and Aubusson Tapestries

visits.text: The medieval ruins of the Château de Fère-en-Tardenois rise on a wooded hill. Built from 1206 onwards, it was extensively remodelled during the Renaissance, notably with the addition of its famous gallery bridge. The medieval towers and curtain walls emerge from the vegetation in a romantic atmosphere.

Sainte-Macre Church was rebuilt in the 16th century using remains from an earlier building. Its still-Gothic architecture foreshadows the Renaissance. Badly damaged in 1918, it was restored during the 1920s and notably preserves stained-glass windows by Maurice Denis.
The Villemoyenne Chapel stands in a hamlet of Fère-en-Tardenois. This historic building, listed as a Monument historique, is a discreet example of the area’s religious heritage.
The picturesque village retains its rural charm with old houses and quiet lanes. The green surroundings invite leisurely exploration.

activities.text: Fère Forest offers hiking trails around the village. The forest paths run alongside streams and clearings through unspoilt woodland. Several marked loops provide walks lasting from 2 to 4 hours.
Surrounding ponds welcome anglers in a peaceful setting. Predatory fish and non-predatory freshwater fish populate these managed waters. Fishing permit required.
Country roads connect the villages of Tardenois through rolling landscapes and cereal farmland. The rural heritage is best explored at the leisurely pace of a bicycle.

days_plan.itin_title: Aisne Itinerary: Gothic Cathedrals and the Picardy Countryside

places.name: Ferrette

visits.text: Ferrette is one of southern Alsace's best-kept secrets. Nestled in a small water gap in the Alsatian Jura, this former capital of the Counts of Ferrette is dominated by the ruins of its castle, built in 1105 by Frederick of Montbéliard, first Count of Ferrette. For two centuries, seven counts ruled over a territory that was nearly a sovereign state—the county passed to the Habsburgs in 1324 through the marriage of Joan of Ferrette to Albert II of Austria. Today, Prince Albert II of Monaco still bears the title of Count of Ferrette, through a chain of inheritances passing through Mazarin and the Grimaldi family. The ruins are freely accessible year-round—allow 10 minutes for the climb and 45 to 60 minutes for the entire site.

The upper castle, the oldest, preserves a residential tower carved directly into the limestone on several levels — one of the first of its type in Alsace. From the summit platform at 612 meters altitude, the panorama is exceptional: the rolling hills of Sundgau, the Alsace plain, the Vosges to the north and, on clear days, the Swiss Alps to the south. The lower castle, built from a 12th-century keep, was remodeled in 1488 and has several round towers still standing.

In the lower town, the 1572 town hall is an elegant example of Rhenish Renaissance architecture with triple-light windows—its small belfry houses a 1592 bell cast in Basel that still rings the curfew at 10 p.m. The two coats of arms on the facade tell the story: on the left, the House of Austria; on the right, the two fish of the Counts of Ferrette. The Church of Saint Bernard of Menthon, listed as a Monument Historique since 1902, completes the historic center's heritage.

activities.text: Head out on the trail leading to the Cave of the Dwarves—a legend widespread throughout Sundgau tells of dwarves with webbed feet who inhabited these limestone gorges and helped residents with their chores, until the day the villagers mocked their feet and drove them away forever. The hike to the cave takes 40 minutes from the village. The complete 6 km loop, passing by the castle, cave, and viewpoints over the Jura, is the best route for discovering the site.

If you have the energy, climb to the Rossberg tower—a lookout a few kilometers from Ferrette offering a 360° view of the three countries: the Alsace plain, the Swiss Jura, and the German Black Forest.
