The Sundgau's culinary specialty is fried carp—several regional inns serve it year-round in a slightly vinegary sauce.

days_plan.itin_title: The 15 Most Beautiful Villages of Alsace

map_keywords: Château de Ferrette ruines piton rocheux
Hôtel de Ville Ferrette Renaissance rhénane

places.name: Figeac

visits.text: The Champollion Museum—Writings of the World occupies the birthplace of the man who deciphered hieroglyphics. Its contemporary facade is inlaid with a thousand writing symbols in copper and glass. Inside, 5,300 years of writing history unfolds: Sumerian cuneiform, Egyptian hieroglyphics, Chinese ideograms, Mayan glyphs. The oldest piece, a Sumerian pictographic tablet, dates back to 3200 BCE.

Just beside the museum, Place des Écritures features a giant reproduction of the Rosetta Stone cast in black granite by American artist Joseph Kosuth in 1991. In the adjacent courtyard, the French translation is engraved on a glass plate suspended above a map of the Nile Delta.

On Place Champollion, the Maison du Griffon dates from the mid-12th century—the town's oldest dwelling. All around, half-timbered medieval houses and typical Quercy soleilhos compose an intact historic setting. The 14th-century former hospice completes the ensemble.
The Hôtel du Viguier du Roy, a 14th-century palace, served as the royal representative's residence. Its interior courtyard, cloister, formal French gardens, and royal tower are open to visitors.
The Church of Saint-Sauveur grew from a 9th-century Benedictine abbey. Romanesque and Gothic styles blend through successive renovations. The carved capitals and austere atmosphere merit a stop.

Wander Figeac's historic center, designated a Town of Art and History. Merchants' houses from the 12th–15th centuries with ogival arcades, open soleilhos beneath the roofs, Renaissance mansions, and 18th-century bourgeois facades form a remarkably preserved ensemble.

activities.text: Follow the Clés de Figeac circuit, a marked route through the old town. An illustrated booklet guides you from one monument to the next in a coherent loop.
Figeac's market fills Place Carnot every Saturday morning beneath the 19th-century metal hall. Find cabécous, Rocamadour cheeses, walnuts, Quercy saffron, and fouace—a local orange-blossom brioche.

days_plan.itin_title: Lot Itinerary: Cahors, Rocamadour & the Lot Valley
The Most Beautiful Villages of Lot and Périgord in 6 Days

map_keywords: Hôtel du Viguier du Roy Figeac

visits.text: Le Corbusier Site, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List. Le Corbusier's largest architectural ensemble in Europe brings together five buildings in the Firminy-Vert district. The Maison de la Culture, the only building constructed during the architect's lifetime, between 1961 and 1965, has a façade tilted at 53 degrees, punctuated by undulating panels designed by the composer Xenakis. The curved roof rests on unstressed cables. An auditorium, performance halls and visual arts rooms occupy the building's 5,000 square meters.

Saint-Pierre Church. Built between 1973 and 2006, this church shaped like a truncated cone rises to 33 meters. In the nave, an 11-second echo creates surprising acoustics. The constellation of Orion pierced through the east façade fills the interior with golden rays in the morning sun. The lower level, originally intended for parish activities, hosts exhibitions on Le Corbusier's work, with original maquettes and sculptures.

Unité d'Habitation. The fifth unit built worldwide, completed in 1967 by André Wogenscky after Le Corbusier's death. The building is 130 meters long and 56 meters high, resting on imposing pilotis. Its 414 apartments, from 25 to 113 square meters, house around 600 residents nicknamed “les Corbus”. Seven multicolored interior streets serve the dwellings. The Modulor system, a scale based on a man 1.83 meters tall, guided the proportions. Guided tours only.

Firminy stadium and swimming pool. The stadium, completed in 1968, is the only one in France classified as a historic monument. Its 4,000 seats are arranged in tiers entered from above, recalling Greco-Roman arenas. Spectators come in and go out at the top. The municipal pool, built between 1969 and 1971 by Wogenscky, was restored in 2006. These facilities illustrate Le Corbusier's wish to combine culture of the body with culture of the mind.

activities.text: Discovering the Firminy-Vert district. Created in the 1950s to address the housing crisis in this former mining town, the district offers a modernist vision of urban planning. Social housing, schools, a shopping center and garages form a town within the town. The architects designed a more open, healthier and more functional space than the 19th-century workers' quarters. The site attracts 20,000 visitors a year from all over the world.

days_plan.itin_title: Loire Circuit: Wild Gorges and Industrial Heritage

visits.text: As soon as you arrive in Flavigny, a sweet scent of anise greets you. Anis de Flavigny sweets have been made since the 16th century in the former Benedictine abbey - an anise seed is coated for 15 days in flavored sugar syrup. Visit the factory - it is free, and you will leave with your pockets full of sugar-coated sweets flavored with rose, violet or lemon.

Wander the cobbled streets of this hilltop village, listed among the Plus Beaux Villages de France. Medieval ramparts, fortified gates, Renaissance houses with ornate facades—Flavigny served as the setting for the film Chocolat with Juliette Binoche and Johnny Depp. The 13th-century Saint-Genest church, with its carved choir stalls, deserves a detour.

Walk around the ramparts to discover views over the valleys of the Ozerain. The village sits on an isolated plateau at an altitude of 400 meters, offering 360-degree panoramas over the Burgundian countryside.

activities.text: Take the rural trail that descends toward the Ozerain valley and climbs back through the orchards. Along the way, you'll cross the Alesia archaeological site—the plateau where Vercingetorix surrendered to Julius Caesar in 52 BC is just 8 km away. If the subject fascinates you, the MuséoParc Alésia is worth the detour.
In the evening, settle onto the ramparts with a glass of Crémant de Bourgogne. The sunset over the hills of Auxois is one of the most beautiful along the route.

days_plan.itin_title: Burgundy's 15 Most Beautiful Villages
Burgundy-Franche-Comté: The Most Beautiful Villages in 7 days

visits.text: Fleurance is a bastide founded in 1274. Its central covered market with Gothic arcades dates from the 14th century and still hosts the market. The church has fine contemporary stained-glass windows created by Arnaud Moles, the same artist as at Auch cathedral.

Take the time to walk around the central covered market, the heart of the bastide. Its arcades and timber frame recall the trading activity that has enlivened the square for centuries. All around, the arcaded streets trace the checkerboard plan characteristic of Gascon bastides.

activities.text: Tuesday morning market is one of the liveliest in the Gers. Local producers sell foie gras, duck, cheeses, and vegetables. It's the perfect time to discover regional products and chat with the Gersois.
Stroll through the arcaded streets surrounding the central square. The typical bastide architecture is clear here with the grid layout and central plaza. Half-timbered houses add charm to the scene.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Garonne Road Trip: From Toulouse to the Pyrenees

visits.text: Fleurie lives up to its poetic name. One of Beaujolais' most celebrated crus, it produces elegant, fragrant wines across 870 hectares of granite hillsides. The winegrowing village spreads its pink-stone houses along the road winding through the vineyards. The Chapelle de la Madone, perched on the heights, watches over this blessed terroir where Gamay expresses all its finesse.

The Maison du Cru Fleurie welcomes visitors in the heart of the village and introduces them to the appellation and its winegrowers. A selection of wines reveals the diversity of Fleurie's granite terroirs and the distinctive qualities of its wines. Information about the vineyard, local estates and tasting opportunities completes the visit.

Discover family-run wine estates preserving expertise handed down over several generations. Stone-vaulted cellars hold the barrels in which wines patiently mature. The winegrowers share their passion with sincerity, explaining the characteristics of the pink granite terroir that gives Fleurie wines their distinctive floral delicacy.

The Chapelle de la Madone crowns the hill with its glazed Burgundian tiles. From the forecourt, the view takes in the entire vineyard as it descends in green waves towards the plain. The harvest in early September transforms these hillsides into a hive of activity, with pickers and carriers working among rows of vines laden with black grapes.

activities.text: Follow the Wine Route through Fleurie, linking the major Beaujolais crus. Signposts guide you from cellar to cellar and estate to estate. Each stop reveals a different side of Beaujolais: fruity wines served chilled, age-worthy crus that improve in the cellar and light rosés for summer.

Take part in tastings organised at the estates. The winegrowers introduce their different cuvées: traditional Fleurie with floral notes, single-vineyard wines expressing a specific terroir, and concentrated, complex old-vine wines. The art of tasting is learned from these enthusiasts, who speak about their wines as if they were their children.

Hike along the marked trails that cross the terraced vineyards. The ridge circuit offers exceptional panoramas over the surrounding valleys and neighbouring winegrowing villages. Educational signs explain work in the vineyards through the seasons, from winter pruning to the autumn harvest.

Taste Beaujolais cuisine in the village's bouchons and restaurants. Saucisson brioché, cervelle de canut, quenelles and andouillettes: Lyonnais cuisine finds its way onto the plates. The food and wine pairings are carefully considered, highlighting the versatility of Fleurie wines, which go equally well with charcuterie, poultry or cheese.

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip from Bresse to Bugey via Beaujolais and Lyon

places.name: Florac

visits.text: Florac's château, beside the Vibron stream, houses the headquarters of Cévennes National Park. Its courtyard, shaded by centuries-old plane trees, provides a peaceful setting. The building hosts exhibitions on Cévenol heritage.

In a quiet park, the Pêcher spring gushes from a rocky scree through several outlets. It channels water from the Méjean causse toward the Tarnon. Its name derives from the Occitan "pesquièr" (fish pond), inherited from the old mills that once lined the watercourse.

Cross the stone Pont du Tarn, Florac's architectural emblem. It offers unobstructed views of the river and surrounding cliffs. Downstream, the metal bridge of the old station, built in 1890 following Eiffel's design, recalls when trains opened up the Cévennes.

The Maison du Tourisme et du Parc national des Cévennes occupies the renovated building of the old railway station. An interactive display presents the Park, its ecosystems and the issues it faces. Shop and nature bookshop on site.

Florac-Trois-Rivières lives up to its name: the Tarn, Tarnon, and Mimente converge here. Stroll the Vibron's banks between schist houses, the 1833 neoclassical temple on the Esplanade, and Parc Paul Arnal.

activities.text: Paddle down the Tarn by canoe from Florac to Sainte-Énimie. The gorges gradually tighten, cliffs rise higher, pebble beaches invite breaks. Rental companies provide shuttle service back.
The Rochefort via ferrata offers two interlinked routes along the river, with an optional 50-metre zip line. There is a chance to stop for a swim between sections.

The GR70, Robert Louis Stevenson's trail, passes through Florac. Follow a section to reach Col de Jalcreste or Barre-des-Cévennes, a hilltop village with history-laden facades and panoramic views over the National Park.

days_plan.itin_title: Lozère Circuit: Tarn Gorges and Cévennes

map_keywords: Maison du Parc national des Cévennes Florac

visits.text: Dive into the medieval heart of Foix, a small prefecture where cobblestone lanes wind between half-timbered houses. The Abbey of Saint-Volusien reveals its Romanesque architecture, while the pontils suspended between facades bear witness to a unique heritage. Look up to see the three towers of the castle dominating the confluence of the Arget and the Ariège.

The Castle of the Counts of Foix rises from its rocky pinnacle, a symbol of feudal power since the 11th century. Pass through the walls to explore the three towers, the museum space, and reconstructed rooms furnished with period pieces. The siege engines on the terraces (trebuchet, stone-thrower, drum winch) bring medieval sieges back to life. From the summit, the panorama sweeps across the Pyrenees to the Corbières.

The Forges de Pyrène in Montgailhard transport you to a recreated village of the 1900s. Over 5,000 antique tools bear witness to vanished skills, while the demonstrators keep alive the ancestral gestures of the blacksmith, the clog-maker, the basket-weaver and the baker. The 15th-century trip-hammer forge, listed as a Historic Monument and the last still working in France, still echoes with the song of the anvil.

activities.text: At the Forges de Pyrène, join workshops led by artisans in period costume: try your hand at traditional forging, handle crossbows and bows under supervision, or discover the stone-cutting techniques of the builders. These immersive experiences work even in bad weather, under cover.

days_plan.itin_title: Ariège Circuit: Cathar Castles, Prehistoric Caves & Mountain Lakes
Ariège Road Trip: Cathars and Prehistoric Caves

places.name: Fondation Louis Vuitton

visits.text: The Fondation Louis Vuitton, built by Frank Gehry and inaugurated in 2014 in the Bois de Boulogne, is one of Paris's most spectacular buildings: 12 blown-glass sails wrapped around an iceberg-like structure of white concrete, comprising 3,600 curved glass panels across 11 galleries. The foundation exhibits a permanent collection of modern and contemporary art—Basquiat, Richter, Hirst, Koons—and organizes major temporary exhibitions. The terrace at the top offers a 360° view of the Bois de Boulogne, the Eiffel Tower, and La Défense. Book your ticket online. Free shuttles depart from Porte Maillot every 20 minutes.

activities.text: The Bois de Boulogne surrounds the foundation—take advantage of it for a walk or bike ride around the Lac Inférieur after your visit. The Bagatelle gardens, a 10-minute walk away, are renowned for their rose garden with 1,200 varieties in bloom from May to July.

days_plan.itin_title: The Great Museums of Paris

map_keywords: Fondation Louis Vuitton Paris Bois de Boulogne
Collections art contemporain Fondation Vuitton Paris

visits.text: The Odeillo Solar Furnace stands 50 meters tall. Built in 1969 with 1,000 adjustable mirrors, it concentrates solar energy to reach 3,500°C at the focal point. Research center for high-temperature materials.
The Hermitage of Notre-Dame de Font-Romeu dates from 1693. This baroque chapel on the Camino de Santiago houses a 13th-century statue of the Virgin. The sacred fountain gives it its name.
The twentieth-century Christ the King church overlooks the center. Built of concrete, it is home to a monumental statue of Christ the King.
The National High-Altitude Training Center has welcomed Olympic athletes since 1967. Its facilities are open to the public: swimming pool, ice rink, weight room.
The Grand Hôtel, built between 1910 and 1914, dominates the resort. Listed as a historical monument, this Belle Époque establishment symbolizes the rise of climate therapy.

activities.text: Ski in the Font-Romeu Pyrénées 2000 ski area. France's sunniest resort with 43 slopes at elevations between 1,600 and 2,213 meters, 500 snow cannons, and 110 km of cross-country skiing.
Take the Yellow Train from Font-Romeu station. Century-old line connecting Villefranche to Latour-de-Carol through Cerdagne landscapes.
Hike on the Cerdagne plateau. Hundreds of kilometers of marked trails run through pine forests, past lakes, and across clearings at an altitude of 1,800 meters.
Relax in the hot sulfurous waters of the baths. Llo, Dorres and Saint-Thomas offer peaceful havens surrounded by nature. For Saint-Thomas, allow for a round trip by road from Font-Romeu.

days_plan.itin_title: Pyrénées-Orientales Road Trip: French Catalonia and the Côte Vermeille

visits.text: Fontaine-de-Vaucluse gave its name to the department: "Vallis Clausa," the enclosed valley, attested as early as 979. The Sorgue spring that gushes at the foot of a 230-meter limestone cliff is France's most powerful resurgence, with an average annual flow of 630 million cubic meters. It's fed by waters from Mont Ventoux, the Albion plateau, and the Vaucluse Mountains. The first explorations of the chasm began in 1878; in 1985, divers reached a depth of -308 meters without finding the bottom. The walk from the village to the chasm takes 15 to 20 minutes on foot. The view is most spectacular in spring, when the waters boil at high flow.

The Musee-Bibliotheque Francois Petrarque, on the left bank of the Sorgue, is dedicated to the Tuscan poet who settled in Fontaine-de-Vaucluse from 1338 onward to escape the tumult of the papal court in Avignon. Here he wrote much of his Canzoniere, 366 poems dedicated to Laure de Sade, who died of the Plague in 1348. The museum also exhibits a modern art collection bringing together names such as Braque, Picasso, Miro and Giacometti, all connected to the work of the poet Rene Char, a native of L'Isle-sur-la-Sorgue.

The Church of Saint-Véran, classified as a Historic Monument since 1840, is built on the remains of a Roman temple. It's one of the oldest in the diocese of Cavaillon, with an 11th-century Romanesque nave. It houses the sarcophagus of Saint Véran, 6th-century bishop of Cavaillon, reputed to have slain a legendary beast—the Coulobre—in the Sorgue waters.

activities.text: Round trip to the chasm from the parking lot (15-20 min walk each way). The path follows the Sorgue and its waterwheels. Note: access has been reduced for safety reasons (possible rockfall), the observation point has been moved 50 meters upstream.

Trail along the left bank of the Sorgue, shaded section under the plane trees (45 min). The emerald green waters of the Sorgue allow kayaking and aquatic hiking—providers offer these activities from the village.

days_plan.itin_title: The 15 Most Beautiful Villages of the Luberon
Vaucluse: Avignon, Luberon Villages & Ventoux Routes

visits.text: The Château de Fontainebleau commands 130 hectares of parks and gardens. Eight centuries of monarchs lived here continuously, from the 12th to the 19th century. With 1,500 rooms, it's the most furnished royal palace in France.
Walk through the François I Gallery, 60 meters long. The frescoes and stuccowork by Rosso Fiorentino depict mythological scenes commissioned by the king to transform Fontainebleau into a "new Rome".

The Napoleon I Museum occupies the Louis XV wing. Uniforms, weapons, imperial jewels, and personal items trace the emperor's life—he called the château "the true home of kings, the house of centuries".
Step into Empress Eugénie's Chinese Museum. Cloisonné vases, jade, and porcelain form an Asian cabinet of curiosities installed during the Second Empire.

The Imperial Theatre, commissioned by Napoleon III and inaugurated in 1857, was rediscovered after 150 years of neglect. Its refinement echoes that of the Versailles opera house. Accessible by guided tour only.

Descend to the Court of Honor, known as the "Farewell Court". The horseshoe staircase marks the exact spot where Napoleon bid farewell to the Imperial Guard on April 20, 1814, before his exile to Elba.

activities.text: Stroll through the English Garden, landscaped under Napoleon I, then follow the Grand Canal dug under Henri IV. Rowboats let you glide across the water facing the château.

The Fontainebleau Forest stretches across 22,000 hectares. Its sandstone boulders are the world reference for bouldering, drawing climbers from across the globe. Over 30,000 boulders across 270 sectors are mapped, from beginner to expert.
Follow the marked forest trails: the GR 1, 2, 11, and 13 cross the massif. Landscapes alternate between sandstone chaos, oak groves, and sandy plateaus.

days_plan.itin_title: Seine-et-Marne Circuit: Fontainebleau and Châteaux

places.name: Fontenay Le Comte

visits.text: Fontenay-le-Comte is Vendée's only town with the Ville d'Art et d'Histoire designation—Francis I described it as the “Fountain and Source of Fine Minds.” Begin by wandering through the Renaissance old town, where private mansions—the Maison Billaud, Hôtel de la Sénéchaussée and Hôtel Grimouard—line the cobbled lanes. Look up and you will spot caryatids and sculpted details on almost every façade.

Château de Terre-Neuve, built between 1584 and 1594 for poet Nicolas Rapin, a comrade-in-arms of Henry IV, is a Renaissance jewel. Don't miss the fireplace bearing alchemical symbols—studied by Fulcanelli—and the thirteen suns gilded with gold leaf from Louis XIV's bedroom at Château de Chambord. Georges Simenon lived here from 1940 to 1943. A guided tour is required to visit the interior, and you'll soon understand why once you see the coffered ceilings.

The Notre-Dame church, a Gothic building from the 15th century, conceals an 11th-century Romanesque crypt beneath its foundations. Its bell tower rises to over 80 meters. Step inside and you'll pass through several centuries at once: Renaissance chapels, a 17th-century altarpiece and an 18th-century pulpit.

Go down a few steps to discover the Fontaine des Quatre Tias, built in 1542. This listed monument, shaped like a small ancient temple with a pediment and Doric columns, bears the city's Latin motto. It is the symbol of Fontenay—small but highly photogenic. You will come across it in a narrow lane, almost by surprise.

Vouvant, listed among the Plus Beaux Villages de France since 1988, is Vendée's only fortified town. Perched on a rocky spur in a bend of the La Mère River, it was founded around 1010 by William the Great, Duke of Aquitaine. Allow a good half-day to explore it: you will find ramparts, lanes lined with hollyhocks and artists' studios.

Climb to the top of the Tour Mélusine, a 13th-century circular keep standing 35 meters high—the last remnant of the Lusignan castle. According to legend, the fairy Mélusine, half-woman, half-serpent, is said to have built the castle in a single night “with an apronful of stones and a mouthful of water.” From the top, you will have a 360° panorama of the village, the river and the Mervent-Vouvant forest. Keys are available at the tourist office on Place du Bail.

The Romanesque church of Notre-Dame-de-l'Assomption, whose oldest section (the Théodelin nave) dates to the 11th century, has a north portal with exceptionally rich carving for Bas-Poitou—animal imagery, interlace and human figures. Inside, you will discover contemporary art exhibitions in the Théodelin nave. The contrast between Romanesque stone and modern works is surprising.

Pass through La Poterne, the sole surviving fortified gate among the three original town entrances. From there, descend toward the La Mère River between limewashed houses and painters' and sculptors' studios. You'll encounter about fifteen artists' studios open to the public from April to October—step inside; the craftspeople enjoy chatting.

activities.text: Set off on a rowing boat trip through the Marais Poitevin from the landing stages near Fontenay. Canals shaded by ash trees and poplars crisscross the “Green Venice”—you will glide through complete silence, outside time. Allow 2 hours. Several landing stages offer boat rentals.

Climb to Parc Baron, the former site of Fontenay's medieval fortress. The remains of the Romanesque keep, the Guinefolle bastion and the Boulaye tower offer the finest view over the town's rooftops. You will probably have the place to yourself—it is a quiet, little-visited spot.

Hike in the Mervent-Vouvant forest, Vendée's largest woodland with 5,000 hectares of oak and beech. The Orée de la Forêt route starts at Café Mélusine on Place du Bail and covers about 12 kilometers (3 to 4 hours). For something shorter, the Bocage loop (4 km, 1 hour 30 minutes) is suitable for families.

If the weather permits, travel down the La Mère River by rowing boat or canoe. The calm water winds between wooded cliffs and the bends that have made Vouvant a strategic defensive site since the 11th century. From the water, you will have the finest view of the ramparts and the Tour Mélusine.

days_plan.itin_title: Vendée Itinerary: Noirmoutier Island, Puy du Fou and the Coastline
Vendée Itinerary: Noirmoutier Island, Puy du Fou and the Coastline

map_keywords: Fountain of the Four Tias, Fontenay-le-Comte

visits.text: The Royal Abbey of Fontevraud, founded in 1101, is one of the largest monastic cities in Europe with its 13 hectares. A UNESCO World Heritage site, it was led for 700 years by 36 abbesses.

In the abbey church lie the polychrome effigies of Eleanor of Aquitaine, Henry II Plantagenet, Richard the Lionheart, and Isabelle of Angoulême. This royal necropolis bears witness to the Plantagenet empire that once stretched from Scotland to the Pyrenees.
The 12th-century Romanesque kitchens are unique. Their 20 tuffeau stone chimneys rise beneath an octagonal structure topped with slate scales.
The Grand-Moûtier cloister invites contemplation. Its 16th-century galleries frame a garden where silence reigns.
The chapter house served as the nuns' daily meeting place. Converted into a prison in the 19th century, it has been restored to reveal its Gothic beauty once more.

activities.text: The abbey hosts artists in residence, contemporary art exhibitions and concerts in its history-laden spaces.
The village of Fontevraud-l'Abbaye, classed among France's Most Beautiful Villages, is best discovered on foot. Its white tuffeau houses line flower-filled lanes.
The Saumur vineyards surround the abbey. Several estates within a few kilometres offer tastings.

days_plan.itin_title: Maine-et-Loire Road Trip: Anjou and Loire Valley Châteaux

visits.text: Fontvieille owes its fame to Alphonse Daudet and his "Letters from My Windmill." But know this: Daudet never lived in this windmill. He stayed at the nearby Château de Montauban, one of whose owners was his friend. The mill called Daudet's, built in 1814 and stopped in 1915 (when wheat was requisitioned for war), served as his setting and inspiration. Now a museum, it sits on a hill of olive trees and pines with panoramic views of the Alpilles. The walk from village center takes 20 minutes.

Fontvieille's white limestone quarries have been exploited since the 15th century. The same blonde stone dressing the village served to build the Arles and Nîmes arenas, Château de Tarascon (1429-1434), and even Marseille's Palais Longchamp and Stock Exchange. The large underground galleries — some converted into Carrières de Lumières at Les Baux — are a geological feature of the Alpilles limestone massif.

The Roman aqueduct of Barbegal, 2 km from Fontvieille, is an exceptional archaeological site: a series of 8 water wheels superimposed on two parallel channels, fed by water from the Caume mountain. Built in the 2nd century AD, it's the largest collective hydraulic mill known from antiquity — it produced enough flour daily to feed 12,000 people. Free access, roadside parking.

activities.text: Loop of Fontvieille windmills (marked trail, 2h): the trail starts from Daudet's mill and follows garrigue hills on rocky tracks to Château de Montauban, where Daudet wrote. Several viewpoints over the Arles plain and Alpilles punctuate the route.

Discovery of capitelles and oratories around Fontvieille: capitelles are small circular dry-stone constructions, built without mortar, used as shelters by shepherds and wine growers. The Alpilles area is particularly rich in them. Several marked circuits reveal these witnesses to Provençal rural architecture.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpilles, Aix-en-Provence & Arles Circuit

visits.text: The citadel crowns the hill above Forcalquier. Notre-Dame-de-Provence Chapel stands watch at the summit, offering an all-around panorama of the Alps, the Luberon and the Montagne de Lure.

The Cordeliers convent displays its 13th-century Franciscan monastic architecture. The Gothic cloister, with its vaulted galleries, surrounds a medicinal herb garden. Temporary exhibitions and concerts regularly bring this carefully restored, history-filled place to life.

Notre-Dame-du-Bourguet cathedral blends Romanesque and Provençal Gothic. The 13th-century sculpted portal opens onto a harmoniously proportioned nave. Side chapels house richly decorated Baroque altarpieces.

Walk through the lanes of the old town, lined with private mansions and Renaissance residences. Medieval gates mark the course of the former ramparts. Restored fountains and washhouses line the shaded little squares, where the easy pace of Provençal life prevails.
The cemetery offers a haven of peace away from the town. The terraced graves follow the slope of the hill. The cypresses stand like sentinels in this serene place.

activities.text: Forcalquier market brings the town to life every Monday morning. Considered one of Provence's most beautiful markets, it spreads its colorful stalls across several squares. Local producers, artisans and market gardeners offer goat cheeses, lavender honey, olives and local specialties.

The Montagne de Lure rises north of Forcalquier; allow for a round trip from Forcalquier within the day. Forest roads wind through beech woods and alpine grasslands, then the final approach to the summit at 1826 meters is on foot. The astronomical observatory benefits from the clear sky for its observations.
Hiking trails radiate around Forcalquier. The loop around the Montagne des Mourres offers a moderate route through garrigue and oak trees. Medieval ruins and views of the Alps punctuate the routes.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpes-de-Haute-Provence Tour: Lavender and Hilltop Villages

visits.text: Isolated and austere at high tide, the Fort d'Ambleteuse, also known as fort Mahon or fort Vauban, becomes accessible on foot again as soon as the sea recedes. It was built between 1680 and 1690 on the orders of Louis XIV at the mouth of the Slack. Listed as a historic monument since 1965, it owes its survival to a volunteer association. Check the tide times before going, as access is quickly cut off.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Villages from Flanders to the Bay of Somme

visits.text: A medieval fortress planted in the middle of an oil port: Fort de Bouc guards the mouth of the Caronte channel, now surrounded by Lavéra installations. Vauban passed through in 1686 and added bastions and bartizans. The tower still carries a lighthouse, electrified in 1936.

activities.text: Book at Martigues Tourist Office: Fort de Bouc is in a Seveso zone, the road is closed and access is by boat from the canals, around 30 minutes. Children under 10 are not admitted, ID required.

If you're afraid of heights, be aware that the rampart walk at Fort de Bouc doesn't have guard rails meeting current standards: yet that's where you get the view of Port-de-Bouc harbour and its industrial landscape. Uneven ground, flat, closed-toe shoes compulsory.

days_plan.itin_title: Côte Bleue and Camargue: the lower coastal route in 7 days

visits.text: Fort Freinet occupies a rocky peak at 450 meters above La Garde-Freinet, protected by a ditch cut into the rock, 8 to 10 meters deep. The outlines of the 12th-century walls and main street can still be made out on the ground. The site was long wrongly attributed to the Saracens. Access is via a steep trail: about 45 minutes uphill, with suitable footwear.

activities.text: If you want to understand what you're looking at, book the guided tour of Fort Freinet through the Conservatoire du Patrimoine du Freinet: the guide recounts the history of the archaeological site and its abandonment. It's free for members and children under 8. Book online for a specific date: slots are scarce outside the tourist season.

days_plan.itin_title: Roquebrune-sur-Argens: sea, villages and the Var in 10 days
Var in 4 Days: From Bormes to the Most Beautiful Villages of the Verdon

visits.text: The 11th-century keep of the fortress of Montbazon rises on a rocky spur overlooking the Indre. Erected by Fulk Nerra, the formidable Count of Anjou, this 28-meter square tower is one of France's oldest stone keeps.
Climb to the top of the keep to take in the Indre valley, the village rooftops, and the Touraine countryside. The panorama extends several kilometers on clear days.
The fortified enclosure shelters the remains of a seigneurial residence and a chapel. Explanatory panels trace the history of Fulk Nerra, a fortress builder and major figure of medieval Anjou.

activities.text: Medieval activities and demonstrations regularly take place within the enclosure: crossbow shooting, blacksmithing, calligraphy, and knightly combat bring the fortress to life during school holidays.

days_plan.itin_title: The Essential Châteaux of the Loire Valley

visits.text: The royal fortress of Chinon stretches 500 meters along the top of a rocky spur overlooking the Vienne. Three fortified enclosures follow one another: Fort Saint-Georges, Château du Milieu, and Fort du Coudray.
In the great hall of the royal residence, Joan of Arc recognized Charles VII among his courtiers in March 1429. Interactive displays recount this foundational episode in French history.
The Tour du Coudray preserves graffiti carved by Templars imprisoned here in 1308 on the orders of Philip the Fair. Crosses, inscriptions, and mysterious symbols cover the tuffeau limestone walls.

The royal apartments have been recreated using a digital system that projects furniture, hangings, and characters onto the walls. The contrast between the ruins and the virtual reconstruction is striking.
From the ramparts, the view looks down over the Vienne, the slate roofs of old Chinon, and the vine-covered hillsides that produce the famous Chinon red wine.

activities.text: Descend into old Chinon via the cobbled lanes. Half-timbered houses from the 15th and 16th centuries, cave cellars dug into the tuffeau limestone, and small shaded squares form a preserved historic center.
The cave cellars in Chinon's hillsides house wine producers who offer tastings of the local cabernet franc, the appellation's emblematic grape.

days_plan.itin_title: The Essential Châteaux of the Loire Valley

visits.text: Fougères Castle. Dominating the Nançon Valley from a rocky outcrop, this 2-hectare fortress is the largest in Europe in this state of preservation. Built between the 12th and 15th centuries to defend the Breton Marches, it has 13 towers connected by imposing curtain walls. The guided tour reveals the ingenuity of its defensive system: drawbridge, arrow slits, machicolations, rampart walkways, and the spectacular 31-meter-high Mélusine Tower. From the top of the ramparts, the panorama takes in the entire lower town with its colorful half-timbered houses, offering one of France's most beautiful medieval landscapes.

Bourg-Vieil Medieval Quarter. At the foot of the castle stretches Fougères' oldest quarter, miraculously preserved with its 17th-century half-timbered houses. Place du Marchix with its terraces, Rue de Savigny with its colorful facades, and Rue des Fontaines winding down to Saint-Sulpice Church form a picturesque maze where time seems frozen. The Baroque Saint-Sulpice Church contains two medieval altarpieces among the oldest in Brittany and stained glass windows recounting the local legend of the Virgin of the Marshes.

Public Garden and Jardin du Val Nançon. From Place aux Arbres, laid out on high ground, a magnificent panorama looks down over the castle, medieval quarter, and Saint-Sulpice Church in a postcard-worthy composition. The Jardin du Val Nançon winds across 2 hectares at the foot of the northern ramparts, offering a succession of themed gardens: family vegetable plots, a botanical garden, a priest's garden, and even a cage made of plants. Chèvre des Fossés goats, a local breed, maintain the site through conservation grazing, while beehives and insect hotels make this space a biodiversity haven in the heart of the city.

La Coursive - Heritage Interpretation Center. At the foot of the castle, this new interactive museum space serves as a living encyclopedia of Fougères' history. Multimedia exhibitions and playful installations trace the city's evolution from its medieval origins, explain the strategic role of the Breton Marches, and reveal the fortress's construction secrets. A combined ticket for the center and the castle provides a particularly enriching, comprehensive visit.

activities.text: A walk at the foot of the ramparts. A path runs along the fortifications of Fougères Castle, following the Nançon Valley from the medieval quarter of Bourg-Vieil. The route passes beneath the curtain walls and towers of the fortress, then reaches the Jardin du Val Nançon, laid out at the foot of the walls. From there, the view down over the green valley creates a striking contrast with the austere stone of the castle.

Fougères Forest. This 1,600-hectare state forest has a network of marked trails for hiking, mountain biking, and horseback riding. Forest roads cross century-old beech groves and jumbles of granite boulders, remnants of old quarries. Breton folklore permeates the place, with sites evoking stories of fairies and korrigans dear to local storytellers.

days_plan.itin_title: Ille-et-Vilaine Tour: Saint-Malo, Dinard and the Emerald Coast

visits.text: The Écomusée du Pays de la Cerise, housed in a former distillery dating from 1829 and listed as a Historic Monument, traces 150 years of expertise in cherries and AOC kirsch. Tour the manor house, discover the stills, the cellar with its oak barrels, and the attic where eaux-de-vie age in their glass demijohns.

The conservation orchard brings together nearly 40 heritage cherry tree varieties, some threatened with extinction: Béchat, Caraude, Jean Blanc, Marie Jean Diaude, Tinette, Chapendu. In spring, the blossoms offer an enchanting spectacle evoking a Japanese atmosphere.

activities.text: Follow the Route des Chalots, a tourist route that lets you discover chalots, traditional grain stores typical of Vosges architecture, while meeting local artisans who keep the craft of distillation alive.

Meet the fruit growers who distill their own spirits and have kept the tradition of Kirsch de Fougerolles AOC alive for generations. Today, about a hundred producers cultivate 10,000 cherry trees that produce 500 tonnes of cherries for 35,000 liters of eau-de-vie annually.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Saône Tour: Comtois Plateaus and Heritage

visits.text: Fourcès is one of France's rare circular bastides, listed among the Most Beautiful Villages. Founded in the 13th century, it's organized around a round square bordered by arcades. Half-timbered houses and flower-laden façades create a picturesque atmosphere. The 15th-century château overlooks the village.
The church of Saint-Laurent has a fortified bell tower typical of the region. Inside, 15th-century frescoes are still visible.

activities.text: In late April, the flower market transforms the circular square into an ephemeral garden. It's one of the Southwest's most beautiful flower markets with hundreds of exhibitors. The atmosphere is festive.
Wander beneath the arcades of the round square. The galleries shelter small shops and restaurants. Sit at a terrace to admire this unique architecture.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Garonne Road Trip: From Toulouse to the Pyrenees

places.name: Fox Amphoux

visits.text: Fox-Amphoux is a double village: "new Fox" down in the plain holds the school, the town hall and the post office; Old Fox sits perched at 540 meters on a spur and has kept all its medieval character. The remains of the Blacas castle, first mentioned in 1200, stand above the stepped lanes. On the church square, do not miss the hackberry tree, more than 400 years old and 5 meters round — it stays cool there even in the middle of July. The panorama from the viewpoint on rue de la Prison takes in the whole of the Var, as far as the Sainte-Baume and the Alpilles in clear weather. This is also the birthplace of Paul Barras, born here in 1755: this revolutionary viscount voted for the death of Louis XVI, helped bring down Robespierre in 1794 and sat in the Directory before being pushed aside by Napoleon.

Descend from Old Fox on a cobbled path to the Chapel of Notre-Dame du Bon Secours, set within a grotto at the foot of a limestone tufa cliff. The way is marked by several oratories and a peaceful forest atmosphere. Inside the grotto, behind the gates, the altar is adorned with flowers and the vault covered with small ex-votos. A discreet and touching place, off the tourist circuits.

activities.text: At the former cooperative cellar at the village's base, the DinoFox Museo displays fossils and dinosaur bones discovered in the area — notably the Variraptor mechinorum, discovered between 1992 and 1995 by amateur paleontologists, which provided the first proof of a dromaeosaur (velociraptor cousin) in Europe. The visit is free and fascinating for the whole family.

In late afternoon, settle on the Old Fox viewpoint to watch the sun descend over the wooded hills of the Haut-Var. The perched village then stands out as a dark silhouette against the horizon — one of the most distinctive views in the backcountry.

days_plan.itin_title: The 10 Most Beautiful Villages of the Haut-Var

map_keywords: Chapelle Notre-Dame du Bon Secours Fox-Amphoux grotte

visits.text: Fréjus' amphitheater divides opinion, and it's easy to see why: the restoration begun in 2007 extended the ancient ruins with modern materials rather than reconstructing them. Built in the 1st century and measuring 113 meters by 85, it could accommodate up to 12,000 spectators. Victor Hugo saw horses grazing there in 1839. If the concrete makes you bristle, seeing the outside is more than enough.

Fréjus is nicknamed the Provençal Pompeii, and place Formigé explains why: Saint-Léonce cathedral, the cloister, baptistery and episcopal palace form a single episcopal complex. The octagonal 5th-century baptistery is one of the oldest in France and is still used for baptisms. A guided tour is included in the ticket: take it, as it's the only way to enter the baptistery.

A fantastical bestiary looks down at you from the ceiling: the larch ceiling coffers in the cloister of Saint-Léonce cathedral in Fréjus are covered with figures painted in the 14th century, human, animal or somewhere in between. They've darkened over time, but many can still be made out. An indoor room shows an explanatory video: watch it before, not after.

If the arena left you cold, the Fréjus aqueduct makes up for it: it brought water from the Siagnole, in Mons, over about forty kilometers. Its remains are distributed between avenue des Aqueducs, rue Henri Vadon and the Villa Aurélienne park, which preserves the largest portion. The park is free and shaded.

activities.text: Get the Fréjus Pass if you plan to visit several sites: €6 for four sites, valid for seven days, versus €3 for the amphitheater alone. It covers the ancient and medieval heritage of the city, which holds the Ville et Pays d'art et d'histoire label. The pass pays for itself from the second site: easy enough in Fréjus.

If you prefer the unusual to the Roman, head to the north of Fréjus: the Missiri mosque rises among holm oaks and stone pines, and the Hong Hien pagoda completes the picture. Two colonial legacies you would not expect here, ten minutes from the arena. The mosque cannot be visited and is seen from the outside only; for the pagoda, check the opening hours, they are irregular.

days_plan.itin_title: Var Road Trip: French Riviera & Provence Verte
Roquebrune-sur-Argens: sea, villages and the Var in 10 days

visits.text: Fresnay-sur-Sarthe has perched on a rocky spur above the Sarthe since the 9th century—William the Conqueror besieged it several times in the 11th century. Labeled Petite Cité de Caractère since 1995, it represented the Pays de la Loire region on the television show France's Favorite Village in 2021. Its absolute jewel: the carved oak door of Notre-Dame church, created in 1528 by the Dienis brothers, two local artists. The left panel illustrates the Tree of Jesse (Old Testament), the right the Twelve Apostles (New Testament). The church itself, built in warm-toned russet stone, was constructed in the second half of the 12th century by the counts of Maine.

Climb to the château park for two discoveries: the ruins of the old medieval keep and the plunging view over the Sarthe meanders and the Creusot quarter where weavers' houses still line up. These houses have very particular architecture—the weaving workshop was installed slightly underground to maintain the humidity necessary for hemp thread solidity, the living room upstairs, accessible by an external staircase. The château's postern, two 14th-century circular towers, marks the entrance to the public garden.

The Bonnet Museum exhibits 180 19th-century Sarthe bonnets—from the simple bonnette to the Bise-moi vite—restored and presented on hat stands by the local association's seamstresses. Each bonnet tells an era and social status: the most elaborate, entirely handmade in lace, could represent weeks of work. A precious ethnographic document on Sarthe women's lives.

activities.text: Descend rue du Bourgneuf, partly paved, which runs along the Sarthe at the foot of the promontory. Typical houses open directly onto the river and benches allow you to sit and watch the water pass. It's one of the most peaceful and authentic streets in Sarthe—take your time.

The Coteau des Vignes, accessible from a marked path from the bottom of the village, offers a fantastic view over the Sarthe valley and its meanders. This sensitive natural site hosts rare plant species specific to limestone grasslands—its almost Mediterranean feel is surprising in the Maine region.

days_plan.itin_title: Sarthe Road Trip: Le Mans and the Loir Valley

visits.text: Fresnes Prison was built between 1895 and 1898 by Henri Poussin to replace Paris's old Mazas, Sainte-Pélagie, and Grande-Roquette prisons. At its opening, it was the world's largest prison: 1,800 individual cells, running water, steam heating, electric lighting. Its "telephone pole" layout — cell wings perpendicular to a 200-meter central corridor — was copied for a century in the United States, notably at Rikers Island. During the Occupation, the Germans detained resistance fighters and British SOE agents there. The prison was liberated on August 24, 1944, by Leclerc's 2nd Armored Division. You can't go inside — it's an active prison — but the exterior and history are worth the detour. It's been listed as national cultural heritage since 1995.

The Parc de Sceaux, a few kilometers away in Hauts-de-Seine, is one of the best-preserved formal French gardens in Île-de-France. Le Nôtre designed it for Colbert—large cascades, a grand canal, ornamental parterres. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes for the full circuit.

activities.text: The Verrières forest, at Fresnes's doorstep, is one of the best-preserved peri-urban forests south of Paris. Several marked trails allow walking or running in an environment that contrasts sharply with the concrete and prison walls nearby.

Fresnes's Saint-Sulpice church dates in part from the 12th century. The village has preserved some old buildings around it that remind you that Fresnes was a rural village before the prison transformed its identity in 1898.

days_plan.itin_title: Val-de-Marne Road Trip: Castles and the Banks of the Marne

places.name: Fresselines

visits.text: Fresselines still bears the mark of Claude Monet's stay from March to May 1889. The Impressionist master created 23 canvases here, including ten depicting the confluence of the two Creuse rivers, nicknamed “Les Eaux Semblantes.” This series is considered his first true exploration of the same motif in different light, a technique he would perfect with the Haystacks and then the Cathedrals.

The Espace Monet-Rollinat, an art center opened in 2018, pays tribute to the two figures who left their mark on the village. A memorial room is dedicated to Monet and displays reproductions of his Creuse paintings. The other recalls Maurice Rollinat, author of Les Névroses, who lived here for twenty years and hosted artists and writers. Temporary exhibitions of contemporary art bring this creative space to life.

On the wall of the Fresselines church, a bas-relief by Rodin entitled 'The Poet and His Muse' pays homage to Maurice Rollinat. The sculptor, a friend of the poet, offered this work to the town after Rollinat's death in 1903. Inside, contemporary stained glass windows created by a local glass artist add a modern artistic touch to the building.

activities.text: The “Dans les pas de Monet” trail starts in the village and winds for 3 kilometers along the Petite Creuse. A suspension footbridge crosses the river, leading to the painter's favorite viewpoints. Interpretive panels display the paintings created at each location, allowing visitors to compare today's landscape with the Impressionist vision of 1889.

The Rocher de la Fileuse, in the neighboring commune of Saint-Plantaire, offers the most beautiful panorama of the valley and the confluence of the Creuse and Sédelle. It was here that Monet created his series of 24 canvases. A 3-kilometer hiking trail leads there through the woods. The late afternoon light enhances the colors the master sought to capture.

days_plan.itin_title: Creuse Tour: Valley of the Painters and Aubusson Tapestries

map_keywords: In the Footsteps of Monet Trail Fresselines

visits.text: Saint-Michel Abbey, founded in 972, dominates the Tarn riverbanks. In its vaulted cellars, the museum traces Gaillac's history through the Gallo-Roman mosaic discovered on site, sacred art, and the journeymen's guild tradition.
Head to the Quai Saint-Jacques quarter, the oldest part of town. From here, gabarres loaded with woad and wine once departed, sailing down the Tarn to the Gironde and European ports.
Continue to the Portanelle quarter. Its houses with overhanging upper floors, timber framing, and sun-dried or fired bricks mixed with pebbles illustrate typical Tarn riverside architecture.
Château de Foucaud houses the Fine Arts Museum. Its park, laid out as a listed Italian-style garden, descends in terraces to the Tarn's banks, with small pools and unobstructed views.
Saint-Pierre Church, built in the 10th century, features a 14th-century stone portal and an understated façade. Inside, marble altars and the nave's proportions warrant a visit.

activities.text: Visit a wine estate for an introduction to wine tasting. The Gaillac wine region, one of France's oldest with over 2,000 years of history, produces powerful reds and dry, sweet, or sparkling whites.
Follow a wine-themed hiking trail through the Gaillac AOP vineyards. These marked walks cross rolling landscapes nicknamed “Occitan Tuscany.”
Stop at Gaillac's weekly market to discover regional products: foie gras, duck confit, local saffron, and sheep's milk cheeses from the Lacaune Mountains.

days_plan.itin_title: Tarn Road Trip: Albi & Hilltop Villages

visits.text: Take the road that climbs the Fango valley for 15 km from Galéria—a forest of cork oaks and chestnuts descending from the heights of Monte Cinto (2,706 m, Corsica's highest point) down to the sea, classified as a UNESCO biosphere reserve. Solitude is almost total on weekdays. The Fango's waters are among the island's most transparent, shifting from blue to green depending on depth and light.

Don't leave without stopping at the Fango's natural pools—a series of basins and potholes carved in granite between two Genoese stone bridges. The main swimming spot is about 5 km from the village, past the old bridge. The water is cool and limpid even in August.

activities.text: In Galéria, rental operators offer canoes to explore the Fango delta in season. The outing takes place on calm channels near the river mouth, between the vegetation along the banks and the water lilies. It is ideal in the morning, before the wind picks up offshore.

Picnic beside the Fango pools: bring your supplies from Galéria. Settle on the flat rocks beside the water - the cool shade and the sound of the stream do the rest. The spot is quiet on weekdays and crowded on Saturdays in July.

days_plan.itin_title: Complete Tour of Corsica

visits.text: Start with the Musée Muséum départemental, and don't skip the showpiece: the mausoleum of Lesdiguières, the last Constable of France, a mass of black-and-white marble standing more than four meters tall and installed here since 1912. The rest blends archaeology, fine arts and natural history under one roof. Admission is free, which is not that common for a museum of this size. Allow a solid hour, more if the mountain ethnography section appeals to you.

Notre-Dame-et-Saint-Arnoux Cathedral anchors the center with its neo-Gothic silhouette. Rebuilt in the nineteenth century over an older Romanesque sanctuary, it makes full use of polychromy: alternating light and dark stone, local marble columns. Not a major monument by Alpine standards, but a logical stop right in the pedestrian heart of town. Twenty minutes does it if you're not an ecclesiastical architecture buff.

Gap is best explored on foot. The old town's colorful facades rise in tiers along shady boulevards, with its pedestrian lanes, café terraces and the fountain on Place Jean-Marcellin. A little fact to slip into conversation: at 740 meters, Gap is France's highest prefecture. The market fills Place de la République on Wednesday mornings, the right time to come across alpine pasture cheeses and local honey.

activities.text: Four kilometers from the center, Domaine de Charance stretches over 220 hectares of terraced gardens, forest, and a pond, with an eighteenth-century château as a backdrop. The Botanical Conservatory watches over thousands of wild alpine plant species. It's the green escape for Gap locals: picnic areas, marked trails, views over the city from the heights. Free access year-round, free parking.

A short geological detour about twenty minutes from Gap, in the municipality of Théus: the Salle de bal des Demoiselles coiffées. These fairy chimneys are columns of friable clay capped with a stone block that protects them from erosion, lined up by the dozens in a spectacular cirque. A marked trail loops around them. Go late in the day—the low-angle light sculpts the silhouettes even better.

days_plan.itin_title: Hautes-Alpes Road Trip: High Mountains and Alpine Valleys

visits.text: Gargilesse village. Listed among the Plus Beaux Villages de France, Gargilesse nestles in the verdant Creuse valley. Its houses with steep roofs covered in small brown tiles are harmoniously grouped around the Romanesque church and château. This village captivated George Sand, who owned a house here as a retreat, and later numerous Impressionist painters like Armand Guillaumin and Léon Detroy.

Notre-Dame Church and its crypt. Built in the 12th century, this Romanesque church reveals 120 superb historiated capitals where the 24 Elders of the Apocalypse and carved biblical scenes coexist. A small staircase leads down to the crypt adorned with 13th and 16th-century frescoes illustrating the instruments of the Passion and episodes from the lives of Christ and Mary.

Villa Algira. George Sand discovered Gargilesse one June evening in 1857 during a walk with Alexandre Manceau, who gave her this small house. The writer stayed here regularly between 1857 and 1864, finding inspiration for several novels in this romantic refuge. The museum presents natural history collections, drawings by Maurice Sand, and everyday objects that tell the story of George Sand's life in Berry.

Gargilesse Castle. Built in the 13th and 14th centuries, the château was expanded in the 16th and 18th centuries. Access to the estate is through the ancient 12th-century gate flanked by two towers, the sole remnant of the old fortress. The square tower dates from the 17th century and originally served as a tomb for the lords of Gargilesse.

activities.text: International Harp Festival. Gargilesse has become the world capital of the harp thanks to Pierre Jamet, who founded this festival in 1968. It is now directed by his daughter Marie-Claire. Concerts, courses, and masterclasses take place throughout the year, with a particularly prestigious summer festival in August. The international harp academy offers courses in April and August.

Creuse riverside trails. Hiking paths follow the banks of the Creuse and reveal the landscapes that inspired so many artists. The changing reflections on the water, lush vegetation, and viewpoints over the village create a uniquely romantic atmosphere.

Art galleries and artisan workshops. The village continues its artistic tradition with several galleries exhibiting paintings, sculptures, and artistic crafts. Workshops open seasonally allow you to meet the artists and artisans and discover their works in an unpretentious, warm atmosphere.

days_plan.itin_title: Indre Road Trip: Secret Berry and the Vallée Noire

visits.text: Century-old hackberry trees on Place deï Barri in Gassin shade one of the finest balconies over the Gulf of Saint-Tropez, with views of the Hyères islands and the Massif des Maures. Perched at an altitude of 201 meters, this village is among the Plus Beaux Villages de France. The Androuno alley, the narrowest in the village, admits only one person at a time. Come early—restaurant terraces take over the square from noon onward.

activities.text: Locals tell how Germaine L'Hardy-Denonain single-handedly cleared the abandoned terraces below the ramparts to create the botanical garden that bears her name. Awarded the Jardin Remarquable label, it brings together over a thousand Mediterranean species on former agricultural terraces. The entrance hides behind the restaurant tables on Place deï Barri—easy to miss.

days_plan.itin_title: Var in 4 Days: From Bormes to the Most Beautiful Villages of the Verdon

visits.text: The Cirque de Gavarnie, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List since 1997 as part of the cross-border site “Pyrénées – Mont Perdu,” is a natural amphitheater 6.5 km in circumference whose limestone walls rise to 1,700 meters high. Glacial erosion sculpted it approximately 50 million years ago; its concentric tiers of striking symmetry are surrounded by peaks exceeding 3,000 meters. Victor Hugo called it an “impossible and extraordinary object.”

The Grande Cascade de Gavarnie, with its 423-meter drop, is the highest waterfall in mainland France. Fed by snow and the Marboré glacier, it unfolds in long white veils on the cirque wall. Its flow varies considerably by season, with the spring melt months offering the most powerful spectacle.

The Brèche de Roland, at an altitude of 2,804 meters, is a natural notch 40 meters wide and 100 meters high in the rock wall separating France from Spain. According to legend, the knight Roland, Charlemagne's nephew, is said to have opened it by striking the rock with his sword Durandal in an attempt to destroy the sword so it would not fall into enemy hands.

The village of Gavarnie, the starting point for the cirque, retains traditional Pyrenean architecture with stone houses and slate roofs. A historic stop on the routes to Santiago de Compostela, it is also the birthplace of Pyreneanism, the movement devoted to exploring and climbing the Pyrenees that began in the 18th century.

The Refuge des Sarradets, at an altitude of 2,587 meters below the Brèche de Roland, dates from 1955–1956. Its terrace offers one of the most striking panoramas of the Pyrenees, with the Cirque de Gavarnie and the Grande Cascade as a backdrop. It serves as a stop for hikers climbing toward the Brèche.

The Cirque de Gavarnie is part of a group of three glacial cirques together with Estaubé and Troumouse, forming the UNESCO-recognized site “Pyrénées – Mont Perdu.” The area is home to remarkable wildlife: Pyrenean chamois on the slopes, marmots in the high-altitude meadows, the bearded vulture (2.80 m wingspan), and the golden eagle riding the updrafts.

activities.text: From the village, walk for about an hour and a half on the main trail to the foot of the cirque to see the Grande Cascade up close. The path presents no technical difficulty, crosses meadows, and follows the mountain river—it can also be traveled on horseback using the village's horse rental services.

For seasoned hikers, reach the Brèche de Roland from the Col des Tentes (2,208 m) via the Sarradets mountain hut. Allow 5 to 6 hours round trip for this demanding hike (approximately 1,000 m of elevation gain, with possible snowfield crossings even in summer).
Tour the medieval village of Gavarnie, observing the stone architecture of Pyrenean houses and barns, and stop at one of the small restaurants to taste garbure or sheep's milk cheese from the valley.
Stay until evening if you can: the sunset light on the cirque walls transforms the rock into gradients of ochre and pink, a spectacle that photography struggles to reproduce.

days_plan.itin_title: Hautes-Pyrénées Circuit: From Tarbes to Cirques and Valleys

visits.text: Discover the Écomusée de la Baie, an enlightening interpretation center dedicated to the natural wonders of the Mont-Saint-Michel bay and its protected ecosystems. Spread across 400 square meters, this engaging museum features films, detailed scale models, and interactive terminals that explain the unique environment of Europe's greatest tidal bay. The museum offers unobstructed views toward the iconic silhouette of the mount.

Explore the charming coastal village of Genêts, a quintessentially Norman settlement that serves as the traditional starting point for guided bay crossings. This picturesque harbor community retains its authentic maritime character with stone cottages, fishing boats, and a peaceful atmosphere that contrasts beautifully with the drama of the surrounding tidal flats.

activities.text: Embark on the legendary barefoot crossing of the Mont-Saint-Michel bay, an unforgettable adventure through one of the world's most dramatic tidal landscapes. Accompanied by an expert guide, wade through shallow channels, discover the phenomenon of quicksand safely, and experience the vast scale of this UNESCO-listed natural site. The bay witnesses Europe's highest tidal variations, creating an ever-changing seascape of extraordinary beauty.

Observe the remarkable wildlife that thrives in the bay's unique ecosystem, including elegant egrets, graceful seals, and the famous pré-salé sheep that graze the salt marshes. The herbus — coastal meadows regularly covered by the tides — support extraordinary biodiversity and produce the distinctively flavored lamb that is a regional culinary treasure.

days_plan.itin_title: Normandy's Bay of Mont-Saint-Michel: Coastal Drives & the Sacred Abbey

visits.text: Lac de Gérardmer, the largest natural lake in the Vosges, stretches across 115 hectares at an altitude of 660 meters. Glacial in origin, it measures 2.2 km long and reaches a depth of 38 meters. A 6 km trail allows you to walk around it.
Climb the Tour de Mérelle (observation tower) for 360° views over the lake, fir forests, and Vosges ridges. On clear days, you can make out the Hohneck to the south.
The Cascade de Mérelle nestles in the forest, accessible only on foot. Water tumbles from a porphyry slab into a setting of ferns and moss—one of the most photographed sites in the Vosges.

Visit the Confiserie des Hautes-Vosges, allowing for a return trip from Gérardmer, to watch the traditional production of certified organic Vosges candies. You can taste the candies while they are still warm as you leave the workshop.
La Mauselaine is a ski resort in the Vosges. Outside the ski season, follow the forest trails on foot up to the Tête de Grouvelin to discover the mountain scenery.

activities.text: On the lake, rental shops offer pedal boats, canoes, paddleboards, and electric boats. Only electric motors are allowed, ensuring calm on the water.
Thursday and Saturday mornings, the market at Place du 8-Mai gathers farm producers, Vosges honey, smoked charcuterie, and local textiles.

Head to a farmhouse inn for a marcaire meal: Vosges meat pie, smoked meat, tofailles (simmered potatoes and bacon pieces), and bilberry tart (wild blueberries). A hearty meal typical of the high pastures.

days_plan.itin_title: Vosges Road Trip: Lakes, Mountains & Thermal Spas

visits.text: Gerberoy has more rose bushes than inhabitants—barely 100 souls in this village listed among France's Most Beautiful Villages since 1982. Half-timbered houses from the 17th–18th centuries, wattle and daub, red brick and flint: a unique Picard-Norman blend in the Oise.

The Le Sidaner gardens occupy 4,000 m² on the ruins of the old château, across three terraced levels. Twenty-five rose varieties, a rose garden, a pergola and a Temple of Love: the post-impressionist painter designed them as a living canvas. Awarded the Jardin Remarquable label.

Push open the door of Saint-Pierre collegiate church, rebuilt in the 15th century after a fire set by the English. Choir stalls with carved misericords from the 15th century, Aubusson tapestries from the late 17th century and an 18th-century cope cabinet form a remarkable collection of furnishings.
The Jardin des Ifs harbours specimens whose age is unmatched in France. More intimate than the Le Sidaner gardens, it can be explored like a cabinet of botanical curiosities.
The 15th-century market hall, with its orange arcades, triangular pediment and timber frame, welcomed merchants for centuries. Beside it, the town well plunges to a depth of 70 m.

Spot the blue house from 1691 at the entrance to the ramparts: its woad-blue colour (a dye made from woad, grown in the Middle Ages in the Beauvaisis) covers the timber framing, shutters and door. On rue du Logis-du-Roy, the inn where Henry IV stayed in 1592 after the Battle of Aumale still bears his name.

activities.text: Walk the circuit of the ramparts via the tree-lined promenade, protected since 1913. The route offers views over the Beauvaisis countryside from the hilltop (188 m altitude) where the village perches.
If you visit on the first Sunday of June, the Fête des Roses transforms the village into an open-air garden, as it has done since 1928. Collectors' roses, floral activities and a village atmosphere.
Gerberoy hosts artists' workshops—painter, potter, glass artist—in its lanes. Take time to push open gallery doors to discover crafts inspired by the village.

days_plan.itin_title: Oise Circuit: châteaux, forests and history
Opal Coast Villages and Flemish Heartlands

visits.text: Gien Château overlooks the Loire from its polychrome brick platform — an Early Renaissance façade commissioned from 1482 onwards by Anne de Beaujeu, daughter of Louis XI and regent of France. It was she who transformed the former medieval fortress into a comfortable residence. Since 1952, the château has housed the Museum of Hunting, holder of the Musée de France label: falconry, venery and shooting are illustrated through paintings by Desportes and Oudry, 17th-century tapestries, antique weapons and mounted Chambord stags. A collection of 4,000 hunt buttons and hunting horns completes the display.

The Gien pottery works were founded in 1821 by an Englishman, Thomas Hall, who had spotted the site's advantages: siliceous pebbles from the Loire for the pastes, the state forest for the kilns, and the canals for transport. For two centuries the manufactory has kept alive the famous Gien Blue. The museum retraces the firm's history through its historic collections — armorial tableware, tile panels, fine faience — and a guided tour of the works (by reservation, every Wednesday morning) lets you see the artisans at work.

The stone bridge spans the Loire opposite the château. The view from the bridge — brick château against the sky, river and wooded islands — is Gien's postcard image. To the left, looking upstream, Sainte-Jeanne-d'Arc Church raises its red and black brick tower at the top of the mound, right beside the château.

activities.text: On Saturday mornings, the market enlivens the Loire quays opposite the château. It's the chance to find Gien faience pieces at factory prices in the surrounding shops — seconds and end-of-line stock available at the manufactory shop. Several local artisans also exhibit at the town's seasonal markets.

Use the afternoon to explore the Faience Route between Gien and Briare. This circuit links workshops, museums and ceramic and faience shops within a radius of about thirty kilometres. Gien is also a stop on the Jacques-Cœur tourist route and on the Loire à Vélo.

days_plan.itin_title: Loiret Road Trip: Orléans and the Châteaux of the Loire

visits.text: Vaison-la-Romaine is an anomaly: an almost complete Roman town whose layout can still be traced beneath the present-day town. The Villasse quarter and Puymin quarter together cover several hectares of open excavations—paved streets, columns, baths, houses with their original door thresholds. The restored Roman theater from the 1st century still hosts performances in summer. And the Roman bridge has spanned the Ouvèze for 2,000 years, still in service for pedestrians. Allow half a day to see everything properly.

The Dentelles de Montmirail are jagged limestone ridges that rise 600 meters above the plain—the effect is striking seen from below, from the vineyards of Gigondas or Beaumes. From the ridges themselves, the panorama takes in Mont Ventoux, the Alpilles and, on clear days, the Alps. Several marked trails leave from Gigondas village—allow 2 hours for the classic loop.

Beaumes-de-Venise and its naturally sweet fortified Muscat: here, white Grenache is fortified with alcohol during fermentation, which stops the conversion of sugars and yields a golden, lusciously sweet wine with 15 to 21° alcohol and aromas of orange blossom and apricot. Completely different from Sauternes—simpler, more direct, less complex, much more affordable. Serve chilled as an aperitif or with a dessert that is not too sweet.

activities.text: Lunch at L'Oustalet in Gigondas—one Michelin star in a village of 600 inhabitants, which says something about the concentration of good food in this corner of Provence. Vaucluse regional cuisine with local ingredients prepared with precision. The wine list is naturally centered on the Dentelles: Gigondas, Vacqueyras, Beaumes—a lesson in wine geography as you eat. Book ahead.

Tasting at Domaine du Cayron or Château de Saint-Cosme in Gigondas, an AOC recognized in 1971. Grenache dominates here (often over 80%), complemented by Syrah and Mourvèdre. These are fleshy, sun-filled wines with firm tannins that need 5 to 8 years to soften. Saint-Cosme also offers Vacqueyras cuvées from just next door—the chance to compare the two appellations with the same winemaker.

days_plan.itin_title: Rhône Valley: From Northern Syrahs to Southern Grenaches

visits.text: Saint-Pardoux Church. Church from the late 15th century housing an exceptional treasure: the reliquary shrine of Saint Stephen, a masterpiece of 12th-century Limoges enamel. Also several old statues and liturgical objects.
Notre-Dame du Rosaire Chapel. White Penitents' chapel located on the village's main street.
Ruins of Roche Haute Castle. Medieval ruins overlooking the village, visible from the main street.

activities.text: Gimel Waterfalls - Parc Vuillier. The Montane river plunges in three spectacular falls totaling 143 meters: the Grand Saut (45 m), the Redole (38 m) and the Queue de Cheval (60 m), which plunges into the “gouffre de l'Inferno.” Painter Gaston Vuillier developed this park between 1893 and 1899 with staircases and observation points. Abel Hugo, Victor's brother, was the first to describe the site's beauty in “La France pittoresque” (1883). Listed site since 1912.

Hike to the 4th waterfall and Pont du Péage. A free route taking about 1 hour 30 minutes one way leads to an additional waterfall outside the park that charges admission. The “cascadelles” are also accessible via the Petit Circuit in the forest.

days_plan.itin_title: Corrèze Road Trip: Villages and Dordogne Valley

visits.text: At the summit of the Ballon d'Alsace (1247 m), the statue of Jeanne d'Arc, erected in 1909, marks the boundary between three departments. The orientation table created in 1888 by the Club Alpin offers views of the Alps in clear weather. From Giromagny, reach the Ballon d'Alsace by road, then walk from the parking area to the summit.
Fort Dorsner was built in 1875 as part of the Séré de Rivières system to guard the Savoureuse valley. This pink sandstone fortress towers over Giromagny and the Ballon d'Alsace road.
The Église Saint-Jean-Baptiste in Giromagny houses a remarkable Verschneider organ. Neoclassical architecture from the 19th century.

activities.text: Arrange a road transfer from Giromagny to the start at the Ballon d'Alsace. Hike along the GR5 from the Ballon d'Alsace to Giromagny. A 13 km stage with 224 m of descent, marked with the Club Vosgien's red rectangles. The route passes the Chaumière and Wissgrut farm restaurants.
The mining trail crosses former argentiferous lead mines. The industrial history of the Haute-Savoureuse valley from the Middle Ages to the 20th century.

days_plan.itin_title: Territoire de Belfort Road Trip: The Citadel and the Lion

visits.text: The Clos Normand extends before Monet's house. Metal arches support nasturtiums and roses. Flower beds arranged by height and color compose a living painting that changes monthly, from April to October.

Cross the underground passage to reach the water garden. Weeping willows, bamboo, and water lilies surround the pond. Monet painted his Japanese bridge 45 times—it's made of beech wood, covered with wisteria planted by the painter himself.

The pink stucco house preserves its original interior: sun-yellow dining room, kitchen with blue Rouen tiles, and an exceptional collection of Japanese prints covering the walls from floor to ceiling.

The former Water Lilies studio, where Monet painted his large panoramic canvases, houses the foundation's shop. It was in this vast 300 m² space that he worked on the panels destined for the Orangerie in Paris.
The Museum of Impressionisms, a short walk away, presents temporary exhibitions linking Giverny to the Impressionist legacy. Its formal garden offers another perspective on the village.
Sainte-Radegonde Church, at the end of the main street, houses Monet's grave in its cemetery. The painter passed away in Giverny in 1926 after 43 years of residence.

activities.text: Wander through art galleries and studios in the village. Giverny still attracts painters and photographers who exhibit along Rue Claude Monet.
Bike ride on the Seine by Bike route between Vernon and Giverny. The route follows the river then crosses Norman countryside to the village.
Arrive early at the gardens' opening to enjoy the low-angle light on the pond—the very light Monet sought for his Water Lilies.

days_plan.itin_title: Complete Normandy Road Trip: Cliffs, D-Day Beaches and Mont-Saint-Michel
The 20 Most Beautiful Villages in Normandy

visits.text: Fort Charlemont. This stone colossus erected by Charles V in 1555 then remodeled by Vauban dominates the Meuse from an 80-meter rocky spur. The 60 hectares of successive fortifications testify to five centuries of military architecture evolution. Underground galleries, casemates, and bastions offer striking panoramas across the valley and nearby Belgian border.

Old Town of Givet. The Meuse separates the town into two historic quarters: Grand-Givet and Petit-Givet linked by the Pont de l'Europe. Cobbled lanes reveal old houses, Saint-Hilaire Church, and remnants of urban fortifications designed by Vauban. Lively quays border the river where barges and cruise boats dock at the river port.

Collegiate Church of Saint-Hilaire. Built in the 15th century, this Gothic church preserves a remarkable sculpted Renaissance rood screen and Baroque organ case. Restored stained glass and liturgical furnishings testify to the artistic wealth of this frontier town. Engraved tombstones tell the history of Givet families.

Vauban Towers and urban enclosure. Remnants of fortifications encircling Givet illustrate the genius of the royal architect who made the town impregnable. Monumental gates, watchtowers, and dried moats punctuate an urban route steeped in history. The Mont d'Haurs fortified camp completed the defensive system capable of accommodating 20,000 men.

activities.text: Hike in the Ardennes forest. Marked trails traverse the Pointe de Givet nature reserve surrounding Fort Charlemont. Limestone grasslands, rocky outcrops, and dense forests shelter remarkable fauna and flora. Viewpoints over the Meuse meanders reward climbs through fragrant undergrowth.

Cruise on the Meuse. Come aboard to discover the valley and the fort from the river. The commentary enriches the trip between limestone cliffs and riverside villages. Sightseeing trips, gourmet meals or musical evenings are offered from the port.

Ardennes gastronomy. Local restaurants showcase regional specialties including the famous boudin blanc de Rethel (white pudding), Ardennes pâté, and forest game. Craft breweries offer local beers including La Charlemont brewed in neighboring Belgium. Markets feature farm products, cheeses, and local cured meats.

days_plan.itin_title: Ardennes Road Trip: Forests & Fortresses (3 Days)

visits.text: Abbaye Notre-Dame de Sénanque nestles in a narrow valley, 4 km from Gordes. Founded in 1148 by Cistercians, this Romanesque jewel is still inhabited by monks. Its cloister with round arches, church oriented northeast, roofs of lauze stone.
Lavandin fields surround the abbey. From mid-June to mid-July, purple rows ripple in the mistral. The monks cultivate, harvest and distil the essence to finance the monastery's upkeep.

Gordes stands on a rocky spur facing the Luberon. Voted most beautiful village in the world by Travel + Leisure, its golden stone houses cling to the slopes in tiers. Steep cobbled lanes, shaded squares, Renaissance façades.

Château de Gordes, a medieval fortress remodelled in the 16th century, dominates the central square. Now transformed into a cultural centre, it hosts contemporary art exhibitions. Monumental Renaissance fireplace, spiral staircase.

The Village des Bories brings together dry-stone huts built without mortar, simply by stacking stones. These examples of vernacular architecture date from the 18th century and housed shepherds and farm tools. About ten restored bories.
Roussillon raises its ochre and blood-red façades on a rocky peak. Natural pigments have coloured the village walls for centuries, from pale yellow to deep purple.
The Sentier des Ocres winds through former quarries. Striated cliffs, fairy chimneys, bright red sand beneath the pines. Two possible circuits: 30 or 60 minutes of walking.
