Bonnieux clings in tiers to the north slope of the Luberon. Climb by staircases between stone houses, upper church perched at 400 m altitude. Panorama over the Calavon valley and Mont Ventoux.

Ménerbes stretches its lanes along a limestone ridge. Listed among the Plus Beaux Villages de France, it preserves Renaissance houses, ramparts and a 16th-century citadel. Views down over vineyards and cherry orchards.

activities.text: Stop at the viewpoint on the D15 before Gordes. The village spreads out in an amphitheatre, houses stacked in terraces. Golden light late in the day, cypresses punctuating the landscape.
Gastronomic dinner on a Gordes terrace. Panoramic views over the Calavon valley and Luberon in the distance. Refined cuisine, AOC Côtes du Luberon wines, attentive service.
Relaxation break at the mas or hotel pool. Provençal sunshine, cicadas, lounger in the shade of olive trees. Reading, nap, swim.

days_plan.itin_title: The 15 Most Beautiful Villages of the Luberon
Vaucluse: Avignon, Luberon Villages & Ventoux Routes
The Most Beautiful Villages: From the Alps to the Luberon in 3 Days
Provence & French Riviera Road Trip: Lavender, Villages & Beaches
Provence & French Riviera Road Trip: Lavender, Villages & Beaches

visits.text: The water is cold, the rock is red and the bottom of the Pennafort gorges stays cool when the coast swelters. The Rioufreid tumbles from pool to pool for about 400 meters, down to the waterfall. Be aware: a 1996 decree prohibits swimming, despite what most visitors do, and you can be fined.

Built in 1855 on the remains of an 11th-century tower, the Notre-Dame de Pennafort chapel crowns a rocky spur where two valleys meet, in a Greek Revival style unusual for the region. A footpath leads up from the picnic area. Unobstructed views over the gorges, and usually nobody around.

activities.text: Follow the Rioufreid riverbed from the Pennafort gorges parking lot, on the D25 between Callas and Le Muy: 2.6 km round trip, some rocks to cross, feet sometimes in the water. Parking is free and quite large. Come in spring: in summer, the river dries up and there's not much left to see.

days_plan.itin_title: Roquebrune-sur-Argens: sea, villages and the Var in 10 days

visits.text: Colorado in Provence: the Blavet gorges owe their red color to amaranth-red rhyolite, a volcanic rock from the Estérel massif. The Blavet, a tributary of the Argens, has carved a canyon of cliffs and rock spires here. The contrast with the cork oaks is stark. Low-angle morning or evening light brings out everything the rock has to offer.

Rhyolite was extracted here until the 18th century to carve millstones for flour and oil mills. Remains of millstones survive along the Blavet gorges trail. The wild scenery is therefore partly a former industrial site. Spotting them requires attention: they're not signposted on the ground.

activities.text: Park at the Blavet gorges parking lot on the D47, on the Bagnols-en-Forêt side, for the orange-marked loop. Two fords, a steep, stony descent and a viewpoint orientation panel as your reward. Avoid this route in rainy weather: the rocks become as slippery as bars of soap and water levels at the fords rise quickly.

If you're a climber, climbing is the best reason to come to the Blavet gorges: the rhyolite has a texture very different from the Var's limestone, and the site attracts climbing teams from far beyond the region. A climbing guide is sold at the Bagnols-en-Forêt tourist information office. There is a small but real risk of falling rocks below the cliff faces.

days_plan.itin_title: Roquebrune-sur-Argens: sea, villages and the Var in 10 days

visits.text: The gorges du Loup cut deep into the limestone between Bramafan and Pont-du-Loup. The Loup, a river flowing down from the plateau de Caussols, has carved natural pools here called “giant's kettles”, polished by erosion over millennia. Plan a stop at the entrance to the Saut du Loup for your first viewpoint.

The Saut du Loup is the main stop in the gorges: a 40-meter waterfall plunging into an emerald basin surrounded by rocks sculpted into hollows. A privately owned site with an admission fee (a few euros), open from April to October. Allow 30 minutes on-site to look around and take photos. Just downstream, the Courmes waterfall (also 40 m) can be seen from the road for free.

activities.text: The Gorges du Loup are one of the most renowned canyoning spots in the Alpes-Maritimes. In summer, local outfitters offer half-day and full-day trips: jumps, natural slides, rappels into pools. Rates range from €60 to €90 per half-day depending on the route. Beginner routes are accessible from ages 10–12. Book a few days ahead in July–August.

days_plan.itin_title: Nice's hinterland: 8 days of hilltop villages and the Mercantour

visits.text: Gorron is a small character town set on the granite foundations of the Armorican Massif, at the historic crossroads of the Breton and Norman marches. The Colmont river flows through it, creating a green setting bordered by old wash houses.

Saint-Martin church, rebuilt from 1868 to 1874 in neo-Romanesque style, dominates the town from its tall square bell tower that forms the entrance porch. Inside, an altarpiece depicting the stoning of Saint Stephen deserves attention.

Rue des Chauvinettes, quite steep, runs within the outline of the old fortress built around 1162 by Henry II Plantagenet, King of England. The granite flanks of the Colmont riverbanks served as natural fortification. The castle, contested between the lords of Mayenne and the English crown, was destroyed during the Hundred Years' War.

Stroll the lanes to spot the town hall housed in the old market halls, 19th-century bourgeois houses and the metal footbridge above the street—remnant of the former furniture factory that brought industrial fame to Gorron after the clog makers.

activities.text: The Colmont trail (n°11, yellow markers, FFRandonnée certified) starts from the church and circles the town between sunken lanes, hedgerows and Colmont riverbanks. Along the way, the Roche menhir has stood since approximately 4,000 BC beside a stream: 4.40 meters tall, classified Historic Monument. Legend says that on Christmas night, at the twelve strokes of midnight, the stone turns twelve times on itself.
The Colmont Leisure Park offers in season treetop adventure courses, kayaking, swin-golf, outdoor laser tag and paintball in a preserved natural setting.

days_plan.itin_title: Mayenne Circuit: Hedgerows and Medieval Towns

visits.text: Goudargues fully deserves its nickname of “little Venice of Gard.” The La Fontaine canal that runs through the village is fed by a Vauclusian spring with a constant flow (1,400 m³/h) and a stable temperature of 14°C year-round. The Benedictine monks who developed the site in the Middle Ages chose their location well. Roman remains attest to human presence as early as the 3rd century—the village name itself comes from “Gordanicus,” the name of a Roman villa that occupied the site. The plane trees lining the canal were planted in 1821. Sit on a terrace on the quay and watch the water flow between the plane trees: it's the most representative image of southern Gard.

The Notre-Dame-et-Saint-Michel abbey church is a surprise for those expecting a simple village church: it's a 12th-century abbey building, listed as a Historic Monument, which ranks among the most interesting Romanesque buildings in Languedoc. It developed around a Benedictine cloister — the refectory and chapter house have survived and now host cultural events. The choir and apse still date from the original Romanesque period.

Walk through Goudargues' narrow streets: the large washhouse with its emblematic bronze frog, the fountains, the bridges over the canal, the shaded squares. The village has local craft shops and tasting cellars for wines from the Gard Côtes du Rhône. In summer, the Wednesday evening market is one of the week's most pleasant moments.

activities.text: The bike loop from Goudargues to the surrounding wine-growing hamlets (15 to 20 km, gently rolling terrain) is one of the best ways to explore the Gard countryside. The roads between vineyards and garrigue have virtually no traffic.

The Cèze is accessible on foot from Goudargues in 10 minutes via the path that starts from the washhouse. Swimming spots in limestone pools upstream and downstream from the village allow you to enjoy the clear water in summer, with fewer crowds than at La Roque-sur-Cèze.

days_plan.itin_title: Cèze Valley and Ardèche Gorges Circuit

visits.text: Goult is worth the effort: less known than Gordes or Roussillon, this village perched in the heart of the Luberon has retained genuine authenticity. Its château (private) belonged to the powerful Agoult family, whose name gave the village its identity. As you wander through its lanes with vaulted passages, arcades and old archways, you'll discover stone and ochre facades that change color with the light. The Thursday morning market on the Place de la Libération is a good excuse to meet local producers.

The Moulin de Jerusalem is the village's crowning glory. Perched atop the hill behind the chateau, this late-17th-century windmill operated until 1919. It owes its unusual name to the surrounding quarter, so called in reference to the Crusades in which the lords of Agoult took part. After serving as an astronomy teaching centre for the Institut Geographique National from 1947 to 1990, it was restored to its original state by the municipality between 1994 and 1997. It still has its sails and its interior mechanism, a rarity in Provence. Panoramic view over the Calavon valley from the summit.

activities.text: Heritage trail up to the windmill and the old communal oven (30 min from the center). The path is well marked and offers beautiful views over the Claparèdes plateau and the Luberon.

Trail between dry-stone terraces, olive trees and vines—a short loop (approximately 1h) starting from the Conservatoire des terrasses de cultures, a restored landscape site showcasing local agricultural heritage. Make the detour to the Romanesque Chapel of Saint-Véran, nestled in a pine forest away from the village.

days_plan.itin_title: The 15 Most Beautiful Villages of the Luberon

visits.text: Goumois is a Franco-Swiss village split in two by the Treaty of Vienna in 1815, with the Doubs serving as the border. Nestled in the valley hollow, it is surrounded by the Corniche road, the Rocher du Singe, and the ruins of the medieval castle of Franquemont. Jean-Jacques Rousseau came to botanize here as early as 1748 with botanist Gagnebin. The bridge over the Doubs connects the two namesake communes.

The Corniche de Goumois viewpoint offers an exceptional panorama over the Doubs gorges and the Swiss Jura. The very picturesque road that leads there dominates the gorges and offers a series of varied viewpoints. It is the meeting place for lovers of wild and authentic nature.

The Maîche plateau extends between 800 and 1,000 meters altitude, bounded by the deep valleys of the Doubs and Dessoubre. This characteristic area of the Haut-Doubs offers vast expanses dotted with old Comtoise farms. Maîche, the canton's chief town near the Swiss border, is integrated into the Doubs Horloger regional natural park.

activities.text: Goumois is an internationally renowned fishing spot for trout and grayling. The Franco-Swiss Doubs offers 150 km of marked hiking trails. The most daring will take the Échelles de la Mort, installed in a wild and spectacular site near Charquemont.

Le Russey, at nearly 1,000 metres above sea level on the Maîche plateau, offers views over the surrounding plateaus. The 19th-century town hall is listed as a Historic Monument. The church of Saint-Nicolas and the Saint-Roch chapel reflect the local religious heritage. It is the birthplace of the Almanach Vermot, founded by Joseph Féréol Vermot, born here in 1828. About 20 km from the base town, a 30-minute drive.

days_plan.itin_title: Doubs Circuit: Watchmaking and Swiss Border

visits.text: The Church of Saint-Pierre sits atop Gourdon's hilltop. Its southern Gothic facade, flanked by two defensive towers, conceals a richly decorated interior: an 18th–19th-century tribune organ, altarpiece, and bas-reliefs. The 14th-century rose window on the main portal and the large apse window play with light throughout the day.

Reach the château esplanade at the hilltop's highest point, 286 meters elevation. From the site of the former castle and its ramparts, panoramic views extend across Gourdon's rooftops, the Bouriane countryside, and the distant plateaus.

The Maison du Sénéchal, built in the 13th century, was the residence of the royal official responsible for justice and local administration. Now converted into a Center for Architecture and Heritage Interpretation, it presents the history of the town and of the Bouriane.

The Gardens of the Hilltop nestle in Gourdon's medieval heart. The Zig-Zag Gardens recreate the medieval atmosphere; the Sénéchal Gardens shelter a performance courtyard adorned with a topiary butterfly; the Fairy Tale Garden blends wicker structures, wooden characters, and ornamental grasses. All maintained by passionate volunteers.

The Cougnac Caves, 3 kilometers from Gourdon, comprise two cavities discovered in 1949 and 1952. The first cave displays a mineral forest of rare density: stalactites, translucent tubular formations, delicate draperies. The second contains Paleolithic paintings about 30,000 years old—ibex, mammoths, giant deer, and rare human figures called "wounded men." Listed as Historic Monuments.

activities.text: Original sensory tours invite you to discover Gourdon blindfolded, guided by touch, hearing, and smell. An unconventional approach to heritage that engages all the senses.

Walk the medieval lanes of the historic center: golden stone houses, pointed arches, covered passages. The marked pedestrian circuit leads from one building to the next in a village founded in the 11th century.
Gourdon's market gathers local producers and artisans. Black truffles in winter, porcini mushrooms in autumn, goat cheeses, walnuts, and honey year-round.

visits.text: Goury marks the northwestern tip of Cotentin. Its small harbor, wedged between moorlands and rocks, faces the Cap de la Hague lighthouse and Raz Blanchard, one of Europe's most powerful currents.
The Goury lighthouse, built in 1837 on a wave-battered rock, is visible only from the coast. The old lifeboat shelter, built into the cliff face, testifies to the dangers of the raz.
The Nez de Jobourg drops 128 m into the sea. The path runs along the edge through a landscape of low heath and wind-battered gorse.
Écalgrain Bay, accessible on foot from the GR223, offers a wild beach framed by green cliffs. Sunsets are spectacular, facing the Channel Islands.
The hamlet of Port Racine, a few kilometers away, claims the title of France's smallest harbor. Two or three boats fit in its natural granite basin.

activities.text: Hike on the GR223 (customs officers' path). The section between Goury and Nez de Jobourg crosses bare moorlands swept by wind with plunging views over the Channel.
Seabird observation from the Nez de Jobourg cliffs. Fulmars, European shags, and gannets soar above the precipices.
Sunset at Écalgrain Bay, facing the Channel Islands. In clear weather, Alderney and Jersey's coasts stand out on the horizon.

days_plan.itin_title: The 20 Most Beautiful Villages in Normandy
Cotentin, Pays d'Auge: 5 days exploring the most beautiful villages

visits.text: Start with Écalgrain Bay in La Hague. It's one of the wildest panoramas in the Cotentin - schist cliffs plunging into turquoise water, with the Channel Islands as a backdrop on clear days. The coastal path along the ridge offers breathtaking views. Bring a windbreaker - even in summer, the wind blows hard here.

Continue to Nez de Jobourg, the highest point of the Norman cliffs - up to 128 meters above the sea. From the viewpoint, you'll see sea caves carved into the rock below. In rough weather, waves crash into them with thunder. A marked path allows you to walk safely along the ridge.

Make a stop at the Vauville mare nature reserve, protected by a thin dune cordon. From the Thot viewpoint, you overlook this 67-hectare coastal pond owned by the Coastal Conservatory. It's a remarkable Natura 2000 site for observing migratory birds - binoculars recommended.

Heading south, stop at Flamanville Castle. Built in the 17th century from local granite, it's visited mainly for its gardens and park - the castle itself is private. The view of the coast from the terraces is worth the detour.

Finish at Gouville-sur-Mer, where colorful beach cabins lined up on the sand are the classic photo spot of the Cotentin's west coast. At low tide, oyster parks stretch as far as the eye can see - if you meet an oyster farmer, don't hesitate to buy a dozen directly from them.

activities.text: Coastal hike between dunes and tidal flats on a marked section of the GR 223. You'll alternate between sandy paths, passages over rocks, and views of oyster parks. Allow 1 to 1.5 hours depending on your pace.

days_plan.itin_title: Complete Normandy Road Trip: Cliffs, D-Day Beaches and Mont-Saint-Michel

visits.text: The Grand Palais—240 meters long, a nave 45 meters high topped with 15,000 m² of glass canopy—is one of Paris's largest exhibition spaces. Built in 1897-1900 for the Universal Exposition, it hosts major temporary exhibitions at the Galeries Nationales and significant cultural events. Its central nave, the largest in France, is open to the public during certain events. Check the current program before coming—exhibitions change every two to three months and require advance booking.

activities.text: Walk or rent a bike up the Champs-Élysées to the Arc de Triomphe—1.9 km of perspective from Place de la Concorde. The panorama from the top of the Arc (284 steps, open daily) embraces the 12 radiating avenues and, on clear days, the towers of La Défense on the horizon.

days_plan.itin_title: The Great Museums of Paris

visits.text: The highlight of the trip: Mont-Saint-Michel. Plan a day trip from Granville. Arrive early - before 9 a.m. if possible. Park in the main car park (paid) and take the free shuttle or walk 2.5 km along the footbridge. The Mont reveals itself gradually - first its distant silhouette, then the ramparts, then the village, then the abbey at the top. A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1979, it welcomes 3 million visitors a year.

First climb along the Grand-Rue through the medieval village—narrow lanes, half-timbered houses, shops (lots of tourism, but the village as a whole is authentic). Then climb to the abbey. The tour with an audio guide lasts about 1½ hours. The story begins in 708 when the Archangel Michael supposedly appeared in a dream to Bishop Aubert to command him to build a sanctuary on this 92-meter-high rock. Benedictine monks settled here in 966. The “Merveille”—the 13th-century Gothic building clinging to the north face—is an architectural marvel, with its three stacked levels of halls.

Walk the circuit of the ramparts. Built from the 12th to 14th centuries, they enabled the Mont to withstand an English siege from 1423 to 1434 during the Hundred Years' War—one of the rare Norman sites never to have been taken. The western terrace in front of the abbey church offers the most open view over the bay.

A day in the Norman bocage. Thirty minutes from Granville, Villedieu-les-Poêles has been the "copper city" since the 12th century. The Cornille-Havard bell foundry, operating since 1865, is one of France's last—it cast bells for Notre-Dame de Paris. The museum tour shows you the manufacturing stages, from the clay mold to the bronze pouring at 1,150°C.

Wander through Villedieu's artisan lanes—you'll pass workshops of coppersmithing (working copper), pottery and lacemaking. The Cour du Foyer, former cloister of the Hospitallers, is a haven of calm in the center of town. Push open the doors of workshops that are open—artisans readily demonstrate their skills.

Continue to Mortain-Bocage (about 62 km from Granville, a 1-hour drive). The Grande Cascade, 25 meters high, is the tallest waterfall in western France. You reach it along an easy 800-meter path from the town center. The Petite Cascade is less well known but just as pretty. Do not miss the Abbaye Blanche, founded in the 12th century at the foot of the waterfall.

Final day in Granville, the "Monaco of the North." Begin with the fortified Haute-Ville, perched on a rocky promontory. Pass through the Grande Porte and climb the granite lanes to the Église Notre-Dame-du-Cap-Lihou. The ramparts offer a panorama over the harbor, the Chausey Islands offshore and, in fine weather, Jersey on the horizon.

At the far tip, the Pointe du Roc—a rocky spur battered by waves where the old signal station stands. It's the best spot to watch the spring tides. The Granville lighthouse, steps away, has guided boats to the harbor since 1828.

Don't miss the Musée Christian Dior, housed in the villa Les Rhumbs, the couturier's childhood home. Purchased by the Dior family in 1906, it stands above the cliff facing the sea and the Channel Islands. His mother Madeleine created an English-style garden there, and young Christian designed the pergola and reflecting pool around 1920. The museum presents a new themed exhibition each year—haute couture dresses, accessories, perfumes. The garden is open to everyone, free of charge, year-round.

If you have time, continue to the Musée d'Art Moderne Richard Anacréon in the Haute-Ville. Richard Anacréon, a Parisian bookseller born in Granville, bequeathed his hometown a collection of rare books and works by Derain, Vlaminck, Utrillo or Signac. A small museum offering a brief but worthwhile visit.

activities.text: If the tide schedule allows, watch the rising waters from the walkway bridge or from the ramparts. Mont-Saint-Michel Bay experiences the greatest tides in continental Europe—up to 15 meters of tidal range during equinoctial spring tides. Legend says the sea rises “at the speed of a galloping horse”—in reality it's about 6 km/h, but it's still impressive.

For a different experience, book a guided walk across the bay. Qualified guides take you across 7 km of tidal sands (14 km round trip), telling the legends of the Mont and showing you how to avoid quicksand. Depart from Genêts (about 22 km from Granville, a 25-minute drive) or the Bec d'Andaine - be prepared to go barefoot and wear clothes that can get wet.

From the Mortain viewing point (beside the Chapelle Saint-Michel), you sweep your gaze across the entire Norman bocage—and in clear weather, the silhouette of Mont-Saint-Michel appears on the horizon. It's one of Normandy's highest points. In August 1944, the German counteroffensive at Mortain (Operation Lüttich) was one of the fiercest battles of the Battle of Normandy.

End the journey with a stroll along the Plat Gousset seawall and the beach of the same name. This crescent-shaped beach of fine sand, protected by the seawall, is Granville's family beach. The Art Deco casino and bathing cabins complete the seaside picture. If you're there on a Saturday morning, Granville's covered market is one of the best in Manche—fish, seafood, salt-marsh lamb.

visits.text: Grasse has been the world's perfume capital since the late 18th century - perfumery gradually replaced tanning, which had previously made the town wealthy. Local expertise (growing perfume plants, extracting essences, composing fragrances) has been inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list since 2018. The old town has ocher and yellow façades, where 17th- and 18th-century buildings stand alongside 19th-century mansions.

The International Perfume Museum is the world's most important museum of its kind. Created in 1989 and renovated in 2008, its 3,500 m² trace 4,000 years of perfume history, from the Egyptian canopic jar to Lalique bottles. Over 50,000 objects in the collection. The olfactory trail, with around a hundred essences to smell, is the standout experience. Allow at least 90 minutes. Closed Tuesdays in low season.

Visit one of the three historic perfumeries: Galimard, founded in 1747 (the oldest), Molinard, operating since 1849, or Fragonard, operating since 1926. Guided laboratory tours are free—copper stills, enfleurage trays, packaging rooms. No obligation to buy, but the shop is part of the tour. Galimard offers an archival video on rose picking in the 1950s—worth the visit on its own.

Notre-Dame du Puy Cathedral, a 12th-century Romanesque building, houses three paintings by Rubens (The Crowning with Thorns, Saint Helena and the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, and The Raising of the Cross), which arrived in Grasse in the 19th century after an eventful journey from Italy. Alongside them, a Fragonard (The Washing of the Feet, 1754)—one of the few religious works by the Grasse-born painter—and an altarpiece attributed to the school of Louis Bréa. A short but memorable visit for painting enthusiasts.

The Fragonard Villa-Museum, elegant 17th-century bastide, exhibits works by Jean-Honoré Fragonard in the garden where he stayed with his cousin during the Revolution. The Grasse painter (1732-1806) is represented by drawings, copies and his famous "Progress of Love in the Heart of a Young Girl" cycle (copies, the originals being at the Frick Collection in New York).

activities.text: Perfume creation workshop in Grasse: guided by a “nose,” you learn to distinguish fragrance families and blend your own custom fragrance. Galimard, Molinard and Fragonard all offer sessions lasting 1 to 2 hours, around €50–80. Booking essential, especially in high season.

The market on place aux Aires, on Saturday mornings: tapenades, olive oils from Cagnes and Nice, Marseille soaps, local fruit and vegetables. The square itself, beneath its century-old plane trees and around its 18th-century fountain, is one of the liveliest spots in the old town.

The Jardins du MIP in Mouans-Sartoux (10 km from Grasse) are a living collection of perfume plants: 700 species including May roses, Grasse jasmine, tuberoses and violets that supply the perfumeries. Awarded the “Jardin remarquable” label. Peak bloom in May–June for roses, August for jasmine.

Make a detour to Vallauris, about a 25-minute drive away. Picasso discovered ceramics there in 1946 at the Madoura workshop before settling in this potters’ village in 1948. Over about twenty years, he created nearly 4,000 original works there. At the Musée national Picasso, you can admire “War and Peace,” two monumental panels painted in 1952 and installed in the château’s former chapel. The Madoura workshop is currently closed for renovation.

Provence & French Riviera Road Trip: Lavender, Villages & Beaches

visits.text: Gravelines is France's only fortified town entirely surrounded by water. Founded in the 12th century by the counts of Flanders at the mouth of the Aa, it has preserved its star-shaped bastioned walls intact—ramparts, ravelins, counterscarps and moats fed by the river.

In 1525, Charles V had the counts' castle rebuilt and ordered the construction of the first bastioned ramparts with six large bastions. After the French conquest in 1658, Vauban remodelled the fortifications from 1678, tripling the width of the defensive perimeter and adding a second ring of ravelins in 1699, plus a flushing sluice system capable of flooding the surrounding area in the event of an attack.

The château-arsenal houses the musée du Dessin et de l'Estampe originale—France's only museum devoted exclusively to prints. Vauban's powder magazine presents the history and techniques of printmaking; the salle du Pilier, a former defensive casemate, hosts temporary exhibitions.

The Porte aux Boules, the first listed Historic Monument in Gravelines, owes its name to the two decorative balls atop its stone masonry. The former Dunkirk gate retains its drawbridge and opens onto the rampart walk, which allows a complete circuit of the walls.

Gravelines belfry, inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage list, towers over the town hall. Saint-Willibrord church, the town's oldest building, recalls Gravelines' Flemish origins—Saint-Omer's outer port in the Middle Ages.

The gardens laid out in the bastions are worth a detour: the formal French-style jardin de l'Arsenal, the jardin de la Liberté (awarded the Jardin remarquable label) with its 19th-century bandstand and old rose varieties, and the vegetable gardens along the rampart walk. Gravelines holds the Ville 4 Fleurs label and received the Fleur d'Or in 2016.

activities.text: The Embarcadère Vauban Promenade offers electric boats, rowing boats and pedalos for exploring the moats and fortifications from the water. A route of about an hour, skimming alongside vegetation-covered brick ramparts.

The Son et Lumière de Gravelines brings together 350 costumed extras each summer to recount 1,000 years of history. Cannon fire, mounted combat and over 1,500 costumes: a night-time show to experience within the ramparts.

The beach at Petit-Fort-Philippe, Gravelines' seaside resort, offers a vast sandy foreshore with blue-and-white beach huts. The marina, at the mouth of the Aa, provides a waterside stroll among masts and sea spray.

days_plan.itin_title: Opal Coast Villages and Flemish Heartlands

visits.text: The Baron Martin Museum occupies an 18th-century château that hosted the Count of Provence (future Louis XVIII) from 1777 to 1783. Awarded the Musée de France designation, it has 14 fine art galleries with sumptuous decor: overdoors, female mascarons, trumeaux, and stuccowork. The collections feature Prud'hon, Tissot, Boucher, Van Loo, Van Kessel, and Monticelli.
The museum's medieval cellars house 600 archaeological pieces, including the famous pagan sarcophagus from Mantoche (1844) and Greek vases from the 4th-5th centuries BC.

Look up at Notre-Dame Basilica, a Gothic edifice dating from the 15th–16th centuries and dominating the upper town. Built after the 1477 fire, it has housed the heart of Saint Peter Fourier since 1641 and the miraculous statue of Our Lady of Gray since 1802, which earned it the title of minor basilica in 1948.

Inside the basilica, admire the 11.1-meter Tree of Jesse, made in the 16th century by the Flemish sculptors of Brou. The sacred art treasures include reliquaries, chalices, monstrances, and sculptures.
Discover the Hôtel de Conflans, built in the 16th century, with its remarkable Renaissance-style staircase tower (viorbe), impressive for its size.

activities.text: Stroll through the museum's park, laid out in the French formal style, which offers a stunning view of the Saône valley from its terrace graced with two ceremonial cannons. The entrance is marked by the Paravis tower, a crenellated remnant of the former medieval fortress.

Climb the Saint-Pierre Fourier tower with its pivoting staircase, unique in France, leading to a small Renaissance room where Peter Fourier, a priest from Lorraine fleeing his homeland, hid in 1636. Once rotated, the staircase conceals access to this secret hideaway.

Board the Audacieux, a solar-electric boat, for a narrated cruise on the Saône. Admire the river landscapes and discover the history of river trade that made Gray prosperous from the 12th century onward.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Saône Tour: Comtois Plateaus and Heritage

places.name: Grenoble

visits.text: Stop in Chambéry in the morning (about 58 km from Grenoble, a 40-minute drive). The capital of the Duchy of Savoy from 1295 to 1563, the town has retained an understated elegance. The Château des Ducs overlooks the old town - you can walk through its courtyards and around its exterior, and glimpse the Sainte-Chapelle, which housed the Holy Shroud before it was moved to Turin. On your way down, do not miss the fontaine des Éléphants in the central square - four elephants without hindquarters, earning them the local nickname “the four without backsides”. The vaulted passages and alleyways of the old center are a pleasure to explore, especially on Saturday mornings when the market is in full swing.

In Grenoble, the Musée de Grenoble is one of France's most important museums for older and contemporary art—Matisse, Chagall, and Picasso are all represented. The light-filled modern building is pleasant to explore even if you're not a dedicated museum enthusiast. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes for a proper visit.

Take a stroll through Grenoble's old center along the banks of the Isère. The city is wedged between three massifs—Chartreuse, Vercors, and Belledonne—giving it a spectacular mountain backdrop visible from every street. The area around Place Saint-André and Rue Très-Cloîtres retains a medieval character.

activities.text: Ride up to the Bastille in Grenoble's famous 'bubbles'—those spherical plexiglass cabins that have been a city symbol since 1976, designed by engineer Denis Creissels and manufactured by local company Poma. The cable car, inaugurated in 1934, is one of the world's first urban cable cars, following those in Rio and Cape Town. In 4 minutes and 266 meters of elevation gain, you reach the 19th-century fort at 476 m altitude. The panorama over Grenoble and the three surrounding massifs is spectacular—on clear days, you can see Mont Blanc. Walk back down the trails if you have time (45 min).

days_plan.itin_title: From the Alps to the Ardèche Gorges: Lakes, Peaks and Garrigue

map_keywords: Château des Ducs de Savoie Chambéry

visits.text: In the hamlet of Gruchy, you'll be shown the house where Jean-François Millet was born on 4 October 1814 to a peasant family. The painter, who moved to Barbizon in 1849, rarely returned, but the moors and cliffs of La Hague left their mark on his entire body of work. The path towards the sea complements the visit well.

days_plan.itin_title: Cotentin, Pays d'Auge: 5 days exploring the most beautiful villages

visits.text: Visit the largest Renaissance château in southeastern France, perched on a 33-meter rocky promontory. Mentioned as early as the 11th century as a fortress, it was transformed during the Renaissance into a sumptuous residence. The Marquise de Sévigné stayed here during three long visits and died here in 1696. Admire the Adhémar Gallery, the Tinel hall, the Prelates' wing, and Madame de Grignan's chamber in the former medieval keep.

Stroll the famous terraces built atop the Saint-Sauveur collegiate church that offer unforgettable 360° panoramas of Provence. The view extends to La Lance mountain, Mont Ventoux, and the Dentelles de Montmirail. Madame de Sévigné wrote: 'It is even pleasant not to be tempted to leave your beautiful terraces.'

Explore this charming medieval village ranked among France's Most Beautiful Villages that hugs the contours of the rocky promontory. Reach the village via steep alleys where you can admire the 14th-century belfry and superb 15th-century houses. The village cultivates both its literary heritage and its terroir: AOC vineyards, truffle grounds, lavender fields.

Visit this collegiate church built in the 16th century, one of the first buildings listed as a Historical Monument in 1840. The Renaissance façade features two symmetrical square towers. Madame de Sévigné was interred in this collegiate church on April 18, 1696. She still rests in this history-laden place.

activities.text: Discover Madame de Sévigné's apartments, the painting collection from the 16th to 20th centuries, and the interpretation space tracing the château's architectural evolution. Guided tours illuminate daily life of Provençal nobility in the 17th century. Possibly attend one of the many concerts held in the Adhémar Gallery.

Walk through the surrounding landscapes where vineyards, lavender, and truffle grounds create a typically Provençal mosaic of colors. In June-July, blooming lavender fields offer an unforgettable spectacle with the château as backdrop.

Visit producers directly and the village's fine restaurants to discover local gastronomy. Taste AOC Grignan-les-Adhemar wines, Cotes-du-Rhone, Tricastin black truffles, Nyons olive oil, and goat cheeses.

days_plan.itin_title: Drome Provencale Road Trip: Villages and Terroirs

visits.text: Grimaud Castle, built in the 11th century, preserves its three defensive walls, two large round towers, and a medieval keep. Pillaged during the Revolution, it still offers a panorama over the Gulf of Saint-Tropez and the Maures massif despite its ruined state. In summer, the ramparts provide the backdrop for the Grimaldines festival.

Saint-Michel church, Romanesque and dating from the 12th century, is a listed historic monument. Its typically Provençal architecture contrasts with the Penitents' and Saint-Roch chapels, whose mural paintings have been restored.

Get lost in the village's cobbled lanes: Rue des Arcades houses the Templars' house, a fine 16th-century Renaissance building adorned with three Gothic arches. Mullioned windows and doorways framed with serpentinite punctuate the stroll.

The Saint-Roch mill, a 17th-century windmill restored in 1990 by the Compagnons du Tour de France, overlooks the village from its hill. On the ground, a large slab was used for threshing wheat; beside it, an old press produced olive oil.

Reach the Pont des Fées via a 3 km loop from the mill. This 15th-century arched bridge spans the Garde and served as an aqueduct to supply the village with water. The trail follows the river through a cool, shaded valley.

activities.text: Port-Grimaud, a waterside town created in the 1960s by architect François Spoerry, can be explored by boat on its canals. Each house has direct water access and a mooring ring. “Provençal Venice” can also be discovered on foot from the village.
The Provençal markets of Grimaud and Port-Grimaud alternate through the week. Local producers and artisans offer fruit, cheese, olive oil, and art objects.
Several wine estates around the village offer tastings of AOC Côtes de Provence wines. The Grimaud wine cooperative lets you sample the local vintages.

days_plan.itin_title: Var Road Trip: French Riviera & Provence Verte
Roquebrune-sur-Argens: sea, villages and the Var in 10 days
Var in 4 Days: From Bormes to the Most Beautiful Villages of the Verdon

visits.text: The cave mouth suddenly comes into view at the foot of the cliff: Mueron Cave has a monumental entrance and extends far into the rhyolite. It was occupied in 10,000 BC, then served as a Bronze Age campsite. South-facing, with a commanding view over the valley and a stream below: it had everything. It still shelters hikers caught in thunderstorms.

Two natural arches are tucked against the cliff face, about ten meters above the trail, a few steps from Mueron Cave. They go unnoticed unless you look for them. The cave itself is not very deep despite its monumental entrance. Look up just after the cave, or you'll walk past without seeing them.

activities.text: Approach along the orange-marked trail: there are two fords to cross before reaching Mueron Cave. The overhanging routes beneath the cave mouth make it one of the Var's major climbing spots. Good footwear is essential: the descent just beyond is steep and rutted by erosion.

If you're not a climber, continue to the viewpoint orientation panel above Mueron Cave: the panorama takes in the Estérel, Roquebrune Rock and the Fréjus-Saint-Raphaël coast. Return along the Bayonne track, lined with chestnut trees.

days_plan.itin_title: Roquebrune-sur-Argens: sea, villages and the Var in 10 days

visits.text: The Caves of Baume-les-Messieurs wind roughly 1 km beneath the rock, with an entrance 70 meters high worthy of a church nave. The guided tour lasts 55 minutes and passes through several chambers, including the Lake Hall. Open April through September only.

days_plan.itin_title: Burgundy-Franche-Comté: The Most Beautiful Villages in 7 days

visits.text: The old village of Gruissan is built in a "circulade" — its lanes spiral like a snail shell around a large limestone rock crowned by the Barberousse Tower, remnant of a 10th-century medieval castle. Climb up: the 360-degree view over the lagoons, pink salt marshes, sea and Massif de la Clape is spectacular, especially late afternoon.

The Plage des Chalets is Gruissan's most famous image. Its 1,330 colorful chalets arranged in 11 rows facing the sea are the invention of Narbonne families in the mid-19th century, who came seeking sea bathing and gradually raised their huts on stilts to protect them from storm surges. Destroyed in 1943 by Germans fearing a Mediterranean landing, they were rebuilt in the 1950s — this time in a staggered pattern so everyone would have a sea view. Jean-Jacques Beineix's 1986 film "Betty Blue" ("37°2 le matin") made it an iconic location: Betty and Zorg's chalet no longer exists, but cinephiles still make the pilgrimage.

The Salt Marshes of Île Saint-Martin cover 400 hectares exploited since Antiquity. In summer, the salt tables turn bright pink due to a micro-algae, dunaliella salina. Guided tours allow you to see salt workers at work and encounter pink flamingos, stilts and avocets. Bring good shoes — the path runs along the basin edges.

activities.text: The Plage des Chalets and the Massif de la Clape offer 15 km of sand. If you have energy after swimming, climb to Pech Redon (214 m) via the trail from the beach: plunging view over the lagoons and sea, with AOC Clape vineyards in between.
Oyster farms around the Gruissan lagoon offer tastings directly from the producer, waterside. A simple, flavorful moment, typical of the Aude coast.

days_plan.itin_title: Aude Road Trip: Carcassonne, Cathar Country & the Mediterranean

visits.text: Guebwiller is nicknamed 'the town of three churches' — and each represents a different style. The Romanesque Church of Saint-Léger with its two 12th-century towers is the oldest. Its sculpted portal and Gothic choir make it a remarkable example of Rhenish art: take time to examine the historiated capitals before entering.

The Dominican Convent, a listed historic monument, is another surprise: construction began in 1294, and its rib-vaulted choir dates to 1322. The building was converted into a hospice and then a market hall after the Revolution. In 1838, an industrialist and patron had a concert hall built in the choir—Clara Schumann performed there as early as 1862. The acoustics of this nave are considered among the finest in Europe. Since 2013, the site has hosted exhibitions, concerts, and digital arts.

The Notre-Dame church, built between 1765 and 1785 in a Neoclassical style, completes the trio of churches. Its Callinet organ resonates beneath the central dome — it became a parish church in 1792 after the abbey of Murbach, to which it belonged, transferred its canons there. Continue to the remains of the abbey of Murbach, a masterpiece of Alsatian Romanesque art whose 12th-century choir and transept survive.

The Théodore Deck Museum traces the work of this Guebwiller-born ceramicist, born in 1823, who became director of the Sèvres National Manufactory. His glazed earthenware and Art Nouveau creations are displayed in this small municipal museum that preserves the memory of a brilliant craftsman.

activities.text: Guebwiller's vineyard is unique in Alsace: it's the only commune in the region to produce four Grands Crus — Kessler, Kitterlé, Saering, and Spiegel. The slopes are vertiginous, some reaching 50 degrees, supported by 50 kilometers of dry-stone walls. Operators offer guided tours in electric 4x4s across these terraces for those who don't want to climb on foot. The tasting that follows helps you understand why these steep terroirs produce wines of exceptional minerality.

The marked vineyard trail climbs among the Grands Crus from lower Guebwiller to the viewpoint overlooking the four terroirs. Allow two hours for the complete loop—sturdy shoes are essential on these steep slopes. The view from the top over the Alsace plain and the Rhine is worth the effort.

days_plan.itin_title: Haut-Rhin Road Trip: Colmar and the Southern Wine Route

visits.text: Guérande's ramparts are among the best preserved in France—1,300 meters of intact walls, six towers, and four fortified gates, listed as a historic monument since 1877 and built mainly in the 15th century under Francis II. A third of the wall walk can be visited, via the stretch between the Saint-Jean tower and the Sainte-Anne tower. Enter through the Saint-Michel gate, the main entrance: this fortified 15th-century residence now houses the Guérande castle museum, which traces the town's history from its origins. From up there, the view over the slate roofs and the Guérande countryside is worth the admission.

Saint-Aubin Collegiate Church has stood at the heart of the town since the 12th century—its Romanesque foundations, burned in 1342, were built upon during a Flamboyant Gothic reconstruction in the 15th and 16th centuries. It has a rare feature: five centuries of construction layered on top of one another and visible in a single building. Listed as a historic monument in 1840. The 19th-century stained glass is remarkable, including the windows depicting Margaret of Antioch. Free admission.

Wander the cobbled lanes of the medieval center, lined with half-timbered houses and private mansions. The market is held Wednesday and Saturday mornings inside the ramparts, in the covered market halls and on place de la Collégiale—around 200 producers and traders. If you're there on a Saturday morning, it's one of the liveliest markets on the peninsula. A daily fish market (except Monday and Thursday) rounds out the offering.

The Château de Careil preserves Renaissance furniture and 15th-century roof timbers in remarkable condition. Its water-filled moats reflect the fortified silhouette of the manor house, built between the 14th and 15th centuries by the Careil family. The guided tour, organized by the owners, gives access to the interior rooms, which are still furnished.

activities.text: Join the salt workers in the crystallization pans to observe the salt harvest. From June through September, they rake coarse salt and gather precious fleur de sel from the water's surface with a wooden skimmer—a movement passed down since the Middle Ages essentially unchanged. The 2,000 hectares of salt marshes around Guérande produce one of Europe's most renowned varieties of fleur de sel. Guided visits with a salt worker are organized; book ahead in peak season.

Cycle the trails between the salt marshes' basins and dikes. The light is especially beautiful in late afternoon when the mirror-like pools reflect the sky. Bike rental companies are available in town. The circuit connecting Guérande, Saillé, and Le Croisic spans roughly 15–20 km and remains accessible to all.

days_plan.itin_title: Loire-Atlantique Road Trip: Nantes and the Côte de Jade

visits.text: The Musée d'Art et d'Archéologie de Guéret, housed in the Hôtel de la Sénatorerie, is closed to the public for renovation and work on its collections. During the closure, its outdoor trail in the town center introduces the museum's history and collections through panels covering, among other subjects, the painters of the Creuse valley and Limousin enamels. A map of the trail is available from the tourist office or town hall.

The Hôtel des Moneyroux itself deserves attention: this Renaissance residence, with its mullioned windows and sculpted stair tower, reflects the prosperity of the Creuse bourgeoisie in the 15th century.

The town center of Guéret, the administrative capital of Creuse, retains several mansions and Place Bonnyaud, lined with old houses. Saint-Pierre Church, altered over the centuries, has a Romanesque portal. The town remains compact, ideal for strolling among shops and café terraces.

activities.text: The Parc animalier des Monts de Guéret, in the heart of Chabrières forest, offers an immersion in wolf territory. Established in 2001, it houses about fifty wolves roaming freely within six enclosures, the largest covering 19,000 m². European gray wolves, Canadian white wolves, black wolves: observe their natural pack behavior from the observation points and watchtower.

The Labyrinthe géant des Monts de Guéret, near the wolf park, has hedges extending over more than 6 hectares. Themed quizzes guide visitors through the hedge maze. A mini farm, a skills course, an educational area about sustainable development, and a water slide round out this fun attraction, ideal for families.

Chabrières forest surrounds the tourist attractions of the Monts de Guéret. Hiking and mountain biking trails crisscross this woodland, where stands of oak, beech, and conifers alternate. The woodland atmosphere contributes to the character of the wildlife park, giving the wolves an almost natural environment.

days_plan.itin_title: Creuse Tour: Valley of the Painters and Aubusson Tapestries

visits.text: Notre-Dame-d'Aquilon Church is Guillestre's pride: built between 1507 and 1532 in local pink marble, its porch (also called a réal) is directly inspired by Embrun Cathedral and reuses two column-bearing lions from the Romanesque church that preceded it. The spire-topped bell tower is visible from everywhere in the town. Less glorious anecdote: part of the ceiling collapsed during Christmas Mass in 2013—the church has since been restored and reopened.

Explore Guillestre looking up at its painted sundials and their mottoes on the facades, one of the valley's finest collections. Add the Saint-Sébastien chapel with its trompe-l'œil, the pastel-hued Ruelle Sainte-Catherine, and the remnants of medieval ramparts with the Saint-Jean-Baptiste gate. A crossroads town that also serves as the gateway to Queyras. Allow an hour of wandering.

About fifteen kilometers up the Guil gorges, Fort Queyras guards the valley entrance from its rocky chokepoint. A medieval fortress taken over and modernized by Vauban, it has vaulted rooms, a main courtyard, and wall walks above the torrent. It's the logical excursion of the day from Guillestre. Winding but short road; factor in the round trip with the visit time.

activities.text: The Guil gorges are Queyras' whitewater playground: the torrent plunges between vertical walls, and outfitters offer rafting, kayaking, and canyoning from beginner to expert. The road above them is already a spectacle in itself. Book according to water levels, higher in early summer during snowmelt. Gear and supervision provided by local operators.

The Château-Queyras via ferrata climbs the walls above the Guil: cables, ladders, and exposed walkways make for a dizzying but secured climb, with views down into the gorges. Book the experience if you're already comfortable with this type of route. Harness, lanyards, and helmet required, available for rental on-site. Avoid in stormy weather.

days_plan.itin_title: Hautes-Alpes Road Trip: High Mountains and Alpine Valleys

visits.text: The Basilica of Notre-Dame-de-Bon-Secours, built from the 12th to 16th centuries, blends three styles across its south facade: Romanesque, Gothic, and Renaissance. It houses a rare Black Virgin, one of the few in western France, a paved labyrinth, and a magnificent 1654 organ case. Every year, on the Saturday before the first Sunday of July, the Pardon brings the town to life—a nighttime procession of the Black Virgin, followed by the lighting of three bonfires on Place du Centre. A tradition documented since the 16th century.

La Plomée, a Renaissance fountain on Place du Centre, is adorned with allegorical figures and dolphins. Vestiges of the medieval castle, residence of the Dukes of Brittany, can still be glimpsed in the urban fabric. Guingamp was the duchy's third stronghold after Rennes and Nantes.
The banks of the Trieux, below the old town, reveal themselves via an 80-meter footbridge. Stone bridges, old washhouses, and terraced gardens border the river. A haven of calm steps from the center.

Guingamp's former prison, an unusual and rare heritage site, can be visited on days when guided tours are offered. Period cells, prisoner graffiti, and 19th-century prison architecture—a little-known facet of the town's history.

activities.text: Guided tour of Guingamp, a Petite Cité de Caractère. From the town's origins to today, among cobbled streets, half-timbered houses, former convents, and 18th-century mansions. The guide leads you from castle ruins to the basilica.

La Vapeur du Trieux, a tourist steam train between Paimpol and Pontrieux. The century-old locomotive travels down the Trieux valley at 30 km/h through a preserved natural landscape. Castles, manor houses and grey herons pass by along the estuary. Allow for a return trip during the day from Guingamp to reach the departure point in Paimpol.

days_plan.itin_title: Côtes-d'Armor Road Trip: Dinan, Pink Granite Coast, Bréhat Island & Lake Guerlédan

places.name: Haguenau

visits.text: Haguenau, nicknamed the 'City of Barbarossa' (Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa had his imperial palace here in the 12th century), is the only town in northern Alsace to offer a Christmas market open daily for five weeks — from November 21 to December 30, without interruption. About sixty chalets spread across five downtown squares, in a pleasant and well-designed pedestrian area. This family-friendly, accessible market, 20 minutes from Strasbourg, is perfect for those wanting to experience Alsatian Christmas away from weekend hordes.

Haguenau is also the birthplace of nativity scenes in Alsace: a register dated 1420 preserved in the Municipal Archives mentions creating a nativity scene at the Église Saint-Georges — the oldest known mention in Alsace. The clay nativity scene created by potter Vincent Remmy of Betschdorf, fashioned with clay from Haguenau forest, is exhibited with free access throughout the market at Place de Neubourg. Exhibitions of nativity scenes from around the world are also visible at several town locations during Advent, notably at the Basilica of Marienthal.

activities.text: The entertainment that delights everyone in Haguenau? The magnificent 1900 carousel — period wooden animals (horses, donkeys, lions, and an Alsatian stork) whose original mechanism still turns. Children clamor for more, adults smile watching it. The bike-tree is another homemade innovation: by pedaling this stationary bike, you power the large tree on the square with electricity. A symbolic and playful gesture at once.

Haguenau's Forêt d'Exception — France's largest lowland state forest, a stone's throw from town — offers marked Christmas trails for families. In December, snow-covered paths beneath pines, with their riddles and explanatory panels, provide welcome fresh air between two markets. Inquire at the tourist office for December programs.

days_plan.itin_title: Alsace's Most Beautiful Christmas Markets
The Most Beautiful Villages of Alsace in 4 Days

map_keywords: Marché de Noël Cours de la Décapole Haguenau

visits.text: Château d'Haroué displays 365 windows, 52 chimneys, 12 towers and 4 bridges. Germain Boffrand integrated the medieval castle's towers and moats into his baroque construction between 1720 and 1729.
Marc de Beauvau-Craon commissioned this residence from the same architect as the Lunéville château. The princely family still lives here after eight generations.
The grand staircase features ironwork by Jean Lamour, who also created the gates of Place Stanislas. The Beauvau family tree covers the wall.
The Pillement salon reveals Chinese paintings in a round tower. This boudoir also served as a music room.

activities.text: The French-style gardens spread before the château. Emilio Terry designed them in 1957 with perspectives over the Saintois region.
The château moats are still fed by the Madon river. The walk around the moats offers different perspectives on the baroque architecture.

days_plan.itin_title: Meurthe-et-Moselle Road Trip: Art Nouveau Nancy & Fortified Cities

visits.text: Perched on a rocky spur of the Meuse Heights, Hattonchâtel village overlooks the Woëvre plain by 80 meters. Fortified in the 9th century by Hatton, Bishop of Verdun, it preserves the 12th-14th century vaulted house, the 14th-century arcaded house, and a 1921 washhouse inspired by medieval and Japanese design.

The Saint-Maur collegiate church houses the Hattonchâtel altarpiece (1523), attributed to sculptor Ligier Richier. This polychrome stone triptych depicts three Passion of Christ scenes in a setting borrowed from the Italian Renaissance: scroll pilasters, interlaced motifs, and basket-handle arches.

The 14th-century cloister, of which only one gallery remains, adjoins the church. Stained glass windows by Jacques Grüber, Nancy master glassmaker, illuminate the nave with colored reflections. The 16th-century calvary outside completes this ensemble classified as Historic Monuments.

The castle, rebuilt in the 1920s thanks to American patron Belle Skinner, blends medieval fantasy with Norman checkerboard stonework. A private property housing a hotel, it can be visited by appointment. From the esplanade, the panorama extends over the Meuse Heights, mirabelle orchards, and Lake Madine.

Climb up to the Butte de Montsec (375 m) to discover the American memorial raised in honor of the troops who reduced the Saint-Mihiel salient in September 1918. Allow about 13 kilometers from the stage town, 15 minutes by road. The bronze orientation table and the circular colonnade offer a 360° panorama over the Woëvre plain and Lake Madine.

activities.text: Cycle around Lake Madine: a 20-kilometer bike path circles this large body of water ideal for water sports, swimming, and observing migratory birds.
Wander through Hattonchâtel's lanes following the arcaded street. Bucolic gardens border village houses and viewpoints offer views over the vineyards and orchards of the northern Meuse Heights.
Want to taste the terroir? Producers of the Meuse Heights offer gray, white, and red wines from Lorraine grape varieties with tangy and fruity aromas.

days_plan.itin_title: Meuse Circuit: Verdun and the Citadels

visits.text: Perched at 755 meters, the Château du Haut-Koenigsbourg was given to Emperor Wilhelm II in 1899 while in ruins. He commissioned a complete restoration to symbolically assert the German identity of annexed Alsace. The architect Bodo Ebhardt relied on rigorous archaeological surveys to reconstruct the fortress as it appeared around 1500. The work lasted eight years, from 1900 to 1908. Allow half a day—the site is among the most visited in Alsace and fills up quickly in July and August.

activities.text: The castle's lower courtyard contains a reconstructed former inn, forge, and mill, offering a glimpse of daily life at the foot of the fortress. The large artillery bastion, added during the restoration, provides the most unobstructed view over the Alsace plain and, on clear days, the Black Forest.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Villages of Alsace in 4 Days

visits.text: The plateau du Retord stretches at an altitude of more than 1,000 metres, a vast expanse of upland pastures and coniferous forests. Plan a round trip from Hauteville-Lompnes for this visit. This remote, wild limestone plateau offers exceptional views of the Alps and the Jura mountains. Winter transforms the landscape into a Nordic skiing area where cross-country skiers and snowshoers explore the vast snowy expanses.

Plateau d'Hauteville, which includes the former municipality of Hauteville-Lompnes, has been a renowned health resort since the 19th century and enjoys invigorating clean air at an elevation of 850 metres. The former sanatoriums reflect its past medical role, when tuberculosis patients were sent to breathe the mountain air. Today, the town remains a popular destination for the quality of its environment.

Panoramic viewpoints dot the roads crossing the plateau. From the Signal de Hauteville, the view takes in the Alpine range from Mont Blanc to the Chartreuse and Vercors massifs. Peak-identification panels help you identify the summits silhouetted against the blue-tinged horizon.

Spruce and fir forests cover much of the plateau. These conifer stands, harvested for timber, shelter elusive mountain wildlife. Roe deer, wild boar and, more rarely, lynx frequent these wooded areas, where silence is broken only by birdsong.

activities.text: Go mountain biking on the many trails that criss-cross the plateau and surrounding combes. The marked routes offer every level of difficulty, from easy-rolling forest tracks to technical single tracks. Steep climbs are rewarded with exhilarating descents through conifer forests and fragrant woodland.

Explore the chasms and sinkholes that pierce the limestone plateau. Bugey has numerous underground cavities explored by cavers. Some developed caves can be visited with a guide, revealing formations, underground rivers and majestic galleries carved by water through the limestone over millions of years.

Observe high-altitude flora and fauna along the hiking trails. Flower-filled meadows are home to wild orchids, gentians and martagon lilies. Birds of prey soar on the thermals, watching for voles and lizards. Nature enthusiasts will find an ideal observation area for photographing plant and animal species.

Go cross-country skiing and snowshoeing when winter arrives. The snow-covered plateau becomes a Nordic paradise with 150 kilometres of marked routes suitable for all abilities. Snow-laden fir trees, muffled silence and low-angled light create an enchanting atmosphere. The Nordic centres provide information about open routes, snow conditions and equipment hire.

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip from Bresse to Bugey via Beaujolais and Lyon

visits.text: The Church of Saint-Sindulphe houses the tomb of Dom Pérignon at the centre of the choir. The Benedictine monk Pierre Pérignon (1638–1715) was cellarer of the abbey of Hautvillers from 1668 until his death: 47 years spent perfecting his techniques for blending grapes from different crus, a revolution that lies behind champagne as we know it. The abbey itself, founded in 650 and owned by Moët & Chandon since 1823, cannot be visited, but the church is open to the public all year round. The tomb slab is plain, almost austere for a man whose legend has endured through the centuries.

Look up as you wander the lanes: nearly 140 wrought-iron signs adorn the façades throughout the village. This tradition dates to the Middle Ages and was revived in the 1950s. Each sign reflects the trade or passion of the residents — winegrowers, artisans, private homes. It's distinctive and often beautifully crafted.

In the Pierre Cheval park, a bronze statue weighing 700 kg depicts Dom Pérignon, the work of the sculptor Juan Carlos Carrillo. A mural retraces the wine-growing history of the village since the beginnings of the abbey. A good starting point for understanding the man before visiting the tomb.

activities.text: Take the waymarked paths through the vines that surround the village. Hautvillers sits on a natural amphitheatre of slopes facing the Marne: this is the landscape Dom Pérignon looked out on as he selected his grapes. The trails of 5 to 8 km pass through UNESCO-listed plots and offer views down into the valley. Set off early in the morning when the light is beautiful.

Visit the village's independent winemakers — about twenty producers welcome visitors. You'll taste champagnes made on the historic hillsides that inspired Dom Pérignon, often quite different from the major industrially produced cuvées. Ask the tourist office for the addresses of producers who receive visitors without an appointment.

days_plan.itin_title: Marne Road Trip: Reims, Épernay and Champagne

visits.text: Pass through the Broërec'h Gate, dating to the 13th century, built under Duke John I the Red. Flanked by two massive towers with pepperpot roofs, it guarded the entrance to the walled town. Inside, don't miss the small museum retracing the town's history—the brigand Marion du Faouët was imprisoned here in 1746 before her execution. After the 1944 bombing, the towers were carefully restored.

Walk the wall-top path of the restored ramparts. The views plunge over the town and the Blavet below. These fortifications played a defensive role for three centuries—notably in 1342, when Jeanne of Flanders, called 'Jeanne the Flame', defended the town during the Breton War of Succession. Gardens now replace the old ditches.

The Notre-Dame-du-Paradis basilica grew out of a farrier's project: François Michart laid the first stone in 1514 to build a chapel dedicated to the Virgin Mary. The spire rises to 65 metres - a landmark visible from afar to sailors. The organ, installed in 1652, is one of the oldest in Morbihan. Check access before your visit - the basilica was damaged during Storm Ciaran.

The National Stud occupies the former Cistercian abbey of Joie since 1856. Inaugurated by Napoleon III on 15 August 1858, it's the birthplace of the Breton draft horse. The wooded park shelters century-old specimens, including a linden over 200 years old. The site has been a listed monument since 1995. Take time to stroll the avenues—the place is as beautiful as the horses.

Tour the Napoleonic stables at the Stud. The museum space recounts the crafts linked to horses: farrier, saddler, blacksmith. The ceremonial saddlery preserves its original tools. If you come during the school holidays, equestrian shows are often scheduled.

Hennebont Harbour spreads at the foot of the railway viaduct on the Blavet's banks. Once a busy trading hub for timber, grain and salt, it's now a peaceful promenade far from commotion. Head to the waterside in the evening—the calm and light are pleasant.

activities.text: If you're here on a Thursday, don't miss the market—the largest in the Lorient area. It fills the square around the basilica. Breton products, salted-butter crepes and kouign-amann rule here. Taste the Guémené andouille, a speciality of the area.
If visiting during school holidays, catch an equestrian show at the Stud. Riders present Breton draft horses and harnessing acts under a marquee. Book ahead; seats sell quickly.

Treat yourself to a break at the Kerbihan botanical park, 10 hectares on the town's edge. Over 400 species of trees and flowers from around the world are planted here, including a bamboo grove that's refreshing in summer. Free entry, ideal for a walk with children.

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip Morbihan: Gulf, Carnac and Breton Coast

visits.text: Henrichemont is a 17th-century utopian town. Founded in 1609 by the Duke of Sully, minister to Henry IV, it was meant to be the capital of the Principality of Boisbelle — an independent micro-state where no taxes were paid. The planned layout: a perfect square 500 metres on each side, eight streets radiating from a central square towards the town gates. Inspired by the Italian ideal cities and by Charleville, its contemporary.

Henry IV's assassination in 1610 and Sully's fall from favour froze the project. Only the pavilions around the central square were completed. You recognise the style of Salomon de Brosse — architect of the Palais du Luxembourg in Paris — in the pedimented façades and ornate dormer windows. The Hôtel du Bœuf, the Hôtel des Monnaies and the Maison du Procureur fiscal speak to what should have been.

The Principality of Boisbelle, whose capital was Henrichemont, remained independent until 1779. No royal taxes, its own judicial system, coins minted on site. Louis XV eventually bought back these privileges, ending four centuries of autonomy.

activities.text: The “Balade de Sully” is a 4-hour-50-minute circuit around Henrichemont. The route takes you through oak and beech forests and sleepy hamlets, past ponds rich in fish. Cher Pas-à-Pas waymarking. Bring water and a picnic.

From Henrichemont, the vineyards of Menetou-Salon are less than 20 minutes away; for Sancerre, allow around half an hour's drive from Henrichemont. Menetou-Salon produces white wines (Sauvignon) and reds (Pinot noir) in the same style as its neighbor, often at more affordable prices. The Château de Menetou-Salon, owned by the Prince d'Arenberg, is open for visits during the season.

days_plan.itin_title: Cher Loop: Romanesque Berry and the Route Jacques-Cœur

visits.text: Discover downtown Héricourt, Haute-Saône's second most populous town, which developed thanks to its 19th- and 20th-century industry. Its urban architecture and modern facilities testify to its economic dynamism in the Lizaine valley.

activities.text: Explore this town marked by its industrial history, particularly in metallurgy and mechanical engineering. The architecture of former factories and working-class neighborhoods tells the story of this working-class town's development near Montbéliard and the Territoire de Belfort.
Relax in Héricourt's parks and gardens, which offer breathing spaces in the heart of this dynamic town, with facilities for families and sports enthusiasts.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Saône Tour: Comtois Plateaus and Heritage

visits.text: Hérisson, a Petite Cité de Caractère® nestled in a bend of the Aumance, spreads its medieval town below its fortress. Founded in the 5th century, the town was enclosed by a wall flanked by 22 towers; the Porte de Varenne and Porte de la Rivière survive (listed historic monuments). The three main streets converged on the Place du Chapitre, dominated by the 12th-century Saint-Sauveur bell tower.

The pink sandstone ruins of the Castle of the Dukes of Bourbon (13th–14th centuries) crown a rocky spur. The duchy's main stronghold facing the English sphere of influence during the Hundred Years' War, this fortress endured numerous sieges. Its remnants pierce the sky, testifying to its past power. The view from the ramparts takes in the surrounding Aumance valley.

The 12th-century Romanesque Saint-Pierre de Châteloy church houses remarkable polychrome frescoes from the 13th and 16th centuries. Each summer, this architectural gem hosts the Festival de Musique en Bourbonnais (founded in 1966), with five or six chamber music concerts performed in the nave. This cultural festival prompted the restoration of the building.

Old houses from the 15th, 16th and 17th centuries line the village's cobbled lanes. The house La Synagogue (early 14th century) stands out for its remarkable murals and roof timbers. The Musée du Terroir Hérissonnais brings together collections and accounts of local life through the centuries.

activities.text: The banks of the Aumance invite peaceful walks along the river, whose course was diverted in the Middle Ages to form a natural obstacle protecting the town. Walks lead to the Butoir mill (1 km upstream), with its 10-tonne waterwheel restored in 1995 and awarded the Fondation du Patrimoine label in 2023. The old mechanism and the history of the mills can be discovered on a visit.

The Calvary Chapel is reached by a path offering beautiful panoramas over the medieval village and the Aumance. Further on, the Church of Châteloy completes the discovery of Romanesque heritage. The Castle of Roche-Othon (3 km northwest), a 14th-century vestige, also dominates the valley from its hilltop.

The Arts Mêlés festival in July offers an eclectic programme combining theatre, music, photography, circus, puppetry and painting. Hérisson maintains a strong theatrical and cultural tradition through exhibitions, folk gatherings and events throughout the year. The medieval town becomes a place for living and creating.

days_plan.itin_title: Allier Road Trip: Vichy, Thermal Baths and Bourbonnais Bocage

visits.text: Hesdin's belfry rises 70 m above Place d'Armes. A three-storey square tower built in 1878, it houses a bell of nearly 2 tonnes and has been listed as a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2005.

The town hall, built in the 16th century in red brick on a sandstone base, bears Charles V's coat of arms. Inside, the tapestry room displays Flemish hangings from the La Marche series, listed as Historic Monuments. The 16th-century fireplace displays the arms of Robert de Melun.
Notre-Dame church, whose foundation stone was laid in 1565, combines Gothic architecture, brick and chalky stone beside the Canche. Restoration work is underway after the vaults collapsed in 2022.

The birthplace of the abbé Prévost - the author of Manon Lescaut - has a large carriage entrance opening onto a paved courtyard with a view of the church. This 17th-century residence has been converted into a cultural venue.

The 17th-century “maison du Père Brassart” is Hesdin's oldest house. It belonged to a companion of Napoleon Bonaparte. The cavalry riding hall of 1821, with its imposing timber roof structure supported by brick walls, now serves as a community hall.

The municipal museum, housed in two former prisons, recounts the town's tumultuous history: destroyed by Charles V in 1553, rebuilt six kilometres away the following year, annexed to France in 1477 under Louis XI.

activities.text: Hesdin state forest stretches over 1,014 ha of century-old beech groves. The Fond Notre-Dame trail (14 km) crosses this green lung where roe deer, green woodpeckers, and buzzards soar over the high forest.
Explore Hesdin from the Canche by canoe: the river passes under the town's nine bridges, offering an unusual perspective on the belfry and half-timbered façades.
In spring, the forest floor is carpeted with wild bluebells. A short walk from the forest car park is enough to enjoy this fleeting blue carpet.

days_plan.itin_title: Opal Coast Villages and Flemish Heartlands

visits.text: The Vieux Bassin forms the heart of Honfleur. Its narrow slate-covered facades rise six or seven stories high—sailors lived as close to the harbor as possible. Number 44, classified as a Historic Monument, showcases the typical slate cladding.

Step through the door of Sainte-Catherine Church, the largest wooden church in France. Built after the Hundred Years' War by ship carpenters, its vaulted ceiling evokes an upturned ship's hull. The bell tower, separated from the nave to prevent lightning fires, stands across the square.
La Lieutenance, the last vestige of 14th-century fortifications erected under Charles V, houses a heritage interpretation center. From its terraces, enjoy a 360° panorama of the harbor and estuary.

The Eugène Boudin Museum brings together 92 paintings by the master along with works by Monet, Courbet, and Jongkind. One room traces the artistic ferment of the Auberge Saint-Siméon, birthplace of Impressionism.
Take Rue Haute—which, despite its name, is the lowest street in town—to admire the old shipowners' timber-framed houses with polychrome half-timbering.
The Salt Warehouses, two vast 17th-century stone buildings, stored up to 10,000 tons of salt for fish preservation. They now host exhibitions and concerts.

Cross the Pont de Normandie, a cable-stayed bridge stretching 2,141 meters and inaugurated in 1995. Its 214-meter pylons (the height of the Montparnasse Tower) dominate the Seine estuary. A striking viewpoint over the mudflats and nature reserve.
The Maisons Satie pay tribute to the composer born in Honfleur. The visit unfolds with headphones on: surreal rooms, moving objects, and absurdist music—true to the character.
Saint-Léonard Church preserves a 15th-century Flamboyant Gothic facade. The interior, rebuilt in the 17th-18th centuries after the Wars of Religion, displays murals and a wooden vault.
The Naturospace houses an 800 m² tropical greenhouse where butterflies and exotic birds fly freely among orchids and banana trees.
Head to the Garden of Personalities, a landscaped park by the sea. Bronze busts commemorate artists and explorers linked to Honfleur, from Boudin to Champlain.
Quai Sainte-Catherine offers a row of tall, colorful houses. Restaurant terraces and art galleries line up facing the Vieux Bassin.

activities.text: Climb to the Notre-Dame de Grâce Chapel via the Côte de Grâce path. Ex-votos from sailors have lined the walls for centuries. Panoramic view over the Pont de Normandie and the estuary.
The Honfleur market sets up Saturday mornings around Sainte-Catherine Church (organic market on Wednesdays). Norman regional products, cider, cheeses, and fresh fish.
Evening stroll around the Vieux Bassin. The slate facades capture the changing twilight that inspired Boudin and Monet.
Wander through galleries and artists' studios. Honfleur has several dozen, spanning painting, sculpture, and photography.
Cycle the estuary trail. The route follows a section of the Seine by Bike and Vélomaritime routes, passing wet meadows and mudflats.
Relax in the cobbled streets of the Sainte-Catherine quarter: designer boutiques, antique dealers, and tea rooms in half-timbered houses.
