visits.text: Houdan's keep, a 25-meter cylindrical tower flanked by four corner turrets, was erected between 1125 and 1132 by Amaury III de Montfort. Restored between 2014 and 2016, its 250 steps lead to panoramic views over the Yvelines countryside.
The Saint-Jacques-Saint-Christophe church blends Flamboyant Gothic and Renaissance styles. It houses a Clicquot organ from 1734 and a 1582 fresco depicting the pilgrimage to Montserrat.
Houdan's market hall recalls the commercial past of this rural town. 17th- and 18th-century half-timbered houses line neighboring streets, forming a preserved setting.

activities.text: The traditional Houdan market brings the town center to life each week. Free-range poultry, cheeses, and seasonal vegetables: local producers hold their stalls in the shadow of the keep.
Walk through the old town to spot half-timbered façades, interior courtyards, and carved details on door lintels.
Take country paths around Houdan for a pastoral walk between grain fields and groves. The rolling landscape evokes nearby Normandy.

days_plan.itin_title: Yvelines Road Trip: Versailles and Impressionist Villages

visits.text: Mont Saint-Michel de Brasparts—not to be confused with its Norman namesake—is a 380-meter summit crowned by a white 17th-century chapel, with 360-degree views across all of inland Finistère. It's from here that you understand the geography of fear: the Yeun Elez spreads below you due north, a vast basin of peat bogs and marshes with Lake Brennilis in the middle. For medieval shepherds who brought their livestock to graze here, the Yeun literally appeared as the vestibule of Hell—not a metaphor, but geography. The word 'Elez' in Old Breton means 'hell.' It's a place name, not marketing. Fifteen minutes' walk from the parking area.

Brennilis is a village of 467 inhabitants sadly known for two things. The first is a nuclear power station, built in 1962; its dismantling, begun in 1985, is scheduled to run until 2040. The second reason is older: the Youdig, a specific area of shifting peat bogs on the edge of the village, which Breton tradition unambiguously designates as the gate of Hell. In 1893 Anatole Le Braz documented the local practice: when a ghost haunted a house, a priest from the Monts d'Arrée was fetched, who exorcised the soul by turning it into a black dog, then led the dog to the Youdig and threw it into the bog. A practice attested until the 19th century. The howls heard at night in the marsh? Modern ornithologists lean towards Eurasian bitterns, a bird with a foghorn-like call. The villagers of the time did not have that information.
The Maison des Fées in Brennilis is a V-shaped dolmen 13 meters long, dating from around 3,000 BC. Free access, 10 minutes' walk from the village. It is understated and needs to be nothing more.

activities.text: Loop around Lake Saint-Michel, created in 1936 by the Nestavel Dam, which drowned a third of the original Yeun Elez under its waters. 450 hectares of dark water, frequent fogs, almost Irish landscape. Marked trail of 15 km loop, or simple stroll from the EDF parking area on the north side. The best time is twilight, when the low light and first mists transform the site into something that fully justifies its reputation.

If you book a storytelling evening at the Auberge-Expo du Youdig in Brennilis (Kerveguenet, 25-35€ with a meal), it may well be the most memorable event of the trip. The tales come from the local folklore collected by Anatole Le Braz - not a folk re-enactment, but genuine work of transmission. Booking essential.

days_plan.itin_title: Haunted Brittany in 6 days: From Brocéliande to the Lands of the Ankou

visits.text: The fortified Church of Saint James the Greater is one of the iconic images of Alsatian wine country. Perched on a knoll above the village and surrounded by a hexagonal enclosure with six bastions pierced by arrow slits, it served as a fortified refuge for residents in case of attack—a keep dressed as a church. Built in the 15th and 16th centuries on the remains of an 11th-century sanctuary, it's been listed as a Monument Historique since 1972. The interior reveals a curiosity unique in Alsace: the 16th-century pink sandstone pulpit is only accessible via a staircase passing through a church pillar. Since 1687, Catholics and Protestants have taken turns using it under the simultaneum arrangement—a coexistence imposed by Louis XIV that continues today.

Below the church sits the Fontaine Sainte-Hune, from which the village takes its name: according to legend, the 7th-century holy washerwoman transformed water into wine during a bad harvest. Beside the washhouse, the 1517 town hall still bears on its facade the coats of arms of Hunawihr's overlords: the antlers of Württemberg, the lozenges of the Duchy of Teck, the double-headed eagle of the Holy Roman Empire, and the two fish of the County of Montbéliard.

activities.text: Walk the circuit through the vines around the church to enjoy panoramas of Ribeauvillé, Zellenberg, and Riquewihr—you'll see all three villages from the path around the vineyards. The Grand Cru Rosacker, whose name comes from the wild roses planted at the vineyard edges, produces high-class Rieslings and Gewurztraminers here. Easy loop of 3 to 4 km, 1 hour.

The NaturOparC in Hunawihr is the reintroduction center for white storks in Alsace — the regional symbol that nearly disappeared in the 1970s. Fishing shows feature otters and cormorants. The Exotic Butterfly Garden, located right next door, lets hundreds of tropical butterflies live freely in a greenhouse and botanical park. Both sites are worth the visit, especially for families.

days_plan.itin_title: The 15 Most Beautiful Villages of Alsace
Grand Est Road Trip: Vineyards, Ramparts and Forests
The Most Beautiful Villages of Alsace in 4 Days

places.name: Hunspach

visits.text: In Hunspach, Alsace changes its palette. Forget the multicolored facades of the south—here, everything is white. The half-timbered houses, built between the 18th and 19th centuries with local wood and lime, create an understated and striking harmony of color. Voted Village Préféré des Français in 2020, the village owes its fame to two architectural details: the convex windowpanes on the facades—baroque glazing that allowed residents to look out onto the street without being seen—and the well sweeps dotting the courtyards that open onto the street. Strict rules still require white facades and green or blue shutters today.

Push on to Fort Schoenenbourg, 5 kilometers north of Hunspach—it's one of the most important fortifications of the Maginot Line in Alsace, built between 1931 and 1935. Its underground galleries stretch for 3 kilometers, dug 30 meters underground, and the fort could house 600 men for three months while remaining entirely self-sufficient. It was the most heavily attacked fortification of World War II and withstood nine days of intense bombardment in 1940. The guided tour lasts about 1 hour 30 minutes—bring a jacket, it's cool even in summer.

activities.text: Follow the village's marked historical walk—about 45 minutes to spot remarkable facades, well sweeps, and hidden symbols on lintels. The tourist office also offers guided tours with anecdotes about each house. If you want to learn more about rural life in the past, the Petite Ferme d'Antan in the heart of the village displays its tools and utensils.

Explore Seebach, 5 km to the northeast, another village of white half-timbered houses in the Outre-Forêt, laid out like a “ladder” with two parallel streets linked by three cross streets. Cyclists can combine the two villages on the 49 km route that then runs along the Rhine.

days_plan.itin_title: The 15 Most Beautiful Villages of Alsace
The Most Beautiful Villages of Alsace in 4 Days

visits.text: Built in the 1920s by architect Robert Mallet-Stevens, Villa Noailles is a masterpiece of modern architecture listed as a historic monument. Gabriel Guévrékian's cubist garden offers a panoramic view of the Golden Islands. The venue hosts exhibitions and fashion and design festivals throughout the year.
Below the villa, Parc Saint-Bernard unfolds its narrow terraces linked by stone staircases. The botanical garden gathers Mediterranean and exotic species: rosemary, wisteria, and rare plants.

The Olbius-Riquier gardens spread across seven hectares of greenery. An exotic greenhouse shelters palms, bamboo, banana trees, and cacti. The pond and its cascade offer welcome coolness in summer. Free admission year-round.

Climb up to the Collégiale Saint-Paul, adorned with ex-votos, then wind back down through the steep alleys of the old town. The Templars' Tower, a medieval vestige of the order, can be visited with a treasure hunt for children.

The ruins of the medieval castle crown a rocky peak at the town's summit. Dating from the 11th century, it offers a panorama over Hyères Bay, the Golden Islands, and the Maures massif. Free access via the ruin trail from Villa Noailles.
Visit the archaeological site of Olbia, a Greek trading post founded in the 4th century BCE. Excavations reveal ramparts, dwellings, and Roman baths by the sea.

activities.text: On Saturday mornings, the Îles d'Or market takes over the old town. Seasonal fruit, tapenade, soaps, and local crafts fill the stalls under the plane trees.

Follow the coastal trail around the Giens peninsula. Between salt pans, pine groves, and coves, the route runs along the salt road and its marshes, where greater flamingos and gray herons come to rest.
In the mood for the beach? L'Almanarre beach, a long ribbon of sand between the sea and the salt pans, is renowned for windsurfing and kitesurfing thanks to its steady winds.

days_plan.itin_title: Var Road Trip: French Riviera & Provence Verte
Southeast France Road Trip: Perched Villages and Gorges

visits.text: The Île d'Or is mainly worthwhile for its history: a doctor, Auguste Lutaud, supposedly won it at cards at the beginning of the 20th century, proclaimed himself Auguste I and had a square tower built there in red stone from the Estérel. Many think Hergé drew inspiration from it for The Black Island. It has remained private property since 1897: content yourself with the view.

activities.text: Rent a kayak at Débarquement beach and paddle around the Île d'Or: the water is clear, the rocky seabed is worth bringing a mask for, and the red tower comes into view from every angle. Landing is prohibited; the islet is private. Calm seas are essential: choppy waves build quickly in the passage.

days_plan.itin_title: Roquebrune-sur-Argens: sea, villages and the Var in 10 days

places.name: Ile De Batz

visits.text: The crossing between Roscoff and Île de Batz takes fifteen minutes, with boats running every day of the year. The island is 3.5 km long, with about 500 inhabitants, not a single car, and a lighthouse whose 198 steps lead to a view over the entire bay of Morlaix. Allow at least half a day. Rent a bike at the landing stage if you want to circle the island without spending all day.

activities.text: A twenty-minute walk from the landing stage on the île de Batz, the Georges Delaselle garden brings together nearly 2,500 exotic species that the Gulf Stream allows to thrive at this latitude: palms, agaves and cacti. Allow an hour there, longer if you stroll to the eastern tip. Open from April 1 to November 1, closed for the rest of the year.

map_keywords: Georges Delaselle garden Ile de Batz

visits.text: Passenger boats link Audierne to Île de Sein in about an hour, with several sailings daily in season. The island is barely 2 km long, with no cars and lanes narrow enough to break the westerly wind. Its inhabitants were among the first to head to London in June 1940. The sea can be rough in the Raz: if you're prone to seasickness, take something before boarding.

Housed in the former seamen's shelter on the quay, the Île de Sein ecomuseum tells the story of sea rescue, shipwrecks in the Raz, and the departure of virtually all able-bodied men for England after the June 18, 1940 appeal. A second space, the Rescue Museum, displays lifeboat models and wreck artifacts near Men Brial. Allow an hour for both. Open mainly in summer: check with the town hall before crossing.

activities.text: Walking around Île de Sein takes barely two hours: it's 1.8 km long by 500 meters wide, and its highest point excluding the lighthouse tops out at seven meters. The path passes the Goulenez lighthouse, with 249 steps and visits possible only in summer, then heads toward the rocks at the western point facing the Raz. Metal-tipped walking poles are forbidden, as they damage the paths. Remember to bring cash, as there's no ATM on the island.

days_plan.itin_title: Brittany 7 days: Pink Granite, Lighthouses & Peninsulas

visits.text: Despite its name, Île Renote can be reached on foot from Grève Blanche in Trégastel: its coastal loop of about 2 km passes one jumble of granite boulders after another in very clear water. The rocks bear nicknames: the Painter's Palette, the Crab Claw, the Stack of Crêpes. Direct views of the Sept-Îles and Ploumanac'h lighthouse. One hour 30 minutes at a stroll, free, and never as crowded as Ploumanac'h.

days_plan.itin_title: Brittany 7 days: Pink Granite, Lighthouses & Peninsulas

visits.text: You'll cross to Tatihou Island aboard the amphibious boat Tatihou III, which drives across the foreshore depending on the tide. The maritime museum, designated a Musée de France, preserves remains of ships sunk during the Battle of La Hougue in 1692. Book the crossing in advance: places are limited in high season.

days_plan.itin_title: Cotentin, Pays d'Auge: 5 days exploring the most beautiful villages

places.name: Illiers Combray

visits.text: Maison de Tante Léonie - Musée Marcel Proust, a literary pilgrimage site of worldwide renown. In this 19th-century bourgeois home, young Marcel spent his vacations between 1877 and 1880. The quaint kitchen and the bedrooms of Marcel and Tante Léonie inspired the immortal pages of “Swann's Way”.

Pré Catelan of Illiers-Combray, exotic garden created by Proust's uncle that became 'Swann's park' in In Search of Lost Time. From this haven of greenery, the Beauce plains stretch as far as the eye can see, inspiring the writer's contemplative descriptions. A place for literary meditation.

Church of Saint-Jacques in Illiers-Combray, whose timber framework painted in shimmering colors and boat-shaped vault captivated young Marcel. This is where he would set Combray's church in his novel, with its stained glass windows filtering light like “a historical sun”.

Proustian circuit through Illiers-Combray, renamed in 1971 for the writer's birth centenary. The streets, squares, and houses correspond to locations in In Search of Lost Time: discover the 'Méséglise way' and the 'Guermantes way' that the narrator walked as a child.

activities.text: Tasting of artisanal madeleines at La Madeleine de Proust, those little scallop-shell-shaped cakes that made Illiers world-famous. The flavor of this madeleine dipped in tea triggered in Proust the flood of memories that became the most celebrated in French literature.

Hike along the paths of the surrounding Beauce countryside, where wheat fields undulate to the horizon as in Proust's time. The landscape has hardly changed in a century, offering total immersion in the world of In Search of Lost Time.

days_plan.itin_title: Eure-et-Loir Tour: Chartres, Châteaux and Proust

map_keywords: House of Aunt Léonie Marcel Proust Museum

visits.text: Saint-Austremoine Abbey Church in Issoire, listed as a Historic Monument since 1840, is Lower Auvergne's largest Romanesque church, measuring 65 meters long with a height of 17 meters beneath the vault. Its east end is a masterpiece of tiered volumes, adorned with small columns, capitals, sculpted modillions, geometric mosaics, and medallions depicting the signs of the zodiac. Inside, the polychromy restored by Anatole Dauvergne between 1857 and 1860 bursts into vivid hues that transform the building into an unexpected jewel box of color amid the austerity of the golden arkose stone.

The abbey church choir's historiated capitals depict a complete cycle of Christ's Passion and Resurrection with exceptional narrative quality. The celebrated Last Supper, carved with remarkable expressiveness, is considered one of Auvergne's finest Romanesque capitals. In the crypt, the 12th-century reliquary shrine of Saint Austremonius and a 15th-century painting of the Last Judgment complete this major heritage ensemble.

Issoire's historic center, set in the Val d'Allier, can be explored through its colorful facades and red roofs, which contrast with the volcanic stone of its monuments. The Georges-Duby Romanesque Art Center, housed in a listed chapter room, exhibits collections devoted to Auvergne's Romanesque art and hosts temporary exhibitions.

activities.text: Join guided tours of the abbey church organized in July–August and by reservation for groups during the rest of the year. A free activity booklet for children aged 6–12, available at the Tourist Office, turns a visit to the church into an architectural treasure hunt. The abbey church is open daily from 8:30 AM to 6:30 PM.

Festival Art roman d'Issoire, a major cultural event scheduled from late July to early August. Concerts, lectures, performances, and themed tours celebrate the Romanesque heritage of the town and its surroundings in a program that attracts specialists and curious visitors.
Walk along the Allier River near Issoire. The Val d'Allier offers wild river landscapes with pebble beaches, riparian forests, and volcanic cliffs—ideal for walking, cycling, or simply contemplation.

days_plan.itin_title: Volcanoes and Auvergne traditions

visits.text: Tour Blanche. Erected in 1195 at Richard the Lionheart's request and completed in 1202 under Philip Augustus, this 27-meter tower has dominated the town for over 830 years. Never conquered despite numerous attacks, it returned to the Kingdom of France with Blanche of Castile's dowry. The new exhibition installed in 2014 includes a video projection on the first level about the history of this unjustly forgotten queen. From the top, there is a remarkable panorama over the town and its surroundings.

Musée de l'Hospice Saint-Roch. Housed in the former Hôtel-Dieu beside the Théols, this museum holds an exceptional collection of heritage treasures. The 15th-century chapel features decoration unique in France, and the patients' wards bear witness to the history of hospital care. Gallo-Roman and medieval archaeological collections, an apothecary's shop dating from the 17th and 19th centuries, and a splendid carved Tree of Jesse enrich the tour. A modern extension hosts prestigious contemporary art exhibitions.

Belfry and Clock Gate. The 12th-century belfry testifies to medieval communal independence. The Clock Gate, rebuilt after the Wars of Religion, presents remarkable Renaissance decorations. Two round towers connected by a vaulted passage, one adorned with a clock and bell, constitute this ensemble that served as a prison until World War I.

Saint-Cyr Church. This Gothic church dominates the historic center with its splendid 15th-century stained glass window. The interior architecture testifies to the town's religious importance in the Middle Ages.

activities.text: Ramparts promenade. Boulevard Champion runs along the old ramparts and offers a remarkable view of the château quarter, town hall, and Tour Blanche. A panoramic elevator installed in a gap in the ramparts allows easy access to Parc François Mitterrand.

Parc François Mitterrand. This two-hectare green space extends on both sides of the Théols. Children's play facilities, benches, and landscaping that changes with the seasons make it a popular walking spot. At night during the season, the park and ramparts are artistically illuminated as part of the Paysages de Lumières.

Saturday market. A major center for fairs since the Middle Ages, Issoudun continues this tradition with its weekly market. Regional produce, goat cheeses, seasonal vegetables, and Berry specialties bring the town center to life in a friendly atmosphere.

days_plan.itin_title: Indre Road Trip: Secret Berry and the Vallée Noire

visits.text: The Courvoisier house has its château on the banks of the Charente. Tour of the cellars including the famous “Paradis” where the oldest eaux-de-vie age. Tasting overlooking the river.
The church of Saint-Pierre blends eras: 11th-century Romanesque foundations, a 12th-century crypt where the former Counts of Jarnac rest, later alterations. Tomb of the local lords in the crypt.

The Musée Donation François-Mitterrand occupies a former cognac warehouse. Closed to the public in 2026. State gifts received during his terms in office: paintings, sculptures and ceramics from around the world. The former president was born here and is buried here.
Jarnac's quays are lined with trading houses and bourgeois residences. The Charente flows peacefully, white façades reflected in the water. Starting point for river cruises.

activities.text: Tour of the Courvoisier house. More low-key than the Cognac giants, with a family feel. The 'Paradis' cellar holds century-old eaux-de-vie. Tasting included.
River cruise Jarnac–Cognac. Licence-free barge for the day or guided gabare. The river winds between vineyards and villages. Manual locks, contemplative pace.
Visit to François Mitterrand's birthplace. The house where the former president was born in 1916. Guided tour by appointment, intimate atmosphere.

days_plan.itin_title: Charente Tour: Cognac and Romanesque Heritage in 4 Days

places.name: Joigny

visits.text: Saint-Thibault Church, built between 1490 and 1529, blends flamboyant Gothic with early Renaissance influences. Its choir leans curiously to the left. Inside, admire the hanging vault keystones and Renaissance pulpit.
Château des Gondi, a Renaissance edifice, overlooks Joigny from the heights of the Saint-Jean quarter. The panorama embraces the entire town and Yonne valley.
At Place du Pilori, the Tree of Jesse House displays half-timbered carvings of Christ's genealogical tree, enhanced with polychrome ceramics. It's one of Burgundy's finest half-timbered houses.
The Bailli House, at 36 rue Montant-du-Palais, is a 16th-century tower house. Its façades bear Latin and Greek inscriptions dated 1573; its half-timbers are carved with scales and lozenges.
Saint-Jean Church, a castle chapel turned parish church in the 11th century, contains the tomb of Countess Aélis de Joigny (early 13th century) and a Renaissance Entombment of great refinement.
Cross the Pont Saint-Nicolas, long the only passage on the Paris-Lyon route. From the Baltard market halls, the view of half-timbered houses tiered in an amphitheater is striking.

activities.text: Climb into the vineyards of Côte Saint-Jacques, an AOC Bourgogne appellation. The trail offers an open view over the Yonne valley, between forests and grain fields.
Wander through Joigny's three historic quarters—Saint-Thibault, Saint-Jean, and Saint-André—linked by steep lanes, stairs, and narrow passages. Each quarter has its own personality and church.
The river port of Les Maillotins, at the foot of the old town, welcomes boaters between the Seine, the Canal de Bourgogne, and the Yonne. Landscaped banks invite strolling.
The Museum of the Resistance traces the action of Groupe Bayard, created in Joigny in 1940. Documents, photos, and period objects testify to the fight against the occupier.

days_plan.itin_title: Yonne Circuit: Northern Burgundy & Chablis

map_keywords: Maison de l'Arbre de Jessé Joigny

visits.text: The Grand Jardin Castle stands as one of France's most exquisite Renaissance pleasure pavilions, built between 1533 and 1546 by Claude of Lorraine, first Duke of Guise. Local tradition claims he built it to win forgiveness from his wife Antoinette of Bourbon for his infidelities—yet the reality is also political: above all a stage for a duke of voracious ambition, close to François I. In November 1546, the king himself was received here. Visit the Saint-Claude Chapel: its coffered vault bears the letters C and A (Claude and Antoinette), the year 1546, and relief fruit. Two marble caryatids—remnants of Claude of Lorraine's monumental tomb designed by Le Primatice—represent Temperance and Justice.

The Renaissance garden, recreated in the 1990s from 16th-century written sources, sprawls across the first third of the 4.5-hectare site: 139 boxwood topiaries sculpted in geometric forms, a verdant maze, an orchard of 364 heritage fruit trees, trellised arbors. The 19th-century romantic park beyond shelters rare species: ginkgo biloba, giant sequoia, tulip tree. The nationally designated boxwood collection, recognized in 2018, comprises 153 varieties. Designated a Historic Monument and Remarkable Garden.

Wander Joinville's narrow lanes, a Small Town of Character. The Renaissance Auditory of Justice, the Sainte-Croix hospital, and several manor houses attest to the Guise patronage that made Joinville a princely Renaissance capital. The marked trail through the medieval townscape leads from the vanished upper castle to the Peceaux Wharf, where the Marne flows.

activities.text: At Thonnance-lès-Joinville, a few kilometers away, My Mill Gardens display 6,000 square meters of three peony collections: tree peonies, Itoh hybrids, and herbaceous types. The May to June bloom transforms the site into a flaming tableau. Outside this window, clematis collections and rose varieties still reward a visit.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Est Road Trip: Vineyards, Ramparts and Forests
Haute-Marne Circuit: Langres and Heritage

visits.text: Joinville was nicknamed “Hollywood-sur-Marne”—and it wasn't a metaphor. The Pathé studios, established in 1910 in a furniture rental warehouse on Avenue du Général Gallieni, produced up to 40% of French cinema between 1910 and 1987: Children of Paradise, Marius, and Les Misérables were shot there. The buildings were demolished in 1991 for a residential development, but the GTC laboratories' chimney still stands on the quay—look for it. The La Belle Équipe footbridge (1933, used in the 1936 film of the same name) still spans the small Polangis channel.

Île Fanac is accessible by elevator from the Joinville bridge. Head down to it: 17 hectares, the École municipale des Arts with its turrets and chimera weather vane, and the Boat House of the Société Nautique de la Marne, founded in 1876. This is also where Zola set Jullien's tavern in The Ladies' Paradise.

Walk along Quai Gabriel Péri from the bridge: Art Deco and Art Nouveau villas line the banks, remnants of when wealthy Parisians had weekend houses built here. The former Pathé factory, converted into post-production workshops, is still active on this quay.

activities.text: Chez Gégène has been around since 1918—Eugène Favreux, known as Gégène, built the building himself on the site of a burned barge. He also ran the Pathé studios' canteen, which brought him Jean Gabin, Édith Piaf, and pretty much the entire film industry. Red checkered tablecloths, moules-frites, community dances on weekends from May to September. Book if you're going on a Saturday.
Operators offer electric boats that do not require a license, departing from the marina.

days_plan.itin_title: Val-de-Marne Road Trip: Castles and the Banks of the Marne

visits.text: Josselin Castle has overlooked the Oust for more than a thousand years—the first wooden castle dates to around 1008. On the river side, three medieval towers linked by curtain walls present an austere, martial face. But turn to the courtyard side: the Renaissance façade commissioned by Jean II de Rohan between 1490 and 1510 is a lacework of carved granite, with the Rohan motto 'A Plus' chiselled into the stone. Richelieu, furious with the Protestant Rohans, had the keep and three towers dismantled in 1629, but spared this façade. The Rohan family still lives in the castle—one of France's longest family occupations.

Detour to the former stables: the Dolls and Toys Museum displays the Rohan family's private collection—nearly 5,000 pieces begun by Herminie de Rohan in the late 19th century. Breton-costumed dolls, Japanese sets, doll houses and period toys. Your children will love it; so will you.

Take time to walk in the castle gardens: four hectares and three moods. The formal French garden, designed by Achille Duchêne (who also worked at Vaux-le-Vicomte), spreads century-old box hedges before the Renaissance façade. The rose garden holds 160 rose bushes across 40 varieties. And the English-style park, redesigned by landscape architect Louis Benech in the 2000s, drops into the valley with hydrangeas and rhododendrons.

Notre-Dame-du-Roncier Basilica blends Romanesque and flamboyant Gothic. The effigies of Olivier de Clisson and Marguerite de Rohan lie in the nave. Legend says in 808 a peasant discovered a Virgin statue in a bramble bush—hence 'Roncier'. Push the door and gaze upward at the vaults.

If energy permits, climb the 138 steps of the basilica bell tower. The panorama embraces the Oust, castle and entire medieval town. It's the best vantage point on Josselin—the effort is well rewarded.

The Sainte-Croix quarter climbs the hillside above the Oust. Restored in 2006, it ranks among Josselin's oldest areas. The 11th-century Sainte-Croix chapel commands the valley. Half-timbered houses, cobbled alleys—lose yourself here.

The Caryatid House, dated 1538, is one of Josselin's oldest dwellings. Its carved half-timbered façades are listed historic monuments. The caryatids adorning the façade give it its name—look for them on the first floor.

activities.text: From the riverside quay below the castle, paddle, kayak or take an electric boat on the Nantes-Brest Canal. The view of the castle towers from the water is breathtaking. Rental shops nearby offer equipment April to October.

Cycle along the canal towards Rohan - 25 kilometres through the countryside. You can stop at Timadeuc Abbey, approximately 11 km from the stage town, an 11-minute drive away. Founded in 1841, it is where the monks make Timanoix cheese, matured with walnut liqueur. A good excuse for a tasty break.

Every other year on 14 July, the medieval festival fills Josselin's streets. Armoured knights, jugglers, musicians and craftspeople recreate the Breton dukes' era. If your dates coincide, don't miss it.

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip Morbihan: Gulf, Carnac and Breton Coast

visits.text: Joyeuse's medieval lanes spread out around the shaded central square. The historic village retains town mansions and old facades that bear witness to its commercial past.

activities.text: The weekly market brings Joyeuse to life every Wednesday morning. Local producers and artisans offer specialties from the Cévennes, cheeses, and regional products.

days_plan.itin_title: Ardèche Road Trip: Wild Gorges and Villages with Character

visits.text: Ancient Noviodunum, now the commune of Jublains, is western France's most important Gallo-Roman site. Capital of the Gallic Diablintes people and founded in the 1st century AD, the city counted 3,000 to 4,000 inhabitants at its peak and served as a road junction connected to a dozen cities.
The Gallo-Roman temple on the road to Mayenne marks the town's origin. Rebuilt in stone after 65 AD, it testifies to the acceleration of Romanization in the mid-1st century.

The fortress is the site's most spectacular element and a monument unique in the Roman Empire. This fortified trapezoid measuring 117.50 × 104.25 meters wasn't a military camp as long believed, but probably a warehouse where taxes in kind and precious metals transited to Rome.

The theater, built around 80 AD and gifted to the city by merchant Orgétorix, sits on the plateau slope facing the Coëvrons hills. Initially fully circular in the 1st century, it was rebuilt as a semicircle in the 2nd. It still hosts cultural events today.

Beneath the current church hide the Roman baths, transformed into a place of worship as early as the 5th century. They occupied a square urban block 60 meters on each side with porticos, bathing rooms and shops—the heart of Roman social life.

The departmental archaeological museum, labeled Tourism and Disability, presents collections from the Bronze Age to the early Middle Ages: pottery, jewelry, coins, game pieces, terracotta Venus statuettes and fragments of the 'pillar with masks' evoking a theater scene.

activities.text: Follow the archaeological trail by spotting the 12 bronze discs set into the ground. They mark a pedestrian circuit between the temple, baths, theater and fortress, crossing the ancient Roman town's layout.
Continue to the Crafts Forum, a venue dedicated to artisanship built after the discovery of an ancient artisan quarter whose activity continues today.

Excavations have been ongoing since 2010 at Jublains: archaeologists and student volunteers are uncovering a vast Gallo-Roman complex—domus or macellum—along the Grazay road. A temporary exhibition accompanies each year's excavation season closing.

days_plan.itin_title: Mayenne Circuit: Hedgerows and Medieval Towns

visits.text: Jujurieux describes itself as the “village of thirteen castles”—an exceptional concentration of medieval fortified residences and 19th-century industrialists' châteaux in a Bugey village. The coexistence of these two types of architecture, fortified and industrial, reflects the complex economic history of this Albarine valley, alternately a stronghold and a production center. Stroll among the façades and let local guides tell you about the rivalries between noble families that shaped this built landscape.

The urban fabric between the Ain valley and the Bugey hillsides deserves slow exploration. The historic 19th-century workshops bear witness to the transition from agriculture to the textile industry in this part of the Ain.

activities.text: “Castles and viewpoints” loop (3–4 km, ~1 hour 30 minutes), taking you from one castle to another while climbing above the Ain valley.
Heritage tour of the historic center: façades, old workshops, and the architecture of 19th-century manor houses. Allow 45 minutes at a leisurely pace.

days_plan.itin_title: Loop Around Lyon: Villages and Pierres Dorées

visits.text: According to local tradition, the name Juliénas is linked to Julius Caesar and the Roman presence in the region during the conquest of Gaul. The winegrowing village stretches across the granite slopes of Mont de Bessay, at elevations ranging from 250 to 470 metres. The vines struggle in this poor soil to draw their resources, producing lively, full-bodied wines that are both robust and elegant, with subtle spicy notes reflecting the varied terroirs.

La Vieille Église stands in the heart of the village, bearing witness to the long winegrowing history of this Beaujolais cru. Its ancient stones have seen generations of winegrowers shape these hillsides. The Caveau de Juliénas, a historic establishment, offers tastings in a traditional setting where the spirit of the old brotherhoods still lingers.

The Château de Juliénas, built in 1582 with extensions dating from 1740, houses the longest cellar in Beaujolais: 350 metres of underground galleries arranged in a square. These century-old vaults hold barrels and large wooden casks, some a hundred years old, in which wines mature peacefully for eight to eighteen months. The eight hectares of vines are cultivated without herbicides or fertilisers.

The Château du Bois de la Salle and the Maison de la Dîme complete the village's architectural heritage. These winegrowers' buildings tell the story of a community united around tending the vines. The golden-stone façades are adorned with climbing vines that turn red in autumn, creating a living picture of the winegrowing seasons.

activities.text: Step inside the family-run wine estates dotting the hillsides. Passionate winegrowers share their expertise, handed down from generation to generation. In the cool cellars, the four Juliénas cuvées reveal different profiles, from fruity wines to wines with great ageing potential that improve with time, expressing the complexity of the granite and sedimentary terroirs.

Follow the hiking trails that wind through the vineyards up to the Col du Fût d'Avenas. The panorama takes in the terraced vineyards, hilltop villages and, on clear days, the Alpine range on the horizon. Marked trails cross woods and vineyards, offering a three-dimensional view of this exceptional terroir.

Join the Nuits du Vin held in late June, two days of celebration, conviviality and wine discovery. The village comes alive with tasting workshops, musical entertainment and opportunities to meet winegrowers. The festive atmosphere, enjoyed by all, celebrates winegrowing tradition with the warmth typical of Beaujolais.

Discover the gastronomic specialities served with Juliénas wines: fine cured meats, full-flavoured cheeses and roast chicken with baby potatoes. The village restaurants offer carefully considered food and wine pairings that highlight the subtle blend of fruit and spice characteristic of this distinctive cru.

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip from Bresse to Bugey via Beaujolais and Lyon

visits.text: Set off to discover the 18 fountains that have made this Cité de Caractère famous. The Marianne Fountain (Place de la Libération), listed as a Historic Monument, is the oldest public representation of the Republic in France. The Lions Fountain displays its elegant sculptures.
Saint-Pierre Church, rebuilt between 1750 and 1760, houses a remarkable high altar and superb woodwork created by Jean Gerdolle, testament to the craftsmanship of 18th-century artisans.
The Maison Cordienne features a main residential building and staircases listed as Historic Monuments, a characteristic example of Jussey's medieval secular architecture.

Nearby, discover Château de Bougey, founded in the 14th century and transformed in the 16th-17th centuries. Its strategic defensive position on the heights bears witness to its past as a medieval stronghold.

activities.text: Climb Mont des Capucins, the town's highest point, to enjoy exceptional panoramas over the surrounding countryside and verdant valleys.
Embark on an adventure with the Baludik app, which offers trail games and treasure hunts through the streets—perfect for exploring the town with family.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Saône Tour: Comtois Plateaus and Heritage

visits.text: Kaysersberg's fortified bridge is unique in Alsace. Built in 1514 of pink sandstone, it spans the Weiss and is equipped with parapets and arrow slits to prevent any attack via the river. At the bridge's center, a shrine houses an 18th-century polychrome Virgin—residents once came to pray here before leaving the town. It also served as an “open prison” for petty offenders exposed to public ridicule. Crossing this bridge means entering the oldest part of Kaysersberg, whose 15th- and 16th-century half-timbered houses number among the finest examples of Rhenish Renaissance architecture in Alsace.

Climb to the ruins of the imperial castle, erected shortly before 1227 by a bailiff of Emperor Frederick II of Hohenstaufen to control the passage between Lorraine and Alsace. Its circular keep—with walls 4.42 meters thick—stands 50 meters above the town. The castle was destroyed in 1632 by Swedish mercenaries during the Thirty Years' War. From the summit platform, the view takes in terraced vineyards, the Weiss valley, the Alsace plain, and, on clear days, the Black Forest.

Kaysersberg was the birthplace of Albert Schweitzer, born here in 1875. Physician, theologian, philosopher, and musician—and Nobel Peace Prize laureate in 1952—he founded the hospital in Lambaréné in Gabon and developed his philosophy of “reverence for life.” The museum dedicated to him in the house where he was born traces his exceptional life; his personal objects, organ scores, and correspondence are displayed in a contemplative atmosphere.

activities.text: Walk Rue du Général-de-Gaulle from the fortified bridge to the end of the historic center—800 meters of Renaissance houses where every facade holds a detail to notice: carved oriels, wrought-iron signs, twisted posts. The 1521 town hall, the Renaissance well decorated with dolphins in the inner courtyard, and the 1594 Maison Brève Faller, which belonged to a cooper, are the centerpieces of this open-air museum.

Reach the terraced vineyards above Kaysersberg via the ramparts trail for panoramas of the Vosges and Black Forest. Local cellars offer tastings of Grand Cru Schlossberg—the name evokes the castle and mountain, and the wines produced combine finesse and power. If you're there in December, Kaysersberg's Christmas market is renowned for its authenticity.

Alsace's Most Beautiful Christmas Markets
Grand Est Road Trip: Vineyards, Ramparts and Forests

The Most Beautiful Villages of Alsace in 4 Days

visits.text: The Château de L'Aigle, completed in 1730 to plans by Hardouin-Mansart, stands on the site of an 11th-century fortress where an eagle's nest gave the town its name. Its rubble and brick walls now house the town hall.

In the château's outbuildings, the June 1944 Museum, inaugurated in 1953, was France's first talking museum. Life-size reconstructions, authentic BBC voices, and a 36 m² animated strategic map recount the Battle of Normandy.
The Church of Saint-Martin, Gothic in style, survived the 1944 bombings that destroyed 80% of the town. Its ancient stained glass filters soft light.

On April 26, 1803, a shower of meteorites fell on L'Aigle. The permanent exhibition in the town hall displays fragments and recounts scientist Jean-Baptiste Biot's investigation, which proved the stones' extraterrestrial origin.
In the Square Eugène Pasquis, two 300-year-old plane trees—designated 'remarkable trees'—take root between two arms of the Risle. Botanists believe they could become thousand-year-old specimens.

activities.text: Every Tuesday, the L'Aigle market stretches across kilometres of stalls selling Norman regional produce, cheeses, poultry and crafts.
In Saint-Sulpice-sur-Risle, a factory still in operation makes needles and pins using know-how more than 190 years old. The tour reveals period machinery still running.
Trails along the Risle reveal the bocage landscape of Pays d'Ouche, the former domain of Countess de Ségur, who wrote many of her novels at the nearby Château des Nouettes.

days_plan.itin_title: Orne Road Trip: Norman Bocage and Stud Farms

places.name: L Arbresle

visits.text: Three kilometers from the center of L'Arbresle, on the heights of Éveux, stands one of the most important architectural works of the 20th century: the Couvent Sainte-Marie de la Tourette, designed by Le Corbusier between 1953 and 1960 for the Dominican friars. It's Le Corbusier's last great work in France, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2016 along with 16 other Le Corbusier sites. Father Couturier, who commissioned it, had chosen Le Corbusier—a non-Catholic—because he had “a sufficient sense of mystery”. The result: a block of raw concrete set on pilotis in a steep-sided valley, where light is a material in its own right—light cannons, horizontal slit openings, undulating glass panels designed by composer Iannis Xenakis. You can stay overnight on site, attend services, and visit the convent on a guided tour. Book in advance.

The old center of L'Arbresle, built at the confluence of the Brévenne and Turdine, preserves some lanes and 19th-century façades from the era of silk merchants. Less spectacular than the convent, but pleasant for a late-afternoon stroll along the quays.

activities.text: Urban route of L'Arbresle's bridges and quays (2 km, flat, ~45 min). The town was once an important textile trading center between Lyon and the Beaujolais.

Hillside trail above Éveux for views over the Lyonnais Mountains. The Tourette estate, acquired by the Dominicans in 1943, spans more than 70 hectares — a forest and agricultural setting that provides striking contrast with the convent's raw concrete.

days_plan.itin_title: Loop Around Lyon: Villages and Pierres Dorées

map_keywords: Couvent Sainte-Marie de la Tourette Éveux L'Arbresle

visits.text: You'll spot it from far away on the chalky plain — the Basilica of Notre-Dame de L'Épine rises in the middle of nowhere, in a village of 600 inhabitants, with the proportions of a cathedral. Construction began in 1406, in the midst of the Hundred Years' War, and ended in 1527. A masterpiece of Flamboyant Gothic, it takes its name from a statue of the Virgin and Child that, according to legend, shepherds discovered around 1400 in a burning thornbush. The church was listed as a historic monument as early as 1840 — among France's first — and is inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage list as part of the Routes to Santiago de Compostela.

Walk around the outside before going in. The gargoyles on the chevet are among the most elaborate in Champagne, fantastical creatures of remarkable delicacy. The detail of the Flamboyant carving across the whole façade shows the ambition of the builders: for such a small village, the building is staggering.

Inside, the 15th-century stone rood screen separates the nave from the choir. Its right-hand arcade houses the statue of the Virgin, the origin of the site's fame. The great organ, completed around 1552, is one of the oldest in France still in working order: its Renaissance case, carved with Greek gods and apostles, is exceptional.

activities.text: Look up at the two unequal spires. The left spire was cut down in 1798 to install a Chappe telegraph relay station — bell towers were used as transmission pylons at the time. It was rebuilt later. This little story says a great deal about how heritage buildings were used during the revolutionary period.

L'Épine lies on the Routes to Santiago de Compostela. Walk the road crossing the chalky plain around the village — the basilica, visible for kilometres, gives a sense of its role as a landmark for pilgrims over six centuries.

days_plan.itin_title: Marne Road Trip: Reims, Épernay and Champagne

visits.text: Forget the polished postcard: L'Estaque harbour lines up concrete jetties and fishing boats at the foot of the hills, 10 km from the Vieux-Port. The heart of the village beats around Place Maleterre, in front of the church, where the view opens onto the bay and the Côte Bleue viaducts. Come in the morning—the light is better and parking is possible.

Painted by Cézanne, Braque and Dufy between 1870 and 1914, the subjects of their L'Estaque paintings are still here: the horizontal line of the sea, factory chimneys, viaduct arches. A walking circuit, the painters' path, starts from the harbour jetty. Allow an hour and wear good shoes, as the climb towards the Falaise is steep.

Surprisingly clear water for Marseille: the beaches at Corbière, on the edge of L'Estaque, were reclaimed from the sea with rockfill and a breakwater. Sloping lawns, pines and picnic areas make it a family spot. They fill up quickly on summer weekends—arrive before 11am.

activities.text: Try the chichis fregis at L'Estaque harbour, sweet fritters sold from stalls, with panisses as the savoury option. It's the neighbourhood speciality, not a tourist invention. The stands close early out of season.

If you come on a Sunday, L'Estaque's jousting club practises in the harbour: two knights standing on boats, lance in hand, until one falls. A Provençal tradition still alive here. Free access from the quay.

days_plan.itin_title: Côte Bleue and Camargue: the lower coastal route in 7 days

places.name: L Hay Les Roses

visits.text: Jules Gravereaux made his fortune as a business partner of the Boucicaut family at Le Bon Marché. On retiring in 1892, he bought a property in L'Haÿ—then an unknown village—and began collecting rose bushes. By 1894, he had 1,600 varieties. In 1899 he called in landscape architect Édouard André, who created a 1.5-hectare formal French garden around his collection. By 1910, all known forms of the genus Rosa were gathered here. The town changed its name in 1914 to L'Haÿ-les-Roses, in direct homage to this garden. Today: 13 collections, 3,000 varieties, 11,000 plants. Some varieties exist nowhere else in the world. Come between late May and mid-June for peak bloom—after that, the flowers thin out quickly.

At the Roseraie du Val-de-Marne, walk along the Allée de l'histoire de la rose: the rose bushes trace the evolution of wild and cultivated varieties. Jules Gravereaux also spent four years developing scented roses for the perfume industry: “Roseraie de L'Haÿ” and “Rose à parfum de L'Haÿ” were the result.

activities.text: Guided tours are offered on Saturdays during the season by departmental staff — the people who maintain the collections and know the stories behind each lost variety. Groups must book in advance. In 2026, the rose garden is open only from April 25 to September 20.

The Jardins du Val de Bièvre, on Avenue Flouquet, stretch across 44,000 m² with 300 trees and two wooden pontoons on a pond. If you still have energy after the rose garden, it's an easy 20-minute walk.

days_plan.itin_title: Val-de-Marne Road Trip: Castles and the Banks of the Marne

map_keywords: Jardins du Val de Bièvre L'Haÿ-les-Roses

visits.text: You will arrive at Port-Joinville after a 30-minute ferry ride from Fromentine, or 1 hour from Saint-Gilles between April and September. It is the beating heart of the island: façades with colorful shutters, café terraces and trawlers unloading sea bass and shellfish in the morning. Rent a bike as soon as you step off the ferry—it is the best way to explore the island's 23 km².

The Vieux Château is the island's landmark monument. Perched on a rocky spur surrounded by the sea, it was built in the 14th century by the lords of Belleville at the beginning of the Hundred Years' War. It was listed as a Historic Monument in 1890. Its silhouette recalls the castle in Hergé's The Black Island, and with good reason: the author is said to have drawn inspiration from it. Visits are available by reservation. Approach along the southern coastal path for the most spectacular view.

Climb the Grand Phare, rebuilt after its destruction by the Germans in 1944. Its tower stands 41 meters tall (56 meters above sea level), and its beam reaches 30 nautical miles. From the top, the entire island unfolds before you. The original lighthouse dated to 1829 and was built after numerous shipwrecks in the area.

Port de la Meule, on the wild coast, is a tiny fishing haven lined with colorful huts. The Notre-Dame-de-Bonne-Nouvelle Chapel overlooks the cove from the path. Dating from the 11th century, it was where sailors came to pray before setting out to sea. Sit down on the rocks and you will feel as though you are at the end of the world.

Stop at the Church of Saint-Sauveur, a Historic Monument since 1906—one of the island's oldest structures, built atop a former priory. Medieval frescoes from the 12th century were uncovered during recent restoration, alongside contemporary stained glass. The contrast is striking.

activities.text: Hop on a bike for the island's Grand Tour: 28.5 kilometers of roads and trails alternating between wild coast, low-growing heathland, hedgerow countryside and coves of golden sand. Allow 3 to 4 hours with stops. Go via Pointe du But for the most wind-exposed viewpoint—you'll feel the full force of the Atlantic.

Lay down your towel on Plage des Vieilles, the island's best-known beach. Lined with typical island houses, this fine-sand cove is an unspoiled natural spot sheltered from the prevailing wind. Outside the summer season, you will have it entirely to yourself.

days_plan.itin_title: Vendée Itinerary: Noirmoutier Island, Puy du Fou and the Coastline

visits.text: Place Paoli spreads its century-old plane trees through the heart of L'Île-Rousse. Founded in 1758 by Pasquale Paoli to compete with Genoese Calvi, the town retains its orthogonal layout. The covered market with its 21 columns in antique style, built between 1844 and 1846 and classified as a Historic Monument, hosts stalls of charcuterie, cheese, and honey every morning.

The island of La Pietra is reached by a causeway from the marina. Red porphyry rocks give the town its name (Isola Rossa in Italian). The white lighthouse built in 1875, fully automated and solar-powered, offers panoramic views of the coast and the islets of Roccio, Roccetto, and Piano. The 15th-century Genoese tower stands watch over the waves.

The Church of the Immaculate Conception overlooks Place Paoli. Inaugurated in 1893, partially destroyed by fire in 1914, then rebuilt in 1935. Architecture blending baroque and neoclassical styles. Two 17th-century paintings from the Fesch collection adorn the interior.

activities.text: The Marinella promenade runs along Napoléon beach on the waterfront. A pedestrian path beneath palms with views of the island of La Pietra. The bronze Siren statue (A Sirenella di l'Isula Rossa) has perched on a granite rock since 2016. Best at sunset when the rocks turn crimson.

The beach train connects L'Île-Rousse to Calvi along the coast. U trinichellu stops at all the Balagne beaches: Bodri, Ghjunchitu, Algajola. A scenic journey at leisurely pace discovering coves and maquis. A relaxing alternative to driving for exploring the coastline.

The beaches of Bodri and Ghjunchitu lie to the southwest, 3 to 5 kilometers away. Fine sand, translucent water. A naturist area at the northern end of Bodri. Reached by the coastal path from L'Île-Rousse or by paid parking in season.

days_plan.itin_title: Upper Corsica Road Trip: Cap Corse and Balagne
Complete Tour of Corsica

places.name: L Isle Adam

visits.text: The L'Isle-Adam river beach is France's largest in a river setting: created from 1895 onward, it extends over 3.5 hectares between the Oise and the forest. Its 44 wooden beach cabins from the 1920s, large semicircular pool opening onto the river, and bandstand give it a Belle Époque resort atmosphere that attracted Mistinguett and Vlaminck in the 1930s. Awarded the Patrimoine d'intérêt régional designation, it opens during the summer season. Even off-season, the quays and promenade are worth exploring.

The Parc de Cassan, steps from the beach, shelters a late 18th-century Chinese pavilion listed as a Historic Monument - one of the rare examples of this style in Île-de-France. The estate with its pond and foliage is a quiet, little-visited spot.

The L'Isle-Adam state forest stretches over more than 1,500 hectares of oaks and beeches immediately outside town—a former hunting reserve of the Princes of Conti that became state property during the Revolution. Crossed by the GR1 and broad avenues laid out by Le Nôtre, it's easily explored in 2 hours from the center. If you have time, look for the Provost Oak, the forest's oldest tree at about 350 years old—forest rangers can point you to its location.

activities.text: Hiking on the GR1 in L'Isle-Adam forest: from the beach, the trail climbs into the woods northward and offers viewpoints over the Marais de Stors, a riverside nature reserve. Easy loop of about 8 km, well marked. Avoid after heavy rain: the clay paths become sticky.

Rental outlets offer canoes and paddleboats on the Oise from the beach in season (generally May-September, 10 AM-5 PM). The backwaters between the Île du Prieuré and Île de la Cohue are the calmest - ideal in the morning before pleasure boats pass through.
