visits.text: L'Isle-Jourdain developed around the Save River. The church of Saint-Martin dates from the 14th century with its characteristic octagonal bell tower. The town center preserves some half-timbered houses.
Lac de L'Isle-Jourdain is a leisure base with a developed beach. In summer, it's a swimming and water sports spot popular with families.

activities.text: Walk along the Save River that flows through town. The banks are landscaped and offer a pleasant setting for walking.
Saturday morning market offers local products from the Toulouse region. You'll find vegetables, cheeses, and charcuterie.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Garonne Road Trip: From Toulouse to the Pyrenees

visits.text: Nicknamed the “Venice of the Comtat,” L'Isle-sur-la-Sorgue is crossed by willow-lined canals. About fifteen waterwheels still turn, remnants of the old textile and paper industries that once made the town wealthy.

The Collégiale Notre-Dame des Anges surprises with its 17th-century baroque interior: 222 sculpted and gilded angels populate the nave, chapels, and chancel. The whole is listed as a historic monument.
Over 300 permanent antique dealers are spread across seven clusters of antique shops, making L'Isle Europe's third-largest center for the art and secondhand goods market.

Visit the Partage des Eaux, a natural site where the Sorgue divides into two branches according to a historical allocation: five-twelfths toward Velleron, seven-twelfths toward Entraigues. A small shaded path follows the river.
The medieval Tour d'Argent and Renaissance mansions on Rue Ledru-Rollin testify to the city's past prosperity, built on the silk and paper trade.

activities.text: Sunday and Thursday markets bring life to the Sorgue quays. In summer, the floating market sends boats loaded with goods along the canals, following the nego-chin (“butt-soaker”) tradition.
Rent a canoe or kayak to descend the Sorgue from Fontaine-de-Vaucluse to L'Isle. Transparent water flows between white cliffs and foliage.
Casual bargain hunters or knowledgeable enthusiasts: move from stall to stall during the major secondhand goods fairs held at Easter and around August 15, attracting hundreds of vendors.

days_plan.itin_title: Vaucluse: Avignon, Luberon Villages & Ventoux Routes

visits.text: La Baule's Grande Plage stretches 9 kilometers of fine sand in a crescent between Pornichet and Le Pouliguen—one of the longest in Europe. The resort was born in 1879 when two representatives of the Paris-Orléans Railway Company had the bright idea of building a seaside resort on what was then just a marshy spot called La Bôle. The pine forest, planted as early as 1849 by a Nantes ship owner to stabilize the dunes, made the town's reputation. The seafront esplanade gradually filled with villas between 1880 and the Roaring Twenties: the town counts more than 4,000 today, in Art Deco, neo-Breton, neo-Basque, and Belle Époque styles. The bay has belonged to the Club of the World's Most Beautiful Bays since 2011.

To appreciate the architectural heritage, stroll residential neighborhoods set back from the seafront. Themed guided tours of villas and architecture are offered by the tourist office (roughly 1.5 hours). Fifteen villas are distinguished as exceptional heritage in the architectural heritage protection zone. The Sainte-Anne Chapel, built between 1880 and 1904, regularly hosts exhibitions and concerts—check the program on-site.

La Baule's market runs every morning along the seafront and in the covered market halls. Regional oysters, Guérande fleur de sel, and local Loire products are sold side by side. A must-visit market for putting together a beach picnic or bringing edible souvenirs home.

activities.text: La Baule Bay is ideal for water sports thanks to regular westerly winds. Operators offer lessons in sand yachting, kitesurfing, catamaran sailing, and stand-up paddleboarding, along with equipment rentals, directly on the beach. If you're a beginner, try sand yachting—La Baule's signature sport, practiced on the beach at low tide.

days_plan.itin_title: Loire-Atlantique Road Trip: Nantes and the Côte de Jade

places.name: La Borne

visits.text: La Borne has been a potters' village since the 15th century. A seam of stoneware clay and abundant wood made its fortune. In the 19th century, 80 artisans among 700 inhabitants produced salting pots, terrines and milk jugs for the whole of central-western France. Today, around a hundred ceramic artists of 12 nationalities continue the tradition, but functional ware has given way to contemporary art.

The Centre Céramique Contemporaine La Borne (CCCLB) showcases the work of local and international artists in a 665 m² glass gallery. Exhibitions change each season, artist residencies, lectures. It's the ideal starting point before visiting the studios.

The Pottery Museum, set in the former Saint-Jean-Baptiste chapel, presents traditional production: functional pieces, folk imagery, throwing tools. You can gauge the shift from rustic 19th-century salting pots to contemporary sculptures.

The Ivanoff Museum occupies the former studio of Vassil Ivanoff, “the first expressionist in ceramics”. 300 pieces donated by his family: monumental stoneware, tortured forms, fractured glazes. A distinctive world that left its mark on a whole generation of ceramicists.

activities.text: Going from studio to studio is the heart of the visit. You push open the doors, watch the artisans at the wheel, handle the pieces. Each ceramicist has their own style: raw or glazed stoneware, pared-down or organic forms, gas or wood firing. Prices range from €20 for a bowl to several thousand euros for a sculpture.

Les Grands Feux de La Borne (late October) bring together ceramicists and enthusiasts for a week of collective firings. Traditional wood-fired kilns reach 1,280°C. Open days, demonstrations, lectures, market. The major event on the French ceramics scene.

Beginner ceramic workshops at the CCCLB: hand-modelling, wheel-throwing, glazing. Courses from half a day to several days, for adults or children. You leave with your creation after firing (postal shipping possible).

Five minutes from La Borne, Jean Linard's Cathedral is a work of art brut in the middle of fields. The artist spent 30 years building this structure of mosaics, ceramics and salvaged materials. Visits by appointment only.

days_plan.itin_title: Cher Loop: Romanesque Berry and the Route Jacques-Cœur

map_keywords: Musée de la Poterie La Borne

visits.text: La Bourboule preserves the elegance of its Belle Époque heritage along the upper Dordogne at an altitude of 850 meters in the Massif du Sancy. The spa town owes its renown to its 58°C waters rich in bicarbonate, sodium chloride, and arsenic, reputed to help with respiratory, skin, and mucous membrane conditions. The Grands Thermes, luxury hotels, former casino, and Parc Fenestre form a coherent architectural ensemble from the turn of the 20th century. Illustrious guests of the resort have included the Queen of Romania, Sacha Guitry, and Buster Keaton.

The Funiculaire du Capucin at Le Mont-Dore is France's oldest electric funicular, built in 1898 and listed as a Historic Monument. Its Art Deco departure station, expanded in 1930, provides access to a car that climbs at one meter per second to the Salon du Capucin at an altitude of 1,245 meters. From there, hiking trails lead off, and there is a Sylvatorium for forest therapy, a forest adventure park, and a via ferrata.

Parc Fenestre offers a cool, green space in the heart of La Bourboule. This spa garden bordering the Dordogne brings together rare tree species and Belle Époque features in a mountain resort atmosphere. The pure air at this moderate mountain altitude, naturally low in allergens, makes the resort popular with families—La Bourboule holds the Famille Plus label.

activities.text: Hike to Puy de Sancy, the Massif Central's highest point at 1,886 meters. From Le Mont-Dore, the resort cable car provides summit access after a short ridge walk. The panorama embraces the entire volcanic massif, the Limagne plain, and on clear days, the Alps.

Discover the Grande Cascade du Mont-Dore, one of Auvergne's highest waterfalls. Accessible by a shaded forest trail from Le Mont-Dore, the waterfall offers a refreshing spectacle amid greenery in the volcanic landscape.

Stroll through the streets of the spa towns of Le Mont-Dore and La Bourboule to admire the architecture of their Belle Époque villas and hotels. Ornate facades, wrought-iron canopies, and sculpted pediments testify to the heyday of spa treatments in Auvergne.

days_plan.itin_title: Volcanoes and Auvergne traditions

visits.text: The Maison de la Préhistoire in La Bouverie is devoted to Bouverian man, the Upper Paleolithic human who gave his name to the region's last Paleolithic industry. Points, scrapers and knapped flint come from excavations led in 1967 by Jean Landréat and François Puigdellivol. Free entry, open only for half-day periods: call ahead.

Four caves discovered in the 1970s at the foot of the Blavet gorges: the La Bouverie caves were occupied almost continuously during the last 20,000 years of the Upper Paleolithic. South-facing, with a stream nearby and shelter from the wind. You can see them from the trails, rather than on guided tours.

activities.text: If you're passing through on a Saturday morning, La Bouverie's market offers local produce in the northern district of Roquebrune-sur-Argens. Wine estates and an apiary round out the stop after your hike. It's the best place to stock up before tackling the Blavet gorges.

days_plan.itin_title: Roquebrune-sur-Argens: sea, villages and the Var in 10 days

places.name: La Bresse

visits.text: Lac des Corbeaux, nicknamed "the black eye," is a 9-hectare glacial lake perched at 887 meters. Enclosed in a cirque of dark firs, it owes its nickname to the almost black reflections of its deep waters (27 m).
La Bresse extends between 600 and 1,363 meters altitude (the Hohneck). La Bresse-Hohneck resort is the largest ski area in the Vosges, with summer chairlift access to high-altitude pastures.

The summit of the Hohneck rises to 1 363 meters. Allow for a return trip from La Bresse to reach it. From the summit, the view takes in the Alsace plain, the Black Forest and, in clear weather, the Bernese Alps. Chamois sometimes graze on the slopes.
The Route des Crêtes, laid out during World War I to stay out of sight of the enemy, winds between 900 and 1,300 meters. It offers alternating panoramas over the Vosges and Alsatian slopes.

activities.text: Hike to the Roche du Lac, 200 meters above Lac des Corbeaux. The climb is steep (alt. 1,050 m), but the view down over the lake below is spectacular.

Ascend the Hohneck via the farmhouse inns: Firstmiss then Kastelberg. Lunch is a marcaire meal (meat pie, Munster cheese, bilberry tart), overlooking the high pastures and surrounded by white-banded Vosges cattle.
In summer, descending by electric scooter from the heights of La Bresse is a fun way to explore the forest trails under the supervision of instructors.

days_plan.itin_title: Vosges Road Trip: Lakes, Mountains & Thermal Spas

map_keywords: Lac de la Lande La Bresse

visits.text: The Abbey of La Chaise-Dieu (Casa Dei, "House of God") was founded in 1043 by Robert de Turlande. The 14th-century Gothic abbey church shelters the white marble tomb of Pope Clement VI, surrounded by 55 sculpted figures.
The famous Danse Macabre, a 15th-century fresco painted on the north aisle, is one of the few surviving in France. Three dead and three living dance together: "Death spares neither small nor great."

Admire the 14 Flemish tapestries from the early 16th century, totaling 65 m (213 ft) in length. Commissioned by Abbot Jacques de Saint-Nectaire, they illustrate biblical scenes from the Poor Man's Bible.
The 144 carved oak stalls surround the choir. Chimeras, monks in grotesque poses, grimacing faces: Flemish sculptors let their imaginations run wild here.
Visit the Echo Room, a genuine acoustic curiosity. Stand in one corner and whisper: your companion, in the opposite corner, hears you perfectly.
The flamboyant Gothic rood screen separates the nave from the monks' choir. Above the main entrance, the 17th-century Baroque organ case adorns the interior façade with sculpted musical angels.
The Clémentine Tower, an imposing 14th-century fortified keep at the church's chevet, once housed the abbey's treasures. The neighboring stables have been converted into an auditorium.

activities.text: Wander through the medieval town built below the abbey. The rue des Casernes, narrow and paved with pebbles, is the oldest. Some façades preserve bartizans, mascarons, and coats of arms.
Each August, the La Chaise-Dieu Music Festival, founded in 1966, hosts classical music concerts beneath the abbey's vaults. Check the program.
Step inside the Chapelle des Pénitents, the former monks' refectory transformed into a chapel after the Revolution. Free access year-round.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Loire Road Trip: Le Puy-en-Velay and Volcanoes

visits.text: La Chapelle-en-Vercors is the central town of the Drôme Vercors, at the bottom of a basin surrounded by meadows and forests. During summer 1944, it too was struck by German occupation: several memorial sites in the village recall civilian massacres. A memorial site in the village recounts these events. If you visited Vassieux the day before, La Chapelle offers a complementary perspective on the same events—here, the civilian aspect predominates.

The Combe Laval road departs La Chapelle westward: it's one of the Vercors' most spectacular roads, carved into the cliff face 300 meters above the Lyonne valley. The view from developed viewpoints plunges onto the forest below and extends to Royans. The road itself is the attraction: don't leave it too quickly.

activities.text: The village-meadows-forest edge circuit (4-5 km) exits the village via farm roads and follows the basin's wooded rim. It's typical Drôme Vercors landscape: meadows in the basin floor, spruces on slopes, gray cliffs on ridges.

The climb to a high point for basin views from Trois Châteaux (south slope, accessible via forest path) offers the overall geography of La Chapelle-en-Vercors nestled in its plateau. Allow 1h round trip from the village.

days_plan.itin_title: Royans-Vercors Road Trip: Hilltop Villages and Gorges

visits.text: Founded in 1059 by the Cluniac order, La Charité's priory earned the nickname "eldest daughter of Cluny." In the 12th century, the church stretched 120 meters long with over 400 dependencies across Europe.

Notre-Dame Church, inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage list in 1998 as a major stop on the Way of St. James, displays a radiating chapel apse and two carved tympana. The ambulatory capitals illustrate Cluniac inspiration.
The conventual buildings, rebuilt in the 18th century, preserve two cloister wings and staircases with ornate railings. They host exhibitions and cultural events year-round.
The Monks' Garden offers magnificent views of the church's chevet. Excavations have unearthed the foundations of buildings that preceded the current church.
The 14th-century medieval ramparts encircle the town. Two towers and several fortified gates survive, testifying to La Charité's strategic importance along the Loire.

activities.text: La Charité holds the "Book Town" label, with some fifty secondhand bookshops and bouquinistes. Browse through the shelves—each shop has its specialty.
Wander along the Loire quays, redesigned for pedestrians. The royal river once served to transport goods from the Nivernais forges.
The Centre Culturel de Rencontre hosts concerts and exhibitions. The medieval town comes alive with cultural events.

days_plan.itin_title: Nièvre Road Trip: Morvan and Ducal Heritage

visits.text: La Châtre historic center. A town with a three-flower rating, La Châtre astonishes with the quality of its heritage. The 15th-century keep, which became a prison then a museum, dominates the old town. The mysterious lantern of the dead and the picturesque tanners' quarter with its half-timbered houses plunge you into the medieval atmosphere. A marked route with 20 stops follows the history-laden streets.

Chauvigny Keep. This massive tower stands out above the old town of La Châtre. Once the fortress of the local lords, it long served as a prison before housing collections devoted to George Sand. The building can no longer be visited, but its mass of stone remains the landmark of the historic center and the best place to understand the town's defensive position above the Indre.

Parish church. The church in the town center has distinctive architecture and testifies to La Châtre's spiritual history. Its belfry is visible from afar and serves as a landmark in the urban landscape.

activities.text: George Sand's estate at Nohant. A few kilometers away, George Sand's house is open year-round. This 18th-century residence preserves the famous writer's furniture and belongings. The salon and dining room welcomed Balzac, Chopin, Delacroix, Flaubert, and Liszt. The six-hectare park, designated a Jardin Remarquable, features a rose garden, meadow-orchard, and vegetable garden. The puppet theater created by the family completes the visit.

Saint-Martin Church in Vic. In Nohant-Vic, this 11th-century Romanesque church houses remarkable 12th-century frescoes, preserved thanks to George Sand and Prosper Mérimée's intervention in 1851. The biblical scenes with striking colors and expressions constitute a unique testimony to Berry Romanesque art.

Saturday market. The weekly market brings the town center to life with stalls selling regional produce. Goat cheeses, seasonal vegetables, honey, Berry wines, and local culinary specialties create a friendly atmosphere typical of Berry.

days_plan.itin_title: Indre Road Trip: Secret Berry and the Vallée Noire

visits.text: First, step through the doors of Eden-Théâtre at 25 boulevard Clemenceau. Built in 1889, it's the world's oldest cinema still in operation. The Lumière brothers organized a private screening here as early as September 21, 1895—weeks before Paris—and the first paid public screening took place here on March 21, 1899. The Lumière family spent vacations in La Ciotat at their Clos des Plages château, and the town's streets were where they filmed their first movies, including the famous “Arrival of a Train at La Ciotat Station.” The building, listed as a historic monument, was saved and renovated by passionate volunteers. Guided tours on Wednesday and Saturday afternoons.

Next, head down to La Ciotat's Old Port. The quays are lined with 17th-century houses in colorful façades. At the quay's end, the old Town Hall (1864) houses the Ciotat museum with maritime history and Lumière brothers memorabilia. Did you know pétanque was invented here in 1907 or 1910, depending on sources? A monument commemorates it near the port.

Continue on foot to Parc du Mugel, 20 minutes from the port. This 12-hectare botanical park nestles in a red-rock calanque, sheltered by the Bec de l'Aigle. Climb to the belvedere at 82 meters elevation: the view of ochre cliffs plunging into the turquoise Mediterranean is probably La Ciotat's finest. The vegetation is lush—pines, eucalyptus, palms. Bring proper shoes for the trails.

Right next to Mugel, stop at Figuerolles calanque. Smaller and more intimate than those near Cassis, it's distinguished by strangely shaped rocks sculpted by erosion and crystalline waters. If you're there late afternoon, the grazing light on the red rocks is superb.

activities.text: To extend the day by the sea, take a shuttle boat from the port to the Île Verte, a wooded island. The crossing takes 10 minutes. On the island you will find hiking trails, a small beach and a restaurant - a peaceful break facing the mainland. Allow half a day.

Stroll the waterfront in the evening. In summer, the port comes alive with nighttime artisan markets and open-air concerts. Try the local bouillabaisse—each restaurant has its own recipe, and locals claim theirs is better than Marseille's.

days_plan.itin_title: From Marseille to Aix-en-Provence: Calanques, Hilltop Villages and Provençal Light

visits.text: The Gorges du Fier form a spectacular canyon carved by the river of the same name. A footbridge suspended 25 meters above the torrent follows the walls sculpted by erosion. Allow for a round trip during the day from La Clusaz.
Faces in the rock naturally appear in the limestone walls. Visitors' imagination discerns human profiles and animal silhouettes.

The Château de Montrottier overlooks the valley from its rocky promontory. This medieval fortress houses collections of antique weapons, faience and artworks from around the world. Allow for a round trip during the day from La Clusaz.
The castle's circular keep offers a panoramic view of the gorges and surrounding mountains. Vaulted rooms preserve monumental fireplaces.

The Château de Menthon-Saint-Bernard stands on a spur overlooking the lake. This fairytale residence is said to have inspired Walt Disney's Sleeping Beauty castle. The site is about 25 km from La Clusaz, a 30-minute drive.
Still inhabited by the same family for a thousand years, the castle opens its furnished rooms to visitors. The library holds over 12,000 antique volumes.
La Clusaz displays its authentic Savoyard village at the foot of the Aravis range. Wooden chalets and a pointed church steeple compose a postcard setting.
The Aravis Pass peaks at 1,486 meters offering a grandiose panorama of Mont Blanc on clear days. The winding road crosses pastures and fir forests.
The Balme, Torchère, and Fernuy cirques carve into the massif with their hanging valleys. These natural amphitheaters shelter remarkable alpine flora.
The Burgeat Waterfall tumbles down rocks in the Manigod Valley. A short forest trail leads to this refreshing curtain of water.
The Sulens chalet perched in the alpine meadow welcomes hikers with its farmhouse cheeses. Cows graze the rich grass that gives Reblochon its incomparable taste.

activities.text: Walk along the Gorges du Fier footbridge above the torrent and observe the limestone walls sculpted by the water. Allow for a round trip during the day from La Clusaz.
Discover the Mer des Rochers at the exit of the Gorges du Fier, where erosion has shaped striking limestone formations. Allow for a round trip during the day from La Clusaz.
Visit the Château de Menthon during its summer evening openings, when candles and torches recreate a medieval atmosphere. The site is about 25 km from La Clusaz, a 30-minute drive.
Explore the Château de Menthon's kitchen garden, where fruit, vegetables, flowers and aromatic plants grow below the residence. The site is about 25 km from La Clusaz, a 30-minute drive.
Taste PDO farmhouse Reblochon made in the Aravis alpine pastures. This raw-milk cheese is enjoyed aged or melted in tartiflette.
The Yves Pollet-Villard via ferrata in La Clusaz follows an airy route across the cliff. Ladders, rope bridges and walkways provide dizzying thrills.
Hiking trails crisscross alpine meadows where herds graze. The climb to the Aravis Pass rewards walkers with an unforgettable panorama.
In summer, ski lifts transport mountain bikers to the summits for descents through flowering alpine meadows.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Savoie Road Trip: Alpine Lakes & Mont Blanc
Grand Tour Ain & Savoie Mont-Blanc: Lakes, Mountains and Heritage
Grand Tour Ain & Savoie Mont-Blanc: Lakes, Mountains and Heritage

places.name: La Colle Sur Loup

visits.text: La Colle-sur-Loup was the perfume rose capital until the mid-20th century, and the Centifolia rose, known as the May rose, is one of the signature flowers in Chanel N°5 alongside Grasse jasmine. The fields have receded but the identity holds.

The Espace Rose de Mai, Rue Clemenceau, is the former perfume flower producers' cooperative, active from 1907 to 1995. It's now a municipal hall, but it's the anchor point of the village's horticultural history.

The Saint-Jacques-le-Majeur church, in the old centre, houses an altarpiece and a polychrome wooden Virgin and Child. A sober building, not ostentatious, in the lineage of 16th-century parish churches.
The old village spirals around the hill, its golden stone houses linked by stairways and vaulted passages. The oldest well, at Place Saint-Giaume, dates from 1633.

activities.text: If you visit in mid-May, the “Autour de la Rose” festival fills the lanes with rose growers, alembic distilling and a craft market.
The terraced trail crosses olive groves and vineyards with views over the Loup gorges. Budget 1h30—easy and well shaded.

For olive oil, the nearest active mill is the Moulin de la Brague in Opio, about 15 km away, which presses over 60% of the department's olives. In La Colle itself, ask the tourist office about producers open for tastings.

days_plan.itin_title: Secret valleys of the Nice hinterland in 6 days

map_keywords: Rose de Mai space La Colle-sur-Loup

places.name: La Courneuve

visits.text: Georges-Valbon Park covers 417 hectares. More than 310 hectares are designated as a Natura 2000 site, home to over 140 bird species.
The park's rose garden contains 15,000 rose bushes. In spring, fragrance fills the paths and colors burst from the carefully tended beds.
The Maison du parc Victoria Montou, by the Grand Lac, hosts free exhibitions and events year-round. Nearby, artist Rachid Koraïchi's sculpture Le Vigilant overlooks the water.

The Terrain des Essences, 13 hectares restored to a natural state after the Paris Games, has become part of the park. An observation point offers a view of this still-young ecological reserve, a refuge for local wildlife.

activities.text: Take the 10 km hiking loop offered by the Fédération de la Randonnée. The trail winds between seven lakes, woodlands, clearings, and viewpoints.
In fine weather, pedal boats and rowboats are available on the Grand Lac. Families enjoy playgrounds, the carousel, and orienteering courses.
The park's equestrian center offers introductory pony riding sessions for children. Horse-drawn carriage rides are organized from April to September.

days_plan.itin_title: Seine-Saint-Denis Tour: Basilica and Urban Culture

map_keywords: Maison du parc Victoria Montou La Courneuve
Lac du parc Valbon La Courneuve

places.name: La Couvertoirade

visits.text: La Couvertoirade rises from the Larzac plateau like a mirage. Its intact ramparts, built by the Hospitallers in the 15th century, encircle a village of 25 permanent residents. Two monumental gates topped by square towers and round towers at corners form the defensive system.

The Templar castle, erected in the late 12th century, is the only castle built by the Templars in France. Classified as a Historic Monument, it houses a space dedicated to the history of the Order of the Temple: armor, iconographic documents, plans. The keep is carved into rock.

The church of Saint-Christol, built by the Hospitallers in the late 13th century in flamboyant Gothic style, replaced a Templar chapel that had become too small. Its position on a rocky spur dominates the entire village.

From the rampart walk, the view embraces lauze roofs, the castle, paved lanes, and beyond the walls, the Larzac causse expanses to the Cévennes. Arrow slits and loopholes testify to the medieval defensive system.

The lavogne, an artificial pond lined with slabs, served as a watering trough for flocks on this limestone plateau where water is scarce. Along with houses' roof cisterns, it illustrates the ingenuity of causse architecture for capturing every drop.

The Maison de la Scipione, starting point of the visit, recounts the village's history through films and exhibitions. The communal oven, Redounel mill (17th century), and 16th-17th century mansion houses complete the architectural panorama.

activities.text: The hiking loop around La Couvertoirade crosses Larzac's agropastoral landscape: dry-stone walls, lavognes, sheepfolds, and expanses of limestone grasslands. Ideal for understanding inhabitants' daily life in the Templars' era.

The network of the five Templar and Hospitaller sites of the Larzac (La Couvertoirade, Sainte-Eulalie de Cernon, La Cavalerie, Le Viala-du-Pas-de-Jaux and Saint-Jean-d'Alcas) can be visited with a joint pass. The commandery of Sainte-Eulalie, the mother house of the network, is especially worth the detour: about 17 km from the stopover town, 17 minutes by car.

The Larzac plateau, inscribed as World Heritage for the agropastoral landscapes of the Causses and Cévennes, is crossed by marked trails. Shepherds still lead flocks of sheep whose milk produces Roquefort cheese.

days_plan.itin_title: Occitanie's 13 Most Beautiful Villages

map_keywords: Maison de la Scipione La Couvertoirade

visits.text: The Grande Arche, inaugurated in 1989, anchors Paris's historic axis. Danish architect Johan Otto von Spreckelsen conceived this 110-meter hollowed cube as a modern echo to the Arc de Triomphe.
The CNIT, built between 1955 and 1958, displays a triangular concrete vault spanning 220 meters per side. This shell rests on just three support points.
La Défense towers embody glass-and-steel architecture. Tour First, Tour Total, and Tour EDF compose Europe's premier business district.

activities.text: The La Défense esplanade spreads across 3 hectares punctuated by modern sculptures: César's Thumb, Barrias's La Défense statue, and Takis's fountains.
The Quatre Temps shopping center features 220 boutiques. When it opened in 1981, it was Europe's largest shopping mall.

days_plan.itin_title: Hauts-de-Seine Road Trip: Royal Heritage & Gardens

visits.text: The Prytanée National Militaire is an institution of uncommon historical density. In 1603, Henry IV donated his château of La Flèche to the Jesuits to found a college there—his declared objective: "to instruct youth and make them lovers of learning, honor, and virtue." René Descartes was one of its first students, from 1607 to 1615, and traced in the Discourse on Method the intellectual formation he received there. In 1808, Napoleon transferred the military Prytanée from Saint-Cyr here. The Henri IV quarter, 16 hectares classified as historic monuments in the heart of the city, can be visited in summer: three courtyards in succession, the Jesuit library, the halls of honor. Above all, don't miss the Church of Saint-Louis.

The Church of Saint-Louis, built between 1607 and 1621, is La Flèche's Baroque jewel. Its interior decoration was completed in 1693 and revolves around three major pieces: Pierre Corbineau's great altarpiece (1633), the organ and its gallery (1640), and the royal cenotaphs. Henry IV had promised, in his lifetime, to bequeath his heart to this church. His promise was kept—but during the Revolution, in 1793, representative Thirion had the two royal hearts thrown onto the pyre in the public square. A local surgeon collected some ashes in a glass vial, returned to the Prytanée in 1814. Today, a small gilded heart-shaped urn in the north transept arm preserves these mingled ashes of Henry IV and Marie de Medici.

The Zoo de La Flèche truly deserves a visit, and not just with children. Founded in 1946 by naturalist Jacques Bouillault—France's first private zoo—it extends over 18 hectares and gathers 1,500 animals representing 160 species. It regularly features in the top 5 most visited zoos in France and was the subject of the documentary television series broadcast on France 4. The gibbons, lemurs, and okapis alone are worth the trip. Allow at least two hours.

activities.text: Walk along the Loir riverbanks from the Parc des Carmes, where picturesque ruins of the old château remain. The landscaped banks follow the river for several kilometers—a flat, shaded walk, perfect midday. In season, you can continue to the Monnerie lakes which offer a beach and cycling path along the water.

The Cré-sur-Loir marsh, a regional nature reserve about ten kilometers from La Flèche, offers several marked trails to discover the Loir valley's wetland fauna. Herons, spoonbills, and sometimes otters are regularly observed here—bring binoculars and boots if you go after rain.

days_plan.itin_title: Sarthe Road Trip: Le Mans and the Loir Valley

places.name: La Flotte

visits.text: Cross the Île de Ré bridge (2.9 km) and head to La Flotte, classified as one of France's Most Beautiful Villages. You'll discover this small harbor with flowered lanes and white houses with green shutters is one of the island's most charming. The morning medieval market (daily in summer) is excellent—fish, goat cheeses, island salt.

Continue to Saint-Martin-de-Ré, whose Vauban citadel (17th century) is a UNESCO World Heritage site. The harbor is protected by star-shaped fortifications. The shopping lanes are lively yet remain human-scale—you'll find the area's most authentic atmosphere.

Climb the Phare des Baleines at the island's northern tip—257 steps to reach the top (57 meters). Built in 1854, it takes its name from the whales that once beached on this coast. The view sweeps across the ocean and straits. The 1682 lighthouse stands right beside it.

Detour through Ars-en-Ré—its black-and-white bell tower painted like a seamark has served as a landmark for sailors for centuries. You'll find a tiny pedestrianized village with art galleries and peaceful terraces.

activities.text: Get on a bike to explore the salt marshes—Île de Ré has over 100 kilometers of flat, marked cycling paths. You'll pass salt harvesters collecting fleur de sel, donkeys in trousers (a Ré tradition), and migratory birds. Allow 2 hours for a medium loop.
Settle in at Plage de la Conche des Baleines, one of the island's wildest beaches—long, bordered by dunes and pine forest. Few visitors outside July-August. Bring a picnic; there's nothing on-site.

days_plan.itin_title: Nouvelle-Aquitaine Loop: Villages, Vineyards & Dordogne
Nouvelle-Aquitaine Loop: Villages, Vineyards & Dordogne

visits.text: A free museum dedicated to cork, silkworms and chestnuts: the Conservatoire du Patrimoine du Freinet, housed in the Saint-Jean chapel, tells the story of what sustained the Maures massif before tourism. A model of Fort Freinet and finds from excavations complete the visit. Open Monday to Friday: it's closed on weekends for most of the year.

activities.text: Head down into the lanes of La Garde-Freinet: the village took shape at the pass in the 14th century, when the inhabitants of Fort Freinet abandoned the rocky peak. Houses grew up around the Saint-Clément church, and fountains, a washhouse and a threshing floor line the route. A printed guide is available free at the tourist office.

Chestnut honey and candied chestnuts are the signature of La Garde-Freinet, along with farmhouse goat cheeses and AOC olive oil. The village market is the place to taste all that at once. In autumn, it's chestnut season, and that changes everything.

days_plan.itin_title: Roquebrune-sur-Argens: sea, villages and the Var in 10 days
Var in 4 Days: From Bormes to the Most Beautiful Villages of the Verdon

visits.text: 1970s architecture of La Grande-Motte, visionary seaside resort created from scratch by Jean Balladur. Residential pyramids with staggered white facades draw inspiration from pre-Columbian and modern architecture. The Grande Pyramide, iconic 14-story building, dominates the seafront. Seaside residences with bold geometric forms—Point Zéro, Grande Motte, Acapulco—illustrate the seaside utopia of the post-war boom years. The 20th-century architectural heritage classified with Heritage of the 20th Century label attracts modern architecture enthusiasts. Green spaces integrated into buildings create a unique garden city on the coast.

Port de plaisance of La Grande-Motte, modern marina with 1,600 berths nestled between dunes and pyramids. Pontoons welcome yachts, sailboats, and pleasure boats in a protected basin. Lively quays border restaurants, ice cream shops, and nautical boutiques in relaxed seaside atmosphere. Sailing school offers introductions and courses for all levels. Developed promenades invite strolling between boats and brutalist architecture. Sunsets set ablaze white pyramid facades reflecting in calm waters.

Beaches of La Grande-Motte, three miles of supervised fine sand bordered by protected dunes. Grande Plage facing the pyramids offers lifeguard stations, nautical clubs, and deckchair rental. Themed beaches—Plage du Couchant, de l'Esplanade—adapt to different practices: family swimming, water sports, sunbathing. Breakwaters create calm swimming zones for children. Handicapped access with tiralos allows swimming for all. Beaches with Blue Flag label guarantee water quality and preserved environment.

activities.text: Water sports at La Grande-Motte, premier destination for aquatic activities. Schools offer lessons in optimist sailing, catamaran, dinghy, or windsurfing. Kitesurfing practiced on windy spots with professional supervision. Paddleboarding and kayaking allow discovering coast and lagoons at peaceful pace. Scuba diving reveals Mediterranean seabeds, posidonia meadows, and local fauna. Nautical centers rent equipment and organize supervised outings. The tramontane wind guarantees optimal conditions for gliding sports.

Thalassotherapy and wellness at the resort's specialized centers. Marine cures use seawater, algae, and mud for restorative treatments. Heated seawater pools, massaging jets, and whirlpool baths relax after an active day. Facial and body treatments with marine products regenerate skin. Relaxing massages, wraps, and scrubs complete wellness offerings. Half-day or full-day packages include access to facilities and personalized treatments. The zen atmosphere invites a relaxing break facing the Mediterranean.

Evening at La Grande-Motte casino, gaming and entertainment establishment by the sea. Air-conditioned rooms offer slot machines, roulette, blackjack, and Texas Hold'em poker. Weekly tournaments gather skilled players in competitive atmosphere. The panoramic restaurant offers gourmet cuisine with sea views. Shows, concerts, and stand-up comedy animate cultural programming. The lounge terrace allows cocktails facing the waves. The building's brutalist architecture integrates into the resort's pyramidal style.

days_plan.itin_title: Gard Circuit: Roman Nîmes, Pont du Gard and Camargue

places.name: La Malene

visits.text: La Malène occupies a meander of the Tarn at the bottom of the gorges. Its château of the barons of Montesquieu, remodelled in the 16th century, overlooks the lauze stone roofs. Narrow lanes drop down to the boatmen's landing stage.
Climb up to the Roc des Hourtous or the Roc du Serre. These two viewpoints, reached by road from the causse, offer a vertical drop of 600 m over the gorges. Griffon vultures often glide below.
Aven Armand, on the Méjean causse, shelters a forest of more than 400 stalagmites. The tallest reaches 30 m, a world record. The funicular descent leads to an underground chamber of 60,000 m².

The Belvédère des Vautours, above the Jonte gorges, about 13 km from the stopover town, 20 minutes by road, is a museum space devoted to the raptors reintroduced since the 1970s. Viewing scopes and live cameras let you follow griffon, black and Egyptian vultures on the cliffs.

The Méjean causse stretches between the Tarn and Jonte gorges. An almost lunar landscape of sparse grasslands, dolines, and dry-stone walls. Isolated farms perpetuate a UNESCO-recognized agropastoral tradition.

activities.text: Embark from La Malène for the flat-bottomed boat descent to the Baumes cirque. Boatmen navigate through Les Détroits, where cliffs plunge vertically into the Tarn.
Walk down the Jonte gorges from the Méjean causse. The path winds between the cliffs where the vultures nest. Just look up to catch sight of the birds, with wingspans of nearly 3 m.
Swim in the Tarn at pebble beaches upstream or downstream from La Malène. The turquoise water is brisk but invigorating. Cliffs frame natural spots sheltered from wind.

days_plan.itin_title: Lozère Circuit: Tarn Gorges and Cévennes

places.name: La Palud Sur Verdon

visits.text: La Palud-sur-Verdon is a village full of character nestled at the foot of the gorges. Stone houses rise in tiers around the Romanesque church. Flower-filled little squares offer refreshing stops in the shade of lime trees.

Point Sublime offers a vertiginous viewpoint over the entrance to the gorges. The view looks down on the Verdon 180 meters below. It's the starting or finishing point of the Martel trail, depending on the direction you choose.

Viewpoints along the Route des Crêtes follow one another on the clifftop. La Carelle, Tilleul, l'Escalès... each promontory reveals a different facet of the canyon. The setting sun sets the cliffs ablaze in golden and pink hues.

The Maison des Gorges du Verdon presents the canyon's exceptional ecosystem. Interactive exhibitions and documentaries reveal the geology, fauna and flora of this protected natural site. Griffon vultures and golden eagles reign over these rock faces.

activities.text: Paddle upstream along the Verdon by kayak from Lake Sainte-Croix; allow for a round trip from La Palud-sur-Verdon within the day to reach the lake. The kayak glides over turquoise waters between the canyon walls. Limestone cliffs rise on either side, creating the atmosphere of a natural open-air cathedral.

River hikes combine walking and swimming in the Verdon's tributaries. Jumps into pools, passages under waterfalls and whitewater swimming punctuate the route. The secondary gorges offer an intimate, unspoiled setting.

Climbing in the gorges attracts climbers from around the world. Over 1500 bolted routes trace their lines on the limestone. Climbing areas offer grades from 3 to 9, providing challenges for all levels in a spectacular setting.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpes-de-Haute-Provence Tour: Lavender and Hilltop Villages
Alpine Hinterland and Verdon Gorges: From Thorenc to Riez

map_keywords: Belvédère de la Dent d'Aire Verdon

places.name: La Petite Pierre

visits.text: La Petite-Pierre occupies a pink sandstone spur overlooking the forests of the Vosges du Nord in one continuous sweep. Its castle — whose earliest traces date back to the 13th century — was extensively remodelled by Vauban in 1684 for Louis XIV, who made it a strategic control point between Alsace and Lorraine. Today, the castle is the headquarters of the Parc naturel régional des Vosges du Nord. Entry to the courtyard is free.

The Staedtel—the old fortified town—rises in tiers on the sandstone outcrop with its ramparts, underground cisterns carved directly into the rock, and pink sandstone houses. The church preserves remarkably well-preserved 15th-century painted frescoes depicting biblical figures in ochre and blue tones. One of Alsace's least-known treasures.

The Alsatian Seal Museum and the Museum of Popular Arts and Traditions of La Petite-Pierre respectively exhibit the heraldic history of Alsatian families and local popular traditions, notably Springerle—these little white cookies molded in shapes of flowers and animals that are part of Alsatian Christmas bredele.

activities.text: The Northern Vosges Regional Nature Park has been a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve since 1989—one of northeastern France's most extensive protected natural areas with 135,000 hectares of pine and sandstone forests, streams, and ruined castles. Over 2,600 km of marked trails cross the park. From La Petite-Pierre, several hiking circuits reach directly to spectacular sandstone rocks and medieval castle ruins buried in the forest.

The rampart path circles La Petite-Pierre's outcrop and follows the fortifications for about 250 meters long by 80 wide. The underground cisterns—carved into the sandstone to supply the garrison during sieges—open for guided visits at certain times. Inquire at the Park House.

days_plan.itin_title: Alsace and the Wine Route: Strasbourg to the Vosges

map_keywords: Parc naturel régional Vosges du Nord

visits.text: A view down onto turquoise water as soon as you round the bend: the Calanque de la Redonne reveals itself from above, whether you arrive by road or by train. Below, a tiny harbour under the viaduct, a few surviving cabins among newer villas. The car park has about fifteen spaces, which means none in summer.

There are just two small beaches at the calanque de la Redonne: the sandy plage de la Dugué and a second beach of large pebbles beneath the viaduct. The rest consists of rocks that are difficult to access.

activities.text: Take the Marseille-Miramas TER and get off at Ensuès-la-Redonne station: the track runs along the cliff face and the road down to the harbour passes under the viaduct. Twenty-five minutes from Marseille, and the parking problem disappears.

days_plan.itin_title: Côte Bleue and Camargue: the lower coastal route in 7 days

visits.text: La Réole is a medieval town founded in 977, one of Gironde's oldest urban centers. Awarded the Ville d'Art et d'Histoire designation, it's France's smallest commune to carry this label. The town clings to a rocky promontory overlooking the Garonne. It was protected by three successive defensive enclosures, of which vestiges remain. Wander cobbled lanes to discover half-timbered houses, vaulted passages, and small squares. The atmosphere is authentic and peaceful.

The Benedictine Priory of Saint-Pierre stands majestically above the Garonne. Founded in the 10th century, it gave rise to the town's development. The 18th-century classical façade hides older buildings. The priory now houses the town hall, municipal services, and library. The 18th-century wrought-iron entrance gate is an ironwork masterpiece. The forecourt offers beautiful river and hillside views.

La Réole's Town Hall is one of France's oldest civic buildings, dating from the 12th century. This remarkable Gothic building originally served as a covered market and municipal hall. The architecture testifies to La Réole's political and economic importance in the Middle Ages. The square-facing façade preserves its Gothic arcades. The interior houses municipal services. The building can be visited on guided tours organized by the tourist office.

Château des Quat'Sos is an imposing 13th-century medieval fortress. Built to protect the town, it had four corner towers (hence its name, Quatre Sous). The château was dismantled on Richelieu's orders in 1629. Two imposing round towers and part of the curtain walls survive. Transformed into a bourgeois residence in the 18th century, it's now private. Visible from outside, it is open for occasional visits during Heritage Days or on guided tours booked in advance.

Saint-Pierre Church in La Réole combines several architectural styles from the 12th to 15th centuries. The Gothic building features Romanesque and Flamboyant Gothic elements. The sculpted capitals and stained glass deserve attention. The church preserves interesting furnishings, including a Baroque altarpiece. It forms part of the stop on the Vézelay Way, one of the pilgrimage routes to Santiago de Compostela. Its remarkable acoustics make it a venue for classical music concerts.

activities.text: Guided tour of La Réole. The tourist office and the Ville d'Art et d'Histoire service offer themed guided tours: medieval heritage, town history, architecture. The standard tour lasts 1.5 hours and covers the main monuments and neighborhoods. You'll discover the fascinating history of this town that alternated between French and English control during the Hundred Years' War. Passionate guides bring La Réole's past to life. Reservations recommended.

Stroll along the Garonne banks. The quays developed in the 19th century offer a pleasant riverside walk. You'll enjoy views of vineyard-covered hillsides on the opposite bank and the Rouergue suspension bridge. A towpath follows the river upstream and downstream. It's a peaceful spot for walking or picnicking. Some benches let you settle in facing the river. Sunset here is particularly beautiful.

La Réole Market is held every Saturday morning on the Garonne quays. This traditional market gathers local producers and artisans. You'll find seasonal fruits and vegetables, cheeses, charcuterie, honey, Entre-deux-Mers wines. The atmosphere is friendly and authentic. It's an opportunity to chat with producers and discover regional specialties. Some stalls offer on-site dining for breakfast.

Discovering La Réole's gastronomy. Several restaurants showcase local Gironde products: duck, foie gras, porcini mushrooms, asparagus, prunes from nearby Agen, regional cheeses. Entre-deux-Mers wines pair perfectly with these dishes. The town also retains its pastry specialties. For an authentic experience, choose a restaurant in the old town with a terrace on the quays in summer.

A walk in Charros Park, developed at the foot of the medieval ramparts. This peaceful landscaped garden follows the course of the former Charros stream that served as the château's moat. Interpretive panels and benches invite you to relax and discover the heritage. The park offers lovely views of the fortifications and the remains of the third defensive enclosure. It's a green haven appreciated by La Réole residents. Children's playground.

days_plan.itin_title: Gironde Circuit: Bordeaux, Vineyards & Arcachon Bay

places.name: La Roche Bernard

visits.text: La Roche-Bernard, a Petite Cité de Caractère, clings to a rocky spur overlooking the Vilaine. The “Promenade du Ruicard” follows the cliff and offers a dizzying view over the river, 30 meters below.

The old quarter preserves captains' and shipowners' houses from the 16th–17th centuries. Rue du Ruicard is lined with granite facades with arched doorways and exterior staircases typical of the tidal Vilaine.
The port, at the foot of the cliff, once housed shipyards that built Vilaine barges. A museum recounts this maritime and river history—the Vilaine was navigable as far as Redon.

The current suspension bridge replaced the bridge of 1839—Brittany's first suspension bridge, swept away by a storm in 1852. From its deck, the view takes in both banks and the meanders of the Vilaine.
The Notre-Dame chapel, perched atop the rock, dates from the 16th century. During the Revolution, the town mayor took refuge there before being executed—a tragic episode of the local Chouan uprising.

activities.text: Descend to the port via the staircase carved into the rock, then follow the Vilaine on the towpath. Old warehouses and launching ramps dot the route.
Cross the bridge and reach the Arzal dam on foot or by bike. This maritime lock, the largest in France, separates fresh water from salt water and regulates tides on the Vilaine.
The Thursday morning market on Place du Bouffay is a gathering place for local producers. Pénestin oysters, buckwheat pancakes, and farmhouse cider make up a complete Breton breakfast.

days_plan.itin_title: Brittany Road Trip: Villages with Character, Sea and History

map_keywords: Château des Basses Fosses La Roche-Bernard

visits.text: La Roche-Guyon is the only village in Île-de-France awarded the “Plus Beaux Villages de France” designation. The castle overlooking it is one of the region's most unusual: backed by the chalk cliff since the Middle Ages, it combines a medieval 12th-century keep on the ridge, linked to the lower castle by a rock-cut underground passage with 250 steps, and 18th-century state rooms. In June 1944, Rommel had established his headquarters here and had chambers dug into the cliff to store ammunition for 500,000 men - these casemates can be visited. Claude Monet and Georges Braque painted the village; Lamartine stayed here in 1819. Open from April 1 to November 1, daily 10 am-6 pm.

Cross the road to reach the château's vegetable garden and orchard, awarded the “Jardin Remarquable” designation: 3 hectares restored following original 18th-century plans, organized into four large squares and groves cultivated with organic farming methods. Allow 30 to 45 minutes to walk around it. The view from the terraces over the Seine and cliff is one of the Vexin's finest—don't miss it.

Descend into the village to wander its lanes. The Church of Saint-Samson, built from 1404 with authorization from Charles VI, houses the tomb of François de Silly, first Duke of La Roche-Guyon, who died at the siege of La Rochelle in 1628—a kneeling sculpture by Nicolas Guillain. The cave houses (the “boves”) carved into the cliff and half-timbered houses form a cohesive and preserved architectural ensemble.

activities.text: Hiking on the ridge trail above the village: from the château, climb to the Vexin plateau for a view looking down over the Seine's meanders. Allow about 1 hour 30 minutes for the loop. Avoid after rain—wet chalk is very slippery.

Farms in the Vexin offer cider and apple juice tastings in season (mainly in fall). Local providers also organize visits to cellars and cider presses in the villages around Théméricourt and Chars - ask at the La Roche-Guyon tourist office. Plan a same-day return drive from La Roche-Guyon for these visits.

days_plan.itin_title: Val-d'Oise Tour: Impressionist Villages and Heritage

places.name: La Roche Sur Yon

visits.text: Begin at Place Napoléon, the heart of La Roche-sur-Yon. Laid out in 1804 by order of the emperor, this 3-hectare esplanade was completely redesigned between 2010 and 2014 by architect Alexandre Chemetoff. Since then, 13 mechanical animals made of wood and steel—an 8.70-meter crocodile, a hippopotamus, a dromedary and flamingos—have inhabited its planted pools. They are the work of François Delarozière, creator of the Machines de l'île in Nantes. Operate the cranks and levers to set them in motion: it is free, they run on hydraulic and pneumatic power, and you will see that adults have just as much fun as children.

Step inside the Haras de la Vendée, a ten-minute walk from the square. This stallion depot was authorized by Louis-Philippe in 1842, and construction began in 1843 under the direction of architect Malet. The site spans 4.5 hectares in the town center and housed up to 220 stallions at its peak. Now owned by the Vendée Department, the stud farm offers guided tours and a daily equestrian show in July and August. Even outside the main season, you can stroll through the English-style gardens free of charge.

Saint-Louis Church, facing Place Napoléon, is the largest religious building in Vendée. Construction began in the early 19th century as part of Napoleon's urban development plan. Its neoclassical façade with columns and pediment is reflected in the square's pools—one of the city's most photographed sights. If you step inside, the imposing proportions of the nave are worth a look.

Head to the Historial de la Vendée in Les Lucs-sur-Boulogne, 20 minutes away by car. Opened in 2006, this museum traces 7,000 years of Vendée history across 3,100 m², with 3,000 objects and 85 audiovisual stations spread over seven areas - from Prehistory to the 21st century. Don't miss the Musée des enfants, designed for families. Just next door, the Mémorial de la Vendée commemorates the 564 victims of the February 1794 massacre in Les Lucs. Allow at least 2 hours for the whole visit.

activities.text: At the end of the day, follow the Vallée de l'Yon on foot or by bike. The parc de la Vallée offers a walk just a few minutes from the town center. To reach the rock formations at Piquet, allow approximately 19 km from La Roche-sur-Yon, a 20-minute drive, followed by a walk between the river and rocks covered in vegetation. You'll be surprised to find such a wild corner of nature.

days_plan.itin_title: Vendée Itinerary: Noirmoutier Island, Puy du Fou and the Coastline

map_keywords: Royal Stud Farm Vendée, La Roche-sur-Yon

visits.text: The Château de La Rochefoucauld has belonged to the same family since 1019 — a French record. The three-storey Renaissance galleries recall Italian palaces. Legend has it the spiral staircase was designed by Leonardo da Vinci.
The castle's four libraries hold 21,000 volumes. The guided tour (compulsory for this section) includes the Treasury room where the guide handles archives dating back eight centuries. Impressive.

The town at the foot of the castle is worth a stroll: half-timbered houses, cobbled lanes along the Tardoire. This is where the charentaise was born — the slipper, not the local woman. Specialist shop on Rue des Halles.

activities.text: Full castle visit. Self-guided section (salons, kitchens, galleries) + guided tour of the libraries and archives. Allow 2 hours total. Children can dress up as knights or princesses — costumes provided.
Chocolaterie d'Antan at the foot of the castle. Artisans can be seen at work from the shop. Local speciality: the pichotte, a sweet made with chocolate, almonds and icing sugar. Open even on Sundays.
Hike along the Tardoire. Waymarked trails from the castle into the rolling countryside. Landscapes that hint at the neighbouring Périgord. Several loops from 5 to 15 km.

days_plan.itin_title: Charente Tour: Cognac and Romanesque Heritage in 4 Days

places.name: La Rochelle

visits.text: The three towers of the Old Port are remnants of La Rochelle's medieval fortifications. The Saint-Nicolas Tower (14th century), slightly tilted like the tower in Pisa, rises to 37 meters. A chain once linked it to the Chain Tower to close the harbor each evening—the original chain is visible at the tower's base.

The Lantern Tower, with its 55-meter octagonal Gothic spire, served as both lighthouse and prison. Some 600 graffiti carvings made by English, Spanish and Dutch privateers adorn its walls—ships, figures, and even a locomotive. Rabelais mentions it in his Fifth Book.

La Rochelle's Old Port was the largest port on the Atlantic coast in the 15th century. Stroll along Cours des Dames and Quai Duperré, lined with outdoor seating areas. In the evening, the illuminated towers are reflected in the harbor basin—one of the most beautiful scenes on the French coast.

The arcades of the city center have sheltered passersby since the Middle Ages. Over 3 km of covered galleries line the shopping streets. Under stone and wooden vaults, half-timbered houses and Renaissance mansions tell of the prosperity of La Rochelle's shipowners.

La Rochelle Aquarium is one of the largest private aquariums in Europe. Over 12,000 marine animals in 3 million liters of water. The shark tank and jellyfish gallery are spectacular. Allow 2 to 3 hours for the visit.

The New World Museum occupies Hôtel Fleuriau, an 18th-century shipowner's mansion. Collections on the triangular trade, the French West Indies and the slave trade. An unflinching look at La Rochelle's wealth built on slavery.

The Gabut district, a former bastion converted into a colorful village. Brightly painted wooden houses, artists' studios, outdoor seating areas facing the marina. An unexpected Scandinavian atmosphere on the Atlantic shore.

activities.text: Visit the tour de la Chaîne and tour de la Lanterne in La Rochelle. A single ticket grants access to both monuments. The tour Saint-Nicolas is closed to visitors. Allow 2 hours for the whole visit.

Walk along the rampart walkway between the Chain Tower and Lantern Tower. This section of rampart, called 'Rue sur les Murs', overlooks the Saint-Jean-d'Acre esplanade and offers stunning views of the port.

La Rochelle central market. Beneath the wooden and wrought-iron market halls, producers sell Marennes-Oléron oysters, Pineau des Charentes, mogettes (white beans) and tourteau fromager. Lively atmosphere every morning.
The Bus de Mer and the Passeur connect both sides of the port. A 5-minute crossing, a pleasant alternative to walking around. The electric Passeur operates year-round.

Concurrence Beach, the closest to the city center. Fine sand, calm water, view of the towers. Lifeguarded in summer. The Mail promenade lined with tamarisk trees runs along the coast toward Les Minimes.
Self-service yellow bike rentals (Yélo). La Rochelle pioneered bike-sharing in France. Cycle paths lead to Les Minimes beaches and the marina.

Charente-Maritime Road Trip: La Rochelle, Île de Ré, Fort Boyard and Roman Saintonge
Nouvelle-Aquitaine Loop: Villages, Vineyards & Dordogne
