Museum of the New World La Rochelle

visits.text: La Rochepot Castle rises above the forest like a fairytale castle, with polychrome glazed-tile roofs identical to those of the Hospices de Beaune and instantly recognizable. Dismantled during the Revolution, it was then restored in the 19th century by the son of President Sadi Carnot.

Walk down to the tiny but charming village below—a few stone houses, a church, and above all an open view over the vineyard slopes. Look for public viewpoints where the château's polychrome tiles stand out against the sky.

activities.text: Follow the vineyard paths that lead from the village toward the hillsides. You're here on the edge of the Côte de Beaune—plots of Pinot Noir and Chardonnay rise in tiers between murgers (dry stone walls), clos, and cabottes (small vineyard huts). The landscape is listed as a UNESCO World Heritage site as part of the Climats, terroirs of Burgundy.
Walk on to the hamlet of Evelle for a panorama over the entire vineyard slope. The trail crosses landscapes of “strips”—the long, narrow plots that shape the geography of Burgundy's appellations.

days_plan.itin_title: Burgundy's 15 Most Beautiful Villages
Burgundy-Franche-Comté: The Most Beautiful Villages in 7 days

visits.text: La Romieu's Saint-Pierre Collegiate Church is listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site as part of the Ways of Saint James. Built in just six years (1312-1318) by Cardinal Arnaud d'Aux, cousin of Pope Clement V, it displays southern Gothic architecture with a single nave, cloister and two towers. One contains one of Europe's oldest double-helix staircases. Climb the octagonal tower for a panorama over the hillsides and discover recently restored 14th-century murals in the sacristy.

On the arcaded square, dozens of stone cats keep watch from window ledges. They tell the legend of Angéline: during a terrible famine in 1342, this orphan hid her cats when villagers got rid of theirs. When rats threatened the following year's harvest, her twenty kittens saved La Romieu. The sculptures are the work of Maurice Serreau, who fell in love with this story.

The Gardens of Coursiana, classified as a Remarkable Garden, spread across fifteen acres facing the collegiate church. An arboretum with 700 species, an English garden, a family vegetable garden and 350 rose varieties compose a botanical journey created in 1974 by botanist Gilbert Cours-Darne.

activities.text: Guided tour of the collegiate church and its secrets. The route leads from the church to the cloister, then into the towers with passage along the wall-walk and the sacristy paintings. Audio guides available.

Hike on the GR 65 starting from La Romieu. The village sits at the crossroads of the Le Puy-en-Velay route and the Rocamadour route. Marked trails wind through Gascon hills, between vineyards and sunflower fields.
Stone cat hunt through the village. Try to find all of Maurice Serreau's sculptures hidden on façades, windows and doorsteps. A bust of Angéline reigns over the square. Children love it.

days_plan.itin_title: Gers Road Trip: Gascon Bastides, Armagnac & Musketeers

visits.text: La Roque-Gageac clings to a 120-meter limestone cliff above the Dordogne, its golden stone houses and slate roofs mirrored in the water below. It has been listed among the Plus Beaux Villages de France since 1982. The dramatic setting and medieval architecture make it instantly unforgettable.

A 12th-century fort is carved directly into the cliff face 40 meters above the village. Climb 140 steps hewn from living rock to reach the summit, where panoramic views sweep across the Dordogne Valley and the rival castles of Beynac and Castelnaud. The fort was never conquered—its position made it impregnable.

An exotic garden thrives at the cliff base, nurtured by a south-facing microclimate that shields it from northern winds. Palm trees, banana plants, orange trees, cacti, and towering bamboo grow together in improbable abundance. Admission is free—a botanical surprise tucked into medieval Périgord.

activities.text: Traditional flat-bottomed gabarres—the cargo boats that once carried wine, timber, and salt along the Dordogne—now offer one-hour river cruises. Two companies operate from La Roque-Gageac. Guides recount the history of river commerce and point out the castles of Castelnaud, Beynac, Fayrac, and Marqueyssac rising from the valley cliffs.

The Gardens of Marqueyssac, just 3 km away, feature 6 km of pathways bordered by 150,000 hand-trimmed boxwood shrubs—some over a century old. The belvedere perched 130 meters above the Dordogne offers one of the most breathtaking viewpoints in all of Périgord. Come for sunset if you can.

days_plan.itin_title: Dordogne: Prehistoric Caves, Medieval Fortresses & Périgord Delights
The Most Beautiful Villages of Lot and Périgord in 6 Days

visits.text: A local saying sums up La Roque-sur-Cèze well: “Anyone who goes to La Roque gets hooked.” Listed among Les Plus Beaux Villages de France since 2007, the village is perched on its rocky peak, crowned with an 11th-century castle and a 12th-century Romanesque chapel with an apse adorned with cog-tooth decoration. To enter, you cross the Charles-Martel bridge, classified as a Historic Monument: built in the 13th century, it measures 155 meters long and has twelve stone arches. It is so narrow that only one car can cross at a time. From the village center, climb up to the castle esplanade—a viewpoint guide helps you identify Mont Ventoux on clear days.

The Cascades du Sautadet, below the village, are the most spectacular natural site in the Cèze valley. For 5 million years, the river has been carving a series of cascading falls with a total drop of 15 meters into the limestone rock, sculpting “giant's kettles”—cylindrical cavities several meters in diameter swirling in the rocky riverbed. The nickname “devil's leap” is well deserved: swimming is strictly forbidden due to currents and whirlpools responsible for fatal accidents. Stay on marked trails and designated viewpoints. A little downstream, a beach allows safe swimming.

La Roque-sur-Cèze's lanes paved with rounded pebbles, steep stone-paved streets, golden stone houses with tiled eaves and old facades with Romanesque vaults deserve a stroll of at least 45 minutes. Thirteen heritage panels mark the route through the village—pick one up at the entrance so you don't miss anything.

activities.text: The La Roque-sur-Cèze and Cascades du Sautadet loop hike (8 km, about 2 hours 30 minutes, easy to moderate difficulty) links the village, the Charles-Martel bridge and both banks of the waterfalls, returning through vineyards and garrigue. It's the ideal way to combine heritage and nature in one outing. Follow the instructions: swimming is forbidden in the waterfall area.

days_plan.itin_title: Cèze Valley and Ardèche Gorges Circuit

visits.text: La Sône is a boating village perched on the right bank of the Isère, between Royans and Vercors. Its church and former watermen's houses recall the era when the river was an active commercial route connecting the Valence plain to Royans villages. Take time to walk the quays and observe the terraced gardens on the opposite bank—the village opens entirely onto the river.

La Sône's mills long operated using the current's power. Though the industrial buildings have nearly all disappeared, their locations along the quays remain visible in the landscape. Sit on a waterside bench to gaze at the green Royans hillsides across the way: it's one of the valley's most peaceful views.

activities.text: The quays and nearby hamlets loop—2-3 km with no elevation change—follows the Isère then climbs to the first hamlets perched on the hillside. You'll see the architectural variations between lowland houses and the first stone constructions typical of Royans.

The path to riverside viewpoints upstream from the village reveals the river's geography: across the way, the limestone foothills of the Vercors begin to rise, heralding the Bourne gorges you'll reach in two days.

days_plan.itin_title: Royans-Vercors Road Trip: Hilltop Villages and Gorges

visits.text: The Church of Notre-Dame de La Souterraine stands out with its 60-meter bell tower, the tallest in Creuse. A masterpiece of the transition from Romanesque to Gothic, built from the 11th to the 13th century by the monks of Saint-Martial de Limoges, this austere granite building has a façade with a multifoil portal showing Mozarabic influence, evidence of the passage of pilgrims to Compostela along the Via Lemovicensis. Inside, the vast proportions of the nave invite contemplation.

Descend into the thousand-year-old crypt via Place d'Armes. This underground church, which gave the town its name (Subterranea in 1268), was built around 1020 on a Gallo-Roman necropolis. Under the Romanesque vaults reinforced with ribs, three chapels follow one another: the main one under the chancel, Sainte-Anne to the north, and Saint-Martial to the south. The Espace Patrimoine displays archaeological finds from the ancient site of Bridiers. Open in summer, free admission.

The Saint-Jean Gate, a remnant of medieval ramparts, stands near the church with its two corbeled turrets, crenellations, and machicolations. Built in the 13th and 15th centuries, it preserves the notches that supported the drawbridge chains. Ask for the key at the Café du Marché to access the top: the view over the town and surrounding countryside rewards the ascent.

At the cemetery of La Souterraine, a 12th-century lantern of the dead intrigues with its silhouette of a hollow tower topped by an openwork pavilion. According to tradition, the lamp lit there guided the souls of the deceased toward eternal rest. This funerary construction typical of Limousin testifies to medieval beliefs about death.

Four kilometers to the east, the site of Bridiers reveals the remains of a Gallo-Roman settlement of the Lemovices. The Tower of Bridiers, the 12th-century keep of a former fortress, overlooks reconstructed medieval gardens. In August, the site hosts the Fresque Historique: a nighttime show combining sound, light, and pyrotechnics with more than 300 costumed actors.

activities.text: A visit to the lake of Sagnat requires a return trip by car from La Souterraine. It offers a fully equipped leisure area in natural surroundings. A supervised beach for swimming in summer, shaded walking paths and fishing pontoons make it an ideal spot for a refreshing break after exploring the local heritage.

The Cheix pond, two kilometers from the center, offers a peaceful setting for fishing or a simple walk by the water. The landscaped banks provide opportunities to observe local wildlife in an unspoiled environment.

days_plan.itin_title: Creuse Tour: Valley of the Painters and Aubusson Tapestries

visits.text: Labeaume sits at the foot of impressive limestone cliffs riddled with troglodyte caves. Its houses built of river pebbles crowd along narrow cobbled lanes and vaulted passages—a labyrinth where it's pleasant to get lost. The submersible bridge, built in 1877, spans the Beaume: it's designed to be covered by water during floods, giving it a silhouette flush with the current—spectacular. Park at the lower village lot (paid in season, forbidden to motorhomes July-August) and walk up.

The Jardins Suspendus du Récatadou are one of Labeaume's most astonishing curiosities. These small cultivated terraces were created in the 18th century right on the cliff overlooking the Beaume gorges, in rocky crevices where farmers carried soil on their backs. They were worked until the mid-20th century. To reach them, cross the submersible bridge and follow the yellow-and-white blazed trail toward Saint-Alban-Auriolles for 1.2 km. Guided visits are organized Friday mornings from Easter to mid-September.

From the upper village, climb to the viewpoint on the cliff—figure 15 minutes from the submersible bridge. The panorama over the Beaume meanders, white cliffs opposite and village rooftops below is one of the finest views in the area. In summer, the Labeaume en Musiques festival sets up stages on the river, in caves and in clearings—concerts Thursdays and Fridays mid-July to mid-August.

activities.text: The Sentier des Belvédères circles the cliff above the village for 3 to 5 km, with sections on developed ledges. The start is from the village parking lot. The climb is fairly athletic with stairs carved into rock, but the view is well worth the effort. Bring proper shoes—limestone rock can be slippery in wet conditions.

The natural beach at Labeaume, at the village base in the Beaume riverbed, is renowned for its clear waters and skipping stones. It's unsupervised—check bathing conditions before going with children. You can also walk along the river to Ruoms (roughly 5 km) on a shaded trail.

days_plan.itin_title: The 18 Most Beautiful Villages of Ardèche

visits.text: Lac de Saint-Point stretches 7.2 km in length and 800 m in width at an altitude of 860 meters. Fed by the Doubs, it is surrounded by upland meadows and spruce forests. The Maison de la Réserve in Labergement-Sainte-Marie, by the lake, presents the ecosystem of upland wetlands and nearby peat bogs through educational exhibitions. From the belvédère des 2 lacs (reached on foot from the parking lot), the view down over Saint-Point and Lac de Remoray is striking.

Fort Saint-Antoine, built in 1879 on General Séré de Rivières' orders to watch the Swiss border, has served as a Comté aging cellar since its conversion in 1966. Perched at an altitude of 1,100 m, it houses between 65,000 and 100,000 wheels slowly aged for 10 to 20 months in its vaulted galleries of dressed stone. The guided tour takes you through cathedral-like courtyards 120 meters long, followed by a tasting in the heart of the cellars. Reservation required—slots are limited.

In Labergement-Sainte-Marie, an artisan foundry makes bronze bells using methods inherited from the 19th century. The visit, by appointment, lets you see the clay molds, furnaces and sometimes the metal casting. A rare experience in one of the last artisan bell foundries still active in France.

activities.text: Operators offer pedal boat, canoe and windsurfing board rentals on Lake Saint-Point. In winter during severe cold, the lake freezes and becomes one of France's largest natural ice rinks. The complete lake loop on foot or by bike is 24 km—suitable for all ability levels.

days_plan.itin_title: Doubs Road Trip: Nature and Heritage of Franche-Comté

visits.text: Lake Génos-Loudenvielle ranks among the most beautiful bodies of water in the Pyrenees. Nestled at the bottom of the Louron Valley at 987 meters elevation, it mirrors the surrounding peaks — on calm days, the reflection is almost flawless. Walk or cycle around the shore in late afternoon: the path follows the water's edge for several kilometers and the views shift at every turn. The late afternoon light on the ridges is particularly striking.

Loudenvielle is a typical Bigorre mountain village: stone houses, slate roofs, narrow lanes. Wander through the center between spa sessions. The Peyragudes ski resort — where the opening scene of the James Bond film Tomorrow Never Dies was filmed in 1997 — sits 12 km above the lake, which gives you an idea of the setting.

activities.text: The Balnéa thermal spa complex is the first leisure thermal facility in the French Pyrenees, opened in 2000. Water is captured from two boreholes at 170 and 600 meters depth above the Saoussas Baths, and flows naturally at 30–33°C into the pools. Across 4,000 m², five themed spaces — Roman, Amerindian, Incan, Mayan, Tibetan — each offer a distinct atmosphere. The outdoor Incan and Mayan baths at 36°C allow you to bathe in open air facing snow-capped peaks: it's one of the most memorable experiences of the route. Online booking available.
After your soak, walk along the lake at sunset. Light fades slowly on the ridges, reflections turn orange and rose. It's one of the finest moments of the day to appreciate the Louron Valley setting.

days_plan.itin_title: Pyrenean Thermal Route: Spa Towns

visits.text: Lake Guerlédan, Brittany's largest freshwater expanse, was born from the construction of a hydroelectric dam between 1923 and 1930. Its 51 million m³ of water stretch through the Blavet valley, between schist ridges and forests. The dam submerged a section of the Nantes-Brest canal.

The Cistercian Bon-Repos Abbey, founded in 1184 by Alain III de Rohan and Constance of Brittany, stands on the banks of the Nantes-Brest canal. Legend says the viscount fell asleep at the confluence of the rivers and saw the Virgin in a dream: “This place shall be the site of your prayers and your eternal rest.” Sold as national property during the Revolution, restored since 1986 by volunteers.

Quénécan forest, over 3,700 hectares of oak-beech woodland south of the lake, rises to 290 meters. For three centuries, charcoal burners produced the charcoal that fed the blast furnaces of the Forges des Salles. Chestnut trees, holly, and Scots pines form a dense canopy.

The Forges des Salles, an intact ironworking village since operations ceased in 1877, nestle in the heart of Quénécan forest. Blast furnace, ironmaster's house, workers' housing, canteen, school, and chapel—time has stood still. Classified as a Historic Monument since 1980.

The Liscuis moors and their Neolithic gallery graves, dating from 3,000 BCE. These schist megalithic tombs are among the best preserved in Brittany. The panorama from the moors extends over the Blavet valley.

activities.text: Hike the Lake Guerlédan circuit. The 37 km trail can be covered in 2–3 days or in sections. The Trégnanton viewpoint offers the finest panorama—moorland yellow with gorse, bluish waters, and slate schist.

Water sports on Lake Guerlédan. Beau Rivage beach offers kayaking, paddleboarding, waterskiing, and tubing. Anse de Sordan, on the south shore, provides a wilder setting for canoeing at the foot of Quénécan forest.

Visit Bon-Repos Abbey. Self-guided tour, guided tour, or digital tour with augmented reality tablets. In summer, a sound and light show projects the history of Central Brittany onto the facade—a two-hour historical pageant on a 2-hectare stage.

days_plan.itin_title: Côtes-d'Armor Road Trip: Dinan, Pink Granite Coast, Bréhat Island & Lake Guerlédan

visits.text: A former sand quarry turned lake: Lake Aréna, also called Lake Perrin, covers some thirty hectares of fresh water at the foot of Roquebrune Rock. The site has Natura 2000 status and wildlife has reclaimed it. The best photo angle is from the south shore, early in the morning, when the rock glows red above the still water.

Aréna Beach borders Lake Perrin on the water sports center side: sand, deck chairs and a head-on view of Roquebrune Rock. It's a lake beach, not a sea beach: fresh water, no waves, no salt. A flat, easy trail circles the lake, ideal for letting your meal settle before heading out.

activities.text: Rent a paddleboard at the Arena Plage water sports center on Lake Aréna, and head as far as the passage toward the Argens: the corridor of vegetation linking the lake to the river takes a little paddling effort to reach. The lake waters stay calm, and children can stand on their boards without any drama. The center is open from May 1 to September 30, not before.

The inflatable water park at Aréna Plage is mainly worthwhile for kids: slides, obstacle courses and a separate Aquakids area for little ones, all set up on Lake Aréna. The multi-activity packages advertised by the regional tourist office cost around €35 per adult and €30 per child. In July–August, arrive when it opens at 9:30am.

If you're passing through on a Sunday morning, the weekly flea market is held right next to Lake Aréna, summer and winter. It's more a local gathering than a tourist market. Follow up with the fruit and vegetable market at the water sports center to put together a picnic and eat it by the water.

days_plan.itin_title: Roquebrune-sur-Argens: sea, villages and the Var in 10 days

visits.text: A lake born of a catastrophe: EDF began the Saint-Cassien dam project after the Malpasset dam failed in 1959, and completed it in 1966. The reservoir holds about 60 million m³ across more than 400 hectares, between the Var and Alpes-Maritimes. The Maison du Lac, on the Tanneron side, serves as a gateway with its exhibition area about the Pays de Fayence.

activities.text: Rent a pedal boat or paddleboard on Lake Saint-Cassien: combustion engines are prohibited, leaving the water surprisingly calm for a lake this size. Several water sports centers share the shores, with a sailing school and mountain bike rentals. The free summer shuttle saves you the parking headache at the Maison du Lac.

If you're traveling with young children, head for the beach below the Maison du Lac on Lake Saint-Cassien: swimming supervised by Var firefighters in summer, a first-aid station, and beach volleyball and pétanque nearby. Supervision runs from July 1 to August 31, from 11am to 7pm. Outside those dates and hours, nobody is on duty.

days_plan.itin_title: Roquebrune-sur-Argens: sea, villages and the Var in 10 days

visits.text: An artificial lake dug for firefighting, now a bird refuge: Lake Escarcets, in the heart of the Plaine des Maures National Nature Reserve, belongs to the Conservatoire du littoral. Its reed bed provides a nesting area. A trail circles it, with information panels along the way. Access is via the piste de la Tire off the D558 toward La Garde-Freinet.

At sunset, the pink sandstone slabs of the Plaine des Maures, dotted with umbrella pines and cork oaks, evoke a savanna. The reserve, created in 2009, covers 5,276 hectares. The August 2021 fires destroyed a large part: the landscape is rebuilding before your eyes. Stay on marked trails, the grasslands are very sensitive to trampling.

activities.text: If you're looking for Hermann's tortoise, it's here or in Corsica: the Plaine des Maures is its most important population stronghold in Provence and is covered by a national action plan. The European pond turtle and the ocellated lizard also live there. In the morning, tortoises warm up at the edges of bushes. Look, don't touch, don't collect anything.

Bring binoculars on your walk around Lake Escarcets: harriers, teal, ducks and European bee-eaters visit the reed bed depending on the season. The walk is flat and short, suitable for families. Access to the Var's forested hills is restricted from June 21 to September 20 due to fire risk: check the prefecture's decree for the day.

days_plan.itin_title: Roquebrune-sur-Argens: sea, villages and the Var in 10 days

visits.text: The Fontaine des Pisseurs stands on Place du Griffoul. Listed as a historic monument in 1913, this 15th-century fountain depicts four figures—Lacaune's former consuls—and symbolizes the diuretic properties of the town's thermal waters.

The Musée du Vieux Lacaune occupies the 16th-century consular house facing the fountain. Fifteen themed rooms recreate daily life for Lacaune's inhabitants from the 18th to the 20th century: costumes, tools, vanished trades.

Step into the Maison de la Charcuterie to understand how the harsh mountain climate—800 meters above sea level, north winds—favored the art of salt-curing. The exhibit traces this craft's evolution since the 18th century.
The Filature Ramond, founded in 1841, preserves working carding and spinning machines listed in the historic monuments inventory. The visit immerses you in Haut-Languedoc's textile heritage.
On the outskirts of the town, the Peyro Levado is a statue-menhir. These engraved and sculpted stones, scattered across the Monts de Lacaune, bear witness to a Neolithic past that remains mysterious.

activities.text: Visit an artisanal meat-curing workshop to discover the production stages: salting, drying in the north wind, and aging. The end-of-tour tasting lets you sample award-winning hams, salami, and dry-cured sausages.
Take the Roc du Montalet trail for a hike in the Lacaune Mountains. Beech forests, heather moorlands, and valley panoramas unfold along the route.

Head to the Plateau des Lacs, allowing for car journeys from Lacaune: four lakes offer swimming, fishing in first-category waters and water sports in the heart of the Parc Naturel Régional du Haut-Languedoc.

days_plan.itin_title: Tarn Road Trip: Albi & Hilltop Villages

places.name: Lacoste

visits.text: Lacoste is one of the Luberon's most distinctive villages, and not only because of its most famous resident. Built on the flank of a limestone hill, its cobbled lanes climb among stone houses up to the summit esplanade, where the view embraces the Bonnieux plain and Mont Ventoux. The village owes its fame to the Marquis de Sade, whose family has owned the chateau since 1716. The author of The 120 Days of Sodom lived here several times to escape censorship and legal prosecution, notably from 1769 to 1772. The Revolution nearly destroyed it entirely, and Sade, learning the news in Paris, wrote: "What a loss! It is beyond expression. I am in despair!"

The château, purchased in 2001, now hosts contemporary art exhibitions each summer and an opera festival in the adjoining quarries that have been transformed into a natural theater. The inner courtyard and grounds are open to visitors. From the summit, the panorama is exceptional: Bonnieux in the foreground, the Vaucluse Mountains behind, and on clear days the Alps on the horizon.

As you descend the stone lanes, look for the galleries and artists' studios scattered throughout the village. Lacoste has attracted painters and sculptors for decades, drawn by the light and atmosphere—the ambiance is quite different from Gordes or Roussillon, more intimate and less touristy.

activities.text: Climb to the castle plateau up to the summit viewpoint (20 min round trip from the center). The view over the Calavon valley and the Luberon ridges is one of the broadest in the northern Luberon.

Walk along the stone lanes between terraces and dry-stone retaining walls, descending toward the old underground quarries that supplied the village's building stone. An impressive network of galleries, visible from certain access points along the path.

days_plan.itin_title: The 15 Most Beautiful Villages of the Luberon

map_keywords: Château du Marquis de Sade Lacoste

visits.text: From the road coming from Lézignan-Corbières, Lagrasse reveals itself at a bend: the medieval village nestled in the valley, the winding Orbieu River, and the massive abbey on the other side. Fifteen buildings in the town are protected as Historic Monuments.

The abbey of Sainte-Marie-d'Orbieu was founded in 779 under Charlemagne's protection. For over a thousand years, Benedictine monks lived here. The Revolution split it in two: the public part (abbatial palace, cellar, dormitory, chapels) and the private part, administered since 2004 by a community of canons.

The humpback Old Bridge connects the town to the abbey. It appears on a seal from 1303, and its three unequal arches were once topped by two 18-meter crenellated gate-towers. They were demolished because their weight was causing the bridge to sag.

The medieval hall, arranged in 1315, marks the market's transfer from outside the walls. One can easily imagine the bustle of merchants from that era. Saturday morning's market perpetuates this tradition under the same vaults.

The Heritage House occupies the former 15th-century presbytery. Three rooms display 131 painted medieval ceiling panels, classified as Historic Monuments. The permanent exhibition 'Forgotten Images of the Middle Ages' offers a fresh look at medieval daily life in Languedoc.
The parish church of Saint-Michel, built between 1359 and 1398, is a typical example of the region's single-nave Gothic. Since the Revolution, it contains furnishings mainly from the abbey.

activities.text: In summer, a swimming area is set up in the Orbieu, facing the abbey. Clear water, 'beach space,' and shaded spots under trees. Supervised swimming in July-August.
Lagrasse is classified 'Towns and Crafts of Art.' Ceramics, leatherwork, luthiery, jewelry, sewing, stained glass: push open the doors of workshops lining the village lanes.
The Corbières hills around the village are ideal for hiking. The view from the D212 toward Lézignan offers a remarkable panorama of Lagrasse and its bridges.

days_plan.itin_title: Aude Road Trip: Carcassonne, Cathar Country & the Mediterranean
Occitanie's 13 Most Beautiful Villages

visits.text: Visit the cutlery workshops in the heart of Laguiole village. The cutlers handcraft each piece with the forged bee, chiselled spring, and guillochage patterns. Several manufacturers offer tours and assembly demonstrations.

The Forge de Laguiole lets you watch the complete making of a knife. The artisans hot-forge the blades, sculpt the bee with a file and punch, then assemble the different parts. Handles are made from precious wood, Aubrac horn, or stag antler.

Laguiole village is also the birthplace of the Aubrac cattle breed and the Laguiole AOC cheese. Burons dot the plateau where the cows graze. Aligot is the local speciality made from fresh tome cheese and potatoes.

activities.text: Explore the Aubrac plateau between 1,000 and 1,400 metres altitude. The landscapes alternate between summer pastures and peatlands. The traditional burons were used to make cheese during the transhumance.
Taste the aligot in the village restaurants. This mashed potato dish mixed with fresh tome cheese is beaten at length until it forms long ribbons. Each inn has its own recipe and technique.

days_plan.itin_title: Aveyron Road Trip: Causses, Tarn Gorges and Villages

visits.text: Lambesc is often called the "Little Versailles of Aix" — and for good reason: under the reigns of Louis XIV, XV, and XVI, the town hosted the General Assemblies of the Communities of Provence for 140 years. This distinction earned it a profusion of 17th and 18th-century townhouses that still line its main streets. Look for the fountain from 1646, topped with an obelisk and adorned with the coat of arms of the Dukes of Guise, former princes of Lambesc.

The Jacquemard is Lambesc's emblematic clock — a 25-meter-high tower, built between 1526 and 1646 and classified as a historic monument. Its uniqueness: four carved wooden automatons strike the hours and quarters — Jacquemard and Margarido for hours and half-hours, Jaquet and Jaqueto for quarters. Right at its feet, Place des États-Généraux recalls the era when it was at the heart of Provençal political life. This ground is said to still conceal the old cellars of houses destroyed in the 1909 earthquake.

On June 11, 1909, at 9:15 PM, Lambesc suffered a magnitude 6.2 earthquake — the most devastating in 20th-century metropolitan France. The village was completely destroyed, with 46 deaths and 250 injuries throughout the region. You'll still see traces of this early 20th-century reconstruction in "Post-1909" style houses that replaced the old buildings. The heritage trail (brochure available at the tourist office) will guide you to the witness sites of this history.

activities.text: Vineyard-olive grove loop on the Trévaresse hillsides — it's the geological fault (Trévaresse fault) that caused the 1909 earthquake. Marked trails circle the massif among vineyards, olive groves, and fragrant garrigue. Views of the village bell towers from the heights.

Provençal market on Friday morning at Place des États-Généraux: local products (honey, jams, cheeses, seasonal vegetables), Provençal crafts. A farmers' market also takes place on Tuesday afternoon at the same square year-round.

Bertoire windmill (open Saturday morning): one of the rare windmills still standing in the Aix region. The tour traces the path from grain to flour, in a typically Provençal dry-stone setting. Accessible on foot from Lambesc center in 20 minutes.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpilles, Aix-en-Provence & Arles Circuit

visits.text: The Château de Langeais, built in 1465 under Louis XI's orders, rises dramatically from a promontory overlooking the Loire. Facing the town, it displays all the attributes of a medieval fortress: massive towers, a still-functioning drawbridge—one of the last in France—and a machicolated walkway. On the garden side, the façade opens up with large windows heralding the early Renaissance.

The richly furnished rooms recreate the atmosphere of a 15th-century noble residence: chests, millefleur tapestries, monumental carved fireplaces. The highlight is the recreation of the secret marriage of Charles VIII and Anne of Brittany, celebrated here at dawn on December 6, 1491—an event that sealed Brittany's union with France.

In the grounds, the remains of Foulques Nerra's keep (late 10th century) stand among the oldest stone donjons in France. A reconstructed medieval scaffold with period lifting equipment demonstrates the building techniques of the year 1000. Climb into the tree house perched in a bicentennial cedar, then head to the belvedere for sweeping views over the Loire.

Cross the Langeais bridge to admire the chateau's silhouette dominating the river from the left bank. Here, the UNESCO-listed Loire unfurls its sandbanks and ever-changing light. The village retains an old market hall and tufa stone houses typical of Touraine.

activities.text: Drawbridge demonstration. Each summer, the château's drawbridge is manually operated in front of visitors—a rare sight in France. The counterweight system requires two people to maneuver.
Cycling on La Loire à Vélo. This cycling route passes below the château, connecting Tours to Saumur along the river. Langeais is 18 miles from Tours on flat terrain.

Tasting of AOC Bourgueil and Saint-Nicolas-de-Bourgueil wines in the troglodyte cellars of the right bank, about 21 km from the stopover town, 25 minutes by road. Cabernet franc, the king grape of the Loire, produces fruity, full-bodied reds here.

days_plan.itin_title: Indre-et-Loire Road Trip: Loire Valley Châteaux, Secret Valleys & Touraine Vineyards

visits.text: Saint-Gervais-Saint-Protais Church, founded in 998, preserves a 12th-century Romanesque nave flanked by two side aisles. Fifteenth-century Gothic chapels house a 17th-century Virgin statue. The flamboyant Gothic portal opens to a sober, light-filled interior.

The 18th-century grain hall is one of the largest surviving market halls in France. Its Tuscan-order granite columns support an imposing timber frame covered with lauze stone from the Tournel. The market is still held here every Saturday.

The Filature des Calquières, a historic monument, is the oldest spinning mill in France still in operation. Its 19th-century machinery, driven by a larch paddle wheel on the Langouyrou, turns fleece into yarn before your eyes. A living witness to the time when Lozère had three times more sheep than inhabitants.

Langogne is a thousand-year-old town with a circular layout unique in Lozère. Remnants of ramparts and six medieval towers—one housing the town hall—still trace the fortified perimeter. The 15-monument heritage walk comes with a brochure from the Tourist Office.

The ruins of Château de Luc, 12 km southeast, overlook the Allier valley. Built between the 10th and 12th centuries on the Voie Régordane, it displays remarkable "opus spicatum" (herringbone) masonry. Dismantled by order of Richelieu in 1630, it was converted to a chapel in the 19th century.

activities.text: Lake Naussac covers 1,050 hectares at 950 m above sea level. Sailing, paddleboarding, kayaking, kitesurfing and electric boats are on offer from two water sports centres. Supervised beach in summer.

Langogne sits at the crossroads of major trails: the GR70 (Stevenson Trail), GR700 (Voie Régordane), GR4, and GR470 (Sources et Gorges de l'Allier). Follow a section toward the Mercoire forest, 11,000 hectares where the Allier and Chassezac rivers rise.
Langogne's market runs Saturday mornings under the grain hall and in adjacent streets. A second market operates Tuesdays in summer. Cheeses, charcuterie, mountain honey, and Margeride lentils.

days_plan.itin_title: Lozère Circuit: Tarn Gorges and Cévennes

places.name: Langres

visits.text: Langres' ramparts stand as one of France's rare intact medieval fortifications: 3.5 kilometers of walls, 12 towers, and 7 preserved gates, constructed and reinforced from the 3rd century through the Napoleonic era. The Tower of Navarre—28 meters in diameter, 7 meters of wall thickness—is dizzying. Walk the full circuit from the Saint-Jean gate: allow 45 minutes without stopping, longer if you take time for the views across the Champagne plain at 400 meters altitude. In the evening, the illuminations are particularly beautiful.

The Gallo-Roman arch, built into the ramparts near the Market Gate, dates from the 1st century AD. It is the oldest monument still visible in Langres: the town was then called Andemantunnum, capital of the Lingones, a crossroads of the Roman roads linking Trier, Lyon, Besancon and Sens. A striking detail: in the 19th century, the ancient stones were simply set into the medieval wall rather than moved.

Saint-Mammes Cathedral, built between 1150 and 1196, is a masterpiece of transition between Burgundian Romanesque and Gothic. It measures 94 metres long and 23 metres high under the vault, and yet Langres today is only a small town. That is because until the 18th century it was the seat of a vast and influential bishopric, whose holders carried the sceptre at the coronation of the kings of France. If you have the energy, climb the 227 steps of the south tower for a spectacular view.

Do not miss the Chapel of the Holy Cross, built from 1547 to 1549 on the left side of the nave: its carved coffered vault, its altar and its polychrome Rouen faience floor are among the finest examples of the Renaissance in the region. Two 16th-century tapestries depicting the life of Saint Mammes, attributed to Jean Cousin the Elder, adorn the transepts.

The Diderot House of Enlightenment celebrates the philosopher born in Langres in 1713, who spent his first 15 years here. A curious detail for enthusiasts: a cutlery knife from Nogent artisans on display belonged to Diderot's father, himself a cutler—the father of the Encyclopédie came from artisan stock.

activities.text: Taste Langres AOC cheese in the cheese shops and delicatessens of the town centre. This cheese, washed with salted water, has a characteristic hollow on top: local legend advises pouring in a dash of Champagne or Marc de Bourgogne before eating it. The AOC has protected the cheese since 1991.

Take the time to visit the Guy Baillet Museum of Art and History in Langres. Its collections combine Gallo-Roman archaeology, sculpture and painting. Allow an hour or two, easily slotted in between two walks along the ramparts.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Est Road Trip: Vineyards, Ramparts and Forests
Haute-Marne Circuit: Langres and Heritage

map_keywords: Langres Guy-Baillet Art and History Museum

places.name: Lans En Vercors

visits.text: Lans-en-Vercors is the southeastern gateway to the plateau, 30 km from Grenoble via the Furon gorges. The gateway village has preserved its shopping streets and mountain architecture blending old and new. From the heights above the village, the Grenoble cluse suddenly opens up—the city and Chartreuse in the background, with the Belledonne massif on the horizon. It's one of the northern Vercors' most frequented panoramas by Grenoble residents.

The Lans-en-Vercors plain, vast and open, contrasts with the gorges and cliffs of previous days. In winter, the Nordic domain offers 15 km of marked trails. In summer, it's a space for gentle walks with views of the Vercors' eastern ridges. The village church and several century-old Dauphiné farms dot the village.

activities.text: The balcony path above the village (3-4 km) climbs to the plateau's western rim for a plunging view of the Isère valley. It's a loop route marked from the village center, accessible in about 1h30.

The climb to the Col de l'Arc, above Lans-en-Vercors, starts from the Barnets car park at the eastern edge of the village. Allow about 2 hours of walking and 450 metres of ascent, with no technical difficulty, to reach the pass. From up there, the view opens onto the Grenoble cluse, the Furon gorges and the Belledonne range.

days_plan.itin_title: Royans-Vercors Road Trip: Hilltop Villages and Gorges

map_keywords: Plaine de Lans ski de fond

visits.text: Lantosque stretches along a rocky ridge in the heart of the Vésubie valley. The town is a major stop on the old salt route, and the Rivet quarter, once a station on the Nice-Vésubie tramway that ran until 1928, made it an important transit point.

The Saint-Pons church dates from 1668 and has a cruciform plan unique in the valley. Its low, squat façade was designed to withstand earthquakes, and the interior holds relics of Saint Sulpice gifted by the Pope.
The Notre-Dame-de-la-Balma sanctuary, downstream from the village, is the only cave-sanctuary example in the Vésubie. A White Penitents procession took place there annually.
The Rivet quarter preserves the old stagecoach and post office hotels. It's a discreet witness to a time when reaching Nice took nearly a day on horseback.

activities.text: The Lantosque canyons via ferrata follows the Vésubie gorges for 1.2 km with footbridges and rope bridges. Budget 3h—it's strenuous, and equipment rental is available on site.
The Laune de l'éléphant, about 2 km south, is a natural pool accessible via a 15-minute trail. Turquoise but cold water—perfect for a swim after a hike.
The Vésubie gorges trail follows the river between waterfalls and reddish cliffs. Flat, shaded, ideal for late afternoon.
Chestnuts are the local speciality, with a festival dedicated to them each autumn. Mountain tomme and chestnut ravioli can be found at producers and restaurants in town.

days_plan.itin_title: Secret valleys of the Nice hinterland in 6 days

visits.text: The Cathedral of Notre-Dame crowns the hilltop like stone lace. Built between 1150 and 1235, it stands as one of the first major buildings of French Gothic architecture. Sixteen sculpted oxen adorn its towers, recalling the legend of a miraculous ox that descended from heaven to transport the stones. The interior is astonishingly bright thanks to its tall windows and white limestone.

Climb the 209 steps of the tower to reach the lapidary museum housed in the galleries. This repository, unique in France, displays around a hundred sculpted stones dating from the original construction and the 19th-century restoration. Gargoyles, capitals, and medieval sculptures can be viewed up close. The panorama over the upper town and surrounding plains rewards the climb.

Explore the medieval underground passages with an audioguide on a one-hour tour through the network of galleries carved beneath the city. These former quarries, later converted into cellars, recount Laon's geological and political history. The recently inaugurated exhibition design turns the visit into a true journey through time beneath the crowned city.

Medieval ramparts encircle the upper town for several kilometres. Discover fortified gates, notably the Ardon Gate, and admire the views down over the Aisne countryside. Walls punctuated with towers bear witness to Laon's strategic past.

activities.text: Stroll through the cobbled streets of the medieval upper town. Half-timbered houses line the narrow streets, including Laon's oldest house with its round chimneys in ruelle Pourrier. Private mansions and courtyards reveal themselves as you wander.

The Euromédiévales festival brings the ramparts to life each year with performances, craftspeople recreating medieval trades, and entertainment for the whole family. The festival immerses the city in the atmosphere of the Middle Ages for one festive weekend.

days_plan.itin_title: Aisne Itinerary: Gothic Cathedrals and the Picardy Countryside

places.name: Larressingle

visits.text: Larressingle is France's smallest fortified village. Nicknamed 'little Carcassonne of Gers,' it preserves intact its 13th-century ramparts, crenellated towers, dry moat, and recently restored old drawbridge.

Cross through the vaulted gateway with broken barrel arch, topped by a bretèche. Inside, a handful of medieval houses lean against the curtain walls. The entire village can be toured in twenty minutes, yet the atmosphere suspends time.

At the heart of the enclosure, ruins of the castle of the abbots then bishops of Condom occupy the entire center. The building is private but its massive 13th-century walls dominate the village at full height.

The fortified Romanesque church of Saint-Sigismond, from the 12th and 13th centuries, combines architectural purity with modern stained glass. The atmosphere holds absolute calm, far from tourist bustle.
The Medieval Siege Engines Park, installed around the ramparts, recreates a medieval siege camp. Trebuchets, bricoles, and full-scale assault engines are presented with demonstrations.
A few minutes' walk away, the Lartigue Bridge spans the Osse River. Inscribed as UNESCO World Heritage as part of the Ways of St. James, it sits exactly 1,000 km from Santiago de Compostela.

activities.text: Larressingle sits on the Via Podiensis (GR 65). Walk a portion of the Way of St. James toward Condom or Montréal-du-Gers through the Gers wine country.
Estates producing Armagnac and Floc de Gascogne surround the village. Visit one to understand distillation and taste these two local specialties.

For families, try the treasure hunt 'Conquering the fortified citadel of Larressingle,' available at tourist offices in Condom, Larressingle, and Montréal-du-Gers. Two versions depending on children's ages.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Garonne Road Trip: From Toulouse to the Pyrenees
Occitanie's 13 Most Beautiful Villages

map_keywords: Cité des Machines du Moyen Âge Larressingle

visits.text: Lassay-les-Châteaux, a Small Town of Character, boasts three castles. Victor Hugo, passing through in 1836, wrote to his wife that he'd seen 'Lassay, a charming half-wild little town with three castles, two of them admirable, which I sketched.'

The fortress, rebuilt in one campaign in 1458-1459 by Jean II de Vendôme after the Hundred Years' War, is a remarkable example of 15th-century military architecture. Its eight massive towers linked by curtain walls and ramparts, its barbican and drawbridge form an irregular octagon that has survived intact to this day—an exceptional occurrence in France.

The guided tour opens furnished rooms: bedroom, armory, kitchen with its granite cooking range and collection of antique copper. Arrive at the first tour to witness the drawbridge opening, or at the last to see it close.

A kilometer from the center, the ruins of Bois-Thibault castle raise their century-gilded towers amid the ivy. Built on a castle mound, it was home to the Du Bellay family—that of poet Joachim. Classified as a Historic Monument in 1925, it's maintained by a volunteer association.
Saint-Fraimbault church is dedicated to the 6th-century evangelizing hermit buried at Lassay, who allegedly inspired Chrétien de Troyes to create the character of Lancelot of the Lake.

The historic center in local granite can be explored on foot: picturesque lanes, houses from the 14th-18th centuries, colorful storefronts and preserved period signs. Spot the lintel carvings and turrets at street corners.

activities.text: Wander through Lassay's rose garden, near the old convent, where some 300 rose varieties offer an olfactory experience in season.
The medieval garden, connected to the castle, presents plants and herbs cultivated according to Middle Ages practices—aromatic, dye, medicinal.
Follow the Lassay river to discover the numerous old wash houses lining the waterway, witnesses to daily life of yesteryear.
The King Arthur legend interpretation trail connects the town's three castles (Lassay, Bois-Thibault and the Bois-Frou vestiges) through verdant landscapes and built heritage.

days_plan.itin_title: Mayenne Circuit: Hedgerows and Medieval Towns

visits.text: The four castles of Lastours, Cabaret, Tour Régine, Surdespine and Quertinheux, rise in tiers between 260 and 285 metres above sea level along a 600-metre rocky ridge, encircled by the Orbiel river and the Grésilhou stream. By the early 13th century Cabaret was already a Cathar stronghold of the Carcassès, frequented by bishops and the perfecti. In 1209 Simon de Montfort besieged it in vain. Allow 1 hour 30 for the full visitor trail. Then drive to the Montfermier viewpoint, 2 km away, to see the four silhouettes lined up against the Montagne Noire: the panorama is worth the detour.

The Gouffre géant de Cabrespine, about 16 km from Lastours, 25 minutes by road, is one of the largest open chasms in Europe: 250 metres deep and up to 80 metres wide. Balconies suspended 200 metres above the void, a glass walkway, and red and white aragonite crystals in the galleries. The temperature stays at a constant 14°C, so bring a jacket even in high summer.

Montolieu is a hilltop village on the edge of the Montagne Noire that has reinvented itself as a book village: some fifteen bookshops and second-hand booksellers occupy the stone houses of the historic centre. The Musée des Arts et Métiers du Livre traces the history of printing since Gutenberg. Plan a break to browse the shelves on a terrace with a view of the hills. About 23 km from Lastours, 30 minutes by road.

activities.text: The complete castle circuit is actually a hike: you pass through all four fortresses and the castrum of Cabaret, with an elevation gain of about 250 meters. Good shoes essential — the terrain is rocky and exposed to the sun. Set off early in the morning in summer.

days_plan.itin_title: Aude Road Trip: Carcassonne, Cathar Country & the Mediterranean

places.name: Laudun L Ardoise

visits.text: Camp de César is one of the least-known and most impressive ancient towns in the Rhône corridor. Perched on the Lacau plateau at an altitude of 264 meters, this 18-hectare oppidum overlooks the confluence of the Cèze and Tave, with views as far as the Alps on clear days. What we know: occupation lasted over 1,000 years. The Gauls founded a fortified oppidum in the 5th century BC, the Romans expanded it in the 1st century AD with a forum, a civic basilica and a courthouse—structures visible in the excavations—then the Benedictines occupied the site until the 13th century. Access is free year-round.

On the plateau, two viewpoint guides help you locate notable features: the Rhône, Cèze, Tave, Cévennes and Alpilles in the distance. Visible remains include the Roman rampart with a gateway for carts and a vaulted pedestrian gate, the foundations of the 1st-century forum and basilica, and late-period sarcophagi. A permanent exhibition in the village presents the most significant objects from the excavations.

A few hundred meters from Camp de César, the Balouvière aqueduct is a little-known 19th-century curiosity: built in 1870 to supply Laudun with drinking water, it measures 62 meters long and 10 meters high, its limestone rubble masonry recalling its illustrious ancestor, the Pont du Gard, about thirty kilometers away. Both sites are freely accessible.

activities.text: The Camp de César archaeological loop (3 to 5 km, easy difficulty, about 1 hour 30 minutes) starts from the signposted parking area in the hills above Laudun and crosses the plateau along the course of the ancient ramparts. The garrigue vegetation (holm oaks, rosemary, thyme) contrasts with the cut stones of the Roman fortifications. On clear days, the view over the Rhône valley from this vantage point is one of the most expansive on the circuit.

days_plan.itin_title: Cèze Valley and Ardèche Gorges Circuit

map_keywords: Forum basilique Camp de César Laudun

places.name: Lautrec

visits.text: The La Salette windmill, dating from 1688, dominates the village from its hilltop. It's one of the last mills in Occitania that still grinds flour. In season, it welcomes visitors for a demonstration of milling skills.

The Saint-Rémy collegiate church, listed as a historic monument since 1996, extends for 40 meters in the heart of the village. Its marble altarpiece is remarkable, and the pastel-blue interior tones recall that you're in the Pays de Cocagne.

Pass through the Porte de la Caussade, a remnant of medieval fortifications. Behind it, the quarter contains underground silos carved directly into the rock beneath homes: these flat-bottomed, jar-shaped cavities with a capacity of 2 m³ stored grain during wartime.

Stroll around the central square bordered by arcades and houses with covered walkways. The 14th-century houses with overhanging upper floors and the half-timbered façades testify to prosperity linked to the woad trade.
Climb to the Calvaire de la Salette for the finest panorama of the Lautrec region. The view takes in the Agout valley, the Montagne Noire, and, on clear days, the Pyrenees.

activities.text: Walk the “garlic trail,” an 8 km loop through the Lautrec countryside. The path passes farms equipped with traditional drying facilities where pink garlic hangs in bunches called “manouilles.”

Want to taste Label Rouge pink garlic from Lautrec? Friday mornings from mid-July through December, the garlic market sets up in the village. Its sweet, subtle flavor works equally well raw or roasted.
Visit a faithfully reconstructed clog-maker's workshop, with restored tools and machinery. This nearly vanished trade was practiced in Lautrec until the early 1960s.

days_plan.itin_title: Tarn Road Trip: Albi & Hilltop Villages

map_keywords: Moulin à vent de la Salette Lautrec

visits.text: Place des Cornières forms a medieval bastide founded in 1241 by the Count of Toulouse. Its semicircular arcades frame Gothic and Renaissance houses from the 15th to 18th centuries.
Saint-Barthélemy Church houses a 17th-century gilded wooden Baroque altarpiece. The building testifies to the growing wealth of this medieval trading town.
The defensive barbican offers panoramic views over the Quercy Blanc's limestone plateaus and valleys. Vistas extend across the Barguelonne and Lendou rivers.
The Jardin du Pèlerin, designated a Remarkable Garden, features a life-size Game of the Goose. Each stage traces the history of the pilgrimage route to Compostela.
Wander lanes lined with half-timbered houses and stone dwellings. Ornate facades recall the prosperity of medieval merchants.

activities.text: Walk the Via Podiensis passing through the bastide. Lauzerte is a major stop on the Way of Saint James between Le Puy-en-Velay and Spain.
Head to the promenade de l'Éveillé for sweeping views over the valleys. The hillsides are adorned with orchards of Moissac chasselas and Quercy melons.
Visit art galleries and artists' studios housed in old residences. Lauzerte nurtures a vibrant cultural scene with exhibitions and summer concerts.

days_plan.itin_title: Tarn-et-Garonne Road Trip: Bastides and Orchards

visits.text: Laval, prefecture of Mayenne and a Town of Art and History, has stretched along the riverside for a thousand years. Dominated by its medieval castle, the historic city abounds in half-timbered houses, steep lanes and townhouses.

The Old Castle, founded around 1020 by Guy de Dénéré on a hill overlooking a ford, is the town's emblematic monument. Its 34-meter cylindrical keep, crowned with a defensive hoarding, houses an exceptional 13th-century timber frame. The 12th-century Romanesque chapel boasts beautiful carved capitals.

The MANAS (Museum of Naïve Art and Singular Arts), installed in the castle since 1967, is France's first naïve art museum. It displays major collections across 1,100 m² including three canvases by Le Douanier Rousseau, a Laval native born in 1844, and works by Séraphine de Senlis. Free admission to permanent collections.

Pass through the Beucheresse Gate, one of the old fortified gates: it was in this tower that Le Douanier Rousseau was born. From the other side of the Old Bridge, the panorama of the castle and quays is Laval's most photographed view.

The Basilica of Notre-Dame d'Avesnières, on the right bank, is a fine Romanesque building from the 11th-12th centuries. Its chevet with radiating chapels is one of the most harmonious in western France.

The municipal Public Baths, labeled '20th-century Heritage,' are a jewel of Laval Art Deco. Their mosaics by Isidore Odorico play with blue and yellow contrasts in each cabin, following a pattern inspired by Viennese art.
The Saint-Julien wash-boat, last survivor of the fleet that animated the Mayenne riverbanks, recalls the time when washerwomen beat their laundry along the water.

activities.text: Climb up to the Perrine Garden, a haven of peace in the heart of town. This park overlooking the Mayenne shelters century-old trees, a rose garden and panoramic views of the river. At Le Douanier Rousseau's grave, read the verses engraved by his friend Guillaume Apollinaire.

Descend to Laval's port for an electric boat ride on the Mayenne. Southward, the river leads to the Abbey of Notre-Dame du Port-du-Salut (birthplace of the famous cheese) and the Gallo-Roman baths of Entrammes.
The towpath along the Mayenne is part of the Vélo Francette (from Caen to La Rochelle). Rent a bike to pedal along the river between manual locks and hedgerow landscapes.

days_plan.itin_title: Mayenne Circuit: Hedgerows and Medieval Towns

visits.text: Lavaudieu's Romanesque cloister is the only one in Auvergne to have escaped destruction. Its single or paired columns, crowned with sculpted capitals, support rounded arches beneath a 12th-century wooden gallery.

Enter the refectory adjoining the cloister. A monumental Byzantine-influenced fresco depicts Christ in Majesty above the Virgin surrounded by the Apostles. Classified as a Historic Monument as early as 1862.

The Abbey Church of Saint-André, crowned by its octagonal Romanesque bell tower, conceals a collection of 14th-century murals from the Italian School: Passion scenes and a curious allegory of the plague, the "Black Death."
The Benedictine abbey was founded in 1057 by Robert de Turlande, also founder of La Chaise-Dieu. Nuns lived here until the Revolution, in this place baptized Lavaudieu—"Valley of God."
Visit the Museum of Folk Arts and Traditions, housed in the former baker's home. Over a thousand objects recreate an Auvergnat interior from days past.
Notice the abbey's bell tower, truncated during the Revolution: a pike and Phrygian cap still ornament its summit, an unusual republican vestige.

activities.text: Stroll along the Senouire River and cross the Romanesque bridge. From both sides, the view of the golden stone wine-growers' houses and their rounded tiles is exceptional.
Meander through the cobbled lanes of the village, classified as one of France's Most Beautiful Villages. Kitchen gardens nestled around the abbey and an 18th-century iron cross punctuate the walk.
In summer, the village hosts its traditional wine festival, a custom born during the Revolution when locals seized barrels destined for the monks of La Chaise-Dieu.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Loire Road Trip: Le Puy-en-Velay and Volcanoes

visits.text: Saint-Alain Cathedral, a masterpiece of southern French Gothic, was built from 1255 onward. Its single nave rises 23 meters high. The carved polychrome wooden organ case from 1523 is a jewel of Midi Renaissance art.

Look up at the tower: the Jacquemart, a 17th-century wooden automaton, still strikes the hours. It's the only working example in southwestern France. Legend has it that a Protestant prisoner built it to escape.

The jardins de l'Évêché, north of the cathedral, form a French formal garden with carefully arranged flowers from May to October. The subtly colored beds descend in terraces with views over the Agout.
Follow the path to the Tour des Rondes, remnant of medieval fortifications. Here in 1211, during the Albigensian Crusade, 400 Cathars perished in the crusade's largest mass burning.

Place du Plô overlooks the Agout. The paved streets of the medieval quarter are lined with half-timbered houses and brick mansions, witnesses to the era when Lavaur was capital of the Pays de Cocagne.
Saint-François Church, built in the 17th century by Franciscans, offers a contrast of simplicity and intimacy after the cathedral's grandeur. Its modest nave invites a contemplative pause.

activities.text: The large Saturday morning market takes over Lavaur's avenues. It's one of the region's most important: farm products, fattened poultry, foie gras, cheeses, and local crafts fill the stalls.

Follow the Roman road between Lavaur and Puylaurens, which runs along the crests of the hills in the Pays de Cocagne. The landscape of woad fields, dovecotes, and white stone houses recreates the atmosphere of a dazzling era.
Attend an organ concert at the cathedral when the schedule allows. The grand 1876 Cavaillé-Coll organ attracts international organists for regular recitals.

days_plan.itin_title: Tarn Road Trip: Albi & Hilltop Villages

visits.text: The Cluniac Priory of Sainte-Croix was founded in 1025 by Odilon de Mercoeur, 5th Abbot of Cluny. The buildings visible today date mainly from the 15th and 18th centuries, their hemicycle form hugging the Allier's meander.
Step inside the Priory Church of Sainte-Croix, in Gothic style (15th c.). It preserves a Romanesque door called Saint Odilon's Door (12th c.) and a polychrome wooden Christ from the mid-12th century.
Look for the statuette of Notre-Dame-Trouvée: in 1496, two girls playing by the Allier discovered this 1.5 cm (0.6 in) Virgin inside a broken pebble. She is preserved in a silver reliquary.
Cross the humpbacked medieval bridge linking the village's two quarters. One of its arches dates back to the 11th century—it has resisted centuries of violent Allier floods.
The Maison des Oiseaux et de la Nature, in the priory courtyard, presents around fifty bird species from the Allier gorges, sculpted life-size in wood against a fresco backdrop.
Explore the Barrys quarter, the village's oldest, with its traboules, the characteristic narrow passageways allowing a quick descent to the river.

activities.text: Descend the Allier gorges by canoe or kayak. Outfitters offer trips suited to all levels departing from the village.
Take the belvedere loop (PR001, 2 km / 1.2 mi) for a unique view of the Allier's perfect loop around the priory. Family-friendly.
In summer, swim in the Allier from the beach near the bridge. This river, one of the last wild rivers in Europe, is also ideal for family fishing.
The GR 470 "Source et Gorges de l'Allier" crosses the village. The Lavoûte-Chilhac–Langeac stage (19 km / 12 mi) offers gorge landscapes hemmed between volcanoes and forests.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Loire Road Trip: Le Puy-en-Velay and Volcanoes

visits.text: Village of Le Bec-Hellouin. Eure's second village labeled among France's Most Beautiful Villages, this Norman gem enchants with its colorful half-timbered houses, flower-filled cobbled streets, and preserved atmosphere. Nestled in the Bec valley hollow, it offers a condensed essence of authentic charm that echoes its neighbor Lyons-la-Forêt.

Notre-Dame Abbey of Le Bec. Founded in 1034 by knight Herluin, this Benedictine abbey became one of Europe's greatest spiritual and intellectual centers. Two of its abbots, Lanfranc and Anselm, became Archbishops of Canterbury. The 15th-century Saint-Nicolas tower, the site's symbol, dominates the cloister and Maurist buildings with their elegant facades. Monks perpetuate monastic life and sell their delicate handcrafted ceramics in the shop.
Saint-André Church of Le Bec-Hellouin. Erected in 1039 and dependent on the abbey until the Revolution, this neo-Gothic parish church houses the tomb of Blessed Herluin, the abbey's founder.

Sainte-Françoise Romaine Monastery. Two kilometers from the abbey, 26 Benedictine nuns live according to the Rule of Saint Benedict in buildings constructed since 1950. You can buy handcrafted candles there and enjoy absolute calm for a spiritual retreat.

activities.text: Le Bec-Hellouin Organic Farm. This permaculture farm, located 500 meters from the abbey, is a global reference in agroecology. Training sessions and tours reveal this productive agriculture without tractors or pesticides, where ecosystems interact harmoniously.

Château d'Harcourt and arboretum. Eight kilometers from Le Bec-Hellouin, this 12th-century medieval castle is surrounded by one of France's oldest arboretums (1802). Nearly 500 species of century-old trees compose this remarkable park.

Château du Champ de Bataille. Twelve kilometers away, this 17th-century château restored by decorator Jacques Garcia presents sumptuous interiors and exceptional French formal gardens. A journey into the French art de vivre.

days_plan.itin_title: Eure Road Trip: From Giverny to Normandy's Most Beautiful Villages
Cotentin, Pays d'Auge: 5 days exploring the most beautiful villages

visits.text: The hamlet of Le Boréon is Saint-Martin-Vésubie's alpine outpost, at an altitude of 1,473 meters at the foot of the Gélas massif. A few chalets, a reservoir shaped like a glacial basin, a waterfall. It's the starting point for the Mercantour's major hikes on the Vésubie side. The air changes abruptly compared with the village below: you're deep in the mountains.

Lac du Boréon, fed by torrents flowing down from the Gélas, takes on an intense blue-green hue in summer. The walk around the lake takes 30 minutes on a flat trail accessible to everyone. The Boréon waterfall, just downstream, is visible from the road. Free parking is available nearby and fills quickly in July–August.

activities.text: Hike to Lac de Trécolpas from Le Boréon: 8 km round trip, 600 meters of elevation gain, 3.5 hours of walking, an alpine setting with marmots on the rocks and ibex on the ridges. Check the weather; afternoon thunderstorms are common in summer in the Mercantour. Start in the morning and head back down before 3 p.m.

days_plan.itin_title: Nice's hinterland: 8 days of hilltop villages and the Mercantour

visits.text: Strange that this is the world's only museum dedicated to Bonnard, given his attachment to the place: the painter bought the Villa Le Bosquet in 1926, lived there over twenty years, painted nearly 300 canvases there, died there in 1947. The Bonnard Museum opened on June 25, 2011 in the Hôtel Saint-Vianney, the last Belle Époque witness in Le Cannet, partnership with the Musée d'Orsay since 2012. Collections focused on 1922–1947: landscapes, nudes, interiors (The Dining Room at Le Cannet, 1932; Nude in Profile). Closed Mondays.

activities.text: Then climb into old Cannet, ten minutes on foot from the museum. Rue Saint-Sauveur, Place Bellevue, and the seven hills offer the same views Bonnard painted from Le Bosquet: red rooftops, the Estérel range, Cannes Bay in the distance. Allow 45 minutes for the complete loop.

days_plan.itin_title: French Riviera Art Museums and Galleries: An 8-Day Journey

visits.text: Enter Le Castellet village through the Grand Portail, one of only two fortified gates pierced in the ramparts—there's no other access. Listed among France's Most Beautiful Villages, this perched medieval village offers 360° views over the Bandol vineyards. Sloping lanes climb toward the 15th-century château (now town hall, interior not open to visitors). Marcel Pagnol filmed “The Baker's Wife” here in 1938 with Raimu—you can still see Place de l'Ormeau where scenes were shot.

Look for the “Trou de Madame”—an opening in the ramparts, left of the château. It's a discreet but spectacular viewpoint: the entire Brûlat wine plain spreads before you, bordered by olive groves and pine forests, with the white line of the Sainte-Baume massif as a backdrop. On clear days, the contrast between golden garrigue and blue sky is striking.

Push on to La Cadière-d'Azur, 5 minutes by car. This hilltop village, also labeled a Var Village of Character, is less touristy than Le Castellet but equally charming. Its orientation table offers a panorama over vineyards, the distant sea, and Var hills. Lanes are quiet, stone façades golden—this is Provence in its authentic form.

In Le Castellet, take time to browse artists' workshops—potters, ceramicists, painters, leatherworkers. The village has specialized in art crafts, and the Parcours des Arts lets you discover them shop by shop. Saint-Sauveur church, built in 1030 by the Marseille bishopric and oriented toward Jerusalem, deserves a look for its three-arch bell tower and campanile.

activities.text: Take advantage of your visit for a tasting at a Bandol AOC wine estate. Vineyards spread at Le Castellet's foot on sunny terraces. Mourvèdre dominates the reds—powerful, tannic wines that age remarkably well. Several estates offer visits and tastings without reservation in off-season, but call ahead in summer.

At the end of the day, drive down to Bandol (15 minutes by car). The small marina is lined with terraces where you can have a last drink facing the boats. The Provençal market on Tuesday mornings is worth a detour if your schedule allows.

days_plan.itin_title: From Marseille to Aix-en-Provence: Calanques, Hilltop Villages and Provençal Light

places.name: Le Cateau Cambresis

visits.text: The Matisse Departmental Museum occupies the Palais Fénelon, the former palace of the archbishops of Cambrai. Founded by Matisse himself in 1952 in his hometown, it gathers 783 works by the master: 26 paintings, 21 sculptures, 479 drawings and cut-outs, including Window in Tahiti and the Oceania series.

The collection of Auguste Herbin, another native of Le Cateau-Cambrésis, presents 92 works by this pioneer of geometric abstraction. His stained-glass window Joie, with vivid colours and pure forms, encapsulates his quest for a universal visual language.

What did publisher Tériade's dining room contain? The museum displays this entire room, decorated by Matisse and Giacometti. The Tériade donation comprises 590 works by Picasso, Chagall, Miró, Giacometti and Léger – a panorama of 20th-century art assembled by one man.
The Palais Fénelon itself merits attention. This 18th-century edifice, former residence of Cambrai's archbishops, presents an orderly classical façade overlooking Place du Commandant-Richez.

The French formal garden, laid out in the late 17th century in Le Nôtre's style, extends behind the palace. One hundred and seventy-five trees, including three-hundred-year-old lime trees, border its straight paths laid out according to classical principles of perspective.

activities.text: Take time to sketch in the museum's galleries. Sketching workshops are regularly offered in front of Matisse's works – a way to grasp the simplification of line that characterises his late work, between pared-down forms and colour.

Walk through the centre of Le Cateau-Cambrésis, from the market square to Saint-Martin Church. The small town has preserved a coherent urban fabric, with 19th-century brick houses aligned along narrow streets leading to the Selle.

Le Cateau-Cambrésis holds France's third Matisse collection, after Nice and Paris. Compare the cut-outs exhibited here with those you may have seen elsewhere: the display illuminates the master's creative process, from sketch to finished work.

places.name: Le Chambon Sur Lignon

visits.text: Le Chambon-sur-Lignon Memorial Site. Opened in 2013, this unique museum retraces the story of the rescue of thousands of persecuted Jews during the Second World War. The exhibition explains what was particular about the Vivarais-Lignon plateau and what motivated the inhabitants in their civil, spiritual and armed resistance. The memorial room plays testimonies from rescuers, refugees and resistance fighters. Nearly 90 people have been proclaimed Righteous Among the Nations. The Memory Garden, designed by the landscape architect Louis Benech, offers a space for contemplation.

Le Chambon-sur-Lignon Protestant Church. Built around 1821 on Valla Chomier's land, it replaced the first Protestant church, destroyed in 1679 during the Wars of Religion. On the granite porch, the inscription “Love one another” recalls the village's tradition of hospitality. It was here, on June 23, 1940, that pastors André Trocmé and Edouard Theis called on their parishioners to resist with “the weapons of the spirit”. The building bears witness to the plateau's long Protestant tradition.

Le Chambon Historic Center. Place de la Fontaine brings together shops and events. All around, pine woods, groves and paths create a soothing atmosphere even in the middle of the village. Its 2,400 inhabitants live in a setting where nature and built heritage blend harmoniously. Old houses, historic hotels and public buildings tell the story of the village's tourist development, which began in the early 20th century with the arrival of the railway from Saint-Étienne.

activities.text: Hiking on the Vivarais-Lignon plateau. The Plateau des Justes route offers beautiful panoramic views of the volcanic peaks, the Pic du Lizieux and Mont Mézenc. Distance: approximately 16 km. Marked trails cross pine woods, groves and meadows at elevations between 874 and 1,139 meters. The village's natural body of water allows swimming and water sports in summer. The 18-hole golf course extends across a wooded, hilly site.

Memory Trail through the village. Guided tours are offered year-round for groups and on Tuesdays in summer for individual visitors. The route begins at the station with a historical introduction, continues with the exhibition “Accueil et Paroles de nos villages”, then a walk through the village takes in Tante Soly, the parsonage, the old village and the school. The visit ends with a moment of sharing at the Protestant church. Reservations at the Tourist Office.

days_plan.itin_title: Loire Circuit: Wild Gorges and Industrial Heritage

map_keywords: Place de la Fontaine Le Chambon
Jardin de la Mémoire Le Chambon

visits.text: Board here for Ushant and Molène: Le Conquet has preserved an old town center of granite houses spared by rebuilding, huddled around a still-active port. Several old facades recall the wealth of shipowners before the town was burned by the English in 1558. Passenger boats to the islands depart from the slipway, with several sailings daily in season. Book in July–August, as crossings fill up.

activities.text: Cross the Croaë footbridge and you're on the Kermorvan peninsula in Le Conquet: a narrow tongue of land ending at a lighthouse put into service in the mid-19th century, with the Chenal du Four due west. The flat loop covers about 4 km along paths and across low-growing heath. Opposite, Blancs Sablons beach stretches out for nearly 2 km of light-colored sand protected by its dune. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes with the beach stop.

days_plan.itin_title: Brittany 7 days: Pink Granite, Lighthouses & Peninsulas

visits.text: The port of Le Croisic comes to life early in the morning. From the 16th century onwards, proud shipowners and captains ensured the prosperity of this town, now one of the peninsula's most architecturally beautiful. The Ministry of Culture has listed several houses dating from the 15th to the 17th century along the granite quays. Take time for a stroll before the day's influx of tourists.

The Océarium du Croisic grew out of a family story in 1968, when a fish wholesaler set up an aquarium to keep his customers occupied while they waited. It has since become one of France's largest private aquariums, with over 4,000 animals across 56 tanks. From Australian sharks to penguins, by way of an 800,000-liter Pacific ray tank—unique in Europe according to its designers—there's enough for 1.5 to 2 hours. The daily events (penguin feeding, shark presentations) are included in the ticket. No reservation required, but come early in peak season.

Climb Mont Esprit to take in the whole peninsula at a glance. This artificial mound was formed by the stone ballast that foreign ships dumped on arriving in port to load their cargo of salt—over time, the stones built up into a hill. The 360° panorama over the salt marshes, the ocean, and Le Croisic harbor is worth the climb.

The Côte Sauvage stretches south of Le Croisic, between granite cliffs and windswept heathland. A maintained path follows the ocean from the La Vigie parking lot, offering views of coves and rocks. One of the peninsula's best spots, with few visitors outside weekends.

activities.text: Cycle the Guérande Peninsula between ocean and salt marshes. Bike paths connect Le Croisic, La Baule, and Guérande on a 25–30-kilometer loop. The route between the salt pans is particularly beautiful in late afternoon when the sun catches the mirror-like pools. Bike rental companies are available locally.

days_plan.itin_title: Loire-Atlantique Road Trip: Nantes and the Côte de Jade

places.name: Le Crotoy

visits.text: Le Crotoy has the only south-facing beach in the North. At low tide, fine sand stretches to infinity and the bay becomes a mirror reflecting the sky—painters Seurat, Toulouse-Lautrec, and Sisley came here to capture this unique light.

The little fishing harbour preserves old-time charm. In the 17th century, it was one of the Channel's most important ports. A few sauterelliers—flat-bottomed boats—still set out to catch grey shrimp on the sandbanks.

On Place Jeanne d'Arc, a statue recalls that Joan of Arc, a prisoner of the English, was held in Le Crotoy's fortified castle in 1430 before being taken to Rouen. Remnants of the 12th-century castle survive among the town's buildings.

The Jules-Noiret promenade runs along the beach for 2 km, lined with beach huts. It passes the monument to the Caudron brothers, aviation pioneers who tested their first aircraft on the bay's firm sand.

Saint-Pierre church dates back to the 13th century. Modest but endearing, it bears witness to the long history of this fishing village, which became a seaside resort when sea bathing began here in the mid-19th century.

activities.text: On Saturday mornings, fishermen sell directly to customers at the fish market hall facing the harbour. Brown shrimp, sole and plaice: the bay's best on improvised stalls.
Board the Somme Bay steam train at Le Crotoy station. The metre-gauge line crosses salt marshes and wet meadows to Saint-Valery-sur-Somme.
At low tide, the immense beach lends itself to land yachting, kite flying, or simply a long barefoot walk on wet sand. Check tide times before setting out.
The Marquenterre Ornithological Park, a few kilometres away, shelters 365 bird species on a 19,000 ha Ramsar site. Observation hides, marked trails, and nature reserve atmosphere.
