visits.text: The Herisson waterfalls trail is the iconic hike of the Jura lakes: in 3.7 km and 250 meters of elevation gain (one way), the Herisson tumbles down 31 drops including 7 major waterfalls. The tallest is the Eventail waterfall, a 65-meter drop whose width increases as it descends, which is where its name comes from. It's followed by the Grand Saut (60 meters) then the Gour Bleu, an emerald-hued pool that few photographers can resist capturing. Before the first mills were built on this torrent in the Middle Ages, a local legend spoke of a giant living behind the Grand Saut, who had the power to summon lost objects to him. Bring waterproof shoes: the footbridges and rocks are slippery in wet weather.

The 4 Lakes viewpoint perched at 900 meters altitude is one of the most photographed panoramas in the Jura. From the La Chaux-du-Dombief parking lot, count 5 minutes on foot to reach this viewpoint that simultaneously embraces Lakes Ilay, Narlay, Petit and Grand Maclu — four glacial lakes of different origins and hues. Lake Narlay stands out for its 48-meter depth, which earned it the nickname "black lake." An orientation table helps read the landscape. In clear weather, the view extends all the way to Mont Blanc from the nearby Pic de l'Aigle (993 meters).

activities.text: Picnic by Lake Bonlieu: this small wild lake, source of the Hérisson, is surrounded by dense forests and flowering meadows. Access from the village of Bonlieu is easy, the setting is perfectly preserved. This is where the river originates before tumbling down the 31 waterfalls toward the valley — a good spot for a quiet midday break before the big hike.

Hike to Pic de l'Aigle (993 m) from the La Chaux-du-Dombief parking lot: the round trip to the summit takes about 1 hour. The 360° view over the Frasnois plateau, the Hérisson valley and the Grandvaux is striking. This hike can be extended into a 9 km loop to descend toward Lakes Ilay and Maclu — then count 3h30 and sturdy shoes, some descents are steep.

days_plan.itin_title: Jura Lakes Route: Emerald and Turquoise Waters

visits.text: Head to Étretat (about 27 km from Le Havre, a 30-minute drive), then start with the Aval cliff - Étretat's star attraction. The natural arch towers more than 80 meters above the sea, and right beside it stands the famous Aiguille, 51 meters high. Maupassant compared the Amont arch to an elephant dipping its trunk into the sea. Climb the steps from the beach - allow 20 minutes for the ascent - and stop at the viewpoint above the arch for the best photo. Caution: stay 5 meters back from the edge, as rockfalls are frequent.

Continue along the path toward the Manneporte, 500 meters to the southwest. This arch is even more massive than the Aval arch: 50 meters high and 40 meters wide. Maupassant claimed that a ship could sail through it with all its sails set.

Head back down to Étretat beach and cross toward the Falaise d'Amont via the 263-step staircase behind the Hôtel des Roches Blanches. At the summit, you'll find the Chapelle Notre-Dame-de-la-Garde, protector of fishermen. The current building replaces a chapel destroyed by the occupying forces during World War II. Right beside it, the bird-shaped monument honors Nungesser and Coli—it was from here that their aircraft L'Oiseau Blanc was last sighted in 1927 before vanishing over the Atlantic.

The Jardins d'Étretat occupy the top of the Falaise d'Amont. Originally created in 1905 by Madame Thébault, an actress friend of Monet, they were reimagined between 2015 and 2017 by landscape architect Alexander Grivko. Seven themed gardens follow one another along the cliff—the Émotions garden with its large resin faces, the Zen garden with suspended sculptures, the Impressions garden with its statue of Monet before his easel. Allow a good hour. The panorama over the Needle and the Channel from the Amont terrace is the finest at the site.

Return to town and step into the Clos Lupin, the home of writer Maurice Leblanc. He lived here from 1919 onward and it was here that he imagined the adventures of Arsène Lupin. The museum tour traces the story of The Hollow Needle, published in 1909, in which the gentleman thief discovers a royal treasure hidden inside the Needle. If you've seen the Netflix series, you'll recognize the locations.

Head to Honfleur this morning - about 25 km from Le Havre, a 30-minute drive via the Pont de Normandie (toll). Start with the Vieux-Bassin, the historic harbor surrounded by tall, narrow timber-framed houses dating from the 16th and 17th centuries. Arrive before 9:30 a.m. if you want to see the façades reflected in the water without the crowds - Honfleur welcomes 5 million visitors a year. Stroll along rue des Petites Boucheries and rue de la Prison, the oldest streets in the neighborhood.

A stone's throw from the harbor, you can't miss the Église Sainte-Catherine. It's the largest wooden church in France. Built in the second half of the 15th century after the Hundred Years' War, it was constructed by shipwrights who used oak from the Touques forest and their boat-building techniques. Result: the vault resembles an inverted ship's hull. The bell tower stands separate from the rest of the church—a precaution against lightning. Entry is free.

Next, climb up to the Chapelle Notre-Dame-de-Grâce, a 15-minute walk up the Côte de Grâce. Since Pentecost 1861, every year Honfleur's children have carried model boats in procession from the Église Sainte-Catherine to here. The chapel is lined with sailors' ex-votos. The view from the esplanade over the Seine estuary and the Pont de Normandie is worth the climb.

After lunch in Honfleur, take the coastal road to Deauville (30 min). Head straight for Les Planches, the famous wooden boardwalk along the beach. Each cabin bears the name of a director or star who participated in the American Film Festival. Stroll to the end—the view down the coast is unobstructed and the chic seaside atmosphere is unique in Normandy.

Cross the bridge spanning the Touques to reach Trouville-sur-Mer, Deauville's more down-to-earth neighbor. Half-timbered houses line the Quai Fernand-Moureaux, facing the fishing port. Go to the fish market at the port—even if you don't buy anything, the display is a spectacle. The Église Notre-Dame-des-Victoires, in the heart of town, dates from the 11th century.

A day devoted to Le Havre. Begin with the Église Saint-Joseph—impossible to miss, its 107-meter lantern tower dominates the entire city. Built between 1951 and 1957 by Auguste Perret after the destruction of Le Havre by the September 1944 bombings, it's as much a memorial as a church. From outside, the raw concrete is startling. But push open the door: inside, 12,768 pieces of mouth-blown colored glass created by master glassworker Marguerite Huré line the octagonal tower. The light shifts with every hour of the day. The city center reconstructed by Perret has been UNESCO-listed since 2005.

Next, walk to Le Volcan, the national performing arts venue designed by Brazilian architect Oscar Niemeyer and inaugurated in 1982. You'll immediately recognize its white curved forms set beside the Bassin du Commerce—locals long dubbed it the “yogurt pot.” The Petit Volcan now houses the municipal library. Cross the Passerelle François-Le-Chevalier spanning the basin—the view of Le Volcan and the water is a postcard image of modern Le Havre.

The MuMa (Musée d'art moderne André Malraux) sits by the sea at the port entrance. This glass-and-steel building houses one of the finest Impressionist collections outside Paris—Boudin, Monet, Renoir, Sisley. The view over the sea through the large windows is part of the visit. Allow 1 to 1½ hours.

After the MuMa, head to the Porte Océane, the monumental gateway between city and sea designed by Perret. Two 11-story towers frame a 600-meter boulevard bordered by low-rise buildings. Continue to the seafront—Le Havre's pebble beach stretches 2 km. You'll see the colorful cabanas and the sculpture UP#3 by Sabina Lang & Daniel Baumann.

Climb to the Jardins Suspendus, laid out in a former 19th-century military fort on the heights of Le Havre. The tropical greenhouses and themed gardens are pleasant, but it's mainly the 360° panorama over the city, the port and the Channel that's worth the trip. Free entry.

activities.text: In the late afternoon, follow Étretat's seafront promenade along the central beach. From the promenade, look at the Aval arch and the Aiguille, then the Amont arch. The chalk arches stand out above the pebbles and the sea. Stay opposite the promenade, in the authorized section of the beach: access to the rocks and beaches at the foot of the cliffs is prohibited.

If the late-day light is beautiful, return to Honfleur's Vieux-Bassin for the golden hour. The façades glow on the western side and it's photographers' favorite time—Monet, Boudin and Jongkind had already discovered the spot in the 19th century.

In Deauville, if the tide allows, walk barefoot on the wet sand. The beach is immense at low tide—you can venture far out toward the open sea. Bring a windbreaker, even in summer: the breeze from the open sea is cool.

In the evening, go down to the pebble beach for sunset. The sky over Le Havre is famous for its light—it's no accident that Monet painted “Impression, Sunrise” in the harbor in 1872, giving its name to the Impressionist movement.

places.name: Le Mans

visits.text: The Gallo-Roman ramparts of Le Mans are one of the most astonishing things you'll see anywhere in France. Built in the early 4th century to encircle ancient Vindinum—the red city, as the Romans called it, referring to its blood-colored bricks—it originally ran 1,300 meters and today preserves about 500 meters, with 12 towers and 3 posterns still standing. On certain sections, polychrome geometric friezes run more than 8 meters high—a decorative richness unique in the entire former Roman Empire. Le Mans is, in fact, a candidate for UNESCO listing for these ramparts. For the best view, descend the Pans-de-Gorron staircase to the left of the bishop's palace and look up.

The Cité Plantagenêt—old Le Mans, renamed in 2003—spreads across 20 hectares atop the promontory. This is where the Plantagenet dynasty shaped medieval England's history: in 1128, Geoffrey Plantagenet married Matilda, heiress to England's throne, in the cathedral here, and their son Henry II, future King of England, was baptized in the same place. Since then, little has really changed—15th-century half-timbered houses, Renaissance mansions, and cobbled lanes so picturesque that scenes from the film Cyrano de Bergerac were shot here. Walk along rue de Vaux with its climbing roses and look for the houses called des Deux-Amis and du Drapier: their carved signs alone tell the quarter's story.

The Cathedral of Saint-Julien has dominated the city since the 11th century—in reality far longer, its foundation dating according to archives to the 4th or 5th century. Its Romanesque nave and Gothic choir completed in 1254, signed notably by Jehan de Chelles who also worked on Notre-Dame de Paris, make it one of France's most complex buildings, at 134 meters long and 5,000 m² in area. Don't miss two curiosities: the Ascension window in a side chapel, dated late 11th century and considered the oldest stained glass still in place in any cathedral in the world; and the pink sandstone menhir attached to the west facade, nicknamed Saint Julien's Stone, which legend says brings fertility to those who touch its navel.

The Musée Jean-Claude-Boulard – Carré Plantagenêt, in central Le Mans, presents local history and archaeology, from prehistory to the Middle Ages. Its collections offer a chance to discover, in particular, the Gallic treasure of Les Sablons, Gallo-Roman artefacts and the history of Le Mans. The museum is therefore a good introduction to the Cité Plantagenêt and its wall.

Three kilometers from the center, the Royal Abbey of Épau is one of the finest Cistercian foundations in northwestern France. Founded in 1229 by Queen Bérengère of Navarre—who died a year after construction began and never saw it completed—the abbey houses her white marble effigy in the abbatial church. Sculpted in the style of Eleanor of Aquitaine at Fontevraud, she is depicted crowned, with a purse at her belt and a lion at her feet. The effigy had been discovered under bales of straw in 1816 then transferred to Le Mans cathedral, before returning here in 1970. The site extends through a 13-hectare park.

The 24 Hours of Le Mans Museum retraces the greatest endurance race in the world, run without interruption since 1923 on the same 13.6 km course using local roads south of Le Mans. The permanent collection brings together more than 120 authentic vehicles: the 1924 Bentley 3 Litre Sport that opened the podium of the second edition, the Bugatti Type 57G that won in 1937, the Jaguar D-Type, the Ford GT40 victorious in 1969, the Porsche 917, the Audi R18... A display case of 4,236 models at 1/43 scale represents every car entered since 1923.

The guided tour of the 24 Hours of Le Mans circuit lets you access behind the scenes: the paddocks, starting line, the Hunaudières straight where cars reach over 350 km/h, the legendary corners of Tertre Rouge, Mulsanne, and Arnage. The permanent Bugatti circuit—4.2 km—is an integral part of the 24 Hours layout. Local operators also offer sports car tours or karting sessions within the complex.

The Tessé Museum, in Le Mans city center, holds a fine collection of paintings from the 13th to 20th centuries. Don't miss the enameled copper copy of Geoffrey Plantagenet—one of the oldest figurative representations in champlevé enamel in France—and the Egyptian archaeology collection that stands out in this context.

activities.text: In summer, don't miss the Nuit des Chimères: every evening from July to early September, the Gallo-Roman ramparts and cathedral become giant projection screens with sound and light. Wander freely through the Cité's lanes to discover the eight visual spectacles animating the medieval facades—Le Mans heritage seen as you never imagined it.

Stroll the Cité's lanes searching for underground passages that once connected the cathedral to other strategic points in the city. Gallo-Roman baths from the 1st century are partially preserved beneath the Beaux-Arts school—fragments of mosaics following Italian rules of the period—and the tourist office offers audioguides to explore these superimposed layers of history.

Operators offer karting or track driving sessions within the 24 Hours complex—karting on the Maison Blanche circuit, driving simulators, or introductory rides in a sports car on the Bugatti Circuit. For serious enthusiasts, it's even possible to drive a homologated sports car on the legendary track. Book online before arrival to guarantee your slot.

The official 24 Hours of Le Mans shop, at the circuit entrance, is one of France's largest automotive merchandising stores: jerseys, caps, scale models, artwork, car accessories. Even if you don't drive, it's a temple of motorsport that no enthusiast can miss.

visits.text: Documented as early as 1252, the Tour Charles Quint in Le Muy was called Tour Notre-Dame before 1536. That year, residents barricaded themselves inside to try to assassinate the emperor invading Provence. They fatally wounded a well-dressed man they mistook for him: it was the poet Garcilaso de la Vega. They surrendered on a promise that their lives would be spared, and were hanged anyway.

An 18th-century oil mill filled with gliders and jeeps: the Musée de la Libération du Muy, next to the Tour Charles Quint, tells the story of the airborne operation of August 15, 1944. Le Muy was one of the first towns liberated in Provence. Free entry, run by volunteers, but open only a few half-days: check the opening hours before you come.

activities.text: If you're there on a Thursday or Sunday, Le Muy's market coincides with the opening of the Tour Charles Quint and the Musée de la Libération. Visit all three in one go, between 9:30am and 12:30pm. The rest of the week, the village is very quiet and the doors are closed.

days_plan.itin_title: Roquebrune-sur-Argens: sea, villages and the Var in 10 days

visits.text: Carrouges Castle in the Perche Regional Natural Park is a national monument. Built from the 14th to 16th centuries, it's surrounded by moats and you access it via a brick-and-stone entrance gatehouse. The interior preserves period furniture and monumental fireplaces. Enjoy the 10-hectare park, freely accessible.

Château du Champ-de-Bataille, near Le Neubourg, is one of Normandy's most fascinating castles. Built in the 17th century, it was restored by a decorator who recreated monumental French formal gardens over 45 hectares. You'll see geometric parterres, ponds and linden alleys that rival Vaux-le-Vicomte. If the grand apartments are open, don't miss them - the painted ceilings and furniture are remarkable.

activities.text: Enjoy the Champ-de-Bataille gardens for a picnic in permitted areas. The estate's scale allows you to settle in peace, away from other visitors. Bring farmhouse cider and raw-milk Camembert - you're in Normandy, might as well make the most of it.

days_plan.itin_title: Complete Normandy Road Trip: Cliffs, D-Day Beaches and Mont-Saint-Michel

visits.text: The Vauban Citadel has dominated Le Palais harbor since 1549. Expanded by Fouquet then fortified by Vauban in 1683, it served as a state prison—political detainees were imprisoned there until the 20th century. The rampart walk offers a complete panorama over the roadstead.
The Aiguilles de Port-Coton, rocky pyramids battered by waves, fascinated a famous Impressionist who painted them 39 times in 1886. Colors change with each hour depending on light and tide.
Pointe des Poulains, at the island's northern tip, takes its name from the “poulains”—rock scree extending beyond it. A 19th-century military fort is accessible at low tide via a tidal causeway.
The Grand Phare, commissioned in 1836, rises 52 meters. Its 247 steps lead to a panoramic view taking in the Côte Sauvage, the mainland, and, on clear days, Noirmoutier island.
Le Palais harbor, protected by two jetties, displays colorful houses facing the boats. Pastel facades - pink, yellow, blue - date from the 19th century when shipowners competed in elegance.
Donnant Beach: wedged between two black schist cliffs, this wild beach receives Atlantic swells head-on. Surfers frequent it; swimmers remain cautious of currents.

activities.text: Explore the Côte Sauvage by bike (rental at the port). The road follows cliffs 30 to 60 meters high, interspersed with inaccessible coves and sea caves.
The coastal path from Port-Coton to Port-Goulphar winds along the cliff edges through heather and gorse heathland. Views of the rock needles and sea caves are spectacular.
Reach Pointe des Poulains at low tide to access the small fort. Be sure to check tide times: the causeway is submerged in 20 minutes as the tide rises.

days_plan.itin_title: Brittany Road Trip: Villages with Character, Sea and History

places.name: Le Poet Laval

visits.text: The 12th-century keep towers over the village with its pale yellow stone walls. The Knights Hospitaller of Saint John of Jerusalem founded a commandery here, one of the most important in Provence.
Step through the gates of the Château des Hospitaliers, restored in 1996 by the Historic Monuments authority. The Renaissance wing adjoining the keep hosts permanent and temporary exhibitions.
The Chapelle Saint-Jean-des-Commandeurs dates from the early 13th century. From rue Neuve, the view of its nave and choir, both still standing, is striking.

Wind through the covered rue de la Chalanque, then the lower rampart street. Vaulted passages, steps with uneven cobbles and terraces follow one another in a labyrinth without cars or street furniture.

The former 17th-century Protestant temple, one of the few preserved in France, houses the Museum of Dauphiné Protestantism. It traces the history of the Reformation, the Wars of Religion and the exile of the Huguenots.
The Yvon Morin Art Center occupies handsome rooms restored using materials salvaged in the village. Each summer it hosts a major exhibition and concerts.

activities.text: Make your way to the Grand Portail, the village's old entrance through a vaulted chicane passage, then climb to the benches facing the Jabron Valley. Panorama over the wooded hills and the lavender fields.

Le Poët-Laval is the starting point of the "On the Huguenot Trail" path, a 1,800-km European route retracing the exile of Dauphiné Protestants to Germany. The first few kilometers cross the surrounding hills.
Curious about local pottery? The town of Dieulefit, a few minutes away, keeps alive an ancient ceramic tradition. The studios open their doors to visitors.

days_plan.itin_title: Rhône-Alpes Circuit: Perched Villages and Mountain Peaks

map_keywords: Musée du Protestantisme Dauphinois Le Poët-Laval
Centre d'Art Yvon Morin Le Poët-Laval

places.name: Le Raincy

visits.text: The Church of Notre-Dame du Raincy, the world's first church built entirely in reinforced concrete, was erected in just thirteen months in 1922–1923. Its bell tower rises to 43 meters. Le Corbusier called it “the Sainte-Chapelle of reinforced concrete.”
Inside, 32 slender columns support barrel vaults. Load-bearing walls are replaced by openwork concrete screens fitted with stained glass, transforming the walls into walls of light.

The stained glass, designed by the Nabi painter and created by a pioneering female master glassmaker, adorns all the walls. Ten large figurative windows illustrate the life of the Virgin and the departure of the Marne taxis for the Battle of the Ourcq in September 1914.
Le Raincy retains beautiful villas from the turn of the 20th century along its tree-lined avenues. Walk down Allée des Tilleuls to admire buhrstone facades and enclosed gardens.
Le Raincy high school occupies a historic property surrounded by a vast park. Its gates and ceremonial courtyard are worth a glance as you pass.

activities.text: Walk to the Allée de Montfermeil, an urban street in Le Raincy. Stroll past the houses and gardens, then return toward the town center along the nearby streets.
Look up at Le Raincy's modern architecture: the town served as an urban planning laboratory with its early-20th-century subdivisions conceived as garden cities.

days_plan.itin_title: Seine-Saint-Denis Tour: Basilica and Urban Culture

map_keywords: Parc du Plateau d'Avron Le Raincy

visits.text: Le Touquet-Paris-Plage owes its nickname as the pearl of the Opal Coast to its Anglo-Norman villas nestled in a century-old pine forest, with turrets, bow windows, and half-timbering. The resort, also dubbed the garden of the Channel, has 12 kilometers of white sand beach. Rent a bike to explore the forest without tiring your legs.

You'll wander through Le Touquet's covered market, listed as a historic monument since 1996, open Thursday and Saturday mornings year-round. Seafood, regional specialties, and a convivial atmosphere mix well, steps from Rue Saint-Jean and its shops. Come early; the best stalls empty quickly in season.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Villages from Flanders to the Bay of Somme

visits.text: Cliffs of Le Tréport — These chalk cliffs rise to 106 meters. The Calvaire des Terrasses offers a panorama over the Bay of the Somme, the slate roofs of the harbor, and the Picardy coast as far as Mers-les-Bains.

Le Tréport Funicular — This funicular inaugurated in 1908, renovated in 2006, climbs the 106 meters of elevation in 47 seconds through a tunnel carved into the cliff. Free to ride, it connects the port to the upper town and the Calvary panorama.

Le Tréport Fishing Port — Leading fishing port for scallops in the Eastern Channel, Le Tréport perpetuates centuries of maritime tradition. Trawlers unload sole, mackerel, and shellfish onto lively quays.

activities.text: Mers-les-Bains — This neighboring seaside resort on the Picardy coast lines 300 Belle Époque villas with polychrome façades listed as historical monuments. Their carved wooden balconies, bay windows, and ceramics form a unique architectural ensemble.
Le Tréport Beach — This pebble beach bordered by cliffs has welcomed Parisians since the railway arrived in 1873. Colorful beach huts and seafood restaurants perpetuate the seaside tradition.

Saint-Jacques Church at Le Tréport — This flamboyant Gothic church from the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries dominates the port with its massive silhouette. Its pendant vault keys and Renaissance porch testify to the port's prosperity in the Middle Ages.

days_plan.itin_title: Seine-Maritime Road Trip: The Cliffs of Étretat, Rouen & Jumièges Abbey

visits.text: The Rochers des Parcs are a well-known climbing site in western France, with routes for all levels. You can explore the site on foot as well as by climbing.

days_plan.itin_title: Cotentin, Pays d'Auge: 5 days exploring the most beautiful villages

visits.text: Lectoure stands on a limestone promontory overlooking the Gers valley. Two miles of ramparts from the 13th to 17th centuries encircle the city, former capital of the Counts of Armagnac. On clear days, the Pyrenees chain cuts across the southern horizon. This part of Lomagne is nicknamed "French Tuscany."

Saint-Gervais-et-Saint-Protais Cathedral, built in the 12th century on the site of a Roman temple dedicated to Cybele, dominates the town with its 150-foot bell tower. The stone spire that once topped it, doubling the current height, was destroyed by a storm on the eve of the Revolution. The interior houses remarkable furnishings.

The Eugène Camoreyt Archaeological Museum, housed in the former bishop's palace—now the town hall—preserves a unique collection of twenty Gallo-Roman taurobolic altars dedicated to Cybele. The Hall of the Illustrious and the pharmacy room complete the visit to this building that also served as Marshal Lannes' residence.

Step through the doors of the Bleu de Lectoure workshops. Pastel, the blue pigment extracted from woad, made Occitanie's fortune in the 15th and 16th centuries. Here, the workshop perpetuates the tradition: dyeing scarves, dresses and cosmetics in that deep blue that once seduced kings and nobles.

The old castle of the Counts of Armagnac, now transformed into a hospital, closes off the western end of town. Opposite, the Gothic Fontaine de Diane supplied the city with water since the Middle Ages. The fountain trail leads from one to another, between stone stairways and hanging gardens.

activities.text: Climb to the cathedral bell tower. The 150 feet offer stunning views of the town, the Gers valley and, on clear days, the Pyrenees chain from Pic du Midi to Canigou. Guided tours available through the tourist office.
Lectoure market on Friday mornings. In the town center lanes, producers sell Lectoure melons, foie gras, local saffron and Lomagne garlic. A must for Gascon flavors and temperaments.

Lectoure thermal spa. Housed in an 18th-century mansion, the thermal center draws its water from more than 3,000 feet deep, at 108°F. Pool at 90°F, jacuzzi, hammam and sauna—accessible for half-day sessions without medical treatment.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Garonne Road Trip: From Toulouse to the Pyrenees
Gers Road Trip: Gascon Bastides, Armagnac & Musketeers

visits.text: The Louvre-Lens is the region's architectural shock. Opened on 4 December 2012 — Saint Barbara's Day, patron saint of miners — on the site of the former Pit 9, it embodies the cultural regeneration of the mining basin. The Japanese firm SANAA (Kazuyo Sejima and Ryue Nishizawa) designed this long box of glass and aluminium that blends into the grey sky. On overcast days, the museum seems to float. It brings together in a single room masterpieces that Paris keeps hidden in storage.

The Gallery of Time is the centrepiece of the Louvre-Lens: 3,000 m² with no partitions at all, where more than 200 Louvre masterpieces are displayed in a chronological journey from the 4th millennium BC to the mid-19th century. Mesopotamia, Egypt, Greece, Rome, the Renaissance, the Baroque — everything flows on without a wall between them, in an open space that invites comparison between civilisations. Allow at least 1.5 hours to appreciate it properly.

The Cité Pavillonnaire No. 9, next to the museum, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2012 as part of the Mining Basin listing. These 19th-century workers' terraces retain their voyettes (small paths between the gardens) and their carins (outbuildings). A guided tour organised from the museum takes you into the heart of this working-class life frozen in time.

The Base 11-19 site in Loos-en-Gohelle preserves the industrial buildings of the pit yard and offers free access all year round. It is one of five mining basin sites listed by UNESCO. A Timescope terminal on the forecourt plunges you into virtual reality in the shoes of a miner. Understated, free and moving.

activities.text: Climb the twin slag heaps of Loos-en-Gohelle — the highest in Europe at 186 metres. They resulted from 10 years of intensive mining between 1960 and 1970 and represent 24 million m³ of extraction waste over 90 hectares. Access is free and the round trip takes about an hour. From the summit, on a clear day, you can see the Stade Bollaert, the Louvre-Lens, the Vimy Memorial, and even the slag heaps of Mont des Flandres. Wear good shoes — the slopes are steep.

Stroll through the landscaped park of the Louvre-Lens: 6,600 trees, 26,000 shrubs, and grass banks that echo the shape of the slag heaps. The old railway paths that once linked the mine pits have become walking trails. An unexpectedly peaceful moment a stone's throw from the museum.

Explore the town centre of Lens, entirely rebuilt after 1918 in a style blending neoclassicism, regionalism and Art Deco. Lens station, built in 1926 by architect Urban Cassan, evokes the silhouette of a steam locomotive. Its interior stained-glass windows by Auguste Labouret pay tribute to the mining heritage — a curiosity not to be missed.

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip Pas-De-Calais: The Opal Coast and Belfries

places.name: Les Andelys

visits.text: Château Gaillard. Richard the Lionheart's proud fortress has dominated one of the Seine's most beautiful loops for 800 years. Built in just two years (1196–1198), this feat of military architecture prompted the King of England to exclaim: 'How beautiful she is, my one-year-old daughter!' The keep offers breathtaking panoramas over the valley and Petit-Andely below. Guided tours available April through November.

Petit-Andely. This medieval village born in the castle's shadow retains its picturesque charm. The 12th-century Saint-Sauveur church and narrow streets lined with old houses invite wandering. Facing the Seine, the quays offer the finest view of the perched fortress.

Notre-Dame Collegiate Church of Grand-Andely. Founded in the 6th century by Queen Clotilde, wife of Clovis, this church blends styles from the 13th to 17th centuries. Its 16th-century Renaissance stained glass windows rank among Normandy's finest. The Sainte-Clotilde fountain, a miraculous spring that appeared during construction, still draws pilgrims.

Nicolas Poussin Museum. Housed in a 17th-century mansion, this museum honors the classical painter born in Les Andelys in 1594. Local history collections, paintings, and art objects trace this strategic city's past.

activities.text: Richard the Lionheart Loop hike. This 8 km walking trail starts from the Seine riverbanks, crosses Petit-Andely, and climbs to the castle via limestone hillsides. The viewpoints over the river's meanders are spectacular, especially at sunset.
Seine river cruise. Cruise ships dock at Les Andelys to admire Château Gaillard from the river. Boat tours reveal this majestic loop from a unique perspective.

days_plan.itin_title: Eure Road Trip: From Giverny to Normandy's Most Beautiful Villages
Complete Normandy Road Trip: Cliffs, D-Day Beaches and Mont-Saint-Michel

map_keywords: Richard the Lionheart loop hiking trail

places.name: Les Arcs Sur Argens

visits.text: Locals call it the Tour Sarrasine; it's actually the keep of the Villeneuve family, Catalan lords who settled in Les Arcs-sur-Argens from the 13th century onward. Standing 19 meters tall, it dominates the village and survived the castle's destruction, ordered by Barras during the Revolution, thanks to his secretary, a native of the village. Climb up along the cobbled lanes: they're steep and paved.

Le Parage is the medieval quarter of Les Arcs-sur-Argens: its name comes from the Occitan paratge, meaning nobility. Four gates punctuate the defensive walls, including the Porte du Miracle des Roses. The clock tower, formerly a 14th-century flanking tower, is topped by a bell frame dating from 1662. The quarter was saved from ruin in the 1960s by a handful of enthusiasts.

It houses a Louis Bréa altarpiece dated 1501: the Saint-Jean-Baptiste church in Les Arcs-sur-Argens replaced the old Parage church in the 19th century. There's also an animated Provençal nativity scene. Visit it on your way down from the upper quarter, so save it for the end of the route.

activities.text: Step inside the Maison des Vins Côtes de Provence in Les Arcs-sur-Argens: several hundred wines gathered in one place, to help you understand the appellation without visiting estate after estate. Taste in moderation, with a designated driver. Rosé is the obvious choice, but ask for the reds: that's where the surprises lie.

If you're traveling with children, the Réal Max Carzoli walk, in Les Arcs-sur-Argens, is less than a kilometer between the stream and the countryside. It's a shaded green corridor, accessible from the center. Perfect for a quiet hour waiting for the afternoon opening of Sainte-Roseline chapel.

days_plan.itin_title: Roquebrune-sur-Argens: sea, villages and the Var in 10 days

map_keywords: Le Parage medieval city Les Arcs

places.name: Les Baux De Provence

visits.text: Les Baux-de-Provence perches at 245 meters on a limestone spur — its name comes from the Provençal "bauç" meaning precipitous place. The first Lord of Les Baux appears in 10th-century chronicles, his family claiming descent from Balthazar, one of the three Magi. At their peak, they ruled over 79 towns and villages of Provence. Their fortress was dismantled by order of Richelieu in 1632 to punish their rebellion. Here in 1821 bauxite (aluminum ore) was discovered, named after the village by geologist Pierre Berthier. Arrive at opening (9 AM) in high season — after 10 AM tour buses arrive.

The Château des Baux-de-Provence spans 5 hectares of ruins. The audio-guided tour (in 10 languages, included in ticket) leads you through the keep, the Sarrazine and Paravelle towers, the castle chapel, and the former Quiqueran hospital. Reconstructed war machines — trebuchet, catapult — feature in summer demonstrations. From the summit, on clear days, the view reaches the sea and Mont Ventoux.

The Carrières de Lumières occupy former limestone quarries where the Alpilles' blonde stone was extracted — the same that built the village, the Arles arena, and Nîmes' Roman amphitheaters. This underground space of 6,000 m² hosts monumental digital projections on the walls (about 45 minutes of show). The temperature remains constant at 14-16°C year-round — bring an extra layer even in summer. Programs change annually.

The medieval streets of the pedestrian village merit slow wandering — restored Renaissance houses, mullioned windows, art galleries. The Saint-Vincent church (12th century) preserves contemporary stained glass offered by the Prince of Monaco in the 1980s. The Val d'Enfer, accessible on foot from the lower village, is a narrow valley with rocks sculpted by erosion — its bizarre shapes inspired medieval legends and served as film locations.

activities.text: Viewpoint over the Arles plain from the château ramparts: on clear days, the Camargue plain spreads to the horizon. It's the panorama that made the site photographically famous — arrive late afternoon for raking light on the Alpilles.

Hiking in the Alpilles from Les Baux: several marked trails start from the parking area (paid parking below the village). The GR6 follows limestone ridges toward Maussane, offering alternating views over the Baux valley and the Camargue plain. Access to the massifs is prohibited by order during high fire risk (particularly July-August).

days_plan.itin_title: Alpilles, Aix-en-Provence & Arles Circuit
The Most Beautiful Villages: From the Alps to the Luberon in 3 Days

map_keywords: Église Saint-Vincent Les Baux XIIe siècle

places.name: Les Epesses

visits.text: Dedicate this day to Puy du Fou, France's second-most visited theme park. The park stages its historical shows in a century-old forest in Les Epesses. Do not miss Le Bal des Oiseaux Fantômes: falcons, vultures, storks and owls—more than 200 birds of prey—fly over the ruins of a medieval castle in a breathtaking display. You will also see Le Signe du Triomphe in a 6,000-seat Roman arena, and Vikings attacking a Frankish village with a 20-meter longship.

On the way to Puy du Fou, stop at Mont des Alouettes in Les Herbiers. Two windmills dominate the ridge overlooking the Vendée bocage. During the Wars of the Vendée, the position of their sails was used to signal the enemy's location to the Royalist armies. In clear weather, there are unobstructed views over the bocage.

Spend a second day at Puy du Fou, devoted to the shows you could not see the previous day and the latest attractions. Le Dernier Panache takes you into a revolving theater where the stage rotates around the audience to tell the story of a naval officer during the Revolution. Le Mime et l'Étoile uses mapping and hologram technology. In the evening, the Renaissance château in the background becomes the setting for the sound-and-light show.

activities.text: Explore Puy du Fou's reconstructed villages: the medieval town with its craftspeople, the 18th-century village and the 1900 town. The craftspeople demonstrate period techniques before your eyes—blacksmithing, pottery and manuscript illumination. Take time to wander between shows, as this is where the park reveals all its charm.

If you are lucky enough to be there on a Friday or Saturday evening from June to September, attend the Cinéscénie. Created in 1978, it is the world's largest nighttime show: 2,550 volunteer actors (the “Puyfolais”), 28,000 costumes and a 1-hour-40-minute performance on a 23-hectare stage, featuring 3D video mapping, drones and pyrotechnic effects. The show traces the history of Vendée through the fate of the Maupillier family, from the Middle Ages to the Second World War. Be sure to book in advance—tickets sell very quickly.

days_plan.itin_title: Vendée Itinerary: Noirmoutier Island, Puy du Fou and the Coastline
Vendée Itinerary: Noirmoutier Island, Puy du Fou and the Coastline

map_keywords: Ghost Birds Ballet, Puy du Fou
The Last Flourish, Puy du Fou

places.name: Les Eyzies

visits.text: The National Museum of Prehistory in Les Eyzies holds more than 18,000 artifacts spanning 400,000 years of human history. Paul Dardé's imposing statue of Primitive Man towers over the entrance, a fitting welcome to the birthplace of paleoanthropology.

Font-de-Gaume Cave is one of the last painted sanctuaries of the Ice Age still open to the public. Discovered in 1901, its galleries shelter approximately 230 polychrome images—bison, horses, mammoths, and reindeer—painted 14,000 years ago. To preserve these fragile masterpieces, visits are strictly limited to 13 people at a time. Book weeks in advance.

Combarelles Cave contains 800 engraved figures etched along 300 meters of narrow galleries. Discovered just three days before Font-de-Gaume in September 1901, it stands out for its 48 human representations—an unusual subject in Ice Age art. The engravings are subtle, rendered in fine lines that emerge slowly from the rock as your eyes adjust.

activities.text: The Vézère Valley concentrates about fifteen UNESCO-listed prehistoric sites within a few kilometers. Beyond the painted caves, you can explore the Pataud Shelter (14 distinct occupation levels), the Cro-Magnon Shelter (where the first anatomically modern humans in Europe were discovered in 1868), and the Cap-Blanc Shelter, famous for its sculpted frieze of life-sized horses.

days_plan.itin_title: Dordogne: Prehistoric Caves, Medieval Fortresses & Périgord Delights

map_keywords: Musée National de Préhistoire Les Eyzies
Statue de l'Homme Primitif Les Eyzies

visits.text: Les Issambres has 8 km of coves and beaches between the Gulf of Saint-Tropez and Fréjus: it's Roquebrune-sur-Argens' window onto the sea. Its heart beats on place San-Peïre, around the port and café terraces. San-Peïre beach and its port have Blue Flag status. Parking is difficult in August: come before 10am or leave the car and take the bus.

In winter, you smell the mimosa in the La Gaillarde valley before you even see it: the flowering trees turn the trail into a yellow avenue above Les Issambres. Below, La Gaillarde beach also has Blue Flag status. There are three routes to choose from depending on your fitness. February is mimosa month, not July.

activities.text: Take the coastal path at Les Issambres: 8 km one way with no elevation gain, following the old customs officers' path from the First Empire. It runs between coves, rocks and umbrella pines, with the Gulf of Saint-Tropez and the Estérel as a backdrop. Check bus schedules for the return, or you'll walk 16 km instead of 8.

The municipal sailing center at Les Issambres remains the simplest way to get out to sea without breaking the bank: courses and rentals, with options for all levels. You can also go diving, water skiing and jet skiing in the bay. Book the day before in summer; morning slots go first.

days_plan.itin_title: Roquebrune-sur-Argens: sea, villages and the Var in 10 days

places.name: Les Riceys

visits.text: The southernmost commune in Champagne, Les Riceys lines up three formerly fortified villages (Ricey-Bas, Ricey-Haute-Rive, Ricey-Haut) strung out over 3 km along the Laignes. A singular feature: each belonged to a different bishopric (Sens, Dijon, Langres), creating rivalry and emulation, hence three listed Renaissance churches. Add two châteaux, six chapels, seven washhouses, an imposing covered market hall and countless white-stone winegrowers' houses, some of them Renaissance.

Les Riceys reigns over 866 hectares of vineyards, the largest vineyard area in Champagne. An absolute achievement: it is France's only commune holding three distinct AOCs (Champagne, Coteaux Champenois, Rosé des Riceys). The latter, a still rosé wine obtained by controlled maceration of Pinot Noir, was Louis XIV's favorite. AOC since 1947, production remains confidential: maximum 50,000 bottles in good years, crafted on the steepest, sunniest slopes by some twenty winemakers jealously guarding this treasure.

activities.text: Marked routes wind between vineyards and forests to reveal the cadoles—dry-stone winegrowers' shelters that bear witness to the ancestral labor carried out on these Kimmeridgian slopes. Three routes cross valleys and paths bordered by low stone walls, with panoramic views over villages and vineyards. Maps are available from the Tourist Office. These authentic Champagne hikes combine vernacular heritage with vineyard landscapes.

In their centuries-old vaulted cellars, the winegrowers of Les Riceys reveal the legendary Rosé des Riceys. Guided tastings explain the famous Riceys flavor—a distinctive combination of red fruit, dried fruit and spice aromas—for which only a native winegrower can identify the exact moment to stop the maceration. This legendary wine, aged for 3 to 10 years, accompanies foie gras, red meat and mature cheeses. Champagnes and Coteaux Champenois complete the selection. Reservations are recommended.

days_plan.itin_title: Aube Tour: Champagne, Medieval Heritage and the Lakes of the Forêt d'Orient

map_keywords: Rosé des Riceys wine tasting cellars

visits.text: Les Salles-sur-Verdon is no ordinary village. The old village was pulled down house by house from 1973 to make way for Lake Sainte-Croix—the church itself was dynamited on March 5, 1974, at 4:45 PM, and the last inhabitants were forcibly evacuated by the gendarmerie a few days earlier. The new village, rebuilt on the Bocouenne plateau from 1970, carries the memory of that sacrifice in every stone: the fountain and washhouse in the center come from the submerged village, and the church bells were saved from the water. Follow the ten-stage historical trail—the panels put up by the association “Mémoire des Salles sur Verdon” recall the vanished buildings with unsettling precision.

The permanent exhibition at the Tourist Office recounts the dam's construction and the story of the submersion. Testimonies from former inhabitants are preserved here—if you're lucky, you might meet one of them still living in the village, since direct descendants of the expelled families still live here. The lake itself, France's fourth-largest reservoir at 2,200 hectares, filled the valley over a year between 1973 and 1974, extending from the 95-meter-high double-curvature arch dam.

Head down to the lakeshore to admire Costebelle Island, a small wild island facing the village that you can reach by swimming or pedal boat. In summer, the lake welcomes up to 40,000 tourists per day along its shores—but in spring and September, you'll find rare tranquility here, with the Verdon's turquoise waters in all their splendor.

activities.text: Take the Toine Nature Trail — an easy 14-station loop through the Provençal garrigue that follows the lakeshore for part of the route. Interpretive panels guide you through the local flora: kermes oaks, rock roses, rosemary, and lavender that perfume the air from spring onwards. Allow 1.5 to 2 hours depending on your pace.

Local providers offer pedal boats, paddleboards, and electric boats from the village's water sports center. Plan to book ahead in July-August — slots fill up fast. Since motorized boats with combustion engines are banned across the entire lake, the atmosphere remains remarkably peaceful.
Thursday mornings, the Provençal market sets up in the main square. Honey, cheeses, marinated olives, lavender from the nearby Valensole plateau — a delicious stop before hitting the road.

days_plan.itin_title: Lake Sainte-Croix and Verdon Circuit

visits.text: The Franciscan friary of Les Thons is a treasure that nobody knows about—and that's exactly what makes it so precious. Founded in 1452 by Guillaume de Saint-Loup and his wife Jeanne de Choiseul with the support of John II, Duke of Lorraine, it is today the best-preserved Franciscan complex in all of northeastern France. The central part houses a restaurant serving farmhouse cooking and a museum where you can see a reconstructed friar's cell, a prison established by order of King Louis XV, the cloister, the Saint-François fountain and the refectories. The friary church (consecrated in 1483), a masterpiece of late Gothic, is undergoing restoration thanks in part to the Loto du Patrimoine—work is progressing, so check access before arriving.

activities.text: The friary restaurant serves farmhouse cooking in a large Louis XIII fireplace—if you arrive at lunchtime, it's a stop you won't regret. After the meal, stroll between Petit-Thon and Grand-Thon, the two hamlets that make up the commune. This landscape of hedged farmland in the southwestern Vosges, silent and intact, has a rare charm.

days_plan.itin_title: Vosges Abbey Trail: Monastic Heritage

visits.text: The stone houses of Les Vans rise in tiers at the foot of the first Cévennes foothills. Place du Marché buzzes with Provençal life every Saturday morning. The authentic market town retains its mountain character with cool lanes and singing fountains.

activities.text: The colorful market brings Les Vans to life every Saturday morning year-round. Local producers, Cévennes market gardeners, and artisans offer chestnuts, goat cheeses, lavender honey, and mountain specialties.

days_plan.itin_title: Ardèche Road Trip: Wild Gorges and Villages with Character

places.name: Leucate

visits.text: The limestone cliffs of Cap Leucate plunge 40 to 51 meters straight into the Mediterranean — the town's name reportedly comes from the Greek leukos (white) for the rock's whiteness. The Sentier du Guetteur (4.3 km round trip) runs along the plateau edge between the lighthouse, semaphore and cliff to La Franqui. On clear days you'll glimpse the Canigou at 2,784 meters and the entire Pyrenees range. Morning light is best for photographs.

The Plage des Coussoules at La Franqui stretches 8 km, classified Natura 2000, wild and battered by the tramontane — a wind that blows here about 300 days a year. It's one reason Leucate has become Europe's kitesurfing and windsurfing mecca. Every spring, the Mondial du Vent has gathered the international elite here since 1996. Outside competitions, it's one of the most unspoiled and spacious beaches on the Aude coast.

The Leucate lagoon spans 5,400 hectares between sea and maritime Corbières. Its 280 bird species (89 protected) make it a major ornithological site — pink flamingos, egrets and terns appear seasonally. On the Grau, colorful oyster farmers' huts offer their oysters waterside.

The village of Leucate just above its cliff has all the hallmarks of an ideal Mediterranean village: shaded square, colorful lanes, castle ruins. Climb to the ruins for sunset over the lagoon — the golden light on the water and salt marshes is one of the coast's finest spectacles.

activities.text: Leucate is the best kitesurfing and windsurfing spot on the French Mediterranean coast. Local operators offer beginner courses on the lagoon (flat water, ideal for learning) and more committed sessions on the sea side. Book ahead in high season.

visits.text: Levens sits perched at 600 m altitude between the Var and Vésubie valleys, on the old road linking Nice to Lantosque. The village has kept its steep lanes and golden stone houses stacked in an amphitheatre.

The Masséna family house, on Rue Masséna, is the former residence where the future Marshal of the Empire grew up with his grandmother after his father's death. A plaque marks it, but note—Masséna was born in Nice in 1758, not here. The house dates from 1722.
The Saint-Antonin church, in the village heart, is a fine example of Niçoise baroque with its gilded altarpieces and hushed atmosphere. You'll encounter few others inside.
The Place de la République retains its fountain and plane trees. It's the spot to pause five minutes before heading to the village heights for views over the Nice coastline and Bay of Angels.

activities.text: The Férion trail climbs to 1412 m for an exceptional viewpoint over the coast and Pre-Alps. Budget 4h round trip and 800 m elevation gain—a proper half-day hike.
The Grand Pré, a 13-hectare municipal leisure park with summer pool and playgrounds, is handy if you're travelling with family. Note the pool only opens July-August.
Sunday morning market on the square sells mountain honey, cheeses and olives. Handy for picnic supplies before heading to Lantosque.
Try raviolis à la daube in a village inn. It's the local speciality, inherited from the County and far heartier than the seaside Nice versions.

days_plan.itin_title: Secret valleys of the Nice hinterland in 6 days

visits.text: Rouen to Lille: direct TER from Rouen Rive-Droite to Lille-Flandres (6 departures per day), 2h38–3h, from €30. Alternative with one change at Amiens (TER, 3h30, €35–55). Faster via Paris: TGV Rouen–Paris Saint-Lazare 1h15 + metro across to Gare du Nord + TGV Paris–Lille 1h, total 3 hours including the Paris crossing, €70–100. Hotel near the Grand'Place or in Vieux Lille. Lille is the capital of the Hauts-de-France region, 230,000 inhabitants, right on the Belgian border — warm, carnival-spirited Northern atmosphere.

The Grand'Place (officially Place du Général-de-Gaulle, but nobody calls it that). The Colonne de la Déesse (1845), commemorating Lille's successful resistance to the Austrian siege of 1792. Flemish façades from the 17th and 18th centuries in red brick and white stone with scroll gables. La Voix du Nord (the regional newspaper) occupying a 1936 Art Deco building. Christmas market in December — among the finest in France.

The Vieille Bourse, an architectural gem. Built 1652–1653 during the Spanish era (Lille was Spanish until 1667, when Louis XIV annexed it). A masterpiece of Flemish architecture — 24 houses arranged as a quadrilateral around an inner courtyard. A sculpted façade: caryatids, garlands, grotesque masks, coats of arms. Second-hand booksellers fill the courtyard every afternoon (except Mondays). Chess and draughts players. Listed monument. Free.

Vieux Lille — the quarter that escaped Haussmannian planning, entirely pedestrianised. Cobbled lanes, brick-and-stone façades, 17th-century Flemish mansions. Rue de la Monnaie, Rue Esquermoise, Rue Basse. Designer boutiques, concept stores, chocolate shops (Meert, since 1761 — a Lille institution, serving a waffle filled with Madagascar vanilla favoured by De Gaulle). Notre-Dame-de-la-Treille Cathedral with its contemporary translucent marble façade (2000).

The Opéra de Lille (1913, monumental neo-classical) and the Chamber of Commerce with its 76-metre belfry flank Place du Théâtre. The Beffroi de l'Hôtel de Ville (1929–1932): France's tallest belfry at 104 metres, UNESCO since 2005 as part of the Belfries of Belgium and France. Lift then 100 steps (€7) for a 360° panorama over Lille, the Flemish plain and — on a clear day — Belgium. The legendary giant figures Lydéric and Phinaert carved into the belfry.

Palais des Beaux-Arts, Place de la République. The second-largest museum in France after the Louvre, inaugurated in 1892. A monumental neo-Renaissance building. Five centuries of collections: Donatello, Raphael, Rubens (Descent from the Cross), Van Dyck, Goya, David, Courbet, Monet, Renoir, Degas, Toulouse-Lautrec, Picasso. Basement: relief maps — 15 military scale models of French fortified towns commissioned by Louis XIV in the 17th century to plan sieges. €7, closed Tuesdays. Allow 2 hours.

Sunday morning (or Wednesday/Friday/Saturday): the Wazemmes market — Lille's largest and most popular, an emblem of the cosmopolitan city. Covered 1869 market hall plus outdoor stalls. Three hundred vendors, produce from around the world. Music, florists, cheesemongers, rotisserie, Maghrebi, Italian and Portuguese specialities. Roast chicken with chips to take away, €9, a local institution. 7am–2pm. Metro Gambetta.

Afternoon in Roubaix for La Piscine — one of the most memorable visits in France. Art and industry museum installed in a 1932 Art Deco municipal swimming pool, converted into a museum in 2001. The main pool with its original mosaics, zenithal lighting and a sunset stained-glass window serves as the main gallery — sculptures facing one another in the still, reflecting water. Paintings, sculptures and textiles (Roubaix was France's textile capital). Metro Gare Jean-Lebas then 10 minutes. €11, closed Mondays.

The Vauban Citadel, a masterpiece of the great military architect. Built 1667–1670 after Louis XIV's annexation of Lille. Known as the Queen of Citadels for its perfect pentagonal shape with five bastions, it is still operational as a military barracks. The surrounding 70-hectare park is free and popular with Lille joggers. The Lille Zoo is inside (free, 70 species).

The birthplace of Charles de Gaulle (9 Rue Princesse, Vieux Lille) — a museum in the house where the General was born on 22 November 1890. A late-19th-century bourgeois home, restored and furnished as it was. A biographical trail, 1,500 personal objects. €7, closed Mondays and Tuesdays. Worth visiting even for non-Gaullists, for the atmosphere of a Flemish Catholic bourgeois childhood.

activities.text: Dinner. Estaminet Chez la Vieille (Rue de Gand): carbonade flamande (beef stewed in beer), waterzooi, potjevleesch (a 3-to-5-meat terrine in aspic), moules-frites in season. La Chicorée (26 Rue de Béthune), open 24 hours, cult address. €25–40. Local beers: Goudale, Jenlain amber, Ch'ti blonde. Meert waffle for dessert.

Rue Royale, Rue de la Barre, Place Louise-de-Bettignies for bars and cocktails. Le Barbue d'Anvers, an estaminet and live-music bar on Rue Saint-Étienne. Festive: Rue Solférino and Rue Masséna for students — Lille has 120,000 of them. First weekend of September: the Braderie de Lille, Europe's largest flea market since 1127, two million visitors, 10,000 sellers spread across 100 km of pavements.

Last dinner of the tour. Bloempot by Florent Ladeyn (Rue des Bouchers): a bistronomic table that is resolutely locavore, a single set menu at €48, 100% regional produce. Or T-Rex Café (Rue Saint-André) for a Northern burger and craft beer. Welsh rarebit is unmissable (bread, melted Cheddar, beer, fried egg) — caloric but iconic. Genièvre as digestif (a Flemish juniper berry spirit, 40%).

Last night of the grand tour. A drink in a rooftop bar or a signature cocktail. Le Comptoir Volant (Rue Esquermoise), creative cocktails in a cosy room. Open Gallery (Place du Lion d'Or) for something trendier. Or go back to the hotel and get ready for tomorrow's return to Paris — 1 hour on the TGV, arriving at Gare du Nord in the morning.

visits.text: The Musée national Adrien Dubouché showcases 5,000 ceramic pieces from a reserve collection of 18,000. The circular route spans antiquity to contemporary porcelain, centered around the world's richest Limoges collection.

Step through the doors of Gare des Bénédictins, a classified Historic Monument. Built between 1924 and 1929, it blends Art Nouveau, Art Deco, and Neoclassical styles. Its campanile rises 61 meters high, while the copper dome crowns a hall bathed in light from Francis Chigot's stained glass depicting Limousin chestnut trees and foliage.

The Four des Casseaux, a classified Historic Monument, is a former porcelain kiln built in 1900. It bears witness to the titanic work of porcelain workers during 19th-century firings and hosts temporary exhibitions of contemporary ceramics.

Walk down to Cathédrale Saint-Étienne, the only monument in Limousin with a uniform Gothic style. Construction stretched from 1273 to 1888. Admire the Flamboyant Gothic Saint-Jean portal, the Renaissance rood screen commissioned in 1533, and the three sculpted tombs in the ambulatory.

The Jardins de l'Évêché are laid out on terraces at the foot of the cathedral, with views down over the Vienne. The botanical garden brings together medicinal plants and poisonous species. The Musée des Beaux-Arts, housed in the former 18th-century episcopal palace, holds a remarkable collection of medieval enamels.
Cross the Pont Saint-Étienne, built around 1210 over the Vienne. Its medieval arches link the Cité quarter to the left bank and offer one of the finest views of the cathedral.

Visit the workshops of a porcelain factory for an immersive guided tour. From raw material to finished product, you'll follow the manufacturing stages: modeling, slip casting, glazing, and high-temperature firing. Artisans work before your eyes.

The Église Saint-Michel-des-Lions, built between the 14th and 16th centuries, takes its name from two granite lions flanking its portal. It preserves the relics of Saint Martial and Saint Valérie, displayed during the septennial Ostensions.
The Église Saint-Pierre-du-Queyroix features a typically Limousin bell tower and beautiful stained glass. Its late Gothic atmosphere contrasts with the dark granite facade.

Head to the Cour du Temple, an elegant 17th-century Renaissance courtyard tucked between Rue du Temple and Rue du Consulat. Its arcades and terraces create an unexpected setting in the heart of downtown.
The Pavillon du Verdurier, an octagonal Art Deco building designed by the railway station's architect, is adorned with porcelain and enamel tiles. It regularly hosts exhibitions.

activities.text: Wander through the Quartier de la Boucherie, Limoges' most picturesque neighborhood: half-timbered houses, narrow lanes, and the 15th-century Chapelle Saint-Aurélien, owned by the butchers' brotherhood. The Maison traditionnelle de la Boucherie traces the techniques and tools of this guild, which was active in the Middle Ages.

Beneath Place de la République, the Crypte Saint-Martial preserves vestiges of the Benedictine abbey founded in the 9th century. This medieval scriptorium spread the art of illumination and polyphonic music — the word 'troubadour' was born here, from the 'tropes' composed by monks.
Head back up to Place de la Motte at the end of the day to enjoy the terraces and illuminated half-timbered facades. The atmosphere is lively in the evenings.
The Halles centrales de Limoges are a gathering place for food lovers. Fine-grained Limousin meat, farmhouse cheeses, chestnuts, and clafoutis: taste the spirit of Limousin among the market stalls.
Try your hand at modeling or painting on porcelain in a workshop. Beginners welcome — you'll leave with your own creation.
Stroll along the Vienne riverbanks in late afternoon for a peaceful walk between medieval bridges. Limoges boasts 52 m² of green space per inhabitant: nature is never far away.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Vienne Tour: Limoges, Porcelain and Villages
Haute-Vienne Tour: Limoges, Porcelain and Villages
Haute-Vienne Road Trip: Castles and Périgord-Limousin

visits.text: Place de la République in Limoux hosts the world's longest carnival: from January to March, every Saturday and Sunday, the costumed bands of "Fécos" parade three times daily (11am, 4:30pm, 10pm) under the medieval arcades. Each band represents a neighborhood of the town. The ritual concludes each year with the "Nuit de la Blanquette" and the burning of His Majesty Carnival on Place de la République. If you're not there in season, stroll under the arcades and seek out the medieval Pont Vieux over the Aude.

Blanquette de Limoux is the oldest sparkling wine in the world: in 1531 a monk at the Benedictine abbey of Saint-Hilaire discovered by chance that wine bottled and sealed with cork formed bubbles, a century before champagne was invented. The abbey of Saint-Hilaire, whose origins go back to the 9th century, also holds a marble reliquary sarcophagus attributed to the mysterious Master of Cabestany, one of the great anonymous Romanesque sculptors of the 12th century, whose works are scattered across Languedoc and Catalonia. Cellars in Limoux and estates in the area offer tours and tastings.

Make the 3 km detour to the sanctuary of Notre-Dame de Marceille. This 14th-century Gothic church houses a Black Virgin venerated since the Middle Ages and a spring pilgrims consider miraculous. From the esplanade, the view of the Pyrenees in clear weather ranks among the region's finest.

activities.text: At a cellar in the Limoux area, a guided tour takes you down into underground galleries to see manual riddling, disgorgement and corking — the traditional method inherited from the monks of Saint-Hilaire. The final tasting includes Blanquette méthode ancestrale (100% Mauzac, under 7° alcohol) and Crémant de Limoux. Allow 1 hour.

If you're in Limoux between January and March, the carnival is free and open to all. Three daily outings on Saturdays and Sundays — the evening session (10pm) is the liveliest and most authentic. The masked "Goudils" dance from café to café offering wine to spectators.

days_plan.itin_title: Aude Road Trip: Carcassonne, Cathar Country & the Mediterranean

visits.text: Porte Haute, flanked by two towers, guards the medieval town entrance. It ranks among the finest examples of fortified gates in Meurthe-et-Moselle.
The 12th-century Collégiale Saint-Pierre features a Romanesque tower topped with a modern bell tower. The organ, restored in 1999, dates from 1847.
Château Corbin was built on the ramparts between two towers. Its park offers views over the Moselle loop and now houses a media library.
Place de la Fontaine reveals 16th-century arcades. The Renaissance facades testify to the architectural wealth of this summer residence of the Bishops of Toul.
The 18th-century presbytery houses the tourist office. From its windows, views extend over the Moselle loop.

activities.text: Head to the viewpoints over the Moselle loop from Porte Haute or Château Corbin park. The Moselle draws a spectacular meander around the promontory.
Explore the medieval town's cobbled lanes. Corner statuettes served as landmarks for visitors.

days_plan.itin_title: Meurthe-et-Moselle Road Trip: Art Nouveau Nancy & Fortified Cities

places.name: Livry Gargan

visits.text: La Poudrerie forest park covers 137 hectares. Established by decree of Napoléon III in 1865, the national gunpowder works produced gunpowder for civilian and military use for a century. Around thirty brick and stone buildings remain among the century-old oaks.

The Technical Museum of Gunpowder and Armament traces the history of this pioneering factory. The first steam-powered gunpowder plant, it employed up to 3,300 workers during World War I, producing 28 tonnes of powder daily.
The entrance pavilions of the Cour d'honneur, built in 1884, mark the threshold of the estate. Their brickwork with stone quoins is characteristic of 19th-century state factories.
The Canal de l'Ourcq runs through the park and divides it into two worlds: the woodland side with the Bois des Sablons, and the leisure side with ponds, an educational farm, and playgrounds.
In La Poudrerie forest park, observe the ponds from paths open to the public and look at the vegetation along their banks. Stay on the marked paths: the Bois de la Tussion is closed to the public.

activities.text: Take the park's marked trails for a hike among giant sequoias, sessile oaks, and century-old chestnut trees. Clearings left by demolished buildings are home to butterflies and rare insects.
In fine weather, a water sports center offers introductory canoeing sessions on the Ourcq canal in a wooded, quiet setting. Paddle in the shade of century-old trees.
Join free events organized year-round by the park's eco-rangers: birdwatching, nocturnal outings in search of amphibians, nature workshops for families.

visits.text: The royal citadel of Loches, one of France's finest medieval fortresses. Built on a rocky spur overlooking the Indre valley, it unfurls over a mile of ramparts protecting both keep and royal lodgings. Five centuries of construction, from the 11th to 16th century, can be read in its stones.

The keep of Loches, 120 feet high, built by Foulques Nerra starting in 1013. A masterpiece of Romanesque military architecture, it's one of the best-preserved in Europe. Transformed into a state prison by Louis XI, it still bears graffiti and frescoes painted by prisoners—including Ludovico Sforza, Duke of Milan.

The royal lodgings welcomed Joan of Arc on May 23, 1429, after the victory at Orléans, when she convinced Charles VII to proceed to Reims for his coronation. The king installed his mistress Agnès Sorel here in the 1440s. Anne of Brittany's oratory, in Flamboyant Gothic style, is the jewel of the wing added by Charles VIII and Louis XII.

The collegiate church of Saint-Ours, between keep and lodgings, presents a profile unique in France: its nave is topped by two octagonal pyramids called "dubes." The polychrome portal is one of the finest Romanesque testimonies in the Loire Valley. Inside, the alabaster tomb of Agnès Sorel watches over the "lady of beauty" for eternity.

Descend into Loches' lower town through winding medieval lanes. Half-timbered houses, Renaissance mansions, and hanging gardens compose a historic town scenery. The Cordeliers Gate and Saint-Antoine Tower punctuate the promenade.

activities.text: Interactive scenographic tour of the royal citadel. Tactile model, projections, video animations and sound markers immerse you in the monument's great moments. At the keep, the Histopad offers an augmented reality visit.

Stroll in the royal citadel's medieval gardens. At the base of the thousand-year-old keep, a "hortus deliciarum" inspired by medieval illuminations offers a peaceful haven with aromatic, medicinal and heirloom plants.

Walk along the Indre from Loches. The verdant, peaceful valley offers waterside trails with views of the perched citadel's silhouette. The abbey church of Beaulieu-lès-Loches, visible from the lodgings terrace, merits a detour.

visits.text: The Grand Menhir Brisé lies in four pieces on the ground. At 21 meters long and 280 tonnes, it was the largest monolith ever erected in Europe. Transported 10 km from a gneiss deposit, it was raised around 4500 BC.

The Table des Marchands, a 30-meter-long cairn, houses a dolmen whose capstone bears a spectacular carving: a crook or hafted axe symbol. This fragment fits with another found at Gavrinis, 4 km away by sea.

The Er Grah tumulus, 140 meters long, is one of the largest funerary monuments of the European Neolithic. Built in several phases between 4600 and 3900 BC, it contained cist burials accompanied by polished axes.

The Dolmen des Pierres Plates stretches 24 meters along the seaside. Its L-shaped angled corridor is covered with Neolithic carvings: axes, crooks, shield-shaped idols. One wall bears a stylized face nicknamed the 'Mother Goddess.'

The port of Locmariaquer faces the entrance to the Gulf of Morbihan. The tidal current reaches 9 knots—one of the strongest in Europe. Oyster beds form a grid across the foreshore as far as the eye can see.
The Notre-Dame-de-Kerdro church, from the 11th century, preserves Romanesque elements. On the square, a 16th-century cemetery cross bears sculptures of the Virgin and Christ.

activities.text: Visit the megalithic complex (Grand Menhir, Table des Marchands, Er Grah) in one go. The interpretation center at the site entrance explains megalith transport and erection techniques with models and films.
Follow the coastal path (GR34) to Pointe de Kerpenhir, facing Port-Navalo. The view takes in the entrance to the Gulf of Morbihan, Gavrinis island, and the Rhuys peninsula.

Embark on the crossing to Gavrinis island (15 min). The Neolithic cairn houses the most beautiful known megalithic carvings: 23 of 29 slabs are entirely sculpted with spiral motifs, chevrons, and arches.

days_plan.itin_title: Brittany Road Trip: Villages with Character, Sea and History

visits.text: Village of Locronan, Small City of Character ranked among France's Most Beautiful Villages. The central square paved with granite is encircled by remarkably preserved 15th and 17th-century Renaissance dwellings. Pale stone façades testify to prosperity brought by sail canvas trade. The absence of electric wires and ban on automobile traffic freeze the town in a medieval atmosphere. Artisans perpetuate traditional crafts in their workshops.

Saint-Ronan Church, a 15th-century Gothic sanctuary dedicated to the Irish patron saint who founded Locronan. The stone pulpit carved in granite displays remarkable statuary of apostles and evangelists. Saint Ronan's tomb has attracted pilgrims for centuries during the Grande Troménie. Jean-Pierre Le Bihan's contemporary stained glass windows flood the nave with colored light. The adjoining Pénity chapel houses a gilded baroque altarpiece.

Locronan Mountain, a 289-meter-high sacred hill dominating Douarnenez Bay. The Petite Troménie trail winds through moorland and woods following the steps of the millennial pilgrimage. Twelve stations marked by oratories punctuate the 6-kilometer route. From the summit, the panorama embraces the ocean, Monts d'Arrée, and Menez-Hom. The site has held spiritual significance since Celtic times, later Christianized by Saint Ronan.

Arts and crafts workshops and galleries scattered through the village lanes. Glassmakers, potters, sculptors, weavers, and jewelers perpetuate ancestral techniques in their shops. Demonstrations allow observing precise glassblowing or weaving gestures. Boutiques offer unique pieces inspired by Breton heritage: decorated ceramics, traditional pattern fabrics, granite sculptures. The medieval atmosphere inspires numerous filmmakers for their shoots.

activities.text: Hiking the Petite Troménie circuit, a 6-kilometer pilgrimage performed annually in July. The marked trail crosses century-old beech woods, heather moorlands, and granite chaos. The twelve stations correspond to stages in hermit Saint Ronan's life. The sunken path bordered by dry stone walls reveals rural landscapes and panoramic views. The location's spiritual dimension transcends beliefs creating an atmosphere of serenity.

Tasting Breton specialties in the village's authentic crêperies. Buckwheat galettes garnished with local products—Guéméné andouille sausage, goat cheese, free-range eggs—are savored in rooms with exposed beams. Wheat crêpes topped with salted butter caramel or flambéed with lambig liqueur prolong the feast. Farmhouse cider traditionally accompanies these simple, flavorful dishes. The convivial atmosphere of wooden tables invites sharing.

Visiting the Grande Troménie during holy years, a monumental 12-kilometer pilgrimage performed every six years. Over 10,000 participants in traditional costumes follow the ancestral route punctuated by Breton hymns and parish banner processions. The cortège crosses villages, chapels, and sacred fountains in impressive collective fervor. The next edition will occur in 2025 perpetuating this millennial tradition inscribed on intangible heritage lists.
