visits.text: Lodève is a city of art and history nestled at the foot of the Larzac plateau. Its medieval center preserves beautiful old houses, cobbled lanes, and shaded squares. The city was the seat of a bishopric until the Revolution and an important cloth-making center. The atmosphere is peaceful with cafés on squares, lively Saturday market, and local shops. Lodève is also the gateway to the Haut-Languedoc Regional Natural Park and the Salagou-Mourèze Grand Site. It's an ideal base for exploring the Hérault hinterland.

Saint-Fulcran Cathedral dominates Lodève with its two massive towers and fortifications. Built in the 13th-15th centuries, it testifies to the bishopric's power. The southern Gothic architecture is austere outside, brighter inside. Modern stained glass contrasts with stone walls. The adjoining cloister has preserved Romanesque elements. 12th-century sculptures adorn the portal. The cathedral is freely accessible. The 18th-century organ is remarkable.

The Museum of Lodève, housed in an 18th-century private mansion (Hôtel de Fleury), is a museographic gem. Permanent collections present the region's exceptional geology and paleontology: fossils, Permian animal prints, minerals. A section is dedicated to sculptor Paul Dardé, a local son whose works are in the Musée d'Orsay. High-quality temporary exhibitions attract national audiences. The museum is playful and accessible to families. Allow 2 hours for the complete visit.

Former cloth factories testify to Lodève's industrial past. The city was an important wool cloth production center from the Middle Ages to the 20th century, notably supplying the army. Some industrial buildings survive, transformed into housing or public facilities. Industrial heritage can be discovered on walks through former working-class neighborhoods. This activity's history is recounted at the Museum of Lodève. The city successfully reconverted after factories closed in the 1960s.

activities.text: Lodève market takes place every Saturday morning in the covered market and city center squares. It's a lively, authentic market with local producers, market gardeners, cheese makers, and charcutiers. You'll find seasonal fruits and vegetables, goat and sheep cheeses from Larzac, honey, olives, wines. The atmosphere is friendly and typically southern. Lodève residents do their weekly shopping here. It's the best time to discover local life. Some stalls offer prepared dishes to eat on-site.

Discover the Terres d'Hérault Geopark, with Lodève as its gateway. This 2,000 km² territory presents exceptional geological heritage with rocks of all ages and remarkable fossils. The Geopark is seeking UNESCO recognition. Several major geological sites are accessible: La Lieude slab with 951 Permian animal prints, quarries, cliffs. The Museum of Lodève is the starting point for understanding this richness. Discovery circuits are offered. It's a unique destination for geology enthusiasts.

Excursion to Lake Salagou, 10 km from Lodève. This reservoir created in 1969 covers 750 hectares amid spectacular scenery. The red soils, known as ruffes, contrast with the blue waters of the lake. The site is classified a Grand Site de France. You can go round it by car (a 25 km loop), by bike or on foot. Several beaches allow swimming. Water sports are plentiful: sailing, paddleboarding, canoeing. It is a must-see in the Hérault.

Hike to the Cirque de Mourèze from Lake Salagou (about 15 km from the base town, around 15 minutes by car). This dolomitic chaos of 340 hectares dates back 160 million years. The eroded limestone rocks form chimneys and natural sculptures with strange shapes. The lunar landscape fascinates visitors. The main path crosses the cirque in 1 hour. For the sportier, the climb up Mont Liausson (2 hours there and back) offers an exceptional view over the cirque on one side and the lake on the other. Significant height gain at the end of the climb. No shade, avoid summer. Paid parking, but the ticket can be reused all year.

days_plan.itin_title: Hérault Road Trip: Montpellier, Beaches and the Hinterland

visits.text: Vauban's fortifications have formed a star on the plateau since 1679. Longwy ranks among the nine new towns built ex nihilo by King Louis XIV's engineer.
Porte de France resembles a triumphal arch. Vauban gave this monumental entrance the prestige worthy of the Sun King.
The Siege Well and cross-shaped casemate complete the stronghold's equipment. The military bakery and powder magazine served the garrison's needs.
The Musée des Émaux et Faïences occupies the former military bakery. Faience produced since 1798 and cloisonné enamels appearing in the 1870s illustrate this unique craft.
The enamels with their distinctive blue acquired worldwide renown. The collections present tableware, vases, and sculptures from the 19th and 20th centuries.

activities.text: Walk the UNESCO ramparts to discover Église Saint-Dagobert and the town hall. The promenade offers views over bastions and curtain walls.
The manufactories perpetuate the craft of outlined enamels. Some workshops open by reservation to discover the production stages.

days_plan.itin_title: Meurthe-et-Moselle Road Trip: Art Nouveau Nancy & Fortified Cities

visits.text: Prepare to be impressed: the Keroman submarine base sprawls across 26 hectares on the peninsula of the same name. Built between 1941 and 1944 by the Organisation Todt, it's the largest submarine base Nazi Germany built outside its own territory. Three concrete blocks (K1, K2, K3) bear roofs 3.5 to 7.5 metres thick—they withstood the most powerful bombing of the era. This base is why the Allies razed Lorient in 1943.

The Flore-S645 submarine, a Daphné-class boat, is moored at the quay at Lorient La Base. Slip through the narrow passageways, the engine room and the command post—you'll quickly grasp the confined life of submariners. The museum space beforehand explains how diesel-electric submarines work and retraces the Battle of the Atlantic. It's one of four submarines open to visitors in France.

Éric Tabarly's Sailing City opened in 2008 in a building by architect Jacques Ferrier. It's Europe's only venue entirely dedicated to offshore racing. Navigation simulator, 4D cinema, interactive displays—the visit is dynamic and engages both adults and children. The Pen Duick yachts (I through VI) are displayed on the quays outside. Budget 2–3 hours to see everything.

Stroll the pontoons of the offshore racing hub. The 32-metre Ultim trimarans and the Vendée Globe IMOCAs are moored here between races. Lorient has been the 'Sailing Valley' of French sailing since the 2000s—the leading skippers have their technical bases here. You might come across them preparing their boats.

If time allows, cross the roadstead to Port-Louis and the Company of Indies Museum, housed in the citadel. Lorient in fact owes its name to this company—'L'Orient' was the ship of that name under construction here in 1666. The museum displays Chinese porcelain, spices and objects brought back by the ships in the 17th and 18th centuries. The citadel itself, built by the Spanish then strengthened by Vauban, is worth the detour.

activities.text: Join a guided tour of Block K3, the most impressive of the three bunkers. A guide takes you into the submarine pens, the slipway (the ramp for putting submarines into the water) and the technical installations. The crushing scale of the concrete and the stories told there give you goosebumps.

Settle on a terrace at La Base for a break facing the moorings. You'll have views of racing yachts, converted bunkers and busy harbour life. Crepes, seafood or cocktails—the spot buzzes with energy, especially late afternoon.

Keroman fishing harbour ranks among France's busiest. If you're an early riser, visit the auction between 6am and 10am to watch fish move from sea to market. Organised tours explain how this modern port operates.

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip Morbihan: Gulf, Carnac and Breton Coast

visits.text: The Tour Carrée towers over Loudun, with 156 steps leading to the top. Built between 1162 and 1185 under Henry II Plantagenet, it's the sole remnant of the fortress dismantled by Louis XIII to suppress the Protestants. The panorama sweeps across the city and the crossroads of Anjou, Touraine, and Poitou.

Sainte-Croix Collegiate Church, an 11th-century Romanesque building, was the setting for exorcism sessions during the trial of Urbain Grandier in 1634. Accused of witchcraft by the Ursuline nuns, the priest was tortured and then burned alive. The interior preserves painted decorations from the 12th and 14th centuries, restored in 1995.
The Porte du Martray, sole survivor of the four gates in the fortified enclosure designed by Philip Augustus in the 14th century, opens onto one of Loudun's oldest quarters.

The Renaudot Museum occupies the birthplace of Théophraste Renaudot, physician to Louis XIII and founder of La Gazette de France in 1631. You'll discover a reconstructed print shop, a period herbalist's, and the library with original issues of the Gazette.
The Charbonneau-Lassay Museum houses eclectic collections bequeathed by the local scholar: archaeological objects, antique books, swords, and artifacts from the Loudun area.

activities.text: At the foot of the Tour Carrée, the garden inspired by medieval gardens features medicinal plants in square beds edged with woven chestnut, including those used in “Polychreston,” a remedy devised by Renaudot in 1619.
Walk along the Philippe-Auguste and Foulques Nerra promenades that follow the old ramparts. Views of slate rooftops and bell towers form a well-preserved scene.

Join the guided tour “L'Affaire des Possédées” offered by the tourist office. Various stops in Loudun help explain this famous 17th-century witchcraft case, orchestrated by Richelieu against the parish priest Urbain Grandier.

days_plan.itin_title: Vienne Road Trip: Futuroscope and Romanesque Heritage

visits.text: Lined with 157 arcades, the Grande Rue in Louhans hosts one of Burgundy's liveliest weekly markets. Every Monday morning, the poultry market on Place de la Charité showcases the Bresse chicken, with its blue legs, white feathers, and red comb.

activities.text: By noon, the smell of roasting chickens drifts across the square. Sample the corniotte, a local pastry made with Bresse AOP butter, before continuing to the church of Saint-Pierre and its glazed-tile bell tower.

days_plan.itin_title: Burgundy-Franche-Comté: The Most Beautiful Villages in 7 days

places.name: Lourdes

visits.text: The Grotte de Massabielle, on the banks of the Gave de Pau, is the site where Bernadette Soubirous reported eighteen apparitions of the Virgin Mary in 1858. This rock cavity (3.80 m high, 9.50 m deep) houses a Carrara marble statue sculpted by Fabisch, placed in the niche of the apparitions. The spring discovered by Bernadette still flows, captured and channeled to fountains accessible to visitors. The site is protected as a Historic Monument.

The Basilica of the Immaculate Conception, built from 1866 to 1871 atop the Massabielle rock, is in neo-Gothic style. Its single nave of five bays is adorned with ex-votos, and the pointed arches bear the words that the Virgin addressed to Bernadette. The bell tower rises to 70 meters.

The Basilica of Our Lady of the Rosary, constructed between 1883 and 1889 below the previous one, adopts a Greek cross plan and Romano-Byzantine style. Its interior walls are covered with mosaics over more than 2,000 m² depicting the mysteries of the Rosary. It can accommodate 1,500 worshippers.

The Underground Basilica of Saint Pius X, inaugurated in 1958 for the centenary of the apparitions, is one of the world's largest churches with a capacity of 25,000 people. Its gemmail stained-glass windows cast a distinctive light in this elliptical concrete space buried beneath the esplanade.

The Château Fort, erected in the 11th century on a rocky outcrop, dominates the town and surrounding valleys. Classified as a Historic Monument, it houses the Musée Pyrénéen (with the Musée de France designation), dedicated to Pyrenean cultures, traditions, and expertise from the 18th to the 20th century. A botanical garden enhances the visit.

The Pic du Jer, accessible by a funicular inaugurated in 1900, rises to an altitude of 1,000 meters. At the summit, a 360° panorama takes in the Pyrenees, the Tarbes plain, and the town of Lourdes below. Caves equipped for visitors can be explored on site.

activities.text: Cross the sanctuary esplanade to the grotto, then climb back toward the basilicas built one above the other using the ramps that follow the Gave de Pau.
Climb to the Château Fort by the steep paths and enjoy the view looking down over the sanctuaries and rooftops of Lourdes before touring the Musée Pyrénéen collections.
Take the Pic du Jer funicular for a fifteen-minute ascent, then explore the caves at the summit before descending on foot via the wooded trail.
In the evening, from Easter to late October, attend the torchlight procession that takes place every evening within the sanctuary grounds - a moment that touches believers and visitors alike.

Take an excursion to the Grottes de Bétharram, located between Pau and Lourdes, about 15 km from your overnight base, a 20-minute drive. The visit, lasting about 1 hour 20 minutes, combines walking through five levels of underground galleries, descending 250 steps, a boat crossing on the underground river and a return journey by miniature train over 700 metres.

days_plan.itin_title: Hautes-Pyrénées Circuit: From Tarbes to Cirques and Valleys

map_keywords: Basilica of the Immaculate Conception Lourdes

visits.text: Lourmarin is the southern gateway to the Luberon—and one of the region's most vibrant villages. Its cobbled lanes, plane-tree-shaded squares, and numerous art galleries make it both a heritage destination and a living community. This is where Albert Camus chose to settle in 1958 with his Nobel Prize money, purchasing an old silkworm farm that he furnished entirely as a gift to his family. He died on January 4, 1960, in a car accident while leaving the village; Lourmarin's footballers carried his coffin to the cemetery. You can reach it on foot in five minutes from the center: the grave, simple and covered with laurels, is one of the most visited in Provence.

The Château de Lourmarin is often described as Provence's first Renaissance castle. Its construction began in the 15th century under the d'Agoult family and extended until 1560, featuring an elegant Italianate loggia. The Renaissance section—the only part open to the public—houses furnished apartments and stairways of surprising geometry. Each summer it also serves as the venue for the Summer Music Festival, whose starlit evening concerts are worth the trip in themselves.

The village contains two symbolic religious buildings standing side by side: the Church of Saint-Andre and the Protestant Temple, a direct reflection of the Wars of Religion that marked the region. In 1545, a tragic episode unfolded here: the massacre of the Vaudois of the Luberon, during which the village was almost entirely destroyed before being repopulated by families from Piedmont and the Brianconnais.

activities.text: Lourmarin's market takes place Friday mornings—one of the region's most renowned. Browse among stalls of cheeses, olives, lavender, and local products. Arrive before 9 AM to have space and avoid the high-season crowds.

Walk toward the orchards and dry-stone walls south of the village (30 to 45 min). The trail climbing toward the Lourmarin valley offers beautiful views of the village and château, particularly in the golden late-afternoon light.

days_plan.itin_title: The 15 Most Beautiful Villages of the Luberon

visits.text: Sant'Antonino is one of France's most beautiful villages—and one of Corsica's oldest, perched at 500 meters altitude on a granite outcrop since the 9th century. The lanes are so narrow you can barely pass. The view from the summit over the Balagne beaches and sea is breathtaking. Count on 45 minutes to walk around—cars stay below in the parking lot.

Occi is a ghost village: abandoned in the 1950s by its inhabitants who left for the coast, it sleeps on its spur facing the sea with its roofless houses overgrown by maquis. The hike from Lumio takes 45 minutes one way. It's a silent and slightly melancholy place that neatly sums up the depopulation of Corsica's interior in the 20th century.

Speloncato, 600 meters above sea level in the heart of Balagne, is a hilltop village overlooking the plain on one side and the ridges on the other. Cardinal Pietro Casini came from here. Allow for a round trip by road from Lumio.

activities.text: The Balagne village loop by car takes a whole day: Lumio, Lavatoggio, Zilia, Montemaggiore, Cateri follow one another on the hillsides. Stop in Zilia for its olives and renowned spring water, in Montemaggiore for the church perched above the vineyards. Local producers sell olive oil, honey, and figatellu directly.

days_plan.itin_title: Complete Tour of Corsica

visits.text: Germain Boffrand built Lunéville château between 1703 and 1723 for Duke Leopold I. Mansart's student created this 'Lorraine Versailles' after Louis XIV occupied Nancy.
Stanislas Leszczynski settled in Lunéville in 1737. He had the gardens embellished with fabriques, the exotic pavilions designed by Emmanuel Héré.
The ducal chapel, restored after the 2003 fire, now welcomes visitors. The Livery Room and Guards Room pay tribute to the reconstruction workers.
The château museum displays 18th-century paintings and decorative arts. Three rooms trace the history of the château from the year 1000 onwards.
Église Saint-Jacques was built between 1730 and 1747 under Francis III and Stanislas. Its organ, designed by Emmanuel Héré, is entirely concealed by magnificent decoration.

activities.text: The Parc des Bosquets spreads over 21 hectares of formal French gardens laid out by Yves des Hours. Visitors wander freely between the classical vistas and the wilder groves.
The Lunéville Embroidery Conservatory perpetuates this recognized and transmitted Lorraine craft. Introductory workshops are offered regularly.

days_plan.itin_title: Meurthe-et-Moselle Road Trip: Art Nouveau Nancy & Fortified Cities

visits.text: Wander through the historic center of Lure, the department's third most populous commune after Vesoul and Héricourt. Its architecture bears witness to its industrial past and 19th-century development.

activities.text: Discover the Southern Vosges landscapes from Lure, gateway to the forests, heather moorlands, and peaks of the Ballons des Vosges. The trails offer panoramas over the valley and the first mountain foothills.
Discover the street art works displayed on the M.u.r (Modular, Urban, Responsive), a wall dedicated to urban art and regularly refreshed with creations by recognized artists like Stom500.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Saône Tour: Comtois Plateaus and Heritage

visits.text: Lurs stands at an altitude of 612 metres on a rocky spur above the Durance. Designated episcopal land by Charlemagne in 812, the town was the summer residence of the bishops of Sisteron until the Revolution — this past is visible everywhere: the castle of the prince-bishops, the Clock Tower, whose bell dates from 1599 and is the oldest in the department, and the seminary built between 1738 and 1742. Enter the village along the Chemin des Écritures, inaugurated in 2010: 42 stelae trace the development of Latin script and typography. The idea was born here because Jean Giono and typographer Maximilien Vox founded the Rencontres Internationales de Lure in 1952 — they are still held during the last week of August each year.

Don't leave without taking the Promenade des Évêques: from the castle, an avenue lined with 15 oratories dedicated to the Virgin (built in 1864) leads to the Chapel of Notre-Dame de Vie (1552, with a columned entrance). From the terrace, there is a 360° view over the Durance valley, the Valensole plateau, Montagne de Lure and the Luberon — in clear weather, the Alpine range appears on the horizon. It's one of the finest views in Haute-Provence.

The Lurs olive grove is one of the five most beautiful in Provence — often centuries-old olive trees cascade down towards the Durance. The local Aglandau variety produces an AOC olive oil. Follow the calade path downhill for a walk among the trees.

activities.text: The Pont Romain loop (3 hours 15 minutes, 270 m elevation gain) crosses the village, the Promenade des Évêques and a forest before reaching a bridge built between 121 and 145 CE on the Via Domitia — the Roman road linking Italy and Spain passed at the foot of Lurs. A phallus deeply carved into a large dressed-stone corner block has long intrigued archaeologists. The return climb follows a path lined with dry-stone walls and olive groves.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpes-de-Haute-Provence Tour: Lavender and Hilltop Villages
Forcalquier & Verdon Gorges Road Trip

places.name: Lusigny Sur Barse

visits.text: A 70,000-hectare natural haven, the Forêt d'Orient Regional Natural Park combines ancient forests, wet meadows and 5,000 hectares of artificial lakes—three giants created to regulate the flow of the Seine: Orient, 2,500 ha; Temple, 2,000 ha; and Amance, 490 ha. An internationally recognized birdwatching paradise, it is home to more than 265 recorded species, including thousands of migrating common cranes, extremely rare black storks, Eurasian spoonbills and white-tailed eagles. The Maison du Parc in Piney provides information, exhibitions and nature activities.

The oldest and largest of the three, Lac d'Orient spreads its 2,500 hectares between dykes, peninsulas and wild coves. Fine sandy beaches with the Blue Flag label at Mesnil-Saint-Père, Géraudot and Lusigny-sur-Barse turn summer into a Champagne Riviera. The Maison des Lacs (Mesnil-Saint-Père) provides information, rents equipment and offers guidance. To the north-east, the bird reserve protects nesting areas - purpose-built hides offer a winged spectacle all year round. Lac Amance (490 ha), about 30 km from Lusigny-sur-Barse, 30 minutes by road, resounds with the roar of engines: the largest motorboating area in Europe (jet skiing and water skiing allowed).

activities.text: Lac d'Orient is a haven for non-motorized water sports. From March to November, sailing—dinghies, catamarans and windsurfing—kayaking, canoeing, paddleboarding, kitesurfing and wingfoiling share 2,500 hectares of calm water protected from strong winds. Sailing schools offering courses for all levels, affiliated water-sports clubs and professional rental operators provide equipment and supervision. Regular competitions, summer courses and club outings punctuate the season. The modern water-sports center has changing rooms, toilets and a snack bar.

42 km of safe greenway link Troyes to the lakes along a family cycle path. The Lac d'Orient loop (27 km) is a delight: panoramic dikes, shaded woodland and beaches in turn. Waymarked walking routes (150 km) and bridle paths (117 km) crisscross the Park. Mountain bikes, road bikes and e-bikes for hire. Picnic stops, water points and free maps at the Tourist Offices.

Four strategically placed birdwatching observatories at Lac d'Orient and Lac du Temple reveal the secrets of Champagne's birdlife. Highlights include the autumn migration of common cranes—40,000 birds in some years—the spring arrival of Eurasian spoonbills, black storks nesting in the forest and noisy colonies of terns, gulls and cormorants. Binoculars are essential. Guided outings with Park naturalists—reservation recommended—explain behavior, identify species and explore wetland ecology. Spring and autumn are the best seasons.

days_plan.itin_title: Aube Tour: Champagne, Medieval Heritage and the Lakes of the Forêt d'Orient

map_keywords: Forest of Orient Regional Natural Park

visits.text: The Saint-Pierre Basilica, the fourth church erected on this site where Saint Columbanus founded one of Europe's first monasteries in 590, harmoniously blends Romanesque and Gothic styles. Built between 1215 and 1330, its pink Vosges sandstone walls lend it unique beauty. The bell tower contains Haute-Saône's largest bell at 3,563 kg.

Look up at the basilica's crown jewel: its 17th-century organ case (1617, expanded in 1685), one of the oldest in Franche-Comté. Supported by a statue of Atlas, this instrument with 3,137 pipes and 44 stops evokes in its sculpted form the prow of a royal vessel.
Stroll through the abbey cloister, built from pink sandstone in the late 15th century. On the vault keystones, discover the coats of arms of the abbots who contributed to its construction.

The Abbey of Saint-Pierre-et-Saint-Paul, founded in 590 by Saint Columbanus on the ruins of ancient Luxovium (ravaged by Attila in 451), was a leading religious and intellectual center. Its scriptorium gave rise in the 7th century to Luxeuil script, the first calligraphic script in lowercase letters.

Discover the thermal baths, a classical pink Vosges sandstone building constructed in the 18th century under Louis XV, listed as a Historic Monument in 1862. Since Celtic and Roman times, the thermal waters gushing at over 63°C have been renowned for their curative properties. The Art Deco architecture with its refined mosaics makes this establishment a remarkable place.

The Maison François Ier with its three arcades is the last vestige of the arcaded houses that once lined the main street. Also admire the Maison Espagnole with its Flamboyant Gothic façade, the Maison du Bailli with its balcony and crenellated polygonal tower, and the Maison du Cardinal Jouffroy adorned with France's oldest suspended stone balcony.

Visit the 33-meter-high Tour des Échevins, built in the 15th century, which houses one of France's oldest museums. The collections trace Luxeuil's history through Gallo-Roman archaeological remains, and one floor is dedicated to the famous painter Jules Adler.

activities.text: Follow the 2-km Sentier du Patrimoine, marked by bronze suns embedded in the ground, with 14 stops featuring QR codes for audio explanations. It takes you past the 17 historic monuments: basilica, cloister, thermal baths, Ecclesia archaeological site, Renaissance houses, and rue des Balcons.

Look up along Rue Carnot to admire the 52 wrought-iron and cast-iron balconies that testify to the golden age of Haute-Saône foundries in the 19th century. These foundries notably manufactured Monaco's war memorial and ornaments for Cuba's Parliament Palace.
Explore the Ecclesia archaeological site presenting over 2,000 years of history with 150 sarcophagi, one of eastern France's principal sites for early Christian and Merovingian periods.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Saône Tour: Comtois Plateaus and Heritage

visits.text: The Church of Saint-André, known as the “Templars' Church,” is actually the work of the Hospitallers of Saint John of Jerusalem, who fortified it in the 14th century to protect pilgrims traveling to Santiago de Compostela from miquelets, Aragonese bandits. Its battlements, arrow slits, and defense towers give it a fortress-like appearance. Classified as a Historic Monument as early as 1840—one of the very first Pyrenean monuments to receive this distinction—it contains a painted 16th-century vault depicting Christ surrounded by the four evangelists in tetramorphic form, and an 18th-century Baroque high altar.

The Pont Napoléon spans the Gave de Gavarnie at a height of 63 meters, with an arch spanning 68 meters. Constructed between 1859 and 1861 under Napoleon III, it was erected in gratitude to the valley inhabitants after Empress Eugénie stayed at the Saint-Sauveur thermal baths. The site has become a bungee jumping spot.

The Solférino Chapel, built in 1859 at Napoleon III's request to commemorate the victory at the Battle of Solferino in Italy, stands on a promontory overlooking the valley. Its Byzantine-inspired tower and surrounding benches make it a peaceful viewpoint over Luz and the surrounding mountains.

The Gorges de Luz carve a narrow passage through rock walls downstream from the village. The road that crosses them offers a striking view of the erosive power of the gave, with geological strata visible on the cliff faces.
The Château Sainte-Marie, in ruins on the heights at 630 meters altitude, preserves two medieval defense towers. The remains offer a viewpoint over the confluence of the Barèges and Gavarnie valleys.

Luz-Saint-Sauveur itself comprises two joined towns: Luz, a commercial center enlivened by its Monday morning market at the foot of the fortified church, and Saint-Sauveur, a spa resort where Second Empire elites stayed. Victor Hugo described the light of this valley by comparing its name—Luz—to the word “light.”

activities.text: Visit the fortified church, paying attention to the sculpted Romanesque tympanum on the north facade, the polychrome painted vault, and the sacred art treasury displayed in the Notre-Dame-de-la-Pitié chapel.

Cross the Pont Napoléon on foot, then descend the small trail on the right that leads to the gave's edge, at the foot of the bridge - a cool spot for a break, with a view looking up at the monumental arch.
Climb to the Solférino Chapel for a peaceful panorama over the valley. On market days (Monday morning), first stock up on local products below before climbing up for a picnic.
Explore the town of Saint-Sauveur, its spa building facades and alleys, climbing toward the Château Sainte-Marie ruins for an overall view of the Pays Toy.

days_plan.itin_title: Hautes-Pyrénées Circuit: From Tarbes to Cirques and Valleys
Pyrenean Thermal Route: Spa Towns

visits.text: Saint-Jean-Baptiste Cathedral, built between 1175 and 1480, blends Romanesque and Gothic styles across 260 feet in length. Its 14th-century astronomical clock—one of Europe's oldest—calculates the positions of the sun, moon, and stars above Lyon. Henry IV and Marie de Medici were married here in 1600.

Old Lyon's traboules form a network of over 300 covered passages connecting streets through interior courtyards. The earliest date to the 4th century, others to the Renaissance. During World War II, the Resistance used them to escape the occupiers. A gilded lion's-head plaque marks their entrance.

Rue du Boeuf and Rue Saint-Jean hold the finest Renaissance mansions in the district. Italian merchants, drawn by the four great fairs granted by Charles VII, built houses with inner courtyards and Italian-style galleries. The Gadagne museum traces the history of Lyon and houses the museum of puppets of the world.

Place du Change, the 15th-century bankers' square, preserves the Exchange Lodge built by Soufflot in 1748. The half-timbered houses surrounding it recall when Lyon was Europe's leading financial center, before Paris seized that title.

Saint-Georges quarter, south of Old Lyon, was the craftsmen's domain. More working-class than Saint-Jean, it retains a village atmosphere with narrow lanes and its 19th-century church on the Saône's banks. Stunning views of the footbridge and Fourvière hill.

Notre-Dame de Fourvière Basilica, completed in 1884, towers over Lyon from the 'hill that prays.' Its neo-Byzantine interior astonishes with exuberant golden mosaics, stained glass, and sculptures. Guided visits access the rooftop and Observatory Tower for 360° panoramas of the city, the Alps, and the Pilat mountains.

The great Roman theater, built around 15 BC under Augustus, is the oldest in Roman Gaul. Expanded in the 1st century, it could seat 10,000 spectators. Its orchestra preserves polychrome marble paving and a stage curtain pit whose mechanism is reconstructed in the neighboring museum.
The odeon, smaller than the theater, was reserved for musical performances and recitations. Its paving of colored marbles, brought from across the Empire, is one of the finest in the Roman world.

The Lugdunum Museum, embedded in the hillside by architect Bernard Zehrfuss (1975), houses one of France's richest archaeological collections. The Claudian Tablet—Emperor Claudius's speech before the Senate—and the Vaise Treasure rank among the masterpieces. Virtual reality tours available to relive the Roman city.

Fourvière esplanade offers Lyon's most celebrated panorama: the peninsula, both rivers, the Part-Dieu tower, Croix-Rousse, and on clear days, the Alpine chain from Mont Blanc to Vercors. Locals gather here for the Festival of Lights on December 8.

Place Bellecour, one of Europe's largest pedestrian squares, opens between the Rhône and Saône. Louis XIV's equestrian statue has stood at its center since 1825. The name likely derives from 'Bella Curtis'—beautiful garden in Latin. At no. 29, lion statues guard the pedestrian street entrance. The Little Prince and Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, Lyon-born, have had their statue on the square since 2000.

Place des Terreaux, at the foot of Croix-Rousse, lines up the Bartholdi fountain (originally intended for Bordeaux), the Fine Arts Museum in the former Saint-Pierre Convent, and the City Hall rebuilt after a 1674 fire. At night, Daniel Buren's 69 water jets illuminate the ground.

Lyon's Museum of Fine Arts, installed in a 17th-century former convent, is France's second most important after the Louvre. Its collections span from antiquity to contemporary art. The cloister garden, free and open to all, is a peaceful haven in the city center.

Lyon Opera House, renovated by Jean Nouvel in 1993, preserves its neoclassical façade crowned by a contemporary glass dome—a striking contrast between the 18th century and modernity. Eight muses on the pediment contemplate the Place de la Comédie.

Les Halles de Lyon Paul Bocuse, 'Lyon's belly,' gathers over 60 merchants across 145,000 square feet. The first covered market opened in 1859 at Place des Cordeliers. Moved to Part-Dieu in 1971, it took the multi-starred chef's name in 2006. Aged Saint-Marcellin cheese, quenelles, charcuterie, praline brioches, and seafood—Lyon's gastronomy concentrated in one place.

The Mur des Canuts, on Boulevard des Canuts, is Europe's largest trompe-l'oeil: 13,000 square feet of fresco depicting neighborhood life. Created in 1987 by CitéCréation, it's updated every ten years—characters age, shops change. Spot Guignol, the Vélo'v bikes, and the loom between the windows.

La Maison des Canuts, on Rue d'Ivry, is the living conservatory of Lyon's silk-making heritage. Weaving demonstrations on hand looms, explanations of 19th-century techniques. The canuts—silk-weaver workers—lived in workshop apartments with 13-foot ceilings, necessary to accommodate Jacquard looms.

Croix-Rousse's traboules, built in the 18th century, served to protect silk bales transported from street to street. During the 1831 Canut Revolt—one of history's first workers' uprisings—they allowed insurgents to move under cover. Their motto: 'Live working or die fighting.'

The Fresque des Lyonnais, on Quai Saint-Vincent, features 30 local personalities across 8,600 square feet of façade: Paul Bocuse, the Lumière brothers, Abbé Pierre, Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, Louise Labé. Recognizing them is a game for visitors—painted balconies and windows blend with real ones.

The 'Silk Roads' fresco, at Clos Jouve, traces 3,000 years of silk history across 1,600 square feet: from Lei Tsou to Genghis Khan, from Charlemagne to Francis I. The Croix-Rousse quarter is the birthplace of this industry that made Lyon's fortune from the 16th to 19th centuries.

activities.text: Guided tour of Old Lyon's traboules. Guides unlock Renaissance courtyard doors normally closed to the public. Spiral staircases, carved wells, and Italian-style galleries reveal themselves behind golden stone façades.

Dinner at a traditional Lyonnais bouchon in Old Lyon. Tablier de sapeur, pike quenelle, cervelle de canut, and pink pralines compose the traditional menu. The mâchon—a sort of workers' brunch inherited from silk weavers—is savored in the morning.
Sunset stroll along the Saône quays. Warm light illuminates the cathedral façade and Renaissance houses. The buildings' reflections in the water give the quarter its nickname: 'little Florence.'

Funicular ride from Old Lyon to Fourvière. Two lines: one to the basilica, another to the Roman theaters (Minimes station). Descend on foot through the Rosary Gardens—flowered staircases with views of the Saône and Old Lyon.

Les Nuits de Fourvière transforms the ancient theaters into a summer festival stage each year. Concerts, plays, circus acts, and dance under the stars—the antique setting gives performances magical dimension.

Visit Lugdunum Museum with virtual reality journey. Six immersive stations plunge you into the Roman city of Lugdunum, capital of the Three Gauls. Mosaics, sculptures, and a 3D model of 80 km² of the 2nd-century metropolis.

Gourmet stroll through Les Halles Paul Bocuse. Sample quenelles, aged cheeses, and oysters paired with a glass of Condrieu at the counter. Early morning brings a producers' market atmosphere; late morning, starred chefs do their shopping.

Visit the Museum of Fine Arts. The collection spans five millennia: Egyptian antiquities, paintings by Rubens, Rembrandt, Monet, Picasso, and a fine contemporary art ensemble. The cloister garden is free and open to everyone.

Shopping and wandering on Rue de la République, carved out in the 19th century by Prefect Vaïsse (Lyon's Haussmann). Covered passages—Passage de l'Argue, Passage Thiaffait—preserve the charm of 19th-century galleries.

A walk among the painted walls of La Croix-Rousse. Starting from the Mur des Canuts, head down the slopes past the best-known frescoes. Allow 1h30 for the loop to the Fresque des Lyonnais, cutting through the traboules and courtyards along the way.

Croix-Rousse market, one of Lyon's largest and liveliest. Boulevard de la Croix-Rousse, a UNESCO site, fills with producers' stalls on Tuesday, Thursday, Friday, and Saturday mornings. Cheeses, charcuterie, fruits, and vegetables from the Lyon region.

Visit La Maison des Canuts. Weaving demonstration on period Jacquard looms. Soierie Vivante workshop, in the quarter's last remaining workshops, extends the experience with guided tours in authentic facilities.
