visits.text: Château Gaillard overlooks a bend of the Seine from its rocky spur. Built in a single year (1196-1198) by Richard the Lionheart to protect the duchy of Normandy, it fell to Philip Augustus in 1204. The keep is still accessible. About 18 km from the stage town, 18 minutes by road.

Le Petit-Andely spreads out at the foot of the fortress, facing one of the loveliest bends of the Seine. Half-timbered houses, quiet quays and a sweeping view of the chalk cliffs. About 18 km from the stage town, 18 minutes by road.

The collegiate church of Notre-Dame in Les Andelys has kept 16th-century stained glass and a Renaissance doorway. The Nicolas Poussin museum, housed in a 17th-century building, pays tribute to the painter born here in 1594. About 18 km from the stage town, 18 minutes by road.

In Lyons-la-Forêt, the 18th-century market hall stands at the square's center. Its oak timber frame, restored under the Duke of Penthièvre, sheltered markets and fairs. It served as the agricultural fair setting in two adaptations of Madame Bovary (Renoir 1933, Chabrol 1991).
Half-timbered houses from the 17th and 18th centuries line the spiral streets around the former castle mound. On Rue d'Enfer, a half-timbered manor house hosted composer Maurice Ravel.
The town hall, former seat of the bailiff's court, has retained its courtroom with period furniture and an 18th-century fleur-de-lis tapestry. Free visit during opening hours.

activities.text: Hike in the Lyons State Forest, 10,700 hectares of cathedral beech forest—the largest in France. Beeches reach 45 meters high. The Fontaineresse trail (6.5 km) starts from the village center.
Viewpoint over the Seine from the ruins of Château Gaillard, ideally at sunset. The panorama embraces Le Petit-Andely, limestone hillsides, and river meanders.
Stroll in the Parc des Trois Moulins in Lyons-la-Forêt, along the Lieure. Centuries-old trees, meadows, and bucolic atmosphere.

days_plan.itin_title: Eure Road Trip: From Giverny to Normandy's Most Beautiful Villages
The 20 Most Beautiful Villages in Normandy

places.name: Macinaggio

visits.text: Macinaggio is the port at Cap Corse's northern tip—the very end. Tour operators offer narrated cruises to the Giraglia islets and the cape's limestone cliffs, accessible only from the sea. The crossing follows a coast almost free of buildings, with cliffs plunging directly into the water.

Nonza, on the west coast of Cap Corse, is one of the island's most photographed villages: a 17th-century Genoese tower perched on a black cliff, with a black pebble beach below - its color comes from the mountain's schist. It was in Nonza that a lone woman, Catarina Gentili, defended the tower against the French in 1768 by making them believe a whole garrison was entrenched inside. Go in the late afternoon for the light on the cliff. Allow for a round trip by road from Macinaggio.

If you still have time, continue to Erbalunga, 10 km north of Bastia - a small Genoese fishing village with houses clustered around a tower that has collapsed into the sea. It is one of the most picturesque places on the cape's east coast, often photographed as the backdrop to seafood restaurant terraces, which are among the region's best. Allow for a round trip by road from Macinaggio.

activities.text: The sentier des douaniers between Macinaggio and Barcaggio is a 12 km one-way hike along the northern coastal ledge of Cap Corse, between maquis and sea cliffs. It is Corsica's wildest coastal trail - allow 4 hours round trip or walk it one way with a return shuttle. Bring water.

The Patrimonio wine route crosses Corsica's first PDO vineyards (the appellation dates from 1968) at the foot of the cape. Muscat de Cap Corse and red nielluccio are the two mainstays of this black-schist terroir. Estates offer tastings without an appointment, particularly around the village of Patrimonio. Allow for a round trip by road from Macinaggio.

days_plan.itin_title: Complete Tour of Corsica

map_keywords: Nonza plage galets noirs Cap Corse

visits.text: Mercurey, Rully, Givry - the same grape varieties as the Côte d'Or, two to three times cheaper. This is where Burgundians themselves stock up, and they don't say it too loudly. Rully produces 60% of its volume in Crémant de Bourgogne, Mercurey dominates in Pinot Noir, Givry in aging reds. Stop at a Rully producer and compare a Premier Cru Rully with a Meursault from the same vintage: the price difference is enormous, the difference in the glass is smaller than you'd think.

This 493-meter limestone promontory doesn't look like much from the plain - and then you look up and understand. For 25,000 years, Paleolithic hunters brought down their prey at the foot of this rock: tens of thousands of horse bones were uncovered during 19th-century excavations, one of Europe's richest prehistoric hunting sites. Mitterrand climbed it every Pentecost for 23 years, with a circle of friends whose composition changed according to the political ambitions of the moment. The ascent via the south trail takes 45 minutes. The view over the Pouilly-Fuisse vineyards is the day's finest.

The first Mâconnais Chardonnay to win premiers crus recognized by INAO - 22 climats classified in 2020, after years of lobbying by local winemakers. The result in the glass: powerful, buttery whites with a finish that rivals some Meursaults at twice the price. End-of-route tasting at Château de Fuissé or at an independent producer in the village - and compare with the Chablis from day one: same grape, opposite terroirs, two wines that have nothing in common.

activities.text: Final tasting in Pouilly-Fuissé: the village of Fuissé has about ten producers open for direct visits, most without appointment in season. It's a chance to compare the Pouilly-Fuissé style with what you've tasted all week - Mâconnais whites are more solar, less acidic than Chablis, rounder than Meursault. One more glass to decide which one you'll pack in your luggage.

Arrive in Mâcon in the late afternoon and stroll along the Saône quays opposite the old town. Mâcon is the birthplace of Alphonse de Lamartine (1790-1869). In the evening, Lyon-style bouchons begin to appear in the narrow streets: the food becomes heartier, foreshadowing Lyon 70 km away.

days_plan.itin_title: Saône-et-Loire Road Trip: Bibracte, Cluny, Solutré & the Mâconnais Vineyards
Burgundy Grand Crus Route - 7 Days from Chablis to the Mâconnais

visits.text: Maillane is inseparable from Frédéric Mistral (1830-1914), Provençal poet, co-founder of the Félibrige in 1854, and 1904 Nobel Prize in Literature winner. Here he grew up, built his house in 1876 (the year of his marriage), and died. The house-museum, classified as a Historic Monument since 1930, has retained its original appearance with its 2,120 objects, 60,000 letters received by the poet, and intact furnishings. Its facade is sculpted with figures of Mireille and Estérelle, heroines of his two Provençal epics. Book ahead: visits are by appointment.

Mistral's tomb in Maillane cemetery deserves a discreet visit: he himself had this mausoleum built in 1906 modeled on the Love Pavilion of Queen Jeanne of Les Baux-de-Provence. A gesture consistent with his works that celebrated medieval Provence. Mistral also used his Nobel Prize funds to finance the development of Arles' Museon Arlaten, the Provençal ethnographic museum.

The Maison du Lézard is the small family house where Mistral lived with his mother from 1855 to 1875 before moving into his purpose-built house. He wrote part of Mirèio and Calendau here. Now the municipal library and tourist office, it still features a sundial adorned with a lizard that he had installed in 1903 — a discreet symbol of his permanent presence in the village.

activities.text: The "Discovering the village heritage" trail: a marked route with 12 information panels starts at the house-museum and guides visitors around the village's Mistral-related sites, fountains, wayside shrines and old wells. Allow 1.5 hours.
A walk into the farmland west of Maillane: the farm tracks heading that way cross the Rhône plain, an open landscape of vines and almond trees.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpilles, Aix-en-Provence & Arles Circuit

visits.text: Founded around the year 1000 by Duchess Emma of Aquitaine, Maillezais Abbey was Poitou’s wealthiest Benedictine abbey for five centuries—its revenues reportedly exceeded those of the Archbishopric of Bordeaux. Built on a former island in the heart of the marsh, it became a cathedral in 1317 by order of Pope John XXII, before being devastated in 1562 during the Wars of Religion, used as a stone quarry after the French Revolution, and listed as a historic monument in 1924. What you see today—majestic ruins still reaching 25 meters high—is only a shadow of a cathedral that measured 105 meters long, 33 meters wide, and 60 meters high beneath its vaults. Take time to examine the outline on the ground: it reveals the colossal footprint of the vanished building.

Climb the remaining tower to take in the surrounding marsh—the same landscape seen by the monks who dug the first canals of the Marais Poitevin as early as the 11th century, in partnership with four other abbeys, including Saint-Maixent. François Rabelais spent five years here as secretary to Bishop Geoffroy d’Estissac: the abbey appears in his works, and it was here that he discovered the first romaine lettuces sent from Rome.

The monastic buildings preserve the pilgrims’ refectory, the kitchen, the salt cellar, and what is known as “Rabelais’s dungeon.” An immersive film projected onto three walls in the former refectory traces the abbey’s history from its foundation. It’s worth 30 minutes of your attention.

activities.text: A picnic in the shaded area within the grounds, with a direct view of the ruins. The contrast between the broken walls, the sky, and the surrounding marsh vegetation is particularly striking at this time of day.

Set off from the abbey’s boat landing to explore the canals of the wet marsh. Compared with Coulon, the waterways here are narrower, shadier, and less crowded. The landscape feels more enclosed and mysterious—a different experience.

days_plan.itin_title: Deux-Sèvres Tour: Marais Poitevin and Romanesque Heritage

visits.text: Château de Maintenon, home of Françoise d'Aubigné, Louis XIV's secret wife. This architectural jewel blends medieval remains with Renaissance and classical elements. The 17th-century apartments reveal Madame de Maintenon's private life through portraits, period furniture, and the Noailles gallery adorned with paintings by masters.

Vauban's unfinished aqueduct, a monumental testament to Louis XIV's ambition. Commissioned in 1685 to channel Eure waters to Versailles' fountains, this colossal project was abandoned in 1688 for lack of funds. Its romantic ruins majestically cross the park for nearly 4 kilometers.

French formal gardens designed by Le Nôtre, restored in 2013 according to the original 1686 plans. The flower parterre of blue sage, rose bushes, and impatiens surrounds a canal bordered by two paths named Racine and Le Nôtre. Facing the aqueduct, deck chairs offer a place to contemplate this grand setting.

activities.text: Walk along the Eure through the château park, where the river has been transformed into a canal passing beneath the aqueduct's majestic arches. White swans glide on the water while century-old linden trees create an atmosphere of aristocratic serenity.

Explore the village of Maintenon with its old houses and Saint-Nicolas church, connected to the château by a wing built under Louis XIV. A peaceful village that has preserved its old-world charm in the shadow of the royal estate.

days_plan.itin_title: Eure-et-Loir Tour: Chartres, Châteaux and Proust

visits.text: The Fragonard Museum was founded in 1766—older than the Louvre. It's housed in the grounds of the École nationale vétérinaire d'Alfort, itself created the same year by Louis XV in the Château d'Alfort. The collection is dizzying: 4,200 pieces, hundreds of animal skeletons, natural “monsters” (two-headed calves, a five-legged sheep, a cyclops), and especially Honoré Fragonard's 21 écorchés—human and animal bodies preserved for 250 years thanks to a larch resin varnish. His painter cousin used the same resin for his paintings. The most famous depicts a rider on a galloping horse, muscle by muscle. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes. Children under 8 are not admitted, and for good reasons.

The Sainte-Agnès church, built between 1928 and 1936 by architects Teisseire and Pelletier, is Val-de-Marne's finest example of Art Deco and is listed as a historic monument. Stained glass, frescoes, sculptures, wrought iron—everything was conceived as “total art.” The founder of Suze, a gentian-based aperitif, financed much of the construction: his factory facade is still visible right next door.

End on the Marne banks at the Saint-Maurice dam. This is where the Promenade Paul Cézanne from Saint-Maur terminates. The Maisons-Alfort bridge, with its stone pier topped by a ship's prow and RF letters, dates from 1911 — built by the same engineers as the Pont du Petit-Parc in Joinville.

activities.text: The dam creates eddies that local kayakers train to paddle upstream against. Vendors offer license-free boat rentals between May and September from the Maisons-Alfort banks.

The Maisons-Alfort neighborhood is home to a large Eastern European community—residents call the local market “the Russian market.” Slavic grocery stores, Polish and Russian bakeries: an unexpected change of scenery 10 km from Paris.

days_plan.itin_title: Val-de-Marne Road Trip: Castles and the Banks of the Marne

visits.text: Lake Saint-Point is the 3rd largest natural lake in France at 7.2 km long, 950 m wide, and 40 m deep at an altitude of 849 m. Crossed by the Doubs, it is separated from Lake Remoray by a protected wetland. It frequently freezes in winter and becomes a natural ice rink. Five villages border its shores: Saint-Point-Lac, Les Grangettes, Labergement-Sainte-Marie, Montperreux, and Malbuisson.

Malbuisson has been a Station Verte since 2009, recognized for its hotel and gastronomic tradition. The village overlooks the lake and serves as the starting point for the lake loop trail (23 km, pedestrians only). The Aqua2lacs water complex offers overhanging pools with panoramic lake views, jacuzzi, and relaxation area.

Mont d'Or rises to 1,463 meters, the highest point in the Doubs department. From its summit, accessible by the Morond chairlift or on foot via the GR5, you discover an exceptional panorama of more than 300 Alpine peaks including Mont Blanc, as well as the Haut-Doubs, Haut-Jura, and neighboring Switzerland. The site is classified as a Sensitive Natural Area for its remarkable flora including some protected species.

activities.text: Four water sports centers offer sailing, catamaran, stand-up paddle, canoe-kayak, and pedal boats on Lake Saint-Point. The beaches at Les Grangettes and Oye-et-Pallet are supervised in July-August. The water remains cool even in summer (18-22°C in August).

The Mont d'Or ridge hike (approximately 2h round trip, 6 km) connects the Morond summit to the Mont d'Or summit via a panoramic trail. A museum space in the snow factory presents the history and biodiversity of the massif. Free trail guides are available at the station ticket offices.

days_plan.itin_title: Doubs Circuit: Watchmaking and Swiss Border

visits.text: Malicorne-sur-Sarthe became France's capital of artistic faience thanks to a fortunate combination: quality clay deposits at Ligron, abundant wood for kilns, and a port on the Sarthe to distribute production. In 1747, Jean Loiseau, a faience maker from Touraine, opened the first manufactory here in a former inn called the Plat d'Étain. Push open the door of Faïencerie Bourg-Joly Malicorne—the direct heir of that foundation, still in operation—and watch the artisans work. Their openwork baskets are Malicorne's signature: the technique involves cutting the raw clay piece with a pointed blade to create fine openings reminiscent of lace. In 2011, during Monaco's princely wedding, Bourg-Joly delivered 342 of these baskets to decorate the Opera reception tables.

The Museum of Faience and Ceramics, labeled Musée de France, is housed in a former 19th-century stoneware manufactory with its kilns and chimney. The tour traces the history of Malicorne faience from the 18th century to contemporary creations—decorations inspired by Rouen, Quimper, or Moustiers, and especially the famous openwork invented in 1924 by Émile Tessier. He had the idea of piercing the still-raw piece with a pointed blade before firing. Slip-casting workshops are offered for young and old—a good way to leave with a piece made by your own hands.

The Malicorne color mill houses the Arts and Crafts shop on the upper floor. This is where faience makers once ground their stones under millstones to extract colored pigments. The building is worth seeing even if you don't buy anything.

activities.text: Embark on an electric boat ride on the Sarthe. Operators offer these outings from Malicorne port—an original perspective on the village from the water, with its tuffeau facades and poplar-lined banks. Allow an hour for the short version, two hours to reach Sablé-sur-Sarthe downstream.

Operators offer Sarthe descents by canoe-kayak from Malicorne. Successive locks punctuate the navigation and allow stops on wild banks. Bring spare clothes—even in calm weather, lock crossings can hold surprises.

days_plan.itin_title: Sarthe Road Trip: Le Mans and the Loir Valley

places.name: Mamers

visits.text: The Halles aux Grains of Mamers, built in 1818 replacing an older building, still host Monday, Friday, and Saturday markets today. Countess de Ségur mentioned them in Memoirs of a Donkey, published in 1860. These halls fit into a monumental triptych around Place Carnot: facing them, the Italian-style theater—one of the region's rare examples—occupies the ground floor of the festival hall building; behind, Saint-Nicolas church built between the 13th and 14th centuries raises its remarkable tower-belfry and Renaissance portal classified as a historic monument.

On Place de la République, look up to spot Mamers' Eiffel Tower: a 1:100 replica, built in 1889—the same year as the Paris Tower—by a local tinsmith who had worked on the Parisian construction site. Restored in 1997, it sits on a roof and remains probably the oldest known copy of the Eiffel Tower in the world. The story says it was commissioned to attract officers from the local garrison.

The Convent of the Visitation, founded in 1630 by Marie-Augustine Davoust, was confiscated at the Revolution to install the town hall and state prisons. Graffiti from royalist prisoners are still visible on the walls of the former cells. Also stroll through the coulées mamertines—these paved passages so narrow they can't be distinguished from the square—and along rue de Cinq-Ans with its hemp weavers' houses.

activities.text: Tasting Sarthe rillettes is an obligation in Mamers. The Brotherhood of Knights of Sarthe Rillettes, founded here in 1968, organizes a National Contest of Best Rillettes each year. Maine rillettes are slowly cooked in their own fat—melting texture, concentrated and slightly caramelized pork flavor. Market butchers will offer you several producers to compare.

The Maine Saosnois Greenway, a former railway line converted to a gentle path, extends 12 kilometers from Mamers through the Sarthe Perche countryside. Accessible on foot, by bike, or stroller—flat, natural, and with views over bocage. Operators rent bikes at the start.

days_plan.itin_title: Sarthe Road Trip: Le Mans and the Loir Valley

map_keywords: Halle aux Grains Mamers place Carnot

visits.text: Mane is a village of pale golden stone set on a hill of safre, the local ochre-coloured rock. Its name may come from Mana Genita, the Roman goddess of funerals — the site has been inhabited since prehistoric times, and the Via Domitia passed below. The 12th-century citadel, built on the rocky peak, is the only feudal fortification to have remained intact in Haute-Provence. Wander through the calade-paved lanes and look for the pointed cabanons, or bories, scattered across the area: these mortarless dry-stone structures, built between 1850 and 1950, bear witness to a lost rural craft.

Salagon Priory is the key visit at this stop. Listed as a Historic Monument, this vast 50 x 30 m complex comprises a 12th-century Romanesque church (barrel vaults, carved capitals, a rare 15th-century wall fresco), a 15th-century prior's residence and 6 hectares of ethnobotanical gardens. The surprise inside: a series of six contemporary stained-glass windows by Aurélie Nemours (installed in 1998) bathe the nave in intense red — a striking contrast with Romanesque austerity. The gardens feature more than 1,700 plants and include a medieval garden and a poisonous plant garden. The museum traces 2,000 years of occupation of the site, from the Neolithic to monastic life.
The château de Sauvan (18th century) is an architectural curiosity amid the Provençal scrubland. Period furniture and formal gardens, with guided tours in season.

activities.text: Walk the route through the village's calades and fountains, then continue to the medieval Romanesque bridge over the Laye, which once allowed pilgrims to reach Salagon Priory without getting their feet wet. The round trip from the village takes about 45 minutes and offers lovely views of Mane's rocky peak.

days_plan.itin_title: Forcalquier & Verdon Gorges Road Trip

visits.text: The historic center displays its winding streets between two medieval gates. Porte Saunerie and Porte Soubeyran guard the fortified old town entrance. Renaissance mansions reveal their inner courtyards and spiral staircases behind heavy wooden doors.

The Jean Giono Center celebrates the locally born writer. The house and urban trail trace the author's life and work. Manuscripts, first editions and personal belongings evoke the world of the man who celebrated Provence and its inhabitants.

Saint-Sauveur church blends Provençal Romanesque and southern Gothic. The 14th-century sculpted portal precedes a nave with soaring vaults. Side chapels house Baroque altarpieces and Renaissance baptismal fonts.
The couvent de la Présentation occupies a vast monastic complex.

Discover shaded little squares where fountains and washhouses murmur. Place de l'Hôtel de Ville brings the heart of Manosque to life. Café terraces invite you to watch daily life unfold in this authentic Provençal town.

activities.text: The Route Napoléon follows the Emperor's historic route on his return from the island of Elba in 1815. Commemorative markers and signs line this legendary road between Golfe-Juan and Grenoble. Allow for a round trip from Manosque within the day to reach the Route Napoléon.

The Valensole plateau stretches just outside Manosque. Lavender fields form fragrant geometric patterns from June to July. Hilltop villages and distilleries punctuate country roads through this iconic landscape.
Hiking trails crisscross wooded hills around Manosque. Mont d'Or offers a moderate ascent rewarded by a panorama over the Durance and Luberon. Aleppo pines and kermes oaks punctuate the routes.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpes-de-Haute-Provence Tour: Lavender and Hilltop Villages

visits.text: The Collégiale Notre-Dame de Mantes-la-Jolie, built between 1140 and 1240, bears striking resemblance to Notre-Dame de Paris. Its Last Judgment rose window, dated 1210-1220, and Burgundian glazed tile roof set it apart.
The Saint-Maclou Tower, remnant of a 14th-century Gothic parish church, stands sentinel above the old town rooftops. It serves as a landmark visible from the Seine quays.

The Hôtel-Dieu Museum holds the largest collection of works by Maximilien Luce, the neo-Impressionist painter born in the town. A lapidary display presents carved fragments from the collegiate church.

activities.text: Stroll along the Seine quays to the Île aux Dames, reached by a pedestrian footbridge. The island offers lawns, playgrounds, and a view of the collegiate church from the opposite bank.
Wander through the old town of Mantes-la-Jolie: medieval alleyways, fountains, and half-timbered façades surround the collegiate church.
Listen to the 1897 Merklin organ at the concerts held regularly beneath the vaults of the collegiate church.

days_plan.itin_title: Yvelines Road Trip: Versailles and Impressionist Villages

places.name: Marche Des Enfants Rouges

visits.text: The Marché des Enfants Rouges, opened in 1615 on Rue de Bretagne in the Marais, is Paris's oldest covered market—its name supposedly comes from children at the neighboring hospice who wore red clothes, the uniform of charity orphans at the time. Closed and fallen into disrepair in the 20th century, it was classified as a historic monument in 1982 and reopened in 2000 after restoration. Today about ten stalls offer Moroccan, Japanese, Lebanese, Creole, and French cuisine under the original metal and glass canopies. It's a place to eat on-site, standing or sitting on benches, like Parisians from the neighborhood.

activities.text: Lunch at the Marché des Enfants Rouges—choose your dish at one of the counters, settle on the communal benches under the arcades. The neighborhood market atmosphere, between onlookers and regulars, nicely sums up what's lively and informal about Paris far from the museums. It's a fitting way to end this cultural tour.

days_plan.itin_title: The Great Museums of Paris

map_keywords: Marché des Enfants Rouges Paris Marais

visits.text: Lupiac, a castelnau perched at 243 metres on a Gascon hill, is the cradle of the most famous of the musketeers. Charles de Batz de Castelmore was born there around 1613 in the family château, before leaving to conquer Paris around 1630. He became captain-lieutenant of King Louis XIV's Musketeers and died at the siege of Maastricht in 1673. About 14 km from the base town, 15 minutes by road.

On the central square, the first equestrian statue of d'Artagnan rears skyward—an 11-foot monumental bronze inaugurated in 2015. Sword brandished, the rider seems ready to resume his journey to Paris. The village preserves Saint-Barthélemy Church, whose four bells date from the musketeer's era.

The d'Artagnan Museum, housed in the Saint-Jacques Chapel classified as a Historic Monument, traces the life of the real musketeer. Wax figures in Grand Siècle costume, period documents, editions of Dumas's Three Musketeers and movie posters. A twenty-minute film draws parallels between legend and reality.

Nine miles southwest, the Tower of Termes-d'Armagnac rises 120 feet above the Adour valley. Classified as a Historic Monument, it's the last vestige of the palace of the lords of Termes, vassals of the Counts of Armagnac (late 13th century). Its most famous resident, Thibault de Termes, accompanied Joan of Arc at the siege of Orléans in 1429 and remained faithful to her until the end. From the summit, spectacular views of the Pyrenees.

Inside the Termes keep, climb the 150 steps of the spiral staircase. Reconstructed armory, seigneurial chamber, reception hall—each floor plunges into the life of a 13th-century Gascon palace. Children can duel with foam swords in a mini-arena above the weapons room.

Marciac, a royal bastide founded in 1298 through a paréage between the Abbot of Case-Dieu and the Seneschal of Toulouse, has preserved its grid plan intact. Its impressively vast central square is bordered by elegant arcades with imposing wooden pillars. This is where jazzy Gascony's heart beats.

Notre-Dame Church raises its bell tower above the terracotta rooftops. Its painted portal exemplifies southern Gothic. Nearby, the spire of the former Augustinian convent chapel recalls that Marciac also lies on the Arles route leading to Santiago de Compostela.

Les Territoires du Jazz offers a journey into the heart of the history of jazz. With infrared headphones on, walk through twelve sets: from the Africa of the origins to New Orleans, from feverish blues to New York clubs, all the way to Europe as a land of welcome for jazzmen.

L'Astrada, a modern performance hall inaugurated to extend the festival spirit year-round. Dance, circus, theater, classical music and of course jazz take turns here. The Augustins cultural center, arranged in the former convent, houses the tourist office and exhibitions.

activities.text: Visit the d'Artagnan Museum with activity booklet for children. Pencil in hand, young musketeers embark on an adventure through the rooms. Written guide available in six languages for adults.

Walk around Lake Lupiac, a few hundred yards from the village. Shaded trail, swimming possible in summer, fishing and picnic areas. The bucolic setting of Gascon hillsides lends itself to a peaceful break.

Medieval events at the tower of Termes in summer: jousting tournaments, costumed guided tours, medieval banquets. In August, the d'Artagnan chez d'Artagnan festival turns Lupiac into a seventeenth-century village.

Stroll beneath the medieval arcades of the central square. Terraces, shops and art galleries animate this bastide that has vibrated to the rhythm of jazz since 1978. In summer, the free off-festival takes over the square with impromptu concerts on every corner.

Walk around Lake Marciac, a third of a mile from the bastide. Created in 1963, this body of water offers jogging, fishing, paddle boats and swimming in summer. The landscape setting, ringed by hills, invites a pause between visits.

Tasting of Saint-Mont wines and armagnac. The Saint-Mont AOC vineyard holds a curiosity: the Sarragachies vine, dating from the early nineteenth century and listed as a Historic Monument, one of the oldest pre-phylloxera vines in France, with 21 grape varieties of which 7 are unidentified. About 30 km from the base town, 30 minutes by road.

Visit in summer for Jazz in Marciac (late July through mid-August). Created in 1978 by a handful of friends, the festival now attracts 250,000 spectators and the biggest names in world jazz. A 6,000-seat big top in the evenings, free concerts on the square during the day.

days_plan.itin_title: Gers Road Trip: Gascon Bastides, Armagnac & Musketeers
Gers Road Trip: Gascon Bastides, Armagnac & Musketeers

visits.text: Brouage, a citadel asleep in the marshes. Founded in 1555, it was Europe's leading salt port before silting up. Richelieu made it an impregnable stronghold between 1628 and 1633 under Pierre d'Argencourt, then Vauban reinforced the fortifications in 1685. Samuel de Champlain, founder of Quebec, was born here around 1570. Today, 500 inhabitants and an uncanny silence.

The Brouage rampart walk (2 km) offers views over former salt marshes turned into a bird reserve. Black-winged stilts, egrets and spoonbills nest here. The restored powder magazines, forge and church can be visited.

Marennes, oyster capital. The Marennes-Oléron basin produces 45% of French oysters. The Saint-Pierre church bell tower (85 m) is the tallest in Charente-Maritime. The Cité de l'Huître explains maturation in claires, brackish water ponds that turn the oysters green and refine their flavor.

activities.text: A visit to an oyster shack. Producers open their premises to explain oyster farming and maturation. Tasting on site with views of the claires—a glass of local white wine accompanies the oysters.
Walk in the Brouage marshes. Marked trails through former salt marshes. Binoculars recommended for watching migratory birds. The sunset over the pools is memorable.

days_plan.itin_title: Charente-Maritime Road Trip: La Rochelle, Île de Ré, Fort Boyard and Roman Saintonge

visits.text: The Margaux appellation is one of six commune-level Médoc appellations, renowned for its elegant and aromatic wines. The vineyards extend over 1,500 hectares across four communes: Margaux-Cantenac, Soussans, Arsac, and Labarde. The appellation has 21 growths classified in 1855, including the celebrated Château Margaux. The gravelly terroir (pebbles) brings finesse and complexity to the wines. Margaux village itself is small but charming.

The Maison du Vin et du Tourisme de Margaux welcomes you to explore the appellation. The exhibition area explains the terroir, vineyard history, and the 1855 classification. A selection of wines is available for tasting and purchase. Staff can advise you on châteaux to visit and help with reservations. It's the ideal starting point for planning your exploration of the vineyards.

The Margaux-Cantenac château loop is a 15 km route to walk or cycle. This waymarked trail crosses the vineyards past 18 of the appellation's 21 classified growths. You pass alongside prestigious estates such as Château Margaux, Château Palmer and Château Lascombes. The path offers fine views over the estuary and Île Margaux. Allow 2 hours by bike, 4 hours on foot, excluding stops for visits.

Saint-Michel Church in Margaux, built in the 19th century in neo-Romanesque style, stands in the village center. Its square bell tower is visible from afar across the flat Médoc landscape. The simple interior houses some interesting stained-glass windows. The forecourt opens onto the main village square where the market is held. It's a useful landmark for finding your way around Margaux.

activities.text: Visit and tasting at a Margaux château. The appellation offers a wide diversity of wine tourism experiences, from classified grands crus to more accessible family properties. Guided tours help you understand vineyard work, vinification, and barrel aging. Tastings reveal the elegance characteristic of Margaux wines. Reservations essential, sometimes several weeks in advance for the most prestigious estates.

Cycling through Margaux vineyards. The Médoc's flat terrain and quiet minor roads make cycling very pleasant. Several rental shops offer conventional or electric bikes. You can follow the château loop or create your own itinerary. The rows of vines stretching as far as the eye can see are magnificent. Plan breaks to admire châteaux and take photos.

Margaux Golf offers an 18-hole, 6,000-meter course spread over 45 hectares. Designed in a natural setting amid vineyards, it's renowned for its beauty and the quality of its maintenance. Greens are bordered by century-old elms and ash trees. The clubhouse offers views over the course and surrounding vineyards. On-site restaurant. Affordable green fees; reservations recommended.

Margaux Saveurs is an annual event of the appellation. Many châteaux open their doors for tastings, activities, concerts and gourmet meals. It is a festive and friendly way to discover the Margaux appellation from another angle. The program combines wine discoveries with a musical atmosphere. Tickets and bookings on the event website.

days_plan.itin_title: Gironde Circuit: Bordeaux, Vineyards & Arcachon Bay

visits.text: Lake Chalain is the largest natural lake in the Jura, nestled in a typical glacial recess framed by 60 to 80-meter limestone cliffs. Its 232 hectares, 2,700 meters in length and maximum depth of 30 meters make it a body of water of striking clarity — the blue-turquoise waters contrast sharply with the dark green forests that envelop it. To capture the full beauty of the lake in one glance, climb up to the Fontenu viewpoint on the north shore: the plunging view over the entire recess is considered one of the most beautiful in the Jura.

Beneath the waters of Lake Chalain lies an exceptional archaeological site, on the UNESCO World Heritage list since 2011. Stilt villages occupied these shores between 4000 and 750 BC, from the Neolithic to the Bronze Age. Excavations carried out since 1904 have yielded thousands of objects (tools, weapons, shoes, pottery) remarkably preserved by the lake sediments, along with a 9.35-metre dugout canoe hollowed from an oak trunk, precisely dated to 959 BC. All of this can be seen at the archaeological museum of Lons-le-Saunier, about 19 km from the stopover town, 29 minutes by road. The site itself is not open to visitors.

activities.text: Swimming in the turquoise waters of Lake Chalain: with its gently sloping developed beaches and water reaching 24°C in summer, Chalain is one of the most popular swimming spots in Franche-Comté. Motor navigation is prohibited — only non-motorized craft (canoe, kayak, sailing, stand-up paddle) are allowed, which preserves rare tranquility. Check access before you go: since the campsite closed in 2022, visits are now day-use only.

Sunset walk around Lake Ilay (4 Lakes site): from the hamlet of Ilay in La Chaux-du-Dombief, a trail follows the shores of this glacial lake nicknamed "Motte Lake" for the Neolithic island it contains. The shades of green and blue of the 4 lakes vary with the seasons and evening light — a spectacle that locals themselves call "Little Scotland." Swimming tolerated at Lake Ilay only (access at designated areas).

days_plan.itin_title: Jura Lakes Route: Emerald and Turquoise Waters

visits.text: Notre-Dame Church in Marmande, listed as a historic monument since 1862, is a fine example of southern Gothic architecture built between the 13th and 14th centuries. In 1672, lightning struck the bell tower, where the town’s consuls had foolishly stored its gunpowder reserves. The explosion destroyed the choir and shattered the bell tower. Only the copper cockerel from the original spire survived. Inside, do not miss the Entombment, the 17th-century Baroque altarpiece in gilded wood and the 19th-century organ by Cavaillé-Coll, a world-renowned organ builder.

Adjoining the church's south flank, the Renaissance Cloister bears the date 1540 carved at its north entrance. It's among the region's finest, with elegant arcades and balanced gallery proportions. Only the south galleries and part of the east gallery remain—the Wars of Religion between 1560 and 1569 destroyed the rest. A stroll under the arcades ranks among Marmande's most pleasant moments.

The Cloister Garden, laid out as a formal topiary garden in the 1950s, has held the Remarkable Garden label since 2007. Inspired by the gardens of the Château de Langeais, it features boxwood parterres and yews clipped into cones, spheres and pyramids around a central pool. It is a cool, peaceful space in the very centre of town, perfect for a midday break.

Stroll Rue Labat and its 16th-century half-timbered houses. These dwellings with overhanging upper stories testify to Marmande's Renaissance merchant prosperity. Richard the Lionheart had granted it a charter of customs as early as 1182, conferring privileged status on the Garonne's left bank.

On Place Clemenceau, look for the Pomme d’Amour statue, named after the local nickname for the tomato. Marmande has been France’s capital of the beefsteak tomato since the 19th century, when market gardeners from the Garonne plain popularised it throughout France. The Albert Marzelles Museum, awarded the Musée de France designation in 2002, presents exhibitions throughout the year.

activities.text: Walk around Marmande market to taste the famous local tomato: growers from the Garonne plain display their harvest from June to September. Red, ribbed and perfectly sweet, the Marmande tomato bears no comparison with industrial varieties. The market is held three times a week, early in the morning.

Follow the banks of the Garonne across the Plaine de la Filhole, the green meander west of the centre. The towpath runs alongside the river through poplars and willows, a walk of 3 to 5 km depending on how you feel, flat and easy.

Walk behind the church to find the remains of the Chemin de Ronde and the Tour du Passeur, the only surviving traces of Marmande’s medieval fortifications. These ruins frame a secluded municipal garden that few visitors discover.

days_plan.itin_title: Lot-et-Garonne Road Trip: Bastides and Villages

visits.text: Maroilles owes its name to the cheese—or vice versa. Maroilles PDO, a 13 cm square of soft cheese with an orange washed rind, was reportedly created around 960 in the Benedictine abbey founded in 652. A 7th-century ordinance already required peasants to turn their milk into cheese on 24 June and deliver it to the abbey a hundred days later.

The superbly restored abbey watermill spans the Helpe Mineure. Built in 1576, enlarged in 1634 and modified in 1770, it bears on its lintel the Latin motto of Abbot Frédéric d'Yves, diplomat and adviser to Philip II of Spain: “It is good to cling to God”.

The tithe barn, a massive brick-and-stone building where monks stored tithes in kind, now houses the visitor centre of the Parc naturel régional de l'Avesnois. A 200 m² interpretation centre covering the hedgerow landscape, fauna, flora and local produce.

The triumphal arch, erected in 1807 to glorify Napoleon's armies, incorporates elements from the portal of the abbey destroyed during the “Maroilles tumult” in 1789; these account for two-thirds of the arch. Saint-Humbert church, rebuilt in the 18th century, preserves the shrine containing the first abbot's relics.

The village streets are lined with pink-brick and blue-stone houses, former abbey residences and chapels typical of the Avesnois. The Frère-Portier building (no. 32 Grand-Rue) has become the tourist office; the town hall occupies the former aldermen's hall of 1704.

activities.text: Visit Cerfmont farm, the last farm producing Maroilles in the municipality, or the Leduc cellars (2,200 m², 55 m visitor corridor) to follow the production and maturation of the PDO cheese. Tasting flamiche au Maroilles is a must.

The flamiche and Maroilles festival, on the Sunday before 15 August, is the village's flagship event. Outside the season, the Caves de l'Abbaye (a walkers' café) and the France Terroir shop offer tastings throughout the year.

The hedgerow landscape of the Avesnois can be explored on foot or by bike from Maroilles: hawthorn hedges, meadows along the Helpe Mineure, wayside shrines and chapels. The signposted Parcours des Sens crosses a landscape of green pastures reminiscent of Normandy.

days_plan.itin_title: Opal Coast Villages and Flemish Heartlands

visits.text: Start with La Bonne Mère—that's what locals call Notre-Dame-de-la-Garde, and it's the first thing you should do upon arrival. Perched at 154 meters atop a limestone outcrop, this Romano-Byzantine basilica consecrated in 1864 dominates everything. The gilded statue of the Virgin at the summit measures 11.20 meters and weighs nearly 10 tons—it was crafted by the Christofle house and requires regilding every 25 years. Inside, the walls are covered with 1,200 m² of gold-backed mosaics and sailors' ex-votos: suspended ship models, thank-you plaques, and naïve paintings. Go up in the morning for the light and avoid weekends.

Head back down to the Old Port and climb up into Le Panier district, Marseille's oldest neighborhood—this is where Greek settlers from Phocaea landed 2,600 years ago. Today, narrow alleys are covered in street art, hidden squares shelter artists' workshops and improvised terraces. Don't look for a precise route: get lost, that's the whole point. Place des Moulins, the district's highest point, makes a good landmark if you lose your bearings.

Leaving Le Panier toward the sea, you'll encounter La Major cathedral. Built between 1852 and 1893 in neo-Byzantine style, it's massive—142 meters long, the largest religious building constructed in France during the 19th century. The contrast between white Carrara marble and green Florence stone gives it a striking striped appearance. Glance inside at the choir mosaics, then exit on the sea side for views over the port of La Joliette.

End the day with a stroll along the Old Port. It's been Marseille's beating heart for 26 centuries. In the morning, the fish market on quai des Belges is a spectacle—fishermen sell their catch directly from boats, shouting in Provençal. By late afternoon, the terraces take over. The Vieux-Port ombrière, Norman Foster's immense polished steel structure, acts as a mirror reflecting the crowds—it's become one of modern Marseille's symbols.

Devote the morning to MuCEM—this concrete cube wrapped in an openwork lattice facing the sea was designed by Rudy Ricciotti. Opened in 2013 when Marseille was European Capital of Culture, it entered the world's 50 most visited museums the following year. Collections cover anthropology, archaeology, and contemporary art around the Mediterranean. Even if exhibitions don't appeal, head to the rooftop terrace: the view over the Old Port and the open sea is free and spectacular.

Cross the 130-meter footbridge linking MuCEM to Fort Saint-Jean—suspended above the harbor basin, it offers a vertiginous view of the sea. The fort, built on Louis XIV's orders from 1668 onward, dominates the Old Port entrance from its 20-meter height. It served as much to protect Marseille as to watch over it—cannons were aimed at the city in case of revolt. Free entry, it houses the Garden of Migrations, a 12,000 m² Mediterranean botanical space with lavender, rosemary, and orange trees. Look for the Fanal tower (17th century) that served as a lighthouse and King René's tower (15th century), whose terrace offers plunging views over the port.

Return landward via the second footbridge leading directly into Le Panier district. Take rue du Petit-Puits to La Vieille Charité, a former 17th-century hospice built by Pierre Puget around an arcaded courtyard and oval chapel. Today, the building houses the Museum of Mediterranean Archaeology and the Museum of African, Oceanic, and American Indian Arts. Even without entering the museums, the courtyard is magnificent and free.

activities.text: Walk up to Notre-Dame-de-la-Garde on foot from the Old Port via Saint-Victor Abbey—one of France's oldest, founded in the 5th century, with crypts and early Christian sarcophagi. Allow 30 minutes uphill. Alternatively, bus 60 departs from the Old Port and drops you at the basilica's foot.

Late afternoon, walk along Corniche Kennedy heading south. It's a 25-minute walk from the Old Port to reach Vallon des Auffes, a tiny fishing harbor wedged between two concrete cliffs. This is postcard Marseille, with colorful pointus (traditional boats) and little bouillabaisse restaurants. The spot is perfect for an aperitif facing the sunset.

If you enjoy contemporary art and alternative spaces, make a detour to Friche Belle de Mai—a former tobacco factory converted into a 45,000 m² cultural center. Galleries, artists' studios, concert hall, rooftop skatepark, restaurants. This is creative Marseille, far from tourist circuits. Take bus 49 from the Old Port.

In the late afternoon, head down to the Prado beaches or the Escale Borély for a seaside stroll. Parc Borély is a large green space in Marseille, with its 18th-century château, its botanical garden and its lake. The atmosphere is relaxed - joggers, families, pétanque players. Have a drink on a terrace facing the sea before heading to Cassis the next day.

From Marseille to Aix-en-Provence: Calanques, Hilltop Villages and Provençal Light

The Grand Tour of France in 5 Weeks, Car-Free

visits.text: Martel, the "Town of Seven Towers," is listed among France's Most Beautiful Villages. A merchant city founded in the 11th–12th centuries by the viscounts of Turenne, it has preserved its intact medieval layout encircled by 12th–14th-century ramparts.
Place des Consuls forms Martel's beating heart. An 18th-century market hall shelters stalls beneath stone pillars. All around, half-timbered houses and arcaded dwellings compose a preserved setting.

The Palais de la Raymondie, built between 1280 and 1330, raises its square tower above the square. The former seigneurial residence houses the Uxellodunum Museum—Gallo-Roman collections and Quercy history. Designated a Museum of France.

The fortified Church of Saint-Maur impresses with its 40-meter bell tower-keep built for defense. A carved 12th-century tympanum adorns the portal. Inside, entirely painted decoration, surprisingly colorful, contrasts with the facade's austerity.

Spot the seven towers that gave the town its nickname. The 13th-century Tour Tournemire, a former prison, offers panoramic views from its summit. The Tour des Cordeliers is the sole remnant of a Franciscan monastery founded in 1230. The Maison Fabri recalls a dark episode: here a young Anglo-Norman king allegedly breathed his last after pillaging Rocamadour.

activities.text: The Truffadou tourist train follows the former Bordeaux-Aurillac line carved into the cliff 80 meters above the Dordogne. The 13-kilometer route between Martel and Saint-Denis offers plunging views of the valley from open wagons.
Browse Martel's market on Wednesday and Saturday mornings beneath the 18th-century hall. Seasonal truffles, walnuts, Quercy terroir products, and local specialties.
Visit a traditional walnut oil mill near Martel. Périgord walnuts, with AOC designation, are pressed using artisanal methods. Tastings and on-site sales.

days_plan.itin_title: Lot Itinerary: Cahors, Rocamadour & the Lot Valley

visits.text: The Miroir aux Oiseaux, listed since 1942, is a tiny spot: a stretch of water bordered by ochre and pink fishermen's houses, south of the Île quarter. The pointu boats moored at the foot of the façades make the scene. Come early in the morning, when the water is flat and the terraces empty.

Opened in 1908, the Musée Ziem holds more than 8,000 works in a former customs barracks in Martigues: Ziem canvases, works from the Marseille school, Fauvist landscapes, archaeological collections. Free entry, closed Tuesdays.

The people of Martigues call it the Venice of Provence without irony: the Canal Saint-Sébastien, one of the town's three canals, cuts through the Île quarter between two rows of coloured façades. You can stroll without a map, taking turns at random. Car parks on the outskirts, as the centre is narrow.

activities.text: If you are here in summer, the Miroir aux Oiseaux turns into a milonga dance floor: tango on the quays in July and August. Free, with a village atmosphere. The Flâneries au Miroir, featuring Venetian costumes, take over in September.

Take advantage of everything being free at the Musée Ziem: permanent collections, temporary exhibitions, lectures and concerts are open to all, without a ticket. The programme changes throughout the year, so check it before coming.

days_plan.itin_title: Côte Bleue and Camargue: the lower coastal route in 7 days

visits.text: Hard to find older roots: Pape Clément's vineyards date back to 1300, when Bertrand de Got—future Pope Clement V—bequeathed the estate to the Archbishopric of Bordeaux. Seven centuries later, it's still a Graves Cru Classé, one of the rare high-quality reds from the left bank outside the Médoc. What surprises inside: ultra-modern cellars carved into limestone, in total contrast with the 18th-century facade. Paid visit, booking on the website.

Two former ski champions buy a Bordeaux château in 1990 and turn it into one of Pessac-Léognan's most sought-after estates—sounds like the start of a joke, but Smith Haut Lafitte is very real. Daniel and Florence Cathiard invested heavily: cedar cellars (extremely rare in Bordeaux), five-star hotel, Caudalie vinotherapy spa. The result in both red and white holds its own against the appellation's finest. The shop sells futures directly—interesting opportunity.

If Bordeaux rhymes with red in the collective consciousness, Domaine de Chevalier is here to correct the error: it produces one of France's greatest dry white wines, barrel-aged Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon, in an appellation—Pessac-Léognan—that most wine lovers don't cite spontaneously. The visit is understated, the cellars functional. It's the right place to understand that Bordeaux doesn't only make red.

activities.text: Getting wrapped in grape marc or soaking in a barrel bath—that's the concept Mathilde Cathiard launched here in 1999 under the name vinotherapy. Kitschy, but the experience is genuine—and the Sources de Caudalie spa, with its grape polyphenol treatments, is now copied in about ten countries. Here, it's the original. Book treatments when you book the room: they sell out before rooms do.

Ask the sommelier at Sources de Caudalie to arrange a comparative red/white tasting in Pessac-Léognan. The exercise is particularly revealing here: Haut-Brion, Smith Haut Lafitte, Domaine de Chevalier excel in both colors—an almost unique case worldwide. An hour is enough to leave with a far more nuanced vision of Bordeaux than you arrived with.

days_plan.itin_title: Bordeaux in 7 Days: Médoc, Saint-Émilion, and Sauternes

places.name: Mas Du Pont De Rousty

visits.text: The Musée de la Camargue has occupied the sheepfold of the Mas du Pont de Rousty, on the road to Saintes-Maries, since 1978. Renovated in 2013 beneath its original roof timbers, it presents the permanent exhibition “Le fil de l'eau, le fil du temps”. It's the best introduction before exploring the delta. Allow an hour.

activities.text: Follow your museum visit with the Pont de Rousty discovery trail: it runs along the canal and rice fields to the marsh, passing a reed-thatched hut and an observatory. Free access, around an hour and a half. Tadashi Kawamata's work Horizons marks the start.

If you come between November and March, the Musée de la Camargue only opens Monday to Friday outside school holidays. From April to September, it opens every day from 9am to 6pm, and every day from 10am to 5pm in October. Check before travelling the 10 km from Arles.

days_plan.itin_title: Côte Bleue and Camargue: the lower coastal route in 7 days
