visits.text: Massat, a Couserans mountain village, climbs at the foot of peaks over 2,000 meters, with stone houses under slate roofs and a slender Gothic bell tower surprising for a town this size. A quiet, authentic stop, it's the gateway to several wild passes and valleys. A peaceful nature halt to close your journey far from the crowds.

Above Massat, the Col de Port (1,249 m) links Couserans to the Ariège Valley: a passage used since Roman times, between Atlantic slope and Mediterranean slope. From the pass, the panorama opens over both Pyrenean flanks. Cyclists know it well; hikers use it as a starting point. Quick car stop, or springboard for a walk.

activities.text: For a final big hike, the Pic des Trois Seigneurs (2,199 m) is reached from valleys around Massat: climb through fir forests then panoramic ridges over the frontier chain, chamois and marmots included. Demanding full-day outing, reserved for fit hikers and stable good weather. Early start, water, and windbreaker essential.

Nature detour toward Aulus-les-Bains in the neighboring valley for the Cascade d'Ars, one of the Pyrenees' tallest waterfalls: a three-tier drop at the end of a forest trail. Allow about 3 hours round trip from Aulus, moderate difficulty, in a setting of forest and torrent. Do it if you have half a day and the desire for a beautiful refreshing walk.

days_plan.itin_title: Ariège Road Trip: Cathars and Prehistoric Caves

visits.text: Vauban's fortifications still encircle Maubeuge along two-thirds of their original layout. Erected in record time from 1679 to 1685 on Louis XIV's orders, they transformed the city into a sentinel of the Pré Carré, that line of strongholds protecting the kingdom's northern frontier.

The Porte de Mons, classified as a Historic Monument since 1924, is the rampart's last intact gate. Built in 1682, this monumental gate preserves its complete defensive complex: drawbridge, guardhouse and ravelin.

The Corps de Garde Museum occupies a building erected in 1683 following Vauban's directives. Beneath its old timber roof structure, it traces Maubeuge's military history. On the ground floor, a 19th-century relief model clarifies the fortifications' geometry.

Saint-Pierre-Saint-Paul Church, erected between 1955 and 1958, is built entirely of reinforced concrete. Its 43-metre bell tower, pierced with glass bricks, houses a 28-bell carillon. The tympanum is adorned with a mosaic designed by Jean Lurçat, brother of architect André Lurçat.

The Salle Sthrau, listed as a Historic Monument since 1958, is a unique Art Deco ensemble housed within a former baroque chapel of the Jesuit college. Rebuilt between 1923 and 1927, it comprises a two-level music hall with characteristic geometric decoration.

Maubeuge was 80% destroyed in 1940. André Lurçat, charged with reconstruction, designed a city centre of remarkable modernist uniformity: concrete and brick buildings, spacious vistas, green spaces integrated into the ramparts. Architecture that still divides opinion but leaves no one indifferent.

activities.text: Maubeuge Zoo occupies 7 hectares within Vauban's very ramparts. Tour the bastions while observing over 300 animals of 60 species, in a setting where the fortifications' moats and embankments serve as natural enclosures.

Walk along the Monier ponds southeast of the fortifications. Set against the rampart, these former defensive basins bordered by willows now form a peaceful haven popular with walkers and anglers, a few steps from the city centre.

Follow the fortifications' covered way from Porte de Mons to the Oratoire bastion. Artillery access ramps, embrasures and casemates punctuate the route—you can imagine horses pulling cannons to firing platforms.

days_plan.itin_title: Nord Tour: Lille, Belfries and Flemish Culture

visits.text: The Basilique Notre-Dame-des-Miracles rises at the heart of Mauriac, a sanctuary founded in the 6th century by Théodechilde, daughter of Clovis. The carved 12th-century Romanesque portal hints at the majesty of the building. Inside, the Gothic choir and the relics of Saint Marius (an evangelising disciple whose name is said to have inspired “Puy Mary”) bear witness to the age-old religious influence of this town between the Dordogne and the Cantal mountains.

The old town retains the charm of Auvergne towns with its bourgeois houses, small shaded squares and volcanic stone façades. Stroll through the lanes climbing towards the basilica, discover the local shops and the peaceful atmosphere of this Cantal sub-prefecture with its preserved character.

activities.text: The weekly market brings the central square to life in a bustle of colours and flavours. Farm producers, market gardeners and artisans offer aged cheeses, local cured meats, sourdough breads and seasonal vegetables. The perfect opportunity to meet passionate livestock farmers and taste Cantal's authenticity.

The outing to the Château d'Anjony requires a return trip during the day from Mauriac. It reveals one of the most beautiful castles in the Cantal, a medieval fortress from the 15th century overlooking the Doire valley. Its four corner towers frame a remarkable square keep. The chapel's Renaissance frescoes and the wall paintings in the apartments are exceptional artistic treasures in this austere military setting.

days_plan.itin_title: Cantal Road Trip: Auvergne Volcanoes and Mountain Traditions

visits.text: Maussane-les-Alpilles is the olive-growing heart of the Baux Valley — its cooperative mill processes olives from several hundred members to produce a PDO oil recognized among France's finest. Several local varieties enter the blend: Aglandau (also called Beruguette), Grossane, Salonenque, and Verdale des Bouches-du-Rhône. Providers offer visits and tastings — a gustatory experience differentiating the two typicities (fruity green and fruity black) that the valley's millers passionately defend.

Maussane's central square with its fountain and southern facades is the quintessential Provençal village image: café terraces under plane trees, local merchants, tractors crossing the town. It's also one of the rare Alpilles squares not overrun by tourist shops. Settle on a terrace and observe.

activities.text: Olive grove-vineyard walk on agricultural tracks: from Maussane center, unpaved rural paths wind between olive groves and plots of PDO Les Baux-de-Provence vines. Morning light on century-old olive trees is remarkable. Allow 2 hours for a 7 km loop.

Oil mill visit (according to opening): several artisanal and cooperative mills in the valley welcome visitors, especially during extraction season (November-January). Outside the season, guided tours explain the process from olive to oil, from manual harvest (November) to cold pressing.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpilles, Aix-en-Provence & Arles Circuit

visits.text: Mayenne Castle overlooks the river of the same name. Over 1,100 years old, it houses Europe's best-preserved Carolingian palace, classified as an archaeological site of national interest. The reception hall, cellar and residential tower are still legible in the masonry.

The museum, labeled Museum of France and starred in the Michelin Green Guide, traces 2,000 years of history through an interactive journey. The collections from excavations are exceptional: chess and backgammon pieces from the 10th-12th centuries, ceramics, coins, arrowheads and funerary furnishings testifying to the life of Mayenne's lords.

In the upper courtyard, a medieval-inspired garden has been recreated from period documents. Plants and shrubs are classified as in the Middle Ages: simples, aromatics, edibles, medicinals or 'magical' plants.

The Basilica of Notre-Dame-des-Miracles, on the right bank, is a composite edifice from the 12th, 16th and 19th centuries. The west façade is original Romanesque (circa 1110). The 19th-century choir draws inspiration from Le Mans Cathedral's chevet. A chapel houses the 15th-century polychrome wooden statuette of Our Lady of Miracles.

The basilica's current stained glass windows, designed by Maurice Rocher and installed between 1952 and 1962, replaced those destroyed during the June 1944 bombings that devastated the town. The basilica remained closed for thirteen years for restoration.

Stroll through Place de Hercé with its octagonal fountain, then reach Place Cheverus surrounded by 17th-18th century townhouses. On the left bank, the 11th-century Saint-Martin church stands out with its russet granite.
The Calvary Sisters Chapel, last vestige of a vast 17th-century convent, now houses an art center devoted to contemporary creation.

activities.text: Walk along the Mayenne quays for a riverside stroll. The castle park, right in the town center, offers a bandstand, towering trees and a stunning view from the ramparts.

Drive 5 km to Fontaine-Daniel, a village of character nestled in a clearing in the Salair woods. Founded around a Cistercian abbey in 1205, it became the birthplace of Toiles de Mayenne in 1806 when the abandoned abbey was transformed into a spinning mill. The factory, labeled Living Heritage Company, still weaves on site.
In season, board the pleasure boat departing from the river stop for a narrated cruise on the Mayenne River. Wildlife, flora, local history and manual lock operation on the program.

days_plan.itin_title: Mayenne Circuit: Hedgerows and Medieval Towns

places.name: Mazamet

visits.text: Hautpoul clings to its rocky outcrop, 300 meters above Mazamet. According to legend, this village was founded in 413 by a Visigothic king. Once a Cathar refuge and later a Protestant stronghold, the village retains remnants of medieval fortifications along its steep streets.

Climb to the Rocher de la Vierge and the old castle terraces for an exceptional panorama over the Arnette valley and Mazamet below. The neighboring medieval garden displays medicinal plants and plants used for dyeing during that period.
The Maison du Bois et du Jouet offers more than 1,500 m² of exhibitions on the journey from forest to tree, tree to wood, and wood to toy. Children and adults alike linger here.

On the way back down toward Mazamet, the Jardins Cormouls Houlès, dating from the mid-19th century, offer a spectacular botanical trail overlooking the valley, punctuated by viewpoints toward the Montagne Noire.

Follow the self-guided heritage routes in Mazamet, which has the “100 Plus Beaux Détours de France” label. The architecture tells of the era when the city was the world center for processing wool imported from Australia and Argentina.

activities.text: Cross the Mazamet footbridge, suspended 70 meters above the Arnette valley. 140 meters long, it sways gently underfoot and connects the town to Hautpoul village. Free and open daily.
Take the Jamarié path, a former salt road and Roman road, to reach the footbridge via a route steeped in history. You can return along a different trail to complete a loop.
In the evening, return to admire the illuminated footbridge: each night it lights up in changing colors until 2 a.m., creating a luminous spectacle above the gorges.

days_plan.itin_title: Tarn Road Trip: Albi & Hilltop Villages

map_keywords: Maison du Bois et du Jouet Mazamet

places.name: Meaudre

visits.text: Méaudre is one of the "Four Villages" of the northern Vercors plateau, with its aligned chalets, gallery farms, and grassy squares. Autrans and Méaudre have now merged into a new commune. The village is distinguished in winter by its Narces Nordic domain, 300 meters above the village, and its biathlon stadium. In summer, the flowering meadows surrounding the village are the typical Vercors image between hay and firs.

The church and gallery farms in Méaudre's center constitute the essential heritage elements. The covered wooden galleries served to store hay and shelter animals—functional architecture adapted to 1,000 meters altitude.

activities.text: The gentle valley-floor loop between Méaudre and Autrans (5-7 km, flat) follows the plain connecting the two villages. In summer, it's a walk through meadows with views of wooded ridges on both sides. In winter, it's the Nordic traverse route, one of the classics of the 180 km trail network.

The short forest-edge climb to the Gève plateau from Autrans (30-minute drive from Méaudre, then hike) offers a panorama of the entire Alps chain in clear weather. This is the site that hosted the Olympic cross-country skiing events in 1968, on the domain's legendary yellow trail.

days_plan.itin_title: Royans-Vercors Road Trip: Hilltop Villages and Gorges

map_keywords: Foyer de ski de fond Méaudre

visits.text: The Saint-Étienne Cathedral of Meaux, begun around 1175, displays four centuries of Gothic styles layered: classical, rayonnant, and flamboyant. Five richly sculpted portals frame a central tympanum depicting the Last Judgment. The vaults reach 33 meters.

Inside, look for the 14th-century Crucifixion stained glass window above the choir, the great 15th-century rose window, and Bossuet's tomb—the famous 17th-century bishop and orator nicknamed "the Eagle of Meaux".

The Bossuet Museum occupies the former episcopal palace, built from the 12th to 17th centuries. Its vaulted rooms house a collection of 17th and 18th-century paintings. Wood paneling, paved ramp, and garden views make the site remarkable.

The Bossuet Garden, attributed to Le Nôtre, extends over 8,500 square meters in the shape of an episcopal mitre. Boxwood parterres, a pool, centuries-old linden trees, and views of the Gallo-Roman ramparts make it one of the finest formal gardens in Île-de-France.

The Museum of the Great War of the Pays de Meaux, inaugurated in 2011, is one of the largest museums dedicated to World War I in Europe. It stands on the very spot where the German advance was halted in September 1914.

The Gallo-Roman ramparts, erected in the late 3rd century, line the Boulevard Jean Rose for 250 meters. Their brick chains alternating with small stone courses are characteristic of late Roman architecture.

activities.text: Visit the Maison du Brie de Meaux for a discovery tour: from milk collection to a recreated 19th-century aging cellar. The visit concludes with a tasting of the "king of cheeses".
Walk along the Marne and Ourcq Canal. The Parc naturel du Pâtis, one of the largest urban parks in Île-de-France, offers hiking trails, lakes, and birdwatching.
In summer, the Grand Spectacle historique de Meaux brings together over 500 costumed actors to retrace the town's history outdoors.

days_plan.itin_title: Seine-et-Marne Circuit: Fontainebleau and Châteaux

visits.text: Accessible by gondola, this calvary stands at 1,840 meters on Mont d'Arbois. It offers an exceptional 360° viewpoint over the Mont Blanc massif, whose summit at 4,809 meters can be clearly made out.

The chicest resort in the French Alps, Megève has preserved its soul as a Savoyard village. The center gathers superb wooden chalets with flower-filled balconies and excellent gastronomic restaurants.

activities.text: Set off to discover the flowering Alpine pastures surrounding Megève. Several trails climb gently through meadows and forests. The mountain farms offer Beaufort, Tomme de Savoie, and Reblochon.
Stroll the cobbled lanes dotted with elegant boutiques. Discover Savoyard specialties in the fine grocery shops: mountain charcuterie, aged Alpine cheeses, and artisan honeys.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Savoie Road Trip: Alpine Lakes & Mont Blanc

visits.text: Mehun-sur-Yèvre Castle was King Charles VII's favoured residence during his reign at Bourges. It was here, on 29 December 1429, that he received Joan of Arc to grant her letters of nobility. Before him, Duke John of Berry had transformed the 9th-century defensive castle into a princely residence. Only romantic ruins remain — lightning, a fire and the Revolution accounted for the rest — but the night tour on 14 August recreates the medieval atmosphere with jousts and musicians.

The Porte de l'Horloge (1219) is the finest surviving remnant of the medieval ramparts. Three successive archways topped by a watch chamber, converted to a prison during the Revolution. The bell cast in 1394 at Duke John of Berry's request still tolls the hours. From here, you can see the silhouette of the ruined castle on the hill.

The Pôle de la Porcelaine traces the story of Berry's “white gold”. Exceptional collections from the Pillivuyt manufactory, which won numerous awards at 19th-century world's fairs. An exhibition display explains how kaolin is transformed into fine porcelain. Each year, a temporary exhibition highlights local artistic crafts.

The Pillivuyt factory has produced porcelain cookware and tableware since 1818. It is one of the few in France to control the entire process: mold making, preparing the porcelain body, firing and decoration. At the factory shop in Mehun-sur-Yèvre, you can discover its porcelain plates and dishes. Tours of the production workshops are temporarily suspended.

activities.text: The Berry Canal runs alongside Mehun for several kilometres. Completed in 1830, it enabled porcelain manufactories to flourish before being decommissioned in 1955. Today, its shaded banks delight walkers and cyclists. A quiet alternative to La Loire à Vélo.

The Venetian Carnival in Mehun (spring): 140 costumed participants wander through the streets and castle gardens. Venetian masks, studied poses, photographers on the lookout. A strange journey to Venice in the heart of Berry.

days_plan.itin_title: Cher Loop: Romanesque Berry and the Route Jacques-Cœur

visits.text: The Notre-Dame-et-Saint-Privat Cathedral dominates Mende with its two uneven bell towers. Founded in 1368 at the request of Pope Urban V, a native of the Gévaudan, it housed the Non-Pareille, the largest bell in Christendom in 1516. Only its clapper remains, displayed at the foot of the organ.

Step into the Musée du Gévaudan, spread over 1,200 m² and three floors. Its twelve rooms present more than 500 objects, from prehistory to the present day, around two themes: Nature and Culture. The legend of the Beast of Gévaudan is documented here with real rigour.
The Pont Notre-Dame, medieval in origin, spans the Lot upstream from the centre. The houses along the water have roofs shaped like an upturned boat hull, characteristic of Mende's architecture.
The Tour des Pénitents is the last remnant of the medieval ramparts. From its top, the view takes in the lauze stone roofs of the old town and the cathedral's two bell towers.

Head to the pharmacy of the former hospital, built between the 17th and 19th centuries. Its walnut furniture and apothecary objects make it one of the ten finest historic pharmacies in France. Accessible by guided tour only.

The cobbled lanes of the historic centre are best discovered along the heritage trail marked by 28 posts. Old doorways, fountains on small squares, an 18th-century town hall with a lauze stone roof: a free leaflet is available at the Tourist Office.

activities.text: Climb Mont Mimat to the summit cross. The orientation table offers a complete panorama: Mende at your feet, the Margeride mountains to the north, the Mende causse plateau to the south. Best at sunset.
Craving thrills? Mende's via ferrata features routes for all levels on cliffs above town. Suspension bridges, ladders, and a zipline punctuate the course.

days_plan.itin_title: Lozère Circuit: Tarn Gorges and Cévennes

visits.text: A guardhouse wedged between two granite blocks that serve as its walls: Meneham, in the commune of Kerlouan, resembles no other Breton village. The lookout post dates to 1756, built to monitor the coast and later smuggling; the surrounding thatched cottages were built in the 19th century for customs officers, then occupied by farmers who also gathered seaweed. After falling into ruin, the hamlet was restored between 2004 and 2009. The site is freely accessible year-round at no charge.

At Meneham, the farmer's house, fisherman's house, and stonemason's workshop have understated displays telling the story of life in Pays Pagan, divided between land and sea. Hour-long guided tours are offered, plus a storytelling version at nightfall centered on legends of wreckers. An inn housed in a thatched cottage serves lunch. Limited hours outside school vacations.

activities.text: The wild beaches of Kerlouan around Meneham offer white sand and protected dunes, with few people on weekdays outside July and August. Swimming calls for caution; the currents are not marked anywhere. Bring something to drink.

days_plan.itin_title: Brittany 7 days: Pink Granite, Lighthouses & Peninsulas

places.name: Menerbes

visits.text: Ménerbes is one of the most evocative villages in the Luberon: a long rocky spur resembling a stone ship resting on the garrigue, it has remained in the world's imagination thanks to Peter Mayle, who wrote A Year in Provence there in 1989. But before Mayle, there was Picasso — who owned a house there — and Dora Maar, his photographer muse. As you wander through the lanes, you will still find the Maison Dora Maar, a beautiful 18th-century residence that has become an artists' residency and is open for visits on Tuesdays and Saturdays.

The Maison de la Truffe et du Vin du Luberon has occupied the Hôtel d'Astier de Montfaucon since 2004, a 17th-century building classified as a Historic Monument on the Place de l'Horloge. You'll discover over 170 wine references from the Luberon appellation, sold at estate prices, and a shop specializing in truffle products. If you're here in winter, the small black truffle market (tuber melanosporum) on the last Sunday of December is an event in itself.

The Tour de l'Horloge and the belfry of Ménerbes date from the 15th century. From the vaulted passage beside it, a view opens onto the plain and the neighbouring villages. Below the village on the road to Bonnieux, the Dolmen de la Pitchoune bears witness to human occupation since the Neolithic.

activities.text: Loop walk along the viewpoints on the northern slope — views over the Petit Luberon and the Calavon plain.

Descent toward the wine terraces at the foot of the village. The Côtes du Luberon appellation produces typical red and rosé wines here, and some estates welcome visitors for tastings. Call ahead before stopping by.

days_plan.itin_title: The 15 Most Beautiful Villages of the Luberon

map_keywords: Maison de la Truffe et du Vin Ménerbes

visits.text: An ochre and yellow facade with asymmetric bell towers, a forecourt paved with black and white pebbles forming the Grimaldi coat of arms: Saint-Michel-Archange Basilica is Menton's most photographed sight. Its construction began in 1639 at the instigation of Honoré II of Monaco, who wanted to make it the jewel of his future capital. The forecourt was redone in 2006 with 250,000 pebbles laid one by one. Inside, gilding, polychrome marble and a 19th-century Italian organ in pure Nice Baroque style.

Get lost in Old Menton: cobbled streets climbing toward the basilica, pastel facades pressed against each other, turquoise and pale yellow shutters. The architecture recalls Ligurian villages—Ventimiglia is only 8 km away, and you can really feel Italy beginning in the air. Flaubert stopped here and noted: “Menton. Italy begins, you feel it in the air.” The Chapelle des Pénitents Blancs, a second Baroque jewel, deserves a stop.

The Cocteau Bastion Museum: the large Wunderman museum designed by Rudy Ricciotti has been closed since the 2018 floods (Storm Adrian), but the Bastion—a small 17th-century fortress standing on the seafront—remains open. Cocteau chose it in 1957 to exhibit his works during his lifetime and decorated it himself. Some of the 1,800 works from the Wunderman donation are displayed on rotation, with additional displays at the Palais de l'Europe. Admission €5.

The Val Rahmeh Botanical Garden, managed by the National Museum of Natural History since 1967, features 1,700 species over 1.5 hectares. Awarded the “Jardin remarquable” label, it houses a specimen of Sophora toromiro, a tree native to Easter Island that no longer exists in the wild—Val Rahmeh is one of the only sites in the world to conserve it outside major botanical collections (Kew Gardens, Gothenburg). In summer, giant Amazonian water lilies cover the pool. Closed Tuesdays. Admission €7.

Serre de la Madone is a secluded garden above Menton: created between 1924 and 1939 by the British major Lawrence Johnston (the creator of Hidcote Manor in England), it is one of the Riviera's most refined botanical gardens. Terraced pools, rare plants brought back from expeditions to Yunnan and South Africa, a meditative atmosphere. Less visited than Val Rahmeh, richer for botany enthusiasts.

Climb to the Vieux-Château cemetery: terraces stacked on the rocky promontory, exceptional view over the ochre roofs and Mediterranean. Here rests William Webb Ellis, the inventor of rugby, who died in Menton in 1872—his tomb has become a pilgrimage site for rugby fans. Alongside, dozens of Grand Tour travelers who came to die gently under the sun.

activities.text: The Halles market, beneath its Belle Époque structure dating from 1898, is one of the liveliest covered markets on the Côte d'Azur. Menton lemons in all their forms (jams, limoncello, soaps), truffle tapenades, olive oil from the hinterland, Italian cheeses - the border is 8 km away. Every morning.

If you're there between mid-February and early March: the Fête du Citron transforms the Biovès gardens into citrus madness—floats made of oranges and lemons (around 145 tonnes of citrus fruit used each year), processions, entertainment. Created in 1934, listed as part of France's intangible heritage in 2019. 200,000 visitors over 15 days. Book your hotel well in advance.

Promenade du Soleil: 1.5 km along the seafront between the beach and palm trees, perfect for a walk late in the day. Menton is one of France's sunniest cities thanks to its location in a basin sheltered from the wind.

Menton lemon tart on a terrace: local pastry-making works with lemon to achieve a fruity intensity that ordinary lemons cannot match. Served with an ice-cold limoncello, it is a Menton afternoon ritual. Maison Au Baiser du Mitron (rue Saint-Michel) has been a benchmark since 1965.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpes-Maritimes Road Trip: Riviera and Mercantour, 13 days
The 15 Gems of the French Riviera and Backcountry
7-Day French Riviera Circuit: Villefranche to Antibes
French Riviera Art Museums and Galleries: An 8-Day Journey

visits.text: Your first encounter with highland Ariège takes place in Merens-les-Vals, cradle of the Merens horse: small, jet-black, indestructible, and present in these valleys for millennia. In summer, you'll spot them roaming free across the high pastures. They're the local pride and a postcard subject in their own right. Ask local breeders where to observe them depending on the season.

Above the old village, sulfurous hot springs bubble up in the wild and feed stone basins with free open access, facing the peaks. Nothing monumental or manicured: this is the hikers' wild bath, a few minutes' walk from the road. Nearby stand the ruins of the Romanesque church of Saint-Pierre, a remnant of the Merens that existed before the fire of 1811. Pack swimsuit and towel.

activities.text: Merens is a gateway to the high mountains, a stone's throw from Andorra and on the route of the GR10 long-distance trail. Paths climb through pine forests before opening onto glacial cirques dotted with mountain lakes. Chamois watch hikers from the ridges. Allow 3 to 5 hours depending on which lake you're aiming for, 8 to 12 km, moderate difficulty, and June through September only (snow lingers late up here).

days_plan.itin_title: Ariège Road Trip: Cathars and Prehistoric Caves

visits.text: Acquired in 1784 by the Marquis de Laborde, this estate was transformed into a picturesque garden by Hubert Robert. The Juine River was diverted to create islands, meanders, and lakes.
The neoclassical château from the 13th and 15th centuries overlooks artificial rock formations. It occupies pride of place in the composition of this Anglo-Chinese park.
The Pont aux Boules d'Or by Jean-Michel Othoniel has spanned the Juine since 2023. Four large golden spheres and three thousand mirrored beads reinterpret the 18th-century work.
Picturesque ruins dot the park: artificial grottoes, remnants of bridges, and spectacular rock formations. Châteaubriand called this place a romantic oasis.
The 33-meter Tour Trajane was built between 1790 and 1792 by masons from Limousin. It was used to measure the Earth's meridian as early as 1793.

activities.text: Explore the 90-hectare park, designated a historic monument. Seven hundred artisans worked for ten years to create this landscape of open meadow encircled by trees.
Follow the diverted Juine that flows through the estate. The restored water system has just been inaugurated following extensive restoration work.
The estate reopened in 2018 and received the Jardin Remarquable label in 2019. Guided tours are offered by the tourist office on Sunday afternoons.

days_plan.itin_title: Essonne Tour: Castles and Valleys

visits.text: Metz’s Saint-Étienne Cathedral displays 6,500 m² of stained glass, an absolute French record ahead of Chartres with its 2,600 m². Nicknamed the “Good Lord’s Lantern”, it is bathed in changing light, where Marc Chagall’s mystical blues converse with Hermann de Münster’s medieval windows. Its naves rise 42 metres beneath the vaults, the third-highest elevation in France. Between 1958 and 1970, Chagall created Old Testament-inspired windows for the ambulatory and north transept, including the Sacrifice of Isaac and Jacob’s Dream in shades of supernatural blue, cosmic green and mystical red.

Centre Pompidou-Metz rises like a spaceship set down on the landscape, with an 8,500 m² hexagonal woven-timber roof inspired by a Chinese hat. Designed by Japanese architect Shigeru Ban and Jean de Gastines and inaugurated in 2010, it offers 5,000 m² of exhibition space beneath a structure comprising 18 km of glued-laminated timber beams. Its spire reaches 77 metres, a reference to the creation of the original Paris Centre Pompidou in 1977. The 15 m-wide galleries frame views of the cathedral, railway station and Parc de la Seille.

On Place Saint-Louis, the 13th-century medieval arcades form a setting of golden stone where the footsteps of Lombard money changers and merchants once echoed. The half-timbered façades and wrought-iron signs recount eight centuries of international trade. Take time for a coffee beneath the vaults, where the heart of Metz has beaten since the Middle Ages.

The Temple Neuf raises its 1904 neo-Romanesque silhouette on the Petit-Saulcy island, surrounded by the waters of the Moselle. Built during the German period for the Protestant garrison and equipped with its 1904 Walcker organ, it forms a romantic scene with the weeping willows, particularly popular with photographers at dusk, when its grey Vosges sandstone takes on pink hues.

Saint-Pierre-aux-Nonnains Church, built in the 4th century, is one of the oldest churches still standing in France. Its 3 m-thick Gallo-Roman walls have survived sixteen centuries, from a Roman civic basilica to a Benedictine abbey church founded in 972. Its carved 7th-century Merovingian capitals are among the jewels of Lorraine’s pre-Romanesque art. The building now hosts concerts and exhibitions.

The Château de la Grange unfolds its French formal gardens, an eighteenth-century aristocratic residence miraculously preserved. Allow about 28 km from the stage town, 30 minutes by road. Gilded panelling, Aubusson tapestries and Louis XV-Louis XVI furniture make up a refined interior untouched since 1731. The 25-hectare terraced gardens designed by Achille Duchêne offer a soothing view over the Moselle countryside and the Belle-Isle water tower.

activities.text: Stroll through the German Imperial Quarter, an architectural laboratory built between 1902 and 1918 under Wilhelm II. Avenue Foch is lined with neo-Romanesque and Art Nouveau villas with polychrome façades, while the monumental 1908 railway station in grey sandstone evokes Rhineland castles with its 40 m central tower. This kaleidoscope of Wilhelmine styles offers a unique immersion in Belle Époque Prussian urban planning, with more than 800 listed buildings.

The Musée de la Cour d’Or reveals 2,000 years of Metz history in the former Petits Carmes convent. First-century Gallo-Roman baths, Roman mosaics and Romanesque sculptures stand beneath centuries-old vaults. Its Merovingian collections rank among the richest in France and include the treasure from the Metz-Sablon necropolis. Do not miss the medieval Greniers de Chèvremont incorporated into the tour.

Explore the islands of Metz on foot, a string of green spaces set on the Moselle between the Temple Neuf and Jardin Boufflers. From the lake to the banks of Parc de la Seille, footbridges link these havens of urban nature where Metz residents come for fresh air. Pedal boats and rowing boats await those who enjoy leisurely boating along 3 km of landscaped riverbanks.

The Jean-Marie Pelt Gardens, a former botanical garden created in 1866, contain more than 2,500 plant species across 4.4 hectares. Tropical greenhouses covering 800 m², a rose garden with 80 varieties and a Japanese garden create a botanical journey across the continents. Collections of medicinal and aromatic plants perfume the air in fine weather. The koi pond and ecological garden complete this haven of urban biodiversity.

days_plan.itin_title: Eastern France by Train from Paris
4-Day Moselle Tour: Metz, Bitche Citadel and Chagall’s Stained Glass
4-Day Moselle Tour: Metz, Bitche Citadel and Chagall’s Stained Glass

visits.text: The Château de Meung-sur-Loire is nicknamed the château of two faces — with good reason: on the town side, the 13th-century façade shows its medieval defensive towers; on the garden side, an elegant 18th-century classical façade, bishop's blood red in colour, opens onto a 7-hectare park. The château was the residence of the bishops of Orléans from the Middle Ages until the Revolution. It welcomed Louis XI, Francis I, and Joan of Arc herself, who took it back from the English on 14 June 1429. Its darkest part: the oubliettes. The poet François Villon was imprisoned there in 1461 by Bishop Thibault Daussigny — he spent four months there in terrible conditions. These underground chambers can still be visited and the staging is worth the detour.

The Saint-Liphard Collegiate Church raises its Romanesque bell tower at the heart of the town. The crypt goes back to the 6th century and holds the tomb of Saint Liphard, the hermit who gave the town its name. The present collegiate church dates mainly from the 12th century; note the carved capitals and the Romanesque arches of the nave. It was around this sanctuary that the episcopal lordship of Meung developed.

Water mills line the channels of the Mauves that runs through the town. These medieval installations driven by the river bear witness to the milling activity that made Meung prosperous for centuries. Some buildings are still recognisable as you walk along the town-centre watercourses.

activities.text: Stroll the château's 7-hectare park. Beneath the foliage you can still make out the layout of the English-style garden created on the eve of the Revolution. Lime-tree alleys, the bed of the landscaped rivers and the ghost of a music pavilion — designed by Le Camus, architect to the Duke of Choiseul — compose a romantic tableau. Bishop Jarente de la Bruyère had invested his entire fortune to recreate a little Versailles here; the Revolution drove him out before he could enjoy it.

Wander Meung's medieval centre streets. The town has preserved its period urban fabric: narrow lanes, half-timbered houses, and a few hundred metres on, remnants of the old Loire bridge that Joan of Arc attacked on 15 June 1429 to cut English reinforcements before the Beaugency victory.

days_plan.itin_title: The Essential Châteaux of the Loire Valley
Loiret Road Trip: Orléans and the Châteaux of the Loire

visits.text: Beaune is the wine capital of Burgundy, and its landmark, the Hôtel-Dieu, ranks among the finest secular buildings of the Middle Ages in France. It was founded in 1443 by Nicolas Rolin, chancellor to the Duke of Burgundy, and his wife Guigone de Salins as a “palace for the poor”—Rolin, immensely wealthy, sought in this way to buy his salvation. The Flamboyant Gothic building served as a hospital only until 1971. Inside, the Salle des Pauvres measures 50 meters long and can accommodate 30 beds. The collection's masterpiece is Rogier van der Weyden's Last Judgment polyptych, commissioned by Rolin—allow at least 1 hour 30 minutes for the visit. Every third Sunday of November, 41 cuvées from the Hospices wine estate are auctioned in the Halles de Beaune, the world's most famous charity auction.

Beaune's ramparts form Burgundy's finest fortified enclosure: built in the 15th and 16th centuries, they remain virtually intact and enclose several kilometers of cellars carved into limestone rock. Walk the complete circuit on foot—35 towers and 12 bastions—to see the town from the outside before diving into its medieval lanes. The 12th-century Collégiale Notre-Dame also deserves a visit for its Flemish tapestries depicting the Life of the Virgin.

Savigny-lès-Beaune, 5 km northwest of Beaune, is worth a detour for its 14th-century château and its “unusual collections”: some fifty racing motorcycles and a collection of military aircraft. Savigny's vineyards produce fruity, approachable Pinot Noirs; the appellation is often the best value for money on the Côte de Beaune.

Aloxe-Corton marks the entrance to the Côte de Beaune with its emblematic hill. Corton and Corton-Charlemagne are red and white grands crus of the Côte de Beaune—Charlemagne is said to have owned vines here in the 8th century. Stop at the viewpoint to see the wooded crown of the Corton hill rise above the rows of vines: it is the most photographed image in the area.

Pommard, whose name alone sets the tone, is the Côte de Beaune's best-known Pinot Noir village with its 28 premiers crus. The village is classic: a Romanesque church, stone winegrowers' houses, a small square. But tasting cellars abound, and the Clos des Épeneaux vineyard, a monopole parcel at the heart of the appellation, is visible from the road.

activities.text: Guided tasting in the Côte de Beaune at an estate or wine merchant: Pinot Noir here tends to be suppler than in the Côte de Nuits, and Chardonnay begins to appear. It's an opportunity to compare the two côtes in a single glass. Ask to taste a village wine alongside a premier cru from the same estate—the price difference always makes more sense in the glass.

days_plan.itin_title: Burgundy's Route des Grands Crus: Dijon to Santenay
Burgundy's 15 Most Beautiful Villages

visits.text: Meyrueis, at the confluence of the Jonte, Béthuzon, and Brèze, is ringed by mountains. Its narrow streets weave between Renaissance houses and covered passages. The Tour de l'Horloge, a remnant of medieval fortifications, marks the town's heart.
The Château de Roquedols, 2 km from the centre, is a restored 16th-century seigneurial residence. It houses the Cévennes National Park centre for the southern side of the Méjean causse.

The Dargilan cave, known as the 'pink cave' for the shade of its concretions, opens onto the Causse Noir. Its immense chambers, including the Grande Salle 142 m long, display draperies, columns and stalactites with orange tints. Discovered in 1880 by a shepherd.

The Mont Aigoual Observatory stands at 1,567 m, about 13 km from the stopover town, 20 minutes by road. On a clear day the view stretches from the Alps to the Pyrenees and as far as the Mediterranean. The exhibition traces the history of meteorology.
Drive back up the Jonte gorges from Meyrueis. Dolomite cliffs frame a narrow road carved into rock. Natural balconies offer views of griffon vulture colonies in flight.

activities.text: Hike on the Méjean causse starting from Meyrueis. The trail crosses dry grasslands, skirts lavognes (pastoral ponds), and passes causse farmsteads built of stone. A landscape of magnificent solitude.
Canyoning in the Tapoul or Jonte gorges. Jumps, natural slides, and rappels in crystalline water between limestone walls. Outfitters provide full equipment.
Meyrueis market runs Wednesday and Friday mornings beneath the plane trees. Causse sheep cheeses, chestnut honey, country charcuterie, and seasonal porcini mushrooms.

days_plan.itin_title: Lozère Circuit: Tarn Gorges and Cévennes

visits.text: The Millau Viaduct, inaugurated in 2004, is the world's tallest cable-stayed bridge—its highest pylon rises to 343 meters, 19 meters taller than the Eiffel Tower. Designed by engineer Michel Virlogeux and architect Norman Foster, it spans the Tarn valley for 2,460 meters. The best viewpoint is from the belvedere in the village of Peyre, ranked among France's Most Beautiful Villages, where you'll see the viaduct with troglodyte houses in the foreground.

Old Millau deserves a stop. Its octagonal 12th-century belfry (44 meters) dominates the Place du Maréchal Foch. The town was a major leather glove production center since the Middle Ages—the Millau museum traces this tradition. You'll find good restaurants on the central squares, with views of the causses.

activities.text: If you enjoy thrills, several operators offer canoeing and kayaking in the Tarn gorges, about a 20-minute drive north of Millau. Otherwise, simply drive the gorge road between Millau and Les Vignes—allow for a full day's round trip from Millau. Limestone cliffs 500 meters high frame the turquoise river for 50 km. It is one of Europe's most beautiful canyons.

days_plan.itin_title: Aveyron Road Trip: Causses, Tarn Gorges and Villages
Southeast France Road Trip: Perched Villages and Gorges

visits.text: The 15th-century timber-framed market hall has miraculously survived the centuries. Its massive beams shelter a traditional market every Thursday where Milly mint is sold.
The Chapel of Saint-Blaise des Simples was a 12th-century leprosarium. In 1959, Cocteau decorated it with frescoes depicting medicinal plants and Christ's resurrection.
Mint, valerian, and belladonna grow in the medicinal herb garden surrounding the chapel. These medicinal plants recall a tradition in Milly dating back to the Middle Ages.
Step inside the Maison de Jean Cocteau. The office, bedroom, studio, and large drawing room immerse visitors in the mythological world of the poet who lived here from 1947 to 1963.
The national plant conservatory brings together more than 1,500 medicinal and aromatic species. The museum displays explain the history of medicinal herbs and their use.
The Château de la Bonde, dating from the 13th and 15th centuries, stands with its two crenellated towers near the stone bridge. Cocteau lived in a former outbuilding here.

activities.text: Venture into the forest to discover Tinguely's Cyclope. This giant head, 22 meters tall and made of 300 tonnes of steel, surveys the forest with its single golden eye.
Enter the bowels of the Cyclope via stairs and walkways. Works by Niki de Saint Phalle, Spoerri, Arman, and César fill this mechanical labyrinth.
The Trois-Pignons massif extends south of Milly. Its boulder fields attract climbers, while its forest trails draw hikers.
Reach nearby Fontainebleau Forest. The sandstone plateaus and maritime pine groves create surprising landscapes just a few kilometers from Milly.

days_plan.itin_title: Essonne Tour: Castles and Valleys

visits.text: Sainte-Marie gatehouse bell tower: Remnant of a 12th-century Benedictine priory inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List as part of the Routes of Santiago de Compostela. The sculpted 13th-century portal ranks among the finest in southwestern France. Remarkably preserved 15th-century murals. The Musée Prieuré completes the visit with archaeological collections.

Courant de Mimizan: A winding 7km coastal river connecting Lake Aureilhan to the ocean. This natural boundary separates Mimizan-Nord from Mimizan-Sud. Developed walking paths along the banks with views of fishing boats and pleasure boats. Renowned spot for sea bass and sea trout fishing.

Lake Aureilhan and Promenade Fleurie: Over 400 plant species line the route around the lake. Open-air botanical garden with remarkable trees and exotic plants. The 350-hectare lake offers calm waters for swimming and water activities. View over the Landes forest and dunes in the distance.

Monument des Ailes: Commemorates the first North Atlantic crossing by the French crew of the Oiseau Canari (Assolant, Lefèvre, Lotti), who made a water landing off Remember Beach in June 1929. Stele erected facing the ocean. The Château de Woolsack, built in the Tudor style in 1910, testifies to the resort's aristocratic past.

activities.text: Hiking on marked trails: 40km of routes through forest, dunes and lakes. Loops lasting 2 to 5 hours depending on the route. The coastal trail offers ocean panoramas and passes bunkers. Maps available at the tourist office. Welcome shade in summer.

Ocean beach swimming: 10km of beaches, including 4 lifeguarded in season (Nord, Sud, Lespecier, Courant). Beware of baïnes (dangerous currents). Swimming flags must be strictly observed. Beach access mats for people with disabilities on certain beaches. Lifeguard stations June to September.

Canoeing on the Courant: A peaceful 7km paddle downstream between the lake and the ocean. Rentals at the lake, with a return shuttle or a one-way trip to the sea. Observation of wildlife (herons, cormorants) and riverside plants. An easy outing suitable for accompanied children aged 6 and up.

Landes Aventure treetop adventure park: 120 obstacles spread across 9 courses among the pines. Heights from 1m to 15m depending on the level. 160m zipline. Open April to November with nighttime sessions in summer. Equipment provided, mandatory safety briefing. Online booking advised.

days_plan.itin_title: Landes Road Trip: Ocean, Pine Forest and Landes Traditions

visits.text: Minerve is a spectacular Cathar village perched on a rocky spur at the confluence of the Cesse and Brian rivers. Fortified in the Middle Ages, it was the scene of a tragic 1210 siege during the Albigensian Crusade: 140 Cathars were burned here. Access to the village is via a bridge spanning the gorges. Narrow streets, stone houses, ramparts, and the octagonal tower (castle remnant) testify to the medieval past. The village has fewer than 150 inhabitants but attracts many visitors drawn by its history and exceptional natural setting.

The Cesse gorges were carved by the river through limestone over millions of years. The geological spectacle is impressive with steep cliffs, natural bridges, and tunnels. In summer, the Cesse disappears underground, leaving its bed dry, which allows access to the Grand Natural Bridge and Petit Natural Bridge, genuine curiosities. These rocky arches are remnants of collapsed ancient caves. The site is classified as a Grand Site de France. Hiking trails allow you to discover them from Minerve.

The Musée Hurepel in Minerve traces the history of Catharism and the 1210 siege. Collections present archaeological objects, documents, and models explaining the siege's unfolding and Cathar life. One room is dedicated to the gorges' geology and the natural bridges' formation. The visit helps understand the site's historical importance. The museum is small but information-dense. Allow 45 minutes for the visit.

activities.text: Hike to Minerve's natural bridges. A marked trail descends into the Cesse gorges from the village. You reach the Grand Natural Bridge, an impressive arch 250 meters long and 30 meters high. The smaller Petit Natural Bridge upstream is more modest but equally spectacular. In summer, the river is dry and you walk on the pebble bed. The route is about 4 km round trip with elevation change. Good shoes essential. Avoid summer's intense heat as there's little shade.

Discover Minervois vineyards. The appellation extends over the foothills of the Montagne Noire with varied soils and exposures. Red wines, the majority, are powerful and structured, made primarily with Syrah, Grenache, and Carignan. Cooperative cellars and wine estates offer tastings and visits. The Minervois Wine Route crosses landscapes of vines, garrigue, and character villages. It's a wonderful way to discover the terroir while combining heritage and gastronomy.

Stroll through Minerve village at sunset. It's the ideal time to enjoy the place's unique atmosphere when visitors have left. Low-angle light illuminates the golden stone houses and ramparts. The view from viewpoints over the gorges is magnificent. Silence returns to the village; you hear cicadas singing and wind in the trees. A few restaurants and an inn allow you to dine and spend the night on-site to fully enjoy this unique atmosphere.

days_plan.itin_title: Occitanie's 13 Most Beautiful Villages
Hérault Road Trip: Montpellier, Beaches and the Hinterland

visits.text: Mirande is a 13th-century bastide organized in a grid pattern around its central square. The covered wooden market hall has sheltered the market for centuries. The church of Sainte-Marie has a characteristic octagonal bell tower.
The Museum of Fine Arts displays paintings and sculptures from the 17th to 20th centuries. The collection includes works by regional and national artists.

activities.text: Monday morning market is renowned throughout the Gers. Producers sell poultry, foie gras, and Gascon specialties. It's an authentic market where locals do their shopping.
Taste the gastronomy of the Gers at restaurants in the center. Duck confit, seared foie gras, and garbure (peasant soup) are specialties. Regional wines accompany these hearty dishes perfectly.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Garonne Road Trip: From Toulouse to the Pyrenees

visits.text: The first shock on arriving in Albi: the cathedral looks like a prison. Blank red-brick walls without side windows, a 78-meter bell tower, a massive layout - it is deliberate. The inquisitor bishop Bernard de Castanet began construction in 1282; he had good reason to fear a popular uprising, because his predecessors had burned heretics a few hundred meters away. A fortress-cathedral was the only model he considered viable. Completed in 1480, it is the largest brick cathedral in the world - 113 meters long, 200 years of construction. Then you step inside. A complete reversal: 18,500 m² of vaults painted blue, a choir of Flamboyant Gothic stone lacework. A prison-like exterior, an opulent interior. The message is as political as it is spiritual. Admission to the nave is free, €5 for the choir.

The Last Judgment fresco (1474–1484), 270 m² beneath the organ, is clinically disturbing. The damned to the right of Christ aren't vaguely tormented—they're flayed with anatomical precision, muscles and viscera visible, tortured according to their sin: misers drink molten metal, gluttons eat toads, the lustful are impaled. It's fear propaganda, made by people who had burned heretics for real and wanted the people to understand what awaited them. A detail added by a 17th-century bishop: a doorway cut right through the middle of the fresco to access a chapel, destroying Christ the Judge and half of Paradise. The damage has never been repaired. Local peasants of the time saw this as a sign that the bishop didn't like looking Christ in the face.

Thirty meters to the left of the cathedral, the Berbie Palace was the former bishop's palace and prison—heretics tried in Albi awaited their sentences in its basement. Today the building houses the Toulouse-Lautrec Museum, the world's largest collection of works by the artist born here in 1864. The paradox is clear: the place where the Inquisition locked up its suspects now preserves posters for Parisian cabarets. The former 14th-century dungeons, with prisoners' graffiti still visible on the walls, aren't accessible to the public—access is reserved for researchers with authorization. What you can't see sometimes has more presence than what's shown. Ticket €12.

activities.text: Lunch in Albi: L'Épicurien for fine dining (€50–80), or Le Lautrec near the cathedral for something simpler (€35–50). The Vieux Pont over the Tarn, built in 1040 and one of the oldest bridges in France still in use, is worth the 15-minute walk from the cathedral.

En route to Mirepoix (2 hours southeast), a possible stop at Cordes-sur-Ciel (30 minutes north of Albi)—a medieval bastide founded in 1222 by Raymond VII of Toulouse for Cathar refugees driven from the plains. Perched at 287 meters, often wrapped in morning fog that makes it appear suspended in the clouds. Explore independently. Overnight in Mirepoix: Hôtel Le Comptoir Saint Hubert (€90–150) or Maison de Mirepoix (€130–200). The arcaded square of Mirepoix, with its carved half-timbered houses from the 13th–15th centuries, is one of the most beautiful medieval spaces in the Southwest.

days_plan.itin_title: Occitanie's 13 Most Beautiful Villages
Haunted Southwest - 5 Days from Périgord Noir to the Cathar Castles
Ariège Road Trip: Cathars and Prehistoric Caves

visits.text: Climb to the top of the village to reach the Église Sainte-Foy, a jewel of 12th-century Romanesque art. Now deconsecrated, it hosts regularly changing exhibitions from April to September.

From the orientation table near Sainte-Foy, the view embraces the Rhône Valley, the Vivarais mountains and the foothills of the Vercors. On clear days, the panorama stretches for dozens of kilometers.
Sloping lanes lead past superb stone facades. The Adhémar de Monteil family built the first fortifications in the 12th century, and the ramparts still trace the silhouette of the village.

The Église Saint-Pierre, in the heart of the village, dates from the mid-19th century. Inside hangs a 17th-century painting depicting Saint Ursula and Saint Augustine contemplating the mystery of the Trinity.

Artisan workshops dot the narrow streets: ceramics, jewelry, sculptures. A cubist painter settled here in the 1920s and founded a summer academy, igniting an artistic tradition that thrives to this day.
Mirmande once flourished through sericulture—silkworm farming. Panels throughout the village recount that era when magnaneries (silkworm nurseries) provided livelihoods for local families.

activities.text: Follow the Sainte-Foy trail winding through orchards and olive groves below the village. You'll be rewarded with panoramic views of Mirmande's rooftops against the backdrop of the Drôme hills.
The region is renowned for its orchards. In season, farmers open their properties to visitors: cherries, apricots, peaches, nectarines, and kiwis available for pick-your-own or direct purchase.

The village of Cliousclat, just a few kilometers away, preserves its pottery-making heritage. A historical trail traces the story of the kilns and artisans who have worked the clay here for generations.

days_plan.itin_title: Rhône-Alpes Circuit: Perched Villages and Mountain Peaks

visits.text: Mittelbergheim differs radically from its Alsatian neighbors: no colorful half-timbering here, but pink Vosges sandstone cut into regular blocks, Renaissance houses with carved gables and flower-filled courtyards. The village was founded by the Franks in the early 6th century under the name “Berge,” and its prosperity from winemaking in the 16th and 17th centuries allowed it to build this exceptional architectural ensemble. The town hall dates from 1620 and houses, in its vaulted cellar, a treasure unique in Alsace: the Weinschlag, a wine accounting register kept since 1456 that records wine prices, harvests, and landmark village events over more than five centuries.

Don't miss the Musée Mémoire de Vignerons, open since 2008, which presents a collection of old tools related to viticulture in a preserved rural setting. In the town hall cellar, a wine library preserves bottles from village winemakers—the oldest, a Sylvaner Zotzenberg, dates to 1959. This is where you'll understand why Mittelbergheim is different: its medieval ramparts surround not houses but vineyards, a configuration unique in Alsace.

activities.text: Head out on the Grand Cru Zotzenberg trail—the vineyard that built the village's international reputation. This south-facing terroir, on Jurassic marls and limestone at elevations between 215 and 315 meters, is the only Grand Cru in Alsace where Sylvaner has been permitted since the 2005 vintage. Tasting a Sylvaner from Zotzenberg at a local winemaker's means tasting a wine found nowhere else. Plan 2 to 3 hours for the loop, with panoramas of Mont Sainte-Odile and the plain.

Stroll the cobbled streets to spot dated lintels and cart entrances — gateways wide enough to let grape-laden wagons through. Every house hides a wine cellar in its limestone foundations. The wine festival takes place the last weekend of July: estates open their cellars and the atmosphere is especially convivial.

days_plan.itin_title: The 15 Most Beautiful Villages of Alsace
Grand Est Road Trip: Vineyards, Ramparts and Forests
The Most Beautiful Villages of Alsace in 4 Days

visits.text: The Forts de l'Esseillon form an ensemble of five fortifications built between 1819 and 1834 by the Kingdom of Piedmont-Sardinia on a natural glacial lock. Listed Historic Monuments, they bear the names of the royal family: Victor-Emmanuel, Marie-Thérèse, Marie-Christine, Charles-Albert, and Charles-Félix.

Fort Victor-Emmanuel, the most imposing of the complex, could house 1,500 soldiers. You wander through casemates, vaulted corridors, and guard posts. A scenario-based treasure hunt invites families to slip into the role of a 19th-century French spy.

Redoute Marie-Thérèse, horseshoe-shaped, houses a fortified heritage interpretation center. Scale models, panels, and artifacts trace the history of the military lock, from its construction to Savoy's annexation in 1860.
Walk down to the Pont du Diable, a suspension bridge above the Arc gorges, linking Fort Victor-Emmanuel to Redoute Marie-Thérèse. The plunging view into gorges more than 100 meters deep is dizzying.

At Modane's outskirts, on the Valfréjus road, spot the "maison penchée." This former 1939 blockhouse, an observation post at the railway tunnel entrance, was hurled dozens of meters by the explosion of two explosives wagons in 1944. It replanted itself in the ground, nearly intact but tilted.

The monumental entrance to the Fréjus railway tunnel (the Alps' first boring, 1857-1871) stands on the Modane-Valfréjus road. The cut-stone portal marks the beginning of one of the 19th century's great engineering projects.

activities.text: Via Ferrata du Diable. Seven routes of increasing difficulty spread across the Esseillon site, between rock walls, monkey bridges, and metal ladders overhanging the Arc gorges.

Hike on the old Esseillon road, starting from Modane. The trail winds between Le Bourget and Aussois via the Saint-Benoît waterfall and chapel, then passes the forts one by one. Drinking water points all along the route.
Treetop adventure course in the Parc du Diable, near Redoute Marie-Thérèse. Walkways between the trees and zip lines above the gorges, in a spectacular setting blending forest and military heritage.

days_plan.itin_title: Savoie from Lakes to Glaciers: Yenne to Haute-Maurienne

places.name: Moirans En Montagne

visits.text: The Toy Museum of Moirans-en-Montagne was born in 1989 to celebrate a local tradition dating back to the Middle Ages. It all began at the Abbey of Saint-Claude in the 13th century: monks turned wood to produce devotional objects for pilgrims, then peasants took up the craft during winters. The first turned wooden toys in Moirans-en-Montagne date from 1820 — whistles and recorders. Around 1850, the town was nicknamed "Bibiville" for its thousands of "bibis," whistles topped with a balloon. Today, the museum labeled "Musée de France" houses 16,000 pieces covering 5,000 years of play history. Count at least 1h30 for the visit, 2h if you have children — there are many interactive spaces.

Lake Vouglans is the third-largest artificial reservoir in France by capacity, after Serre-Ponçon and Sainte-Croix: 605 million m³ of water, 35 km in length, 1,600 hectares. The dam was built between 1963 and 1968 by EDF on the Ain River — 545,000 m³ of concrete and an arch of remarkable thinness (25 meters at the base, 6 meters at the top). The filling took 18 months and submerged several hamlets as well as the Chartreuse de Vaucluse, a 12th-century Carthusian monastery. From the viewpoints overlooking the shores, the emerald waters are reminiscent of fjords — one understands the appellation "Land of Emerald" for the region.

activities.text: Cruise or kayak trip on Lake Vouglans: providers offer boat excursions and kayak rentals from the three lake ports (la Saisse, la Tour-du-Meix, la Mercantine). The shores are wild and largely inaccessible other than by boat — it's the best way to discover the cliffs plunging into the lake and isolated coves. The speed limit zone of 5 km/h within 50 meters of the shores guarantees the tranquility of non-motorized navigation.

Scenic walk to the Vouglans Dam viewpoint: from the village of Lect, a marked trail climbs toward the ridges overlooking the dam (height 103 meters, crest width 427 meters). The view plunges over the entire reservoir and, in clear weather, all the way to the Alps. The dam itself has for several years carried a monumental fresco created by scraping lichens — visible from the left bank and right bank viewpoints.

days_plan.itin_title: Jura Lakes Route: Emerald and Turquoise Waters

map_keywords: Lake Vouglans Pont de la Pyle

visits.text: The cloister of Saint-Pierre Abbey, finished in 1100, has 76 carved capitals, 46 of them with narrative scenes. Arcaded galleries frame a quiet garden where every capital tells a biblical or medieval story.
The tympanum of the south portal measures 6.5 meters by 4.5 meters. Carved between 1110 and 1130, it shows Christ in Majesty surrounded by the 24 Elders of the Apocalypse according to Saint John.
The abbey church combines Romanesque stone and Gothic brick. Its upper sections were rebuilt in the 15th century after destruction during the Albigensian Crusade.
The Marcel Durliat Center for Romanesque Art exhibits reproductions of manuscript illuminations created by monks in the 11th and 12th centuries. A specialized library complements the collection.
Walk through the cloister galleries of Saint-Pierre Abbey in Moissac. The arcades frame the garden and offer a view of the carved capitals.

activities.text: Walk the Way of Saint James. Moissac is a major stop on the Via Podiensis, where thousands of pilgrims converge every year.
Follow the Canal des Deux Mers cycle path. From Toulouse to Bordeaux, the route runs beside calm waters conducive to contemplative stops.
Taste the chasselas de Moissac, harvested from late August until the first frosts. This golden white grape has held an AOC designation since 1971.

days_plan.itin_title: Tarn-et-Garonne Road Trip: Bastides and Orchards

visits.text: Mollégès derives its name from the Latin "molle gesium" (soft lands) — an allusion to the rich alluvium of the Crau d'Orgon plain surrounding the village. Nestled among orchards and cypress hedges, this plain settlement has retained a Renaissance facade behind the church (remains of an old château) and parts of a monastery cloister partially converted into dwellings. Place du Lavoir, with its draft horse monument in Luberon marble (1989), pays tribute to the horses that worked these fertile lands.

Wednesday morning market offers a chance to take the pulse of this agricultural village: local produce farmers, cheese makers, antique dealers. The Mollégès plain is one of the most productive in Bouches-du-Rhône — intensive greenhouse market gardening and orchards as far as the eye can see. Don't miss the Saint-Thomas chapel in the cemetery, surrounded by tall trees.

activities.text: Agricultural paths through hedgerows and orchards toward Saint-Andiol: rural roads connecting Mollégès to Saint-Andiol (5 km) cross a mosaic of Provençal crops — cherry, apricot, olive, and sweet cherry trees — separated by cypress hedges planted to protect crops from the mistral. An ideal bike ride (completely flat terrain) or walk in the morning.

Easy cycling loop in the plain: rental providers operate from Saint-Andiol and Eygalières. The flat terrain of the Crau d'Orgon lends itself perfectly to leisurely cycle touring. Roads are lightly trafficked and views of the Alpilles to the north accompany the entire route.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpilles, Aix-en-Provence & Arles Circuit

visits.text: The Rock of Monaco, a limestone outcrop 800 meters by 300, has housed the old town and Prince's Palace since the 13th century. This is where Francesco Grimaldi took the fortress in 1297, disguised as a Franciscan monk—an anecdote that is probably legendary but explains the family motto “With God's Help.” The Rock's streets have a surprising air of calm a short walk from Monte-Carlo's bustle. Park at the Pêcheurs parking lot; access is on foot or by shuttle.

Sainte-Marie-Immaculée Cathedral, also called Notre-Dame-Immaculée, houses the tombs of the Grimaldi princes—including that of Grace Kelly, who died in 1982. The neo-Romanesque building, made of white stone from La Turbie, was consecrated in 1875 on the site of the former Saint-Nicolas church. An altarpiece by Louis Bréa from 1500 stands in the side chapel. The line to see Grace's tomb can get long—come early.

The Oceanographic Museum has been plunging into the abyss since 1910. Founded by Prince Albert I—nicknamed the “Navigator Prince” for his 28 scientific expeditions—the imposing neo-Baroque building rises 85 meters along the cliff face. Jacques Cousteau directed it from 1957 to 1988. Over 6,000 specimens in the aquariums, including a superb recreated coral lagoon. Allow at least 2 hours; the detour is worth the expense (€19). A very good educational program for children.

Casino Square and the Monte-Carlo Casino: the current building is by Charles Garnier (the architect of the Paris Opera), inaugurated January 25, 1879. Sarah Bernhardt performed at the opening evening—but at the adjoining Salle Garnier (the Monte-Carlo Opera), not in the gaming rooms. The onyx hall, 28 marble columns and symbolist paintings can be visited even without gambling. Verified anecdote: Monegasques have been forbidden to gamble there since Charles III, who didn't want to see his subjects ruined. Proper attire required in the evening.

Monaco's Exotic Garden, perched 100 meters above the sea, presents nearly 1,000 species of cacti and succulents clinging to the cliff. The highlight: the Observatory Cave that descends 60 meters below the garden, formed 200 million years ago, where human bones of Grimaldi Man (Upper Paleolithic) were discovered in 1916.

activities.text: Attend the changing of the guard in front of the Prince's Palace at 11:55 AM sharp: carabiniers in white uniform in summer, black in winter, executing the ceremony with military precision. Short spectacle (10 minutes) but photogenic, beware crowds in high season.

Stroll along Port Hercule: yachts exceeding 100 meters, a chance to trace the F1 circuit that runs through the city each May. Permanent safety barriers mark the tightest turns on the calendar (Sainte-Dévote, Mirabeau, Casino corner). It's one of the few street circuits where single-seaters exceed 280 km/h in the tunnel.

The Princess Grace Rose Garden, created in 1984 in memory of the actress, gathers over 8,000 rose bushes in a 3,500 m² park. Roses often bear the names of celebrities. Maximum bloom in May-June. Free admission, it's a peaceful corner away from Monaco's bustle.

Larvotto Beach: Monaco's only public beach, completely renovated in 2021. Imported sand, crystal-clear water, beach facilities and lifeguards in summer. Locals have a quick lunch here between appointments. Avoid Saturdays in July–August—it's packed.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpes-Maritimes Road Trip: Riviera and Mercantour, 13 days
7-Day French Riviera Circuit: Villefranche to Antibes

places.name: Moncontour

visits.text: Moncontour, designated one of the Petites Cités de Caractère, preserves its medieval ramparts almost intact. Six towers and two fortified gates encircle the upper town, perched on its rocky spur since the 11th century.

The Saint-Mathurin church contains six 16th-century stained glass windows classified as Historic Monuments. The windows depict the lives of Breton saints with a palette of blues and reds of rare intensity.
Overhanging 15th and 16th-century houses line the narrow streets. Half-timbered facades, sometimes leaning to the point of almost touching, testify to the prosperity of linen cloth merchants.
On Place Penthièvre, granite mansions stand in a row with their carved porches. The central fountain dates from the 18th century. This is where the cloth fair that made the city wealthy was held.

From the rampart walk, the panorama takes in the Penthièvre countryside and the Côtes-d'Armor hills. The crenellations and machicolations are remarkably well preserved for a defensive enclosure of this size.

activities.text: Follow the ramparts circuit (marked in yellow), which makes a complete circuit of the medieval walls. Six towers punctuate the route, each offering a different view of the valley.
Descend to the medieval washhouse below the ramparts. Water still flows there. The trail joins the terraced gardens built on the former moats.
Browse the artisan workshops housed in former medieval shops. Potters, weavers, and painters occupy the vaulted ground floors of Rue des Dames.

days_plan.itin_title: Brittany Road Trip: Villages with Character, Sea and History

map_keywords: Maisons à pans de bois Moncontour

visits.text: Monflanquin is one of the best-preserved bastides in south-western France. Founded in 1256 by Alphonse of Poitiers, brother of Saint Louis, it has an oval layout that is very unusual for a hilltop bastide, with streets arranged in a grid around the central arcaded square. Its fortifications, strengthened in 1282 after the territory was ceded to the English, were dismantled in 1632 on Richelieu’s orders. The village has since been classed among France’s Most Beautiful Villages. Begin at Place des Arcades: it has been the vibrant heart of the bastide for 770 years, and the Thursday market has been held here without interruption since 1256.

On the square, look out for the Black Prince's House with its 14th-century mullioned windows with bilobed tracery. Edward of Woodstock, known as the Black Prince and son of King Edward III of England, is said to have stayed here during the Hundred Years' War, at a time when Monflanquin passed alternately into French and English hands.

Saint-André Church retains its 13th-century portal. Burned in 1559 during the Wars of Religion and subsequently left in ruins, it was rebuilt: a major restoration took place in 1715, the vaults were redone around 1860 and the current bell tower dates from 1923. The somewhat composite building clearly reflects the turbulent history of this frontier bastide.

Lose yourself in the carrerots, the medieval lanes spanned by pontets, small bridges linking the houses at upper-floor level. The grid plan has remained intact since 1256 and every passageway offers a different view of the rooftops and the surrounding countryside. It is the best way to understand the urban logic of these medieval new towns.

The Bastide Museum, housed above the tourist office, recounts the creation of the 350 bastides of south-western France between the 13th and 14th centuries, covering the Franco-English rivalry, urban layouts, charters of customs and everyday life. The displays combine models, audio recordings and period costumes. A medieval escape game is also available for families.

Climb up to the Cap del Pech, the highest point of the bastide at 181 metres. On a clear day you can make out the Chateau de Biron to the south and the rolling countryside of the Haut Agenais stretching to the horizon, a landscape that really does recall Tuscany, with its rows of plum trees and rounded hills.

activities.text: Stroll around the Place des Arcades market on Thursday morning, the very same market that has been held here since 1256. Local producers from the Haut Agenais sell fruit, vegetables, farmhouse poultry, cheeses and Bergerac wines. In summer, an evening market takes over in a festive atmosphere.

Book a guided tour with Janouille la Fripouille, the theatrical jester-guide who has made the bastide his playground for years. His storytelling blends verified historical anecdotes, Gascon humour and banter with the audience. The night tours in summer are especially popular, so book ahead.

In August, the Medieval Days transform the village over the weekend of 15 August, with troubadours, knights fighting on Cap del Pech, fire shows and a grand period banquet in a thoroughly festive atmosphere.

days_plan.itin_title: Nouvelle-Aquitaine Loop: Villages, Vineyards & Dordogne
Lot-et-Garonne Road Trip: Bastides and Villages

visits.text: Monpazier, founded in 1284 by Edward I of England, is considered the model bastide among the 300 scattered across southwestern France. Its rectangular checkerboard plan remains perfectly intact. With 32 classified monuments, Monpazier ranks among France's Most Beautiful Villages—a medieval town that seems to have resisted time itself.

Place des Cornières is bordered by 23 arcaded houses in golden limestone, built between the 13th and 17th centuries. The central chestnut market hall still contains the old grain measures (bushels) used for centuries. This is one of the best-preserved medieval squares in France—architecture textbooks cite it as the definitive bastide plaza.

Le Bastideum is an interpretation center dedicated to bastide history, offering a playful approach to medieval life through interactive exhibits, an escape game, and a reconstructed period garden. It's engaging for families and provides context for understanding these planned medieval towns.

activities.text: Monpazier's market has convened every Thursday morning for 700 years—since the 13th century. Stalls spread under the market hall and around Place des Cornières, selling regional products and local crafts. It's a living tradition that connects the present directly to the Middle Ages.

Monpazier's narrow streets shelter artisan workshops and shops selling regional specialties. Despite enduring the Wars of Religion and the bloody Croquants peasant revolts (1594, 1637), the village has preserved its medieval character—a testament to the durability of stone and civic memory.

days_plan.itin_title: Dordogne: Prehistoric Caves, Medieval Fortresses & Périgord Delights
The Most Beautiful Villages of Lot and Périgord in 6 Days

visits.text: Mont-Dauphin is a fortified town built from scratch by Vauban from 1693 onwards, set on a rocky spur above the confluence of the Guil and the Durance. Listed by UNESCO in 2008 along with Briançon, it is twinned with Mont-Louis in the Pyrenees, the Sun King's twin fortresses. An unusual feature: its ramparts are built of Guillestre marble, which turns pink in the setting sun. Fewer than 200 inhabitants still live within the walls.

Once past the gates, the village feels like a stage set frozen in time: ruler-straight lanes, an unfinished church, wells, the Rochambeau barracks and arsenal. The star-shaped layout, with triangular bastions and ravelins, is easier to make out from the ramparts, which offer views down into the Durance valley. The Centre des monuments nationaux manages the site and offers guided tours. Allow a solid hour to walk around it at a leisurely pace.

activities.text: Several artisan workshops have opened in Mont-Dauphin's barracks and shops: a glassblower, potters, designers, who take advantage of the timeless setting. It's a pleasant way to extend the visit without museum displays, chatting with the people who bring the fortress to life today. Hours vary by workshop and season.

For walkers, trails link Mont-Dauphin to Vauban's outworks, like the lunette d'Arçon, connected to the fortress by underground passages. The military paths offer viewpoints over the confluence and surrounding peaks. A short, easy loop, ideal for understanding the defensive logic of the site from outside. Decent shoes recommended.

days_plan.itin_title: Hautes-Alpes Road Trip: High Mountains and Alpine Valleys

visits.text: Musée Despiau-Wlérick: the permanent collections are closed for renovation. From Place Marguerite de Navarre, view the Lacataye keep, a medieval building housing the museum devoted to local sculptors Charles Despiau and Robert Wlérick. Continue on foot through central Mont-de-Marsan with the Musée dans la Rue: its outdoor sculptures let you discover the city's sculptural heritage without entering the closed galleries.

Arènes du Plumaçon: Built in 1889 and expanded in 1933, the bullring has been awarded the Patrimoine du XXe siècle designation. It comes alive with tradition during the famous Feria de la Madeleine every July. The course landaise has been practiced here with passion for over a century.

Historic center: A stroll along the Midou and Douze rivers, which converge at the city's heart. The shaded quays and bridges offer beautiful views of local architecture. The Parc Jean-Rameau stretches peacefully along the water's edge.

activities.text: Musée dans la Rue trail: Discover monumental sculptures scattered throughout the city. This free urban art trail lets you admire major works outdoors. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes for the complete walking circuit.

Saturday morning food market: Local producers offer foie gras, Tursan wines, and Landes asparagus. The convivial atmosphere and Gascon specialties make this market unmissable. Vendors set up from 8am around the central market halls.

Fêtes de la Madeleine in July: 5 days of Landes tradition with courses landaises in the bullring, street bands, and concerts. Over 500,000 festivalgoers gather annually for this major feria in southwestern France. Accommodation must be booked several months in advance.

places.name: Mont Des Recollets

visits.text: The scent of freshly clipped boxwood greets visitors at the entrance to the Jardins du Mont des Récollets. Across 1.5 hectares, this garden—classified as Jardin Remarquable—recreates Flanders' history through topiaries and orchards, channeling the spirit of Brueghel's paintings. Entry costs eight euros for adults; allow an hour for a leisurely stroll. The on-site tea room rounds out the visit nicely, shaded by sculpted yews.
