places.name: Mont Dore

visits.text: Climb Puy de Sancy, the highest summit in the Massif Central at 1,885 meters—and the highest volcano in mainland France. This stratovolcano began forming 5 million years ago and went dormant about 250,000 years ago. The cable car, in service since 1936 (one of France's first), deposits you at 1,790 meters in 4 minutes from the resort base. Then 864 wooden steps lead you to the summit in 20 more minutes. From the top on clear days, the Chaîne des Puys, the Cantal mountains, Forez, and even the Alps spread before you.

Descending from the cable car, search out the sources of the Dordogne. The Dore and Dogne rivers rise on the flanks of Sancy at 1,680 and 1,640 meters altitude respectively—joining at 1,370 meters, they form the Dordogne, which then flows 483 km to the Gironde estuary. An interpretive panel on the trail guides you to the sources, which seem to spring from nowhere on a plateau covered in broom.

Back in Mont-Dore, visit the Art Nouveau thermal establishment, open since 1817. The town is a renowned spa resort for respiratory treatments—the waters rich in bicarbonate and arsenite gush forth at 44°C. Even without taking a cure, the interior architecture of the thermal building is worth the detour.

Mont-Dore and surroundings conceal a series of waterfalls worth a full day. The Grande Cascade, Auvergne's highest at 30 meters, is accessible on foot from downtown Mont-Dore via a well-marked trail (45 minutes round trip, easy). The Cascade du Saut du Loup, wilder, is reached after a short forest hike. Cascade de Queureuilh and Cascade du Rossignolet complete this circuit—bring waterproof shoes in wet periods.

Ride up to Salon du Capucin on the Mont-Dore funicular, built in 1898 and one of France's oldest still in service. The arrival station at 1,284 meters opens onto the Capucin plateau with panoramas over the Mont-Dore valley and hiking trails connecting to the Sancy ridges.

activities.text: For the more athletic, the complete ascent of Sancy on foot from the Mont-Dore parking offers a beautiful hike of 500 meters elevation gain over 7 km (about 3h30). Climb via the ridges for plunging views over the Chaudefour valley—a national nature reserve whose basalt cliffs are among Auvergne's most spectacular.

Late afternoon, watch for chamois and marmots on the high meadows above 1,500 meters. Chamois are present year-round on Sancy—spot them on rocky ridges. Marmots hibernate October through April but are very active in summer, especially mornings.

Set out on a loop hike from the Mont-Dore Thermes toward Grande Cascade, the Durbise plateau, and Roc de Cuzeau, with plunging views over the Chambon valley and Murol castle. This roughly 12 km loop (4h, intermediate level) lets you link several waterfalls and viewpoints without descending to the village.

End the day strolling through the lively thermal village of Mont-Dore and its animated lanes. The lower town concentrates small restaurants and shops offering Sancy products: Saint-Nectaire, Auvergne mountain charcuterie, mountain honey, and liqueurs based on volcanic plants.

visits.text: The UNESCO-listed Citadel of Mont-Louis is France's highest fortified town at 1,600 meters. Created from scratch by Vauban in 1679, it forms a square flanked by four bastions. It has housed the National Commando Training Center since 1964.
The Puits des Forçats houses a 17th-century treadwheel. The 28-meter-deep well was operated by two men. Only three original wheels survive in France.
The Mont-Louis solar furnace was the world's first in 1949. Installed by Félix Trombe, it enabled the experimentation that led to the large Odeillo furnace. Power output of 50 kW.
The Church of Saint Louis, dating from 1733, was modeled on the citadel's church. An architectural gem dedicated to Louis XIV's ancestor.
The star-shaped ramparts follow Vauban's plan. Three fortified gates controlled access: Porte Royale, Porte de France, and Porte de secours to the north.

activities.text: Walk the bird trail at the foot of the ramparts. Observe various local bird and insect species while taking in Vauban's ingenious work.
Discover the citadel's parade ground only as part of a guided tour. This esplanade bustles with military activity and reflects the regiment's life today.
Wander through the streets of the department's smallest commune. Saint-Louis fountain, historic town hall, and Catalan architecture await discovery.

days_plan.itin_title: Pyrénées-Orientales Road Trip: French Catalonia and the Côte Vermeille

visits.text: Keolis Armor bus from Saint-Malo to Mont-Saint-Michel: ~55 minutes to 1h15 direct, around €15 single. One to three departures per day depending on season — check keolis-armor.com. Alternative: TER Saint-Malo to Pontorson (1 hour with a change at Dol-de-Bretagne) then Nomad shuttle Pontorson to Mont (15 minutes). From the mainland car park, free Le Passeur shuttles run, or walk the causeway on foot (35 minutes — the new road-dike opened in 2014).

Grande Rue, the only route to the abbey. Four hundred metres, steep climb, uneven cobblestones, medieval houses now converted to shops (many tourist traps, a few good addresses). The Escalier du Gouffre leads up to the abbey. The 15th-century ramparts encircle the mount — built during the Hundred Years' War, Mont-Saint-Michel withstood the English for 30 years despite several sieges. The only place in Normandy never to fall into English hands.

The Abbey of Mont-Saint-Michel, 80 metres tall. Founded in 709 by Bishop Aubert of Avranches after three appearances of the Archangel Michael. Enlarged in the 11th century (Romanesque abbey), then in the 13th century with La Merveille — a three-storey Gothic building constructed on the cliff face, a feat of medieval engineering. UNESCO since 1979. Allow 1h30–2h: the abbey church, the suspended cloister, the refectory, the Guests' Hall, the Knights' Hall, the crypt of the Great Pillars. €13.

The suspended cloister — the jewel of the visit, seemingly floating between earth and sky. A double arcade of 220 small Caen limestone columns with individually carved capitals. A kitchen-garden courtyard in the centre. Looking down through the arcades onto the bay. The abbey church above blends Romanesque (nave) and Flamboyant Gothic (choir rebuilt after it collapsed in 1421). The monks of the Fraternités Monastiques de Jérusalem, who still live in the abbey, may be at prayer.

The rampart walk covers almost the full circuit of the mount. West Terrace: spectacular panoramas over the ever-changing bay. The tides here are the strongest on the continental European coastline — amplitude up to 14 metres, the sea retreating 15 km then surging back at the speed of a galloping horse, according to Victor Hugo (reality: the pace of a brisk walker). Check the posted tidal times. The greatest show is at the equinox tides (March and September).

activities.text: Lunch: be wary on the Grande Rue — prices are inflated. La Mère Poulard (since 1888), famous for its soufflé omelette (beaten for 7 minutes in copper bowls over an open fire), €40 — pricey. Alternative: restaurants on the mainland at La Caserne, cheaper and often better. Or a picnic on the ramparts, with supplies from the intra-muros grocery shop.

Sleeping intra-muros (20 hotels, €120–250, book 2 months ahead): the Mont is magical after the last day-trippers leave around 6pm. Illuminated ramparts, complete silence, empty lanes — the real experience. Otherwise Pontorson (9 km, €50–80) or La Caserne (€80–150). July–August: nocturnal abbey visits Monday to Saturday evenings, €15, classical music and dramatic lighting.

visits.text: Eleven kilometers of cyclopean stone blocks encircle the Mont Sainte-Odile plateau: this is the pagan wall, whose exact function—defensive or ritual—remains debated by researchers. It takes its name from Pope Leo IX, a native of Eguisheim, who described it as pagan in the 11th century. The monastery founded in 738 by Odile, patron saint of Alsace, overlooks the plain from its promontory. Allow a full day's walking to follow the entire wall.

activities.text: The monastery terrace, accessible to visitors and pilgrims alike, offers an unobstructed view over the Alsace plain and, on clear days, the Black Forest. The more low-key Chapelle des Larmes and Chapelle des Anges complete the visit to the site.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Villages of Alsace in 4 Days

visits.text: Montagny is a small medieval village perched on a spur above the Lyonnais hills, with its church's massive bell tower and remnants of its castle history. The narrow lanes and typical Lyonnais rubble-stone walls deserve a brief exploration: the topography itself, between a steep-sided valley and a cultivated plateau, explains why this type of commanding position was so sought after in the Middle Ages.

The viewpoint above the village offers an unobstructed view over the Garon valley and the surrounding terrain. On clear days, the Lyonnais Mountains form a verdant horizon to the southwest—a striking contrast with Lyon's proximity some twenty kilometers to the east.

activities.text: Loop of the spur and viewpoint over the Garon valley (3 km, ~1 hour). The trail follows the old walls and descends toward the valley before climbing back up via a ridge path.

Heritage route through the village's chapels and old gates. Villages of this type, common in the Lyonnais Mountains, bear witness to dense medieval settlement in this buffer zone between Lyon, the Beaujolais, and the Dauphiné.

days_plan.itin_title: Loop Around Lyon: Villages and Pierres Dorées

visits.text: Montargis, the Venice of the Gâtinais, is worth an early start to walk its bridge circuit before the flow of visitors. The town has 132 bridges and footbridges spanning the Briare Canal, the Loing and several watercourses, cutting the old town into small islets. The Pêcherie quarter — the former fishermen's quarter that supplied Paris with live fish via the canals — is the most picturesque: half-timbered houses over the water, footbridges and cobbled lanes. Don't miss the Victor Hugo Footbridge, built in 1881 to plans by the Eiffel company, arching like a rainbow over the canal.

The Girodet Museum is set in the Durzy Garden. It pays tribute to Anne-Louis Girodet-Trioson, born in Montargis in 1767: a pupil of David and winner of the Prix de Rome in 1789, he was one of the pivotal painters between neoclassicism and romanticism. The museum, holder of the Musée de France label since 2002, displays paintings, sculptures and drawings from the 16th to the 20th century, with fine pieces by David, Géricault and James Pradier. The collection brings together more than 6,000 works.

The remains of Montargis château dominate the mound north of the town. Of the royal fortress that welcomed several kings of France, only a few sections of wall and a landscaped park remain. But the view over Montargis and its canals from the heights is worth the detour.

activities.text: Don't leave without tasting Montargis pralines. Legend attributes them to the kitchen officer of the Duke of Plessis-Praslin, who is said to have invented this confection in 1636 — almonds caramelised in cooked sugar. Several confectioners keep the recipe alive in the town centre. If you're lucky, you'll see the artisans working the boiling sugar in copper cauldrons.

From April to October, operators offer 2-hour guided cruises on the Briare Canal from Saint-Roch port. It's the most pleasant way to see Montargis from the water, with lock passages and commentary on the history of the canals. Book ahead in July-August.

On Saturday mornings, a lively market sets up in the town centre. Gâtinais producers, market gardeners and artisans bring the quays and squares to life. It's also the chance to find forest honey, poultry from the region and, naturally, pralines in every form.

days_plan.itin_title: Loiret Road Trip: Orléans and the Châteaux of the Loire

places.name: Montauban

visits.text: Place Nationale forms a quadrangle ringed by double arcades of pink brick. Founded in 1144 and rebuilt after the fires of 1614 and 1649, it retains the covered galleries where merchants once traded.

The Ingres-Bourdelle Museum occupies the former 17th-century bishop's palace. Reopened in 2019 after renovation, it holds 4,500 drawings by Ingres, including La Belle Jardinière, and a major collection of Bourdelle sculptures across five floors.
Pont Vieux has crossed the Tarn since 1335. Its seven pink brick arches span 205 meters. A triumphal arch once adorned one end to celebrate the Peace of Ryswick in 1697.
Saint-Jacques Church exemplifies southern Gothic architecture, with a single nave and massive buttresses. Its octagonal bell tower rises over the old town.
The landscaped banks lead to Port-Canal, where barges moor in the shade of the plane trees.

activities.text: Wander under the arcades of Place Nationale. The red brick and white stone facades form a harmonious classical ensemble.
Explore the Canal des Deux Mers greenway. The cycling route links Bordeaux to the Mediterranean, following the calm waters.
Taste Moissac chasselas at the market stalls. This golden grape with its crisp berries has held an AOC since 1971.

days_plan.itin_title: Tarn-et-Garonne Road Trip: Bastides and Orchards

map_keywords: Canal latéral à la Garonne Montauban

visits.text: The Abbey of Fontenay, a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1981, is the world's best-preserved Cistercian abbey. Founded in 1118 by Saint Bernard of Clairvaux, it has retained its cloister, austere abbey church, water-powered forge, and gardens in remarkable condition. The entire complex nestles in an isolated valley—the silence is arresting. Allow at least 1 hour 30 minutes for your visit, longer if you stroll through the park.

In Montbard itself, climb up to the Parc Buffon—naturalist Georges-Louis Leclerc, Count of Buffon, lived and worked here in the 18th century. He designed this terraced park above the Brenne River. You'll find the remains of the medieval castle. The Tour de l'Aubespin and Tour Saint-Louis offer beautiful views over the town and the Canal de Bourgogne.

activities.text: Walk or cycle along the Canal de Bourgogne from Montbard—the towpath is flat and shaded, and you'll pass leisure barges. Allow an hour for a round trip to the next lock.

days_plan.itin_title: Burgundy Road Trip: Cathedrals, Vineyards and Villages

visits.text: The Château de Montbéliard has dominated the city since the 10th century. Its two hectares include 250 rooms divided between the Henriette and Frédéric towers. The museum presents 15 renovated rooms (875 m²) with history collections (furniture, silverware, weapons from the 15th to 18th centuries), archaeology, natural sciences linked to naturalist Georges Cuvier native to the city, and contemporary art.

The Saint-Martin temple, built between 1601 and 1607 by architect Heinrich Schickhardt, is the oldest French building assigned to Reformed worship. Montbéliard was the only French-speaking Lutheran territory, attached to the Duchy of Württemberg for four centuries. The temple is currently closed for restoration.

The Musée de l'Aventure Peugeot traces the history of the Lion brand from its 19th-century origins. The collections present not only iconic automobiles but also the coffee, pepper, and electric mills that made the company's reputation before the automobile. An immersion into the region's industrial history.

activities.text: Stroll through the historic center of Montbéliard, a City of Art and History. Les Halles (former governmental center of the Principality), the Hôtel du Lion Rouge, the Hôtel Forstner, and the colorful facades testify to the Germanic influence inherited from four centuries of attachment to Württemberg. Saint-Maimboeuf church (1850) completes the architectural panorama.

The Lumières de Noël in Montbéliard is one of the most beautiful Christmas markets in Europe. For four weeks at year-end, 160 artisans set up around the Saint-Martin temple. Shows, entertainment, ice rink, and children's village animate the city. The castle lights up and the streets are adorned with magical decorations.

days_plan.itin_title: Doubs Circuit: Watchmaking and Swiss Border

places.name: Montbrison

visits.text: La Diana Heraldic Hall. Fitted out around 1300 by Count Jean I of Forez, this exceptional hall measures 19 meters long and 8 meters high and wide. Its pointed pinewood vault is decorated with 48 parallel bands, each adorned with 36 repeated shields, making 1,728 compartments in all, depicting the coats of arms of feudal families allied with the counts of Forez. A frieze of 242 shields intertwined with fantastic animals runs around the hall. Francis I was welcomed here in 1536. The site is unique in France for its age. La Diana houses a library of more than 50,000 volumes.

Allard Museum. Set beside a public garden, this is one of the department's oldest museums. Two centuries of continuously enriched collections present archaeology, fine arts, natural history, and regional ethnography. Exhibitions reveal Forez history and its people through objects, paintings, sculptures, and archival documents. The museum occupies a handsome 19th-century building in Montbrison's heart.

Notre-Dame d'Espérance Collegiate Church. An emblematic monument of Forez, this Gothic church, more than eight centuries old, dominates the town. Its unique architecture and thousand-year history make it a must-see. A soaring nave, luminous choir and colorful stained glass characterize the building. Still an active place of worship, the collegiate church has endured through the centuries while retaining its spiritual and heritage importance for the region.

Montbrison Historic Center. Former capital of Forez, Montbrison has retained many reminders of its prestigious past. Private mansions, medieval houses and Renaissance buildings line the streets of the center. Place Grenette, rue Martin Bernard and ruelle du Palais offer a glimpse of Forez architecture through the centuries. The self-guided tour brochure “Laissez-vous conter Montbrison” is available at the Tourist Office.

activities.text: Walk in the Jardin d'Allard. A public park adjoining the museum, this garden offers a place to relax in the heart of the town. Century-old trees, shaded paths and lawns invite visitors to stroll. An ideal starting point for exploring Montbrison's historic center and shops.
