visits.text: The first place on this circuit you'll fall in love with: as you arrive in Montclus, the village comes into view in a bend of the Cèze, clinging to its limestone spur, surrounded by vineyards and lavender. Not a single power pole is visible, and there are no modern buildings—that's why Les Plus Beaux Villages de France awarded it the label in 2012. The Latin name “Castrum Montecluso” appears in a document from 1275: the name literally means “castle enclosed by mountains,” which perfectly describes the site. The 32-meter square keep is the remnant of a castle built that same year, 1275, by the Counts of Sabran, one of the most powerful families in Provence. Climb up to it to appreciate the height of the cliff above the river.

As you descend toward the river via Rue de l'Arceau—the castle's former vaulted medieval entrance—look for the Beaumes site, away from the village: a vast hall carved into the rock, the remnant of a Benedictine cave monastery founded in the 12th century, which later served as a chapel for the Templars. It's one of the valley's least-known curiosities. Check with the tourist office about access conditions.

The Pont du Moulin, built in 1870, is the first crossing of the Cèze after Barjac—before it was built, people and animals alike crossed from one bank to the other on a ferry that charged a fare. From the bridge, the view of the hilltop village with its keep and white stone houses is the one you see on postcards. It also provides access to the Cèze's pebble beaches for a swim.

activities.text: The Dent du Serret hike starts from the village: an accessible trail leading through forests and limestone cliffs to one of the best viewpoints over the Cèze gorges. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes for the 4 km loop. Easy to moderate difficulty. On clear days, the view extends to the hills of the Ardèche.

The Cèze at Montclus is ideal for canoeing, kayaking and swimming in summer. The waters are clear and the summer flow moderate. Operators offer equipment rental in neighboring villages—check with the Cèze Cévennes tourist office for the nearest rental points.

days_plan.itin_title: Cèze Valley and Ardèche Gorges Circuit

visits.text: Perched on Montélimar's heights and accessible within minutes on foot from downtown, this château testifies to the Adhémar family's power. Built in the 12th century, it comprises a seigneurial residence, the 11th-century Saint-Pierre chapel, a square tower, and a fortified enclosure. From the keep, access the sentry path offering 360° panoramic views over the Drôme Pre-Alps and Rhône valley.

Stroll through the entirely pedestrian historic center with alleys lined by Provençal-colored houses. Admire the rehabilitated ramparts and private mansions. Discover Diane de Poitiers' House, a beautiful 16th-century Renaissance building. If you're there Saturday morning, the highly reputed weekly market takes over the market square.

Enter the delicious world of Montélimar nougat at artisanal factories perpetuating tradition since the 19th century. The Arnaud Soubeyran Nougat Museum, the oldest factory founded in 1837, traces this confection's history and offers live viewing of artisanal production. Nougat consists of honey, sugar, egg whites, almonds, and sometimes pistachios.

activities.text: Explore the château through multiple playful visit routes enriched with models, treasure hunts, sound atmospheres, tactile experiences, and augmented reality. This family-friendly discovery imagined by children and Drôme professionals teaches the château's history, lords' lives, and medieval practices.

Visit traditional factories like Le Chaudron d'Or or Arnaud Soubeyran where local expertise unfolds during regular demonstrations. Taste different nougat varieties: white, black, soft, hard, with pistachios, with candied fruits. Learn to distinguish quality genuine Montélimar nougat.
Round off your visit with the Musée de Montélimar, devoted to local history, or the European Fighter Aviation Museum with its combat aircraft still in flying condition.

days_plan.itin_title: Drome Provencale Road Trip: Villages and Terroirs

places.name: Montferrier

visits.text: Mirepoix unfolds around its splendid Place aux Couverts, a gem among medieval bastides, rebuilt after the flood of 1289. Under the wooden galleries of the 15th century, admire the 103 carved heads of the Maison des Consuls: women in headdresses, bearded faces, a tortoise and a grimacing devil adorn the beams. Saint-Maurice cathedral impresses with its single nave 22 metres wide, the second widest in Europe, and its German organ of 1891 listed as a Historic Monument. Allow about 30 km from the overnight town, roughly 35 minutes by road.

Some forty kilometres north, the La Belle Verte leisure centre occupies a tree-shaded 19th-century estate at Le Vernet, on the banks of the Ariège. The century-old park offers safe water access, shaded picnic areas, and direct riverside entry. Landscaped banks let you contemplate the rushing waters before launching onto the rapids.

Montségur raises its enigmatic silhouette at 1,207 meters elevation atop the pog, a vertiginous rocky pinnacle. This last Cathar stronghold where 220 Parfaits perished at the stake in March 1244 crowns a spur reached via a switchback trail from the parking area. At dusk or at dawn, the raking light magnifies this tragic site. The ruins offer 360° panoramas over valleys, the Tabe massif, and plains stretching to Carcassonne.

activities.text: Set off for a white-water stand-up paddle session on the Ariège, supervised by enthusiastic guides. The route from Le Vernet towards Saverdun offers about 8 km of sporty paddling alternating rapids and flat stretches. Paddle standing on your inflatable board and discover the river from a whole new angle. Allow about 60 km from the overnight town, roughly 1 hour by road.

The final ascent to Montségur Castle follows a switchback trail from the ticket office, a 5-minute walk from the car park. Allow 30 minutes to climb this historic path once trodden by the Bonshommes, where stones polished smooth by passing feet make the going slippery. Rest points along the route open onto the valleys and the Tabe massif. Proper walking shoes are essential.

days_plan.itin_title: Ariège Circuit: Cathar Castles, Prehistoric Caves & Mountain Lakes

map_keywords: Base de loisirs La Belle Verte Le Vernet

visits.text: The ruins of the château of the Counts of Montfort overlook the village from a mound 185 meters above sea level. The Anne de Bretagne Tower, a 15th-century Flamboyant Gothic remnant, offers a panoramic view over the Yvelines and the forest of Rambouillet.

The Church of Saint-Pierre, from the 15th and 16th centuries, houses 37 Renaissance stained-glass windows regarded as unique in the Île-de-France. Each window depicts a biblical scene in blues, reds, and golds.

The Maurice Ravel House-Museum, known as "Le Belvédère," keeps intact the piano, the scores, and the collections of curious objects belonging to the composer, who lived here from 1921 to 1937. This is where he composed the Boléro.
The old cemetery, classified as a Historic Monument, surprises with its 15th- and 16th-century galleries evoking a cloister, and its Gothic portal. The Aznavour family vault is located here.

activities.text: Walk the cobbled streets of the medieval village: half-timbered houses, mansions, and the Porte Bardoul trace a circuit through a thousand years of history.
Hike along the edge of Rambouillet forest from Montfort-l'Amaury. Marked trails wind between ponds and clearings.

days_plan.itin_title: Yvelines Road Trip: Versailles and Impressionist Villages

visits.text: Montfuron (200 inhabitants) is one of the Luberon's best-hidden villages. Its name comes from the Latin Monsfurnorum — “mountain of ovens” — a reference to the gypsum fired and ground here to make plaster. The village has one of only two windmills still in working order in Alpes-de-Haute-Provence: the Saint-Elzéar mill, built in 1640. Restored with support from the Luberon Regional Natural Park in 1980 and again in 2000, it retains part of its original wooden machinery and its 13-metre-long sails. It still produces flour during the mill festival on the first weekend of August each year. Guided tours take place on Saturday afternoons in season.

Climb to the Castelas viewpoint (650 m), on the ruins of Jean Garnier's Renaissance castle, sacked during the Wars of Religion. You'll find the stone compass rose, with Provence's 32 winds engraved according to their direction (Tramontane, Mistral, Sirocco…). The toposcope names the mountains visible in the 360° view: Sainte-Victoire, Mont Ventoux, the Luberon, Montagne de Lure and the Alps as far as Italy in clear weather.

activities.text: The Moulins loop (starting in the village, 2 hours 30 minutes) crosses the forest, passes the ruins of the gypsum mill, climbs back up to the ridge with panoramic views and reaches the windmill. The trail is family-friendly and not technically difficult. Right beside the mill, the Jardin à Papillons (7,000 m² of shrubby garrigue, 3,000 plants planted) is home to 60 species of butterflies — a peaceful place to visit depending on the season.

days_plan.itin_title: Forcalquier & Verdon Gorges Road Trip

visits.text: Montgenèvre sits at 1,860 meters, at the foot of one of the Alps' oldest crossings into Italy. The village resort retains its mountain layout beneath its modern facilities, and in summer its slopes turn into flowering alpine pastures. It's a border stop: here you cross over into Piedmont. Drop your bags and enjoy the crisp air before exploring the heights.

The Col de Montgenèvre stands at 1,854 meters. The Via Domitia already passed through it. Today, a commemorative obelisk and sections of the old road recall its role as a crossroads between Gaul and Piedmont for millennia. A few minutes are enough, but the place has its place in the history of travel.

Fort du Janus dominates Montgenèvre with its galleries and casemates. A military structure that was remodeled and extensively modernized through the twentieth century (it was part of the Alpine Maginot Line), it guarded the strategic pass facing Piedmont. Access is by trail from the pass, and the interior can only be visited under supervision. Check before heading up, but the walk and the views are worthwhile.

activities.text: Montgenèvre's bike park descends through larches and alpine pastures, with marked trails for all levels and lifts open in summer. It is one of the good downhill mountain-biking spots near the border, in a Franco-Italian setting. Bike and protective gear rental is available on site. The season generally runs from late June to early September, depending on snow conditions and lift operations.

Cross-border hikes leave from the pass toward Italian Piedmont: the GR5, the great Alpine traverse from Lake Geneva to the Mediterranean, passes through Montgenèvre. Panoramic trails on the Franco-Italian peaks, with the option of overnight stops in mountain refuges. Bring an identity document to cross into Italy. Difficulty ranges from moderate to strenuous depending on the chosen route.

days_plan.itin_title: Hautes-Alpes Road Trip: High Mountains and Alpine Valleys

places.name: Montherme

visits.text: Meuse Loop at Monthermé. The river draws one of its most beautiful meanders here, almost completely encircling the Ardennes massif in a verdant embrace. From the Longue Roche viewpoint, contemplate this geological jewel where the Meuse winds gently 200 meters below. The endless forest and village nestled in the curve compose a grandiose tableau.

Rocks of the Four Sons of Aymon. Four schistose quartzite peaks emerge from the dense forest at 260 meters altitude, evoking the silhouettes of the four knights Renaud, Allard, Richard, and Guichard riding Bayard. The medieval legend inscribes itself in the Ardennes landscape where, it is said, one can still hear the fairy horse neighing. A monumental statue crowns the site accessible by landscaped trail.

activities.text: Walk along the canal. The restored towpath peacefully follows the Meuse for several kilometers between locks and shaded banks. Once a river transport route, it now offers a flat course ideal for walking and cycling. Observe barges, waterfowl, and fishermen in a bucolic atmosphere.

Mountain biking in the massif. Technical trails crisscross the Ardennes forest between rocks, ravines, and panoramic viewpoints. Significant elevation gain and rocky passages delight experienced mountain bikers. Marked circuits reveal Roc la Tour and other rocky chaos hidden in the woods.

Panoramic observation from Roc la Tour. Climb toward this quartzite rocky outcrop surging from the forest to admire the Meuse valley and endless meanders. The remarkable geological site already served as a gathering place in prehistoric times as evidenced by engraved slates discovered. The chaos of tangled blocks both intrigues and fascinates.

days_plan.itin_title: Ardennes Road Trip: Forests & Fortresses (3 Days)

map_keywords: Rochers des Quatre Fils Aymon Monthermé

visits.text: The 13th-century Tower of Montlhéry dominates the plain from its spur. This medieval keep was the seat of a strategic county between Paris and Orléans.
The Linas-Montlhéry racing circuit was built in 1924 by industrialist Alexandre Lamblin. Its 2.5 km high-speed oval with parabolic bends caused a sensation.
Between 1925 and 1939, 86% of world speed records were set at the racing circuit. The track received the Patrimoine du XXe siècle label.
Since 1973, UTAC has managed the facilities. The site now hosts automotive testing and about ten public events per year.

activities.text: The Coupes Auto Légende event takes place in October with six starting grids dedicated to classic cars. Cars ranging from modern classics to pre-war vehicles bring the circuit to life.
The US Motor Show celebrates American cars while the Autodrome Italian Meeting welcomes 400 Italian cars. Track sessions, exhibitions, and parades.
The 3.4 km road circuit lets you relive the atmosphere of grand prix racing. The 51% gradient of the Lapize bend still impresses drivers.

days_plan.itin_title: Essonne Tour: Castles and Valleys

visits.text: The Castle of the Dukes of Bourbon, Montluçon's emblem perched on its rocky spur, has dominated the Cher since the 14th century. Louis II of Bourbon built it to demonstrate the power of his dynasty. From the esplanade, the view takes in the old town nestled in the river's bends, revealing the medieval Saint-Pierre and Notre-Dame churches, timber-framed houses and fifteen buildings listed as historic monuments.

The MuPop (Musée des Musiques Populaires), in the heart of the medieval town, combines renovated mansions with contemporary architecture. A leading French collection of 3,500 popular music instruments (1750 to the present), 150 individual listening stations and spectacular exhibition design: a recreated dance hall, instrument maker's workshop and punk room. Hurdy-gurdies, accordions, bagpipes and electric guitars tell the story of France's festive music.

The medieval Saint-Pierre quarter reveals its narrow lanes, timber-framed houses and preserved heritage. The Saint-Pierre church (testimony to the patronage of the Dukes of Bourbon) and Notre-Dame church punctuate the visit. On market days, the cobbled squares bustle with activity. The town has kept its old-world charm while modernising.

The Jardin Wilson offers a green retreat in the shade of a century-old blue cedar. The Boulevard de Courtais invites shopping in a modern setting. Montluçon, a medieval and festive town and gateway to the Auvergne, has managed to combine its prestigious Bourbonnais past with the turning point of the Industrial Revolution, creating the modern “Ville Gozet” that surrounds the old town.

activities.text: The Canal de Berry, a historic waterway linking Limousin and Berry, runs alongside Montluçon for several kilometres. Towpaths, cycle paths and hiking trails allow visitors to follow its peaceful banks. Locks, bridges and engineering structures bear witness to its waterway heritage. Fishing, cycling or a simple stroll: the canal offers relaxation in nature close to the town.

Concerts and cultural events enliven the year in Montluçon: a strong theatrical tradition (the National Drama Centre attracts families), “Lumières sur le Bourbonnais” (video mapping on the château) and free concerts. The town where Audrey Tautou grew up maintains its cultural dynamism.

The forêt de Tronçais (13,225 ha, one of Europe's finest oak forests) is approximately 41 km from Montluçon, a 45-minute drive. Remarkable centuries-old trees, 560 km of paths and ponds (including the étang de Saloup, 94 ha): this forest offers hiking, mountain biking and horse riding. In autumn, the calls of rutting stags echo at dusk through this legendary forest.

days_plan.itin_title: Allier Road Trip: Vichy, Thermal Baths and Bourbonnais Bocage

visits.text: Montmédy citadel, erected in 1545 by Charles V to defend the Spanish Netherlands, is one of northeastern France's vastest fortresses with over 1.5 kilometers of walls. Conquered by Louis XIV's troops in 1657, it was remodeled by Vauban who added bastions, demi-lunes, and a second ring of fortifications.

At the upper town's heart, the Fortification Museum presents the evolution of Meuse defense systems from prehistory: scale models of works, ancient weapons, aerial views of fortified sites. Maps and reconstructions help understand attack and defense strategies through the centuries.

The Jules Bastien-Lepage Museum, housed in the citadel's former school, exhibits drawings, prints, and paintings by this 19th-century Meuse artist from Damvillers, who painted rural life scenes with realism influenced by the Impressionists.

Upper town lanes twist around small squares where artists' workshops animate the citadel's cultural life. The upper town church houses a remarkable organ and temporary exhibitions in certain casemates transformed into galleries.

Fifteen kilometers away, Avioth basilica is a Gothic marvel rising in the middle of a small village. A highly visited pilgrimage site, it surprises with its dimensions and sculpture finesse. Don't miss the "Recevresse," a structure unique in France designed to receive offerings.

activities.text: Follow the ramparts circuit, a marked route of about 1 kilometer circling the fortifications. Explanatory panels, videos, and quizzes trace the citadel's history. The 360° panorama embraces the Meuse countryside to the Belgian border.
In summer, torchlight visits transform the citadel at nightfall. Underground galleries, artillery casemates, and caponnières take on a striking atmosphere by torchlight.
Make a detour to Marville, 10 kilometers away, a village known for its Renaissance architecture and Spanish-style houses. The cemetery and church merit a stop for old stone enthusiasts.

days_plan.itin_title: Ardennes Road Trip: Forests & Fortresses (3 Days)
Meuse Circuit: Verdun and the Citadels
Grand Est Road Trip: Vineyards, Ramparts and Forests

visits.text: The Jean-Jacques Rousseau Museum occupies Mont-Louis, the house the philosopher rented from 1757 to 1762—a small 17th-century rural house amid a garden where he spent mornings botanizing. This is where he wrote Julie, or the New Heloise, The Social Contract, and Émile. The guided tour (mandatory for the house, about 45 minutes) also recounts the hasty flight of June 9, 1762: condemned for Émile, Rousseau left Montmorency in minutes, leaving his furniture behind. The Donjon, his study at the far end of the garden, is where he wrote his Letter to d'Alembert in three weeks. Open Tue–Sun, 2–6 PM (high season), Tue–Sat, 2–6 PM (low season).

A few steps away, push open the door of the Collégiale Saint-Martin—Montmorency's oldest church, built between the 15th and 16th centuries. Its Renaissance stained-glass windows are of rare quality for a church this size: Rousseau visited regularly, and the Marshal of Luxembourg, his protector at the château, had his own reserved pew. Take a few minutes to sit and let the light filtered through colored glass do the rest.

If you still have energy late in the day, climb into the Montmorency forest—2,600 hectares of chestnut trees and oaks five minutes' walk from the center. The GR1 and numerous marked trails run through the forest. From clearings on the ridges, on clear days, you'll glimpse Paris to the south and the Vexin hills to the north—an unexpected view at this distance from the capital.

activities.text: Hiking in Montmorency forest: the GR1 enters the woods from the northern edge of town and climbs toward the ridges along old avenues laid out in a star pattern. A loop of about 10 km from town, easy and well-shaded.
In the evening, the café terraces on Place du Marché come alive with locals. It's Montmorency's most central spot for a drink before dining in the restaurants on the adjoining streets.

days_plan.itin_title: Val-d'Oise Tour: Impressionist Villages and Heritage

visits.text: Cross the old 14th-century Gothic bridge over the Gartempe to enter the Cité de l'Écrit et des Métiers du Livre. Since 2000, some thirty booksellers, secondhand booksellers, bookbinders, and illuminators have occupied this restored medieval quarter.
Outside Notre-Dame church, a statue of the Virgin, regarded as miraculous since 1789, is still venerated.
The Octogone is a 12th-century funerary chapel with an octagonal shape. It is part of the listed Maison-Dieu complex, founded in the 11th-12th centuries to welcome pilgrims and the sick.

Climb up to Saint-Laurent Chapel, whose façade and bell tower date from the 12th century. It preserves frescoes and the tomb of Étienne de Vignolles, known as "La Hire," Joan of Arc's companion and lord of Montmorillon.

The Montmorillon Art and History Museum (free admission) presents varied collections from prehistoric archaeology to fine arts. A permanent museum showcases over 200 antique typewriters and calculating machines.

activities.text: Taste Montmorillon's macarons, a local specialty since the 17th century. The Macaron Museum traces the history of this confection in the lower town.
Stroll along the banks of the Gartempe, the river that separates upper and lower town. From the quays, the view of the medieval city and Notre-Dame Church is especially photogenic.
Visit the open-air theater set in the gardens of the Maison-Dieu, overlooking the town. The magnificent 17th-century monastic buildings dominate the panorama.

days_plan.itin_title: Vienne Road Trip: Futuroscope and Romanesque Heritage

visits.text: Saint-Gilles Chapel in Montoire-sur-le-Loir houses exceptional 12th-century Romanesque frescoes. These remarkably preserved murals depict biblical scenes and saints in colors still vivid after nine centuries. Christ in Majesty enthroned in the apse dominates the whole with his monumental presence. Apostles and angels spread their wings in harmonious compositions. This small chapel is a little-known gem of Romanesque art that is well worth a detour. Specialists consider it one of the region's most important groups of wall paintings.

Montoire's medieval bridge spans the Loir with its centuries-old stone arches. This fortified bridge from the Middle Ages connected the two banks of the walled town. Its massive piers have withstood floods for centuries without fail. The view from the bridge takes in old façades reflected in tranquil water. Restored washhouses testify to the work of washerwomen in the past. Landscaped banks invite strolling along the willow-lined river. The area's river heritage can be discovered along the water in a peaceful atmosphere.

The old town of Montoire-sur-le-Loir reveals its old lanes and half-timbered houses. The ruined château dominates the town from its rocky promontory. Saint-Laurent Church features restrained Gothic architecture. Old middle-class residences testify to past prosperity. Flower-filled interior courtyards can be discovered while wandering. The preserved architectural heritage invites leisurely exploration of this characterful small town. Shops and cafés cluster around the lively central square.

activities.text: Discovering the Loir valley as it winds between limestone hillsides and green meadows. The river's peaceful, poplar-lined meanders invite cycling or walking along towpaths. Wine-growing villages dot the waterside, offering picturesque stops. Restored mills testify to the area's once-flourishing economic activity. Bucolic landscapes inspired writers and Impressionist painters. The gentle atmosphere of Anjou can be felt in this valley spared from mass tourism.

Exploring cave dwellings carved into the tuffeau cliffs lining the Loir. Former quarries turned into cellars and mushroom farms can sometimes be visited on open days. Underground galleries maintain a constant temperature ideal for storing wine. Some caves converted into dwellings reveal the ingenuity of vernacular architecture. Underground shelters dug during wars dot the hillsides. This fascinating underground heritage is worth discovering with passionate local guides.

Vineyards on the Vendômois hillsides produce AOC wines little known to the general public. Chenin, Pineau d'Aunis, and Gamay grape varieties flourish on sunny slopes overlooking the Loir. Winemakers open their cellars to introduce their crisp whites and light reds. The Coteaux du Vendômois and Cheverny appellations testify to the region's wine revival. Tastings let you appreciate these characterful wines paired with local goat cheeses. Panoramas from the vineyards take in the entire verdant valley.

days_plan.itin_title: Loir-et-Cher Itinerary: Royal Châteaux and the Loir Valley

visits.text: Place de la Comédie, nicknamed the "Egg Square" due to its oval shape, is the beating heart of Montpellier. At its center stands the Fountain of the Three Graces, sculpted in 1776 from Carrara marble. The square is bordered by the 19th-century Opéra Comédie, whose neoclassical façade is remarkable. Street performers, bustling café terraces, and crisscrossing trams make this an essential meeting point. The square has been entirely pedestrianized since the 2000s and serves as the ideal starting point for exploring the historic center.

The Musée Fabre is one of Europe's most important art museums, with over 900 works displayed across 9,000 square meters. Founded in 1828 thanks to a donation from painter François-Xavier Fabre, it presents a journey from the Renaissance to contemporary art. The collections include major works by Rubens, Delacroix, Courbet, and an exceptional Soulages room. The 19th-century Griffons Gallery and Colonnade Gallery are spectacular. The entrance is through the former Jesuit college, featuring a mosaic designed by Daniel Buren. Allow at least 2-3 hours for your visit.

The Écusson is the name given to Montpellier's historic center because of its shape, which resembles a heraldic shield. This maze of cobbled medieval lanes contains 80 private mansions from the 17th and 18th centuries. You'll discover façades adorned with mascarons, hidden inner courtyards, and monumental staircases. The Promenade du Peyrou, with its triumphal arch and neoclassical water tower, offers beautiful views over the city. The quarter blends boutiques, restaurants, art galleries, and architectural heritage. Get lost in the narrow streets to uncover these treasures.

Saint-Pierre Cathedral, built in the 14th century, dominates the Écusson with its impressive fortified porch supported by two massive towers. The austere Gothic architecture contrasts with the brighter interior, where the single nave rises to 28 meters. Connected to the medical school founded in 1220, one of the oldest in the Western world, the cathedral testifies to Montpellier's historical importance. The forecourt offers a peaceful space to rest after exploring the Écusson.

The Antigone quarter, designed by architect Ricardo Bofill in the 1980s, is a striking example of neoclassical urban planning. The buildings with their monumental façades, columns, and pediments create a theatrical atmosphere. The long axis leading from the city center to the Lez River crosses geometric squares and esplanades. The architecture divides opinion but doesn't leave anyone indifferent. The walk to the banks of the Lez is pleasant, with basins, fountains, and views of the modern Port Marianne district.

activities.text: The Jardins du Peyrou extend over 3 hectares at Montpellier's highest point. Laid out in the 17th century, they offer a shaded promenade with panoramic views of the Cévennes and the Mediterranean on clear days. The Saint-Clément aqueduct that feeds the neoclassical water tower is impressive with its 22-meter arches. The atmosphere is peaceful, ideal for a break after visiting the historic center. Montpellier locals love to picnic here at sunset.

Montpellier's tram system is a convenient way to discover the city and its different neighborhoods. The network has 4 lines, with trams featuring designs by contemporary artists. Lines 1 and 2 intersect at La Comédie. Line 3 serves the Mosson area and connects to surrounding villages. It's a pleasant and economical way to get around. A ticket costs a few euros for one hour of travel.

The Arceaux market takes place every Tuesday and Saturday morning under the arches of the Saint-Clément aqueduct. It's one of Montpellier's most authentic and lively markets, with local producers, market gardeners, cheese makers, and fishmongers. The atmosphere is friendly and Provençal. You'll find seasonal fruits and vegetables, olives, goat cheeses, and Mediterranean specialties. Perfect for immersing yourself in local life and discovering regional products. Arrive early to get the best selection.

Walk along the Lez River to Port Marianne. The landscaped riverbanks are pleasant for walking or cycling. The route passes gardens, green spaces, and contemporary architecture. You'll pass the Hôtel de Région designed by Ricardo Bofill, the modern City Hall, and the business district. Pontoons allow you to settle by the water. The journey to the sea (Port Marianne) is about 5 km. Bike rentals available in the city center.

days_plan.itin_title: Hérault Road Trip: Montpellier, Beaches and the Hinterland

visits.text: Montpeyroux is one of this circuit's surprises. Classified among France's Most Beautiful Villages, this medieval village is built almost exclusively of arkose—a golden feldspathic sandstone quarried locally, lending it a surprisingly southern air at this latitude. Its name, from Latin mons petrosus, means 'stony mount'—it has been since antiquity. Enter through the 14th-century fortified gate, remnant of the old ramparts, and lose yourself in the calades (lanes paved with river pebbles) winding between winegrowers' houses.

Climb to the 13th-century medieval keep—33 meters of circular tower dominating the village and the Allier valley. It's the last vestige of the fortress that once guarded the seigneury, which passed notably to Madeleine de La Tour d'Auvergne, whose daughter married Lorenzo de Medici—Montpeyroux was thus, via her granddaughter Catherine de Medici and then Queen Margot, a possession linked to French history until 1610. From the summit platform, your gaze carries to the Chaîne des Puys westward and Puy de Dôme, Sancy to the southwest, and the Allier valley below.

15 km from Montpeyroux, make the detour to Issoire and its Saint-Austremoine abbey church—one of Auvergne's five great Romanesque churches and one of the best preserved. Its polychrome interior decoration, restored in the 19th century, blends ochres, earth tones, and lapis in a striking result. The apse capitals illustrate John's Apocalypse with rare narrative force.

activities.text: Local outfitters offer tastings of PDO Côtes d'Auvergne Montpeyroux wines. Vines planted on the sunny slopes of the hill produce mainly gamay for reds and chardonnay for whites. This vineyard, which nearly disappeared after the phylloxera crisis, has since the 2000s seen a renaissance driven by several passionate winemakers.

Wear good shoes for the 'On the arkose path' circuit (8.5 km, 2h30, easy) departing the village and skirting the old arkose quarries, passing near the Allier and Château de Chadieu. Along the way, you'll see outcrops of the blonde rock that 19th-century quarrymen exploited to supply Clermont-Ferrand, Issoire, and even the streets of Paris.

days_plan.itin_title: Auvergne Volcanoes Road Trip: Puy de Dôme and Lakes

visits.text: Saint-Martin Collegiate Church has stood over the village since the 14th century. Its 16th-century Flemish tapestries, listed as Historic Monuments, retrace the life of Saint Martin.
Explore the bastide center with its white stone houses. Arcades and covered passages testify to Quercy's medieval architecture.
Discover the collegiate church's side chapels adorned with murals. Liturgical furnishings include carved choir stalls and gilded altarpieces.

activities.text: Stroll cobbled lanes lined with half-timbered houses and dovecotes. The tranquil atmosphere reflects rural Quercy life.
Stroll around the central square of Montpezat-de-Quercy, a short walk from the collegiate church of Saint-Martin. The covered walkways and white stone façades invite you to take a break.

days_plan.itin_title: Tarn-et-Garonne Road Trip: Bastides and Orchards

visits.text: Montréal-en-Ardèche is a medieval village perched on the foothills of the Tanargue massif, overlooking the valley below. Its square keep and church are the village's two architectural landmarks, visible from approach roads. Cobbled lanes link the upper village to agricultural terraces below—dry-stone terraces testifying to considerable clearing and development work over several centuries.

From the village's high point, the view over southern ridgelines—Tanargue, Cévennes plateaus, first Cévennes heights—is particularly striking. On clear days, you can make out the silhouettes of Gerbier-de-Jonc and Mont Mézenc to the north. Climb to the keep for the best panorama.

Viewpoints over the southern ridgelines are reached by signposted trails from the village. Pick up the hiking map at the tourist office before you set off, as the routes can be wet or overgrown depending on the season.

activities.text: Take the trail climbing toward the high point behind the keep for a 3 to 4 km round trip offering an extended panorama over southern ridges and the network of old terraces. Figure 1h30 to 2h. The path crosses chestnut groves and follows dry-stone walls characteristic of southern Ardèche.

The short heritage loop within the enclosure and outskirts (2 km) can be done in under an hour. It lets you read the village's medieval layout and spot defensive elements still visible in the built fabric. Access is entirely free.

days_plan.itin_title: The 18 Most Beautiful Villages of Ardèche

visits.text: Montréal-du-Gers is a 13th-century hilltop bastide, listed among France's Most Beautiful Villages. Its central square is bordered by Gothic arcades. The fortified church dominates the village with its square bell tower that served as a keep.

activities.text: Stroll through the cobbled lanes descending from the central square. Houses of honey-colored stone and half-timbering, vaulted passages, and small squares give the village tremendous charm.
The panorama from the church terrace embraces the Gers countryside and Armagnac hills. On clear days, you can glimpse the Pyrenees to the south.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Garonne Road Trip: From Toulouse to the Pyrenees

visits.text: Montréjeau is a hilltop bastide dominating the confluence of the Garonne and Neste rivers. Its 19th-century market hall marks the town center. The architecture follows the grid pattern typical of bastides.
The panorama from the terrace embraces the entire Pyrenees chain. On clear days, the view extends from Pic du Midi to the peaks of Spain. It's one of the finest viewpoints over the central Pyrenees.

activities.text: The Monday morning market draws people from all over the region. You will find mountain produce and Pyrenean specialties there.
From Montréjeau, Saint-Bertrand-de-Comminges is visible in the distance on its rocky outcrop. The road leading there crosses landscapes of hills with the Pyrenees as backdrop.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Garonne Road Trip: From Toulouse to the Pyrenees

visits.text: The Murs à pêches span 34 hectares of undeveloped orchards. From the 17th to the early 20th century, these three-meter-high walls of plaster and flint made it possible to grow exceptional peaches served at the tables of Louis XIV and the Russian tsar.
Within the teaching garden, the horticultural museum is France's only museum devoted to the tools and techniques of espalier peach cultivation from the 16th to 19th centuries.
The Maison populaire de Montreuil, a contemporary art center, hosts exhibitions, seminars, and events in a brutalist building at the heart of the town.
Climb up to Parc des Beaumonts for an unobstructed view over the capital. This 24-hectare natural park harbors calcareous grasslands rare in Île-de-France and a bird observatory.
Bas-Montreuil blends workers' housing built of brick and buhrstone, former workshops converted into lofts, and cultural third places. The alleyways hold surprises at every turn.

activities.text: Wander the paths of the Murs à pêches between plots maintained by local associations: gardening, beekeeping, theater, and land art coexist here.
The Croix-de-Chavaux neighborhood brings together shops, cafés, and restaurants with flavors from around the world. Looking for a change of scenery just steps from Paris?
Spot the murals and collages scattered throughout downtown streets. Montreuil hosts one of the most vibrant street art scenes in the eastern suburbs.

days_plan.itin_title: Seine-Saint-Denis Tour: Basilica and Urban Culture

visits.text: The Château de Montreuil-Bellay raises its 15 towers and 600 metres of ramparts above the Thouet valley. Founded in 1025 by Foulques Nerra, it combines medieval and Renaissance architecture.
The 15th-century medieval kitchen with its central hearth is exceptionally well preserved. Dry moats and vaulted underground passages testify to the fortress's defensive past.
The collegiate church and the canons' lodge, built in the 15th century, display the richness of Flamboyant Gothic architecture.
The 15th-century vaulted cellars house the château's wine estate. Sixteen hectares of organically farmed vines produce Saumur reds, whites and crémants.
The chamber of the Duchess of Longueville retains its period furniture. This cousin of Louis XIV was exiled here after the Fronde.

activities.text: The village of Montreuil-Bellay, a medieval walled town, is explored on foot. Its cobbled lanes climb towards the château between white tuffeau houses.
The Saumur vineyard surrounds Montreuil-Bellay. The flinty clay slopes produce powerful Cabernet Francs and elegant Chenins.
The Thouet cycle route follows the river. This cycling itinerary links Montreuil-Bellay to the neighbouring châteaux along bucolic paths.

days_plan.itin_title: Maine-et-Loire Road Trip: Anjou and Loire Valley Châteaux

visits.text: Montreuil-sur-Mer is nicknamed the 'Carcassonne of the North', and rightly so. Its 3 km of ramparts, perfectly preserved and lined with centuries-old trees, offer a panoramic walk over the Canche valley, the hills of the Montreuillois and the rooftops of the lower town. Take the time to walk the full circuit — it takes a good half hour, and every angle reveals a different view.

The star-shaped citadel, built in the 16th century on the foundations of a castle of Philip Augustus, houses the Roger-Rodière museum: collections of sacred art, medieval sculptures and paintings by 19th-century American painters drawn by the light of the Canche. But above all, this is where the son et lumière show “Juliette et les Misérables” is held every summer — 500 volunteers in costume, projections on the façades. Book well in advance if you're there in July-August.

Saint-Saulve abbey church is the soul of the upper town. It was while visiting this church in September 1837 that Victor Hugo saw a young girl crying on the forecourt — this memory would become Fantine in Les Misérables, published in 1862. The abbey church holds an exceptional treasury of sacred art, assembled after the revolutionary destruction of 1793 thanks to relics received in the 19th century.

Wander through the medieval lanes: the Rue du Clape-en-Bas, cobbled and sloping, lined with timber-framed houses leaning against one another, inspired Hugo's scene of the cart hurtling down the hill in Les Misérables. The Cavée Saint-Firmin, steep and cobbled, is the town's finest lane. The Porte de Boulogne, rebuilt in 1828 as an exact replica of a medieval gate, marks the northern entrance to the fortified town.

Discover the Chartreuse Royale, at the foot of the ramparts. Founded in the 14th century, it served as the general printing house of the Carthusians and then as a Belgian military hospital during the First World War — the largest in Europe at the time. Now converted into a cultural venue, it hosts exhibitions, artists' residencies and concerts.

activities.text: Descend via the Poterne tower for a walk at the foot of the ramparts. The path runs along the Canche valley and the lower town on an easy 8 km loop — ideal for understanding the strategic position of the fortified town on its promontory.

Stroll through the 40 eighteenth-century townhouses of the upper town — the prosperity of the cloth and wool merchants left behind refined residences that mass tourism has yet to discover. The town was already a thriving trading port in the Middle Ages, the only Capetian port for a time, before the silting up of the Canche put an end to its maritime calling.

days_plan.itin_title: Opal Coast Villages and Flemish Heartlands
The Most Beautiful Villages from Flanders to the Bay of Somme
Road Trip Pas-De-Calais: The Opal Coast and Belfries

visits.text: Montségur crowns its pog at 1,207 meters, the ultimate symbol of Cathar resistance. After a steep 20- to 30-minute climb through rockrose and thorn, you emerge onto the wind-battered ruins and the vertiginous panorama. Here unfolded the 11-month siege that ended on March 16, 1244: some 225 Perfects, refusing to recant, climbed onto the pyre lit at the foot of the rock, in the field known as the Champ des Crémats. The castle visible today was rebuilt after the surrender. Closed shoes essential.

activities.text: In the village below, the archaeological museum of Montségur displays the results of excavations conducted on the pog since 1968: everyday objects, coins, weapons, fragments of the last defenders' lives. A useful stop to put faces to the legend before or after the climb. Small museum, allow thirty minutes to an hour.

The Montségur area and the Pays d'Olmes are beautiful hiking terrain: trails toward neighboring ridges, views over the isolated pog and the Pyrenean chain. The simple round trip to the castle can extend into a loop for energetic legs. Check at reception for marked routes departing from the village.

days_plan.itin_title: Ariège Road Trip: Cathars and Prehistoric Caves

visits.text: Pass through the Porte de Bourgogne, remnant of the 1,400 meters of fortifications erected by Philippe Auguste in the 12th century. Its defensive systems—portcullis, murder hole, and machicolations—remain visible.

The bridge over the Loing, immortalized by the Impressionist painter who lived here his last twenty years, offers one of the most photographed views in town. Enameled lava plaques mark the exact spots where he set up his easel.
Notre-Dame Church, Gothic from the 13th to 15th centuries, was painted fourteen times by the same artist. Its two-tower facade frames a richly sculpted portal.
The keep, remnant of the royal castle, has dominated the town since the 12th century. The ramparts still preserve several turrets and the Porte de Samois, the town's second fortified entrance.
Step into the Maison du Sucre d'Orge (Barley Sugar House). This confection, created in 1638 by Benedictine nuns, has been made here for nearly four centuries using a closely guarded secret recipe.
The so-called François I Gallery, dating from 1527, features a Renaissance facade adorned with detailed sculptures. Ancient facades line the town's cobbled streets.

activities.text: Follow the "In Sisley's Footsteps" trail: a route marked by enameled plaques at the locations where the artist set up his easel. Reproductions of his paintings are visible on-site.
Cycle along the banks of the Loing. A cycle route links Moret-sur-Loing to Souppes-sur-Loing along the towpath of the Loing canal.
Visit the Halle de Moret-sur-Loing on market days to taste local Brie specialties: valley cheeses, forest honey, and barley sugar drops.

days_plan.itin_title: Seine-et-Marne Circuit: Fontainebleau and Châteaux

visits.text: Six sea caves carved into the cliff border Morgat beach, and some have ocher and violet walls colored by iron oxides. They're accessible only by boat: tour boats depart from Morgat harbor for outings of about 45 minutes, with the Grotte de l'Autel the tallest cave. Departures are canceled as soon as the seas pick up, so aim for the morning and keep a backup plan.

Sheltered from westerlies by the point, Morgat beach offers the mildest water for swimming on the Crozon peninsula, along nearly a kilometer of light-colored sand. Behind it, Belle Époque villas recall that the resort was launched in the late 19th century by the Peugeot family. Lifeguarded in July–August, nearly deserted in June.

activities.text: Renting a sea kayak in Morgat remains the best way to approach the caves without depending on tour boat schedules: two to three hours suffice to paddle along the cliffs toward Cap de la Chèvre. Rental operators require a briefing and won't let you go out above a certain wind strength. Reservations recommended in July–August.

days_plan.itin_title: Brittany 7 days: Pink Granite, Lighthouses & Peninsulas

places.name: Mortagne Au Perche

visits.text: The Saint-André Crypt is all that remains of the old Toussaint collegiate church, founded by Countess Mahaut of Bavaria around 1200. Its low vaults and carved capitals evoke the medieval Perche.
The Church of Notre-Dame, in Flamboyant Gothic style, was built with support from Marguerite of Lorraine in the late 15th century. Its 18th-century woodwork frames a luminous interior.
Climb up to the Porte Saint-Denis, a remnant of the old fortifications.
The Saint-François Cloister and Chapel, built by Marguerite of Lorraine in the 16th century, form a well-preserved monastic ensemble at the heart of the town.
The Musée Alain pays tribute to the philosopher Émile-Auguste Chartier, known as Alain, who was born in Mortagne. Manuscripts, photographs and personal objects trace his life and career.
Stroll the formal gardens of the town hall, planted in the French style. The surrounding cobbled lanes reveal handsome limestone houses in shades of rose and ochre.

activities.text: Mortagne-au-Perche is the capital of black pudding. Visit an artisan butcher to discover variations: farm-style, with apples, with walnuts, with chili. The Brotherhood of Knights of the Black Pudding has upheld the tradition since 1963.
The Saturday morning market sets up in the square. Percheron regional products, cheeses, and farmhouse cider fill the stalls.
Want fresh air? Trails around Mortagne wind through the Percheron bocage. Gentle hills, hedgerows, and stone manors punctuate the route.
A few kilometres away, stud farms offer encounters with the Percheron, the region's emblematic horse breed. Visits, rides, or introductory sessions are available.

days_plan.itin_title: Orne Road Trip: Norman Bocage and Stud Farms

map_keywords: Jardin de l'Hôtel de Ville Mortagne-au-Perche

visits.text: The Saut du Doubs is a 27-meter waterfall on the Franco-Swiss border, classified as a Grand National Site. Created 12,000 to 14,000 years ago by a landslide, it marks the end of Lake Brenets (or Lake Chaillexon). The Basins of the Doubs that precede it form a 3.5 km long canyon, 100-200 m wide and 30-40 m deep, bordered by high limestone cliffs with sometimes strange shapes. The level varies by nearly 20 meters between floods and low waters. The site attracts 200,000 visitors per year.

Morteau is the birthplace of the eponymous sausage, protected by PGI since 2010 and Label Rouge since 2006. Its cylindrical shape with wooden peg is recognizable among all. Smoking with coniferous wood (fir, spruce, juniper) in traditional tuyés is inscribed on UNESCO's intangible heritage. Production reaches approximately 5,000 tons per year. The town, labeled Cité de Caractère, preserves beautiful monuments including the Town Hall (1590) and the Renaissance-facade Château Pertusier.

The Pays Horloger saw the birth of the French watchmaking industry in the mid-18th century. This know-how is inscribed on UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage. The watchmaking museum, installed in Château Pertusier, is currently closed for renovation and will reopen in 2026 under the name Cité des Horlogers with new exhibition spaces.

activities.text: Two boat companies offer commented one-hour cruises to the Saut du Doubs from Villers-le-Lac. You can also access it on foot (2.5 km from Vions parking), by carriage from La Courpée, or by car to the viewpoint. The sporty hike to the Châtelot dam offers superb views of the gorges.

Visit a tuyé farm to discover traditional Comtoise architecture and the meat smoking process. These buildings with large roofs house a central room with a chimney that can reach 15 meters where coniferous smoke slowly perfumes sausages, bresi, and hams for several weeks. The Ferme-musée du Beugnon in Grand'Combe-Châteleu presents this heritage.

days_plan.itin_title: Doubs Circuit: Watchmaking and Swiss Border

visits.text: Ten kilometers from Grasse, Mouans-Sartoux is home to the garden branch of the Musée International de la Parfumerie: the Jardins du MIP, a living collection of nearly 700 species of fragrant plants across 3 hectares. Centifolia roses, jasmine, tuberose, violet, lavender, geranium: the same flowers that still supply Grasse's perfume houses. The site holds the “Jardin remarquable” designation. Allow 1 hour for a leisurely visit.

The 15th-century Château de Mouans-Sartoux houses the Espace de l'Art Concret: a leading contemporary art center for European concrete art, with the Albers-Honegger donation comprising several hundred works. Combine it with the Jardins du MIP if you have a taste for geometric abstract art. Admission fee, closed Mondays.

activities.text: May and June are good months for the Jardins du MIP: May roses in full bloom and intense fragrances. In fall, it is quieter and you can see the harvest of autumn fragrance plants. Tastings of flower syrups (rose, violet) are sometimes offered at reception.

days_plan.itin_title: Nice's hinterland: 8 days of hilltop villages and the Mercantour

visits.text: In the morning, the winding lanes of Mougins still have room to breathe before the outdoor cafés open: this is a good time to explore this hilltop village at 260 meters between Cannes and Grasse. Flower-covered facades, fountains, and art galleries are yours alone. At the village entrance, a monumental bronze sculpture reminds visitors that Picasso lived at Mas Notre-Dame-de-Vie from 1961 until his death on April 8, 1973. Practical tip: park at the Val de Mougins parking lot below; you reach the village center on foot.

The Centre de la Photographie de Mougins has occupied the former rectory since 2020, taking over from the Musée André Villers. Villers, Picasso's friend and a portrait photographer, photographed the master throughout his years in Mougins. His collection is preserved here, including the Rolleiflex given to him by Picasso. Temporary exhibitions change frequently, so check the program before visiting: the quality of the visit depends on what's on.

The FAMM (Femmes Artistes Musée Mougins) is the first private museum in Europe dedicated exclusively to female artists, from the 17th century to today. Opened in 2024, it complements the Centre de la Photographie nicely, making Mougins a true village of museums. Allow 1 hour and 15 minutes for the visit, longer if you want to explore the galleries in the lanes: over 30 art studios occupy the old village streets.

The Mougins bell tower can be climbed from April to October: 360° panorama over Cannes Bay, the Lérins Islands, the Grasse hills, and north, the snow-capped Pre-Alps. Locals simply call it 'the view,' which says it all. In summer, nocturnal climbs are organized—a smart choice if you want to avoid the heat and enjoy soft light over the bay.

activities.text: Les Étoiles de Mougins is the village's food festival, launched in 2006 as a tribute to Roger Vergé. Le Moulin de Mougins, opened by Vergé in 1969, made the town a hub of Michelin-starred cuisine for several decades. Demonstrations, workshops, and culinary competitions fill the lanes one weekend in September. If you're here during that time, book several months ahead—the festival sells out very early.

The Parc de la Valmasque spreads over 427 hectares between Mougins and Sophia Antipolis. The trail around the Fontmerle pond takes an hour at a leisurely pace. Aim for July–August to see the lotus flowers in full bloom, an unexpected spectacle at this Mediterranean altitude. Few visitors know the spot; it's the ideal quiet walk for late afternoon.

Dining in Mougins isn't limited to Michelin-starred restaurants: even neighborhood restaurants use local ingredients. Roger Vergé's cuisine du soleil, blending Provence and the Mediterranean, has left a real mark. For lunch without breaking the bank, head to restaurants off the main street, toward Place de l'Église: reasonable prices and reliable quality.

days_plan.itin_title: French Riviera Art Museums and Galleries: An 8-Day Journey
Nice's hinterland: 8 days of hilltop villages and the Mercantour

visits.text: On the road climbing toward Gassin, you'll encounter the Moulin de Paillas, the last survivor of a group of five mills built between the 16th and 19th centuries. Restored in 2002, its wooden mechanism remains in working order. The access road is narrow—better to walk from the village, about 30 minutes uphill.

days_plan.itin_title: Var in 4 Days: From Bormes to the Most Beautiful Villages of the Verdon

visits.text: The Centre National du Costume de Scène (CNCS), the flagship of Moulins' museums, preserves 10,000 stage costumes in the former 18th-century cavalry barracks. The Nureyev collection and costumes from the Comédie-Française and the Paris Opera: each temporary exhibition (renewed once or twice a year) reveals a different museum. Innovative architecture and spectacular exhibition design pay homage to live performance.

Notre-Dame-de-l'Annonciation Cathedral elegantly combines Romanesque and Gothic styles. Its Flamboyant Gothic choir (15th century), built of orange-yellow sandstone, contrasts with the neo-Gothic nave (19th century), which alternates white limestone from Chauvigny with black stone from Volvic. Its two 82-metre spires rise a further 20 metres above the Allier.
The Château of the Dukes of Bourbon (14th century) retains only the Mal Coiffée keep, a flat-roofed tower gutted by fire in 1755.

The Musée Anne-de-Beaujeu, a 15th-century Renaissance pavilion, houses the art collections of Louis XI's daughter. Bourbonnais sculptures, medieval and Renaissance paintings, ceramics, cutlery and archaeology make up an exhibition as varied as it is interesting. The building surprises visitors with its Italian architecture and was the first Renaissance building constructed in France.

activities.text: The recently redeveloped banks of the Allier invite walks along the Réserve naturelle nationale du Val d'Allier. Three options from Moulins Bain: the Sentier des castors (6 km round trip), the 9 km cycle path, or simply a contemplative pause on a bench by the water. The wild river offers coolness and fresh air between two cultural visits.

The “Moulins entre en scène” show illuminates five monuments from late June to late August: the Sacré-Cœur church, Jacquemart, Hôtel de ville, château des Ducs de Bourbon and CNCS. Projections lasting 10 to 20 minutes each and immersive music fill the 1-hour-30-minute night-time walk with wonder. The façades come alive throughout the evening.

The historic quarter can be explored on a guided tour or with a smartphone audio guide. Place d'Allier and its Grand Café (an institution since 1899), the Italian-style theatre in the Hôtel de Ville, the Jacquemart and timber-framed houses: every corner reveals the history of Moulins, a town with the Ville d'Art et d'Histoire designation. Art Nouveau shops (Nouvelles Galeries, chocolatier Serardy) delight enthusiasts.

days_plan.itin_title: Allier Road Trip: Vichy, Thermal Baths and Bourbonnais Bocage

visits.text: Mouriès is France's premier olive-growing commune by number of trees: 91,000 trees spread across the Alpilles' south slopes. The Mouriès cooperative mill, whose origins go back to the 17th century (the primitive mill called Mas-Neuf dates from this period), produces a regularly award-winning PDO Vallée des Baux-de-Provence oil. In November, it's a family celebration for 450 members bringing their harvests: weighing, de-leafing, washing, then pressing within 24 hours.

The village center — a few small squares linked by limestone alleys, a fountain, the 17th-century church — looks unassuming but conceals flowery back courtyards and carefully restored manor houses. It's also a bull-running village: its arena hosts Camargue-style races in summer, a discipline where men armed with hooks face bulls (without killing).

activities.text: Eastern Alpilles ridge trails: from Mouriès' north slope, marked trails climb toward limestone ridges for magnificent views toward the Crau and Camargue. Fire risk may close these trails from mid-July to mid-September. Inquire before departing.

Olive oil tasting and purchase directly at the mill: the Moulin Coopératif de Mouriès offers visits and direct sales. It's an opportunity to understand differences between typicities and varieties — and leave with a PDO oil that Parisian restaurants snap up.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpilles, Aix-en-Provence & Arles Circuit

visits.text: Look up as soon as you arrive in Moustiers: between the two limestone cliffs that hem in the village, a golden star gleams at the end of a 135-meter chain. Popular legend—recounted by Frédéric Mistral in 1885—attributes this votive offering to the knight of Blacas, taken prisoner during the Crusades in 1210 and freed after promising to hang a star in honor of the Virgin if he returned alive. The mystery remains unsolved. In any case, the star you see dates from 1957, after the previous one fell. The village, classified among France's Most Beautiful Villages since 1983, also takes its name from its original monastery: monks from Lérins settled here in the 5th century.

The church of Notre-Dame-de-l'Assomption is an often-underestimated Romanesque gem. Its 12th-century Lombard bell tower, classified as a Historic Monument since 1913, dominates the village with its squat silhouette. Inside, a five-bay nave with pointed barrel vaults and an altar carved from a 5th-century sarcophagus—one of the rare examples of reusing an early Christian piece in a medieval Provençal building.

The Musée de la Faïence presents more than 300 pieces and traces five centuries of an art that Moustiers made famous throughout Europe. It all began in 1668 when Pierre Clérissy obtained the secret of white glaze from a monk at Lérins Abbey—it is said that Louis XIV's financial crisis, which forced him to melt down his gold tableware, opened the market for luxury faience. From then on, the products of the Moustiers workshops graced the tables of the kingdom's elite. Today, workshops carry on the craft in the village center—step into those with open doors to watch the artisans at work.

activities.text: Climb the 262 steps of the calade (paved path) leading to the Notre-Dame-de-Beauvoir chapel. This chapel blends 12th-century Romanesque with 16th-century Gothic—it was formerly called Notre-Dame-d'Entreroches, “between the rocks.” Along the Way of the Cross, the stations are decorated with faience tiles. From the esplanade, the panorama takes in all of Moustiers' rooftops, Lake Sainte-Croix below, and the first foothills of the Verdon. Avoid the climb at midday in summer—the slope is exposed. Coming back down, take the alternate path passing by the Sainte-Madeleine grotto.

Friday mornings, the market sets up on Place Montelupo, opposite the faience museum. It's a chance to leave with Haute-Provence honey, herb-marinated olives, fresh goat cheese, or a Provençal kougelhopf. Then spend the morning exploring the faience workshops that also operate as shops—some offer demonstrations of wheel-throwing.

Providers based 5 km away on the shores of Lake Sainte-Croix offer canoe rentals to paddle upstream along the stretch of water at the entrance to the Verdon gorges—a unique experience where the water changes from the blue-green of the lake to the emerald hue of the canyon. Allow half a day for the round trip.
