places.name: Nantua

visits.text: Lake Nantua, a 141-hectare glacial gem, lies amid limestone cliffs at an elevation of 478 metres. Its waters, reaching a maximum depth of 43 metres, reflect the mountains surrounding this narrow cluse. Listed for its natural beauty, the lake displays turquoise and emerald shades as the light changes. Historic rockfalls, such as the collapse of La Colonne in 1973, have shaped this spectacular landscape where nature and geology meet.

The Saint-Michel Abbey Church, Cluny's elder sister, has displayed its Cluniac Romanesque art since the 12th century. Its sculpted portal, pointed vaults and finely carved capitals bear witness to the refinement of the Benedictine abbey. The listed 1845 organ, with its 2,800 pipes, resounds during summer concerts. Do not miss Eugène Delacroix's painting The Martyrdom of Saint Sebastian, a Romantic masterpiece housed in a side chapel.

The Departmental Museum of the Resistance and Deportation occupies Nantua's former prison. The emotionally charged atmosphere of the site intensifies the visit. Objects, testimonies, documents and reconstructions retrace the struggle of the Bugey and Haut-Jura resistance fighters. The immersive display lets visitors experience a weapons airdrop inside the reconstructed fuselage of a Hudson aircraft. The individual stories of resistance fighters make this period of history tangible.

The Pierre district preserves medieval shops clinging to the slope. Cobbled streets, vaulted passages and overhanging houses create a preserved medieval setting. The Doye spring rises in the town centre, a karst resurgence whose pure water once supplied fountains and washhouses. The Lâte Tower, the last remnant of the ramparts, watches over this exceptional architectural heritage.

activities.text: Swim in the lake's clear waters from the developed Albert Griot beach. In summer, lifeguard supervision allows families to enjoy this exceptional natural setting safely. The cool but invigorating water offers memorable swimming beneath the towering cliffs. Shaded lawns invite you to nap after a dip, lulled by the lapping waves.

Enjoy water sports on the lake: sailing, paddleboarding, canoeing, kayaking and pedal boating. Sheltered from the wind, the lake offers ideal conditions for learning or improving your skills. Rental operators on the shores provide equipment and advice. In summer, water-skiing engines roar as spectators laugh at the skiers' acrobatics.

Fish in this lake, renowned for its pike, perch, trout and Arctic char. Local anglers know the best spots depending on the season and conditions. Trolling, casting or still fishing can yield some fine specimens. Local regulations require compliance with minimum sizes and quotas in order to preserve fish stocks.

Enjoy the famous pike quenelles with Nantua sauce. This essential speciality combines the delicate flesh of local fish with a creamy crayfish-butter sauce. Lakeside restaurants preserve this gastronomic tradition, which has made Nantua famous worldwide. A side of Creole rice and the freshness of a Cerdon wine complete this regional feast.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour Ain & Savoie Mont-Blanc: Lakes, Mountains and Heritage
Road Trip from Bresse to Bugey via Beaujolais and Lyon

map_keywords: Museum of Resistance and Deportation Nantua

places.name: Narbonne

visits.text: The Cathedral of Saint-Just-et-Saint-Pasteur is the city's most soaring monument. Begun in 1272 in the Rayonnant Gothic style, it was never completed — Narbonne's consuls refused to demolish the ramparts to allow the nave to extend. Result: only the choir exists, but what a choir — 41 meters under vault, making it France's fourth tallest cathedral, after Beauvais, Amiens and Metz. Climb the Gilles-Aycelin keep (1295-1306, 42 meters) for the best view over the city and the Canal de la Robine.

Head to rue Rouget-de-Lisle and go down into the Roman Horreum. These underground galleries from the 1st century BC, probably a public market or warehouse, run beneath the heart of the city. Narbonne, the first Roman colony in Gaul, founded in 118 BC, was then the capital of Gallia Narbonensis and the leading port of the region. Allow 45 minutes for the visit.

The Palais des Archevêques, built and extended over eight centuries, takes up an entire side of the place de l'Hôtel-de-Ville. Its art and history museum houses Flemish paintings and Orientalist rooms. In front of the palace, the paving stones of the Via Domitia can be seen directly in the ground of the square. Take time for the Passage de l'Ancre, a covered lane linking the palace to the cathedral.

The Canal de la Robine is a UNESCO-listed branch of the Canal du Midi. Its Pont des Marchands — one of France's rare inhabited bridges with its colorful houses perched on seven arches (only one is visible from the canal side) — links the Roman quarter on the right bank to the medieval quarter on the left. The Promenade des Barques, running along the quays, is Narbonne's loveliest stroll in fine weather.

The Narbonne Covered Market, built in the early 20th century in a Baltard-style of metal and glass, opens every morning. Fishmongers, butchers, cheese shops, olives, oysters from the lagoon — it's the liveliest spot in town to lunch standing at the counter or to pick up a picnic.

activities.text: In the evening the quays of the Robine come alive with terraces and street musicians in summer. Sunset over the canal is worth the detour.

days_plan.itin_title: Aude Road Trip: Carcassonne, Cathar Country & the Mediterranean

map_keywords: Canal de la Robine Pont des Marchands Narbonne

visits.text: The Navacelles cirque is a massive abandoned meander carved 300 meters deep into the limestone causses by the Vis River. From the northern belvedere (Causse de Blandas side), you overlook this verdant chasm—it's one of Europe's largest natural cirques. The tiny village of Navacelles nestles at the bottom with its waterfall and medieval bridge.

Descend to the bottom of the cirque via the winding road (watch for tight turns). The Vis waterfall, in the village heart, flows over moss-covered rocks. You're standing in the “Cirque de Navacelles” Grand Site of France. The climb up the southern side (Causse du Larzac) offers equally spectacular views.

activities.text: Hike the causse around the cirque—several marked trails depart from the belvederes. The Mediterranean vegetation (boxwood, juniper, wild lavender) contrasts with the austere limestone. Allow 1.5 hours for the loop from the northern belvedere.

days_plan.itin_title: Southeast France Road Trip: Perched Villages and Gorges

visits.text: The ramparts of Navarrenx are the first examples of bastioned fortifications in France — built between 1538 and 1547 by the Italian architect Fabricio Siciliano on the orders of Henry II of Albret, king of Navarre and grandfather of Henry IV. Vauban visited the place in 1685 and found nothing to change, so far ahead of its time was the Italian design. These walls, 1.7 km long, 10 metres high and 4.50 metres thick, encircle the medieval bastide founded in 1316. Listed as Historic Monuments, they can be walked freely from the rampart walkway.

The Porte Saint-Antoine, also called the Gate of Spain, is the main entrance to the bastioned town. It is UNESCO-listed as part of the Roads to Santiago de Compostela — Navarrenx is a stage on the Via Podiensis, the Le Puy route, three days' walk from Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port. Once past the medieval bridge, 873 km still separate the pilgrim from Santiago de Compostela.

The Church of Saint Germain was built between 1550 and 1560 on the site of the old church of the bastide, demolished because it stood too close to the new walls. Jeanne d'Albret had Calvinism recognised there as the official religion; Louis XIII had the first Catholic mass celebrated there in 1620. The U-shaped Arsenal, built in 1680 on the site of the House of the Kings of Navarre, today houses an interpretation centre on the bastioned town, with models and plans.

activities.text: The gave d'Oloron flows at the foot of the ramparts. It is reputed to be one of the best salmon rivers in France and hosts a fishing championship every year. The fish ladder near the Massey dam allows you to watch salmon during their migrations. Operators offer canoeing and kayaking from April to October.

Do the full circuit of the ramparts from the rampart walkway — about 2 km of panoramic walking. From the watchtower above the Porte Saint-Antoine, the cannon pointing due west offers a surprising view of the medieval bridge and the gave. On clear days, the Pyrenees stand out on the horizon.

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip Pyrenees-Atlantiques: Basque Country and Bearn

visits.text: Naves sits at the gates of the Parc Naturel Régional des Monts d'Ardèche, a preserved territory where settlement has kept its traditional form. The village, with its tightly packed houses and paved cobbled lanes, looks straight out onto the Chassezac valleys, a river tumbling down from the high Cévennes plateaus. The church and the shaded squares form the heart of the village, a quiet place off the usual tourist circuits.

Remnants of the enclosure and arched passages are visible in old village lanes. Look for faïsses—these small terraces in restanques developed on slopes for cultivation—from village heights: it's one of the most typical landscapes of Cévennes Ardèche, shaped over centuries by peasants to gain land on hillsides.

Viewpoints near the village offer views over the Chassezac valleys and its tributaries. The watercourse below is renowned for its clear waters and pebble beaches. In summer, some unsupervised swimming spots are accessible via trails from the village.

activities.text: The old village and nearby viewpoints discovery loop (2 to 3 km, 1h) is signposted from the church square. It passes the main viewpoints over the valleys and returns through medieval lanes. An accessible circuit for all, without significant elevation change.

The walk toward faïsses and traditional terraced cultivation (3 km round trip) starts from village heights and descends toward restanques developed on slopes. It's an opportunity to understand concretely how these dry-stone structures retained earth on steep hillsides. Allow 1h15.

days_plan.itin_title: The 18 Most Beautiful Villages of Ardèche

visits.text: The Château-Musée de Nemours rises above the Loing River. Built in the late 12th century by Gauthier I de Villebéon, it's one of the rare medieval urban castles still standing in Île-de-France. Its rectangular keep is flanked by four corner turrets.
Climb the turret to discover the oratory, a Gothic architectural gem on two levels. The château houses 25,000 objects, from 19th-century paintings to antique prints.

The Saint-Jean-Baptiste Church, founded in 1170, was rebuilt after the 1358 fire during the Hundred Years' War. The choir dates from the 15th century. The stained glass windows and high altar were added in the 19th century.

The Prehistory Museum of Île-de-France occupies a building designed by Roland Simounet, classified as 20th-century heritage. The collections span 500,000 years of human history, from early hunters to Gallic metalworkers. A 9th-century Carolingian boat completes the tour.
Head to the banks of the Loing from the château. The picturesque streets of Nemours preserve the charm of an ancient town, with stone bridges and medieval facades.

activities.text: Extend your museum visit with the Nemours communal forest loop. This marked trail crosses a sea of sand, old quarries, and strangely shaped boulders.
Paddle down the Loing by canoe from Grez-sur-Loing to Moret-sur-Loing. The river winds between willows, meadows and painters' villages.
The nearby village of Larchant deserves a detour for its spectacular Saint-Mathurin church ruins and the Dame Jouanne rock, one of the highest bouldering spots in the massif.

days_plan.itin_title: Seine-et-Marne Circuit: Fontainebleau and Châteaux

places.name: Nerac

visits.text: The Henri IV Chateau-Museum is one of the rare surviving Renaissance buildings in Lot-et-Garonne. Of the original four-wing quadrangle, only the north wing remains, the sole survivor of the Revolutionary destruction. What it reveals is elegant: an exterior gallery with twisted columns and carved capitals, characteristic of the so-called Louis XII style. Built in the 15th century by Alain d'Albret the Great, great-great-grandfather of Henri IV, the chateau became a royal residence in 1484 when the Albrets came to the throne of Navarre. This is where Henri of Navarre, the future Henri IV, lived with Marguerite de Valois between 1577 and 1582. Allow an hour to walk through the rooms devoted to the Albret saga and the Renaissance court of Nerac.

Behind the château lies Parc de la Garenne, where Queen Margot had the Allée des 3,000 Pas laid out, a walk of more than 2 km beneath centuries-old oaks along the Baïse. Marguerite of Angoulême, sister of François I, turned Nérac into a literary court where she welcomed Clément Marot and Lefèvre d’Étaples and influenced Calvin. Her daughter Jeanne d’Albret converted to Protestantism here. Take the time to follow the avenue to its end: the atmosphere truly feels timeless.

Along the walk, spot the Renaissance fountains: Saint-Jean Fountain, Fleurette Grotto, and Dauphin Fountain. These ornamental elements attest to the refinement of the Albret court in the 16th century. Fleurette Grotto takes its name from a local legend connected to young Henri IV.

In Petit Nérac, on the right bank of the Baïse, meander through Rue Séderie lined with half-timbered houses. The Old Bridge offers beautiful views over the port and former wharves. This is where barges loaded with Armagnac and flour once departed for Bordeaux.

Four kilometres to the north-west, the Moulin des Tours de Barbaste is a fortified mill. Built in the 12th century and bought by the Albret family in 1308, it was a favourite stopover of Henri IV himself, who sometimes signed his letters as the 'Miller of the Tours de Barbaste'. The ten-arch Romanesque bridge beside it is one of the oldest in the region. Make the detour if you can.

activities.text: The market runs on Allées d'Albret, featuring farmhouse cheeses, Quercy melons, cèpes in season, and products from Pays d'Albret. Arrive early—the best producers sell out quickly.

Head to Nérac port to board La Gabare Le Prince Henry, a boat ascending the Baïse to Nazareth Lock. The cruise lasts roughly an hour and follows Parc de la Garenne from the water—the perspective on wooded banks and château is breathtaking. Inquire for current schedules at the Albret tourism office.

days_plan.itin_title: Lot-et-Garonne Road Trip: Bastides and Villages

map_keywords: Allée des 3000 pas (3,000 Steps Walk), Nérac
Moulin des Tours (Mills of Barbaste), Barbaste

visits.text: The Gallo-Roman pools (originally 80 metres long by 60 wide) testify to the importance of the ancient spa town of Aquae Nerii. Three Roman pools have been visible in the Parc des Chaudes since 1924. The Roman amphitheatre, where circus games and theatrical performances took place, completes this exceptional ancient heritage. Néris was one of Gaul's major spa towns.

The current thermal baths (19th century), built on the site of ancient baths, were completely modernised in the early 2000s. Their lithium-rich thermal water has sedative, analgesic and relaxing properties: Néris is a leader in the comprehensive treatment of nervous conditions (stress, anxiety, sleep disorders) and rheumatism. The majestic building retains its Belle Époque décor.

The Casino-théâtre (1896) displays a façade adorned with murals in shades of brown by Émile Ledoux (1899), depicting allegories of dance, operetta and comedy. The north pavilion houses the theatre, where shows and concerts take place. Belle Époque architecture, sculpted medallions and ironwork create a unique setting for entertainment.

The Pavillon du Lac, the former Néris-les-Bains railway station (1930), listed as a historic monument, surprises visitors with its Art Deco architecture. Pink and yellow sandstone and multicoloured glazed tiles make up this majestic building. Now a multipurpose hall, it hosts weddings, exhibitions and conferences. The medieval Saint-Georges church and the Merovingian necropolis complete the historic heritage.

activities.text: The Spa Thermal Les Nériades (1,000 m²), built behind a historic Moorish façade, is a haven of wellbeing. Indoor and outdoor thermal-water pools, a sauna, hammam and treatment rooms: the sensory area offers a restorative break. Massages from around the world (Hawaiian, Californian, Balinese, Swedish), body and facial rituals, balneotherapy: stress becomes a distant memory.

The 17 hectares of flower-filled parks planted with rare species invite strolling and botanical discovery. Lake Cournauron offers an ideal setting for a picnic or a walk. The 'Rue jardin' and the 'Incroyables Comestibles' (shared vegetable gardens) bring nature into the town. A tree trail and walking and mountain-biking routes satisfy outdoor lovers.

The golf course, covering more than 60 hectares, offers technically challenging play in an unspoilt setting. Varied sports facilities (tennis complex, swimming pool) will delight sports enthusiasts. Néris-les-Bains, with its Plus Beaux Détours de France designation, comes alive throughout the season: organic and local produce markets, concerts, theatre, the Belle Époque celebration on 14 July (the town returns to the 19th century), exhibitions and fairs from April to November.

days_plan.itin_title: Allier Road Trip: Vichy, Thermal Baths and Bourbonnais Bocage

places.name: Neuf Brisach

visits.text: Neuf-Brisach is a real curiosity: a town created from scratch in 1698 on the Alsace plain after France lost the fortress of Vieux-Brisach following the Treaty of Ryswick. Louis XIV himself chose this perfect octagonal plan from three projects submitted by Vauban—which cost him 4 million livres. To transport the pink sandstone from the Vosges, a special canal was dug. The fortifications were completed in 1702, the Church of Saint-Louis in 1736. The entire site has been listed as UNESCO World Heritage since July 2008, as the sole example of Vauban's “third system”. The best way to appreciate it is from the air—operators offer ultralight flights that reveal the geometric perfection of the sixteen-pointed star.

The place d'Armes is a large square 120 meters on each side occupying the geometric center of the octagon. Around it, 48 rectangular blocks follow a relentlessly logical grid plan: barracks against the ramparts to protect civilians, government buildings around the central square. Walk to the royal fountain and observe the symmetry of streets converging toward you from all cardinal directions.

The Vauban Museum, housed in the Porte de Belfort, uses models and original plans to trace the construction of this ideal fortress town. Here you'll understand the genius of the double defensive enclosure: the inner defensive wall surrounding the town directly, then the outer works—ravelins, counterguards, bastions—which multiply the angles of fire to make any enemy approach suicidal.

The Royal Church of Saint-Louis, whose foundation stone was laid on October 11, 1731, and whose construction was completed in 1736, expresses the restrained classicism of 18th-century Alsace. Its clean lines survived the American bombing of 1945 that devastated much of the town. The façade of the military hospital built in 1765 to plans by architect Gabriel-Ignace Ritter is also worth a look.

activities.text: Walk the rampart walkway, which makes a complete circuit of the defensive enclosure over 2.4 kilometers. A marked historical route starts from the place d'Armes and guides you through the different military works. Contemporary artworks have also been installed in the ramparts, which since 2013 have housed France's second street art museum (MAUSA).

Operators offer ultralight flights from a nearby airfield. From the air, the geometric perfection of Neuf-Brisach's sixteen-pointed star makes complete sense—it's the only angle from which you truly understand Vauban's military genius.

days_plan.itin_title: The 15 Most Beautiful Villages of Alsace
Haut-Rhin Road Trip: Colmar and the Southern Wine Route

map_keywords: Musée Vauban Porte de Belfort Neuf-Brisach

visits.text: The Cistercian abbey of Notre-Dame de l'Étanche is the most unassuming monastic foundation on this itinerary. In 1148, Mathieu I, Duke of Lorraine, had it built at the request of his mother Adélaïde, widow of Duke Simon I, who wanted to end her days near her children. The monastery's possessions eventually spread across about forty parishes. Of the medieval buildings, nothing remains—the church was destroyed during the Thirty Years' War, and the nuns had to flee to Neufchâteau in 1636, taking their deeds and silverware with them. A 1778 convent building with a mansard roof survives, now private property. You can walk along the perimeter from outside—the melancholic atmosphere of the wooded valley is a visiting experience in itself.

From Neufchâteau, allow for a day trip to discover the Romanesque Saint-Martin church in Vomécourt-sur-Madon. Built by the Knights Templar in the 12th century, it overlooks the Madon valley and is considered one of the four most beautiful Romanesque churches in Lorraine. Its portal depicts the holy women at the tomb — the sculptural details are remarkably precise for a rural building. Allow 20 minutes.

The church of Saint-Nicolas is a fascinating architectural puzzle — and that's what makes it so endearing. Founded at the end of the 11th century by Duke of Lorraine Thierry II, it has two superimposed levels: an 11th-century Romanesque crypt below, a 12th–13th-century Gothic upper church above, each with its own stacked chapels. You've never seen this anywhere else in Lorraine — even specialists say so. In the upper church, don't miss the 15th-century polychrome stone Entombment: nine life-size figures of striking expressiveness. Outside July-August, visits are by guided tour only — book at the Tourist Office.

The church of Saint-Christophe, first mentioned in 1094, dates in its main structure from the 13th century and shows a Burgundian influence that is rare in Lorraine. Don't leave without seeing the Wiriot chapel (1505): it's the only chapel with pendant vaulting in France to have a vault entirely without vault webs—a technical feat that has intrigued architects for centuries.

The historic center of Neufchâteau is the first Site Patrimonial Remarquable of the Vosges — labeled Petite Cité de Caractère and ranked among the 100 Plus Beaux Détours de France. The Hôtel de Houdreville hides a 16th-century Renaissance staircase and medieval cellars that can be visited. On Place Jeanne d'Arc, look for the Maison des Goncourt, which belonged to the grandfather of writers Jules and Edmond — an unexpected literary connection in this Vosges town.

activities.text: A walk around the Étanche site and through the surrounding forest—the wooded, secluded setting of this small valley helps explain why the Cistercians chose places away from the world to settle. Then head to Neufchâteau for the evening stop.

Push open the door of the former Le Scala theater, housed in the outbuildings of a convent of Augustinian nuns sold as national property in 1791. Its interior plasterwork and painted decoration date from renovations in 1891–1893. The Tourist Office offers guided tours of the town throughout the year by reservation—the VIP package includes access to normally closed sites.

days_plan.itin_title: Vosges Abbey Trail: Monastic Heritage
Vosges Abbey Trail: Monastic Heritage
Vosges Road Trip: Lakes, Mountains & Thermal Spas

places.name: Neuilly Sur Seine

visits.text: The Île de la Jatte stretches two kilometers between Neuilly and Levallois, once home to the Château de Neuilly where Louis-Philippe resided. Square Jatte preserves a Temple of Love pavilion originally from Parc Monceau.
Georges Seurat immortalized this island in A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte. Monet, Sisley, and Van Gogh also painted these bucolic riverbanks and riverside cafés.
The 19th-century Saint-Pierre church dominates the residential quarter. Haussmannian buildings line the tree-lined avenues.

activities.text: Parc de l'Île de la Jatte occupies the island's northern tip. Discover the educational apiary, the garden, and the Seine embankments where barges and rowing boats sail past.
The Bois de Boulogne unfolds across 850 hectares south of Neuilly. Once the royal hunting grounds, it shelters the Parc de Bagatelle and Jardin d'Acclimatation.
The Fondation Louis Vuitton, designed by Frank Gehry, reflects unique architecture. Its glass sails evoke ships.

days_plan.itin_title: Hauts-de-Seine Road Trip: Royal Heritage & Gardens

map_keywords: Jardin du Temple de l'Amour Neuilly

visits.text: Saint-Étienne Basilica. Listed as UNESCO World Heritage as part of the Routes of Santiago de Compostela, this 11th- and 12th-century Romanesque basilica presents an architectural design unique in France. The building combines a central nave with side aisles and a three-level rotunda with an ambulatory, modeled after Jerusalem's Holy Sepulchre. The rotunda, 22 meters in diameter, is supported by 11 columns representing the eleven apostles.

Rotunda and relics. The rotunda evokes Jerusalem's Holy Sepulchre and was built by Eudes de Déols in the 11th century. In 1257, Cardinal Eudes de Châteauroux gifted three drops of Christ's Precious Blood, initiating an important pilgrimage celebrated each Easter Monday. Each column is adorned with carved capitals depicting the battle between forces of Good and Evil.

Église Saint-Pierre de Dampierre. Allow for a return trip from Neuvy-Saint-Sépulchre to reach this village, which has a 12th-century Romanesque church listed as a historic monument. With its beautiful proportions, the church is distinguished by its bell tower clad in chestnut shingles. The chapel on the right contains the tombstone of Pierre de Muzard, lord of Chanlebon.

activities.text: Multimedia guided tour. A smartphone app allows you to discover the basilica independently. The great figures who marked the monument's history tell the story: Eudes de Déols the founder, Eudes de Châteauroux donor of the relics, Viollet-le-Duc who saved it from ruin. This audio tour of 8 stops is enriched with anecdotes, photos, and unpublished documents.

Summer concerts. The basilica regularly hosts sacred and classical music concerts that showcase the site's exceptional acoustics. The Romanesque atmosphere and circular rotunda create a unique sonic experience for music lovers.

days_plan.itin_title: Indre Road Trip: Secret Berry and the Vallée Noire

visits.text: The Clarée valley is the grand finale, and quite a finale it is: designated a protected natural site since 1992, 20,000 hectares of wilderness along a crystal-clear river bordered by larches that blaze in autumn. Often cited among the most beautiful valleys in the Alps, it narrowly escaped a uranium mine and a road tunnel in the 1980s. Drive slowly—the upper valley closes to cars in the middle of the day in summer; the shuttle is mandatory.

Névache's hamlets are strung out along the valley, with larch-log houses and old sundials, including the one at Le Rosier, dated 1740 and bearing an enigmatic motto. The old village of Ville-Haute has preserved its narrow lanes, wooden fountains and bread ovens. Do not miss the Baroque chapels with their colorful frescoes, evidence of the faith of these isolated high-altitude communities. Allow an hour to wander between two hikes.

activities.text: Hiking in the upper Clarée is a sure bet: more than 30 high-altitude lakes (Long, Rond, Laramon, des Muandes) are accessible by marked trails for all levels, from family walks to demanding outings. The scenery alternates between alpine pastures, larches and turquoise water. The Buffère and Drayères refuges offer overnight stops. Take two liters of water for long outings, and keep the shuttle timetable in mind when traveling to the upper-valley trailheads.

For seasoned hikers, Mont Thabor rises to 3,178 meters: a 3,000-meter peak with no major technical difficulty, but a long route of about 18 km and more than 1,500 meters of elevation gain, often completed over two days with a night in a refuge or bivouac. At the summit, the Notre-Dame-des-Sept-Douleurs chapel and a 360-degree panorama from the Écrins to Mont Blanc. Attempt it only from July to September, take three liters of water and start early.

The Vallée Étroite, incorporated into France in 1947, stretches deep toward Italy through a wild, rocky landscape. From Névache (via the Col de l'Échelle), you reach the hamlet of Les Granges then Lac Vert, nestled in a cirque facing the Thabor. A Franco-Italian valley with a character all its own, quieter than the main Clarée valley. Easy to moderate hike to the lake.

days_plan.itin_title: Hautes-Alpes Road Trip: High Mountains and Alpine Valleys

places.name: Nevers

visits.text: The cathedral boasts two opposing choirs, bearing witness to fifteen centuries of history. The 11th-century Romanesque choir features a fresco depicting Christ in Glory, while the 14th-century Gothic choir blazes with 1,052 square meters of contemporary stained glass.
Climb the Bohier Tower to discover panoramic views of the Loire and Nevers' slate rooftops.

Completed in 1491, the Ducal Palace is considered the first Loire château. Its Renaissance façade is adorned with sculptures inspired by Sebastiano Serlio's architectural treatise. Two medieval round towers dominate the Place de la République.
The Ducal Palace Heritage Centre traces the town's history through Nevers stone, Loire waters, and traditional crafts. An aquarium showcasing Loire fish species completes the visit.
The Faïence Museum houses 1,950 pieces of Nevers pottery from the 16th to 20th centuries, plus a collection of enameled glass on loan from the Louvre. The museum gardens provide a peaceful setting.
Saint-Étienne Church stands as one of France's best-preserved Romanesque churches. Built in the 11th century, it belonged to the Abbey of Cluny. Listed as a historic monument in 1840.
The Espace Bernadette Soubirous occupies the former Saint-Gildard convent where Bernadette lived from 1866 to 1879. Her body has rested intact in a glass shrine in the chapel since 1925.

activities.text: Follow the Faïence Route, a blue line traced on the sidewalks that connects historic pottery workshops to the town's monuments.
Stroll along the Loire quays, complete with an urban beach in summer. The royal river offers views of the Ducal Palace and cathedral.
Explore the Gardens of La Baratte, a centuries-old site with vegetable gardens, fountains, and wash houses. Restored former market gardeners' houses dot the landscape.

days_plan.itin_title: Nièvre Road Trip: Morvan and Ducal Heritage

map_keywords: Faïence and Fine Arts Museum Nevers

visits.text: Vertiginous: the Nez de Jobourg forms one of the highest cliffs on the French Channel coast, facing the Raz Blanchard and its currents, reputed to be among the strongest in Europe. The viewpoint, accessible via a short path, offers views of the Channel Islands on clear days. Avoid getting too close to the edge.

days_plan.itin_title: Cotentin, Pays d'Auge: 5 days exploring the most beautiful villages

visits.text: The Promenade des Anglais stretches for seven kilometers between the Baie des Anges and Belle Époque luxury hotels, and it's on one of the blue chairs that you grasp its spirit. It was launched in 1822 by Reverend Lewis Way to provide work for Nice residents during a food shortage: a promenade financed by British winter visitors that became the city's symbol. The famous blue chairs, designed in the 1950s, have become so iconic they've entered the MAMAC collections. Walk early in the morning if possible: the light is better and you avoid the crowds of evening joggers.

Get lost in Old Nice: laundry hanging from windows, green shutters against ochre facades, cool alleyways opening onto unexpected little squares. The color palette comes from Genoese and Piedmontese influence—at times, you'd swear you were in Genoa, not France. Important note: Old Nice itself isn't UNESCO-listed—it's the entire 522-hectare ensemble of the "Winter Resort Town of the Riviera," including Old Nice, Promenade des Anglais, Port Lympia, and Cimiez, that was inscribed as a World Heritage site on July 27, 2021. Avoid noon to 2 PM in summer when the heat in the narrow streets becomes crushing.

Probably the least-known Baroque palace in France, the Palais Lascaris is tucked away on Rue Droite, a street so narrow that it is easy to walk past without looking up. Built from 1648 for Jean-Baptiste Lascaris, a descendant of the Byzantine aristocracy, it now houses one of France's two most important collections of historical musical instruments: more than 500 pieces bequeathed in 1904 by prominent Nice resident Antoine Gautier. Standard admission is €5, with free or reduced admission available to eligible visitors. Closed on Tuesdays.

On Place Rossetti, Sainte-Réparate Cathedral raises its 17th-century baroque facade. Inside, gilding and polychrome marble compete in pure Nice baroque style—overloaded side chapels, painted vaults. The square itself, with café terraces open late into the evening and a fountain at its center, is one of the liveliest in the quarter. The Fenocchio ice cream parlor on the square's edge offers 94 flavors, including lemon thyme and Provence calisson: worth a detour even when you're not hungry.

Climb Castle Hill: free elevator from the seafront, or 400 steps if you want to earn the view. At the top, a wooded park overlooks the entire city, an artificial waterfall murmurs, and the panorama opens across the Baie des Anges as far as the Pre-Alps. The castle itself was razed by Louis XIV in 1706—only ruins and the seaside cemetery remain, where Gaston Leroux, among others, rests. Go an hour before sunset, when the light on the ochre rooftops is superb.

Port Lympia, dug in the 18th century at the mouth of the Paillon, lines up its red and yellow facades in pure Piedmontese baroque style. It's one of Nice's most photogenic spots in late afternoon—facade reflections on the water, colorful boats, modern yachts side by side. An atmosphere between fishing village and chic marina, without Monaco's frenzy. The fish restaurants around quai Lunel are worth the detour for lunch.

On Cimiez hill, the 2nd-century Roman arena sleeps beneath century-old olive trees. Right next door, the Matisse Museum occupies a red Genoese villa from the 17th century: the collection traces the entire oeuvre of the painter, who lived in Nice and died there in 1954. In the neighboring Franciscan monastery rest Matisse and Raoul Dufy, beneath the same stones. It's less crowded than Old Nice; allow 90 minutes for the museum alone. Closed Tuesdays.

The Marc Chagall Museum, a stone's throw from the Matisse Museum, presents the “Biblical Message”: 17 large canvases that the painter donated to the French state in 1966 so a museum would be built around them. The building, designed by André Hermant, is itself very well designed—soft light, a Mediterranean garden, a mosaic and stained glass by Chagall. A museum devoted to a single artist with a rare sense of coherence. Closed Tuesdays.

Saint Nicholas Orthodox Cathedral rises behind the train station like an apparition: five colored onion domes reaching 50 meters high. Erected between 1903 and 1912 at the request of Tsar Nicholas II and financed by his mother, Empress Maria Feodorovna, it's the largest Russian Orthodox cathedral outside Russia. The interior, adorned with icons and frescoes, testifies to the Russian colony that wintered in Nice from 1856. Proper attire required, photos forbidden inside.

MAMAC, the Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, occupies a 1990 modernist building at the end of the Promenade du Paillon. Its collections are particularly strong in New Realism (Yves Klein, Arman, César, all from Nice or connected to the city) and American Pop Art (Andy Warhol, Roy Lichtenstein). The museum is currently closed for major renovation work and is expected to reopen in 2028. In the meantime, a selection of its works can still be seen through exhibitions and events held outside the museum.

The Palais Masséna is a Belle Époque villa, built in 1898 for Victor Masséna, a descendant of the marshal of the Empire. Today it is a museum of Nice's history: Empire furniture, Joséphine's dresses, Napoleonic memorabilia and the history of vacationing on the Côte d'Azur. The garden on the Promenade, with its palms and pool, is a special place—cool, shaded, free. Ideal for catching your breath before returning to the beach.

activities.text: Stroll through Cours Saleya first thing in the morning: flower market stalls exploding with color, socca vendors calling out to each other, smells of tapenades and spices. This is where you get a sense of Nice's character—loud, generous, Mediterranean. On Mondays, antique dealers replace the florists, creating a different atmosphere. Avoid Sundays in high season—it's packed.

The Promenade du Paillon is the 12-hectare green corridor that crosses Nice from Old Nice to MAMAC. Opened in 2013 above the old channeled river, it features a reflecting pool with 3,200 jets where children splash in summer. It's become the city's green lung—Nice residents gather here at all hours. Ideal for catching your breath between museums.

On Place Masséna, bright red buildings and black-and-white checkerboard paving form the gateway to Avenue Jean Médecin and its shops. At the center, seven illuminated statues represent the seven continents—an installation by Catalan artist Jaume Plensa that lights up at nightfall. The most photogenic moment: just after sunset, when the figures start changing colors.

Taste authentic Niçoise cuisine: golden socca sizzling on the griddle at Cours Saleya, melt-in-the-mouth pissaladière, and chard pie in both sweet AND savory versions (yes, the same base). For dinner, restaurants in Old Nice serve pan bagnat, Niçoise beef stew, herb ravioli and stockfish. It is Niçoise cuisine, distinct from Provençal cuisine—not olive oil everywhere, but rather onion, anchovy and slow-cooked vegetables.

Finish with a swim off the pebble beaches along the Promenade des Anglais. The water is generally calm in summer, but bring water shoes—the pebbles are treacherous as you enter and the seabed slopes steeply. Private beaches rent lounge chairs and umbrellas if you prefer comfort. Tip: Beau Rivage beach, opposite the opera house, is less crowded than those near the Negresco.

Try socca at Chez Pipo, on the edge of Old Nice: this chickpea flour pancake cooked over a wood fire is THE Nice street food. Crispy on top, soft underneath, with pepper and nothing else. Pipo (rue Bavastro) has been around since 1923 and has turned down all offers to franchise. Expect to pay €3–4 per portion.

Place Garibaldi marks the northern border of Old Nice: its yellow arcades and bustle recall Turin (and for good reason, Nice was Sardinian until 1860). Garibaldi was born here in 1807—the central statue honors him. It's also the starting point for Tram 1 which runs throughout the city.

For modern art fans: Villa Arson, 10 minutes by car from the center, is simultaneously an art school, contemporary art center, and artist residency. Impressive 1960s brutalist architecture, always cutting-edge exhibitions. Free admission. Not suitable for families with young children.

The Nice Carnival, if you are there in February: 15 days of parades, flower battles and illuminated processions, created in 1873 and listed as part of France's intangible heritage. It is one of the three largest carnivals in the world, alongside Rio and Venice.

Leave time for a short walk along the Promenade des Anglais if your departure from Nice allows a little flexibility. The waterfront follows the Bay of Angels and offers the loop’s first coastal scenery. This stop is optional: set off toward Liguria without delaying the stops planned for later.

Back on the Bay of Angels, head up to Castle Hill for a final walk above Nice. The park offers views of the bay and shaded paths around its waterfall. Keep this stop optional and enjoy the terraces before heading back down, leaving enough time for your return.

visits.text: Arènes de Nîmes, one of the world's best-preserved Roman amphitheaters at 436 feet long and 69 feet high. Built in the 1st century AD, it held 24,000 spectators who came to watch gladiatorial combat. The two-tiered exterior arcade in honey-colored Vers-Pont-du-Gard stone demonstrates Roman engineering mastery. The free audioguide in seven languages recreates the atmosphere of ancient games. Today the monument hosts férias, concerts, and historical reenactments including the Roman Days of Nîmes each late April.

Maison Carrée, a Roman temple from the 1st century BC added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2023. The Corinthian facade with its 30 fluted columns illustrates the harmony of classical proportions. The innovative display, with the immersive projection "Nemausus, the birth of Nîmes", retraces 2000 years of history on the interior walls. The building served in turn as a consular house, a church, a prefecture and departmental archives.

Tour Magne, remnant of Roman ramparts dominating Nîmes from atop Mont Cavalier at 105 feet high. Built under Augustus, it marked the northwestern corner of fortified walls that stretched nearly four miles. Climbing the 140 steps leads to a panoramic platform offering 360° views over the city, garrigue scrubland, and on clear days, Mont Ventoux and the Cévennes mountains. The octagonal tower integrated into the most imposing defensive system in Roman Gaul.

Jardins de la Fontaine, an 18th-century public park designed around the sacred spring that gave birth to Nemausus. Majestic tree-lined pathways bordered by balustrades and neoclassical statues follow a monumental perspective inspired by Versailles. The Temple of Diana, a mysterious Roman sanctuary with collapsed arcades, stands at the garden's heart. Terraced pools capture spring waters while staircases climb toward Mont Cavalier and Tour Magne. In summer, the garden becomes a cool refuge beneath centuries-old plane trees.

Musée de la Romanité, contemporary building opened in 2018 facing the Arena. The pleated glass facade reflects the amphitheater, creating dialogue between ancient heritage and modern architecture. The 5,000 pieces displayed across 37,500 square feet trace 25 centuries of history from Nemausus to Nîmes: exceptional mosaics, statues, everyday objects, augmented reality reconstructions. The multimedia immersive experience uses interactive technologies and monumental projections. The panoramic rooftop overlooks the city's roofs and Roman arena.

Nîmes Old Town, medieval historic center with winding streets lined by Renaissance facades and private mansions. Notre-Dame-et-Saint-Castor Cathedral combines Romanesque and Gothic styles with its sculpted frieze depicting the Old Testament. Shaded small squares shelter café terraces and artisan shops. The 19th-century central market halls offer Provençal products: olives, tapenades, Costières de Nîmes wines, brandade. The southern atmosphere comes alive at daily markets in a colorful, fragrant ambiance.

activities.text: Experience the Nîmes Férias, major bullfighting events in May (Pentecost) and September. For five days, corridas in the arena, lively bodegas, musical peñas, free concerts, and marching bands invade downtown. Aficionados in white outfits stroll from bar to bar in a festive, convivial atmosphere. Abrivados and bandidos see Camargue bulls running through the streets. Goyesque corridas feature bullfighters in period costumes. The electric atmosphere celebrates Camargue and Spanish bullfighting culture.

Taste brandade de Nîmes at a traditional restaurant in the historic center. This specialty made from desalted cod, milk, olive oil, and garlic is served hot with croutons. Family establishments perpetuate ancestral recipes passed down since the 18th century. Brandade houses also offer versions with truffles or gratinéed. This emblematic Nîmes dish pairs with white Costières wine or chilled rosé.

Stroll through the Provençal markets of Nîmes, especially the one on boulevard Jean-Jaurès on Friday mornings. The stalls overflow with fruit and vegetables from the Gard, pélardon AOC goat cheese, olives and oils, artisan cured meats and cut flowers. Local producers sell garrigue honey, homemade jams and aromatic plants. The lively atmosphere echoes with accents from the Midi and cheerful bargaining. The aromas of roast meats, socca and paella drift between the aisles.

visits.text: A military fort from 1860 turned diving centre: the Calanque de Niolon, in the commune of Le Rove, fits almost entirely within this building. The hamlet consists of just a few cabins, two restaurants and a tiny beach, facing the Frioul islands. You can walk around it in twenty minutes.

The Niolon railway viaduct spans the calanque with its giant arches, and it's what makes the photograph, not the harbour. A small path from the quay climbs up onto the cliff for a view of the whole scene. Slippery rock in wet weather.

activities.text: Take the TER on the Côte Bleue line to Niolon station: around 20 minutes from Saint-Charles, with views down over the sea. The station overlooks the village. If you drive, barriers restrict access and the vehicle impound service does the rest.

The real reason to visit Niolon lies underwater: the UCPA centre housed in the old fort is a FFESSM federation base and offers introductory dives. A field of Italo-Roman amphorae lies at a depth of around 13 metres, accessible to divers with a Level 1 qualification or above.

days_plan.itin_title: Côte Bleue and Camargue: the lower coastal route in 7 days

visits.text: The Niort Keep is the most striking remnant of the Plantagenet empire in Poitou. Henry II of England commissioned its construction beginning in 1180—the very year he wanted to make Niort his capital on the Sèvre—with walls 3.50 meters thick built of dressed stone fitted with narrow joints. Its two square towers rise to 28 meters (the south tower) and 23 meters (the north tower, which collapsed in 1749 and was rebuilt to a lower height). It was Niort’s first building to be listed as a historic monument, back in 1840. Inside, the permanent exhibition “1000 Years of History” traces the keep’s evolution across five rooms, with scale models and 3D animations.

Climb to the terrace for sweeping views of the old town to the southeast and the Sèvre Niortaise to the northwest. A panoramic guide will help you identify the rooftops and bell towers. From this terrace, you can appreciate Niort’s strategic position along the route through the marshes to the Atlantic.

On the floor beneath the roof timbers, do not miss the collection of traditional Poitou furniture, with its large solid-wood wardrobes, and the recreation of a 19th-century interior. Even more haunting are the graffiti left by English sailors imprisoned in the 18th century, carved into the walls of the south tower, where officers were held after their ships were seized. They left their names, their regrets, and sometimes drawings of boats—look for them.

Follow the banks of the Sèvre Niortaise to Espace Épona, which displays remains from the ancient sanctuary at Port Boinot, including a series of goddess statues discovered during the 2018 excavations. Among them is Épona, goddess of equines. This little-known archaeological site is well worth a detour.

activities.text: Stroll through the historic district among the covered market halls, half-timbered facades, and carved dragons adorning some downtown buildings. The market in the halls is especially lively on Saturday mornings—a good time to sample candied angelica, a specialty of the Niort area.

The Bernard d’Agesci Museum brings together fine arts, decorative arts, and natural history collections in a single space, in the spirit of a cabinet of curiosities—a surprisingly rich collection for a city of this size. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes to explore at a leisurely pace.

days_plan.itin_title: Deux-Sèvres Tour: Marais Poitevin and Romanesque Heritage

visits.text: Head for the Cutlery Museum, housed in a former trading house founded in 1725: the Georget house. Nogent is not Thiers: here knives are not made in bulk, this is fine cutlery made for Hermes, Christofle and the great French houses. In Jean Renoir's film La Bete Humaine (1938), the character Roubaud exclaims: "That's a fine knife... but it's a Nogent!" You will understand when you see the 8,000 pieces in the collections: embroidery scissors like lace made of steel, a zeppelin knife inspired by the airship L 49 shot down near the village in October 1917, surgical instruments of goldsmith precision.

The Nogent cutlery basin spreads across 20 kilometers surrounding the city—some forty villages, each specializing in a distinct production type. At the 1862 Universal Exposition, Nogent scissors were hailed as "the finest manufactured anywhere in the world." Stroll the old town to see facades bearing witness to the 19th-century golden age, when 6,000 workers labored in the surrounding cutlery trades.

The Marne riverbanks beckon for a gentle walk. The river threads through well-preserved bocage, and several hydraulic mills recall that it was precisely water power that propelled the cutlery trade's rise in the region from the 14th century onward.

activities.text: Follow the Route des Vallees Coutelieres, a waymarked circuit that takes you to meet the workshops and craftsmen keeping the Nogent know-how alive. Along the way you can admire two plates from Diderot's Encyclopedie devoted to the cutler's trade, a trade which, as a reminder, Diderot's own father practised in Langres. The Cutlery Fair, held every year in April, is also a chance to watch live demonstrations.

The museum shop stocks handcrafted knives, scissors, and items produced throughout the Nogent basin. It's the ideal place to take home an authentic piece—contemporary works sit alongside reproductions of historic models.
If you're in town Friday morning, don't miss the market. Haute-Marne produce and local specialties fill the square.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Marne Circuit: Langres and Heritage

visits.text: Carné filmed Nogent-sur-Marne in 1929 in Nogent Eldorado du dimanche—Parisians arriving on the Bastille train for Sunday boating, riverside taverns packed, the Marne as a substitute for the sea. But before the taverns, the town was aristocratic: from the 17th century, nobles and members of the bourgeoisie had country houses built there. The Hôtel des Coignard, an 18th-century building in the town center, is the most visible reminder of this heritage.

The Maison nationale des artistes occupies two 17th and 18th-century mansions bequeathed to the state by the Smith sisters — Madeleine, a painter, and Jeanne, a photographer. The 10-hectare park has been classified as a picturesque site since 1909. It now houses both a retirement home for artists and MABA, a contemporary art center. Free entry, daily 9am to 6pm.

The Musée intercommunal de Nogent-sur-Marne is France's only museum dedicated to the history of the Marne's meanders. Founded in 1962, it holds over 6,000 items: glass photographic plates from the early 20th century, paintings by Ferdinand Gueldry, Belle Époque postcards. This is where the golden age of riverside taverns truly comes to life.

activities.text: The Nogent viaduct spans 800 meters with 34 arches—it was built to bring the train from Mulhouse, which transformed the town into a fashionable residential suburb. At its base stand Art Nouveau villas designed by Nachbaur father and son, architects from Nogent who built much of this neighborhood between 1900 and 1914. The Vallée de la Marne tourist office organizes guided walks exploring this heritage in season.

Nogent's marina carries the France Station Nautique label. Clubs offer kayaking, rowing, and paddleboarding on the Marne—this is where Belle Époque nautical festivals and regattas were held. On spring weekends, the place regains some of that bustle.

days_plan.itin_title: Val-de-Marne Road Trip: Castles and the Banks of the Marne

visits.text: The Passage du Gois is worth the trip in itself. This 4.125 km tidal causeway connects the mainland to Noirmoutier and is the longest in Europe. It is passable only at low tide, for about 1 hour 30 minutes before and after low water. Depending on the tidal coefficient, it disappears beneath 1.30 to 4 meters of water. The first known crossing dates back to 843. Refuge markers line the route for anyone caught out by the tide. Always check the tide times before setting off; otherwise, use the Noirmoutier Bridge, built in 1971.

Noirmoutier Castle dominates the town center. The lords of La Garnache erected fortifications as early as the 9th century to fend off Vikings, and the present castle dates to the 12th century. Climb the keep: you'll have a commanding view of the island, salt marshes, and coast.

Saint-Philbert Church stands on the foundations of a Benedictine abbey church founded around 674 by the monk Philbert. The crypt contains the saint's empty tomb—his relics were transferred to Tournus during the Norman invasions of the 9th century. Go down into it and you will feel the weight of fourteen centuries of history in the dim light.

Wander through the Banzeau district, one of the oldest on the island. White houses with colorful shutters, hollyhocks and climbing vines—this is picture-postcard Noirmoutier. Continue to the Bois de la Chaise, where maritime pines, holm oaks and strawberry trees lead you to Plage des Dames and its iconic white beach huts.

At day's end, detour to the village of Le Vieil, an old fishermen's hamlet with white houses right at the waterline. Its narrow lanes and tranquil coves make it one of the island's most photogenic corners—and the best spot for sunset.

activities.text: Join a salt worker to learn how salt is harvested. Salt marshes cover around a third of the island, and techniques passed down from generation to generation transform seawater into coarse salt and fleur de sel. In summer, guided tours are available almost every day.

Follow the bike paths on a loop around the island—about 25 kilometers connecting Barbâtre, La Guérinière, L'Épine and Noirmoutier-en-l'Île. The terrain is flat, the ride is easy, and you can bring the children along without any difficulty.

days_plan.itin_title: Vendée Itinerary: Noirmoutier Island, Puy du Fou and the Coastline

visits.text: Built in the 14th century, the Market Halls of Nolay are medieval halls still in use today. Their four-sided roof, covered with limestone slabs, rests on original framing. The Monday market is still held here.

activities.text: Locals nickname their town the city of Lazare Carnot, after the scientist born here who became the organizer of the Republic's armies. His statue, a pair of compasses in hand, stands prominently on the village's main square.

days_plan.itin_title: Burgundy-Franche-Comté: The Most Beautiful Villages in 7 days

visits.text: Built in 1519 following apparitions of the Virgin Mary, the sanctuary of Notre-Dame de Grâces overlooks Cotignac from Mont Verdaille. In 1660, Louis XIV and his mother Anne of Austria came to thank the Virgin for the king's miraculous birth. Access to the surrounding forest areas is regulated from June to September when there is a fire risk.

days_plan.itin_title: Var in 4 Days: From Bormes to the Most Beautiful Villages of the Verdon

places.name: Noyers

visits.text: Noyers-sur-Serein, classified among France's Most Beautiful Villages since 1982, nestles in a meander of the Serein River. The village counts 78 buildings listed as Historic Monuments, most dating from the 15th century.

Look up at Place du Marché-au-Blé and Place de la Petite-Étape-aux-Vins. The half-timbered façades bear carved pinnacles, small columns, and stone decorations testifying to medieval commercial prosperity.
The Notre-Dame church, built between 1491 and 1515 in the Flamboyant Gothic style, contains a light-filled nave.

The Museum of Naïve and Popular Arts occupies the former 17th-century college. It presents donations of naïve art, popular art works from Southern Europe, Asia, and Latin America, plus Hokusai albums.
Walk the ramparts and their 19 defensive towers, still partially visible. The Venoise Tower, called 'cave au loup,' preserves its intact vaulted room and feeds a local legend.
The ruins of the medieval castle, destroyed in the 14th century, offer beautiful viewpoints over the village below and the Serein's loop. The climb follows a short path from the center.

activities.text: Follow the Serein riverbanks along the path starting beneath the ramparts. Reflections of half-timbered houses in the calm water create one of the village's loveliest scenes.
The village hosts artists' workshops and artisan studios open to the public. Galleries, potters, and sculptors occupy shops along the cobbled lanes.
In autumn, attend the Burgundy truffle market. Tastings and activities celebrate the 'black diamond' in a convivial atmosphere.

places.name: Noyers Sur Serein

visits.text: Built between the 15th and 18th centuries, the half-timbered houses of Noyers-sur-Serein line up beneath arcades carved with human figures. The village, spared by wars, has kept remarkably uniform architecture. Allow an hour for a full walking tour.

activities.text: Noyers' winemakers still retain their old cellars dug beneath the houses, vestiges of a forgotten winemaking past. Several village wine cellars offer guided tastings. In autumn, the Burgundy truffle market enlivens the main square.

days_plan.itin_title: Burgundy-Franche-Comté: The Most Beautiful Villages in 7 days

visits.text: Notre-Dame Cathedral was begun in 1145 as a landmark of early Gothic. Its double transept with apsidal chapels remains unique, together with Soissons, in French Gothic architecture.

The Chapter Library has stood on wooden pillars since 1506. A rare European example of a half-timbered building, it preserves 3,000 volumes including editions of works by Calvin, Pascal and Montaigne.
The Morienval Gospel Book dates from the 9th-century Carolingian period. Its wooden binding inlaid with ivory and illuminations illustrating Aesop's fables make it a major bibliophilic treasure.

The Jean Calvin Museum occupies a building erected between 1927 and 1930 on the site where the reformer was born in 1509. The history of Protestantism and rare 16th-century engravings trace the Reformation.
The Noyonnais Museum occupies the former episcopal palace. Two thousand years of local history are displayed there, from Gallo-Roman vestiges to the coronation of Charlemagne in 768.

activities.text: Wander through the cathedral quarter among canons' houses from the 17th and 18th centuries. The chapter house and episcopal outbuildings line the cobbled streets around Notre-Dame.

days_plan.itin_title: Oise Circuit: châteaux, forests and history

visits.text: Admire this elegant medieval bridge built in the 14th century that spans the Eygues with a single daring arch 43 meters long and 18 meters high. Construction began in 1340 but wasn't completed until 1409. Listed as a Historical Monument in 1925, it's a masterpiece of medieval engineering and Nyons' iconic symbol.

Wander the picturesque alleys of the old village with its ancient houses bathed in the warm atmosphere of Drôme Provençale. The Randonne Tower emerges from the rooftops, crowned with a curious pyramid of arcades topped by a Virgin statue. Nyons has earned the France's Most Beautiful Detours and Remarkable Taste Site labels.

Visit one of the historic olive oil mills at the foot of the Roman Bridge. The Dozol-Autrand Mill, established in 1750, has seen 14 generations of millers. A video traces an olive's journey to its transformation into oil. The Vieux Moulins Mill offers heritage unique in France with two old mills from the 18th and 19th centuries and a soap works.

Contemplate the olive groves stretching across the surrounding hills, often terraced. The Tanche olive, a unique local variety grown only in the Baronnies Provençales territory, can withstand temperatures down to -10°C. The Nyons black olive stands out with its monk's robe color and gentle taste with red fruit aromas. Nyons olive oil, France's first PDO oil in 1994, is characterized by its golden color and buttery taste.

activities.text: Explore the traditional mills and discover the complete olive oil production process. Possibly attend a demonstration of scourtins weaving at La Scourtinerie, France's only such workshop. Taste different Nyons PDO olive oils and preserved black olives. The ideal period to observe production is December through January during harvest and pressing.

Don't miss Thursday morning's colorful market, a true Nyons institution. Browse stalls overflowing with local products: Nyons PDO olives and oils, Picodon goat cheese, lavender honey, aromatic herbs. The market comes alive beneath century-old plane trees.

Discover local craft shops, art galleries, and creator workshops. Visit the World of Olives Institute and the Olive & Sens exhibition that engages all five senses to explore the olive universe. Culinary and cosmetic workshops centered on olives are regularly offered.

days_plan.itin_title: Drome Provencale Road Trip: Villages and Terroirs
From the Alps to the Ardèche Gorges: Lakes, Peaks and Garrigue

visits.text: Obernai concentrates the best of medieval Alsace on a single square. At Place du Marché—where the weekly market has been documented since 1301—the Renaissance Town Hall (1523, remodeled in 1610), the 1554 Corn Exchange (originally a butcher shop and salt store), the 1579 Six-Bucket Well, and the Kappellturm belfry form a remarkably cohesive ensemble. Arrive in the morning for the light and before the tour buses descend.

The Kappellturm belfry dominates the square at 60 meters tall. It's what remains of a chapel built in the late 13th century—the chapel was destroyed in 1873 but the bell tower survived, with its six bells, the two oldest dating from 1429 and 1474. The gallery with its watchtowers was added in 1596-97. On the northeast buttress, you'll find the official measurements of the ell and dagger carved into the stone—medieval measurement standards.

Obernai is the legendary birthplace of Saint Odile, patroness of Alsace, born blind in the 7th century and said to have regained her sight on the day of her baptism. The medieval ramparts that still encircle the center—1,400 meters of walls with towers and moats—testify to the town's strategic importance. In 1354, Obernai joined nine other cities to found the Decapolis, the league of free imperial cities of Alsace. A walk along the rampart path gives you a good sense of the scale of the work.

Saints Peter and Paul Church, built between 1867 and 1872 in monumental neo-Gothic style, preserves two classified treasures: the 1882 Merklin organ and the 1504 Holy Sepulchre altar, which depicts the risen Christ surrounded by the Holy Women with striking realism for its time.

activities.text: Climb to Mont Sainte-Odile, 15 km from Obernai, Alsace's foremost pilgrimage site since the 7th century. The Abbey of Hohenbourg perches at 764 meters and offers views on clear days as far as the Bernese Alps and the Black Forest. Around the abbey runs the Pagan Wall—a 10 km enceinte of cyclopean stones whose origin remains debated, probably Celtic. An 11 km hiking circuit allows you to walk its full perimeter.

In the evening, linger in Obernai's lanes to taste Alsatian specialties in a winstub: tarte flambée, baeckeoffe, choucroute garnie, and sweet kouglof for dessert. The town is the Bas-Rhin's second tourist destination after Strasbourg—restaurants are numerous and quality is generally good.

visits.text: Oingt, listed among the Plus Beaux Villages de France, spreads its golden-stone houses along a steep ridge. This former fortified medieval town has preserved its enclosing walls, vaulted gateways and stone-paved lanes winding between ochre façades. The local limestone, extracted from nearby quarries, takes on warm hues that set the village ablaze in the light of the setting sun.

Rue Tyre-laine and the village lanes are lined with winegrowers' houses and golden-stone dwellings. Carved lintels, studded doors and inner courtyards reflect the former prosperity generated by the wine and stone trades. Each façade deserves close attention for its architectural details, finely carved into the soft limestone.

The medieval tower, the last remnant of the fortified castle, offers an exceptional 360-degree panorama. The view takes in the Monts du Lyonnais, the Beaujolais vineyards, the Azergues valley and, on clear days, Mont Blanc on the horizon. From the top of this watchtower, you can understand Oingt's strategic role in watching over trade routes.

Saint-Mathieu Church displays the restrained Romanesque architecture characteristic of rural Beaujolais buildings. Its golden-stone vaults create remarkable acoustics appreciated during concerts. The chancel contains restored wall frescoes and an 18th-century altarpiece bearing witness to local religious devotion.

activities.text: Stroll through the stone-paved lanes, where stones laid on edge form traditional geometric patterns. These calades, a distinctive feature of the Pierres Dorées region, require ancestral expertise handed down from one specialist paver to the next. Craftspeople patiently restore these pavements, which drain away water while enhancing the narrow lanes.

Visit the artists' and artisans' workshops housed in former winegrowers' homes. Painters, sculptors and potters have made their homes in this inspiring village, where light plays across the golden façades. Art galleries display contemporary works in medieval settings, creating a dialogue between past and present.

Walk the vineyard trails descending from the village towards the valley. Hillside vineyards produce quality Beaujolais and Beaujolais-Villages wines. Family estates preserve traditional methods, favouring hand harvesting on these steep slopes that machines cannot reach.

Visit the Carrières de Glay in Saint-Germain-Nuelles to discover the heritage of the golden stone that shaped the region's landscape and architecture. This former open-air quarry reveals the methods once used to extract and work the limestone. The quarry faces display shades ranging from creamy white to golden yellow, depending on the geological layers.

days_plan.itin_title: Rhône Road Trip: Lyon, Golden Stone Villages of Beaujolais & Condrieu Vineyards
Loop Around Lyon: Villages and Pierres Dorées
Road Trip from Bresse to Bugey via Beaujolais and Lyon

visits.text: Oiron Castle stands apart among France’s heritage sites: a 16th- and 17th-century Renaissance residence that has housed a unique contemporary art collection since 1993, conceived around the theme of cabinets of curiosities—the eclectic collections that fascinated Renaissance scholars. More than 63 artists have filled the historic rooms with their work: some pieces are puzzling, others make you smile, and all engage with the 17th-century painted and carved woodwork. One ticket covers both eras.

The 55-meter-long Renaissance gallery is the highlight of the historical tour. Its 16th-century frescoes illustrate the story of Troy. They were commissioned by Claude Gouffier, Henry II’s Grand Equerry. Take time to examine them closely: the scenes tell a story, almost like a novel.

The adjoining collegiate church, whose construction began in 1499 under Gabrielle de Bourbon-Montpensier to house the Gouffier chapel, stands immediately beside the castle. Its Flamboyant Gothic features and the tombs of the family of local lords round out a visit to the estate.

activities.text: Stroll through the castle park, landscaped between 2005 and 2008 by a contemporary landscape designer who incorporated works of art into the green spaces. It is a natural extension of the collection inside.
The village of Oiron itself has welcomed a few contemporary artworks in its squares and narrow streets—a walk of about 30 minutes that extends your wanderings from the castle into the village.

days_plan.itin_title: Deux-Sèvres Tour: Marais Poitevin and Romanesque Heritage

places.name: Oloron Sainte Marie

visits.text: The Cathedral of Saint Mary is Oloron's flagship monument. Its 12th-century Romanesque portal — created by two different artists including the "Master of Oloron" — is one of the finest in the Southwest. It depicts preparations for a medieval banquet with scenes of local life: wild boar hunting, salmon fishing, bread and cheese cutting. Glass beads were inserted into the eyes of the figures to bring them to life — look closely. Listed as UNESCO World Heritage in 1998 under the Roads to Santiago, the cathedral was in service from the 12th century onward and was reworked several times. The Gothic chevet with ambulatory dates from the 14th century.

The Sainte-Croix quarter, perched on its hill, is the medieval heart of Oloron. The Tour de Grède rises above the rooftops and offers a panorama over the Pyrenean chain. The paved lanes and half-timbered houses create the atmosphere of a medieval town barely altered by the centuries.

Head to the confluence where the gave d'Aspe and the gave d'Ossau meet to form the gave d'Oloron. This meeting point offers a panorama over the first Pyrenean summits and marks the start of the two great valleys running down towards Spain. Operators offer canoeing and whitewater sports on the gave.

activities.text: The Basque-Bearnese beret is still made in Oloron. Workshops have kept this craft alive since the 19th century — one local factory has been producing berets since 1840. A workshop visit lets you see the fulling and shaping stages. Ten kilometres away, Tissages Lartigue have carried on the art of weaving Basque linen for more than four generations.

The Aspe valley opens due south from Oloron. An hour's drive brings you to the Somport pass at 1,632 metres, the French-Spanish border and a stage on the Road to Santiago — pilgrims coming via Arles crossed this pass. The road follows the gave d'Aspe between beeches and firs, with some chance of spotting vultures and, more rarely, the brown bears of the Basque Country.
