visits.text: You'll make a short detour to the cemetery of Omonville-la-Petite, where the poet Jacques Prévert rests, having spent the final years of his life here. The tiny village can be visited in a few minutes on foot from Port Racine.

days_plan.itin_title: Cotentin, Pays d'Auge: 5 days exploring the most beautiful villages

visits.text: The Manoir du Tourp, a 16th-century seigneurial farm converted into a cultural space, tells the history of La Hague through permanent and temporary exhibitions. The port of Hâble d'Omonville-la-Rogue, one of the few natural shelters on this rocky coast, remains a pleasant stopping point between coastal walks. Free admission to the manor on certain days.

days_plan.itin_title: Cotentin, Pays d'Auge: 5 days exploring the most beautiful villages

visits.text: Oppede-le-Vieux is perhaps the most moving of the Luberon villages: half-ruined, half-restored, it feels frozen in the Middle Ages. The original village was gradually abandoned from the 20th century onward in favour of the lower village in the plain. In 1940, only six inhabitants were still holding out there. It was not until the 1960s that artists and heritage enthusiasts began restoring houses and stone lanes. Wear good shoes: the path from the car park climbs for 15 to 20 minutes along steep cobbled lanes before emerging onto the church esplanade.

The Collégiale Notre-Dame-d'Alydon crowns the village. Its origins likely date to the 10th or 11th century, with significant alterations in the 16th and 17th centuries: the hexagonal bell tower dates from 1500-1501. The interior preserves an 18th-century gilded wooden altarpiece and a painting by Provençal artist Reynaud-Levieux (The Presentation of the Rosary). The building was saved from ruin through the efforts of a network of artists united by an annual festival. Free entry, irregular hours outside summer.

The feudal castle ruins at the summit are inaccessible for safety reasons, but the silhouette is spectacular. A dark anecdote haunts this site: in 1545, Jean Maynier d'Oppède, lord of the château and First President of the Parliament of Aix, ordered the destruction of neighboring Waldensian villages, causing nearly 3,000 deaths. This massacre of the Vaudois of the Luberon remains one of the darkest episodes in Provençal history.

activities.text: Climb via the stone lanes to the summit esplanade—360° view over the Calavon valley, Ventoux, and the Alps. The light is fantastic at midday on the honey-colored stones.
Below the parking lot, the Jardins de Sainte-Cécile offer fifteen terraces of Mediterranean plants with over 80 hardy species. An unexpected natural respite at the foot of a medieval village.

days_plan.itin_title: The 15 Most Beautiful Villages of the Luberon

visits.text: The Centre de la Mémoire d'Oradour, inaugurated in 1999, is the sole entrance to the martyred village ruins. Its permanent exhibition traces, through archival documents and filmed testimonies, the context of World War II and the events of June 10, 1944.

The martyred village preserves intact the ruins of the Limousin town destroyed on June 10, 1944, by the SS Das Reich division. 643 victims — men, women, and children. The cleared streets, reinforced walls, and bullet marks left untouched allow you to measure the massacre's full extent. Classified as a Historic Monument since 1946, the site receives 300,000 visitors annually.

The martyred village church is the most emotionally charged place: here 450 women and children were locked inside and killed. Traces of fire and bullet impacts are carefully preserved during each restoration.
The memorial crypt, designed in the 1950s, houses in its display cases personal objects of victims found in the rubble — stopped watches, toys, keys — relics of shattered daily life.

activities.text: Take time to walk the esplanade linking the Centre de la Mémoire to the new town, rebuilt after the war. The new Oradour church faces the ruins — two eras, one village.
At the municipal cemetery, the Tombeau des martyrs holds the victims' ashes. Votive offerings placed over the decades bear witness to enduring remembrance.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Vienne Tour: Limoges, Porcelain and Villages

visits.text: The ancient theatre of Orange awaits you with its stage wall 103 metres long and 37 metres high — Louis XIV called it “the most beautiful wall in my kingdom”. Built in the Augustan era, it is one of the best-preserved Roman theatres in the world. The cavea could seat 9,000 spectators on 34 tiers arranged according to their social rank. In the large central niche of the stage wall, a colossal statue 3.50 m high watches over the performances — probably an Augustus, although some historians dispute that attribution. UNESCO-listed since 1981. Since the 19th century, the theatre has hosted the Chorégies d'Orange every summer, an open-air opera festival among the oldest in France — book if you are there in June-July.

At the northern entrance to town, Orange's triumphal arch stands 19 meters long and 20 meters high in the middle of a crossroads. It was erected between 10 and 25 AD under Tiberius to honor the veterans of Caesar's Second Gallic Legion, founders of the colony of Arausio. Its three archways bear exceptional decoration: shields, helmets, military standards and—even rarer—maritime motifs evoking the Battle of Actium. Its bas-reliefs of chained Celtic captives recreate the atmosphere of Roman conquest in Gaul. Since spring 2023, a 12-station audio trail has surrounded the monument.

activities.text: The Orange Museum of Art and History, facing the ancient theater, preserves the most complete collection of Roman land registers from the ancient world—engraved marble slabs that precisely mapped the colony's properties. These unique documents help explain how Rome organized land distribution to veterans. An ideal complementary visit to put what you've seen in the theater into context.

days_plan.itin_title: Roman Provence Road Trip: Ancient Remains and Villages
Vaucluse: Avignon, Luberon Villages & Ventoux Routes

visits.text: Orcières-Merlette 1850 gives it away in the name: the resort sits at 1,850 meters on the sunny slopes of the Champsaur. Out of ski season, the slopes turn to alpine pasture and the resort center keeps its mountain architecture. It's mostly a base camp for the surrounding mountains rather than a visit in its own right. Spend a night here to tackle the heights early the next morning, before the heat sets in.

Ride the Télémix gondolas, open in summer, up to the Drouvet summit at 2,650 meters. Up top, the panorama takes in Écrins National Park, the Champsaur, and Valgaudemar in a single glance. Marmots and occasionally a golden eagle complete the picture. It's the easiest starting point for the Monde des 6 Lacs hike; otherwise just enjoy the high-altitude terrace at Rocherousse.

activities.text: Orcières' flagship hike is the Monde des 6 Lacs: a high-altitude loop through glacial lakes and wide-open spaces, accessible from the top of the lifts to avoid most of the elevation gain. Allow half a day, depending on your pace. Marmots guaranteed in the scree. Take at least 2 liters of water, as the sun is intense at this altitude even in cool weather.

For thrills, the Roll Air Cable zip line is one of Europe's longest: 1.8 km of cable, launching headfirst from the Drouvet summit (2,650 m) toward Lac Long, roughly 1 minute 20 seconds of flight high above the ground. Access via Télémix Drouvet I and II. Book ahead, and give it a miss if heights make your stomach knot.

Orcières Bike Park offers 11 trails for all levels, with wooden features, bridges, and teeter-totters for downhill mountain biking fans. Beyond the park, 500 km of marked trails descend from the Drouvet to the recreation area at 1,350 meters. Bike and protective gear rental on-site. Open roughly early July to early September.

days_plan.itin_title: Hautes-Alpes Road Trip: High Mountains and Alpine Valleys

visits.text: The basilique Notre-Dame d'Orcival is one of Auvergne's five major Romanesque churches and has preserved its original bell tower intact. Built in the 12th century, it displays remarkably harmonious architecture, with its pyramidal tiered east end and transverse tower base. In the choir stands the celebrated Virgin in Majesty, a silver and silver-gilt statuette that has drawn pilgrims since the Middle Ages. Painted capitals adorn the nave and choir, while the crypt can be visited by descending from the side aisles.

The Porte Saint-Jean, the basilica's side entrance, deserves careful attention. Its cedar door leaves predating the 13th century bear extraordinary ironwork adorned with animal heads and human faces, rare evidence of Romanesque ironworking. Nicknamed Notre-Dame des Fers, the church preserves chains and iron balls offered as votive offerings by former prisoners grateful for their release. A 16th-century sundial engraved with the image of a chained prisoner recalls this unusual devotion.

Château de Cordès stands at an altitude of 900 meters, two kilometers north of Orcival. This estate dating from the 15th–18th centuries is most notable for its French formal gardens designed by André Le Nôtre's workshop in 1695. The hornbeam bowers and the hornbeam and beech hedges—unique at this altitude—form a geometric landscape listed as a Historic Monument and awarded the Jardin Remarquable label. Visits take place during the summer season.

activities.text: Join a free guided tour of Orcival Basilica offered in summer by parish volunteers. These passionate guides reveal the capitals' iconographic subtleties, the Virgin in Majesty's eventful history, and the architectural secrets of this exceptionally harmonious Romanesque building.

Le prisonnier d'Orcival tablet game, available at the Tourist Office. This fun, interactive trail invites families to solve puzzles tied to the history of the village and its basilica while exploring the lanes and the area around the church.

Hike the volcanic landscapes around Orcival in the Parc naturel régional des Volcans d'Auvergne. Several marked trails wind through summer pastures dotted with burons and through the beech forests surrounding the village, offering views of the Chaîne des Puys peaks.

days_plan.itin_title: Volcanoes and Auvergne traditions

visits.text: Begin at Sainte-Croix Cathedral, one of France's five largest Gothic cathedrals: 140 metres long, 53 metres wide, with a spire reaching 106 metres. Its construction spans from the 13th century until 1829 — King Charles X inaugurated the portal on 8 May of that year, exactly 400 years after Joan of Arc lifted the siege. Henry IV financed its reconstruction from 1601 onwards, and Louis XIV had his royal sun added to the transept's rose windows, with his motto Nec Pluribus Impar. Don't miss the stained glass of the lower nave: ten grand scenes recount Joan of Arc's life, from Domrémy to Rouen. The great bell, named Sainte Jeanne d'Arc, weighs six tonnes.

In Place du Martroi, Joan of Arc's equestrian statue was cast in 1855. Look at the bas-reliefs on the pedestal: they retrace the whole epic, from the appearance of the voices to the liberation of Orléans. The originals are kept at the Museum of Fine Arts — the bronzes you see are casts. Every 7 May in the evening, during the Johannic Festivals, the city solemnly hands over the banner from this square.

The Joan of Arc House is a 1960s reconstruction of the residence of Jacques Boucher, treasurer to the Duke of Orléans, where Joan stayed from 29 April to 9 May 1429 during the siege. The original was burned in 1940. On the ground floor, a multimedia room screens a 15-minute panoramic film on the Hundred Years' War and the Maid's epic, with interactive terminals and mapping of her route. Upstairs sits the world's largest documentary collection dedicated to Joan of Arc: 37,000 books, journals, maps, engravings and films, accessible by appointment.

The Hôtel Groslot is among Orléans's most distinctive monuments. Its façade of red bricks arranged in lozenges was built between 1549 and 1558 by Jacques Groslot, bailiff of the city, under architect Jacques Androuet du Cerceau. King Francis II — married to Mary, Queen of Scots, son of Henry II and Catherine de Medici — died there on 5 December 1560, aged 16, while presiding over the Estates-General. The room where it happened is now the wedding hall, where 450 civil unions are celebrated each year. The visit is free: salon d'honneur, Aubusson tapestries, coffered ceilings.

The Museum of Fine Arts of Orléans occupies a building facing the cathedral. Its collections span from the 15th to the 20th century: Italian primitives, French school from the 17th and 18th centuries, pastels by La Tour. The bequest of Aignan-Thomas Desfriches in the late 18th century formed its core collection. You'll also find the original bas-reliefs from the pedestal of the Joan of Arc statue and works by Girodet. Allow at least 90 minutes for a proper visit.

activities.text: Walk along the redeveloped Loire quays to the George V bridge. The tree-lined promenade offers a panorama over the royal river — UNESCO-listed in 2000 — and its sandbanks. Guinguettes set up in season between May and September. It's one of the best places to take the measure of France's longest river from the bank.

Every year from 29 April to 8 May, the Johannic Festivals commemorate the city's liberation in 1429. Period-costumed processions, medieval markets, concerts and sound-and-light shows on the cathedral: it's France's oldest national festival still celebrated. If planning a visit during this window, book accommodation well in advance.

Wander Place du Châtelet and the pedestrian streets of the centre. On Saturday mornings, the market sets up under the plane trees with local producers, flowers, and Loire Valley specialities such as cotignac, a quince paste sold in small round wooden boxes — a typically Orléans souvenir since the Middle Ages.

days_plan.itin_title: Loiret Road Trip: Orléans and the Châteaux of the Loire

visits.text: On the way to Ornans, make a detour to the Musée des Maisons comtoises in Nancray. Allow for a round trip from Ornans for this visit. This open-air museum brings together around thirty rural buildings dismantled in their original villages in the 17th, 18th and 19th centuries and reassembled on the site—a cooperative Comté dairy, a farmhouse with a traditional smoking chimney, a pink sandstone house and a half-timbered barn. The themed gardens (witch's vegetable garden, heritage orchard) complete the visit.

At Étalans, just before Ornans, the Poudrey chasm is worth the detour. Discovered in 1899, it's the largest chasm in France equipped for visitors, with a main chamber of about 1 million m³. A sound and light show highlights its stalagmites and stalactites. Constant temperature of 10°C—bring a jacket.

Ornans is nicknamed the “little Venice of Franche-Comté” for its houses built to project over the Loue—a protected site. The Courbet Museum, relocated to the painter's birthplace and then expanded in 2011 to cover over 2,000 m², displays more than 70 original works across 21 rooms. Gustave Courbet (1819–1877), a leading figure in realism, painted these Loue landscapes more than 13 times. The museum's large glass windows directly frame views of the river and cliffs—a remarkable architectural effect.

In Ouhans, the source of the Loue is well worth a detour. Allow for a round trip from Ornans, then walk to the source from the parking lot. It is not a true spring: it is a resurgence of the Doubs, spectacularly demonstrated in 1901 when a fire at a distillery in Pontarlier gave the waters of the Loue the scent of absinthe. The waterfall gushes out at the foot of a 100-meter rocky box canyon. A protected site since 1912—among the earliest site designations in the history of environmental protection in France.

activities.text: Operators offer canoe rentals on the Loue from Ornans. Paddling down the valley between limestone cliffs and forests is one of the trip's finest moments in nature. Allow 2 hours for a leisurely trip.

days_plan.itin_title: Doubs Circuit: Watchmaking and Swiss Border
Doubs Road Trip: Nature and Heritage of Franche-Comté

places.name: Ospedale

visits.text: Climb to the Ospedale forest, at 900 meters altitude above Porto-Vecchio: an oasis of coolness among laricio pines and holm oaks, with an artificial lake built in the 1960s shimmering at the basin's bottom—a surprising image at this altitude. From the forest road you'll have some of the finest views over the Bay of Porto-Vecchio. Stop at the viewpoints on the village road.

The Piscia di Gallo waterfall - “rooster pee” in Corsican, which gives you an idea of the local poetry - has a 60-meter drop. It is a 30-minute walk from the forest parking lot. The only catch: it is spectacular in spring and after the autumn rains, but can dwindle to a trickle in August.

activities.text: Two-hour round-trip hike to Piscia di Gallo waterfall from the forest parking lot: well-marked trail in the pines, moderate 200 m elevation gain. Hiking shoes required—the path is rocky.
From the Ospedale forest belvedere, the Bay of Porto-Vecchio spreads below with its islets and green waters. Stop there in late afternoon: the declining light turns the gulf to gold.

days_plan.itin_title: Complete Tour of Corsica

map_keywords: Point de vue baie Porto-Vecchio Ospedale

visits.text: Créac'h Lighthouse, one of Europe's most powerful lighthouses with its 55-meter tower striped black and white. Lit in 1863, it marks the boundary between the English Channel and Atlantic and guides ships into the Ouessant traffic separation scheme used by over 50,000 vessels annually. Its luminous range reaches 32 nautical miles thanks to xenon lamps. At nightfall, the beams majestically sweep the moorland and horizon in a mystical, grandiose atmosphere.

Lighthouses and Beacons Museum, installed in Créac'h's former engine room. Collections trace the technical evolution of maritime signaling with Fresnel optics, monumental lenses, and historic lanterns. Keepers' narratives illustrate the isolated life on offshore lighthouses like La Jument or Kéréon. The space dedicated to constructing these sentinels reveals engineering feats against raging elements.

Stiff Lighthouse, built in 1700 on Vauban's advice to Louis XIV. Perched at the island's highest point at 63 meters, its two adjoining round towers overlook the harbor of the same name. Climbing the 104 steps leads to a circular panorama over the island's wild coasts, the Brest roadstead and, in clear weather, the mainland. The neighboring military semaphore station and the radar tower watch over maritime traffic.

Niou Huella Ecomuseum, a traditional 19th-century Ouessant house preserved in its original state. The two restored rooms reveal island life of yesteryear with furniture, utensils, and everyday objects. The box bed, central fireplace, and painted furniture testify to ingenuity facing the harsh climate. The reconstituted vegetable garden shows subsistence crops adapted to violent winds.

Village of Lampaul, Ouessant's sole settlement concentrating the island's 870 inhabitants. The parish church and its bell tower dominate lanes bordered by low houses with blue shutters. The "leaning house" with slanted walls housed the island's first hotel in the early 20th century. Lampaul harbor welcomes boats when easterly winds prevent docking at Stiff. The cemetery houses a tiny mausoleum for proëlla crosses, wax symbols representing sailors lost at sea.

activities.text: Cycling to Pointe de Pern, the island's western extremity and mainland France's westernmost point. Roads cross windswept bare moorland where black Ouessant sheep graze. Steep cliffs plunge into foaming seas while jagged rocks testify to the elements' violence. Violent currents between Ouessant and Molène maintain water at 15°C, ideal temperature for grey seals. The spectacle is breathtaking in its power and savage beauty.

Observing offshore lighthouses from Pointe de Porz-Doun in the island's southwest. On clear days, three maritime sentinels stand out against the horizon: Nividic, France's westernmost built in 1936, La Jument famous for storm images since 1911, and Kéréon emerging from the Fromveur passage with currents reaching 16 km/h. These "Hell" lighthouses, built on isolated reefs, symbolize the courage of now-vanished keepers. The Runiou pyramid serves as a navigation landmark.

Geocaching along Ouessant's lighthouse trail, a modern treasure hunt marking the island's iconic sites. Caches hidden near lighthouses, megaliths, and viewpoints invite exploration of every corner. The app reveals historical anecdotes and natural curiosities while collecting finds. A fun, interactive way to tour the island as a family.

Tasting Ouessant mutton stew cooked under peat, an island specialty simmered according to ancestral tradition. The lamb, fed on salt-seasoned grasses, develops a unique flavor, tender and aromatic. Lampaul and Stiff port restaurants offer this authentic recipe accompanied by garden vegetables. Buckwheat galettes and crêpes complete the Breton gastronomic tableau.

days_plan.itin_title: Finistère Circuit: Breton Headlands, Islands & Artists' Villages

activities.text: The Padirac Chasm opens as a shaft about thirty meters in diameter. The descent, by elevator or via a staircase of several hundred steps, leads 103 meters underground, where a boat takes you onto the subterranean river, discovered in 1889 by speleologist Édouard-Alfred Martel.
The Grand Dôme chamber, an underground cathedral, soars to nearly 90 meters high. Allow around 1.5 hours for the visit, audio guide included in several languages.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Villages of Lot and Périgord in 6 Days

visits.text: Paimboeuf was Nantes' outer port in the 17th and 18th centuries: deep-draft vessels could not sail up the river to Nantes, and it was here, 50 km from the mouth, that goods changed ships. The town numbered nearly 9,000 inhabitants on the eve of the Revolution, while Saint-Nazaire had only 700—the roles were reversed in the 19th century. Stroll the redesigned quays: the colorful facades of fishermen's houses alternate with elegant ship owners' residences with wrought-iron balconies and dormer-windowed roofs. The Chaussée Neuve lighthouse, erected in 1854, is the only lighthouse on the Loire estuary—its signal is visible more than 15 kilometers away.

Saint-Louis Church, built between 1875 and 1884, will surprise you with its neo-Byzantine style, extremely rare in the region—a dome, vaults, and Eastern arcading in a Loire town make an unforgettable sight. Inside, admire the listed high altar made from fourteen precious marbles, and the large painting by Alexis Douilard depicting La Mort de Saint-Louis à Tunis.

The Jardin Étoilé, a permanent work on the Estuaire art trail created by Japanese artist Kinya Maruyama during the 2007 biennial, sits on the banks of the Loire east of town. Inspired by the Great Bear constellation and the four cardinal points, this garden with viewing platforms and walkways offers one of the best vantage points over the estuary. Ideal for ending this road trip facing the river as it widens toward the Atlantic.

activities.text: Follow a few kilometers of the Canal de la Martinière by bike or on foot from the Carnet locks. This 15-km ship canal, built in the 19th century to link Nantes to Saint-Nazaire while bypassing the Loire's sandbanks, was a feat of hydraulic engineering for its day: 55 meters wide, over 5 meters of draft, ten years of work. During the Cold War, between 1958 and 1968, the United States had established a NATO base here to store strategic equipment—an episode that appears in no tourist guide.

days_plan.itin_title: Loire-Atlantique Road Trip: Nantes and the Côte de Jade

visits.text: Paimpol port, awarded the Port d'Intérêt Patrimonial label, was the departure point for the schooners immortalized by Pierre Loti in “An Iceland Fisherman”. Colorful houses of shipowners and privateers line the quays. The memorial to those lost at sea recalls the toll paid by Paimpol families.

Beauport Abbey, founded in 1202 by Premonstratensian canons, stands facing the bay and Bréhat archipelago. A stop on the Way of Saint James—scallop shells carved on the walls bear witness. The 120-hectare estate, owned by the Conservatoire du Littoral, contains a conservation orchard of old apple varieties.

Paimpol's historic center features cobbled streets, painting galleries, and handsome granite townhouses. Place du Martray hosts the Tuesday market—Coco de Paimpol AOC, scallops, blue lobsters, and farmhouse cider fill the stalls.

Bréhat Island, 3.5 km long and 1.5 km wide, became France's first listed natural site in 1907. There are no cars on the island. The lush southern island resembles the Mediterranean with its agapanthus, mimosas, and fig trees. The wilder northern island is covered in moorland and heather facing the open sea.

Pont ar Prad, built by Vauban in the 18th century, links the two islands that form Bréhat. From this stone bridge, the view takes in pink granite rocks, flowering gardens, and the turquoise sea. The passage between the two islands is one of Brittany's most photographed spots.

Paon lighthouse, at the island's northern tip, overlooks a spectacular granite boulder field. Jagged rocks plunge into seas churned by currents. In heavy weather, waves can reach the cliff top. The lighthouse was rebuilt after its destruction in 1944.

Bréhat's citadel, built in the 17th century, now houses the Verreries de Bréhat glassworks. Glassblowers create unique pieces inspired by the island's colors—sea blue, granite pink, garden green. You can watch glassblowing demonstrations.

Port de la Corderie was the departure point for Newfoundland fishermen. In 1508, the Bonaventure was the first vessel known in Europe to return from Newfoundland with holds full of cod—16 years after the “discovery” of the Americas. Small pink granite houses still line the quays.

activities.text: Visit Beauport Abbey. The restored buildings host contemporary art exhibitions and artist residencies. The natural estate is freely accessible, with routes through meadows, salt marshes, reed beds, and foreshore. Unobstructed views over Bréhat Island.

Hiking the GR34 along the cliffs of Plouézec and Plouha. The Plouha cliffs rise to 104 meters—the highest in Brittany. The path passes the Shelburn memorial stele, commemorating the escape of 135 Allied airmen during the Second World War. The site is about 21 km from the town for this stage, a 35-minute drive.
Oyster tasting at an oyster farm on Pointe de Kérarzic, feet in the sand facing the bay. Paimpol oysters, which have won awards several times, are briny and meaty.

Walk around Bréhat Island. Paths cross gardens where exotic plants grow—agapanthus, hydrangeas, eucalyptus—in a mild microclimate. Allow 3 to 4 hours for the complete circuit, with contemplative pauses.

Tour the archipelago by motorboat or sailboat. The 86 islets and reefs of the Bréhat archipelago reveal themselves from the water. Cormorants to the east, sea bass and sand eels to the west, seals on isolated rocks. Navigating among the markers and currents is a spectacle in itself.

days_plan.itin_title: Côtes-d'Armor Road Trip: Dinan, Pink Granite Coast, Bréhat Island & Lake Guerlédan
Côtes-d'Armor Road Trip: Dinan, Pink Granite Coast, Bréhat Island & Lake Guerlédan
Brittany Road Trip: Villages with Character, Sea and History

visits.text: Forty-five minutes west of Rennes, the Paimpont Forest begins without warning—the road narrows, the trees close in, and you're in Brocéliande. First stop: Comper Castle in Concoret, a 13th-century fortress perched on the edge of a pond where tradition holds that the fairy Viviane was raised before becoming the Lady of the Lake and raising Lancelot. The Centre de l'Imaginaire Arthurien housed within is serious and educational—a solid entry point before encountering the sites themselves. Allow 1.5 hours, €8 admission, open April through October.

The Château de Trécesson, in Campénéac, is the highlight of the day. Its reddish-purple schist walls are reflected in the moat with mirror-like precision. Built at the end of the 14th century, listed as a historic monument in 1922. What sets Trécesson apart is that its legends were published: the most famous, the Bride of Trécesson, first appeared in 1824 in the Lycée armoricain, collected from the château's caretaker. Around 1750, one autumn night, a poacher hiding in the orchard sees a carriage stop. Two gentlemen bring out a young woman in a wedding dress and bury her alive in a freshly dug pit. They are, depending on the version, her own brothers. The poacher waits for them to leave, then runs to alert the lord. The woman is dug up at dawn - she is still breathing, but dies without having said her name. Her dress, her bouquet and her crown remained on display on the chapel altar until the Revolution. Five legends in all in this single château, including the Ghost Card Players - a trial before the Parlement of Brittany really did take place over gold coins left on a table after two players vanished. The trial is documented. View from the embankment: free access all year round. Interior: July-August only, 8€.

activities.text: Lunch in Paimpont, capital of the forest. Le Relais de Brocéliande or La Forge: try kig ha farz if you want something authentic—it's Breton pot-au-feu with far cooked in a cloth bag, the winter staple of Breton peasantry and nearly impossible to find elsewhere. Expect €18-30.

Evening at the Manoir du Tertre in Paimpont if you're staying there: 16th-century manor house, €110-180 per night, with an on-site restaurant. The place has the merit of matching the journey's atmosphere—stone, woodwork, no hotel chains.

days_plan.itin_title: Brittany Road Trip: Villages with Character, Sea and History
Haunted Brittany in 6 days: From Brocéliande to the Lands of the Ankou

visits.text: The Pain de Sucre is reached by a steep but short climb from the hamlet of Le Vey, on the north bank of the Orne. The promontory overlooks Clécy and the river's meanders, with the Lande viaduct visible below from the Route des Crêtes. Bring good shoes, as the final ascent is steep.

days_plan.itin_title: Cotentin, Pays d'Auge: 5 days exploring the most beautiful villages

visits.text: The historic Palais de la Découverte is closed for renovation, with its reopening at the Grand Palais announced for March 2027. In the meantime, science experiments are presented at Les Étincelles du Palais de la Découverte in the 15th arrondissement, while some family activities take place at the Palais des enfants in the Grand Palais. Check the program and address before your visit.

activities.text: In the 8th arrondissement, walk down Avenue Montaigne to see the façades of the major fashion houses, including Dior at no. 30 and boutiques belonging to Parisian labels. A café terrace on the avenue remains one of the most classic spots in the 8th for watching Parisian life go by.

days_plan.itin_title: The Great Museums of Paris

places.name: Pantin

visits.text: The Magasins Généraux, former customs warehouses built in 1929, rise along the Ourcq canal with their concrete silhouette. Nicknamed the “cathedral of graffiti” before their conversion, they host exhibitions and cultural events.
The Grands Moulins de Pantin, a former industrial flour mill, bears witness to the town's manufacturing past. Its brick facade towers over the canal banks.
The Centre National de la Danse occupies Pantin's former administrative center. Its rehearsal studios regularly open to the public for work-in-progress presentations.
The Church of Saint-Germain, in the heart of old Pantin, retains a 13th-century bell tower and 19th-century stained glass. The forecourt opens onto the quiet lanes of the old village.
Head to Place de la Pointe, a public space designed between the harbor basin and the Magasins Généraux. Engravings on the ground recall the site's port history.

activities.text: Follow the Ourcq canal by bike or on foot from La Villette to Pantin. Along the towpath, street art murals alternate with barges hosting cultural activities and floating terraces.
The Bas-Pantin neighborhood teems with artists' studios housed in former warehouses. Visit during open-studio days to discover ceramicists, painters, and designers.
The canal banks host guinguettes and barges in summer. Settle on a waterside terrace to watch the ballet of joggers, cyclists, and pleasure boats.

days_plan.itin_title: Seine-Saint-Denis Tour: Basilica and Urban Culture

map_keywords: Centre National de la Danse Pantin

visits.text: Le Paradou is an endearing Provençal village that owes its gentleness to its network of irrigation canals — these "roubines" that wind at the foot of houses creating unexpected freshness in the heart of the Alpilles summer. A medieval village established on the Alpilles flank, it has preserved its stone wash houses, roadside oratories, and blonde limestone houses without transforming into a tourist attraction. An hour wandering its streets is enough to understand why artists and photographers prefer it to its more famous neighbors.

Le Paradou's canal network has fed olive groves and gardens on the Alpilles' south slope since the Middle Ages. A walk along these plane-tree-shaded canals, accompanied by the sound of water running over stones, is one of the most restful moments of the entire itinerary. Look particularly for the old open-air wash house where village women still came to wash clothes in the early 20th century.

activities.text: Shaded walk along the irrigation canals (about 4 km round trip, flat terrain). Marked rural paths follow the roubines between olive trees and market gardens. An authentic Provençal quality of life, without crowds.

Walking loop toward Maussane-les-Alpilles (3 km one way): a marked trail links the two villages through olive groves. The return route can take the heights for views over the Baux valley and limestone ridges. Allow 2 hours for the complete loop.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpilles, Aix-en-Provence & Arles Circuit

visits.text: The Basilica of the Sacred Heart in Paray-le-Monial is a miniature replica of the abbey church of Cluny—it's the best way to imagine what the vanished great church looked like. Built between 1090 and 1109 under Abbot Hugh of Semur (the one you encountered in Semur-en-Brionnais), it's considered a masterpiece of Cluniac Romanesque art. The play of light in the nave at sunrise alone is worth the visit.

Stop by the Musée du Hiéron, right next to the basilica. Its collection of sacred art spans from the 12th to the 20th century. Look for the white marble Romanesque tympanum from the former Abbey of Anzy-le-Duc—it's the centerpiece, one of the finest in Burgundian Romanesque art. Admission is inexpensive and the museum is rarely crowded.

The Hôtel de Ville of Paray, a former Renaissance mansion, deserves a look for its turreted facade and sculptures. Continue to the banks of the Bourbince for a shaded stroll—a lovely way to end this Burgundian road trip.

activities.text: Treat yourself to a final walk along the Bourbince and the Canal du Centre. Pleasure barges, flower-decked locks, and reflections of the basilica in the water—the loop covers 4 km, it's flat, and it's a beautiful way to conclude the journey.

If you have a bit more time, visit the Chapelle des Apparitions within the grounds of the Visitation convent. This is where Marguerite-Marie Alacoque had her visions of the Sacred Heart in the 17th century—an event that made Paray a major pilgrimage site. Even without religious conviction, the place has a particular atmosphere.

days_plan.itin_title: Saône-et-Loire Road Trip: Bibracte, Cluny, Solutré & the Mâconnais Vineyards
Burgundy's 15 Most Beautiful Villages

visits.text: Before you spot a single bird, the Marquenterre landscape surprises with its contrasts: golden dunes, pine forest, and marshes succeed one another across 200 protected hectares within the Bay of Somme nature reserve. The visitor center offers a shop and dining area to extend your visit without driving away. Binoculars available for rent on site. Families appreciate the short trail, accessible to all-terrain strollers.

activities.text: The guides at Parc du Marquenterre like to remind you that here, you observe without disturbing: binoculars are mandatory, and you must keep your distance from every bird. Open since 1973 at the heart of the Bay of Somme nature reserve, the site has recorded over 300 migratory species across its 200 hectares of dunes, forests, and marshes. About ten observation hides allow you to get close to storks and avocets along three trails, ranging from 500 meters to 6 kilometers. Reduced hours in winter; check before leaving.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Villages from Flanders to the Bay of Somme

places.name: Parc Saint Donat

visits.text: A phonograph museum in the heart of Provence is unexpected: the Musée du Phonographe et de la Musique mécanique is in parc Saint-Donat, between Sainte-Maxime and Le Muy, with more than 300 devices. Hours are limited and seasonal. Call before making the trip; it would be a shame to find it closed.

activities.text: If these machines appeal to you, ask for a demonstration at the Musée du Phonographe in parc Saint-Donat: some of the devices still work more than a century later. The museum is private and has no fixed hours. Calling ahead is not a formality; it's a condition of entry.

days_plan.itin_title: Roquebrune-sur-Argens: sea, villages and the Var in 10 days

map_keywords: Phonograph and Mechanical Music Museum Sainte-Maxime

visits.text: Oil heritage: discover the oil field found on March 25, 1954. The deposit lies between 2,000 and 2,500m deep beneath Lake Parentis-Biscarrosse. From the shores you can see the drilling installations, wellheads and derricks operated by the Canadian company Vermilion, producing a few thousand barrels a day. This activity funded the village's development.

Arènes Roland Portalier: built in 1927 and fully renovated in 2021. Typical Landes bullring architecture with wooden seating tiers. The Feria Sen Bertomiu in August draws thousands of festivalgoers for courses landaises, concerts and street bands over 5 days. Free access to view the exterior outside events.

Lake Parentis-Biscarrosse: 3,540 hectares shared with Biscarrosse, Gastes and Sainte-Eulalie. Moutéou Pipiou and Calède lake beaches with fine sand and fresh water. Picnic tables and play equipment for children. Spectacular sunsets over the oil installations create a special atmosphere. 15th-century Saint-Pierre church in the village center.

activities.text: Lake fishing: A paradise for anglers fishing for predatory fish (pike, zander, perch) and carp. Numerous designated fishing spots along the banks. Rowboats and float tubes permitted. Fishing permit required, available at the tobacco and news shop. Catch-and-release recommended to preserve fish stocks. Best months: April–May and September–October.

Lake beach swimming: Moutéou Pipiou beach (tables, play equipment for children) and Calède (wilder). Warm fresh water in summer, with a pleasant temperature higher than in the ocean. Lifeguards in July–August. Gently sloping sandy bottoms. Ideal for young children and beginner swimmers.

Water sports: Paddleboard, canoe, kayak and pedal boat rentals. The lake's calm waters are perfect for beginners. Water sports centers on the main beaches. Lessons and courses in July–August. Life jackets provided. Exploration of quiet coves and observation of lake wildlife.

Bike paths around the lake: Loops connecting Biscarrosse and neighboring villages through the forest. Flat shaded routes. Designated viewpoints over the lake and oil installations. Bike rental in the village. Bring water and a picnic for longer outings.

days_plan.itin_title: Landes Road Trip: Ocean, Pine Forest and Landes Traditions

visits.text: Start at the Trocadéro on the Right Bank. This is where you get the best straight-on view of the Eiffel Tower, especially in the morning when the light hits the ironwork head-on. The terraced gardens descend to the fountains, and the esplanade of the Palais de Chaillot frames the classic postcard panorama you've seen a thousand times.

Cross the Pont d'Iéna and head for the Eiffel Tower. Standing 330 metres including its antenna, it was built by Gustave Eiffel for the 1889 World's Fair and was originally meant to be dismantled after 20 years — it survived only because of its usefulness as a radio antenna. Book online several weeks ahead, or expect a two-hour queue. The second floor (115m) offers the best balance between views and vertigo.

Take metro line 8 to Concorde. The square covers 8.6 hectares — the largest in Paris. The Luxor Obelisk at its centre dates from the 13th century BC (the reign of Ramesses II) and was gifted by Mehemet Ali, Viceroy of Egypt, in 1830 and erected on the square in 1836. Louis XVI was guillotined here in 1793. So was Marie-Antoinette.

Walk up the Champs-Élysées to the Arc de Triomphe — 1.9 km of avenue. Napoleon commissioned the arch in 1806 after Austerlitz, but never saw it completed in 1836. There are 284 steps to the top. Under the vault, the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier and its flame, rekindled every evening at 6:30pm.

Arrive at the Louvre the moment it opens at 9am sharp. Use the Carrousel entrance (the underground passage on the Rivoli side) rather than the pyramid — the queue is shorter. The world's largest museum holds 380,000 works, with 35,000 on display across 73,000 m². Prioritise the Mona Lisa (Denon wing, 1st floor, room 711), the Venus de Milo, the Winged Victory of Samothrace, and the Napoleon III apartments.

Walk through the Tuileries Garden to Place de la Concorde — 25 hectares, created in 1564 for Catherine de' Medici, the oldest garden in Paris. The green metal chairs scattered around the central pond are one of the city's best-loved details.

At the far end of the Tuileries, step into the Orangerie for Monet's Water Lilies. Eight monumental compositions totalling 91 metres, housed in two oval rooms designed by architect Camille Lefèvre following Monet's own instructions. He offered the gift to the French state on 12 November 1918, the day after the armistice; the deed was signed on 12 April 1922, and the rooms inaugurated in May 1927, a few months after his death. The Walter-Guillaume collection downstairs features Renoir, Cézanne, Utrillo, and Soutine.

Head up towards the Palais-Royal via Rue de Rivoli. The inner courtyard contains Buren's Columns (1986) — 260 black and white marble cylinders. The rear gardens, lined with arcaded galleries of antique shops and cafés, are an unexpected haven of calm right in the city centre.

Finish at the Opéra Garnier. Completed in 1875, 11,000 m², 2,000 seats. Its Italian-style red-and-gold auditorium, ceiling painted by Chagall in 1964, and grand staircase in 30 different marbles are among the great theatrical interiors of Europe. Self-guided visit €15.

Île de la Cité — the historic cradle of Paris. Notre-Dame reopened in December 2024 after five years of post-fire restoration following the blaze of 15 April 2019. The new spire is a faithful recreation of Viollet-le-Duc's 1859 design. Entry is free; booking a time slot is not mandatory but strongly recommended on notredamedeparis.fr to avoid the queue.

Two hundred metres away, the Sainte-Chapelle. Saint Louis had it built in seven years (1242–1248) to house the Crown of Thorns. The upper chapel: 15 stained-glass windows standing 15 metres tall, depicting 1,113 biblical scenes, with 90% of the original 13th-century glass still in place. When the sun is out, the kaleidoscope effect is breathtaking. €13.

Cross to the Latin Quarter. Shakespeare & Company, the English-language bookshop opened in 1951 by George Whitman — Hemingway, Fitzgerald, and Ginsberg all slept here. Climb to the Panthéon, a former church converted into a national mausoleum in 1791: Voltaire, Rousseau, Hugo, Zola, Curie, and Joséphine Baker (2021) are all interred here. Foucault's pendulum has been demonstrating the Earth's rotation since 1851.

Descend to the Luxembourg Garden — 25 hectares, created by Marie de' Medici in 1612 on the model of the Boboli Garden in Florence. It is laid out around the Luxembourg Palace, seat of the French Senate since 1799. Children rent toy sailboats to race on the octagonal pond.

The Musée d'Orsay, a former railway station built for the 1900 World's Fair and converted into a museum in 1986. Monumental clock, 138-metre nave. The world's finest Impressionist collection: Monet, Renoir, Van Gogh, Manet, Degas, Cézanne, Gauguin. Allow at least two hours. €16, closed Mondays.

Metro to Abbesses — the deepest station within Paris proper (36 metres), surpassed since January 2025 by Villejuif-Gustave Roussy on line 14. Original Art Nouveau Guimard canopy. Walk up to the Wall of Love: 612 declarations in 311 languages on blue ceramic tiles. Then Rue Lepic, where Amélie Poulain worked at the Café des 2 Moulins (no. 15).

Climb via Rue Tholozé to the Moulin de la Galette, the last surviving original windmill of Montmartre (17th century). Renoir painted his Bal du moulin de la Galette here in 1876. Rue Girardon and Rue Norvins bring you to the Place du Tertre, the historic heart of the village.

The Sacré-Coeur basilica, completed in 1914, crowns the top of the Butte at 130 metres. Its Château-Landon limestone actually whitens in the rain. The dome (€7) offers the second-highest viewpoint in Paris — but the view from the steps in front is already exceptional. The basilica itself is free.

Descend on the north side past the Montmartre Vineyard — 2,000 vines planted on Rue des Saules in 1933, with a festive harvest in early October. Le Lapin Agile, a cabaret open since 1860 where Picasso, Modigliani, and Utrillo used to drink. The Moulin Rouge on the Boulevard de Clichy, open since 1889.

Afternoon: metro to République for the Canal Saint-Martin. 4.5 km dug by Napoleon in 1825 to supply Paris with drinking water. Iron swing bridges painted dark green, 9 working locks, pedestrianised banks at weekends. This is the Paris of bobos and intellectuals — cocktail bars, vintage shops.

Metro to Saint-Paul for the Marais, the best-preserved neighbourhood in old Paris — largely spared by Haussmann in the 19th century. The Place des Vosges, inaugurated in 1612 by Henri IV, was Paris's first royal square: 36 identical pavilions in red brick and white stone. Victor Hugo lived here for 16 years, at no. 6.

The Musée Picasso, on Rue de Thorigny, occupies the Hôtel Salé — a private mansion from 1659. Some 5,000 works by Picasso: paintings, sculptures, ceramics, engravings. The collection came to the state as a donation from his heirs in lieu of inheritance tax. €16, closed Mondays.

Lunch on Rue des Rosiers, the heart of the historic Jewish quarter. L'As du Fallafel (or Chez Hanna directly opposite) — €7–9 for a stuffed pitta. Lenny Kravitz and Scarlett Johansson both stop here whenever they're in Paris.

The Centre Pompidou closed on 22 September 2025 for a five-year renovation, with reopening scheduled for 2030. The exterior architecture remains spectacular: the Renzo Piano and Richard Rogers building (1977) with its colour-coded pipework (blue=air, yellow=electricity, green=water, red=circulation). The Place Beaubourg attracts street performers and musicians. During construction, the collections are touring via the Constellation programme (Centre Pompidou-Metz, the Grand Palais, and the Tripostal in Lille for temporary shows); a new Centre Pompidou Francilien is due to open in Massy between late 2026 and 2027.

Metro to Père-Lachaise. 44 hectares, Paris's largest cemetery, 70,000 graves since 1804. Notable tombs: Jim Morrison (division 6), Edith Piaf (97), Oscar Wilde (89, covered in lipstick kisses), Chopin (11), Molière (25), Apollinaire (86). Free map at the entrance.

The Musée Rodin, on Rue de Varenne, is housed in the Hôtel Biron (1732), where Rodin had his studio at the end of his life. In 1916 he bequeathed to the state 6,600 sculptures, 8,000 drawings, and his personal collection including works by Van Gogh and Monet. The three-hectare garden holds The Thinker, The Burghers of Calais, and The Gates of Hell. €14, closed Mondays.

Les Invalides. Commissioned by Louis XIV in 1670 to house wounded soldiers — still a functioning hospital today. The gilded dome rises to 107 metres and shelters the church of Saint-Louis and Napoleon's tomb, a sarcophagus of red porphyry placed here in 1861. The Army Museum covers 12 centuries of French military history. €15.

Metro to Bercy (line 14). Bercy Village, a 19th-century wine warehouse complex converted into a cobblestoned shopping and dining promenade in 2001. The Parc de Bercy is right next door — 14 hectares with three themed gardens, and the original railway tracks preserved in the ground.

Metro to Buttes-Chaumont (line 7bis). This 25-hectare park was inaugurated in 1867 by Napoleon III — one of the four great Haussmann parks. Built on a former gypsum quarry, it plays on the terrain with artificial cliffs, a stalactite cave, a lake with a central island topped by a Temple of the Sibyl, and a suspension bridge designed by Gustave Eiffel. Completely unlike any other park in Paris.

Walk down towards Belleville and Ménilmontant. Belleville is Paris's second-highest point after Montmartre. Street art, world cuisine (the best Asian neighbourhood in Paris on Rue de Belleville). The Cité Fleurie, with its pedestrian lanes, offers a glimpse of the Paris that escaped Haussmann.

Leave early on RER C from Saint-Michel, Musée d'Orsay, Invalides, or Champ-de-Mars. Direction: Versailles Château Rive Gauche, 40 minutes, €8 return. Book your entry slot online — the 9am–10am windows are the least crowded.

The Palace of Versailles has 2,300 rooms across 63,000 m². Louis XIV moved the court here in 1682, after 21 years of construction. Walk through the King's Grand Apartments (seven drawing rooms dedicated to the planets, ceilings by Le Brun) to the Hall of Mirrors. Seventy-three metres long, 357 mirrors opposite 17 arched windows, completed in 1684. The Treaty of Versailles was signed here on 28 June 1919.

The Queen's Apartments are as impressive as the King's. Marie-Antoinette's restored four-poster bed, the Salon des Nobles, the Antichambre du Grand Couvert where the royal family ate in public. Don't miss the Royal Chapel completed in 1710, with Corinthian columns on two levels and a vaulted ceiling painted by Antoine Coypel.

The gardens, designed by André Le Nôtre: 800 hectares in total, 93 of which are formal French gardens. Geometric parterres, hidden groves, 400 sculptures, and up to 1,400 fountains in Louis XIV's time (around 670 today, including 55 main basins). Tuesdays and weekends from April to October: the Grandes Eaux Musicales, fountains choreographed to music by Lully and Rameau. €10–12 supplement.

Walk to the Grand Trianon (20 minutes on foot) or take the small train (€8). A pink marble palace built by Mansart in 1687. The Petit Trianon was given by Louis XVI to Marie-Antoinette in 1774. Behind it, the Queen's Hamlet: a fake Norman village built in 1783 with a farm, a mill, and a dairy — Marie-Antoinette's pastoral retreat.

TER train from Paris Montparnasse to Chartres, a direct 1h–1h15, around €21 full fare (from €7 with the Rémi card). Aim to arrive around 9:30–10am to see the cathedral in the morning light — its two mismatched spires dominate the Beauce plain and are visible from 30 kilometres away.

The Notre-Dame Cathedral of Chartres, UNESCO-listed since 1979, was built almost entirely between 1194 and 1220 — a remarkable pace. Its 176 stained-glass windows from the 12th and 13th centuries cover 2,600 m², the majority original. The famous Chartres blue came from a manufacturing secret that has since been lost.

In the middle of the nave, the Labyrinth — 13 metres in diameter, 261.5 metres of path, inlaid in the floor since 1205. Pilgrims once walked it on their knees. Visible on one Friday per month outside liturgical periods.

Descend into the crypt, the third largest in Europe — 220 metres long. It houses the Veil of Our Lady, a relic gifted by Charles the Bald in 876. The Well of the Strong Saints dates from the Gallo-Roman era. Guided visit only, €3.

Head down to the lower town via Rue des Écuyers. The banks of the Eure: half-timbered houses, stone bridges, medieval washhouses, converted mills. The Maison Picassiette is worth the detour — a house covered entirely in mosaic by a visionary worker between 1938 and 1962. €6.

Direct TGV from Lille-Flandres to Paris Gare du Nord: 1 hour, €40–75. Many departures. You arrive in the heart of Paris, with the metro everywhere. If your train or flight departs in the afternoon or evening, you have the morning for one last neighbourhood. If you have an international flight during the day, allow a generous buffer — at least 2h30 before an international departure.

Saint-Germain-des-Prés, which you may not have explored at the start of the trip. The Church of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, the oldest in Paris (6th century, rebuilt in the 11th), where Descartes is buried. Café de Flore and Les Deux Magots (Boulevard Saint-Germain) — the bastions of existentialism where Sartre, Beauvoir and Camus held court. Coffee €6–8, but the atmosphere is unchanged. Rue Jacob, Rue de Buci, Rue de Seine: galleries, boutiques, covered market.

Alternative: Place Vendôme and Rue Saint-Honoré for the Paris luxury experience. The Vendôme Column (1810) erected by Napoleon from the bronze of cannon captured at Austerlitz, a copy of Trajan's Column in Rome. Classical façades by Mansart (1702). The Hôtel Ritz at no. 15 (Coco Chanel lived here for 37 years; Proust and Hemingway were regulars). Boutiques of Chanel, Dior, Cartier, Van Cleef & Arpels. Place de la Madeleine with the neo-classical Madeleine church (1842) and the luxury food shops (Fauchon, Hédiard, Maille).

A final Parisian lunch to match the occasion. Le Grand Véfour (Palais-Royal, an institution since 1784, frequented by Napoleon, Victor Hugo and Colette; chef Guy Martin — the setting is a listed monument and still sumptuous, €75–135 at lunch). Bouillon Chartier (Rue du Faubourg-Montmartre, a popular institution since 1896, dishes from €5 to €15). Or Clamato (Rue de Charonne, oyster bar and small plates, €35–55). Or the simplest and most genuine: a baguette-tradition, Paris ham, a wedge of cheese and a glass of wine on a bench in the Tuileries.

activities.text: In the evening, head back to the Eiffel Tower for the light show — every hour on the hour after dark, 20,000 LED bulbs flash for five minutes. Spread out on the Champ-de-Mars with a picnic: it's a proper Parisian ritual.

For dinner, head down rue Cler in the 7th arrondissement, a lively pedestrian market street in the evening with decent bistros. Expect to pay €25-40 for a main course and a glass of wine in a classic bistro such as Le Petit Cler.
Stop at Angelina, 226 Rue de Rivoli, for a L'Africain hot chocolate — the thickest in Paris since 1903, served with homemade whipped cream. €9. Proust and Coco Chanel were regulars.
Dinner in the Palais-Royal neighbourhood — Le Grand Colbert (a grand 1900s brasserie), Le Gabriel, or Le Soufflé, a restaurant devoted to sweet and savoury soufflés since 1961. €40–60.

For lunch, try Polidor on Rue Monsieur-le-Prince — a workers' soup kitchen open since 1845, still serving honest food at honest prices (€15–20), with checked tablecloths and numbered cloth napkins. Hemingway, Joyce, and Verlaine all ate here.

End the day on the Left Bank quays, UNESCO-listed since 1991. Between the Pont Neuf and the Pont des Arts, the bouquinistes have been setting up their 900 green boxes since the 16th century. The bridges are illuminated after dark.

In Montmartre, skip the Place du Tertre — it's a tourist trap. Head instead to Rue des Abbesses or Rue Lepic: Le Relais Gascon does a generous warm goat's cheese salad for €14; Pink Mamma is the go-to for trendy Italian.

Spend the evening by the canal Saint-Martin. Try Le Verre Volé, a cult wine bar and bistro in the 10th arrondissement, or head towards place Sainte-Marthe, an almost secret little cobbled square with a very local atmosphere.

End of the day at Place de la Bastille. The July Column commemorates those who died during the Three Glorious Days (1830), not the storming of the Bastille in 1789. Have a drink on Rue de Lappe, or on the quieter Rue de la Roquette.

Dinner in the Marais. Breizh Café for gourmet Breton crêpes (€16–22), Chez Janou for a Provençal bistrot with unlimited chocolate mousse, or Miznon on Rue des Écouffes for Israeli-style pittas. €35–50.

If you still have energy: Parc de la Villette in the 19th — 55 hectares, Paris's largest park, designed by Bernard Tschumi in 1987. Cité des Sciences, the Géode, the Philharmonie de Paris, the Zénith. Free outdoor cinema in summer.

Farewell dinner in Paris at a bistrot in the 11th or 10th. Le Chateaubriand on Rue Parmentier remains one of the best tables in the city at €75 (book a month ahead). Budget option: Bouillon Pigalle, with dishes from €4 to €15.
Lunch at La Flottille in the gardens (on the edge of the Grand Canal, €30–40). Alternative: Angelina inside the palace, or head out to the Place du Marché Notre-Dame.

Back in Paris by late afternoon. Dinner in an unexplored neighbourhood — the 9th arrondissement (South Pigalle) has been one of the city's top dining destinations for the past decade: Hôtel Amour, Buvette, Le Pantruche. €40–60.

Lunch in the old town — Le Saint-Hilaire on Rue du Pont-Saint-Hilaire at €25–35. Alternative: La Picoterie on Rue du Bourg, lunch menu at €16. Local specialities: pâté de Chartres, cochelins, mentchikoff.
April to January: Chartres en Lumières after dark — 22 sites lit up with video mapping every evening until 1am. Completely free. Otherwise, catch the TER back to Paris (last train around 10pm).

If your train or flight is in the evening: one last hour on the Pont des Arts, the Pont Neuf or the Seine quays. A final look at Notre-Dame, the Louvre, the Eiffel Tower in the distance. Thirty-seven days ago you were discovering Paris for the first time on this trip. You have made a complete loop around the hexagon. This time you look at Paris carrying everything you've been through — Loire, Alsace, Alps, Mediterranean, Atlantic, Brittany, the North. You have seen the whole of France: it will never look the same again.

Airports: Charles de Gaulle (RER B from Gare du Nord direct, 35 minutes, €12; taxi €55–65 from the centre, 45 min–1h depending on traffic), Orly (Orlyval from Antony or tram T7, 30–40 minutes, €12; taxi €40–50). Allow 3 hours before international non-Schengen flights, 2 hours for domestic or Schengen flights. Gare du Nord for the Eurostar. Gare de Lyon for the south-east, Montparnasse for the west, Austerlitz for the centre.

visits.text: Bois de Vincennes — Paris's largest green space with 995 hectares, this royal forest landscaped by Haussmann contains four lakes, a racetrack, a velodrome and the award-winning Parc Floral. Its bridle paths and bike trails offer a natural escape at the gates of Paris.

Château de Vincennes — Medieval fortress dominated by Europe's tallest keep (52 meters), this royal castle served as residence to seven kings of France before Versailles. The 14th-century Sainte-Chapelle, replica of Paris's, preserves remarkable Flamboyant Gothic stained glass.

Bercy Village — Former 19th-century wine warehouses converted into a commercial and cultural village, this pedestrian district with original cobblestones houses cinemas, restaurants and boutiques under century-old plane trees. Frank Gehry's Cinémathèque française completes the ensemble.

activities.text: Coulée Verte René-Dumont — World's first elevated linear park (1993) built on the former Bastille railway line, this 4.7 km tree-lined promenade crosses the 12th arrondissement at 10 meters height before descending to the Bois de Vincennes.

Parc Floral de Paris — This 35-hectare botanical garden in the heart of the Bois de Vincennes features over 3,000 plant species around a central pond. Its seasonal flower exhibitions and summer jazz festival make it unmissable.

Bastille Quarter — This historic crossroads where the fortress was stormed on July 14, 1789 now vibrates to the rhythm of trendy bars and clubs on rue de Lappe. Carlos Ott's Opéra Bastille and Port de l'Arsenal add a contemporary cultural touch.

days_plan.itin_title: Paris Must-Sees

visits.text: Trocadéro — This monumental esplanade facing the Eiffel Tower offers the most beautiful viewpoint on the Iron Lady from the Palais de Chaillot gardens. Its Trocadéro cascading fountains, created for the 1937 Exhibition, illuminate at dusk in a water show.

Musée Marmottan Monet — This 19th-century private mansion houses the world's largest collection of Claude Monet works, including Impression, Sunrise that gave its name to the Impressionist movement. The monumental Water Lilies and Berthe Morisot collection complete this unique ensemble.

Bois de Boulogne — Former 846-hectare royal hunting ground landscaped by Haussmann, this green lung of western Paris contains two romantic lakes, the Longchamp racecourse, the Auteuil greenhouses and the Bagatelle rose garden with 10,000 rose bushes.

activities.text: Serres d'Auteuil — This 1898 botanical garden houses five tropical greenhouses where palms, orchids and exotic plants thrive under Art Nouveau glass roofs. The Japanese garden with koi carp and century-old azaleas offers an unexpected zen break.

Musée de l'Homme — Set in the Passy wing of the Palais de Chaillot, this museum renovated in 2015 explores human evolution through 700,000 years of history. Its ethnographic and prehistoric collections coexist with reflections on our species' future.

Cité de l'Architecture — World's largest architecture center set in the Palais de Chaillot, this museum presents life-size casts of Romanesque and Gothic portals, models of radiant cities and a reconstructed Le Corbusier show apartment.

days_plan.itin_title: Paris Must-Sees

visits.text: Sacré-Cœur Basilica — Built between 1875 and 1914 in Romano-Byzantine style by Paul Abadie, this white stone basilica from Château-Landon rises to 130 meters altitude on Montmartre hill. Its 475 m² mosaic of Christ in Glory is one of the world's largest. Since 1885, perpetual prayer has been maintained day and night.

Village of Montmartre — Former wine-growing village annexed to Paris in 1860, Montmartre has preserved its cobbled lanes, secret stairways and bohemian atmosphere. Picasso, Van Gogh and Toulouse-Lautrec lived there, immortalizing its windmills and cabarets in their works.

Place du Tertre — Artistic heart of Montmartre since the 19th century, this cobbled square gathers painters and portrait artists under umbrellas. Despite tourist crowds, it retains the charm of Belle Époque studios where Utrillo painted white facades.

Montmartre Vineyards — Last wine-growing vestige of Paris planted in 1933 on 1,556 m², this vineyard produces about 500 bottles of Clos Montmartre each year during festive October harvest. A reminder of the wine-growing tradition that once covered the entire hill.

activities.text: Moulin Rouge — Founded in 1889, this legendary cabaret with its red sails saw the birth of the French cancan and hosted Toulouse-Lautrec, who immortalized its dancers. Its feathered revues perpetuate the tradition of Parisian music hall in Pigalle.

Fondation Louis Vuitton — Glass vessel conceived by Frank Gehry and inaugurated in 2014 in the heart of the Bois de Boulogne, this contemporary art museum unfolds twelve translucent sails over 46 meters high. Its terraces offer panoramic views of La Défense and Paris.

Palais de Tokyo — Europe's largest contemporary art center with 22,000 m², this 1937 Art Deco palace programs bold exhibitions and performances until midnight. Its Monsieur Bleu restaurant facing the Eiffel Tower attracts creative Paris.

days_plan.itin_title: Paris Must-Sees

visits.text: Louvre Museum — Former medieval fortress that became a royal palace then museum in 1793, the Louvre houses over 35,000 works across 60,600 m². The glass pyramid designed by I.M. Pei in 1989 marks the entrance to this temple of art where the Mona Lisa by Leonardo da Vinci, the Venus de Milo and the Winged Victory of Samothrace reign.

Tuileries Garden — Created by Catherine de' Medici in 1564 then redesigned by Le Nôtre in 1664, this French formal garden extends over 23 hectares between the Louvre and Place de la Concorde. Sculptures by Maillol and Rodin punctuate the paths lined with century-old chestnut trees.

Place Vendôme — Jewel of elegance designed by Hardouin-Mansart in 1699, this octagonal square with classical facades houses the world's greatest jewelers. The central column, cast from bronze of 1,200 cannons captured at Austerlitz, rises to 44 meters.

activities.text: Palais Royal — Pass through the arcades to discover Buren's columns in the courtyard of honor and the secret gardens surrounded by galleries where antique dealers and fashion boutiques line up. This haven of peace was the theater of the beginnings of the French Revolution.

Comédie-Française — Founded in 1680 by Louis XIV, the world's oldest theater company perpetuates French dramatic art. Admire the neoclassical facade of the Salle Richelieu where Molière performed his final shows.

Rue de Rivoli Arcades — Stroll under the 2.5 km of Napoleonic arcades lined with shops and cafés. This monumental perspective offers protection from the weather while revealing the uniform facades desired by Percier and Fontaine.

days_plan.itin_title: Paris Must-Sees

visits.text: Père-Lachaise Cemetery — Paris's largest necropolis at 44 hectares established in 1804, this garden cemetery with romantic paths houses the graves of Jim Morrison, Édith Piaf, Oscar Wilde, Chopin and Molière. Its neo-Gothic chapels and Art Nouveau mausoleums make it an open-air museum.

Parc de Belleville — This 4.5-hectare park, laid out in 1988 on the Belleville hill (108 metres), offers an outstanding panorama over the capital from its belvedere terrace. Its waterfalls, playground and Maison de l'Air make it a much-loved green space.

Ménilmontant Quarter — This working-class village absorbed by Paris in 1860 preserves its secret passages, artists' studios and authentic bistros. The walls covered in street art and the guinguettes of Parc des Buttes perpetuate its roguish and creative spirit.

activities.text: Rue Oberkampf — Trendy artery of eastern Paris, this street with colorful facades lines up cocktail bars, world cuisine restaurants and concert venues. In the evening, its giant terrace invades the sidewalks for a festive and cosmopolitan atmosphere.

Street Art in Belleville — The streets of Belleville form an open-air gallery where the greatest names in world street art express themselves. Rue Dénoyez with entirely covered walls and murals on Boulevard de Belleville constantly renew this free urban museum.

Place Gambetta and 20th arrondissement town hall — This working-class neighborhood with village charm is organized around Place Gambetta and its Second Empire town hall. The Belleville market, one of Paris's largest and cheapest, animates its streets on Tuesdays and Fridays.

days_plan.itin_title: Paris Must-Sees

visits.text: Notre-Dame Cathedral — Masterpiece of French Gothic built between 1163 and 1345, the cathedral reopened its doors in December 2024 after five years of restoration following the 2019 fire. Its 12,000 oak timbers of the new framework, its spire rebuilt identical to Viollet-le-Duc's and its restored 13th-century rose windows once again dazzle visitors.

Île de la Cité — Historical cradle of Paris where the Parisii settled in the 3rd century BC, this island houses the vestiges of royal and religious power. Stroll along the Quai des Orfèvres immortalized by Simenon and discover the century-old flower market.

Sainte-Chapelle — Jewel of Rayonnant Gothic erected in just seven years (1241-1248) by Saint Louis to house the Crown of Thorns. Its 1,113 m² of 13th-century stained glass, among the oldest in Paris, diffuse celestial light depicting 1,113 biblical scenes.

activities.text: Place des Vosges — Paris's oldest square inaugurated in 1612, this perfect 140-meter square charms with its red brick and blonde stone pavilions. Victor Hugo lived there for six years at No. 6, now a free museum dedicated to the writer.

The Marais — Wander the narrow streets of the 4th arrondissement, among private mansions, cobbled courtyards and old façades. Galleries, shops and cafés bring life to this quarter a short walk from the Place des Vosges.

Musée d'Orsay — Former train station transformed into a temple of Impressionism, the museum displays masterpieces by Monet, Renoir, Van Gogh and Cézanne under a monumental glass roof. The great clock offers a unique view of Montmartre.

days_plan.itin_title: Paris Must-Sees

visits.text: Latin Quarter — Paris's intellectual heart since the Sorbonne's founding in 1257, this neighborhood owes its name to Latin spoken by medieval students. Its cobbled lanes lined with bookshops, art cinemas and bistros perpetuate the bohemian and rebellious spirit of May '68.

Panthéon — Commissioned by Louis XV in 1744 as Sainte-Geneviève church then transformed into a republican mausoleum in 1791, this neoclassical temple by Soufflot houses the remains of Victor Hugo, Voltaire, Rousseau, Marie Curie, Jean Moulin and Simone Veil. Foucault's pendulum demonstrated Earth's rotation there in 1851.

La Sorbonne — Founded in 1257 by Robert de Sorbon to train theologians, this legendary university rebuilt under the Third Republic preserves its 17th-century chapel where Cardinal Richelieu rests. Its amphitheaters have seen the greatest thinkers pass through.

Luxembourg Gardens — Created by Marie de' Medici in 1612 to accompany her Florentine palace, this 25-hectare garden blends French and English styles. Its iconic metal chairs, pond where small sailboats glide and statues of French queens make it Parisians' favorite green lung.

activities.text: Latin Quarter Bookshops — Explore the legendary Shakespeare and Company facing Notre-Dame, Gibert Joseph and its seven floors, or the bouquinistes along the Seine quays listed as UNESCO heritage. These temples of books perpetuate the neighborhood's literary tradition.

Boulevard Saint-Germain — This 3 km Haussmannian artery crosses the intellectual heart of the Left Bank where Sartre and Beauvoir philosophized at Café de Flore and Deux Magots. Antique dealers, galleries and publishing houses perpetuate this cultural heritage.

Théâtre de l'Odéon — Opened in 1782, this neoclassical Italian-style auditorium hosted the first performances of Beaumarchais's The Marriage of Figaro. Now the Théâtre de l'Europe, it programmes contemporary creations alongside great classics.

days_plan.itin_title: Paris Must-Sees

visits.text: Saint-Germain-des-Prés — Paris's oldest church founded in 543 by Childebert I, this neighborhood was the heart of postwar existentialism. Jazz cellars, art galleries and antique dealers perpetuate the bohemian atmosphere dear to Boris Vian and Juliette Gréco.

Saint-Sulpice Church — Paris's second-largest church after Notre-Dame, this 17th-century monument impresses with its asymmetrical facade and two unfinished towers. Its astronomical gnomon and Delacroix frescoes in the Chapel of the Holy Angels fascinate visitors.

Historic Cafés — Café de Flore and Les Deux Magots face each other on Boulevard Saint-Germain, witnesses to 20th-century intellectual ferment. Their heated terraces under red umbrellas perpetuate the tradition of the Parisian philosophical café.

activities.text: Canal Saint-Martin — This romantic 4.5 km canal dug under Napoleon I crosses northeast Paris through nine locks and two swing bridges. Its tree-lined banks, immortalized in the film Amélie, attract picnickers and pétanque players.

Parc des Buttes-Chaumont — This 25-hectare park landscaped by Haussmann in 1867 on former gypsum quarries offers Paris's unique steep terrain. Its Temple of the Sibyl perched on a 50-meter rock dominates the lake and artificial waterfalls.

Montmartre Cemetery — Third-largest Parisian necropolis, this romantic cemetery with shaded paths houses the graves of Dalida, François Truffaut, Edgar Degas and Émile Zola. A peaceful haven overlooked by the Caulaincourt Bridge.

days_plan.itin_title: Paris Must-Sees

visits.text: Eiffel Tower — Built in 2 years, 2 months and 5 days by Gustave Eiffel for the 1889 Universal Exhibition, this 330-meter, 7,300-ton "Iron Lady" of puddled steel assembled by 2.5 million rivets was meant to be dismantled after 20 years. Saved by its usefulness for wireless telegraphy, it now welcomes nearly 7 million visitors per year.

Champ-de-Mars — This 780-meter esplanade extends from the Eiffel Tower to the Military School where Bonaparte studied. Former parade ground, this English-style garden hosted five Universal Exhibitions and remains the preferred spot for Parisian picnics facing the Iron Lady.

Hôtel des Invalides — Commissioned by Louis XIV in 1670 to house wounded soldiers, this masterpiece by Libéral Bruant then Hardouin-Mansart houses under its 107-meter golden dome Napoleon I's tomb, in six nested coffins of red quartzite.

activities.text: Musée Rodin — Set in the 18th-century Hôtel Biron where the artist lived, this museum presents The Thinker, The Kiss and The Burghers of Calais in a verdant setting. The sculpture garden is among Paris's most romantic.

Musée du Quai Branly — Designed by Jean Nouvel and inaugurated in 2006, this museum of indigenous arts houses 300,000 objects from Africa, Asia, Oceania and the Americas. Its 800 m² plant wall signed by Patrick Blanc makes it a unique vertical garden.

Place de la Concorde — Paris's largest square where Louis XVI was guillotined in 1793, it displays the Luxor obelisk offered by Egypt in 1836. Its monumental fountains and eight statues representing great French cities frame a unique perspective toward the Champs-Élysées.

days_plan.itin_title: Paris Must-Sees

visits.text: Avenue des Champs-Élysées — Nicknamed "the most beautiful avenue in the world," this 1.9 km artery connecting Concorde to the Arc de Triomphe was laid out by Le Nôtre in 1667. Its wide sidewalks planted with chestnut trees host July 14th military parades and the Tour de France finish.

Arc de Triomphe — Commissioned by Napoleon in 1806, this 50-meter-high monument celebrates the victories of the Grande Armée. The flame of the Unknown Soldier has burned there since 1923, rekindled each evening at 6:30 pm. The panoramic terrace offers a 360° view of the twelve radiating avenues.

Grand Palais — Built for the 1900 Universal Exhibition, this Beaux-Arts palace features Europe's largest glass roof covering 13,500 m². Its 45-meter-high nave hosts major international exhibitions and fashion shows from the great houses.

Petit Palais — Harmonious counterpart to the Grand Palais, this City of Paris Fine Arts Museum presents collections from Antiquity to 1914 for free. Its peristyle inner garden, inspired by Pompeii, offers an unexpected bucolic break.

activities.text: Église de la Madeleine — Neoclassical temple surrounded by 52 Corinthian columns 20 meters high, this church without bell tower or cross was desired by Napoleon as a temple to the glory of the Grande Armée. Its richly decorated interior hosts concerts and prestigious ceremonies.

Musée de Cluny — Set in a 15th-century medieval mansion and 3rd-century Gallo-Roman baths, this National Museum of the Middle Ages preserves the famous Lady and the Unicorn tapestry, six 15th-century Flemish tapestries illustrating the five senses and a mysterious sixth.

Arènes de Lutèce — Vestige of the 1st-century Gallo-Roman amphitheater that could hold 15,000 spectators, these arenas rediscovered in 1869 during Haussmann's works now form a peaceful square where Parisians play boules.

days_plan.itin_title: Paris Must-Sees

places.name: Parthenay

visits.text: The Saint-Jacques Gate is the symbol of Parthenay. Built in the early 13th century at the town’s northern entrance, it opens onto the Plantagenet Way leading to Santiago de Compostela—the route taken by pilgrims from the British Isles and Mont Saint-Michel. Its vaulted passage, defended by a portcullis and a murder hole, is flanked by two massive elliptical towers and approached by a fortified bridge over the Thouet. Reinforced in the 14th and 16th centuries, it was fitted with a gunport as early as the 16th century. From the tower, the view of the Saint-Paul neighborhood below and the river is worth the modest effort of climbing the stairs.

Rue de la Vau Saint-Jacques extends for 334 meters. The town’s main thoroughfare in the Middle Ages, it owes its name to its location at the bottom of a well-sheltered valley. More than a hundred 15th-century half-timbered houses survive here. Some facades still show traces of the textile crafts that brought Parthenay wealth through trade reaching as far as England and Flanders. A neighborhood of weavers, innkeepers, and money changers, Vau Saint-Jacques bustled with life when pilgrims stopped here.

Don’t miss the Romanesque portal of Notre-Dame-de-la-Couldre church, the former castle chapel dismantled during the Wars of Religion. This surviving portal, with sculptures depicting the Announcement to Zechariah and various animal motifs, is a fine example of Poitou’s Romanesque art. Take the opportunity to continue to the ruins of the 11th-century lord’s castle. It had a triangular layout, and granite defensive elements survive in the ramparts that line the citadel.

The Georges Turpin Museum in the Maison des Cultures traces the town’s history from the Middle Ages to the 20th century, with archaeological collections of coins and carved stonework, Parthenay faience from the late 19th century, and an educational area devoted to the pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostela.

activities.text: Follow the path along the ramparts from the citadel to La Prée. On the flood meadow side, the circular towers are reflected in the Thouet, and goats sometimes graze at the foot of the walls. Allow 45 minutes for this walk around the outside.

Cross the bridge at the Saint-Jacques Gate toward the end of the day to admire the reflection of the fortifications in the calm waters of the Thouet. The evening light on the elliptical towers and the old bridge is particularly beautiful.

days_plan.itin_title: Deux-Sèvres Tour: Marais Poitevin and Romanesque Heritage

map_keywords: Rue de la Vau Saint-Jacques Parthenay

visits.text: Pau Castle is the most visited monument in Bearn — around 100,000 visitors a year. Its 33-metre brick tower was built by Gaston Fébus in the 14th century. This is where Henry IV was born on 13 December 1553, a fact attested by an 18th-century inscription. At his birth, his grandfather rubbed his lips with a clove of garlic and had him breathe in Jurançon wine — a Bearnese custom. He was then placed in a giant tortoise shell, his legendary cradle, kept ever since in the king's chamber. That shell remains the national museum's most emblematic object. The visit is by guided tour only and lasts about an hour.

The boulevard des Pyrénées unrolls 1,800 metres of panoramic promenade, created gradually between 1893 and 1899.
