On clear days — winter and spring are the best seasons — the Pyrenean chain unfolds from the Pic du Midi d'Ossau to the Pic d'Anie, and the Spanish Pyrenees can be made out on the horizon. It is one of the most spectacular urban panoramas in France.

The Museum of Fine Arts presents a European collection from the 15th to the 20th century: El Greco, Rubens, Degas share space with regional painters. Plan 1.5 hours to tour it completely. The building itself, from the 19th century, is an example of classical museum architecture.

activities.text: Take the Pau funicular, put into service in 1908 and free from the start. In a few minutes it links the railway station to the boulevard des Pyrénées at the level of the place Royale. A century-old technical curiosity that remains the pleasantest way to get up to the town centre from the station.

Beaumont Park spreads its 11 hectares in the heart of the town. Century-old sequoias, a rose garden, a lake and a bandstand adorn this 19th-century English-style garden. The Jurançon hillsides are 10 minutes away by car: the vineyards produce two very different AOC wines — a dry wine with character and a sweet moelleux renowned ever since Henry IV was baptised with it.

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip Pyrenees-Atlantiques: Basque Country and Bearn

visits.text: Pauillac is the capital of the Médoc wine country, known worldwide for its 18 classified growths. The village stretches along the Gironde estuary over 1.3 km of quays lined with 18th- and 19th-century townhouses. The Pauillac appellation holds 3 of the 5 first growths classified in 1855: Château Lafite Rothschild, Château Latour and Château Mouton Rothschild. The vineyard covers around 1,200 hectares, tended like formal French gardens.

The Maison du Tourisme et du Vin de Pauillac is the ideal starting point for discovering the vineyards. You'll find a selection of wines from the 8 Médoc appellations sold on consignment at estate prices, advice for organizing château visits, and tourist information. The team can book visits to wine estates for you. A shop offers wine accessories and local products.

Saint-Martin Church in Pauillac, built in the 19th century on the site of a former church, overlooks the waterfront. Its neo-Gothic architecture contrasts with the classical quayside façades. The interior is simple yet bright. The forecourt offers lovely estuary and marina views. The weekly market takes place in the adjacent square every Saturday morning.

Pauillac marina welcomes boats passing through the estuary. The landscaped quays are pleasant for strolling with views over the Gironde. On clear days, you can see the right bank and the Blaye vineyard. Several restaurants and cafés line the waterfront. It's a peaceful spot to pause while watching the movement of boats and tides.

activities.text: Visit a Médoc wine château. Prestigious properties and more accessible estates alike offer guided tours of their facilities. You'll discover the vines, the cellars where wines age, and the property's history. The final tasting helps you understand the Médoc wine style, marked by Cabernet Sauvignon. Reservations required, often several weeks in advance for classified grands crus.

The Médoc Château Route (D2) crosses the prestigious appellations of Margaux, Saint-Julien, Pauillac, and Saint-Estèphe. This 60-kilometer route between Bordeaux and Pointe de Grave runs along the estuary passing dozens of wine châteaux. Landscapes of meticulously aligned vines and varied château architecture make this route unmissable. Plan a full day to enjoy the journey with some estate visits.

A hike around Pauillac's châteaux. Two marked walking loops of 8 and 14 km let you discover the Pauillac AOC wine estates on foot. The circuit crosses vineyards between prestigious châteaux and offers beautiful estuary views. It's a pleasant, active way to discover the terroir. The route is flat, accessible to all. Maps available at the Maison du Tourisme.

Boat tour on the Gironde estuary. Several companies offer cruises departing from Pauillac to discover the estuary, Europe's largest (75 km long). You'll pass vine-planted banks, glimpse islands and port facilities. Some cruises include guided commentary on river heritage and Médoc wine tasting. Duration typically 2 to 3 hours.

Tasting and lunch at a wine estate. Several Médoc estates offer gastronomic experiences combining cellar visits, guided tastings, and lunch with food and wine pairings. Dishes highlight local products: Pauillac lamb, garden vegetables, regional cheeses. It's a convivial way to deepen your wine knowledge while enjoying the exceptional château setting.

days_plan.itin_title: Gironde Circuit: Bordeaux, Vineyards & Arcachon Bay
Bordeaux in 7 Days: Médoc, Saint-Émilion, and Sauternes

places.name: Peau De Meau

visits.text: A desert of pebbles in Provence is disorienting: the Peau de Meau trail crosses the coussoul, a semi-arid steppe grazed by sheep since the Neolithic, in the Coussouls de Crau nature reserve. 4.7 km, fifteen information panels, an observatory. No dogs; staying on the trail is compulsory.

The sheepfold and its observatory, halfway along the Peau de Meau trail, provide the only hide on the circuit. The Crau remains the main area for transhumant sheep farming in Lower Provence, grazed mainly in winter and spring before the sheep leave for the Alps. Stay on the marked trail.

activities.text: Bring binoculars and two liters of water for the sentier de Peau de Meau: pin-tailed sandgrouse, lesser kestrels and little bustards can be seen here. No shade along the trail, and the mistral blows frequently. Early morning is best.

days_plan.itin_title: Côte Bleue and Camargue: the lower coastal route in 7 days

map_keywords: Sentier de Peau de Meau Saint-Martin-de-Crau
Réserve naturelle des Coussouls de Crau

places.name: Penne D Agenais

visits.text: Penne-d'Agenais is one of the most strikingly perched medieval strongholds in Lot-et-Garonne. From below, you can spot the gleaming zinc dome of the Basilica of Notre-Dame de Peyragude from afar. Park at the bottom and walk up through the cobbled lanes — it is the best way to discover the village layer by layer. The first stone of the Romano-Byzantine basilica was laid on 14 May 1897, but it was not completed until 1948. Inside, 47 stained-glass windows created between 1946 and 1956 by master glassmaker Jacques Leuzy depict the life of Mary. Behind the building, a grotto houses the original church where the Virgin has been venerated since the year one thousand — according to legend, a Marian apparition in 1562 called for it to be rebuilt after its destruction by the Protestants.

The basilica's summit offers a breathtaking panorama over two valleys: the Lot to the north and the Boudouyssou to the south. Sunset from the terrace ranks among the department's most spectacular. Plan to be there late afternoon.

On the way down, pass through the Porte de Richard, one of the village’s surviving fortified gateways and a remnant of the defensive network that made Penne ‘the key to the Duchy of Guyenne’, as the English called it in the Middle Ages. Richard the Lionheart, son of Eleanor of Aquitaine, built a powerful fortress here in the 12th century because of the site’s strategic position above the Lot.

On Place Aliénor d'Aquitaine and Mercadiel Square—the old medieval market square—admire restored half-timbered houses and white-stone façades characteristic of Agenais. Art galleries and artisan studios lining the steep lanes make Penne an active village, not merely a setting.

activities.text: Walk down to the Port de Penne on the banks of the Lot. The site has yielded Azilian remains, the Azilian being a Mesolithic culture dating from around 10,000 years before our era. Today, boaters moor here in complete tranquillity. The contrast between the stronghold perched above and this quiet port below is striking.

Penne-d’Agenais holds its market on Sunday mornings in a friendly atmosphere. A few local producers sell cheeses, jams, preserves and locally grown vegetables. It is small but authentic, with no mass tourism.

Penne-d'Agenais lies on the Santiago de Compostela route. Local operators offer boat trips on the Lot from the port—hour-long or half-day cruises to explore the river's meanders between cliffs and orchards.

days_plan.itin_title: Lot-et-Garonne Road Trip: Bastides and Villages

map_keywords: Basilica of Notre-Dame de Peyragude, Penne-d'Agenais

visits.text: Saint-Front Cathedral rises above Périgueux with five Byzantine domes—an architectural anomaly in France that looks more at home in Constantinople than the Dordogne. Designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1998 as part of the Santiago de Compostela pilgrimage routes, it became the blueprint for Paris's Sacré-Cœur when architect Paul Abadie sought inspiration. Victor Hugo famously dubbed it 'the great mosque of Périgueux.' Guided tours take you onto the rooftops for sweeping views across the medieval city.

The Vesunna Museum encloses the ruins of a grand Gallo-Roman villa (1st-3rd century AD) beneath a striking structure designed by Jean Nouvel. The collection showcases murals, jewelry, and ceramics from the Petrocorii, the Gallic tribe who once ruled this territory. Adjacent stands the Vesunna Tower—a 27-meter remnant of a 2nd-century temple that once dominated the Roman cityscape.

Périgueux's medieval quarter is an architectural treasure trove: 65 protected monuments packed into narrow, winding streets. Half-timbered houses lean over cobblestones, Renaissance townhouses display ornate stonework, and shaded squares invite lingering. The Maison des Dames de la Foi and its Renaissance staircases speak to the wealth that flowed through this city during the Middle Ages.

activities.text: Périgueux market erupts into life at Place du Coderc every Wednesday and Saturday morning. The stalls overflow with foie gras, seasonal truffles, tangy goat cheeses, and Périgord walnuts. This is one of the region's largest and most authentic markets—a sensory immersion into Périgord's culinary soul.

The restaurants around the Saint-Front quarter serve the robust classics of Périgord cuisine: foie gras seared to golden perfection, duck confit with crispy Sarladaise potatoes, earthy porcini omelets. Périgord cooking is unabashedly rich—a cuisine that rewards the hungry.

days_plan.itin_title: Dordogne: Prehistoric Caves, Medieval Fortresses & Périgord Delights

places.name: Peronne

visits.text: The Historial de la Grande Guerre brings together the perspectives of the belligerents within the 13th-century castle. Over 70,000 items, including Otto Dix's engravings, tell the story of the Battle of the Somme.
The Thiepval museum presents a 60-meter panorama drawn by Joe Sacco depicting the first day of the battle, July 1, 1916. Approximately 27 km from Péronne, a 35-minute drive.

activities.text: The Thiepval memorial, a 45-meter triumphal arch inaugurated in 1932, bears the engraved names of 72 000 missing British soldiers. Approximately 27 km from Péronne, a 35-minute drive.
Explore the battlefields where over one million people fell between July and November 1916.

days_plan.itin_title: Somme Road Trip: Bay of Somme and War Remembrance

map_keywords: Historial of the Great War Péronne

visits.text: Pérouges, Ain's only village with the Plus Beaux Villages de France designation, unfolds its streets paved with rounded pebbles like an intact film set. Perched on its tuff spur, the fortified medieval town has survived the centuries without losing the spirit of a 15th-century weavers' village. Eighty historic monuments bear witness to this exceptional heritage in a town where the powerful Dukes of Savoy once lived.

The fortified church of Sainte-Marie-Madeleine stands like a stone bastion, unique in the entire department. Built in the 15th century, it combines defensive and spiritual functions in an unusual architectural design. Its thick walls and Gothic vaults have withstood the Wars of Religion and the ravages of time, protecting villagers who took refuge within.

The Maison des Princes, a splendid 14th-century residence, accommodated the Counts of Savoy during their stays. Now home to the Musée du Vieux Pérouges, it preserves period furniture, weavers' tools and everyday medieval objects. The medieval garden, or hortulus, grows aromatic and medicinal plants according to ancestral traditions. Climb the watchtower for sweeping views over the stone-slab roofs, the Dombes plateau and the Ain plain.

Place du Tilleul, also known as Place de la Halle, is dominated by the liberty lime tree, planted in 1792. Half-timbered houses with projecting upper storeys create a coherent architectural ensemble, miraculously preserved. Behind these façades, eighty permanent residents still live: craftspeople and designers who uphold the spirit of the village.

activities.text: Taste Pérouges' famous galette au sucre, a speciality created in 1912 by Marie-Louise Thibaut. This lemon-flavoured yeast dough, topped with butter and sugar cream, crunches between your teeth in the village inns. A registered trademark and local culinary emblem, it is equally suited to breakfast, dessert or an afternoon snack.

Explore the artisan workshops housed in medieval shops. Potters, ceramicists, fine bookbinders and master glassmakers preserve traditional skills in this exceptional setting. Each workshop tells a story of skills passed down and a passion for the artistic crafts that keep this village alive throughout the year.

Join a guided tour of the medieval town to discover its fortified gateways, cobbled lanes and historic houses. The tour recounts the history of this former stronghold and explains how the village was organised during the Middle Ages. Check with the tourist office for tour dates and times.

Discover the Rose de Pérouges, a variety created especially for the medieval town. Its fuchsia and garnet flowers bloom from May until the first frosts. This unscented rose adorns the lanes and gardens of the fortified village.

days_plan.itin_title: Loop Around Lyon: Villages and Pierres Dorées
Grand Tour Ain & Savoie Mont-Blanc: Lakes, Mountains and Heritage
Eastern France by Train from Paris
Road Trip from Bresse to Bugey via Beaujolais and Lyon

places.name: Perpignan

visits.text: Built in 1274 by James II, the Palace of the Kings of Majorca commands the city from its promontory. Its southern Gothic architecture is arranged around a central courtyard, with two chapels, one above the other, featuring pink and white marble archivolts.
The Castillet's tower of red brick and golden stone has stood since 1368. This former city gate houses a Catalan museum and offers panoramic views over Perpignan's rooftops and the Pyrenees.
The Cathedral of Saint John the Baptist blends Romanesque and Catalan Gothic styles. Its 80-meter single nave houses the Dévot Christ, a 14th-century crucifix carried during Easter processions.
The Campo Santo stands as one of France's largest medieval cloister-cemeteries. Its 13th-century arcades still bear sculpted coats of arms and Gothic interlacing.
The Hyacinthe Rigaud Museum occupies two renovated townhouses. Its collections span five centuries, from Catalan Gothic art to Rigaud's portraits, with works by Picasso, Maillol, and Dufy.

activities.text: Stroll through Place de la République, Perpignan's beating heart. Café terraces come alive from morning onward around the central fountain.
Climb to the top of the Palace of the Kings of Majorca for the panorama. The view sweeps across the city, vineyards, and snow-capped Canigou.
The market on Place de la République displays fruit, vegetables and Catalan specialties. A local atmosphere is guaranteed from 7 a.m.

days_plan.itin_title: Pyrénées-Orientales Road Trip: French Catalonia and the Côte Vermeille

map_keywords: Palais des Rois de Majorque Perpignan

visits.text: Ploumanac'h's granite boulder field defies the laws of balance. Enormous blocks of pink granite, sculpted by wind and sea over millennia, compose a landscape unique in the world. The copper color comes from iron oxide impurities in the crystal lattice. Voted Village Préféré des Français in 2015.

Mean Ruz lighthouse ('red stone' in Breton), emblem of the Pink Granite Coast, has watched over sailors since 1860. The current lighthouse, in pink granite, replaced one destroyed by bombing in 1944. Depending on the sun's angle, the building and rocks change color—a living masterpiece.

Saint-Guirec beach, nestled among granite boulder fields, shelters an oratory dedicated to its namesake saint. According to tradition, young women would stick a pin in the granite statue's nose to find a husband within the year. Château de Costaérès stands silhouetted on its islet in the background.

The Maison du Littoral, near the lighthouse, explains the Pink Granite Coast's geology and the Conservatoire du Littoral's role in protecting the site. Exhibitions on granite formation, coastal flora and fauna.

Trestraou beach, Perros-Guirec's large fine-sand beach, faces the Sept-Îles archipelago. Lined with seaside villas from the late 19th and early 20th centuries, it blends a family atmosphere with Belle Époque architecture.

Trestrignel beach, more intimate than Trestraou, is bordered by cliffs and seaside villas. Its clear waters attract kayakers and swimmers. From Pointe du Sphinx, the panorama extends over the Sept-Îles archipelago.

Perros-Guirec port, on Quai de la Douane, is the departure point for excursions to Sept-Îles and Bréhat Island. Fishing boats and sailboats mingle here. On Wednesdays, the La Rade market sets up facing the sea.

The Renote peninsula in Trégastel, connected by a causeway since 1885, is classified as one of France's scenic sites. The path circles the island between jumbles of pink granite, sandy coves and sweeping views of the Sept-Îles archipelago. The loop takes just under an hour.

Trégastel's Marine Aquarium is built beneath a mound of pink granite boulders. Natural caves shelter tanks populated by fish, crustaceans, and anemones from the Breton coast. A setting unique in the world for an aquarium—granite blocks serve as tank walls.
The Grève Blanche in Trégastel, a fine sandy beach framed by pink rocks, offers swimming in clear waters with views of the Sept-Îles.

activities.text: Hike the coastal path from Trestraou to Ploumanac'h. The GR34 winds among pink granite boulder fields for 4 km, each turn revealing a new scene. Allow 2 hours for the loop, more if you take time for photos—and you will.

Motorboat excursion to the Sept-Îles archipelago, France's largest bird sanctuary. Protected since 1912, classified as a National Nature Reserve in 1976, the archipelago shelters France's only northern gannet colony, Atlantic puffins, and about forty gray seals. Departures from Trestraou beach.

Exploration of the Traouïéro Valley, between Ploumanac'h and Trégastel. Two deep valleys where the Kérougant stream winds beneath a canopy of oaks and giant ferns. Caves, granite boulder fields, and korrigan legends—a shady refuge ideal for summer.

Sea kayaking on the Pink Granite Coast. Paddle among the granite boulder fields to immerse yourself in the scenery at water level. The rocks take on even more surprising shapes when viewed from the sea. Guided outings suitable for beginners.

Walk around the Renote peninsula. The coastal path winds among granite boulder fields, pebble beaches, and hidden coves. The island is the Pink Granite Coast in miniature—perfect for those wanting to extend the magic of Ploumanac'h.
Seafood tasting at Perros-Guirec port. Terraces facing the boats serve oysters, lobsters, and scallops in season. A glass of Muscadet accompanies it all.

days_plan.itin_title: Côtes-d'Armor Road Trip: Dinan, Pink Granite Coast, Bréhat Island & Lake Guerlédan
Côtes-d'Armor Road Trip: Dinan, Pink Granite Coast, Bréhat Island & Lake Guerlédan
Brittany 7 days: Pink Granite, Lighthouses & Peninsulas

visits.text: Perched above the Ognon, the Château de Pesmes dates partly from the 10th century and dominates the valley from its promontory. Partially in ruins, it can't be visited but remains visible from the ramparts. The village preserves several buildings listed as historic monuments.

activities.text: Stroll along the banks of the Ognon before climbing back up to the church of Saint-Hilaire, which preserves a painted 17th-century triptych. In summer, canoeing and kayaking offer a way to discover the village from the river.

days_plan.itin_title: Burgundy-Franche-Comté: The Most Beautiful Villages in 7 days

places.name: Petit Palais

visits.text: The Petit Palais, built by Charles Girault for the 1900 Universal Exposition, houses the City of Paris's Museum of Fine Arts—and permanent admission is free. The architecture itself is worth the visit: a trapezoidal plan around an interior garden with colonnades, a central rotunda crowned by a dome, mosaics and Belle Époque murals. The collections span 5,000 years of history: Greek and Egyptian antiquities, medieval enamels, paintings by Courbet, Monet, and Cézanne, sculptures by Carpeaux. Allow 90 minutes at your own pace—the rooms are rarely crowded.

activities.text: The Petit Palais faces the Grand Palais—the two buildings connected by Avenue Winston Churchill form a cohesive architectural ensemble from the 1900 era. Stroll between the two to observe their façades: the allegorical sculptures, glass canopies, and friezes from the period testify to the decorative ambition of the Third Republic.

days_plan.itin_title: The Great Museums of Paris

map_keywords: Musée des Beaux-Arts Petit Palais Paris

visits.text: Pézenas is a classified city of art and history, intimately linked to Molière, who stayed here several times in the 1650s with his troupe. The remarkably preserved pedestrian historic center features cobbled lanes, Renaissance private mansions, artisan shops, and ornate façades. The atmosphere is that of a tranquil small city where it's pleasant to stroll. Pézenas was the residence of Languedoc governors and hosted the Estates-General, explaining its rich heritage. The city still cultivates a passion for theater with its Molière festival in June.

The Musée de Vulliod Saint-Germain occupies a 16th-century private mansion in Pézenas's heart. The rooms recreate the atmosphere of a bourgeois residence with period furniture, tapestries, and objets d'art. A section is dedicated to Molière and his stays in Pézenas. You'll discover the famous chair of barber Gély where the author sat to observe common people. The interior architecture with its monumental staircase and painted ceilings is worth the visit. The museum helps you understand 16th and 17th-century Pézenas.

The Maison des Métiers d'Art, housed in the former 17th-century consular house classified as a Historic Monument, exhibits and sells artisan crafts. You'll find unique pieces and limited series: sculptures, jewelry, ceramics, textiles, tableware. Creators are both local and national. It's the ideal place to discover artisan skills and purchase an authentic object. The building itself merits a visit with its Renaissance architecture.

The Theatre of Pézenas, created in 1803 and reopened after restoration in 2012, is a cultural landmark. Academician Marcel Pagnol pronounced the famous phrase here: "If Jean-Baptiste Poquelin was born in Paris, Molière was born in Pézenas." The Italian-style hall is elegant with balconies and gilding. Classified as a Historic Monument in 1995, it hosts theatrical performances, concerts, and shows year-round. Programming honors Molière and the classical repertoire. Visits possible outside performances.

activities.text: Taste the petits pâtés de Pézenas, a culinary specialty since the 18th century. These bobbin-shaped bites (4 cm wide by 5 cm tall) are filled with lamb, brown sugar, and lemon. The recipe was brought by Lord Clive's Indian cook when the Viceroy of India came to Montpellier for treatment in 1768. The sweet-savory taste is surprising. These pastries are enjoyed warm as an appetizer or with salad. A brotherhood jealously protects the recipe. Several pastry shops in the historic center make them by hand.

Stroll through Pézenas's artisan workshops. The city has numerous creators perpetuating ancient crafts: cabinetmakers, glassblowers, potters, jewelers, milliners, wood gilders, ceramicists, stained glass artists. Many open their workshops to visitors. The Mirondela dels Arts association, created in 1966, promotes craftsmanship and organizes exhibitions. It's an opportunity to see these artisans at work and discuss their craft. Their creations are visible in the center's numerous shops.

Pézenas market has been held every Saturday morning for over 600 years. It fills the historic center streets and brings together local producers, market gardeners, and cheese makers. You'll find seasonal fruits and vegetables, goat cheeses, honey, olives, and regional wines. The atmosphere is lively and friendly. It's the best time to see the town come alive and meet locals. Some stalls offer specialties like petits pâtés or artisan products.

days_plan.itin_title: Hérault Road Trip: Montpellier, Beaches and the Hinterland

visits.text: Phalsbourg, a fortified town founded in 1570 by Count Palatine Georges-Jean de Veldenz-Lützelstein, retains its two monumental gates dating from 1680: Porte de France to the south and Porte d'Allemagne to the north, witnesses to its strategic role as the lock barring the Vosges passage. The arcaded Place d'Armes, the 1770 Lastours barracks and 18th-century townhouses evoke the period when 4,000 French garrison troops defended this passage. The history museum recounts the story of the town that inspired the Lorraine writers Erckmann-Chatrian and their Histoire d'un conscrit de 1813.

The Saint-Louis crystalworks have carried on a centuries-old glassmaking craft since 1586, becoming a royal manufactory in 1767. Allow about 25 km from the stage town, 25 minutes by road. Visit the workshops where master glassmakers blow crystal at 1,450°C with age-old gestures: gathering the parison, blowing and hand-shaping vases, glasses and art objects. The museum displays 2,000 exceptional pieces. The shops offer contemporary creations and end-of-series items at gentle prices.

activities.text: The Saint-Louis-Arzviller inclined plane, Europe’s only transverse boat lift, was inaugurated in 1969. It raises barges through a height difference of 44.55 m in 4 minutes, instead of the full day formerly required to pass through 17 locks. Board a boat for a spectacular crossing in which it glides inside a huge water-filled caisson weighing 5,000 tonnes, travelling along rails inclined at 41%. Guided tours cover the 108 m-long machinery room and the counterweight mechanism. More than 8,500 boats and 100,000 visitors discover this technical achievement designed by engineer Robert Vadot each year.

The Marne-Rhine Canal runs for 314 km through tunnels and forests between Alsace and Lorraine, with 178 locks. Its renovated towpaths offer 45 km of pleasant walks and cycle rides through the Zorn Valley, in a peaceful atmosphere where only the lapping of the water accompanies your progress. Remarkable engineering structures and chamber locks punctuate this route, inaugurated in 1853.

days_plan.itin_title: 4-Day Moselle Tour: Metz, Bitche Citadel and Chagall’s Stained Glass

visits.text: Built between 1829 and 1834 with 11,000 granite blocks, Gatteville Lighthouse rises to 75 metres, making it the second tallest in France. The 365 steps, one for each day of the year, lead to a view across the entire Val de Saire. The climb is not recommended in strong winds or for those with heart conditions.

days_plan.itin_title: Cotentin, Pays d'Auge: 5 days exploring the most beautiful villages

places.name: Phare De La Canche

visits.text: Le Touquet-Paris-Plage owes part of its identity to the Phare de la Canche, designed by local architect Louis Quételart and commissioned in 1949 on the site of two twin towers destroyed by the German army in 1944. Standing 57.6 meters high, it has 274 steps to climb for a 360-degree view over the forest, beach, and estuary. The former lighthouse dated from 1852. Book the guided tour at the Maison des Phares if you want to discover all its secrets.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Villages from Flanders to the Bay of Somme

map_keywords: Phare de la Canche Le Touquet

visits.text: Built in 1882, the Phare de la Gacholle is only 18 metres tall and stands inland: the sandbanks couldn't support anything taller. Partially destroyed during the war and restored in 1947, it now serves as the reserve's visitor reception point, with a glass-fronted room for observing birds.

activities.text: Cycle along the Digue à la mer from the Comtesse car park: built in the 19th century to keep the sea out, it opens up around twenty kilometres of trails between Saintes-Maries and Salin-de-Giraud. Motorised vehicles forbidden. The access track to the car park is seriously bumpy.

If you set off without water, the Phare de la Gacholle sells it at weekends and during school holidays, from 11am to 5pm. It's the only supply point on the route. An area shaded by reed screening provides a place to picnic.

days_plan.itin_title: Côte Bleue and Camargue: the lower coastal route in 7 days

visits.text: Photograph the Petit Minou lighthouse from the arched bridge leading to its rock: it is the quintessential Breton scene, especially in rough seas. Commissioned in 1848, it marks the entrance to the strait in alignment with Portzic. The path from the parking area to Minou beach takes a quarter of an hour. Ideal at sunset.

days_plan.itin_title: Brittany 7 days: Pink Granite, Lighthouses & Peninsulas

visits.text: The UNESCO-listed Calanques de Piana display red porphyry formations rising 400 meters in height. The D81 road winds between Porto and Piana offering spectacular viewpoints over natural sculptures. Rocks sculpted by erosion evoke animal and fantastical forms. This World Heritage site ranks among the Mediterranean's geological wonders.

The village of Piana, built on a plateau at 438 meters, overlooks the Gulf of Porto. White houses arranged in an amphitheater reveal themselves along narrow shaded lanes. The baroque Church of the Assumption, completed in 1792, dominates the heart of the village with its elegant campanile. A stroll reveals the authentic atmosphere of one of the Plus Beaux Villages de France.

The Les Roches Rouges hotel, built in 1912, marks the approach to Piana with its Belle Époque architecture. Awarded the Architecture contemporaine remarquable label, the hotel overlooks the gulf from high ground. The dining room, protected as a historic monument, displays preserved Art Deco décor. Views from the terrace take in the Gulf of Porto and Scandola reserve.

activities.text: Hikes in the Calanques de Piana reveal rock formations and sea views. The Château Fort trail reaches a viewpoint overlooking the gulf in 1 hour. The Sentier des Muletiers crosses the calanques via the old path linking villages. The hike to Capo Rosso and its Genoese tower takes 4 hours, with exceptional views at an altitude of 331 meters.

Boat excursions from Porto explore the Calanques de Piana by sea. Tours lasting 1 hour 30 minutes follow the red cliffs and reveal inaccessible sea caves. Longer tours lasting 3 to 5 hours combine the calanques and Scandola reserve. Crystalline waters invite swimming in wild coves.

Ficajola Beach nestled below Piana offers an intimate setting between red cliffs. The winding 4-kilometer descent from the village reveals spectacular landscapes. The beach has sections of fine sand and pebbles; turquoise waters invite swimming. The old fishing harbor preserves its authenticity far from crowds.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Corsica Tour: Bonifacio, Porto-Vecchio and Mountains

visits.text: The ruins of the medieval castle dominate the Somme valley from the promontory. A testament to the power of the vidames of Picardy during the Middle Ages.
The Saint-Martin collegiate church has a Flamboyant Gothic facade. Its carved tympanum dates from the early 16th century.

activities.text: Walk along the Somme quays where barges and boats glide between ponds and wet meadows.

days_plan.itin_title: Somme Road Trip: Bay of Somme and War Remembrance

visits.text: Viollet-le-Duc started on Pierrefonds in 1857, working from the ruins that Richelieu had ordered demolished in 1617 - Louis XIII had the original fortress razed because its owners, the Orléans branch of the Valois, were considered too independently powerful. What Viollet-le-Duc built between 1857 and 1885 is openly a reconstruction: he invented as much as he restored, and the result is more medieval than the Middle Ages ever managed to look. That's not a criticism. The Salle des Preuses alone - an immense banqueting hall decorated with the armour and heraldry of the nine female heroines of medieval chivalry - is worth the 80km from Paris. The 'haunted' angle is local legend: Viollet-le-Duc died in 1879 before the project was finished, and keepers in the 1920s and 1930s reportedly claimed to see him in the corridors, checking his own unfinished work. No documentation survives. But the story fits the building precisely. Ticket 9.50€, 2.5 hours minimum.

The Clairière de l'Armistice at Rethondes, 30 minutes northwest of Pierrefonds: this is the clearing in the Compiègne forest where Foch and the German delegation signed the armistice of 11 November 1918 in a railway carriage. And it's the place where Hitler, by deliberate calculation, forced France to sign its own armistice on 22 June 1940 - in the same carriage, on the same spot. He then had the carriage taken to Germany, where it was destroyed in 1945. The replica carriage in the museum is meticulous. The esplanade with the sculpture of a French soldier crushing an eagle, the plaques for both armistices, the silence of the forest around it: it's one of the most charged sites in France, and almost no one outside the region knows it's there. Ticket 7€, 1 hour.

activities.text: Lunch in Pierrefonds village, directly below the château: Restaurant Aux Blés d'Or or L'Aubergeade - cuisine bourgeoise, 30-45€. The view of the keep from the terrace is enough reason to eat slowly.

If the schedule allows, make a third stop at the Château de Compiègne — the autumn residence of Napoleon III and Empress Eugénie, with imperial rooms preserved as they were left, offering a tangible example of the refined domestic life of the Second Empire. Admission 8€; 1 hour is enough for the state apartments.

days_plan.itin_title: Oise Circuit: châteaux, forests and history
Haunted Île-de-France: 5 Days of Royal Ghosts and Revolutionary Prisons
Opal Coast Villages and Flemish Heartlands

visits.text: Pigna perches at 400 meters elevation overlooking the Balagne valley. The quintessential artisan village, its lanes reveal workshops of potters, glass blowers, luthiers, and sculptors. The Casa Musicale perpetuates the tradition of Corsican polyphonic singing and hosts concerts and workshops.

Sant'Antonino crowns its peak at 500 meters, one of Corsica's oldest villages. Classified among France's Most Beautiful Villages, its granite houses spiral around the rocky pinnacle. Vaulted lanes and covered passages create a medieval labyrinth. 360-degree panorama over Balagne and the sea.

Corbara terraces its ochre houses between olive groves and vineyards. The 19th-century Convent of Saint-Dominique dominates the village. The baroque Church of the Annunciation preserves paintings and sculptures. The terraces offer plunging views of the sea and L'Île-Rousse.

activities.text: The Balagne artisan route winds through Pigna, Corbara, Lumio, and Sant'Antonino. Workshops open to visitors offer demonstrations of ancestral techniques: pottery, ceramics, lutherie, woodworking. A hilltop village atmosphere far from mass tourism.

Polyphonic music concerts are organized at the Casa Musicale in Pigna. Male voices a cappella interpreting traditional Corsican repertoire. Reservations recommended for summer evening performances. Intimate atmosphere beneath stone vaults.

Panoramic hikes depart from the villages toward the Balagne ridges. Marked trails crossing maquis and century-old olive groves. Sea views at every turn. Easy to moderate difficulty depending on chosen routes.

days_plan.itin_title: Upper Corsica Road Trip: Cap Corse and Balagne

visits.text: Piriac-sur-Mer is designated a Petite Cité de Caractère, and the label is deserved. The village has preserved its Breton stone lanes with an unusually harmonious appearance. Set off on foot from the harbor: white houses with blue shutters, fishing pots stacked on the quays, pleasure boats in the basin. Saint-Pierre-ès-Liens Church (1766), with its square tower clearly visible from the sea, deserves a look inside—the votive offerings and hanging ship models recall that Piriac was a port for deep-sea fishing off Newfoundland as early as the 17th century. Émile Zola stayed here in 1876 while writing L'Assommoir, and Alphonse Daudet spent two consecutive summers here, in 1874 and 1875.

Castelli Point, at the far end of the municipality, is a geosite of major interest: its outcrops of mica schist and gneiss, 477 million years old, rank among the geological curiosities of the Armorican Massif. From the rocks you'll spot Dumet Island—the only maritime island in Loire-Atlantique, owned by the Conservatoire du littoral since 1990 and now a bird reserve. A panorama of wild coastline worth the detour.

activities.text: The coastal path from Piriac toward La Turballe is one of the finest walks on the peninsula. Over 5 kilometers, ochre mica-schist cliffs alternate with sandy coves, and you pass close to the famous Tombeau d'Almanzor, a granite block that stays above water even at high tide and around which a medieval legend has grown. It is in fact a geological curiosity, with holes drilled during 19th-century tin mining. The walk is easy, there and back or as a loop.
Fishermen sell their daily catch each morning on the quays, facing the boats. Fish and shellfish at their freshest—your chance to put together a good picnic before setting off on the coastal walk.

days_plan.itin_title: Loire-Atlantique Road Trip: Nantes and the Côte de Jade

visits.text: Europe's last major wild camping area closed in 2016, and Plage de Piémanson has benefited: several kilometres of sand without a single building, between dunes, lagoons and the Mediterranean. Driftwood polished by the Rhône litters the shore. Parking outside the designated area, bivouacking and caravanning are now forbidden.

activities.text: Walk ten minutes from the Piémanson car park and you'll be more or less alone: the area patrolled by lifeguards in July–August is concentrated in the centre, while the rest is empty. A naturist area occupies the end of the beach. Outside the lifeguarded area, swimming is at your own risk.

Out of season, Plage de Piémanson is worth it mainly for the emptiness: cool sea, no lifeguards, kitesurfers and flamingos for company. The water reaches 24–26°C between July and September. Take your rubbish away, don't trample the dunes.

days_plan.itin_title: Côte Bleue and Camargue: the lower coastal route in 7 days

visits.text: Lac au Duc spreads across 250 hectares—one of inland Brittany's largest bodies of water. It was created in the 12th century by Benedictine monks who dammed the Yvel river to power their mills. Walk at least part of the circuit to enjoy the viewpoints over the wooded shores.

The Hydrangea Circuit unfolds 3 kilometres through woodland beside the lake. Over 5,000 hydrangeas in numerous varieties form a remarkable botanical collection. Blooming runs June to September—July is peak. Free, accessible to all.

Saint-Armel Church preserves Gothic architecture with a 15th-century carved portal. The colourful stained glass and Baroque furnishings merit a look. Saint Armel, founder of Ploërmel in the 6th century, is depicted with a dragon he is said to have tamed and thrown into the river—look for his statue in the church.

Head to Place La Mennais to see Ploërmel's astronomical clock: a complex mechanism displaying lunar phases, tides and the positions of the planets. It is a curious object rarely found in a town of this size.

Wander the cobbled streets around the place du Roi Arthur and the rue Beaumanoir—the half-timbered houses of the historic centre are well preserved. Ploërmel sits at the gates of Brocéliande Forest—if you're drawn to Arthurian legend, you've arrived.

activities.text: Circle Lac au Duc on foot: 14 kilometres of marked, flat trail. Wetlands shelter otters, roe deer and grey herons. Budget 3–4 hours at an easy pace with photo stops.

If you feel like getting some exercise, Lac au Duc offers windsurfing, dinghy sailing, catamaran sailing, canoeing and kayaking, stand-up paddleboarding and water skiing. Local providers offer equipment hire and lessons on site. The water is calm—perfect for learning, even if you have never set foot on a board.

The V3 greenway links Mauron to Questembert over 53 kilometres via Ploërmel. An old railway converted for bikes, walkers and riders crosses Ploërmel country and skirts the lake. Tackle a section if you lack a full day.

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip Morbihan: Gulf, Carnac and Breton Coast

visits.text: The Thermes Napoléon, commissioned by Napoleon III in 1857, impress with their 18-meter-high vault crowning a 65-meter corridor in cut stone. The entire complex is listed as a Historic Monument.
The remains of the Roman Baths bear witness to 2,000 years of thermal bathing. The Romans built a concrete raft foundation with shafts to bring up the hot water, a technique still visible today.

The Pavillon des Princes served as Napoleon III's residence. It was here that the secret meeting between the Emperor and Count Cavour took place on July 21, 1858, laying the groundwork for Italian unification.
Wander the sloping alleyways to admire the thousand balconies in wrought iron, molded cast iron, or carved wood. Each balcony is unique—hence the town's nickname: "the city of a thousand balconies."
The Church of Saint-Amé, in neo-Gothic style inspired by Viollet-le-Duc, dates from the 19th century. It's listed as a Historic Monument and sits near the terraced gardens.
The terraced gardens form Plombières' “1,001st balcony.” Ponds, sculptures, rare plant species: the view looks down over the entire Augronne valley.

activities.text: Climb to the Coteau de la Vierge to reach the statue of Notre-Dame des Eaux (1855), a work by Joseph-Hugues Fabisch. The panorama takes in the spa town set deep in its valley.
Walk through the Parc Impérial in Plombières-les-Bains, laid out under Napoléon III. Its landscaped paths, pond and musical trail provide a setting for a stroll in the heart of the spa town.
Taste the Plombières ice cream, created during the 1858 meeting between Napoleon III and Cavour. This blend of candied fruits and ice cream is a local source of pride that every tearoom serves.
Head to Val-d'Ajol, 10 km away, to discover the Faymont waterfall and the Vallée des Roches, lined with granite formations bearing evocative names: la Roche du Renard, la Citerne aux Ours.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Est Road Trip: Vineyards, Ramparts and Forests
Vosges Road Trip: Lakes, Mountains & Thermal Spas

visits.text: The monumental calvary of Plougastel-Daoulas, erected between 1602 and 1604, has 181 figures sculpted in kersanton stone. Built to celebrate the end of a plague epidemic, it's one of Brittany's three great calvaries, along with those of Guimiliau and Plougonven.

Scenes of Christ's Passion, arranged in a continuous frieze around the base, blend biblical figures and 17th-century Breton costumes. Look for the Roman soldier dressed as a Breton gentleman—a deliberate anachronism.

The Strawberry and Heritage Museum traces the history of strawberry cultivation, which made the peninsula's fortune in the 19th century. Strawberry plants were imported from Chile in 1714 by a naval officer, and Plougastel strawberries became an export product.
Sainte-Christine chapel (16th century), set by the sea on the Tinduff foreshore, is accessible only at low tide. Its miniature parish close includes a calvary, an ossuary, and a devotional fountain.
Pointe de l'Armorique, at the peninsula's tip, offers a panorama over the Brest roadstead, the Albert-Louppe bridge, and military vessels at anchor. A viewpoint panel identifies the landmarks.

activities.text: Hike the peninsula's coastal path, between Anse de l'Auberlac'h and Pointe de l'Armorique. The trail alternates between coves, pebble beaches, and viewpoints over the Brest roadstead.
Visit the strawberry fields (in season, May to July). Some farms offer pick-your-own—Plougastel's heritage varieties have an incomparable fragrance.
Head to Daoulas Abbey (5 min by car). Its 12th-century Romanesque cloister, the only one preserved in Brittany, houses a garden of medicinal plants from five continents.

days_plan.itin_title: Brittany Road Trip: Villages with Character, Sea and History

visits.text: Ploumanac'h's jumble of granite boulders features pink granite blocks sculpted by 300 million years of erosion. Some bear nicknames: Napoleon's Hat, the Turtle, the Die, the Overturned Bottle. Each weighs between 50 and 500 tonnes.

The Mean Ruz lighthouse (1945), in pink granite, replaces a 19th-century coastal signal station destroyed during World War II. Its color blends with the surrounding rocks—you have to search among the boulders to find it.

Saint-Guirec beach, a cove of fine sand framed by pink rocks, shelters an 11th-century oratory on the foreshore. According to tradition, girls of marriageable age stuck a needle in the nose of the saint's statue to find a husband within the year.

Costaérès castle, built in 1892 on a rocky islet, is the iconic image of the Pink Granite Coast. Accessible only at low tide, it served as a summer residence for a Polish engineer passionate about literature.

The Maison du Littoral explains the geology of pink granite: formed 300 million years ago at a depth of 6 km, it owes its color to iron-rich feldspars. Only three sites worldwide have granite of this hue.

activities.text: Walk the customs officers' path from Ploumanac'h to Perros-Guirec. The trail winds between pink granite blocks, gorse moors, and turquoise coves. It's one of the GR34's most spectacular sections.
Embark for the Sept-Îles, France's largest bird sanctuary. Northern gannets (France's only colony), puffins, guillemots, and gray seals populate this protected archipelago.
At sunset, pink granite turns orange then purple. Best viewpoint: the path between Saint-Guirec beach and Mean Ruz lighthouse.

days_plan.itin_title: Brittany Road Trip: Villages with Character, Sea and History

visits.text: Ploumanac'h's pink granite color comes from iron oxides trapped in the crystals. The Sentier des Douaniers crosses the jumble of boulders between Trestraou beach and the harbor: the blocks bear nicknames—the Turtle, the Mushroom, Napoleon's Hat. Allow 2 hours on foot, 4 hours if you're taking photographs. The path sometimes requires using your hands; closed-toe shoes are mandatory.

You look for it and walk right past it: Men Ruz Lighthouse, red stone in Breton, is built from the same pink granite as the surrounding blocks. Fifteen meters high, it was erected between 1946 and 1948 to replace the one German troops blew up in 1944. It is closed to visitors. The light at the end of the day turns it distinctly orange.

On Saint-Guirec beach in Ploumanac'h, a small granite oratory shelters the statue of a saint whose nose young women pricked with a needle hoping to marry within the year. The 14th-century wooden statue, ruined by the ritual, was replaced by a granite version in 1904. From here, Château de Costaérès stands out on its islet, a private property closed to visitors. Low tide for the beach, high tide for the photo.

Stop at the Maison du Littoral before the walk rather than after: at the entrance to Ploumanac'h's jumble of boulders, it explains for free how this granite, hundreds of millions of years old, was rounded by erosion into stacked spheres. Small exhibitions, guided nature outings in season, and people who know the terrain better than any printed guidebook. Seasonal opening.

activities.text: The Sentier des Douaniers between the Trestraou parking lot and Ploumanac'h harbor covers 6 km round trip, and the best time to go is sunrise or sunset, when the low-angle light reddens the granite. A shuttle links both ends in season, saving you from retracing your steps. Walking poles may only be used with rubber tips, as the rock scratches easily.

Passenger boats depart from Trestraou beach for the Sept-Îles archipelago, France's oldest bird reserve, created in 1912: thousands of northern gannets on Rouzic, Atlantic puffins, and gray seals resting on rocks. The outing lasts about 2 hours without landing, longer with a stopover on Île aux Moines. Reservations are mandatory in summer, and the seas can be rough on the crossing.

days_plan.itin_title: Brittany 7 days: Pink Granite, Lighthouses & Peninsulas

places.name: Point De Vue Du Sel

visits.text: Pearly pink, blinding white, stark blue: the Point de vue du sel, on the Piémanson road, overlooks the salt evaporation ponds and the camelles, salt mounds about ten metres high. The pink comes from a microalga, Dunaliella salina, and is at its strongest between June and September. Free stop, on-site parking, ten minutes is enough.

activities.text: Stop here rather than on a random roadside verge: the Point de vue du sel is the only purpose-built viewpoint overlooking the salt evaporation ponds, with parking and free access. Late-afternoon backlighting washes out the colours, so come in late morning instead.

days_plan.itin_title: Côte Bleue and Camargue: the lower coastal route in 7 days

map_keywords: Point de vue du sel Salin-de-Giraud

visits.text: Further west than Pointe Saint-Mathieu and Pointe du Raz, Pointe de Corsen in Plouarzel is the westernmost point of mainland France, and a marker notes this on site. The viewpoint overlooks the Chenal du Four; in clear weather, Ushant and Molène stand out on the horizon. Just above, CROSS Corsen monitors maritime traffic from this promontory. It's more symbolic than spectacular: allow thirty minutes, free parking.

days_plan.itin_title: Brittany 7 days: Pink Granite, Lighthouses & Peninsulas

places.name: Pointe De Pen Hir

visits.text: Pointe de Pen Hir is the Crozon peninsula's showpiece: cliffs over 60 meters high and, extending from them, the Tas de Pois, a line of islets planted in the Iroise Sea. At the summit, a Cross of Lorraine honors Bretons who left for London after 1940. Come at sunset, when the low-angle light does all the work. Constant wind, free parking.

Ten minutes' walk from Camaret harbor, the Lagatjar alignments consist of nearly 150 standing stones on flat heathland, re-erected in 1928 after centuries of neglect. Some exceed three meters. It's free, never crowded, and the site takes on a downright unsettling air at the end of the day. Twenty minutes suffice, unless you're counting the stones.

activities.text: Pen Hat beach, between Pointe de Pen Hir and Pointe du Toulinguet, is a large, wild stretch of sand with not a single shop. Swimming is inadvisable: currents are notoriously treacherous and there are no lifeguards. On the other hand, climbing to the bunkers overlooking it gives an unbeatable view due west. Allow an hour on site.

days_plan.itin_title: Brittany 7 days: Pink Granite, Lighthouses & Peninsulas

map_keywords: Pointe de Pen Hir Tas de Pois

visits.text: The Hourdel lighthouse, green and white, marks the southern entrance to the Bay of Somme from this still-active small fishing port. On the neighboring shingle bank rests an overturned blockhouse, a remnant of the Atlantic Wall planted in the pebbles. The Route Blanche, 3.5 kilometers between dunes and sea buckthorn, links Le Hourdel to the hamlet of La Mollière on foot or by bike. Park at the Route Blanche entrance; the harbor parking lot fills quickly in summer.

activities.text: You'll reach the Hourdel shingle bank to observe, at a safe distance, France's largest seal colony, a mix of harbor seals and gray seals. The animals gather on the sandbanks roughly two and a half hours before low tide, never quite visible to the naked eye. The 300-meter safety distance is imperative: a seal raising its head is a stressed seal. A guided outing with Picardie Nature remains the best option to make sure you don't miss anything.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Villages from Flanders to the Bay of Somme

places.name: Pointe Du Raz

visits.text: Heavily visited, yet Pointe du Raz holds up: since the 1990s rehabilitation, parking lots and buildings have been moved back several hundred meters, the heath has regrown, and you must walk to earn the view. The cliffs drop 72 meters to the Raz de Sein, a strait where currents remain violent even in calm seas. Notre-Dame des Naufragés keeps watch, balanced at the edge. Paid parking from April through late October, flat daily rate per vehicle.

Seen from Pointe du Raz, La Vieille Lighthouse rises on its rock amid the current: first lit in 1887, it wasn't automated until 1995, after changes of lighthouse keepers that remain famous for their difficulty in heavy weather. Behind it, the Île de Sein appears in clear weather, so flat it seems to float. The Maison du Site lends binoculars, and that changes everything.

activities.text: From the Maison du Site at Pointe du Raz, the loop along the GR34 to the point and then along the north coast covers about 5 km and takes 1 hour 30 minutes to 2 hours. The marked trail stays back from the sheer drops, but the wind blows constantly: a windbreaker is essential even in July. Seabirds nest in the cliffs, and binoculars can be borrowed at reception.

days_plan.itin_title: Brittany 7 days: Pink Granite, Lighthouses & Peninsulas

map_keywords: Maison du Site Pointe du Raz

visits.text: Free parking, hardly anyone about, and the chapel of Saint-They standing alone on the edge of the void: the Pointe du Van is the exact opposite of the Pointe du Raz, its famous neighbor some ten kilometers to the south. From here the eye takes in the Baie des Trépassés and the Pointe du Raz seen head-on, which frankly makes the best photo in the area. Flat 30-minute walk from the parking area.

days_plan.itin_title: Brittany 7 days: Pink Granite, Lighthouses & Peninsulas

visits.text: A lighthouse planted amid abbey ruins: Pointe Saint-Mathieu in Plougonvelin has no equivalent in France. The Abbey of Saint-Mathieu de Fine-Terre dates to the 11th century, and its Romanesque facade, nave arcades, and choir vaults remain, with free access. The lighthouse, first lit in 1835, rises to 37 meters: 163 steps to the gallery and a view over the Iroise Sea that makes the climb worthwhile. Climbing is suspended in heavy weather.

Families still come looking for a specific name: the National Memorial to Sailors Who Died for France at Pointe Saint-Mathieu was erected in 1927 on Admiral Guépratte's initiative. Below, a cenotaph displays photos and biographies of several thousand sailors from the French Navy, merchant marine, and fishing fleets. This is not a decorative monument. Free access, and silence comes naturally.

activities.text: A 4 km loop, the remembrance trail, links Pointe Saint-Mathieu to the Mémoires 39-45 museum, housed in a former German command bunker on the Atlantic Wall. The interior is stark, cramped, and poorly heated, and tells the story of the siege of Brest in 1944 without flourishes. Allow an hour of walking plus an hour for the visit. Seasonal opening.

days_plan.itin_title: Brittany 7 days: Pink Granite, Lighthouses & Peninsulas

visits.text: Villa Savoye, inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2016, embodies Le Corbusier's five points of modern architecture: pilotis, roof terrace, free plan, ribbon windows, and free façade. Built between 1928 and 1931, it appears to float above the lawn.

The Collégiale Notre-Dame de Poissy, built in the 12th century, blends Romanesque and Gothic styles. Its baptismal font is where Saint Louis was christened in 1214. Two octagonal towers crown the transept.
Step into the Toy Museum, housed in the 14th-century royal priory gatehouse. Over 600 toys and games from 1850 to 1950 tell the story of childhood across the ages.
Parc Meissonier offers a manicured rose garden and a curiosity: the Maison de Fer, a 19th-century prefabricated metal structure and a survivor of the earliest days of industrial architecture.

activities.text: Walk the banks of the Seine in Poissy: the towpath links the town center to the Île de la Dérivation, a pleasant spot for a picnic or a break in the open air.
Explore Poissy's old town on foot to spot the medieval façades and narrow streets around the collegiate church.

days_plan.itin_title: Yvelines Road Trip: Versailles and Impressionist Villages

places.name: Poitiers

visits.text: The façade of Notre-Dame-la-Grande displays 12th-century sculpted decoration among the richest in Poitou. Prophets, apostles and biblical scenes cover the stone in two tiers.

Step into the Saint-Jean Baptistery, one of France's oldest preserved Christian buildings. Built in the 4th century, it houses an octagonal baptismal font, Merovingian sarcophagi, and Romanesque wall paintings.

The Palace of the Counts of Poitou, residence of the Dukes of Aquitaine, preserves a Great Hall in Angevin Gothic style, rebuilt around 1200 by the Plantagenets. The Maubergeon Tower offers sweeping views over the old town.

Saint-Pierre Cathedral, commissioned by Eleanor of Aquitaine from 1160 onward, blends Angevin Gothic with influences from the Île-de-France. Marvel at the 12th-century Crucifixion window—one of Europe's largest Romanesque stained-glass panels—and the 13th-century choir stalls, the oldest in the country.

Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site on the Routes to Santiago de Compostela, Saint-Hilaire-le-Grand Church is dedicated to Poitiers' first attested bishop, who died around 367. Its Romanesque murals and carved capitals are well worth exploring.
The Sainte-Croix Museum brings together collections spanning from prehistory to the 20th century. You'll find medieval sculptures, Gallo-Roman artifacts, and works by Camille Claudel.

Futuroscope offers over 40 immersive attractions 10 km north of Poitiers. L'Extraordinaire Voyage, voted Europe's best attraction, sends you soaring above the five continents with your feet dangling in midair. Chasseurs de Tornades uses Europe's largest circular LED screen.

activities.text: Wander through the medieval lanes of the historic center. Half-timbered houses, Hôtel Fumé, and Hôtel Berthelot bear witness to the rich past of this city of a hundred bell towers.
Stroll through Parc de Blossac, 10 hectares of greenery laid out as a French formal garden, an English garden, and the Jardin des Roches. Unobstructed views over the Clain Valley.
Watch Futuroscope's nighttime show, “La Clé des Songes,” combining projections onto water, flames, and lights.

days_plan.itin_title: Vienne Road Trip: Futuroscope and Romanesque Heritage

map_keywords: Palais des Comtes de Poitou Poitiers

visits.text: Polignac Fortress rises from a 3-hectare basalt platform at 806 m (2,644 ft) elevation. The 14th-century keep soars 32 m (105 ft) high, commanding a 360° panorama across the Puy basin and the Meygal and Mézenc massifs.
Follow the 14-stop circuit through the ruins: 800 m of ramparts, 6 fortified gates, the armory hall, a vertiginous well 83.5 m (274 ft) deep, and the medieval-inspired garden.
On the keep's ground floor, the mask of Apollo testifies to an ancient Roman temple. Pilgrims once consulted an oracle here—a priest hidden behind the mask dictating prophecies.
Step inside Saint-Martin Church, a Romanesque jewel classified as a Historic Monument since 1902. The choir shelters 14th-century frescoes depicting the Last Judgment, paradise, and hell.

In the south apsidiole, 15th-century paintings illustrate the Annunciation, the Visitation, and the Nativity. Notice the polychrome statue of Saint Anne from the 13th century, typical of medieval folk art.

The village counts over 100 rural heritage features scattered across twenty hamlets: crosses, fountains, bread ovens, and wash houses. The one at Bilhac preserves a cross inscribed as a Historic Monument since 1930.

activities.text: Climb to the top of the keep to embrace the Velay volcanoes. On clear days, the view reaches all the way to the Chaîne des Puys.
Follow the Pinatelle du Zouave trail winding around the basalt dike. The walk reveals the volcanic geology of this site, over 2.5 million years old.
Wander the lanes of this village labeled one of France's Most Beautiful Villages. Houses built from volcanic breccia and lava stone fountains punctuate your stroll.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Loire Road Trip: Le Puy-en-Velay and Volcanoes

visits.text: Maison du Comté, an interpretation center completely rebuilt in 2021 with modern architecture reimagining the traditional farm buildings of Haut-Doubs. The 3,000-square-meter interactive journey offers a sensory voyage discovering that there isn't just one Comté but multiple varieties with ever-changing flavors. Films, sensory games, and testimonies from industry actors tell of terroirs, know-how, and production techniques. The visit concludes with a guided tasting.

Collégiale Saint-Hippolyte from the 15th century, whose first stone was laid in 1415 by the Archbishop of Besançon. The church, enriched by donations from wealthy Poligny lords, owes its renown to Claus de Werwe, sculptor to the Duke of Burgundy. The building testifies to the Burgundian golden age with its sculptures and imposing architecture. The stained glass windows and furnishings tell the religious history of the capital of Comté.

Circuit de la Tour, marked on the ground, traversing Poligny's heritage. The itinerary reveals vestiges of the old Château de Grimont ramparts, the wine-growing quarter of Charcigny with its traditional houses, the Jacobins' crypt, and the Ursulines' Courtyard. Monasteries, cloisters, and churches unfold like hidden treasures. A free map and audio guide are available at the Tourist Office.

Old Pharmacy of the Hôtel-Dieu on the ground floor of the current hospital. This prestige room built in the late 17th century preserves its wood paneling, pharmacy jars, and period furniture. It testifies to Poligny's level of medical development at that time. Apothecaries prepared remedies and potions here according to doctors' prescriptions.

activities.text: Ascent of Croix du Dan, a 12-meter-high cross dominating Poligny and visible from the town center. The trail winds through forests and meadows to the summit offering panoramic views over the valley, vineyards, and first Jura plateaus. On clear days, the view extends to the foothills of Burgundy. The effort of the climb is rewarded by this 360-degree spectacle.

Walk through the vineyard between the Monts Martin, Grands Roussots, and Chevraudes terroirs. The trail crosses these three entities with different soils beneath the limestone cliff that generates the gravels characterizing Poligny's terroirs. Panoramas unfold over the town, the Collégiale Saint-Hippolyte, and the wine-growing slopes. In the Charcigny quarter, traditional wine-growing housing with trappon cellars tells the local story.

Visit to Comté cheese dairies. Poligny concentrates an impressive number of dairies and creameries dedicated to France's first AOC cheese by tonnage. Dairies like Poligny-Tourmont offer tours of aging in their cellars and the production of this cheese—1.65 million wheels produced annually. Tasting reveals the differences between young and aged Comté.

days_plan.itin_title: Jura Road Trip: Lakes, Waterfalls & Mountains

visits.text: Abbaye des Prémontrés presents its classical 18th-century facade along the Moselle. Built between 1705 and 1735, it was bombed in 1944 then restored until 1974.
The Sainte-Marie-Majeure abbey church follows a hall church plan. The grand staircase and library rank among the jewels of this listed monument.
The abbey gardens cover 2.5 hectares. The Scent Garden, the French garden, and the Moselle garden offer three distinct atmospheres.
Triangular Place Duroc features Renaissance arcades around its entire perimeter. It's one of the largest arcade ensembles still visible in Lorraine.
Église Saint-Martin, consecrated in 1335, blends 14th and 15th-century styles. The Entombment of Christ required four years of restoration.

activities.text: The Musée Au Fil du Papier traces the town's history since the founding of the University of Lorraine in 1572. Its collection of papier-mâché objects reflects Belle Époque style.
Drive 10 minutes to climb the Mousson hill. The castle ruins offer valley views.

days_plan.itin_title: Meurthe-et-Moselle Road Trip: Art Nouveau Nancy & Fortified Cities

visits.text: Pont-Audemer, the Norman Venice. Crisscrossed by Risle canals, this former tanners' city has retained its medieval charm. Classified among France's Most Beautiful Detours and labeled a City of Art and History, it reveals its treasures along the water: 15th and 16th-century half-timbered houses, old skin-drying sheds, private mansions, and small stone bridges.

Saint-Ouen Church of Pont-Audemer. This imposing church blending Romanesque, Gothic, and Renaissance styles impresses with its 15th and 16th-century stained glass windows and remarkable organ case. The building dominates the town from the main street.

Ruisseau des Pâtissiers and Ruisseau des Carmes. These canals crisscrossing the old town bear names evocative of local history. Views from the small bridges strangely recall Venice, with reflections of colorful facades in the water.
Alfred Canel Museum. Housed in the former home of the historian and politician, this cabinet of curiosities presents local history collections, antique library holdings, and temporary exhibitions.

activities.text: Kayaking on Pont-Audemer's canals. Trade the gondola for a kayak to glide along Risle branches through medieval quarters. The route passes under picturesque stone bridges and along the tanners' old wharves.

Mirliton tasting. A local specialty created in 1340 by Guillaume Tirel, known as Taillevent, cook to the kings of France, this biscuit roll filled with praline cream and sealed with chocolate is the pride of Pont-Audemer's pastry makers. This is where Thierry Hermès lived before founding his famous Parisian house.

Marais Vernier. A few kilometers away, this largest peat marsh in France (4,500 hectares) is a paradise for migratory birds. Ramsar-labeled, it offers 44 hiking trails and wild basketry workshops in this preserved setting.

days_plan.itin_title: Eure Road Trip: From Giverny to Normandy's Most Beautiful Villages
The 20 Most Beautiful Villages in Normandy

visits.text: Village of Pont-Aven, city of painters made famous by Paul Gauguin and the Pont-Aven School. Fourteen watermills that once punctuated milling activity line the tumultuous Aven. White granite houses reflect in the river creating changing tableaux according to light. Art galleries succeed workshops perpetuating artistic tradition born in the 19th century. The bucolic atmosphere that seduced Gauguin, Bernard, and Sérusier endures despite tourist influx.

Pont-Aven Museum, an exceptional collection devoted to the Pont-Aven School and Synthetism. Major canvases by Gauguin, Bernard, Sérusier, and Denis trace the artistic revolution born here between 1886 and 1896. The chronological route reveals evolution from Naturalism toward Synthetism then Symbolism with flat colors and simplified forms. Temporary exhibitions explore aspects of Breton art history. The building's contemporary architecture harmoniously integrates the site.

Trémalo Chapel, a 16th-century sanctuary housing the crucifix that inspired Gauguin's famous painting. The polychrome carved rood beam represents the Crucifixion surrounded by the Virgin and Saint John. The secluded chapel's meditative atmosphere in the countryside contrasts with the town's animation. Manessier's modern stained glass windows illuminate the choir. The external calvary dates from the 15th century.

Bois d'Amour, a romantic walk along the Aven immortalized by numerous painters. The shaded path winds between mossy rocks, waterfalls, and meanders where the river takes changing hues. The Trou de l'Enfer, a spectacular granite chaos, attracted Gauguin and his disciples. Century-old beeches create a vegetal cathedral preserving coolness even in summer. Benches invite contemplation facing light playing on water.

activities.text: Hiking along the Aven to Pont-Aven harbor on the painters' path. The marked 6-kilometer route follows riverbanks crossing landscapes that inspired the Pont-Aven School. Reproductions of famous paintings punctuate the path allowing comparison of works and reality. Restored mills, old washhouses, and locks mark the bucolic walk. The river mouth opens onto the estuary and salt marshes sheltering herons and egrets.

Tasting famous Pont-Aven cookies, pure butter biscuits created in 1886 by Isidore Penven. Artisan biscuit factories perpetuate the original recipe with salted butter and wheat. Shops offer shortbreads, palets, traous-mad, and other Breton specialties in traditional packaging. Tea rooms allow tasting warm cookies accompanied by cider or hot chocolate. The Belle Époque atmosphere of shops adds to the gourmet charm.

Visiting contemporary art galleries exhibiting regional and national artists' creations. About fifteen galleries succeed open studios where painters, sculptors, and ceramists work live. Styles vary from figurative to abstract through naive in the Pont-Aven School lineage. Openings and artist meetings regularly animate the town. The vibrant pictorial tradition perpetuates the village's artistic influence.

Dining in a traditional crêperie tasting buckwheat galettes garnished with local products. Authentic recipes favor Guéméné andouille sausage, free-range eggs, smoked bacon, and aged cheese. Wheat crêpes topped with homemade salted butter caramel or flambéed with Lambig brandy prolong the feast. Farmhouse cider served in bowls traditionally accompanies this convivial meal. Rooms with exposed beams create a warm, rustic atmosphere.

days_plan.itin_title: Brittany Road Trip: Villages with Character, Sea and History
Finistère Circuit: Breton Headlands, Islands & Artists' Villages
Brittany 7 days: Pink Granite, Lighthouses & Peninsulas

places.name: Pont De Gau

visits.text: Opened in 1949 as a zoo, Pont de Gau became an ornithological park in 1974 and now covers 60 hectares of marshes, reed beds and salt marshes. The birds roam freely here and pointedly ignore you, which changes everything. A rehabilitation centre takes in injured birds each year. Adult €8.50, child €5.

activities.text: Allow two hours for the 7 km of trails at the Parc ornithologique de Pont de Gau: herons, egrets, storks, kites, and an observatory overlooking the Ginès marsh, where bulls graze in the warmer months. You can leave at any time until sunset.

If you come in winter, the gatherings of flamingos at Pont de Gau are the densest of the year. The park organises guided tours and twilight walks during school holidays. A tripod and telephoto lens will come in handy.

days_plan.itin_title: Côte Bleue and Camargue: the lower coastal route in 7 days

map_keywords: Parc ornithologique de Pont de Gau Saintes-Maries-de-la-Mer

visits.text: A former aqueduct bridge, the Pont des Fées supplied Grimaud with water before becoming a walking destination. It marks the village's lowest point, tucked into a valley in the Maures massif. Be aware: routes suggested by apps sometimes lead to a dead end. Start from the cemetery parking lot; it's a few minutes away on foot.

activities.text: Start from the Saint-Roch mill to reach the Pont des Fées on foot: the trail winds through the scrubland, with views of Grimaud Castle reappearing on the way back. The route is marked and short. Avoid midday in July: there's nowhere to get water along the route, and the valley radiates heat.

days_plan.itin_title: Roquebrune-sur-Argens: sea, villages and the Var in 10 days

visits.text: The abbey church of Saint-Antoine-l'Abbaye, built between the 13th and 15th centuries, is one of the most remarkable Gothic achievements in the Dauphiné. Listed as a Historic Monument since 1840, it preserves wall paintings, walnut panelling and an organ from the 17th and 18th centuries. About 15 km from Pont-en-Royans, 25 minutes by road.

The Treasury room, in the sacristies with walnut and Hungarian oak woodwork, displays the collection of the Order of the Antonines: a 17th-century ivory Christ, antiphonaries, medieval surgical instruments and an exceptional rotating vestment chest. Approximately 15 km from Pont-en-Royans, a 25-minute drive.

Walk through the “goulets”, narrow, partly covered lanes leading to the top of the village. The houses become more ornate as you climb: mullioned windows, glazed tiles in the “Dauphiné roof” style and sculpted decorations. Approximately 15 km from Pont-en-Royans, a 25-minute drive.

The departmental museum, housed in the former 17th- and 18th-century novitiate, is devoted to the Hospitallers of Saint Anthony, an order of physician-monks who treated “Saint Anthony's fire”. A medieval garden completes the visit. Approximately 15 km from Pont-en-Royans, a 25-minute drive.

In Pont-en-Royans, the suspended houses appear to spring from the rock face above the Bourne River. Built in the 16th century to facilitate timber trade from the Vercors, their ochre, yellow, and pink façades have been protected as Historic Monuments since 1944.

Cross the Pont Picard for the village's most iconic view: the colorful houses stand out against the deep green waters. The buildings are constructed directly into the rock spur, with wooden overhangs projecting into empty space.

The Musée de l'Eau occupies a former convent that became a silk mill and then a power plant. It houses a water bar featuring 1,500 bottles from around the world, plus an exhibit on aquatic biodiversity.

activities.text: Climb to the Belvédère des Trois Châteaux above Pont-en-Royans. The ascent is short but steep, passing through the medieval quarter and its terraced gardens. The panorama takes in the Royans region and the entrance to the Bourne gorges.
The landscaped banks of the Bourne invite relaxation: picnic tables, a waterfall, and swimming areas in summer. The water is crystal-clear and cool, flowing straight down from the Vercors.

The Gorges de la Bourne road connects Pont-en-Royans to Villard-de-Lans over 24 km. Carved into the cliff face in the 19th century, it hangs above the gorge with vertiginous drops and tunnels bored through solid rock.

days_plan.itin_title: Rhône-Alpes Circuit: Perched Villages and Mountain Peaks
Royans-Vercors Road Trip: Hilltop Villages and Gorges

visits.text: Two monumental arches frame a single arched span: Pont Flavien, at the entrance to Saint-Chamas, is a Roman bridge that has preserved both its arches, a very rare case. It crosses the Touloubre on the Marseille-Arles road and measures 22 metres between the arches. Listed as early as 1840.

The four lions standing at the ends of the Pont Flavien entablatures watch over the passage, but only one is ancient: the other three were remade in the 18th century. Also look for the crowned eagles at the top of the Corinthian pilasters.

activities.text: Look for the ruts worn into the vault of Pont Flavien: once the ancient paving had disappeared, carts rolled directly over the stone for centuries. Journeymen on their tour of France carved their names here in the 17th century. Blue-zone parking near the roundabout.

days_plan.itin_title: Côte Bleue and Camargue: the lower coastal route in 7 days

visits.text: Pontarlier was the world capital of absinthe in the 19th century. In 1805, the first distillery opened its doors. In 1900, 25 distilleries employed 3,000 people (38% of the population) and produced 66,000 liters per day. Banned on March 17, 1915, absinthe was rehabilitated in 2001 and has enjoyed PGI status since 2010. The municipal museum recounts this history with a collection of objects, posters, and period documents.

The last historic distillery in Pontarlier, founded in 1890, perpetuates the tradition at 49 rue des Lavaux. Its century-old copper stills and vats produce absinthe using ancestral methods. Labeled Living Heritage Company, it offers free tours with tasting of its products: absinthe, Pontarlier-Anis, and fir liqueur.

The Château de Joux has overlooked the Pontarlier cluse since the 11th century, controlling the passage to Switzerland. Its 5 enclosures, 3 moats, and 3 drawbridges extend over 2 hectares with 250 rooms. Classified as a Historic Monument, it was fortified by Vauban at the end of the 17th century then served as a state prison. Toussaint Louverture, hero of Haitian independence, died there on April 7, 1803, after seven months of imprisonment in a freezing cell. The site is inscribed on the Route of the Abolitions of Slavery.

activities.text: Participate in a guided tour of the Château de Joux to discover the evolution of fortification from the Middle Ages to Vauban. Guides also recount the history of famous prisoners: Mirabeau, Toussaint Louverture, and German writer Heinrich von Kleist. Toussaint Louverture's cell is a memorial site for the abolition of slavery with commemorations every April 7 and May 10.

Taste Comtoise specialties in Pontarlier restaurants: Morteau sausage, Comté fondue, morel croute, warm Mont d'Or in winter. The city maintains a gastronomic tradition linked to its past as a commercial crossroads between France and Switzerland.

days_plan.itin_title: Doubs Circuit: Watchmaking and Swiss Border
Doubs Road Trip: Nature and Heritage of Franche-Comté

places.name: Pontivy

visits.text: Merlin's Tomb, on the edge of the Val sans Retour, is a calculated disappointment: two standing stones, a holly tree, and nothing else. What was once a Neolithic alignment of several megaliths was largely destroyed in 1894 by treasure hunters convinced that Merlin was buried beneath with his gold. They found nothing. What remains is a place for leaving offerings—folded papers tucked between the holly branches with written wishes. The fact that people continue to do this, without anyone asking them to, is more interesting than the dolmen itself. Thirty minutes is enough.

The Fontaine de Barenton has to be earned: a 30-minute walk from the Folle Pensée car park over uneven ground, closed shoes essential. The tradition is precise: pouring its water onto the stone slab unleashes the storm. Celtic druids held ceremonies here, the Knights of the Round Table stopped here, and processions from nearby villages were still coming in the 19th century to bring rain in times of drought - an attested and documented practice. If you go, pour the water onto the slab. At worst, nothing happens.

The Grail Church in Tréhorenteuc is unique in France. Father Henri Gillard restored this small village church between 1942 and 1962 with an entirely Arthurian iconographic program: stained glass, frescoes, and mosaics blend Christianity and Grail legend within the same nave. The idea was to make this modest place a pilgrimage site for Brocéliande enthusiasts. It worked. Free admission, 1 hour.
