The Hôtié de Viviane is a Neolithic megalithic chamber—roughly 3,000 BCE—positioned on the heights of the Val sans Retour, with a panorama across the entire forest. The walk from the Arbre d'Or (a monumental sculpture installed in 1990 as a tribute to the forest burned that year in a 900-hectare fire) takes 1 hour round-trip. Best in late afternoon when the light grazes the moorland.

activities.text: Lunch in Tréhorenteuc before or after the church—the village is tiny (1,200 inhabitants) but has a few simple options. Otherwise, picnic in the forest with supplies from Paimpont.
Drive to Pontivy in the evening, about 1 hour on the road. Overnight in the historic old town. Dinner in the centre - classic Breton cooking, no fine dining to be expected at this stop.

days_plan.itin_title: Haunted Brittany in 6 days: From Brocéliande to the Lands of the Ankou
Road Trip Morbihan: Gulf, Carnac and Breton Coast

map_keywords: Hôtié de Viviane Val sans Retour

visits.text: Saint-Maclou Cathedral is an architectural lesson in itself: construction began around 1140–1165, and it brings together styles spanning four centuries—a Romanesque chevet, a Gothic nave with ribbed vaults, a 15th-century Flamboyant façade with a rose window and grand portal, and 16th-century Renaissance chapels. It only officially became a cathedral in 1966 with the creation of the Diocese of Pontoise. A listed historic monument since 1840 and owned by the city (an extremely rare case in France), it houses little-known treasures: six 16th-century Renaissance stained-glass windows in the northern chapels, an “Entombment” sculpture by Nicolas Leprince, and a Deposition from the Cross signed by Jean Jouvenet (1708). The grand Baroque organ of 1716, enlarged by Cavaillé-Coll, is the largest in Val-d'Oise. Don't miss the Chapel of the Passion to the left of the entrance.

The Musée d'Art et d'Histoire Pissarro-Pontoise (MAHPP) occupies a late 19th-century bourgeois house built on the site of the former medieval castle—the view of the Oise from the terrace alone is worth the visit. Created in 1980 for the 150th anniversary of Camille Pissarro's birth, the museum traces the painter's time in Pontoise (1866–1868 and 1872–1884) and presents a collection that extends far beyond his work: Caillebotte, Daubigny, Matisse, Rodin, Arp, and over 3,000 drawings and prints in its collection of works on paper. Open Wednesday–Sunday, 11 AM–6 PM (closed from 12:30–1:30 PM). First Sunday of the month: free admission.

Take time to descend into Old Pontoise, around the Mont Bélien district and Place du Petit-Martroy. Medieval lanes reveal half-timbered houses and stone façades that Pissarro painted many times from the hillsides. Climb to the northern ramparts: the view over the Oise Valley toward Auvers is exactly what the painter saw from his studio.

activities.text: The Pontoise market on Place du Général-de-Gaulle takes place on Wednesday afternoons. Pick up cheeses and local produce for a picnic on the banks of the Oise.

Walk along the Oise banks from Quai du Pothuis: the bridges and islets of Pontoise are those Pissarro depicted in his paintings from the 1870s. Take your time to identify the angles he chose—a loop of about 3 km for taking photographs.

days_plan.itin_title: Val-d'Oise Tour: Impressionist Villages and Heritage

visits.text: Begin exploring Pornic from the Gourmalon corniche, opposite the castle and the old harbor: it offers the best view of the town. Pornic Castle, whose origins date back to the 10th century, dominates the old harbor from its cliff. Its present silhouette, with romantic turrets, is chiefly the result of a 19th-century restoration—it is privately owned and cannot be visited, but the view of it from the quays is worth a look. Below, stroll around the old harbor lined with colorful fishermen's houses. At low tide, the boats lean to one side on the mud while the quayside restaurants come alive.

Noëveillard Beach, sheltered near the marina, is Pornic's most family-friendly: it remains accessible even at low tide. To discover some of the wilder coves dotting the coast toward La Bernerie-en-Retz, take the coastal path from the Gourmalon garden—the scenery shifts at every turn.

activities.text: Pornic's main walk is the sentier des Douaniers. Within the municipality, it follows 14 kilometers of coastline, from Saint-Michel-Chef-Chef to Les Moutiers-en-Retz. The stars of the route are the fishing huts: these wooden huts on stilts above the water are used for lift-net fishing—a square net measuring 25 m² is hauled up at high tide with a winch. They are all privately owned and cannot be visited, but seeing them from the path is a spectacle in itself. Bring water and good shoes; the route is easy but long.

Head to Pointe Saint-Gildas, some twenty kilometers north of Pornic. This rocky headland, designated a Regional Nature Reserve, offers a panorama over Bourgneuf Bay and the island of Noirmoutier on clear days. The sentier des Douaniers passes here too: the easily accessible loop around the headland is 7.5 km long.

days_plan.itin_title: Loire-Atlantique Road Trip: Nantes and the Côte de Jade

visits.text: Fort Sainte-Agathe, strengthened in 1531 under Francis I, has dominated the harbor since Antiquity. Managed by Port-Cros National Park, it hosts exhibitions on the island's marine and terrestrial biodiversity. The view from the ramparts sweeps over the village and Courtade beach.

Notre-Dame beach, voted the most beautiful beach in Europe, stretches along a bay lined with eucalyptus trees. Its shallow turquoise waters make it ideal for swimming. Allow about 45 minutes on foot or 25 minutes by bike from the village.
Near the fort, the Moulin du Bonheur, a Provençal windmill restored by the National Park, offers a glimpse of island agricultural life. Free guided tours for visitors under 18, from May to September.

Porquerolles village nestles behind the harbor, around the shaded Place d'Armes. Sainte-Anne church and the houses with colorful shutters compose a postcard scene. In the evening, once the ferries have left, calm settles over the village.

Fort de la Repentance, an underground artillery battery dating from 1893, offers an unobstructed view over Notre-Dame Bay and the harbor. The interior can be visited during Heritage Days. The final stretch is steep by bike.

activities.text: Bike rental shops are set up at the harbor. Four trails marked out by the National Park let you cross the island from north to south between vineyards, pine groves, and maquis.

Follow the forts circuit: 9.5 km of trails linking Forts Lequin, Alycastre, Repentance, and Sainte-Agathe. The route retraces the stages of the island's military life through four centuries of fortifications.
The island's wine estates devote 70% of their output to AOC Côtes de Provence rosé. Tastings are by reservation in a unique island setting, between vines and pine groves.
Two dive centers offer explorations of the seabed around the island, classified as the core of Port-Cros National Park. Posidonia seagrass meadows, groupers, and barracudas populate these waters.

days_plan.itin_title: Var Road Trip: French Riviera & Provence Verte

visits.text: The fishing port of Port-en-Bessin brings the small coastal village to life with its ballet of colourful trawlers. The quays echo with the cry of seagulls and the bustle of fishermen unloading their fresh catch. The authentic atmosphere of this working port contrasts with the neighbouring seaside resorts.
Stroll between the nearby D-Day beaches. Gold Beach lies just a stone's throw away, a reminder that Port-en-Bessin served as a fuel port during the Battle of Normandy thanks to the PLUTO pipeline.

activities.text: Savour seafood at one of the port's fish auctions. Scallops, oysters and fresh fish come straight from the boats to the restaurant stalls on the quayside.
Climb up to the Vauban tower overlooking the port. The panorama encompasses the Bessin coast and offers an unbeatable view of Gold Beach.

days_plan.itin_title: Calvados Tour: D-Day Beaches and Normandy

visits.text: Morning boat shuttle from Port Grimaud to Saint-Tropez. Cross the gulf in 20 minutes, views of coastal villas and Cap de Saint-Tropez. Arrival at the Vieux-Port.
The Vieux-Port of Saint-Tropez comes alive from the morning onwards. Moored luxury yachts, Provençal pointu fishing boats, colourful façades in a semi-circle. An atmosphere both chic and laid-back.
Breakfast on the terrace at Café Sénéquier, a Saint-Tropez institution since 1887. Iconic red armchairs on the Quai Jean-Jaurès, unbeatable views of the boats' dance.

The market on Place des Lices runs at full tilt on Tuesday and Saturday mornings. Stalls of Provençal fruit and vegetables, fresh fish, olives, goat cheeses, Provençal fabrics. Century-old plane trees, pétanque players in the shade.

The Citadelle de Saint-Tropez, a hexagonal 17th-century fortress, watches over the town from its hill. Well-preserved ramparts, maritime history museum, poop deck from a royal galley. 360° panorama over the gulf and the Maures massif.
Return to Port Grimaud late afternoon. Final swim on the fine sandy beach at the entrance to the canal town, calm shallow waters ideal for cooling off.
Scenic drive between Grasse and the Gulf of Saint-Tropez. Descent to the Mediterranean through the Var hinterland, hilltop villages, forest of cork oaks and umbrella pines.

Port Grimaud can be explored from the entrance car park. A canal town conceived by François Spoerry in 1966, built on former marshland. 2,500 colourful houses along 14 km of canals, each residence with its own private mooring.
The church of Saint-François-d'Assise, modern and fortified, dominates Port Grimaud. Climb to the top of its bell tower to take in the entire canal town, the canals and the Gulf of Saint-Tropez.

activities.text: Lunch with your feet in the sand in Saint-Tropez. Salade niçoise, grilled fish, chilled rosé. Views over the bay, relaxed summer atmosphere.
Electric boat ride through the Port Grimaud canals. Peaceful cruising between colourful houses, under bridges, along hanging gardens. Unique perspective on the town's waterside architecture.
Seafood dinner on a quayside terrace. Platters of oysters, stuffed mussels, gulf fish. Maritime atmosphere, boats returning at sunset.

Day at Pampelonne beach, 5 km of fine sand near Saint-Tropez. Private beach clubs with loungers and restaurants at the water's edge, or a quieter public beach. Crystal-clear waters, views of Cap Camarat.
Dinner on the Port Grimaud quays. Tables on the terrace facing moored boats, reflections of colourful façades in the calm canal water. Grilled fish, Mediterranean cuisine.

days_plan.itin_title: Provence & French Riviera Road Trip: Lavender, Villages & Beaches
Provence & French Riviera Road Trip: Lavender, Villages & Beaches
Roquebrune-sur-Argens: sea, villages and the Var in 10 days
Var in 4 Days: From Bormes to the Most Beautiful Villages of the Verdon

visits.text: Just a handful of boats barely larger than a rowing boat: Port Racine, described as the smallest port in France, can be explored in a few minutes at Saint-Germain-des-Vaux. The garden honouring Jacques Prévert, who lived nearby in Omonville-la-Petite, extends the walk to the cemetery where the poet is buried.

days_plan.itin_title: Cotentin, Pays d'Auge: 5 days exploring the most beautiful villages

visits.text: Porticcio stretches along the southern shore facing the Gulf of Ajaccio as a lively seaside resort. Colorful houses line the marina where yachts and traditional fishing boats are moored. The Genoese tower of Capitello, dating from the 16th century, overlooks the beach of the same name and offers panoramic views over the gulf.

The megalithic site of Filitosa spreads across 3 hectares of hills planted with thousand-year-old olive trees; plan a round trip by car from Porticcio. The rows of anthropomorphic menhirs date from 3300 BC, and warrior statues engraved with weapons and faces testify to Torrean ingenuity. The central Torre monument features Cyclopean architecture. The adjoining museum displays archaeological objects and explains 8000 years of human occupation.

The village of Grosseto-Prugna in the hinterland overlooks Porticcio from an altitude of 500 meters; plan a round trip by car from Porticcio. Its characteristic lanes wind between traditional Corsican houses and shaded squares. The village retains its authentic character away from the coast's summer bustle.

activities.text: Porticcio's beaches offer alternating stretches of fine sand and sheltered coves over several kilometers. Plage de la Viva boasts panoramic views of Ajaccio and shallow turquoise waters. Agosta Beach to the south stretches for 2 kilometers in a wilder setting. Plage Mare e Sole and Plage de Verghia rank among the finest with their immaculate white sand.

The Muvimare ferry links Porticcio to Ajaccio year-round with several daily crossings. The 20-minute crossing offers unique perspectives on the gulf and lets passengers avoid winding roads. Extra evening services run in summer so passengers can enjoy the imperial city's nightlife.

Water sports abound on Porticcio's beaches. Paddleboarding, sea kayaking, windsurfing, and jet skiing let you explore the coast. Water sports clubs offer introductory sessions and equipment rentals. Scuba diving reveals remarkable seabeds with caves, wrecks, and abundant marine life.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Corsica Tour: Bonifacio, Porto-Vecchio and Mountains

visits.text: Don't miss the Calanques de Piana under any circumstances—listed as a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1983 along with the Gulf of Porto and the Scandola reserve. These 250-million-year-old red porphyry formations rise up to 400 meters above the sea across 11,800 hectares. The D81 road between Porto and Piana winds through them for 2 kilometers: stop at the viewpoints to make out the wind-sculpted silhouettes—a fortress, a bishop, petrified lovers. Maupassant crossed these same rocks in 1880 and wrote: “these are the marvels of Corsica, one might say one of the marvels of the world.” By car or on foot, plan to be there late in the day when the sun sets the rock ablaze.

Girolata is a fishing hamlet accessible only by boat or by a 2.5-hour hike from the Col de la Croix—no roads, no cars, just colorful houses on the edge of a green gulf. Also within the UNESCO-listed area, it has barely a few dozen year-round residents. If you take the boat from Porto, you'll glimpse it while passing the Scandola reserve.

Porto's Genoese tower—square and red like the rocks—has dominated the harbor since the 16th century. It was built to watch for Barbary raids and alert the inland villages. The climb takes 10 minutes and the view over the gulf from its summit is worth it, especially at golden hour.

activities.text: The boat excursion from Porto to Scandola, Girolata and the calanques de Piana is an essential outing during your stay. The Scandola nature reserve - created in 1975 and listed by UNESCO in 1983 - is home to peregrine falcons, ospreys and giant groupers that you will see diving beneath the hull. The cruise generally lasts 3 to 4 hours. Operators depart from Porto's harbor every morning. Book the day before in high season - trips are often fully booked.

Hike the calanques trail starting from Roches Bleues: from the parking area on the D81, a marked trail winds through the red porphyry formations for 3 to 4 km. The route offers views you can't get from the road—count on 2 hours round-trip. Closed-toe shoes required; no flip-flops on these sharp rocks.

days_plan.itin_title: Complete Tour of Corsica

visits.text: Porto-Vecchio's Genoese citadel has dominated the gulf since the 16th century. The Bastion de France protects the upper old town where cobbled lanes and vaulted passages wind. Place de la République is home to cafés and restaurants beneath plane trees. The ramparts offer panoramic views over the marina and Alta Rocca mountains.

The old town preserves its character with traditional Corsican houses and artisan boutiques. The 19th-century Saint-Jean-Baptiste church dominates the main square. Art galleries and artisan workshops punctuate the narrow lanes. The Provençal atmosphere flourishes in the evening when the terraces come alive.

The archaeological sites of Ceccia and Tappa reveal distinctive Torrean casteddi. These Bronze Age fortresses bear witness to Corsica's prehistoric civilizations. The views from the sites take in the gulf and the surrounding mountains.

activities.text: Palombaggia and Santa Giulia beaches rank among the finest in the Mediterranean. Palombaggia stretches for 3 kilometers, with white sand bordered by umbrella pines and translucent turquoise waters. Santa Giulia forms a perfect arc of fine sand in a protected bay. Water sports abound: paddleboarding, kayaking, windsurfing.

Rondinara beach forms an almost perfect arc surrounded by green hills; plan a round trip by car from Porto-Vecchio. The shallow turquoise water suits families. The listed site remains well preserved, with few buildings. Tamaricciu beach offers fine sand and century-old pine trees in a more intimate setting.

The Cavu valley winds through maquis and forest to the natural pools; plan a round trip from Porto-Vecchio. The pools of crystal-clear fresh water invite swimming in a wild setting. Hiking trails follow the river between granite rocks. The site, accessible from Porto-Vecchio, attracts families and hikers.

days_plan.itin_title: Complete Tour of Corsica
Southern Corsica Tour: Bonifacio, Porto-Vecchio and Mountains

visits.text: Pradelles perches at 1,150 meters on a volcanic spur above the upper Allier valley. Ranked among France's Most Beautiful Villages, this town is inseparable from the Via Régordane — that ancient route between the Massif Central and the Mediterranean that muleteers called the 'Régourdans road,' hauling wine, salt, and olive oil from Languedoc into Auvergne. King Saint Louis himself stopped here in 1254. Start at Place de la Halle: surrounded by arcades and Renaissance houses from the 15th–17th centuries, it forms the historic heart of Pradelles. The Maison Frévol (16th century) and the covered gallery deserve close attention.

Walk the circuit of the remaining ramparts: Porte de la Verdette is the only medieval gate still standing, and Tour Rochely recalls the town's defensive strength. Beneath the town, pass under the arch of the 17th-century former road hospice — one of only four such surviving structures left in Europe. This building once sheltered travellers and pilgrims heading down to Saint-Gilles-du-Gard. Pradelles also preserves the Notre-Dame chapel (built in 1613, literally straddling the road) with its miraculous statue of the Virgin discovered, according to legend, in a buried chest in 1512.

Before leaving Pradelles, walk up to the calvary hill: on clear days, you can see the statue of the Virgin on the keep of Luc castle from here, the next stop on the Via Régordane. The two fortresses once communicated by fire signals. The view of Lake Naussac spreading through the valley below makes a striking contrast with this high-altitude Auvergne landscape.

activities.text: In 1878, the Scottish writer Robert Louis Stevenson passed through Pradelles with his donkey Modestine on the journey he recounted in “Travels with a Donkey in the Cévennes”. A 2-to-3 km loop over the heights around the village offers beautiful views of the Devès plateau and Lake Naussac — allow 1 hr 15 min to link the two main viewpoints.

The former Le Puy-Langogne railway line has been converted to a vélo-rail (pedal-powered railcar) starting from Pradelles station: trips from 1h to 5h (return on 18 km) let you cross the gorse moorlands, lentil fields, and peat bogs of the plateau. It's an ideal family activity for exploring volcanic landscapes at a leisurely pace. Book ahead in high season.

days_plan.itin_title: Auvergne Circuit: Perched Villages and Volcanoes
Haute-Loire Road Trip: Le Puy-en-Velay and Volcanoes

visits.text: Fort Lagarde, built by Vauban between 1677 and 1682, guards the entrance to the Haut-Vallespir. Its star-shaped keep surrounds a medieval signal tower. Climb via the zigzagging path or the underground passage with 142 steps.
The medieval ramparts have encircled the upper town since the 14th century. Vauban remodeled them in the 17th century to create a remarkable defensive complex.
The Church of Saints Justus and Rufina has stood out for its imposing size since the 9th century. Rebuilt in the 13th and 16th centuries, its 1245 portal displays ironwork from Catalan forges.

The Tour de Mir bears witness to the medieval defensive system. This watchtower offers a view over the valley. Access from Prats-de-Mollo is on foot along a hiking route, so plan it as a separate outing.

View La Verneda, a former textile factory in Prats-de-Mollo, from outside. The interpretation center devoted to the history, heritage and Catalan traditions on both sides of the Pyrenees is currently closed to visitors.

activities.text: Wander through the medieval streets of the upper town. The colorful facades contrast with the austerity of Vauban's fortifications.
Head up to La Preste, a spa town nestled at an altitude of 1,130 meters. Its sulfurous waters have treated rheumatism and respiratory ailments since the 16th century.
Discover the col d'Arès leading into Spain, allowing for a round trip by road from Prats-de-Mollo. A historic crossing point between France and Catalonia at an altitude of 1,513 m.

days_plan.itin_title: Pyrénées-Orientales Road Trip: French Catalonia and the Côte Vermeille

places.name: Propriano

visits.text: Sartène overlooks the Rizzanese valley from its granite spur. Prosper Mérimée called it “the most Corsican of Corsican towns” for its tall stone houses, medieval lanes, and 15th-century projecting watch turret. Place de la Libération is home to cafés beneath the elms; Sainte-Marie church preserves the chain and cross of the Catenacciu. The Pietraggi quarter reveals vaulted passages and centuries-old stairways.

The Musée de Préhistoire et d'Archéologie de Sartène displays statue-menhirs, Neolithic ceramics, and Bronze Age artifacts. Collections from excavations at Cauria and Filitosa trace 10,000 years of human occupation. A room dedicated to megalithic alignments and Torrean artifacts rounds out the picture of prehistoric Corsica.

AOP Sartène wine estates cultivate Sciaccarellu, Niellucciu, and Vermentino on unique granite terroir. Tastings reveal structured reds, full-bodied rosés, and rich whites with green highlights. Family vineyards open their cellars and winemaking facilities for guided wine tours. The vineyard landscape extends from Propriano to the Lion de Roccapina.

activities.text: The megalithic sites of Cauria comprise the Stantari alignment, the Fontanaccia dolmen and the Renaghju alignment. Menhirs erected 4000 years ago dot a pastoral plateau 15 kilometers from Sartène; plan a round trip by car from Propriano. The Fontanaccia dolmen remains Corsica's best-preserved funerary monument, with its 2.4-ton covering slab. A marked trail connects the three groups in a 90-minute walk.

The Genoese bridge of Spin'a Cavallu has spanned the Rizzanese with its humpback profile since the 13th century. Its single dry-stone arch follows the natural rock in a landscape of maquis. Natural pools downstream offer swimming in cool river water. The site is accessible via a 20-minute walk along a forest trail.

The hike to the Genoese tower of Campomoro follows the Conservatoire du littoral's coastal path; plan a round trip by car from Propriano. Corsica's largest tower has overlooked a wild bay since 1586, its 6-meter-thick walls bearing witness to Genoese defensive architecture. The panorama stretches from the Valinco gulf to the Bouches de Bonifacio. The 2-hour round-trip walk follows coves and flowering maquis.

days_plan.itin_title: Complete Tour of Corsica
Southern Corsica Tour: Bonifacio, Porto-Vecchio and Mountains

map_keywords: Sartène Museum of Prehistory and Archaeology

visits.text: The Tour César, a 12th-century keep, is unique in France: an octagon set on a square base, raised on an artificial mound. From the top, the panorama embraces the medieval town and the Brie plain.
The upper town's ramparts, 1,200 meters long with 22 varied towers, were erected from 1226 to 1314 to protect the wealth of the Champagne Fairs. A walkway runs along their length.

Descend into Provins' underground passages. These galleries carved in limestone served as merchant cellars during the fairs. The guided tour crosses vaulted rooms with sculpted capitals, in groups of 25. Constant temperature: 13°C.

The Grange aux Dîmes, a 13th-century merchant house once rented to Toulouse traders, recreates the atmosphere of the Champagne Fairs. An audio-guided exhibition presents the trades and merchants of the era.

The Saint-Quiriace Collegiate Church, begun in the 12th century, was never completed. Its Gothic choir and 17th-century dome create a striking contrast with the unfinished nave. The Place du Châtel, at the church's foot, was the heart of comital power.
The Saint-Ayoul Priory, whose forecourt hosted the first fairs born from pilgrimages, preserves a thousand-year-old architectural ensemble with its crypt and Romanesque sculpted capitals.

activities.text: Watch "Les Aigles des Remparts" (Eagles of the Ramparts): equestrian falconry at the foot of the fortifications. Eagles, falcons, and horses recreate medieval life in 50 minutes.
"The Legend of the Knights," a chivalry show in the ramparts' moats, features sword fights, jousting, and equestrian stunts.

The Provins Rose Garden spreads across three hectares at the foot of the upper town. The Provins rose, reputedly brought from Damascus by a Count of Champagne, appears in jam, crystallized petals, and rosewater.
Wander through the upper town's streets to the half-timbered houses. Artisans offer medieval specialties: honey, hypocras, and Provins rose products.

days_plan.itin_title: Seine-et-Marne Circuit: Fontainebleau and Châteaux

places.name: Pujols

visits.text: Pujols stands at 180 metres on a spur overlooking the Lot Valley and is classed among France's Most Beautiful Villages. Enter the village through the 15th-century Saint-Nicolas Church, which is literally part of the fortifications: its bell tower rises above the north gateway and forms a single structure with the defensive walls. This rare and original architectural solution says a great deal about the military role of the site in the Middle Ages.

Open the door of Sainte-Foy Church, on the southern edge of the village overlooking the hillside. Built in the first half of the 16th century, it has a Latin-cross plan with two additional side chapels. Inside, 16th-century frescoes depict Saint Catherine, Saint George and the Assumption of Mary. The paintings have been weathered by the centuries but remain perfectly legible. Look towards the top of the castle painted on the wall, where figures acclaim Saint George as he leaves for battle. In summer, the deconsecrated church hosts contemporary art exhibitions.

At the western end of the village, the Porte des Anglais is a far more modest fortified entrance than the main gate. Local tradition holds that English soldiers fled through this passage during the Hundred Years' War. In the 13th century the village was still one of the most important strongholds in the Agenais, until the Albigensians were driven out in 1229 and its walls demolished.

Wander the lanes of Pujols between half-timbered houses and houses of white stone. Rue de la Citadelle and the covered passageways hide finely worked doorways and unexpected hanging gardens. Art galleries and craft workshops line the main street: the village has managed to attract a creative community.

The 19th-century market hall on the main square hosts the Sunday market from May to September. Its oak beams shelter local producers and craftspeople. The atmosphere is relaxed and unfussy, very different from the tourist markets of the region.

activities.text: Head to the viewpoint for a 180-degree panorama over the Lot Valley. On clear days, you can see for up to 30 km: the pink-brick buildings of Villeneuve-sur-Lot spread out below, the River Lot winds across the plain and the hills roll away towards the horizon. The sunset from this viewpoint is particularly beautiful.

Browse the Sunday market in the market hall to taste the local specialities of Lot-et-Garonne: melons, tomatoes, prunes, preserves and Buzet wines. This producers' market runs from May to September on Sunday mornings.
If visiting in summer, inquire about concerts and exhibitions organized in Sainte-Foy Church. The building's acoustics are excellent and musical evenings in this medieval setting are often memorable.

Pujols is a stop on the Vézelay route, the GR 652, towards Santiago de Compostela. Even if you are not walking all the way to Spain, follow the GR downhill from the village to Villeneuve-sur-Lot: the view of the bastide from above is completely different from the perspective below.

days_plan.itin_title: Lot-et-Garonne Road Trip: Bastides and Villages

map_keywords: Gate of the English (Porte des Anglais), Pujols

places.name: Puy De Dome

visits.text: From the Maison de Site at the volcano's base, board the Panoramique des Dômes—an electric rack railway inaugurated in 2012 that whisks you to 1,465 meters altitude in 15 minutes over 5.6 km of track. Book online in summer: queues can be long on weekends. At the summit, the 360° panorama embraces 80 volcanoes of the Chaîne des Puys, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2018. On exceptionally clear days, you can even make out Mont Blanc on the horizon.

Don't miss the ruins of the Gallo-Roman Temple of Mercury at the summit. Built in the 1st-2nd centuries AD, it was the largest mountain temple in Roman Gaul—pilgrims came from across the region to leave offerings. A detailed interactive museum space completes the visit with artifacts unearthed on site. Bring warm clothing whatever the season: at the summit it's typically 5 to 10°C cooler than in the plains.

activities.text: Set out on one of the marked trails at the Puy de Dôme summit. Three themed paths are offered: the Pilgrims' Path, the Conquerors' Path, and the Curious Path. If you're athletic, descend on foot via the Chemin des Muletiers (1h30, 575m descent), the old path used to haul construction materials for the Roman temple.

Late afternoon, weather permitting, make the round trip to Puy Pariou, a neighboring volcano with a perfectly preserved crater 100 meters deep, visible from the ridge. Accessible on foot from the Maison de Site parking (2h30 round trip, easy level), it's one of the most beautiful craters in the Chaîne des Puys.

days_plan.itin_title: Auvergne Volcanoes Road Trip: Puy de Dôme and Lakes

map_keywords: Panoramique des Dômes gare départ Orcines
Temple de Mercure Puy de Dôme
Maison de Site Puy de Dôme

visits.text: Puy-l'Évêque rises on a rocky spur 30 meters above the Lot. Golden-stone medieval dwellings tier in arcs from the seigneurial tower at the summit down to the old port below. From the bridge across the Lot, the overall view of the terraced town and its reflection in the water forms the village's emblematic image.

The 13th-century episcopal tower rises 23 meters—the last vestige of the bishops' palace of Cahors, who gave the town its name in 1228. Its four levels, connected by a staircase within the wall thickness, served as a watchtower. The top floor preserves a fireplace and latrines carved into the stone.

The Church of Saint-Sauveur, a Historic Monument from the 14th–15th centuries, occupies an unusual position: outside the castrum, on the heights. Its Gothic nave with ribbed vaults and its bell tower—a former watchtower—dominate the valley. A remarkable feature: the church possesses the Lot department's only historic carillon, composed of 15 bells, the oldest dating from 1632.

Descend through the hanging gardens, created in 2016 on the site of ruined medieval houses. This terraced pedestrian pathway connects the upper town to the river, punctuated by rest stops with open views across the Lot Valley and the rooftops of the town.

At the village base, Rue de la Cale leads to the old port where gabarres moored, loaded with wine barrels bound for Bordeaux. Street names preserve the memory of former trades: boatmen, nailsmiths, dyers, washerwomen. On Place Guillaume de Cardaillac, admire medieval houses from the 13th–16th centuries and a beautiful half-timbered dwelling.

activities.text: Board an electric gabare at the foot of the village. This replica of 19th-century boats glides silently on the Lot. The guide recounts river navigation history while vineyards, cliffs, and mills slip past.

Puy-l'Évêque is the capital of the Cahors vineyard. Malbec, planted here since Roman times, produces a deep, structured AOP wine. Several estates open their cellars to visitors for tastings guided by the winemaker.
The Lot Valley cycle route winds between vineyards and river. From Puy-l'Évêque, ride toward Albas and its steep lanes, or toward Luzech and its peninsula, for panoramas of the Lot's meanders.

days_plan.itin_title: Lot Itinerary: Cahors, Rocamadour & the Lot Valley

visits.text: The Wild Coast stretches 8 kilometres from Percho Point to Turpault Castle. The GR 34 follows the shoreline—jagged cliffs, inaccessible coves, Atlantic rollers crashing against the rock. It's one of Brittany's most beautiful stretches of the customs officers' path. Never venture onto wet rocks—the waves here are treacherous.
At Percho Point, ruins of an old military guardhouse overlook the cliffs. The view is raw and spectacular—in heavy swell, waves rise metres high. Pack a windbreaker; it always blows here.

The Port Blanc arch pierces the coastal rock—a natural formation sculpted by erosion, now the iconic image of the peninsula. At low tide, you can go down to the foot of the arch and photograph it from the beach. Check tide times before going.

You can't miss Turpault Castle at the southern entrance to the Wild Coast, perched on Beg-er-Lann Point. This Anglo-medieval manor was built between 1904 and 1910 by Georges Turpault, a Cholet spinner who named it 'the Castle of the Sea'. It's private, not open to visitors, but photograph it from the road—its silhouette against the ocean is one of Morbihan's most iconic shots.

Conguel Point juts a kilometre into the sea at the peninsula's south-eastern tip. Walk the full circuit: views embrace Belle-Île, Houat, Hoëdic and the Teignouse lighthouse. On the rocky shelves, spot remnants of old seaweed-burning kilns.

Haliguen Harbour shelters both a fishing port and a pleasure marina. Its small 11-metre lighthouse was inaugurated in 1856. Stroll the quays in the evening, when the boats come in and the evening light softens the stone.

activities.text: Take the Tire-Bouchon, the tourist train linking Auray to Quiberon along the coast. The journey crosses the whole peninsula with views over the beaches and the Penthièvre isthmus. An original, relaxing way to reach Quiberon without the car—and without the summer traffic jams.

The Great Beach faces Belle-Île, oriented due south. Turquoise water, fine sand, supervised bathing in season. Hippocampe beach wheelchairs are available for visitors with reduced mobility. Arrive before 11am in summer if you want to lay down your towel without jostling for space.

From Port-Maria, ferries link Belle-Île-en-Mer, Houat or Hoëdic in 45 minutes to 1 hour. If you have time for one island, choose Belle-Île—the Monet-painted Port-Coton sea stacks merit the crossing. Book in season, especially weekends.

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip Morbihan: Gulf, Carnac and Breton Coast

visits.text: Rennes-le-Château, home to 89 people on a rocky spur 450 metres above sea level, lies about 16 km from Quillan, 20 minutes by road. It all begins with Abbé Bérenger Saunière, appointed priest of this poor parish in 1885: from 1891 he spent considerable sums renovating the church and building a luxurious villa (the Villa Béthanie), a crenellated neo-Gothic tower (the Tour Magdala), gardens and an orangery, all in the name of his servant Marie Dénarnaud. Where did the money come from? Treasure of the Visigoths, the Templars, the Cathars, a secret of the Church? Nobody knows. Saunière died in 1917 without revealing anything. Step into the church of Sainte-Marie-Madeleine: at the porch a Latin inscription warns “This place is terrible”, and on the left a devil named Asmodée, guardian of treasures, holds up the holy water stoup. Entry to the church is free.

Then climb to Tour Magdala, built from 1900 at the hill's edge. Saunière used it as a library and meditation retreat. From the crenellated platform, you can see some twenty villages of the Corbières and Pyrenees. The estate (villa, gardens, presbytery converted to museum, rampart walk) charges admission — allow 1.5 hours to see everything.

From Quillan, head south into the Gorges de l'Aude: the Gorges de Pierre-Lys (a road cut into the cliff), between Quillan and Axat, then the Gorges de Saint-Georges, just past Axat, around twenty minutes by road from Quillan. Two spectacular passages that take you along the river between limestone walls several dozen metres high.

activities.text: Operators in Axat and Quillan offer rafting descents on the Aude ranging from 7 to 17 km. Class III-IV rapids, passages named "triple chute" and "flipper". Accessible from age 6 or 12 depending on routes. Book the day before or morning — the activity depends on river flow.

days_plan.itin_title: Aude Road Trip: Carcassonne, Cathar Country & the Mediterranean

visits.text: Saint-Corentin Cathedral, a masterpiece of Breton Gothic art erected between the 13th and 15th centuries. Twin 76-meter spires dominate the city while the choir's curious slight deviation intrigues visitors. Fifteenth and 16th-century stained glass windows flood the nave with colored light depicting biblical scenes and Breton saints' lives. Remarkable statuary includes legendary Saint Corentin, Quimper's first bishop. The monumental Cavaillé-Coll organ resonates during regular concerts.

Departmental Breton Museum, installed in the former episcopal palace. Collections trace Breton history and identity through traditional costumes, furniture, faience, and everyday objects. The room devoted to headdresses displays the extraordinary diversity of women's ornaments according to regions. The chronological route reveals Breton society's evolution since Gallo-Roman times. Temporary exhibitions explore specific cultural themes.

Quimper Fine Arts Museum, a rich pictorial collection from the 14th to 21st centuries. French, Italian, and Flemish schools stand alongside the Pont-Aven school with major works by Gauguin, Bernard, and Sérusier. Canvases evoke Breton landscapes, rural life scenes, and peasant portraits in traditional costume. The Silguy donation groups rare furniture and precious objects. The 19th-century Italian palace adds to the visit's charm.

HB-Henriot Faience Factories, a manufactory perpetuating Quimper faience craftsmanship since 1690. Workshop tours reveal artisanal manufacturing stages: throwing, molding, freehand painting, glazing, and firing. Traditional Breton motif decorations—little Breton figures, stylized flowers, rural scenes—are transmitted generation to generation. The museum displays rare pieces and three centuries of stylistic evolution. The shop offers contemporary creations perpetuating tradition.

Quimper Old Town, a preserved medieval heart between the Odet and Steïr rivers. Cobbled lanes bordered by 15th and 16th-century half-timbered houses wind to the cathedral. Place au Beurre retains its painted façades and old shops. Rue Kéréon, the main shopping street, lines traditional boutiques and artisan workshops. Bridges spanning the rivers offer photographic perspectives on colorful façades reflected in water.

activities.text: Strolling along the Odet, a coastal river crossing Quimper in a verdant setting. Landscaped banks allow following quays from downtown to peripheral residential districts. Restored washhouses, watermills, and flowered footbridges punctuate the bucolic route. Swans and ducks animate calm waters while weeping willows create a romantic atmosphere. The Bishop's Gardens offer a haven of peace facing the cathedral.

Participating in the Cornouaille Festival in July, the largest Breton cultural festival created in 1923. For a week, concerts, costume parades, fest-noz, and bagad competitions animate the historic heart. The Grand Parade gathers 3,000 participants in traditional dress from different Breton regions. Stages host international Celtic and traditional music artists. Stalls offer local crafts and gastronomic specialties in a festive, popular atmosphere.

Traditional market at Les Halles Saint-François, an unmissable meeting for Quimper residents every Saturday morning. Stalls overflow with Cornouaille terroir products: market garden vegetables, farmhouse cheeses, artisan charcuterie, auction fish. Breton producers offer farmhouse cider, warm kouign-amann, salted butter cookies. The convivial atmosphere resonates with discussions in Breton and French. The 19th-century metal hall also houses restaurants and crêperies bustling all week.

Cruise on the Odet from Quimper to Bénodet, a river descent nicknamed France's most beautiful river. The boat glides between wooded banks dotted with Renaissance castles and manor houses. Meanders reveal secret coves, fishing villages, and wild islets. Commentary enlightens about history, fauna, and bank flora. The estuary opens onto the ocean offering spectacular views over Bénodet's fine sand beaches.

days_plan.itin_title: Brittany Road Trip: Villages with Character, Sea and History
Haunted Brittany in 6 days: From Brocéliande to the Lands of the Ankou
Finistère Circuit: Breton Headlands, Islands & Artists' Villages
Brittany 7 days: Pink Granite, Lighthouses & Peninsulas

visits.text: Built in a spiral around its bell tower, the village of Ramatuelle rises on Paillas hill and overlooks Pampelonne bay. The tight, inward-facing architecture once protected against Barbary invasions. Place de l'Ormeau, enlivened by terraces and the Provençal market, is now its beating heart. Park on the village outskirts—traffic within the village is restricted in summer.

days_plan.itin_title: Var in 4 Days: From Bormes to the Most Beautiful Villages of the Verdon

visits.text: The Château de Rambouillet, a 14th-century fortress that became a royal and then a presidential residence, preserves outstanding rocaille woodwork and the chamber where Francis I died in 1547. The first G6 summit was held here in 1975.

The Queen's Dairy, commissioned by Louis XVI for Marie-Antoinette between 1785 and 1787, houses Pierre Julien's sculptural group "Amalthea and the Nymph" in a neoclassical setting of marble and stucco.
The Shell Cottage conceals beneath its thatched roof one of Europe's finest mother-of-pearl and seashell decorations, created between 1779 and 1780 for the Princess de Lamballe.

The National Sheepfold, created by Louis XVI in 1786, houses France's only flock of Rambouillet merinos, direct descendants of sheep imported from Spain. Cows, goats, horses, and poultry complete the educational farm.

activities.text: Hike in Rambouillet forest, 14,550 hectares of oaks and pines classified as a "protected forest." The Étang d'Or trail or the Coupe-Gorge loop are among the most pleasant routes.
Head to the Espace Rambouillet to watch red deer, hinds, roe deer, and wild boar in open enclosures across 250 hectares of forest. The Forest of Eagles puts on a free-flight show of birds of prey.

Stroll through the gardens of the Château de Rambouillet, 150 hectares awarded the "Jardin remarquable" label, with canals, six islands, a formal French garden, and an 18th-century English garden. Access to the park is free.

days_plan.itin_title: Yvelines Road Trip: Versailles and Impressionist Villages

visits.text: Enter the heart of Réalmont to discover this royal bastide founded in 1272 on Philip the Bold's orders. The arcaded square, bordered by a double row of covered galleries, preserves the geometric rigor typical of medieval bastides.

Notre-Dame-du-Taur Church has a distinctive history: it began as a 17th-century Protestant church, converted into a Catholic church in 1628. Its square bell tower dates from 1712, and the nave contains four richly decorated chapels on each side.

Look for the Fontaine de la Fréjaire, a traditional 17th-century spring, and the washhouse dating from 1880. These small heritage features lie along a signposted historical route passing houses with overhanging upper floors and traces of former fortified gates.

Walk the streets that intersect at right angles, a hallmark of southwestern bastides. Here, every façade tells of builders past: half-timbered houses, upper floors wider than the ground floor, details carved in brick and stone.
The small Protestant church, understated but steeped in history, recalls that Réalmont was the scene of conflicts between Catholics and Huguenots during the Wars of Religion.

activities.text: On Wednesday mornings, Réalmont hosts the Tarn's oldest market. Local producers display cured meats, cheeses, fruits, and vegetables beneath the arcades. A friendly atmosphere is guaranteed.
Plan a return trip by car from Réalmont to reach the cascades d'Arifat, southeast of the town. A wooded footpath leads to these waterfalls deep in the forest, ideal for a refreshing break.
Go cycling or mountain biking on the rolling trails of central Tarn. Lake Bancalié, 15 minutes from Réalmont, offers canoeing, pedal boats, and fishing in a preserved natural setting.

days_plan.itin_title: Tarn Road Trip: Albi & Hilltop Villages

visits.text: The Nice refuge, managed by the CAF, sits at 2232 m altitude in the heart of the Mercantour, on the balcony opening toward the Cime du Gélas and the Vallée des Merveilles. It's the most iconic high-altitude bivouac in the Gordolasque, with a dormitory and classic alpine refuge half-board.
The Countet bridge, the valley-end parking area, is the starting point for the ascent. It's also where routes depart for Lac de la Fous and the Vallée des Merveilles on the western side.

activities.text: Climb to the Nice refuge from the Countet bridge, a waymarked granite trail. Budget 4h for the ascent, 900 m elevation gain, strenuous but without technical passages. Refuge reservation essential in summer.
Overnight at the refuge on half-board, early wake-up to see dawn over the border peaks. Option to continue next day to the Cime du Gélas (3143 m) or cross over to the Vallée des Merveilles.

days_plan.itin_title: Secret valleys of the Nice hinterland in 6 days

visits.text: Begin with Notre-Dame Cathedral: you will immediately understand why it was called the “queen of the churches of France” in the Middle Ages. Built from 1211 on the ruins left by a fire, it measures 149 metres long and 87 metres high and has 2,303 statues on its façade, a world record. This is where 33 kings of France were crowned, from Henry I in 1027 to Charles X in 1825. The Smiling Angel, on the left portal, has become the emblem of the city. Allow at least 1 hour 30 minutes, and arrive early in the morning to enjoy the light on the stained glass before the influx of tourists.

Right beside the cathedral, view the Palais du Tau from the outside, the former residence of the archbishops. This is where the kings prepared for their coronation and held their banquet that evening. The palace is closed to the public for renovation until 2027, so interior visits and access to the treasury are currently unavailable. The chasuble worn by Charles X at the last coronation in 1825, fragments of the cathedral's original statues and the reconstructed Sainte Ampoule cannot be seen during this closure.

Then push open the door of the Basilica of Saint-Remi, a few minutes' drive to the south. Its Romanesque nave dates from the 11th century and is 122 metres long, almost as long as the cathedral. The tomb of Saint Remi, who baptised Clovis in 496, stands at the centre of the Gothic choir beneath a 12th-century canopy. The whole site has been UNESCO-listed since 1991. The crowds are far thinner than at the cathedral: make the most of it.

activities.text: Go down into the Taittinger cellars, 18 metres underground in UNESCO-listed Gallo-Roman chalk quarries from the 4th century. What is remarkable here is the setting: galleries dug in a pyramid shape into the white chalk, the remains of the 13th-century Abbey of Saint-Nicaise destroyed during the Revolution, and the 15 million bottles ageing in total darkness at 10–12°C. The house completely renovated its tour in 2024. Booking in advance is essential.

The Pommery cellars are in a category of their own. In 1868 Madame Pommery launched “the construction project of the century”: 18 kilometres of galleries dug 30 metres down, linked by a monumental staircase of 116 steps. The galleries bear the names of the great cities of the world won over by the house over time. What sets Pommery apart is the contemporary art exhibition that changes every year in the heart of the chalk quarries — monumental installations by international artists in the chalk cellars. An unexpected sight.

In the evening, stroll around the cathedral quarter. Place du Parvis and Rue Chanzy are home to a good proportion of the city's café terraces. Take the chance to taste the pink biscuit of Reims, a must with a glass of champagne.

days_plan.itin_title: Eastern France by Train from Paris
Marne Road Trip: Reims, Épernay and Champagne

visits.text: In Relanges, Notre-Dame church is an extremely rare surviving example of 11th-century Romanesque art in southern Lorraine. A Cluniac priory was founded here around 1030 by Ricuin de Darney and his wife Lancède—in the pure Cluniac tradition of intercession for the souls of the deceased. The priory disappeared without a trace, but the church's facade gable is one of the few 11th-century remains still standing in the region. The nave and side aisles were rebuilt in the 16th century. Do not miss the upper washhouse in the village.

7 km north, the ruins of the priory of Bonneval at Saint-Baslemont deserve a stop for lovers of abandoned sites. Only walls and the outlines of a former church remain, but the chapel of Notre-Dame-des-Neiges (1861) still stands as guardian of the place. In Saint-Baslemont itself, the 16th-century church of Saint-Jean-Baptiste and the remains of the 11th-century Tour Séchelles complete the visit.

activities.text: This part of the southern Vosges—hedged farmland, agricultural plateaus, hamlets built of golden stone—is one of the least visited in the entire department. Take the opportunity to simply walk from Relanges along the marked trails around the village. There is something special about the late-afternoon light over these meadows, especially in May–June. The peace is absolute.

days_plan.itin_title: Vosges Abbey Trail: Monastic Heritage

visits.text: Remiremont has a distinction that few French towns can claim: its 18th-century canonesses' quarter has remained practically intact. The noble canonesses who belonged to this chapter—reserved for the aristocracy, it wasn't open to everyone—lived in these elegant residences around the abbey church of Saint-Pierre. The Romanesque crypt of the abbey is one of the last surviving traces of the monastery founded in the 7th century on the neighboring Saint-Mont by the monks Amé and Romaric. Audio guides are available at the Tourist Office to explore the quarter at your own pace.

The Musée Charles Friry is going to surprise you. Housed in a canoness's residence built in 1750 for the chapter's last dean, it preserves the collection assembled by Charles Friry, a prosecutor under King Louis-Philippe who bought the house in 1833 and spent fifty years filling it with paintings and art objects. The centerpiece: Le Vielleur à la sacoche by Georges de La Tour—one of forty known works by this 17th-century painter from Lorraine, long overlooked before being rediscovered in the 20th century. There are also prints by Rembrandt, Callot and Goya. The garden retains two 18th-century rocaille fountains listed as historic monuments. Open Wednesday to Sunday.

activities.text: Stroll along Rue de la Xavée, lined with arcaded porticoes and one of the most picturesque streets in Lorraine. Finish the day on the quays of the Moselle. For a panoramic view of the town and valley, climb to the chapel of Notre-Dame du Calvaire—the climb takes about twenty minutes from the center, and the view over the rooftops and wooded hills is worth the effort to end this itinerary in style.

days_plan.itin_title: Vosges Abbey Trail: Monastic Heritage
Vosges Road Trip: Lakes, Mountains & Thermal Spas

visits.text: Rencurel sits at the outlet of the Bourne gorges, where the valley opens onto meadows and hamlets scattered through forests. The village preserves a chapel and rural architecture typical of the Vercors—steep roofs, gallery farms, and stone walls. It's a transition village between the limestone cliff Royans and the gentler plateau that heralds Villard-de-Lans.

From the viewpoint above the village, you have a plunging view of the Bourne gorges you arrived through. The wooded ridges of the Quatre Montagnes extend to the east. It's a different framing from the cave: here, it's the overall geography of the Vercors that imposes itself.

activities.text: The hamlets and clearings loop around Rencurel (4-6 km, minimal elevation gain) crosses meadows and forest edges between the commune's scattered hamlets. In May-June, meadows blooming with gentians and wild orchids are spectacular. This kind of pastoral mid-mountain landscape is exactly what justifies the designation "Vercors Regional Natural Park."

The round trip to the gorges viewpoint from the village heights (about 45 minutes) follows a marked forest path. The view of the Bourne gorge cut between cliffs gives the measure of the relief you've just traversed from Pont-en-Royans.

days_plan.itin_title: Royans-Vercors Road Trip: Hilltop Villages and Gorges

visits.text: Palace of the Parliament of Brittany. A 17th-century masterpiece designed by Salomon de Brosse, this iconic monument still houses the Brittany Court of Appeal. Miraculously saved from the 1994 fire, it reveals on guided tours the splendor of the Grand'Chambre and its coffered ceilings adorned with paintings by Noël Coypel, the only intact example of Charles Errard's work in France. The carved and gilded woodwork embodies all the prestige of grand French royal decoration.

Portes Mordelaises. This twin-towered medieval gatehouse marks the former main entrance to the fortified city. Rebuilt in the 15th century, it testifies to Rennes' defensive past with its double drawbridge and characteristic machicolations. The coats of arms of the Dukes of Brittany still adorn the stone, recalling that future dukes had to swear here to defend Breton liberties before being crowned at the cathedral. The rampart gardens, landscaped in 2022, offer a peaceful walk along the ancient walls.

Rennes Historic Center. The multicolored half-timbered houses of Place des Lices and Rue Saint-Michel form one of the finest medieval ensembles in Brittany, miraculously spared by the great fire of 1720. Wander the cobbled streets to Saint-Pierre Cathedral with its neoclassical interior, then discover Place de la Mairie with its town hall designed by Jacques Gabriel. The blend of medieval and classical architecture creates a unique atmosphere, where nearly 400 half-timbered houses stand alongside elegant 18th-century facades.

Thabor Park. Designated a Jardin Remarquable, this 10-hectare green lung was originally the orchard of Saint-Melaine Abbey. Landscape architect Denis Bühler transformed it in the 19th century into a romantic haven blending a French formal garden, an English landscape garden, and a botanical garden. Over 3,000 plant species flourish among the shaded paths, the rose garden has 2,000 varieties, and the old aviaries house exotic birds. Sculptures from the School of Fine Arts punctuate the walk, creating living tableaux at every turn.

Palace of the Parliament of Brittany. A 17th-century masterpiece where the prestige of Breton power still resonates, this palace designed by Salomon de Brosse continues to house the Court of Appeal. The Grand'Chambre's coffered ceilings, gilded woodwork, and paintings by Noël Coypel testify to the splendor of French royal decoration. The guided tour reveals these historic spaces and their spectacular rescue after the 1994 fire.

Portes Mordelaises. This fortified gatehouse flanked by two massive towers marked the ceremonial entrance to the former ducal city. Future Dukes of Brittany swore here to defend Breton liberties before being crowned. The 15th-century fortifications, with their ducal coats of arms, drawbridge, and machicolations, recall the defensive strength of the Breton capital. The rampart gardens invite a peaceful walk along the former defenses.

Historic Center and Half-Timbered Houses. Place des Lices and Rue Saint-Michel bring together nearly 400 colorful medieval half-timbered houses, miraculously spared by the great fire of 1720. This exceptional architectural ensemble contrasts with the elegant 18th-century neoclassical facades built after the disaster. Saint-Pierre Cathedral and its sumptuous interior, Place de la Mairie with Jacques Gabriel's town hall, and the cobbled lanes create an urban setting rich in heritage.

Thabor Park. This 10-hectare remarkable garden combines a French formal garden, an English landscape garden, and a botanical garden in a romantic ensemble masterfully designed by Denis Bühler in the 19th century. Its 3,000 plant species, rose garden with 2,000 varieties, old aviaries housing exotic birds, and sculptures from the School of Fine Arts create an enchanting world of greenery. This former orchard of Saint-Melaine Abbey has become Rennes residents' favorite green lung.

activities.text: Marché des Lices. Every Saturday morning, this century-old market brings the square to life with over 300 vendors offering the finest Breton local products. The convivial and authentic atmosphere makes it one of France's most beautiful markets, where galettes-saucisses, farmhouse cheeses, artisanal cider, and organic vegetables attract locals and visitors. Arrive early to enjoy the freshness of the fish and seafood delivered directly from Breton ports to the stalls.

Promenade des Bonnets Rouges and Street Art. Along the Saint-Martin Canal and in the Maurepas-Bellangerais neighborhood, Rennes displays one of France's most important street art collections. The signposted route reveals monumental murals, stencils, and installations by international artists. The Teenage Kicks festival enriches this open-air museum each year. The canal banks also offer a pleasant green walkway popular with joggers and cyclists.

Shopping and Gastronomy on Rue Saint-Georges. This pedestrian shopping street brings together designer boutiques, concept stores, independent bookstores, and trendy restaurants. The Saint-Georges neighborhood blends historic heritage with contemporary life, with private mansions transformed into art galleries and vaulted cellars converted into wine bars. Terraces come alive in fine weather, creating an unexpectedly Mediterranean atmosphere in the heart of Brittany.

Écomusée du Pays de Rennes. Fifteen kilometers from Rennes, this reconstructed 16th-century Breton farm presents traditional rural life with its period buildings, local-breed animals, and vegetable gardens. Craft demonstrations (blacksmithing, weaving, bread-making) and children's workshops bring ancestral skills back to life. The outdoor route passes through orchards preserving heritage varieties, an educational pond, and a display of old agricultural machinery.

Promenade des Bonnets Rouges and Street Art. Along the Saint-Martin Canal and in the Maurepas-Bellangerais neighborhood, Rennes displays one of France's most important street art collections. The signposted route reveals monumental murals, stencils, and installations by international artists. The Teenage Kicks festival enriches this open-air museum each year. The canal banks also offer a pleasant green walkway popular with joggers and cyclists.

Saint-Georges Pool. This Art Deco jewel, listed as a historic monument since 1995, continues to operate as a municipal pool while offering an exceptional architectural setting. Polychrome mosaics, colored stained glass, wooden changing cubicles, and ornamental sculptures create a unique atmosphere dating from 1926. It's one of France's most beautiful historic pools still in operation, allowing visitors to swim in a preserved period setting.

Shopping and Gastronomy on Rue Saint-Georges. This pedestrian shopping street brings together designer boutiques, concept stores, independent bookstores, and trendy restaurants. The Saint-Georges neighborhood blends historic heritage with contemporary life, with private mansions transformed into art galleries and vaulted cellars converted into wine bars. Terraces come alive in fine weather, creating an unexpectedly Mediterranean atmosphere in the heart of Brittany.

visits.text: The Fondurane biological reserve covers about forty hectares west of Lake Saint-Cassien and has been protected by a habitat protection decree since 1988. Wetlands, birds and a quiet atmosphere: it's the exact opposite of the lake's recreation areas. Fishing is restricted and regulated here. Come in the morning, when the shores are silent.

activities.text: Take the Fondurane trail from Montauroux: it follows an arm of Lake Saint-Cassien, passes a bird hide and crosses the Biançon bridge. The mosaic of habitats attracts many migratory birds. The tracks are wide and also used by mountain bikers. Binoculars are essential; otherwise, you'll see water and trees.

days_plan.itin_title: Roquebrune-sur-Argens: sea, villages and the Var in 10 days

visits.text: Church of Saint-Nicolas. This 16th-century Flamboyant Gothic church dominates the town with its high square tower. The interior shelters beautiful Renaissance stained glass windows and remarkable liturgical furnishings. Ribbed vaults and side chapels testify to the prosperity of this merchant town on the route to Flanders.

Museum of the Rethel Region. Housed in the former town hall, the museum presents local history from Gallo-Roman times. Archaeological collections, sacred art objects, and testimonies from both World Wars tell the turbulent past of this frontier town. The section dedicated to boudin blanc evokes Rethel's gastronomic renown.

Old town and built heritage. Pedestrian streets reveal ancient stone and brick dwellings typical of Ardennes architecture. The central square bordered by arcades once hosted the three annual fairs that enriched the town. Restored half-timbered houses stand alongside 18th-century private mansions.

activities.text: Tasting boudin blanc de Rethel. World capital of this specialty benefiting from PGI certification, Rethel has perpetuated since the 17th century the recipe for this delicate dish. Composed solely of pork, milk, eggs, and shallots without breadcrumbs or starch, it's enjoyed pan-fried in butter accompanied by apple compote. Artisan charcuteries also offer truffle or forest mushroom versions.

Traditional market. The weekly market unfolds its stalls of farm products, cheeses, cured meats, and Ardennes specialties. Local producers offer seasonal vegetables, honey, craft beers, and homemade pastries. The friendly atmosphere and authentic flavors invite discovery of the terroir.

Stroll along the Ardennes Canal. Follow the shaded banks of this waterway connecting the Meuse to the Aisne over 88 km. The restored towpath offers a flat route ideal for walking or cycling between locks and old bridges. Observe pleasure barges, fishermen, and aquatic birds in a peaceful atmosphere.

days_plan.itin_title: Ardennes Road Trip: Forests & Fortresses (3 Days)

places.name: Revin

visits.text: Viewpoint of the Dames de Meuse. Perched at 393 meters altitude, this belvedere offers vertiginous panoramas over the loop the Meuse draws 200 meters below. The river almost completely encircles the Dames peninsula in a spectacular meander. Legend tells that three sisters transformed into rocks eternally watch over the valley.

Museum of Old Revin. Housed in an ancient dwelling, the museum traces the industrial history of this working-class town marked by metallurgy. Collections of tools, period photographs, and testimonies evoke work in forges and rolling mills. The section devoted to slate recalls the importance of this extractive industry in the massif.

activities.text: Hike in the Ardennes forest. Steep trails climb toward ridges dominating the Meuse through century-old beech and oak groves. Outcropping rocks, deep ravines, and fern undergrowth compose a wild and mysterious setting. Viewpoints reward effort with grandiose panoramas over the narrow valley.

Canoeing on the Meuse. Descend the river with the current between steep cliffs and forests plunging into the water. The tranquil route allows observation of riparian wildlife and access to viewpoints unreachable by road. Rental companies offer various packages from a few hours to a full day.

Climbing on schistose rocks. Schist and quartzite cliffs attract climbers to equipped routes of all levels. Walls overhanging the Meuse offer spectacular setting and quality rock. Climbing sites are distributed throughout the valley with free access for autonomous practitioners.

days_plan.itin_title: Ardennes Road Trip: Forests & Fortresses (3 Days)

map_keywords: Point de Vue des Dames de Meuse Revin

visits.text: Richelieu is a unique masterpiece of 17th-century urban planning. Founded in 1631 by the Cardinal and designed by Jacques Lemercier (architect of the Sorbonne), this "ideal city" follows a grid plan enclosed by ramparts and moats, accessible through three monumental gates.

Walk down the Grande Rue, 12 meters wide, lined with 28 identical townhouses, all listed as historic monuments. Regularity, symmetry, and perfect alignment: the Cardinal's spirit can be seen in every façade.

The market halls, completed in 1638, are a fine example of functional architecture from the Grand Siècle. They still host a market on Friday mornings, opposite the Notre-Dame-de-l'Assomption Church in classical style.

The Espace Richelieu, housed in a restored townhouse, offers an interactive exhibit on the Cardinal, his city, and new towns. 3D glasses let you immerse yourself in the splendor of the château that no longer exists.

The Richelieu Museum displays art collections that belonged to the Cardinal, a great patron and collector: portraits by Philippe de Champaigne, engravings by Jean Marot showing the château as it was, and a model of the town.

Stroll through the château park, 475 hectares enclosed by walls. Of the palace that inspired Versailles, what remains is the Dome Pavilion, the orangery, the cellars, and the entrance bridge. Nearly 2,000 workers labored on this titanic construction project.

activities.text: Hop on a bike along the Richelieu-Chinon Greenway, 20 km on a former railway line through unspoiled nature in the Loire-Anjou-Touraine Regional Nature Park.
Walk around the ramparts and moats. The fourth gate, a fake, was created solely to respect the ensemble's symmetry—a detail that sums up the Cardinal's spirit.
In summer, visit the shops of artisans and secondhand dealers occupying some fifteen premises in the city.

days_plan.itin_title: Vienne Road Trip: Futuroscope and Romanesque Heritage

visits.text: The Cathedral of Sainte-Marie in Rieux, despite its small size, was the seat of a bishopric. Built in the 14th century, it presents a rare octagonal plan. Its tower-belfry dominates the Arize valley.
The medieval bridge spans the Arize River. Rebuilt several times over the centuries, it links the two banks of Rieux.

activities.text: The Volvestre is known for foie gras and ceramics. Pottery workshops continue an ancient tradition. You can visit some workshops by appointment.
The Arize River is renowned for trout fishing. The shaded banks offer lovely spots to fish or simply walk.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Garonne Road Trip: From Toulouse to the Pyrenees

visits.text: At the entrance to Riez, in a field on the left-hand side of the road, you will come across four monolithic columns of grey Estérel granite, 5.90 metres high and topped with white marble Corinthian capitals. They are all that remains of a tetrastyle temple dedicated to Apollo, erected in the 1st century CE, and were included on the first list of Historic Monuments in 1840. Riez is no ordinary village: under the name Colonia Julia Augusta Reiorum Apollinaris, it was one of the 13 cities with Latin rights in Gallia Narbonensis. At its height in the 2nd century, the town covered 20 hectares and had two bath complexes, a theatre and several necropolises.

The early Christian baptistery (5th century) is one of the few buildings of its kind preserved in Provence. Behind its austere square exterior lies an octagonal room with eight granite columns, Corinthian marble capitals and a baptismal immersion pool used one night a year during the Easter ceremony. Comparable to the baptistery in Fréjus, it has been listed as a Historic Monument since 1840.

In the old town, enter through the Porte Saint-Sols to reach the Grande-Rue and its Renaissance façades. Look for the Hôtel de Mazan (1523): its staircase with four twisted columns is adorned with gypseries, the moulded and carved plasterwork for which Riez is known. As there was no dressed stone nearby, the people of Riez covered everything with sculpted plaster: façades, fireplaces, ceilings and staircases. Then climb to the 17th-century Chapel of Saint-Maxime on the hill for a panoramic view over the three valleys.

activities.text: The Wednesday and Saturday morning market is one of the largest in the region — held for centuries under the plane trees on the central square. In winter (December–February), a truffle market takes place on Wednesday mornings. The transhumance festival (third or fourth Sunday in June) is a major event: sheep cross the village heading up to the mountain pastures.

Riez sits at the heart of Verdon Regional Natural Park: Lake Sainte-Croix (2,200 hectares, the largest of the Verdon lakes) is 14 km away. If the weather is favourable, an afternoon on or beside the water is a fine option before heading to Moustiers the next day.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpes-de-Haute-Provence Tour: Lavender and Hilltop Villages
Forcalquier & Verdon Gorges Road Trip
Alpine Hinterland and Verdon Gorges: From Thorenc to Riez

places.name: Riom Es Montagnes

visits.text: The old town of Riom-ès-Montagnes has old houses clustered around the parish church, with the atmosphere of an authentic mountain town. The nerve centre of the Pays Gentiane, this small town retains the character of Cantal villages where lava stone bears witness to the territory's volcanic origins.

The Maison de la Gentiane et des Plantes d'Auvergne reveals the secrets of this iconic plant with its yellow root that grows on high-altitude pastures. Interactive museum displays, a botanical garden and an educational distillery trace the history of traditional harvesting and processing into liqueur. The yellow gentian, hand-picked on the summer pastures, remains a powerful symbol of mountainous Auvergne.

activities.text: A visit to a gentian distillery reveals the ancestral techniques for producing the famous liqueur. The roots macerate for several years before distillation to release their characteristic bitter aromas. A comparative tasting between different expressions (Avèze, Salers Gentiane) allows you to appreciate the nuances of this quintessentially Auvergnat spirit.

Hiking on the plateau offers scenic escapes through summer pasture landscapes where Salers cattle graze. These vast green expanses dotted with abandoned burons tell the pastoral story of Cantal. Trails wind between heather moors and flowering meadows with views of the surrounding mountains.

days_plan.itin_title: Cantal Road Trip: Auvergne Volcanoes and Mountain Traditions

map_keywords: House of Gentian and Auvergne Plants

visits.text: Riquewihr had the fortune to pass through both world wars without a single bombing—its relative geographic isolation earned it this miraculous preservation. The result: 300 half-timbered houses from the 13th to 18th centuries, intact, in a village of 1,200 inhabitants surrounded by 368 hectares of vineyards. Listed among France's Most Beautiful Villages since 1982, it attracts over 1.5 million visitors per year. Arrive at opening time or late afternoon—during the day, the main street is packed.

The Dolder, a 25-meter bell tower erected in 1291 along with the first fortified enceinte, is Riquewihr's symbol. Its Alsatian name means 'the highest point.' On the exterior side, it's austere and defensive; on the town side, it presents a half-timbered façade. Climb to the museum at the top for views over the rooftops and vineyard—from up there you understand better why the two grand crus Schoenenbourg and Sporen surround the village.

The 13th-century Thieves' Tower—former prison of the Wurtemberg seigneury—preserves its medieval torture instruments and the interior of a 16th-century winemaker's house. The atmosphere is dark and authentic, very different from the picturesque main street. Not to be confused with the castle of the counts of Wurtemberg-Montbéliard, a 16th-century Renaissance building that today houses a museum of communication in Alsace.

activities.text: Push through the doorways into interior courtyards—behind the main street façades lie winemakers' cellars that welcome visitors for tastings. About fifteen family estates still produce the village's two grand crus: Schoenenbourg, renowned since the 16th century for its rieslings of remarkable minerality and longevity, and Sporen, more clay-and-marl, the preferred terrain of gewürztraminer.

The vineyard trail of the Grands Crus starts from rue de la Piscine and winds through the vines of Schoenenbourg and Sporen. In summer, winemakers lead guided tours followed by free tastings. Allow 90 minutes for the complete circuit. It's the best way to understand the soils and topography that make Riquewihr wines distinctive.

Make the 5 km detour to Ribeauvillé, at the foot of the Vosges. A marked 7 km circuit (2h30) connects its three ruined medieval castles perched on the ridges: Saint-Ulrich castle, Girsberg, and Haut-Ribeaupierre. The panorama from each embraces the Alsace plain and the vineyards below.
