visits.text: Riverie is a small upland village ringed with remnants of medieval ramparts, with cobbled lanes and a keep. The village attracts few visitors, which is precisely its charm: you feel as though you're discovering a place everyone has forgotten. The view from the lookout over the Rhône valley and the Pilat foothills is one of the finest on the Lyonnais Mountains section of the route.

The viewpoint facing the Pilat and the Rhône valley deserves a long pause. On the horizon, on clear days, you can make out the terrain of the Massif Central to the west and the Pilat to the south—a panorama that gives a full sense of the scale of the circuit you're following around Lyon.

activities.text: Rampart tour and climb to the village's high point (~1 km, 30 min). The walkway follows the vestiges of the medieval walls.
Ridge walk toward neighboring terraces with views over the Lyonnais valleys (2–3 km, ~1 hour). The landscape of meadows and bocage is typical of this part of the Lyonnais Mountains.

days_plan.itin_title: Loop Around Lyon: Villages and Pierres Dorées

visits.text: Joseph-Déchelette Museum. This art and archaeology museum occupies a beautiful 18th-century townhouse. Collections trace Roannais history from prehistory onward. Gallo-Roman ceramics, archaeological artifacts from the Joeuvres site, paintings, and sculptures fill the galleries. Joseph Déchelette, an eminent early 20th-century archaeologist, contributed enormously to local heritage knowledge. The museum notably preserves bronze statuettes from the 1st century BCE discovered at the Celtic oppidum of Joeuvres.

Marina and Roanne–Digoin Canal. The Loire riverbanks, redeveloped in 2021, offer a pleasant place to walk just steps from the town center. Water play areas, slides and sports grounds enliven the banks. The marina welcomes barges and river cruise boats. The Roanne–Digoin Canal connects the Loire to the Saône, a route popular with cyclists on the Véloire. Contemporary architecture integrated into the landscape completes this urban development.

Old town of Roanne. Shopping streets, the Halles Diderot and the place du Marché form the historic heart. The market halls host local producers, charcuterie sellers, cheesemongers and vegetable growers. On Fridays, a large weekly market takes over the place du Marché. Old quarters with burgher houses and restored façades bear witness to the past prosperity of this town of 35,000 inhabitants, situated at the crossroads of Burgundy, Beaujolais and Forez.

activities.text: Roanne Gastronomy. Roanne is world-famous for Maison Troisgros, a restaurant with three Michelin stars since 1968, now located in Ouches on the Bois sans Feuilles estate. César Troisgros carries on the family tradition. Le Central, the Troisgros family's brasserie in the town center opposite the station, serves inventive home-style cooking in a convivial atmosphere. The Praluline, a brioche with pink pralines created in 1955 by Auguste Pralus, is sold still warm at the Halles Diderot every morning. Numerous quality restaurants in the town center.

Roanne market. On Fridays, the market takes over the town center. Producers from haut-Beaujolais, Forez and the Côte Roannaise offer charcuterie, goat cheeses, organic vegetables and AOC wines. A lively atmosphere brings together residents and visitors. The Halles Diderot operate every morning with their permanent shops.

days_plan.itin_title: Loire Circuit: Wild Gorges and Industrial Heritage

visits.text: Thirty-five meters in diameter, a seventy-five-meter drop before reaching the underground river. In the Middle Ages, local tradition in the Lot said the frustrated Devil had dug this hole with a kick of his hoof—as good an explanation as any for a chasm nobody understood. More down-to-earth: villagers threw the bodies of executed criminals and people who had died by suicide into it, since they couldn't be buried in consecrated ground. Édouard-Alfred Martel, in 1889, found several medieval human skeletons at the bottom. Today the underground network spans 50 km of identified passages—including some branches that nobody has yet explored. The boat ride on the river covers 500 meters at a constant 13°C. Bring a jacket, really. Ticket €17, booking required in season.

Arriving via the l'Hospitalet viewpoint—on the east side, before descending into town—is a must. You look down over the entire town: village, sanctuaries, castle, each at a different level of the cliff, with a 150-meter difference in elevation. It's dizzying and somewhat absurd, like a town built by someone who wasn't afraid of heights. Park at l'Hospitalet and walk down rather than taking the shuttle—the descent gives you a sense of the scale of the place. The sanctuary originated around 1166 with the discovery of an incorrupt body in a cave; in the 12th–13th centuries, hundreds of thousands of pilgrims climbed here each year. The third-ranking pilgrimage destination in Western Christendom after Rome and Santiago de Compostela. Henry II Plantagenet comes here barefoot in 1170—shortly after indirectly commissioning the assassination of Thomas Becket. Kings confess too.

Pilgrims used to climb the 216 steps of the Pilgrims' Stairway on their knees, stopping at each step to pray, weighed down with chains symbolizing their sins. Henry II did this for a full week. In the Notre-Dame Chapel at the top: the Black Virgin, a 70 cm walnut-wood statue from the 12th century, still venerated today. And embedded in the cliff above, Durandal—Roland's sword. According to tradition, the dying Roland is said to have thrown it from Roncesvalles toward Rocamadour in 778 to protect it from the Saracens. Six hundred kilometers as the crow flies. Physically impossible, but the sword has been there since the 12th century. For 800 years, the neighboring pilgrims' cemetery receives those who die en route—notably in 1348–1350, when thousands of sick people flock to the Black Virgin during the Black Death. Most die there. Castle ticket €3, sanctuaries free.

activities.text: Lunch in Padirac village or at Auberge de Padirac, regional Lot cuisine, €25-40. No particular atmosphere, but the meal between the chasm and Rocamadour is welcome.

Overnight in Rocamadour (Chez Anne-Marie, simple food €30–40, or Le Balcon au Château with a view down from above €60–90) or in Cahors (1 hour southwest, Michelin-starred Le Balandre €60–100). Cahors is worth the detour for the 14th-century Pont Valentré—6 fortified towers over the Lot, and the local legend of the Devil who is said to have helped build it in exchange for the first soul to cross it.

days_plan.itin_title: Lot Itinerary: Cahors, Rocamadour & the Lot Valley
Haunted Southwest - 5 Days from Périgord Noir to the Cathar Castles
Midi-Pyrénées Circuit: Bastides, Cliffs and Abbeys
The Most Beautiful Villages of Lot and Périgord in 6 Days

visits.text: The wind often whistles across this viewpoint: the Roche d'Oëtre overlooks the Rouvre gorges from a height of 118 meters, at Saint-Philbert-sur-Orne. The viewpoint is free to access and has been developed for visitors.

days_plan.itin_title: Cotentin, Pays d'Auge: 5 days exploring the most beautiful villages

visits.text: Le Chalard is one of the most unassuming and surprising villages in Limousin; allow for a round trip during the day from Rochechouart. The village grew around an abbey founded in 1088 by Saint Geoffroy, and the Romanesque church built from 1096—consecrated in 1100—is its heart. It houses Saint Geoffroy's tomb, protected by a 15th-century cabinet, and a chapel decorated with frescoes. The English occupied the site from 1419 to 1421 during the Hundred Years' War and fortified its walls—the supports of the wall walk are still visible. Then open the small door at the church's eastern end: you discover the monks' cemetery, around forty graves from the 12th to 15th centuries whose carved stones display symbols of trades (weaver, blacksmith, cleric). It is one of the most intact groups of medieval tombs in France.

Right next to the church in Le Chalard, do not walk past the Maison de l'Or without going in; allow for a round trip during the day from Rochechouart. Limousin is one of France's most gold-rich regions, and Le Chalard has kept the memory of this most alive—gold mines were worked here as far back as the Gallic period, and the permanent exhibition traces this entire history through models, films and objects. Allow 45 minutes. If you are visiting with children, the gold-prospecting workshop is a great choice.

The Château de Châlus-Chabrol is an 11th-century fortress perched on a rocky spur above the town of Châlus; allow for a round trip during the day from Rochechouart. Its history revolves around one date: on March 26, 1199, Richard the Lionheart, King of England and Duke of Aquitaine, is inspecting the defenses of the castle he is besieging when Pierre Basile hits him with a crossbow bolt fired from the keep. Gangrene does the rest: Richard dies in this castle on April 6, 1199, aged 42, in the arms of his mother, Eleanor of Aquitaine. Before dying, he requested that his entrails be placed in the castle chapel. You can still see the chapel and the keep from which the fatal bolt was fired. The view from the ramparts over the Limousin countryside is worth the detour.

activities.text: After Le Chalard, stop on the medieval Pont de la Tour below the village; allow for a round trip during the day from Rochechouart. This bridge with pointed arches and cutwaters marks the historic boundary between Limousin and Périgord. It is a good place for a photo stop.

The route between Châlus and Rochechouart crosses through the heart of the Périgord-Limousin Regional Natural Park. Take the small roads—the D87 or secondary routes toward Dournazac—rather than the main highway: granite hamlets, ponds, and chestnut forests roll past at a pace that makes you want to stop. These roads are lightly trafficked and pleasant to drive in any season.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Vienne Tour: Limoges, Porcelain and Villages
Haute-Vienne Road Trip: Castles and Périgord-Limousin

visits.text: Rochecolombe is one of Ardèche's most discreet villages, but its rocky peak and medieval lanes deserve the detour. The Château de Rochecolombe, mentioned as early as the 11th century, was long the residence of the lords of Vogüé before they moved to Vogüé in the 17th century. What remains of the castle is the Chapelle Saint-Barthélémy, several of whose architectural elements were transferred to Vogüé castle during reconstruction: the 16th-century bas-relief of the twelve Apostles, a monstrance and a 13th-century coat of arms. Climb to the ruins for views over the surrounding hills and valleys.

The lower village lanes cling to the limestone peak's flank: tightly packed medieval houses, remnants of the enclosure surfacing between buildings, small covered passages. Take time to wander between upper and lower village to read how the village developed on the rocky ledge over the centuries. Near the village, the hamlet of Sauveplantade shelters a small Romanesque church dating to the Early Middle Ages.

The Cascade de Rochecolombe, accessible via a short trail (20 min one-way), is particularly spectacular after Cévennes rains. The stream tumbles through a setting of cliffs and wild vegetation. In dry weather, the trickle is modest, but the setting remains pleasant for a cooling break.

activities.text: The short loop around the peak (2 to 3 km) starts from the parking lot and circles the castle rock with interpretive points about the site. Ideal in late afternoon when low light enhances the limestone. Figure 1h to 1h30 with stops.

From Rochecolombe, the small road circuit that reaches the viewpoint above the village lets you appreciate the site's layout from outside. You'll have an overview of the peak, village and surrounding wooded hills—useful perspective for understanding the defensive choice of this site.

days_plan.itin_title: The 18 Most Beautiful Villages of Ardèche

visits.text: The Corderie Royale in Rochefort, built between 1666 and 1669, is 374 meters long—longer than the Eiffel Tower is tall. This factory supplied rope to the French royal navy for two centuries. The Centre International de la Mer presents the arsenal's history and ropework techniques.

The Louis XV dry dock saw the rebirth of the Hermione, a replica of the frigate that carried La Fayette to America in 1780, rebuilt over 17 years by shipwrights. The ship has now left for restoration and can no longer be visited in Rochefort. The dock and the arsenal workshops can be seen from the quays, a short walk from the Corderie Royale.

The National Naval Museum occupies Hôtel de Cheusses, Rochefort's oldest civilian building. Models of ships built at the arsenal, navigation instruments, figureheads. The arsenal produced 550 ships between 1666 and 1927, including France's first submarine (Le Plongeur, 1863).

activities.text: Accro-mâts, in the Louis XV dry dock, recreates the Hermione's masts. A high ropes course 30 meters above the ground lets visitors experience the sensations of 18th-century topmen. Spectacular final zip line.

A walk through the Arsenal gardens: the Jardin des Retours, the Jardin de la Marine and the potager du Roy. Palm trees, tulip trees, begonias—plants brought back from maritime expeditions. Peace and shade overlooking the Charente.

The Rochefort transporter bridge (1900), the last of its kind in France, connected both banks of the Charente by a suspended gondola. Listed as a Historic Monument in 1976, restored between 2016 and 2020. Gondola crossings available.

days_plan.itin_title: Charente-Maritime Road Trip: La Rochelle, Île de Ré, Fort Boyard and Roman Saintonge

visits.text: Rochefort-en-Terre perches on a rocky outcrop overlooking the Gueuzon valley. Voted France's Favourite Village in 2016, classified Most Beautiful Villages of France and a Petite Cité de Caractère—the accolades are deserved. The village was born in the 12th century to control the passage between La Roche-Bernard and Malestroit. Arrive early in summer, before tourist coaches.

Climb to the castle, rebuilt in the early 20th century by American painter Alfred Klots, smitten with the village on first sight in 1903. He purchased the ruins of the 12th-century medieval fortress and transformed them into a home using reclaimed Gothic and Renaissance elements. Klots championed the village—he launched the flower-window contest whose tradition endures. The park is free to explore; enjoy the panoramic views.

Don't miss the Naïa Museum, housed in Alfred Klots's former studio glasshouse in the castle park. Opened in 2015, this private museum displays nearly 300 works of fantastical and visionary art—sculpture, painting, digital art—by over 100 international artists. The name comes from 'Naïa', a marginalised woman nicknamed the witch of Rochefort, who lived in the castle ruins at the turn of the 20th century. Go down into the medieval underground passage that forms part of the route—atmosphere guaranteed.

Reach the place du Puits, ringed by corbelled houses from the 16th and 17th centuries. Restored half-timbered façades, geraniums and ivy spilling from planters—this is the village postcard. In summer the historic centre is pedestrianised, which makes the wander even more pleasant.

Step into Notre-Dame-de-la-Tronchaye Church, blending Romanesque and flamboyant Gothic. A former chapel enlarged in the 16th and 17th centuries for a college of canons, it preserves a listed façade and listed choir stalls. Also take a look at the calvary in the adjoining graveyard.

The cobbled alleys climb between flower-decked granite houses. The rue Saint-Michel and the place des Halles concentrate the craft shops and art galleries. Every shop sign is styled in wrought iron—an attention to detail that adds to the charm. Don't miss the south-facing façades, where balconies overflow with flowers from May to October.

activities.text: Flower-planting is a Rochefort-en-Terre tradition since Alfred Klots created the window-flower contest in 1911, even offering his greenhouse to residents to overwinter plants. Since 1945 the custom continues; locals rival each other's creativity in balcony and façade displays. Look up—every house has its character.
Artisan studios line the village alleys. Potters, glassmakers, sculptors and local creators share their craft. Push open the welcoming doors and chat—one of Rochefort's pleasures.
If travelling with children, descend 15 minutes to Moulin Neuf recreation area: kayaking, paddling, pedaloes and zip-line on 15 wooded hectares. A perfect active break before the road ahead.

In December, the Christmas market transforms the village. Lights, decorated trees and craft stalls create an atmosphere famous region-wide. If you're in Morbihan this season, it's a worthwhile detour.

days_plan.itin_title: Brittany Road Trip: Villages with Character, Sea and History
Road Trip Morbihan: Gulf, Carnac and Breton Coast

visits.text: Roquebrune Rock rises to 373 meters and can be spotted from the A8 highway: a red mass set between the Maures and the Estérel, without truly belonging to either. At the summit, the monumental Trois Croix are the work of Bernar Venet, and the panorama stretches through 360°, from the sea to the Maures. Expect to use your hands as much as your feet: the last few meters require climbing with the help of cables.

Built in the 16th century, the Notre-Dame de la Roquette chapel belonged to a former Trinitarian convent, some ruins of which remain nearby. A forest fire severely damaged it in 1962, and tile thefts did the rest in the 1980s–1990s. The site is listed and the building is fragile: look, don't climb on it.

Locals call it the Saint Trou: a very narrow cleft in Roquebrune Rock with a legend attached. A young woman being pursued supposedly implored the Virgin, and the rock opened to let her pass; they say only virtuous souls can cross it. Trail markers peter out in this area and cairns take over: don't set out without a map.

activities.text: Park at the Pont d'Argens parking lot, facing the Saint-Roch chapel, to tackle the climb to the Trois Croix on Roquebrune Rock via the marked trail. Views of the Argens plain and the Estérel open up at the large rock slab halfway along. Access to the hills is restricted in summer according to fire risk: the prefecture publishes a map daily.

The Hautes Roques alternative route is not a family walk: sections equipped with cables, rock steps and a summit perched above the cliffs of Roquebrune Rock. It starts at the Hautes Roques parking lot, north of the hills. Hiking boots are essential, and turn back immediately if the rock is wet.

days_plan.itin_title: Roquebrune-sur-Argens: sea, villages and the Var in 10 days

places.name: Rocroi

visits.text: Fortress of Rocroi. Unique in France for its perfectly preserved star-shaped plan, this fortified town was created in 1555 by Henri II. Two concentric enclosures—the 16th-century pentagon and Vauban's decagon—encircle the town over nearly 4 km. Bastions, demi-lunes, and counterguards compose an exemplary defensive system of bastioned military architecture.

Museum of the Battle of Rocroi. In the former 17th-century guardhouse, relive the celebrated victory of young Duke d'Enghien over Spanish tercios on May 19, 1643. A model of 2,000 lead soldiers recreates the battle that marked the end of Spanish invincibility. The relief map details the town's fortified architecture in the 18th century.

Place d'Armes. The nerve center of the town, this pentagonal square sees ten radio-concentric streets converging toward the ramparts. The central fountain and ancient well recall urban organization designed for military life. Gray stone facades shelter cafés and boutiques in a timeless atmosphere.

activities.text: Walk the ramparts. The complete 4 km circuit on the covered way reveals the ingenuity of Vauban's system. Cross bastions, powder magazines, and casemates while enjoying panoramic views of the Ardennes plateau. Explanatory panels detail the evolution of fortifications from the 16th to 19th centuries.

Panoramic observation. From the heights of the bastions, contemplate the Ardennes landscape stretching to the horizon. The marshes that once protected the town have given way to undulating bocage and forests. On clear days, the Belgian Ardennes massif appears on the northern horizon.

days_plan.itin_title: Ardennes Road Trip: Forests & Fortresses (3 Days)

map_keywords: Musée de la Bataille de Rocroi

visits.text: The Soulages Museum opened in 2014 with nearly 500 works by the Rodez-born painter. The architecture by Catalan firm RCR Arquitectes features Corten steel that develops a patina over time. The galleries alternate between varying heights and half-light to showcase Soulages' creative periods.

Notre-Dame Cathedral required 300 years of construction, from the 13th to the 16th century. Its bell tower reaches 87 metres and offers a 360° view after climbing 400 steps. The interior houses ancient and contemporary stained glass windows, a monumental organ, and richly decorated choir stalls.

The Fenaille Museum holds the largest collection of statue-menhirs in Europe. These sculptures from the 3rd millennium BC remain enigmatic. The building occupies the Hôtel de Jouéry, saved from demolition in the early 20th century by Maurice Fenaille.

activities.text: Follow the historic centre trail available from the tourist office on Place de la Cité. The numbered route takes you past the Maison d'Armagnac, the bishop's palace, and Renaissance façades.

The market takes place on Wednesday and Saturday mornings. You'll find Aveyron specialities there: farçous, aligot, and Aubrac beef. The brasseries in the centre serve these dishes throughout the week.

days_plan.itin_title: Aveyron Road Trip: Causses, Tarn Gorges and Villages

visits.text: Rogliano gathers seven hamlets scattered across the mountains between 110 and 500 meters elevation. Bettolacce, Magna, Vignale, and Olivo reveal medieval chapels and square towers. The Church of San Michele in Bettolacce features a bell tower separated from the main building following the Pisan tradition.

Macinaggio centers around its marina, the largest in Cap Corse. This is where Pasquale Paoli landed in 1790 after 20 years in exile. The marina hosts shops and artisans in a peaceful atmosphere. Offshore, the Finocchiarola islands are classified as a nature reserve.

Barcaggio spreads its blonde sand beach at the tip of Cap Corse. The isolated hamlet faces the Giraglia islet crowned by its lighthouse. Corsican cows sometimes graze on the sand. The end-of-the-world atmosphere contrasts with the bustle of the east coast.

activities.text: The customs officers' trail runs from Macinaggio toward Centuri for 35 kilometers of wild coastline. The first section to Tamarone beach crosses maquis and secret coves. Count on 3 hours to Barcaggio with spectacular views of the sea and islands.

The beaches of Macinaggio and Tamarone attract visitors with their crystalline waters. Fine sand bordered by pines and eucalyptus. Popular snorkeling spot for observing fish and rocky seabeds in the marine reserve.

days_plan.itin_title: Upper Corsica Road Trip: Cap Corse and Balagne

visits.text: Discover this imposing collegiate church built from 837 onwards. Listed as a Historical Monument since 1840, it blends Romanesque and Gothic architecture. Admire the 14th-century murals in the choir and the embroidered tapestry of the Mystery of the Passion from the 16th century.

Immerse yourself in 4,000 years of footwear history in this former 17th-century convent. Romans was France's luxury shoe capital. The museum displays 16,000 pairs from around the world, including creations by Charles Jourdan and André Pérugia.

Wander the cobbled streets of the historic center, designated a City and Land of Art and History. Admire the 47-meter-high Jacquemart Tower built in 1370, and visit the Old Bridge spanning the Isère since the 11th century. The Sunday morning market was voted France's favorite market.

Explore this medieval village, listed among the Most Beautiful Villages of France and named Favorite Village of the French 2025. Founded in 1070 around the abbey, which became a major pilgrimage site. Wander the maze of picturesque lanes paved with river stones and discover the craft workshops. About 19 km from Romans-sur-Isere, 20 minutes by road.

Visit this remarkable abbey church built between the 12th and 15th centuries, considered one of the most remarkable Gothic achievements in the Dauphiné. Listed as a Historic Monument since 1840, it has a magnificent sculpted doorway and the high altar holding the reliquary of Saint Anthony the Egyptian. About 19 km from Romans-sur-Isère, 20 minutes by road.

activities.text: Discover shoe manufacturing workshops still in operation. Observe every step of shoemaking. Workers share Romans' long tradition and the current revival of small local businesses.

Follow the playful trail of 12 giant shoes scattered throughout Romans' city center. These monumental sculptures pay tribute to the local shoe industry's history. The route covers approximately 3.4 kilometers and is accessible to all.

Housed in the former novitiate and the Grandes Écuries, the museum presents two permanent exhibitions on the history of the abbey in the Middle Ages and on cloister gardens. Discover the abbey's medieval garden. About 19 km from Romans-sur-Isère, 20 minutes by road.

days_plan.itin_title: Drome Provencale Road Trip: Villages and Terroirs

visits.text: The Musée de Sologne in Romorantin-Lanthenay is housed in the Moulin du Chapitre beside the Sauldre. This ethnographic museum unveils the secrets of a fascinating area through an immersive sensory journey. Collections trace Sologne's history, its natural environment of heaths and ponds, its pink-brick architecture, and ancestral customs. Old trades, hunting, and poaching are evoked through authentic objects and detailed reconstructions. Temporary exhibitions regularly enrich the visit. The connection to Francis I reveals Romorantin's prestigious past, when it nearly became the kingdom's capital.

Romorantin's Renaissance heritage bears witness to the era when Francis I considered establishing his capital here. The Hôtel Saint-Pol preserves its spiral staircase and remarkable Renaissance galleries. The chancellery has a sculpted façade with medallions and friezes. Half-timbered houses line the old lanes of the historic center. Canals and bridges spanning the Sauldre lend Venetian charm to the town. Saint-Étienne Church dominates the town with its tall tower. The remains evoke Leonardo da Vinci's wild project to divert the Loire and create a large navigable canal.

The Espace automobile Matra in Romorantin celebrates the history of this innovative car brand, which left its mark on French motor racing. The models on display trace Matra's technical and stylistic evolution since the 1960s. Racing cars that won the 24 Hours of Le Mans stand alongside production models like the Bagheera and Murena. Prototypes reveal the boldness of pioneering engineers. Period documents and photographs recount the saga of this French industrial adventure born in Sologne.

activities.text: Romorantin market in the covered market hall in the town center on Wednesday and Saturday mornings, bringing the whole neighborhood to life. Sologne producers offer game, poultry, goat cheeses and vegetables grown locally on family farms. Specialties such as Easter pâtés and fruit tarts delight food lovers. Flowers and vegetable seedlings attract amateur gardeners. The friendly atmosphere of the market is a chance to chat with locals and discover regional produce. The cafés welcome their regulars.

Walk through the Sauldre valley as it winds through wild Sologne. Marked trails follow the river lined with alders and weeping willows. Shimmering ponds attract herons, egrets, and kingfishers in an aquatic ballet. Forests of maritime pines and oaks shelter roe deer and wild boar. Heather-covered heaths evoke Maurice Genevoix's descriptions in Raboliot. The undisturbed silence invites contemplation and observation of unspoiled nature.

Discovering Sologne's architecture, characterized by red-brick houses and flat-tile roofs. Traditional farms have enclosed courtyards with living quarters, barns, and cattle sheds arranged around them. Bull's-eye dormers light the grain lofts. Monumental chimneys testify to the importance of heating in this damp region. Villages preserve Romanesque churches, communal washhouses, and restored bread ovens. This preserved vernacular architecture defines the visual identity of authentic rural Sologne.

days_plan.itin_title: Loir-et-Cher Itinerary: Royal Châteaux and the Loir Valley

visits.text: Cap Moderne brings together Eileen Gray's Villa E-1027 and Le Corbusier's Cabanon at the foot of Cap-Martin - one of the world's most important ensembles of modern architecture, now managed by the Centre des monuments nationaux. Villa E-1027 was designed between 1926 and 1929 by the Irish designer Eileen Gray and the architect Jean Badovici, her partner. Its name is a romantic code: E for Eileen, 10 for the J in Jean (the 10th letter), 2 for the B in Badovici, 7 for the G in Gray. Visits are by guided tour only, exclusively from April to October; booking on the CMN website is essential. Allow 2 hours for the visit; access is on foot from Roquebrune station.

Next to Villa E-1027, Le Corbusier built his famous Cabanon in 1952: exactly 3.66 m on each side, designed according to the Modulor, his proportional system based on the human body. He spent every summer there until his death by drowning on August 27, 1965, 50 meters away during his morning swim. The Cabanon has been inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage list since 2016 as part of "The Architectural Work of Le Corbusier" (17 sites, 7 countries). The site also includes l'Étoile de Mer (former bar-restaurant of Thomas Rebutato, Le Corbusier's friend) and the 1957 Camping Units.

Roquebrune Castle overlooks the medieval old village. Built in the 10th century by the counts of Ventimiglia to resist Saracen invasions, it's one of the oldest Carolingian castles still standing in France. It belonged to the Grimaldis from 1355 to 1848, when Roquebrune and Menton declared themselves free towns before voting to join France in 1860. The climb to the keep offers a view down over Monaco and the Mediterranean. Admission €5.

The medieval streets of old Roquebrune, perched 200 m above the sea, are among the Riviera's most intact: vaulted passages, narrow stairs carved in rock, houses clinging to the peak. The famous thousand-year-old olive tree (officially 2,000 years according to dating) stands apart, on the path descending toward Menton. A few tables on shaded squares for lunch without crowds.

activities.text: The Le Corbusier path (former customs officers' path) runs along the foot of Cap-Martin for about 6 km between Cabbé and Monte-Carlo Beach. Mediterranean vegetation, pebble coves, crystal-clear water. The path passes in front of Plage du Buse, a former haunt of Coco Chanel when she lived in her villa La Pausa on the heights above. Good shoes recommended; some rocky sections.
Swimming in coves along the path: Plage du Buse in particular, with warm water fed by underwater freshwater springs. Accessible only on foot. Pebbles, no facilities—bring water and a towel.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpes-Maritimes Road Trip: Riviera and Mercantour, 13 days
The 15 Gems of the French Riviera and Backcountry
7-Day French Riviera Circuit: Villefranche to Antibes

visits.text: Start with the Castrum: it's the part of Roquebrune-sur-Argens that has changed least since the year 1000. The fortified walls date from around the 10th century, and rue des Portiques below is lined with 16th-century arcaded houses beneath the belfry. Walk through in late afternoon, when the arcades cast patterns of shadow and the groups have left.

Built on remains from the 11th and 12th centuries, the Saint-Pierre-Saint-Paul parish church hides a far more spectacular interior than expected behind its restrained Gothic façade. It's listed on the historic monuments inventory. Step inside as you leave the Castrum—it's two minutes away: the contrast between outside and inside is what gives the visit its charm.

A free museum with an ice house beneath your feet: the Maison du Patrimoine occupies a former stable built in 1883 on impasse Barbacane, and its glass floor protects a 17th-century ice house discovered in 2002. The rest tells the story of the town from prehistory to the cork industry. Free entry, but closed on weekends outside the tourist season: check before heading up to the village.

activities.text: The smell of cocoa gives away the Maison du Chocolat et Cacao before you even see it: it occupies a former chapel in the old center of Roquebrune-sur-Argens and opened in June 2015. Inside, you follow the village's chocolate history and its famous Rocher, a lavender-honey nougat coated in chocolate.

If you have an extra hour, follow the 7 Fontaines route through the lanes and small squares of Roquebrune-sur-Argens. You'll pass the 18th-century Fontaine Vieille and the clock tower rising above the 16th-century ramparts. The map is free at the tourist office, and the route stays in the shade: perfect between 2pm and 4pm in summer.

days_plan.itin_title: Roquebrune-sur-Argens: sea, villages and the Var in 10 days

visits.text: The Roquefort Société caves welcome over 100,000 visitors a year. The one-hour guided tour takes you through natural caves carved beneath the Combalou rock. The fleurines naturally ventilate the caves at 10°C with 80% humidity.

Penicillium roqueforti develops spontaneously in the caves. This mould gives the cheese its characteristic blue-green marbling and flavours. The master refiners carefully select and cultivate their own strains.

Roquefort was the very first AOC in history, granted in 1925. It celebrates its centenary in 2025. The AOP requires raw Lacaune ewe's milk, daily pasturing within the Roquefort area, and ageing in natural caves.

activities.text: A tasting of the three Roquefort AOP cheeses concludes the visit. The caves also offer workshops pairing wine and cheese. The standard tour costs €7.50, or €15 for the tour with a guided tasting.
The village is home to seven Roquefort producers. Maison Gabriel Coulet offers a free self-guided tour with a presentation film. The Papillon caves also provide discovery tours.

days_plan.itin_title: Aveyron Road Trip: Causses, Tarn Gorges and Villages
Southeast France Road Trip: Perched Villages and Gorges

visits.text: Look at the outer walls of Roscoff's Notre-Dame-de-Croaz-Batz church: caravels are carved into the stone, paid for by shipowners who financed the building and sought divine protection for their fleet. Built between 1522 and 1545, with a Renaissance bell tower from 1575–1576, and listed as a historic monument as early as 1886. Also look for the carved figures of people and animals at the ends of the gables. Free entry, fifteen minutes suffice if you know where to look.

Selling onions door-to-door in the UK, by bicycle, sometimes for months: the Maison des Johnnies et de l'Oignon de Roscoff tells a story you'd think was invented. These Roscoff merchants crossed the Channel with their strings of onions, and the British called them Johnnies. The pink Roscoff onion earned its designation of origin in 2009. Guided tours at fixed times, reservations recommended.

People made a lot of money here, and it still shows: Roscoff's old port is lined with 16th- and 17th-century shipowners' houses, complete with turrets and carved dormers. The long pier extending into the sea allows you to board boats for Île de Batz even at low tide. It has undergone recent work, with departures shifted to Port du Bloscon depending on the tide: check the boarding point on the day.

Southern Hemisphere plants thriving in northern Finistère: Roscoff's Exotic and Botanical Garden grows amid a jumble of granite boulders, protected by both the Gulf Stream and rocks that block the wind. It brings together thousands of species. Climb the central rock for an unobstructed view over the bay of Morlaix and Île de Batz. Allow an hour. Closed in midwinter.

activities.text: The GR34 heading west from Roscoff passes Pointe de Perharidy, then reaches the forest of Santec and Pointe du Dossen, facing Île de Siec. About 10 km if you go all the way, flat and sandy, with stretches through pine woods that offer a change from the bare coast. At low tide you can reach the islet of Siec, but watch the time: the crossing is covered by the tide quickly.

Brittany 7 days: Pink Granite, Lighthouses & Peninsulas

visits.text: Saints-Pierre-et-Paul church (12th century) is one of the finest Romanesque edifices in Alsace. Its frieze of human and animal figures runs along the external cornice. Inside, sculpted capitals blend foliage, masks and fantastical motifs.
The Maison romane (circa 1152), on rue du Général-de-Gaulle, is considered one of the oldest stone civic constructions in Alsace. Its façade preserves Romanesque arcading and twin windows.
Four medieval gates survive in the ramparts: Porte du Lion, Porte de l'École, Porte Basse and Porte de la Vierge. Each retains sculpted door crowns, a unique vestige of Rosheim's medieval décor.
The six-bucket well on Place de la Mairie, and the 16th and 17th-century half-timbered houses complete a dense and homogeneous intra-muros heritage.
Follow the marked heritage route: panels explain the history of this former free imperial city, fortified as early as the 13th century.

activities.text: The Alsace Vineyard Green Way leaves from Rosheim on a disused railway line. By bike or on foot, it crosses vineyards and orchards to Saint-Nabor.
Drive up to Mont Sainte-Odile (13 km): the Pagan Wall, a 10-km megalithic enclosure, rings the summit. The monastery offers a panorama over the Alsace plain.
Rosheim winegrowers cultivate mainly Riesling and Pinot Gris. Cellars open along the main street offer tastings.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Est Road Trip: Vineyards, Ramparts and Forests

visits.text: La Piscine in Roubaix is a former Art Deco Olympic swimming pool dating from 1932, transformed into a museum of art and industry. A sheet of water remains from the pool, reflecting coloured glazing depicting the sun. The old shower cubicles now house a vast ceramics collection, and rooms display paintings, sculptures and textiles.

In Croix, Villa Cavrois is a manifesto of modernist architecture. Built between 1929 and 1932 for a textile industrialist, its 60-metre yellow brick façade overlooks a reflecting pool. The interior, entirely designed by the architect, features central heating, telephones in every room, and indirect lighting – visionary luxury for the era.
Walk through Parc Barbieux, a 34-hectare landscaped garden designed in the 19th century. Its paths wind between rolling lawns, flower beds and century-old trees.
La Condition Publique, a former 19th-century warehouse where wool was weighed and conditioned, has become a cultural and arts venue. Its vast red brick halls host exhibitions and performances.

activities.text: Follow the blue line painted on the ground from Roubaix station: it leads straight to La Piscine, through the town centre and past its repurposed industrial façades.
Roubaix was nicknamed the "city of a thousand chimneys" for its textile mills. Walk among the old red brick factories, some converted into lofts or cultural spaces.
The gardens of the Villa Cavrois extend the walk through a geometrically landscaped setting dotted with contemporary structures.

places.name: Rouen

visits.text: Great Clock — This fourteenth-century Gothic belfry houses one of Europe's oldest astronomical clocks, with a mechanism dating to 1389. The Renaissance arch, built between 1527 and 1529, spans the pedestrian street with its 2.5-meter gilded dial showing a sun with 24 rays against a starry blue background. A single hand marks the hour while a globe indicates the moon's phases.

Old Market Square — This is where Joan of Arc was burned on May 30, 1431. The Church of Saint-Joan of Arc, inaugurated in 1979, features an audacious architecture shaped like an inverted flame and houses Renaissance stained glass windows from the former Church of Saint-Vincent, destroyed during the war.

Saint-Ouen Abbey Church — A masterpiece of Rayonnant Gothic built between the fourteenth and sixteenth centuries, this former Benedictine abbey impresses with its 137 meters of length and fourteenth-century stained glass windows among the most complete in France. Its grand Cavaillé-Coll organ from 1890 features 64 stops.

Le Secq des Tournelles Museum — Housed in the former fifteenth-century Church of Saint-Laurent, this museum, unique in the world, presents 12,000 pieces of decorative ironwork from the third to the nineteenth centuries: signs, locks, grilles, and everyday objects testifying to the craftsmanship of master ironworkers.

Saint-Catherine Heights — From this 150-meter-high hill overlooking the left bank, embrace all of Rouen in one sweeping view: the cathedral painted by Monet, the spires of Gothic churches, the Seine's meanders. The viewpoint immortalized by Impressionist painters in the nineteenth century.

Jumièges Abbey — Founded in 654 by Saint Philibert, this "most beautiful ruin in France" according to Victor Hugo raises its 46-meter twin towers in the heart of a 15-hectare English-style park. Destroyed by the Vikings in 841 and later turned into a quarry after the Revolution, its Romanesque remains bear witness to Norman monastic power. About 20 km from Rouen, 20 minutes by road.

Rouen Cathedral — Immortalized by Monet in 30 paintings, this Gothic cathedral built from the twelfth to sixteenth centuries boasts the highest spire in France, reaching 151 meters. Its lace-like stone façade, the Butter Tower funded by Lenten dispensations, and the tomb of Richard the Lionheart make it a Norman heritage jewel.

activities.text: Joan of Arc Historical Museum — Set in the archbishop's palace where Joan was condemned and later exonerated, this immersive scenographic journey traces the Maid's destiny through testimony, projections, and reconstructions of the 1431 trial.

Eau-de-Robec Street — This picturesque cobbled street runs alongside a canal where dyers once washed their fabrics. Its half-timbered houses from the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, restored after the 1944 bombing, transport visitors into medieval Rouen.

Rouen Botanical Garden — This 8.5-hectare botanical garden, created in 1840, shelters over 5,600 plant species, tropical greenhouses, and a rose garden. A green haven in the city's heart, perfect for wandering among botanical collections and century-old trees.

Seine Meanders — Take the free ferry route crossing the river between Jumièges and Duclair. These landscapes of meandering waters bordered by orchards, limestone cliffs, and Norman villages inspired Impressionist painters in the nineteenth century.

Fruit Route — Between Rouen and Le Havre, this scenic route winds through the apple and cherry orchards of the Pays de Caux region. In spring, blossoming trees offer an enchanting spectacle along the Seine's meanders.

Village of Villequier — This romantic village on the banks of the Seine is home to the house where Victor Hugo lost his daughter Léopoldine, drowned in 1843. The museum devoted to the writer displays manuscripts, letters and mementoes of the tragedy that inspired Les Contemplations. About 30 km from Rouen, 30 minutes by road.

visits.text: The Church of Notre-Dame de l'Assomption is an unusual building: its construction began in the 11th century in Romanesque style, continued in the 13th and 14th centuries in Gothic style, and was never really finished—the south tower remained incomplete until 1875, when it was raised in neo-Gothic style. This mixture produces a strange and fascinating result. On your way out, look for traces of an old practice: deep notches in the stone at the east end of the church—winegrowers once sharpened their pruning knives on the church stone, which was supposed to ensure good grape harvests. And don't miss the “Smile of Rouffach”: two delicate carved faces—a young woman and a young man—flanking the door of the old sacristy.

The Witches' Tower, last tower surviving from Rouffach's medieval fortifications, is attached to the old town hall. Its round base dates from the 13th century, its square upper part from the 14th and 15th centuries. It served as a prison for centuries, notably for women accused of witchcraft during the Inquisition era — hence its name. A stork's nest tops it today, giving it a more peaceful air.

The Récollets Church, built between 1280 and 1300 by the Franciscans, is one of the very few surviving mendicant-order churches in Alsace with an outdoor pulpit. These outdoor pulpits allowed popular preachers to address the crowd directly in the square. Inside, the austerity sought by the Franciscan order contrasts with the richness of the neighboring Notre-Dame church.

On place de la République, take time to observe the group of monuments: the old 16th-century Halle aux Blés with its characteristic gables, the old town hall with its double Renaissance pediment, the houses with stepped gables that bear witness to the town's golden age under the prince-bishops of Strasbourg. Rouffach was long the capital of the Haut-Mundat, their possession in Upper Alsace.

activities.text: The Vorbourg Grand Cru vineyard trail winds across the south-facing limestone slopes above Rouffach. As you climb, views gradually open up over Rouffach, its medieval monuments, the Alsace plain, and, in clear weather, the Black Forest. A marked 4-kilometer trail loops through rows of Gewurztraminer and Riesling.

Climb to the Notre-Dame de Schauenberg sanctuary via the forest path from Pfaffenheim. This pilgrimage site perched among beech trees overlooks the valley and vineyards. The path starts in the vineyard, crosses meadows, then heads into the woods—the round trip takes about 2 hours and 30 minutes.

days_plan.itin_title: Haut-Rhin Road Trip: Colmar and the Southern Wine Route

visits.text: The ruins of Château de Rougemont crown the Montagne des Boules at 736 meters altitude. Built in the late 12th century by Count Frédéric II of Ferrette, it guarded the southern gateway to Alsace and the Roman road from Langres to Basel. Besieged in 1375 by Enguerrand de Coucy's mercenaries, it was abandoned and later demolished on Louis XIV's orders in 1673. Restored between 1977 and 1980, the ruins have been a classified historic monument since 1996.

The Chapelle Sainte-Catherine, rebuilt in 1876, stands beside a spring reputed to cure eye ailments. A popular pilgrimage destination in the 18th and 19th centuries: the offerings collected were 75 times greater than those at the parish church.

From the summit, the panorama stretches from the Vosges to the Jura with views of the Swiss Alps on clear days. Rougemont, set against the mountain, offers a broad horizon at an average elevation of 450 meters.

activities.text: Climb to the castle along forest trails from the Plainot picnic area. This 3-hour circuit passes through 1,249 hectares of municipal forest within the Natura 2000 site and the Ballons des Vosges Regional Natural Park.
Follow the botanical trail at Mont Marty. Discover Vosges flora with valley views. This 247-hectare Natura 2000 site preserves forest habitats.

days_plan.itin_title: Territoire de Belfort Road Trip: The Citadel and the Lion

visits.text: Roussillon is listed among the Plus Beaux Villages de France. Its ochre-rendered facades display every shade from pale yellow to blood red, depending on the pigments extracted from nearby quarries.

The Sentier des Ocres, nicknamed the "Giants' Causeway", winds between cliffs of red, orange, and yellow ochre sculpted by erosion and former quarrying. Two marked routes of 30 and 50 minutes cross this mineral landscape shaded by pines.
The Conservatoire des Ocres et Pigments Appliqués, housed in the old Mathieu factory, traces the history of Provence's ochre industry. Demonstrations of pigment production and hands-on workshops.

The Église Saint-Michel dominates Place de la Mairie with its square bell tower. From the nearby panoramic viewing table, the view extends over the Vaucluse plateau, the Luberon mountains, and Ventoux.

Allow time for a return drive from Roussillon to the Colorado Provençal in Rustrel to discover thirty hectares of wilder ochre formations. The hoodoos, the Sahara cirque and the Désert Blanc create a landscape worthy of the American Wild West.

activities.text: Walk the Belvédère circuit in the Colorado Provençal in Rustrel; allow time for a return drive from Roussillon. This two-hour trail climbs through the forest to a viewpoint overlooking the orange dunes and hoodoos.
Stroll through art galleries and painters' studios in the village. Ochre has inspired artists for centuries: natural pigments, watercolors, and colored earth appear on the canvases.
Late in the day, head to the Castrum overlook to watch the setting sun ignite the ochre cliffs. The colors shift in intensity minute by minute.

visits.text: Royan, a seaside resort rebuilt after the 1945 bombings. The 1950s architecture, called 'Cinquante Glorieuses', now holds the Ville d'Art et d'Histoire label. Modernist villas, curved seafronts, luminous concrete.

Notre-Dame Church of Royan (1958), a raw concrete masterpiece by Guillaume Gillet. A 45-meter-long elliptical nave, inverted V-shaped vault, abstract stained glass. Controversial when it was built, it is now a listed Historic Monument.

Royan central market, a concrete and glass structure by Louis Simon and André Morisseau (1956). Undulating dome 52 meters in diameter, spectacular natural light. Seafood, orchard fruits, Charentes specialties. One of the finest covered markets in France.

Royan's seafront stretches across 5 beaches: Grande Conche, Foncillon, Chay, Pigeonnier, Pontaillac. A walk past modernist villas, the casino and the convention center. Elegant seaside atmosphere facing the Gironde estuary.

activities.text: Guided tour “Royan in the 1950s.” The tourist office offers architectural tours with commentary: the Parc district villas, convention center, Protestant church, bus station. A fresh look at 20th-century heritage.

Grande Conche beach, 2 km of fine sand in an arc. Lifeguarded in summer, surf and sailing schools, outdoor seating areas facing the ocean. The Cordouan lighthouse, “Versailles of the sea,” is silhouetted on the estuary horizon.

Royan-Le Verdon ferry. The crossing of the Gironde estuary (20 min) offers a unique view of the Charente and Médoc coasts. You can continue to the phare de Cordouan by boat, landing at low tide (guided excursion).

days_plan.itin_title: Charente-Maritime Road Trip: La Rochelle, Île de Ré, Fort Boyard and Roman Saintonge

visits.text: Small in size, immense in its stonework: the Chapelle du Saint-Esprit de Rue remains one of the three great examples of Flamboyant Gothic architecture in Picardy, alongside the collegiate church of Abbeville and the abbey church of Saint-Riquier. Built between 1440 and 1514 to house a crucifix washed up on the shore, it displays vaults adorned with pendant keystones and a façade carved in stone lacework. Pillaged in 1793, it was restored as early as 1839 by the Duthoit brothers.

The belfry of Rue, a 15th-century tower listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, overlooks the square right beside the chapel. The guided tour offered by the tourist office generally combines the belfry, the chapelle de l'hospice and the chapelle du Saint-Esprit in around two hours. Climb up to the roof if access is open; the view over the Marquenterre makes it worthwhile.

visits.text: Joséphine de Beauharnais purchased Château de Malmaison in 1799. Between 1800 and 1802, alongside the Tuileries, it became the seat of French government where Bonaparte received his ministers.
Architects Percier and Fontaine redecorated the château in antique style. The Council Room shaped like a military tent, the library, and Joséphine's oval bedroom exemplify the Consulate style.
The second floor presents objects from Napoleon's exile in Saint Helena: the campaign bed on which his body was displayed, his furniture, and death mask.

activities.text: Joséphine designed the park in English landscape style with help from Scottish gardeners. She cultivated every rose variety known at the time. The restored rose garden now features 150 antique varieties.
Parc des Impressionnistes evokes Giverny with its water garden. Monet, Renoir, and Sisley painted along Rueil's riverbanks.

days_plan.itin_title: Hauts-de-Seine Road Trip: Royal Heritage & Gardens

visits.text: Ruoms conceals behind its lively shopping street one of Ardèche's best-preserved medieval defense systems. The old village was founded in the 10th century around a Benedictine priory of Cluny Abbey—only the Chapelle Notre-Dame-des-Pommiers survives, which you'll find in the historic center. The rectangular ramparts flanked by seven round towers were built in the 14th century during the Hundred Years' War, in local limestone and Ardèche river pebbles. Look for the Maison des Gardes, whose facade preserves a Renaissance fresco depicting Saint Christopher carrying the Christ Child, and the Maison de Justice with its lintel naively carved with a cross, scales and key. The self-guided circuit takes about an hour.

From the eastern exit of the village, the scenic Route des Défilés de Ruoms offers a striking geological spectacle: carved into rock in the 19th century (completed 1866), it plunges through a limestone corridor via a succession of tunnels and vaults, then follows a deep canyon formed by the Ardèche and Ligne rivers. Drive the route but stop at the viewpoints—the exposed rock strata are worth the pause.

Leaving the village northward, don't miss the Renaissance Château de Chaussy: visible from the road, it makes a lovely composition with its corner turrets and mullioned facade. It's not open to the public, but its silhouette amid the greenery deserves a photo. Ruoms is also known for hosting Ardèche's largest breweries, which closed in 1967—wine has since largely replaced them, and the department's largest wine cooperative is located in the commune.

activities.text: The signposted pedestrian loop inside the walls lasts about an hour and is entirely free to access. Panels along the route explain the defensive elements. If you want a guided commentary tour, ask at the tourist office—guided visits are organized in season by reservation.

Local operators offer canoe or kayak descents on the Ardèche from Ruoms. The pebble beaches beside the river, accessible from the municipal campground, are also ideal for a peaceful swim after visiting the village. The river is supervised July-August at this location.

days_plan.itin_title: The 18 Most Beautiful Villages of Ardèche

visits.text: The Château de Sablé-sur-Sarthe, rebuilt in the 18th century, dominates the confluence of the Sarthe and Vègre from its promontory. It replaced the old medieval fortress of the lords of Sablé—including Geoffroy the Old, who founded in 1010 the priory that would become Solesmes Abbey. From the terrace, the view over the two rivers and city rooftops is particularly beautiful in late afternoon. Black marble extracted from Sablé quarries was used for certain exterior facings of the Palace of Versailles.

The Marble Ecomuseum traces the marble industry that made Sablé and its region wealthy from the 17th to 20th centuries, employing at its peak over 2,000 workers. Discover quarrymen's tools, extraction and polishing techniques, and some remarkable pieces from royal commissions. It's a fascinating and little-known local economic history.

The Saint-Nicolas suburb preserves some half-timbered medieval houses adorned with ironwork and ridge finials. Their winding lanes open onto the Sarthe pleasure port—the busiest in the West—where boaters travel up and down the river between May and October.

activities.text: Operators offer river cruises from Sablé: the navigable Sarthe reveals its wooded meanders and tuffeau villages from the water. Allow two hours for a round trip to Solesmes—the view of the abbey from the river is one of the circuit's great moments.

The weekly market of Sablé-sur-Sarthe is one of the department's liveliest. Taste Sarthe rillettes—slowly cooked for hours in their own fat, they have a melting texture very different from industrial rillettes—accompanied by goat cheeses from local producers and shortbread cookies made according to the original recipe of the eponymous village.

days_plan.itin_title: Sarthe Road Trip: Le Mans and the Loir Valley

visits.text: Écomusée de Marquèze: Exceptional immersion in an authentic 19th-century Landes hamlet, accessible only by historic train dating from 1903–1910 (carriages listed as historic monuments) from Sabres. After a 10-minute journey through the forest, discover the 25-hectare airial where 30 to 40 people once lived. Half-timbered manor houses and Landes tenant farms dating from the 18th and 19th centuries, sheepfolds, a mill on stilts relocated from Geloux, bread ovens under century-old oaks.

Traditional craft demonstrations: Costumed interpreters explain pine resin tapping, spinning, weaving, bread making and pastoral life with shepherds on stilts. Traditional Gascon games (palet, rampeau, skittles). The ecomuseum traces the evolution of the Landes landscape, from wet heathland to the industrial forest imposed by Napoleon III in 1857. Tasting of pastis landais baked in a wood-fired oven.

Le Pavillon: A contemporary building presenting a permanent exhibition on the history of the Landes de Gascogne and an annual temporary exhibition. Modern architecture contrasting with the airial's traditional buildings. An interactive museum trail accessible to people with reduced mobility. Video screenings and recorded accounts complete the visit.

activities.text: Historic train journey: Boarding at Sabres station in carriages dating from 1903–1910 and listed as historic monuments. A 10-minute journey through the forest on the former Sabres-Labouheyre-Mimizan line. Rear platform recommended on the return journey for a panoramic view. Regular departures throughout the day. A single ticket includes the train journey and access to the airial.

Hands-on workshops: An introduction to walking on Landes stilts, Gascon games, straw weaving and handmade soap making, depending on the program. Activities for all ages. Activity booklets for children turn the visit into a treasure hunt. Short theatrical sketches on certain days with costumed actors. Digital tour with tablets available at reception.

Full day at the ecomuseum: On-site dining with Landes specialties. Shaded picnic area. Shop selling artisanal products (pastis landais, soaps, honey). Allow 4 to 6 hours to fully enjoy the site. Themed guided tours on certain days. Hours: 10am–7pm in high season (April 1–September 28). Booking advised for groups.

days_plan.itin_title: Landes Road Trip: Ocean, Pine Forest and Landes Traditions

visits.text: Saignon magnificently concludes this tour of the Luberon. This eagle's nest above Apt takes its name from the Latin "signum"—the rock dominating the village served as a light signal for Gallic populations before the Romans arrived. From the Place de la Fontaine, with its centuries-old hackberry tree and cool fountains, wander through narrow, steep lanes where every doorway deserves a glance. The village counted up to forty different lords in the 14th century—which is to say, a tumultuous history.

The Church of Notre-Dame-de-Pitié dates back to the 11th and 12th centuries. Classified as a Historic Monument, this Romanesque church houses Carolingian baptismal fonts, red marble columns, and a 16th-century reliquary. In the Middle Ages, it was a stop on the Via Domitia for pilgrims en route to Santiago de Compostela. The portal with three doors and its large Gothic arch is particularly beautiful.

The Rocher de Bellevue is the village's highest point—about thirty meters above the houses. It served as the base for three medieval fortress-châteaux whose ramparts and sentry paths are still visible. An orientation table at the summit allows you to identify Mont Ventoux, the Montagne de Lure, and the Alps.

activities.text: Climb to the Rocher de Bellevue via the fitted-out stairs (10 min from the village). 360° view over the Apt valley, the Luberon, Ventoux, and on clear days the Alps. The most beautiful panoramic ending imaginable for an itinerary.

Circuit of the two wash-houses fed by the Valsorgues springs, and of the bories and clapas that mark the paths around the village. The Claparèdes Plateau trail connects Saignon to Sivergues through a landscape of garrigue and dry stone.

places.name: Saint Affrique

visits.text: Saint-Affrique stretches along the banks of the Sorgues in the heart of the Grands Causses Regional Natural Park. The Pont-Vieux, listed as a Historic Monument, connects the two banks. The centre retains stone houses, small squares, and vaulted passageways.

The Rocher de Caylus offers a panoramic view over the town and surrounding hills. A cross tops this landmark site. The Notre-Dame de la Miséricorde Church features a tall Gothic spire visible from afar.

The Maison de la Mémoire du Pays Saint-Affricain displays objects, stories, and photographs of daily life in times past. The Tribunal des Arts occupies the former courthouse and exhibits works by local artists.

activities.text: The Saturday morning market brings the town centre to life. Producers sell local cheeses (Pérail, Roquefort, Recuite), charcuterie, and regional specialities. The atmosphere is friendly and Aveyron delicacies are plentiful.

The landscapes around Saint-Affrique range from blazing red-soil rougiers to wild causses and green valleys. The Rougier de Camarès to the south offers spectacular red earth, about 20 km from the stopover town, a 20-minute drive. Hiking, mountain biking and climbing are all possible nearby.

days_plan.itin_title: Aveyron Road Trip: Causses, Tarn Gorges and Villages

map_keywords: Notre-Dame de la Miséricorde church Saint-Affrique

visits.text: The abbey tower of Saint-Amand-les-Eaux, 82 m high, is one of northern Europe's most remarkable Baroque monuments. Built from 1626 to 1640 under Abbot Nicolas Dubois, it served as the entrance to the church of the Benedictine abbey founded in the 7th century by the monk Amand. Its Avesnes stone façade is carved with ribbons, fantastical masks and eight reptilian buttresses—coiled serpents evoking the legend of Saint Amand slaying a monster.

The musée de la Tour abbatiale holds temporary exhibitions on the ground floor beneath a monumental carved vault. Upstairs, the permanent collections bring together religious sculptures from the 16th–18th centuries and more than 300 pieces of Saint-Amand faience with original decorative designs—locally produced in the 18th-century Desmoutiers and Fauquez workshops.

At the top, the 48-bell carillon dating from 1640 rings out through openings carved in the stone. Les Carillonnades brings together carillonneurs from across Europe each August. A school for carillonneurs keeps the tradition alive in the town.

The Échevinage, another remnant of the abbey on the Grand-Place, and the fountain paved with blue stone representing the former moats complete the picture. During recent excavations, a 17th-century bridge was discovered below ground—it will be restored with a wooden drawbridge.

The thermal baths of Saint-Amand-les-Eaux, the only spa resort north of Paris, use waters known since Roman antiquity. Nearly 10,000 spa visitors come each year for treatments for rheumatic and respiratory conditions—or simply a wellness treatment on the edge of the forest.

activities.text: The state-owned forest of Raismes-Saint-Amand-Wallers (4,800 ha) is crossed by walking, cycling and riding trails. Marshes, ponds and varied tree species; the Sabatier spoil heap provides an unexpected viewpoint.
The Porte du Hainaut river port, on the Scarpe canal, offers kayaks, canoes, paddleboards, pedalos and bicycles for hire. An outing on the water with the abbey tower as a backdrop.

The Scarpe Valley tourist steam train runs on Sundays from May to September. The Arenberg mining site (UNESCO) and the legendary Trouée d'Arenberg section of Paris–Roubaix, 10 km away, round off the visit.

days_plan.itin_title: Opal Coast Villages and Flemish Heartlands

visits.text: Founded in 1136, Noirlac Abbey ranks among the best-preserved in Europe. The Cistercian architecture is intact: absolute austerity, pure lines, light filtered through round-arched windows. You visit the vaulted cellar, the cloister with paired columns, the abbey church with exceptional acoustics, the chapter house where monks met in council, the warming room (the only heated room), the refectory and dormitories. Allow at least 1.5 hours to see everything.

Noirlac's gardens were redesigned by landscape architect Gilles Clément (creator of the Parc André-Citroën in Paris). Paths lined with grasses, a reflecting pool, roses that change with the seasons. The cloister shelters a garden of medicinal and aromatic plants around the central well. Beyond, an avenue of two-hundred-year-old lime trees leads towards the bocage.

Since 2024, the “RésoNance” sound trail has offered an immersive musical experience in the abbey. Eight artists created pieces specifically for each space, played every afternoon. The abbey church's acoustics — used for classical concerts — take on another dimension with this contemporary installation.

Saint-Amand-Montrond is a town of goldsmiths. Gold jewellery making has been established here since the late 19th century and still supports many workshops and craft artisans. Strolling through the centre, you understand why Jacques Cœur, the king's treasurer, had connections in this region.

The ruins of Montrond Fortress overlook the town. Dismantled on Louis XIV's orders after the Fronde, it preserves impressive remains: ramparts, towers, underground passages. The view spans the Cher valley and the first foothills of the Massif Central.

activities.text: The Les Traversées festival (June–July) presents concerts in Noirlac's abbey church. Classical music, traditional music, jazz — the Cistercian acoustics enhance voices and acoustic instruments. Dinner in the gardens after the concert is available.

The bocage around Noirlac is designated an Espace Naturel Sensible. Damp meadows, century-old hedges, ponds where great crested newts splash about. 427 species recorded, including the European bee-eater and the great capricorn beetle. Guided nature walks are offered from April to October.

The Monastic Products Market (November) brings together abbeys from across France: Trappist beers, cheeses, honeys, jams, candles, cosmetics. Two days of tasting and direct sales in the conventual buildings.
A stroll along the Cher and Berry Canal. The two waterways run side by side for several kilometres, offering a flat route ideal for families. Restored locks, old towmen's houses, riverside wildlife.

visits.text: Saint-Andiol was founded in the 10th century by monks from Saint-Victor Abbey in Marseille, who drained the marshes enabling agricultural development of the plain. The Saint-Vincent parish church is a fortress in itself: built in Romanesque style in the 11th-12th centuries, fortified in the 14th with machicolations and crenellations, its massive bell tower and thick walls give it the appearance of a keep. Sundials are visible on the south-facing wall. Free admission.

The Château de Saint-Andiol belonged successively to the d'Albe, Varadier, and d'Estourmel families — the latter had it elevated to a marquisate in 1656. Its beautiful double-revolution staircase from the 16th-17th century, Renaissance style, merits a visit to the 5-hectare wooded park planted with century-old plane trees and chestnuts. The château now houses a community socio-cultural center.

Saint-Andiol has a direct link to Resistance history: Jean Moulin, future founder of the National Resistance Council, grew up here at 35 Route Nationale. On January 2, 1942, after being parachuted near Fontvieille, he walked to the Saint-Andiol family home to coordinate the REX mission. The Jean Moulin Museum, inaugurated in 2018, traces his life from Béziers to the Panthéon, where his father Antonin was a schoolteacher.

activities.text: "In the footsteps of Antonin Moulin" trail: a marked route with explanatory panels starts from the Jean Moulin museum to tour the key sites in the village and Moulin family history. Allow 1h30 to complete the communal heritage tour.

Rural route through orchard-olive country: the commune dedicates 66% of its territory to permanent crops (orchards, olive groves). Agricultural paths cross cherry orchards, apricot trees, and olive groves along the banks of the Durance and irrigation canal. The Sainte-Croix chapel (before the year 1000) on the road to Mollégès is one of the oldest monuments of pure Romanesque style in the region — listed as a historic monument.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpilles, Aix-en-Provence & Arles Circuit

visits.text: Saint-Antoine-l'Abbaye was voted France's Favorite Village in July 2025, and arriving from the plain makes it clear why: the Gothic abbey church rises at the end of an avenue of centuries-old linden trees like a vessel of stone. Its construction spanned from 1130 to the late 15th century—nearly four centuries of building. The structure measures 32 meters wide by 22 meters high, an unusually wider-than-tall format. Inside, don't miss the walnut choir stalls, Aubusson tapestries, and the 17th-18th century organ. Classified as a Historic Monument by Prosper Mérimée as early as 1840.

The village's history began in 1070 when Geilin, a local lord, brought back the relics of Saint Anthony the Great from Constantinople—believed to cure "St. Anthony's fire," ergot poisoning that caused gangrene and hallucinations. The Antonine Order, these monk-physicians, eventually established a network of 300 commanderies across Europe. You'll find their treasury in the church sacristies: liturgical vestments, medieval surgical instruments, and an ivory Christ. Plan for a guided tour to access these pieces—schedules vary by season.

The museum housed in the former novitiate offers two permanent exhibitions—"Chronicles of a Medieval Abbey" and "Healing Soul and Body"—and provides access to the medieval garden in the former stables. Medicinal plants, herbs, and fruit trees are cultivated according to Antonine pharmacopoeia. The garden is free; allow an hour for the complete visit.

Wander through the goulets—narrow cobblestone alleys—between half-timbered houses and facades adorned with mullioned windows from the 14th and 15th centuries. The village is also a stop on the Way of St. James. Climb to the viewpoint above the abbey courtyard to take in the entire site with the Chambaran hills as backdrop.

activities.text: The 2-3 km heritage loop within the village walls connects the abbey church, medieval alleys, market hall, and rampart remnants. Interpretive panels mark the route. Start from the abbey courtyard square in late afternoon when the light gilds the molasse facades—the local golden, slightly rosy stone.

The trail to Saint-Jean-le-Fromental chapel follows the old Antonine pilgrim paths for about 7 km (2h45 round trip). Along the way, you'll pass walnut groves overlooked by the Vercors rim on the horizon. A map is available at the tourist office.

days_plan.itin_title: Royans-Vercors Road Trip: Hilltop Villages and Gorges

visits.text: The Maison Romane, built around 1150, was restored by Viollet-le-Duc in the 19th century.
Explore medieval lanes lined with half-timbered houses and carved facades. The Maison de l'Amour features two lovers carved in stone in the 15th century.
Descend to the Bessarel quarter where old tanneries survive. Canals once channeled water for treating hides that made the town's fortune.
The 19th-century market hall rises at the square's center. The Sunday market has attracted pilgrims and residents for centuries.
Reach the belvedere at the foot of Roc d'Anglars. This 90-meter limestone cliff dominates the confluence of the Aveyron and Bonnette rivers.

activities.text: Canoe downstream through the Aveyron Gorges. Sheer cliffs, old bridges, and natural beaches line the river's emerald waters.
Climb the equipped routes on the limestone cliffs. Roc d'Anglars and Pech Dax offer climbs for all levels.
Browse the Sunday morning market renowned for local products. Goat cheese, honey, and charcuterie are displayed in the market hall and on the square.

days_plan.itin_title: Tarn-et-Garonne Road Trip: Bastides and Orchards

visits.text: Saint-Nabor Abbey Church in Saint-Avold is one of Moselle’s most important religious monuments. The abbey was founded in 722 by Sigisbaud, Bishop of Metz, and in 765 Bishop Chrodegang placed the relics of Saint Nabor there, a Roman soldier martyred for his faith—making the site a regional pilgrimage center. The current building was rebuilt from 1754 to 1769 to plans by Dom Léopold Durand, a monk and architect, using variegated sandstone from the Saint-Avold quarries. Its bell tower rises to 45 meters. Listed as a Historic Monument since 1930, it houses an Entombment in the Burgundian style dating from 1510, an oak statue of Saint Nicholas carved in 1773, and Baroque wood paneling created between 1755 and 1762. The traditional nativity scene is on display from December 4 through the end of January, daily from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.

Take a detour to Boulay-Moselle, about 20 km from Saint-Avold, a 20-minute drive. This former medieval fortified town, elevated to a county in 1615, has preserved the two “Dada” towers, the last remains of its fortified walls, destroyed in 1635. Saint-Étienne Church, dating from 1782 and topped with a bell tower with an onion dome from 1863, was once renowned for its monumental organs—Boulay was home to the organ manufactory founded in 1863 by Dalstein-Haerpfer. The nativity scene occupies the altar of Mary and depicts Bethlehem and Jerusalem with plaster figures from the mid-20th century.

In Longeville-lès-Saint-Avold, don’t miss Saint-Magne Church. It dates from 1740 and was remodeled and enlarged in 1889 in the Gothic Revival style. The organ, built in 1905–1906 by the Manufacture Lorraine des Grandes Orgues, was fully restored in 2008 by the Manufacture d’Orgues Bernard Aubertin. Its stained-glass windows depict Gospel scenes and parables. The sculpted Stations of the Cross from 1896 are among the finest in the region.

In Saint-Avold, Sainte-Jeanne-d’Arc Church houses a nativity scene measuring 4 meters by 2 meters, depicting the Nativity with landscapes and a pastoral scene—one of the most richly detailed on the entire route. On view from mid-December to mid-January during services, every other Sunday.

In Folschviller, the Résidence Sainte-Barbe sets up a traditional nativity scene made by volunteers each year, on view from December 15 to January 14, from 2 p.m. to 5 p.m. The one in Altviller is also worth a detour: nativity figurines dressed by hand by the village’s patchwork club form a handcrafted village nativity scene.

activities.text: A few minutes from the abbey church lies the American military cemetery in Saint-Avold, the largest American World War II cemetery in Europe. It holds the graves of American soldiers who fell during the fighting of 1944–1945. A somber, moving visit that places Christmas in Lorraine within the context of its turbulent history. Open to the public, with free admission.

Each year, Saint-Avold hosts an extensive program of Christmas festivities centered on the market square, with a Santa’s village and musical entertainment. Saint Nicholas’s arrival in a horse-drawn carriage, accompanied by the municipal band and a torchlight procession, brings the town to life in early December.

days_plan.itin_title: 4-Day Moselle Tour: Metz, Bitche Citadel and Chagall’s Stained Glass
Christmas Nativity Scene Route in Moselle

visits.text: Saint-Béat is the marble village. Quarried since Roman times, this white marble was used for numerous monuments including the Paris Opera Garnier. The village church is entirely in marble. The old quarries on the mountainside can be visited.
The 11th-12th century château dominates the town. Its ruins testify to Saint-Béat's strategic importance controlling the passage to Spain.

activities.text: The Spanish border is very close. The valley narrows between mountains. The landscapes become truly mountainous with peaks exceeding 2,000 meters.
Hikes depart from Saint-Béat toward surrounding peaks. The trails often follow ancient Roman roads. The Garonne here is just a mountain torrent.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Garonne Road Trip: From Toulouse to the Pyrenees

visits.text: Medieval village. Listed among the Plus Beaux Villages de France, Saint-Benoît-du-Sault perches on a rocky spur overlooking the Portefeuille valley. The village has preserved its proud medieval character with winding cobbled streets, houses from the 15th and 16th centuries, and remnants of fortifications. The 14th-century Portail, the Beffroi with its still-functioning clock, and place de la Demi-lune bear witness to this past.

Church and priory. The 11th-century Saint-Benoît church features a remarkable timber roof frame shaped like an inverted boat hull. The priory, founded at the end of the 10th century by the Abbey of Saint-Benoît-sur-Loire, served as an outpost in Aquitaine. The current building dates from the 18th century and regularly hosts art exhibitions.

Maison de l'Argentier. This house, listed as a historic monument, has a remarkable medieval façade. The finely carved door lintel features two warriors' heads with helmets, a geometric rosette, and two hearts. Its architecture remains a historical enigma that fascinates visitors.

Valley viewpoint. From the church terrace, a stunning view extends over the verdant Portefeuille valley. The colors change with the seasons and create a natural tableau that has captivated numerous artists over time.

activities.text: Le Temps Suspendu Festival. Each summer in August, this baroque music festival pays tribute to the village's exceptional heritage. Concerts take place in the church and its surroundings, creating an intimate experience between musicians and audience. Open-air dinners and concerts with aperitifs punctuate the festival.

Rencontres Photographiques. In early August, the priory hosts exhibitions of fine-art photography for about ten days, along with talks, portfolio reviews, workshops, and concerts accompanied by projections. A photo contest open to all completes the program.

Portefeuille Gorges. This fast-flowing river runs below the village in a steep-sided valley. Hiking trails allow you to explore this preserved natural environment where flora and fauna thrive freely. The contrast between the perched medieval village and the verdant valley creates a remarkable landscape.

days_plan.itin_title: Indre Road Trip: Secret Berry and the Vallée Noire

visits.text: Saint-Bertrand-de-Comminges, awarded the “Plus Beaux Villages de France,” “Grand Site Occitanie,” and “Site Patrimonial Remarquable” designations, occupies a promontory at an altitude of 515 meters overlooking the Comminges plain.
