The medieval town extends along winding, steep streets around the cathedral, with a fortified enclosure called the “scepte” that contained the episcopal palace, canons' houses, cemetery, and cloister. The town walls incorporate numerous stones and sculptures reused from ancient Lugdunum Convenarum.

The Cathedral of Sainte-Marie, classified as a Historic Monument as early as 1840 and inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1998 as part of the Routes of Santiago de Compostela, is a Romanesque-Gothic building whose construction dates to around 1100. Bishop Bertrand de l'Isle (1083–1123), canonized in 1218, had the Romanesque cathedral and first cloister built. In 1307, Bertrand de Got, who had become pope under the name Clement V, launched the reconstruction of the Gothic apse and Gothic choir, and had Saint Bertrand's relics transported in 1309.

The cathedral interior holds exceptional treasures. The carved Renaissance choir stalls, commissioned by Bishop Jean de Mauléon (1523–1551), are among France's finest. The organ, built in the 16th century in a corner on five Corinthian oak columns, rises to sixteen meters high and has three manuals, a thirty-note pedalboard, forty stops, and 2,621 pipes—it is considered one of Europe's most beautiful classical organs. The treasury preserves embroidered copes donated by Clement V, including the Chape de la Passion depicting scenes from Christ's Passion, and Saint Bertrand's pastoral staff, carved from a narwhal tusk.

The Romanesque-Gothic cloister, dating from the 12th to the 14th centuries and adjoining the cathedral, comprises four galleries from different periods: the western Romanesque gallery is the oldest, the southern and eastern galleries date from the first half of the 13th century, and the northern gallery, the only vaulted one, dates from the 14th century. Its openings onto the surrounding landscape, created in the early 20th century, offer an unexpected view of the Pyrenees.

The remains of Lugdunum Convenarum, a Gallo-Roman city among the most important in Roman Aquitaine, extend at the foot of the hill. Founded in the Augustan era, the city had up to ten thousand inhabitants at its peak before being destroyed in 585 during Frankish succession wars. Excavations, conducted from 1913 to 1970 then resumed from 1985 to 2006, have uncovered a 1st-century theater seating five thousand spectators, a temple dedicated to the imperial cult built of Pyrenean marble, a forum, baths, and a Christian basilica. The Augustan trophy, in white Saint-Béat marble, is one of the most complete found in France. The upper town ramparts, from the 5th century, are listed as a Historic Monument.

The Basilica of Saint-Just de Valcabrère, classified as a Historic Monument and inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List on the same basis as the cathedral, is an isolated Romanesque building in the middle of fields, a few hundred meters from Saint-Bertrand. Built on the site of a Roman necropolis whose stones it reuses, it is mentioned as early as Bishop Bertrand's time (1083–1123). Remains of a cloister and ancillary buildings testify to a former house of canons regular.

activities.text: Devote the morning to the cathedral, taking time to admire the carved choir stalls, climb to observe the monumental organ, and tour the cloister to the openings onto the Pyrenees - morning light is particularly beautiful there.

Descend to the ancient site of Lugdunum Convenarum to walk among the remains of the theater, forum, and baths. A single ticket sold at the Musée Les Olivétains gives access to the cathedral, basilica, and archaeological site.
Walk to the Basilica of Saint-Just de Valcabrère via the path through fields—the gradual approach to this solitary Romanesque building in its green setting is one of the stay's highlights.
Visit Les Olivétains, housed in a former convent, which offers shared ticketing, a bookshop, exhibitions and local products. Guided tours can be booked on site.
If the schedule permits, attend a Festival du Comminges concert in the cathedral: the acoustic qualities of the organ and nave give works performed here exceptional resonance.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Garonne Road Trip: From Toulouse to the Pyrenees
Hautes-Pyrénées Circuit: From Tarbes to Cirques and Valleys
Occitanie's 13 Most Beautiful Villages

visits.text: Notre-Dame Collegiate Church. For more than 600 years, the Gothic collegiate church has dominated Saint-Bonnet-le-Château from its promontory. Built between the early 15th and the 16th century, it impresses with its restrained design and size. From the square in front of the church, an exceptional panorama takes in the Forez plain, the Massif Central, the Pilat and, on clear days, the Alps. The lower chapel holds early 15th-century murals, among the best preserved in France. The crypt houses mysteriously preserved natural mummies, discovered in a 17th-century burial vault.

Fortified Old Town. The 14th-century ramparts partly surround the medieval town. Cobbled lanes lined with 15th- and 16th-century burgher houses testify to its past prosperity. The Porte Louis Mandrin and Porte de la Châtelaine mark the old fortified entrances. The village retains its medieval character with its aristocratic residences, vaulted passages and small squares. The architectural ensemble tells the story of the tanners, weavers, armorers and locksmiths who lived in the town.

International Pétanque and Boules Museum. Set in the heart of the town, birthplace of the OBUT boule created in 1955, the museum traces the history of pétanque and local craftsmanship. In 1955, locksmith Frédéric Bayet joined forces with mechanic Antoine Dupuy to create the brand of “playing boule” that would conquer the world. The exhibitions present the evolution of manufacturing techniques, the different types of boules and the history of the game. Saint-Bonnet has mastered the art of metalworking for centuries.

activities.text: Walk along the Aventure du Rail. A greenway laid out between Estivareilles and Saint-Marcellin-en-Forez on a former railway line. A family route of several kilometers crossing the Forez countryside. A railway worker mascot accompanies visitors along this walking and cycling path. A 1950s tourist train is also available for families and is a great favorite with children.

Discovering Medieval and Renaissance Heritage. Self-guided walk with a visitor map available at the Tourist Office. Quiz game for children. Walk along the ramparts with views of the surrounding area. Weekly market on Fridays, where local producers offer regional products.

days_plan.itin_title: Loire Circuit: Wild Gorges and Industrial Heritage

visits.text: Saint-Brieuc's Saint-Étienne Cathedral, built from the 13th to 15th centuries, is one of the rare fortified churches in Brittany. Its two massive towers, pierced with arrow slits, resemble a fortress entrance more than a religious edifice—it served as a citadel during several 14th-century sieges. Enter when the sun reaches its zenith: the south transept's rose window projects brilliant colors. A baroque altarpiece from 1745 and a 1540 organ case rank among the interior treasures.

Saint-Brieuc's old town centers on the cathedral. Pedestrian streets, half-timbered houses from the 15th to 17th centuries, and granite mansions tell the story of its past as an episcopal city. The Hôtel des Ducs de Bretagne (1572), with carved lion heads and Renaissance plant motifs, welcomed Mary Stuart in 1548.

The Saint-Brieuc fountain, below the cathedral, marks the site of the monastery founded in 580 by Welsh monk Brieuc. This is where everything began: an oratory near a spring, a land grant from Breton chief Riwal, and a monastery that gave birth to the city.

The Cesson Tower, on a rocky spur overlooking the bay, once guarded the Gouët estuary entrance. This strategic site has been occupied since Viking and Roman times. The ruins offer an unobstructed panorama over the entire Saint-Brieuc bay.

activities.text: Guided tour of the historic center. Between sacred monuments and half-timbered houses, decipher carved facades, shop signs, and ornaments that showcase Breton craftsmanship from the Middle Ages to the Renaissance.
Walk through the nature reserve of the baie de Saint-Brieuc. At low tide, the mudflats attract thousands of migratory birds. Bring binoculars to observe brent geese, sandpipers and oystercatchers.
Saint-Brieuc market, Wednesday and Saturday mornings around the metal market halls listed as a Monument Historique. Fish from Légué, local cider, galettes, and kouign-amann.

days_plan.itin_title: Côtes-d'Armor Road Trip: Dinan, Pink Granite Coast, Bréhat Island & Lake Guerlédan

visits.text: Saint-Céneri-le-Gérei has been classified as one of France's Most Beautiful Villages since 1983—and seeing the ensemble from the stone bridge spanning the Sarthe, you immediately understand why. The 11th-century Romanesque church perched on its granite spur reflects in the river's peaceful water. Arrive via the RD56 to enjoy this emblematic viewpoint before entering the village. Inside the church, frescoes from the 12th and 14th centuries were covered with whitewash in 1650 then rediscovered in the late 19th century: a Virgin extending her blue mantle above a crowd, a Christ in Majesty, and the hermit Saint Céneri himself. Also look for the bee's nest carved in stone—present according to tradition since the 9th century, the bees are said to be guardians of the holy place ever since they attacked soldiers who threw themselves into the Sarthe to escape them.

The Chapel of Petit Saint-Céneri, dating from the 15th century, stands in a vast meadow on the other bank of the Sarthe—facing the village. Its chestnut framework forms an inverted boat hull. This is where, according to legend, founder Céneri's hermitage was located, an Italian monk who came to evangelize the Alpes Mancelles in the 7th century. Tradition holds that young women wishing to marry within the year come to plant a needle in the saint's statue's feet.

The Auberge des Sœurs Moisy, transformed into a tourist information office from April to September, was until 1908 the haunt of Impressionist and Naturalist painters who came for inspiration in the Alpes Mancelles. Corot, Courbet, Harpignies, Boudin, Mary Renard all stayed here. Go up to the first floor to see the Decapitated Room: by candlelight, visiting painters amused themselves by tracing on the whitewashed walls, in charcoal, the shadow puppet profile of their guests—sixty decapitated silhouettes still watching you today.

activities.text: Walk the Saint-Céneri on the motif pedestrian trail, set up by the Normandie-Maine Regional Natural Park. This route leads to places appreciated by 19th-century painters for the particular quality of light on the valley—panels indicate the exact position from which such and such a painting was made. A playful booklet is available at the tourist office.

Hikes in the Alpes Mancelles from Saint-Céneri offer landscapes of cliffs, rocks, and wild river that surprise in this corner of France. The Haut-Fourché and Toyères cliff sectors offer marked circuits of 2 to 4 hours in the Regional Natural Park. Local operators also offer Sarthe descents by canoe from the village.

days_plan.itin_title: Sarthe Road Trip: Le Mans and the Loir Valley
The 20 Most Beautiful Villages in Normandy

visits.text: Few industrial wastelands are this beautiful: the park of the former Royal Gunpowder Factory, established in 1690 under Louis XIV and closed in 1974, covers 118 hectares on the edge of the Étang de Berre. Thirty years of abandonment have let ivy, ruins and reed beds mingle. Storks nest here.

The Chapelle Saint-Vincent, at the far end of the Poudrerie park in Saint-Chamas, dates from the 12th century and has a canal running through it, with an old wash-house below. The interpretive trail passes it after the mills and the bird observatory. Allow a good hour for the lower loop.

activities.text: Check the opening times before leaving: the Poudrerie park in Saint-Chamas only opens on certain days, which vary with the season, and closes when the fire risk requires it. In July–August, it opens in the morning from 7am to noon.

days_plan.itin_title: Côte Bleue and Camargue: the lower coastal route in 7 days

visits.text: Saint-Cirq-Lapopie clings to a limestone cliff 100 meters above the Lot River. France's Favorite Village, it boasts thirteen listed historical monuments and fewer than 200 residents. Houses from the 12th to 15th centuries, with brown-tile roofs, cascade toward the river below.

Climb to the Rocher de Lapopie, the village's highest point. Ruins of a 10th–12th-century fortress occupy the summit. The 360° panorama embraces the Lot Valley, the limestone cliffs, and the village rooftops below.

The 12th-century fortified church dominates the village from its rocky promontory. Its bell tower doubled as a defensive structure during troubled medieval times. Inside, simple furnishings and understated decor invite quiet contemplation.

Walk down the medieval main street, lined with craft workshops and houses with stone arcades. Place du Sombral, the heart of the village, offers a shady pause. At the far end, the Pélissaria gate opens onto the path down to the Lot.

The former Mariniers Inn, on the cliff edge, won over the Surrealist poet who settled there and declared he never wanted to be anywhere else. His house-studio, now an artists' residency, is recognizable by its facade opening onto the void.
Pass through the Porte de Rocamadour, a fortified gateway in the medieval ramparts. Remnants of the defensive wall are still visible along the path that circles the upper village.

activities.text: Walk the towpath between Bouziès and Saint-Cirq-Lapopie, carved into the cliff face 80 meters above the Lot between 1843 and 1847 for horses pulling barges. Along the way, a 30-meter bas-relief sculpted into the rock depicts the valley's fauna, flora, and fossils. The route passes through the manual lock at Ganil.

Board a traditional flat-bottomed gabare from Bouziès. These historic boats navigate the Lot, passing through locks with commentary on river navigation history and views of the cliffs and perched village.
Rent a canoe, kayak, or stand-up paddleboard at the river's edge below the village. Outfitters offer routes of varying lengths, with shuttle service or loop options.

days_plan.itin_title: Lot Itinerary: Cahors, Rocamadour & the Lot Valley
Occitanie's 13 Most Beautiful Villages
Southeast France Road Trip: Perched Villages and Gorges
Midi-Pyrénées Circuit: Bastides, Cliffs and Abbeys
The Most Beautiful Villages of Lot and Périgord in 6 Days

visits.text: Saint-Clar, a bastide founded in 1274 through a paréage between the King of England and the Bishop of Lectoure, possesses a rarity: two arcaded squares. On Place de la Garlande, the hall classified as a Historic Monument raises its 20 weathered wooden pillars supporting a 13th-century timber frame. The rear, rebuilt in stone in the 18th century, is topped with a neoclassical bell tower.

The second arcaded square, the Plaçote (Place de la République), preserves its "cornières"—covered galleries beneath golden stone houses. The old-fashioned storefronts hint at interior courtyards and a prosperous commercial past. Remarkably rare, these two squares lie just dozens of yards apart.

Head up to the Château-Vieux, Saint-Clar's original core. The old 12th-century Romanesque church, with its handsome bell tower, overlooks half-timbered houses packed into medieval lanes. The Garden of Four Seasons, created on the site of collapsed houses, pays tribute to Gascon poet Dastros (1594-1648).

Saint-Clar is the capital of Lomagne white garlic, cultivated here since the 13th century and protected by a PGI since 2009. The House of Garlic offers visits to understand the cultivation, drying and uses of this Gascon specialty. In summer, garlic braids adorn the market stalls.

activities.text: Saint-Clar market on Thursday mornings. Under the wooden-pillared hall, tradition dates back to the Middle Ages. White garlic, fattened poultry, seasonal fruits and vegetables—a concentrate of Lomagne terroir. In summer, the garlic market runs from July through September.

Guided tour of Saint-Clar bastide. The tourist office offers commentary-led circuits to understand the singular architecture of this two-square bastide. Medieval lanes, ramparts, wash houses and Gascon pigeon houses complete the picture.

Hike the hillsides around Saint-Clar. Marked trails offer views of the Arrats valley and Lomagne countryside—fields of sunflowers, garlic, wheat and vines compose a patchwork of colors depending on the season.

days_plan.itin_title: Gers Road Trip: Gascon Bastides, Armagnac & Musketeers

visits.text: Saint-Pierre Cathedral dominating the town nestled in the Bienne gorge. The imposing religious edifice testifies to Saint-Claude's historical importance as a religious center. The architecture blends different construction periods with its Gothic choir and remodeled nave. The 15th-century carved choir stalls rank among the finest in Franche-Comté. The treasury contains remarkable pieces of religious goldwork.

Pipe and Diamond Museum tracing the two industries that made Saint-Claude's renown. The town was the world capital of pipes until the decline of smoking, with hundreds of workshops producing millions of briar pipes. Diamond cutting developed there thanks to local artisan know-how. The collections present tools, techniques, and exceptional pieces. Demonstrations allow understanding of the precision of these art crafts.

Bienne Gorges carved by the river between spectacular limestone cliffs. The impressive natural site can be discovered from the road or via hiking trails. The vertical walls dominate the tumultuous watercourse creating wild landscapes. Developed belvederes offer plunging views over the gorges and valley. The vegetation clinging to the rocks adds to the dramatic character of the place.

Fort des Rousses, about 19 km from the stopover town, 29 minutes by road, one of the largest forts in France, built between 1840 and 1862 under Louis-Philippe. The underground galleries run for several kilometres into the mountain. Part of them now houses the Comté maturing cellars, where 100000 wheels age in ideal conditions of temperature and humidity. The guided tour reveals the imposing military architecture and includes a tasting of the cheese matured in these unusual surroundings.

Lake des Rousses at 1060 metres altitude in the heart of the village resort, about 19 km from the stopover town, 29 minutes by road. This peaceful stretch of water surrounded by fir forests offers a rural setting made for relaxing. The flat path around the lake suits families. In winter the frozen lake turns into a natural ice rink. The laid-out shores offer picnic areas and supervised swimming zones in summer.

Les Rousses resort, a mountain village on the Swiss border, about 19 km from the stopover town, 29 minutes by road. The alpine feel comes through in the chalet architecture and the lively streets. In winter the French-Swiss ski area offers downhill runs and 200 kilometres of cross-country tracks. In summer, walking and mountain-bike trails criss-cross the high plateaux. The village keeps its authenticity despite tourist development.

activities.text: Hike to the Flumen waterfalls. The forest trail leads to these impressive falls gushing in a rocky amphitheater. Water cascades over several levels creating a striking sound and visual spectacle. The coolness released by the spray provides welcome relief on hot days. The route crosses varied landscapes between dense forests and flowery clearings.

Hike to Lake Lamoura in a preserved mountain cirque. The trail climbs through alpine pastures flowering in summer offering panoramas over the surrounding mountains. The high-altitude lake with cold waters reflects the surrounding peaks. The high mountain atmosphere contrasts with the cirque landscapes of the lower Jura. Montbéliarde cows graze in the meadows bordering the path.

Mountain biking in the Haut-Jura forests on numerous marked trails. The varied routes adapt to all levels from family trails to technical singletracks. Playful descents alternate with sustained climbs rewarded by open views. Electric mountain bike rentals allow less athletic riders to enjoy the itineraries. Themed circuits like the GTJ VTT cross the massif over several days.

Visit diamond-cutting workshops perpetuating century-old know-how. Artisans explain faceting techniques that reveal the stone's brilliance. The millimeter precision of the gesture and necessary patience impress. Contemporary creations sit alongside historical pieces testifying to the evolution of styles. Possibility to purchase directly from the cutters.

days_plan.itin_title: Jura Road Trip: Lakes, Waterfalls & Mountains

visits.text: Catherine de' Medici acquired the estate in 1577. Louis XIV gifted it to his brother Philippe d'Orléans in 1658. The château, set ablaze in 1870 during the Franco-Prussian War, was razed in 1891.
The Grande Cascade, a 17th-century hydraulic masterpiece, spans 92 meters. Jets, bubbling fountains, and basins compose a water spectacle. The Grand Jet basin shoots water over 40 meters high.
Pavillon de Breteuil houses the International Bureau of Weights and Measures. Two exemplars of the meter and kilogram standards are preserved here.

activities.text: The 460-hectare national park unfolds with formal French gardens designed by Le Nôtre, groves, and terraced allées. The summit at 161 meters offers views over Paris.
The Rock en Seine festival takes over the estate each summer.

days_plan.itin_title: Hauts-de-Seine Road Trip: Royal Heritage & Gardens

visits.text: The marina features 1,885 berths, making it Europe's third-largest port by capacity. Developed since 1967 with three protected basins, a modern harbor master's office, and services for boaters.
The Saint-Cyprien Collections display 19th- and 20th-century paintings. Eugène Boudin, Barbizon School, Utrillo, Marquet, Modigliani, and François Desnoyer enrich the galleries.
The Jardin des Plantes spans five hectares in the Villa des Capellans park. Over 800 plant species, a bamboo grove, old garden roses, and contemporary sculptures.
The Golf de Saint-Cyprien Resort offers an 18-hole and a 9-hole course. Links-style atmosphere with views of the Pyrenees and Mediterranean.

activities.text: Go sailing or motorboating. The Yacht Club offers lessons and boat rentals for cruising along the coast.
Enjoy the water sports center on the golf lake. Water skiing, wakeboarding, towable tubes, paddleboarding, and windsurfing are available.
Relax on the long fine sandy beach. Six kilometers of Blue Flag coastline with beach clubs and entertainment.
Discover the port fountain that cleans the waters. Built in 1991, it draws seawater and injects it into the harbor to eliminate odors.

days_plan.itin_title: Pyrénées-Orientales Road Trip: French Catalonia and the Côte Vermeille

places.name: Saint Cyr Au Mont D Or

visits.text: Ternand, a Petite Cité de Caractère, perches its old village on a rocky spur partly made of white marble, overlooking the Azergues valley. Once the summer residence of the archbishops of Lyon, the village still has a rampart walk along the old walls, with views over the vineyards and the Beaujolais hills. Allow about 15 miles from the base town, 35 minutes by road.

The Romanesque Church of the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist houses beneath its chancel an 11th-century crypt decorated with Carolingian frescoes - rare and precious, they probably date from the 8th century. Access to the crypt is restricted (Heritage Days or upon request), but reproductions are on display. It is about 25 km from the stage town, a 35-minute drive.

The ruins of the 12th-century castle, destroyed in 1562 by the Huguenot troops of the Baron des Adrets, have been turned into a public garden. The remains of the keep and the lanes lined with golden-stone houses, mullioned windows and medieval vaults create a timeless village. It is about 25 km from the stage town, a 35-minute drive.

Mont Thou (2,005 feet), the accessible high point of the Monts d'Or, offers exceptional panoramas over greater Lyon, the Saône plain, Beaujolais, and the Alpine chain—from Mont Blanc to Vercors. The orientation table at the summit helps identify peaks on clear days.

The Mont Cindre Hermitage (1,542 feet) directly overlooks Lyon. Its esplanade is a natural belvedere over the city and its two rivers. The Monts d'Or, a small limestone massif at the metropolis's gates, shelters golden stone quarries and cabornes—dry-stone huts built by winegrowers.

activities.text: Morning walk through old Ternand. The wall walk, medieval lanes and views over the Azergues Valley can be explored in about an hour. Taste Gamay at a village winegrower's before getting back on the road. It is about 25 km from the stage town, a 35-minute drive.

Afternoon hike from Mont Thou to Mont Cindre. The 6-mile loop connects both summits through forests, meadows, and heathland. Wild orchids in spring, dry-stone cabornes, and the Birds of Prey trail marked with panels about local species.

Mont d'Or villages—Saint-Cyr, Saint-Romain, Curis, Poleymieux—preserve surprising rural charm at the metropolis's doorstep. Golden stone houses, washhouses, and fountains compose a preserved Lyon countryside landscape.

days_plan.itin_title: Rhône Road Trip: Lyon, Golden Stone Villages of Beaujolais & Condrieu Vineyards

places.name: Saint Denis

visits.text: The first masterpiece of Gothic art, the cathedral basilica houses over 70 recumbent effigies sculpted from the 12th to 16th centuries. Forty-two kings and thirty-two queens rest beneath its vaults, from Dagobert to Louis XVI.

Descend into the crypt to discover the burial pit of Saint Denis, martyred around 250 AD. The eight recumbent effigies commissioned by Saint Louis lie alongside the monumental tomb of Francis I and Catherine de' Medici.

The Paul Éluard Museum of Art and History occupies a former Carmelite convent founded in 1625. Its collections trace the history of the 1871 Commune, the Hôtel-Dieu apothecary shop, and the life of the surrealist poet.
Step into the Fabrique de la Ville, an educational center dedicated to archaeology and excavations that reveal two thousand years of Saint-Denis history.
The Saint-Denis market brings together nearly 220 permanent merchants. Stalls overflow with spices, fabrics, and products from around the world.

activities.text: Follow Saint-Denis's historic trail: 20 markers chart the route between the Stade de France and the basilica, tracing 2,000 years of history along the canal.
The Street Art Avenue runs along the Saint-Denis canal for 5 km between the Stade de France and Parc de la Villette. Some forty monumental murals bring color to the banks.
Stroll through Parc de la Légion d'Honneur in the heart of downtown. In spring, the Tulip Festival transforms the lawns into a botanical rainbow.

days_plan.itin_title: Seine-Saint-Denis Tour: Basilica and Urban Culture

map_keywords: Musée d'art et d'histoire Paul Eluard Saint-Denis
Parc de la Légion d'Honneur Saint-Denis

visits.text: The cathedral complex at Saint-Dié is going to throw you off balance—in a good way. Three pink sandstone buildings connected together: the cathedral, the small church of Notre-Dame de Galilée, and their Gothic cloister. The cathedral dates back to the 7th century and was founded by Saint Déodat, an Irish monk who gave his name to the town. Its current walls date from the 12th–13th centuries, but the 18th-century Baroque facade (designed by Giovanni Betto) contrasts with everything else. The surprising detail: the cathedral was dynamited by the Germans in November 1944, then rebuilt to match the original with new stained glass windows designed by Jean Bazaine. If you look carefully on the cloister, you'll find the gargoyle nicknamed l'Iroquoise—because of its feathers, not because of any link to America. It had been torn off by the 2003 earthquake; it returned to its place in 2017.

Don't walk past the cloister without entering—it's one of the largest in eastern France, rebuilt from 1444 thanks to indulgences granted by Pope Eugene IV (Charles VII and Duke René I had put their weight behind it). The galleries blend Flamboyant Gothic and early Renaissance touches. On the cloister floor, look for the stylized map of the New World inlaid in the paving: this is where, in 1507, a small printing house published the first map to bear the printed name America.

The Musée Pierre-Noël is right next to the cathedral and worth a 45-minute visit: it preserves the documents and works of the master stained glass artists who worked on the reconstruction of the building after 1944. A good way to better understand what you just saw in the cathedral.

activities.text: At the end of the day, climb up to the Roche Saint-Martin via the trail at the edge of town. Allow 1 hour round trip. The view down over the Meurthe valley and the cathedral's pink sandstone bell towers is well worth the effort, especially in late afternoon when the light warms the stone.

days_plan.itin_title: Vosges Abbey Trail: Monastic Heritage

visits.text: Lake Der-Chantecoq is the largest man-made lake in France, 4,800 hectares and 77 kilometres of shoreline. Created between 1969 and 1974 to control the flooding of the Marne upstream of Paris, it swallowed three villages: Chantecoq, Nuisement-aux-Bois and Champaubert-aux-Bois. When the water drops in autumn, remains sometimes surface, walls and the lines of old roads, and the melancholy sight is striking. To understand the story of these lost villages, head for the Village-Musee du Der at Sainte-Marie-du-Lac, about 16 km from the overnight town, 16 minutes by road: the timber-framed church of Nuisement was dismantled piece by piece and rebuilt there exactly as it was.

The Route of the Timber-Framed Churches is one of the most unusual architectural legacies in France. Unlike regional building traditions based on stone, the inhabitants of the wet Champagne built their churches in oak and cob from the 15th century onwards, for lack of accessible quarries. About a dozen survive, six of them near Lake Der. The one at Chatillon-sur-Broue, about 22 km from the overnight town, 22 minutes by road, is the most photographed. Allow half a day to see three or four.

In Saint-Dizier proper, pause before the façade of "Petit Paris" at 478 Avenue de la République: executed in faience tile and shell mosaics in an Art Brut style, it expresses popular 20th-century creativity. Notre-Dame Church preserves an Entombment and is ringed by timber-framed 16th-century houses.

activities.text: Watch the common cranes between October and mid-March. Every autumn up to 300,000 birds pass through Lake Der, their great migratory stopover between northern Europe and the wintering grounds of Spain and Africa. In 1977 there were 40,000; today the yearly peak sometimes exceeds 300,000. Get up before dawn to watch them take off from the dykes: hundreds of birds rise into the pink sky with their distinctive krou-krou call, a sight and a sound that stay with you. The Chantecoq and Champaubert hides, about 18 km from the overnight town, 18 minutes by road, are the best spots.

Cycle the lake's 38-kilometer circuit on dedicated paths and green ways. The route traverses Champagne bocage and follows the supply canal from Saint-Dizier. Bike rentals operate near the lake. A full day allows completion without undue haste.

The lake offers six sandy beaches for summer swimming. Sailing, windsurfing, kayaking, and water skiing round out available water sports through local providers. The season runs primarily from June through September.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Marne Circuit: Langres and Heritage

visits.text: Lynch-Bages, a Fifth Growth since 1855, has traded at Second Growth prices for decades—and nobody's complaining, except perhaps the other Fifths. The Cazes family has owned the estate since 1939 and had the intelligence to build an entire renovated village around Château de Bages: café, bakery, gourmet grocery, wine shop. It's touristy, but well done—and genuine. La Cave de Bages sells older vintages directly from the estate, which is a rare enough opportunity to be worth mentioning.

Oriental pagodas on the banks of the Gironde—that's what Louis Gaspard d'Estournel built in the 19th century after bringing back his teak doors from Oman. Cos d'Estournel is the most photogenic château in the Médoc, by far. A Second Growth, it produces a powerful Saint-Estèphe that needs at least ten years of aging before becoming approachable. The exterior visit is free—and more than enough for the photo.

Take the small road that runs along Calon-Ségur—the only classified Médoc château whose label bears a heart, ever since an 18th-century owner wrote to friends: 'My heart is at Calon.' A walk through the vineyards of Saint-Estèphe, between parcels sloping down toward the Gironde, does more to explain Médoc terroir than any lecture: the gravel and blue clay soil underfoot retains moisture from the estuary. That's why the wine is different here.

Imagine a church 38 meters long, 20 wide, 11 high—carved entirely by hand from limestone bedrock, without a single added load-bearing wall. That's Saint-Émilion's monolithic church, excavated between the 8th and 12th centuries, one of the largest underground churches in Europe. Even in mid-August, the coolness inside is striking. Visit is obligatorily guided via the local tourist office—book early morning to avoid groups. The catacombs and Trinity Chapel below complete the ensemble.

62 spiral steps, narrow staircase—fair warning if you're claustrophobic—and at the top, the best view on the circuit: 360° over Pomerol's vineyards, the Côtes de Castillon, and the Dordogne valley. The Tour du Roy dates from the 13th century, built by Louis VIII during the siege of the town. Combined ticket possible with the monolithic church.

Three levels of cellars carved into the limestone cliff, 13°C year-round without air conditioning: Beau-Séjour Bécot offers Saint-Émilion's most educational visit on how a Premier Grand Cru Classé B operates. The Bécot family clearly explains the appellation's dual nature—limestone on the plateau, clay and sand at the foot of the slope—and why Merlot here produces wines far softer than in the Médoc. Booking required.

Pomerol has no official classification—no 1855, no hierarchy carved in stone—and yet Château Pétrus, 11.4 hectares of almost pure Merlot on a mound of blue clay, produces 30,000 bottles per year selling for between €3,000 and over €20,000 depending on the vintage. The estate doesn't receive the public. The building is discreet, almost modest. The lesson is right there: in viticulture, reputation always precedes architecture.

activities.text: For estuary lovers, the Relais de Médoc in Lamarque, facing the Gironde, offers the same spirit with a different view. Allow approximately 50 km from Saint-Émilion, 50 minutes by road.

If you arrive in Saint-Émilion late afternoon via the D670, the Roman-tile roofs and the bell tower of the monolithic church emerge from the vineyards in the golden late-day light. It's one of the best arrivals on the circuit—don't miss it by leaving too late. An hour of free wandering through the narrow streets before dinner, to take the village's temperature without any set plan.

The terrace at Belles Perdrix overlooks Saint-Émilion and its vineyards in a 360° sweep—and David Charrier's cooking (two Michelin stars) lives up to the setting. Landes and Bordeaux terroir worked with precision, flawless wine pairings. The lunch menu is significantly more affordable than dinner—it's the right time to go. Book several weeks ahead, it fills up fast.

Late afternoon, when the tour buses leave, Saint-Émilion becomes a village again. Rue Guadet, Place du Marché, the terrace at the foot of the bell tower—everything's walkable in twenty minutes. Independent wine merchants in the village offer tastings from small producers you'll never hear mentioned elsewhere: that's where you'll find the trip's best deals.

days_plan.itin_title: Gironde Circuit: Bordeaux, Vineyards & Arcachon Bay
Nouvelle-Aquitaine Loop: Villages, Vineyards & Dordogne
Bordeaux in 7 Days: Médoc, Saint-Émilion, and Sauternes
Bordeaux in 7 Days: Médoc, Saint-Émilion, and Sauternes

visits.text: Puits Couriot, Mining Museum. The museum occupies the former mining site operated until 1973. In the reconstructed underground galleries, machinery sounds and atmospheric lighting recreate the miners' working environment. The famous hanging room, where equipment was suspended, evokes the daily lives of these men, who employed up to 1,500 people at this pit. The exhibitions trace Saint-Étienne's mining history through objects, photographs and personal accounts.

Museum of Art and Industry. Three themed routes present the local industrial heritage. The bicycle section shows the evolution of the bicycle from draisines to modern bikes made of composite materials. France's first bicycle is said to have been built here in 1886. The arms collections trace the history of the arms factory, displaying swords, rifles and muskets from an artistic and historical perspective. The textile section highlights Saint-Étienne's decorative trimmings and ribbon-making.

Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art. France's second-largest collection with nearly 20,000 works, the museum presents contemporary art from 1960 onward. Geometric abstraction, Nouveaux Réalistes, Pop Art and Art Brut sit side by side in this building clad in black ceramic tiles. Temporary exhibitions draw more than 60,000 visitors a year. Didier Guichard's architecture combines modernity with international openness.

Saint-Étienne Historic Center. Place Marengo, with its bandstand and tree-lined esplanade, forms the heart of city life. Rue des Martyrs de Vingré preserves 18th-century houses with their exposed beams and rusticated façades. The Grand'Église, the city's only Gothic survivor, built in the 15th century in Forez sandstone, shelters a Renaissance Entombment and a flamboyant Gothic choir.

activities.text: Cité du design. Housed in the restored former arms factory, the Cité du design stages the International Design Biennial every two years. Permanent and temporary exhibitions explore the links between design, innovation and industry. The site reflects Saint-Étienne's industrial redevelopment; the city has joined the UNESCO Creative Cities Network for design.

Walk through the renovated districts. The Saint-Charles district combines redeveloped former industrial sites with new urban spaces. The Bancs d'essai, design installations scattered across the city, invite unusual breaks in the urban setting. The Châteaucreux district, around the station, brings together modern buildings and redesigned public spaces.

days_plan.itin_title: Loire Circuit: Wild Gorges and Industrial Heritage

visits.text: Saint-Étienne-du-Grès is a peaceful gateway to the Alpilles between the Crau and the massif's piedmont. Its old center, spared by tourist flows, preserves side streets and small squares where little has changed since the 1970s. A few minutes north of the village, the Romanesque chapel of Saint-Gabriel (11th-12th centuries, classified historic monument) stands alone amid olive trees. Its sculpted facade represents the Annunciation — one of the finest examples of primitive Romanesque sculpture in the region.

Domaine Dalmeran, at the village's north exit, is one of the last large olive and wine estates in this part of the Alpilles, certified PDO Les Baux-de-Provence. Providers offer visits to vineyards and olive groves, plus tastings. The "Les Baux-de-Provence" designation covers only 8 communes — including Saint-Étienne-du-Grès — and produces 85% organic, an exceptional proportion.

activities.text: Agricultural paths toward the Alpilles foothills: from the village, agricultural tracks gradually climb toward the first limestone ridges. Views open toward the Crau plain south and the Alpilles garrigue north. Allow 2 hours for an 8 km loop.

Heritage trail (wash houses, oratories, fountains) through Saint-Étienne center: an hour of quiet walking in the old town reveals a dozen small dry-stone structures — the communal wash house fed by a spring capture, roadside oratories with their flower-filled niches, and some sculpted 17th-century doorways.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpilles, Aix-en-Provence & Arles Circuit

visits.text: Château de Saint-Fargeau, a 'giant of pink brick,' unfolds its five corner towers crowned with bell turrets around a pentagonal courtyard. Its origins date to 980, when the Bishop of Auxerre built a fortified hunting lodge here.

Tour the furnished apartments of La Grande Mademoiselle, cousin of Louis XIV, exiled here in 1652. The wooden library, trophy room, and reconstruction of her bedroom transport you to the Grand Siècle.
The château's timberwork, open to the public, forms a spectacular labyrinth of beams. An attic full of old-fashioned toys is arranged under the rafters—children can handle the toys from yesteryear.
The château chapel preserves wall paintings and a grand stone staircase. The 120-hectare English-style park extends behind the ramparts.

Near Saint-Fargeau, the Guédelon construction site is building a fortified castle using only 13th-century techniques. Stonemasons, carpenters and blacksmiths have worked before visitors’ eyes since the late 1990s.

activities.text: In summer, the château's historical pageant brings together 600 volunteers and 50 horsemen to retrace 1,000 years of history in 90 minutes. On Friday and Saturday evenings in July-August, the château blazes at nightfall.
Lake Bourdon, the Yonne's largest lake, spreads at the village's foot. Supervised swimming in summer, hiking trails, and fishing enliven its wooded shores.
On Thursday summer evenings, candlelit night tours of the château reveal private apartments. Costumed characters guide visitors between legend and reality.

days_plan.itin_title: Yonne Circuit: Northern Burgundy & Chablis

places.name: Saint Florent

visits.text: Saint-Florent is nicknamed the Corsican Saint-Tropez—an upscale marina on the Gulf of Saint-Florent, with its white yachts, waterfront restaurant terraces, and evening buzz. The 15th-century Genoese citadel dominates the harbor from the hill. It's well preserved and you can walk its ramparts. Below the harbor, wander the old town's lanes before joining the evening stroll.

The Santa Maria Assunta cathedral in Nebbio, 1 km from Saint-Florent on the Bastia road, is one of Corsica's finest examples of Pisan Romanesque architecture: built in the 12th century in white limestone with a half-domed apse and sculptures of serpents and animals on the capitals. The austere, cool interior contrasts with the heat outside. Take 20 minutes to walk around.

The beaches of Saleccia and Lotu, in the Désert des Agriates, are among the most beautiful unspoiled beaches in the Mediterranean - white sand, turquoise water and no buildings on the horizon. They are accessible by boat shuttle from the harbor of Saint-Florent (a 30-minute trip). Shuttles depart several times a day from May to October. Do not miss Saleccia: a kilometer of white sand surrounded by umbrella pines.

activities.text: Stroll through Saint-Florent's lanes and enjoy an aperitif on the harbor in late afternoon: the waterfront terraces come alive around 6 PM. It's a chance to taste Cap Corse, the local aperitif made from macerated Corsican wines that the Italians copied to make their Martini.

Tour operators offer sea kayak rentals by the day to reach the Désert des Agriates beaches from Saint-Florent. The sea route follows a coast free of any buildings—count on 2 hours of paddling one way, with swimming stops along the way. Ideal for travelers who like getting away from crowds.

days_plan.itin_title: Upper Corsica Road Trip: Cap Corse and Balagne
Complete Tour of Corsica

map_keywords: Plage du Lotu Désert des Agriates

visits.text: Saint-Floret nestles against the rock at the entrance to a narrow gorge the Couze Pavin has carved through granite — Stendhal wrote there was 'nothing more picturesque.' The village developed around a seigneurial castle built from the 13th century by the Dauphins of Auvergne. Dare to push open the door of the castle's lower hall: you'll discover 13 exceptional frescoes painted around 1370 recounting the Romance of Tristan and Iseult — the only French depiction of this version of the medieval romance. The colours are vivid, the figures life-size. Visits are guided only, April to September (check times with the Issoire tourist office). In June 1944, the village was bombed by the Luftwaffe in reprisal — one section of town remains in ruins, deliberately preserved as a witness.

Cross the old Pont de la Pède from the 15th century: a single arch topped by an oratory housing a polychrome Romanesque Virgin in Majesty from the 13th century. This bridge is said to be miraculous since, during the 1944 bombing, the only bomb that failed to explode fell precisely here. Then climb to the Chastel site on the granite mound: a 12th-century Romanesque church surrounded by a necropolis with anthropomorphic tombs carved in rock, a pyramidal ossuary, and 14th-century frescoes inside — an archaeological site of rare density.

A few kilometres upstream from the village, don't miss the Tête de Lion spring: an impressive limestone concretion with a feline profile formed by deposits of calcium carbonate carried by the water (travertine). It's one of the most spectacular mineral springs among the 600 catalogued in Auvergne. The path follows the Couze Pavin — allow 20 minutes from the spring car park.

activities.text: The Couze Pavin gorge trail (3–5 km, moderate elevation gain, ~2h) follows the river upstream through its canyon between granite walls. Rock climbing sites line the river for enthusiasts — local operators offer introductions in the gorges. The Couze flow can be strong during rainy periods: check locally on conditions.

days_plan.itin_title: Auvergne Circuit: Perched Villages and Volcanoes

visits.text: Saint-Pierre Cathedral dominates the Place d'Armes with its two square towers rising to over 80 metres. Built between the 14th and 15th centuries in dark lava stone, it holds the record as Europe's highest Gothic cathedral by altitude (892 m at the forecourt). The massive austerity of its façade contrasts with the riches inside: the “Beau Dieu noir”, a 12th-century figure of Christ carved in walnut wood, and an organ that resounds during regular concerts bear witness to its spiritual grandeur.

The upper town stands like a stone vessel on its basaltic promontory at an altitude of 900 metres. Designated a Ville d'Art et d'Histoire, it reveals cobbled lanes, Renaissance townhouses and medieval ramparts in a setting of volcanic stone. The ancient fortified gates recall its motto: “None took me by force but the wind”. From the heights, the view plunges down to the Ander valley and the Cantal mountains.

The Musée de la Haute-Auvergne, housed in the former episcopal palace, presents ethnographic and archaeological collections tracing the territory's history. Discover pastoral traditions, local craftsmanship and evidence of daily life in this historic capital of Haute-Auvergne.

activities.text: The weekly market fills the upper town in a convivial atmosphere. Auvergne cheeses, artisanal cured meats, honeys and regional products are displayed on the stalls of local producers. Cantal's cuisine reveals all the generosity of its mountain traditions here.

The ramparts route follows the natural and medieval fortifications that once protected the city. This walk reveals the vertiginous basaltic escarpments, preserved fortified gates and panoramas over the surrounding valleys. Saint-Flour's defences reveal their full strategic strength.

days_plan.itin_title: Cantal Road Trip: Auvergne Volcanoes and Mountain Traditions

visits.text: The Collegiate Church of Saint-Pierre-et-Saint-Gaudens dates from the 11th century. Its Romanesque bell tower and sculpted portal are remarkable. Inside, historiated capitals narrate biblical scenes.
The municipal museum presents local archaeology and sacred art collections. You'll also see works on the history of Saint-Gaudens.

activities.text: Thursday morning market is one of the most important in Comminges. Mountain and plain producers gather to sell poultry, cheeses, and vegetables.
Walk in the Garonne valley which begins to narrow here. The Pyrenees draw closer and the landscape changes with the first mountain reliefs.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Garonne Road Trip: From Toulouse to the Pyrenees

places.name: Saint Germain En Laye

visits.text: En route, stop at the Museum of the Royal Estate of Marly: scale models and engravings trace the history of Louis XIV's vanished château and the workings of the famous Marly Machine.

Visit the remains of the Marly Machine, dubbed the "eighth wonder of the world" when built between 1681 and 1684. Its 14 hydraulic wheels, each 12 meters in diameter, pumped water from the Seine to feed Versailles' fountains.

The Château of Saint-Germain-en-Laye houses the National Museum of Archaeology and its 29,000 objects spanning Paleolithic to Merovingian times. The Lady of Brassempouy, a tiny ivory face carved 21,000 years ago, is the centerpiece.
The Saint-Louis Chapel, built between 1230 and 1238, is a jewel of Rayonnant Gothic that inspired the Sainte-Chapelle in Paris. Its tall stained-glass windows flood the nave with light.

Climb up to the Grande Terrasse designed by Le Nôtre: 2.4 kilometers in a straight line, with a panoramic view over the Seine Valley and the western suburbs of Paris. On a clear day, the outline of La Défense stands out on the horizon.

activities.text: Follow the Impressionists' Path from Bougival to Chatou along the Seine. Enameled plaques reproduce paintings created at each spot, including Monet and Renoir's La Grenouillère.
Browse the Saint-Germain-en-Laye market, one of the finest in Yvelines, to taste regional produce from the Île-de-France.

days_plan.itin_title: Yvelines Road Trip: Versailles and Impressionist Villages

map_keywords: Musée du Domaine royal de Marly Port-Marly

visits.text: Saint-Gilles-Croix-de-Vie is the leading sardine port on the Atlantic coast, with around 3,000 tonnes of sardines landed each year. It is also the only port in France designated a “Site Remarquable du Goût,” a distinction awarded in 1998. If you stroll along the quays in the morning, you will see the trawlers returning—the fish auction, computerized since 1995, handles the catches of around forty vessels. Saint-Gilles sardines have even received the Label Rouge quality mark, a first for a wild fish.

Get lost in the Maroc district, also known as la Petite-Île, the city's oldest neighborhood. In the 16th century, descendants of Moors from Spain settled here and taught local fishermen the gillnetting technique, which revolutionized the region's economy. Houses are built from ballast stones unloaded from merchant ships. Seek out Rue Torterue, the main thoroughfare since the Middle Ages.

Le Remblai runs alongside the Grande Plage for about 3.5 km. Head to the viewpoint for a panorama of the two harbors—fishing and recreational boating, with Port La Vie offering more than 1,200 berths. If you are looking for somewhere quieter, the smaller, sheltered Boisvinet Beach is nearby and is well suited to families.
Saint-Gilles Church, restored in the 20th century, houses a series of Stations of the Cross by Vendée painter Henry Simon and remarkable stained glass. In summer, free guided tours are offered.

Visit the Atelier de la Sardine to understand the history of Vendée's last cannery. A video traces the sardine's entire journey—fishing, selection and canning by hand—and you can sample the products at the end of the visit. The museum also tells the story of fishing in Saint-Gilles since the 17th century.

activities.text: Walk along the Corniche Vendéenne between Saint-Gilles and Saint-Hilaire-de-Riez. This 3-kilometer coastal path, designated a protected natural site since 1926, winds along cliffs and coves with unobstructed views of the Atlantic. Belle Époque seaside villas overlook the rocky shore. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes for the round trip—you will have no difficulty.

If the season allows (April to September), detour through the salt marshes of Saint-Hilaire-de-Riez. Salt farmers harvest using ancestral methods and explain the difference between coarse salt and fleur de sel. Count on 1 hour for a guided tour.

days_plan.itin_title: Vendée Itinerary: Noirmoutier Island, Puy du Fou and the Coastline

visits.text: Saint-Girons is the lively capital of Couserans, set at the confluence of the Salat and its tributaries. The town is organized around the river: tree-lined riverside walks, old bridges, sidewalks of local gray-blue marble. Less monumental than neighboring Saint-Lizier, it has the active charm of a Pyrenean market town. Good base camp for exploring the valleys.

The big event is Saturday morning market on Place du Champ-de-Mars: one of the most important in the Ariège Pyrenees, where Couserans producers gather—cow and sheep cheeses, mountain charcuterie, and the famous croustillon. Arrive in the morning for the atmosphere and the best stalls. Guaranteed buzz on a fine-weather Saturday.

activities.text: From Saint-Girons, 18 valleys fan out toward the frontier peaks: this is the terrain of still-confidential hiking, toward summer pastures, passes, and lakes, with Mont Valier (2,838 m), emblem of Couserans, as the landmark. Perched villages, Romanesque churches, and slate-roofed farms dot the valleys. Choose a valley according to your level and available time.

The Salat and its tributaries rank among the Pyrenees' most renowned trout rivers: fly-fishing in swift, cool waters, in a mountain setting. Varied beats for beginners and experts alike, supervision possible with a local guide. Remember your fishing license before casting the first fly.

days_plan.itin_title: Ariège Road Trip: Cathars and Prehistoric Caves

visits.text: Gellone Abbey, founded in 804 by Guillaume, Duke of Aquitaine and Charlemagne's cousin, is a masterpiece of Languedoc Romanesque art. Listed as UNESCO World Heritage in 1998 as part of the Routes of Santiago de Compostela, it houses two major relics: those of Saint-Guilhem and a fragment of the True Cross given by Charlemagne. The abbey church impresses with its nave's height (18 meters for 6 wide). The cloister, partially reconstructed, preserves beautiful carved capitals. Part of the original cloister is in New York's Metropolitan Museum. It's a major spiritual site attracting pilgrims and visitors.

The medieval village of Saint-Guilhem-le-Désert, one of France's Most Beautiful Villages, stretches through the Gellone valley at the foot of vertiginous cliffs. Honey-colored stone houses with weathered tile roofs nestle in narrow cobbled lanes. Arcades, paired windows, and carved lintels testify to the medieval past. Place de la Liberté with its bicentennial plane tree planted in 1855 is the village heart. The atmosphere is preserved despite tourist crowds. Artisan shops, restaurants, and galleries animate the streets without spoiling the place's character.

The Devil's Bridge has spanned the Hérault gorges since 1031. It's one of France's oldest medieval bridges, UNESCO-listed. Built by the abbeys of Aniane and Gellone, it connected the river's two banks. Legend says the Devil offered to build the bridge in exchange for the first soul to cross it. Saint Guilhem tricked him by throwing a bone so a dog would pass first. Enraged, the Devil threw himself into the water, creating the "Devil's Hole." The site is magnificent with emerald waters and limestone cliffs. A beach allows swimming.

The Hérault gorges form a spectacular canyon carved through limestone. Steep cliffs, Mediterranean vegetation, and the Hérault's clear waters create remarkable landscapes. The site is classified as a Grand Site de France with the Cirque de l'Infernet. Hiking trails wind through the gorges with vertiginous viewpoints. The Cirque du Bout du Monde, accessible from Saint-Guilhem, is an impressive natural amphitheater. Fauna and flora are rich: eagles, eagle owls, cade junipers. It's a paradise for hikers and nature lovers.

Clamouse Cave, located between Saint-Guilhem and the Devil's Bridge, is internationally recognized for its exceptional concretions. Limestone formations—stalactites, stalagmites, draperies, fistulas—create a fairytale setting. The guided 1-hour tour takes you through several evocatively named rooms. The constant 16°C temperature is pleasant in summer. Light displays highlight the crystallizations. Several tour circuits are offered depending on preferences. Reservation advised in high season.

activities.text: Hike to the Cirque de l'Infernet, also called Cirque du Bout du Monde. The trail starts from Saint-Guilhem and plunges into the Gellone valley between vertiginous cliffs. The Chemin des Fenestrettes, built in the 18th century by monks as a corbelled path above the void, is spectacular. Arrival at the cirque rewards the effort: a natural amphitheater surrounded by 300-meter walls. The trail is 6 km round trip with moderate elevation gain. Allow 2-3 hours. Exceptional landscapes guaranteed. Bring water as there's little shade.

Swimming at the Devil's Bridge. The landscaped beach at the foot of the medieval bridge is very popular in summer. The Hérault's clear, cool waters invite swimming. The site is supervised in season and suitable for families with children. Water is shallow near the shore. The natural setting between limestone gorges and Mediterranean vegetation is magnificent. Beware of strong currents in the river's middle. Arrive early as the site is crowded in summer. Free shuttles from the Maison du Grand Site parking.

Canoe-kayak descent of the gorges. Several routes are offered between Saint-Bauzille-de-Putois and the Devil's Bridge. The descent crosses gorges between limestone cliffs and rapids. Water is cool and clear. The level is accessible to beginners on short routes. Rentals and shuttles are organized by providers. Allow 2 hours for a short route, 4 hours for the complete descent. Guaranteed thrills with fun passages. Life jacket provided. Reservation advised in summer.

A visit to the village of Saint-Jean-de-Fos, the potters' village 5 km from Saint-Guilhem. Pottery has been made here since the Middle Ages. Several workshops keep the tradition alive and welcome visitors. You can watch work on the wheel and buy handmade pieces. Argileum, the House of Pottery, presents the history of this craft with exhibitions and workshops. The village itself is charming with its narrow streets and its covered market hall. It is a pleasant stop to round off your discovery of the Hérault valley.

days_plan.itin_title: Occitanie's 13 Most Beautiful Villages
Southeast France Road Trip: Perched Villages and Gorges
Hérault Road Trip: Montpellier, Beaches and the Hinterland

places.name: Saint Haon Le Chatel

visits.text: Medieval Fortified Village. Perched on a rocky porphyry outcrop, Saint-Haon-le-Châtel retains its 14th-century ramparts, a configuration unique in the Loire department. At just 87 hectares, it is the department's smallest commune. Seventeen towers punctuate the medieval walls. Cobbled lanes lined with timber-framed houses, Renaissance manors such as the Fleur de Lys with its unusual turrets, and 17th- and 18th-century private mansions make up this village awarded the Village de Caractère label. The Hôtel Pelletier, a beautiful Renaissance residence, is built against one of the rampart towers.

Saint-Eustache Romanesque Church. A massive 12th-century Romanesque building anticipating the Gothic style with its pointed arches and lancet windows. The bell tower, set over the first bay of the nave, dominates the village. Chapels were added in the 15th century on the north side. A 17th-century five-sided chevet with tall round-arched windows. Statuary and murals decorate the interior. A porch adjoining the west façade gives access to the historic cemetery, which offers an exceptional panorama over the surroundings from the top of the hill.

Petit Chateaumorand and Gardens. A manor house accessible on guided tours. The medieval garden, reconstructed in the 1990s, presents medicinal and aromatic plants cultivated in the Middle Ages. Informational panels explain the uses of the plants. The garden is freely accessible. The Maison du Cadran Solaire, Maison Maret and Maison de la Murette complete the village's remarkable architectural heritage.

activities.text: Guided Village Tour. Historical walks are offered year-round by reservation, including at night for a special atmosphere. Guides introduce visitors to streets, alleys, inner courtyards, ramparts and the medieval garden. Anecdotes and historical explanations enrich the visit. Jean-Jules Jusserand, French ambassador to the United States from 1903 to 1925, vacationed in Saint-Haon-le-Châtel. A street and a tower bear his name.

Medieval Treasure Hunt. A scavenger hunt for families with children. The adventure “Le Boulet perdu de Charles VII” immerses participants in the village's history in 1440, when Charles VII confronted his son Louis XI. Capucine and Colline guide the searchers through medieval lanes to find the king's favorite cannonball. Booklet sold at the Tourist Office.

days_plan.itin_title: Loire Circuit: Wild Gorges and Industrial Heritage

map_keywords: Manoir de la Fleur de Lys Saint-Haon

visits.text: The Cirque de Consolation is a wild blind valley 350 metres deep with magnificent limestone cliffs, at the heart of the Doubs Horloger regional nature park. This is where the Dessoubre rises, fed by the Lançot, Tabourot and Source Noire springs. The Minim monastery, built in 1670 with stones from the château of Châtelneuf-en-Vennes destroyed during the Ten Years' War, forms a square 40 metres on each side. The 1682 chapel holds works of art and the mausoleum of Ferdinand-François de Rye. About 23 km from the base town, a 35-minute drive.

The Lançot waterfall drops 47 metres into the Cirque de Consolation. It flows during heavy rain or snowmelt. The path leading to it crosses a magical setting of streams, tufa formations and small caves. The lush vegetation creates an atmosphere that invites contemplation. About 23 km from the base town, a 35-minute drive.

Saint-Hippolyte, a character town of Bourgogne-Franche-Comté, nestles at the confluence of the Doubs and Dessoubre (the 'Revirot'). Freed by Jean II de la Roche in 1298, it preserves its 14th-century collegiate church of Notre-Dame where the Shroud of Turin was kept for 35 years (1418-1452), the 18th-century Ursuline convent, and 16th and 17th-century mullioned houses. It is the historic capital of the Franche-Montagne.

activities.text: The Roche du Prêtre viewpoint offers a dizzying panorama over the Cirque de Consolation and the Dessoubre valley, 350 metres below. Reached by car or on foot via a demanding hike. Legend has it that a priest was thrown from the top of the cliff by the friends of a giant he had shut in a cave. Picnic tables provided. About 23 km from the base town, a 35-minute drive.

Descend the Dessoubre valley to Saint-Hippolyte. This picturesque 33 km valley, where many water mills once sang, offers exceptional environmental richness. It is paradise for fishermen (trout, grayling) and walkers who appreciate the ambient calm. In summer, the cool water invites you to dip your feet.

days_plan.itin_title: Doubs Circuit: Watchmaking and Swiss Border

visits.text: The Thermal Baths, inaugurated in 1855, display neoclassical architecture with 1900 windows adorned with Briare enamels. The establishment opens onto a century-old six-hectare park.
Three springs feed the baths: "Romains," "Crevasse," and "Garenne." These chlorinated, sodic, and mildly sulfurous springs treat rheumatism and respiratory ailments.
The thermal park displays century-old oaks, plane trees, and cedars. Benches, basins, and stairways in Briare enamels take up the springs theme in Art Deco style, in Morvan colors: yellow and green.
Belle Époque villas adorned with carved fretwork, decorative red brick bands, and wrought-iron canopies dot the town. The bourgeoisie and aristocracy had them built in the 19th century.

The Château de La Montagne (16th century), entirely remodeled in the 18th by Jean-Baptiste Caristie, occupies a 25-hectare hamlet listed as a Historic Monument. Félix Duban redecorated the interiors in 1840.

activities.text: Enjoy the thermal SPA for a moment of relaxation: essential oil massages, hydrotherapy treatments, beauty rituals in a preserved natural setting.
Follow the heritage trail punctuated with markers discovering Belle Époque monuments linked to spa tourism: villas, casino, classified resort infrastructure.
Hike 10 kilometers between Bazois and Morvan, mainly through open landscapes with beautiful scenery and charming hamlets. Departs from the Tourist Office.
Relax at the Étang des Sources with its accessible fishing dock and "Family Fishing" label. Playground and picnic area complete the 8-hectare space.

days_plan.itin_title: Nièvre Road Trip: Morvan and Ducal Heritage

visits.text: Villa Ephrussi de Rothschild is the ultimate pink palace of the Riviera, perched on the narrowest part of Cap-Ferrat. Baroness Béatrice Ephrussi de Rothschild competed for the land in 1905 with King Leopold II of Belgium, who wanted to expand his neighboring property—she won by paying the price. Five years of construction (1907–1912), nine themed gardens, an Italian Renaissance facade. Famous anecdote: the baroness asked her gardeners to wear sailors' berets so she could imagine herself surrounded by a crew at sea. She bequeathed the villa and 5,000 works to the Académie des beaux-arts in 1934. Allow 2 hours for the villa and gardens.

The nine gardens of Villa Ephrussi are an experience in themselves: French (the main one, shaped like a ship's deck), Spanish, Florentine, stone, Japanese, exotic, Provençal, rose garden, Sèvres garden. Every half hour, the French garden comes alive with water jets synchronized to classical music—unashamedly kitsch, rather pretty. The view from the Temple of Love over the Villefranche roadstead on one side and Beaulieu bay on the other is the high point of the tour.

Make a detour to Villa Kérylos in Beaulieu-sur-Mer, five minutes by car from Cap-Ferrat. Inspired by the aristocratic houses of the island of Delos, it was built between 1902 and 1908 for archaeologist Théodore Reinach by architect Emmanuel Pontremoli. It cost nine million gold francs at the time, financed largely by the fortune of Reinach's wife, who belonged to the Ephrussi family. Reinach bequeathed the villa to the Institut de France in 1928. The villa is currently open to the public. Nevertheless, check the opening hours before your visit.

The Cap-Ferrat lighthouse, at the southern tip of the peninsula, is one of the most powerful on the French Mediterranean coast. Its range reaches 45 km. Built in 1827 and rebuilt after the destruction of 1944, it offers a 270° view from the surrounding grounds over Beaulieu, Villefranche and Monaco in the distance. Access inside is limited to a few Heritage Days—the exterior is more than enough.

activities.text: The Cap-Ferrat coastal path makes a complete loop of the peninsula over about 10 km. Limestone cliffs, wild coves, Aleppo pines, alternating panoramas over Beaulieu and Villefranche. Halfway along, the Saint-Hospice tower marks the former hermitage of the saint it is named after. Allow 3 hours for the complete loop, or choose a section. Closed-toe shoes are essential; there are no drinking water points on the route.

Swimming at Plage Paloma (pebbles, eastern exposure, clear water) or Plage de Passable (west side, well sheltered, direct view of Villefranche). Paloma is the most frequented and chicest, Passable more family-friendly. For more tranquility, head down to the small coves accessible from the coastal path.

Kayak or paddleboard from Plage de Passable: the cape waters are remarkably clear, pleasure boat traffic remains moderate outside July-August. The complete loop of the cape by kayak takes about 2.5 hours depending on your pace. Several operators on site, rental from €25 per hour.

Promenade Maurice Rouvier: flat, easy 2 km path connecting Beaulieu to Saint-Jean-Cap-Ferrat along the sea. The ideal walk in late afternoon—constant views over the roadstead, golden light, terraces to stop at. Doable even in dress shoes.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpes-Maritimes Road Trip: Riviera and Mercantour, 13 days
The 15 Gems of the French Riviera and Backcountry
7-Day French Riviera Circuit: Villefranche to Antibes

visits.text: Saint-Jean-de-Côle is one of Périgord Vert's most charming villages, classified as one of France's Most Beautiful. The central square, bordered by the Château de la Marthonie (15th-17th century), the market hall, and the Romanesque church, is among Dordogne's most harmonious. From the old humpback bridge, you'll capture the village's postcard view.

activities.text: Walk the village heritage loop—a 3-kilometer marked trail takes you through the lanes, along the river, and back via the old bridge. Allow 45 minutes. In May, the village hosts the Floralies, one of southwestern France's finest flower markets.

days_plan.itin_title: Nouvelle-Aquitaine Loop: Villages, Vineyards & Dordogne

places.name: Saint Jean De Luz

visits.text: The church of Saint-Jean-Baptiste is one of the most beautiful in the Basque Country — and one of the most closely tied to French history. It was here that Louis XIV married Maria Theresa of Austria on 9 June 1660, after the signing of the Treaty of the Pyrenees. The church was still a building site that day; temporary facades had been put up for the occasion. The gilded wooden baroque altarpiece, one of the largest in the Basque Country, was completed in 1669. The three tiers of carved oak galleries frame the nave on three sides — a feature of the churches of Labourd. Look for the walled-up door on the right-hand side: this is where the royal couple left, and it was sealed immediately afterwards so that no one else could use it.

The Maison Louis XIV, built in 1643 for the shipowner Joannis Lohobiague, was the king's lodging for forty days. Louis XIV called it his "Little Louvre." It is one of the few houses in France to have belonged to the same family since it was built. Its pink sandstone facades and corner towers reflect 17th-century shipowner architecture. Check the opening hours before you come — it is open only part of the year.

The House of the Infanta, built around 1640 by the shipowner Joannot de Haraneder, hosted Maria Theresa of Austria for her wedding to Louis XIV. The two newlyweds were 22 years old and doubly first cousins. Its two galleries with five Italian-style arcades overlook the port. The inscription carved above the door says it all: "I received the Infanta in the year sixteen sixty, I have been called the Infanta's castle ever since."

activities.text: The Port des Pêcheurs comes alive at dawn. Trawlers unload anchovies, tuna and hake from the bay of Saint-Jean. Stroll among the colourful boats and drying nets, then head to the covered market to buy fresh fish and gâteau basque.

The Rhune Train departs from Col de Saint-Ignace station, 7 km from Saint-Jean-de-Luz. This rack railway built in 1924 climbs in 35 minutes to 905 meters altitude at Mount Rhune's summit. At the top, pottoks — semi-wild Basque ponies — and griffon vultures roam free, and the view encompasses the ocean, beaches and the Pyrenees. Book your ticket online in season: queues can be very long in summer. The train does not operate in winter.

Watch a game of Basque pelota at the fronton by the harbour or in the trinquet. Chistera, bare hand, cesta punta — each variant has its own rules and champions. Games are held all summer long, and some are free. This is the national sport of the Basque Country, played here since the 16th century.

days_plan.itin_title: Bordeaux to Toulouse Road Trip: Ocean, Pyrenees and Heritage
Road Trip Pyrenees-Atlantiques: Basque Country and Bearn

map_keywords: Church of Saint John the Baptist Saint-Jean-de-Luz

visits.text: The Cathédrale Saint-Jean-Baptiste, founded in the 6th century, rebuilt in the 11th, and enlarged in the 15th, possesses one of France's oldest timber frames (wood dated to 1075). In the choir, 82 walnut Gothic stalls carved in 1498 depict saints, apostles, fauna, and flora—each one different from its neighbor.

The cloister, built around 1450 between the cathedral and the canons' refectory, unfolds its tufa vaults reinforced with local gypsum ribs. From the south bay, you access the Romanesque crypt, rediscovered in 1958 beneath the Gothic choir.

The neoclassical portico (1771) shelters the cenotaphs of three of the first princes of the House of Savoy: Humbert the White-Handed, founder of the dynasty, Amadeus I, and Boniface. The bell tower, a former 11th-century capitular keep, lost its Gothic spire during the Revolution.

The Musée Opinel occupies nearly 700 m² dedicated to the famous Savoyard knife. From the old forge to modern workshops, the exhibition traces the adventure of a tool created in 1890 in the nearby hamlet of Gévoudaz, today distributed in over 70 countries. Free entry, personalized engraving in the boutique.

Opposite the cathedral, the former bishop's palace (listed Historic Monument) houses the Musée des Costumes, Arts et Traditions Populaires. The collection of traditional Maurienne costumes, among the Alps' most original, displays embroidered headdresses, festive aprons, and dresses from the Arvan valleys.

Stroll through the historic center: the cathedral square hosts the market, lanes reveal the Tabellion block (medieval tribunal), the Art Deco festival hall (1933) that became the Théâtre Gérard Philipe, and at the town entrance, two giant Opinel knife sculptures mark local pride.

activities.text: Excursion to the Lacets de Montvernier. This spectacular road chains together eighteen tight hairpins on a vertical wall above the Maurienne valley. Plunging view guaranteed, a legendary Tour de France passage since 2015.
Cycling on the Maurienne greenway. The bike path follows the Arc through the valley, linking villages between orchards and valley-floor meadows. E-bike rental available on-site.

Tasting of Mauriennais specialties: Saint-Jean local cheese, diots (smoked sausages cooked in white wine), corn polenta, and crozets (small square buckwheat pasta). Restaurants around the cathedral square offer these traditional dishes.

days_plan.itin_title: Savoie from Lakes to Glaciers: Yenne to Haute-Maurienne

visits.text: Village of Saint-Jean-du-Gard, typical Cévennes town in the heart of Cévennes National Park. Schist houses with slate roofs tier along the Gardon. The 12th-century Romanesque church stands beside a Protestant temple testifying to Cévennes Huguenot history. Paved streets lined with artisan workshops wind between fountains and shaded squares. Tuesday morning market animates the center with local products and friendly atmosphere. The multi-arched medieval bridge spans the Gardon offering views of surrounding mountains.

Musée des Vallées Cévenoles – Maison Rouge, ethnographic collection tracing traditional lifestyles. Reconstructions present authentic Cévennes interiors: rustic furniture, daily utensils, regional costumes. The silk-farming department evokes the epic of magnaneries and flourishing silk industry until 1900. Thematic rooms document terraced agriculture, sheep farming, century-old chestnut groves. The Camisard space relates Wars of Religion and Protestant resistance in the 18th century. Temporary exhibitions deepen intangible Cévennes heritage.

Saint-Jean-du-Gard outdoor summer pool, a municipal facility where visitors can cool off on hot summer days. The pools provide an enjoyable aquatic break in the heart of the village. This family activity offers a relaxing pause between two visits in the Cévennes.

activities.text: Hike the Stevenson Trail (GR70) crossing the Cévennes. The Scottish writer covered 137 miles in 1878 with his donkey Modestine, recounted in "Travels with a Donkey in the Cévennes." The mythical trail winds through chestnut groves, schist ridges, deep valleys, and isolated hamlets. Stages around Saint-Jean-du-Gard discover typical Cévennes landscapes: cultivated terraces, pastoral drailles, mountain panoramas. Gîtes d'étape dot the route welcoming hikers. Donkey rental perpetuates the Stevensonian tradition.

Discover Cévennes chestnut groves, cultivated forests shaping terraced landscapes. The chestnut tree, the "bread tree," ensured Cévennes subsistence providing flour, building wood, and heating. Century-old orchards with gnarled trunks tier on slopes arranged in terraces supported by dry-stone walls. Autumn sees fallen chestnuts gathered and transformed into cream, jam, flour. Clèdes, vaulted buildings for drying, dot the chestnut groves. Interpretive trails explain this heritage silviculture inscribed by UNESCO.

Visit a traditional magnanerie, silkworm breeding building. Restored magnaneries testify to prosperous silk-farming industry in the 18th-19th centuries. Vaulted rooms sheltered racks supporting millions of worms devouring mulberry leaves. The complete process—from egg to cocoon, silk reeling, weaving—unfolds through exhibitions and demonstrations. Mulberry trees planted on terraces fed seasonal breeding operations. The Cévennes silk epic exported to Lyon enriched the region before declining against Asian competition.

days_plan.itin_title: Gard Circuit: Roman Nîmes, Pont du Gard and Camargue

visits.text: The Porte Saint-Jacques marks the historic entry of pilgrims into the town and is part of the UNESCO property inscribed in 1998. At 39 rue de la Citadelle you will find the pilgrims' welcome office — this is where walkers have their credencial stamped before tackling the crossing of the Pyrenees. More than 60,000 pilgrims pass through each year on their way to Roncevaux, 8 km away.

The Citadel stands 80 metres above the town on the hill of Mendiguren. Built around 1625 on the site of the castle of the kings of Navarre, it was reworked by Vauban after his inspection in 1685 — he found almost nothing to change, so excellent was the existing work. Now a listed Historic Monument occupied by a secondary school, it can be visited in summer on guided tours that go down into the underground passages and reveal the period bread oven. The view over the Cize valley and the Pyrenees is exceptional.

Walk down the rue de la Citadelle, paved and lined with pink sandstone houses. The carved lintels bear the names of the houses, the year of construction and the initials of the first owners. The Church of Notre-Dame, 14th-century Gothic with its facade of pink Arradoy sandstone, is a listed Historic Monument. Look for the gateway that incorporates the bell tower, on the left as you enter — this arrangement is rare.

The Prison of the Bishops, at 41 rue de la Citadelle, takes its name from the presence of three bishops of Bayonne during the Western Schism, between 1383 and 1417. The building later served as a prison until the 20th century. Its vast pointed-arch vaulted hall in the basement, with chains still fixed to the walls, today houses a permanent exhibition on the Road to Santiago.
