activities.text: Walk the full rampart walkway that runs along the walls of the upper town — 269 steps lead up to the terrace from the place des Casernes. The view from the watchtower above the Porte Saint-Antoine is one of the finest in the inland Basque Country: the gave, the green valley and the first Pyrenean peaks.

The Monday morning market is held on the place des Remparts. Sheep cheeses, Banca trout, Irouléguy AOP wines — one of France's smallest wine regions, a few kilometres away — and Itxassou cherry jam fill the stalls. A producers' market is added every Thursday in summer.

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip Pyrenees-Atlantiques: Basque Country and Bearn

places.name: Saint Jean Saint Maurice Sur Loire

visits.text: Château de la Roche. Anchored on its rocky outcrop in the middle of the Loire since the 13th century, this castle, an emblem of the gorges, seems to float on the water when the river is high, or to rest on its Scottish plinth when the Loire is low in autumn. A theatrical tour is offered by actor-guides playing Mr. and Mrs. Roustan, the owners between 1900 and 1930. The recreated interiors of their summer residence immerse visitors in the Belle Époque and the castle's history. The four-leaf clover, a symbol of good luck, adorns the façades and interior decoration. Two escape games allow visitors to discover the castle's secrets.

Medieval village of Saint-Maurice. Perched on a promontory overlooking the Loire, the medieval town retains its 12th-century keep, 17 meters high. A spiral staircase leads to the top, offering a 360° panorama over the waters of the Villerest reservoir and the meanders of the Loire. The castle walls, the 17th-century Manoir de la Mure with its doorway topped by a carved lintel and finely decorated stair tower, and the Maison du Cadran Solaire make up this village awarded the Village de Caractère label. Ruelle Guy de la Mure, lined with ivy-covered houses, offers a peaceful atmosphere.

Saint-Maurice Church. The choir, entirely covered with listed 13th-century frescoes, forms an exceptional group of paintings. In a window recess on the south wall, a painting depicting Saint James attests that Saint-Maurice was on the pilgrimage route to Santiago de Compostela. The Cluny/Le Puy-en-Velay Way of Saint James still passes through the village. Saint-Jean Church, rebuilt around 1870, retains its 12th-century bell tower incorporating an entrance porch, the only surviving part of the Benedictine priory dismantled during the Revolution.

Joeuvres Archaeological Site. On the Loire's right bank, this hamlet shelters a Celtic oppidum inhabited since prehistoric times. Excavations led notably by Joseph Déchelette in 1911 revealed two 1st-century BCE bronze statuettes representing a horse and a wild boar, visible at Roanne's Joseph-Déchelette Museum. Ionian and Phocaean amphora shards prove Mediterranean trade via the Rhône and Ardèche. A bronze workshop operated on this strategic site.

activities.text: Pêt d'Âne viewpoint. In the commune of Vézelin-sur-Loire, this panoramic site offers the finest view over the meanders of the Loire, about 28 km from the stopover town, a 40-minute drive. A bench for contemplation faces the largest meander on the river. Below, kayaks and paddleboards glide along the wild river. The medieval silhouettes of Saint-Jean-Saint-Maurice-sur-Loire form a living postcard. Parking and easy access from the road.

Ridge path. A short walk offering the best views over the meanders of the Loire and the tower of Saint-Jean-Saint-Maurice. An elevated route overlooking the river. Trails through woods and meadows. Several craftspeople based in the village open their studios and shops by appointment.

days_plan.itin_title: Loire Circuit: Wild Gorges and Industrial Heritage

visits.text: Saint-Jeannet is a hilltop village at the foot of the Baou, a Provençal word for a steep rock with a flat summit. About twenty kilometers from Nice. The oldest neighborhood, Queirard, has “calades”: sloping lanes interrupted by steps to prevent gullying, a technique inherited from Roman roads. Saint-Jeannet was long a land of vines and wine; the Rasse family continues this tradition on Route des Sausses toward Gattières.

The panorama from the village stretches from the Col de Braüs (Italian border) to the Estérel mountains in the west. In clear weather, Corsica appears on the horizon. Artists began settling here in the 1950s, drawn by the tranquility. Dada poet Georges Ribemont-Dessaignes lived here from 1944 to 1974 and invited his friends: Tristan Tzara and Jacques Prévert stayed in Saint-Jeannet.

activities.text: The hike to the Baou de Saint-Jeannet is the area's signature excursion. The summit rises to about 800 meters (exactly 802 m according to the IGN), and the Baou towers 300 meters above the village. From the René Veyssi parking lot, the round trip is 6 km and takes 2.5 to 3 hours of walking. At the summit, a 360° panorama of the Côte d'Azur, the Mercantour, and Italy: one of the region's best panoramic views. The Baou is also a major climbing site, with 470 routes across 17 sectors. Start early; the parking lot fills quickly in summer.

For a longer circuit, the trail passes the ruins of a 14th-century fortified sheepfold (the Castellet) and Baou de la Gaude (796 m), with vestiges of a Ligurian enclosure and a centuries-old oak nearly 7 meters in circumference. Allow 5 hours for the complete loop. Signposted route, but less frequented than the main Baou.

On the way down, refresh yourself at the village fountains. Artisans offer herb ravioli to go, a local specialty inherited from the County of Nice. If you have access to a kitchen tonight, this is what I recommend: 5 minutes in boiling water and a drizzle of olive oil, and there's your dinner after the hike.

days_plan.itin_title: The 15 Gems of the French Riviera and Backcountry
Nice's hinterland: 8 days of hilltop villages and the Mercantour

places.name: Saint Junien

visits.text: The Collégiale de Saint-Junien, one of the largest and oldest Romanesque churches in Limousin, was built from the 11th to 13th centuries in local granite. Its tomb of Saint Junien, carved around 1100 in La Rochefoucauld limestone, bears on three faces the twenty-four elders of the Apocalypse and Christ in a mandorla.

In the nave, look up: the 12th-century fresco of the twenty-four elders of the Apocalypse echoes the tomb's iconography. The Saint-Martial chapel preserves Romanesque paintings showing the display of relics attended by pilgrims who came seeking healing.

The Chapelle Notre-Dame-du-Pont, in Flamboyant Gothic style, has guarded the Vienne bridge entrance since 1451. Enlarged thanks to the generosity of King Louis XI, who came on pilgrimage in 1463, it remains a place of popular devotion.

The Cité du Cuir, opened in late 2025 on the banks of the Vienne at the site of former tanneries, traces the complete luxury glove manufacturing cycle. The immersive museum route runs from raw hide to finished product, passing through reconstructed workshops.

The Maison des Consuls, built in the 14th century, testifies to the medieval town's prosperity. A few steps away, the Bourse du Travail on Place Lénine recalls the working-class social history of Saint-Junien, a town with a glove-making tradition dating back to the 11th century.

activities.text: Every seven years, Saint-Junien celebrates the Septennial Ostensions, inscribed by UNESCO: 1,500 costumed participants parade through the town in a procession around the relics.
Follow the banks of the Glane to the Site Corot, designated a Natural Area of Ecological Interest.
Visit a glove-making workshop to observe artisan craftsmanship, from cutting leather to assembling gloves. Saint-Junien has supplied the greatest fashion houses since the 19th century.

visits.text: Saint-Lary-Soulan was formed by the 1963 merger of the villages of Saint-Lary and Soulan to enable the ski resort's expansion. Located in the Aure valley and designated a Pays d'Art et d'Histoire, the village is a historic stop on the Way of Saint James. The main street bears the name of Vincent Mir, founder of the resort. The Pyrenean architecture of its stone houses and their enhanced facades, the Pic Lumière cable car, and the Vignec gondola linking the village to the slopes create an authentic mountain setting.

The Maison du Patrimoine, located at 41 rue Vincent Mir on the Tourist Office square, houses several exhibition spaces dedicated to Pyrenean heritage: traditions, wildlife, architecture, schooling, and livestock farming in the past. Upstairs, an interactive 3D map lets visitors explore the valley's trails, passes, and lakes. Temporary exhibitions of painting, photography, and sculpture are presented throughout the year. Guided village tours are organized by the Pays d'Art et d'Histoire Aure-Louron association.

The Church of Saint-Bertrand, built between 1950 and 1952 and consecrated in October 1952, replaced the old Saint-Hilaire church. Nearby, the Sainte-Marie Chapel and the Romanesque chapels from the 11th and 12th centuries in surrounding villages testify to the valley's rich religious heritage. The restored Moulin Debat can be visited, as can the Moulin de la Mousquère in Soulan village, renovated and dating from the Middle Ages.

Soulan, an unspoilt, sunny pastoral village, overlooks Saint-Lary from the heights towards the ski resort. Three kilometres away, Vielle-Aure offers a typical village with cobbled lanes and a 12th-century Romanesque church. Further on, Ancizan (six kilometres), a former village of cloth merchants and weavers, retains the church of Saint-Blaise-et-Saint-Martin. Gouaux and Grailhen enjoy a particularly favourable exposure and sweeping views of the peaks, with the goat farm in Gouaux available to visit.

The Rioumajou Valley, accessible from the Frédancon parking lot at an altitude of 1,380 meters (twelve kilometers from Saint-Lary), offers an easy two-hour round-trip family hike on a forest track following the Neste du Rioumajou. The pastoral valley opens out into vast meadows crossed by a mountain stream winding to the Hospice du Rioumajou, a mountain hut and restaurant at an altitude of 1,560 meters with 27 beds. Awarded the “Esprit Parc national” label, it is open from June to September. For more experienced walkers, the Balcon de l'Hospice (1,969 m) offers a viewpoint overlooking the site, accessible in two and a half hours round trip. Vehicle access is regulated from July to August between 12 pm and 4 pm.

The Néouvielle Nature Reserve, created in 1936 and one of France's first nature reserves, covers 2,313 hectares at altitudes between 1,800 and 3,091 meters. It is home to seventy lakes (Aubert, Aumar, Orédon, Cap-de-Long, l'Oule), mountain pines that hold records for longevity and altitude, 1,250 vascular plants, 370 animal species, and 570 algae species. Access is via the lakes road from Saint-Lary, with shuttles between Orédon and Aubert in season. Bivouacking is permitted from 7 pm to 9 am in designated areas; dogs and swimming are prohibited.

activities.text: Stroll through Saint-Lary's streets starting from the Maison du Patrimoine, then climb toward Soulan village for a sunny panorama over the Aure valley and its peaks.

Hike in the Rioumajou Valley to the Hospice, an easy and bucolic two-hour round-trip walk along the mountain stream, ideal for families—the mountain hut's restaurant serves cuisine awarded the “Esprit Parc national” label.

Follow the lake road towards the Réserve du Néouvielle, allowing for a day excursion there and back from Saint-Lary, to discover the lakes of Aubert and Orédon amid their thousand-year-old mountain pines - shuttle services make access easier in summer.
Visit the villages of Vielle-Aure and Ancizan to discover traditional Pyrenean architecture, cobbled streets, and Romanesque churches, before stopping at the Gouaux goat farm.
Thrill-seekers will find a wide choice of activities in Saint-Lary: canyoning, rafting on the Neste, mountain biking in the bike park, paragliding, via ferrata, and downhill electric scooters.

visits.text: Saint-Laurent-sous-Coiron places you at the foot of the Coiron massif, an imposing basalt plateau that visually contrasts with lower Ardèche's white limestone. The village occupies a plateau edge with exceptional views in every direction. Remains of the old castrum can still be read in the village fabric: a partly preserved enclosure, houses crowded around the church square, the defensive layout typical of perched villages in Bas-Vivarais.

The geological interest of the Coiron is spectacular. The basalt flows that form the plateau have created landscapes of organ-pipe columns and dykes visible along the ridges. From the heights of the village, on a clear day, the view takes in the Cévennes to the west and the first lines of ridges leading towards Aubenas.

The church square atop the village is the quietest spot for a break: houses shelter the square's corners and an old fountain sometimes runs. The view south over valleys descending toward the Ardèche is particularly beautiful late in the day.

activities.text: The ridge trail on the Coiron rim (3 to 5 km from the village) is the area's signature walk. It follows the break in slope between the basalt plateau and limestone hills, with views north over the plateau and south over valleys. Allow 1h30 to 2h at your pace.

Stop on the road reaching the plateau to observe basalt columns on the cliff face—these hexagonal columns formed by cooling lava flows are visible from the road without requiring a walk. A good moment of geological reading to understand where the black stones omnipresent in local construction come from.

days_plan.itin_title: The 18 Most Beautiful Villages of Ardèche

visits.text: Limeuil, at the confluence of the Dordogne and Vézère rivers, is classified as one of France's Most Beautiful Villages. Climb to the Jardins Panoramiques for views across both rivers—you'll look down over the entire confluence from the former château site. In summer, the pebble beaches are perfect for a swim.

Saint-Amand-de-Coly shelters a fortified 12th-century abbey—one of Dordogne's most beautiful. You'll see the fortress-church, with its 2-meter-thick walls and wall-walk, served as a refuge during wartime. The honey-stone village is tiny and silent.

Saint-Léon-sur-Vézère is a small town nestled in a meander of the Vézère. Its 12th-century Romanesque church, right at the water's edge, is one of Périgord's most harmonious—you'll see it reflected in the river from the bridge.

activities.text: Canoe down the Vézère from Saint-Léon—the section toward Les Eyzies is easy, flat, and passes through landscapes of limestone cliffs. Allow 2 to 3 hours depending on the distance you choose—you'll make the most of it.

days_plan.itin_title: Nouvelle-Aquitaine Loop: Villages, Vineyards & Dordogne

visits.text: The Collégiale de Saint-Léonard, inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List as part of the Routes of Santiago de Compostela, dominates the town from its seven-story bell tower rising 52 meters. Pass through the Limousin portal to discover the barrel-vaulted nave, the octagonal lantern tower, and the vast choir with ambulatory encircled by seven radiating chapels.

At the heart of the collegiate church, Saint Leonard's tomb is covered with chains of “freed prisoners”. Tradition holds that women touch the saint's lock bolt to have their prayers answered. Small slippers are still placed on the tomb in thanks.

The baptistery rotunda, vaulted with a cupola resting on eight columns, was erected around 1100, during the time of the First Crusade. It illustrates Limousin Romanesque architectural mastery at its finest.

The Moulin du Got, Limousin's last working paper mill, brings to life handmade papermaking and printing techniques from the 15th to 20th centuries. Take home a souvenir made from paper crafted on-site.

The Musée Gay-Lussac, awarded the Maison des Illustres label, honors the chemist born here in 1778. Personal clothing, laboratory instruments, and publications trace the life and work of this scientist who gave his name to several fundamental laws of gas physics.

activities.text: Roam the lanes of the medieval town between the round tower and the square tower. Gothic facades, secret passages, and remnants of the gates in the town walls mark the route. Saint-Léonard is listed among the “Plus Beaux Détours de France”.
Walk down to the old 13th-century stone bridge over the Vienne. The small 4 km loop offers views of the viaduct and surrounding countryside — ideal for a post-meal stroll.
Taste the massepain de Saint-Léonard, a cookie made from ground almonds, sugar, and egg white. Legend says this Mediterranean-flavored delicacy was brought back by pilgrims returning from Compostela.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Vienne Tour: Limoges, Porcelain and Villages

visits.text: Saint-Lizier, a former Gallo-Roman city that became the religious capital of Couserans, has been listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1998 as part of the Routes of Santiago de Compostela, and holds a curiosity: two cathedrals in the same village. The one in the lower town, the parish church, preserves an exceptional ensemble of Romanesque frescoes dated 1060–1080, among the oldest in the Pyrenees, and a treasury with the reliquary bust of Saint Lizier. Open year-round, the interior truly merits the stop.

Adjacent to this cathedral, the 12th-century Romanesque cloister is Ariège's only cloister: vaulted galleries, twin columns, and carved capitals around a peaceful garden—Pyrenean Romanesque art at its peak. You'll gladly linger longer than planned, especially in morning light. Included with cathedral admission.

In the upper town, the Bishops' Palace overlooks Saint-Lizier and the Salat Valley: 77 bishops succeeded one another here, and it now houses the Ariège departmental museum. It adjoins the second cathedral, Notre-Dame-de-la-Sède, nicknamed the Ariège Sistine Chapel for its Renaissance paintings and twelve sibyls, all encircled by a 5th-century Gallo-Roman wall, one of the best preserved in southern France. Beautiful view over the Pyrenees from the terrace.

activities.text: Saint-Lizier is also savored on foot, without specific monument in mind: cobbled lanes, half-timbered and overhanging houses, former canons' residences, clock tower, and little squares open onto the mountains. Slip down to the old Hôtel-Dieu and its 18th-century pharmacy, remarkably preserved. An hour's wander, effortlessly.

days_plan.itin_title: Ariège Road Trip: Cathars and Prehistoric Caves

visits.text: The abbey church of Saint-Maixent has weathered fifteen centuries, bearing the scars: founded in the 5th century on the site of the monk Maixent’s cell, plundered by the Normans, ravaged by a series of fires in the 11th and 12th centuries, and largely destroyed by Protestants in 1568. The Benedictine Congregation of Saint-Maur began rebuilding it in 1633, entrusting the work to architect François Le Duc, known as Toscane—the same man who would rebuild Celles-sur-Belle. What you see today is therefore a 17th-century Gothic building standing on 11th-century Romanesque foundations. At 92 meters long and 24 meters wide, the nave impresses with its height and Late Gothic vaults. Admission is free.

The Saint-Léger crypt is one of the oldest surviving funerary structures in France. Built around the 7th century to house the relics of Saint Léger—the sixth abbot of Saint-Maixent, who became bishop of Autun before being martyred and beheaded in 678 on the orders of Ebroin, mayor of the palace—it was remodeled and redecorated in 1681 by François Le Duc. The crypt can only be visited on a guided tour: ask at the tourist office.

The cloister and chapter house, adjoining the abbey church, host exhibitions and cultural events. They belong to the military complex that occupied this site for many years—the École nationale des sous-officiers d’active still operated here until 2011.

activities.text: Stroll along the banks of the Sèvre Niortaise among half-timbered houses and 16th-century mansions—some have miraculously survived fires and wars. On Place du Marché, look for the house with an arcaded gallery dating from 1470: a fine example of Poitou’s secular architecture.
Markets have been held on Saturday mornings on Place du Marché since 1469—by royal decree. That’s a useful historical reference point. Local products from Haut Val de Sèvre are well represented here.

days_plan.itin_title: Deux-Sèvres Tour: Marais Poitevin and Romanesque Heritage

visits.text: Saint-Malo Intra-Muros. Reconstructed stone by stone after the 1944 bombardments, the privateers' city stands behind granite ramparts facing the ocean. The complete circuit of the walls takes 1 hour along 2 kilometers of rampart walkways, offering breathtaking panoramas of the emerald sea, Fort National at high tide, and the Grand Bé and Petit Bé islands. Inside, the grid of cobbled streets leads to the castle of the Dukes of Brittany, which houses the city museum, while Saint-Vincent Cathedral has watched over the city since the 12th century. The maritime atmosphere permeates every alley, where shipowners' mansions testify to the wealth born of privateering and overseas trade.

Fort National. Built by Vauban in 1689 on a rocky islet, this defensive fort is accessible only at low tide via Éventail Beach. The guided tour reveals the underground passages, drawbridge, ramparts, and the dark history of 1944, when 380 hostages were imprisoned there by the Germans. From the top, the 360° view of Saint-Malo, the bay, and the Emerald Coast as far as Cap Fréhel makes the climb worthwhile. Wear good shoes and be sure to check tide times before going to avoid being stranded on the rock for six hours.

Grand Bé and Chateaubriand's Tomb. Three hundred meters from Intra-Muros, this granite islet shelters the simple tomb of François-René de Chateaubriand, facing the sea as he wished. The Romantic writer has rested facing the ocean since 1848, with a simple inscription on the rock: “A great French writer wished to rest here to hear only the sea and the wind. Passerby, respect his last wish.” Accessible only at low tide, the walk offers an exceptional panorama of the ramparts and a moment of contemplation imbued with literary emotion.

Grand Aquarium. Beyond the historic center, this modern aquarium takes visitors into the world's oceans through 600,000 liters of seawater and 11,000 animals. The touch pool allows visitors to touch rays and dogfish, the underwater tunnel in the Anneau des Mers literally immerses them among sharks, and the Abyssal room presents strange creatures from the deep. Shipwreck reconstructions and the Nautibus virtual submarine voyage complete a fun visit particularly appreciated by families on rainy days.

activities.text: Sillon Beach and Promenade. This immense 3-kilometer beach of fine sand stretches between Rochebonne and the fort de la Cité, bordered by a seawall promenade ideal for walking and jogging. Blue-and-white striped beach huts create a retro seaside atmosphere, while water sports clubs offer sand yachting, kitesurfing, and sailing. The uninterrupted view of the Intra-Muros ramparts gives every swim an exceptional setting.

Route du Rhum. Every four years in November, Saint-Malo comes alive for the start of this famous solo transatlantic race to Guadeloupe. For two weeks, the race village takes over the quays with exhibitions, activities, and boat presentations. Even between editions, the city museum traces the history of this legendary event and the great Saint-Malo sailors who have left their mark on world sailing.

days_plan.itin_title: Brittany Road Trip: Villages with Character, Sea and History
The Grand Tour of France in 5 Weeks, Car-Free
Ille-et-Vilaine Tour: Saint-Malo, Dinard and the Emerald Coast

visits.text: In the 15th century, Saint-Marcellin was the stronghold hosting the region's largest market, held three times weekly. This market gave its name to the town's emblematic cheese—an 80-gram disc with soft paste and bloomy rind, first documented in King Louis XI's household accounts from 1461. Saved from a bear in 1447, Louis XI allegedly received bread and cheese—Saint-Marcellin—from two local woodcutters. According to legend, he promised them fortune and nobility. The cheese earned its PGI designation in 2013, covering 274 communes across Isère, Drôme, and Savoie.

Saint-Marcellin's old center preserves a medieval layout around its church with arcades, narrow streets, and remnants of ramparts. Then descend to the Isère riverbanks: the tree-lined promenades along the river offer open views of the Royans hillsides.

activities.text: The historic gates and suburbs circuit of Saint-Marcellin covers about 2 km on flat ground and reveals the different layers of occupation from the medieval town onward. If you're there Wednesday or Saturday morning, the weekly market is a perfect opportunity to taste Saint-Marcellin PGI in its two states: dry with blue rind, Dauphiné style; or soft and creamy, Lyon style.

The riverside walk along the Isère, downstream from the town center, leads to the confluence with the Bourne. It's a bucolic route with no elevation gain, perfect for evening strolls with reflections on the water and Royans hillsides in the background.

days_plan.itin_title: Royans-Vercors Road Trip: Hilltop Villages and Gorges

visits.text: Saint-Martin-d'Ardèche marks the spectacular end of the Gorges at their confluence with the Rhône. The village, with its Station Verte designation, offers developed beaches and family activities. The Famille Plus label guarantees infrastructure and entertainment suited to all ages.

The scenic road winds for 29 km between Vallon and Saint-Martin, offering eleven developed lookout points. The belvédère de la Cathédrale, the Rocher de la Cathédrale, and la Madeleine reveal dizzying views over the river's meanders. The limestone cliffs drop from heights of up to 300 meters.

The beaches of Saint-Martin line the Ardèche with tranquil coves. Pont Cassé beach offers a peaceful setting for swimming and picnics. The calm waters downstream from the gorges are perfectly suited for families with young children.

The lanes of the medieval village of Saint-Marcel-d'Ardèche rise in tiers, paved with pebbles from the Rhône. Ochre facades and vaulted passages create an authentic Provençal setting. The nearby Saint-Marcel cave reveals a spectacular underground network.

activities.text: The bois de Païolive spreads its forest of downy oaks among rugged limestone rocks; plan a day trip from Saint-Martin-d'Ardèche. Rock formations sculpted by erosion create a unique mineral labyrinth. The Chassezac winds through this geological jumble, designated an Espace Naturel Sensible, with opportunities to swim in natural pools.

The weekly market brings Saint-Martin to life every Wednesday morning in summer. Colorful stalls offer local produce, olives, goat cheeses, and specialties from Ardèche. The lively Provençal atmosphere celebrates local flavors beneath the plane trees.

days_plan.itin_title: Ardèche Road Trip: Wild Gorges and Villages with Character

visits.text: Saint-Martin-de-Brômes is a village of endearing simplicity: Jean Giono nicknamed it “the curled-up fox”. It was built in an amphitheatre-like arrangement on the slope of Castelleras Hill, at the confluence of the Colostre and the Pontet. The village emblem is the Clock Tower — a former keep built by Boniface de Castellane in the 14th century, standing 24 metres high and equipped with machicolations and arrow slits. Listed as a Historic Monument since 1921, it has housed one of France's smallest museums (10 m²) since 1972. On the ground floor are a 4th-century Gallo-Roman sarcophagus with a 300 kg lead lid and an intact skeleton, discovered during roadworks in 1972, and a milestone of Emperor Carus (282–283 CE) that marked the Roman road between Aix-en-Provence and Riez.

The Romanesque Church of Saint-Martin (12th–14th centuries), listed as a Historic Monument, is known for its 19th-century murals by Esprit Michel Gibelin — a student in Cézanne's studio — depicting the lives of Saint Martin and the Virgin in the blind arcades of the nave. Also look for the church's oldest statuette: Saint Anthony the Hermit, patron saint of truffle growers, in gilded and polychrome wood.

activities.text: 7 km away, Lake Esparron-de-Verdon opens onto turquoise water — an artificial reservoir created in 1967, but set in a landscape of limestone gorges that gives it a wild appearance. Operators offer pedal boats, canoes, and electric boats for rent. It's one of the best swimming spots in the region, ideal for an afternoon.

The GR4 crosses the commune and offers beautiful ridge trails above the Colostre — views of the Valensole plateau on one side and the emerging Verdon gorges on the other. A 2-hour loop suffices for the most interesting viewpoints.

days_plan.itin_title: Forcalquier & Verdon Gorges Road Trip

visits.text: Welcome to the Crau plain — a landscape unique in France: 55,000 hectares of pebbles rolled by the ancient Durance three million years ago, forming Western Europe's only dry grassland steppe. The Crau sèche, an area classified as a national nature reserve covering 7,400 hectares, harbors species existing nowhere else in France — little bustard, pin-tailed sandgrouse, ocellated lizard. The Crau ecomuseum offers a complete introduction to this singular ecosystem.

The irrigated Crau's canal irrigation system is a hydraulic work dating back to Adam de Craponne (16th century) — the engineer who created the canal bearing his name to bring Durance water to the Crau. This network transformed part of the dry steppe into Crau hay meadows (PDO since 1997, the only PDO for hay in France). Irrigated meadows are easily recognized by their grass's intense green in midsummer.

activities.text: Wildlife observation on Crau sèche tracks: according to regulations (inquire at the ecomuseum), marked circuits allow observation of steppe fauna — little bustards (during display period, April-May), pin-tailed sandgrouse, short-toed snake eagles, and lesser kestrels. The Crau is an ornithologically exceptional area for open Mediterranean habitat species.

Cycling loop in the irrigated plain (completely flat terrain): agricultural paths crossing the irrigated Crau among hay meadows, shepherds' huts, and market gardens offer a ride completely off ordinary marked trails. A few 17th-18th century farmhouses dot the route.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpilles, Aix-en-Provence & Arles Circuit
Côte Bleue and Camargue: the lower coastal route in 7 days

visits.text: The bridge to the île de Ré, 2.9 km long, has linked the mainland to the island since 1988. There is a toll on entering the island (free on leaving).

The fortifications of Saint-Martin-de-Ré, built by Vauban between 1681 and 1691, form a 14 km star-shaped rampart. UNESCO World Heritage since 2008, they could shelter the entire island population in the event of an English invasion. Walking or cycling the ramparts is spectacular.

The port of Saint-Martin-de-Ré, nestled within the fortified walls, has quays lined with outdoor seating areas. Convicts bound for Cayenne departed from here—the citadel served as a holding depot. Climb the church tower for a panoramic view of the island.

The phare des Baleines, at the western tip of the island, stands 60 metres tall. 257 steps lead to the top - a 360° view of the ocean and the island. The name comes from the whales that once washed ashore on this coast. The old Vauban tower (1682) and a lighthouse museum complete the site. Plan a return trip during the day from Saint-Martin-de-Ré.

activities.text: The île de Ré by bicycle: 110 km of cycle paths connect the island’s ten villages. Bicycle rental in every village. The Saint-Martin → Phare des Baleines route crosses the salt marshes and the pine forest.

A visit to the salt marshes of Loix or Ars-en-Ré. Salt workers harvest fleur de sel by hand using techniques that date back millennia. Guided walks in the marshes, explanations of the work and tastings.

Île de Ré beaches: fine sand on the south coast (Bois-Plage, La Couarde), wilder to the north. Fish traps, semi-circular stone walls, catch fish on the ebb tide—an ancestral technique still practiced.

days_plan.itin_title: Charente-Maritime Road Trip: La Rochelle, Île de Ré, Fort Boyard and Roman Saintonge

visits.text: Saint-Martin-en-Vercors is a valley village nestled at the foot of the Drôme Vercors ridges. The Romanesque church and surrounding hamlets compose a tableau of peaceful mountain countryside, crossed by combe streams. Wet meadows and beech forests descend to the first houses—an atmosphere that changes from Vassieux's open plateau.

The Combe de la Balme, downstream from the village, is a wooded corridor between two series of cliffs. Looking east from the village bottom, you see ridges culminating around 1,500 meters—a continuous wall marking the boundary between plateau and Die plain. The gray-orange cliffs change hue according to time of day.

activities.text: The hamlets and stream banks loop (3-4 km) connects the various hamlets composing the commune via farm roads. Combe streams are cool even in summer. It's a gentle hike, ideal before the final stage to Corrençon.

The Herbouilly Nordic area, 8 km from Saint-Martin-en-Vercors, is one of three gateways to the High Vercors Nordic domain. In summer, paths winding between beech forests and pastures with Scandinavian accents allow car-free walks. Pack a picnic to enjoy views of the High Plateaus at 1,000 meters altitude.

days_plan.itin_title: Royans-Vercors Road Trip: Hilltop Villages and Gorges

visits.text: If observing wolves in the mountains appeals to you, discover Parc Alpha “Le Temps du Loup” in Saint-Martin-Vésubie. Opened in 2005, it houses two packs in semi-natural enclosures, which you can observe at feeding time from wooden hides. Wolves returned naturally to the Mercantour in November 1992 from Italy's Abruzzo region. The park explains the animal's biology, behavior and return, at the heart of an ongoing debate between livestock farmers and naturalists. Book ahead in high season.

Saint-Martin-Vésubie, nicknamed “the little Switzerland of Nice's hinterland,” is the Mercantour's tourist capital, at an altitude of 1,000 meters. Stroll through its lanes, with their wooden chalets, murmuring fountains, and the canal running down the middle of the main street. The village is a gateway to thousands of hectares of larch forests and alpine pastures, with summits exceeding 3,000 meters.

If you have time, push on to the Sanctuaire de la Madone de Fenestre at 1,903 meters. Accessible by a winding road from Saint-Martin, generally open June to October. This medieval pilgrimage site offers unobstructed views of the Gélas, the Alpes-Maritimes' highest point at 3,143 meters. The road is a journey in itself—don't rush.

activities.text: Outfitters offer canyoning and aqua-hiking in the crystalline gorges around Saint-Martin: jumps, natural slides, rappels into pools at 8–10°C. Family outings are accessible from age 8, with expert options for technical gorges. The water is cold year-round; plan to wear a wetsuit supplied by the outfitter.

The Saint-Martin-Vésubie market runs on Sunday mornings on Place Félix-Faure, in the heart of the village: producers from the upland valleys, alpine pasture cheeses, charcuterie, chestnut honey, mountain herbs. It's a good opportunity to taste the cuisine of the Vésubie valley before exerting yourself at altitude. Then stroll along the canal running down the main street, a distinctive feature inherited from medieval waterworks: few mountain villages have preserved this system intact.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpes-Maritimes Road Trip: Riviera and Mercantour, 13 days
Nice's hinterland: 8 days of hilltop villages and the Mercantour

places.name: Saint Maur Des Fosses

visits.text: Saint-Maur-des-Fossés forms a peninsula with 14 km of banks surrounded by the Marne's last major loop. When the Marie-Thérèse canal was cut through in 1825, barges stopped navigating these meanders — and the now-useless towpaths were colonized by riverside taverns, boaters, and painters. Cézanne came to set up his easel here. Follow the Promenade Paul Cézanne for 4 km from Quai Fernand Saguet to the Maisons-Alfort bridge. You'll pass islands classified as a departmental nature reserve — some were never developed.

As you walk along the banks, spot the vacation villas that sprang up from the late 19th century: flamboyant neo-Gothic, Anglo-Norman chalets, Art Nouveau in millstone masonry. When the Bastille line opened in 1859, Parisians poured in by the thousands on Sundays, and architects from Nogent like the Nachbaurs had work for thirty years. Some of these houses carry the Patrimoine d'intérêt régional label.

The Abbey of Saint-Maur was founded in the 9th century and received the relics of Saint Maurus—a disciple of Saint Benedict—on November 13, 868. It gave the town its name and dominated the municipality's development for several centuries before being dismantled during the Revolution.

activities.text: The Guinguette de l'Île du Martin-Pêcheur is accessible via a footbridge. During the Belle Époque, there were more than 200 guinguettes between Joinville and Chelles. In 2026, the venue is open from July 10 to November 1; if you are there on a weekend, book a table for the evening. The accordion music, paper lanterns and checkered tablecloths have not disappeared.

Operators rent out electric boats that do not require a license from May to September. Rent one — from the water, you will understand why Cézanne and Lebasque kept coming back here to paint the reflections and islands.

days_plan.itin_title: Val-de-Marne Road Trip: Castles and the Banks of the Marne

map_keywords: Guinguette de l'Île du Martin-Pêcheur Saint-Maur
Réserve naturelle îles de la Marne

visits.text: Saint-Michel-l'Observatoire is a Provençal village of light-coloured houses — it owes its name and worldwide reputation to the Observatoire de Haute-Provence (OHP), founded in 1937 after measurements taken as early as 1925 revealed 260 to 280 nights of excellent skies per year above the plateau. The OHP's crowning achievement: in 1995, astronomers Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz discovered the first confirmed exoplanet there (51 Pegasi b) using the T193 telescope (1.93 m mirror) and its Élodie spectrograph — a discovery rewarded with the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2019. Today, 13 domes are scattered through the oak grove. Guided tours of the large dome are organised regularly; tickets are sold online or at the Centre d'Astronomie, not on site.

The village itself is worth a look around: the Church of Saint-Michel dates from the 12th century, while ramparts and a Romanesque tower (the Tour de Porchères) recall its medieval past. Seven educational displays line the “Chemin des Étoiles” on the hill overlooking the village — an astronomy discovery trail accessible to everyone and open at all times.

activities.text: The Centre d'Astronomie (on the Moulin plateau, a few minutes from the village) hosts year-round activities for the public: telescope observing evenings, sessions in the 64-seat planetarium and solar observation. In summer, the Été Astro festival brings together more than 10,000 visitors. Book your places in advance — observing evenings fill up quickly in July–August.

The Observatory walk (6 km loop, 2 hours, easy) skirts the oak grove around the scientific site and offers beautiful views of Montagne de Lure and the Valensole Plateau. It is a rural walk among terraces, ruined mills and country chapels.

days_plan.itin_title: Forcalquier & Verdon Gorges Road Trip

places.name: Saint Mihiel

visits.text: Saint-Étienne church preserves Ligier Richier's absolute masterpiece: the Sepulcher, composed of thirteen figures slightly larger than life, carved from Euville stone between 1554 and 1564. The dead Christ, carried by Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea, is surrounded by Mary Magdalene, the Virgin, and the Holy Women. Classified as a historic monument as early as 1840.

The Benedictine Library, on the second floor of the former abbatial palace, is considered one of France's five most beautiful libraries. Its two architecturally remarkable rooms contain 8,780 books, including 74 manuscripts from the 9th to 16th centuries and 86 incunabula. Some volumes still bear the scars of a 1915 shell.

Saint-Michel abbey church, founded in the 8th century, preserves a Romanesque tower-porch. Inside, Ligier Richier's Swoon of the Virgin - two life-size walnut wood figures - shows Mary fainting in Saint John's arms after Christ's death.

The Museum of Sacred Art, in the monks' former refectory, gathers religious objects, paintings, and sculptures from the 13th to 19th centuries deposited by departmental communes. The Saint Elisabeth attributed to Ligier Richier is an exceptionally refined piece.

Walk through Saint-Mihiel's Renaissance streets: the Gondrecourt mansion with its gargoyles representing a ram, dog, and lion; the Bousmard mansion (1520); Ligier Richier's house; the 16th-century Café des Arcades. An open-air museum of Lorraine architecture.

activities.text: Hike to the Seven Rocks, limestone cliffs over twenty meters high overlooking the Meuse valley. The 7-kilometer trail crosses forests and rock formations with panoramic viewpoints.
The Meuse Greenway follows the river: a bike and pedestrian path crossing several picturesque villages. Bike rental shops offer equipment suitable for the whole family.
Taste local specialties: croquets and rochers de Saint-Mihiel, traditional dry cookies that accompany Lorraine coffee.

days_plan.itin_title: Meuse Circuit: Verdun and the Citadels

map_keywords: Église Saint-Étienne Saint-Mihiel Sépulcre Ligier Richier

visits.text: Saint-Montan welcomes you with one of Ardèche's most remarkable stories: in the 1970s, the old medieval village was a field of ruins. Volunteers rebuilt it stone by stone over forty years—an estimated 20,000 people contributed to the effort, including scouts, students and volunteers from around the world. Wander the cobbled lanes climbing toward the castle: ochre facades catch the southern sun, and every corner reveals an ornate doorway or medieval vault. The free exhibition at the village entrance tells this extraordinary restoration story.

The Château de Saint-Montan sits atop Rocher de l'Agache, a limestone spur above the village. The original keep dates to the 12th century, with written mention of a "De Saint-Montan" family as early as 1110. The castle expanded until the 14th century, reaching a total area of two hectares by the 15th century with an enclosure and three main gates. It was sacked in 1570 when Coligny's army of 3,000 men and 400 horses passed through, then abandoned until its modern resurrection. From the ramparts, views stretch across the Rhône valley and on clear days to Mont Ventoux. During high season, costumed medieval reenactments fill the courtyard, so check the dates before you go.

Head down to the church of San Samonta at the village base: it comprises a 10th-century chapel and a 12th-century Romanesque nave, joined into one discreet building. Local legend holds that the village owes its name to a 5th-century hermit, Montanus, who supposedly lived thirty years in a cave in the neighboring valley. A bit further along, the Curé Garden—formerly the scented garden—is freely accessible year-round, planted with aromatic herbs beside the stream.

activities.text: Take the trail to the Ermitage de la Sainte-Baume from the village, a loop of roughly 3 hours that crosses the gorges before rejoining Larnas. Warning: the trail is fairly steep and not recommended for inexperienced hikers. Along the route, you'll pass the Grotte de l'Ermite Montanus, carved into the cliff face, with an exceptional viewpoint over the entire village from above.

For a gentler approach, walk down to the valley floor and climb the opposite side to read the castle site as a whole—the silhouette of the castle perched on its rock and the village's layout on the southern slopes are particularly legible from this vantage point. Figure 2 km round trip.

days_plan.itin_title: The 18 Most Beautiful Villages of Ardèche

visits.text: Go down into the submarine Espadon, moored in the fortified lock of the submarine base—the only submarine in France that can be visited afloat. 77 meters long and commissioned in 1960, the Espadon became famous in May 1964 when it became the first French submarine to cross the Arctic Circle beneath the ice pack, together with its sister ship Le Marsouin. The visit lasts about 45 minutes and takes you through every compartment: torpedo room, control room, quarters for the 65 crew members. Book ahead in peak season.

Escal'Atlantic, housed in the submarine base built by the German army between 1941 and 1942 to shelter its U-boats, is a 3,500 m² museum recreating an ocean liner. The recreated interiors immerse you in the world of legendary transatlantic liners: luxury cabins, engine room, bar, promenade deck—you step into the 1930s and cross the Atlantic in your imagination. Allow 1.5 hours for the visit, with timed entry. Reservations recommended.

Climb onto the panoramic terrace of the fortified lock for a 360° view of the whole site: the port, Chantiers de l'Atlantique shipyards, the Loire estuary and the Saint-Nazaire bridge, which spans the river for 3.356 kilometers. From the terrace, you can also see the works by Felice Varini painted on the concrete of the bunkers, a large-scale contemporary installation.

activities.text: The Chantiers de l'Atlantique, founded in 1862, extend across 100 hectares and assemble the world's largest cruise ships. Guided bus tours take you through the shipyard to observe thousands of workers and technicians at work. The guide explains the entire process, from plate cutting to block assembly. A unique experience for understanding the industrial scale of contemporary shipbuilding. Booking is required on the tourist office's website.

The Écomusée de Saint-Nazaire traces the city's industrial and port history: postwar reconstruction (the city was 85% destroyed in 1942–1943), shipbuilding history, workers' lives. A more intimate museum than the technical sites, but useful for placing Saint-Nazaire in its human context.

days_plan.itin_title: Loire-Atlantique Road Trip: Nantes and the Côte de Jade

visits.text: Upon entering Saint-Nazaire-en-Royans, the aqueduct greets you—without warning. This structure, 235 meters long and 35 meters high with 17 arches, was built between 1873 and 1876 to irrigate the Valence plain. It was presented at the 1878 Paris Universal Exposition as a masterpiece of hydraulic engineering. A panoramic elevator beside the artificial lake formed in 1958 by the EDF dam lifts you to the pedestrian walkway above the Bourne. From up there, the view extends to the entrances of the Bourne gorges on the right and Combe Laval on the left. Allow 1 hour.

The medieval village below the aqueduct deserves a stroll: steep streets, old houses, and remnants of the 12th-century Delphinale tower recall that Saint-Nazaire was a stronghold of the Dauphins. During World War II, on June 29, 1944, the village was bombed by German aviation—it was a strategic crossroads between Valence, Grenoble, and the Vercors maquis. Some forty resistance fighters were executed in the castle park.

The Thaïs cave at the village entrance is a prehistoric cavity inhabited during the Magdalenian period. An hour-long guided tour reveals galleries rich in archaeology. Don't confuse it with Choranche cave: Thaïs is smaller but older in terms of human occupation.

activities.text: Local operators offer paddlewheel boat cruises on the Isère from the artificial lake's shores. The 1.5-hour outing circles the limestone cliffs of the Vercors foothills and travels upstream to Pont-en-Royans. A guide narrates the history of villages crossed and the birds nesting in the cliffs.

The hike to the Vanille viewpoint (3-hour round trip) climbs the western hillside and offers a 360° panorama of the aqueduct, village, and three breaches in the Vercors cliff face. Yellow and red trail markers from the lakeside.

days_plan.itin_title: Royans-Vercors Road Trip: Hilltop Villages and Gorges

visits.text: Perched on Mont Cornadore, Saint-Nectaire's Romanesque church is one of Auvergne's five major Romanesque churches. Its lava stone nave, topped by a dome and flanked by two towers on the facade, houses 103 polychrome sculpted capitals of striking expressiveness. The treasury is one of France's most remarkable collections of Romanesque metalwork: the reliquary bust of Saint Baudime in gilded and enameled copper, the Notre-Dame-du-Mont-Cornadore Virgin, and several reliquaries testify to Auvergne's artistic influence in the Middle Ages.

The grottes du Cornadore reveal 1st-century Gallo-Roman baths carved into the rock. The route recreates the Roman bathing ritual: from the tepidarium, the warm room, to the caldarium, the hot room, passing two perfectly preserved bathtubs out of the twenty in the original complex. Thousand-year-old stalactites, an ancient pool, and tanks of hot, mineral-rich water with a high CO2 content feature along the guided tour.

The Maison du Fromage devotes an exhibition space to Saint-Nectaire PDO, one of France's oldest cheeses. Traditional production, the history of the local terroir, and tasting reveal why this uncooked pressed cheese, aged on rye straw, became the region's gastronomic emblem.

Saint-Nectaire-le-Bas spreads its villas and parks along more than forty thermal springs. The 19th-century spa development left architectural heritage still visible in former bathhouse facades and shaded walkways connecting the springs.

activities.text: Attend music concerts in Saint-Nectaire's Romanesque church, scheduled throughout the year. The Romanesque nave's exceptional acoustics enhance the sound and offer a musical experience in an extraordinary heritage setting.

Join a guided tour of Saint-Nectaire's Romanesque church offered in summer. Guides detail the 103 capitals' iconography, decode biblical and secular carved scenes, and present the metalwork treasury's masterpieces.

Hike around Mont Cornadore with views over the Monts du Sancy and Couze Chambon valley. Several marked trails leave from the village and reveal volcanic landscapes, thermal springs, and high pastures.

days_plan.itin_title: Volcanoes and Auvergne traditions

visits.text: Notre-Dame cathedral in Saint-Omer is a Gothic cathedral begun in the 13th century and completed three hundred years later. Measuring 105 metres long, 51 metres wide and 22.9 metres beneath the vault, it has been listed as a historic monument since 1840. Don't miss its 16th-century astrolabe clock — it still shows the position of the stars — nor the black-and-white marble labyrinth set into the floor, a copy of an older labyrinth from Saint-Bertin Abbey. Medieval pilgrims walked it on their knees as a substitute for a journey to the Holy Land.

The Sandelin Museum occupies an 18th-century mansion on a lovely cobbled street. Its fine art collections and 750 pieces of ceramics make it one of the finest small museums in northern France. Delft earthenware, silverware, Flemish paintings — the quality is consistently high. Allow 1.5 hours.

The 20-hectare public garden stretches over the town's former ramparts. It alternates French formal garden, English landscape garden and arboretum. An artificial waterfall and an open-air theatre make it a pleasant place for a walk in any season. This is where the people of Saint-Omer come to unwind — and you should too, after the museums.

The ruins of Saint-Bertin Abbey overlook the lower town. Founded in the 7th century by Saint Bertin himself, it was destroyed during the Revolution. What remains — a few sections of wall and ghostly arcades — evokes the religious power that made Saint-Omer a major intellectual centre in the Middle Ages. The abbey notably hosted Irish scholars in exile.

The 18th-century town hall, locally nicknamed the coffee grinder for its cubic shape topped with an octagonal dome, now houses an Italian-style theatre. Its façade has a sober elegance that contrasts with the flamboyant belfry of Arras.

activities.text: Set off on a bacôve boat trip through the Audomarois marsh, covering 3,400 hectares crossed by 160 km of watergangs (drainage canals). These flat-bottomed boats let you glide past the floating gardens where market gardeners grow cauliflowers and leeks that are unreachable by land. Book ahead in season: it's a quintessential experience of the region.

10 km from Saint-Omer, don't miss La Coupole d'Helfaut: an immense bunker built by the Organisation Todt in 1943-1944 as a launch base for V2 rockets against London. This 75-metre-diameter concrete dome was never used, as it was destroyed by British bombs. It now houses a remarkable history centre covering the Second World War and the conquest of space.

Stroll through the medieval lanes of Saint-Omer's historic centre. Mansions from the 17th and 18th centuries stand one after another among the yellow-brick Flemish houses. The town has retained a discreet charm that mass tourism has yet to reach.

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip Pas-De-Calais: The Opal Coast and Belfries

places.name: Saint Ours

visits.text: Vulcania is Europe's volcanism theme park, inaugurated on February 20, 2002—a symbolic date deliberately chosen: 20-02-2002. Set on 57 hectares in the heart of the Chaîne des Puys, 15 km northwest of Clermont-Ferrand, it has welcomed over 8 million visitors since opening. The main building, largely buried beneath an earth mound, reveals only a monumental cone evoking the neighboring volcanoes—architecture by Hans Hollein. The science center covers three themes: volcanoes, natural phenomena (earthquakes, tsunamis), and Earth in Space. Plan a full day: visits easily exceed 6 hours.

A few minutes from Vulcania, the Lemptégy volcano offers a radically different experience: you literally descend into the guts of a volcano laid bare by an old pozzolana quarry. The guide leads you on foot or by small train among volcanic chimneys, lava flows, and volcanic bombs. It's geology at full scale—nothing like a theme park.

activities.text: At Vulcania, don't miss the Awakening of the Auvergne Giants—a dynamic experience projecting you into a volcanic eruption—and the Namazu roller coaster that lets you experience an earthquake. The planetarium, France's largest, offers shows on a hemispheric dome. In summer, nighttime animations and the light show on the park's façades are worth the evening.

days_plan.itin_title: Auvergne Volcanoes Road Trip: Puy de Dôme and Lakes

map_keywords: Maison de Site Puy de Dôme Orcines

visits.text: Saint-Paul-de-Vence is the quintessential artists' village. Fortified by Francis I in the 16th century, it attracted a colony of artists from the 1920s onward who paid their bills at the Colombe d'Or with paintings: Picasso, Matisse, Chagall, Léger. Marc Chagall lived here from 1966 until his death in 1985 and rests in the village cemetery. Pass through the 14th-century Porte de Vence to enter the fortified town—one of the cannons on the ramparts was captured from Charles V in 1536. Avoid 11 AM–4 PM in high season, when the village becomes a sea of people.

Rue Grande crosses the village from end to end for 300 meters, with art galleries and artists' studios in a row between medieval beige limestone facades. About forty galleries in total in the village—variable quality, but some contemporary heavyweights alongside the inevitable souvenir sellers. A marked route with 12 information stands lets you find the viewpoints that inspired 20th-century painters.

The Chapelle des Pénitents Blancs, from the 17th century, was entirely decorated between 1997 and 2008 by Belgian artist Jean-Michel Folon: floor mosaics, stained glass, wall frescoes and a monumental sculpture transform the space into a poetic world of winged figures and deep blues. A total surprise in this medieval setting, not to be missed.

The Rosary Chapel in Vence (10 minutes by car) is Matisse's spiritual testament, completed in 1951—he was 81 and considered it his masterpiece. Stained glass in three colors (yellow, green, blue), wall ceramics, liturgical furniture and vestments: a total work of art. The colored light from the stained glass changes with the hours. Open Tuesday, Thursday and Friday mornings, closed certain months—check hours.

activities.text: The Maeght Foundation is France's first independent private art foundation, inaugurated on July 28, 1964, by André Malraux. Art dealer Aimé Maeght had it built in memory of his son Bernard, who died at 11 in 1953. Catalan architect Josep Lluís Sert designed the building in direct collaboration with the artists: the Giacometti courtyard, Miró labyrinth, Chagall mosaics, Braque pool and Calder stabile are part of the architecture itself. Over 13,000 works in the collection. Allow at least 2 hours. An extension was inaugurated for the 60th anniversary in 2024.

Walk around the ramparts along the Chemin de Ronde: views down over the village rooftops and the countryside around Nice. The loop takes 20 minutes. In late afternoon, the low-angle light on the ochre facades is particularly beautiful for photos.

Place du Général de Gaulle: legendary pétanque games beneath the plane trees, where Yves Montand, Lino Ventura and Simone Signoret competed in the 1960s-70s. The tradition continues with local players from morning to evening. Café terraces all around.

Tourrettes-sur-Loup, 15 minutes by car, is the “violet village.” La Bastide aux Violettes presents the cultivation of the Victoria violet, the only violet in France grown as a main crop (harvest October to March). The medieval village, quieter than Saint-Paul, houses about forty artisan workshops. The Fête des Violettes has taken place in early March every year since 1952.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpes-Maritimes Road Trip: Riviera and Mercantour, 13 days
The 15 Gems of the French Riviera and Backcountry
7-Day French Riviera Circuit: Villefranche to Antibes
French Riviera Art Museums and Galleries: An 8-Day Journey
Nice's hinterland: 8 days of hilltop villages and the Mercantour

visits.text: The Chartreuse de Valbonne is one of this circuit's most unusual curiosities—nestled at the bottom of a wooded valley, it is reached by a winding road through 1,500 hectares of state forest harboring tree species rare in the Mediterranean region. It was founded in 1204 when Guillem de Vénéjean, Bishop of Uzès, ceded a then-marshy estate to the Carthusian order; the monks cleared and drained the site, naming it “vallis bona”—the good valley, the origin of Valbonne. Pillaged in 1585 during the Wars of Religion, rebuilt from 1593, expropriated during the Revolution, bought back by the Carthusians in 1836, then transformed into a leprosarium from 1929 by Pastor Philadelphe Delord—who welcomed up to 400 patients and died on site in 1947—the monastery's history spans the entire modern era.

The Chartreuse is instantly recognizable by the Burgundy-style glazed tiles covering the towers and the bell tower of the conventual church - a surprising detail for a Provençal charterhouse. The great cloister has a perimeter of 355 meters; around it, the monastic cells are marked with letters from A to Y (Q is not used). The visit provides access to the conventual church with its complex stereotomic vaults, the work of the Franque brothers from Avignon, and to the small cloister dating from the early 13th century. The Chartreuse has been listed as a Historic Monument since 1959. Check visiting hours before setting off.

The Chartreuse vineyard produces organic Côtes du Rhône—a tasting is offered on site. Around the buildings, the Valbonne forest offers shaded trails with downy oaks, Scots pines and strawberry trees mixed with Mediterranean tree species.

activities.text: The Chartreuse de Valbonne forest trail (5 to 7 km loop, moderate difficulty, about 2 hours) crosses the state forest around the monastery and offers a striking contrast between the silence of the woods and monastic architecture. You encounter old dry stone walls, capitelles (shepherds' shelters) and more open garrigue areas with views of the surrounding landforms.

days_plan.itin_title: Cèze Valley and Ardèche Gorges Circuit

visits.text: Saint-Pierre-de-Mézoargues is a discreet Rhône-side commune — a few hundred inhabitants, orchards as far as the eye can see, and the Rhône dike as horizon. It's one of those villages existing only in regional literature and local memories. Its 12th-century church (remodeled) and 17th-18th century farms witness an ancient settlement on this fertile alluvial land that Saint-Victor monks began draining in the 10th century. The spirit of "deep Provence" is total here.

The village's rural fabric deserves an hour's walk: 17th-18th century closed-courtyard farms, stone irrigation canals, old wells, and oratories at crossroads. Careful observation reveals architectural and agricultural details typical of Rhône-side Provence — the same sober architecture as in Camargue villages.

activities.text: Rural walking loop among hedgerows and orchards: rural roads and paths surrounding Saint-Pierre-de-Mézoargues cross a mosaic of cherry, apricot, plum trees, and market garden plots. The terrain is completely flat, ideal for a 2-hour walk without difficulty.

Observation from the Rhône dike: the several-kilometer-long dike offers direct views of the Grand Rhône, its pebble banks, and riparian vegetation (black poplars, white willows, ash trees). A spot of absolute calm for observing river birds — grey herons, great cormorants, kingfishers, and in autumn, migrating waders.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpilles, Aix-en-Provence & Arles Circuit

visits.text: The Saint-Pourçain wine-growing area, awarded AOC status in 2009 and one of the oldest in France, covers 600 hectares and 19 communes around the Sioule and the Allier. Served at the table of the kings of France as early as the 13th century, these wines (red, white, rosé) blend Gamay and Pinot Noir for the reds, Chardonnay and Tressallier (a unique native grape variety) for the whites. Seventeen independent winegrowers and the cave de l'Union welcome visitors for tastings.

The Musée de la Vigne et du Terroir occupies the Maison du Bailli (16th century), a Renaissance building that houses the magnificent spiral staircase of the belfry, listed as a historic monument. Eleven rooms present more than 1,000 objects tracing 2,000 years of winegrowing history: tools, labels, clothing, an 1889 horse-drawn still with four vessels. The life of the winegrower in the 17th and 18th centuries feels less distant.

The Sainte-Croix abbey church extends its immense nave through the heart of the wine town. The belfry or clock tower, the Cour des Bénédictins and the lanes of the historic centre reveal medieval and Renaissance architecture. The town, with its southern feel and lined with plane trees, sits on the boundary between the langues d'oïl and the langue d'oc, retaining that pivotal position in its identity.

The Île de la Ronde and Les Cordeliers offer pockets of greenery in the heart of the town. The Jardin des Némusiens, a genuine hidden Garden of Eden, grows more than 300 varieties of plants. Hundreds of colours and fragrances fill this secret place. The banks of the Sioule invite visitors to stroll along the river.

activities.text: Tasting with the winegrowers reveals the diversity of the terroirs: sandy soils to the north-east (Chemilly, Besson), granite slopes to the west (Bresnay, Meillard), clay-limestone ground to the south (Saint-Pourçain, Saulcet). The white wines made with Tressallier develop a unique character, the reds blend Gamay and Pinot with finesse. The local 'Ficelle' keeps alive the legend of the innkeeper Gaultier, who dipped a string into the jugs to measure how much had been drunk.

The Wine Route winds through the 19 communes of the appellation, offering views over south-east-facing slopes along the Allier and the Sioule. A route by bike or car, cellar visits, stops with passionate winegrowers: each stage reveals a different terroir. Explanations of growing, winemaking, and winegrowing history enrich the tasting experience.

The Festival viticole et gourmand in August enlivens the 27 communes of the Pays Saint-Pourçinois for 10 days. Markets, walks and horse rides, vineyard visits by horse-drawn carriage, country buffets, a parade of flower-covered floats and concerts: the wine cellars of Saint-Pourçain celebrate. The tourist pass and gourmet pass allow visitors to fully enjoy the events and festival menus.

days_plan.itin_title: Allier Road Trip: Vichy, Thermal Baths and Bourbonnais Bocage

visits.text: The basilica of Saint-Quentin rises with a Gothic silhouette 123 metres long and 34 metres high. The second-largest Gothic building in Picardy, it was built from the late 12th to the late 15th century. Its double-transept plan and front porch tower give it a distinctive character. An ancient 260-metre labyrinth winds through the nave's paving. The crypt houses the relics of Saint Quentin.

The Antoine Lécuyer Museum houses the world's most important collection of pastels by Maurice-Quentin de La Tour, official portraitist of Louis XV. These 18th-century works sit alongside Sinceny faience and paintings from the 19th and 20th centuries.

The Art Deco town hall has a Flamboyant Gothic façade adorned with more than 170 sculptures. Built in the early 16th century, this architectural jewel dominates the Grand Place. The neo-Gothic hall and wedding room with its Renaissance fireplace are open to visitors.

The Art Deco station restaurant dazzles with its grey maple furniture, period stained glass, and mosaics. Master glassmaker Auguste Labouret created a glass partition inspired by the Hôtel Lutetia in Paris. The station, rebuilt in 1926 after the fire, reflects the splendour of Art Deco.

Saint-Quentin has around 3,000 façades featuring Art Deco elements, including nearly 300 buildings designed entirely in the Art Deco style. A walk through the city reveals colourful façades, bay windows and decorative ironwork between the Grand-Place and the Conservatory.

activities.text: The Marais d'Isle nature reserve spans 48 hectares in the heart of the city, making it unique in France. This remnant of the alkaline marshes of the Upper Somme valley is home to 600 living species. Reed beds, ponds and riverside woodlands shelter nearly 160 bird species. Observation paths run alongside the protected wetlands.

Board a bacôve for an hour of silent boating on the Étang d'Isle. These traditional flat-bottomed boats, crafted from oak, glide between the reed beds. The guide recounts the history of the marshes as moorhens and herons take flight when you pass.
Parc d'Isle offers fitness trails, children's play areas, a small educational farm, and picnic spaces. Its 11 hectares of greenery offer opportunities for jogging, cycling, and family strolls.

days_plan.itin_title: Aisne Itinerary: Gothic Cathedrals and the Picardy Countryside

visits.text: The priory church (1722) surprises with its three onion-domed bell towers that draw a baroque silhouette in the hollow of the Vosges hills. Inside, the Silbermann organ of 1746, a listed Historic Monument, is the only authentic survivor of Jean-André Silbermann's work.

The Haute Chapelle, a 12th-century Romanesque construction, overlooks the village from a wooded relief. According to legend, the mule transporting Saint Quirin's relics from Rome stopped here in 1049 and refused to go further.
Walk around the priory to find the miraculous fountain below. For centuries, it has been attributed with healing powers for skin diseases.
The archaeological site of Croix Guillaume, accessible by a marked forest trail, reveals a Gallo-Roman hamlet: traces of dwellings, necropolis, sandstone quarries and cult remains.

In Lettenbach, the Verriers chapel (1756), rococo style, sports an onion-domed bell tower and folk art stained glass. The monks had established a glassworks here in the 15th century that became a Royal Manufacture under Louis XV.

activities.text: Take the Club Vosgien marked trails around ponds and deciduous forests. The village counts 75 listed or registered buildings, from Lorraine farms to wayside crosses.
Seven churches and chapels scattered around the village form the "7 Roses" circuit. Each tells its story, between Christianized Celtic sanctuaries and forest hermitages.
In summer, the Silbermann Musical Days offer organ recitals in the priory church: a rare moment in an exceptional setting.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Est Road Trip: Vineyards, Ramparts and Forests

places.name: Saint Raphael

visits.text: San Rafeu church, a 12th-century Romanesque structure, is a classified historic monument. Its foundations rest on a site occupied since Roman times. The adjoining presbytery houses the municipal archaeological museum, with collections ranging from prehistory to underwater archaeology.

Climb the 129 steps of the San Rafeu Tower, a 13th-century fortified tower standing 25 meters high. From the top, the 360-degree panorama takes in the basilica's domes, the red rocks of the Estérel, the Mediterranean, and the bay of Saint-Tropez.

The Basilica of Notre-Dame de la Victoire, with its Byzantine domes, has dominated the seafront since the late 19th century. Its neo-Romanesque architecture blends golden stone and pink sandstone from the Estérel.
The archaeological museum displays amphorae, anchors, and objects raised from wrecks off the coast. One section is devoted to the Paleolithic, with remains discovered in the region.
The old harbor and its daily Provençal market make up a lively Mediterranean scene. The shaded lanes of the “village quarter” preserve the atmosphere of an old farming town.

activities.text: Take the Corniche d'Or, a 40 km road between Saint-Raphaël and Cannes. Beneath the umbrella pines, the red porphyry rocks of the Estérel plunge into the turquoise Mediterranean. Stops are possible at the coves of Agay, Dramont, and Anthéor.
The Agay roadstead, sheltered between Cap Dramont and Pointe de la Baumette, offers calm water ideal for swimming, kayaking, and paddleboarding. The sandy beach is bordered by pines and red rocks.

Several dive clubs offer outings around Cap Dramont, Île d'Or and the wrecks along the coast. Further east, the protected seabed around Cap Roux is home to groupers, brown meagres and gorgonians, among other species.

Hike in the Estérel massif towards the pic de l'Ours or Mont Vinaigre (614 m, the highest point). The trails wind among red rocks, fragrant scrub, and coastal views. Plan a return trip during the day from Saint-Raphaël to reach the trailheads by car, then continue on foot.

days_plan.itin_title: Var Road Trip: French Riviera & Provence Verte
Roquebrune-sur-Argens: sea, villages and the Var in 10 days

map_keywords: Basilique Notre-Dame de la Victoire Saint-Raphaël

visits.text: The Château des Baux sits atop a rocky spur at 245 meters, and the vertical drop to the base of the rock is about 200 meters. That's important to know before entering: it's from here that Raymond de Turenne had his prisoners thrown. Nicknamed “scourge of Provence”, excommunicated by Pope Clement VII in 1393, condemned to death by the Parliament of Aix the same year—he openly disregarded it all and carried on. His indictment before the seneschal of Provence explicitly cites “the execution of his enemies thrown from the top of the rock of Les Baux”. The castle was finally demolished in 1631 on the orders of Richelieu, who feared Protestants might use it as a base. What you see today are the ruins left by that demolition. Worth seeing: the chapel of Sainte-Catherine (12th century, where the Turenne-Boucicaut marriage was celebrated on December 23, 1393), the keep, and the south cliff face. Ticket €12, allow 2.5 hours.

The Carrières de Lumières are the old limestone quarries where Jean Cocteau filmed Testament of Orpheus in 1959. Since 2012, the walls—vertical, 6 to 16 meters high—have served as screens for immersive sound-and-light shows (Klimt, Van Gogh, Cézanne depending on the season). The atmosphere is strange, and not only because of the projections: the quarries were worked from the 16th to 19th centuries, accidents were frequent, and several workers were buried by rockfalls. This isn't folklore—it's in the safety records of the time. Ticket €14, a 35-minute show on a loop, allow 1 hour.

The Val d'Enfer is the steep valley north of the village, a jumble of rocks where Provençal legend has placed witches' sabbaths since the Middle Ages. The rumor that Dante Alighieri drew inspiration from it to describe Hell during his passage through Provence in 1309 is plausible but undocumented—Dante did pass through Avignon, but no source places him at Les Baux. The legend predates tourism, which gives it a different status. Walk freely along marked paths, 30 minutes.

You are visiting a memory, but the memory is still alive. Saint-Paul-de-Mausole is a Romanesque priory that has served as a psychiatric institution since 1605, with a break during the Revolution: nationalized in 1791, reopened in 1807. Today it is a clinic for women, and in the part closed to visitors, patients are being treated while you walk through the cloister. On May 8, 1889, Van Gogh voluntarily admitted himself here, a few months after cutting off his left earlobe in Arles. Dr. Théophile Peyron diagnosed him with epilepsy and prescribed alternating hot and cold baths twice a week, the standard treatment of the time. In 53 weeks, Van Gogh produced 143 oil paintings and more than 100 drawings. The Starry Night (June 1889) is at MoMA. Irises (May 1889, the first canvas painted here, in the garden) is at the Getty. He also tried to swallow his own tubes of oil paint in July 1889. He left on May 16, 1890, declared cured. He killed himself on July 29 in Auvers-sur-Oise. Ticket €8, allow 1.5 to 2 hours.

200 meters south of Saint-Paul-de-Mausole, the ruins of Glanum suddenly come into view from the road. A Greek and then Roman city active from the 4th century BC to the 3rd century AD, abruptly abandoned around 270 during barbarian raids. What remains is remarkable: the 1st-century BC triumphal arch and the Mausoleum of the Julii—a 19-meter Roman funerary tower, one of the best preserved in the world, erected around 30–20 BC by the grandsons of one of Caesar's soldiers. The site museum explains how 20th-century excavations uncovered baths, a forum, and a temple beneath Provençal fields. Ticket €8, allow 1.5 hours.

activities.text: Lunch at L'Oustau de Baumanière (3 Michelin stars, founded in 1945 by Raymond Thuillier, one of France's very finest restaurants for 80 years): €200–350 per person. For a more reasonable budget: La Reine Jeanne on the village's main square, traditional Provençal cuisine, €35–55.

Arrival in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence in late afternoon, 15 minutes north of Les Baux. Lodging: Hôtel de Tourrel (18th-century residence, €250–400) or Hôtel des Ateliers de l'Image (€200–350), or the simpler Le Mas des Carassins (€130–200). Dinner at Bistrot Découverte or restaurant L'Aile ou la Cuisse, €30–60.

Morning: before visiting Saint-Paul, walk the circuit of 19 large-format reproductions of Van Gogh's works that line the streets of Saint-Rémy from the Musée Estrine in the town center to the priory. 25-minute walk, marked route. Each panel shows the canvas and the exact spot where it was painted—the cypress along the path, the olive grove, the roadside ditch. Free.

The art therapy workshop of the Valetudo association inside Saint-Paul-de-Mausole deserves special attention: current female patients create works that are exhibited and sold on site. The workshop operates in the same rooms where Van Gogh painted. It's not presented as an attraction—it's an actual therapeutic activity. Buying a work directly funds the program. Pay what you wish starting at €20.

Roman Provence Road Trip: Ancient Remains and Villages
Haunted Provence - 5 Days Through Cursed Castles, Asylums, and Ancien Régime Crimes

visits.text: Saint-Saturnin perches on a basalt flow overlooking the Monne gorges, 15 km south of Clermont-Ferrand. Its monumental duo seen from the road — Romanesque church and medieval castle in golden arkose and Volvic lava — is one of Auvergne's most photographed sights. Notre-Dame church is one of five so-called 'major' Romanesque churches in Auvergne, alongside those of Issoire, Orcival, Clermont, and Saint-Nectaire — listed as a Historic Monument in 1862. Built in the 12th century, its octagonal bell tower is one of the best preserved in Auvergne, and its capitals are carved from local volcanic lava. Allow 45 minutes for the interior visit in season (guided tours in July-August).

Right next to the church, the Royal Château de Saint-Saturnin was built in the 13th century by the La Tour d'Auvergne family, then embellished in the Renaissance by Catherine de' Medici — Countess of Auvergne — who added a formal French garden. In 1566, King Charles IX and his entire court stopped here. In 1586, Queen Margot passed through before her exile in Usson. The visit (about 50 minutes, guided) grants access to the keep, wall-walk, and furnished rooms.

Walk along Rue de la Boucherie with its medieval shop and houses from the 15th–17th centuries, then reach the Renaissance fountain from the 16th century between the church and castle — its decoration bears the La Tour d'Auvergne coat of arms. The 12th-century Romanesque Sainte-Madeleine chapel adjoins the former cemetery transformed into a garden. On the lintel of the door, read the 1668 inscription: 'We have been like you, one day you will be like us, Think well on it.' Rarely has an invitation to contemplation been so direct.

activities.text: The washhouses walk descends to the Monne from the Renaissance fountain, following the flank of the basalt flow. On the south-facing slopes (the Serre mountain), old vineyard terraces and dry-stone huts recall that Puy-de-Dôme was France's second-largest wine-producing department in the 19th century. If you search carefully in the walls, you'll find fossilized stromatolite impressions 25 million years old.

Saint-Saturnin is 15 km from Clermont-Ferrand and makes a lovely final stop before the city. Several marked loops explore the Monne valley and its steep-sided gorges, accessible on foot or by mountain bike from the village.

days_plan.itin_title: Auvergne Circuit: Perched Villages and Volcanoes

visits.text: Saint-Saturnin-lès-Apt is a medieval town that underwent three successive expansions in the 13th, 15th, and 17th centuries, each leaving its traces in the urban fabric. As you climb the cobbled lanes toward the château, you'll cross the remains of several fortified enclosures. The Portail Eyguier, a 15th-century corner tower, is the sole survivor of the second enclosure. From the summit ramparts, the panorama embraces the Alpilles, the Vaucluse Mountains, and both Luberon massifs—a 180° view over all of Provence. In the village center lanes, look for the carved doors and window frames classified as Historic Monuments, as well as the 18th-century public fountain whose sculpted pediment was a gift from the last Marquis de Monclar—guillotined in 1794.

The Castle Chapel, consecrated in 1056, is perched atop the original rock on the remains of a 6th-century early Christian church. Accessible on request at the town hall, it's worth the detour.
