In 1850, a villager named Rosette Tamisier reportedly saw a painting bleed here—the affair caused quite a stir before she was imprisoned for fraud. Two 17th-century windmills dominate the hill, one of which still has its sails—a rarity in Provence.

activities.text: Climb to the castle plateau via the cobbled lanes (20 min round trip). View from the orientation table over the Apt basin and the ochres of Roussillon on the horizon.

Trail of the Aiguiers—a discovery loop around the cisterns carved into the limestone rock to collect rainwater. Allow 1h30 for a short loop. A rare hydraulic heritage, well explained by the Luberon Park panels.

days_plan.itin_title: The 15 Most Beautiful Villages of the Luberon

visits.text: Colette's birthplace, in the village heart, has been restored according to the writer's own descriptions. Wallpaper, parquet, woodwork, and vegetable garden recreate the setting of her childhood in Puisaye.

The Musée Colette occupies the château rebuilt in the 17th century. It offers a sensory discovery of the writer's life: manuscripts, photographs, personal objects, and immersive artistic installations.

The Tour Sarrasine, an ovoid 11th–12th century keep, is the last vestige of the old medieval fortress. Colette evokes it in 'Claudine at School': 'the Saracen tower, thick, low, sheathed entirely in ivy, crumbling at the top.'
The village church, recognizable by its absent bell tower, stands on the main square. Dating from the 13th century, it's part of the 'Following Gabrielle's Footsteps' trail through the village.

On the road to Moutiers, the Poterie de la Bâtisse perpetuates ten generations of know-how. The old 18th-century reclining kiln and 1930 workshop are still in operation. Colette's pencil pot is among the iconic creations.

activities.text: Take the 'Following Gabrielle's Footsteps' walk through the village. The one-hour route passes places evoked in Colette's work, from the Petit Saint-Jean washhouse to woods that 'ripple to infinity.'
Puisaye has been the land of potters since the Middle Ages. Visit the open workshops of Saint-Amand-en-Puisaye and discover the region's characteristic blue stoneware.

The Puisaye countryside—a bocage of ponds and forests—lends itself to peaceful hikes. Sunken lanes bordered by hedges lead from village to village through a landscape Colette described as 'the most beautiful country in the world.'

days_plan.itin_title: Yonne Circuit: Northern Burgundy & Chablis

visits.text: Saint-Savin occupies a promontory balcony above the Gaves valley at 430 meters elevation. This village of fewer than 400 inhabitants houses one of the most remarkable abbey churches in the Pyrenees. The Benedictine abbey founded around 945 by the Count of Bigorre owned in the Middle Ages the entire territory up to the upper Cauterets valley — and the thermal baths found there. The current abbey church dates from the 12th century and has been listed as a historic monument since 1840. Inside, don't miss the Renaissance organ from 1557 — one of the oldest in France still in working condition. Listed as a historic monument since 1840, the building was restored between 1855 and 1863 thanks to Prosper Mérimée's intervention. Free entry.

Take advantage of the day to explore the Azun Valley, this broad preserved valley radiating from Argelès-Gazost toward the high massifs. About fifteen typical villages succeed one another between meadows and forests: Bigourdan stone houses, barns, fountains, small chapels. It's ideal territory for a walk or a leisurely drive between hamlets.

activities.text: The Jardin des Bains, located in Argelès-Gazost 2 kilometers from Saint-Savin, is the thermal spa that ideally closes this circuit. Installed since 2011 in the historic Argelès-Gazost thermal building — constructed between 1880 and 1885, with a remarkably preserved Pyrenean marble hall — it offers three themed spaces: the Emerald Forest with its plant and floral decor, the Mesopotamian Ziggurat with its Hanging Gardens of Babylon, and the walking circuit with its outdoor jacuzzi. The chloro-sulfurous sodium waters of Argelès are recognized for treating venous conditions. The plant setting and light effects between the glass roofs make it one of the most original spaces on the route.

The Pyrenees Animal Park in Argelès-Gazost houses about 100 mountain animal species — izards, marmots, vultures, bearded vultures — in enclosures integrated into the natural terrain. It's an interesting complement to the day for those traveling with family or wishing to observe Pyrenean wildlife up close before heading home.

days_plan.itin_title: Vienne Road Trip: Futuroscope and Romanesque Heritage
Pyrenean Thermal Route: Spa Towns

places.name: Saint Suliac

visits.text: Saint-Suliac has held the Plus Beaux Villages de France designation since 1999. The narrow lanes, so tight that two people cannot pass side by side, wind between granite houses with arched doorways and thatched roofs. Fishing nets still hang from the facades.
The 6th-century church, founded by the monk Suliau, houses stained glass windows, wooden sculptures, and maritime votive offerings left by the families of Newfoundland fishermen.
Walk down the Ruette des Petits Puits - a 17th-century well gives the lane its name. Legend says it concealed an underground passage connecting the church to the harbor.
At the harbor, dories - flat-bottomed boats of the Newfoundland fishermen - sway facing the Rance River. Sailors from Saint-Suliac departed each year to fish for cod off the coast of Newfoundland.
The Beauchet tidal mill, listed as a Historic Monument, used tidal energy to grind grain. Rebuilt in stone after a fire, it operated until 1980.

At low tide, stone foundations emerge in the Vigneux cove. Listed as a Historic Monument since 1986, this site is believed to be an ancient fortified Viking camp where longships sheltered on the landward side.

activities.text: Climb to the summit of Mont Garrot (73 m) for a 360° panorama over the Rance estuary, the harbor, and the Viking remains below.

Reach the Grainfollet oratory via the coastal path. In 1874, fishermen promised to build this sanctuary if all returned safely from Newfoundland. Twenty years later, the vow was fulfilled. At sunset, the view over the Rance is sublime.
The Saint-Suliac peninsula loop follows the old salt marshes, Beauchet mill, and the Chablé menhir (5 m high, nicknamed 'Gargantua's tooth'). Warning: some passages are submerged at high tide.

days_plan.itin_title: Brittany Road Trip: Villages with Character, Sea and History

map_keywords: Moulin à marée de Beauchet Saint-Suliac

visits.text: Saint-Symphorien-sur-Coise is a town full of character in the Lyonnais Mountains that has preserved a remarkably intact historic heart: a Gothic church, houses with projecting upper stories, old market halls, and sections of ramparts. Take time to get lost in the lanes: the façades tell the story of several centuries of prosperity linked to trade between Lyon and the Massif Central. Don't miss the climb to the panoramic view over the Lyonnais Mountains—on clear days, the view extends far toward the Pilat.

The ramparts and their fortified gates remain partially visible. The town's position overlooking the Coise valley illustrates the medieval defensive logic characteristic of this corridor between the Rhône plains and the Massif Central plateaus.

activities.text: Intramural heritage loop (2–3 km, ~1 hour). The circuit passes by the main fortified gates, the market halls, and the lanes connecting the different levels of the town.
Ridge path to a high point to explore the landscape of the Lyonnais Mountains. This mountain range, little known to tourists, offers unspoiled nature less than an hour from Lyon.

days_plan.itin_title: Loop Around Lyon: Villages and Pierres Dorées

visits.text: Île d'Oléron, the largest French Atlantic island (30 km long). The free viaduct (1966, 3 km) links it to the mainland. Varied landscapes: pine forests in the south, salt marshes in the north, fine sand beaches on the west coast.

The phare de Chassiron, at the northern tip of the island, has sported its black and white stripes since 1836. 224 steps lead to the lantern - views of Fort Boyard and the île d’Aix in clear weather. The spiral garden at the foot of the lighthouse echoes the patterns of oyster shells. Plan a return trip during the day from Saint-Trojan-les-Bains.

Le Château d'Oléron, former stronghold at the island's entrance. The Vauban citadel guarded the estuary. Today, its ramparts house a market for local artisans and producers (summer). The colorful port cabins have become artists' studios.

Fort Boyard, oval fortress built between 1801 and 1857 between Oléron and Île d'Aix. Never used militarily, it became famous through the TV game show. No visits inside, but cruises circle it – an iconic silhouette set on the ocean.

activities.text: Cruise around Fort Boyard. Departures from Boyardville or Saint-Denis-d’Oléron. A complete circuit of the fort, passing near the île d’Aix. Commentary on the history of its construction and anecdotes from filming. Boyardville is approximately 17 km from Saint-Trojan-les-Bains, a 15-minute drive.

Oyster tasting at the port of La Cotinière, the leading small-scale fishing port in Charente-Maritime. Fish auction in the morning, tasting huts in the afternoon. The fines de claire and spéciales oysters from Oléron have an incomparable briny flavour. Allow approximately 14 km from Saint-Trojan-les-Bains, a 20-minute drive.

Île d'Oléron beaches: Grande Plage at Saint-Trojan, Les Saumonards at Boyardville, Vert-Bois in the south. Maritime pine forests stretch to the sand. The little Saint-Trojan train crosses the forest to Gatseau beach.

days_plan.itin_title: Charente-Maritime Road Trip: La Rochelle, Île de Ré, Fort Boyard and Roman Saintonge

visits.text: The Musée de l'Annonciade, housed in a former 16th-century chapel, holds a first-rate collection: Pointillist, Nabis, and Fauvist paintings. Signac, Matisse, Derain, and Marquet are all represented. The place is a reminder that Saint-Tropez was a major center of avant-garde painting.

The Citadel, erected in 1602 under Henry IV, has dominated the harbor for four centuries. The hexagonal keep, a listed historic monument since 1921, houses the Museum of Maritime History. Models, artifacts, and immersive displays tell the stories of sailors from Saint-Tropez, from whaling to trade with the Ottoman Empire.

Place des Lices, lined with century-old plane trees, has been the village's beating heart since the 19th century. On Tuesdays and Saturdays, the Provençal market takes over the square. The rest of the time, pétanque games enliven the café terraces.

Notre-Dame de l'Assomption church, with its characteristic ochre and pink bell tower, has watched over the village since the 16th century. Inside, the bust of Saint Torpès recalls the founding legend of the town.
On the Citadel ramparts, some thirty peacocks roam freely. The view down over the rooftops of Saint-Tropez, the seaside cemetery, and the gulf forms one of the finest panoramas on the coast.

activities.text: Follow the coastal path from Graniers beach. This seaside trail runs along the coves and headlands, offering panoramas between pine groves and turquoise water. Swimming is possible in the wild coves.
The old harbor is made for strolling: fishing boats sit alongside yachts, and the colorful facades are reflected in the water. Head to Quai Jean-Jaurès for the ever-present spectacle.
Carry on to Ramatuelle, a medieval village perched on Paillas hill overlooking Pampelonne Bay. Its spiraling lanes and its ramparts offer a quiet counterpoint to the bustle of Saint-Tropez.

days_plan.itin_title: Var Road Trip: French Riviera & Provence Verte

visits.text: Saint-Vaast-la-Hougue, voted France's Favourite Village in 2019, reaches into the sea like a ship's prow. Its quai Vauban runs along a working fishing port, the third largest in the Manche department.

Walk the causeway from the Sailors' Chapel, the choir of the first 11th-century parish church dedicated to those lost at sea, to the Fort de la Hougue. The 20 m Vauban tower, UNESCO-listed since 2008, commands the bay from its granite promontory 40 m above sea level.

Take the amphibious boat to Tatihou Island, 28 hectares of protected nature. Its twin Vauban tower, 21 m high and 20 m in diameter, crossed fire with the one at La Hougue to close off the bay after the naval defeat of 1692.

Tatihou's maritime museum holds the archaeological collections from the wrecks of the royal fleet sunk during the Battle of La Hougue in 1692. Shipboard objects, cannons and remains tell the story of this defeat against the Anglo-Dutch fleet.

Tatihou's gardens shelter a surprising flora protected between dykes and granite walls. Palm trees from the Val de Saire, exotic plants and wildflowers sit alongside a bird reserve where more than a hundred species nest.

activities.text: Walk over to Tatihou at low tide, following the tidal path between the oyster beds. At high tide, the amphibious boat rises onto its wheels for the return trip by land.
Discover the oyster beds between Saint-Vaast and Tatihou, in the Cul de Loup inlet. Saint-Vaast oysters, known for their hazelnut taste, can be tasted on the spot at the oyster farms.
In summer, the Traversées de Tatihou festival puts on concerts of music from the sea on the island. The atmosphere of an island festival reachable only by water.

days_plan.itin_title: Manche Road Trip: Cotentin Peninsula & Mont-Saint-Michel
Cotentin, Pays d'Auge: 5 days exploring the most beautiful villages

visits.text: Saint-Valery-sur-Somme's medieval town overlooks the bay from a limestone promontory. Chequerboard walls of flint and sandstone, half-timbered houses with jettied upper floors from the 15th–16th centuries, and cobbled lanes filled with valerian and hollyhocks.

Pass through the Porte de Nevers (16th century, Historic Monument): above the entrance, two bays once let through the drawbridge chains. The coat of arms of the Duke of Gonzague-Nevers and the motto 'FIDES' still mark the pediment.
Climb to the Guillaume towers for a 180° panorama over the bay. From here in 1066, William the Conqueror assembled his fleet before crossing the Channel to England.
Saint-Martin church surprises with its two naves and walls where flint, sandstone, and limestone mingle—intact for 500 years. Inside, sailors' ex-votos testify to the town's maritime past.
Descend to the Courtgain quarter, former fishermen's village. Its low houses with coloured façades line narrow lanes—a striking contrast with the fortified upper town.

The chapelle des Marins stands on the site of the tomb of Saint Valery, an Irish hermit who founded an abbey here in the 7th century. From the neighbouring viewpoint, the view over Cap Hornu and the bay is one of Picardy's finest.

The Herbarium des remparts, nestled in the former nuns' garden, grows medicinal plants, dye plants and plants cultivated in medieval times. Some chefs from the region come here to source edible flowers.

activities.text: Join a guided outing on the salt marshes of Somme Bay to observe common seals—France's largest colony. Nature guides know the channels and tide times.
At low tide, the bay transforms into a giant mirror. Set off by sea kayak or pirogue from the harbour to approach the sandbanks where seals rest.

The Somme Bay Railway links Saint-Valery to Le Crotoy by steam train on the former Réseau des Bains de Mer (metre-gauge). Wooden carriages, a whistling locomotive and salt-marsh sheep passing by—an hour-long journey out of time.

days_plan.itin_title: Opal Coast Villages and Flemish Heartlands
Somme Road Trip: Bay of Somme and War Remembrance
The Most Beautiful Villages from Flanders to the Bay of Somme

visits.text: Welcome to 2,042 meters - the highest commune in Europe. Saint-Véran stretches for a kilometer along the mountainside, divided into five quarters separated by firebreaks after the fire of 1526. The traditional chalets, built in fuste style (larch wood on stone foundations), served as dwelling, stable, and hayloft all at once. Look up: some thirty painted sundials adorn the facades, several signed by Giovanni Francesco Zarbula, a 19th-century sundial maker from Piedmont.

Step inside the 17th-century church, built atop the foundations of an earlier structure. Outside, notice the sculpted lions clutching a child in their paws - a rare motif. On the wall, the sundial bears the village motto: “Lou plus aouto coumunoutas inte se mangeu lou pan de Diòu” - the highest commune where one eats the bread of God.

The Musée Le Soum occupies the village's oldest house, dated 1641. You'll discover how Queyras families lived: box beds positioned near livestock for warmth, carved wooden tools, and the everyday objects of harsh mountain life at 2,000 meters. It's compact but richly detailed.

activities.text: Wander from quarter to quarter through the village - each section had its own bread oven, larch fountain, and mission cross. Stop at the fountains: the round section served as a trough for animals, the rectangular one as a wash house. In summer, the artisan market offers sheep's cheese, mountain honey, and herbal teas.

If you're a confident hiker, climb toward the Clausis chapel (1.5 hours one way). The trail crosses alpine meadows where you'll spot marmots and possibly chamois. Near the chapel, remnants of the ancient copper mine remind us the site was worked as far back as the late Neolithic period.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Villages: From the Alps to the Luberon in 3 Days

visits.text: The Château de Bonneval, in Coussac-Bonneval, has existed in its present form since the 14th century—but a fortress already stood here in 930, as a stone embedded in the masonry of the entrance tower attests. The Bonneval family has owned it since 1055, making it one of the castles held longest by the same family in France. The guided tour takes you through ten rooms and two galleries furnished in Louis XIII and Louis XVI styles, including tapestries from Aubusson and Fontainebleau. Do not miss the room of Count Claude-Alexandre, nicknamed “the Pasha with Three Tails” for his adventures in the East in the 18th century. Note: the castle only opens in the afternoon, and a guided tour is mandatory—plan to start your day in Coussac so you are there when it opens.

Stop at Place Attane: the collegiate church of Saint-Yrieix commands attention immediately with its 12th-century Romanesque façade, built by the canons thanks to the generosity of the Dukes of Aquitaine. Inside, the carved capitals are worth examining, but don't leave without asking to see the 12th-century Bible preserved in the municipal library—376 vellum sheets covered in illuminations, classified as a historic monument and considered the finest Romanesque manuscript in the Limousin. It weighs 23 kilograms. An extraordinary object that few visitors know about.

Right next to the collegiate church stands the Tour du Plô, the oldest secular monument in town. Standing 24 meters tall, built of schist slabs in the early 13th century by the Viscount of Limoges to assert his authority over the canons, it served successively as a prison (on the ground floor, with no windows), a residence for the viscount on the third floor, and a lookout post at the top. Restored and reopened to the public in 2021 after years of closure, it offers an unobstructed view from its terrace over the medieval rooftops and countryside. Make the climb—it's the best viewpoint in town.

activities.text: Wander through the village of Coussac-Bonneval before your castle tour: the Place aux Foires and the lanes around the castle give you a good sense of the medieval village. The Church of Saint-Saturnin, just steps away, houses the tombs of Bonneval family members—a natural extension of your castle visit.

Saint-Yrieix-la-Perche holds the “Plus Beaux Détours de France” designation, and a stroll through its medieval lanes shows why it deserves it. The town is also the birthplace of kaolin: it was here that Jean-Baptiste Darnet discovered this white clay in 1768, essential for manufacturing Limoges porcelain. The archaeological site at Marcognac, on the edge of town, helps you understand this industrial adventure. If you're there in the morning, the weekly market sells local specialties: Bijou madeleines, cul-noir pork, cheeses from the Limousin countryside.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Vienne Road Trip: Castles and Périgord-Limousin

visits.text: Sainte-Agnès claims the title of Europe's highest coastal village at an altitude of 800 meters. Listed as one of France's “Most Beautiful Villages,” its pebble-paved lanes climb to the ruins of the feudal castle—built by the Counts of Ventimiglia and later demolished on the orders of Louis XIV. From the summit, the view stretches from Cap Martin to the Italian Riviera. Legend attributes the village's founding to a Roman princess named Agnès, who, having survived a hurricane, built a chapel in gratitude.

Don't leave without visiting the Maginot fort of Sainte-Agnès, part of the Maginot Line. Built between 1932 and 1938 (an irony of history: by an Italian company), it could house 350 men, fully self-sufficient for three months, with electricity, central heating, a hospital and an internal railway. Its artillery fired 1,201 shells at Italian troops in June 1940, holding back the invader for five days. Book your guided tour by text message 48 hours in advance.

activities.text: Ridge trail from the Saint-Sébastien chapel (17th century): several marked circuits lead toward Mont Ours (1,239 m) or Pic du Baudon (1,264 m). Moderate level, but the panoramas over the coast and Mercantour reward the effort.
Village square: taste local produce (ravioli-daube, honey products) on the central square. The village's glassmakers and jewelers display their creations in the surrounding lanes.

days_plan.itin_title: The 15 Gems of the French Riviera and Backcountry

visits.text: Sainte-Croix-du-Verdon perches on a rocky promontory facing the lake at the outlet of the gorges. The village nearly disappeared: the dam's original plans called for flooding it, before the planned water level was lowered. The stone Provençal houses, flower-filled squares, and narrow alleyways retain the character of Haute-Provence's hilltop villages. From the main overlook, the 180° panorama across the lake, the dam to the west, and the Verdon ridges to the east is one of the broadest on the circuit.

The 16th-century parish church on the central square is open to visitors. The Musée conservatoire des Arts et Traditions Populaires de Sainte-Croix-du-Verdon traces Provençal peasant life before the dam—agricultural tools, costumes, everyday objects—and gives a sense of what the valley was like when it lived off lavender, truffles, and honey. It's a moving complement to a visit to Les Salles-sur-Verdon.

Head down to the dam to see up close the structure that changed everything. Its double-curvature arch, 95 meters high and built with only 55,000 m³ of concrete to hold back 760 million m³ of water, makes it one of Europe's most “efficient” dams in terms of concrete-to-water ratio. Though closed to direct visits for safety reasons, it can be admired from the D111 bridge spanning the lake just downstream.

activities.text: The Sainte-Croix-du-Verdon water sports center offers windsurfing, kayaking, pedal boats, and sailing on the turquoise waters of the lake. It's one of the best sailing spots on the lake thanks to the wind that regularly blows up from the gorges in the afternoon. Providers offer introductory lessons and hourly or half-day rentals.

Hiking the hills overlooking the lake from Sainte-Croix-du-Verdon offers different views at every hour — in the morning, the lake reflects the cliffs in absolute calm; at sunset, the water takes on orange and pink hues. Allow 1.5 to 2 hours for the loop from the village.

On Tuesday mornings, from June to September, a market brings together local producers. Honey from the Alpes de Haute-Provence, dried herbs, goat cheeses and local olive oils. One last chance to take the flavors of the Verdon home before getting back on the road.

days_plan.itin_title: Lake Sainte-Croix and Verdon Circuit

visits.text: Here is one of the most improbable sites in France: a medieval charterhouse entirely transformed into a village during the French Revolution. Founded in 1281 by Béatrix de la Tour du Pin, the charterhouse of Sainte-Croix-en-Jarez housed Carthusian monks for five centuries—prayer, solitude, and silence—before being sold as national property in 1792. Since then, inhabitants have literally lived in the cells, cloisters, and monastic buildings. It's the only Carthusian monastery in the world to have become a municipality. It's been listed among the “Plus Beaux Villages de France” since 1982 and has fewer than 500 inhabitants. Take the guided tour: it gives access to otherwise closed interior spaces (14th-century wall paintings, a restored Carthusian priest's hermitage) that you won't see without a guide.

The small squares and houses built against the monastic structures tell the story of the unique coexistence between secular life and Carthusian heritage. A school has operated in the brothers' courtyard since 1839. On a self-guided stroll, observe how inhabitants have converted the former cells into ordinary homes—it's both strange and touching.

activities.text: Hike to the Roches de Marlin in the heart of the Pilat Regional Natural Park (7.3 km, ~3 hours, yellow blazing). This unusual megalithic site nestled in the Jarez hills offers views over the Gier and Rhône valleys. Hiking boots recommended.

Nighttime storytelling walks organized every Thursday evening from late July to late August: about 1 hour 15 minutes by lantern light in the charterhouse with a local storyteller. A rare experience—check the program at the Pilat tourist office before arriving.

days_plan.itin_title: Loop Around Lyon: Villages and Pierres Dorées

visits.text: Sainte-Énimie clings to the flank of the Sauveterre causse, between 600-meter-high cliffs. According to legend, the Merovingian princess Énimie, sister of King Dagobert, was cured of leprosy by bathing in the Burle spring and founded a monastery in the 6th century.

The Burle spring gushes at the village heart in a turquoise-water basin. This karst resurgence, explored by divers through 400 meters of underground galleries, constitutes one of the major outlets of the Sauveterre causse.

The church of Notre-Dame-du-Gourg, backed against the causse, dates from the 12th century and was remodeled in the 14th. Its Romanesque portal with round arch and two voussoirs opens onto a three-bay nave. Inside, a chapel illustrates Saint Énimie's story in contemporary ceramics.
The chapter house of the former Benedictine monastery, restored in 951, housed the monks' refectory and passing pilgrims. Its walls preserve acanthus decorations and carved human faces.
The wheat hall preserves one of the last stone grain measures in Gévaudan. The old village around the hall reveals its half-timbered houses, vaulted passages, and broad stone steps worn by centuries.

Castelbouc, a troglodyte village one kilometer upstream, can be visited from the riverside path. Its houses are pressed against the cliff, dominated by ruins of a medieval castle destroyed in 1592 to prevent it serving as Protestant refuge.

activities.text: The hermitage trail climbs from the Tarn bridge to the cave where Énimie supposedly retreated. Short but steep (45 min round trip), it offers a plunging panorama of the village and river's bend.

Outfitters offer Tarn canoe descents on several routes (from 30 min to over 5h). The stretch between Sainte-Énimie and La Malène crosses the Défilé des Détroits, the gorges' narrowest and most spectacular passage.

Aven Armand, 30 minutes by car on the Méjean causse, shelters a forest of 400 giant stalagmites, the largest reaching 30 meters. The funicular descent accesses an underground hall of cathedral dimensions.

Saint-Chély-du-Tarn, one kilometer downstream, offers a spectacle of cascades plunging into the Tarn from the cliff. Its 11th-century Romanesque church and semi-troglodyte chapel of Cénaret complete the visit.

days_plan.itin_title: Lozère Circuit: Tarn Gorges and Cévennes
Occitanie's 13 Most Beautiful Villages

visits.text: Opened in 1927, the Russian Cemetery is the largest Orthodox necropolis in Western Europe. More than 15,000 Russian émigrés who fled the 1917 revolution rest here.
The 5,200 graves include those of Rudolf Nureyev, Serge Lifar, Andrei Tarkovsky, and Princess Obolensky. Princes, artists, and resistance fighters lie alongside entire families.

The Church of Our Lady of the Dormition was inaugurated in 1939. Its green roof symbolizes the earth, its blue onion dome the sky. The architecture draws inspiration from 15th- and 16th-century Novgorod.
The portico features a fresco of the Assumption; the dome shows Christ bestowing blessings. The crypt houses the tombs of bishops and architect Albert Benois.
Orthodox crosses, carved steles, and frescoes testify to the spiritual richness of the Russian diaspora. Birches, spruces, and pines create an authentically Russian atmosphere.

activities.text: Stroll among the graves beneath the towering birch trees. The Russian-style landscaping with small benches and trees creates a pastoral setting unique in France.
The municipal park runs along the Orge on the edge of town. Walking paths and playgrounds invite you to take a break in nature after visiting the cemetery.

days_plan.itin_title: Essonne Tour: Castles and Valleys

visits.text: L'Île-Bouchard, an unusual town made up of two suburbs separated by an island on the Vienne, about 15 km from the stopover town, 15 minutes by road. The Saint-Léonard priory, founded in 1067, retains only its Romanesque choir and its ambulatory with three apsidioles. Its capitals carved around 1130-1140, showing scenes from sacred history, form one of the most complete sets of Romanesque sculpture in Touraine.

The church of Saint-Gilles in L'Île-Bouchard, about 15 km from the stopover town, 15 minutes by road, reworked in the 15th and then the 19th century, overlooks the right bank of the Vienne. The Cordeliers convent, with 12th- and 17th-century remains listed as a Historic Monument, rounds off this discreet heritage. Joan of Arc, on her way to Chinon in 1429, is said to have stopped here before the Romanesque doorway of Saint-Gilles.

Sainte-Maure-de-Touraine, the small town that gave its name to the famous AOP goat cheese. The truncated cone-shaped log pierced by an engraved rye straw has been produced here since Carolingian times. Legend says it was Moorish women, who remained after the 732 defeat, who transmitted their cheesemaking knowledge to the people of Touraine.

The market hall of Sainte-Maure, built in the 17th century, houses a lively market. Nearby, a dolmen and remains of a Roman camp testify to ancient occupation of the plateau. The 11th-century church and 16th-century houses complete this Touraine market town's heritage.

activities.text: Visit to a goat farm and Sainte-Maure-de-Touraine AOP tasting. Farm producers open their doors to explain the raising of Alpine and Poitevine goats, lactic coagulation, ladle molding and aging. The rye straw, laser-engraved, guarantees the cheese's authenticity.

Walk in the Vienne valley around L'Île-Bouchard, about 15 km from the stopover town, 15 minutes by road. The Loire-Anjou-Touraine regional nature park offers waymarked paths between vine-covered slopes, riverbanks and tuffeau villages. Bucolic scenery and absolute quiet.

Sainte-Maure-de-Touraine market. Under the 17th-century market hall, producers display goat cheeses, rillettes, honey and seasonal fruit. Sainte-Maure AOP pairs perfectly with a red Chinon or dry Vouvray.

days_plan.itin_title: Indre-et-Loire Road Trip: Loire Valley Châteaux, Secret Valleys & Touraine Vineyards

visits.text: Construction of Sainte-Maxime's Tour Carrée began in 1520 under the abbey of Le Thoronet. Until 1935, it served as a lord's residence, a gun tower, a granary, a prison, a school and a town hall. The dungeon remains accessible within the walls. Listed in 1977, it now houses the Maison des Traditions. The town offers guided tours: ask in advance.

The Maximois nickname the Pointe des Sardinaux little Corsica: rocks, pines and clear water, a few minutes from the center of Sainte-Maxime. It is the least built-up spot along the town's 11 km of coastline. Wear closed-toe shoes: it is more slippery than it looks.

activities.text: Walk through Sainte-Maxime's covered market in the morning: Provence AOC olive oil, Côtes de Provence wines and local produce from the Maures. It's the natural starting point for a stroll toward the port and its roughly 800 boats. Your best bet: go before 10am, then have a coffee on promenade Aymeric Simon-Lorière.

If you want to see Saint-Tropez without dealing with parking, board the Bateaux Verts from the port of Sainte-Maxime: the gulf crossing takes about twenty minutes. Sailings are frequent in season. Take the first morning departure; the 6pm return is packed.

days_plan.itin_title: Roquebrune-sur-Argens: sea, villages and the Var in 10 days

visits.text: Here they still recount the night of 5–6 June 1944, when American paratrooper John Steele was left hanging from the church bell tower, his parachute caught on the roof ridge. A dummy is fixed there in memory of the episode. The Airborne Museum, just opposite, displays a glider and a C-47 that participated in the landing.

activities.text: The Airborne Museum offers a guided village tour on Wednesdays at 2:30 pm during school holidays, focused on the retaking of Sainte-Mère-Église by paratroopers. Booking recommended as places are limited.

days_plan.itin_title: Cotentin, Pays d'Auge: 5 days exploring the most beautiful villages

visits.text: Sainte-Suzanne crowns a rocky spur rising 70 meters above the Erve valley. Listed among France's Most Beautiful Villages and as a Small Town of Character, it was the only stronghold to resist the assaults of William the Conqueror in the 11th century.

Step into the castle courtyard to discover the Renaissance lodge, built between 1608 and 1613 by Guillaume Fouquet de la Varenne, Henri IV's Postmaster General. It now houses the CIAP (Centre for Architecture and Heritage Interpretation) with scale models, audiovisuals and tactile displays exploring Mayenne's heritage.

The 11th-century quadrangular keep, erected by the Beaumont family from around 1020, stands protected by round towers equipped with arrow slits—the flour tower and the powder tower. The entrance was on the first floor via a ladder, designed to protect the lord during attacks.

Walk the patrol path along the double rampart walls. The 360° view sweeps across the Coëvrons hills, the Mayenne hedgerow countryside and the Erve valley. Head to the Watch Tower and West Tower for the finest panoramas over the town's rooftops.

The church, remodeled in 1884, preserves a Renaissance portal and remarkable statues from the 14th to 17th centuries, including those of Saint John the Baptist and Saint Suzanne, patron saint of engaged couples.

Push open the door to the municipal museum, housed in the former 17th-century courthouse. Nine rooms trace 3,000 years of local history through models, weapons from the Hundred Years' War and elements of Celtic vitrified walls. The centerpiece: France's oldest suit of armor, dating from 1410-1430, restored by the Musée des Invalides.

Descend toward the Grand Moulin, the oldest mill in the lordship. Transformed from a grain mill into a paper mill, it's still run by a master papermaker who crafts pure rag paper by hand using 13th to 18th-century techniques. The town once boasted 16 paper mills from the 17th to 19th centuries.

activities.text: The Mills Walk follows the Erve for 3.6 km below the fortified town. This family-friendly path passes the vestiges of old water mills installed along the river.
Visit the Erves dolmen, Mayenne's oldest monument. This Neolithic megalith, approximately 6,500 years old and classified in 1889, once sheltered the burials of 14 individuals.
Climb to Tertre Ganne in the late afternoon. This former strategic post from the Hundred Years' War offers the finest panorama of the medieval town and castle—spectacular at sunset.

days_plan.itin_title: Mayenne Circuit: Hedgerows and Medieval Towns

visits.text: The Arch of Germanicus (AD 19), a Roman arch with two openings that marked the entrance to the bridge over the Charente. Moved stone by stone in 1843 to escape demolition. Dedicatory inscriptions to Tiberius, Germanicus and Drusus Caesar are legible on the attic story.

The Gallo-Roman amphitheater of Saintes (1st century) could hold 15,000 spectators. Carved into a valley in the hillside, it retains its tiers, vomitoria and elliptical arena. Summer concerts and shows in this ancient setting.

The Abbaye aux Dames (11th-12th century), the first women's monastery in Saintonge. Romanesque facade sculpted with grimacing heads and fantastic animals. Conical bell tower covered in stone scales. Now a cultural center and home to an early music festival.
Saintes' old town stretches between the Charente and the hillsides. Saint-Pierre Cathedral (rebuilt after the Wars of Religion), 18th-century mansions, medieval lanes. Wrought-iron market halls.

activities.text: Guided tour of Gallo-Roman Saintes. The tourist office offers a complete circuit: Arch of Germanicus, Saint-Saloine baths, amphitheater, archaeological museum. Mediolanum Santonum was capital of the Aquitaine province.
Cruise on the Charente departing from Saintes. Landscapes of meadows, weeping willows and grey herons. Commentary on the history of river transport of cognac.
Pineau and cognac tasting. Regional producers open their cellars for guided visits. Pineau des Charentes, a blend of grape must and cognac, is enjoyed chilled as an aperitif.

days_plan.itin_title: Charente-Maritime Road Trip: La Rochelle, Île de Ré, Fort Boyard and Roman Saintonge

visits.text: The church of Notre-Dame-de-la-Mer looks more like a keep than a church: thick walls, arrow slits, no exterior ornamentation, built from the 9th century onwards to defend against Saracen incursions. Inside, a long nave without side chapels and sailors' votive offerings. It's visible from ten kilometres away in every direction.

Stifling heat and hundreds of candles: the crypt of the church of Notre-Dame-de-la-Mer houses the statue of Saint Sara, covered with robes and jewellery offered by pilgrims. You go down by a small staircase. The place is venerated all year, not just in May. Appropriate dress required.

The best view in Saintes-Maries-de-la-Mer is from the roof terrace of the church of Notre-Dame-de-la-Mer, reached by a staircase from the upper chapel where the reliquaries are kept. Views of the village, marshes and sea. The staircase is narrow and steep.

activities.text: If you visit on 24 and 25 May, the Gypsy pilgrimage takes over the whole village: Sara's procession to the sea on the 24th, the boat of the saints escorted by gardians on horseback on the 25th. Sara's procession only dates from 1935, when the Marquis de Baroncelli secured permission for it. Parking is impossible: arrive very early.

Rent a bike in Saintes-Maries-de-la-Mer and head towards the Bac du Sauvage and the Petit-Rhône, west of the village: rice fields, bull and horse herds, and drainage channels, without going back via the dyke. The route is flat; the mistral provides all the difficulty. Bring 1.5 litres of water per person.

days_plan.itin_title: Côte Bleue and Camargue: the lower coastal route in 7 days

visits.text: Salernes is the French capital of the hexagonal tomette — the small red terracotta tile that has paved floors all over Provence since the early 19th century. From 1830 onwards, local factories specialized in this tiling, prized for its thermal inertia: cool in summer, mild in winter. The Terra Rossa museum, housed in a former tile factory converted by the architect Jean-Michel Wilmotte, traces 7,000 years of ceramic activity in the Salernes area. The visit takes in a palaeontology room showing local digs, a full reconstruction of the early 20th-century workshops with their period machinery, and an exceptional collection of more than 2,000 decorated tiles from the Middle Ages to the 19th century, some of them unique in Europe. Allow at least an hour and a half to make the most of it.

The rest of Salernes can be explored leisurely on foot: about fifteen pottery and ceramics workshops are established in and around the village, most open to the public. Step inside two or three to watch artisans at work and understand the techniques that transform the red clay from local hills into tomettes or decorated faience. The old town's lanes, fountains and the Bresque River below complete the stroll.

activities.text: On Sunday morning, the Salernes market is one of the liveliest in the Haut-Var. Local producers sell honey, fresh figs (the white Salernes fig is renowned), olive oil and goat cheeses. It's also an opportunity to find artisan ceramic pieces directly from exhibitors. Arrive between 8 AM and 10 AM for the best selection.

Salernes' old mill and oil press allow you to complete your discovery of traditional local industry. Guided tours combining all three sites — mill, oil press and Terra Rossa — are offered on certain Tuesdays in July and August. Check with the tourist office for dates.

days_plan.itin_title: The 10 Most Beautiful Villages of the Haut-Var

visits.text: The village of Salers displays its Renaissance houses of black lava stone around the Place Tyssandier d'Escous. Perched at an altitude of 950 metres, this Plus Beau Village de France preserves its 16th-century heritage intact: turrets, carved lintels, mullioned windows and ramparts recall its status as the former seat of the Bailliage des Hautes Montagnes d'Auvergne. The church of Saint-Mathieu houses a 15th-century Entombment and Aubusson tapestries.

Puy Mary rises in a pyramidal silhouette to 1787 metres in the heart of the Cantal massif. Designated a Grand Site de France, this iconic summit offers a 360° panorama from its orientation table over radiating glacial valleys, triangular summer pastures and the rocky peaks of Europe's largest stratovolcano (2700 km²). Plan a return trip from Salers to Pas de Peyrol (the Massif Central's highest road pass at 1589 m), then follow a maintained trail for 30 minutes on foot to reach this exceptional viewpoint, with views as far as Mont Blanc on a clear day.

The Esplanade de Barrouze forms a dizzyingly high balcony overlooking the Maronne valley and the Cantal mountains. This grassy terrace, a true Salers postcard view, reveals the Puy Violent and the entire chain of puys in a landscape where the green of pastures meets the blue of distant ridges.

activities.text: Tasting Salers AOC cheese is a must in this town that gave the cheese its name. Produced exclusively on farms and in summer from raw milk of Salers cows, this cheese aged at least 3 months reveals an incomparable rustic intensity. Farms offer visits to burons and meetings with producers.

The hike to the summit of Puy Mary requires a return trip from Salers to the start of the maintained trail, whose steps climb 195 metres in 30 minutes. The Grand Site area offers 350 km of marked trails, from the GR®400 circling the massif to family loops. The more adventurous aim for sunrise or sunset for a magnificent spectacle over the dormant volcano.

Plomb du Cantal, the massif's highest summit at 1855 metres, is reached by cable car from the resort of Le Lioran; allow for a return trip from Salers to the resort before the ascent. This mechanical ascent offers hikers a spectacular alternative for reaching the ridges of Europe's largest volcano and admiring the Chaîne des Puys, Cézallier and Monts du Forez.

days_plan.itin_title: Cantal Road Trip: Auvergne Volcanoes and Mountain Traditions
Auvergne Circuit: Perched Villages and Volcanoes

places.name: Salies De Bearn

visits.text: The Salies-de-Béarn thermal baths occupy a Moorish-inspired building opened in 1889 — the architect Adrien Lagarde drew inspiration from the mosque of Cordoba for the two-tone facade and the minaret tower. An earlier establishment had opened in 1857; a fire in 1893 led to a complete rebuild. The virtues of the thermal waters were recognised by the Academy of Medicine in 1891 for rheumatology, gynaecology and childhood development disorders. The spring, 200 million years old, contains 300 grams of salt per litre.

Descend into the crypt of Place du Bayaà to see the salt spring fountain. Since 1587, only the Corporation of Share-Holders — descendants of Salies' original inhabitants — has the right to exploit this source. Their ownership right was recognized by Henry III of Albret in 1588. According to founding legend, the spring was discovered by a wounded wild boar that took refuge in the marshes and emerged covered in salt crystals before dying.

The Salies salt works produce around 2,000 tonnes of salt a year, a salt used to cure PGI Bayonne ham. Extraction goes back to the Bronze Age — pottery fragments dating from 1500 BC bear witness to it. The site houses a museum space on the history of production, along with shops selling salt and cured products.

The Church of Saint Vincent blends 11th-century architecture with Gothic style. Its Baroque altar dominates a nave restored several times. The historic quarter around the church is full of Bearnese half-timbered houses on stilts from the 14th to the 17th century, some of them straddling the Saleys — the river that runs through the town and earns it the nickname of the Bearnese Venice.

activities.text: Spa operators offer baths and treatments using the salt water of Salies, heated to 32°C and rich in 26 trace elements. An experience open to everyone, including outside a medical cure. The water makes you float naturally — as in the Dead Sea. Book ahead.

Stroll along the Saleys, which runs through the historic quarter. The half-timbered houses on stilts, the stone bridges and the colourful facades make up a scene that the people of Salies compare to Venice. In September, the Salt Festival enlivens the whole town centre for several days.

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip Pyrenees-Atlantiques: Basque Country and Bearn

map_keywords: Place du Bayaà salt spring Salies-de-Bearn

visits.text: Rows of workers' housing in the Camargue: the Solvay district of Salin-de-Giraud has long red-brick buildings, built with materials and workers from northern France. Straight streets, workers' estates, no Provençal farmhouses. The village grew up in the late 19th century around salt and soda ash.

The Orthodox church of Salin-de-Giraud, a long, low building repainted in blue and white, was given by Salins du Midi to the village's Greek community. Salin still has many descendants of Greek, Armenian, Spanish and Italian immigrants who came to work in salt production.

Small and unpretentious, the Salin-de-Giraud arena is a reminder that the village is also part of the Camargue, despite its industrial town planning. It stands right in the centre, on Rue des Arènes, a stone's throw from the workers' estates. Check the local calendar: bull races only take place on a few days each year.

activities.text: Take the Barcarin ferry rather than the road via Arles: it crosses the Grand Rhône between Port-Saint-Louis and Salin-de-Giraud, a crossing of around 450 metres. It's the prettiest way to approach the Camargue, and the shortcut to Martigues or Marseille.

If you want to understand salt, the Salin-de-Giraud tourist office, housed in the renovated Cercle Solvay, offers guided walks around the village between April and late September. The saltworks itself can be explored on a circuit, on foot, by bike or by car.

days_plan.itin_title: Côte Bleue and Camargue: the lower coastal route in 7 days

visits.text: Grande Saline of Salins-les-Bains, UNESCO site inscribed on the World Heritage list since 2009. The mandatory hour-long guided tour descends into underground galleries built in the 13th century in the image of a cathedral, extending 165 meters long and 10 meters high. The two saltwater extraction wells are protected by majestic vaults. France's last salt pan, the tools, carts, and timbers impregnated with salt testify to 1,200 years of operation until closure in 1962. The Salt Museum completes the visit.

Fort Saint-André watching over Salins since the 17th century on the heights of the town. Rebuilt by Vauban after 1674 following Franche-Comté's attachment to France, this fort of medieval origin can be visited with a guide. The view from the ramparts embraces the entire Furieuse valley and the rooftops of the spa town. The visit concludes with a tasting of wines, Comté, and cured meats in the old vaulted rooms.

Old town and its private mansions testifying to past prosperity. Salins counted 8,500 inhabitants on the eve of the French Revolution, the second city of Franche-Comté thanks to white gold. Transverse lanes hide architectural treasures: fountains, covered passages, Renaissance houses, terraced gardens. The Collégiale Saint-Anatoile dominates the heights with its imposing architecture. The city stretches along the Furieuse between the two forts.

ThermaSalina spa, a thermal establishment completely renovated in 2017 over 2,800 square meters. The naturally salty waters denser than those of the Dead Sea provide a unique sensation of weightlessness. The richness in trace elements like magnesium, iron, and zinc plays a therapeutic role for rheumatism and joint flexibility. The wellness area open Monday to Saturday offers pools, hammam, caldarium, and water jets for passing visitors.

activities.text: Hike to Mont Poupet culminating at 851 meters altitude. The trail climbs through forests and meadows to the summit offering an exceptional panoramic view. On very clear days, you can even glimpse Mont Blanc. It's also the favorite spot for regional paragliders who launch from the summit. The descent allows observation of the cirque, forts, and Jura plateaus from different angles.

Hidden Treasures of the Salt City trail offered by the Tourist Office. Join Léa, Léo, and Lucas to discover how Salins developed thanks to its white gold. Historical anecdotes, prestigious monuments, beautiful viewpoints, and secret places unfold throughout the walking circuit. The elevation gain and stairs on the route provide access to the heights to admire the town.

Relaxation at the spa with saltwater treatments. The wellness area accessible without a cure offers hydro-baths, jet showers, mud applications, underwater saltwater massages, and scrubs. The water temperature between 30 and 34 degrees and exceptional salt content create a soothing floating experience. Half-day or full-day packages allow you to enjoy the therapeutic benefits.

days_plan.itin_title: Jura Road Trip: Lakes, Waterfalls & Mountains

visits.text: Did you know that Salles-Arbuissonnas is the 5th longest municipality name in France? But that's not why we make the detour: it's for its cloister, the last Romanesque cloister in the Rhône department. Built in the 10th century by Cluniac monks, the priory of Saint-Martin-de-Salles houses a 12th-century gallery with ribbed vaults resting on paired columns of golden stone. The site's history is just as colorful: in the 18th century, noble families placed their daughters here as canonesses with the title of countess—pious yet worldly young women who had individual houses built around the forecourt. One of them, Alix des Roys, was the mother of the poet Lamartine. The Musée du Prieuré is open from March 1 to November 30 (closed Monday and Tuesday).

The wine-growing village with its golden stone façades deserves a slow stroll: the vineyards classified under the Beaujolais-Villages AOC hug the hillsides to the horizon, and the panoramas of Mont Brouilly (crowned by its Notre-Dame-des-Raisins chapel) and, on clear days, the Alps are among the most beautiful in the Beaujolais. Take the opportunity to enjoy a tasting in a local wine cellar.

activities.text: Walking loop “cloister–village–vineyards” (3 km, very easy, ~1 hr). The trail follows the vineyard slopes and offers views down over the village. In autumn, during the grape harvest, the atmosphere is particularly lively.
Short climb to a viewpoint over the Beaujolais hills. On clear days, the Alpine range takes shape to the east. It's one of those moments when you understand why we travel.

days_plan.itin_title: Loop Around Lyon: Villages and Pierres Dorées

visits.text: The Château de l'Empéri dominates Salon-de-Provence from a rocky base, the Rocher du Puech. It's the oldest standing castle in Provence, and one of the three largest with the Palais des Papes and the Château de Tarascon. It houses a military museum. The north terrace exists because a tower weakened by the 1909 earthquake was dynamited.

Housed since 1992 in the house that Nostradamus bought in 1547, the Maison de Nostradamus museum traces his life in ten scenes with sound, with a small planetarium. He wrote his Prophecies here and died here in 1566. A 40-minute audio guide, closed Tuesdays.

Small but clever: the Jardin des Simples de Nostradamus, laid out in 2003 in the courtyard of the Château de l'Empéri, brings together the medicinal plants he used, grouped into beds according to his texts. Free entry. Ten minutes is enough, but the visit helps you understand the museum.

activities.text: Visit the Marius Fabre soap factory in Salon-de-Provence to see how Marseille soap is still made: moulding machines, engraved boxwood stamps and stencils are displayed in a former drying room. Two soap factories still operate in the town.

If the Patrouille de France is training, the terrace of the Château de l'Empéri is the best observation post in the town centre. It's been based in Salon-de-Provence since 1964. Training times are not guaranteed: ask at the tourist office.

days_plan.itin_title: Côte Bleue and Camargue: the lower coastal route in 7 days

visits.text: Reach the Montenvers site aboard the red rack railway, running since 1909, about 27 km from the stopover town, 40 minutes by car. At 1,913 metres, discover the Mer de Glace, the largest glacier in the French Alps at 7 kilometres long. Visit the Ice Cave, reached by more than 400 steps.

Discover Samoëns, a village of character classified among the most beautiful flowered villages. Its heart revolves around the Place du Gros Tilleul, where a linden tree planted in 1438 stands. Admire the church of Notre-Dame-de-l'Assomption, completed in 1555.

Explore this exceptional 3.7-hectare Alpine botanical garden, classified a Remarkable Garden. Given in 1906 to her native village by Marie-Louise Cognacq-Jaÿ, the garden presents more than 2,500 mountain plant species along 1.5 km of trails. The Château Chapel offers a panorama over the Giffre valley.

activities.text: Board the historic red train that climbs from Chamonix, about 27 km from the stopover town, 40 minutes by car, up to the Montenvers site facing the Mer de Glace. The commentary along the way covers the history of mountaineering.

Go down the metal stairways (more than 400 steps) to reach the cave carved anew each year into the glacier, about 27 km from the stopover town, 40 minutes by car. Admire the ice sculptures and the translucent blue walls.
Stroll through this unique Alpine garden where every sense is called upon. The winding route allows a gradual discovery of the different recreated Alpine ecosystems.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Savoie Road Trip: Alpine Lakes & Mont Blanc

visits.text: Perched at 312 meters, Sancerre towers over the Loire's bend like a balcony planted with vines. The medieval pedestrian street climbs toward the Esplanade de la Porte César—from there, the view sweeps across the sloping vineyards on one side and the river on the other, with Pouilly-Fumé facing it across the opposite bank. Two rival appellations gazing at each other 4 km apart, sauvignon against sauvignon: the debate is ancient and has no definitive answer.

Sancerre's three terroirs deserve attention before tasting anything. The silex (flint) produces taut, smoky, almost electric wines. The terres blanches—Kimmeridgian limestone, the same rock as Chablis—bring depth and richness. The caillottes, lighter limestone, yield rounder wines that drink well young. Same grape, same sun, three different wines: that's the Loire.

Chavignol, population 200, gave its name to one of the world’s most famous goat cheeses—the crottin. The PDO dates to 1976, the recipe far earlier. The village sits 5 km from Sancerre, nestled among the vines: a handful of houses, a few producers, and goats grazing between the sauvignon plots.

activities.text: Comparative tasting at Vacheron or Alphonse Mellot in early afternoon: request the three terroirs from the same vintage to understand the soil effect rather than the winemaker's influence. Vacheron has been practicing biodynamics since 2004—their silex has a tension you won't forget easily. Reservations recommended during high season.

Chavignol crottin PDO with a glass of white Sancerre: the local pairing that stands the test of time. Young cheese, still moist, calls for a Sancerre from caillottes. Aged crottin, drier and sharper, stands up better to silex. Pick some up at the village cheese shop before heading up to Sancerre for the evening.

Detour to Saint-Andelain for Domaine Didier Dagueneau - the absolute benchmark for Pouilly-Fumé, farmed biodynamically until the founder's death in 2008 and continued by his children. The Silex and Pur Sang cuvées are the most discussed in the Loire Valley. Do not go to the estate without confirmation of an appointment: it does not operate as a public tasting room.

days_plan.itin_title: Loire Valley Wine Route in 8 days
Cher Loop: Romanesque Berry and the Route Jacques-Cœur

visits.text: Grostenquin opens this final day with one of the route’s most spectacular exhibitions: 150 nativity scenes from five continents, brought together in one place. The centerpiece is a large Provençal nativity scene covering approximately 45 m², with around a hundred 27 cm nativity figurines and about fifteen mechanical figures, recreating life in a Provençal village at Christmas. Admission is free. The village’s Gothic Revival church, dedicated to Saint John the Baptist and rebuilt in 1867, is worth a look: when the old church was demolished in 1863, the tomb of a Swedish colonel was discovered inside.

In Destry, the nativity scene is assembled each year by the village children. It features nativity figurines measuring 50 to 60 centimeters from the early 20th century, all carefully restored. Around twenty figures retain their original appearance, sometimes joined by snowmen depending on the mood that year. A lively, much-loved, and touching nativity scene.

Saint-Barthélemy Church in Raville, built in 1758, holds a surprise: it displays nativity scenes made using bobbin lace, the Tiffany stained-glass technique, and ceramics—unusual craft techniques that give these depictions of the Nativity an almost sculptural quality. A detour well worth making for craft enthusiasts.

In Créhange, a family nativity scene covering 7 m² brings together 130 figures and mechanical figures in a meticulously detailed setting. In Bambiderstroff, Saint-Félix de Nole Church displays a wooden nativity scene depicting a Palestinian landscape at the side altar. Bionville-sur-Nied rounds off this overview with the Kahl family’s historic nativity scene, built in 1910 by the grandfather and brought back into the spotlight by his descendants after twenty years packed away in boxes.

The FICI workshop in Sanry-sur-Nied is the route’s final stop and one of its gems. The nativity figurine maker, originally from Poland and trained by a master craftsman in Aubagne, is one of the few members of the Confrérie des Santonniers de Provence based outside Provence. For more than 30 years, she has made hand-painted clay nativity figurines—some 7 cm tall, others much larger and dressed in clothing—including original Lorraine creations such as Saint Nicholas, Père Fouettard, and a Lorraine miner. Awarded the Qualité MOSL label. Workshop visits and on-site sales are available. Groups should contact the workshop in advance.

activities.text: Take time to wander through the villages of the Pays de Nied between Grostenquin and Sanry: Romanesque and Gothic Revival churches dot the country roads of the Lorraine plain. A photography tour of these rural religious buildings, often open without attendants, reveals the diversity of the region’s building craftsmanship from the 18th to the 20th century.

At the FICI nativity figurine makers’ workshop, the exhibition and sale is open on Saturdays and Sundays from late November to late December, according to the published schedule for the season. It is an opportunity to buy handcrafted nativity figurines—some wearing Lorraine regional dress or miners’ clothing—and admire the hand modeling and painting.

days_plan.itin_title: Christmas Nativity Scene Route in Moselle

visits.text: Meursault is nicknamed the “white wine capital of Burgundy”—and the title is well deserved. Its 400-hectare vineyard devotes 95% of its area to Chardonnay, on clay and limestone soils ideal for this grape variety. Tour the village starting with the 14th-century Gothic church, then walk past century-old cellars: the winegrowers' “little châteaux” testify to past opulence. Thomas Jefferson, future president of the United States, wrote to his supplier on January 22, 1789: “I am in urgent need of Meursault... it is the one I prefer!”

Puligny-Montrachet is home to the world's most sought-after white wines: its 4 grands crus—Montrachet, Chevalier-Montrachet, Bâtard-Montrachet and Bienvenues-Bâtard-Montrachet—are often designated as the planet's finest Chardonnays. The Montrachet grand cru itself covers only 7.99 hectares, straddling Puligny and Chassagne. As you walk between the rows, look for the signs marking the parcels—sometimes just a few meters separate a village appellation from a premier cru, and a €50 bottle from a €500 one.

Chassagne-Montrachet, Puligny's neighbor, shares two of the same grands crus but is also known for its red wines—little-known but excellent. Stroll through the village of golden stone to feel the atmosphere of a village where every house conceals a cellar. The commune added Montrachet to its name in 1879, to capture the renown of the grand cru it shares.

Santenay marks the end of the Côte de Beaune—and with it the UNESCO-listed Climats du vignoble de Bourgogne, which stretch from Dijon to here. The commune has two roles: winegrowing, with 12 Pinot Noir premiers crus, and as a spa town—its waters are Europe's richest in lithium and have been known since Roman antiquity. The Château de Santenay overlooks the vines; Philip the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, was one of its owners. From the top of Mont de Sène (521 m), known as “Montagne des Trois Croix”, the view extends on clear days to the Jura and Mont Blanc.

activities.text: The Voie des Vignes cycling route follows small roads between Beaune and Santenay along a 35 km section without excessive climbs: it passes through Pommard, Volnay, Meursault, Puligny and Chassagne. Rental shops offer bikes—standard or electric—in Beaune and the villages. It's the slowest and most pleasant way to read the winegrowing landscape: you'll see the changes in soil, exposure and stone colors from wall to wall.

A hot air balloon flight over the Côte de Beaune, departing from the Beaune or Pommard area, is the experience that makes sense of the geography of this entire vineyard. Seen from above, the Côte resembles a mosaic of puzzle pieces—each parcel has its own soil color, slope and exposure. Flights take place early in the morning or late in the afternoon, depending on the winds. Operators offer regular departures from May to October; book several weeks ahead in summer.

days_plan.itin_title: Burgundy's Route des Grands Crus: Dijon to Santenay

visits.text: The Franciscan monastery of Saorge is one of the architectural rarities of southeastern France: founded in 1633 by Recollect friars who came to help the plague-stricken Roya valley, it exemplifies a Franciscan Baroque style that is both restrained and virtuosic. No marble, no gilding—but 23 frescoes from the 18th century in the cloister recounting the life of Saint Francis of Assisi, and nine sundials painted around 1760–1762 by master mason Calderari from Lugano. The esplanade offers a view down over the village, arranged like an amphitheater, and the gorges. A writers' residence since 2001. Guided tour included in the ticket; closed Tuesdays.

Push open the door of Saint-Sauveur Church at the heart of the village: built in the late 15th century, remodeled in Baroque style in the 18th. Its 1732 high altar is a marvel of marble inlay. But the highlight is the Italian organ made in Ventimiglia, then transported to Saorge in 1847—shipped by boat to Nice, then carried up through the gorges in pieces on muleback. The 19th-century carillon, played by hand and foot by the village carillonneur, still rings during local festivals.

Saorge's streets are worth a visit in themselves: vaulted passages called “pountin,” tall seven-story houses pressed against the slope, roofs of purple stone slabs quarried locally. The entire village is heritage-listed. Thomas Jefferson, future US president, described it as “a castle and a village facing each other, suspended from a cloud.” Look for sundials painted on facades—Saorge has about twenty.

activities.text: The monastery garden, on terraces to the east, is a corner of paradise: a vegetable garden, vines trained over pergolas, fruit orchards, irrigation canals. The spirit of Franciscan self-sufficiency remains intact. Access included in the monastery visit.

Try Roya valley cuisine in one of the village's few restaurants: ravioli with wild herbs, polenta, local cheeses. The valley's cuisine combines influences from Nice and Piedmont. Tende became part of France only in 1947; the Italian identity remains vivid in its dishes.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpes-Maritimes Road Trip: Riviera and Mercantour, 13 days

visits.text: The Caves of Sare descend into the mountain for nearly a kilometer and reveal 45,000 years of human presence. The sound and light tour reveals stalactites, stalagmites and traces of the first inhabitants of the Basque Country. Thirteen species of bats live there. Ideal on rainy days — and Sare sees plenty!

Detour to Ortillopitz House, 3 km from the village. Its foundations date back to 1540 and the house in its current form dates from 1660. It is a typical Labourdin etxe: a self-sufficient farming estate with vineyard, flax, old vegetable garden, stone wash house, spring and traditional livestock. The interior preserves its original furnishings. It is one of the best ways to understand what 17th-century rural Basque life was like.

The Church of Saint Martin in Sare raises its bell tower in the middle of the village. Typical of Labourdin churches with their wooden galleries on several levels, it stands above the fronton — the pelota court — which is the real heart of village social life. Sare has more than 80 carved stone door lintels recorded throughout its streets.

activities.text: Take the Galtzada from the village center. This ancient medieval flagstone path connected Bayonne to Spain over the mountains. The GR8 and GR10 hiking trails follow it in parts, offering scenic loops with views over Mount Rhune. Plan 2 to 4 hours depending on the loop chosen.

Push on to Ainhoa and Ascain at the end of the day. These two Basque villages are listed among France's Most Beautiful Villages — Ainhoa notably for the half-timbered houses lining its pelota square. Compare the architecture of the two villages: same logic, same materials, but each house tells a different story through its carved lintels.

days_plan.itin_title: Nouvelle-Aquitaine Loop: Villages, Vineyards & Dordogne
Road Trip Pyrenees-Atlantiques: Basque Country and Bearn

visits.text: Sarlat survived the Middle Ages by accident: the Hundred Years' War and the Wars of Religion spared it, which was rare enough that André Malraux made it his pilot city for heritage preservation in 1962. Sixty-five protected monuments within 15 hectares - one of the densest concentrations in France. The Maison de La Boétie is worth stopping for: a Renaissance façade with three levels of sculpted windows, built in 1530, and inside (in theory) an 18-year-old philosopher who wrote the Discourse on Voluntary Servitude while his contemporaries fought religious wars. Wander for an hour, note the contrast between the dark stone and tourists in shorts, then take the road to Domme - the real reason for the day.

The Lantern of the Dead is Sarlat's most honest monument: an eleven-meter cylindrical Romanesque tower from the 12th century, and nobody has ever known exactly what it was for. Funerary lantern? Memorial monument? Tomb of an English king trapped by the people of Sarlat in 1147, according to an unverified local tradition? Eight hundred years later, specialists still argue. It's rare for a medieval monument to keep its mystery intact—and not for lack of trying. Free access, five minutes suffice.

On Friday, October 13, 1307—the date does have a history—Philip the Fair orders the simultaneous arrest of all the Templars in France. Sealed orders sent a month in advance to the bailiffs, opened that very morning. Two to three thousand knights rounded up in a single day. At Domme, 70 of them end up in the two towers of the Porte des Tours, built in 1281. For eleven years, knowing that Jacques de Molay burns in Paris in 1314 and that the Order is dissolved, they carve into the stone what they have to say—crosses pattée, crucifixions, inscriptions 'Clemens est antichristus'. In 1970, Canon Tonnelier attributes all this to the Templars. In 2018, an archaeological study challenges this attribution: 'a place for waiting, or even idleness'. The debate remains open. What's certain: the originals are fading, you're watching them disappear. Guided tour €4—without a guide, nothing makes sense.

From the promenoir des Falaises, the Dordogne winds through its meanders 250 meters below, and three medieval castles come into view all at once—Castelnaud, Beynac, Marqueyssac. In October, the low late-afternoon light makes the towers stand out as if they had been cut out with a scalpel. Twenty minutes, free access—it's the best moment of the day to understand why people built in such high places.

activities.text: Lunch in Sarlat: Le Bistrot, place du Peyrou - classic Périgord bistro, duck breast, foie gras, gizzard salad, €25-40. If you're there on a Saturday morning, the market at place de la Liberté (truffles, foie gras, walnuts, porcini in season) is the real first act of the journey.

Dinner and overnight in Domme or Sarlat. For atmosphere: L'Esplanade in Domme, a hotel-restaurant with a panoramic terrace over the valley, €130-220, dinner €45-65. Alternatively, La Belle Étoile on the banks of the Dordogne (€100-180). In Sarlat, Le Présidial occupies a former 17th-century courthouse and serves Périgord cuisine, €45-70.

days_plan.itin_title: Dordogne: Prehistoric Caves, Medieval Fortresses & Périgord Delights
Nouvelle-Aquitaine Loop: Villages, Vineyards & Dordogne
Haunted Southwest - 5 Days from Périgord Noir to the Cathar Castles
The Most Beautiful Villages of Lot and Périgord in 6 Days

visits.text: The Chapelle des Cordeliers, a 13th-century Gothic choir dating from 1265, houses the largest stained-glass window ever created by Marc Chagall: La Paix, a monumental work measuring 12 m high by 7.50 m wide, weighing 900 kg and containing 13,000 pieces of glass. Produced between 1974 and 1976 in the Simon-Marq workshops in Reims by master glassmaker Charles Marq, the window illuminates the choir with celestial blues and blazing reds, depicting the Creation, the Tree of Life and biblical figures in translucent colour. Moses carrying the Tablets of the Law and the prophets seem to float in space. Side windows added in 1977 complete the ensemble.

The Musée du Pays de Sarrebourg, housed in a contemporary building dating from 2004, continues the Chagall theme with the La Paix tapestry, measuring 4.71 m by 6.36 m. Created by Yvette Cauquil-Prince in 1994, it is a textile interpretation of the design for the United Nations stained-glass window in New York. The building also houses remarkable Gallo-Roman archaeological collections: 2nd-century mosaics, polychrome capitals from Tarquimpol and earthenware from the Niderviller factory (1748-1827), whose decoration rivals the refinement of Sèvres.

activities.text: The garden of the Chapelle des Cordeliers is a contemporary 1,200 m² meditation space created in 2007, where Chagall’s recorded voice recites his poems. Glass cubes containing trees and plants with changing colours, hedges of varying heights and fragrant plantings continue the dialogue with the stained glass in a setting of greenery and transparency. Quotations from Cendrars, Aragon and Apollinaire punctuate the walk.

Explore the Gallo-Roman remains around Sarrebourg, the ancient crossroads of Pons Saravi between Metz and Strasbourg on the Roman road. The Croix-Guillaume site at Saint-Quirin, about 15 km from the stage town, 15 minutes by road, reveals a settlement of the Vosges foothills from the first to the fourth century. The baths of Tarquimpol (first to third centuries), about 25 km from the stage town, 25 minutes by road, with their exceptional polychrome capitals, testify to the importance of this territory under the Roman Empire, which numbered 15,000 inhabitants.

days_plan.itin_title: 4-Day Moselle Tour: Metz, Bitche Citadel and Chagall’s Stained Glass

visits.text: The Sarreguemines Earthenware Museum presents two centuries of ceramic expertise in the former apartments of director Paul de Geiger (1871-1914). The Winter Garden, listed as a historic monument in 1979, dazzles with walls entirely covered by 600 m² of earthenware tiles created between 1880 and 1882. Its monumental 3 m majolica fountain, Carl Schuller's allegories of Earth and Fire and its 10 m-high ceiling form an Art Nouveau masterpiece. Fine earthenware, stoneware and porcelain bear witness to 200 years of production that employed as many as 3,000 workers.

The Moulin de la Blies, a museum annex housed in a mill dating from 1725, reveals the secrets of earthenware production. Millstones and grinders prepared the 50 tonnes of clay required by the factory each day. The 11 m-high bottle kiln dating from 1865, the last surviving witness to the first Industrial Revolution, could fire 15,000 pieces per batch at 1,280°C. Throwing and glazing demonstrations bring the traditional skills of the earthenware makers back to life.

The Casino des Faïenceries, a 1906 Art Nouveau building with façades decorated with 800 m² of polychrome ceramics, bears witness to Sarreguemines’ industrial golden age. Floral designs featuring wisteria and climbing roses in glazed earthenware illustrate how the factory’s artisans applied their creativity to architecture. Unfortunately closed to the public, the building can still be admired from outside for its spectacular façades.

activities.text: Stroll along the Sarre and Blies, the two rivers whose confluence gave the town its name. The landscaped Brouazin and Lebrun quays provide 3 km of riverside walks overlooking the converted buildings of the former earthenware factories. Restored barges and sightseeing boats enliven the water in fine weather. The Franco-German garden symbolises cross-border reconciliation.

Discover the borderland heritage of Sarreguemines, a crossroads town between France and Germany, 2 km from Saarland. Its proximity to Germany is reflected in the Wilhelmine architecture, bilingual signs and local cuisine combining quiche Lorraine and fleischnacka. The weekly market, held on Wednesdays and Saturdays, has attracted visitors from both sides of the Rhine since 1297.

days_plan.itin_title: 4-Day Moselle Tour: Metz, Bitche Citadel and Chagall’s Stained Glass

places.name: Sartene

visits.text: Propriano stretches along the head of the Gulf of Valinco as a lively seaside resort. The marina welcomes traditional boats and modern yachts; the quays lined with fish restaurants and artisan ice cream shops attract strollers. The Notre-Dame de la Miséricorde church overlooks the port and houses paintings and statues. The 17-meter Scoglio Longo lighthouse marks the entrance to the commercial harbor.

Roccapina reveals its spectacular rock formations from the viewpoint on the N196, about 21 km from the town on this stage of the itinerary, a 25-minute drive. The pink granite Lion watches over the beach and the Genoese tower in a picture-postcard landscape. The botanical trail of Casa di Roccapina explains the Corsican maquis and the geology of the site. The panorama takes in the Valinco coast as far as Bonifacio.

Roccapina beach forms a crescent of white sand between sculpted rocks and turquoise sea; plan a round trip from Sartène. The translucent water, shallow for several dozen meters, suits families. The 16th-century Genoese tower overlooks the beach and granite formations. The listed site remains free of modern construction.

activities.text: The beaches of the Valinco alternate between fine sand and rocky coves along 40 kilometers of coastline. Cupabia beach forms an arc of white sand facing the flowering maquis; plan a round trip by car from Sartène. Campomoro shelters its 16th-century Genoese tower above a translucent bay. The coastal path connects wild coves and panoramic viewpoints.

Boat excursions from Propriano follow the wild coast of southern Corsica. The trips reveal inaccessible coves, sea caves, and sculpted rock formations. Swimming stops in turquoise waters and sightings of dolphins and seabirds enhance the crossings. Tours extend toward Bonifacio or the Îles Sanguinaires.

Scuba diving explores wrecks and drop-offs of the Gulf of Valinco. Renowned sites include the wreck of the Prado at 42 meters and the Campomoro caves. Crystalline water reveals groupers, spiny lobsters, and red coral in the protected nature reserve. Certified centers offer introductory and exploration dives from April to October.

days_plan.itin_title: Complete Tour of Corsica
Southern Corsica Tour: Bonifacio, Porto-Vecchio and Mountains
