visits.text: Carved out of limestone 320 million years old by the river Erve, this small canyon holds 22 known cavities, listed under Natura 2000, used by humans for at least 300,000 years.

Margot cave, classified Historic Monument since 1926, is the only decorated cave open to visitors in western France. In 2003, archaeologist Romain Pigeaud discovered over 200 prehistoric engravings from the Upper Paleolithic (~25,000 years ago): horses, bison, woolly rhinoceros and engraved birds, the latter very rare in cave art.

Rochefort cave, a human-sized chasm, reveals an archaeological excavation site, spectacular concretions (stalactites, stalagmites) and an underground lake. Excavations have uncovered a Solutrean habitat dated 25,000 to 20,000 years before present.

The Prehistory Museum, opened in 2017, traces the life of the Erve valley's first inhabitants through original archaeological collections: laurel leaves, spear points, reindeer antler harpoons, ibex plaquette. An immersive 3D dome allows virtual visits to Mayenne-Sciences cave, closed to the public, which contains drawings of bison and mammoths 27,000 years old.

Saint-Pierre church, in Saulges village, is a building constructed between the 8th and 10th centuries. A few minutes' walk away, the Céneré oratory perpetuates the memory of the hermit who evangelized the valley.

activities.text: Take hiking trail n°33 from the museum. It crosses the canyon passing Japanese stepping stones over the Erve, follows the limestone cliffs and offers plunging views of cave entrances nestled in the rock faces.
The canyon cliffs count a hundred climbing routes from 3a to 7c, on walls reaching 25 meters. A popular venue for initiation and recreational practice.

The Natura 2000 valley shelters wild orchids, dragonflies, rare butterflies and one of western France's most important bat colonies. Ouessant sheep maintain the site ecologically. Take time to observe wildlife at dusk.

days_plan.itin_title: Mayenne Circuit: Hedgerows and Medieval Towns

visits.text: It was in this fortress, in March 1429, that Joan of Arc identified the Dauphin Charles disguised among his courtiers and convinced him that she heard voices. The story is well known; the place less so. Chinon Fortress stretches for 400 meters above the Vienne - one of France’s largest medieval enclosures - and remains largely ruined, which gives it real character. Allow for a round trip from Saumur for this visit to Chinon.

Rue Voltaire is Chinon's best-preserved street: timber-framed houses from the 15th to the 17th century, cellars cut into the tuffeau behind the façades and the Grand-Carroi fountain. Rabelais was born 6 km from here at La Devinière and described Chinon fondly in Gargantua. The street's bistro is still going. Allow for a round trip from Saumur for this walk in Chinon.

Fontevraud is no ordinary abbey: founded in 1101, it brought monks and nuns together under the authority of an abbess - the pope approved the arrangement by a bull in 1106, which was unusual for the time. The Plantagenets made it their necropolis: Henry II, Richard the Lionheart, Eleanor of Aquitaine and Isabella of Angoulême rest there, with their painted 12th-century effigies still in place. Napoleon turned the abbey into a prison in 1804; it remained one until 1963. Allow for a round trip from Saumur for this visit to Fontevraud.

White, perched above the Loire, Saumur château resembles an illustration from a medieval book of hours—and for good reason: the Très Riches Heures du duc de Berry depicts it exactly this way in September 1412. The current building dates to the 14th century, remodeled in the 15th. It now houses a decorative arts museum and a horse museum—the latter more interesting than it sounds for anyone interested in the Cadre Noir.

The Cadre Noir of Saumur is France's National Riding School and one of the great custodians of the French high-school tradition inherited from the 17th century. Capriole, croupade and courbette: these movements in which the horse rises from the ground are presented by its riders. Demonstrations take place in the morning a few times a month - check the online calendar before booking.

activities.text: Taste at Bernard Baudry in Cravant-les-Coteaux: a benchmark estate for red Chinon, using sustainable farming methods for 30 years. Its Les Grezeaux cuvée, grown on siliceous gravel, is the appellation's entry-level wine. La Croix Boissée, on tuffeau, is the wine for ageing. Visits are by appointment only. Allow for a round trip from Saumur to reach the estate.

Have lunch at Les Années Trente in Chinon - a local benchmark serving unfussy Touraine cuisine: homemade rillettes, Vouvray andouillette and tarte Tatin. Prices are reasonable for the standard. Booking is recommended. Allow for a round trip from Saumur for this lunch in Chinon.

Visit to a sparkling Saumur cave carved into the tuffeau—Bouvet-Ladubay, Ackerman, or Langlois-Château: the three major fine-bubble houses of Saumur. Bouvet-Ladubay's galleries extend 30 km beneath the hillsides; the guided tour lasts 45 minutes and ends with a tasting. Saumur brut lacks Champagne's notoriety but sells at a third of the price for often comparable quality.

Saumur-Champigny tasting at Château de Villeneuve: cabernet franc on limestone, one of the Loire's most consistent red appellations. If Clos Rougeard is inaccessible to you—which is likely, reservations book years in advance—Villeneuve is the honest consolation. Their Grande Vignolle is the reference cuvée.

Coteaux du Layon option in the late afternoon: this vineyard of sweet and dessert Chenin stretches over the slopes of the Layon, a tributary of the Loire. Choose Domaine Ogereau or Château Pierre-Bise for sweet Bonnezeaux or Quarts-de-Chaume wines, the latter classified as a grand cru. Different from Vouvray: sunnier, more jammy and less taut. Allow for a round trip from Saumur to reach these estates.

Loire Valley Wine Route in 8 days
Loire Valley Wine Route in 8 days

visits.text: Less busy than its neighbour Carry, Sausset-les-Pins harbour maintains a real fishing fleet beneath the Château Charles-Roux, a 19th-century building. The commune only gained independence from Carry-le-Rouet in 1924. Pedestrian streets, terraces, and far fewer queues at restaurants.

The Boumandariel reed bed extends across about ten hectares of coastal wetland west of Sausset-les-Pins, with a botanical trail. It's the only one on the Côte Bleue, squeezed between garrigue and sea. Breeding area: stay on the path.

activities.text: Follow the Sausset-les-Pins corniche promenade, 5 km laid out along the old customs officers' path, with views of the bay of Marseille and the islands. The route is flat and easy. No shade: leave early or late in the day.
The people of Sausset shop at the fish market on the west pier, every morning except Thursday: fewer than ten stalls, the day's catch, nothing else. It finishes when it's sold out.

days_plan.itin_title: Côte Bleue and Camargue: the lower coastal route in 7 days

visits.text: Saverne's Château des Rohan astonishes with its proportions. Nicknamed the 'Little Alsatian Versailles,' its neoclassical pink sandstone façade extends exactly 140 meters—no accident: it's the equivalent, horizontally, of the height of Strasbourg Cathedral. Built in the late 18th century by architect Nicolas Salins de Montfort for Cardinal Louis René de Rohan-Guéméné, it's the fourth building erected on this site since the Middle Ages. Its museums (Gallo-Roman collections, art and history, Louise Weiss archives) deserve 90 minutes.

A few kilometers from Saverne, Haut-Barr castle merits the detour. Nicknamed 'the Eye of Alsace,' this 12th-century medieval castle perched at 470 meters on three sandstone rocks offers a panorama over the entire Alsatian plain as far as Strasbourg Cathedral on clear days. The Devil's Bridge footbridge, suspended between two rocks, is a highlight of the visit.

Saverne's rose garden extends at the foot of the pass—France's second-oldest rose garden, it assembles nearly 5,000 rose bushes from 800 varieties. Open from late May through late August, it's particularly spectacular in June during the Rose Festival.

activities.text: The Saint-Louis-Arzviller inclined plane, about ten kilometers from Saverne, is a unique engineering feat in Europe. Opened in 1969 to replace 17 locks over 3.8 km, this transverse inclined plane allows barges to cross 44 meters of elevation on the Marne-Rhine Canal in a single 35-minute operation. Operators offer tourist boat rides on the inclined plane in season.

Stroll along the Marne-Rhine Canal facing the Château des Rohan. The 70-berth marina, installed in the large basin, gives the town particular animation. Operators offer bike rides along the canal toward Arzviller or eastward. The greenway is pleasant and easy.

days_plan.itin_title: Alsace and the Wine Route: Strasbourg to the Vosges

visits.text: Saint-Florent Church looks like no other: a concrete vessel whose bell tower forms a ship's prow pointing toward the lake. All of Savines was hastily rebuilt in the early 1960s, after the old village was dynamited on May 3, 1961, for the flooding of Serre-Ponçon. Architect Achille de Panaskhet designed the entire village and the church with its brightly colored stained glass; the church was inaugurated in July 1962. Awarded the Patrimoine du XXe siècle label, it's the town's most visited monument. Free entry during the day.

The Savines viaduct spans the lake for nearly a kilometer and delivers the postcard shot of the area: turquoise waters, mountains in reflection, Baie Saint-Michel below. Built to cross the reservoir after the old road was flooded, it links both shores. Stop at the village-side viewpoint for the full picture, especially mid-morning when the water is glassy.

activities.text: Savin'Plage, on the lakeshore, is one of Serre-Ponçon's best water-sports centers: supervised swimming in summer, paddleboarding, sailing, kitesurfing that takes advantage of the regular thermal winds. The water reaches decent temperatures in high summer, not a given at 780 meters elevation. Beaches with facilities, food, parking. The ideal spot to break up the drive and take a dip between villages.

Take a cruise on Serre-Ponçon from the Savines pier. Passenger boats follow the shoreline, approach the Saint-Michel chapel perched on its islet (a remnant of the submerged village), and pass under the viaduct. It is the best way to grasp the scale of France's largest man-made lake. Cruises last one to two hours and run more frequently in July and August.

days_plan.itin_title: Hautes-Alpes Road Trip: High Mountains and Alpine Valleys

places.name: Sceaux

visits.text: Colbert acquired the Sceaux estate in 1670. The current château, rebuilt in 1856 by the Duke of Trévise, houses the departmental museum. Collections evoke French art from Louis XIV to Napoleon III.
The Pavillon de l'Aurore preserves a dome painted by Charles Le Brun. The Orangerie, built by Jules Hardouin-Mansart, measures 80 meters long.
Drive to Parc de Saint-Cloud, about 14 km from Sceaux, around 30 minutes by road. The national estate covers 460 hectares along the Seine.

activities.text: The 181-hectare Parc de Sceaux unfolds formal French gardens. André Le Nôtre exploited the terrain's relief to create two perspectives: the château axis and the Grande Cascade descending toward the Octagon Basin.
Montretout, around a 30-minute drive from Sceaux, offers panoramic views of Paris and the Seine valley.

days_plan.itin_title: Hauts-de-Seine Road Trip: Royal Heritage & Gardens

map_keywords: Musée du Domaine départemental de Sceaux

places.name: Sedan

visits.text: Sedan Fortress. Europe's largest fortress spreads its 35,000 m² across seven levels, a legacy of the Princes of La Marck built from 1424 onward. Ramparts 26 meters thick tell six centuries of military history, from the Wars of Religion to the 20th-century commando training center. The scenographic tour plunges visitors into the epic saga of Sedan's princes through armories, casemates, and underground galleries.

Museum of the Battle of 1870. Housed within the fortress, the museum commemorates Napoleon III's defeat by the Prussians on September 1, 1870. An impressive model recreates the 19th-century town entirely surrounded by fortifications. Bavarian painter Ludwig Braun's panorama sketch and the collection of Prussian helmets evoke this dramatic turning point in French history.

Star-shaped stronghold. The bastioned plan drawn in the 16th century and reinforced by Vauban organized the defense of this independent principality until 1642. Four star-arranged bastions connected by imposing curtain walls surrounded the now-vanished urban enclosure. Discover remnants of the defensive system that made Sedan one of Europe's most formidable fortresses.

Felt Museum. This museum bears witness to the major textile industry that flourished in Sedan from the 17th to the 20th century. The collections present the techniques used to make felt and the fine cloth that gave the town its international reputation. Period machines and fabric samples tell the industrial story of the Sedan mills. Allow for the journey from the overnight town, distance and duration to be completed.

activities.text: Historical show at the fortress. During summer, attend chivalric tournaments that transport visitors to medieval times. Stunt fighters clash on horseback or in single combat, bringing to life the codes of honor and the art of the joust. This immersive family show delights young and old in the exceptional fortress setting.

Walk along the Meuse. Shaded banks invite leisurely strolls between gardens and natural areas. The river draws wide meanders at the foot of the castle reflected in calm waters. Landscaped paths connect to the Trans-Ardennes greenway following the old towpath for over 120 km.

Discover felt craftsmanship. Local workshops perpetuate Sedan's centuries-old textile expertise through contemporary creations and traditional pieces. Visit artisan boutiques to observe felting techniques and discover the history of this industry that employed thousands of workers. Craftspeople offer hats, accessories, and decorative objects in natural felt.

days_plan.itin_title: Ardennes Road Trip: Forests & Fortresses (3 Days)

map_keywords: Musée de la Bataille de 1870 Sedan

visits.text: Notre-Dame Cathedral in Sées, built between 1210 and 1310, is the jewel of Norman Gothic architecture in the Orne. Its spires rise to 70 m. The choir, a masterpiece of Île-de-France Gothic, is bathed in the light of splendid old windows. Two stars in the Michelin Guide.
The Basilica of the Immaculate Conception, built in 1854 in neo-Gothic style, was the first in France dedicated to that title. Its interior decoration and distinctive lighting set it apart.

The Palais d'Argentré, built in 1778 for the bishop who tutored the future Louis XVIII, displays neoclassical facades and ordered gardens. It testifies to the clergy's splendor in the Age of Enlightenment.

The Departmental Museum of Religious Art, housed in a 14th-century listed building, displays metalwork, sculptures, paintings, and liturgical vestments from the Middle Ages to today, drawn from rural Orne churches.
Visit the Cours des Fontaines, a classified site with an 18th-century washhouse. This verdant haven follows the remnants of the old fortified wall.
Explore Sées to spot its 13 listed historic monuments, including the remains of the 11th-century Church of Saint-Pierre and the 17th-century chapel of the Hôtel-Dieu, adorned with paintings on wood.

activities.text: The Haras National du Pin, nicknamed the Versailles of the horse, extends over more than 1,000 hectares 20 km from Sées. Founded in 1715 by order of Louis XIV, it houses red-brick stables, a ceremonial saddlery, and a collection of listed horse-drawn carriages.
From June to September, the 'Thursdays at Le Pin' present different horse breeds in the Aure riding hall. Equestrian shows, farrier demonstrations, and carriage rides complete the experience.
The Écouves forest, approximately 15 km from Sées, a 15-minute drive away, reaches its highest point at the Signal d'Écouves (413 m). Marked trails run among sessile oaks and beeches.

days_plan.itin_title: Orne Road Trip: Norman Bocage and Stud Farms

visits.text: The Church of Sainte-Madeleine dominates Segré with its 30-meter-high neo-Byzantine dome. Classified stained glass windows flood the interior with colored light.
From the church esplanade, the view takes in the town and the confluence of the Oudon and the Verzée. The two rivers run through this town founded in antiquity.
The Château de la Lorie, built under Louis XIII, is the northernmost of the Loire châteaux. Its grand salon, entirely made of marble, recalls princely palaces.
The historic centre preserves old houses and listed churches. Rue Pasteur has an example of half-timbered housing listed as a historic monument.

activities.text: La Mine Bleue at Noyant-la-Gravoyère goes 126 metres underground into a genuine slate quarry. The guided tour reveals the miners' working conditions and the techniques used to extract the blue slate.
The banks of the Oudon offer shaded walks. The route follows the peaceful river through rolling landscapes.
The local market puts producers from the Angevin terroir centre stage. Craft workshops and food events regularly liven up the town.

days_plan.itin_title: Maine-et-Loire Road Trip: Anjou and Loire Valley Châteaux

visits.text: Séguret is listed among the Plus Beaux Villages de France. Its cobbled lanes climb at the foot of the Dentelles de Montmirail, between golden stone houses and vine trellises.
Pass through Porte Reynier, the fortified village's main entrance. The 15th-century belfry stands out for its single wrought-iron clock hand, visible from far away in the valley.
The 17th-century baroque Fontaine des Mascarons flows in the small central square. Four sculpted faces spout water into a stone basin worn by the centuries.
The Église Saint-Denis, built between the 10th and 13th centuries, houses a gilded wooden altarpiece and medieval frescoes. Its Romanesque bell gable towers over the village rooftops.
Climb to the feudal castle ruins crowning the rock. The 360° panorama embraces the Rhône Valley, vineyards, and the jagged crests of the Dentelles de Montmirail.
The Place des Arceaux below surprises with its natural pergola formed by plane trees planted around 1860, whose branches have fused together over time.

activities.text: Hike into the Dentelles de Montmirail from Séguret. Trails wind between limestone cliffs and pine forests, with passages carved through rock.
Taste AOC Côtes-du-Rhône Villages Séguret wines directly in the village cellars or surrounding estates. The clay-limestone terroir yields powerful reds and fruity rosés.
In December, Séguret turns into a living nativity scene: villagers act out the scenes of the Nativity in the lanes by torchlight.

days_plan.itin_title: Vaucluse: Avignon, Luberon Villages & Ventoux Routes
The Most Beautiful Villages: From the Alps to the Luberon in 3 Days

places.name: Selestat

visits.text: Sélestat holds a secret very few visitors know: it's here, in this small Renaissance town midway between Colmar and Strasbourg, that the world's oldest known written mention of the Christmas tree is preserved. A modest account register dated December 21, 1521, preserved at the Bibliothèque Humaniste, mentions payment of four schillings to forest guards to 'watch over the maïs from Saint Thomas's Day' — the maïs referring to festive trees cut three days before Christmas. This document is exhibited free of charge at the Salon Erasme each December. Before leaving, reflect on this: every Christmas tree in the world is a distant descendant of those cut in the Vosges forests just a few kilometers from here.

The Église Saint-Georges, a 15th-century Gothic jewel, hosts a unique exhibition each Christmas: about ten trees suspended beneath the nave's arches, decorated according to successive styles from the 16th century to today. The visit is free and open daily except during services. In the nave bathed in stained-glass light, these trees suspended like chandeliers create a breathtaking atmosphere. The Église Sainte-Foy, Romanesque in style, houses for its part an art installation 'Tel un Lustre' — a suspension of Meisenthal Christmas baubles (the famous mouth-blown Alsatian baubles) that changes each year.

activities.text: The Maison du Pain d'Alsace, installed in the former 16th-century bakers' guild Poêle, is a must for food lovers: 300 m² of exhibition on bread history in Alsace, a bakehouse where artisans work before you, and over 25 kinds of bredeles in the shop — anise, butter, schwowe (cinnamon and almonds), with or without chocolate. The tea room offers on-site tastings.

Sélestat's Christmas market spreads across three downtown squares (Place d'Armes, Place du Dr Maurice Kubler, and Place de la Victoire) from late November to late December. Less touristy than Colmar or Riquewihr, it maintains precious authenticity and allows discovering the town's historic heart at your own pace. Look for local producers selling their homemade bredeles and wines from the Haut-Koenigsbourg Appellation.

days_plan.itin_title: Alsace and the Wine Route: Strasbourg to the Vosges
Alsace's Most Beautiful Christmas Markets

map_keywords: Marché de Noël Place d'Armes Sélestat

visits.text: Semur-en-Auxois sits on a pink granite spur encircled by the Armançon gorges. The four round 13th-century towers—including the Tour de l'Orle d'Or, standing 44 meters high—dominate the town and are visible from afar. Climb up to the rampart walk for a view down to the river 30 meters below.

Step through the door of the Collégiale Notre-Dame, built in the 13th and 14th centuries. It preserves remarkable stained glass windows, including one donated by the drapers' guild depicting the stages of cloth manufacture. Outside, linger over the sculpted portals. The Place du Terreau just in front is the heart of the town.

Walk down to the Pont Joly, below the town. From here you'll have the most photographed view of Semur: the towers and ramparts reflected in the Armançon, with medieval houses clinging to the cliff face. Come in the late afternoon for the light.

activities.text: Walk around the ramparts then descend to the banks of the Armançon via the marked trail. The river carves deep gorges here—a striking natural setting for a Burgundian town. Allow 1.5 hours for the complete loop.
Every year in late May, Semur hosts France's oldest horse race—documented since 1639. If your dates coincide, don't miss this popular festival that takes over the town for three days.

days_plan.itin_title: Burgundy's 15 Most Beautiful Villages
Burgundy Road Trip: Cathedrals, Vineyards and Villages
Burgundy-Franche-Comté: The Most Beautiful Villages in 7 days

visits.text: The Collégiale Saint-Hilaire is the jewel of Semur-en-Brionnais—and arguably one of the most beautiful Romanesque churches in Saône-et-Loire. Built in two phases during the 12th century (east end around 1125, west portal around 1180), it's the last great Romanesque church erected in the Brionnais region. Its octagonal bell tower, three apsidioles, and interior corbelled gallery—nicknamed “the ice cream cone” by locals—draw direct inspiration from Cluny III. Look carefully at the west portal's tympanum: it depicts one of the rare scenes of the Council of Seleucia in Romanesque art, an almost unique subject in France. The church is open year-round from 8am to 8pm, with free entry.

A few dozen meters from the collegiate church, the Château Saint-Hugues is the oldest fortified castle still standing in Burgundy, built from the 10th century onwards on a motte. Its 22-meter Romanesque keep retains three stories, including the windowless lower story, which dates from the 10th century. This is where Hugh of Semur was born in 1024, the future abbot of Cluny from 1049 to 1109: under his abbacy, the Cluniac order spread across all of Europe. His architects sent the plans for the collegiate church to Semur in homage to their patron. The castle is open from March 1 to November 15—opt for a guided tour to fully appreciate its rich history.

Wander through the cobbled lanes of the old village among the sandstone houses, the gates of the former ramparts, and the still-legible layout of medieval fortifications. The village was sacked several times: by the English in 1364, burned in 1467 by Louis XI, then again in 1576 during the Wars of Religion. Yet it has retained remarkable architectural cohesion. In late afternoon, the raking light on the golden sandstone façades is worth the journey alone.

activities.text: Heritage loop “collegiate church–castle–old village” (2–3 km, moderate elevation gain). The path around the defenses at the foot of the hill follows the old fortifications and offers a panorama over the Charolais and Brionnais countryside. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes at a leisurely pace.

Walk toward the Brionnais ridges to explore the landscape from above. This region is considered one of the centers of Burgundian Romanesque art, with more than twenty Romanesque buildings recorded within a 20 km radius. A marked circuit starts in the village.

days_plan.itin_title: Loop Around Lyon: Villages and Pierres Dorées
Burgundy's 15 Most Beautiful Villages
Burgundy-Franche-Comté: The Most Beautiful Villages in 7 days

visits.text: Notre-Dame Cathedral was built between 1153 and 1191 with its Portal of the Virgin, a masterpiece of 12th-century Gothic sculpture. Its Gothic spire, dating from 1240, towers over the town at a height of 78 metres.
The Gallo-Roman ramparts from the 3rd century encircle the historic heart for a kilometre. Fifteen towers survive from this six-hectare enclosure built after the Germanic invasions of 275.

The Royal Château stands against the Gallo-Roman walls on the site where Hugh Capet was elected King of France in 987. The medieval remains bear witness to this royal residence associated with the monarchy's foundations.
The Gallo-Roman arena dates from the first century, the era of Augustomagus. It bears witness to the early Romanisation of the town.
The Museum of Art and Archaeology occupies the former episcopal palace. Gallo-Roman vestiges and votive offerings from the forest temple of Halatte trace two thousand years of local history.

activities.text: Stroll through medieval lanes past 15th- and 16th-century half-timbered houses. Rue de la Tonnellerie, Rue de la Tannerie and Rue du Chat Haret still bear their names recalling trades of bygone days.

days_plan.itin_title: Oise Circuit: châteaux, forests and history

visits.text: Senones Abbey is like an adventure novel. Founded around 640 by Gondelbert, bishop of Sens, it came under the protection of Charlemagne—who appointed his own archchaplain as abbot around 768—then was gradually taken over by the Salm family, which created the Principality of Salm-Salm in 1751, a small independent state whose capital was Senones until 1793. You can still see the abbot's palace and its monumental spiral staircase, adorned with a wrought iron railing made by Jean Lamour—the same craftsman who created the gates of Place Stanislas in Nancy. Abbot Dom Calmet (died 1757) had assembled 15,000 volumes here, a library so renowned that Voltaire came to stay for three weeks in 1753, attending all the services and searching through the archives. Guided tours during school holidays and on the 2nd and 4th Saturdays of each month from April to October, with advance registration at the Tourist Office.

Continue to the two remaining wings of the pink sandstone cloister — they now house shops and the Tourist Office. The entire 18th-century building complex is well preserved: large library to the south, farm buildings, abbatial residence. Opposite the abbey, the castles and mansions of the former princely capital deserve a look — you can still sense the ambition of this tiny independent state.

activities.text: Senones is designated a Petite Cité de Caractère—stroll through the narrow streets to spot the 18th-century residences built of pink sandstone quarried on the outskirts of town. A local craft brewery offers tours in season: check with the Tourist Office for time slots. If you like beers with character, it's a good way to end the day.

days_plan.itin_title: Vosges Abbey Trail: Monastic Heritage

visits.text: Begin your road trip at the Cathedral of Saint-Étienne in Sens—quite simply the world's first Gothic cathedral. Construction began around 1135 under Archbishop Henri Sanglier, even before Notre-Dame de Paris. The very wide nave (15.25 m) is covered with sexpartite vaults similar to those in Paris. In 1234, Saint Louis married Margaret of Provence here. Don't miss the Flamboyant transept designed by Martin Chambiges in the late 15th century, or the stained-glass window depicting the assassination of Thomas Becket—the Archbishop of Canterbury had taken refuge in Sens before being murdered in 1170.

Right next door, the Cathedral Treasury occupies the former chapel of the archbishops' palace. You'll see rare pieces: 15th-century Flemish tapestries, Thomas Becket's chasuble, and the Sainte Châsse, an ivory reliquary casket. This is one of France's richest treasuries—allow 30 to 45 minutes.

Wander through old Sens by following the “Circuit de Brennus” (named after the Gallic chieftain of the Senones who captured Rome in 390 BC). Arrows on the ground guide you along narrow streets, past half-timbered houses, and along the quays of the Yonne. Pick up the guidebook at the Tourist Office before you set out.

Return to Sens to complete the loop. If you didn't do it on the first day, climb the south tower of the cathedral (open in summer, by reservation)—the view from the top takes in the town and the surrounding countryside. Otherwise, revisit the nave with fresh eyes after seeing all the Romanesque and Gothic churches along the route—you'll appreciate its pioneering status all the more.

End at the Jardins de l'Orangerie, behind the cathedral—you'll find a carefully designed garden that has regained its 19th-century appearance. Horticultural beds, shaded paths, a view of the cathedral's rear. It's a good final stop, peaceful and free.

activities.text: If you arrive on a Wednesday or Saturday morning, explore the Sens market—it's the best place to sample regional products from the Yonne: goat cheeses, Gâtinais honey, and Burgundy snails.

If you leave on a market day (Wednesday or Saturday), do your last bit of Burgundian shopping - cheeses, mustard, gingerbread and honey from the Gâtinais. Sens has a station with a 1-hour connection to Paris, making the return journey easier.

days_plan.itin_title: Yonne Circuit: Northern Burgundy & Chablis
Burgundy Road Trip: Cathedrals, Vineyards and Villages
Burgundy Road Trip: Cathedrals, Vineyards and Villages

visits.text: The Paul Valéry Museum overlooks the marine cemetery and the Mediterranean from a terrace on Mont Saint-Clair. Its 1970s architecture follows Le Corbusier's design principles. The museum houses around 7,200 works: fine arts collections, Paul Valéry archives (manuscripts, original editions), and the Salah Stétié collection. Temporary exhibitions explore the city's Mediterranean identity. The gardens host outdoor events. The view from the terrace over the sea and cemetery is exceptional. Free admission on the first Sunday of each month.

The marine cemetery, created around 1680 for workers on the Saint-Louis breakwater, was renamed in 1945 in tribute to Paul Valéry's famous poem. Perched on Mont Saint-Clair, it cascades in terraces between sea and lagoon with spectacular views. The academician rests here in his ancestor Giulio Grassi's family vault. Other notable Sète personalities are buried here, including Jean Vilar, creator of the Festival d'Avignon. The architectural chapels and sailors' tombs testify to Sète's maritime heritage. The peaceful atmosphere invites contemplation and strolling.

Mont Saint-Clair rises to 175 meters and offers the finest panorama over Sète, the Thau lagoon, and the Mediterranean. You can climb on foot via staircases or take the winding road. From the summit, you take in the entire "singular island": the canals, port, lido, the Thau lagoon with its oyster beds, and on clear days, the Pyrenees. It's the best place to understand Sète's unique geography. The sunset here is magical. Notre-Dame-de-la-Salette chapel stands at the summit.

The port of Sète is the leading fishing port in the Mediterranean and an important commercial harbor. The quays are lined with restaurants where you can taste the local specialty: tielle, a pie filled with tomato and octopus. Colorful trawlers, the comings and goings of fishing boats, and seagulls create an authentic maritime atmosphere. The Saint-Louis breakwater, built from 1666, marks the city's birth. The canals that cross Sète earn it the nickname "Venice of Languedoc."

activities.text: Water jousting has been a Sète tradition since the 17th century. Two boats propelled by rowers face off, with a jouster on each vessel trying to knock his opponent into the water with a lance. Jousting takes place mainly in summer during the Saint-Louis festivities in August, but also at other events. The spectacle is dramatic and the atmosphere festive. It's a strong element of Sète's identity.

Sète's fish market, in the halls near the canal, operates every morning except Monday. Fishmongers and fishermen offer their catch: sea bass, sea bream, red mullet, tuna, squid, octopus. Freshness is guaranteed and prices are attractive. The atmosphere is friendly, with conversations between vendors and regulars. It's the best place to buy fish if you have accommodation with a kitchen. Otherwise, head to the port restaurants to sample the specialties.

Walk around the Thau lagoon, Languedoc's largest lagoon covering 7,500 hectares. You'll pass the oyster farms where the famous Bouzigues oysters are raised. The villages of Mèze, Marseillan, and Bouzigues border its shores. The landscape of shellfish tables on the water is unique. The lagoon harbors exceptional biodiversity with 300 plant and animal species. Hiking trails and cycle paths allow you to follow the shores. The contrast between the blue-green water and cultivated lands is striking.

Taste oysters from Bouzigues and mussels from the Thau lagoon. The basin produces over 13,000 tons of oysters annually. The oyster farms in Bouzigues welcome visitors directly for tastings overlooking the lagoon. Plump and briny with a sweet note, Mediterranean oysters have a unique taste different from Atlantic ones. Pair them with a glass of white Picpoul de Pinet wine. The atmosphere is authentic and prices are reasonable.

days_plan.itin_title: Hérault Road Trip: Montpellier, Beaches and the Hinterland

visits.text: The Manufacture de Sèvres has produced porcelain since 1756. Founded under Louis XV with Madame de Pompadour's patronage, it supplied European royal courts and still serves the French Presidency.

The workshops reveal the secrets of Sèvres blue. 120 ceramists master about thirty trades: wheel throwing, molding, painting, gilding. Pastes and glazes are crafted on-site using time-honored techniques.
The National Ceramics Museum gathers 55,000 pieces from the Middle Ages to today. Sèvres porcelain, faience, stoneware, and pottery from around the world compose a reference collection.

activities.text: Join the Parc de Saint-Cloud through the gardens. The Manufacture occupies a site bordering the national estate.
The Seine embankments offer peaceful views of the river. Walk between Sèvres and Saint-Cloud.

days_plan.itin_title: Hauts-de-Seine Road Trip: Royal Heritage & Gardens

visits.text: Seyne-les-Alpes first comes into view from the Col de Maure: the Vauban citadel suddenly appears on the rocky spur of La Robine, crowning the village. This former Gallic oppidum became a frontier town facing Savoy under Louis XIV. The 12th-century Grande Tour — Seyne was then known as 'Seyne la Grande Tour' — stands at the very heart of the fortress. Restored and listed as a Historic Monument, its terrace offers a unique panorama over the Blanche Range and the valley. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes for the full visit, including the stalactite-lined cistern, the cannons and the old bread oven.

The citadel itself was built in 1693 by Niquet and Vauban — its narrow, elongated “shark” shape follows the contours of the spur. In addition to the permanent exhibition on military history, you will find a freely accessible contemporary art installation: Le donjon de l'ours qui dort, by American artist Mark Dion, designated as a Viapac work. A full-scale escape game in the fort's underground passages (180 m²) is offered seasonally.

Head down into the old village and follow the pedestrian route from the Porte de Provence to the Place d'Armes: washhouses, half-timbered houses, flower-filled squares and small ecomuseums devoted to the forge, the bugade (traditional laundry) and tailoring line the way. The Church of Notre-Dame-de-Nazareth, overlooking its historic gardens, and the Penitents' Chapel with its rare three-sided bell tower are worth a stop.

activities.text: In summer, the trails around Seyne in the Haute-Provence Geopark offer varied routes through larch forests and along ridges. If you have time, the hamlet of Chardavon is home to the Maison du Mulet, a small, surprising and endearing museum about the mule-breeding tradition of the Pays de Seyne.

days_plan.itin_title: Forcalquier & Verdon Gorges Road Trip

visits.text: Sillans-la-Cascade is a medieval village with 11th-century ramparts built with a unique purpose: not to protect a fortress, but to safeguard a spring. The Bresque River, which rises at Fox-Amphoux, feeds the highest waterfall in the department here. The village has a complex castle history: three castles have succeeded one another on its territory — the first medieval one disappeared, the second was erected in 1609 and destroyed during the Revolution, and the third was built in the 19th century and purchased by the commune in 1992 from the Count of Castellane.

The Sillans waterfall is the village's centerpiece — do not miss it on any account. From the parking area, an 800-meter marked trail runs through a shaded stand of old plane trees before reaching the viewpoint, facing the 42-meter fall. The water of the Bresque drops into a pool coloured emerald and turquoise by micro-algae and the limestone bed. Swimming in the main pool is strictly forbidden for safety reasons — rockfalls are possible — but swimming areas can be reached further downstream. Allow 25 to 30 minutes for the round trip, or 45 minutes if you go down to the river. Come early in summer: parking is paid from April to September and fills up fast after 10 AM.

activities.text: After the viewpoint, continue on a longer circuit along the Bresque to discover the small natural pools open for swimming downstream from the waterfall. The water is cool even in midsummer and the shaded banks are ideal for a picnic break. Marked trails let you climb back up to the heights overlooking the village with views across the entire valley.

days_plan.itin_title: The 10 Most Beautiful Villages of the Haut-Var
Var in 4 Days: From Bormes to the Most Beautiful Villages of the Verdon

visits.text: Simiane-la-Rotonde is perched at 650 metres on a projecting spur of the Albion plateau, at the centre of a Ventoux-Lure-Luberon triangle. The village owes its name to its exceptional keep: the Rotonde, a dodecagonal tower (12 sides) built in the late 12th century by the Simiane-Agoult family. Its interior is the real surprise — on the first floor, a ribbed dome 5 metres high, with capitals adorned with strange, grotesque human masks that fascinate historians. Some associate it with the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, brought back by crusaders. Listed as a historic monument as early as 1841, it can be visited from March to November. In August, an international early music festival (Les Riches Heures Musicales de la Rotonde) has held its concerts here since 1982 — the acoustics are remarkable.

Then wander through the lanes to reach the 16th-century covered market halls: beneath their columns, a panoramic view over the lavender fields below opens up like a painting. Henri Cartier-Bresson immortalised the halls in 1971.

Five kilometres from the village, Valsaintes Abbey has a rose garden containing 600 varieties and permaculture gardens set around the Cistercian ruins. The best time to visit is during the rose bloom, from late May to early June.

activities.text: Simiane is home to the SCA3P cooperative (founded in 1979), France's largest lavender and lavandin cooperative. If you are there between mid-June and mid-July, the flowering Plateau d'Albion is a photographic spectacle not to be missed. A visit to the cooperative or a local estate rounds off the day nicely.

days_plan.itin_title: Forcalquier & Verdon Gorges Road Trip

visits.text: The Sisteron citadel crowns the rocky spur blocking the Durance valley. The imposing fortress's bastioned walls and keep span eight centuries of military architecture. The underground staircase of 258 steps, carved into the rock in the 19th century, links the town to the citadel in a mysterious ascent.

Notre-Dame-des-Pommiers cathedral blends Provençal Romanesque and Lombard influences. The restrained 12th-century building has a harmoniously proportioned nave. Side chapels house Baroque works, and the large 19th-century organ resounds during summer concerts.

Walk through the lanes of the old town, which rise in tiers between the Durance and the citadel. Medieval towers from the 14th century mark the course of the former ramparts. Renaissance fountains and fortified gates line this maze, filled with the atmosphere of Provençal towns.

The Rocher de la Baume rises opposite the citadel on the other side of the Durance. The limestone strata give the impression of stacked slices. This remarkable geological site overlooks the narrow gap where the valley constricts.

Medieval watchtowers punctuate the old town's perimeter. Five of them were preserved thanks to Prosper Mérimée. Rounded on the outside and open on the town side, they bear witness to Sisteron's medieval defensive system.

activities.text: The Rocher de la Baume offers a view down over the Durance and the citadel.

Paragliders take off from the surrounding heights. The Durance valley's powerful thermals carry the wings in an aerial ballet. The panorama takes in the citadel, the Durance and the Alpine valleys during an unforgettable flight over them.

The Route Napoléon crosses Sisteron along the historic route of the Emperor's return. On March 5, 1815, Napoleon passed through the town without resistance during his march to Grenoble. A museum in the citadel traces this epic episode of French history.

Hiking trails radiate around Sisteron. The ascent of the Rocher de la Baume offers a strenuous route rewarded by an exceptional panorama. The nearby Méouge gorges offer swimming and river hikes in an unspoiled setting.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpes-de-Haute-Provence Tour: Lavender and Hilltop Villages

places.name: Solenzara

visits.text: Fautea beach is reached by road from Solenzara, heading south. A round 16th-century Genoese tower overlooks the white-sand beach. Built to watch for Barbary raids, it is now listed as a historic monument. The beach is little frequented - tourists rarely stop here.

Make a detour to the étang de Diane, accessible along a track from the main road: a natural lagoon used for oyster farming since antiquity - the Romans already appreciated its oysters. The site remains unspoiled, lined with tamarisks. Go early in the morning: the low light on the water and the mountains behind is among the most beautiful on the east coast. Allow for a round trip by road from Solenzara.

activities.text: The Côte des Nacres between Fautea and Solenzara is a string of lightly developed beaches with translucent water and smooth granite seabeds. Stop at Canella beach - white sand, no paid parking - for an easygoing afternoon.

Solenzara is the starting point for the Gorges du Solenzara, 10 km west: a mountain road follows the river between granite walls to a series of pools and waterfalls. Ideal for a late-afternoon swim before returning to the village.

days_plan.itin_title: Complete Tour of Corsica

map_keywords: Plage de Fautea tour génoise Solenzara

visits.text: The Abbey of Saint-Pierre de Solesmes has dominated the Sarthe for over a thousand years. Founded in 1010 by Geoffroy the Old, lord of Sablé, who donated a monastery to the monks of Marmoutier, it remained a simple priory until the Revolution. It was Dom Prosper Guéranger who in 1833 made it the pinnacle of Gregorian chant that it is today. Seen from the river, the abbey's silhouette is stunning—austere and massive like a sacred fortress, in the words of a 19th-century traveler. From the bridge spanning the Sarthe, take time to contemplate this emblematic panorama before entering.

Only the abbatial church is freely visited. Once through the medieval door, the Saints of Solesmes await you in the transept: two sculptural ensembles from the 15th and 16th centuries considered masterpieces of French sculpture. The north group represents the tomb of Our Lord in flamboyant Gothic style, the south group illustrates the Assumption of the Virgin. The abbey organ, 39 stops of North European inspiration, resonates under the vaults during services. The crypt, accessible at indicated hours, houses Dom Guéranger's tomb.

Attending a service sung by the community of Benedictine monks is an experience difficult to describe. The sung conventual mass takes place at 10 a.m. every day (about 1h15, 1h45 on Sundays and feast days). Gregorian chant resonates in the abbey's particular acoustics with a depth and purity unlike anything else. Arrive early—seats in the nave fill quickly on Sundays.

activities.text: The abbey shop, open 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. outside services, offers theology books, Gregorian chant recordings by the monks themselves, and monastic products. Solesmes recordings are an international reference in their field—buy one to extend the experience at home.

Continue on the pedestrian path that runs along the Sarthe beneath the abbey to Cri Cri beach. The walk is short and peaceful, perfect after the spiritual immersion of the service. You'll also pass nearby the building of Sainte-Cécile Abbey, founded in 1866, where 45 Benedictine nuns now reside.

days_plan.itin_title: Sarthe Road Trip: Le Mans and the Loir Valley

visits.text: The Abbatiale Saint-Pierre-Saint-Paul de Solignac is a unique case in Limousin: its three-bay nave is covered with hemispherical domes on pendentives, in the manner of Périgord churches. The Benedictine abbey, founded between 632 and 638 by Saint Éloi, goldsmith and advisor to King Dagobert, was Limousin's most powerful from the 10th to 13th centuries.

Look up at the choir capitals: griffins seized by men, figures battling serpents, and stacked palmettes stand out in limestone. The nave capitals, more archaic, show checkered patterns and animal heads.

The oak choir stalls, carved between 1457 and 1484, rank among Limousin's most remarkable. Turn up the misericords: secular scenes appear—grimacing faces, mocking characters, and licentious figures hidden beneath the monks' seats.

In the right transept arm, a 15th-century fresco depicts Saint Christopher carrying the Christ Child, inspired by the Golden Legend. Donors' coats of arms and a detailed ship complete the composition.

The Château de la Borie, a Renaissance residence dating from the 17th century, now hosts contemporary art exhibitions. During public openings between July and September, discover the works displayed in the castle rooms and explore the estate's gardens. The formal French garden, the garden in motion and the vegetable garden form a route combining art and nature.

activities.text: Cross the 12th-century Romanesque bridge, built by monks for Compostela pilgrims. Its three pointed arches and two cutwaters shaped to break the current of the Briance span the river with their elegance intact.

Wander the medieval village lanes, among half-timbered houses and stone foundations. The abbey's turbulent history—Saracen and Norman pillaging, the Wars of Religion, the Revolution—has left scars that the Benedictine monks who returned in 2021 are working to heal.
Follow a section of GR 654 toward the Pont-Rompu, a 13th-century remnant on the old Roman road. The 6 km loop follows the Briance through a preserved landscape of fields enclosed by hedgerows.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Vienne Tour: Limoges, Porcelain and Villages

visits.text: The Rock of Solutré, a spectacular limestone escarpment formed from fossilized coral reefs 160 million years ago, rises to 493 meters amid the vineyards of the Mâconnais. A Grand Site de France, it owes its fame to its prehistoric deposits, rare calcareous grasslands, and François Mitterrand's ritual annual ascent.

The Museum of Prehistory, semi-buried beneath a planted dome at the Rock's foot, presents collections from one of the richest prehistoric sites in Europe. A hunting ground frequented for 55,000 years, the site gave its name to the Solutrean culture (21,000–18,000 BC). The "laurel leaves" of knapped flint represent the apex of prehistoric technique.

The archaeological and botanical garden complements the museum visit. A trail with eight stations traces the geology, hunting techniques, and 150 years of research. Wild orchids, boxwoods, and junipers populate the limestone grasslands at the summit—a unique microclimate protected by Natura 2000.

The Pouilly-Fuissé vineyards spread out at the Rock's foot. This clay-limestone terroir, planted with Chardonnay, produces internationally renowned white wines. The appellation, created in 1936, covers the villages of Solutré-Pouilly, Fuissé, Vergisson, and Chaintré. The Château de Pouilly, a fortified 15th-century manor, overlooks the vines.

activities.text: Ascent of the Rock of Solutré. The 4 km trail from the museum parking lot gains 100 meters in elevation through the vineyards and then the heath. At the summit, a 360-degree panorama over the Mâconnais, the Saône valley, the Beaujolais, and the Alps on clear days.

Pouilly-Fuissé tasting at a winemaker's. The Maison du Grand Site offers an initial introduction, then cellars in surrounding villages let you compare terroirs. Mâcon-Villages and Saint-Véran complete the palette of local whites.

Hike to the Rock of Vergisson, Solutré's twin sister. Less frequented, it offers a comparable panorama and a wilder atmosphere. The loop linking the two rocks via the ridges (8 km) is one of the finest in southern Burgundy.

days_plan.itin_title: Saône-et-Loire Road Trip: Bibracte, Cluny, Solutré & the Mâconnais Vineyards

visits.text: La Gravière and La Nord surf spots: Hossegor's legendary waves are influenced by the Gouf de Capbreton, an underwater canyon reaching a depth of nearly 4,000m offshore. The canyon begins in shallow water near the coast and gradually deepens. These beach breaks, among the most powerful on the planet, attract the world's best surfers during World Surf League competitions each fall.

Basque-Landes villas: An exploration of the seafront and its interwar architecture designed by renowned architects (Godbarge, Lagrange, Pomade, Prunetti). The Sporting Casino, a listed historic monument, dominates the beach. These elegant residences with characteristic half-timbering and steep roofs embody the Basque-Landes style of the 1920s–1930s.

Hossegor's tidal lake: This reshaped natural lagoon offers a 6km promenade lined with traditional oyster huts and elegant villas. The lake's calm waters contrast with the power of the nearby ocean. The complete loop on foot or by bike lets you admire this unique landscape between fresh and salt water.

Place des Landais: Hossegor's beating heart with its cafes, restaurants and designer boutiques. Surfers, families and vacationers mingle in a laid-back atmosphere. The La Vague mural celebrates the town's surf identity. Night markets in summer with local products and crafts.

activities.text: Surf lessons: Schools offer introductory lessons and coaching to improve your skills at spots suited to each level. Plage Sud suits beginners with more accessible waves. Equipment provided, groups of no more than 8. Booking advised in high season.

Cycling around the lake: around Hossegor's tidal lake, use the road shared with cars rather than the pedestrian lakeside promenade. The route offers lovely views of the oyster huts and opportunities to stop for tastings. Bike rentals are available in the town center and near the lake. Allow 45 minutes to 1 hour depending on your stops.

Oyster tasting on the lake: Oyster huts offer tastings facing the water. Marennes-Oléron oysters accompanied by local white wine. Authentic atmosphere lakeside, feet in the sand. Open year-round, arrive before 12:30pm in season.

Bike paths through the forest: 40km of greenways connecting Hossegor to neighboring towns through the Landes pine forest. Shaded and flat routes, perfect for exploring the region. Connection to the Vélodyssée, the European Atlantic bike route. Electric bike rental available.

days_plan.itin_title: Landes Road Trip: Ocean, Pine Forest and Landes Traditions
Bordeaux to Toulouse Road Trip: Ocean, Pyrenees and Heritage

visits.text: Sospel's Old Bridge has spanned the Bévéra since the 13th century: emblem of the village, it carries at its center a tower pierced with an arch that served as a tollhouse on the Salt Road between Nice and Turin via Col de Tende. Destroyed in 1944 by the Germans, it was rebuilt identically in 1953. In late afternoon, the light on the trompe-l'oeil facades of the riverside houses is spectacular. Iconic village photo.

Saint-Michel Cathedral raises its 11th-century Romanesque bell tower at the heart of the old town—one of the region's oldest. The baroque nave, added in the 17th century, contrasts with the tower's sobriety. Inside, altarpiece from the 15th-century Nice school attributed to François Bréa (cousin of Louis Bréa)—the Virgin and Child in the side chapel is remarkable.

Fort Saint-Roch is one of the most impressive fortifications on the Alpine Maginot Line. Built between 1931 and 1933, it required 5,000 m³ of concrete and almost 400 tonnes of steel - a veritable underground town with 2 km of galleries dug 50 metres beneath the rock, designed to accommodate 250 soldiers in complete self-sufficiency for three months. It fired on Italian troops in June 1940 and was never captured. Guided tours led by enthusiastic volunteers, July to August. The temperature inside is 14 °C all year round, so bring an extra layer.

Fort de l'Agaisen, built from 1932 to 1936 on Mont Agaisen, completes the defensive system around Sospel. Less well known than Saint-Roch but airier, it offers a 360° view from its viewpoint marker over the Bévéra valley and all the surrounding fortifications. Guided tours in season by volunteers.

The old town's trompe-l'oeil facades display typically Ligurian ochre and pink hues: painted window frames, wrought-iron balconies, little squares shaded by century-old plane trees. Sospel has retained the atmosphere of an authentic Alpine town, a world away from the bustle of the coast just 18 km away.

activities.text: Col de Turini, 25 minutes by car on a winding road, reaches an altitude of 1,607 meters. It's the legendary stage of the Monte-Carlo Rally, driven each January at night in the snow. In summer, a starting point for Mont Authion and its fortifications, or simply a panoramic view toward the Mercantour.

GR 52 trail in the Bévéra valley: marked routes toward Col de Turini or Cime de Diamant. Chestnut forests, alpine pastures, alternating views of the Mediterranean and the Mercantour. Several difficulty levels, from a family walk (2 hours) to a strenuous hike (full day).
Thursday morning market on Place des Platanes: goat cheeses from the alpine pastures, honey from Mercantour apiaries, local olive oil, garden vegetables. Small, authentic, without mass tourism.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpes-Maritimes Road Trip: Riviera and Mercantour, 13 days

visits.text: The Abbey Church of Sainte-Marie, a masterpiece of Romanesque art, crowns the town with its three domes on pendentives. Founded in the 10th century by Benedictines following the Abbey of Saint-Géraud d'Aurillac, the current church was constructed between 1145 and 1150.

The Romanesque portal, relocated inside the abbey church for protection from the elements, represents a treasure of medieval sculpture. The tympanum recounts the legend of Theophilus; the trumeau interweaves Isaac's sacrifice and original sin. The pillar of the prophet Isaiah, all movement and flowing drapery, is a unique piece of Romanesque art.

Inside, a painting attributed to Chasseriau, "Christ in the Garden of Olives" (1844), and a monumental Stoltz organ (1855), listed as a Historic Monument, complete the visit. The acoustics beneath the domes naturally amplify sound.

Explore Souillac's historic center, crossed by seven viaducts spanning streams and ravines. Ancient alleyways lead to the 19th-century market hall, still active on market days, and to the Dordogne riverbanks where the old river port once stood.

activities.text: Walk along the Dordogne riverbanks downstream from Souillac. The path follows the river through woods and meadows, with views of the hillsides and town rooftops.
The Town of Art and History offers themed guided tours of Souillac and the abbey church, highlighting monastic history and Romanesque sculpture.
Souillac hosts a renowned summer jazz festival. Open-air concerts, performances in the abbey church, and events at various venues animate the summer season.

days_plan.itin_title: Lot Itinerary: Cahors, Rocamadour & the Lot Valley

visits.text: The Basilica of Notre-Dame-de-la-Fin-des-Terres is a jewel of 12th-century Romanesque art, listed as a UNESCO World Heritage site. Built to welcome pilgrims to Santiago de Compostela, it was buried by dunes in the 18th century, then completely cleared of sand in the 19th. The Romanesque architecture is remarkably preserved, with sculpted capitals. The simple, bright interior invites contemplation. Classical music concerts are regularly organized here.

The Village Ancien de Soulac has about 500 Belle Époque villas built between 1860 and 1930. These houses of small pink bricks, with their carved eaves, canopies, arabesques, and colored stained glass, testify to the rise of the seaside resort. Two tour routes reveal the finest: the Soulac villas circuit (1.5 hours) and the architectural circuit (1 hour). Maps available at the tourist office. Some villas bear pretty female names.

Soulac's seafront stretches over 7 kilometers of fine sandy beaches. The landscaped promenade runs along lifeguarded beaches with views of the ocean and Cordouan Lighthouse in the distance. Breakwaters—concrete slabs installed in the 1930s to combat erosion—create natural seawater pools at high tide. Several access paths lead down to the beaches from the promenade. Restaurants and ice cream shops line the seafront.

A 4-meter-tall replica of the Statue of Liberty stands on the seafront facing the ocean. Like the New York original, it was created in the Bartholdi workshops. It faces toward America and the dunes of the Côte d'Argent. It's a charming landmark and a popular photo spot among tourists. A memorial to the northern Médoc fortress stands nearby, recalling the German occupation.

activities.text: Excursion to Cordouan Lighthouse, nicknamed the Versailles of the seas or the king of lighthouses. Built from 1584 under Henry IV, it is the oldest lighthouse in France still in operation. Standing 68 meters tall, it is located at sea, 7 km from the coast. Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2021, it can be visited from April to October. The boat excursion lasts 3 hours 30 minutes, with 1 hour 30 minutes spent visiting the lighthouse. Disembarkation involves wading through the water. Impressive interior with royal apartments and a chapel.

Swimming at Soulac's beaches. The resort has several beaches with lifeguards in summer: the central beach, Plage des Naïades, Plage de l'Amélie du Nord. Atlantic waves attract surfers and bodyboarders. Surf schools offer lessons on two beaches. The beaches are wide and clean, with fine sand. Beware of baïnes, dangerous currents typical of the Atlantic coast. Always swim in lifeguarded areas.

Visit to Pointe de Grave, the northern tip of the Médoc peninsula where the Gironde meets the Atlantic. A monument commemorates the 1917 American troop landing. The site offers spectacular views over the estuary, ocean, and Cordouan Lighthouse. It's the starting point of the GR8 trail running up the entire Atlantic coast. A ferry connects Pointe de Grave to Royan in Charente-Maritime (20-minute crossing). Wild landscapes of dunes and forests.

Cycling through the pine forest. Soulac has a network of bike paths winding through the Landes forest or leading toward the estuary. Routes are shaded and pleasant, away from the heat of the beaches. Several marked circuits let you discover the local heritage and nature. Bikes, pedal-powered quadricycles, and tandems are available to rent in town. Paths are flat and accessible to all.

A visit to the Musée d'Archéologie de Soulac. This small museum presents the history of the Pointe du Médoc from antiquity to the medieval period. Collections include objects discovered during local excavations: ceramics, tools, coins, architectural elements. Several rooms trace the history of the basilica and the pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostela. Low admission fee. Guided tours available by reservation.

days_plan.itin_title: Gironde Circuit: Bordeaux, Vineyards & Arcachon Bay

visits.text: The Saint-Pierre et Saint-Paul priory church (84 metres long), one of the five daughters of Cluny, combines Romanesque architecture (11th–12th centuries) and Gothic vaults. The tombs of the holy abbots Mayeul and Odilon lie in the middle of the nave, making Souvigny one of the most important medieval pilgrimage sites in the West. The double transept testifies to the unique Cluniac style.

The funerary chapels of the Dukes of Bourbon house recumbent effigies and tombs from the 15th century. The old chapel holds Louis II of Bourbon and Anne Dauphine of Auvergne beneath a starry sky filled with musician angels. These mausoleums bear witness to the decision of the Bourbons, the dynasty from which the kings of France descended, to make Souvigny their dynastic necropolis.

The Musée du Grand site clunisien displays the Zodiac Column, a 12th-century carved pillar unique in the world and a masterpiece of Romanesque art. Medieval stone carvings, recumbent effigies, 15th-century Bourbonnais statues (Saint Mary Magdalene) and pages from the famous Souvigny Bible (12th century) make up the collections. The priory garden blends a French formal garden with a medieval one.

The Gothic cloister (15th century) reveals its western gallery and its rib-vaulted bays set in a staggered pattern. From the remains, the view of the priory church's double transept offers a privileged vantage point for understanding Cluniac architecture. The garden's 220 rose bushes and medicinal plants recall the department's winegrowing past.

activities.text: Guided visits allow access to the Bourbon chapels, the Baroque sacristy, and the cloister. Daily (except Tuesdays): church visit at 3:30 PM. Saturdays and Sundays: museum visit at 2:30 PM and bell towers at 5 PM. In high season, daily visits at 10 AM and 3:30 PM. Climbing the bell towers is rewarded with an exceptional panorama.

The pilgrimage at Souvigny, one of Auvergne's major spiritual centres, has been enjoying a revival since 2016 thanks to the initiative of the Bishop of Moulins. The restored Way of Saint James allows visitors to walk in the footsteps of the holy abbots. The sanctuary offers a spiritual audio tour combining history, heritage and spirituality, accessible on a smartphone via a QR code.

Exploring the surrounding Bourbonnais bocage reveals hedgerows, enclosed fields and a characteristic rolling landscape. A tour of nearby Romanesque churches, walks toward the Réserve naturelle du Val d'Allier (a haven for birds) or the Val de Sioule and its wooded gorges: allow for a day trip from Souvigny for these excursions. The area is ideal for gentle hiking.

days_plan.itin_title: Allier Road Trip: Vichy, Thermal Baths and Bourbonnais Bocage

visits.text: The European Museum of Beer occupies the former provisions store of Stenay citadel, transformed into a malthouse in the 19th century. Labeled "Museum of France" and listed as Historic Monuments, it displays 55,000 objects across 2,500 square meters. Six sequences trace brewing history from Mesopotamian origins (12,000 years ago) to the present day.

The museum's highlight: the advertising posters room reveals how graphic art served brewers. It notably features a lithograph by Czech artist Alfons Mucha (1897), created for Bières de la Meuse of Bar-le-Duc, in Art Nouveau style.

Stenay's Saint-Joseph church, rebuilt after Great War destruction, stands out for its sober architecture. The city's coat of arms, adorned with a devil, recalls this former stronghold of the Counts of Bar's rich past.

activities.text: The museum's botanical garden features a hop garden surrounded by herbs and spices used in brewing. The visit stimulates sight, smell and touch.
End at the museum tavern for a tasting of craft beers with top, bottom, or spontaneous fermentation. Local specialties accompany the glasses: beer sausage, cheese, and Stenay madeleines.
Hop on a bike along the Meuse Greenway, a cycle path part of EuroVelo 19. The section from Stenay follows the river through a Natura 2000 zone rich in birds and valley-floor landscapes.

days_plan.itin_title: Meuse Circuit: Verdun and the Citadels

visits.text: The Château de Sully-sur-Loire is one of the finest examples of a medieval fortress on the Loire. Commissioned in 1396 by Gui VI de La Trémoille, it rises on the left bank of the river, surrounded by moats thirty metres wide, still filled with water. Its most precious treasure is invisible from outside: in the keep's roof space, a 14th-century pointed barrel timber frame in oak, in an exceptional state of preservation. Specialists date it precisely by dendrochronology — the trees were felled in the winter of 1388-1389. Voltaire was exiled here in 1716 by the regent; Louis XIV stayed as a child during the Fronde. Don't miss the ten tapestries of the Psyche hanging, Flemish work from the 17th century.

The château's park invites a leisurely wander around the moats. Centuries-old trees, the perspective onto the circular towers and the view over the Loire make for a very photogenic setting. It's also in this park that the Heures Historiques festival is held every May, the largest multi-era gathering in France: between 1,200 and 1,500 costumed reenactors parade from Prehistory to the wars of the 20th century.

The Saint-Ythier Collegiate Church blends 12th-century Romanesque with flamboyant Gothic. It holds the tombs of the lords of Sully. Just nearby, spot the House of Henry IV, a 16th-century dwelling, and the timber spire of Saint-Germain Church — one of the tallest in France.

activities.text: Every year between May and June, the Sully and Loiret Music Festival offers classical, baroque and jazz concerts in the château and other heritage sites in the département. Created in 1973, it's one of the oldest festivals of its kind in the region. Check the programme before your stay if you're coming during this period.

Follow the banks of the Loire by bike or on foot. The Loire à Vélo passes through Sully between levees and wooded islands. The path between Sully and Saint-Benoît-sur-Loire (8 km) is particularly pleasant and takes you to the Benedictine abbey of Fleury, founded in the 7th century, which holds the relics of Saint Benedict.

days_plan.itin_title: The Essential Châteaux of the Loire Valley
Loiret Road Trip: Orléans and the Châteaux of the Loire

visits.text: Suresnes American Cemetery, established in 1917, shelters 1,541 burials from World War I and 24 unknown soldiers from World War II. A chapel watches over the white Carrara marble crosses.

The crosses align in a V-formation on Mont-Valérien's slopes. A wall of the missing perpetuates the memory of 974 soldiers. This is the only American military cemetery in Europe commemorating both World Wars.

activities.text: 4,800 vines spread across Mont-Valérien's slopes, continuing a winemaking tradition dating back to Roman times. The climb rewards you with an unforgettable view of the Eiffel Tower.
Terrasse du Fécheray offers a 180° panorama over Paris. This verdant oasis is cherished for its natural beauty.
Walk along the Seine from the dam and lock. The river structure measures 185 meters long. The embankments preserve a bucolic atmosphere.

days_plan.itin_title: Hauts-de-Seine Road Trip: Royal Heritage & Gardens

visits.text: The Hermitage hill is compact - barely 136 hectares in total - but it produces what some consider France's greatest red wine. Climb on foot from Tain: 30 minutes via the vineyard trail, passing parcels of Chapoutier, Jaboulet, Chave. The Saint-Christophe chapel at the summit dates from the 12th century. The view over the Rhône and the Alps on clear days is worth the breathless climb.
The suspension bridge between Tain and Tournon is still in use for pedestrians. Crossing is free, with a superb view of the Hermitage hill from the middle of the bridge.

Valrhona set up in Tain in 1922 for one simple reason: the quality of Rhône water. The Cité du Chocolat, opened in 2013, traces the journey from bean to bar through well-designed exhibits—and above all, tasting workshops where you learn to distinguish 64% chocolate from 72% in a blind tasting. The result: you leave with different criteria for buying chocolate, and probably too many bars in your bag.

activities.text: Maison Chapoutier offers a guided walk through the Hermitage vineyards with a winegrower—a rare opportunity to walk through the classified plots “Le Méal” or “L'Ermite” and hear why the soil changes character every ten meters. Michel Chapoutier converted the entire estate to biodynamic farming in the 1990s: all labels have been in Braille since 1996. There is a charge for the tour; booking is required.

Comparative tasting of Hermitage red vs. Hermitage white at Chapoutier or Jaboulet: the same hill, the same altitude, but the Marsanne and Roussanne in the white produce a wine of absurd longevity—great white Hermitage vintages last 30 to 50 years in the cellar. Ask to taste a white that is at least ten years old: it's no longer anything like the wine you imagine when you hear “Rhône white.”

days_plan.itin_title: Rhône Valley: From Northern Syrahs to Southern Grenaches

visits.text: Talloires-Montmin nestles in Lake Annecy's most beautiful bay. Cézanne, Napoleon III, and Churchill succumbed to the charm of this village nicknamed the Pearl of the Lake.
The former 11th-century Benedictine priory now houses an American university campus. Its terraced gardens descend to turquoise waters.
The 17th-century Abbey was built by Benedictine monks on the site of a 9th-century monastery. It overlooks the marina.
The Roc de Chère nature reserve preserves 68 hectares of forests and cliffs. Trails lead to viewpoints offering plunging views over the lake.
Saint-Germain's Hermitage and its cave nestle in the cliff. This pilgrimage site offers an exceptional panorama of Talloires and the lake.
The Angon Waterfall plunges 60 meters down a cliff in a green setting. The path follows the rock face to the base of this impressive cascade.

activities.text: Canyoning in Angon Canyon is the region's signature activity. Rappels under waterfalls, natural slides, and jumps spice up this aquatic descent.
Take off paragliding from the Forclaz Pass to soar over the lake and mountains. Tandem flights offer unforgettable sensations facing the Alpine panorama.
The Roc de Chère hike winds through a forest with varied atmospheres: Mediterranean pine groves and mountain beech forests coexist on this promontory.
Rent a kayak or paddleboard to explore Talloires Bay from the water and discover coves inaccessible by road.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Savoie Road Trip: Alpine Lakes & Mont Blanc
Grand Tour Ain & Savoie Mont-Blanc: Lakes, Mountains and Heritage

visits.text: Talmont-sur-Gironde, a village of 100 inhabitants perched on a rocky promontory. Listed as a Plus Beau Village de France, it overlooks the Gironde estuary. Lanes lined with hollyhocks, white houses with blue shutters, artisan shops.

Sainte-Radegonde Church of Talmont (12th century), in the Romanesque style of Saintonge, stands at the cliff edge. Its apse overlooks the estuary—the sea has eaten away at the cemetery. Sculpted facade, single nave, golden light. One of the most photographed churches in France.

The carrelets of Talmont, fishing huts on stilts equipped with square nets. A traditional estuary technique for catching shrimp, eels and mullet. Some can be rented overnight—a unique experience facing the sunset.

activities.text: Talmont market (summer). In the village lanes, local producers and artisans. Pineau, cognac, jams, soaps. Festive atmosphere on summer evenings with concerts on the square.
Talmont cliff path. A 3 km walk along the estuary, between fishing huts on stilts and vineyards. Views of the cliffs of Meschers and their cave dwellings.

days_plan.itin_title: Charente-Maritime Road Trip: La Rochelle, Île de Ré, Fort Boyard and Roman Saintonge
Nouvelle-Aquitaine Loop: Villages, Vineyards & Dordogne

places.name: Tannay

visits.text: Listed as a historic monument in 1840, the Collegiate Church of Saint-Léger marries a 13th-century Gothic choir to a 15th-century Flamboyant Gothic nave. Eight buttresses pierced with arches support the building; the square bell tower adorned with gargoyles culminates with a rooster atop its cross.
The polychrome stone statue of Saint Roch from 1522 adorns the interior. The five bays of the nave are flanked by side aisles the same height as the main vault.
The Claude de La Porte cellar is one of Tannay's oldest known cellars. It once housed the communal wine press and oven.
Tannay preserves numerous towers that dominate the roofs, an architectural peculiarity of the village. Eight châteaux are listed in the area, witnesses to its aristocratic past.
The Coteaux de Tannay vineyard received PGI designation in 2011. Planted by the collegiate's monks as early as 1207 on clay-limestone soil, it now covers 25 hectares farmed by seven winemakers.

activities.text: Taste Coteaux de Tannay wines at local producers. Whites made from Chardonnay and Melon de Bourgogne, reds from Pinot Noir or Gamay perpetuate a thousand-year winemaking tradition.
Walk or bike along the Nivernais Canal. The towpath runs through Tannay, offering a shaded stroll between the Yonne valley and wooded hills.
Follow a section of the GR654, the Way of St. James from Vézelay. A reception center reserved for pilgrims marks this historic stage.

days_plan.itin_title: Nièvre Road Trip: Morvan and Ducal Heritage

map_keywords: Claude de La Porte cellar Tannay

visits.text: The Château du Roi René is one of France's best-preserved medieval castles — and one of the least frequented for a monument of this quality. Built between 1400 and 1434 by the Dukes of Anjou on rock at the Rhône's edge, its 4-meter-thick walls rise 45 meters. René d'Anjou, heir to the County of Provence, furnished it as a pleasure residence between 1447 and 1449. Until 1481, it controlled the Rhône's political border — the opposite bank, Beaucaire, was in the Kingdom of France. The terrace offers exceptional panoramas over the river, Alpilles, and Montagnette.

The Tarasque is Tarascon's legendary monster — a half-ox, half-crocodile dragon that terrorized Rhône boatmen before Saint Martha, who came from Palestine after Christ's death, captured it with her rosary and holy water. The legend, recounted in the Golden Legend (circa 1260), explains the town's very name. The Tarasque festival, created by King René in 1469 and inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Heritage list, is held annually in June. The crypt of the Sainte-Marthe collegiate church (11th century) preserves the saint's tomb.

The old centre of Tarascon is worth an hour's stroll: its streets pack 17th- and 18th-century mansions and medieval houses side by side. The town is also the birthplace of Tartarin, the boastful character invented by Alphonse Daudet.

activities.text: Walk along the Rhône banks and view of Beaucaire: from the quay along the château, the suspension bridge allows reaching Beaucaire (Gard department) on foot. From the opposite bank, the view of the Château du Roi René's facade perched on its rock at river's edge is striking. Return by the same bridge. Allow 1h30.

Circuit of Tarascon's ramparts and medieval gates: the town preserves several vestiges of its medieval fortifications — gates including the Porte du Rhône and sections of ramparts integrated into dwelling facades. A 45-minute walking circuit from the tourist office.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpilles, Aix-en-Provence & Arles Circuit

visits.text: The Niaux Cave holds one of the finest sets of rock paintings in Europe in the famous Salon Noir. The guided route plunges into total darkness, passing through narrow passages and cathedral-like chambers as far as the Salon Noir, 800 metres from the entrance. In the beam of the torches appear bison, horses and ibex painted 14,000 years ago by the Magdalenians with exceptional mastery. The constant coolness at 12°C and the absolute silence heighten the emotion of this prehistoric journey. Booking essential.

Lombrives, billed as Europe's largest cave and part of a 14 km underground network, reveals itself after a 1.4 km approach on foot or aboard a small train. Squeeze through the narrow Passage du Crime before emerging into the Amphithéâtre, an underground cathedral vaster than Notre-Dame de Paris. The grand staircase of 174 steps offers a spectacular plunging view over this titanic chamber. Discover the Galerie du Grand Cimetière, the mythical Tombeau de Pyrène, and admire signatures carved since the 12th century, including that of the future Henri IV, then king of Navarre, dated 1578. Age-old formations, stalactites and stalagmites compose an otherworldly setting.

activities.text: Exploring Lombrives begins with the 1.4 km approach through the forest from the ticket office beside the RN20, either on foot along the hiking trail or aboard the little tourist train, around twenty minutes. The two-hour guided visit winds through a labyrinth of chambers of dizzying scale, between walls adorned with formations and underground lakes of mysterious waters. Concerts and candlelit evening tours create an atmosphere out of time.

days_plan.itin_title: Ariège Circuit: Cathar Castles, Prehistoric Caves & Mountain Lakes
Ariège Road Trip: Cathars and Prehistoric Caves

places.name: Tarbes

visits.text: The Jardin Massey, awarded the “Jardin remarquable” designation, spans eleven hectares in the city center.
