Designed in the 19th century by botanist Placide Massey, former director of the Trianon nurseries in Versailles, it features century-old trees, an orangery, free-roaming peacocks, and the remains of the cloister from the Saint-Sever-de-Rustan abbey, whose 15th-century capitals are classified as a Historic Monument.

The Musée Massey occupies the former residence of the botanist, recognizable by its Moorish tower offering a panorama over the Pyrenees mountain chain. On the first level, the International Hussars Collection brings together more than 15,000 objects tracing four centuries of history of this elite cavalry, from the 16th to the 20th century, across about thirty countries.

The second level of the museum presents a fine arts collection assembled in the 19th century by member of parliament Achille Jubinal. It features works from the Italian, Flemish, Dutch, and French schools from the 15th to the 20th century, with paintings by Girolamo del Pacchia, Frans II Francken, Baron Gérard, and Jean-Léon Gérôme.

The Maison natale du Maréchal Foch, at 2 rue de la Victoire, is an 18th-century house in the local Bigorre style classified as a Historic Monument. Its exterior gallery with balusters, marble-framed windows, and carved wooden staircase exemplify local architecture. Ferdinand Foch spent his first twelve years here before becoming Marshal of France, Great Britain, and Poland.

The Cathedral of Notre-Dame de la Sède is the oldest monument in Tarbes. Still largely Romanesque, it blends Romanesque and Gothic styles. Inside, the Baroque high altar combines local green and red marble, modeled after that of Saint Peter's in Rome. You can also discover Louis XVI's will engraved on a black marble plaque.

The Haras de Tarbes, created by decree of Napoleon I in 1806, occupies eight hectares in the heart of the city. Its Empire-style stables, collection of horse-drawn carriages, ceremonial tack room, and the Maison du Cheval trace the history of breeding the Anglo-Arabian horse, the emblematic breed of the Hautes-Pyrénées developed here by crossing local mares with Eastern stallions.

activities.text: Stroll through the shaded pathways of Jardin Massey to observe the peacocks, then climb to admire the Pyrenean panorama from the museum's Moorish tower.
Tour the rooms of the Musée Massey, taking time to examine the ornate Hussar uniforms, reconstructed on 130 mannequins representing 30 different nations.
Follow the heritage trail marked by studs in the ground through the historic quarter: from the Maison Foch to the cathedral, then toward the stud farm, each stop reveals a chapter of Tarbes history.
Take a guided tour of the Haras to access the stables and see the horses at work—on certain days, the farrier still hammers iron in his forge.

days_plan.itin_title: Hautes-Pyrénées Circuit: From Tarbes to Cirques and Valleys
Bordeaux to Toulouse Road Trip: Ocean, Pyrenees and Heritage

map_keywords: Cathédrale Notre-Dame de la Sède Tarbes

visits.text: If you plan to hike in the Valley of Wonders, be sure to start with the Musée départemental des Merveilles in Tende. Designed by Jean-Michel Wilmotte and inaugurated in 1996, it presents casts, photographs and reconstructions of the Mont Bégo engravings. The petroglyphs date mainly from the Chalcolithic and Early Bronze Age (3,300 to 1,700 BC). Over 40,000 engravings cover 17 km² around Mont Bégo (2,872 m)—one of Europe's largest open-air rock art sites. Allow 90 minutes. Closed Tuesdays.

Tende's medieval village rises in tiers like an amphitheater on the hillside: four- to six-story houses in local green schist, topped with stone-slab roofs, narrow cobbled streets. Once a major stop on the Salt Road between Nice and Piedmont, Tende only became part of France in 1947 after a referendum—Italian identity remains very evident in the architecture, cuisine and family names.

Notre-Dame de l'Assomption Collegiate Church blends Lombard and Baroque architecture: a 12th-century green stone bell tower, a Renaissance facade, an interior remodeled in Baroque style in the 17th century. This mix illustrates the history of Tende, a cultural crossroads between Liguria, Piedmont and France. Inside, gilded wood altarpieces and an Italian organ.

The ruins of Lascaris Castle and the Clock Tower crown the village. The Lascaris reigned over Tende from the 13th to 15th century. The castle was destroyed in 1692. Today, the esplanade offers a panorama over the Roya valley and Mercantour peaks exceeding 3,000 meters. Ideal in late afternoon for golden light on the flagstone roofs.

activities.text: The Valley of Wonders is the must-do excursion from Tende. Over 40,000 rock engravings scattered on glacier-polished rocks around Mont Bégo. Access is unrestricted on marked trails, but an accredited guide is strongly recommended to spot the engravings, which are sometimes hard to see. Departure from the hamlet of Castérino. Allow a full day. Snow makes the site inaccessible from November to June, depending on the year.

The hamlet of Castérino, at an altitude of 1,550 m, is the starting point for hikes to the Valley of Wonders and the Fontanalba valley. Accessible by car from Tende in 30 minutes along a forest road. A mountain refuge with a restaurant is open in season; parking at the end of the road. Chamois, marmots and ibex on the slopes.

Fontanalba valley offers a more accessible alternative to the Valley of Wonders, with its own engravings and remarkable alpine lake landscape. Gentler hike, less frequented. Local guides bookable at Tende tourist office.

Train des Merveilles: the Nice–Tende–Cuneo line is one of France's most spectacular rail journeys. Spiral tunnels through rock, viaducts above gorges, 81 km of engineering feats inaugurated in 1928. The line, partially destroyed by Storm Alex in 2020, has reopened in stages. Check schedules on SNCF Connect.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpes-Maritimes Road Trip: Riviera and Mercantour, 13 days
Nice's hinterland: 8 days of hilltop villages and the Mercantour

visits.text: The Collegiate Church of Saint-Thiébaut is Thann's Gothic jewel and one of the most representative edifices of Rhenish Gothic in Alsace. Its construction lasted over two centuries, from the late 13th century until 1516. The people of Thann like to say: 'Strasbourg has the tallest, Freiburg the biggest, Thann the most beautiful!' — speaking of the bell tower. The stone-lace spire rises to 78 meters. The west portal is carved with three tympana featuring over 500 figures: the Life of the Virgin, the Nativity, and the Crucifixion. Inside, don't miss the 15th-century choir stalls or the stained glass from the same period.

The Witch's Eye watches over Thann from the ruins of Engelbourg castle. In 1673, Louis XIV ordered this fortress dismantled — miners from Giromagny set fire to explosive charges. After three attempts, the great tower broke and a section lifted vertically, forming this cyclopean fragment of stone that resembles an eye scrutinizing the plain. The climb from lower Thann takes twenty minutes and offers a 360° view over the Thur valley, the Rangen vineyard, and the Vosges ridges.

Stroll through Thann's old town among 16th-century houses, their oriel windows and fountains. The place Saint-Thiébaut at the foot of the collegiate church is the heart of local life. The Musée des Amis de Thann, housed in a former grain hall dating from 1519, brings together objects and archives on the history of the town and its vineyard.

activities.text: The Rangen vineyard is Alsace's southernmost and steepest, on south-facing volcanic slopes between 350 and 450 meters above sea level. It's the only vineyard in Alsace entirely classified as Grand Cru—Riesling and Gewurztraminer acquire a unique mineral character linked to the basaltic soil. Operators offer guided tours of the vineyard. It's also the southern terminus of the Alsace Wine Route, which runs for 170 kilometers from Marlenheim.

Climb to Engelbourg castle via the trail starting from the Bungert parking lot in Thann. Cross the bridge over the Thur, follow rue du Rangen for 150 meters, then take the first right. The climb takes thirty minutes and the ruins are freely accessible. The panoramic view from the Witch's Eye over Thann, the ridges, and the plain is well worth the effort.

days_plan.itin_title: Haut-Rhin Road Trip: Colmar and the Southern Wine Route
Alsace's Most Beautiful Christmas Markets

visits.text: Thiers, France's cutlery capital for over six centuries, has carved half-timbered houses and private mansions clinging to a rocky spur facing the Chaîne des Puys. The protected district can be explored from rue de la Coutellerie to the Saint-Jean quarter via the covered passages called pedde, typical of this vertical town. Historic cutlers' shops and craft artisans' workshops line the route. Today, Thiers still accounts for 2,000 jobs and 80% of the knives consumed in France.

The Musée de la Coutellerie, the fourth most visited museum in the former Auvergne region, is spread over three sites: the Maison de l'Homme des Bois, a listed medieval building, and the Maison des Consuls in the town center trace seven centuries of cutlery-making through objects, demonstrations, films, and sound-and-light shows. The third site, the Vallée des Rouets, can be visited three kilometers upstream in the Durolle gorges.

The Vallée des Rouets, awarded two stars in the Michelin Green Guide, meaning “worth a detour,” preserves the last working rouet: this grinding mill allowed knife grinders to polish blades while lying on their stomachs above the grinding wheel, hence their nickname Ventres Jaunes. The walking trail along the Durolle gorges crosses a wild natural landscape dotted with industrial remains and the Chez Lyonnet museum.

Le Creux de l'Enfer, a contemporary art center of national interest opened in 1988, occupies a former cutlery factory that closed in 1956 in the Durolle gorges. Recognizable by the red devil painted on its facade, this venue combines industrial heritage and contemporary creation in a spectacular setting of cliffs and waterfalls. The surrounding Vallée des Usines preserves former cutlery factory sites along the river, including the Maison de l'Aventure Industrielle in the usine du May.

activities.text: Knife-making workshop in Thiers. Participants assemble their own Le Thiers® knife, a protected brand recognizable by the recessed T logo engraved on the blade. A unique handmade souvenir to take home from the capital of French knives.

Hike De l'enfer aux rouets, a 12 km loop connecting the Vallée des Usines to the Vallée des Rouets along the Durolle gorges. The interpretive trail reveals the secrets of papermakers, tanners, and cutlers who harnessed the river's water power for centuries.

Discover Le Thiers® knives in the town's workshops and shops. This protected brand includes pocket, table, and kitchen knives, each piece engraved with the maker's name. The Coutellia festival in May brings together more than 230 artistic knife makers and manufacturers from around the world across 2,500 square meters of exhibition space.

days_plan.itin_title: Volcanoes and Auvergne traditions

visits.text: Thines is this itinerary's most isolated village, and one of the most remarkable. Perched at 550 meters altitude on a rocky promontory above the Thines river, the hamlet is reached only by an old narrow, winding track. The brown schist houses are roofed with schist lauzes, stone slabs whose weight demands particularly robust framing. The houses seem to grow out of the very rock they were cut from. Thines was inscribed as a UNESCO Geosite in 2022.

The church of Notre-Dame de Thines is a Romanesque masterpiece. Built by Benedictines between 1170 and 1190 in polychrome sandstone, a mix of schist, grey granite and red sandstone, it was classified a Monument Historique by Prosper Mérimée himself in 1848. Its monumental portal, carved capitals and facade polychromy are exceptional for a building of this size. Climb the imposing staircase leading to the porch and look at the carved lintel: you can make out Christ's arrest, told with remarkable narrative freshness. The column statues were partly mutilated during the 16th-century Wars of Religion, which paradoxically heightens their presence.

The Maison du Gerboul, at the hamlet base, is the territory interpretation center—documentaries, regional books and local crafts are available. This is where the Rocher de Thines interpretation trail (2 km, 10 thematic panels) starts, guiding geological, architectural and historical reading of the site. The terrace with panoramic views over the Thines valley is ideal for a break.

activities.text: The balcony trail above the thalweg (3 to 5 km from the hamlet, 150 m elevation gain) follows cliffs and offers plunging viewpoints over the river and hamlets on the opposite bank. It's on these heights that the Trois Croix pilgrimage is held each year. The path is sometimes narrow and exposed—avoid in rainy weather; schist can be very slippery.

The hamlet circuit and old cultivation terraces around Thines (2 km, 1h) passes through accols—these small strips of land laboriously developed on slopes—and mule tracks that linked hamlets together. The guide "Voyage au Rocher de Thines" from 2024 is available at Maison du Gerboul to deepen the visit.

days_plan.itin_title: The 18 Most Beautiful Villages of Ardèche

visits.text: The Tour aux Puces, a 14 m medieval keep perched on its mound, has housed Thionville’s museum of history and archaeology since 1905. Its collections retrace 2,000 years of this border town’s history, from its Celtic origins to the two world wars. From the top, the view encompasses the slate roofs of the old town and the meanders of the canalised Moselle. The medieval underground passages contain remains of the former 11th-century fortress.

The casemates of Thionville Castle plunge visitors into the depths of the fortress built by Vauban in the 17th century. These underground galleries, dug beneath the ramparts over 500 metres, served as a shelter for 1,500 soldiers and as an ammunition depot. The cool atmosphere, at 12°C all year round, and subdued lighting recreate the ambience of old strongholds, with their firing positions and wells.

Amnéville Zoo, about 12 km from the stage town, 12 minutes by road, ranks among the finest animal parks in France with 2,000 animals of 360 species over 18 hectares. From the gorillas of the Orangutan Jungle (6,000 m²) to the polar bears of the arctic area, from Siberian tigers to African elephants on the 3-hectare plain, each continent reveals its wildlife in vast, naturalised enclosures. The 1,000 m² tropical vivarium and the lorikeet aviary delight young and old alike. Sea lion shows and free-flying birds of prey punctuate the day.

activities.text: Stroll through the 14-hectare Parc Napoléon, Thionville’s green lung, landscaped in the English style in 1859. Its winding paths follow a 7,000 m² pond where black swans and mandarin ducks glide. A neoclassical bandstand, playgrounds, a rose garden and shaded benches make it a favourite Sunday meeting place for families. The park also contains the 1870 war memorial and several contemporary sculptures.

The 16th-century belfry and the cobbled streets of the old town tell the story of a town shaped by the Franco-German wars. Arcaded squares, Renaissance townhouses and fountains create a setting where French and Germanic influences mingle. The 15th-century Gothic Saint-Maximin Church watches over this preserved architectural heritage.

days_plan.itin_title: 4-Day Moselle Tour: Metz, Bitche Citadel and Chagall’s Stained Glass

visits.text: Lake Coiselet, an artificial reservoir created in 1970, is the southernmost lake in the Jura — it marks the border with the Ain department. Six kilometers long, surrounded by spectacular limestone cliffs, it offers a wild landscape very different from the glacial lakes of the north. From the Condes road that follows the left bank, you'll discover the perched ruins of Oliferne Castle, destroyed in the 16th century by Henry IV's troops — this castle once controlled navigation in the Ain valley. At the end of the lake, the Chancia bridge crosses the Ain toward a village with a small island.

Two kilometers from Thoirette, the small village of Coisia entered the record books in 2004 when roadwork uncovered 140-million-year-old dinosaur footprints, visible from the roadside. Thoirette itself is crossed by the Ain River and serves as the traditional gathering point for fishermen who come seeking pike and trout in its renowned waters. The Thoirette bridge, over a century old, is one of the iconic landmarks marking the end of this lakes route.

activities.text: Canoe-kayak descent through the Ain gorges from Thoirette: providers offer a "discovery route" of 6 to 9 km from the Thoirette put-in. The descent passes through Lake Conflans and its castle, crosses verdant and wild gorges before reaching Corveissiat. Swimming stops are possible at the "Giants' Cauldrons," pools carved into the rock by the current. Count 2h30 to 3h30 of paddling.

Landscape observation from the heights of the Ain valley: several viewpoints line the ridges around Thoirette. From certain vantage points, the view extends over the Vouglans dam upstream and the Ain gorges downstream, framed by the limestone plateaus of the Jura. These ridges are also frequented by raptors — peregrine falcons and red kites are regularly observed on the cliffs.

days_plan.itin_title: Jura Lakes Route: Emerald and Turquoise Waters

visits.text: The Château de Thoiry, built in 1559, functions as an architectural sundial: at the solstices, sunlight passes straight through the entrance hall. Its period-furnished salons complement the wildlife park.
Thoiry's botanical gardens cover 95 hectares awarded the "Jardin remarquable" label. Formal gardens attributed to Le Nôtre, English gardens, and a rose garden make up a varied landscaped whole.

activities.text: Drive the 8-kilometre safari route through the African reserve: bears, elephants and giraffes roam in semi-free conditions. Allow 45 minutes to an hour.
Explore the zoo on foot: over 1,300 animals of 150 species spread across themed enclosures. The tunnel beneath the lion enclosure offers a thrilling viewpoint.
In winter, the Thoiry Lumières Sauvages festival illuminates the park with thousands of giant lanterns depicting animals and landscapes.

days_plan.itin_title: Yvelines Road Trip: Versailles and Impressionist Villages

visits.text: This spectacular Alpine valley stretches between the Bornes massif and the Aravis chain. The limestone peaks rise beyond 2,700 meters and form a grandiose natural amphitheater.
Capital of Reblochon, Thônes has kept its character as a traditional Savoyard market town. Stroll the lanes of the historic center and visit the 18th-century baroque church of Saint-Hippolyte.
This small neo-Gothic chapel from 1861 stands in a magnificent Alpine setting at the hamlet of Les Confins. It marks the starting point for numerous hikes.

activities.text: Set off from Les Confins hamlet to reach this small mountain lake nestled at 1,430 meters. The easy 2 km trail crosses flowering meadows and spruce forests.
The Lake Annecy Golf Club offers an 18-hole course in an exceptional setting facing the lake and the mountains.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Savoie Road Trip: Alpine Lakes & Mont Blanc

visits.text: You come to the Côte d'Azur for the sea, not for bison. And yet, in Thorenc, the Réserve biologique des Monts d'Azur has no equivalent in France: 700 hectares on a plateau at 1,200 meters, where European bison, Przewalski's horses, moose, deer, and wild boar roam completely freely. The project began in 2006 at the initiative of veterinarian Patrice Longour, who was inspired by African reserves to reconstitute the “guild” of large European herbivores. 40 minutes from Grasse and 1 hour from Nice.

The village of Thorenc is a quiet mountain village at 1,250 meters, typical of the Grasse hinterland. A walk through meadows and forests around the plateau makes the contrast with the Côte d'Azur immediately apparent. In fall, the bellowing of stags echoes through the valley at nightfall, a powerful moment few tourists know about.

activities.text: The guided safari on foot (1 hour and 45 minutes) or by horse-drawn carriage (1 hour and 15 minutes) is the only way to enter the reserve: visitor numbers are strictly limited, and reservations are required. In fall, the safari to hear the stags bellow runs in the evening and lasts 2 hours and 30 minutes; it's the most memorable experience of the trip. A naturalist guide accompanies each group. Dress warmly even in summer: at 1,200 m, temperatures stay cool.

Ecolodges let you stay in the reserve for a fully immersive experience: wildlife watching at dusk and dawn from your accommodation, right in the heart of bison territory. It's one of the most unusual experiences in the Alpes-Maritimes. Book well ahead; places are limited and go fast.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpine Hinterland and Verdon Gorges: From Thorenc to Riez
Nice's hinterland: 8 days of hilltop villages and the Mercantour

places.name: Thouars

visits.text: The Castle of the Dukes of La Trémoïlle dominates the rocky promontory where Pepin the Short had already razed a castle in 762. The current building, with its 110-meter-long Louis XIII-style facade, dates from the mid-17th century: in 1638, Marie de La Tour d’Auvergne, the “female pope of the Huguenots” and the duke’s wife, called on architect Jacques Lemercier—the same architect then working on the Louvre and the Sorbonne chapel. He advised her to raze everything and rebuild. The castle now houses a public middle school and is open to visitors only during Heritage Days in September. Walk around it to appreciate its proportions from the esplanade and the orangery attributed to Jules-Hardouin Mansart.

The Notre-Dame Collegiate Church, built from 1499 to 1515 by Gabrielle de Bourbon-Montpensier on the site of the town wall, is a masterpiece of the transition from Gothic to Renaissance architecture. Its facade, unique in France, is topped by a loggia—an open arcaded gallery. Granted collegiate status in 1515 by Pope Leo X, it houses a relic of the True Cross. Enter through the side door if the main entrance is closed.

Saint-Médard Church, at the other end of the plateau, retains a remarkable 12th-century facade in the Romanesque style of Poitou and a north portal with a multifoil arch showing Mozarabic influence—a very rare feature in the region. Its 56-meter Gothic bell tower dominates the town.

Among the half-timbered houses on Place Saint-Médard and Rue du Château is the 15th-century Hôtel des Trois Rois. Then head down toward the Pont des Chouans for a panoramic view from the heights over the bend in the Thouet—one of the most photographed viewpoints in the department.

activities.text: Visit the Henri-Barré Museum, housed in a Neo-Gothic mansion. Its collections of faience, archaeological artifacts, and fine art reflect a town that has always been a cultural crossroads.

Head down toward the Thouet along Rue Imbert and Rue du Château to see the succession of small medieval houses and Renaissance mansions. As you climb back up, the hillside offers a series of views over the river’s meanders.

days_plan.itin_title: Deux-Sèvres Tour: Marais Poitevin and Romanesque Heritage

map_keywords: Château des ducs de La Trémoïlle Thouars

visits.text: The dizzying staircase of L'Échelle du Roi is cut into the basalt flow overlooking the Ardèche. Its 210 steps, suspended above the sheer drop, descend the black lava cliff.

activities.text: The geological hike reveals the wonders of Ardèche volcanism. The lava flow trail passes through basalt formations, organ-pipe lava columns, and jumbles of rock.

days_plan.itin_title: Ardèche Road Trip: Wild Gorges and Villages with Character

visits.text: Fosse Dionne has intrigued visitors since antiquity. This vauclusian spring forms a turquoise pool whose known gallery plunges 61 meters deep over 360 meters. A circular half-rotunda washhouse, listed as a Historic Monument, has surrounded it since 1758.

The Hôtel-Dieu, founded in 1293 by Marguerite de Bourgogne, is Europe's longest medieval hospital. Its patients' hall stretches 90 meters beneath original timberwork. The 15th-century Entombment sculpture is preserved here.

Climb to Saint-Pierre Church, perched on the hill overlooking Tonnerre. Its architecture blends flamboyant Gothic and Renaissance. The interior houses an antique organ, an 18th-century pulpit, and polychrome stained glass.
Notre-Dame Church, in the town center, presents a mix of Romanesque and Gothic styles. Its stones bear witness to Tonnerre's different construction eras—a town destroyed and rebuilt multiple times.
The medieval-inspired gardens, adjoining the Hôtel-Dieu, feature boxwood hedges, hornbeams, and yews. Medicinal plants are identified according to their period uses.
Ten kilometers away, Château de Tanlay rises from its moat amid a vast park. This Burgundian Renaissance residence houses a trompe-l'oeil room and the League Tower adorned with allegorical frescoes.

activities.text: The Canal de Bourgogne cuts through Tonnerre's heart. Take the towpath on foot or by bike for a waterside stroll past locks and barges.
Tonnerrois winemakers open their cellars for tastings. The AOC Bourgogne Tonnerre and Bourgogne Épineuil reveal a discreet but quality terroir.
On Wednesdays and Saturdays, Tonnerre's market offers snails, gougères, Chaourçois cheese, and Armançonnettes—local sweet specialties.

days_plan.itin_title: Yonne Circuit: Northern Burgundy & Chablis
Burgundy Road Trip: Cathedrals, Vineyards and Villages

visits.text: Cathédrale Saint-Étienne was built between 1221 and 1496. Its flamboyant Gothic facade, erected between 1475 and 1496, ranks among the finest in eastern France.
The cathedral's Gothic cloister measures 54 meters long and 42 wide. It's one of the largest in France.
The cathedral towers rise to 62 meters. The spires planned to reach 90 meters were never built.
The 13th-century Collégiale Saint-Gengoult impresses with its bright interior. Its clear glass windows and 16th-century cloister invite contemplation.
Vauban's fortifications have encircled the town since 1678. Star-shaped bastions, casemates, and glacis testify to the marshal's military genius.

activities.text: Toul's cellars have produced vin gris for centuries. This typically Lorraine rosé can be tasted at estates in the surrounding area.
Walk along the Marne-Rhine Canal that runs through Toul. The banks offer a peaceful stroll at the foot of the ramparts.

days_plan.itin_title: Meurthe-et-Moselle Road Trip: Art Nouveau Nancy & Fortified Cities

places.name: Toulon

visits.text: Behind the monumental 18th-century gateway, the National Maritime Museum showcases ship models, galleys and paintings tracing four centuries of naval tradition. The displays explore the history of the Toulon arsenal and the city's major role in French maritime history.

Board the cable car for a six-minute ride and 378-meter ascent to the summit of Mont Faron. At the top, the Memorial to the Provence Landing and Liberation recounts the August 1944 operation through period artifacts and multimedia exhibits.

Notre-Dame de la Seds Cathedral, founded in the 5th century, blends Romanesque and Gothic elements with a unified Gothic nave, a bell tower crowned by a campanile, and an 18th-century organ. The side chapels house the Chapel of the Virgin and the Corpus Domini chapel.

Listed as a historic monument since 1947, the Tour Royale was begun in 1514 under Louis XII and completed in 1524 under Francis I to defend the entrance to Toulon harbor. Its seven-meter-thick walls and moat make it a rare example of an Italian “torrione.” It hosts cultural events in summer.
The Opéra de Toulon was built more than 150 years ago on place Victor Hugo. Its classical façade makes it one of the gems of the old town center.
Step into the Hôtel des Arts TPM, a 400 m² space dedicated to contemporary art. Rotating exhibitions alternate between paintings, sculptures, and installations. Admission is free.

activities.text: Wander through the aisles of the Cours Lafayette market, open Tuesday through Sunday. Herbes de Provence, olives, soaps, and fresh produce line the stalls in a typical Provençal market atmosphere.
Embark on a narrated one-hour boat tour of Toulon harbor. You will see military vessels at the quay, the fortifications, the mussel farms of Lazaret Bay, and the seaside cemetery.
Head to the Mourillon beaches, lined with landscaped gardens, lawns, and playgrounds.

days_plan.itin_title: Var Road Trip: French Riviera & Provence Verte

map_keywords: Musée national de la Marine Toulon
Cathédrale Notre-Dame de la Seds Toulon

visits.text: Fly from Nice Côte d'Azur to Toulouse-Blagnac in 1 hour 5 minutes to 1 hour 15 minutes, for €50-150 depending on how early you book, with direct flights operated by EasyJet and Volotea; Air France routes via Paris-Orly in 3-4 hours and does not offer a direct flight. This is the itinerary's only domestic flight and replaces a 6-hour train journey via Marseille. Book 2 months ahead. Stay around the Capitole or Carmes to explore everything on foot.

Place du Capitole, the city's heart since the 12th century. A 135-metre neo-classical façade with 8 marble columns — town hall and opera house combined in a single building. An Occitan cross in marble on the ground, with four branches each bearing three roundels (12 in total, variously interpreted as the 12 months or the signs of the zodiac). Free open access to the Capitole interior: the Salle des Illustres with Jean-Paul Laurens's monumental frescoes on Toulouse's history, and the Salle Henri-Martin with Pointillist paintings.

The Basilica of Saint-Sernin, the largest Romanesque church still standing in Europe. Built 1080–1220 for pilgrims on the Way of Saint James, UNESCO listed. The octagonal bell tower at 64 metres is the signature of the Toulouse school. A 115-metre nave, sculpted capitals, ambulatory. Shrine of Saint Saturninus, who evangelised the city in the 3rd century and was martyred in 250. Free entry, €4 for the crypt.

Couvent des Jacobins (13th century, work begun in 1230). Southern Gothic style, with its stone palm tree: a central column 22 metres tall whose ribs unfurl like palm fronds under the vault — the pinnacle of Languedoc Gothic. The relics of Thomas Aquinas have rested here since 1369. Between 11am and 3pm, light through the windows illuminates the painted walls. €5.

Hôtel d'Assézat, 1555, built by Pierre d'Assézat, a merchant who made his fortune in woad — the dye plant that enriched Toulouse in the 16th century before Indian indigo ruined the trade. The Renaissance inner courtyard: three tiers of arcaded galleries, mullioned windows. Houses the Bemberg Foundation — Cranach, Canaletto, Gauguin, Bonnard. €12.

TER Toulouse to Carcassonne: 45 minutes direct, €15. Several trains per hour. Leave your bags at the hotel in Toulouse and travel light — you'll be back for a second night. The station is in the lower town (Bastide Saint-Louis), a 25-minute walk from the Cité (2 km) or a €1 shuttle bus (line 4). Wear comfortable shoes — cobblestones and steep climbs ahead.

Enter through the Porte Narbonnaise — late 13th century, built under Philip III the Bold, two massive towers. The Cité has been UNESCO-listed since 1997: 52 towers and a double ring of walls, whose foundations from the 3rd–4th-century Gallo-Roman period are still clearly visible. Four to five million visitors per year, with barely 50 permanent residents. The lices — the strip of ground between the two rings of walls — made a crossed-fire approach impossible to breach.

The Château Comtal, a fortress within the fortress. 12th century, built by the Trencavel viscounts — lords who patronised troubadours and sheltered the Cathars. In 1209, Raymond-Roger Trencavel was imprisoned here, defeated by Simon de Montfort after a 15-day siege during the Albigensian Crusade. He died in his own dungeon a few months later, aged 24. The rampart walk (1.3 km, 35 towers) starts from the castle: views over the Pyrenees and the Montagne Noire. €12.

The Basilica of Saint-Nazaire inside the Cité. Free. Begun in 1096 by the Trencavels, it combines a restrained Romanesque nave with a soaring 14th-century Gothic choir. The 13th-century windows are among the oldest and best-preserved in the South. The 17th-century organ still gives concerts. Visit in late afternoon for the light through the stained glass.

The Pont Vieux (1315–1320), 12 semi-circular arches over the Aude, fully pedestrian. Descend into the Bastide Saint-Louis, founded in 1260 by Saint Louis to rehouse the inhabitants expelled from the Cité after the rebellion of 1240. A medieval grid plan. Place Carnot paved in red marble from Caunes-Minervois (20 km). Saturday morning market, the most animated in the Aude. Neptune Fountain (1771).

The Canal du Midi runs alongside the Bastide from 1810 (a century after the canal's inauguration in 1681, when Carcassonne was finally linked to it). Designed by Pierre-Paul Riquet under Louis XIV: 241 km from the Atlantic to the Mediterranean, UNESCO since 1996. Walk the towpath between the station and Square André Chénier under century-old plane trees. A 1-hour canal cruise (€12) from the port, including passage through a lock.

activities.text: The Garonne quays at end of day. The Pont Neuf (paradoxically the oldest bridge in Toulouse, 1544–1632): seven unequal arches spanning 220 metres. Lit up in gold in the evening. The pink bricks glow orange at sunset — hence the Ville Rose. Restaurants on Quai de la Daurade.

Cassoulet — THE dish of Toulouse. White Tarbais beans, duck confit, Toulouse sausage IGP, pork rind. Its origin has been endlessly disputed with Castelnaudary and Carcassonne, and never settled. Chez Émile (Place Saint-Georges, since 1942) serves a benchmark version at €28. Au Père Louis (Rue des Tourneurs, since 1889). Le Bibent (Place du Capitole, Belle Époque listed interior). Pair with a Fronton or Gaillac red.

Lunch in the Cité. Cassoulet (Carcassonne is one of the three cities that claim its invention). Le Jardin de la Tour (Rue Porte d'Aude) serves a refined version at €22 in a peaceful courtyard setting. Avoid Rue Cros-Mayrevieille — pure tourist trap. Alternative: Brasserie Donjon (Place du Grand Puits), shaded terrace.

Before leaving, return to the Pont Vieux at sunset — the finest viewpoint for the illuminated Cité reflected in the Aude. Photographers love it. Take the last TER back to Toulouse in the evening (last service around 9pm). Free evening in Toulouse.

Bordeaux to Toulouse Road Trip: Ocean, Pyrenees and Heritage
The Grand Tour of France in 5 Weeks, Car-Free
The Grand Tour of France in 5 Weeks, Car-Free

visits.text: The tower at La Hougue, linked to the mainland by a granite causeway, and its twin on Tatihou are archetypal examples of the towers with upper-level gun batteries designed by Vauban. Built from 1694 after the naval Battle of La Hougue, it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2008. The causeway, exposed to the wind, is not suitable for those prone to vertigo.

days_plan.itin_title: Cotentin, Pays d'Auge: 5 days exploring the most beautiful villages

visits.text: Tournemire stretches along a volcanic ridge above the Doire valley, one of thirteen valleys radiating from Puy Mary. The village — one of France's Most Beautiful Villages — centres on its 12th-century Romanesque church, which preserves a relic of the Holy Thorn brought back from the Crusades by a local lord. At the far end of the village, Château d'Anjony rises from its basalt mound with four slender towers reaching 40 meters high. Built around 1430 by Louis d'Anjony, companion-in-arms of Joan of Arc and charged by Charles VII with restoring order in Haute-Auvergne, it has remained in the same family for six centuries. To reach the entrance, you walk through the village from the car park (15 minutes) — factor this into your timing.

The château's interior is worth the visit: the Hall of the Nine Worthies frescoes (around 1575) depict nine legendary knights — Charlemagne, King Arthur, Alexander the Great — life-size on their horses. They were rediscovered in the early 20th century behind 18th-century panelling. The chapel, meanwhile, is decorated with 16th-century Passion scenes. This castle also has a vendetta story worthy of a novel: the Anjony and Tournemire families, neighbours too close for comfort, feuded bitterly for two centuries. In 1523, Claude d'Anjony was assassinated by the Tournemires; in 1623, a duel in front of the church left three dead on each side. The visit is guided, approximately 60 minutes.

activities.text: The viewpoint loop above the Doire (3–4 km, ~1h30) offers sweeping views of the Cantal mountains and pastoral valleys. From the ridges, you can see the basalt organ pipes of neighbouring rocks and, on clear days, Puy Mary. Proper walking shoes essential — paths can be slippery after rain.

Study the houses of Tournemire in detail: lauze stone roofs, dark andesite window frames, carved lintels. This perfectly preserved traditional Cantal architecture represents an open-air manual of volcanic construction. The village is small, but every façade tells a story of craft, century, and family name.

days_plan.itin_title: Auvergne Circuit: Perched Villages and Volcanoes

visits.text: Château-Grillet from the road: 3.5 hectares of walled vineyards, an AOC in its own right since 1936 - the exclusive monopoly of a single family since the 18th century. The wine, a dry, barrel-aged white viognier, sells for around 100 euros a bottle. Visits are not offered. You stop, look at the walls, and realize that in wine, rarity has a very precise geography. Allow for a round trip from Tournon-sur-Rhône.

Saint-Joseph vines stretch over 50 km of terraces on the right bank of the Rhône, from Condrieu down to Cornas. It's the longest appellation in the Northern Rhône—and the most heterogeneous: between the granite plots of the north and the silty soils of the south, the same appellation name can cover very different wines. The road running along the terraces above Tournon offers the best river views of the route.

activities.text: Domaine Georges Vernay in Condrieu is where viognier almost disappeared - in the 1960s, the appellation had only 8 hectares left. Georges Vernay held firm, planted vines, and won people over. His daughter Christine now maintains the estate's status as an absolute benchmark for white wines from the northern Rhône. The tour is understated, the tasting precise. Book in advance. Allow for a round trip from Tournon-sur-Rhône.

Lunch at Beau Rivage in Condrieu - one Michelin star beside the river, Rhône market cooking with a remarkably well-explained list of local wines. It is one of the few restaurants where the sommelier explains why Vernay's viognier and Cuilleron's are so different despite being only 2 km apart. Book ahead. Allow for a round trip from Tournon-sur-Rhône.

Domaine Pierre Gonon in Mauves, in the Saint-Joseph appellation, produces little-known wines that Northern Rhône enthusiasts snap up—and which remain hard to find outside the estate. A tour with the family, no fuss. If you leave with bottles of red, wait at least five years before opening them.

days_plan.itin_title: Rhône Valley: From Northern Syrahs to Southern Grenaches

visits.text: The Abbey of Saint-Philibert in Tournus, founded in the 9th century, is one of the oldest Romanesque structures in France. Its nave, vaulted with transverse barrel vaults—a unique arrangement in Burgundy—is bathed in rosy light filtering through high windows. Monks brought the relics of Saint Philibert here while fleeing the Vikings on Noirmoutier.

The crypt of Saint-Philibert, beneath the choir, preserves pillars and capitals from the 10th century among the oldest in Burgundy. The atmosphere is contemplative, among the squat columns and vestiges of the Carolingian edifice.

The historic center of Tournus stretches between the abbey and the Saône. Medieval streets, townhouses, and half-timbered shops compose a preserved urban ensemble. The Musée Greuze, dedicated to the painter born here in 1725, displays his canvases alongside archaeological collections.

The quays along the Saône offer a peaceful riverside walk. Barges travel upstream toward Chalon and Lyon. The bridge spans the Saône with a view of the abbey and its bell tower reflected in the water.

activities.text: Visit to the Abbey of Saint-Philibert. The nave with transverse barrel vaults, the two-story narthex, the Chapel of Saint-Michel, and the crypt compose a unique architectural journey. Self-guided or audio-guided visit.
Tasting at a Tournus bouchon. The town is renowned for its Burgundian gastronomy: Bresse chicken, snails, gougères, and crème de cassis accompany wines from the Côte Chalonnaise.
Bike path along the Saône. The greenway follows the river between Tournus and Mâcon on a flat, shaded path. Bocage landscapes, stone villages, and barges punctuate the route.

days_plan.itin_title: Saône-et-Loire Road Trip: Bibracte, Cluny, Solutré & the Mâconnais Vineyards
Burgundy-Franche-Comté: The Most Beautiful Villages in 7 days

places.name: Tourrette Levens

visits.text: Tourrette-Levens sits perched on a rocky outcrop 15 km from Nice, in the Paillon valley. The medieval castle was built in 1176 by Raimond Chabaud along a Roman road that became the salt route.

Today the castle houses a free natural history museum, featuring a remarkable collection of butterflies and insects from around the world displayed in the keep. The outbuildings showcase over 300 taxidermy animals in their natural habitats.

The Sainte-Rosalie church, also known as Notre-Dame-de-l'Assomption, is one of the oldest in the region with a 12th-century core. The parish placed itself under Saint Rosalie's protection in 1631 after the plague, and today's baroque building is the result of several expansions up to 1792.

The White Penitents chapel, in the old village below the castle, saw its vault collapse in 1946. What remains is a curious triangular bell tower, one of only two in the County of Nice, built at an angle to save stone.
The old village, partly ruined after a late 19th-century earthquake, retains its cobbled alleys, vaulted passages and the Clock Gate. It's quick to explore but the atmosphere is worth the detour.

activities.text: Climb to the château viewpoint for the sea-to-mountain panorama, from Cap Ferrat to the peaks of the Mercantour. The village's three museums (butterflies and natural history, prehistory, traditional trades) are free and can be visited one after another.

The Mont Chauve hike starts in Tourrette-Levens and offers views of Nice, the village and the mountains. Allow around 3 hours 30 minutes for the 8 km round trip with 680 m of elevation gain; the route is moderately difficult.
Try the tourte de blettes, the real Niçoise version, in one of the village restaurants with terraces. A good introduction to County cuisine before heading to higher altitudes.

days_plan.itin_title: Secret valleys of the Nice hinterland in 6 days

map_keywords: White Penitents chapel triangular bell tower

visits.text: Tourrettes-sur-Loup, the “City of Violets,” is a medieval village perched on a spur above two small valleys. Pass through one of the two gates to discover the crescent-shaped Grand Rue: adjoining 15th-century stone houses, facades flowering with geraniums. The site has been inhabited since prehistoric times and was first mentioned as “castrum de Torretis” in the 11th century. The current 15th-century château, built by the Villeneuve family, now houses the town hall.

The Bastide aux Violettes is both a museum and a working farm. You'll discover the history of the Victoria violet, cultivated in Tourrettes since the 1880s to supply Grasse's perfume houses. The last three families of growers still cultivate them organically on agricultural terraces. Open to visitors year-round, but come from November to March to see the flowers in full bloom: the scent is subtle, almost airy.

The panoramic information panel at the bottom of the village overlooks the Cassan viaduct, the small valleys, and the coast. It also identifies the Pre-Alps summits to the north. Take the time to stay here for a few minutes; it's one of the quietest and least-known viewpoints in Nice's hinterland. Ideal in late afternoon when the light gilds the lanes.

activities.text: On the first weekend in March, the Fête des Violettes transforms the village into a floral parade. The tradition dates to the 1950s, driven by local producers and a Scottish artist who settled in the village. Today, nearly 10,000 visitors flock here. Floats covered in fresh violets in the lanes, a flower battle on Place de la Libération, a producers' market. If you're there, arrive early: the village entrance quickly becomes congested.

Taste violet specialties in the village shops: sugar-crystallized flowers, syrup, eau de toilette, soaps, scented creams. Crystallized flower confectionery is fragile and delicate and keeps for only a few weeks. A good gift to bring home, but it should be eaten soon.

The village is home to a concentration of potters, ceramicists, weavers, jewelers, and sculptors: Tourrettes has always attracted artists, and the trend accelerated in the 1950s. The small Saturday morning market on Place du Scourédou is a good opportunity to meet local makers directly. A relaxed atmosphere and direct contact with artisans.

days_plan.itin_title: The 15 Gems of the French Riviera and Backcountry
Nice's hinterland: 8 days of hilltop villages and the Mercantour

visits.text: Blois stands out halfway as the stop that needs no explanation: it is 195 km from Sancerre to Tours, and the town lies exactly midway. The royal château brings together four wings built under four different dynasties - Gothic, French Renaissance, Italianate Renaissance and Classical - without appearing incoherent. It condenses two centuries of French monarchy into a single building. Allow for a round trip from Tours for this visit to Blois.

Blois old town deserves an hour on foot: timber-framed houses on rue Pierre-de-Blois, the Denis-Papin staircase tumbling towards the Loire, and Renaissance town houses in the lanes below the château. It is less crowded than the valley's châteaux and therefore more pleasant to explore. Allow for a round trip from Tours for this walk in Blois.

Arriving on the Touraine side, Vouvray warrants a stop even if it's evening: caves carved into the white tuffeau line the road between the hillsides and the Loire. A few remain open late afternoon—a chance to understand that chenin isn't a grape variety, it's a question.

Domaine Huet in Vouvray is the address that put chenin on the world map. Gaston Huet planted his first vines in 1928; his son-in-law Noël Pinguet converted the estate to biodynamics in 1990. Three lieux-dits—Le Haut-Lieu, Le Mont, Clos du Bourg—on flint and tuffeau soils. Vintage bottles from the 1940s-1950s still trade at Paris auctions. Cellar tour by appointment.

Vouvray's troglodyte caves: carved into white tuffeau since the Middle Ages, they naturally maintain 12°C year-round—ideal temperature for chenin. Marc Brédif transformed one into an aging cellar and tasting room. Some galleries date to the 15th century; a few still serve as dwellings, which always surprises visitors.

Montlouis-sur-Loire, across the Cher, produces the same grape varieties as Vouvray on different soils—sandier, lighter. Same latitude, same Loire, different bank: the wines are generally rounder, less taut than their neighbors. François Chidaine has been the biodynamics figure here since the 1990s. His dry Clos Habert makes the ideal comparison point with a Huet from the same vintage.

activities.text: If you are in Blois on a Tuesday or Saturday morning, have lunch around the market on place Louis-XII before continuing your journey. The stalls offer fresh produce and Loir-et-Cher specialities: rillons, Berry goat cheeses and cured meats. Allow for a round trip from Tours for this stop in Blois.

First chenin tasting in Vouvray upon late-afternoon arrival—a dry, a semi-dry, a sparkling if the cellar offers it. The goal isn’t to understand everything tonight, it’s to calibrate your palate before the next two days. Marc Brédif or the Vouvray cooperative cellar are open without an appointment.

Comparative chenin tasting in five versions—dry, semi-dry, sweet, dessert, sparkling—from the same Vouvray appellation: it's the circuit's most educational exercise. The same grape, depending on vintage and harvest timing, yields wines with almost nothing in common. A dry Huet and a sweet Huet: same vineyard, same winemaker—and two radically different experiences.

Lunch at Les Halles de Tours or place Plumereau: Tours rillettes with a glass of dry Vouvray—Touraine's essential local pairing. Tours rillettes are fattier and less fibrous than those from Le Mans; the dry Vouvray, with its acidity, cuts through the fat perfectly. Ten-minute walk from the train station.

places.name: Tourtour

visits.text: Tourtour is nicknamed "the village in the Provençal sky" — and at 635 meters altitude, that's no exaggeration. On clear days, the panorama from Place des Ormeaux embraces the entire Var department all the way to the sea. This central square, shaded by two great elms and crossed by eight fountains, is the village heart where residents gather throughout the day. Its stone houses topped with round tiles, vaulted passages and sun-drenched lanes deserve a long stroll. Art galleries and artisan workshops line the streets — Tourtour has attracted creators for decades.

Tourtour's medieval castle, whose walls date from the Middle Ages, was remodeled in the 17th century. Its outer walls front the square and form the backdrop of Place des Ormeaux. The Church of Saint-Denis, Romanesque in its oldest sections, completes this compact, well-preserved built heritage. From the summit plateau, the view of Sainte-Victoire on clear days is striking.

activities.text: The Tourtour Provençal market is held Wednesday and Saturday mornings — it's one of the most popular markets in the backcountry thanks to the altitude and cool site. Honey, olives, soaps, pottery and local wines are offered in a convivial atmosphere. If you're there Saturday, the selection is more extensive.

Several olive oil mills operate around Tourtour and offer visits and olive oil tastings. Check with the tourist office for addresses open to the public. A walking trail descends from Tourtour to Villecroze passing by the Baume waterfall — allow 2.5 hours round trip.

days_plan.itin_title: The 10 Most Beautiful Villages of the Haut-Var
The Most Beautiful Villages: From the Alps to the Luberon in 3 Days
Var in 4 Days: From Bormes to the Most Beautiful Villages of the Verdon

Panorama Tourtour 635 m village dans le ciel

visits.text: A chapel, then fishermen's lodging, then a munitions depot: the cavities beneath the jumble of granite boulders housing the Aquarium Marin de Trégastel had several lives before this one. Three zones follow the rhythm of the tides, with lobsters, conger eels, catsharks, and a touch pool. It's small: one hour maximum. The real bonus is the terrace atop the boulders, at the foot of the rock called Père Éternel.

From Tourony beach in Trégastel, Château de Costaérès stands out on its islet: a neo-medieval building from the late 19th century where Polish writer Henryk Sienkiewicz stayed. Private property, closed to visitors, but the view from the sand is more than enough. Nearby, Coz-Pors beach is exposed for hundreds of meters at low tide. Bring water shoes, as the rocks can cut your feet.

activities.text: The GR34 links Trégastel to Ploumanac'h along about 4 km of coast, with significantly fewer people than the main section on the Perros-Guirec side. Views of Costaérès and the bay come one after another without a break. One hour 30 minutes one way, easy. The return follows the same path unless you arrange a shuttle between the two harbors.

Renting a paddleboard or kayak at Grève Blanche in Trégastel lets you circle the granite blocks at high tide, when they stand alone above the water with their bases submerged. Rental shops operate from April to September and give you a time window based on the tide. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes. A wetsuit isn't a luxury: the water tops out at around 17°C in August.

days_plan.itin_title: Brittany 7 days: Pink Granite, Lighthouses & Peninsulas

visits.text: Saint-Tugdual Cathedral, built from the 13th to 15th century in Caen stone, schist, and granite, blends three eras: the Romanesque Hastings tower (12th century), Gothic nave, and 60-meter openwork spire (1785) adorned with playing card motifs - financed, it's said, by Louis XVI's lottery.

The 15th-century cloister, blessed in 1468, is the most complete in Brittany. Its 46 Gothic arcades, stone flying buttresses, and wooden vault form an irregular trapezoid. It served as a place of prayer, an access route to Saint Yves' tomb, and a covered market.

The tomb of Saint Yves, patron saint of lawyers and the poor, is the focus of a major pardon pilgrimage on the third Sunday of May each year. Born in 1253 in Minihy-Tréguier and canonized in 1347, he is celebrated in a proverb: “Saint Yves was Breton, a lawyer and not a thief—a thing the people found admirable.”

The choir stalls, carved between 1509 and 1512 by two craftsmen, one from the Rhine valley, feature a fantastical bestiary on the misericords. Hidden in residents' homes during the Revolution, they escaped destruction.

Ernest Renan's birthplace, at number 20 on the street bearing his name, is a 16th-century half-timbered shipowner's house converted into a museum. The writer was born there in 1823—his “Life of Jesus” (1863) caused a scandal and earned him the label “European blasphemer” from the pope.

The Calvaire de la Protestation (1904), in kersanton stone, was erected in response to Renan's statue installed on Place du Martray facing the cathedral. The trilingual inscription—Latin, Breton, French—proclaims “This man was truly the Son of God”. A stone summary of the war between clericalists and secularists.

activities.text: Stroll through the historic center designated a conservation area. Place du Martray, Rue Renan, and Ruelle Saint-Yves are lined with 57 half-timbered houses from the 15th and 16th centuries—one of Brittany's best-preserved groups of buildings.
Descend to Tréguier port, nestled in the Jaudy estuary. Two former shipowners' towers once marked the town entrance. The Saint-François footbridge connects both banks.

Walk to Minihy-Tréguier (2 km) to see the Minihy church, where Saint Yves was rector, and the remains of Kermartin manor, where he was born and died. It's the starting point of the annual pardon pilgrimage.

days_plan.itin_title: Côtes-d'Armor Road Trip: Dinan, Pink Granite Coast, Bréhat Island & Lake Guerlédan
Brittany Road Trip: Villages with Character, Sea and History

visits.text: Trévoux, the former capital of the Principality of Dombes, has the remains of its castle standing above the Saône. This medieval fortress, distinct from the Palais du Parlement that later housed the court, dominates the old town with its massive towers. The ramparts offer views down over the river, the tiled rooftops and the Beaujolais hills on the horizon. The turbulent history of this principality, independent until 1762, can be read in every stone.

The Palais du Parlement, constructed between 1697 and 1703 in a restrained Lyonnais architectural style, housed the administration of the principality. Its most remarkable feature is the former courtroom and its historic painted decoration. The building remains connected to the judicial history of Trévoux and can be discovered during guided heritage tours.

Saint-Symphorien Church is a Neo-Romanesque building constructed in the early 20th century. Its façade, rounded arches and bell tower reflect the architectural vocabulary chosen for the new church. Inside, the nave and stained-glass windows create a restrained setting for worship in the heart of Trévoux.

The Trévoux et ses Trésors Museum traces the history of the Principality of Dombes and the skills that shaped the town. Its collections explore coin minting, printing, the Dictionnaire de Trévoux and the work of gold and silver wire drawers. Objects, documents and demonstrations reveal this distinctive heritage to visitors of all ages.

activities.text: Wander through the old town's lanes, which descend steeply from the castle to the quays. Timber-framed houses, Renaissance doors and secret traboules form a remarkably well-preserved medieval heritage. Craftspeople working in the old shops preserve traditional skills in this timeless setting.

Enjoy a river cruise on the Saône. Passenger boats travel up the peaceful river, offering an unusual perspective on Trévoux and its monuments. Green riverbanks, wooded islands and riverside villages pass by in a bucolic landscape. The boatman recounts the river's history, from the boatmen of the past to modern barges.

Explore the quays laid out as a promenade. Restaurant terraces are dotted along the Saône, inviting you to enjoy local cuisine overlooking the river. Barges and pleasure boats sway gently at their moorings. The summer bustle contrasts with the peace of winter, when mist and fog envelop the waterway.

Sample the specialities of the Dombes in one of Trévoux's restaurants. Freshwater fish, Bresse poultry and regional cheeses feature in generous dishes rooted in the local terroir. Depending on the menu and the season, discover traditional recipes accompanied by wines from the nearby Beaujolais or Bugey vineyards.

visits.text: The cave village of Trôo is arranged on three levels on the hillside above the Loir. The dwellings carved into the limestone tuffeau rise from the valley to the top of the hill. Steep lanes and stone stairways wind between the cave houses, which are still inhabited. The exceptional underground heritage includes cellars, mushroom farms and former shelters. The preserved rock-cut architecture bears witness to a thousand-year-old way of life. The underground galleries maintain a constant temperature summer and winter.

Saint-Martin Collegiate Church in Trôo dominates the village with its elegant 12th-century Romanesque bell tower. The church preserves remarkable murals and carved capitals. The building testifies to this fortified village's past religious importance. Contemporary stained glass brings a modern touch to the Romanesque architecture. The vaulted crypt holds little-known architectural treasures. Old baptismal fonts and devotional statues recount the site's spiritual history. The panorama from the forecourt takes in the entire Loir valley.

Trôo's talking well is the village's most famous curiosity. This 45-meter-deep well dug into limestone rock has astonishing acoustic properties that create a spectacular prolonged echo. Visitors enjoy testing the sound phenomenon by calling into the depths. Local legends attribute these mysterious voices to an enchanted spring or ghosts. The carved medieval wellhead testifies to the skill of the well diggers. This unusual place fascinates young and old with its unique acoustic mystery.

activities.text: The Butte aux Anglais overlooks Trôo and offers an exceptional 360-degree panorama of the Loir valley. This medieval castle motte was the strategic defensive point of the fortified village. The climb along the paths reveals the vegetation of the limestone hillsides. The summit unveils a postcard landscape with the tiered village, winding Loir, and green meadows. The viewpoint indicator helps identify visible landmarks. Sunset from this natural lookout creates unforgettable moods.

Cave Yuccas is a cave-dwelling ecomuseum presenting daily life in homes carved into the rock. Reconstructions show how caves were ingeniously fitted out as comfortable living spaces. Tools, furniture, and everyday objects illustrate past living conditions. Explanations detail the techniques used to excavate tuffeau and fit out the spaces. The reconstructed rooms include a kitchen, bedroom, and food-storage cellar. This captivating visit delves into local history and the region's unique vernacular architecture.

Hiking on Trôo's limestone hillsides along marked trails overlooking the valley. Paths wind between vineyards, dry meadows, and downy oak groves. Mediterranean flora surprises with wild orchids and aromatic plants. Successive viewpoints offer changing panoramas over the Loir and surrounding villages. Former tuffeau quarries testify to stone extraction. The 2–3-kilometer loop reveals the natural riches of the preserved hillsides.

days_plan.itin_title: Loir-et-Cher Itinerary: Royal Châteaux and the Loir Valley

visits.text: Troyes emerges as an open book of medieval history, its heart nicknamed the Champagne Cork unfurling nearly 456 half-timbered houses with multicolored facades. Born from the ashes of the terrible fire of May 24, 1524 that ravaged a third of the city, the historic quarter speaks to the ingenuity of Renaissance builders. The Ruelle des Chats winds between facades so close that roofs nearly touch—a testament to an era when property taxes were calculated by land area, pushing houses skyward. Between carved beams, bold corbelling, and paved courtyards, the Maison du Dauphin and the Hôtel du Lion Noir reveal the opulence of the merchant city.

A landmark of the Aube, Saint-Pierre-et-Saint-Paul Cathedral impresses with its dimensions: 114 meters long and 28 meters high beneath the vaults. Yet its luminous adornment is what fascinates visitors: 1,500 m² of stained glass—the equivalent of two handball courts—transform the building into a glass lantern. Built between 1200 and the 17th century and never fully completed—the south tower is missing—it showcases the excellence of the Champagne School of stained glass. Just a short walk away, Sainte-Madeleine Church, the oldest sanctuary in Troyes, preserves an intricately carved 16th-century rood screen, one of the few still standing in France, along with stained-glass windows depicting the Creation and the Tree of Jesse.

Inside the imposing 18th-century Hôtel-Dieu-le-Comte, the Cité du Vitrail celebrates a staggering heritage. Permanent and temporary exhibitions reveal the art of colored light from the Middle Ages to the present day. Not far away, the Maison de l'Outil et de la Pensée Ouvrière occupies the elegant Hôtel de Mauroy (16th century), lovingly restored by the Compagnons du Devoir. In a contemporary display shine 12,000 age-old tools from the 17th to the 19th century, rasps, planes and chisels, witnesses to the trades that shaped France.

activities.text: The historic capital of hosiery since the Middle Ages, Troyes carries on its textile DNA today through four outlet centers totaling 200 shops. Marques City, McArthurGlen in Pont-Sainte-Marie, Villages de Marque or Marques Avenue in Saint-Julien-les-Villas line their aisles with major brands offering discounted designer goods and end-of-line products. The legacy of Troyes' textile industry lives on here through smart shopping and economic heritage.

Four mornings a week (Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday), Troyes vibrates to the rhythm of its traditional markets. The Halles welcome a gourmet ballet of local producers showcasing Troyes andouillette IGP, creamy Chaource AOC, Côte des Bar champagne, and ratafia. Facing the cathedral, the Cellier Saint-Pierre has been distilling the Prunelle de Troyes since 1840—an artisanal liqueur born from the maceration of wild sloe berries in alcohol. Secret recipe, ancestral gesture, exceptional bottle.

days_plan.itin_title: Aube Tour: Champagne, Medieval Heritage and the Lakes of the Forêt d'Orient

visits.text: Notre-Dame Cathedral of Tulle. Built from 1103 on the site of a Merovingian abbey, it blends Romanesque and Gothic styles. Its bell tower with an octagonal spire rises between 73 and 75 meters depending on the source—it's the tallest in Limousin. Inside, the Great Organ from 1839 is listed as a Historic Monument, and the large blue stained glass window by Jean-Jacques Grüber (1979) tells the story of the Lunade, a procession that ended a plague epidemic in the 14th century.

13th-century Gothic cloister. The only remaining cloister in Bas-Limousin, it adjoined the former Saint-Martin Abbey. The "gallery of angels" features sculpted vaults. The chapter house preserves two 14th-century murals depicting the Last Supper and Christ's Entry into Jerusalem. Listed as a Historic Monument since 1840.

Cité de l'Accordéon et des Patrimoines. Opened in April 2024 in the former Banque de France building, it presents three exhibition trails: the accordion (Tulle is the French capital of the instrument, with the Maugein factory established in 1919), “poinct de Tulle” lace and the history of the arms factory. Interactive museum with an audio guide available in Occitan.

Maison Loyac. Architectural masterpiece from the 16th century located in the Enclos quarter. The facade blends Renaissance and Flamboyant Gothic styles, adorned with pediments sculpted with plants and animals (lion, greyhound, wild boar, mermaid). Two projecting watch turrets frame the columned doorway.

activities.text: Stroll through the Trech quarter and the Enclos. Tulle's medieval heart centers on the cathedral. Sloping streets, staircases, tall 15th–16th-century houses with overhanging upper stories and wooden balconies. Don't miss the Coin des Clampes fountain, “the meeting place of chatterboxes” in Occitan, immortalized by a 1984 sculpture.
Tulle Market. The banks of the Corrèze come alive on Wednesday and Saturday mornings. Local products, friendly atmosphere along the river.

days_plan.itin_title: Corrèze Road Trip: Villages and Dordogne Valley

visits.text: Turckheim is one of the few Alsatian towns to preserve all three fortified gates intact: the Porte de France (around 1315, the oldest), the Porte du Brand, and the Porte du Munster. Since Emperor Henry VII elevated the village to the status of an imperial city in 1312 and granted the right to build defensive walls, the town has been part of the Alsatian Décapole. The Porte de France, where storks regularly settle in nests at the top, opens onto Place Turenne—named for the marshal who won the last major decisive battle here in 1675 against the imperial forces, making Alsace definitively French.

The Corps de Garde, built around 1580, now houses the tourist office. It's from this sandstone building, with its double-headed imperial eagle on the facade recalling the town's status as a free imperial city, that the Night Watchman begins his rounds every evening at 10 p.m., from May to October. In period costume—tricorn, halberd, horn, and lantern—he sings out the hours in the alleys, calling to residents to make sure they extinguish their fires and candles. A centuries-old tradition, interrupted from 1939 until the Liberation, makes Turckheim one of the few towns in France to keep this occupation alive.

activities.text: Join the Night Watchman's rounds in the evening—departure from the Corps de Garde at 10 p.m., from May to October. He sings, provides commentary, and reveals the town's secrets in Alsatian and French, followed by a procession of visitors that grows as he makes his way through the alleys. If you want a front-row spot, arrive 15 minutes early.

Climb to the hillsides of Grand Cru Brand, one of Alsace's most renowned vineyards, whose granite soils warm the grapes all day and give the heat back at night — producing particularly concentrated wines. The wine trail from the north ramparts offers views of Colmar and the Rhine plain. The Cave de Turckheim, founded in 1955, brings together the village's winemakers and offers tastings open to all.

visits.text: Caesar's Tower (13th century). Circular keep 18 meters high. The 63 steps of the spiral staircase lead to the top offering a 360° panorama over the Corrèze causse. Turenne was the seat of a powerful viscounty for 10 centuries, virtually independent from the Kingdom of France: the viscounts minted coins and levied taxes. On May 8, 1738, Charles-Godefroy, the last viscount riddled with gambling debts, sold everything to Louis XV. End of the saying "Happy as a viscomtin".

Treasure Tower (13th century). Rectangular keep with buttresses measuring 9.50 m by 12.50 m where the viscounty's archives and treasure were kept. The Guards' Room, with a vaulted ceiling 10 meters high, features a beautiful fireplace and a collection of Louis XIII salt chests.
Collegiate Church of Notre-Dame Saint-Pantaléon. 17th-century church built by the viscounts of Turenne. The interior contains a gilded altarpiece and period woodwork.

activities.text: Climb via Rue Droite. The main street climbs from the bottom of the village to the towers. Houses with turrets, projecting watch turrets and Renaissance windows testify to past prosperity. Good shoes are recommended: the slope is steep and the cobblestones are sometimes slippery.

places.name: Utah Beach

visits.text: The Utah Beach Landing Museum is built on the very spot where American troops came ashore on 6 June 1944. In ten chronological sequences, it retraces the preparation and course of D-Day. An authentic B-26 Marauder bomber takes pride of place in a dedicated hangar.

Step out of the museum and walk on the sand of Utah Beach. At low tide, remnants of the Atlantic Wall, bunkers and anti-landing obstacles, are still visible among the dunes. More than 23,000 soldiers landed here in a single day.

In Sainte-Mère-Église, look up: a parachutist dummy hangs from the church steeple, recalling the night of 5 to 6 June 1944 when paratroopers of the 82nd Airborne were dropped on the town. The church's stained-glass windows depict this episode of the landings.

The Airborne Museum, facing the steeple, spreads over five buildings with immersive displays. Climb aboard an authentic C-47 aircraft that took part in the operations of 6 June, and relive the parachute drops in a flight simulator.
Look for Milestone Zero of the Liberty Road, on the square in Sainte-Mère-Église. This marker opens the historic route that traces the Allied advance from Normandy to Bastogne in Belgium.

activities.text: Follow the 90 'In Honor Of' memorial panels spread across 7 coastal communes around Utah Beach. Each panel pays tribute to the units and soldiers who fought in this sector.
Visit the German battery at Crisbecq in Saint-Marcouf, one of the best preserved of the Atlantic Wall. Its reinforced concrete casemates housed guns able to fire on Allied ships off Utah Beach.
Head to the village of Sainte-Marie-du-Mont to see its distinctive steeple, a landmark visible for kilometres that guided American paratroopers on the night of the landings.

visits.text: Saint-Pierre Abbey Church. Former Benedictine abbey church built from 1030, consecrated in 1095. The gabled bell tower, typical of Limousin, rises from a square base to an octagonal plan. The 11th-century crypt, unique in Bas-Limousin, housed the relics of Breton saints Léon and Coronat, transferred here for protection from Vikings. Listed as a Historic Monument in 1840.
Bécharie Gate. 14th-century fortified gate, sole remnant of the medieval ramparts that protected the town.

activities.text: Walk on the rocky promontory. Uzerche is nicknamed the “Pearl of Limousin.” The local saying goes, “Whoever has a house in Uzerche has a castle in Limousin.” The village perched on a spur overlooks a meander of the Vézère. The towers and turrets of noble houses testify to the town's past importance. Panoramic view from the Lunade esplanade.

days_plan.itin_title: Corrèze Road Trip: Villages and Dordogne Valley

visits.text: Pont du Gard, a masterpiece of Roman engineering on the UNESCO World Heritage list since 1985. The three-tiered aqueduct bridge rises 49 metres high and stretches 275 metres across the Gardon. Built in the 1st century to carry water from Uzès to Nîmes over 50 kilometres, it illustrates ancient hydraulic mastery with a drop of only 12 metres. The 52 stacked arches use blocks of shelly limestone weighing up to 6 tonnes, assembled without mortar. The 165-hectare protected site offers a museum, garrigue trails, Gardon beaches and summer sound and light shows. The monument is about 12 km from the stopover town, 12 minutes by road.

Mémoires de Garrigue trail around the Pont du Gard, a 1.4-kilometre loop through the Mediterranean landscape. The path reveals remains of the Roman aqueduct among holm oaks, Aleppo pines, vines and olive trees. Educational panels explain the construction of the underground channel, Roman techniques and the garrigue ecosystem. Aromatic plants - thyme, rosemary, cistus - perfume the stony path. Rocky outcrops reveal the Urgonian limestone quarried by the builders. The shaded walk invites you to contemplate the monument from different viewpoints. The start is about 12 km from the stopover town, 12 minutes by road.

Duché d'Uzès, France's first duchy created in 1565. The ducal palace's Renaissance facade overlooks Place aux Herbes bordered by medieval arcades. The 11th-century Tour Bermonde, a rectangular keep, stands beside the Gothic Saint-Hubert chapel. Historic apartments reveal period furniture, Flemish tapestries, and family memorabilia of the Dukes of Uzès. 14th-century vaulted cellars host temporary exhibitions. The reconstructed medieval garden cultivates medicinal and aromatic plants. The private residence still inhabited by the ducal family offers guided audio tours.

Fenestrelle Tower in Uzès, France's only circular belfry, dates from the 12th century. The 42-metre-high cylindrical tower is adorned with three levels of twin openings facing the four cardinal points. Its exceptional Romanesque architecture served as the bell tower of the medieval cathedral destroyed during the Wars of Religion. The bells once marked the rhythm of the city's religious life and agricultural activities.

Place aux Herbes, the vibrant heart of Uzès surrounded by medieval arcades and golden-stone ochre facades. The Provençal market on Wednesday and Saturday mornings animates the paved square beneath century-old plane trees. Stalls offer local specialties: black truffle in winter, aged Pélardon, garrigue honey, Picholine olives. Café terraces invite watching the ballet of shoppers and pétanque players. Shopping streets radiate from the square toward Renaissance mansions and potter workshops perpetuating Uzès ceramic tradition.

activities.text: Swimming in the Gardon beneath the arches of the Pont du Gard. The beaches laid out 200 metres from the monument offer supervised swimming areas in summer with play areas for children. The clear, cool waters of the river invite you to cool off after visiting the site. The shaded banks provide picnic spaces under the tamarisks. Swimming opposite the ancient bridge makes for a unique experience combining heritage and nature. The moderate current allows paddling on rings and water games with the family. The site is about 12 km from the stopover town, 12 minutes by road.

Uzès truffle market from November to March, meeting place for truffle hunters and dealers. Every Saturday morning on Place aux Herbes, the black diamond market gathers local producers selling fresh tubers weighed discreetly. The hushed transaction atmosphere contrasts with the square's usual liveliness. Gard truffles, melanosporum variety, rival those from Périgord and Vaucluse. Restaurants offer truffle menus celebrating the precious fungus. The Maison de la Truffe organizes discovery workshops and truffle-hunting demonstrations.

Visit to potters' workshops keeping alive the ceramic tradition of Uzès since antiquity. The craftspeople shape utilitarian and decorative pieces on the wheel from the characteristic red clay. Ancestral techniques sit alongside contemporary creations: Provençal jars, glazed tableware, sculptures. Demonstrations reveal the precise gestures of throwing, glazing and firing in a traditional kiln. Workshop-boutiques line the lanes of the historic centre offering original local production.
