visits.text: The Puymin and Villasse archaeological sites form the largest Gallo-Roman complex open to the public in France. At Puymin, the Maison à l'Apollon Lauré spreads across 2,000 m² of ruins, and the ancient theater dating from the 1st century BCE still hosts summer performances.
Across the avenue, the Villasse quarter reveals the Rue des Boutiques lined with ancient shops, the Maison à la Tonnelle and its 3,000 m², and public baths with their basins and lead pipes.
The Musée Théo Desplans, located on the Puymin site, gathers over 2,000 objects from excavations: Roman marble statuary, mosaics, ceramics, and architectural elements.

Cross the single-arched Roman bridge that has spanned the Ouvèze for two thousand years. It links the lower town to the steep lanes of the medieval Haute-Ville, dominated by the ruins of the Counts of Toulouse's castle built in 1195.
The 11th-century Romanesque Cathédrale Notre-Dame de Nazareth preserves an apse with a semi-dome vault and a cloister with carved colonnettes. Its eastern end rests on reused ancient foundations.
Lose yourself in the cobbled streets of the Haute-Ville. Fortified gates, mossy fountains, a belfry, and shaded small squares compose an intact medieval scene atop the rock.

activities.text: The Tuesday morning Provençal market floods the lower town's streets. Olives, seasonal truffles, Ventoux goat cheeses, and herbes de Provence fill the stalls.
Visit wine estates around Vaison to taste Côtes-du-Rhône Villages. The vines climb in terraces on the Ventoux foothills.
Loop hike from the Haute-Ville toward the surrounding hills. The trails cross garrigue, olive groves, and lavender fields with views of the Dentelles de Montmirail.

From Vaison, the road to Mont Ventoux via Malaucène climbs to the summit at 1,912 meters; allow time for a return drive from Vaison-la-Romaine. The observatory and orientation table overlook a panorama stretching from the Alps to the Mediterranean. The landscape changes from cedar forest to the desert of white stones along the final hairpin bends.

days_plan.itin_title: Vaucluse: Avignon, Luberon Villages & Ventoux Routes
Rhône Valley: From Northern Syrahs to Southern Grenaches

visits.text: The priory of Hérival takes a little effort to reach. Founded in the 12th century by Augustinian canons from Chaumousey, it is tucked away in a wooded valley a few kilometers from the town of Val-d'Ajol. It is not a spectacular site — the surviving parts of the convent buildings are undergoing gradual, discreet rehabilitation — but its atmosphere of a place forgotten by the world is exactly what you are looking for on this itinerary.

activities.text: Le Val-d'Ajol is a commune of 25 hamlets scattered across a landscape of valleys and streams — you will not get lost, but you will linger. For the Belvédère de Mérelle in Gérardmer, allow for a day trip from Le Val-d'Ajol, followed by a climb on foot: the observation tower cannot be reached by car. If textiles interest you, ask the Tourist Office about a possible visit to the Fayetterie, a former water-powered spinning mill still in operation.

days_plan.itin_title: Vosges Abbey Trail: Monastic Heritage

visits.text: Val d'Isère stretches a kilometer in the heart of Haute-Tarentaise, ringed by summits topping 3,700 m. Wander the village center's lanes and admire stone chalets with lauze-slab roofs that remain faithful to traditional rural architecture.

The église Saint-Bernard-de-Menthon, built in the 11th century of cut stone, towers at the village center. Simple and massive, it has marked the rhythm of Avalin life for nearly a thousand years. In front, the larch mission cross (1847) marks Chapelle Saint-Jean, built to protect the village from avalanches descending from Solaise.

Continue to Le Fornet, an authentic hamlet at the very end of the valley. Stone chalets pressed close together, absolute silence: here you touch raw mountain, before the road attacks the hairpin turns of the Iseran pass.

Take the Col de l'Iseran road (2,764 m), the highest paved pass in the French Alps. The panorama sweeps across the glaciers of Vanoise and Gran Paradiso on the Italian side. At the summit, a stone chapel marks the border between Tarentaise and Maurienne.

Parc National de la Vanoise, France's first national park (created 1963), protects 535 km² of core zone. More than 1,400 plant species and remarkable fauna are recorded: ibex, chamois, marmots, bearded vultures, and golden eagles.

Chapelle Saint-Barthélemy, in the hamlet of Laisinant, shelters a restored painting of the Virgin and Child. Built before 1633, it offers a fine starting point for park trails. Nearby, a tapped spring supplies the resort with drinking water.

activities.text: Hike to Refuge du Fond des Fours. From Pont Saint-Charles, the trail crosses the Malpasset gorges, rejoins Val d'Isère village, and climbs the Manchet valley in the heart of the National Park. The refuge (2,537 m) offers a panorama of the Méan Martin glacier.

Family hike to Lac de l'Ouillette (2,350 m). This turquoise alpine lake is reached in 45 minutes from the top of the Solaise cable cars, significantly reducing effort. Beautiful panorama over the Bellevarde rock.
Mountain biking or e-biking on the bike park trails linking Tignes and Val d'Isère. Over 220 km of marked trails between technical descents and panoramic rides overlooking mountain lakes.

days_plan.itin_title: Savoie from Lakes to Glaciers: Yenne to Haute-Maurienne

visits.text: The Cians Gorges form one of the most beautiful routes in the Alpes-Maritimes. The D28 plunges into a canyon where the rock changes color over the kilometers: white limestone at first, then deep red schist at Pra d'Astier. The narrow road runs just a few meters above the torrent, making it difficult to pass buses. Allow 45 minutes to drive through, plus photo stops.

The Daluis Gorges are the most spectacular “Regional Nature Reserve” in the Alpes-Maritimes: vertiginous walls of red pelites 250 million years old, nicknamed the “Nice Colorado.” The Pont de la Mariée spans the void at a height of 120 meters—a must-stop. The road passes through 17 tunnels cut into the red rock, a procession of shadow and light. The Point Sublime viewpoint offers the craziest view of the entire drive.

Valberg, a family resort at 1,669 meters, is one of the few French resorts awarded the “Flocon Vert” label for its environmental commitment—streetlights switched off at midnight, free shuttles between hamlets, a preserved starry sky. Outside ski season, the slopes become hiking trails and the lifts carry mountain bikes. A relaxed atmosphere, with reasonable prices compared to the coast.

Valberg's planetary trail offers an educational loop with a scale model of the solar system: the planets are spaced proportionally, giving a dizzying sense of the distances in space. Explanatory panels, Alpine views; pleasant even without a particular interest in astronomy.

Mont Mounier, at 2,817 meters, is the emblematic summit of the Nice backcountry. Full-day hike from Valberg, rewarded by a panorama over the Southern Alps and Mediterranean on clear days. For the less athletic, the resort's belvederes already overlook alpine pastures and larch forests.

activities.text: Hiking the GR 52A from Valberg: alpine pastures with génépi, rhododendrons and mountain flowers. Several difficulty levels, from a 2-hour family walk to ascents to 2,500 meters. A guide office at the resort offers guided outings.

Mountain biking and road cycling in the Cians and Daluis gorges: the narrow roads bordered by red pelites are among the most photogenic cycling routes in the Alpes-Maritimes. Electric mountain bikes are available to rent at the resort for painless climbs.

Stargazing at Valberg, a resort designated an “International Dark Sky Reserve” since 2019. Far from any light pollution, local astronomy guides set up telescopes and point out constellations during themed summer evenings. Book for moonless nights.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpes-Maritimes Road Trip: Riviera and Mercantour, 13 days

visits.text: Château de Valençay. This Renaissance residence once hosted the Prince of Talleyrand, one of France's greatest diplomats. The château has retained its original Empire furniture, and its salons bear witness to the refinement of the Napoleonic era. The kitchens, pantry, and cellars illustrate the importance of gastronomy for Talleyrand, whose table was renowned throughout Europe. The First Empire theater, a jewel from 1810, still preserves its period sets and backdrops.

Château gardens and grounds. The estate extends over 53 hectares with formal French gardens, the terraced Duchess's garden, and Antonin's garden showcasing 300 species of aromatic plants in tribute to Antonin Carême. The Forêt des Princes offers a 4 km woodland trail with seven historical stops. For children: a mini-farm, scent game, children's château, and Grand Labyrinthe de Napoléon.

Valençay town center. The heritage trail follows medallions set into the ground and leads you to the Halle au Blé, the former spinning mill, Saint-Martin church, and Talleyrand's tomb. The town has two AOC designations bearing its name: the pyramid-shaped Valençay goat cheese and Valençay wine.

activities.text: Valençay cheese and wine tasting. Local producers offer a chance to discover Valençay AOC goat cheese in its truncated pyramid shape, along with Valençay AOC white and red wines. A winemaking and cheesemaking tradition stretching back centuries.

Valençay Automobile Museum. A remarkable collection of over 60 vintage cars, all in working order, traces the history of the automobile. The museum also displays fire trucks, motorcycles, bicycles, garage signs, and period posters.

Train touristique du Bas-Berry. Plan a return trip from Valençay to reach the departure station in Écueillé. This historic line offers scenic journeys through the Berry countryside. The train travels through pastoral landscapes and traditional villages at a pace that lets you appreciate every detail of rural Berry.

days_plan.itin_title: Indre Road Trip: Secret Berry and the Vallée Noire

places.name: Valence

visits.text: The Cathédrale Saint-Apollinaire, founded in the 11th century, was rebuilt identically in the 17th after the destruction of the Wars of Religion. Inside, multicolored stained glass bathes the nave in gentle light.

At 57 Grande Rue stands the Maison des Têtes—a sight that stops every passerby. This mansion, built around 1530, bridges the late Gothic and Renaissance periods. Its façade sculptures represent the Winds, Fortune, Time, Theology, Law, and Medicine.

Step into the corridor of the Maison des Têtes: its vaulted ceiling sits beside medallion busts of Roman emperors. In the interior courtyard, the Church Fathers appear in medallions beneath the gallery arches.

The Musée de Valence, Art et Archéologie adjoins the cathedral. Perched at the edge of the city's first terrace, it offers sweeping landscape views while presenting collections spanning from prehistory to contemporary art.

Parc Jouvet spreads across 7 hectares below the Champ de Mars. Labeled a "Remarkable Garden," it combines formal French style in its central zone with landscape style in its paths. Plane trees over 40 meters high, a rose garden and water features bordered by exotic plants make up the setting.
The Armenian Heritage Center traces the history of the Armenian people's exodus and their arrival in Valence in the 1920s. A place of memory, spare and moving.

activities.text: Head to the Champ de Mars esplanade, inaugurated in 1862. The historic kiosk, now a listed monument, frames a perspective of Crussol Castle and the Vivarais mountains—a vista protected as a natural site since 1942.

Wander through the lanes of old Valence around Place des Clercs. Renaissance townhouses, covered passages, and shaded squares unfold one after another. Le Pendentif, a 16th-century funerary monument, surprises with its unusual form.
Sample the Suisse, a shortbread cookie shaped like a little person and perfumed with orange blossom—a Valence specialty. Pastry shops in the city center keep this tradition alive.
The Parc Jouvet miniature train, in service since 1967, loops around the park. Kids also love the playground, trampoline, and aviary.

days_plan.itin_title: Drome Provencale Road Trip: Villages and Terroirs
Rhône-Alpes Circuit: Perched Villages and Mountain Peaks

places.name: Valence D Agen

visits.text: The market hall on Place Nationale has hosted the market every Tuesday morning since Edward I founded the bastide in 1283. Its arcades shelter producers and artisans.
The del Théron washhouse is the oldest of the three washhouses and is unusual in character. Listed as a historic monument, it recalls a time when washerwomen gathered to scrub their laundry.
The Saint-Bernard washhouse complements this water-related heritage. Restored and adorned with flowers, it remains a gathering place for residents.

Notre-Dame Church, rebuilt in 1902, is neo-Renaissance in style. Its 1865 organ by Vincent Cavaillé-Coll and a gilded wooden Virgin and Child from the 17th century adorn the Rayonnant Gothic interior.
The traditional dovecote exemplifies Gascon rural architecture. Its distinctive silhouette was once a feature of agricultural estates.

activities.text: Follow the cycle route along the Canal des Deux Mers. The canal port offers a shady stop for cyclists and leisure boaters.
Explore the public garden within the former Capuchin convent grounds. Fountains and plantings reflect the town's three-flower classification.
Discover orchards spreading across the Garonne valley. Quercy melons, Agen prunes, and Moissac chasselas ripen under the sun of southwest France.

days_plan.itin_title: Tarn-et-Garonne Road Trip: Bastides and Orchards

map_keywords: Halle de la Place Nationale Valence-d'Agen

visits.text: The Valenciennes Museum of Fine Arts houses a prestigious collection of 17th-century Flemish painting, dominated by Rubens (Triptych of Saint Stephen, Descent from the Cross), Van Dyck and Jordaens. Place Carpeaux at the museum's heart showcases sculptures by the celebrated Valenciennois artist.

Saint-Géry Church, Valenciennes' main church, houses the statue of Notre-Dame du Saint-Cordon. According to legend, in 1008 the Virgin appeared to plague-ravaged residents and encircled the city with a protective scarlet cord. The epidemic ceased immediately.

The Notre-Dame-du-Saint-Cordon Basilica (1852–1864), in neo-Gothic style inspired by Amiens and Chartres, dominates the city with its octagonal spire. Its three-level nave creates a strong sense of light and transparency. Interior decoration was entrusted to local artists.

Walk through the recently renovated streets of Old Valenciennes. Eight information pillars line the route, recounting the history of the city's oldest streets, once part of a fortified town in Hainaut.
The museum's archaeological crypt presents Gallo-Roman and medieval antiquities found in the Valenciennes region: bronzes, pilgrimage badges and bishops' crosiers testify to the city's long history.

activities.text: Stroll through the Rhônelle garden, a landscaped park following the river south of the city centre. Its willow- and plane-lined paths offer a peaceful setting after visiting the museum.
Valenciennes, birthplace of painter Watteau and sculptor Carpeaux, boasts numerous ornate façades. Look up at Place d'Armes and its pilastered buildings to spot traces of this artistic past.
In September, the Tour du Saint-Cordon gathers thousands of pilgrims who follow the legendary path of the Virgin's protective cord through city streets, to the sound of the hymn “Reine des Cieux”.

days_plan.itin_title: Nord Tour: Lille, Belfries and Flemish Culture

places.name: Vallauris

visits.text: Low vault, cool stone, eighteen Masonite panels following the curve: the Romanesque chapel of Vallauris castle houses War and Peace, Picasso's final major political manifesto after Guernica (1937) and Massacre in Korea (1951). The artist lived in Vallauris from 1948 to 1955, painted the fresco in 1952, over 100 m² total. Work donated to the State in 1956, national museum inaugurated in 1959. A third panel, The Four Corners of the World, was added in 1958. Closed Tuesdays.

activities.text: The ticket also grants access to the Magnelli Museum, municipal ceramics museum housed in the same castle (former priory of the Lérins monks). Contemporary ceramics collections from the International Biennial, Alberto Magnelli room, and previously unseen film of Picasso working at the Madoura workshop. Allow 45 additional minutes.

days_plan.itin_title: French Riviera Art Museums and Galleries: An 8-Day Journey

map_keywords: Picasso National Museum War and Peace Vallauris

visits.text: The Vallée des Merveilles is one of Europe's largest open-air rock art sites: about 40,000 engravings pecked into glacier-polished rocks around Mont Bégo (2,872 m). Dating from 3,300 to 1,700 BCE according to Mercantour National Park. The site covers 17 km² at altitudes ranging from 1,900 to 2,700 meters. Listed as a historic monument since 1989.

The hamlet of Castérino (1,550 m) is the main gateway to the valley. A few mountain huts, a parking lot, a national park information point. This is where certified guides set out on day trips to the Merveilles or Fontanalba sectors. The road from Saint-Dalmas-de-Tende climbs through hairpin bends for 12 km.

activities.text: An accredited guide is strongly recommended to identify the engravings, and you are not allowed to leave the GR52 without a guide. The landscape of alpine lakes, scree slopes and marmots is as rewarding as the engravings themselves.

For a shorter option, the Vallée de Fontanalba (also from Castérino) offers its own engravings on a more accessible trail: 9 km round trip, 400 meters elevation gain, 4 to 5 hours. The 'sacred way,' an alignment of late-Neolithic engravings, is one of the route's highlights.

days_plan.itin_title: Nice's hinterland: 8 days of hilltop villages and the Mercantour

visits.text: The Pont d'Arc raises its majestic 54-meter arch over the Ardèche River. This geological wonder sculpted 500,000 years ago marks the gateway to the Gorges, protected as a nature reserve. Turquoise waters glide beneath the natural bridge against a backdrop of spectacular limestone cliffs.

The Grotte Chauvet 2 faithfully recreates the original cave inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage list. This monumental replica unveils 425 cave paintings dating back 36,000 years, humanity's first masterpiece. Horses, lions, and rhinoceroses come alive on the walls in a space reproduced exactly as it was.

The Galerie de l'Aurignacien rounds out the visit with a 700 m² space for playful exploration. Life-size animals and the giant panorama immerse you in the daily life of Aurignacian people 36,000 years ago. Touchscreen terminals, immersive films, and educational workshops reveal the environment of our ancestors.

Vallon-Pont-d'Arc brings its Provençal lanes to life around the main square. The village preserves Aubusson tapestries in the Town Hall and a covered square, a former grain hall. The vibrant summer atmosphere fills terraces and artisan boutiques.

The developed beaches at the foot of Pont d'Arc invite swimming in the clear waters of the Ardèche. The panoramic viewpoint offers a view down onto the arch and gorges. Marked trails allow you to approach the site from different angles.

activities.text: Canoeing down the Gorges is the signature activity of the Ardèche. Several routes await paddlers: a short 8 km descent, a 24 km discovery route, or the physically demanding full 32 km descent. Rental companies provide equipment, return shuttles, and safety instructions for an unforgettable day.

The equipped bivouac sites at Gaud and Gournier allow a two-day descent through the heart of the nature reserve. These campsites provide drinking water, restrooms, showers, barbecue grills, and round-the-clock supervision. A night under the stars in the gorges offers a unique chance to disconnect.

Swimming in the Ardèche provides refreshment after a day of exploration. Pebble beaches and secret coves line the river. The crystal-clear waters invite relaxation in a preserved natural setting under the Ardèche sun.

Hiking along the Gorges offers exceptional panoramas. The long-distance trail crosses the nature reserve over 24 km in two days. The developed lookout points along the scenic road offer eleven spectacular views of the canyon.

places.name: Vannes

visits.text: Saint-Pierre Cathedral has dominated the hilltop of Mené since the 5th century—one of seven cathedrals on the Tro Breiz pilgrimage route. Construction spanned seven centuries, from the 11th to 19th, and it shows: the base of the north bell tower is Romanesque, the nave is 15th-century Gothic, and the Renaissance rotunda from 1537 is a small masterpiece. Inside, don't miss the tomb of Saint Vincent Ferrier in the north transept and the ten Baroque marble altarpieces. Note: the cathedral is under restoration until 2027; verify access before visiting.

Head down toward the Garenne Gardens at the foot of the eastern ramparts. This 15,000-square-metre space was landscaped in the 1950s, but the site served as a pleasure park for Duke John IV as early as 1387. Every year, 30,000 flowers are planted here. Visit in early spring and the Japanese cherry trees in bloom create a spectacular display. The washhouses below, built in the 18th century and restored in 2005–2006, recall the days when Vannes's laundresses beat their linen here.

La Cohue, once a medieval market hall and courthouse, now houses the Fine Arts Museum. Inside you'll find works by 19th-century Breton artists through contemporary pieces. The building itself is worth lingering over—one of Vannes's oldest, with a structure tracing back to the 13th century. Allow a good hour to explore.

Pass through the Saint-Vincent Gate, the main entrance to the walled town. Rebuilt in the 18th century, it's decorated with niches holding statues of saints. This is the ideal starting point for climbing into the historic centre. From here, you can already glimpse the rampart towers and the slate roofs of the intra-muros.

Wander the cobbled streets between Place Henri IV and Place des Lices. The half-timbered and corbelled houses date from the 15th and 16th centuries—Vannes preserves some of Brittany's finest examples. On a corner of Place Henri IV, look for the carved busts of 'Vannes and his wife', two 16th-century figures who became the city's mascot. Nobody really knows who they represent.

The Constable's Tower, the tallest of the ramparts at 20 metres, is recognisable by its large mullioned windows. Built in the mid-15th century, it served as both a defensive tower and residence for the Duke of Brittany's military commander. Victor Hugo sketched it during his 1834 visit. Climb to the top for views over the gardens and the old town.

activities.text: The Place des Lices market runs Wednesday and Saturday mornings. It's one of Brittany's finest—kouign-amann still warm from the oven, far breton, Gulf oysters and farmhouse cider. Arrive early if you want room to move and the freshest produce.

From Vannes harbour, board a cruise into the Gulf of Morbihan—literally 'little sea' in Breton. Boats serve Monks' Island and Arz Island, or offer a full Gulf circuit with its dozens of islets. Allow 2–3 hours depending on stops.

Follow the coastal path from Conleau peninsula to Séné village. The Séné marshes nature reserve harbours avocets, spoonbills and shelducks. The trail is flat and easy—perfect for a late-afternoon stroll when raking light illuminates the mudflats.

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip Morbihan: Gulf, Carnac and Breton Coast

places.name: Vassieux En Vercors

visits.text: Vassieux-en-Vercors is a martyred village and Companion of the Liberation: on July 21-22, 1944, Germans landed by glider on the airstrip built by resistance fighters. Within days, 73 of 430 inhabitants were massacred, 91 resistance fighters killed, and the village 97% destroyed. In total, the summer 1944 Vercors battles claimed 840 French casualties. The departmental Resistance museum, founded in 1973 by former resistance fighter Joseph La Picirella and completely renovated in 2010, houses over 1,000 period objects and interactive terminals. Allow 1h30.

The Vercors Resistance Memorial, inaugurated in 1994 at Col de la Chau 5 minutes from the village, is a contemporary building "camouflaged" in the mountain—a citadel embedded in the terrain referencing the resistance fighters' clandestinity. The 1,200 m² immersive audio-visual journey blends participant testimonies, unpublished archives, and a 3D model. The visit concludes on a viewpoint overlooking Vassieux village and the High Plateaus ridges: a moment of contemplation facing this landscape that witnessed everything.

The national cemetery at the foot of the memorial road gathers the graves of resistance fighters and civilians killed in summer 1944. A sober place of remembrance, surrounded by the plateau's high-altitude grasslands. The white crosses contrast with the limestone ridges in the background.

activities.text: The plateau loop on white trails (6-8 km, very gentle slope) departs Vassieux village and crosses the vast high-altitude grasslands of the Drôme Vercors. In summer, the place is particularly quiet—the high plateaus remain little frequented outside season. The 1944 airstrip track (called "Taille-Crayon") is still visible in the landscape.

days_plan.itin_title: Royans-Vercors Road Trip: Hilltop Villages and Gorges

map_keywords: Mémorial de la Résistance col de la Chau Vassieux

visits.text: Pass through the Porte de France, a medieval remnant through which Joan of Arc left Vaucouleurs on February 23, 1429, to join Dauphin Charles VII at Chinon. Over 13 meters high with 2-meter-thick walls, it's the last of the four gates in the fortified enclosure.

Climb to the castle chapel on the town heights. The crypt houses the statue of Notre-Dame des Voûtes, before which Joan came to pray. The 26 stained glass windows from the Nancy workshop Höner, Benoît et Janin trace Joan's epic journey.

The Joan of Arc Museum, housed in the Town Hall wing, preserves over 300 pieces: drawings, prints, stained glass cartoons, bronze sculptures, and posters. The museum's four sections explore Joan's different symbolisms - virgin, warrior, and martyr.

Next to the Porte de France, the Pagis Towers testify to the city's fortified past. The first castle, built in 1026 by Étienne de Vaux, had 17 rampart towers. Only the King's Tower and the English Tower survive in the lower town.
The 1848 Town Hall contains a monumental painting by Scherrer (1886) depicting Joan's departure, and six Aubusson tapestries inaugurated in 1990 illustrating six stages of Joan's epic.

activities.text: Follow the discovery circuit of Joan of Arc heritage through Vaucouleurs streets: from the Porte de France to the linden tree where Joan reportedly rested, each stop features explanatory panels.
Saturday's weekly market brings together local producers and artisans. Find mirabelles, jams, cheeses, and charcuterie from the Meuse terroir.
Stroll along the Meuse valley. The communal forest surrounding Vaucouleurs offers shaded trails for a nature break between historical visits.

days_plan.itin_title: Meuse Circuit: Verdun and the Citadels

places.name: Vaudreching

visits.text: Vaudreching’s large nativity scene is the highlight of this day—and of the entire route. Every winter since 1954, the parish church council has installed a monumental nativity scene measuring 9.50 meters wide, 8 meters deep, and 5 meters high in the chancel of Saint-Rémi Church (dating from the 18th century and rebuilt by the Benedictines in 1758). More than 200 figures, many made of wax, are animated by 22 salvaged motors. The nativity scene depicts humanity’s reconciliation with God through 12 tableaux, along with scenes of rural life in Lorraine a hundred years ago. Up to 2,000 visitors—more than half of them German—come to see it each year. Admission is free. Installation takes about fifteen volunteers ten days of work.

In Creutzwald, Sainte-Croix du Centre Church—built in 1730, rebuilt from 1763 to 1771, and remodeled in the Romanesque-Byzantine style in 1911 with a dome—houses a carefully restored nativity scene. The figures date from around 1900: a volunteer spent hundreds of hours recreating the original setting from an old photograph. The church has two groups of stained-glass windows: the older ones by the Zettler firm of Munich (1912) and the more recent ones by T. G. Hanssen (1950).
The Villa Notre-Dame de la Clairière in Creutzwald hosts a Christmas nativity scene prepared by young volunteers from the Fédération Pro Europa Christiana.

Step inside Saint-Nicolas Church in L’Hôpital, housed in a former hospital and hermitage that was converted into a chapel after the last hermit’s death in 1695, then rebuilt from 1761 to 1765. Each year, the parish church council installs a nativity scene measuring 7 meters long and 3 meters wide, improving and embellishing it from one year to the next. The chancel’s stained-glass windows, dating from 1882, survived the bombing during World War II.

In Porcelette, Croix-Glorieuse Church, built in the Gothic Revival style between 1885 and 1887, is worth a stop. Every winter, it hosts a beautiful traditional nativity scene. The municipality also preserves the remains of a Roman road and a Gallo-Roman necropolis, evidence of continuous settlement since antiquity.

In Freyming-Merlebach, take a detour to Saint-Maurice Church in the Freyming district, built from 1911 to 1913 and considered a Baroque Revival masterpiece. Its interior decoration and stained-glass windows from the Zettler firm of Munich make it one of Moselle’s finest examples of religious architecture from the Wilhelmine era. The chapel of the Mission Catholique Slovène houses a nativity scene carved from linden and pear wood.

Ham-sous-Varsberg offers two very different nativity scenes: an outdoor display assembled by the municipal public works department, and a family nativity scene on rue de la Bergerie, measuring 2.50 meters high and 4 meters wide. End the day in Valmunster with the thousand-year-old Saint-Jean-Baptiste Church and its live nativity scene, held according to an annual schedule.

activities.text: In Creutzwald, Santa’s Village comes to square de la Bisten every December, with craft stalls and seasonal activities for families. A relaxed, festive stop between church visits.
Christmas services in the churches along the route often feature singing and organ music. Ask the local parish church councils for details: some concerts are open to everyone and free.

days_plan.itin_title: Christmas Nativity Scene Route in Moselle

visits.text: Vaux-en-Beaujolais inspired Gabriel Chevallier's novel Clochemerle, a cheerful satire of French village life. The village cultivates this literary fame while preserving its authentic winegrowing identity. Golden-stone houses line the area around the church, creating a bucolic scene that seems frozen in the 1920s.

The Romanesque church watches over the central square, where the famous urinal that sparked the war of Clochemerle in the novel takes pride of place. Colourful stained-glass windows illuminate the nave, while the bell tower chimes the hours above roofs of glazed tiles. The forecourt offers views down over the vineyards descending in terraces towards the valley.

The Gabriel Chevallier Museum presents the world of the author of Clochemerle through his books, papers, sketches, drawings, paintings and audiovisual documents. The exhibition traces his life, his work and his connections with Vaux-en-Beaujolais, which inspired his famous imaginary village. The visit complements the Clochemerle-themed installations found throughout the village.

Family wine estates welcome visitors for Beaujolais-Villages tastings. Vignerons explain seasonal vineyard work from winter pruning to autumn harvest. Cool cellars shelter barrels where wine develops its characteristic fruity aromas of pink-granite terroir.

activities.text: Follow the literary trail winding through the vineyards around the village. Panels reproduce extracts from the novel at the places that inspired them. The walk lets you discover the terraced vineyards while soaking up the atmosphere of Clochemerle, between reality and literary fiction.

Discover the hilltop villages of Beaujolais dotting the surrounding hills. Each village has its own character: here, golden-stone houses taking on warm hues in the setting sun; there, cobbled lanes climbing towards the church; further on, a restored washhouse where washerwomen once gathered.

Take part in a comparative Beaujolais tasting with a passionate winegrower. Light, fruity Beaujolais nouveau, more structured Beaujolais-Villages and complex crus suitable for ageing: each wine tells a story of terroir and expertise. The winegrower shares their knowledge of Beaujolais winemaking, from carbonic maceration to barrel ageing.

Explore the winegrowing heritage by visiting old communal wine presses and traditional winemaking buildings. These agricultural buildings, sometimes converted into cultural venues, bear witness to the collective organisation of the past, when small landowners pooled their resources to make wine. Their functional architecture accommodates the demands of vineyard work.

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip from Bresse to Bugey via Beaujolais and Lyon

visits.text: Vaux-en-Bugey is a former fortified village with narrow lanes and stone houses, perched above the Albarine valley. The views over the vineyards and meadows below are typical of the Bugey, a little-known region that produces quality white wines (Bugey appellation). Take time to climb to the high points to explore the landscape.
The vestiges of the old fortified village — partial walls, gates, and medieval houses — tell a story of borders and control of passages between the Rhône valley and the Bugey plateaus.

activities.text: Out-and-back walk to the cuves du Buizin: giant's kettles and waterfalls carved into the limestone by the river (marked trail, ~2 hours). These spectacular geological formations are characteristic of Bugey karst. Hiking boots are recommended; the trail can be slippery after rain.
Short loop through the old village and its high points (2 km, ~45 min), with views over the Albarine valley and Bugey vineyards.

days_plan.itin_title: Loop Around Lyon: Villages and Pierres Dorées

visits.text: The Château de Vaux-le-Vicomte was born from the collaboration of three artists in service to Louis XIV's finance superintendent: architect Le Vau, landscape architect Le Nôtre, and painter Le Brun. This 17th-century masterpiece directly inspired the Palace of Versailles.
On the ground floor, the reception salons, library, and king's chamber reveal grandiose decor: exceptional tapestries, period furniture, and ceilings painted by Le Brun.
Climb to the château's dome for a panoramic view over the 33 hectares of formal gardens. The perspective drawn by Le Nôtre extends over three kilometers to the Hercules statue.
In the basement, the period kitchens and cellars remain intact. A permanent exhibition traces Le Nôtre's genius using a large audiovisual model of the garden.
The Carriage Museum assembles coaches, carriages, and harnesses from the 17th to 20th centuries. The collection illustrates the art of travel and aristocratic transport.

activities.text: Tour the formal gardens by electric cart. Flower beds, boxwood embroidery, pools, and fountains unfold across 33 hectares enclosed by a 13-km perimeter wall.
On summer Saturday evenings, 2,000 candles illuminate the gardens for candlelit evenings. A gold and silver fireworks display concludes this magical nocturnal promenade.
Walk to the Hercules statue at the top of the perspective. The viewpoint embraces the garden's different terraced "plateaus" down to the château: the perfect picnic spot with a view.

days_plan.itin_title: Seine-et-Marne Circuit: Fontainebleau and Châteaux

visits.text: Vence is a former episcopal city whose elliptical ramparts, pierced by five gates, are almost completely preserved. The town was an episcopal seat for nearly fifteen centuries, and you can feel it in the density of the old centre.
The Notre-Dame-de-la-Nativité cathedral, founded in the 11th century on an ancient site, houses a mosaic by Marc Chagall, Moses Saved from the Waters, installed in the baptistery in 1979. Free entry.

The Rosary Chapel, completed by Matisse in 1951, is conceived as a total work of art—stained glass, ceramics, furnishings and chasubles included. The yellow, green and blue stained glass windows transform the light throughout the day.
The Place du Peyra, former Roman agora, retains its urn-shaped fountain and remains the heart of old Vence. A good starting point to cross the walled city to the cathedral.
The Château de Villeneuve houses the Émile Hugues Foundation, which programmes modern and contemporary art exhibitions in a 17th-century setting. Combine with Matisse for an art day.

activities.text: The Rosary Chapel is the essential stop in Vence and is best visited in the morning for the light through the stained-glass windows. Allow 30 minutes and check the opening hours: it is closed on Sundays.
The Provençal market sets up at Place du Grand Jardin on Tuesday and Friday mornings, with flowers and local produce. Better than the tourist markets on the coast.
The ramparts circuit is an easy loop around the old centre, a relaxed hour. Combine with a pause at Place du Peyra.
The Col de Vence, 10 km away, opens onto the Pre-Alps and serves as the starting point for hikes to the Baous. Quick round trip by car if you want an open view away from crowds.

days_plan.itin_title: Secret valleys of the Nice hinterland in 6 days
French Riviera Art Museums and Galleries: An 8-Day Journey

visits.text: Trinity Abbey of Vendôme was founded in 1033 by Count Geoffroy Martel after he saw three stars fall into a well. This Benedictine abbey quickly became powerful, housing up to one hundred monks in the 12th century. The abbey church impresses with the dimensions of a small cathedral, harmoniously blending Romanesque and Gothic architecture. The 80-meter Romanesque bell tower has dominated the town for nine centuries. The Flamboyant Gothic façade completed in 1508 by Jean de Beauce is a masterpiece of flame-like forms carved in stone. The preserved cloisters, chapter house, and remains testify to past splendor.

The old town of Vendôme winds between branches of the Loir, which form several islands connected by stone bridges. Medieval lanes reveal half-timbered houses, Renaissance mansions, and flower-filled interior courtyards. The fortified 14th-century water gate guarded access to the walled town. Restored washhouses evoke everyday life of yesteryear along the banks. Terraced gardens descend to shaded riverbanks. The peaceful atmosphere of this city of art and history invites leisurely wandering far from the tourist bustle.

Château de Vendôme overlooking the town from its rocky promontory. The romantic ruins testify to the power of the counts of Vendôme. The medieval ramparts offer a panoramic walk above the Loir valley. The Poitiers tower is the most imposing feature of the fortifications. The gardens laid out within the walls invite contemplation. The public park gives free access to the remains and to outstanding viewpoints over the town.

activities.text: Walking along the Loir's branches flowing through Vendôme and creating an exceptional bucolic setting. Landscaped banks offer shaded paths lined with weeping willows. Green islands connected by stone bridges invite discovery of secret corners. Restored mills and old tanneries recount past economic activity. Reflections of old façades in clear water create changing tableaux throughout the day. Strategically placed benches let you admire the ballet of swans and ducks.

Vendôme's gardens offer green havens in the heart of the historic town. Ronsard Park spreads its lawns and flowerbeds at the foot of the medieval ramparts. The château's terraced gardens overlook the Loir valley, offering panoramic views over the meanders. Green spaces landscaped along the water invite peaceful rest and contemplation. Century-old trees provide welcome shade during hot summer days. Rose gardens perfume the air in June, creating a romantic atmosphere for strollers.

Vendôme market is held on Friday mornings in the streets of the historic center, bringing the whole town to life. Colorful stalls offer farm products, Sologne goat cheeses, Vendôme rillettes and locally grown seasonal vegetables. Producers sell poultry, honey, artisanal jams and traditional Easter pâtés. Flowers, fabrics and bric-a-brac complete the diverse offerings. The convivial atmosphere and conversations among regulars create an authentic provincial market feel. Cafés open their terraces to welcome bargain hunters.

days_plan.itin_title: Loir-et-Cher Itinerary: Royal Châteaux and the Loir Valley

visits.text: Venelles-le-Haut is the old part of the village, perched between 300 and 360 metres above sea level, making it the second highest commune in the Bouches-du-Rhône after Mimet. Walk up to the Place du Château for the viewpoint: from the remains of the 12th-century seigneurial castle, the view takes in the north face of Montagne Sainte-Victoire, the Durance valley and the Luberon. On a clear day you can even make out the château de Meyrargues behind a wooded hill.

The Venelles-le-Haut windmill was built in 1662. It operated until 1904 before being abandoned then restored from 1968 by its current owners, who rebuilt the structure's walls while preserving its original volumes. Even without its sails, its silhouette marks the landscape and forms the village's visual landmark. The facade of the former church from 1876, partially destroyed by the earthquake of June 11, 1909 (magnitude 6.2, the last major earthquake in metropolitan France), is still visible in the streets of Venelles-le-Haut.

Descending toward Venelles-le-Bas, you cross through old dwellings along the historic path with their arches still standing — witnesses to the era when travelers came here for lodging on the road to Sisteron. The Saint-Hippolyte church in the lower village was rebuilt after the 1909 earthquake, which had destroyed the medieval church upstream.

activities.text: Wooded loop on the Venelles hills (marked trails, departure from village center). Aleppo pines and holm oaks dominate gently rolling terrain. The trails offer regular openings onto Sainte-Victoire and the Aix plain. Allow 2 hours for an 8 km circuit with no particular difficulty.

Hike toward the first foothills of Sainte-Victoire: from the east side of Venelles, marked trails lead to the approaches of the massif and Lac du Bimont (dam built in the 1950s). Sainte-Victoire peaks at 1,011 meters and was painted more than 87 times by Cézanne — a figure that conveys the painter's obsession with this mountain.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpilles, Aix-en-Provence & Arles Circuit

places.name: Verdun

visits.text: Descend into the 7 kilometers of galleries of the underground Citadel, dug at the end of the 19th century beneath Vauban's upper citadel. An augmented reality headset puts you in the boots of a 1916 soldier: discover the bread ovens that produced 28,000 rations a day and the memorial chapel where Corporal Thin designated the Unknown Soldier on November 10, 1920.

The World Center for Peace occupies an 18th-century episcopal palace, partially destroyed in 1916 and later restored. Its temporary exhibitions explore Franco-German relations and human rights. The formal French garden at the rear offers an open view over the city.

Step inside Notre-Dame Cathedral, built from the 10th century onward. Its Romanesque-Gothic blend houses a gilded baroque baldachin, restored after the Great War bombardments. Modern stained glass filters colored light into the nave.

Fort Douaumont, the most powerful structure in the fortified complex, fell to German hands on February 25, 1916. Walk through the command room, chapel, combat galleries, and inscriptions soldiers left on the walls. Interior temperature hovers around 7 to 10°C.

The Douaumont Ossuary, inaugurated in 1932, rises like a gigantic shell above 15,000 white crosses. Its 46-meter tower dominates the battlefield. Through the oculi in the base, you glimpse the remains of 130,000 unidentified French and German soldiers.

Renovated in 2016 for the centenary, the Verdun Memorial displays over 2,000 authentic objects at the former station of the destroyed village of Fleury-devant-Douaumont. A 100-square-meter shattered screen reconstructs the battlefield's convulsions. From the top-floor terraces, the panorama reveals scars still visible beneath the forest.

The Trench of Bayonets preserves the memory of June 12, 1916: according to legend, a company of the 137th regiment was buried by a bombardment, their bayonets left stuck in the ground. A sober monument has protected the site since 1920.

activities.text: Walk the Meuse quays at dusk, between stone bridges and facades rebuilt after 1918. The reflection of lights on the river offers a soothing contrast after visiting the battlefields.
Follow the Sacred Way, the former supply route that linked Bar-le-Duc to Verdun during the battle. Milestones carved with poilu helmets mark the 56-kilometer historic route.
Pass through the Porte Chaussée, a 14th-century fortified gate that was part of the city's original ramparts. Used as a prison from 1755 to 1860, it marks the entrance to old Verdun.

The Princerie Museum, housed in a 16th-century mansion, brings together archaeological and artistic collections spanning from prehistory to the 19th century. Sacred art enthusiasts will find remarkable pieces here.

Visit Fleury-devant-Douaumont, a village taken and retaken 16 times in two months. Signs indicate the location of the town hall, school, and church. It's one of nine villages classified as "died for France."

days_plan.itin_title: Meuse Circuit: Verdun and the Citadels
Eastern France by Train from Paris

map_keywords: Centre mondial de la Paix Verdun

visits.text: Claude Monet's House and Gardens in Giverny. Normandy's second-most visited site, this Impressionist sanctuary was the master's refuge for 43 years. The Clos Normand unfolds its flower beds beneath rose-covered arches, while the water garden reveals the iconic Japanese bridge and water lilies that inspired the monumental canvases. The pink stucco house preserves the reconstructed studio, the yellow dining room with its Japanese print collection, and the kitchen with its blue Rouen tiles.

Museum of Impressionisms Giverny. Steps from the Monet Foundation, this contemporary museum presents temporary exhibitions dedicated to Impressionism and its worldwide offshoots. The building blends harmoniously into a landscaped garden that extends the spirit of the place.

Vernon's Old Mill. Perched on the pillars of a 12th-century medieval bridge, this 16th-century half-timbered house seems to defy the laws of balance. A historic monument since 2025, this suspended waterwheel mill immortalized by Monet is one of France's last inhabited bridges. Facing it, the Château des Tourelles once guarded the fortified town's entrance.

Notre-Dame Collegiate Church of Vernon. This church of mixed styles bears witness to eight centuries of religious architecture. The Romanesque façade neighbors Gothic vaults and Renaissance additions. Inside, admire the ancient stained glass windows and the flamboyant rose window.

Old Vernon and Rue Potard. Spared by bombings, this medieval street has preserved its 15th and 16th-century half-timbered houses. The Archives Tower, the castle's former keep, dominates Place de l'Ange. A heritage trail punctuated by interpretive markers retraces this royal city's history.

Eure Valley and its villages. Heading back toward Vernon, pass through the charming Eure valley villages: Chambray, La Croix-Saint-Leufroy, Houlbec-Cocherel. These preserved hamlets bear witness to rural, authentic Normandy.

Pacy-sur-Eure and the Eure Valley Railway. This tourist steam or diesel train covers 22 km of bucolic landscapes between Pacy and Breuilpont. The period station and historic rolling stock transport travelers into the railway atmosphere of the early 20th century.

activities.text: Bike ride along La Seine à Vélo. The cycling route connects Giverny to Vernon following the river. From Vernon station, shuttles and bike rentals allow car-free access to Giverny. The journey crosses landscapes that inspired the Impressionists.

Château de Bizy in Vernon. Nicknamed Normandy's little Versailles, this 18th-century château hosted Louis XV and the Bonaparte family. The monumental stables and park with fountains by Pierre Contant d'Ivry are worth the detour.

Final stroll through Giverny. Before leaving Eure, return to wander the Impressionist village. Visit Claude Monet's grave in the small cemetery near the church, where the father of Impressionism has rested since 1926.
Local produce shopping. Farmhouse cider, Calvados, Camembert, Livarot, and Pont-l'Évêque: Eure's cheese shops and cider houses offer the authentic flavors of Normandy.

days_plan.itin_title: Eure Road Trip: From Giverny to Normandy's Most Beautiful Villages
Eure Road Trip: From Giverny to Normandy's Most Beautiful Villages

places.name: Vers Pont Du Gard

visits.text: At 49 meters high, the Pont du Gard is the world's tallest Roman aqueduct bridge. Built in the 1st century, it forms part of the 50 km aqueduct that carried 30,000 to 40,000 m³ of water per day by gravity from the Eure spring in Uzès to Nîmes—with an average slope of only 25 cm per kilometer over the entire route. The central arch of the first level has a span of 24.52 meters. Nearly 1,000 workers worked on this project, completed in 5 years using 21,000 m³ of limestone extracted from the nearby Estel quarry, without mortar. Classified as a Historic Monument since 1840 and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1985, it's France's most visited ancient monument. Allow at least 1 hour for the self-guided visit.

The Pont du Gard Museum (left bank, in underground spaces invisible from the monument) covers 2,500 m² and traces the history of the aqueduct's construction and operation using multimedia technologies, virtual reconstructions and models. In summer, guided tours provide access to the upper-level gallery—the conduit where water flowed.

The viewpoints on both banks of the Gardon offer very different perspectives on the three levels of arches. The right bank gives the most classic overall view. On clear days, contemplate the monument's reflection in the Gardon from the beach downstream — it's often the best photo of the day.

activities.text: The “Mémoires de garrigue” walking loop (1.4 km, about 40 min, easy difficulty) starts from the site and passes through vineyards, olive trees and holm oaks, revealing the Mediterranean landscape and buried aqueduct remains. More seasoned hikers will take the “Roman aqueduct trail” in the Gardon gorges (8 to 10 km, about 3 hours, moderate difficulty).
Swimming in the river at the foot of the aqueduct is the most memorable experience at the site. Canoe rentals allow you to pass under the arches.

visits.text: Skip the main château. The Trianon domain - a separate ticket (12€, or included in the 24€ full passport) entered via the Grille de la Reine - is where the actual story is. The Petit Trianon is a small neoclassical house built by Gabriel for Madame de Pompadour from 1762, finished after her death, and given by Louis XVI to Marie-Antoinette in 1774 the moment she became queen. Her rules: entry only by personal invitation. No exceptions, not even for the ladies of the court. Fifteen years of humiliated courtiers generated a corresponding fifteen years of savage gossip. On 5 October 1789, she was here, in this house, when she learned that 6,000 women from Paris were marching on Versailles demanding bread. She went back to the main château. The family was taken to Paris by force the following morning. She never returned to Versailles. The Petit Trianon was, for her, the last place she was happy.

The Hameau de la Reine - twelve thatched cottages built by architect Richard Mique between 1783 and 1787, modelled on a Norman village - is the part that most infuriated contemporaries. Marie-Antoinette played at being a peasant: real mill, real cowshed, real dairy, real farm animals (kept clean by a dedicated shepherd so they'd be presentable when the queen came to 'milk' them). It's simultaneously ridiculous and human, and it fed the popular resentment that preceded 1789 more directly than most of her actual decisions. The hamlet has been restored to its 1787 state.

On 10 August 1901, Anne Moberly (54, principal of St Hugh's College Oxford) and Eleanor Jourdain (38, her deputy) visited Versailles with a Baedeker guide. After the main château, they walked toward the Petit Trianon and got lost. What followed - published in 1911 as An Adventure - includes two men in green tricorn hats with spades (matching the Swiss Guard uniform of 1789, not known in 1901), a wooden bridge no longer standing, a Chinese kiosk no longer existing, a man with a pockmarked face beside it (identified afterward as the comte de Vaudreuil, a known friend of Marie-Antoinette who had, historically, a pockmarked face), and a woman in a white summer dress and large straw hat sitting sketching on the lawn, whom Moberly identified from a later portrait as Marie-Antoinette. The skeptical explanation - a costume rehearsal by the writer Robert de Montesquiou - is defensible. The unexplained detail is the kiosk: it didn't exist in 1901, wasn't on any known map in 1901, and a floor plan of the Trianon dated 1774 discovered after publication showed it exactly where the two women described it. Walk the gardens in late afternoon when the tour groups have gone. The probability of apparition is low. The atmosphere is guaranteed.

activities.text: Lunch at Restaurant Angelina in the Pavillon d'Orléans within the château estate: salon de thé, 35-50€, reliably good. Or the Café Trianon on the domain itself for something lighter and quicker if you want to maximise time in the gardens.

Before the RER back, take 30 minutes in the Versailles town market (Tuesday, Friday, Sunday mornings) on the Place du Marché Notre-Dame - four covered halls, local producers, entirely normal after a morning of royal tragedy, and a useful reminder that a town of 85,000 people lives here year-round, mostly indifferent to the ghosts.

days_plan.itin_title: Yvelines Road Trip: Versailles and Impressionist Villages
Yvelines Road Trip: Versailles and Impressionist Villages
Haunted Île-de-France: 5 Days of Royal Ghosts and Revolutionary Prisons

visits.text: The Château de Verteuil dominates the village from its rocky spur. Owned by the La Rochefoucauld family for 1,000 years (sold in 2020), it welcomed Charles V, who planted a yew there that still stands.
The Moulin de Verteuil at the foot of the castle, with its waterwheel still turning. Now a restaurant with a terrace by the water. The castle + mill + Charente view = the perfect photo.

The church of Saint-Médard (12th century) hides a life-size Entombment in polychrome terracotta. Seven figures around Christ, attributed to the workshop of Germain Pilon. One of the Charente's hidden treasures.

The village lanes lead to the fairground shaded by lime trees, on the banks of the Charente. The Maison du Sénéchal (15th century) with its mullioned windows, remains of the old Protestant church, wash houses. As befits a village with the Petites Cités de Caractère designation.

activities.text: A walk around the outside of the castle. The castle can no longer be visited, but the outline of its towers can be seen from the lanes of Verteuil-sur-Charente and from the banks of the Charente. The fairground and the surroundings of the mill offer the best viewpoints.
Lunch at the Moulin de Verteuil. Terrace facing the waterwheel, local cuisine. Booking advised at weekends. Alternative: Jeux de Pots overlooks the Charente.
Hike around the castle. 6.6 km loop through the countryside and hamlets, returning along the Charente banks. Easy, 1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours. Start from the castle car park.

days_plan.itin_title: Charente Tour: Cognac and Romanesque Heritage in 4 Days

visits.text: The Church of Saint-Martin in Vertus is a Romanesque building of the 11th and 12th centuries put up over a former stretch of water. What makes it unique: its Romanesque crypts beneath the choir, dug above the water table, which you visit by going down a few steps. The Saint-Martin well, right beside it, recalls the importance of water in the town's history.

The Baudet Gate, dating to the 13th century, is the sole remnant of medieval ramparts that once ringed the town. Vertus was fortified from 1080 onward and played a significant role under the Counts of Champagne. Today, the former rampart line is replaced by shaded walking paths—a pleasant circuit around the town.

Mont Aimé, a few kilometres to the south, is an outlier hill that rises 50 metres above the plain. From the top, the view takes in the Côte des Blancs and its 20 kilometres of vines climbing towards Épernay. On a clear day, Reims Cathedral is visible on the horizon.

activities.text: Follow the paths winding through the hillsides of the Côte des Blancs. Vertus is the Marne's largest wine-growing municipality with 500 hectares planted, 90% of them with chardonnay. Classified premier cru, it produces blanc de blancs renowned for their chalky minerality. Walking routes of 8 to 12 km cross the plots and offer views down over the Champagne plain.

Visit the independent winemakers of Vertus for a blanc de blancs tasting. The Duval-Leroy house has been established in the village since 1859—one of the last large family-owned and independent Champagne houses. Several grower-producers also welcome visitors for direct tastings. The chalk at the surface gives the wines a distinctive minerality and liveliness, quite different from the pinot noirs of Verzenay or Aÿ. Use this final stage to compare the styles.

days_plan.itin_title: Marne Road Trip: Reims, Épernay and Champagne

visits.text: The fortified churches of Thiérache form a unique heritage ensemble. Sixty buildings were fortified in the 16th and 17th centuries by the villagers themselves to withstand relentless pillaging. Watchtowers, arrow slits and refuge rooms testify to an exceptional blend of military and religious architecture. Burelles, Prisces with its 25-metre keep, and Parfondeval offer the most remarkable examples. Allow for a return trip from Vervins to visit Parfondeval.
Vervins preserves traces of its former fortifications. The upper town reveals its strategic past as a frontier city, with rampart remnants still visible in certain streets.
The Thiérache bocage undulates between meadows and hedgerows. Red-brick villages punctuate this preserved rural landscape where fortified churches dominate green horizons.
Follow the fortified churches tourist route marked on the Pays de Thiérache map. This orange circuit crosses the Brune and Serre valleys, linking the most spectacular buildings.

activities.text: Hiking trails meander through the bocage between fortified villages. Several marked paths allow you to explore this borderland and its unique military heritage on foot.

Explore the fortified château of Guise; allow for a return trip from Vervins. This thousand-year-old stronghold of the Dukes of Guise impresses with its mighty keep and 17 hectares of fortifications overlooking the Oise.

days_plan.itin_title: Aisne Itinerary: Gothic Cathedrals and the Picardy Countryside

visits.text: The Verzenay lighthouse was the idea of a champagne merchant, Joseph Goulet, who decided in 1909 to advertise himself by building a real lighthouse in the middle of the vines. The lantern turned at night, visible from Reims, a bold publicity stunt for the time. The lighthouse is 25 metres high and 101 steps lead to the top, where the 360° view over the Montagne de Reims and its ocean of vines is spectacular. Since 1999 it has housed the Vine Museum, with a 1 hour 30 minute audio-guided tour covering the history and expertise of Champagne. Comprehensive, fun and inexpensive.

The Verzenay mill has watched over the hillsides for several centuries. Owned by the Mumm house, it overlooks parcels of pinot noir classified grand cru. Like the lighthouse, it served as an observation post during both world wars.

If you have half a day, make the detour to the Faux de Verzy, a forest of beeches with twisted shapes, a few kilometres east of Verzenay. These mutant trees, whose mutations nobody can really explain, have been growing for centuries in a forest amphitheatre at the top of the Montagne de Reims.

activities.text: Take the waymarked paths that cross the grand cru vineyards of the Montagne de Reims. The UNESCO-listed slopes reveal a thousand years of labour in an open and very photogenic landscape. The Circuit du Phare starts from the village and follows a loop through the vines: allow 2 hours of walking for 6 to 10 km.

The tasting area at the lighthouse offers cuvées from about fifteen local winegrowers in the Montagne de Reims. Champagnes from the Montagne are dominated by pinot noir — very different from the blanc de blancs of the Côte des Blancs. Take the chance to compare.

days_plan.itin_title: Marne Road Trip: Reims, Épernay and Champagne

visits.text: Climb the Motte hill to reach Notre-Dame Chapel, a pilgrimage site since the Middle Ages. The exceptional panorama sweeps across the Vosges, the Jura mountains, and on clear days, the Alps.

The Musée Georges-Garret occupies a former Ursuline convent built in 1680. Explore 1,200 m² across 14 rooms: the region's most important collection of Gallo-Roman funerary stelae, works by Prud'hon, Tissot, Boucher, Van Loo, and an Orientalist section. The museum pays tribute to the Vesoul painter Jean-Léon Gérôme (1824–1904).
Saint-Georges Church dominates Vesoul's historic center, an imposing religious edifice that bears witness to the local sacred architecture.

activities.text: Enjoy Lake Vesoul-Vaivre below the Motte hill, a developed natural area perfect for a relaxing break with water activities and family walks.
Wander through the streets of old Vesoul, discover its private mansions, and soak up the atmosphere of this administrative capital of Haute-Saône, gateway to the Vosges Saônoises.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Saône Tour: Comtois Plateaus and Heritage

visits.text: The Veules flows 1,149 meters before emptying into the Channel—France's shortest river. A 3.5 km walking circuit, marked with signs, follows its course past mills, thatched cottages, and watercress beds.
At the Veules springs, watercress has been cultivated since the 14th century in watercress beds fed by the chalk aquifer. The water emerges at a constant temperature year-round.
Saint-Martin Church, rebuilt in the 15th century, preserves a 13th-century bell tower. Inside, note the stained glass windows and restored timber frame.
The old château, on the hillside, retains an 18th-century circular dovecote in alternating layers of sandstone and flint—a rare construction in Normandy.
Veules-les-Roses once bore the name Veules-en-Caux. Renamed in 1897, the seaside resort owes its roses to the climbing rose bushes that adorn every facade and street corner.
On the seafront, 19th-century seaside villas stand alongside bathing cabins and old fishermen's houses. The beach offers fine sand at low tide.

activities.text: Follow the circuit of France's shortest river. Allow 1h30 to trace the Veules from its mouth to its springs, passing restored mills, watering troughs, and flowering gardens.
Sample Veulaises, oysters raised in the open sea off the village. Seafront stalls also offer sole, skate, and scallops.
Coastal walk on the Alabaster Coast. White chalk cliffs frame the valleuse sheltering the village. The path offers views of the cliffs and the Channel.

days_plan.itin_title: The 20 Most Beautiful Villages in Normandy

visits.text: On your way to Vézelay, stop at the Caves of Arcy-sur-Cure—an underground network inhabited for 200,000 years. The cave paintings, dating back 28,000 years, are among the oldest in Europe. The guided tour lasts about an hour. Book in advance during summer, as slots fill up quickly.

You'll spot the Basilica of Sainte-Marie-Madeleine from a distance—it overlooks Vézelay from the “eternal hill.” A UNESCO World Heritage site since 1979, this 12th-century abbey church is a masterpiece of Burgundian Romanesque art. Saint Bernard preached the Second Crusade here in 1146 before Louis VII and Eleanor of Aquitaine. In 1190, Richard the Lionheart and Philip Augustus met here before departing for the Third Crusade. The tympanum of the narthex, depicting the Mission of the Apostles, is unique in Romanesque art. If you're here around June 21, watch for the solstice phenomenon: the southern stained-glass windows project a line of light down the center of the nave.

The village of Vézelay itself is worth a stroll—only 450 residents live here, and it's listed among the Plus Beaux Villages de France. Walk up the main street lined with art galleries and medieval houses, follow the ramparts, and continue to the esplanade for the panorama over the Morvan. Take your time.

If you still have time, make a detour to the Château de Bazoches, approximately 13 km from Vézelay, a 15-minute drive. Vauban bought it in 1675 with the proceeds of the spoils from the capture of Maastricht and made it his design office - this is where he drew up most of his fortification plans.

activities.text: From the esplanade behind the basilica, you'll have the finest panorama over the Morvan. It's the ideal spot for a late-afternoon picnic—bring Époisses cheese and white Burgundy wine.

days_plan.itin_title: Yonne Circuit: Northern Burgundy & Chablis
Burgundy's 15 Most Beautiful Villages
Burgundy Road Trip: Cathedrals, Vineyards and Villages
Nièvre Road Trip: Morvan and Ducal Heritage
Burgundy-Franche-Comté: The Most Beautiful Villages in 7 days

visits.text: The old town of Vic-sur-Cère nestles against the eastern slope of the valley at an altitude of 680 metres, sheltered by a spectacular wooded jumble of rocks. Built of lava stone and roofed with schist slabs, this spa village retains the authentic charm of Cantal mountain towns. A renowned climatic resort, it offers a green setting ideal for recharging.

The Rocher des Pendus towers over Vic-sur-Cère and offers an exceptional viewpoint over the upper valley. The nearby Puy Griou rises before the Élancèze and the Peyre-Arse in a grandiose panorama over the Cantal summits. This perspective reveals the full majesty of the volcanic cirque.

activities.text: The Cascades du Pas de Cère tumble through a spectacular canyon where tumultuous water has carved the volcanic rock. The maintained trail follows the gorges amid cool air and greenery, revealing successive waterfalls in an impressive rocky setting. The roar of water echoes between the basaltic walls.

The Pas de Cère canyon offers thrill-seekers a canyoning descent through the wild gorges. Jumps, natural slides and abseils follow one another in the riverbed between vertical walls of black lava. Local activity providers supervise this spectacular aquatic activity.

days_plan.itin_title: Cantal Road Trip: Auvergne Volcanoes and Mountain Traditions

visits.text: The Georges de La Tour Departmental Museum honours the master of chiaroscuro, born in this salt-producing village in 1593. His candlelit paintings illuminate the darkness with mystical, theatrical light, revealing the faces of card players, penitents and meditative saints with poignant realism. The museum displays an exceptional collection of 17th-century Lorraine paintings, including works by Jacques Callot and Claude Deruet, contemporaries of La Tour. Its contemporary 2003 architecture incorporates the former 18th-century salt storehouse.

The 13th- to 15th-century Saint-Marien Collegiate Church retains 16th-century Renaissance stained glass and remarkable liturgical furnishings: 18th-century choir stalls, a 1749 Wegmann organ and Baroque paintings. Its squat 50 m bell tower rises above the village’s interlocking-tile roofs, a sandstone sentinel overlooking the former salt marshes that brought Vic prosperity from the 11th to the 17th century, when 27 salt works produced 60,000 tonnes of salt a year.

activities.text: Discover the history of salt in the Saulnois, a land of 400 salt-water springs exploited since the Gallic and then the Gallo-Roman periods. During the Middle Ages, the salt marshes of Vic, Moyenvic and Marsal produced “white gold” by solar evaporation in lead pans. This little-known heritage shaped Lorraine’s economy until the 18th century and was controlled by the bishops of Metz, who drew immense revenues from it. The flat landscape, with ponds glittering as far as the eye can see, retains its unique character.

Stroll through the narrow streets of Vic-sur-Seille, a characterful village of 1,200 inhabitants with houses built from pink Vosges sandstone. Former salt works with their Gallic salt-production ceramics, 16th- and 17th-century Renaissance townhouses, sandstone fountains and washhouses recount the prosperity of a town that exported its “white gold” by river to Nancy, Metz and even Burgundy. Parts of the medieval walls survive.

days_plan.itin_title: 4-Day Moselle Tour: Metz, Bitche Citadel and Chagall’s Stained Glass

places.name: Vichy

visits.text: The Hall des Sources (1903) reveals its Art Nouveau metal structure, a true vessel of glass and steel designed by Charles Le Cœur. Its ironwork by Émile Robert reproduces the thistles of the park, while five thermal springs flow here: Célestins, Lucas, Hôpital, Chomel and Grande Grille. The mineral water can be tasted free of charge at the drinking fountains set up in this light-filled hall.

Vichy's Opera House (inaugurated in 1903) houses an Art Nouveau hall with 1,486 seats decorated by Léon Rudnicki. Inside the dome, the faces of famous artists such as Sarah Bernhardt adorn the ceiling. This Convention Centre and Opera House, listed as UNESCO world heritage, today combines historic and contemporary spaces in a setting unique in France.

The Thermes des Dômes, recognisable by their neo-Moorish dome, place Vichy among the major spa towns. Built between 1899 and 1903, these first-class baths offer 46 treatment rooms in a preserved Belle Époque setting. Waters rich in sodium bicarbonate have treated digestive ailments and rheumatism for 2,000 years.

The Parc des Sources, created in 1812 by decree of Napoleon I, spreads around the hall of the same name. Its covered wrought-iron galleries (1899–1903) link the park to the Convention Centre and Opera House. The 700-metre-long walkways invite a stroll through this green lung where spa architecture converses with nature.

The Parc Napoléon III (1861) extends over 7.8 hectares of English-style gardens along a 2.5-km dyke protecting against flooding from the Allier. Rare and exotic species (cedars, redwoods, Judas trees) populate this romantic haven. The colonial-style imperial chalets, built between 1863 and 1864, bear witness to the stays of Napoleon III, who made Vichy the queen of spa towns.

activities.text: The Casino du Grand Café, nestled in the Parc des Sources near the Opera House, invites you to try your luck at poker, roulette or one of 100 slot machines. This Belle Époque establishment continues the spa town's gaming tradition, attracting spa guests and visitors in a festive and friendly atmosphere.

The spa quarter reveals its Art Nouveau facades and covered passages with the look of a film set. Rue Alquié lines up its English-style houses, Rue de Belgique displays its baroque facades, while the colonial-inspired Napoleon III chalets recall the splendour of the Second Empire. Vichy's architecture has an openly bourgeois side, a legacy of the golden age of spa life.

The banks of the Allier invite leisurely walks along the artificial lake created in 1963. Plage des Célestins, guinguettes, and green spaces offer relaxation and waterside leisure. The promenade continues for 4 km of cycling paths, perfect for enjoying the golden hour by the river.

days_plan.itin_title: Allier Road Trip: Vichy, Thermal Baths and Bourbonnais Bocage

map_keywords: Thermal Baths of the Domes Vichy

visits.text: The Sainte-Brigitte chapel crowns a 184-meter conical hill above Vidauban. Dating from the 17th century, it commemorates Bridget of Sweden's supposed passage through Provence. Struck by lightning in the 1970s, it had its roof restored in 1998. A winding path climbs to it from a free parking lot: allow just under an hour for the round trip from the center.

activities.text: Canoe down the Argens from Vidauban: the river winds through an alluvial plain between riverside woodland and vineyards. Its tributary, the Aille, has waterfalls and a long rocky plateau nearby. In summer, the flow can be low: call the rental operator before making the trip.

days_plan.itin_title: Roquebrune-sur-Argens: sea, villages and the Var in 10 days

visits.text: Hartmannswillerkopf—nicknamed Vieil Armand by the French infantrymen who couldn't pronounce the Alsatian name—overlooks the Alsace plain at 956 meters. In 1915, it became the scene of extremely violent fighting: the summit changed hands repeatedly over a few weeks, with both armies digging kilometers of trenches into the Vosges sandstone. An estimated 25,000 French and German soldiers fell here, with virtually no tactical gain. The soldiers called it “the man-eater” or “the mountain of death”.

The National Monument, built between 1924 and 1932 and inaugurated by President Albert Lebrun, is one of four Great War national monuments along with Douaumont, Notre-Dame-de-Lorette, and Dormans. You reach it through an 80-meter ceremonial trench that immediately immerses you in the site's atmosphere. The crypt holds the bones of 12,000 soldiers whose identities have been lost. At the entrance, two winged bronze statues are the work of sculptor Antoine Bourdelle. The Altar of the Fatherland, outside, bears the coats of arms of the twelve donor cities.

The Franco-German Historial, inaugurated on November 10, 2017, by Presidents Macron and Steinmeier, is the first Great War museum to present events from both countries' perspectives. The exhibition design follows the evolution of Franco-German relations from the trenches to contemporary reconciliation. Accounts from soldiers on both sides, archival photographs, and objects from everyday military life make up most of the exhibition.

The battlefield preserves kilometers of trenches dug into the Vosges sandstone, underground shelters, barbed-wire networks, and shell craters. A 4.5-kilometer trail with interpretive displays winds through the combat zone. For quiet reflection, the Silberloch military cemetery, inaugurated in 1922, contains 1,264 individual graves of French soldiers and six ossuaries.

activities.text: Follow the marked historical trail through the French and German trenches. Explanatory panels at each junction identify the positions and recount the 1915 offensives. The complete circuit covers about 4.5 kilometers and takes two hours. Wear good shoes—the terrain is uneven and the slopes can be slippery in wet weather.

From the Panorama Rock (Aussichtsfelsen), at the end of the ridge, the view opens up over the southern Alsace plain as far as Mulhouse, across the Belfort Gap, and, in clear weather, over the Bernese Alps. Here you understand why this summit was so fiercely contested—it provided an exceptional strategic vantage point over the entire border.

days_plan.itin_title: Haut-Rhin Road Trip: Colmar and the Southern Wine Route

places.name: Vienne

visits.text: Built around 20–10 BC, the Temple of Augustus and Livia stands in the centre of Vienne, almost intact. It's one of only two Roman temples of this type preserved in France, with the Maison Carrée in Nîmes. Converted into a church then a courthouse, it owes its survival to successive uses. You can admire it free of charge, by day or illuminated in the evening.

Vienne's Roman theatre backs onto the hill overlooking the town, built to accommodate thousands of spectators. Among the largest in Roman Gaul, it still hosts the Jazz à Vienne festival in summer. Climb the tiers for the view over the rooftops. Open to visitors outside performance periods.

Broken columns, arcades and foundations emerge in the Jardin de Cybèle, right in the heart of the city. These remains of the Gallo-Roman forum can be explored for free as you turn into a square. Objects found on-site are exhibited in the neighbouring Museum of Fine Arts and Archaeology. A handy shortcut to the city's Roman past.

activities.text: Cross the Rhône to Saint-Romain-en-Gal, twenty minutes on foot, to see the other face of Roman Vienna. This vast residential and commercial quarter has yielded mosaics and baths, presented in the site's Gallo-Roman museum. Allow half a day if you combine both banks. Separate ticket for the museum.

days_plan.itin_title: Eastern France by Train from Paris

map_keywords: Temple of Augustus and Livia Vienne

visits.text: Viens celebrated its millennium in 1990, and the village wears its age well. On the edge of the Alpes-de-Haute-Provence, it grew up around a fortress built around 990, first mentioned in 1005 under the name "Vegnis." Enter the village through the Porte Sarrasine (also called the Tour de la Pousterle), pierced in the ramparts of the 11th to 13th centuries. It allows only one person through at a time, and its crown of machicolations was partially destroyed around 1960. The Clock Tower above it, with its square belfry, belongs to the 14th-century enclosure. In the narrow lanes, you will come across fine dwellings from the 13th to the 16th centuries with mullioned and transomed windows. A Rue de la Juiverie recalls that a Jewish community found refuge here in the 14th century.

Viens' Renaissance château (16th century, renovated in the 18th and 19th centuries) now serves as the village town hall. Passing through its portal, you'll discover a magnificent octagonal Renaissance staircase—the most remarkable architectural piece in the village. The town hall opens its doors during the day. The Church of Saint-Hilaire (12th century, remodeled in the 17th) is listed as a Historic Monument for its late-13th-century square bell tower with twin bays and Lombard bands.

activities.text: Walk around the ramparts and viewpoint over the Albion plateau from the Montée de la Pousterle (20 min). The view stretches across the Luberon massif.

Rural path toward the terraces and fields (short 1h loop). The surroundings of Viens are located on the border of the Alpes-de-Haute-Provence, with lavender fields beginning to appear on the surrounding plateaus.

days_plan.itin_title: The 15 Most Beautiful Villages of the Luberon

visits.text: Port d'Albret tidal lake: Created artificially between 1966 and 1975 over 40 hectares, this body of water stretches between Vieux-Boucau and Soustons. The central wooded islet nicknamed Île de la tentation remains inaccessible but provides a refuge for birds. The name Vieux-Boucau means old river mouth, a reminder of when the Adour flowed into the ocean here before 1578.
