Promenade du Mail: Connecting downtown to the lake's outlet, this walkway lined with maritime pines features restaurants, bars and ice cream shops. A laid-back summer atmosphere prevails along this pedestrian thoroughfare. Unobstructed view of the lake and water activities. Spectacular sunsets from the sea wall.

The three beaches: Grand Plage in the town center (urban then wild), Sablères beach to the north (high dunes, naturism tolerated), and the tidal lake beach with calm, warm waters. Each beach offers a different atmosphere. Lake waters are 3–4°C warmer than the ocean, ideal for families.

activities.text: Swimming in the tidal lake: Lifeguarded beach in season with calm waters maintained at a constant level. Pleasant water temperature, higher than in the ocean. Ideal for young children and water sports beginners. Inflatable play equipment installed in summer. Lifeguard station and restrooms on site.

Water activities on the lake: Rental of pedal boats, paddleboards, kayaks and small sailboats. The lake's sheltered waters allow beginners to take part safely. Sailing lessons for children and adults in July–August. Family-friendly and convivial atmosphere.

Vieux-Boucau markets: a morning market with local producers runs daily except Sundays and public holidays from mid-June to the end of September, and on Tuesdays and Saturdays during the rest of the year. Special evening markets in summer feature crafts and clothing. A festive atmosphere with musical entertainment. Landes specialties and fresh produce.

Golf de Pinsolle nearby: 18-hole course in a setting of pines and ponds. Accessible to players of all levels. Driving range, pro shop and restaurant on site. Green fees vary by season. Booking advised in high season.

days_plan.itin_title: Landes Road Trip: Ocean, Pine Forest and Landes Traditions

visits.text: Before plunging into the gorge, stop at the Arbois viewpoint, accessible from the D531. You'll overlook the Bourne canyon from a purpose-built walkway—300 meters of empty space below your feet. The gorge was carved 3 to 4 million years ago, then widened by successive glaciers. The white, compact Urgonian limestone creates these spectacular vertical cliffs.

Stop in Pont-en-Royans before entering the gorges. Its houses suspended above the Bourne, clinging to the cliff as if by a miracle, are a striking sight. The village is small - 20 minutes is enough to walk around it, but take the time to photograph the facades from the bridge. Plan a round trip from Villard-de-Lans during the day.

If you enjoy the underground world, make a detour to the grottes de Choranche, about a 30-minute drive from Villard-de-Lans. The soda straw stalactites - hollow calcite tubes as long and thin as drinking straws - are among the most beautiful in Europe. The guided tour lasts about 1 hour, surrounded by underground lakes and translucent mineral formations.

At the Pont de Goule Noire, stop to observe the powerful spring gushing from the cave—it's water from the Autrans-Méaudre plateau re-emerging here after a long underground journey. The spectacle is all the more impressive when water levels are high in spring.

activities.text: Drive the road through the Gorges de la Bourne between Pont-en-Royans and Villard-de-Lans. These 24 km carved into the cliff face required 11 years of work, completed in 1872—workers suspended in mid-air literally sculpted the roadway into the cliff. Every bend reveals a new scene: monumental cliffs, tunnels cut through the rock, waterfalls, and the Bourne snaking below. The road is awarded 3 stars in the Michelin Guide. Caution: the road is narrow and winding; adjust your speed and avoid peak hours in summer.

In late afternoon at Villard-de-Lans, take a short hike on the plateau. The alpine pastures and limestone pavements (rock surfaces sculpted by erosion) give the landscape a lunar quality. The village itself has been a health resort known for its climate since the 1920s, with a pleasant center for a drink on a terrace.

days_plan.itin_title: Royans-Vercors Road Trip: Hilltop Villages and Gorges
From the Alps to the Ardèche Gorges: Lakes, Peaks and Garrigue

visits.text: Villars sits on an isolated hillock between the Vaucluse Mountains and the Grand Luberon, 8 km from Apt. The village's establishment dates back to the late 11th century; a 12th or 13th-century square defensive tower formed the core of the castrum around which it developed. The commune's territory includes twelve hamlets corresponding to the old Gallo-Roman villæ. It's a characterful village that has preserved its authenticity: fountain, shaded squares, and typically Provençal stone houses.

The old center preserves traces of the fortified town—arched passages and narrow lanes—and some fine 16th and 17th-century houses. The Château Saint-Pons wine estate in Villars offers a marked vineyard trail around its parcels in the AOC Ventoux appellation.

activities.text: Rural walk toward the hillsides and dry-stone walls—shepherds' shelters and bories dot the paths around the village. The local economy still cultivates cherry trees (cœurs de pigeon and griottes), apricots and lavender: the landscapes change with the seasons.

Photography route at sunset over the Claparèdes plateau—the raking light on the garrigue and lavandin fields is particularly beautiful in June-July. The plateau overlooks the Calavon valley and extends toward the Colorado Provençal de Rustrel, 5 km away.

days_plan.itin_title: The 15 Most Beautiful Villages of the Luberon

visits.text: The Bird Park of Villars-les-Dombes brings together over 3,000 birds of 300 different species in a green setting of 35 hectares. Immersive aviaries allow close encounters with the rarest species.
Walk the interpretation trail at Chapelier Pond where two ornithological observatories offer prime viewpoints for watching the wild birdlife of the Dombes.
Notre-Dame des Dombes Abbey stands with its Cistercian buildings amid the ponds. The monks' footpath invites a meditative stroll through this landscape of water and sky.
Discover the educational farm where farmyard animals mingle with cows and horses. Children participate in daily care and bread-making workshops.
The land of a thousand ponds spreads its water mirrors as far as the eye can see. These artificial bodies of water dug by monks in the Middle Ages shape a landscape unique in France.

activities.text: Rent bikes and ride the Fairy of a Thousand Ponds circuit, winding between bodies of water where clouds are reflected.
Take off in a hot air balloon to contemplate from the sky this aquatic checkerboard dotted with farms with red-tiled roofs.
Try canicross hiking with sled dogs who guide you along the paths bordering the ponds.
Horse-drawn carriages offer guided tours through the Dombes, set to the tranquil pace of Percheron horses.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour Ain & Savoie Mont-Blanc: Lakes, Mountains and Heritage

visits.text: The Château de Villebois-Lavalette crowns its hilltop with seven round towers visible from kilometres away. Medieval fortress reworked during the Renaissance, two-storey Romanesque chapel. Guided or self-guided tour with booklet.
The covered market hall from the 17th century backs onto the castle walls. Chestnut timber framing and stone pillars.
The village retains some fine old houses, a restored Romanesque church, and an end-of-the-world feel. At the far edge of the Charente, the Périgord is only a few kilometres away.

activities.text: Guided tour of the Château de Villebois-Lavalette. The association's guides bring history to life: two-storey Romanesque chapel (pilgrims below, lords above), medieval towers, 17th-century residence. Family escape games available.
Saturday morning market. Local producers and a village atmosphere. Goat's cheeses, farm-raised chickens, seasonal vegetables and honey. A true country market.
Hike around Villebois. Waymarked trails through wooded hills. Landscapes of mixed crops, isolated farms, views of the castle. Several loops from 5 to 12 km.
Drive to Angoulême on back roads. Through southern Charente: vineyards, villages of golden stone, small valleys. 40 km in an hour at a gentle pace.

days_plan.itin_title: Charente Tour: Cognac and Romanesque Heritage in 4 Days

visits.text: Villecroze is first of all an exceptional natural site: a tufa cliff hollowed out by water over 700,000 years, in which cave dwellings have been occupied since prehistory. The Benedictine monks of the Saint-Victor abbey in Marseille took refuge here during the Saracen raids of the 10th century. In the second half of the 16th century the lord of Villecroze turned them into a stronghold, cutting mullioned windows and arrow slits into them — they have belonged to the commune since 1633 and are classified as a Natural Monument of artistic character. The guided tour (booking required) covers 5 levels, passes behind the waterfall and shows the limestone columns formed by seeping water. Note: closed shoes required, open to children from 6 years old.

The 2-hectare municipal park at the cliff's base hosts the 35-meter waterfall descending from Tourtour — its spring, rich in limestone, helped form the tufa cliff from which the caves hang. The park was created in the 1930s and shelters many Mediterranean species: cedars, fig trees, olive trees, palms, magnolias. It's one of the coolest spots in the Haut-Var in summer. After the waterfall and caves, stroll through the old medieval village: its arcades, seven fountains and flower-filled lanes reveal an authentic atmosphere.

The 11th-century Saint-Victor chapel, south of the village, hosts the Villecroze Music Academy. Free concerts of a high standard are given there in summer — check the dates with the tourist office, some are held in the evening in the chapel or in the open-air theater with its clipped cypresses.

activities.text: On Thursday morning, the Villecroze market sets up under the plane trees on the main square. Local producers of black truffle (in season, November through March), olive oil, saffron, honey and goat cheese — all the flavors of the Haut-Var are represented. Don't leave without a piece of fresh goat cheese.

days_plan.itin_title: The 10 Most Beautiful Villages of the Haut-Var
Var in 4 Days: From Bormes to the Most Beautiful Villages of the Verdon

places.name: Villedieu Les Poeles

visits.text: The Cornille Havard Foundry carries on nine centuries of bell-founding tradition. The listed 19th-century workshop produces more than a hundred monumental bells a year. This is where the bells installed in Notre-Dame Cathedral in Paris during its restoration in 2013 were cast.

Push open the door of the Atelier du Cuivre, which works copper using dinanderie and boilermaking techniques. The craftsmen shape pans, jam basins and decorative objects with hammer blows, like the Sourdins of the past, the nickname given to the inhabitants, deafened by the din of the metal.

The Commandery of the Knights of Malta recalls that Villedieu was for five centuries an independent enclave of the Order of Saint John of Jerusalem. The inner courtyard, the medieval buildings and the herb garden bring back the atmosphere of this commandery founded in the 12th century.

Take the Cour du Foyer, one of the many inner courtyards that give the town its charm. These passages between granite houses once housed the workshops of the copper craftsmen. There are about twenty of them, linked by a maze of lanes.

Notre-Dame Church in Villedieu blends Romanesque and Gothic styles. Its 15th-century porch and octagonal bell tower dominate the town. Inside, the carved wooden pulpit and the stained glass illustrate the religious history of the town.

Villedieu holds the Ville et Métiers d'Art label. Besides copper and bells, the Maison de l'Étain shows how pewter is worked using age-old methods: casting, turning, chasing. The pieces made here are one-off creations.

activities.text: Wander the lanes of the old centre following the route of the courtyards and workshops. Each vaulted passage opens onto a cobbled courtyard where the hammering of copper once rang out.
Villedieu's market is held every Tuesday morning on place de la République. Norman regional produce, farmhouse cider, Villedieu andouille and local cheeses.
Watch a bronze pour at the Cornille Havard foundry. The guided tours follow every stage of making a bell, from the clay mould to the final removal from the mould.

days_plan.itin_title: Manche Road Trip: Cotentin Peninsula & Mont-Saint-Michel
Normandy's Bay of Mont-Saint-Michel: Coastal Drives & the Sacred Abbey
The 20 Most Beautiful Villages in Normandy

map_keywords: Commanderie des Chevaliers de Malte Villedieu-les-Poêles

visits.text: Lake Villefort's 127 hectares nestle in the Cévenol mountains, born from a dam built between 1956 and 1964 on the Bayard valley. Its Blue Flag-certified waters are bordered by developed beaches and an 8.5-km loop trail.

The Château de Castanet, a 16th-century historic monument, was preserved during the dam's flooding. Its name comes from the Occitan "castan" (chestnut tree). Open for self-guided visits in summer, with temporary exhibitions in the vaulted rooms.

La Garde-Guérin, listed among France's Most Beautiful Villages, is a medieval castrum perched at 900 m. Founded in the 12th century by the Bishop of Mende, this fortified settlement protected travellers on the Voie Régordane. Its cobbled streets, lined with houses with mullioned windows and lauze stone roofs, have remained intact.

Climb the 5 levels of the keep at La Garde-Guérin, a 12th-century watchtower 21.5 m high. From the top, the gaze plunges into the Chassezac gorges, 400 m below, and stretches across the Vivarais and Gévaudan uplands.
The Chassezac gorges, a granite canyon 7 km long, cut 400 m below the plateau. From the viewpoint reached on foot, the view of the sheer walls is striking. Locals call it 'the Devil's lair'.

activities.text: Swimming and water sports on Lake Villefort: sailing, windsurfing, canoe-kayak, pedal boats. Lifeguarded beach in July-August.
Villefort's via ferrata unfolds on cliffs above the lake. Two routes (easy and difficult) link ziplines and suspension bridges, with the lake as backdrop.
Fishing on Lake Villefort: brown trout, rainbow trout, and perch populate its waters. Accessible banks and calm zones make it a prized mountain fishing spot.

days_plan.itin_title: Lozère Circuit: Tarn Gorges and Cévennes

visits.text: UNESCO-listed Villefranche-de-Conflent has been enclosed by pink marble ramparts since the 11th century. Vauban created a double covered wall walk, unique in his work, with bastions and fortified gates.

Fort Libéria towers 180 meters above the town. Built by Vauban in 1681, it's reached via an underground staircase of 734 steps. A garrison of 100 men, chapel, powder magazines, and dungeons unfold in succession.
The Canalettes Caves reveal limestone draperies, helictites, and formations thousands of years old. From the couloir des Cupules to the Salle Blanche, water has sculpted wonders.
The Church of Saint James preserves its 11th-century Romanesque architecture. Sculpted portal and capitals testify to Catalan Romanesque art.

activities.text: Board the Yellow Train. This meter-gauge line climbs to an altitude of 1,600 meters, crossing bridges and passing through tunnels and spectacular Pyrenean landscapes.
Stroll through the cobbled streets. Pink marble facades, artisan shops, and café terraces create a medieval atmosphere.
Hike toward the Canigou massif. Several trails start from Villefranche toward the peaks and high-altitude lakes.

days_plan.itin_title: Pyrénées-Orientales Road Trip: French Catalonia and the Côte Vermeille

visits.text: The Saint-Elme Citadel has guarded the entrance to the roadstead since 1557, commissioned by Emmanuel Philibert of Savoy after Villefranche was plundered by Barbarossa in 1543. A star-shaped fortress with five bastions, one of Europe's first bastioned fortifications—its plan would inspire Malta and Vauban. Today it houses small municipal museums (Goetz-Boumeester, Volti) and the town hall. Free admission; allow 45 minutes to walk around the ramparts. Closed Sunday mornings.

The Saint-Pierre Chapel, known as the Cocteau Chapel, is tiny but deeply moving. Jean Cocteau decorated it entirely in 1957 as a sign of friendship for Villefranche's fishermen: five fresco panels illustrating the life of Saint Peter, the Saintes Maries de la Mer and the town's young women. Charlie Chaplin was there at the inauguration on June 30, 1957. Small admission fee (€3), closed mid-November to mid-December. For a concentrated dose of Cocteau, admission is worth every cent.

Rue Obscure is one of the Riviera's most singular passages: 130 meters of 13th-century vaulted gallery, plunged in semi-darkness, running beneath the old town houses. This former patrol path served as shelter for residents during World War II bombings. Cocteau filmed scenes from "Testament of Orpheus" here. Descend from Place du Conseil—atmosphere guaranteed, especially on overcast days.

Saint-Michel Church, at the top of the old town stairs, displays its 17th-century Baroque style beneath imposing vaults. The historic organ in the gallery dates from the 18th century. A remarkable piece not to miss: the recumbent Christ in polychrome wood, carved by a galley slave from fig wood—the expressiveness of the face is striking.

Push on to the Darse, the former military port of the Kings of Sardinia. A quiet basin, remnants of the royal ropeworks, sailboats and traditional pointus—a calm contrast to the bustle of the main marina. A spot almost ignored by tourists. The ropeworks, built in 1769 (260 m long), were used to make ropes for Sardinian galleys.

activities.text: Lay your towel on Plage des Marinières: fine sand and remarkably clear water. The Villefranche roadstead is one of the deepest in the Mediterranean, about 95 meters deep at its center—hence its clarity. The view of Cap-Ferrat is splendid. Visit on a weekday if possible; it gets overcrowded on weekends.

Take a seat on a terrace on Quai de l'Amiral Courbet: pink and orange 18th-century facades reflected in the water, fishing boats returning in the morning, café terraces at noon. It's the classic Villefranche scene, almost a caricature, and yet authentic. Several restaurants serve the day's fish from the local catch.

The roadstead attracts divers and freedivers—often excellent visibility, posidonia meadows and Mediterranean marine fauna. Operators offer introductory dives and guided snorkeling from the port. Expect to pay around €60 for an introductory dive.

Head up to the Moyenne Corniche for panoramic views: the view of the roadstead and Cap-Ferrat, framed by the hills, is the ultimate Riviera postcard scene. Five minutes by car, it's the perfect stop before or after Villefranche.

days_plan.itin_title: Alpes-Maritimes Road Trip: Riviera and Mercantour, 13 days
The 15 Gems of the French Riviera and Backcountry
7-Day French Riviera Circuit: Villefranche to Antibes
French Riviera Art Museums and Galleries: An 8-Day Journey

visits.text: Pérouges is one of France's best-preserved medieval towns, as its 270,000 annual visitors confirm. Perched on a hill at 303 metres, this former town of hemp weavers successfully resisted two thousand Dauphinois soldiers in 1468: the inscription on the Porte d'En-Haut still proclaims it an “impregnable town”. As a reward, the Count of Savoy exempted it from taxes for twenty years. The elliptical ramparts from the 14th and 15th centuries are formed by the continuous frontage of houses, whose outer walls are more than a metre thick. More than 80 buildings are listed historic monuments. Walk through the Porte d'En-Haut and follow the lanes paved with round pebbles nicknamed “cat's heads”. Plan a round trip from Villefranche-sur-Saône for this visit.

The Notre-Dame-des-Marais Collegiate Church displays its Flamboyant Gothic architecture in the heart of the town. This monumental building, begun in the 12th century and completed in the 16th, has a remarkable Renaissance façade. Inside, colourful stained-glass windows, carved choir stalls and an 18th-century organ create an atmosphere of contemplation despite the urban bustle outside.

The Paul-Dini Museum displays its modern and contemporary art collection in two buildings: the former Grenette grain hall and the former Cornil textile factory. Works by regional artists are exhibited alongside those of nationally renowned painters, creating a dialogue between tradition and modernity. The renovated galleries showcase sculptures, paintings and installations along a coherent thematic route.

The covered market comes alive on market days. Local producers and established traders offer Bresse poultry, mature cheeses, fine cured meats and Beaujolais wines. Inaugurated in 1933, this modern covered market provides a fitting setting for the region's culinary produce.

activities.text: Explore the courtyards and passageways hidden behind the buildings of Rue Nationale. Connected to the town's Renaissance residences, these spaces reveal unsuspected architectural treasures. Spiral staircases, galleries and old wells form a hidden heritage that can be discovered along the historic main street.

Stroll along the banks of the Saône, where barges and pleasure boats are moored. The landscaped riverside invites walking and cycling along the Voie Bleue. The lively open-air cafés and floating restaurants contrast with the tranquillity of the public gardens dotted along the riverbanks.

Discover the district of former wine merchants' mansions. These 19th-century bourgeois residences once housed the cellars, offices and apartments of the families who controlled the Beaujolais wine trade. Their Neoclassical façades, imposing porches and cobbled courtyards tell the story of a winegrowing bourgeoisie enriched by commerce.

Enjoy the lively urban atmosphere in the cafés and brasseries of Rue Nationale. Shopping options range from designer boutiques and traditional shops to national chains. This commercial energy makes Villefranche a nerve centre of Beaujolais, where winegrowing tradition meets urban modernity.

days_plan.itin_title: Rhône Road Trip: Lyon, Golden Stone Villages of Beaujolais & Condrieu Vineyards
Road Trip from Bresse to Bugey via Beaujolais and Lyon

visits.text: Gustave Roussy is Europe's leading cancer center and ranks among the world's top 5—50,000 patients per year, including 3,500 children. It all began in 1921 when Professor Gustave Roussy established France's very first clinic dedicated to cancer patients at the neighboring Paul-Brousse hospital. In 1925, the Seine departmental council created the regional center in Villejuif. The campus is still there, never relocated, now surrounded by a biocluster bringing together 5 hospitals, 5 universities, and 48 research teams. It's not a museum—but passing by reminds you that this ordinary suburb houses an institution treating cancers no one else knows how to treat.

The Saint-Cyr-Sainte-Julitte church is a historic monument with parts dating back to the 12th century. Romanesque bell tower, Gothic additions — the church recalls that Villejuif was already a village before hospitals and laboratories took it over in the 20th century.

The Hautes-Bruyères departmental park, near Gustave Roussy in Villejuif, has lawns and walking paths. Walk past the allotment gardens along the edge of the park, then follow the paths to see the plantings and take a break away from the streets.

activities.text: The shopping streets around Léo Lagrange metro station bring together grocery stores, restaurants, and markets reflecting Villejuif's rich cultural diversity—communities from sub-Saharan Africa, the Maghreb, and Asia. An easy culinary change of scenery 15 minutes from central Paris.

For the curious: the Campus Grand Parc under construction around Gustave Roussy aims to become the world's first biocluster dedicated to oncology. The surroundings are freely accessible — you can see how a neighborhood transforms around a scientific institution.

days_plan.itin_title: Val-de-Marne Road Trip: Castles and the Banks of the Marne

visits.text: Nestled in the Noxe Valley, Villenauxe-la-Grande embodies authentic rural Champagne. This peaceful agricultural town has preserved its parish church, stone washhouses and traditional houses, bearing witness to a life governed by the seasons and farm work. The modest but informative Heritage House recounts local history and Champagne traditions—winegrowing, livestock farming and crafts. A restful stop in unspoiled countryside.

activities.text: The banks of the Noxe have been landscaped as a shaded promenade, with flat paths following the river's meanders through wet meadows, willow groves and rustling reeds. Anglers will find peaceful spots to catch pike, zander and carp. This family-friendly route is ideal for a picnic and for observing wildlife—grey herons, moorhens and kingfishers—and riverside plants. Absolute rural peace, far from the tourist crowds.

days_plan.itin_title: Aube Tour: Champagne, Medieval Heritage and the Lakes of the Forêt d'Orient

visits.text: LaM (Lille Métropole Musée d'Art moderne, d'Art contemporain et d'Art brut) houses over 8,000 works by Braque, Picasso, Modigliani, Klee and Miró. Its outsider art collection, France's largest, comes from a donation by the L'Aracine association.

LaM's sculpture park spreads across 23,000 m² of greenery. You'll encounter a monumental mobile by Alexander Calder, a sculpture by Picasso, and works by Richard Deacon, nestled among trees and lawns.
The Château de Flers, a 17th-century Flemish manor surrounded by moats, houses the tourism office. Its brick and stone façade sits within a peaceful small park where ducks patrol.
The Asnapio archaeological park recreates dwellings from the Neolithic to the Middle Ages in the open air using period techniques: Gaulish houses, Gallo-Roman farms and medieval buildings.
The Musée des Moulins, set beside the chain of lakes, traces the history of watermills and windmills in the Flemish region through models, tools and archival documents.

activities.text: Circle Lac du Héron on foot or by bike: 4.6 km of easy trails through a 110-hectare regional nature reserve. Grey herons, grebes and kingfishers inhabit the shores.
The Forum départemental des Sciences features a planetarium and interactive exhibitions on science and nature. Shows under the planetarium dome last about 45 minutes.
Visit the Héron farm beside the park to discover its heritage orchard: over 700 varieties of regional apples, 450 pear varieties, and educational beehives.

days_plan.itin_title: Nord Tour: Lille, Belfries and Flemish Culture

places.name: Villeneuve Les Avignon

visits.text: Fort Saint-André crowns Mont Andaon facing Avignon. This 14th-century royal fortress marked the border between the Kingdom of France and papal lands. Its twin towers frame a fortified gate. From the ramparts, the panorama covers the Palais des Papes, Mont Ventoux, and the Alpilles.

Step through the door of the Chartreuse du Val de Bénédiction, France's largest charterhouse. Founded in 1352 by Pope Innocent VI, it spreads over two hectares with three cloisters, Matteo Giovannetti frescoes in the chapel, and the founding pope's mausoleum.
The Tour Philippe-le-Bel guarded the western end of Avignon's bridge on the French side. Climb its spiral stairs for a view down over the Rhône and Avignon's rooftops.

The gardens of Abbaye Saint-André, landscaped atop Mont Andaon, blend Italian-style terraces, century-old olive trees, and rose gardens. The Romanesque chapel ruins offer a silent setting facing the papal palace.
The Collégiale Notre-Dame houses a 14th-century ivory altarpiece and a copy of Enguerrand Quarton's Pietà, a masterpiece of medieval Provençal painting.

activities.text: Follow the path connecting Fort Saint-André to Tour Philippe-le-Bel along the ramparts. The walk winds through quiet medieval lanes with views of both banks of the Rhône.
In summer, the Chartreuse hosts artist residencies and performances in its cloisters. Check the schedule for the Centre National des Écritures du Spectacle based there.
Settle onto a terrace in the upper part of Villeneuve to watch the sunset over Avignon. The low-angled light sets the Palais des Papes' golden stone ablaze.

days_plan.itin_title: Vaucluse: Avignon, Luberon Villages & Ventoux Routes

map_keywords: Chartreuse du Val de Bénédiction Villeneuve-lès-Avignon

visits.text: Villeneuve-sur-Lot is the largest riverside bastide in south-western France, founded in 1264 by Alphonse de Poitiers under a paréage agreement with the Benedictine abbey of Eysses. Its originality lies in its position astride the Lot. Begin with the Pont des Cieutat, also known as the Old Bridge: its uneven arches have spanned the Lot since the 13th century and three fortified towers once guarded the crossing. The view from the bridge over the pink-brick houses along the river is one of the most photographed in the department.

At the bridge's north entrance, don't miss the Chapel of Notre-Dame-du-Bout-du-Pont in rose brick. This small pilgrimage chapel once welcomed boatmen sailing the Lot before facing the rapids downstream.

Place Lafayette is the heart of the bastide, laid out in the typical grid pattern around a central arcaded square. The market hall and covered arcades house cafés and shops. Sitting at an outdoor café to watch the town come alive is a must: Villeneuve is a living town, not a museum.

The Porte de Paris and Porte de Pujols are two square red-brick towers dating from the 14th century that once closed the northern and southern entrances to the bastide. They contained portcullises and machicolations. Still standing today, they shape the urban landscape and bear witness to the fortifications built from 1313 onwards.

Sainte-Catherine Church, in Romano-Byzantine style and consecrated in 1937, merits a look despite its relatively recent construction. Financed through the support of Georges Leygues, minister and local native son, it rose on the ruins of a 13th-century medieval church. The interior holds splendid 15th-century stained glass windows recovered from the old church, plus five gilded wooden statues that are listed. Note: restoration work began in spring 2024 and will span several years.

Walk through the streets of the old centre in search of the half-timbered houses with corbelled upper floors. Their overhang above the street made it possible to gain living space upstairs without paying more property tax, which was calculated on the ground area. A very pragmatic medieval principle.

activities.text: Visit Place Lafayette market to taste Agen prunes, Quercy melons, and farmhouse cheeses. Villeneuve's market is among the region's liveliest—arrive before 10 a.m. for the best producers.

Head to the water sports base to rent a canoe, pedalo, or electric boat to navigate the Lot. The river is navigable on this stretch and wooded banks offer a peaceful contrast to town life. Allow 2 hours for a leisurely outing.
Follow the Lot's banks on the towpath—routes where horses once towed barges upstream laden with wood, wine, or prunes. The walk is easy and shaded, ideal for late afternoon.

days_plan.itin_title: Lot-et-Garonne Road Trip: Bastides and Villages

places.name: Villers Cotterets

visits.text: The International Centre for the French Language has occupied Francis I's Renaissance château since October 2023. The monarch signed the 1539 ordinance making French the official language of administration here. Four years of restoration revealed sculptural treasures: the royal chapel, the King's Staircase and the Queen's Staircase display salamanders, crowns, fleurs-de-lys and crowned initials. A majestic glass roof crowns the jeu de paume courtyard.

The Centre's permanent exhibition explores the history of the French language through interactive displays, reconstructed voices of historical figures, and fun workshops. Giant puzzles, regional word origins, and personalised reading suggestions punctuate the visit.

The Alexandre Dumas Museum traces the exceptional lives of three generations: General Dumas, the first French general of Afro-Caribbean origin; Alexandre Dumas père, author of The Three Musketeers; and Alexandre Dumas fils, creator of The Lady of the Camellias. Born in Villers-Cotterêts in 1802, the novelist expresses his affection for the town and its forest in his Memoirs.

Follow the “In the Footsteps of Alexandre Dumas” walking circuit offered by the Tourist Office. The route takes you to places from the writer's childhood: his home, Saint-Nicolas Church where he was baptised, and the Henri II pavilion he frequented in his youth.

activities.text: Retz Forest extends over 13,225 hectares, making it the largest state-owned forest in Aisne. This majestic beech forest contains 560 kilometres of paths forming nearly 400 crossroads. Fifteen remarkable trees dot the woodland, which is home to stags, hinds, roe deer, and wild boar. Dumas enjoyed meeting his forester friend near the Maison Neuve forest lodge.
Saint-Nicolas Church, built in 1173 as a castle chapel, was restored in the 16th century. Alexandre Dumas was baptised here on 18 August 1802. The edifice blends medieval and Renaissance elements.

General Mangin's observation tower, a memorial site to the Great War and the offensive of July 1918, is permanently closed to the public. Explore Retz Forest on foot along the royal avenue from the château park in Villers-Cotterêts.

days_plan.itin_title: Aisne Itinerary: Gothic Cathedrals and the Picardy Countryside

map_keywords: International Centre for the French Language

visits.text: Admire Château de Villersexel, which dominates the village and bears witness to local history and the architecture of the nobility of Franche-Comté. The site offers beautiful views over the Ognon valley.

Wander the picturesque lanes of this village full of character, whose preserved architecture evokes centuries past. The parish church and old houses tell the story of this town marked by the 1871 battle during the Franco-Prussian War.

activities.text: Explore the verdant landscapes of the Ognon valley, which runs through Villersexel, with its meadows, forests, and châteaux perched on the heights. The river offers a peaceful setting for walks and nature observation.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Saône Tour: Comtois Plateaus and Heritage

visits.text: The Canadian National Vimy Memorial is one of the finest monuments of the Great War. Its two 27-metre pylons of white Yugoslav limestone stand atop Hill 145, which four Canadian divisions captured on 9 April 1917 — Easter Day — after months of meticulous preparation. It was the first time these divisions had fought together, and this victory is regarded as a founding moment of Canadian national identity. Carved on the monument's walls are the names of 11,285 Canadian soldiers killed in France with no known grave. France ceded this land to Canada in perpetuity in 1922: the 91 hectares still belong to the Canadian people today.

Walk through the open-air trenches, rebuilt in concrete on the original 1917 positions. In places, the Canadian and German lines were just 25 metres apart. The pitted ground around the site still bears the marks of shell craters — some areas remain closed to the public because of unexploded ordnance still buried there.

Go down into the Grange Tunnel — one of 13 tunnels dug ahead of the battle. Running for 1.2 km, it allowed soldiers to advance safely beneath enemy lines. Today 200 metres are open to visitors on a free guided tour (May to November only, 180 steps, not suitable for unaccompanied under-12s). Book as soon as you arrive on site — places are limited to 30 people per tour.

The Notre-Dame-de-Lorette National Cemetery, atop a hill 165 metres high, is the largest French military cemetery. It holds 22,970 individual graves and the remains of 22,000 unknown soldiers in 8 ossuaries — more than 42,000 soldiers in total. The 52-metre lantern tower, visible for miles, watches over this silent space of peace.

The Ring of Remembrance, inaugurated on 11 November 2014 for the war's centenary, forms an ellipse 345 metres in circumference, designed into the hillside by architect Philippe Prost. On 500 gilded steel plates are engraved the names of 580,000 soldiers who died on the fronts of the Nord and Pas-de-Calais — in strict alphabetical order, all nationalities mixed together, friends and enemies side by side. Take the time to look for a familiar surname: the effect is striking.

activities.text: Explore the remains of Mont-Saint-Éloi Abbey a few kilometres from Vimy. Its two 44-metre towers, shelled and collapsed in 1914-1918, dominate the plain with their ghostly silhouette. It is one of the most evocative views in Artois — and from the top of the hill you can see Vimy, Lorette and the slag heaps of the mining basin all at once. Go at the end of the day for the light.

Wander through the landscaped park at the Vimy Memorial. Trees from Canada have been planted here in remembrance of the soldiers, and sheep now graze quietly on the slopes where 35,000 men charged a century ago. The contrast is unsettling. From the monument's high ground, you can see the twin slag heaps of Loos-en-Gohelle and the spires of Arras.

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip Pas-De-Calais: The Opal Coast and Belfries

visits.text: At 52 metres, the keep of Vincennes is the tallest surviving medieval keep in Europe. Charles V had it completed in 1369, and from then until the Revolution it served as both royal residence and state prison - the two functions coexisting without apparent irony. The roll call of inmates is almost comically literary: Henri de Navarre (the future Henri IV, imprisoned 1574-1576, escaped by jumping into the moat), Cardinal de Retz during the Fronde, Nicolas Fouquet briefly after his arrest by d'Artagnan in 1661, Diderot for three months in 1749 for his Philosophical Thoughts, the Marquis de Sade from February 1777 to February 1784 (seven years - this is where he began Les 120 Journées de Sodome), and Mirabeau from 1777 to 1780, imprisoned by his own father's lettre de cachet, during which he wrote his essay on lettres de cachet. The graffiti of prisoners carved into the stone walls - including those of the duc d'Enghien in his final hours - are still visible. Nine floors, roughly 300 steps. Ticket 9.50€.

The duc d'Enghien's story is the one that stays. Louis-Antoine de Bourbon-Condé, 31 years old, was in exile in Ettenheim in Baden when French dragoons crossed the border on the night of 14-15 March 1804 and arrested him on foreign neutral territory - a straightforward violation of international law - then brought him to Vincennes in four days. Trial in the keep on the night of 20-21 March: no defence lawyer, no proper dossier, conducted by a military commission. Condemned to death around 2:30am. Shot in the eastern moat at 3am, in a pit dug in advance. Goethe, Beethoven, and Chateaubriand reacted with public fury. The line 'It was worse than a crime - it was a mistake' is attributed to Bonaparte, though it was more likely Talleyrand or Fouché who said it. Either way, the execution marked the moment many Europeans stopped giving France the benefit of the doubt. A discreet plaque on the eastern exterior wall marks the spot.

activities.text: Lunch at Le Bistrot Vincennois in the centre of Vincennes town, 5 minutes from the château: neighbourhood bistrot, 25-40€, the kind of place that has nothing to do with the 14th century and is the better for it.

Unwind in the afternoon in the Bois de Vincennes — walk around Lac Daumesnil, a 15-minute walk from the château. 995 hectares of woodland and two lake islands. After a morning of moats and executions, the trees feel appropriate. The adjacent Parc Floral is open all year and is worth the 5.50€ admission fee.

days_plan.itin_title: Val-de-Marne Road Trip: Castles and the Banks of the Marne
Haunted Île-de-France: 5 Days of Royal Ghosts and Revolutionary Prisons

visits.text: Vitré Castle. Perched on a schist promontory, this triangular 13th-century fortress is one of the finest examples of fortifications in the Breton Marches. Its tall towers with conical roofs, corbelled rampart walkway, and narrow windows give it the air of a Breton Carcassonne. The museum arranged in the Saint-Laurent, Argenterie, and Oratoire towers offers a journey through seven rooms recreating interiors from the 15th to 19th centuries. From the rampart walk, the panorama takes in the entire medieval city and Vilaine Valley.

Historic Center and Rue d'En-Bas. The walled city stretches at the castle's foot, with narrow streets lined with half-timbered houses and stone mansions. Rue d'En-Bas displays the finest residences of merchants trading overseas who grew rich from the linen and hemp cloth trade in the 15th and 16th centuries: ornate turreted facades, monumental porches, carved half-timbering. Over 50 buildings listed as historic monuments testify to this past prosperity, creating a particularly well-preserved medieval setting.

Ramparts and Promenade du Val. The 500-meter medieval ramparts encircle the rocky outcrop where the castle stands, dominating the verdant Vilaine Valley. The route from the Poterne du Val offers the finest view of the fortress, winding between nature and stone to the Tour Rompue. From the Pré des Lavandières below, the castle is majestically reflected in the Vilaine's waters, creating one of the town's most beautiful scenes.

Notre-Dame Church. Founded, like the castle, around 1060 and then rebuilt in the 15th and 16th centuries, this Gothic church impresses with its south facade and row of seven gables. Inside, the largest 19th-century choir organ stands alongside mural paintings, polychrome wood sculptures, and richly decorated side chapels. The frescoes and vaults testify to Vitré's importance in Breton religious heritage.

activities.text: Vitré Lumières Trail. At nightfall, an illumination trail highlights historic monuments with colorful light displays. The castle, ramparts, and old facades take on fairytale hues that transform the medieval city into a storybook setting. This permanent nighttime spectacle invites visitors to rediscover the town from another angle, in a magical atmosphere particularly appreciated by photographers.

Jardin du Parc. This 7-hectare English landscape garden extends along the historic center's edge, bringing together over 50 plant species in a romantic landscaped setting. Shaded pathways, flowerbeds, and children's play areas make it a place for families to relax. It's also the prime vantage point for photographing the castle from above.

days_plan.itin_title: Ille-et-Vilaine Tour: Saint-Malo, Dinard and the Emerald Coast

places.name: Vittel

visits.text: The Parc thermal de Vittel spans 650 hectares listed as a Historic Monument. You'll encounter the Grand Escalier (1902), the Rotonde Tea-Room (1912), the Pavillon Heudebert (1923)—all designed by architect Fernand César.

The spa building (1884) bears the stamp of Charles Garnier, architect of the Paris Opera. The Moorish-style Grande Galerie (1897–1938) and the Palmarium with its indoor pool (1911) complete the complex.

The Casino, created in 1882 in the park, was rebuilt by Auguste Bluysen in 1929–1930. It preserves the walls of Fernand Nachon's old theater (1908). Art Deco fountains and light fixtures (1934) frame the entrance.

The Musée du Patrimoine et du Thermalisme traces Vittel's transformation from a rural village in the 19th century to a world-renowned spa town, thanks to Louis Bouloumié's acquisition of the Gérémoy spring in 1854.
La Vigie de l'Eau is an interactive discovery space about the world of water and its environmental challenges: workshops, hands-on activities, virtual reality, and immersive sound experiences.

activities.text: Explore the thermal park by Rosalie (pedal car) or bike. The shaded paths pass between a rose garden, a butterfly garden, insect hotels, and an ornithological area.
The Vittel racecourse hosts races in season. On days without races, you can stroll through the grounds and admire the grandstand (1904) designed by Fernand César.
The Golf du Mont Saint-Jean, an 18-hole course in rolling, wooded terrain, is one of the historic courses in eastern France. Non-golfers will enjoy the 18-hole mini-golf in the town center.

days_plan.itin_title: Vosges Road Trip: Lakes, Mountains & Thermal Spas

map_keywords: Musée du Patrimoine et du Thermalisme Vittel

places.name: Vivier Gallo Romain De La Gaillarde

visits.text: Three basins carved into the rock, steps from the departmental road: the Gallo-Roman fish pond of La Gaillarde has been listed as a historic monument since 1939. Fish were kept alive there, and garum was probably made there too, a sauce of fermented fish guts whose smell kept villas at a distance. The low walls are visible a few centimeters below the water: come when the sea is calm, or you'll see nothing.

Aligned north–south in a 20-meter-long cove, the fish pond at Pointe de la Calle used the prevailing winds and swell to refresh its water. It belonged to a villa in the La Gaillarde valley, a kilometer away. There's an explanatory plaque on site and nothing else: don't expect a site with visitor facilities.

activities.text: Walk from Port Ferréol: the stretch of coastal path leading to the Gallo-Roman fish pond of La Gaillarde takes just a few minutes and connects to the corniche des Cigales. There are few suitable places to swim here, and it's almost deserted, even in August. That's precisely what makes it pleasant.

days_plan.itin_title: Roquebrune-sur-Argens: sea, villages and the Var in 10 days

map_keywords: La Gaillarde maritime fish pond Les Issambres
Pointe de la Calle Les Issambres

visits.text: Vogüé is classified among the Most Beautiful Villages of France—and you understand why arriving via the road along the Ardèche: the village rises in an amphitheater on the cliff above the river, with the castle dominating everything. The Château des Marquis de Vogüé has been inhabited by the same family since the 11th century—one of Vivarais's oldest dynasties, a member of which participated in the 1191 Siege of Acre during the Third Crusade. The castle tour (open April to November) includes the Vivarais Estates hall, the 12th-century keep with its kitchens, the chapel with stained glass by Alfred Manessier created in 1980, and the hanging garden called the marquise's garden. Allow at least an hour.

Get lost in the lower village lanes: La Tourasse, one of the first houses of the Vogüé lords, is a tower 15 meters high still standing. Rue des Puces is one of the narrowest streets in France. The medieval arcades supporting the houses give the ensemble a particular atmosphere, especially early morning when tourists haven't yet arrived.

Taking the path that climbs behind the castle, you reach in 40 minutes the Chapelle Saint-Cérice called La Gleyzette—a Romanesque chapel perched on the cliff with plunging views over the castle, village and narrow Ardèche course. The hiking trail continues to a panorama over the Auzon valley. The 1877 railway viaduct, visible below, is now converted to a greenway.

activities.text: The Via Ardèche, a greenway developed on the old railway line, links Vogüé to Gropierre over 25 km. Bike rental is available in the area. The section from Vogüé is particularly pleasant as it follows the Ardèche with viewpoints over the gorges. If you don't do the full 25 km, settle for a 5 to 6 km round trip.

Below Vogüé bridge, the beach supervised July-August attracts swimmers and canoeists. This is the first official launch point for descending the Ardèche Gorges from upstream. Local operators offer water equipment rentals.

days_plan.itin_title: The 18 Most Beautiful Villages of Ardèche

visits.text: Wassy echoes through every history book: on March 1, 1562, François de Guise and his escort forced open a barn where some fifty Protestants were holding their worship. The massacre that followed—around fifty dead, a hundred wounded—ignited the first of eight Wars of Religion that tore France apart until the Edict of Nantes in 1598. The Protestant Museum of the Massacre Barn, housed in the temple built in 1889 on the exact site of the events, rigorously chronicles this founding episode. Panels, display cases, a video presentation in four languages, and period objects—Bibles, Huguenot crosses, engravings—make this turning point in European history comprehensible.

Wassy's Notre-Dame Church exemplifies Champagne Romanesque architecture. Nearby stands the 19th-century circular market hall, witness to the town's commercial past as a sub-prefecture from 1790 onward. The historic center merits exploration: a handful of period buildings and the former theater on Marie-Stuart Square recall Wassy's role as an animated cultural hub.

activities.text: Explore Wassy's historic center on the marked trail. Given the town's modest size, allow an hour for a complete circuit. Weather permitting, venture to the banks of the Blaise nearby.

Lake Der and its Champagne bocage landscapes begin nearby. Use the afternoon to reach the first bird-watching hides if you are traveling between October and March, or for a bike ride on the greenways running alongside the canal.

days_plan.itin_title: Haute-Marne Circuit: Langres and Heritage

visits.text: The Wimereux seafront promenade is a lesson in seaside architecture. Its 1.5 km runs along the beach, lined with Belle Époque villas featuring bow windows, ornate balconies and colourful ceramics — more than 300 Anglo-Norman-style residences, each personalised by its original owner. It is the oldest seaside resort on the Côte d'Opale, born with the arrival of the railway in 1862 and swiftly adopted by visiting English aristocracy and the middle classes.

Wander through the residential lanes to view the villas more closely. Some bear evocative names on their ceramic tiles — “Villa les Goélands”, “Chalet brise-lames” — and each reveals a slightly different style. A signposted “Villas of Wimereux” trail is available from the tourist office.

Wimereux's seaside history was built on three pillars: the tramway, the casino and the golf course. The golf course was created in 1901 and rebuilt after the war. These amenities drew a wealthy clientele who had the villas built. Today the atmosphere is more family-oriented, but the Belle Époque charm remains intact.

activities.text: Head to the Pointe aux Oies north of the village — an area of dunes and coastal grassland protected by the Conservatoire du littoral. On a clear day, the English coast can be seen on the horizon. It is one of the best spots in the region to watch grey seals and harbour seals resting on the sandbanks at low tide. Bring binoculars.

Take the Sentier Impérial, a 14 km loop between the Grande Armée column and Wimereux. The path runs along the cliffs and dunes with remarkable views over the Boulonnais and the Channel. Bring sturdy shoes and a windbreaker — the sea breeze is often sharp even in summer.

Local operators offer introductory lessons in kitesurfing, windsurfing and sand yachting on the beach. The wind that sweeps across the Côte d'Opale creates steady, teachable conditions — Wimereux is an ideal playground for taking up these sports.

days_plan.itin_title: Opal Coast Villages and Flemish Heartlands
The Most Beautiful Villages from Flanders to the Bay of Somme
Road Trip Pas-De-Calais: The Opal Coast and Belfries

visits.text: Cap Blanc-Nez is France's northernmost chalk cliff — its 134 metres above the Channel are striking. On a clear day (which does happen, promise), the white cliffs of Dover can be seen 35 km away. At the summit, a grey stone obelisk pays tribute to the Dover Patrol, the 2,000 Franco-British soldiers who defended these strategic waters in 1914-18. Second World War bunkers are still visible on the cliff face. The chalk grassland atop the cliffs is home to rare flora — orchids, rock roses and the exceedingly rare autumn gentian.

11 km to the south-west, Cap Gris-Nez is the point of France closest to England — just 30.3 km separate its 45-metre sandstone and clay cliff from the Kent coast. Together with Cap Blanc-Nez, it forms the Grand Site des Deux Caps, listed since 2011 — 2.5 million visitors a year. Its cylindrical lighthouse, brought into service in 1957, marks the busiest strait in the world (over 500 ship movements a day).

Between the two capes, the bay of Wissant stretches 12 km of fine sand. This fishing village nestled in the bay is renowned for kitesurfing and windsurfing: the venturi effect created by the two capes concentrates the wind on the beach, making it one of the best spots in the region.

3 km south of Cap Gris-Nez, the village of Audresselles has kept its fishermen's cottages with blue shutters and tarred foundations to withstand the sea spray. The flobarts — traditional coloured beaching boats with flat bottoms for running ashore on the beach — still put to sea. One of the most authentic coastal villages on the Côte d'Opale.

The crans dot the coast between the two capes: the Cran aux Œufs, the Cran Poulet, the Cran du Noirda. These natural notches in the cliffs reveal remarkable Jurassic fossils — the geotope between the two capes is listed for its exceptional scientific interest. Shore fishing is possible here at low tide.

activities.text: The GR120 trail links the two capes over 16 km of cliff path. The chalk grasslands are fragrant with thyme and oregano, orchids bloom in spring, and the panorama alternates between sea views and inland valleys. Allow 4 to 5 hours to walk this route one way; arrange your return journey from whichever cape you finish at.
Operators in Wissant offer kitesurfing and stand-up paddleboarding taster sessions. The vast beach at low tide offers space for all levels — and the wind is never lacking on this coast.

From the summit of Cap Blanc-Nez, watch the shipping traffic in the strait — huge cargo ships and container ships pass by every few minutes along one of the busiest shipping lanes in the world. It is also a major observation site for migratory birds in spring and autumn.

days_plan.itin_title: Opal Coast Villages and Flemish Heartlands
The Most Beautiful Villages from Flanders to the Bay of Somme
Road Trip Pas-De-Calais: The Opal Coast and Belfries

visits.text: Lac de Longemer stretches 2 km at 736 meters altitude, classified as a Remarkable Site with its surrounding 900 hectares. Wilder than Gérardmer, it's ringed by forest—a true mountain lake.
The Saut des Cuves is the valley's iconic waterfall site. The Vologne leaps between enormous granite blocks in successive cascades. The “vats” are holes carved in the rock by swirling pebbles.
A few steps from the Saut des Cuves, the Pont des Fées, rebuilt in 1782, spans the Vologne. Local legend has it that the Pierre Charlemagne still bears the hoofprint of the emperor's horse.
The secluded Lac de Retournemer, the highest of the three Vologne lakes (776 m), is for viewing only: only walking around the lake is permitted, with no swimming or water activities.
The Chapel of Saint-Florent, rebuilt in the 18th century, preserves a bell from 1650. It stands on the shore of Lac de Longemer in a postcard-perfect setting.

activities.text: The walk around Lac de Longemer is an easy, family-friendly loop. The trail passes by the Roche des Vieux Chevaux, which offers a view down over the water framed by fir trees.
From the Col de la Schlucht, take the Sentier des Roches (for experienced hikers). Metal handrails help you cross the exposed passages overlooking the Munster valley.

The Jardin d'altitude du Haut Chitelet, at 1,228 m, brings together 2,700 mountain plant species from around the world. It's also the source of the Vologne, the river that flows through all three lakes.
Want peace and quiet? Lac de Lispach, a peat bog at the foot of La Bresse-Hohneck resort, impresses with its shifting colors and bog vegetation. Easy walk on boardwalks.

days_plan.itin_title: Vosges Road Trip: Lakes, Mountains & Thermal Spas

places.name: Yenne

visits.text: Yenne is a former medieval town built between the Rhône and the Dent du Chat. A marked trail with 29 points of interest crosses the town: the Chambéry Gate, the Novalaise Gate, the salt granary, and noble houses from the 15th to 18th centuries.
Step inside Yenne's church, a listed Historic Monument. Its baroque furnishings sit alongside older elements in a quiet, meditative atmosphere.

Follow the Balcon de Yenne trail—part of the Santiago de Compostela pilgrimage route—up to the Notre-Dame de la Montagne viewpoint. The vista plunges into the Pierre-Châtel gorge, a protected natural site where the Rhône squeezes between cliffs at the border of Ain and Savoie.

The Pierre-Châtel gorge shelters ruins of a 13th-century charterhouse that became a military fortress in the 1800s. From the trail's second viewpoint, you can clearly make out the structure nestled in the canyon below.

Head to the Jongieux-Marestel hillsides, a vineyard classified as national heritage for its scenic beauty. Terraced vines overlook the Rhône. The slopes produce Roussette de Savoie (Altesse grape) and Mondeuse, a bold red wine.

activities.text: Balcon de Yenne hike: the trail climbs through boxwood forest to three successive viewpoints over the Rhône and Pierre-Châtel gorge. Return via the hamlets of Chevru and Curtelod.
Wine tasting in the Jongieux cellars. Marestel vintages and Mondeuse reds are sampled at local producers' estates, set between manicured slopes and Lake Bourget panoramas.
Canoeing and kayaking on the wild Haut-Rhône, at the foot of the Pierre-Châtel gorge. The rushing waters run through a setting of cliffs and forests.

days_plan.itin_title: Savoie from Lakes to Glaciers: Yenne to Haute-Maurienne

places.name: Yvoire

visits.text: Start in Chamonix, at the foot of Mont-Blanc (about 96 km from Yvoire, 1 hour 15 minutes by car). The town hosted the first Winter Olympics in 1924 and has one of France's oldest tourist offices, established as early as 1907. The town center retains an Alpine village feel despite the crowds - the wooden and stone facades on rue du Docteur-Paccard are worth a look. If you are there in the morning, make the most of it: after 10 am, tour buses arrive and the atmosphere changes.

Explore Yvoire on foot—cars stay in the parking areas at the village entrance. Founded in 1306 by Count Amadeus V of Savoy as a stronghold on Lake Geneva, the town has preserved its ramparts, two fortified gates, and its castle (privately owned, not open to visitors). Look up at the onion-domed bell tower of Saint-Pancrace Church, clad in stainless steel with a gold-leaf weathercock—it's typical of Savoyard architecture. Fun fact: in 1844, writer Alfred de Bougy described Yvoire as the most execrable of villages—the turnaround has been total.

Don't miss the Jardin des Cinq Sens, set within the former castle kitchen garden since 1988. This 2,500 m² botanical maze has the Jardin Remarquable designation and contains over 1,300 plant varieties organized by sensory themes—touch, smell, taste, sight, hearing. Allow a good hour to explore it without rushing.

Then head down to the fishermen's harbor east of the castle. It's the most photogenic corner of the village, especially late in the day when the low-angle light turns the stonework golden. From here, you see Lake Geneva opening out toward Switzerland, with the Jura in the background.

activities.text: Take the cable car from Chamonix up to the Aiguille du Midi - 20 minutes to rise from 1,035 m to an altitude of 3,842 m, on France's highest cable car. Up there, the 360° view takes in the French, Swiss and Italian Alps. If you are not afraid of heights, try the Pas dans le Vide: a glass box suspended above a 1,000-meter drop. Bring warm clothing even in summer - it rarely gets above 5°C at the summit. Reservations are required; allow 2 to 3 hours in total. From Yvoire, plan a round trip to Chamonix during the day to reach the cable car.

Transfer from Chamonix to Yvoire along the southern shore of Lake Geneva. The road hugs the lake after Thonon-les-Bains—stop at one of the viewpoints to admire the water and the Swiss mountains opposite. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes for the drive, more if you take breaks.

visits.text: Zellenberg is the village you visit from below—perched at an elevation of 285 meters on a vineyard-covered hill, its closely packed houses stand out from afar against a backdrop of sky and vines. Up close, the curved streets that hug the hill's contours form a compact labyrinth where the church and small square at the top offer unobstructed views of Riquewihr below and across the Alsace plain to the Black Forest. The village retains traces of its old medieval defensive wall, visible at several points.

From the church square, the view takes in a panorama of vineyards that few places in Alsace can match: Riquewihr 2 km away, Hunawihr 3 km away, and the Schoenenbourg and Sporen hillsides opposite. Circle the village via the alleys that follow the remnants of old moats—30 to 40 minutes is enough to see the entire village.

activities.text: Take the path around the hill for a complete circuit on foot—2 to 3 km of easy walking between the vines, with successive viewpoints over the Ribeauvillé valley to the north and the Riquewihr hillsides to the south. The village's wine estates offer tastings of wines from surrounding grands crus—notably Schoenenbourg and Sporen.

visits.text: The village of Zonza, capital of Alta Rocca, clings to the mountainside at an altitude of 780 meters. The village church overlooks stone houses and cobbled lanes. Century-old plane trees shade the main square surrounded by cafés. The panorama from the village takes in the Bavella Needles and Ospédale forest.

The Bavella Needles rise in seven granite towers reaching 1,857 meters. The Col de Bavella at 1,218 meters links Alta Rocca to the eastern coast. The statue of Notre-Dame-des-Neiges has stood at the pass since 1953, welcoming pilgrims every August 5. Corsican pines twisted by the wind punctuate the spectacular rocky landscape.

The Ospédale Forest covers 4,000 hectares with Corsican pines at altitudes between 500 and 1,500 meters. Forest trails wind between granite rocks and waterfalls. The Ospédale dam, built in 1963, forms an artificial lake in a verdant setting. Viewpoints reveal the coast and Gulf of Porto-Vecchio.

activities.text: The Trou de la Bombe hike crosses the Corsican pine forest to an 8-meter natural window in the rock. The marked trail from Col de Bavella offers spectacular views of the Needles. The accessible route takes 2 hours round trip with moderate elevation gain. Panoramas take in all of Alta Rocca.

The natural pools of the Cavu offer swimming in crystal-clear water between granite rocks; plan a round trip from the village of Zonza. The pools follow one another along the river in a landscape of maquis and forest. The easy access path suits families. The cool water provides a welcome break after mountain hikes.

The hiking trails around Bavella cross varied landscapes, from the GR20 to family walks. The alpine variant of the GR20 challenges experienced hikers among the Aiguilles. Routes to the Paliri refuge reveal the massif's wild beauty. Each trail offers distinctive perspectives on the rock formations.
